### Series Title Page

## The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library

Of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continually illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: the first, of subjects, by consulting which one may see at a glance whatever each Father has written on any given theme; the second, of Sacred Scripture, from which it is immediately evident to the reader which Fathers, and in what places in their works, have commented on the individual texts of the books of Scripture.

A most accurate edition, and one easily to be preferred to all others if the following are taken into consideration: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes and its consistent similarity throughout the entire work, the modest price, and especially this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and short works previously scattered here and there, but gathered for the first time in our library from works pertaining to every age, place, language, and form.

### Second Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical science.

The *Patrology* has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. Two hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for 1,000 francs; three hundred volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for 1,800 francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are given in it only in Latin translation.

# In the Year of Our Lord 942. Saint Odo, Abbot of Cluny

[Col. 0009]

## Prolegomena: Historical Eulogy of Saint Odo by Mabillon

(*Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, fifth century, p. 124.)

[Col. 0009]

### Chapter I — The Writers of His Life, and His Parents and Homeland

[Col. 0009A]

1. Although two authors wrote about the deeds of Saint Odo—namely John and Nalgodus, both monks of Cluny—many things were nevertheless omitted by them that deserve to be included in a commentary. Therefore, lest we appear to have investigated too negligently the deeds of men who rendered such outstanding service to the Benedictine commonwealth, it is worthwhile to place before their two writings a historical eulogy of him, in which the matters they left untouched or did not sufficiently explain may be set forth.

First, it is fitting to begin with those two authors. The first, John, recorded his own circumstances here and there in three little books about Odo, which a manuscript from Compiègne reduces to two. [Col. 0009B] He was Italian by nation, Roman by homeland, and a canon by profession. When Odo set out for Rome in 939, he brought John back with him as far as Pavia, and there made him a monk, as appears from Book I, numbers 2 and 4. Then, taking him as a companion on his journey, he subsequently appointed him prior, as is read more than once in Book II, namely numbers 4, 7, and 10—whether at Cluny or at Saint Paul’s in Rome is a question that may arise when numbers 10 and 21 are compared. Finally, John testifies in number 21 that he was “sent to Naples by the necessity of his monastery.” In Book III, number 5, he reckons as two years the entire period during which he was Odo’s companion. During that interval, whatever he was able to observe in Odo’s statements concerning him and in his actions—for so he almost says in his preface—he later committed to writing, omitting other matters [Col. 0009C] that he had learned about Odo from his master Arnulf, from Hubert, Bishop of Tivoli, from the monk Landricus, and from his own provost Hildebrand. Thus he relied only on his own eyes and on Odo’s account—if only he had been less suspicious regarding the testimony of others. We shall try, in some measure, to repair this loss.

John dedicated his work to the monks of Salerno; I do not know whether to those of the monastery of Saint Peter of Salerno “below and near Fistula,” which Ughelli proves was founded by Bishop Peter before the year 958, in volume VII of *Sacred Italy*, column 503. John occasionally wanders into digressions and does not sufficiently observe the sequence [Col. 0010A] of times or the order of events.

2. Wishing to remedy these deficiencies, the monk Nalgodus undertook to reduce John’s work to a summary and arrange it in a better order; he did the same with the life of Saint Majolus. Peter of Rivo, in his Cluniac chronicle, calls Nalgodus Odo’s “disciple,” and says that he was the one who “after the death of Saint Odo himself described his life and miracles with great clarity.” Godefridus Henschenius, in the month of May, understands this as referring to the life of Saint Majolus, and supposes that Nalgodus was his disciple. Yet Nalgodus lived “almost two hundred” years after Odo, and somewhat less than that after Majolus, as he expressly asserts in number 29—namely during the pontificate of Urban II, or certainly after it, according to number 23.

We have decided to place this author’s writing [Col. 0010B] beneath the three little books of John, in smaller type, because of certain details concerning Odo’s death and burial and other circumstances that are not found in John. Many other authors also mention Odo with praise; Chesnius provides a list of them in his notes to the Cluniac library. Among these, Peter Equilinus treats Saint Odo at length in Book X, chapter 8.

3. Before beginning to speak of Odo of Cluny, it will not be irrelevant to observe that, besides him, two other distinguished abbots of the same name existed in the same age: one of Masciacum, the other of Saint Maxentius among the Poitevins. Concerning the monastery of Masciacum among the Bituriges, what we said above in the eulogy of Abbot Berno must be recalled. After Berno, Odo of Cluny appointed there as provost an Odo bearing the same name, who is mentioned in the Masciacum chronicle preserved by Labbe in volume II of the *New Library* as having been “ordained abbot in the year 935.” Concerning the death of this second Odo, the same source also reads: “In the year 967, on the eighth day before the Ides of June, Odo, abbot of blessed memory, died here, and the monk Arduicus on the Nones of September.” The following day is marked in the Thuan-Colbertine Calendar of the Saints, number 99, in these words: “The seventh day before the Ides of June: Odo, abbot of Masciacum.”

The other Odo was abbot at Saint Maxentius, namely in the year 963; Abbot Ramnulf succeeded him in 968, as the chronicler of Maillezais testifies in the same Labbe.

[Col. 0011A] With these matters prefixed, I come to Odo, or Oddo, Abbot of Cluny, whose homeland and parents must first be investigated. His father was named Abbo and belonged to the military order, as is clear from the monk John and others; they contain no mention of Odo’s mother’s name. John reports Abbo’s eulogy from Odo at the beginning of Book I. Nalgodus, following John, says that both parents withdrew to the monastic life at their son’s urging. After recounting the miracle of crumbs changed into pearls, John adds the following in Book I, number 35:

“From that time he began to burn within himself on account of the rescue of his parents, so that he might be able to withdraw them from the bonds of this world. Consequently, not long afterward, having obtained permission, he went away to his father and led him to the monastery [Col. 0011B] and made him a monk. As for his mother, he had her clothed in the sacred veil; if it had been permitted me to write her life”—would that it had been permitted—“it would have seemed more a history than a little booklet.”

Thus Odo was born to such parents in the year 879, since in the year of Christ 939 he was sixty years old, according to John at the beginning of Book I, number 4.

4. It may be inferred that his native home was in the city of the Turonians from his father’s—and his own—inborn devotion to Saint Martin, to whom he devoted himself from the beginning of adolescence, according to John, number 9. The conjecture is strengthened by what the same author reports in Book II, number 16, about Odo’s little nephew being carried off by the Northmen when they were devastating “the borders of Touraine.” Therefore his nephew was living in Touraine.

Nevertheless, in the old Cluniac charter collection there is an eulogy of Odo [Col. 0011C] whose author says that he came from the region of Le Mans. This eulogy was written in the time of Abbot Odilo by the man who, at his command, arranged the charters of the earlier abbots. The principal substance of the eulogy is as follows:

“Thus, as the truthful report of our predecessors relates, he was born of noble stock, arose from the region of Le Mans, was thoroughly imbued with the rules of the liberal arts, was sacristan of the basilica of the blessed Martin of Tours, renowned in speech, and so forth. Therefore, drenched with the fragrance of virtues which at that time the reputation of Cluny”—rather, of Baume—“had spread far and wide, like precious perfumes, he readily accomplished in his mind what he had long desired: he left the dark countryside, while his fellow citizen mourned in his homeland and Christ rejoiced in glory, and submitted his gentle neck to the divine yoke. Finally, having completed the novitiate of his conversion without slackness, and having been ensnared by the entreaty of his father, to whose instructions he had been committed, he accepted, willingly or unwillingly—or, more truthfully, unwillingly—the charge of governing the entire brotherhood.

“Finally, Italy does not fail to know with what severity he sought to humble lofty minds and with what caution to implant virtues; Burgundy bears witness to it, and Gaul likewise reports it. Finally, he is most certainly shown to have been filled with the gift of prophecy when, overtaken by his final lot and asked by the brothers in council who from so great a company should be placed over the others, he is said, inspired by a deep breath, to have answered them as follows:

“‘In this, my sons, while our judgment wavers, the abundant wisdom of Christ the Lord will not be lacking. He will both providently provide his household with a holy shepherd and not deny you, his servants who ask, a worthy father.’

“This is clearer than the sun to those who consider it carefully, since the life and conversion of Lord Heymard provide abundant proof. Here, then, let a brief conclusion suffice concerning the praiseworthy nobility of so great a man, so that from this it may be understood how greatly we ought to adhere to the teachings of one whom we do not doubt was deservedly enrolled among the ranks of the angels.”

Thus far the old author, who in the time of Abbot Odilo—that is, a hundred years after Odo’s death—placed this eulogy before the charters composed under Odo in the Cluniac charter collection.

## Chapter II — Odo’s Childhood and Adolescence, His Canonical Life, and His Studies

5. Odo was brought up partly in the household of Fulk II, Count of Anjou, whom he therefore calls his foster-brother in a letter; partly “within the household of William, Duke of Aquitaine,” according to John at the beginning of his first book. This William, surnamed the Pious, “at that time held Aquitaine and Auvergne by his own right”; he is the man whom we said in Berno’s eulogy laid the foundations of the monastery of Cluny. Abbo, Odo’s father, enjoyed great authority with William himself, according to John in the same place, number 5. Abbo handed the weaned Odo over “to one of his priests, who lived in a more remote place, to be brought up and instructed in literary studies,” number 7.

After this, while Odo was occupied at William’s court with “military exercises,” Christ the Lord called him to a holier service on Christmas Day, “when he was approaching his sixteenth year,” after he had been afflicted for two years by headaches in [Col. 0012C] his ancestral home.

6. Later, dedicating himself to Saint Martin in fulfillment of his father’s vow, in the nineteenth year of his age—which was approximately the year 898 of Christ—he became a cleric and canon there, amid a large gathering of citizens and nobles.

“Among them was Count Fulk, who had brought him up,” and he “immediately granted him a cell beside the church of Blessed Martin, and obtained and granted him his daily sustenance from that canonry.”

Fulk’s surname was the Good. Much remarkable material concerning him is found in the *Deeds of the Counts of Anjou* in volume X of the *Spicilegium*, pp. 402 and 434, including these words on p. 435:

“The Good man’s character was honored at home and in war: he possessed good justice, the greatest concord, and the least avarice.”

Then, concerning Odo:

“This man brought up Saint Odo and granted him a cell beside the church of blessed Martin, together with his daily sustenance from the same chamber. Later, with the support of that count, Odo was appointed master of the school and precentor of the same church.”

7. Beginning at number 12, John then relates Odo’s studies and virtues and his journey to Paris, where, under his teacher Remigius, a monk of Auxerre, he learned the liberal arts, including Augustine’s “dialectic sent to his son Adeodatus.” Returning to Tours, he abridged Gregory the Great’s *Morals on Job*. This abridgment was published in print at Paris in 1617 through the efforts of Dom Martin Marrier, a monk of Saint-Martin-des-Champs.

John says that Odo undertook this work at the request of the brothers—that is, his fellow canons [Col. 0013A]—and that, although he hesitated, he was encouraged to do it after seeing the need. Odo, however, mentions nothing of this in either of his two prefaces, one in prose and the other in verse, perhaps out of modesty; but he suggests that he began it almost of his own accord in these words:

“When, according to the capacity of my smallness, I was devoting myself to the reading of sacred literature in the world, one day a book composed by blessed Gregory in his history of the most holy Job came into the hands of my poverty. For that excellent teacher, inspired by divine breath and drinking from the heavenly fountain, poured himself like a shining river into the history of the aforesaid man and extended it in such eloquent speech that from it, like radiant suns, he produced thirty-five books, which he decided to compress into six codices.

“But while I was reading through the first part of these, my mind, kindled by excessive love and captivated by a certain sweetness, desired, if it could, to devour the entire book. For that wondrous teacher, enriched by divine rains, strove in lucid discourse to unfold the sayings of the Fathers that arose in his mind while expounding the text, and expanded them into numerous volumes concerning the aforesaid history. Those to whom Sacred Scripture is not unknown know that a holy man named Paterius, by a remarkable work, extracted these sayings and restored them to separate volumes.

“From these, two years ago, I too gathered together all the sayings of the Fathers in the Book of Kings, especially those of the most holy Pope Gregory, and joined them into one little book, which I do not think should be despised. Therefore, taking thought for the perception of my frailty, the weakness of my body, and the usefulness of those like me, I raised myself against myself—not swollen with the arrogance of pride, nor puffed up by the spirit of conceit, nor, God knows, relying upon and striving after windy applause—but burning with the fire of reading the aforesaid history. With all my effort I contracted it into this small work so that I might be able to retain its meaning by heart.”

Thus far Odo in the preface to his abridgment.

8. After this, at number 21, John turns his discourse to Count Fulk. He asserts that Fulk, having been afflicted with a deadly illness because he had removed two golden vessels from the treasury of the church of Saint Martin, was restored to health through Odo’s prayers. Some more recent writers, moved by devotion toward Fulk, oppose this account; it was this virtue that gave him the surname “the Good.” Yet the sun itself has its shadows [Col. 0013D], and the writer of the book on the deeds of the counts of Anjou, who records so many distinguished facts about Fulk, did not hesitate to insert this one as well. I mention this in support of John’s authority.

9. I return to Odo’s canonical life. It is useful briefly to explain what discipline prevailed among the Martinian canons at that time. After the abandonment of monastic life, a certain regular form continued in that place. The number of three hundred monks had been reduced to one hundred and fifty canons; continual psalmody had been restricted to appointed hours, as was explained more fully in the eulogy of Alcuin, number 46. Nevertheless, reverence for the cloister was preserved, access was forbidden to women, and most things were arranged according to the appearance of propriety.

The situation deteriorated after the second burning of that basilica, concerning which Odo, already a monk, delivered a sermon at the request of the canons.

“For after that earlier conflagration,” he says, “when you had enclosed the monastery with walls constructed with immense care, you wished above all to prevent the holy house from being harmed by enemies again. But, failing to consider how great the reverence in which this holy place had shone from ancient times, you immediately abandoned religious observance and allowed it to become a common lodging-place, so that the doorkeepers do not resist women coming to draw water or wandering wherever they wish, although we have seen that no one was permitted to enter even slightly within the monastery gates,” and so forth.

To this pertains the letter of Pope Leo VII to Hugh, prince and abbot, published [Col. 0014B] in volume II of the *Spicilegium*, decreeing “that throughout the entire circuit of the old wall, as far as the road that runs beside the northern side of the basilica, no woman should have permission to dwell there, nor even to enter, except solely for the sake of prayer.”

Odo adds:

“Nor is this displeasing in a small degree: certain men brought up in that same place dishonor themselves with somewhat too showy or pompous secular garments, although their manner of life has become such that we have heard it praised even at Rome,” and so forth.

Thus Odo had recalled the canons to better conduct both by his words and by his example, according to John in Book I, number 17.

## Chapter III — The Beginning of His Monastic Life, His Companions, and His Priesthood

10. While Odo was devoting himself in his retreat beside the basilica of Saint Martin [Col. 0014C] to reading and meditating upon the Fathers, he came upon the Rule of Saint Benedict. In accordance with its prescriptions he lay prostrate naked for three years, “and, although not yet a monk, bore the light yoke of monks,” as John says in number 15.

Perhaps he had invited Count Fulk to join his side. But Fulk, alleging that the time had not yet come, introduced Odo to a certain soldier named Adhegrinus, valiant in arms, and brought them together. Both, therefore, “content with a very small hut,” daily yearned for monastic vows. But they could not find a place in which such discipline flourished.

Adhegrinus was sent to Rome to investigate whether he could find such a place; on the journey he turned aside to Baume. The abbot’s kindness and the monks’ religious observance pleased him, and he drew Odo there with him. Odo “moved to that monastery, taking with him one hundred volumes [Col. 0014D] of books.” “He was then thirty years old,” when the year of Christ was approximately 909. These details are excerpted from John beginning at number 21.

Baume was discussed in Berno’s eulogy. After completing his probation, Odo took upon himself the care and education of the boys, or novices, whom John designates by the term “school,” as was not uncommon among the ancients.

11. Adhegrinus, Odo’s companion, “confined himself to a single cell and, with the permission of Abbot Berno, remained in it for three years.” Later he “sought the desert and was confined there in a small cave.” After many anxieties he was granted divine consolation there; he was freed from demonic temptations through the aid of Saint Martin and was also refreshed by a conversation with him, according to John beginning at number 23. In number 28 John continues to write the following about him:

“More than thirty years have now passed, if I am not mistaken, since he has lived within that very desert. Only on Sundays or major feast days has he been accustomed to descend to the monastery of Saint Peter called Cluny, because it is nearly two miles away. He takes with him a little flour, from which he usually makes bread for himself, and a few grains of beans; then he returns to the desert. He never uses wine. His food is not seasoned with fat or oil. At all times he suffers cold and heat: heat between his shoulders, cold in his hands and arms.”

These are altogether remarkable things about Adhegrinus, whom Chesnius testifies in his notes to have been enrolled among the saints. I do not deny his merit; I am seeking evidence. For I find nothing about Adhegrinus in the martyrologies or breviaries, nor among our Cluniacs do I find any memory of his feast or relics.

I do not know whether Droco, a most devout monk of Fleury, was his companion in the desert. Having been tested in the cenobitic way of life, Droco undertook the singular struggle of the desert in the place “called Baume,” according to Aimoinus in the preceding volume, p. 361.

12. The chronicle of Maillezais joins Teuthelo to Odo as a companion in place of Adhegrinus:

“At that same time, while Turpio was still alive, Odo and Teuthelo, most illustrious canons of Saint Martin, fulfilling the evangelical command, left everything and followed Christ, poor among the poor; and at holy Cluny they were clothed in habit and life. Therefore, by God’s will, Odo became the most holy abbot, as we shall say in what follows; while Teuthelo, at the command of his abbot, was unwillingly consecrated archbishop at Tours,” and so forth.

But from what was said above it is understood that this is false concerning Teuthelo, or Teotolo; it will become still clearer from what follows.

13. After some time, Berno considered Odo worthy of the priesthood and “promoted him; and, having summoned the bishop, he had him consecrated a priest against his will.” John explains the matter in number 37, but does not name the bishop. Nalgodus suggests the Archbishop of Besançon, but incorrectly. It is clear from the passage of John cited above that, at the request of the bishop who ordained him and by the command of the abbot, Odo composed three little books on priests “from the prophecy of Jeremiah”—that is, three books of conferences—which were dedicated to Turpio, Bishop of Limoges. That bishop, therefore, conferred the priesthood upon Odo shortly before Odo’s elevation to the abbacy.

## Chapter IV — The Abbatial Dignity and the State of the Monastic Order

14. “For at that time Father Berno began to lie sick with a fatal illness.” He “immediately summoned the neighboring bishops and resigned from every office. Meanwhile he asked the brothers to choose for themselves whichever father they wished. Then,” says John in number 37, “our father was seized by the hands of the brothers, as though forcibly bound, and, while all were shouting that he should be ordained, was brought by force before his abbot”; and “finally, overcome by the excommunication of the bishops, he was ordained” abbot shortly before Berno’s death, which we have said occurred at the beginning of the year 927.

The chronicle of Maillezais dates this event to “the year 926”; but the arguments we have produced suggest otherwise. To these may be added the Limoges Martyrology reported by Chesnius in his notes to the Cluniac library.

Three monasteries were entrusted to Odo: Cluny, Masciacum, and Déols. Four were entrusted to Wido, Berno’s kinsman: Gigny, Baume, Aethic, and the cell of Saint Lautenus. This is explained more fully in Berno’s own eulogy.

15. Odo the abbot accomplished many altogether outstanding deeds. The perfection and dedication of the monastery of Cluny, its privileges, rites, and exact discipline, according to whose standard other monasteries were established or affiliated and from which the body of the Cluniac congregation was formed; the journeys to Rome undertaken for the good of the Church [Col. 0016B]; the concord of princes; charity toward the poor; and other exceptional deeds of this kind made Odo’s fame celebrated everywhere.

On these matters John in Book III and Nalgodus should be read. Here it will suffice to illuminate some of them: namely, the rites and dignity of the monastery of Cluny, the reform or establishment of other monasteries, and the journeys to Rome. I shall first deal with Cluny; but before that, the condition of the monastic order in Gaul at that time must be discussed.

16. After those august rulers, Charles the Great and Louis the Pious, had earnestly undertaken the restoration and improvement of the order of Saint Benedict, and Benedict, Abbot of Aniane, had through their authority brought it about that most of the monasteries of Gaul should live religiously under one head, as a single congregation, it seemed reasonable to hope [Col. 0016C] that this discipline would long endure. But after Benedict died, he who had been its founder and support, storms of both civil and foreign wars brought devastation upon the entire kingdom and upon so excellent an undertaking.

For while the supreme power was being contested in savage disputes among the sons of Louis the Pious, and even against Louis himself, the Northmen suddenly invaded Gaul from the north. For sixty years they grievously weakened a state already violated by domestic wars. At that time districts were reduced to wasteland, cities were captured and burned, churches given over to plunder, monasteries destroyed, monks partly killed and partly driven into exile. Gathering up the relics of the saints and other small possessions, they withdrew wherever the force of war turned, retreating to safer places, if any appeared [Col. 0016D], or scarcely being allowed to lead a miserable, wandering life.

Wherever they were granted even a brief respite, they repaired huts according to the means and circumstances of the moment; in these they were compelled to care not so much for the regular norm as for life and safety. In some places, where the inhabitants of the monastic order had disappeared, a few clerics gathered together, took possession of the former property of the monks, and retained it for themselves even after conditions had become peaceful.

Thus it came about that, at the beginning of the tenth century, when Odo began to think about the monastic life, few monasteries of monks remained, and in those few genuine religious observance was lacking, as is clear from John, Book I, number 22, and from our preface.

[Col. 0017A]

17. In these circumstances, especially under Abbot Odo, Cluny raised its head above all monasteries through the fame of its religious observance, which Odo established there after Berno. In that place emulation in virtue, zeal for sacred matters, exact observance of the Rule, and charity toward the poor flourished so strongly that “in one year seventeen thousand poor people received alms at Cluny at the beginning of Lent, and received two hundred and fifty hams,” as Udalricus testifies in Book III, chapter 11, of the *Customs of Cluny*.

Indeed, this house more than once provided assistance to the Apostolic See, almost like a common treasury of the Church, as Peter the Venerable records. Most of the rites were taken from Abbot Euticius; the rest were added by Berno, Odo, and others. Euticius appears to have been none other than Benedict of Aniane, who collected the institutions of the ancient monks and proposed them for imitation.

John touches upon some of these rites in Book I, number 23, especially number 30 and those that follow. Some concerned the divine office; some regular discipline and monastic virtues; the rest the education of the young and the instruction of others. The holy monk Udalricus, after Bernard, a monk of the same place, describes them all carefully in three books, which our Acherius published in print in volume IV of the *Spicilegium*.

The first book treats of psalmody and the solemnities of Mass, as well as various annual celebrations; the second of regular discipline; the third of the officials.

It was customary to celebrate two solemn Masses each day. Apart from the divine office and the principal Mass, it was considered religiously improper to celebrate private services. Each day everyone offered his own offerings from one or the other choir. Nevertheless, only on five days—Sundays and the three ferial days—did they receive Communion; the others took blessed offerings, in the manner of *eulogiae*, before the common meal.

At solemn Masses for the dead and during the three days of Rogations, both choirs made an offering. At the principal sacred services the deacon always received Communion from the priest’s host; the subdeacon only from other hosts. Communion was provided to everyone during the three days before Easter. Anyone who wished to celebrate privately on Holy Saturday before the principal Mass “did not use a candle, because the new fire had not yet been consecrated.”

But among these matters nothing deserves more consideration than what is read in Book III, [Col. 0017D] chapter 13, concerning the preparation of the hosts. For the grain was “selected grain by grain and carefully washed by the brothers themselves.” It was then gathered into a sack “reserved solely for this purpose.” Next it was carried to the mill by an approved servant, who washed both millstones and covered them “above and below with curtains”; he also clothed himself in white, with a garment covering his face except for the eyes.

The flour was sifted with the same religious care, using a sieve that had been carefully washed. Then the chief custodian of the church, if he was a priest or deacon, completed the remaining tasks, assisted by two others of the same order and one lay brother; if he was neither priest nor deacon, he substituted a deputy.

When Matins had ended, these four washed their faces and hands. Three of them, dressed in white, proceeded as follows: one moistened the flour with the purest water, while the other two baked the hosts in a “marked iron.”

Such was the piety and veneration of the monks of Cluny toward the Eucharist.

### 18

In the regular offices, too, discipline was no less strict. There was uninterrupted silence during the day, and at night it was so sacred that they considered it altogether sacrilegious to break it before Prime, and would rather have faced death itself. Hence communication by signs, which Guigo, the fifth prior of the Charterhouse, nevertheless did not entirely approve, although he too was devoted to silence, “thinking it sufficient to involve only the tongue in the guilt of speaking, and not also the other limbs,” as he himself says in chapter 31 of the *Statutes*.

From the Ides of November onward, the older monks devoted themselves to meditation in the church after the night offices, [Col. 0018B] while the boys applied themselves to singing in the Chapter House. Manual work was performed with psalmody, and the public confession of faults was customary. After Compline guests were not admitted, nor were the brothers permitted to eat. Udalricus reports the notable example of the cellarer, who, although he had been occupied all day receiving wine, could not obtain permission from the abbot to eat after Compline.

The same strictness prevailed in the divine offices. If someone was about to go outside and mount his horse, and the signal for the office sounded, he was obliged to hurry to it. With regard to fasts, they generally observed what Saint Benedict prescribes. From the Ides of September there was only one meal, except on feasts of twelve lessons; and on the octaves of the Nativity of the Lord and of the Epiphany there were two meals. [Col. 0018C] On those feasts of twelve lessons, after the meal and the reading in the cloister, when None had been said, they went to the refectory to drink. On ordinary days, after Vespers there was a reading; then they proceeded to the refectory to drink, afterward there was another reading, and then spiritual *collatio*—that is, a spiritual conference or refreshment.

The remains of bread and wine were distributed by the almoner to poor pilgrims on foot. In addition, eighteen poor people were fed daily at Cluny. Such was their frugality with wine that “eight cartloads of wine sufficed for more than thirty brothers for a year” at the monastery of La Charité, according to Udalricus, book III, chapter 1.

Moreover, following the prescription of Saint Odo, the Ember fast in September was observed during the week in which the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross fell on a Wednesday, Friday, or Saturday, “so that the Cross might be worshiped by fasting.”

[Col. 0018D] Whether Odo allowed the brothers the use of medicine may reasonably be doubted from John, book II, no. 14, and indeed from Peter the Venerable, book VI, letter 39. The Carthusians, according to Guigo, chapter 39, “used medicines very rarely, except cautery and bloodletting.” Bloodletting, moreover, was performed five times a year. As time went on, the Cluniacs likewise had a particular day assigned each month for bloodletting; Udalricus explains the procedure in book II, chapter 21.

I pass over these lesser matters. Of greater importance is what the same Udalricus records about the education of boys: “It can scarcely happen that any son of a king is brought up in the palace with greater care than the least boy in Cluny.” [Col. 0019A] These are his words in book III, chapter 8.

Finally, the administration of this discipline was carried out under the abbot by the major prior, the deans, the cloister prior, the circuitors, the masters of the boys, the precentor, and the armarius, who kept the books—especially those intended for the choir—in the book-chest; by the chamberlain, who was responsible for clothing; the apocrisarius, to whom the church treasury was entrusted; the cellarer; the stable-master; the almoner; and the infirmarian.

### 19

The prerogative of freedom also belongs to the discipline of the place. At the request first of William, its founder, and then of its abbots, the Roman pontiffs conferred this freedom upon Cluny.

Pope Callistus II, in his letter addressed to Abbot Pontius, says that this privilege had been granted to Cluny “from the very beginning of its foundation.” [Col. 0019B] He also recalls the pontiffs who confirmed it, namely John XI, John XII, Agapitus II, Leo IX, Gregory VI and Gregory VII, Alexander II, Stephen X, Victor III, Urban II, Paschal II, and Gelasius II.

Accordingly, when some objected to Peter the Venerable that the Cluniacs did not have a bishop of their own, he replied that they had the Roman pontiff as their own bishop:

> “We glory in having this one, sole, and greatest bishop . . . . The irrefragable authority of the Holy See itself has established this, and not merely the decrees of one pontiff, but of many, are preserved there in our mother church. [Col. 0019C] They established this arrangement in such a way—not to take this church of Cluny, of which we are speaking, away from another bishop who had previously possessed it, but, when requested by the founders who had built it on their own allod, they retained it as their own and decreed that it should be subject forever to the Roman pontiff, confirming this by many privileges . . . . This is not possessed by the Cluniacs alone, but we see it granted to very many others; and we see that, long before Cluny was founded, it was granted by the same apostolic see to many other monasteries.”

Thus Peter, abbot, in book I, letter 28.

For most privileges of this kind, see the *Cluniac Bullary*. Of these, seven were granted to Abbot Odo: one, namely, by John X; two by John XI; one by Leo VI; and three by Leo VII. The privilege of John X, which is wrongly attributed to John XI, was published in the eulogy of Berno.

[Col. 0019D] In the first privilege of John XI, among other matters, Cluny’s right to “coinage,” granted by Rudolf, king of the Franks, is confirmed. It adds:

> “And since, as is all too clearly established, nearly all monasteries now deviate from their purpose, we grant that, if any monk from any monastery should wish to transfer himself to your way of life solely for the purpose of improving his conduct, but his own abbot should neglect to provide him with the regular means of support for overcoming the desire to possess property, you may receive him until the manner of life of his monastery has been corrected. Written in the month of March, in the fourth indiction”—that is, in the year 931.

We shall speak again of the freedom of Cluny in the *Life of Saint Odilo, Abbot*.

### 20

[Col. 0020A] At this point I cannot pass over what Gregory VII decreed concerning Cluny in the Roman synod, in these words:

> “Let our priests—indeed, let this holy synod—know that, although many monasteries have been founded usefully and religiously for the honor of almighty God and the blessed Virgin, among them all there is in those regions a certain monastery called Cluny, which is recognized as belonging properly to blessed Peter and as being joined to this church by a special right. Therefore, from its very beginnings, it deserved to obtain the honor and protection of this holy and apostolic see . . . .
>
> “And by the favor of divine mercy, under religious and holy abbots, it has reached such a degree of dignity and religious observance that, among all the other monasteries, even those much older, it surpasses them—as far as I know—in the service of God and spiritual fervor, and no monastery on earth, so far as I know, can be wholly compared with it. [Col. 0020B] For no abbot has ever been there who was not a saint.”

A truly splendid eulogy from the mouth of a pontiff.

### 21

Thus, according to Peter the Venerable in book I of *On Miracles*, chapter 9, “the monastery of Cluny, almost throughout the whole world, became renowned for religion, discipline, strictness, the number of its brothers, and every observance of the monastic order,” and indeed became:

> “[Col. 0020C] a singular and common refuge for sinners, through which many losses have been inflicted upon hell and very many places have been granted to the heavenly kingdom. There innumerable crowds of people, casting the heavy burdens of the world from their shoulders, submitted their necks to Christ’s gentle yoke. There persons of every profession, rank, and order exchanged worldly pride and luxury for the humble and poor life of monks. There venerable Fathers of the churches themselves, even while fleeing the burdens of ecclesiastical affairs, chose to live more securely and peacefully, and to be subject rather than to rule . . . .
>
> “From there, the whole house of the world was filled with the fragrance of the ointment, as with the nard of spiritual virtues poured out, while the fervor of monastic religion, which at that time had almost grown cold, was rekindled by the example and zeal of those men. Gaul, Germany, and Britain beyond the sea bear witness to this; Spain, Italy, and all Europe acknowledge it, filled with monasteries founded anew by them or restored from ancient decay . . . . [Col. 0020D] But why should I enumerate particular regions of the world, when this reputation has traveled from our furthest West all the way to the East itself, and no corner of the Christian world has remained unaware of it?”

Thus far Peter the Venerable. It would be easy to prove the truth of his statement if our subject did not call us elsewhere. Nevertheless, lest we seem entirely to have abandoned this argument—which certainly pertains most especially to the praise of the Cluniac order and therefore of its founder, Odo—we must now discuss the monasteries founded or restored by him. The same will be done in its proper place for the other abbots of Cluny.

## CHAPTER V  
### Monasteries Reformed by Odo; the Establishment of the Cluniac Congregation

### 22

Here what John writes about Odo in book II, no. 23, appropriately comes to mind:

> “At that time, indeed, the name of our father began to shine far and wide like a most brilliant star. He became known to kings, intimate with bishops, and dear to nobles. [Col. 0021A] For whatever monasteries had been built within their territories, they entrusted to our father’s authority, so that he might correct and order them according to our custom.”

It would be difficult to draw up an exact account of such monasteries; it is enough to note those that come readily to hand. In Gaul I find, among the Lemovices, Aurillac and Tulle; Sarlat in the district of Périgueux; in the district of Bourges, Déols and Massay; in the district of Orléans, Fleury; among the Senones, Saint-Pierre-le-Vif; among the Turones, Saint-Julian; in the district of Vaud, the abbey of Romans; and in the district of Mâcon, Charlieu, along with others.

In Italy we read in John of Pavia, Saint Augustine’s, Saint Paul’s in Rome, Adventinum, Subpentonianum, and Salernitanum. A few observations must be made about all these.

[Col. 0021B] Gerald, count of Aurillac, most devout, “after devoting himself entirely to divine worship, in order to consecrate his possessions also to the Lord, went to Rome and, by a solemn testament, assigned Aurillac, a distinguished estate, to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, together with such appurtenances as could suffice for the entire support of the monks whom he had decided to gather there. He also assigned a census to be paid annually at the shrine (*urna*) of Saint Peter,” namely “ten solidi,” according to Odo in book II of his *Life*, chapters 4 and 17.

Odo adds in chapter 6 that Gerald was extremely anxious to find proven monks who would inhabit the place. When he could not find any, [Col. 0021C] he “sent certain noble boys to the monastery of Vabre,” where “the fervor of regular observance was growing hot,” so that “they might be instructed there under the regular rule.” But when they returned, “because teachers were lacking,” they soon “became softened by childish weakness and neglected the rigor of discipline.” Nevertheless, one person had necessarily been placed over them, who caused Gerald great grief because of their lax ways.

I do not know whether this was Adalgerus, whom the *Chronicle of Aurillac*, published in volume II of the *Analecta*, suggests as the first abbot of Aurillac. He was succeeded by John, from Gerald’s own family. “Odo, venerable abbot, third abbot of Aurillac and of Cluny, at the request of Turpio, bishop of Limoges, and Aimone, abbot of Tulle, wrote the life of blessed Gerald. He had Arnulf as co-abbot.”

[Col. 0021D] Odo was summoned from the monastery of Aurillac, according to Aimoinus in book I of *On the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, chapter 4, to restore discipline in the monastery of Fleury, at the initiative of Count Eliziard, later a monk, as John relates below in book III, no. 8.

At the same time—that is, during the reign of Louis from Overseas—Bernard, count of Périgord, gave the monastery of Sarlat, which eventually became an episcopal see, “to Lord Odo, abbot of Cluny, and to Adacius, his co-abbot.” Letters concerning this matter exist in volume IV of *Gallia Christiana*, though with several blemishes.

[Col. 0022A] The monastery of Tulle, now an episcopal see, was likewise subject to both of them—namely, to Odo, abbot of Cluny, and Adacius, his deputy—after the aforementioned Aimone, who had been brought from the monastery of Saint-Savin in Poitiers to Tulle by Count Ebal.

You will find the diploma for this granted by King Rudolf in Appendix V of Charles Stephen Baluze’s additions to book VIII of *On Concord*, chapter 25.

At that time it was customary that, because one Cluniac abbot could not suffice for several monasteries, pro-abbots or co-abbots were appointed over them in his place; later only the title of prior remained to them. This is clear from Clarius in the chronicle of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif among the Senones, where, after Abbot Samson,

> “Saint Odo succeeded. He summoned Archbishop William and, with the consent of the monks of Saint-Pierre, appointed over that monastery Arigaudus, a religious and God-fearing monk of Saint Benedict’s monastery above the Loire.”

### 23

[Col. 0022B] I believe that Odo performed the same service in the monastery of Saint-Julian at Tours. It had been built in the time of Bishop Gregory but was later destroyed by the Northmen. When Archbishop Teotolo restored it, assisted by his sister Gersende, “he dedicated the church in honor of the Mother of God and Saint Julian; and, wishing to appoint an abbot after assembling the brothers, he summoned Abbot Odo, who was then staying at Saint Benedict’s.”

The *Martyrology of Saint Julian* dates this event to “the year 943, in the eighth year of the reign of King Louis.” But that was the date of the donation made by Teotolo and Gersende, not of Odo’s appointment at Saint Julian, since it is known that he died the previous year, namely in 942. He obtained burial in the church of Saint Julian together with Teotolo, as we shall say later.

[Col. 0022C] I have read a fragment of the chronicle of that place, written five hundred years ago. The chronicle was divided into two books. In the first were contained “the original foundation of the abbey, the impious destruction of the foundation, and the pious restoration of the destruction”; in the second, the condition of the monastery from its restoration onward.

From the tattered membranes of the first book we understand that many bodies of saints, originally placed in the church of Saint Julian, had been buried deeply in the ground during the time of the Danes. Some of them still remained, namely those of Saint Bleviligetus, bishop of Vannes; Saint Laurus, abbot; and Saint Antony, monk.

Of the first, the author says that “Bishop Morvannus,” the “seventh” bishop of Vannes after Bleviligetus, had related certain miracles to him, which he records. [Col. 0022D] Albertus of Monte Relaxo calls him “Blinlivet,” not a saint, and makes him the thirty-third bishop of Vannes; Morvannus, however, the forty-ninth.

The writer of the fragment adds that Laurus, born in Britain, abandoned his homeland and parents but found in their place “Judicael, the excellent leader of the Britons,” who became his helper in all things:

> “With his help, after a monastery had been established, he flourished in all holiness together with those subject to him, and benefited many greatly both by word and by example. His noble life was most religious in the sight of men and precious in the sight of the Lord. The lofty praises of his holiness also continue to be increased by the glory of miracles. For through his holiness debility is remedied and infirmity healed both during his life and after his death, especially in that place where he departed from the world, [Col. 0023A] where his ashes live through the signs that take place.”

Perhaps this was the monastery of Saint John of Gaël, which Judicael restored.

> “And since the book of his life teaches his life, let it suffice to have commended at least the summary of his life.”

We think that this book has been lost. Nor, so far as I know, does anything concerning Saint Laurus appear in Albertus.

Finally, that chronicler writes that Antony lived among the Turones:

> “It is said that Saint Antony lived in you, although it is uncertain to us whether he was from you or came from elsewhere. Delighting in the sweetness of the solitary life, he despised the world for the sake of the solitary life. He inhabited a beautiful and quiet place, enclosed on every side by forest; [Col. 0023B] there was, and still is, a chapel carved in the rock, containing two altars. There the servant of God served God constantly. No woman approaches the spring that is in the chapel.”

This place, which is now a priory, is still visited. It lies three leagues from Tours—Caesarodunum of the Turones—toward Le Mans. Saint Antony is commemorated on the fourth day before the Nones of May in the *Gallican Martyrology*.

Some later writers say that he was one of the companions of Saint Maurus, abbot. A document of John, archbishop of Tours, drawn up in 1407, concerning the relics of Saint Antony and Saint Laurus, calls him abbot of Saint Julian. We may admit that we do not know what antiquity itself did not know. We shall return below to the monastery of Saint Julian.

### 24

[Col. 0023C] Among the monasteries that Odo added to his administration was Romans, situated in the county of Vaud in the district of Lausanne. King Rudolf I of Burgundy granted it to his sister Aleydis in a document issued “on the fourth day before the Ides of June, in the first year of the most devout King Rudolf, from the Incarnation of the Lord 888, in the eleventh indiction,” at Vabrevilla.

These letters, whose complete autograph is in our possession, were published in the notes to the *Cluniac Library*, but with an error in the hundreds digit, where 900 is read instead of 800.

Later Aleys, or Adeleys, herself countess, assigned that abbey, called Romans, to Odo in an excellent diploma, which it is useful to reproduce here, since it remains unpublished, for the elucidation of the history:

> It is clear to all who consider the matter carefully, and so forth. [Col. 0023D] Therefore, let it be known to all who live in the unity of faith and await the mercy of Christ that I, Adeleydis, countess by the gift of God, transfer all the property belonging to me that came to me by the charter of Lord Rudolf, my sweetest and most beloved brother—namely, the monastery called Romans, situated in the district of Vaud, with the whole abbey and all the properties and appurtenances belonging to that abbey, formerly established there by the holy Fathers appointed for that purpose.
>
> That monastery, called Romans, had once been built under the monastic profession in honor of the prince of the apostles, Peter and Paul; but now it has been wholly deprived of monastic inhabitants. Therefore, for love of our Lord Jesus Christ and of those same apostles, I, the aforesaid Adeleydis, transfer it entirely from my right and lordship into the ownership and care of the monks—[Col. 0024A] namely, of the venerable and most reverend abbot Odo, and of all the brothers and the company of monks living under his governance in the monastery of Cluny—on this condition alone: that those monks, as far as they are able, should strive, through the intercession of the apostles and with Christ’s favor, to restore that monastery to its former state.
>
> Let the aforesaid abbot, for as long as he lives, and those monks possess the same monastery in such a way that, although it has been assigned to the apostolic see, just as Cluny has, they may nevertheless always act and be governed as one congregation under one abbot. [Col. 0024B] Thus, when he departs this life, neither group may appoint an abbot for itself without their common consent, nor may these monks, God forbid, presume separately to substitute anyone other than the one whom the others have. For it would be exceedingly unjust if those who might grow up in the monastery of Romans as sons were ever to sever the fellowship of the Cluniacs, who, as fathers, revive that place.
>
> In appointing an abbot, let the constitution of Saint Benedict always prevail, so that, if even the smallest portion of either congregation should wish to choose a better person by sounder judgment, the others may consent to them in accordance with the Rule.
>
> As for brothers to be transferred from one place to the other for the sake of utility, or for resources that may happen to abound more in one place than in the other to be transferred in turn from one to the other, this shall be in the abbot’s power.
>
> And so that a closer fellowship may endure between them, let them also observe jointly the ordinances of divine service, almsgiving, and every good work, so that what is done at Cluny for William of blessed memory, or certainly for others, whether living or dead, may benefit us and our people; and what is done for us at the monastery of Romans according to the will of the Lord may likewise benefit them.
>
> [Col. 0024C] I make this donation first for love of God and of the holy apostles, and then for the soul of my brother and sweetest lord, King Rudolf, the donor of these possessions; then for the repose of my lord Richard, prince of pious memory; and for Queen Willa; thereafter for myself and for my lord King Rudolf, my son, and also King Rudolf, my grandson; for my other sons, Hugh and Boso, and for my grandson Louis; also for our other relatives and for those who adhere to our service; for my father and mother; for the distinguished abbot Hugh and our other kinsmen of either sex; finally, for those who provide aid or protection to the monks residing there; for the state of the whole religious order; and for all Catholics, living or dead.
>
> [Col. 0024D] The monks residing there shall preserve the manner of life that is now transferred from Cluny to instruct those who are to come, so that they in no way diminish that same manner in food and clothing, abstinence, psalmody, silence, hospitality, mutual love and subjection, and the good of obedience.
>
> It has also pleased us to insert into this testament that, from this day forward, the monks gathered there shall not be subjected to our authority, that of our parents, the pride of royal majesty, [Col. 0025A] or the yoke of any earthly power. Nor may any secular prince, any count, any bishop, or even the pontiff of the aforesaid city of Rome—by the Lord and in the Lord, by all his saints, and by the day of the dreadful judgment I bear witness and entreat—invade the possessions of those servants of God, alienate them, diminish them, exchange them, bestow any of them on anyone, or appoint any superior over them against their will.
>
> And so that this wickedness may be more firmly prohibited to all reckless and wicked persons, I add the following further warning. I beseech you, holy apostles and glorious princes of the earth, Peter and Paul, and you, pontiff of pontiffs of the apostolic see, that, by the canonical and apostolic authority which you have received from God, you exclude from the fellowship of the holy Church of God and from eternal life the plunderers, invaders, and alienators of these possessions, which I give with willing and cheerful mind to the servants of God named above. [Col. 0025B] May you be protectors and defenders of the aforesaid place of Romans, of the servants of God dwelling and remaining there, and of all these possessions, for the sake of the almsgiving, clemency, and mercy of our most merciful Redeemer.
>
> If, perchance—and may it not happen; nor do I think it can happen through the mercy of God and the protection of the apostles—anyone, whether among our relatives or strangers, of whatever condition, or by any power or cunning whatsoever, should attempt to bring any disturbance against this testament, which I have decreed to be made for the love of almighty God and the veneration of the princes of the apostles Peter and Paul, let him first incur the wrath of almighty God. May the Lord remove his father from the land of the living and erase his name from the book of life. [Col. 0025C] May his portion be with those who said to God, “Depart from us, Lord,” and with Dathan and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed with open mouth and hell absorbed alive. May he incur everlasting damnation, and, becoming the companion of Judas, the betrayer of the Lord, may he be held shut up in eternal torments.
>
> And lest he appear to human eyes to go unpunished in the present age, may he suffer in his own body the torments of future damnation, receiving a twofold punishment together with Heliodorus and Antiochus, one of whom, restrained by dreadful blows, escaped scarcely half alive, while the other, struck by a heavenly command, died most miserably with his limbs putrefying and swarming with worms. May he share the fate of the other sacrilegious men who dared to profane the treasury of the house of the Lord. Unless he repents, may he have the chief key-bearer of the entire monarchy of the churches, with Saint Paul joined to him, as his adversary and as one who bars the entrance to the pleasant paradise—those whom he could, if he wished, have had as most merciful intercessors.
>
> [Col. 0025D] But according to worldly law, let him be compelled by judicial authority to pay one hundred pounds of gold to those whom he has wronged; let his action be frustrated and have no effect whatsoever. May the force of this testament, supported by every authority, remain forever inviolate and unshaken, with a binding stipulation.
>
> The mark of Adeleydis, countess, royal mother and abbess, authorizing and ordering this testament to be made.
>
> The mark of Hildegangus, an unworthy priest.
>
> The mark of Hulricus.
>
> The mark of Juditta, daughter of King Rudolf.
>
> The mark of Albrada.
>
> The mark of Wido.
>
> The mark of Einricus.
>
> The mark of Hugh, illustrious count and brother of the august King Rudolf.
>
> The mark of Gofredus.
>
> The mark of Rudolf, son of Emperor Louis.
>
> [Col. 0026A] The marks of Stephen, Christian, Gonfredus, Unbertus, Boso, Bavo, Leodfredus, Wlitgerius, and Rudolf.
>
> Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July. I, Hildebrannus the priest, wrote and subscribed this in place of the chancellor, in the fifth year of the reign of the most glorious King Rudolf, in the second indiction. Publicly enacted at the villa of Boiacum.

Thus far the diploma.

Concerning the monastery of Romans, the *Book of Priories* in the Cluniac Library states:

> “The priory of the monastery of Romans (Romansmonstier), in the diocese of Lausanne, where there ought to be twenty-two monks, including the prior, although formerly there were more, as is found recorded; and there ought to be celebrated there three Masses with chant,” and so forth.

### 26

[Col. 0026B] I return to the district of Mâcon, whose abbey, called Charlieu, Pope John XI assigned to Odo, or to the monastery of Cluny, at the request of Hugh, king or duke of Burgundy, “on the seventh day before the Kalends of January, in the eleventh year of his pontificate, in the fifth indiction”—that is, in the year 932.

Louis from Overseas did the same by letters which are preserved in the Cluniac Library, column 276. At the request of Count Siraldus, King Boso had restored this abbey to the monks, as is clear from a charter published by Guichenon in his *History of Savoy*, page 375. There the monastery of Charlieu is said to have been dedicated “in honor of Saint Stephen” and to have been situated “in the county of Mâcon, on the Sornan River.”

The diploma is dated “on the third day before the Nones of December, in the twelfth indiction, in the first year of Boso at the monastery of Charlieu”—that is, in the year 879.

We shall speak of Charlieu again in Aymard, below.

### 27

Finally, besides other Gallic monasteries entrusted to the Cluniacs under Odo, whose records are lacking, [Col. 0026C] certain Italian monasteries also came under the authority of Cluny at that time, namely Subpentonianum, Adventinum, and Saint Paul’s in Rome, as is clear from John; and Salernitanum, to whose brothers John dedicated Odo’s life.

It is highly probable that Saint Peter’s at Pavia also belonged to this number, since, when Odo was returning from Rome, he left John—then a canon, later a monk—there to be educated, as John himself testifies in book I, no. 4.

This is the monastery called Saint Peter in Ciel d’Oro, later called Saint Augustine’s after the translation of his body to that place, which we discussed in part I of the third century.

### 28

[Col. 0026D] Authors write variously about the beginnings of the church of Saint Paul near Rome. Some trace its first origin to Pope Sylvester and the emperor Constantine.

Leo Allatius holds this view in book I of *On the Agreement of the Two Churches*, chapter 6, no. 26. He says that the basilica of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way was originally built by Sylvester in the form of an *eopyla*—that is, with its entrance turned toward the east—but that the emperor Valentinian, at the direction of Pope Siricius, caused it to be transformed into the structure we see today, an *eothola* [the reading is uncertain], with its front turned toward the east.

Peter Damian, however, attributes the Vatican basilica of Saint Peter to Constantine as its founder, and the Ostian basilica of Saint Paul to the elder Theodosius and his son Honorius. The passage occurs in *Opusculum* 4, *Responsio* 4 of the *Defender of the King*:

> “Long afterward, the emperor Theodosius began the basilica of blessed Paul; when he died, his son Honorius brought that same basilica to completion.”

I read the same in a very ancient codex of the church of Noyon, written eight hundred years ago, containing the *Etymologies* of Isidore. There these words occur:

> “[Col. 0027A] In the basilica of Saint Paul the apostle at Rome, where his sacred body is buried…” [The quotation breaks off at this point in the supplied source.]

So much for the origin of the basilica. [Col. 0027B] We must now investigate when it was granted to monks.

That this happened before Odo is suggested by John in book I, no. 27, where he says that Odo, “five years before” he wrote his life, “went to Rome and rebuilt the monastery within the church of the most blessed apostle Paul, as it had formerly been, compelled by the lord pope and by all the orders of the Holy See.”

Therefore, “as it had formerly been” indicates that the place had once been a monastic residence, which Odo restored around the year 937, when he was in Rome, as we shall explain later.

The same John mentions the monastery of Saint Paul and its monks in various places, as well as its abbot Baldwin. He also reports that Saint Odo himself, while he was staying in Rome, was accustomed to live there, especially in book II, nos. 21 and 22.

Nor can this be called into question, [Col. 0027C] since John himself stayed there with Odo.

Yet in the highly reputable book on the life of Saint John, abbot of Gorze, we read that the monk Andrew was sent “to Rome at the request of Pope Agapitus.” Agapitus “had earnestly requested from Lord Einoldus, abbot of Gorze, through a suitable messenger, that some religious men be sent to him, whom he might place, with the assistance of King Alberic, in the monastery of blessed Paul, which he was then endeavoring to transfer to the monastic order. Andrew was brought there together with another brother who had come from the monastery of Luxeuil to Gorze several years earlier. After the place had been instructed in regular discipline, he was not long afterward received by the Lord and buried there.”

[Col. 0027D] Agapitus began to occupy the see in the fourth year after Odo’s death, namely in the year of Christ 946. How, then, could the monastery of Saint Paul, which under Odo had been imbued with monastic institutions, once again have been “transferred to the monastic order” under Pope Agapitus?

This must be understood as a restoration of regular discipline, although it is astonishing that it should have failed there so quickly. Certainly it had failed under the reign of Otto II—or at least that was the pretext used. Otto, according to Glaber Rodulfus in book I, chapter 4, intended to establish canons at Saint Paul in place of the monks, whose conduct had become too lax.

Whatever the truth may be, the Ostian monastery of Saint Paul, although not wholly subject to Cluny, nevertheless repeatedly received its superiors from there. Peter Damian provides evidence of this in *Opusculum* 33, where he discusses Saint Majolus, who was made prior at Saint Paul, as we shall relate in the acts of Saint Majolus.

[Col. 0028A] Finally, Hugh, a monk of Cluny, explicitly confirms this in a letter to Abbot Pontius, in these words:

> “This monastery”—namely, Saint Paul’s—“in the following years was entrusted to your predecessor, Saint Odo, and through him the vigor of the Cluniac order shone there for some time. At last, when the city was disturbed by seditious uprisings, which that city suffers with disastrous frequency, and evils pressed upon them, the monks departed, carrying with them as sacred pledges that vessel of apostolic ashes, namely Saint Paul; and thus they quickly reached Cluny.”

[Col. 0028B] The abbot of the monastery of Saint Paul was that Adam whom Pope Victor III mentioned in book II of *On the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, chapter 25. John Baptist Marus raises a question concerning that passage: to whom was the monastery of Saint Paul then subject, to the Cluniac congregation or to that of Cassino?

The reason for doubt is drawn from the fact that, according to Leo of Marsi in book I of the *Cassinese Chronicle*, chapter 58, the abbey of Saint Paul was entrusted to Abbot Baldwin by Pope Marinus. Hence Desiderius, or Pope Victor, who was also abbot of Cassino, calls the monastery of Saint Paul “ours.”

He could, however, have spoken in this way with reference to the common order, since at that time there was no Cassinese congregation, and indeed not yet a Cluniac congregation in the form in which it was later established under Saint Hugh.

29. To all these and many other monasteries Odo prescribed a uniform rule of life, such as was observed at Cluny, and presided over them no differently than a general abbot. What had first been instituted in the East by St. Pachomius, and attempted in the West by Benedict of Aniane, was finally perfected by Odo. Hence some regarded him as the founder of St. Benedict’s order in Gaul, because he brought together into something like a single body numerous monasteries that had previously been partly ruined and entirely separated from one another. At least Peter the Venerable calls him “the supreme restorer of the monastic order in Gaul and the foremost reformer of the Rule,” and likewise “the first father of the Cluniac order, who undertook to revive the fervor of the monastic vocation, already dead and almost everywhere buried,” in Book VI, Letter 17. In the same sense, before him, Frodoard in his chronicle calls Odo “the restorer of many monasteries and the repairer of the holy Rule”; and Rodulfus Glaber writes:

> He became so great a propagator of this institution that the more important monasteries in the province of Benevento and throughout Italy and Gaul as far as the Ocean rejoiced to be subject to his authority.

[Col. 0028D] So great, finally, was the fame of his name and religious life that not only lay nobles and clerics but also bishops, after resigning their dignities, flocked to him, as John testifies in Book III, no. 10.

## CHAPTER VI — The Increase of the Affairs of the Cluniac Monastery under Odo

30. Odo greatly increased not only the religious observance of the Cluniac institution but also its material resources, which ordinarily follow upon it on almost equal footing. First, at the request of his wife Imma, King Rodulf of the Franks handed over to Cluny the tenanted manses of his brother Hugh, situated in the Mâconnais: three at Salustriac and others elsewhere. The charter was issued “at the villa of Bojaco, on the Kalends of July,” in the tenth year of his reign, indiction 3 (year 44 [uncertain]), that is, in the year 931. In the following year, Berno, bishop of Mâcon, at the request of Archimbold, the prelate—that is, provost—of the Cluniac monastery, and of Hildebrand, sitting “in council” beside the church of St. Vincent at Mâcon “to settle divine commands according to the custom of the preceding Fathers,” granted the tithes of the land at Salustriaco, which King Rodulf had given them. In that same year, namely the tenth year of King Rodulf, the same Bishop Berno consecrated a chapel in the same villa of Salustriaco, which chapel “the little Cluniac community, under the patronage of Odo, its gentle father and abbot, had built.”

31. Two years later, Leotald, count of Mâcon, and his wife Ermengard gave Abbot Odo whatever property they possessed “in the villa of Darbaniac, in the county of Lyon, on the river Salia,” so that God might deign to free the souls of their parents Alberic and Escolana, of Manasses and Irmingard, and also of their friend Gerard, “from the punishments of hell.” After Leotald and Ermengard, Count Gaufred subscribed with others. This charter was published, with a few blemishes, in the Sebusian Library, p. 168; for other documents of the same Leotald, see pp. 236 and 296.

32. In the year 936, a small estate in the villa of Rufiaco—which lies near Cluny—in the county of Mâcon was likewise given to Odo, “in the month of May, when King Rodulf departed from this world. Done at Cluny, confirmed publicly at the castle of Lurdun.” In the second year of King Louis, Abbot Odo and the Cluniac monks purchased a field below the castle of Lordon, commonly called “Lourdon,” which castle was demolished at the command of Cardinal Richelieu.

33. In the same year “in which King Rodulf departed from this world,” Count Gaufred and his wife Ava gave Escozolas in the county of Autun for their souls, “and for the soul of their lord William and his son Boso.” In the fifth year of Louis Transmarinus they likewise transferred Keitaelos in the county of Mâcon, “in the vicariate of Bufarias, for the relief of their souls and of the soul of Gauzbert, the brother of the aforesaid Gaufred.”

34. In the second year of the same Louis, Maimbold, bishop of Mâcon, stated that his predecessor Berno had granted the Cluniac monks that all their churches should remain entirely under their authority; but when these churches had later been destroyed “by the incursion of pagans and the wickedness of evil men,” he reduced the synodal tribute that they paid. The canons subscribed, among them Abbot Ado, who was one of the principal members, and in the twelfth year of that Louis he gave the Cluniac monastery, among other things, the churches of St. Desiderius and St. Julian at Siviac and Davagiac. Likewise, in the second year, Rotmund, bishop of Autun, gave the chapel of St. Leodegarius of Blanciac in the county of Mâcon, which “his most holy predecessor Walo had given for life to a certain priest.” The witnesses were Abbots Hildebod and Girbald.

35. In the third year of the same king, indiction 11—that is, in the year of Christ 938—a mansus in the villa of Madaliac, in the county of Lyon, “in the Ternat district,” was given to the Cluniac monastery, where Odo was abbot. A certain Airich likewise gave Odo a field with a wood in the county of Lyon, “in the Tarnat district,” at the boundary of Denadaliac. “Ternatum” was without doubt the place where the Ternat monastery stood, which everyone is accustomed to confuse with Agaunum. But this Ternatum lies on the Rhône, at the boundary of the counties of Lyon and Vienne, commonly called “Ternay,” where there is now a priory of the order of St. Benedict. Likewise, in the third year of his reign, Louis Transmarinus confirmed by a diploma the Cluniac properties at Quercetum near Dociacum; the diploma survives in the Cluniac Library.

I pass over other smaller donations, such as that by which Count Hugh transferred to the Cluniac monastery and to Abbot Odo one female servant from the villa of “Romanis” in the county of Lyon, in the “sixth year” of King Louis; after that year, donations were made to Abbot Aimard. All the charters under Odo are numbered 188. Furthermore, from all these charters, and from others that we shall discuss under Aimard, it is clear that Mâcon and the county assigned to it were then subject to the king of the Franks, not to the king of Burgundy.

## CHAPTER VI bis — Odo’s Multiple Journeys to Rome on Ecclesiastical Business

36. Odo’s ardent devotion to divine affairs did not confine itself within the retreats of monasteries; rather, it emerged for the benefit of the universal Church. The Roman pontiffs summoned him to Italy once and again, so that by his prudence and authority he might assist the Church in its troubled circumstances.

The cause of his first journey to Rome was as follows. After the death of the emperor Berengar, when Hugh, son of Theobald, count of Arles, had gained control of affairs in Italy, Marozia—the infamous widow of Wido, count of Tuscany, who, together with her son Alberic, had laid hands upon Pope John and reduced Rome to her own power—sent messengers to Hugh inviting him to marry her and assume control of the city. Hugh accepted the proposal, and after contracting the marriage obtained dominion over Rome.

Meanwhile, before the banquet, Alberic, at his mother’s urging, offered water to Hugh so that he might wash his hands, but did so rather clumsily. Hugh struck him in the face as a correction. Offended by this, Alberic incited the Romans to revolt and forced Hugh to flee [Col. 0030D] the city. After Hugh had escaped by flight, Alberic governed the city with consular authority together with his mother Marozia, and restored the ancient discipline of Rome together with the name and office of the consuls.

These events took place around the year 929, during the pontificates of John X, Leo VI, and Stephen VII. In 931 John XI succeeded them, Marozia’s son by her adulterous relationship with Sergius and Alberic’s brother. Thus the holy Roman Church of God was compelled to suffer such things, inflicted by Marozia herself and her son Alberic.

“In the year 933,” writes Frodoardus, “messengers returning to Rome from the Church of Rheims report that Pope John, son of Maria, who is also called Marozia, is being held in custody by his brother, named Alberic; he was also keeping his mother Marozia confined and held Rome against King Hugh.” Shortly afterward: “King Hugh of Italy besieges Rome.” And in the year 936, “after Pope John, Alberic’s brother, had died, a certain servant of God named Leo was established as pope at Rome”—namely Leo VII. Frodoardus immediately adds:

> King Hugh, attempting to capture Rome, at last abandoned the siege after his army had been afflicted by hunger and the death of its horses, having made peace with Alberic and given him his daughter in marriage.

We must now determine in what year Odo was first summoned to Rome by the pontiff.

37. Baronius believes this occurred in the year 936, when King Hugh gave his daughter—whom the deacon Liutprand of Pavia, a writer of that period, calls Alda—in marriage to Alberic and thus ceased his attack on Rome. Baronius is correct. For, as Odo was preparing for his Roman journey, he visited Adhegrin and learned from him, through a revelation of St. Martin, of the anointing of Louis Transmarinus, which took place in 936.

Odo undertook this journey for two reasons. First, he was to reconcile King Hugh with Prince Alberic; Odo himself enjoyed great favor with Hugh, as is evident from three privileges that Hugh obtained from the Roman pontiffs for Odo’s benefit, namely from John XI, Leo VI, and Leo VII. Second, he was to rebuild “the monastery within the church of the blessed Apostle Paul, as it had formerly been,” at the command of the lord pope and “of all the orders of the Holy See,” according to John, Book I, no. 27, where the anointing of Louis Transmarinus is discussed.

At that time, at St. Paul’s in Rome, he corrected the Life of St. Martin and adorned it with glosses, as appears from Book II, no. 22. To this period may be referred what John writes in Book II, no. 9:

> In former times, while the aforesaid King Hugh was besieging the city of Rome because of his hostility toward the aforementioned Prince Alberic, he began to move about inside and outside the city, scattering counsels of peace and reconciliation between the two, so that he might calm the fury of the aforesaid king and defend the city from so great a siege. Meanwhile, one day, while he was walking near the monastery of the blessed Apostle Andrew, which is called by the name of the Clivus Scauri, a certain peasant wished to kill him because of a small flask of water.

Alberic wished to punish the peasant with death, unless Odo had prevented him. Such was the veneration not only of Hugh but also of Alberic for Odo.

Another indication of Alberic’s goodwill toward Odo was that he entrusted to him the reform of the monastery of St. Elias at Suppentonia, as John testifies in Book III, no. 7.

38. Odo’s second journey to Rome took place not in 938 but in the following year, as John explicitly states at the beginning of Book I:

> In the year, therefore, of the Lord’s Incarnation 939, in the sixtieth year of his age and the thirtieth year of his monastic life, when he came to Rome, he found me, wretched man, entangled in earthly bonds; taking pity on me, he caught me in his net and brought me to the monastery of St. Peter at Pavia, where I remained. After I had been detained there for a short time by Hugh, he entrusted me to the aforesaid lord Hildebrand to be educated in the regular disciplines.

John therefore was not Odo’s companion on his first journey, as Baronius thought. John continues:

> Not long afterward, when he came to Rome, he graciously chose to take me as his companion; and the man whom, when departing, he had taken from his parents as a canon, he brought back upon his return as a monk.

From this it is understood that John was born at Rome and had been a canon there. This return to Rome took place while Pope Leo was still alive, and therefore in the year 939 itself, or at least at the beginning of the following year; I do not know whether it occurred before Odo had returned to Gaul.

John confirms this chronology in Book II, no. 7:

> At about the same time we were sent to Italy by Leo, the supreme pontiff, to undertake an embassy of peace between Hugh, king of the Lombards, and Alberic, prince of the city of Rome.

To this period should be referred what John records in Book I, no. 22:
