> Three years earlier, while we were at Rome with the blessed Paul…

John was writing immediately after Odo’s death, which occurred toward the end of the year 942. The same applies to what he reports in Book I, no. 16. Perhaps it was at that time that he made a pilgrimage to Mount Garganus, concerning which he writes in Book II, no. 15.

Finally, in the year 942 Odo was summoned to Rome for the third time by Pope Stephen IX, in order to reconcile King Hugh with the same Alberic. Frodoardus writes under that year:

> The lord Odo, abbot, was laboring with King Hugh of Italy to establish peace between him and Alberic, the Roman patrician.

In these labors undertaken for the Church, the holy man grew old and was worn out. Having contracted an illness at Rome, he obtained from God an extension of life until he could return to Tours, to St. Martin, as we shall soon relate from John.

If Odo did not return to Gaul in 939, then Gerard, bishop of Reggio, mentioned in Book II, no. 6 of the Life, was his companion on the second journey; if, on the contrary, Odo did return then, Gerard accompanied him on the third journey. For these words prove that John was with them:

> At that time when, together with Gerard, bishop of the Church of Reggio, we crossed the Alps and came to Rome…

But anyone who places a fourth journey by Odo to Rome before his final one may perhaps not be far from the truth. For, in addition to the three journeys just mentioned, undertaken on behalf of the Church, John indicates another in Book [I], no. 18, undertaken for the sake of prayer. But enough of this.

## CHAPTER VII — Odo’s Illness, Death, Burial, Relics, and Cult

39. When the holy man realized that death was approaching, he repeatedly recalled in his mind the stains of his former sins, especially those by which he had sinned against his abbot while a private monk. Thus he once addressed John in Book III, no. 6:

> Dearest son, listen to what I tell you. I give thanks to God because, of all the sins I committed from my youth, I have already received punishment for them in this life, except for those that I committed against my abbot; and I have always awaited that day and that time, beseeching God not to reserve them for me in the future.

This occurred shortly before his final journey to Rome, which took place in 942. Before he set out on that journey, however, he appears to have substituted Abbot Aimard in his place, as we shall say below in Aimard’s eulogy.

40. At that time, seized by a sharp and continuous fever, and although he longed for heavenly life, he nevertheless felt a great desire to revisit the tomb of St. Martin, so that he might give up his spirit there, where he had drawn the first years of his holy life. In fact, he obtained this from heaven through the merits of his excellent patron, whom he had always venerated so greatly.

He recovered, returned, and attended the feast he had desired on the fourth day before the Ides of November. But on the fourth day within the octave, the fever flared up again, until at last the blessed man, refreshed by that divine and salutary nourishment and strengthened by the life-giving cup—that is, by the viaticum—departed to heaven under Martin’s guidance on the fourteenth day before December. John relates these events at greater length at the end of Book III.

41. Nalgodus adds several distinctive details: that Odo summoned the brothers, arranged the monasteries entrusted to him, and commended Cluny to God; that he retained only “his chapel,” that is, the sacred furnishings used for the celebration of Mass, and sent everything else back to Cluny. These may perhaps be the author’s conjectures.

More certain is what he adds, namely, that Odo was buried at Tours “in the church of the blessed Julian, which he had built from its foundations”—that is, restored—with the expenses supplied by Archbishop Teotolo, as was said above. This manner of speaking is familiar among authors and in similar passages.

But we should also hear the Necrologium of the monastery of St. Julian:

> After the most reverend man Odo had built many monasteries, corrected very many, taught many to despise the vanities of the world, and written useful works for the Church; after he had composed hymns and antiphons in elegant praise of St. Martin; now in old age, now wearied by the length of his years, as though foreknowing his calling, he desired, once the burden had been laid down, to have the earthly body of his flesh buried beside the body of his special patron, the lord Martin, if possible. He therefore resolved to return to his own monastery at Tours. Meanwhile, when the feast of blessed Martin arrived, the venerable father went forth with his monks to the solemnity of Matins, long before daylight [lacuna]. On the eighth day of his illness, sensing that his final hour was approaching, with all the brothers standing around him, he took care to be faithfully fortified with the viaticum of the Lord’s body and blood. Then he ordered himself to be carried into the church of St. Albin, which was nearby, and, with holy lights and hands raised toward heaven, he surrendered his soul to Christ.

The oratory of St. Albin still survives within the cloister of the aforementioned monastery. “He died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December; he was buried by the often-mentioned Bishop Theotolo in the crypt of St. Julian, beneath the altar of that martyr, on the right-hand side.”

These details come from the local Martyrology, renewed in the form of the older one in the year 1469, in the month of July, under Pope Paul II, King Louis XI, and Archbishop Elias; these names belong to the revised Martyrology.

42. Nalgodus assigns the year of Odo’s death as 945, counting it as the eighteenth year of his ordination. But the authority of Frodoardus, a contemporary writer, must be preferred. He says that Odo died two years earlier, in these words recorded in his chronicle toward the end of the year 942:

> The lord Odo, venerable abbot, restorer of many monasteries and renewer of the holy Rule, died at Tours and was buried at St. Julian.

Nothing clearer can be produced either for fixing the year of his death or for determining the place of his burial. Indeed, this year follows from John’s reckoning, for in Book III, no. 5, he testifies that he had not lived with Odo for a full two years:

> Unhappy me, he says, who did not deserve to serve him for two complete years.

He had attached himself to Odo at the beginning of the year 940, according to what was said in the preceding chapter.

The same year is assigned by Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, in his chronicle:

> In this year the lord Odo, venerable abbot and restorer of many monasteries, after laboring greatly to restore peace between Hugh, king of Italy, and Alberic, patrician of the Romans, died at Tours.

But what follows must be corrected: “and he was buried at St. Martin.” This reading is also found in the margin of Frodoardus’s chronicle in the passage quoted above. Yet this reading is certainly corrupt, as is clear from the same chronicle under the year 945, when Teotolo, archbishop of Tours, is said to have died and to have been “buried in the monastery of St. Julian, which the same holy man had established with the greatest devotion, beside the tomb of the lord Odo”; “and from that time it became evident that this church itself was illumined by divine miracles.”

Therefore the aforesaid Hugh of Flavigny must be corrected; Peter Equilinus likewise must be corrected, since he asserts that Odo was buried “at Cluny.” The anonymous author printed by Chesnius, volume III, p. 341, is entirely correct:

> In that same year—that is, in the seventh year of King Louis— the devout and prudent, learned and eloquent lord Odo, abbot of many monasteries, rested in peace and was buried at Tours, at St. Julian.

The chronicle of Maillezais correctly identifies the place of burial, though it gives the wrong year of death, 938. To all this may be added the chronicle of Dol, printed by Labbe in volume I of the *Bibliotheca nova*, p. 315:

> In the year 942 the holy Odo, second abbot of Dol, died.

Thus Odo departed to heaven in the year 942, at the age of sixty-four, in the fifteenth year of his governance of Cluny.

43. His relics were preserved in the church of St. Julian at least until the fifteenth century. The first evidence of this may be taken from the letters of the association established in October 1117 between Cluny and the monastery of St. Julian. At that time “the lord Pontius, abbot of Cluny, came honorably to Tours to St. Martin for the sake of prayer, and came to us”—so the monks of St. Julian write in their letter—“out of devotion and love for blessed Odo, our patron and his, and on the vigil of St. Dionysius he celebrated Mass concerning that most blessed Odo with our monks and his own. Then, taking with him Bernard Crassus, his prior, and other brothers, he came into our chapter,” and so forth.

Long afterward, namely in the year 1407, John, archbishop of Tours, invited by Robert, abbot of St. Julian, transferred the sacred relics into new reliquaries in the presence of Maria, queen of the Franks, and her daughter Magdalene, John, duke of Bourbon, James, count of La Marche, and other distinguished persons. Among those relics, in the fourth chest, “the body of St. Odo, abbot,” was contained, as the solemn document concerning the matter testifies. It reads as follows:

> John, by divine mercy archbishop of Tours, sends everlasting greetings in the Lord to all who shall see this present letter. Whatever praise or honor we offer to the saints of God, we offer to God himself, as the prophet bears witness, since the Lord commands that he be praised in his saints.
>
> Since the late Brother William, formerly abbot of the monastery of St. Julian at Tours, of the order of St. Benedict, had considered that, although the church of the said monastery was adorned with the bodies, relics, and presence of many saints, through whose intercessions and prayers, together with those of other glorious saints who rest in this city of ours, not only the monastery itself but also the entire city had flourished in prosperous circumstances, nevertheless those bodies and relics had been placed with insufficient reverence and the honor due to them was not being shown, the aforesaid abbot, moved by devoted affection, while he was alive caused five wooden chests to be made, decorated internally with silver and gold, hoping to place these relics and bodies in them.
>
> Overtaken by death, however, as it pleased the Lord, he could not carry out the proposed work himself. The venerable and religious brothers Robert, the present abbot, and the entire convent of the said monastery, embracing his desires and most earnestly wishing to complete the work, devoutly petitioned us that we should deign to place the prepared relics and bodies in the locations constructed for that purpose, as has been said.
>
> We therefore make known that, embracing with the deepest affection the pious wishes of the aforesaid Abbot William, and of the present venerable abbot and convent, for the glory and magnificence of almighty God, on the day of the present document, in the presence of the most Christian lady, the illustrious lady Maria, queen of the Franks, and the noble lady Magdalene, her daughter, and of the noble princes, the lords John, duke of Bourbon, and James, count of La Marche, together with many other barons, knights, noble persons, and the venerable and prudent men listed below, we transferred and deposited with our own hands the bodies and relics from the old sarcophagi into new chests, which we had first sanctified and blessed according to the rite of the Church, in the following order:
>
> Namely, in the first chest, toward the dormitory of the aforementioned monastery, the body of St. Paul, bishop of Léon; in the second chest, the body of St. Anthony, abbot of the said monastery of St. Julian at Tours; in the third, middle, and largest chest, portions of the bodies of St. Pantaleon and St. Columba, together with many other relics whose names are unknown to us; in the fourth chest, the body of St. Odo, first abbot of Cluny and afterward of the said monastery of St. Julian; in the fifth and last chest, the body of St. Laurus, abbot.
>
> After these translations had been carried out, we closed the chests with doors or closures of silver and gilded metal on the outside and fortified them with our blessing, trusting in the divine mercy. We decree, and instruct the aforesaid religious men and their successors, as by this document we decree and instruct them, that henceforth each year they shall celebrate this day of translation festively and solemnize it with the appropriate and due divine offices.
>
> As evidence and testimony of all and each of these matters, we caused two copies of this letter to be made, signed by the notaries listed below, and secured by the attachment of our seal. One of them we placed inside the aforesaid largest chest; the other we granted to the aforesaid abbot and convent to be deposited in the church treasury.
>
> Given in the aforesaid monastery on the twenty-second day of January, in the year of the Lord 1407, in the presence of and with the assistance of the venerable fathers, Brothers Guido of the Greater Monastery near Tours, Robert of the aforesaid St. Julian, and Peter of Cormeriac, abbots of the said order in our diocese; and of the prudent men, the lords John Campidenarius, doctor of decrees, general preceptor of St. Anthony of Thuin in Germany and ambassador of the most illustrious prince, the lord duke of Austria; William Le Picart, treasurer; John Preselli, archdeacon of Transligeria; John Nuloti, archdeacon of Tours; Nicholas Perturelli, official; Victor Hugneti; William Joubert, canon of our church of Tours; and also James of Cormeray, claustral prior and infirmarian; John, the provost’s almoner; Philip, the provost’s chamberlain; John Charretier, sacristan; William Du Vieu, hosteller; John Guibert, cantor; Guido Auger, succentor; William Boutet of Bovo; Michael Belloneau of Guerchia; James Auderon of Château-Regnault; Peter Audebert of St. Anthony; John Selion of Bueil; Robert Helonis of Ambillo, priors; William of Linaye; John Fafeu; Peter Joulain, deacon; Peter Sourdeau; John Lenfant; Aimeric of Mondanier; John of Fonte; John Budet; Andrew of France; and John of the Tower, religious of the said monastery of St. Julian, together with many others.
>
> Thus signed: Thouar and the Masters.

44. From that time onward no mention of St. Odo’s relics remained in the records of the monastery of St. Julian; nevertheless, his shinbone is preserved there. Perhaps the other relics were carried from there to the island of Jordan near Toulouse—whose canons boast that they possess them—when the storm of heresy broke out, and those who scattered the sacred remains of the city of Tours in a profane fire spared not even the relics of St. Martin, which the whole world had always held in honor.

Nor should we accept what is stated in the document quoted above concerning the body of St. Laurus, whose name is not mentioned in the *Martyrologium Gallicanum*. His feast was recently celebrated at St. Julian’s on the first day of October; it has now been transferred to the following day because of the double feast of St. Remigius.

Our Floriacensian monks claim for themselves the body of St. Paul, bishop of Léon, on the authority of Aimoin, who asserts in Book II, chapter 11, *On the Miracles of St. Benedict*, that it was transferred from Bishop Mabbone to the monastery of Fleury.

45. I return to St. Odo, whose cult was accepted among the Cluniacs immediately after his death, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, because the day of his death fell within the octave of St. Martin. For that reason, I think, he is commemorated on that day in the manuscript Martyrology of Brioude and in certain others.

In Udalricus, Book I of the *Customs of Cluny*, chapter 11, where the various annual solemnities are listed, “the deposition of St. Odo” is counted among those celebrated “in white vestments.” His honored memory appears in the Roman, Benedictine, and—among others—the Gallican Martyrologies. In the latter he is mentioned three times, namely on the twelfth and thirteenth days before the Kalends of December and in the Supplement on the fourteenth day before those same Kalends:

> At the island of Jordan near Toulouse: the veneration of the most sacred body of St. Odo, abbot of Cluny, transferred from the bosom of the church of St. Julian at Tours, where, released from the bonds of mortal life, he had first received burial.

Finally, Bernard calls Odo “a saint” in his *Apology to Abbot William*, and before him Gregory VII did so at the Roman council; all the Cluniac abbots before him likewise recognized him as a saint. A sermon on St. Odo is found among the additions to the Cluniac Library and is to be read on his feast day; it is nothing other than St. Maximus’s sermon on Blessed Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli. Finally, Peter Equilinus testifies that St. Odo “lives through miracles.”

## CHAPTER VIII — Odo’s Writings and His Apt Sayings Concerning the Morals of His Age

46. But it is time, leaving the other matters aside, to turn to Odo’s own works, some of which he wrote as a canon, others as a monk, and others as an abbot. As a canon, he abridged Gregory the Great’s *Moralia*, as was mentioned above in chapter 2, and composed hymns and antiphons for St. Martin, according to John, Book I, no. 10.

As a monk, he wrote three little books “from the prophecy of Jeremiah” concerning the priesthood and dedicated them to Turpio, bishop of Limoges, according to John, Book I, no. 37. Some assign these books to him under the title *Occupationes*; in published editions they are called *Collationes*.

Finally, as abbot, he produced other works, namely four books on the life of St. Gerald, count of Aurillac, dedicated to Aimonius, abbot of the monastery of St. Martial at Limoges, as the chronicle of that place reports. The chronicle of Aurillac calls Aimonius abbot of Tulle. Perhaps he presided over both places.

Abbot Odo wrote a little book on the return of St. Martin’s body from Burgundy, at the request of Fulk the Good, count of Anjou; a short work “on why Martin is said to be equal to the apostles”; and various sermons, of which in the printed editions the fourth and last concerns the burning of the basilica of Blessed Martin.

The anonymous chronicler printed by Chesnius, volume III, p. 341, praises a sermon on St. Benedict delivered at his translation at Fleury. All these works are found in the Cluniac Library, together with hymns on the Most Holy Sacrament and on Mary Magdalene.

47. In addition to the works already published, Odo corrected the Life of St. Martin at Rome, at St. Paul’s, and explained it with glosses, as John testifies in Book II, no. 22. The same author, in Book III, no. 11, mentions a book on the arrival of St. Benedict in the county of Orléans; we regret that this book has been lost.

A little book on the life of Gregory, bishop of Tours, of the sort published by Surius, is attributed to “Abbot Odo” in certain manuscript codices. In the codex of St. Sergius at Angers this Life is entitled:

> Prologue to the Life of St. Gregory. Of all the saints, indeed…

After the prologue:

> Here begins the Life of St. Gregory, bishop of Tours, edited by Odo. Gregory, from the Celtic region of Gaul…

The city of Tours and the monastery of St. Julian, which owed much to Gregory and had Odo as its abbot, also support attributing this little book to our Odo.

In a parchment codex of the Discalced Carmelites at Paris, formerly belonging to “the monastery of St. Julian at Tours,” there is an extensive metrical work under the following title:

> Here begins the *Occupation* of the lord Odo, abbot.

It begins with these verses:

> Beloved brother, a most holy love fills you; rejoice;  
> And thirst for justice, which is the honor and glory of the heart.  
> You grieve that the heart is flowing away, and yet you seek from where, from your own [heart].  
> Hence you will desire the poem, perhaps because this may bind it, lest it flow away.

It consists of four books. The first is on God’s work, the second on the creation of man, the third on man’s fall and the corruption of fallen human nature, and the fourth on the Fathers of the Old Testament up to Christ the redeemer. At the end:

> Here ends the *Occupation* of the lord Odo, abbot.

It appears to be the work of St. Odo, both because of the monastery of St. Julian, from which the codex was obtained and where Odo was abbot, and because of the script of the codex, which suggests Odo’s period, as well as because of the title. For his *Collationes* are entitled in the codex of Silviniacum: “The *Occupationes* of St. Odo.” They contain nothing historical but deal quite appropriately with grace.

Baronius—or at least the compiler of the index to volume X of the *Annals*—attributes to our Odo a book on the life of St. Maurus, abbot; it is established that this work belonged to Odo, abbot of Fosses. Certain chronicles are likewise falsely attributed to him. Their author was “Thomas of Loches, who entitled brief chronicles in Odo’s name,” as the writer of the *History of the Consuls of Angers* learned from Thomas’s own mouth, in volume X of the *Spicilegium*, p. 400.

Among others, Sigebert shows that Odo was skilled in composing ecclesiastical chant, in Book [on] Writers, chapter 124:

> Odo the musician, a monk formerly archcantor of Tours and first abbot of Cluny, possessed an elegant talent for writing and delivering homilies, and especially for composing the chants of the saints.

The chant concerning St. Martin appears to be his.

48. In his little works, but especially in the *Collations*, Odo touches upon certain matters worthy of observation. In various places he laments the fallen morals of Christians. In Book II, chapter 17:

> “We say, then, what we can, so that we may at least show that we grieve somewhat over the perversity of the wicked. Is it not deservedly a matter for grief that Christianity, which, the more advanced it is, the more ought to have been strengthened, is instead so bent away from the condition of uprightness that its whole religion seems to have failed? For we all run swiftly and headlong toward evil,” etc.

And in Book I, chapter 41:

> “It must certainly be recognized that, just as in our times almost everything has lost its proper order, many call the extravagant expenditure of their possessions charity, although resources lavished and dispersed for empty glory ought rather to be called feasting or dissipation than charity,” etc.

Then in Book II, chapter 37:

> “He must grieve over the time of the present life, in which everything is so confused that nowhere do you see even a trace of truth, while you observe that all things are filled with wickedness and luxury, and that nothing is preserved justly and rightly. You see the humble, the weak, and the poorer being oppressed, afflicted, and unjustly injured by the proud, the powerful, and the rich; while any honest and peaceful person is disturbed by many injuries. Conversely, you see every worst man heaped with power, made formidable, and increased in evil by his swollen success—men whom neither fear of judges nor reverence for sacred authority can overcome, nor in any way restrain from destruction. But what shall we say about the judges? For those who had been appointed to suppress these evils themselves inflict heavier storms and more destructive ones upon the wretched. This unjust and inequitable inequality is committed and exercised not only in cities but in the countryside, and not only on land but also at sea.”

He adds in chapter 41:

> “But what does more grievous harm amid all evils is that the wicked practice of sinning has now been so strengthened by custom that scarcely anyone is able to distinguish sin by sound judgment. Rather, just as Aaron did not resist the sons of Israel when they were seeking gods, so all are either wicked or yield to wickedness.”

Read also what follows at the end of this chapter and in Book III, chapter 28. He chiefly censures three vices of his age: malice, which belongs to the violent; pride; and luxury. He attacks these vices throughout the first and second books.

49. He adds a fourth in Book II, chapter 28:

> “It is certainly a matter for profound grief that through these three vices, or through the other vices that one is ashamed to enumerate, they appear to apostatize from Christ. But it is much more grievous that they rashly presume to approach that most sacred mystery, namely, the body of the Lord. For this is the greatest benefit among all the good things granted to human beings, and it is what God, in his greater charity, has bestowed upon mortals, because the salvation of the world rests entirely upon this mystery. And indeed, when it is treated unworthily, the divine majesty is daily insulted above all through this very act. This, then, must be grieved; over this one must groan in every way, so that, if we cannot correct it, we may at least show by our protest that the disposition to grieve is present in us—lest perhaps Christ’s voice accuse us, saying: ‘I looked for one who would grieve with me, and there was none.’”

This mystery was not celebrated in the beginnings of the Church as frequently as it is now; nevertheless, the rarer it was, the more reverently it was performed.

Thus writes this most devout man. He reports two notable events, the first concerning the relics of Saint Walburga, or Gualburga, famous for miracles. When her relics had been placed upon the altar, the miracles ceased. While pilgrims were astonished, the virgin appeared to one of the sick and said:

> “For this reason you are not being healed: my relics are upon the altar of the Lord, where the majesty of the divine mystery ought alone to be celebrated.”

When the man reported this to the custodians, they removed the reliquary, and immediately miracles began to occur. “If, then,” Odo adds,

> “out of reverence for that mystery the saints do not wish even their own pledges to be brought near it, what must be thought concerning impurities?”

50. The other event concerns a certain robber who was killed at the very moment of his crime. When his body had been brought to the church, a priest began to celebrate Mass for him.

> “When he was therefore about to come to the words of the Lord’s consecration, a terrifying noise resounded through the roof of the church, and the altar—as is evident to this day—was split down to its very base. Thus the priest, struck with immense fear together with everyone else, fled, and ceased to offer the sacrifice for an apostate. Let this be said against those,”

the holy man remarks,

> “who promise that they will pray for criminals for the sake of their favor.”

Odo seems to have recorded this in order to overturn the opinion of those who, perhaps led to it by a misunderstanding of Augustine’s testimony, said that the sacrifice of the Mass benefited the condemned—either by freeing them entirely from punishment or by making their condemnation more bearable.

A passage expressing this opinion is found in Adrevaldus’s *Book on the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, chapter 21, where he says that the men of Fleury poured out prayers to the Lord for the souls of robbers slain in battle:

> “so that, even if they did not deserve to be released from everlasting torments, at least they might be punished by the strict Judge with lesser penalties.”

In the very old Gellone manuscript there is a Mass “for one whose soul is in doubt,” containing this prayer:

> “Almighty and merciful God, who have power to kill and again to give life, to lead down to the underworld and bring back, and who call things that are not as though they were, whose power stands fully present in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in the underworld: we humbly and tremblingly beseech you on behalf of the soul of your servant, whom you have drawn from the present age without a period for repentance, that, if perhaps on account of the gravity of his crimes he does not deserve to rise to glory, through these sacred libations of offering the torments themselves may at least become bearable.”

These and other passages are taken from volume X of the *Fragments* of our Claudius Stephanotius.

In the *Paralipomena concerning Saint Pachomius*, found in volume III of the May collection of the Bollandists, prayers for the condemned are forbidden, though that punishment is nevertheless thought to contribute to their relief. The body of a deceased monk was being carried out while Pachomius was absent. Meeting the procession, he forbade the singing of psalms. Among other things he said to the dead man’s relatives:

> “For if you wish to perform the funeral rites for him with the singing of psalms, more numerous and more grievous torments will receive the deceased … For this reason I ask you: if you wish to make the dead man’s torments lighter, commit him to burial without psalms. Since God is good and merciful, he might, on account of the dishonor done to him by this, grant him some rest and recall him to the life bestowed from above.”

Papebrochius deletes these final words, although they are found in the Greek, lest they offend anyone.

From a similar belief arose the tale of Trajan; concerning it, see Hepidannus in the *Acts of Saint Wiborada the Recluse*. But even if we remove this final portion, it nevertheless remains that some people believed—or, rather, erred in believing—that the eternal punishments of the condemned could somehow be made lighter.

Whatever may be the case concerning that opinion, which the common consensus of theologians today rejects, it is certain that the audacity of those who do not hesitate to offer the sacred sacrifice of the Mass for anyone indiscriminately, even for those who died in the very act of crime, was rightly condemned. The Second Council of Valence condemned this practice in canon 12 with regard to duelists.

Augustine makes the same determination concerning all the condemned in *The City of God*, Book XXI, chapter 24:

> “The reason, then, why prayer is not offered at that time for those who are punished by eternal fire is the same reason why prayer is offered neither now nor then for the evil angels; and it is likewise the reason why, although prayer is offered now for the living, even for the wicked, prayer is no longer offered either now for deceased unbelievers and ungodly persons.”

When Augustine subsequently explains the opinion of those who extend God’s mercies “even to the torments of the ungodly,” he permits rather than confirms it, so that the ungodly may suffer punishments “milder than their deserts and lighter than they deserve”—not on account of the assistance of intercessors, but on account of God’s mercy.

Nor does the same holy teacher, in chapter 110 of the *Enchiridion*, think that sacrifices benefit the condemned with regard to eternal punishment, but only with regard to temporal punishment:

> “For there is a certain manner of life which is not so good that it does not require these things afterward, nor so bad that these things do not benefit it after death—after death.”

I return to the order of my subject.

51. Odo also gives monks appropriate admonitions and applies a fitting censure, especially against proprietors, meat-eaters, and transgressors of the religious habit and rule, whom he calls “apostates,” adducing a testimony of Gregory from his ninth homily on Ezekiel:

> “For just as he is an apostate who departs from God in faith, so one who returns to a perverse work after professing religion is, without any doubt, reckoned an apostate from almighty God, even if he appears to retain the faith.”

Odo adds:

> “Is it not apostasy to despise the traditions of the Fathers concerning clothing or food, when God has forbidden the boundaries established by the Fathers to be transgressed? And, despising the quality or quantity of food prescribed by blessed Benedict, is it not apostasy to desire bloody dishes with the sons of Israel? Is it not apostasy to reject humble clothing and seek the elegance of dress? And is it not apostasy to cultivate the belly, when Paul, weeping, declares that gluttons [Latin: *ligurgitones*] are enemies of the holy cross and have their belly in place of God? These words concerning apostasy apply to us, I say, since, after the religious habit had been retained through so many past years, various wanton and insolent men among us have dared in our own age to change it.”

This he says in Book III, chapter 17. See also Book II, chapter 7, and Book III, chapter 22.

He also counts among the proprietors

> “those who bring forth from their own little chests an expensive apparatus for celebrating the mysteries, which they acquire from dishonest wealth contrary to the custom and sanction of the holy Fathers, and, as though they would leave it behind for the adornment of the church, possess it securely”

(Book II, chapter 34).

Responding to the objections of proprietors in chapter 36, he says:

> “If they possessed their own property merely through the negligence of their superiors, and not rather through their own greed, they would not presume to have foods or garments other than those established by the rule.”

52. Let this suffice to demonstrate the holy man’s zeal for the Christian and monastic cause. Would that these reprimands did not also apply to our own time, in which—speaking of certain monks—so little religious observance is devoted to the regular institutions that the holy Fathers established and observed with such great reverence.

## CHAPTER IX — Certain Distinguished Disciples of Odo

53. To complete Odo’s eulogy, knowledge of his disciples is necessary, since the reputation of a teacher depends chiefly upon them. But the difficulty in this matter is that ancient records concerning them fail us; and although John presents certain disciples of Odo, he committed little more than their bare names to writing.

Among these must be mentioned Arnulf and Landricus. John reports in his preface that he learned much about Odo from them; he calls one his master and teacher, and the other his confrater.

He adds:

> “Lord Hildebrannus, or Hildebrandus, a man—as the same writer says—truthful, and provost of the monastery of Cluny, and his teacher in the disciplines of the rule.”

Hildebrand is praised in several charters drawn up under Odo’s abbacy, and he subscribed in place of the chancellor to the diploma of Countess Adelaide mentioned above. He was likewise prior of Cluny in the seventeenth year of Louis the Transmariner, according to the hundredth charter under Abbot Aimard.

Another prior of Cluny bearing the same name lived in the eleventh century: he was the man who was later raised to the Roman See and took the name Gregory VII.

Besides these men, John names in his second book Peter the priest; Baldwin, abbot of Casino and of Saint Paul; Firmus, his brother; Lord Gothefredus; and two venerable men from the same congregation, one of whom was called Archembaldus and was “well known” to John, while the other, called Adalasius, was “unknown.” John says of them:

> “They are men of the highest reputation, who have now become Fathers of many monks.”

Archembaldus, “prelate of the monastery of Cluny,” that is, its provost, is praised in a charter of Berno, bishop of Mâcon, dated in the tenth year of King Rudolf. He seems also to have been the man who succeeded Odo in the governance of the monastery of Fleury, concerning whom Aimoinus writes in Book I of *The Miracles of Saint Benedict*, no. 13.

Wlfaldus was his successor; John mentions him in Book III. We shall praise him elsewhere in the *Acts of Saint Abbo the Abbot*.

Aligernus may also be counted among them. He was formerly provost of Saint Paul at Rome and later abbot of Casino; we shall discuss him here under the year 986.

54. Adalasius, whom John mentions shortly afterward, is undoubtedly the same as “Adacius,” to whom, under Odo, the governance of the monasteries of Sarlat and Tulle was entrusted, as we said above in chapter 5.

To this Adacius, as I believe, Count Bernard, “with the assent of his blessed wife and with the support likewise of his sons William, Gausbert—or Arnold—and Bernard,” gave “the monastery of Saint Sur, called Geridia, with the whole abbey,” together with its monks:

> “so that those who wish to live there according to the rule under his authority may possess both the monastery and the whole abbey without any contradiction; and after the death of Lord Adacius the abbot, may choose for themselves, according to the rule of Saint Benedict, whatever abbot they wish,”

with the condition

> “that those monks be subject to the king for the safeguarding of the place, but not for the payment of anything.”

He adjures everyone to carry out this act by all sacred things,

> “and by the merit of blessed Sur, whose body rests in the aforesaid place.”

This charter lacks chronological indications. It is preserved in the cartulary of the monastery of the Rule among the Novempopulani, from which our Stephanotius extracted it.

55. John also counts Adolfus, Theodardus, and Eliziardus, a monk formerly a count, among all these disciples of Odo.

Perhaps that Aribertus was among Berno’s disciples, concerning whom Odo himself relates the following in Book II of *The Life of Saint Gerald*, chapter 19:

> “Once, when he was undertaking that journey—namely, the Roman journey—he took with him a certain monk named Aribertus, a man of great abstinence … On one occasion it happened that there was no stew with which that abstinent man could eat his bread. The elder carefully asked whether the servants had prepared his customary food. When they replied that they had nothing except bread, he was distressed and said: ‘Oh, what has happened to us today! We all have a full meal, while this servant of God will be weakened by fasting.’ It happened to be a day on which abstinence had been relaxed. The time for washing hands had already arrived, and Samuel, who relates this as an eyewitness, ran to fetch water. Suddenly he found a little fish lying exposed on the shore and still moving; before his eyes it had leapt out of the water.”

Gerald gave thanks to God. “Then, when they had sat down at table, that abstinent man ate a sufficient amount” of the prepared fish. Gerald ate the remainder, “and gave pieces to everyone present as a blessing.”

Observe in passing that the word *pulmentarium* can also signify a dish made from fish.

This is enough concerning Aribertus and concerning Odo’s eulogy. Let us now hear his life, first from John and then from Nalgodus.

[Col. 0043]

# THE LIFE OF SAINT ODO, SECOND ABBOT OF CLUNY

Written by John the monk, his disciple.

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, Fifth Age.)*

[Col. 0043]

## AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE

John mentions those who encouraged the work.

[Col. 0043C]

### 1

To the lords and brothers in Christ at Salerno, John, servant of Christ Jesus, brother.

[Note: [Col. 0043C] Monks, and also abbots, assumed the name “brother” when speaking of themselves, as Saint Benedict does below in Book III, no. 8: “Know that I am Brother Benedict,” and likewise in Adrevaldus. Peter the Venerable, Saint Bernard, and others—indeed, sometimes bishops who had come from monasteries—use this designation of themselves continually in their letters.]

When once you compelled me to write the book that the most learned man Palladius composed concerning the life and virtues of the blessed hermit Fathers in the time of the Emperor Theodosius, I did not find the task burdensome. Rather, immediately supporting my body and bending my joints, I applied myself to writing, judging that nothing I could do would be more useful to you.

Therefore, while I was breathlessly trying to bring the work I had begun to its conclusion, I began to be afflicted violently by stomach pain. Meanwhile, one day it happened that the venerable man, Lord Adhelradus, our confrater, was with me, together with John, the collector of the sacred Salernitan palace.

[Note: [Col. 0044C] The collector of the sacred palace was perhaps the official in charge of public funds. Ansegisus the abbot is described somewhat differently under Einhard as “collector of royal works” in the chronicle of Fontenelle. This passage also shows that the term “sacred palace” was in use before Frederick Barbarossa. We demonstrated this earlier against Conringius in Book II of *On Diplomatic Matters*, chapter 11, no. 13.]

Seeing that I was suffering and wishing to provide for my endurance, they began to introduce into my thoughts the pious, venerable, and outstanding memory of our holy father, Lord Odo, knowing that nothing had always been more pious and sweet to me than either to tell others something about him or to contribute something to my own benefit.

But I, remembering what is written, “The peoples recount the wisdom of the saints, and the Church announces their praise,” took up the account of him and began, as they asked me questions, to explain his origins.

When they heard this, they urged me—if I truly loved him, as I was then affirming—to set down without delay what I had spoken, so that the benefits of so good an inheritance might be transmitted to posterity.

Thus, pondering deeply the commands of these men who loved him so greatly [variant: *amans*, “loving”], I first fell silent for a little while, as is customary among monks, fearing that by narrating the life of so great a man with a presumptuous tongue I might dishonor him rather than describe him worthily.

Moreover, I did not think that my speech could adorn its words with the language of grammatical art, nor did I seem worthy to recount the life of this most holy man, even if I had possessed the ability to speak.

The author produces witnesses. He relates what he saw and heard. Why he is silent about the names of many.

[Col. 0045A]

### 2

Having therefore undertaken the work, I began, with marrow-deep tears, to invoke the Creator and Son of the Virgin, and the Holy Spirit equal to him, giver of tongues and distributor of speech, who opens the mouths of the mute and makes the tongues of infants eloquent. I prayed that he who had formerly wished me to grow cold toward the world and to be kindled with love for so great a father would grant me eloquence through his inspiration, though I was deprived of every literary resource.

Therefore, beloved, since compelled by your encouragement I have boldly undertaken so great a work in order to carry it through to the end, deign to assist me with your prayers.

But if anyone should read these words, or hear them read by another, I beg that he neither shudder nor mock, nor presume with a rash tongue to call them fabricated, as though, now that the world had been abandoned by God, the Church could no longer produce such a man—one concerning whom Christ once promised, saying: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age.”

Nevertheless, I call Jesus to witness that my teacher Arnulf, under oath, was accustomed to recount many things about him beyond what I relate here; he testified that he had been present at them. Likewise Hucbertus, bishop of the Tiberine [variant: Tibertine] Church, and one of our brothers named Landricus did so.

[Note: [Col. 0045D] He is absent from the series of bishops of Tibur in Ughelli, *Italy*, volume I, col. 216.]

I deliberately refrained from writing down their accounts, and for no other reason than that, since they did not follow his way with eager devotion, I did not wish to use their testimony. If I chose to record it, I think it would be sufficient to praise any ancient Father or apostolic man.

I was pleased to write those things that, as though I had heard them from another narrator, I took from his own mouth and entrusted to my memory. Then I recorded what Lord Hildebrandus, a truthful man, provost of the monastery of Cluny, and my teacher in the disciplines of the rule, had professed to me and to many others.

Meanwhile, dearest friends, I beg you not to ask me for the names of his ancestors or of the other Gauls with whom he grew up. I neither saw them nor was the opportunity ever given me to see them. Since at that time I was constrained by the disciplines of the rule, I was at least not permitted to question them—especially since Italian soil gave me birth and nourished me within the enclosures of the Church.

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0045]

Summary of Odo’s life.

[Col. 0045B]

### 3

Odo, then, the most blessed man, was descended from the lineage of the Franks.

[Note: [Col. 0045D] Another author says that he came from a military Frankish family. His father was named Abbo. John says the same below. Neither author gives the name of his mother. Odo was born in the year 879 or the following year, as is indicated by no. 4 below.]

He was brought up in the household of William, the most powerful duke of Aquitaine. In the nineteenth year of his age he was tonsured at Saint Martin’s in Tours, and there he was educated in the liberal studies of grammar. Afterwards, at Paris, he was instructed in dialectic and music by Remigius, a most learned man. In the thirtieth year of his life he went to Burgundy, where for fifteen years he led the monastic life under Abbot Berno.

Later, having been ordained abbot, he became the sweetest leader and father of the monasteries situated in the regions of Francia, Aquitaine, and Spain, and in the city of Rome.

The author’s fortune.

[Col. 0045C]

### 4

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 939

[Note: [Col. 0046D] Thus reads the Silviniac manuscript; in all the others that I have seen, the reading is corruptly “839.”]

—and in the sixtieth year of his age, his thirtieth year in the monastic life—he came to Rome and found me, wretched man, entangled in earthly bonds. Taking pity on me, he caught me in his net and brought me all the way to the monastery of Saint Peter at Pavia.

After I had been detained there for a short time by King Hugh, he entrusted me to the aforesaid Lord Hildebrandus to be educated in the disciplines of the rule. Not long afterward, when he came to Rome, he deigned to take me, unhappy man, as his companion. He had taken me away from my parents as a canon when he departed, and later brought me back as a monk when he returned.

Moreover, while we were traveling in those days and conversing together, I set aside my reserve and, as though the monastic path had been placed far from us, boldly broke into speech. I did not hesitate to ask him carefully about the life, conduct, and circumstances of his birth; at the same time I began to beg him more readily to explain these things to me.

As he was always accustomed to do, he remained silent for a little while. Then, wiping the redness from his face and drawing sighs from his innermost heart, he began to explain his origins to me. Yet his words were full of tears and groaning.

Odo tells John about his father’s piety and the beginnings of his own life.

### 5

> “My father,” he said, “was called Abbo, but he seemed to belong to a different character and way of life from the people of the present age. He retained the histories of the ancients, and Justinian’s *Novels*, by heart. At his table, the evangelical word was always heard.
>
> “Whenever a dispute of any kind arose between parties, the truth of his judgment had grown so great that people came from every direction to him for the favor of deciding the matter. For this reason he was dear to everyone, especially to William,

[Note: [Col. 0046D] This is William, surnamed Pious, concerning whom Odo himself writes in Book III of *The Life of Saint Gerald*, chapter 32 and following. We discussed him above in the eulogy of Saint Berno.]

> “the powerful count who at that time held Aquitaine and Gothia [variant: Gaul] by his own right.
>
> “He had long been accustomed to celebrate the solemn vigils of the saints with great watchfulness. On that night when peace was restored to angels and human beings, and Christ the Lord, visiting the world, came forth from a virginal womb like a bridegroom from his chamber, he spent the night in silence, with tears and prayers.
>
> “While he was carefully celebrating this vigil, it was suggested to his mind that he should ask the Lord to grant him a son on account of the Virgin’s childbirth. By such earnestness of prayer he deserved to have a womb already dead become fruitful again. My father often related that this was the manner of my birth.”

### 6

> “During that period of my infancy, it happened that he entered the enclosure of the bedroom and found me there, lying on my cradle without a guardian. Looking around in every direction, and seeing no one, he lifted me in his hands and, looking upward in his heart, said: ‘Receive, jewel of priests, Martin, this child.’ He then placed me upon the same little bed from which he had lifted me, and departed. But he did not wish to reveal to anyone what he had done.”

### 7

> “After I had been weaned, he entrusted me to one of his priests, who lived in a more remote place, to be brought up and instructed in literary studies. Later that priest confessed that during those days he had seen the following vision.
>
> “‘I saw, and behold, the leaders of the Churches began to demand the child from me, even insisting upon him. When I asked what they wanted to do with him—whether they intended to return him to his father’s house—they replied that they had not come for that purpose, but in order to take him to the regions of the East.
>
> “‘But when the priest did not wish to let him go, and was unable to resist them, and did not know what more he could do, he threw himself upon the ground and turned to prayer, begging that they punish him first before taking the child. At one moment he said that he was suffering the father’s vengeance; at another, that he would be called by the parents a betrayer of the child.
>
> “‘One of them was said to have replied: “Lest the child’s father perhaps avenge himself upon the priest, let us leave him until the proper time.”’
>
> “When the priest learned of this revelation, he restored me to my parents. All these things that you ask me about, my son, I heard in this way from my father.”

### 8

> “When I had grown up—the man whom you now see old and unattractive was then being praised as a vigorous and distinguished young man—my father gradually began to withdraw me from the ecclesiastical order and apply me to military exercises. For this reason he handed me over within William’s household to serve the count.
>
> “Eventually I abandoned my literary studies and began to devote myself to the duties of hunters and bird-catchers. But almighty God, who grants salvation to the unwilling and calls things that are not as though they were, began to terrify me in dreams and to show me my life inclined toward evil. Moreover, he turned all my hunting into weariness. For the more I immersed myself in such amusements, the more sorrowfully I returned, exhausted and pierced by fatigue, without accomplishing anything.”

### 9

> “In those days my father urged me to keep the solemn vigils that he himself had been accustomed to celebrate. After several years had passed, I prepared to celebrate the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity. When I had spent part of the night awake, it suddenly pleased my mind to implore the Mother of the Lord Jesus for my life.
>
> “As I prayed, I began to say: ‘O Lady, Mother of mercy, on this night you brought forth the Savior for the world; graciously stand forth as my intercessor. Most merciful Lady, I flee to your glorious and singular childbirth, and incline the ears of your compassion to my prayers. I am exceedingly afraid that my life may displease your Son. And because, Lady, he manifested himself to the world through you, I ask that for your sake he have mercy on me without delay.’
>
> “Between these prayers, the morning praises, and the solemn rites of Mass, the following day dawned. And behold, as usual, the white-robed choir of canons appeared. While a varied modulation of voices was taking place in the praises of so great a solemnity, I sprang into their midst like an impatient young man and began with them to praise the King of the world who had been born.
>
> “I know and confess that I acted improperly; yet, retaining in my heart that saying of David which is written—‘Praise the Lord, all nations, and praise him together, all peoples’—I did not presume to do this without reason.
>
> “Immediately an exceedingly severe pain attacked my head. It crushed me for a little while and then withdrew. After the Gospel reading had been completed, the same headache attacked me again, and unless I had stretched out my arms and held on to the grating of the church, I would soon have fallen lifeless from my upright position.
>
> “That pain tormented me so severely that whenever it came, no hope of life remained in me even for a moment. This happened to me in the sixteenth year of my age, and for the following three years I was furrowed by that plowshare.
>
> “For this reason I was brought back to my parents’ home, and for two full years they applied every kind of treatment to me. But the more extensive and varied the medicines I took, the more the remedies of health fled from me.
>
> “In those days, with deep sorrow and a great sigh, my father explained that my birth had been of this kind. He added: ‘Behold, blessed Martin, what I gratefully offered you, you now demand in full. Truly, as is fitting, you are one whose prayer is heard, but you are dear in the matter itself.
>
> “’When at last all hope of a remedy for my health had been abandoned, I thought that one consolation remained: that I should hasten to him—namely, to the one to whom I had been entrusted without knowing it—cut off the hair of my head, and serve him again, knowing now that this was what had happened.
>
> “’There you have, my son, the origin of my birth and the beginning of my way of life. Take note that I did nothing good of my own accord. Nevertheless, judge my small accomplishments as you deem worthy, provided that you continually proclaim and glorify, with blessing, the mercy that looks upon me.’”

Odo devoted to Saint Martin and composes his hymns.

### 10

Afterwards he seemed to possess such great devotion to blessed Martin that he loved him above all other saints and daily commended himself to his protection—always holding him in his heart wherever he was, proclaiming him with his mouth, and following him in his deeds.

For scarcely more than six years have passed since, while the various orders of the church were celebrating the nocturnal vigil before his body, Odo happened to be present there. But because the antiphons of that office, as is evident to everyone, are short, while the nights of that season are longer, those wishing to prolong the office until daylight sang each antiphon repeatedly after each individual verse of the psalms. The labor became burdensome to them.

Finally, they came to him and, as though with one voice, begged:

> “For a long time we have awaited your arrival, Father, so that you might relieve us from such great labor. Now that you are present, we beg you to compose for us other antiphons concerning the life of blessed Martin, your lord, whose length may suitably remove from us the weariness of these very short ones.”

He began to say that he could not make even these, and that his age denied him all opportunity to learn them, even if they had been composed by someone else. Meanwhile he began to praise the brevity of the antiphons they had and to express disgust at the length of those they were requesting.

But they replied that, if he acted otherwise, he would offend Martin, adding that such an excuse indicated concealed pride.

Overcome by these words and prayers, our father Odo immediately applied himself with great effort to the task of the office.

He composed three hymns in Martin’s praise.

[Note: [Col. 0047] Concerning these, see Udalricus, *Customs of Cluny*, Book I, chapter 23, and Ditmarus, *Chronicle*, p. 107.]

Of these I have decided to insert in this work a copy of only one:

> “Christ the King, Martin’s glory: here is your praise, and you are his. Grant that we may honor you in him, and that we may honor him in you.”

Likewise, he composed twelve antiphons, each having three variations. Their words and the harmony of their melodies agree with one another so perfectly that nothing sweeter seems capable of being found either in their meaning, whether more or less, or in the modulations of the symphony. They are still preserved at Benevento.

Never in the morning or evening was Martin’s memory absent from Odo’s heart and mouth. He held him in his heart while expressing him with his lips:

> “O Martin, O holy one, how holy it is to rejoice in you, O Martin,”

and so forth.

But since the present place has appropriately offered an occasion for the account just written, when, with the Lord’s help, I begin to set forth his life in full, I shall then relate what blessed Martin wished to accomplish through him.

For the moment, let us return to the point from which we digressed.

Odo a cleric in his nineteenth year.

### 11

Thus the most blessed man Odo, fleeing to Saint Martin in the nineteenth year of his age, assumed the office of cleric.

Lest I seem to wrong the poverty with which he was later content, I prefer to remain silent rather than disclose what a crowd of nobles gathered there and with how much display.

Among them was Count Fulco, who had brought him up. The church of Saint Martin promptly granted Odo a cell beside it, and Fulco obtained his daily sustenance from the same canonical community and granted it to him.

But the most blessed man, a lover of poverty, despising the glory of the world, took care to please God alone. Day after day he labored at reading, and by night he devoted himself to prayer, knowing that it is written: “Whoever is ignorant will be ignored” (1 Corinthians 14).

Devoted to Virgil, he is terrified.

12. In those days, moreover, our most skilled sailor, who by his guidance taught us to cross the whirlpools of this world, swam across the immense sea of Priscian. For when he wished to read the verses of Virgil, there appeared to him in a vision a certain vessel, exceedingly beautiful on the outside but within full of serpents. He saw himself suddenly surrounded by them, yet not bitten; and when he awoke, he understood the serpents as the teaching of the poets, the vessel in which they lay hidden as Virgil’s book, and the road along which he walked, greatly thirsting, as Christ.

He Devotes Himself to Sacred Letters

13. Meanwhile, I shall briefly describe how great a power of patience afterward began to shine forth in him. Abandoning the poets’ verses, and deeply instructed by the spirit of counsel [Col. 0049B], he turned himself wholly to the interpreters of the Gospels and the Prophets. Meanwhile, almost all the canons began to rage against him with furious barking.

“What do you intend to do?” they asked. “Why do you seek to undertake another man’s work? You have wasted the work for which you were prized in the flower of your youth. Spare yourself, and, abandoning these letters so intricately joined together, go over to the Psalms.”

But the same Spirit who had formerly taught him to keep silent about good things then taught him to keep silent about evil things. With bowed head, stopped ears, and eyes fixed upon the ground, he turned over in his heart that saying of David: “I said: I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue. I have set a guard over my mouth” (Ps. XXXVIII). Nor was he forgetful of the Lord’s promise: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke XXI). What remains concerning his patience I shall, with the Lord’s help, describe below.

He Becomes Illustrious for His Virtues. He Visits St. Martin’s Tomb by Night, Carrying Writing Tablets. He Is Terrified by Demons

[Col. 0049C] 14. I shall now hasten on to his contempt for worldly things. Let those who wish praise exorcists, healers of corpses, and other men made famous by their virtues. I, the least among them all, shall praise in my Odo first the virtue of patience, then contempt for worldly things; afterward, the winning of souls, the restoration of monasteries, the clothing and food of monks, the peace of the churches, the concord of kings and princes, the safeguarding of all roads, diligence in commandments, perseverance in vigils and prayers, concern for the poor, correction of the young, honor for the old, reform of morals, love for virgins, consolation of the continent, mercy toward the wretched, undefiled observance of the rules, and, finally, an example of every virtue.

In a small cell the good Jesus was then gathering, from diverse groves, a paradise of monks, from which he would water the hearts of the faithful. Content with a tiny cell and withdrawn from the sight of all, he hastened to please God alone. Having distributed among all the poor whatever he had brought with him for temporal use [Col. 0049D], he thought of nothing for the morrow, in accordance with the evangelical precept.

At night he withdrew himself from human sight and went alone to the tomb of blessed Martin for the sake of prayer. It stood nearly two thousand paces from that same cell. He was supported neither by a companion at his side nor strengthened by the protection of a staff, but carried only two tablets in his hand, perfectly suited for writing. They were joined together by skilled workmanship so that they could be opened but not separated, such as schoolmen commonly use on the right thigh.

But the enemy of goodness began to inflict such terrors upon him. From every side, foxes came out of the edges of the road. At first they followed behind him and watched him; then they confronted him face-to-face. When they saw that they could not make him turn aside from the straight road and his purpose, they threatened to strangle him, yelping and rushing upon him with gaping mouths. But he neither fled nor stopped; rather, with his legs crossed and his stiff neck drawn in, he defended himself only with his shoulders and arms. Finally, surrendering his whole body to their teeth, he guarded only his throat against a deadly bite. And suddenly, at great speed, a wolf intervened, freeing him from their attacks; afterward it became his companion and familiar.

And lest anyone think this either impossible or too extraordinary, let him read the life of blessed Paul, written by blessed Jerome; there he will find that the tomb of that same man was prepared by lions. If that one example still seems insufficient, let him turn to the life of blessed Ammon, and he will find that his cell was guarded against robbers by two dragons.

Then let us return to the aforementioned Jerome, and turn also to our Florentius of Nursia, whose life blessed Pope Gregory set forth in his Dialogue. There you will find that Jerome deserved to have a lion as guardian of his donkeys [Note: [Col. 0049D] Hence Saint Jerome is depicted with a lion. But this story was transferred to Jerome through a confusion of names from Abbot Gerasimus of the Jordan, whose lion guarded an ass; marvelous things are read about it in the Spiritual Meadow, chap. 107 [Col. 0050D]. Blessed Odilo followed the same opinion near the end of the Life of Abbot Maiolus.] and Florentius a fierce bear to guard his sheep.

From that time he traveled more securely, always retaining in his heart the testimonies of good Jesus and singing them aloud to him:

“For truly you are faithful, Lord, in your words,  
and holy in all your works.  
You raise up all who fall  
and lift up all who are crushed.”

For, in a reversal of roles, the wolf guarded him from what it sometimes eats, and terrified the foxes by whom it is usually terrified. What temptations, then, the devil invisibly brought against him, let no one ask me to relate. Yet, as evidence by which the matter may be believed—what he may have endured invisibly through patient endurance of suggestion—I think that the visible battle described here should suffice to inspire belief in all who read it.

At night, when he went out from the aforementioned cell in which he lived for the sake of prayer, he did not close its little door [Col. 0050C] behind him, because he feared losing nothing: he was content with a mat laid upon the bare ground and with the clothes he wore.

He Reads the Rule of St. Benedict Repeatedly

15. Meanwhile, as he was reading volumes of various books, it happened that he came upon the Rule of blessed Benedict. When he wished to pass over it hastily, he stumbled upon the very passage in which monks are commanded to sleep clothed (Rule of St. Benedict, chap. 22). Since he plainly did not understand the meaning, he lay clothed for three years and, although not yet a monk, bore the gentle yoke of monks. He took care to obey the precepts of this saint, while wishing to imitate the life of the other. For at that time the Lord Jesus was casting simple seeds into uncultivated earth, from which he expected to receive a hundredfold harvest.

St. Odo Is Vigorous in Body

[Col. 0050D] 16. But this is remarkable: the brightness of his body was not changed by the blackness in which he lay upon the ground, nor was the strength of his spirit weakened by the prolonged continuation of fasting. For during the past two years, when we were visiting together the shrines of the saints inside and outside the city of Rome for the sake of prayer, our youth could neither precede nor even follow his venerable sixty-year-old age.

When we grew tired and begged him to spare both himself and us, he said: “Surely you see that I have lost all my strength. Long old age has made me a *silicernium*—an old man at life’s end. It is now thirty years since I became such as you see me now.”

He himself, groaning, expressed his weakness to us in this manner [Col. 0051A]; but we marveled at his strength with great astonishment, and not without reason: for one who had not allowed himself to be overcome by corruption ought not to have been cast down by bodily decay.

Finally, he thought little of whatever virtue he saw in himself; he considered it a great matter if he could see any virtue in another. During that same period of his youth he was sustained by half a pound of bread and a handful of beans, and—with what is contrary to the nature of the Franks—by very little drink. Having laid aside every corruptible burden, the soldier of Christ, bare-chested and girded as one naked, carried his weapons. To everyone he seemed a raw young recruit, a *triunculus* [uncertain reading], leading the battalions of the old; trusting in Christ, he strove to bring back glorious spoils from the enemy.

All these things took place at the church of blessed Martin at Tours. That place is fertile in every virtue, marvelous in miracles, rich in wealth, and pre-eminent in every form of religious devotion. It is indeed fitting that the place should be marvelous which deserved to have so great an inhabitant. For he was not merely a martyr or a renowned confessor, but the light of the world and the jewel of priests. Kings hasten there, and princes of diverse nations frequently visit it with gifts and vows [Col. 0051B].

He Gives Admonitions to Everyone

17. Meanwhile, it happened that many of these people entered to visit him: those who knew him, to see an acquaintance again; those who did not, to make him known to themselves. But he, like an overflowing spring, offered all the most desired cups; and, as though from an open library, he supplied each person with an appropriate example. To one he prescribed chastity, to another he imposed sobriety. He taught one to despise the world and warned another not to covet what belonged to someone else.

To each person he abundantly supplied whatever was necessary. He wept over this most wretched world and declared that it would soon collapse together with its lovers. He therefore admonished everyone to live sparingly and not to embrace wicked desires. He urged them to restrain completely the gluttony of the belly, saying: “He who stuffs his belly nourishes lust.”

To the lustful he set before them the dragon’s precipice, saying: “Woe to those wretched ones, because the dragon drags a third of the stars after him.” To drunkards and gluttons he said: “Nebuzaradan, captain of the cooks, destroyed the walls of Jerusalem.” To the effeminate and those who sleep with males he set before them the murder committed by Herod and the exile of the scribe.

“How much better,” he said, “is the soul than the body? So much worse than Herod is the man who does such things. Herod killed bodies and sent souls to heaven; this man separates bodies from God and slaughters souls with eternal death. The scribe who examined the recruits was led captive into Egypt; this man, after death, will be led into hell.”

The teacher therefore wept over the precipice and said: “Look, Lord, at the city that has become desolate, though it was full of riches.” And again he said: “Woe to you, Behemoth; you never cease, alas! You spread gold beneath you like mud, and the rays of the sun are beneath you” (Job XLI).

Hearing these things, one man, conscious of his offense, was terrified; another, innocent, rejoiced at his consoling word. Like people taking different foods from a single storeroom [Col. 0051D], they each received something different. I call Jesus to witness: I have never heard such sweetness of speech from the mouth of a man.

In him was fulfilled what the Lord says in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old” (Matt. XIII). Thus, seasoned with divine salt and satisfied with a heavenly dish, they all returned home giving thanks.

He Rejects Gifts

18. Many people finally offered him gifts and presents. He wished to accept none of them, for he had distributed his own so generously that he did not know how he could receive what belonged to others. Once, overcome by his aforementioned lord, he received, whether he wished it or not, one hundred *solidi* sent by him. But the soldier of Christ did not allow them to remain with him even for a moment; as before, he immediately distributed them to the needy [Col. 0052A]. Meanwhile, the pupil began to lead the ranks of teachers and became an example to those who followed.

He Studies at Paris

19. In those days he went to Paris. There he read through the dialectic sent by Saint Augustine to his son Deodatus, and frequently read Martianus in the liberal arts. His teacher in all these subjects was Remigius [Note: [Col. 0051D] He was Remigius of Auxerre, a monk.]. After completing this, he returned to Tours.

He Abridges Gregory’s *Moralia*, Encouraged to Do So after Seeing Gregory

20. During that period, the brothers who loved him asked him to condense the *Moralia* of blessed Pope Gregory into a single volume for them. He declared that he could not possibly do this, adding that even if he had the ability, he ought not to do it, lest he seem to alter in any way the labor of so great a man and the value of so great a work, or to remove anything from it.

They, on the contrary, objected that they would succumb before they could sustain so great a labor, and judged it better to abandon the work altogether and pass on to the remaining Scriptures than to perish beneath it as under a heavy burden. Every day there was considerable dispute among them about this matter.

I know, however, that many will be offended at this account; and, to calm them, I have wished to insert the following explanation. This did not happen through arrogance, but by the Lord’s arrangement, so that a lamp hidden under a bushel might be placed upon a mountain.

The truth of what follows will make the matter clearer. While they persisted in this request, it happened that one night Lord Odo was engaged in his customary prayer inside the church of Lord Martin. Suddenly sleep stole over him, and in the same vision he saw a choir of saints coming down from above and descending into that church. First they blessed the Lord; then they sat in order on the benches. After a little while one of them sprang into the middle and said: “Why are we lingering in this place?”

The others replied that they were waiting for Pope Gregory. Hearing this, our father Odo, like an eager investigator, began looking around in every direction to see from which side he might observe Gregory’s arrival. Then, raising his eyes upward, he saw blessed Gregory as if sent from heaven—far surpassing all those who had preceded him, splendid and adorned in face, appearance, and conduct.

As soon as he arrived, all rose and, bowing their heads, sought his blessing. He did not descend among them to the ground, but stood above the church’s ambo. He called blessed Odo, who was prostrate on the ground, saying: “Rise, brother Odo; do not be afraid.”

When he had risen, he saw a pen clinging above Gregory’s ear, as a scribe would wear it, sharpened and elongated like a teacher’s instrument, and fixed at the top. Blessed Gregory took it and, handing it to him, said: “Go forward confidently, then, and complete the work entrusted to you. The book you compose will not be destroyed; mine, however, will stand forever.”

Immediately awakening, he understood what he had seen. He then took that great volume, read it through carefully, and composed in one volume the sounder portion, as he had foreseen. In this way he silenced the murmuring [Col. 0052D].

He Obtains Health for Count Fulco and Urges Him to Despise the World

21. It happened afterward that the aforementioned Count Fulco, by some means I do not know, took two small golden vessels from the treasury of blessed Martin. But, bridled by the bit of avarice and unwilling to return them, he was struck by a severe punishment. Brought almost to death, he ordered himself to be carried to the tomb of blessed Martin. There he promised very many gifts, but even then he did not receive the gift of health.

After suffering for a very long time, he became so weakened that he awaited the end of death. When Lord Odo entered to visit him, he said: “Return, wretched man, the vessels of blessed Martin that you wickedly took, and immediately you will be healed.”

Fulco promised both to return them and to contribute others, if the truth of the matter proved worthy of belief. Soon, lifted by the hands of our father and those assisting him, he was brought to the body of blessed Martin and prostrated upon the ground. He could not even endure a delay before the promised aid came to him; he who had arrived in others’ hands began to return on his own feet, with his limbs restored, as though carried in a vehicle.

Indeed, it happened that, once corrected, he committed no such acts thereafter and faithfully fulfilled what he had promised. Meanwhile, Father Odo began to admonish him to abandon the world and strive only to please God.

But Fulco replied: “You cannot persuade me of that just now. Yet I have a most beloved soldier, named Adhegrinus, vigorous in arms and prudent in counsel. If he hears you, he will immediately obey your will.” This is what happened later [Col. 0053B]. Within a few days Fulco, completely restored to health, returned home. People came to him from every side to congratulate him on his recovery; and, taking up the story, he began to explain in their presence what and how much he had suffered, adding how promptly he had discovered the power in Lord Odo’s words.

He Draws Adhegrinus to Himself. Adhegrinus Goes to Balma, Where the Rule of Euticius Was Observed

22. Among those standing by was the aforementioned Adhegrinus, an inward hearer—one who listened attentively. Immediately pierced in heart, he arranged all that he possessed and hastened back to Odo. Having put aside his hair and secular military service, he became from that time a champion of Christ.

Our father then took everything he himself had brought for temporal use and distributed it among the poor, as he had previously done with his own possessions. The two former court soldiers remained together, content with a very small hut. Finally, seeing that the world lies in wickedness and that its lovers follow a ruinous road full of enticements, they hastened daily to climb the heights of monastic life.

There was no place within the borders of France where, when they heard that a monastery existed, they did not either go there themselves or send their inspectors. When they found no religious community among them in which they could rest [Note: [Col. 0053D] The same happened to Count Gerald of Aurillac, who searched here and there for monks who were well conducted. But when the scarcity of those to be found caused difficulty, he became anxious, and so forth, in Book II, chapter 6 of the *Life*.], they returned with great sorrow to the aforementioned hut.

For this reason Adhegrinus decided to go to Rome. At last he set out, reached the borders of Burgundy, and arrived at a certain village called Balma, from its name. There stood a monastery recently built by Abbot Bermo. He turned in there and was received by him with the greatest courtesy, according to the rule of blessed Benedict, inside the guesthouse. He wished to remain there for some time in the manner of a guest—not because he needed anything from them, but so that he might learn the customs of the inhabitants and the practices of the place.

The founders of that place were imitators of a certain father, Euticius [Note: [Col. 0053D] It has been shown above that this Euticus or Euticius was none other than Benedict, abbot of Aniane.]. I have not wished to insert into this work what the merit or manner of life of this man was; but I have taken care to commend to your memory the kind of death he deserved.

Who Euticius Was. Odo Enters the Same Community and Is Placed over the School

23. He lived in the time of the great Emperor Louis, beloved by the king and, because he was lovable, by everyone. Although a layman and educated in secular studies, he abandoned those things by which human frailty is accustomed to become proud [Col. 0054A] and devoted himself entirely to the rules and institutions of the blessed Fathers. From these authoritative sources he took various customs and gathered them into a single volume.

Not long afterward he became a monk, and was held in such great favor by the king that the king built a monastery for him within the palace. When he had completed the course of his present life, he suddenly gave up his spirit while brothers stood all around him.

Meanwhile, as the funeral rites were being prepared for the pious father by his disciples, behold, the man who had been dead returned alive. To those who were astonished and amazed, Father Euticus [al., Euticius] said: “Thanks be to God. Know that during these forty years I do not remember having taken food on a single day without first weeping. Today, with my sorrow removed, the Lord has consoled me and granted me a place of rest among the choirs of angels.”

After saying this, he rested forever.

Father Euticus himself was the founder of these customs, which are observed to this day in our monasteries. The venerable Adhegrinus observed them and hastened to report them to our father Odo [Col. 0054B]. Odo then took with him one hundred volumes of books and soon moved to that same monastery. He who had previously been a follower afterward became a *signanus* (standard-bearer).
