Lord Adhegrinus, meanwhile, confined himself to a single cell and, with Abbot Berno’s permission, remained there for three years.

Because Father Odo was a learned man, they assigned him the labor of directing the school [Note: [Col. 0054D] That is, responsibility for the boys, who are designated by the term “school.” If you wish, compare Nalgodum.]. He was thirty years old.

24. I confess, then, that I thought I would pass simply and swiftly through the life of our most holy father. But my small talent, like a violent opponent, wishes to recount together with his life the men whom it understands to have been his companions here. Therefore I ask that, just as I am not deterred from laboring under so great an effort, so you may not find it burdensome or difficult to receive.

For it appears just and well pleasing before God that the examples of those whom he transferred from this pilgrimage to their homeland through a fortunate harbor should be described, together with their lives, as an ornament to our discourse [Col. 0054C].

The Life of Adhegrinus in the Wilderness

25. The venerable Adhegrinus, whom we mentioned above, later obtained permission and sought the wilderness [Note: [Col. 0054D] There were also recluses among the Cluniacs, such as that Gislebert to whom Peter the Venerable wrote Book I, Letter 20.]. There he was confined within a small cave.

One day, overcome by extreme distress, with no one present to offer words of consolation or examples of any father, he descended almost to despair, as Wisdom says: “Woe to him who is alone, for if he falls, he has no one to lift him up” (Eccl. IV). Suddenly a most radiant man stood before him and gently asked what was wrong, or why this had happened to him, that he was plunging himself almost to the precipice.

He replied: “From the time when I began unceasingly to serve the Lord, I have in no way deserved to receive any consolation from him. For this reason I am greatly distressed, because I do not know whether my service pleases him, or whether after so great a labor I shall ever deserve to receive a reward.”

Immediately the other threw himself upon his neck and, kissing him, said: “Believe me: you will never be unworthy of the Lord’s good things.” Having consoled him with these words, he departed.

26. At another time, it happened that the tempter overtook him outside the cell in which he lived. He immediately attacked him and carried him up to the edge of a monstrous cliff, wishing with all his might to throw him down from it.

But what could the soldier of Christ do, unable to stand there with a straight step [Col. 0055A]? He had no idea how he could resist. Yet when he was placed at the very point of death, blessed Martin suddenly appeared to him. Taking his hand, he said: “What is this, and how did you come here?”

He replied: “I do not know, lord.”

Then, strengthening him, Martin restored him to his place.

27. Nearly five years before this, when Father Odo was traveling to Rome in order to rebuild the monastery within the church of the most blessed Apostle Paul, as it had once existed, at the insistence of the lord pope and all the orders of the Holy See, he decided first to revisit the man mentioned above and consult him about this matter, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “Do everything with counsel, and afterward you will not regret it” (Eccli. XXXII).

While they were discussing this matter and conversing for a long time about spiritual things, Father Odo began to ask him to share familiarly whatever had been divinely revealed to him at that time.

Lord Adhegrinus, recalling their former companionship [Col. 0055B] and immediately inflamed by the fire of charity, replied:

“On that day, at that hour, when the course of psalmody had suddenly been completed, blessed Martin appeared to me. After giving his blessing, his splendid face and the familiarity to which I was accustomed immediately gave me confidence. After a few words, I began to ask where he was going or from where he had come.

“He replied: ‘I am coming from Rome and traveling to France. Since you are situated near my route, I have turned aside to visit you.’

“Then, giving thanks, I began to beg him that, since he had deigned to visit a sinner, he might deign to rest beneath his hut, even briefly.

“But he said: ‘Today the coronation of Louis, king of the Franks, is taking place [Note: [Col. 0055] Namely, that of the Transmarinus, whose return from England and coronation occurred in the year 936.], and I am hastening to attend his anointing; therefore I cannot endure any delay.’

“To this I replied: ‘If you wish to leave, I ask that you first deign to bless me.’

“But he said: ‘No, you do not need to be blessed by me. Long ago, the one who blessed me likewise blessed you.’

“When I continued insistently to press him to bless me [Col. 0055C], he immediately added, as if in opposition, that I should bless him in the same way. He further declared that he would in no way agree unless I returned the blessing in kind. Thus a not insignificant and friendly dispute arose between us.

“He resisted because he did not wish to yield; I resisted because I did not presume to bless him. It therefore happened that, after we had first exchanged blessings, he departed, leaving me in great sorrow.

“To establish the truth of this matter, Father Odo, a most faithful arbiter, was present. He ordered that the day and hour be recorded, and afterward, investigating everything carefully, found that it had happened just as Adhegrinus himself had foretold.”

28. More than thirty years have now passed, if I am not mistaken, since he began dwelling in that same wilderness. Only on Sundays or major feast days did he customarily descend to the monastery of Saint Peter called Cluny, since it was nearly two thousand paces away. He took with him a little flour, from which he would make bread for himself, and a few grains of beans, and then immediately returned to the wilderness.

He never drank wine. His food was seasoned neither with fat nor with oil. At all times he endured cold and heat: heat between his shoulders, cold between his hands and arms.

But, as we continue the life of this man, let us return as quickly as possible to the subject from which we have wandered far. Yet again I remember that I promised first to explain Father Odo’s patience, which is the fuel of all virtues, and then, as time allows, to recount his remaining virtues carefully. Therefore, with the Lord’s help, insofar as my strength permits, I shall hasten to fulfill my promise.

Odo Is Tested by False Brothers

29. In the same monastery mentioned above there were certain brothers [Col. 0056A], whose life and conduct you will discover in the following narrative. Hearing that Lord Odo had come there for the sake of religious life, they approached him pretending, and feigned that they were asking why he had come.

When they had received from him an answer to their inquiry, they said: “All of us are seeking to flee this community so that we may save our souls; and you, on the contrary, have come here to lose yours?”

When he asked why they said this, they continued: “Do you know the custom of Abbot Berno?”

“Not at all,” he replied.

“Alas, alas! If only you knew how harshly he treats a monk. His correction is followed by beatings; those whom he beats he then binds in fetters, tames in prison, and afflicts with fasts. After enduring all these things, the wretch cannot even obtain his favor.”

Hearing this, Lord Odo began to waver and retreat step by step from entering. But Adhegrinus, observing him, immediately sprang into the midst and said: “Father Odo, do not be afraid. These words are not those of one speaking (*fantis*), but of one acting as an agent (*administrantis*). Pay attention, and see that the devil is speaking through their mouths.”

At once they withdrew backward in confusion. Father Odo and his companion Adhegrinus bowed their necks beneath the most gentle yoke of Christ.

For this reason blessed Benedict, who foresaw future events, commanded in the disciplinary rules (Rule, chap. 53) that no one should speak with a guest unless permission had been granted by the prior. For how many have been deceived in this way at the beginning of holy religious life, turned back, and changed from the warmth of inward desire to the torpor of a perverse will?

And although Scripture says, “Test the spirits, whether they are from God” (John IV), the testing of the faithful and of those who seek the Lord must not be of this kind—especially since the Lord commands through the prophet those who are inflamed by the warmth of the Holy Spirit: “You who are in the south, hasten to meet those who come from the north with bread.”

But just as the soldier of Christ did not embrace their flatteries, so he was not shaken by their terrors [Col. 0056C]. Of such men blessed Job rightly says: “Let those who curse the day curse it, who are ready to rouse Leviathan” (Job III).

The Customs of the Cluniacs Are Briefly Sketched

30. Meanwhile, I wish to set aside the life of our father Odo for a little while, so that, in explaining the customs of that place, I may linger briefly on certain matters, making the following account clearer.

The custom of that place was that the master of the school should never go anywhere alone with a single boy—not even for the evacuation of nature—and that a boy should not presume to speak with him privately. For the sake of a good reputation, he always took another boy or one of the brothers as a companion, either for travel or conversation.

If it was night and, by some chance, a boy needed to go to the privy, he did not dare set foot outside the dormitory without the light of a lamp and another brother.

At mealtime there was always a reading at both tables [Col. 0056D]. Each person carefully gathered before himself the crumbs produced by cutting the loaves, and before the reading ended he consumed them with thanksgiving. Once the reading had ended, no one dared consume either those crumbs or any other food. They acknowledged these crumbs to be more sacred than other foods.

For they related that, in those same years, a miracle had shone forth through them.

31. There was a certain brother in the same monastery, a very capable man and beloved by all. When he came to the point of death, and the brothers who had gathered around him were commending his spirit to the Lord in prayer, he suddenly cried out loudly:

“Help me, I beg you, lords, for God’s sake! Just now,” he said, “I was snatched away to judgment, and there the devil, accuser of the human race, brought forward against me as testimony a full sack of bread crumbs which I refused to eat according to the custom, and which had fallen from the table” [Col. 0057A].

A little later he began again to cry out terribly and say: “Behold, the devil of whom I told you is here, carrying the aforementioned sack.”

When the frightened brothers looked on in amazement, he added again: “He is standing in that place. Do you not see him?”

Then he armed himself completely with the sign of the cross and, amid words of prayer, gave up his spirit.

From that day forward the crumbs were collected with the greatest care.

32. They also have another method of maintaining silence. At unsuitable hours no one dares speak within the cloister of that monastery or join himself to another brother. When the twelve readings are celebrated [Note: [Col. 0057D] See Udalricus, *On Customs*, Book II, chapters 46 and 55.], no one dares speak within the aforementioned cloister on the following day, except in the chapter house.

On the octave of the Nativity of the Lord and of his Resurrection, the strictest silence was kept among them day and night. They acknowledged that this brief silence signified the eternal silence.

Whenever necessities arose that had to be requested [Col. 0057B], various signs were made among them in order to accomplish what was required. I think grammarians would have wished to call these signs marks made by the fingers and eyes [Note: [Col. 0057D] See Udalricus, Book II, chap. 4.]. Indeed, this system had grown so extensive among them that, I think, even if they had been without the use of the tongue, the signs themselves would have sufficed to indicate everything necessary.

On ordinary days and on the remaining octaves of the saints, however, such moderation was observed. On ordinary days, throughout the courses of day and night, they sang 138 psalms. We have subtracted fourteen of these because of the fainthearted, apart from the special prayers frequently used by our brothers, which seem to exceed the measure of the Psalter. The same applies to the two Masses and the litanies repeated from time to time.

At each canonical hour they bent their knees twice. On the octaves we have mentioned, they sang only seventy-five psalms during the aforesaid courses, bent their knees once, and ate twice.

There are many other matters which, I think, should not be inserted into this work for the sake of readers who might find them tedious.

Odo’s Patience Is Tested

[Col. 0057C]

### 33

Accordingly, when Odo assumed the direction of the school, an opportunity soon presented itself in which his patience might be tested. Night came, and behold, one of the boys signaled that he needed to go out to relieve nature. The place, however, was so close to the dormitory that the lamp burning there by regular authority illuminated the whole area. Father Odo therefore arose, awakened one of the boys, and, content with that light alone, went out with him.

On the following day, as was customary, the brothers assembled in chapter. After the Martyrology, the verse, and the reading of the Rule had been completed, they began to rebuke him severely [Note: “Proclamation” is the term used for this; see also Book II, no. 23, and Udalricus, Book II, chapter 7. Its use is still current among the Cistercians] for having gone after the boy during the night without a candle. But since no one dares to state his case before receiving permission, or to defend his opinion after receiving permission, he immediately fell to the ground and asked forgiveness, saying that the light of the dormitory ought to have been sufficient for him. Yet they not only refused to listen to him but, on the contrary, judged him guilty of a serious offense.

At last, the most blessed man, who had come to follow him by taking the narrow path, when he was suffering, did not threaten, grow indignant, or murmur, nor did he offer any complaints in opposition; instead, seeking brief opportunities, he prostrated himself on the ground and begged forgiveness. His abbot, wishing to test his patience, pretended to be angry and pronounced a sentence involving excommunication, so that he was not to ask forgiveness from him again that day.

But Odo turned over in his heart the words of David:

> “I have become like a beast before you,  
> yet I am always with you”  
> (Psalm 72);

and again:

> “You have laid afflictions upon our backs;  
> you have placed men over our heads”  
> (Psalm 65).

He went away, prostrated himself at the feet of the brothers, and asked them to go and seek forgiveness from the same abbot on his behalf. This was done. Finally, Abbot Bernus [or Berno], astonished at such patience in the young man, summoned him at once and, according to the custom of the Rule, healed that very disturbance with a blessing. From then on, he became dearer to him.

### 34

There were also in that same congregation certain brothers who were young in mind and conduct, whom we mentioned above. Instead of progressing from that point, they were moving toward destruction. For whenever they could find a place or an opportunity, they brought various insults and false accusations against him.

But the peaceful man Odo would lead them aside and, though innocent as a defendant, prostrate himself at their feet, asking forgiveness—not, however, from human fear, but from fraternal love, namely so that by his patience he might correct those whom he saw incurring divine vengeance.

At last they were restrained by his patience; but, like water slipping away, they immediately returned to their former vices. The man whom they ought to have imitated they instead persecuted.

The chief instigator of this plague was called Guido. For often, when he urged one man to insult Odo, the one sent would say:

“Of what use is it to do this every day, when we cannot drive him away or provoke him to an insult? You know that he is more learned than we are. Whatever I have wished to learn from him up to now, he has willingly explained to me. I fear, I say, that one day, broken by such insults, he may begin unwillingly to withdraw what he now gives freely.”

But the other replied:

“It is not as you say. Brother Odo is such that he will endure not only these things and things like them, but even worse; and after all this he will willingly grant you whatever you wish.”

After a short time, however, they were struck by divine vengeance according to the just judgment of God, because fraternal correction could not restrain them. For when Bernus, who was then father of that monastery, had died, they immediately laid aside the religious habit, returned to the world, and later deserved a most dreadful death.

### A Miracle Concerning Crumbs. The Conversion of His Parents

### 35

Indeed, our father is accustomed to relate that this miracle also took place there at that time.

There was in that same congregation a brother who had formed the following habit: when he sat at table, he occupied his entire mind with reading. One day it happened that, after the customary crumbs had been gathered up [Note: The Master’s Rule has another custom concerning crumbs, chapter 25: those lifted daily while the tables are being cleaned are to be kept in one vessel and then cleaned by the weekly servers on Saturday; afterward the resulting mixture, bound with flour or eggs, is to be placed on the abbot’s table before they drink the final warm beverage of the evening], the aforesaid abbot brought his reading to an end before the brother had eaten them.

The brother did not know at all what he should do. After the reading had ended, he did not dare eat them, but he could not leave them lest they perish by accident. He therefore closed his fist and decided that, when they returned after the verse, they ought to be kept for the father of the monastery.

And so it happened that, when they returned from the oratory, he immediately prostrated himself at the father’s feet. When asked why he was seeking forgiveness, he wished to show with his open hand what had happened. But all the aforesaid crumbs had been changed into the appearance of pearls.

They therefore glorified the Lord and were struck with marvelous astonishment. Then, at the father’s command, the pearls were woven into a certain ornament of the church.

He himself is accustomed to recount these events about himself as though about someone else. From that time onward, he began to burn inwardly because of the rescue of his parents, so that he might withdraw them from the bonds of this world. Accordingly, not long afterward, having received permission, he went to his father, brought him to the monastery, and had him made a monk. He also had his mother clothed in the sacred veil. Her life, if it had been permitted me to write it, would seem more like a history than a brief narrative.

### Odo Persuades a Betrothed Virgin to Preserve Her Virginity

### 36

It happened in those days that, one evening, he had turned aside to spend the night in the house of a certain most noble man. The masters of the house were absent, but their daughter was there with the household servants, a grown virgin. Throughout the entire evening she carefully observed his conduct and way of life.

Then, with a contrite heart, she secretly rushed in to him through a back entrance. Prostrating herself at his feet, she quickly declared that she was guilty and destined to be handed over to marriage. She added that, for the sake of God, whose servant he confessed himself to be, he should free her that very night.

When the soldier of Christ heard this, he did not know what to do or how to satisfy the will of so great a virgin, and he began to burn intensely within himself. In his customary manner, he held piety toward God and compassion for the virgin’s tears. He set before himself the judgment of God, the destruction of her soul, and the outcry that parents and people would raise against him: why had a monk presumed to do such a thing?

Yet, overcome by love of God and by the virgin’s sobs, he finally consented to rescue her.

That night, when all the household servants were asleep, he and the brother who was with him mounted their horses and went ahead. At his command, the servants accompanying him took the virgin and followed. The next day they arrived at the monastery.

Near the monastery there was an oratory where women of the highest rank were received for the sake of prayer [Note: From this it is understood that women were not admitted into the principal basilica of the monks. This was once customary in our order, as I have often observed]. He arranged for her to remain there and then went on to the monastery.

On the following day, as was customary, he carefully informed the father of the monastery of everything he had done. When the father heard what he had done concerning the virgin, he was visibly disturbed and began severely rebuking him for presuming to act without permission.

Immediately Odo fell to the ground and, prostrate at his feet, begged forgiveness. Afterward, raised from the ground at the father’s command, he answered the father’s repeated questioning, saying:

“Lord father, from the time you deigned to receive me, wretched man that I am, as far as I have been able to observe, you have never cared about anything except winning souls. The other abbots strive to acquire an abundance of possessions and to please people. But you, relying upon piety and mercy, labor to please God alone for the sake of winning souls. For this reason I desired to be your imitator, and therefore I wished to win this virgin to the praise of your name.

“Although her tears overcame me only after some delay, I did not forget your rebuke, which I knew with complete certainty I could not escape. But I preferred to be beaten by the scourge of a compassionate father rather than to be held guilty concerning her soul. And would that I had been able to win over all the women living in this province who are held by a carnal bond—and that you had needed to scourge me for each one of them in your most compassionate manner!”

By these and similar words he soothed his father’s anger. Nevertheless, the father immediately imposed this obedience upon him:

“Go, and just as you knew how to rescue her from the world, so know how to feed her daily and instruct her with holy admonitions, lest she ever repent and, persuaded by the devil, return to the world.”

After this, Father Odo began carrying her food every day and instructing her by the examples of earlier fathers, until within a few days he brought her to a certain monastery and associated her with the holy virgins. All these things, however, were done in the presence of the brothers, for the sake of a good reputation.

Not long afterward, it happened that she fell asleep in the Lord. When the sisters surrounded her to protect her spirit by prayer, and were holding her as though she were almost dead, she suddenly began to say in whatever voice she still possessed:

“Help me, I beg you; help me rise.”

When they asked her why she said this, she replied:

“Behold, I see the most blessed apostle Paul coming, and I wish to go to meet him.”

She had not yet finished speaking when, extending her arms in order to rise more quickly, she repeated the same words. The others thought that she was delirious.

Meanwhile, as far as she was able, she raised herself onto her knees and, with bowed head, asked the one who was coming to bless her, saying:

“Bless me.”

Then she immediately fell silent forever. For this reason no one doubted that she had been received by the one by whom she had been visited.

### 37

Father Bernus, foreseeing that he would become a man of the highest integrity, advanced him. Then, summoning a bishop, he had him ordained a priest against his will.

Father Odo is accustomed to relate concerning that bishop that no dog dared eat food blessed by him. If this happened by chance, the dog immediately died, as though it had tasted something poisonous in the food.

But I beg no one to reproach me for saying that he had been ordained against his will, lest perhaps anyone who attempts to do such a thing seem to belong among those who do not fear to buy or sell the gift of the Holy Spirit.

On the night following the day of his ordination, he awoke after sleeping through the night. He did not remember his consecration, but he found around his neck—as is customary—the stole given him by the bishop. Immediately he burst into lamentation, as though some great misfortune had happened to him. For a long time afterward, out of extreme shame, he did not know with what expression he could go outside the monastery.

Accordingly, Father Bernus sent him to the same bishop when an opportunity arose. The bishop, chiefly for his own consolation, drew him into a lengthy discourse on the dignity of the priesthood. It happened that the state of the Church became a subject of conversation between them.

Then Father Odo began, from the prophecy of Jeremiah, to expound to him a lament concerning priests. When he had completed it, the bishop began asking him to write down that same discourse for him and arrange it in the form of a little book.

In response, Father Odo brought forward the Rule, which states that a monk may do nothing without the permission of his superior. But that same bishop went to the monastery for this reason. Since he was a close friend of the aforesaid father, he immediately obtained from him what he wanted. Then, at the bishop’s command, Odo composed three little books from the prophecy of Jeremiah, whose text has now been circulated through various churches.

### Odo Elected Abbot Against His Will

### 38

At that time, Father Bernus began to lie ill with a fatal disease. He immediately summoned the neighboring bishops and removed himself from every office. In addition, in a voice full of lamentation, he proclaimed himself guilty and unworthy to have presided over such a ministry.

Amid these words he asked the brothers to choose as father whomever they wished. Then our father was seized by the hands of the brothers, almost forcibly constrained, and, while everyone proclaimed that he should be appointed, was brought by force before his abbot.

Even then he was unwilling to yield or assume the place of shepherd, but at last he was overcome by the excommunication of the bishops. Once he had been ordained, Father Bernus departed to the Lord within a short time.

# BOOK TWO

### Saint Odo Suffers the Attacks of Certain Brothers

### 1

Amid many calamities and frequent illnesses, I have been able to relate only a little about our father Odo, and only what he did under his abbot. Yet from these things your diligence can easily understand from what degree of perfection he began.

But since the beginning of a blessed life brings with it hardships and labors, while the end of struggles brings glory and praise, I shall therefore hasten to pass through his blessed and peaceful life, as though along a straight path, to his death.

Accordingly, after Father Odo had been elected and appointed abbot, the veteran persecutors mentioned above immediately rose up against him. But he preferred to give way and rest in blessed peace rather than live contentiously. He therefore left that monastery, together with everything that had been prepared there by Lord Bernus and handed over to him in the manner of a father, and went to Cluny. There he completed the monastery whose construction had long before been begun.

The elders of that place followed him.

### He Experiences Saint Martin as His Helper

### 2

At that time all the money that he had brought with him for constructing the monastery’s workshop had run out. All this happened around the feast of Saint Martin. It is our custom to celebrate it over a cycle of eight days.

After the morning celebration of the eighth day had been completed, before dawn had yet broken, everyone returned to his own bed, more for rest than for sleep. Our father used to report that an old woman had received the following vision.

She saw—and behold, a venerable man adorned with white hair, dressed in a splendid stole, over which he wore a rain-cloak, and carrying in his hand a staff in the manner of bishops. He approached closely and began inspecting the structure of the monastery all around.

When she asked him who he was, or why he was examining that building, he replied:

“I am the one whose solemnity the brothers celebrate on the eighth day. I have come to visit them. Tell them not to give up, but to persist in the work they have begun.”

The woman then added that all the money he had brought with him had run out. He replied:

“Let them not be afraid. Behold, I am now coming from Rome and going to Tours [Note: That is, into the district of Tours, Touraine. The same word occurs below, no. 16]. I shall make my journey through Gascony and Aquitaine, and from those regions I shall send them such a sum that it will abundantly supply them at this time and remain sufficient for a long while afterward.”

The brothers therefore rejoiced and, confident in the promise of so great a man, began to give thanks to God with complete gladness.

I do not dare to say who this person was, because it was our father’s custom never deliberately to identify a person in his accounts. Whether he had seen something great or something small, he would say in this manner: “One of our brothers, or an old woman, saw this or that.”

For whenever he related these things to me, he repeatedly declared that within a few days after this revelation more than three thousand solidi had been brought there from the borders of Gascony.

He used to tell me of so many and such great things, under such a guise, which had taken place at the monastery of Saint Benedict called Fleury and likewise at Cluny, that if I dared to write them out in full, the length of a little book would exceed the modest capacity of a writer.

But as we recount more fully how Saint Martin’s most faithful promise was fulfilled, the considerable assistance of wild beasts suddenly comes back to mind. This account may perhaps provoke laughter in some readers. But since we have become a spectacle to angels and to human beings, let those who disdain or are unable to imitate us at least derive some benefit from us, seeing us progress from good things to better ones; and finally, leaving behind their mournful life, let them follow with complete rejoicing into eternal joys.

### The Dedication of the Church of Cluny

### 3

When the monastery’s oratory had been built, the brothers went and invited the bishop, as was customary, to consecrate the place. He, however, making light of the monks’ poverty, arrived on the appointed day surrounded by troops and supported by attendants.

When the brothers learned of his arrival, they were overwhelmed with shame, since they did not possess such suitable equipment as would enable them to receive him honorably.

But at dawn that morning, behold, an enormous boar emerged from the forest and hurried toward the monastery. When the church custodian saw it—and since he was outside the monastery, he was thinking about the adornment of the place—he fled into the church and barred its doors against the animal.

The boar, however, setting aside its fierceness in order to be granted entrance by anyone at all, struck the aforesaid doors for a long time and smeared them with the foam from its mouth wherever it could cling.

Indeed, since no one was present who dared open the doors to it out of fear, it remained there until the bishop and his attendants arrived. To them it willingly offered itself to be killed, fulfilling the words of the psalmist:

> “Those who fear the Lord shall not be deprived of any good”  
> (Psalm 3);

and again:

> “They shall not be put to shame in an evil time,  
> and in the days of famine they shall be satisfied”  
> (Psalm 36).

### Odo’s Charity toward the Poor

### 4

Indeed, Father Odo once openly admitted that he had always possessed enough to support the brothers and to give to the poor. No poor person ever withdrew from the embrace of his mercy empty-handed.

Whenever I went with him, he always carefully inquired whether we had anything with which the poor could be supported. Then, once he knew that we had everything necessary, he proceeded secure and without hesitation; and because he gave to all who asked, God’s providence supplied him with everything.

He always had at hand the instruction of Tobit:

> “See that you do not turn your face away from him, and give to everyone who asks you”  
> (Tobit 4).

If someone brought him a gift and appeared poor by his clothing, he immediately asked him what he wanted or whether he needed anything from him. If he asked for something, Odo at once assessed the value of the gift on an equal scale and ordered that twice its value be given to him. I often saw him do this with many things.

I confess my sin: I was frequently distressed by such actions. Since I was prior, and seemed to sympathize with the poverty of the place and to anticipate the needs of the brothers, I would say to him, as though under the pretext of scarcity, that it was wrong to distribute everything so indiscriminately.

I thought I was acting wisely, but rather, enveloped in the darkness of folly, I was being strangled by the blade of greed. He, however, being a most skilled physician of souls, in a certain way touched the pulse of my error with the hand of discernment and treated the wound in my mind by this example.

He would say to me:

“Be quiet. You say this to your own harm.”

There was once a young man devoted to literary studies who, on a winter night, was hastening to Matins so that he might arrive earlier among his fellow students. In the courtyard of that very church he saw a poor man lying there half-naked. Taking pity on his poverty, he removed the scapular he was wearing over his other clothing and, as he passed, threw it to the poor man for his use.

Reflecting on what he had done, he therefore drove fear of the cold far from himself. When the morning praise was finished, he returned to his cell completely stiff with cold. But when he wished to place his frozen limbs in bed to warm them, he found a pound of gold on his bedding. From then on, he had an abundance both to retain for his own use and to give to others.

I do not know of whom Odo was speaking when he told this story. By such examples, and others like them, he treated the wound of my perversity.

### 5

I would like to pass on to other matters, but his many acts of compassion compel me to write and to speak again more fully about his generosity. Yet I know that I cannot do this without exposing my own shame.

Still, I shall write, drive the sword of rebuke into myself, and disclose my faults to everyone, so that, if I cannot now confess these things to him because he has departed, at least I may obtain you as intercessors with him.

On his journeys he would find boys along the road and compel them to sing something. As though rewarding their game, he would order that something from his own possessions be given to them. He used to say that they deserved no small reward.

He would say these and similar things in order to gladden us with his cheerfulness and refresh them with the compassion of his heart. His words were full of rejoicing, and his manner of speaking, because of his excessive happiness, forced us to laugh.

But holding the reins of moderation in his hand, he would immediately cite a chapter of the Rule to us, saying:

“Not to love much or excessive laughter”  
(Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 4, 7);

and again:

“Let a monk not be easily or readily inclined to laughter, because it is written: ‘The fool raises his voice in laughter’”  
(Ecclesiasticus 21).

In this and similar ways he restrained us from laughter; yet his spiritual cheerfulness planted inward joy in our hearts.

But what can I, an unworthy man, suitably say about him, or what can I recount of such joy? Indeed, when we could not otherwise satisfy our minds, we secretly kissed his garments.

But what wonder is that in us, who clung to him without interruption? In truth, whenever he entered the church of Saint Peter, servants of God and those who had gone up there to pray would come running after him from every side. Grasping the edge of the fringe of the birrus with which he was covered, in the manner of a cape, they would kiss it.

He would walk quickly as though fleeing, while they followed him like pursuers. He was like a square cornerstone, both angelic and human, generous and gracious, so that every day he seemed to fulfill what is read in the psalm:

> “Joyful is the man who shows mercy and lends”  
> (Psalm 3),

and the rest; and again, as the apostle Paul says:

> “God loves a cheerful giver”  
> (2 Corinthians 9).

He used to assert that the blind and the lame would become the gatekeepers of paradise. Therefore no one ought to drive them away from his house, lest in the future they close the gates of paradise against him.

If perhaps one of our servants, unable to bear their importunity, answered them harshly with some brief word [Note: Others read “some word,” that is, if I am not mistaken, the French *quelque mot*], or failed to give them the benefits to which they were accustomed, or denied them access to the door of our tent, Odo would immediately rebuke him severely with threats.

Then, while the servant stood there, he would call the poor man and say to him:

“When this man comes to the gate of paradise, repay him in kind.”

He said this to frighten the servants, so that they would not do such things again, and to instruct them in the affection of charity.

If he found an old woman or a disabled person by the roadside—as often happened—he immediately dismounted from his horse and made the person sit upon it. He ordered everyone else to go ahead and instructed one of the servants to stay beside the person and hold him so that he would not fall.

Odo himself would walk on foot among us who were riding, always singing psalms and compelling us to sing with him. If, out of shame or fear of him, someone wished to dismount, he immediately ordered him to remain seated where he was, knowing that the man wished to do this out of reverence for Odo, not for the sake of the poor person. I often saw him do this.

### Odo’s Journey to Rome

### 6

At the time when we crossed the Cottian Alps with Gerald, bishop of the church of Riez [*l’Église de Riez*], and came together to Rome, I remember that Odo did the following for a certain woman possessed by a demon. She was immediately restored to health and came with us as far as Siena [*Sienne*], where she remained ill with dysentery.

Later, at Saint Paul’s in Rome, we saw her there together. Odo immediately gave the signal and ordered that a denarius be given to her.

Since she was sitting there in embarrassment, with bowed head and eyes fixed on the ground, I asked him who that woman was. He replied:

“She is such-and-such a woman.”

He gave me identifying signs by which I could more easily recognize her.

On that same journey, a certain old and weak man was crossing the aforesaid Alps with us. He was burdened with a sack full of bread and garlic, onions and leeks; I could scarcely endure the smells of those herbs.

But as soon as the merciful father saw him, according to his custom he made him sit on his own horse and placed the foul-smelling sack upon himself.

Unable to endure such an odor, I drew my foot farther away from the side of the man whom I was accompanying.

After we had completed the very narrow path over the highest Alpine ridge and had begun descending the slope of the mountain, I saw him standing some distance away, while the poor man was forcing his horse to carry him. Odo had not returned the sack to the poor man, but had hung it from the narrow part of the saddle.

I went ahead of those who had passed me and hurried along, embarrassed, in order to approach him. Shortly afterward, when I had reached him, he said to me:

“Come closer, for there are still psalms that we must sing.”

When I replied that I could not endure the smell of that sack, he immediately rebuked me:

“Alas for me! The poor man can eat what smells foul to you, but you cannot endure its odor! The poor man can carry it, but you say that you cannot even see him!”

He was speaking about himself, for he was truly a poor man of Christ. By these and similar words he rebuked me and so healed my sense of smell that afterward I never again perceived that stench.

### Another Roman Journey of Odo for the Sake of Peace. January and February

### 7

At about the same time we were sent into Italy by Leo, the supreme pontiff, to serve as ambassadors of peace between Hugh, king of the Lombards, and Alberic, prince of the city of Rome.

After several dangers, we finally came to Siena. The city itself was suffering from scarcity of food. At the beginning of that extremely perilous journey, we had received nearly thirty silver solidi, most of which had already been distributed.

I remembered Odo’s custom: he kept nothing in reserve either for himself or for our use. Fearing that both we and all our companions might perish from hunger if we had nothing with which to buy food for everyone, I took the remainder of the aforesaid solidi, secretly left him, and crossed the city without his knowledge.

When he entered the city, needy people came to him asking for their customary gifts. Looking around and not seeing me, he immediately understood what I had done. For although I was not present, he knew that I could not be far away. He therefore gestured to everyone to follow him, and they did so.

As he crossed the city street, he saw three men who were decently dressed in a manner that made them appear unlike beggars, although they too were subject to poverty. He gave them an opportunity to become participants in his blessing.

In front of their houses stood individual small bowls filled with laurel berries. He immediately asked one of them for how much he sold the laurel berries. The man gave some very low price, I do not know what. Our father replied:

“Be quiet. Do not say the price you mentioned; say that they cost so many denarii.”

The man did so. He immediately received that many denarii as a loan, and under the pretext of the price Odo endowed them with his blessing.

Meanwhile, as I watched for his departure, I soon saw him coming from a distance. He advanced like a soldier girded for battle, surrounded by bands of poor people. Yet he was so filled with rejoicing that, after greeting him in our customary manner, he could scarcely return my blessing.

Then I pretended to ask who those people were who walked around him, and what they wanted.

He replied:

“These are God’s household servants and our laborers. So hurry and pay them their wages.”

When this had been done, I again asked him what he needed so many laurel berries for, or where he had obtained them.

He began to say such great and extraordinary things to us as I had never heard from my earliest youth, nor hoped to hear again. He so gladdened everyone that, from excessive joy, none of our companions could restrain his tears well enough to speak to another.

Before those abundant tears of joy had been wiped away, I humbly began asking his fatherliness not to burden us with the load of those berries, but to return them to the sellers.

But he replied:

“No, I will not do so, because I fear that perhaps they may send the price after us.”

At last I could scarcely obtain this from him, by showing him the remoteness of the place and the length of the journey already completed.

That very day he foretold to me that I would become a prior, and many other things that afterward happened to me. Then he began instructing me in how I ought to acquire patience among the other virtues. Beginning with himself, he started to explain how much and what sort of treatment he had endured from his brothers at the time of his ordination.

It is not appropriate to write about this now, because of the most holy conduct they later displayed.

### 8

Before the journey had been completed, and before our money had entirely run out, we met our brother Peter the priest, who was then coming to Rome for the sake of religious observance. Our poverty was enriched by his resources, since we took from him enough to complete our journey.

This happened during the two months of January and February. Our route went through the Ammiate Alps. So great was the snowfall during those days that it erased our knowledge of a route once familiar to us. It filled every hollow so deeply that, with our limbs growing cold, we even lost the ability to articulate speech.

When I saw his aged limbs wasting away, I made him a warm tunic that could protect and heat his inner body.

After our embassy had been completed, our countrymen compelled us to return by the maritime districts. When we reached a place commonly called Burrianum, as the sun was setting over the Ocean, we encountered a half-naked poor man. Just as I was unable to examine his appearance at the time, so afterward I was unable to recall it.

I remember only this: barefoot and with his sides exposed, he was fearlessly treading through the immense snow.

When our father approached him, he stopped, compelled us all to go ahead, and immediately stripped himself. He covered the poor man and ordered me to give him enough money to enable him to complete his journey.

I paused for a moment and asked him where he was going, knowing that there was no place in that vast wilderness where he could turn aside.

He replied that, while daylight lasted, he could reach a shepherds’ fortress.

From his words I understood that the one who had appeared was not an ordinary human being. For the stretch of road that he promised to complete in less than an hour took us almost the whole day to traverse.

The same event had been shown to me in the same order in a terrifying vision the preceding night.

So greatly had his heart been enlarged by mercy that he not only did such things for the faithful, but also opened his hands and extended his palms to his persecutors.

I shall recount another example concerning him, in which Brother Firmus, the brother of Lord Baldwin [Note: He was abbot of Saint Paul’s in Rome, below in number 21, and also of Monte Cassino, according to the chronicle of Leo of Marsica, Book I, chapter 58. He was a Frank by birth, according to chapter 56], was present.

### Odo’s Concern for Peace; His Charity toward a Rustic Hostile to Him
### 9. In Former Times

In former times, while the aforementioned King Hugh was besieging the city of Rome because of his hostility toward Alberic, that man began to move about within and outside the city, spreading counsels of peace and concord between the two sides, so that he might calm the fury of the aforementioned king and protect the city from so great a siege. [Col. 0066B]

Meanwhile, one day, while he was going beside the monastery of the blessed Apostle Andrew—which is called “at the Clivus Scauri” from its name—a certain peasant wanted to kill him because of a small flask of water.

[Note: [Col. 0065D] An outstanding charter concerning this monastery of Prince Alberic appears in volume I of *Italia*, col. 1099, where Benedict, abbot, religious priest, and monk, is said then to have presided; and Sergius, bishop of Nepi, Alberic’s brother, together with his other brothers and sisters, are praised.] For, as Scripture says, “He who walks simply walks confidently” (Prov. 10:9), he proceeded in his accustomed manner, harming no one and suspecting nothing, with his head bowed. Indeed, this practice had become so deeply rooted in him through observance of the Rule (Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 7) that wherever he was—whether standing, walking, or sitting—he always proceeded with bowed head and his eyes fixed upon the ground. For this reason, during the period of his religious life, some people jokingly called him “the Digger.”

Now, while the aforementioned peasant was aiming a blow at his head, everyone who was present beside the road shouted out and caused the attacker to withdraw his hands. Then the most gentle father—though I do not know how many denarii the man had borrowed—returned good for evil, and dismissed him reconciled. But after this reached the ears of the aforementioned prince, he wanted the peasant’s hands to be cut off. When the lord Abbot Odo heard this, he earnestly begged that it not be done, and released that peasant safe and unharmed.

**Also concerning a thief. The discipline of silence**

It has indeed been widely reported, and has reached your ears, what our father once did for a certain bandit when he came to Rome. I would rather set it down so that it is not erased than bring it to the attention of your diligence.

While he remained within the city for the sake of prayer, it seemed best to everyone that our brother, Lord Godefred, should go out into the fields to watch over the horses. It happened that on the following night, while the shepherds, weighed down by sleep, had fallen asleep and he himself remained fully awake, persisting in prayer, a thief appeared, mounted a horse after seizing it, and took flight.

The aforementioned brother preferred to lose the horse rather than break silence; for if he had done so, the thief would immediately have abandoned the horse. He did, however, do this: he went away, touched one of the shepherds, and awakened him, showing him by a sign what had happened. When the night had passed and morning had come, they saw the thief from a distance, sitting on the horse in one fixed place. They seized him, bound him, and sent him to our father. He immediately ordered that five silver solidi be given to him, saying that it was unjust to dismiss him without a worthy reward, since he had endured much labor throughout the entire night.

But after, by God’s drawing, I had entered the monastic life, and thereafter had been elected prior by the brothers as time advanced, our brothers often reminded me of that thief. Since he was the son of our miller, whenever his father opposed the will of the brothers, they compelled me to demand back those aforementioned solidi.

### 11. The Value of Silence

Since the discussion has turned to the practice of silence—without which, plainly, the life of a monk must be regarded as worthless—it remains for us to turn back and travel through it for a little while. For the life of a monk is something only so long as he strives to remain under silence. Once this has been removed, whatever good or honorable thing he thinks he is doing, according to the teaching of the Fathers, will amount to nothing.

### A Remarkable Example

### 12.

At the time when the exceedingly savage people of the Northmen were devastating the territories of the Poitevins and the Tourangeaux with bloody swords, it happened that two venerable men from the same congregation were sent to Touraine, I do not know for what reason. One of them was called Archembald, and was well known to me; the other was unknown to me and is said to have been named Adalasius. They were men of great reputation and have now become fathers of many monks.

As they were undertaking so long a journey and had turned aside to a certain place for the sake of rest, they were captured there that same night by those Northmen. There was a certain town beside the place, upon which they had fallen by night and captured it. Another group of Northmen, which was on the march, arrived at the same place with the booty it had previously seized. They were able to capture the brothers, bind their hands, and threaten them, but they could not make them break their silence.

When morning came, they arrived at the appointed place where they had arranged to assemble. The aforementioned brothers withdrew a little from them and, still bound, cast themselves upon the ground on their faces, so that when they had completed the course of the psalms they might bring their silence to an end. Their prayer was not yet complete when the remaining group arrived, carrying much booty.

Their leader found the aforementioned brothers lying on the ground and asked who they were. They reported everything they had done in order, adding that they had been entirely unable to make the brothers speak. Since he was swollen with barbaric savagery, the barbarian, in excessive arrogance, charged at them on the decorated horse upon which he sat, lowering his spear as if to strike and instilling fear of death in them, wishing to test whether they were afraid. The crowd, which had gathered from every side to watch this spectacle, shouted and clapped their hands in barbarian fashion.

But they, just as they were steadfast in spirit, remained equally motionless in body. This was not some form of mockery among them, but an observance required by the holy Rule, under which they desired to live and die and from which they would never turn aside.

The hand of the Almighty, however, immediately changed their joyful spectacle into mourning. As soon as the barbarian approached them, the horse on which he sat sprang sideways, throwing its rider to the ground and crushing him. A deadly fever immediately followed that injury. Everyone fell silent and, struck with astonishment, began asking one another what they should do with them.

At last, after reaching a decision, they judged it worthy of barbarian custom that one of them should be slain in place of their leader’s life. Then they began casting lots to determine which of them they should kill. But over men of virtue, who had been counted among Christ’s lot, the devil’s lot could in no way prevail. They were therefore amazed at them and, wondering, said that they were more than human beings, since their lot had not been able to fall upon them.

In fact, they had killed one of their servants in this manner. The other servant who remained knew the language of the enemies very well, and secretly reported to the brothers in Latin everything they were saying. We believe that the Consoler of men saved him because of his disclosure.

Then they approached the brothers, quickly released their hands, and through an interpreter began earnestly begging them for the life of their leader. It finally came to pass that afterward they never dared to bind them again.

This too was remarkable: one of the aforementioned brothers wore a golden cross around his neck, and when the Northmen found it, they did not dare to take it away. They were supplied with whatever food and drink they wanted for as long as they remained among them.

Thus that most tested joy was fulfilled in them which produces patience, concerning which the Apostle says: “And not only this, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience, and patience hope. But hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts” (Rom. 5).

And now, all of you who wear monastic garments, I beg you to contemplate with me the examples of these men and at last devote yourselves to silence. Concerning this good of silence Isaiah says: “In silence shall your hope be” (Isa. 30); and Jeremiah: “It is good to await the Lord in silence” (Lam. 1); and again: “It is good for a man, when he has borne the yoke from his youth, to sit alone and keep silent, because he has lifted himself above himself” (Lam. 3:27).

David likewise proclaims concerning it: “I said, I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue. I have set a guard over my mouth” (Ps. 38), and so forth. The Apostle Paul also says: “We command and entreat those who are such, in the Lord Jesus, that, working in silence, they eat their own bread” (2 Thess. 3).

We have cited these words from the ancient prophets so that no one may suppose that this silence was invented in modern times, as some wrongly suspect and acknowledge. The Fathers of the New Testament as well—Paul, Antony, Hilarion, John, and finally the most blessed father Benedict—imitated them, along with many others whom, because of the weariness of some people, we do not list by name. If anyone wishes to seek out their silence diligently, he will find it abundantly in their catalogues.

Therefore, lest anyone oppose us with the solitude and quiet in which those men lived, let us set those matters aside and turn our entire writing toward the teaching of the evangelists, taking our beginning from the works of the Lord Jesus.

### 13.

We have the first testimony in Matthew: “Jesus ordered his disciples to get into the boat and go before him across the lake, until he had dismissed the crowds. And after he had dismissed the crowd, he went up the mountain alone to pray” (Matt. 14).

The second is in Mark: “Jesus compelled his disciples to get into the boat, so that they might go before him across the lake toward Bethsaida, while he dismissed the people. And when he had dismissed them, he went up the mountain to pray” (Mark 6).

The third is contained in Luke as follows: “It came to pass in those days that Jesus went out into the mountain alone to pray, and he spent the night in the prayer of God” (Luke 6).

Likewise, in the same Gospel: “Therefore keep watch at all times, praying that you may be worthy to escape all these things that are to come and to stand before the Son of Man. During the days he was teaching in the Temple, but at night he went out and remained on the mountain called Olivet” (Luke 21).

The fourth testimony concludes in John as follows: “But Jesus went to the Mount of Olives, and at dawn he came again into the Temple” (John 8).

If the Word of God and Creator of the flesh, while living among human beings and proclaiming the Gospel of life, kept silent for a time, you can more easily understand what we ought to do—especially since death and life are placed in the power of the tongue (Prov. 18), and Scripture says: “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Prov. 10), and: “The talkative man shall not be established upon the earth” (Ps. 139).

If the aforementioned brothers, while being beaten, bound, and led away, would not endure breaking their silence with their voices, imitating him of whom it is written, “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53), what will those who suffer no violence and are compelled by no one say when they are brought together for judgment, since the case of both groups will be examined in the sight of God and the angels?

Concerning this examination, holy Church cries out terribly through blessed Job, saying: “You renew your witnesses against me” (Job 10:17). For vengeance is always inflicted most severely upon those who are convicted by witnesses. They receive the curse of the Law who know what belongs to the Law and do not fear rashly to depart from its commandments. Concerning them the Psalmist says: “Cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments” (Ps. 118).

[Note: The material that follows, through no. 22, is placed in Book III in the printed editions.]

### Medicine Is Reluctantly Granted to Sick Brothers

### 14.

There were therefore in our congregation two brothers whose names I do not wish to insert into this work. Because of their very serious illness, they had grown accustomed to praying frequently that he order medicinal remedies to be applied to them, presuming upon recovery.

But he could not endure their persistence and consented to their request. After medicine had been sought, he granted permission, but first summoned them and addressed them with a certain parable:

“I once saw a brother afflicted with a wound like yours, who died before he was restored to his former health. Those men, suspecting nothing about themselves, applied a physician to their case; but after enduring repeated sufferings, they never recovered their health.

“I also know another brother who, at the time of his conversion, while striving to wipe away the stains of his past sins by weeping, abandoned all other pursuits and labored unceasingly day and night in prayer, compunction, and lamentation. When the most patient father asked him why he was not present with the others for teaching or learning, he told him the truth, openly revealed the secrets of his heart, and begged permission to complete this work, knowing with certainty, according to the teaching of the Rule (chapter 49), that what a monk does without the permission of his spiritual father is counted as presumption and vainglory, not as a reward.

“Our father said to him: ‘It remains for this Spirit to depart from you for one year or more, so that your mind may be wounded by the goads of vainglory.’”

Immediately that brother lost the aforementioned compunction, and only after half a year had passed did he deserve to receive it again by entreating our father. His words were filled with an extraordinary weight of gravity, because the holy man, filled with the holy breath, did not know how to speak in vain.

### He Foretells the Episcopate to John

[Col. 0069C]

### 15.

A few days ago, in the presence of our brothers and of others who were with us, Lord John, bishop of the Church of Nola, reported that three years earlier he had gone to Rome twice but had been unable to receive the blessing of the aforementioned episcopate because of the opposition of his enemies.

Meanwhile, Lord Odo was going to Gargano for the sake of prayer. When he saw John grieving, he asked him what was wrong. After John had told him everything that had happened to him, and how, almost despairing of obtaining the episcopal order, he was ashamed to return to Rome for a third time, Odo blessed him and said:

“Go again without fear, and know that God has fulfilled your desire.”

Then he dismissed him. John, having received the blessing, departed, and within fifteen days, just as our father had foretold, the episcopal office came to him. We therefore confidently declare that this man truly possessed the spirit of prophecy, since his words were confirmed with such authority.

### He Obtains Baptism for His Nephew

[Col. 0069D]

### 16.

I want you to remember, brothers, that last year, in your presence, that pilgrim who claimed that he belonged to our father’s household and was hastening to go up to Jerusalem told the story of our father two or three times.

For he said that, during the years when the people of the Northmen were devastating the territories of Touraine, it happened one day that the aforementioned Northmen captured Lord Odo’s nephew, who had not yet been reborn in the baptismal font, together with his nurse. The aforementioned father was then in Tours.

When this was reported to him there, he immediately devoted himself to prayer and prayed to the Lord until he learned that the boy had been freed. He did not grieve for him more than for the other captives, but labored most earnestly for his soul, fearing that by some accident the boy, and his soul with him, might be handed over to Gehenna without the washing of the font.

Among the other things, what the boy’s nurse recounted must not be passed over. “That place,” she said, “to which the captives had been led lay beyond a certain river, whose depth was so great that no one could cross it except by boat or by swimming. It was a journey of eight days from Tours.

“Now the hope of returning to see the boy was being frustrated. While the woman stood in this very danger, she was suddenly inspired by the breath of God to seize the boy and depart; and this she did. She passed so safely through the enemy bands that she was not only not detained by anyone, but was not even questioned.

“She crossed the depth of that great river with dry legs, and completed the distance of so long a journey in three days, without hunger, thirst, or weariness, until she reached Tours.”

The merit of this deed immediately became clear, for as soon as the boy was brought to our father, he had him dipped in holy baptism. Then, lifting his eyes to heaven, he prayed that the boy might die, and three days later the boy returned his spirit to heaven. His father, meanwhile, became a monk.

As for what follows, the blessed father himself explained it—not as though these things had been done by or on behalf of himself, but by recounting the dangers from which the Lord had delivered him.

### He Escapes Shipwreck

### 17.

Once, while crossing the bed of the Rhône by boat, accompanied by the leading men of that region, it happened that one horse wished to strike another with its hoof. The blow was received by a plank of the boat, specifically at a place from which a branch had been cut away when the wood was shaped.

As soon as the top of the plank was torn out, so great a flood of water entered through the opening that the ship was suddenly filled to the surface. Nevertheless, under God’s guidance, it reached the opposite bank while full of water. Father Odo remained inside until everyone had gone out. At last, when he himself had disembarked, the boat sank into the depths.

From this it is plainly evident what merit this man possessed: through his prayers he was able to obtain what Peter and Paul, and afterward our father Benedict, had previously merited.

### Also Concerning a Precipice

### 18.

At about the same time it fell to him to come to Rome for the sake of prayer.

[Note: Compare Book II, no. 16, where John reports that this happened in the year before he wrote.]

Not long afterward, while he was returning to his homeland, his journey was blocked and enclosed among the Alps of Burdon because of the enormous quantity of snow, which that mountain can never be without.

Near that place lives a certain kind of people called Marrones, and I think that they derived this name from the province of Marronea.

[Note: Concerning these same people, see Saint Odo, Book II of the Life of Saint Gerald, chapter 17. The Marruci—inhabitants, that is, of the harsh Alps—considered nothing more profitable than carrying Gerald’s belongings across the mountain passes on pack animals. They are commonly called Marranes.]

They accepted payment and provided him with a guide, as they were accustomed to do for others, since otherwise no one at all could cross those mountains in winter. Before the sun had closed the boundary of daylight, the remaining part of the day was transformed by the mass of snow into darkness.

As they were setting out to pass through that gloomy and dangerous place, suddenly the horse on which our father was sitting placed its foot sideways, and both horse and rider plunged together into the precipice.

Then Father Odo abandoned the reins, raised both hands toward heaven as he fell, and immediately found a branch of a tree between his arms. He clung to it until, summoned by his cries, those who had gone ahead returned and received him.

That branch, however, was never seen again, because no tree is seen or grows there. The horse likewise was never seen again.

### Also Concerning Bandits

### 19.

Indeed, since he burned with an impatient love for the peace of kings and princes and for the correction of monasteries, and for this reason traveled here and there, bandits often laid ambushes for him.

One day forty bandits rose up against him. When one of them, more distinguished than the rest, named Aimon, saw him and the brothers accompanying him continually chanting psalms and making their journey while chanting, he was immediately moved to compunction of heart and said to his companions:

“I do not remember ever having seen such men, nor do I think they have been seen anywhere. Let us withdraw from them. There is also an armed man with them, a vigorous fellow; therefore we cannot harm them without danger to ourselves.”

They replied: “Let us lift that armed man onto the point of our spear, and let us strip the others and allow them to depart.”

He answered: “Turn your weapons against me first; otherwise, while I live, you can do nothing to them.”

Thus they divided among themselves and returned to their homes.

The bandit we mentioned followed our father, did penance for his guilt, and thereafter ceased from the wickedness of banditry. We do not consider this to have happened without cause. So great was the grace of the spirit to which he had clung, filling him, that his joy not only delighted those who were joyful but also restored the sorrowful to true gladness and made them participants in everlasting rejoicing.

For his tongue was, as Scripture sings, “a tree of life,” and his tongue was peaceable; the sweetness of honey was a honeycomb dripping from his lips, and the law of prudence was in his speech.

### He Received a Bandit into Monastic Life; Living Religiously, He Was Called to Heaven by Blessed Mary

### 20.

One day, as he was traveling near the territory of brigands, a young bandit noticed the affability of his face. Immediately moved to compunction of heart, he fell at his feet and humbly begged in a low voice that he have mercy on him.

When our father asked him what he wanted, he begged to be aided by monastic mercy. Our father then asked whether anyone from the same parish knew him.

“Everyone,” he replied.

“Go today,” he said, “and tomorrow, when you come to me, bring with you one of the leading men of that place.”

When he heard this, he departed and did as he had been ordered. The following day, when both men had come before him, Father Odo began questioning that prominent man about the aforementioned bandit’s life and conduct.

“This young man,” he said, “is, father, a most notorious bandit.”

On hearing this, the discerning father said to the bandit: “Go first and correct your conduct; afterward seek monastic discipleship.”

The bandit replied: “Today, rejected by you, I am going to perdition; but God will require my soul from you.”

Then the compassionate father, moved by mercy, ordered him to take the road and precede him to the monastery. This was done.

After he had spent some time under examination according to the Rule, he finally became a monk. They placed him under the obedience of the brother cellarer. Since he was uneducated, they imposed both things upon him: the yoke of obedience and the study of letters.

He carried them out so devotedly that he extended one hand in obedience, while with the other he carried the Psalter, imitating that Israelite people who, while rebuilding Jerusalem, held in one hand the sword with which they drove back their enemies and applied the other to the labor of construction.

Thus, as this brother lived out his life, after a short period of exile he came to the end of his life. When he was struggling at the point of death, he summoned the compassionate father, asking for a private conversation.

When he had sought pardon from him, the father asked whether he had committed any fault after becoming a monk.

“When you questioned me about a certain naked man, through my fault I gave him our tunic, and I took a rope woven from hair from the storeroom.”

When he asked him what he had done with it, the brother replied: “To restrain the gluttony which I had contracted long ago, I tied it around my belly.”

The compassionate father was astonished at this deed. When he wished to loosen it from the man’s entrails, the skin that had adhered to it came away together with the pus.

The brother added: “Father, last night I was lifted up into heaven in a vision. A woman of most glorious appearance and supreme power came to meet me. As she approached me, she said: ‘Do you recognize me?’

“I replied: ‘Not at all, lady.’

“She said: ‘I am the mother of mercy.’

“I asked: ‘What do you command me to do, lady?’

“She answered: ‘After three days you will come here at this hour.’”

And so it happened. On the third day, at the hour she had indicated, he died. It was therefore plainly evident that what he had seen was true, since at the hour he had foretold he departed from this world.

From that time our father adopted the custom of calling blessed Mary “the mother of mercy.”

[Note: Perhaps from this arose the common prayer that begins with these words. This expression is familiar from the acts of Saint Majolus, the abbot.]

### John’s Mission to Naples. Odo’s Revelation Concerning the Death Agony of Two Brothers

### 21.

At that time, necessity compelled me to be sent to Naples on behalf of our monastery. When everything required by necessity had finally been prepared, it fell to me to return to Rome by ship. When I had reached the city of Portus, noblemen received me; they too had come from Rome the day before.

When I asked them about our father, they seemed to rejoice as though over a new acquaintance, and among his other deeds they told me what he had done during my absence at that time.

In the preceding month of August, on the very day of the Assumption of blessed Mary, our father was at the monastery on the Aventine. Lord Abbot Baldwin asked him to celebrate Mass there that day out of love for holy Mary, and to give them communion with the body and blood of the Lord by his own hands.

He replied that he could not do this. But when they persisted, he finally consented unwillingly. Then he entered the church, and after praying for a little while he began to leave the church.

For those who wanted to detain him, he said: “I beg you, let me go, because two of our brothers are at the point of death, and I must hurry to them so that they do not depart while I am absent.”

Then he added: “Behold, the one who compels me to go is at the monastery door.”

He had not yet finished speaking when the messenger arrived, just as he had foretold. When he reached Saint Paul’s, he immediately departed and celebrated Mass for Brother Benedict, giving him the body and blood of the Lord as Viaticum. Thus the aforementioned brother gave back his spirit to the Lord.

[Note: It was once customary, or at least very frequent, for Mass to be celebrated in order to provide Viaticum to the sick, which was usually given at the very point of death. Our Odo, in Book III of the Life of Saint Gerald, chapter 7: “While the others were chanting for his departure, one of the priests hastily celebrated Mass and brought the sacred mystery. When some said that he had already died, he, still retaining consciousness, opened his eyes and showed by this sign that he had not yet died. Then he willingly received the Lord’s body, and so that blessed soul departed to heaven.”]

The other was named Gislebertus, and was my cousin; he followed on the eighth day.

Now let us return, as though in a circle, to the earlier times and proceed for a little while through more important examples.

### He Corrects the Life of Saint Martin at Rome and Explains It with Glosses. The Codex Remains Unharmed by Rain

### 22.

Three years ago, while we were at Saint Paul’s in Rome, Lord Abbot Baldwin asked him to correct and elucidate with glosses a book composed in the form of a dialogue by Gallus and Postumianus concerning the life of the most blessed Bishop Martin.

He immediately agreed to this request and, having summoned Brother Othegarius, assigned the work of correction to him.

While this was being done, the signal was sounded for the evening hour. Immediately, according to the command of the Rule, they left what they were holding in their hands and entered the church, but left the open codex where they had been sitting. Preoccupied with the evening prayers, they forgot the codex.

It was winter. During that night so great a flood of water poured down that it filled all the workrooms of our monastery. The place where the book had been left was situated so that the water flowing from its roof, together with that descending from three other roofs lying below the upper one, was gathered, as it were, into a single channel and fell like a torrent upon that one spot. There the open book remained until morning, while so many floods of water fell around it.

The edge of the book was washed all around, but the writing remained untouched.

In the morning the book was brought before the brothers. While we were all astonished and wondering, the prudent father said:

“Why are you amazed, brothers? Know that the water was afraid to touch the Life of Saint Martin.”

He said this with a certain measure of amusement.

At this, one of our brothers, who was quick to speak, took up the codex and added:

“Look and see: this codex is old, has been eaten away by moths, and was washed by water long ago, so thoroughly moistened that it is now mottled with pale stains. Behold the signs for yourselves. And our father says that a book washed long ago was now afraid to be touched by water? One thing is one thing, and another is another.”

Then the modest father said: “Be quiet; do not say such things. He is not like Martin, who can receive praise among all nations.”

Thus he turned into praise of Martin the things that the Lord had done because of him.

### The Monk’s Unrestrained Speech Is Repressed
23. During that period, our father’s name began to shine far and wide like a most brilliant star. He became known to kings, exceedingly close to bishops, and dear to nobles. Whatever monasteries had been established within their territories, they handed over to our father’s authority, so that he might correct and organize them according to our custom.

Meanwhile, he came to a certain monastery, taking with him a few brothers as companions, one of whom we knew: Adolf by name. He too had departed to the Lord two years before. When that week had ended, as Saturday evening was drawing on and our brothers had begun, according to custom, to prepare the *mandatum* prescribed by the Rule [Note: That is, the washing of the feet, for which the antiphon “I give you a new commandment” is commonly sung. It was performed on Saturday, and the monastery’s utensils were washed according to the prescription of the Rule in chapter 35.], it happened that one of those monks passed through the very place where these preparations were being made.

When he saw our aforesaid brother washing his *subtalares*—that is, his shoes—according to our custom [Note: That is, shoes, also called *sotulares*, which they were accustomed to wash every Saturday. Peter the Venerable abolished this practice in statute 28, considering it superstition to think that shoes, which had originally been worn for labor in rain and muddy roads and had consequently become dirty, needed to be washed; thereafter, once the labor of the hands had been set aside, they were to be sprinkled with two or three drops of water.], he was overcome with anger, broke silence, and began to say:

“Tell me: in what passage did Saint Benedict command monks to wash their shoes?”

The other made a sign according to our custom indicating that he should be silent, because the time was unsuitable. He did not remember what Wisdom says through Solomon: “He who instructs a scoffer does himself an injury” (Prov. 9); and again: “Do not rebuke him, lest he hate you” (Prov. 9:8).

Seeing that the other had not answered him, he became exceedingly enraged and, inflamed with a furious fire, began to spew out these words:
