“O you who used to travel through the provinces of the world doing business—now you have come to preach the Rule to us and correct the life of your betters! By swearing and forswearing yourself, like a hawk, you had grown accustomed to snatching away people’s possessions, and now shamelessly you seek to be acclaimed blessed by us, as though we did not know your actions. God did not make me a serpent, so that I should hiss in your manner, nor an ox, so that I should low; he made me a human being, and gave me a tongue so that I might speak.”

While he incessantly hurled these and similar insults, our aforesaid brother withdrew from him at a quick pace.

The following day, when all these matters had been reported in chapter, the wretched man not only failed to ask forgiveness, but replied that he had done well, adding that it was unbecoming for such a person to rebuke his superior.

Then our father, indignant at his pride, said in agitation:

“Today is the Lord’s Day [Note: In former times it was customary to hold chapter on Sunday, as can be demonstrated by other examples. Observe what follows concerning the restraint of correction on Sunday. The Council of Aachen of 817 agrees in chapter 72: ‘Let the one who is bound by the guilt of an offense be treated more leniently on the Lord’s Day and not be required to ask forgiveness.’ See Saint Bernard’s sermon.]; therefore no one ought to be saddened. For that reason, let this inquiry be postponed until tomorrow.”

And so it was done. Shortly afterward, everyone rose from chapter. But the man suddenly became mute, and after three days died without recovering his speech.

Behold how great is the venom of arrogance! By its sword-edge we have found the lives of many monks wounded up to the present, because, while they think they know what they do not know, they are made fools by their own assertions, according to the Apostle, as Scripture says [Note: Here, and shortly afterward, the term “Scripture” also includes the teaching of the Fathers, in accordance with the solemn usage of the ancients.]: “Whoever does not wish to be a disciple of truth will be a teacher of error.”

Concerning such people the Lord also speaks through Amos: “They turned back, that they might be without a yoke, and became a deceitful bow” (Amos 7).

Without doubt, those who strive to be called teachers before becoming disciples, and desire to ascend the citadel of government before learning to be subject, appear to embody the likeness of these men. Indeed, while still novices, they usurp the victor’s prize, and do not fear to seize, with untrained hands, the weapons of the strongest soldier, neglecting what Scripture says:

“He who is not regularly subject ought not to preside over those who live under a rule.”

But because they do not wish to live according to the law, they do not fear to turn the face of their hearts away from the commandment of the law. Concerning them the Lord speaks through the prophet:

“They turned their backs to me and not their faces” (Jer. 2).

For even Nicodemus, a teacher of the Law, came to Jesus by night, because he first wished to be instructed, so that afterward he might be able to teach others.

This disease has a twofold evil. One is that, through secret presumption, as though under the pretext of holiness, it urges its author to climb to the citadel of teaching authority. The other is that, once ruined himself, he seeks to instruct others according to the sect of his own error; and—something we cannot admit without grief—those who are themselves rushing headlong attempt to drag certain people standing behind them toward the precipice. Of such people the Lord says in the Gospel:

“They are blind guides of the blind. If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit” (Matt. 15).

Their gathering is more properly called a tavern than a congregation, because there each person does what he pleases and does not do what he dislikes. Of such people Solomon says:

“A bundle of tow is the assembly of sinners” (Ecclus. 21).

Blessed Benedict calls this kind of monk most abhorrent (Rule, chapter 1). He says that their way of life is most wretched, and so pitiable that he judges it better to remain silent about it than to say anything.

Therefore, leaving these matters aside, let us return to the complaint of the aforesaid monk and see what blessed Benedict prescribes concerning the monastery’s possessions.

“Let them regard all the vessels of the monastery and all its property as sacred vessels of the altar.”

And again:

“If anyone treats the monastery’s possessions in a dirty or negligent manner, let him be corrected” (Rule of Saint Benedict, chapters 31–32).

For what else are the brothers’ shoes and clothing except the monastery’s property? If elsewhere he himself commands the weekly servers to return the vessels used in the ministry, clean and sound, to the cellarer—vessels that are earthen and cheap and assigned to kitchen duties—what should be thought of shoes, which are valuable in price and meant to adhere to the church floor?

But just as it seems a serious fault for monks to take careful care of another’s property, so it is much more serious to neglect their own. If the rich man is condemned because he feasted splendidly every day, then surely the servant of God is gravely condemned who daily desires to make himself splendid, especially since blessed Benedict commands in the sixth degree of humility that the monk be content with every kind of lowliness and the most meager condition.

For this reason, someone who is negligent does not wish to wash his shoes, so that he may throw them into some corner and allow them to wither under the pallor of mud; and finally they become useful neither to him nor to the poor, although the aforesaid father commands that everything old be distributed to the poor.

We say this not so that they may walk about dirty or shining like hypocrites, but so that they may use all their garments clean and washed, as a certain wise man says:

> If you desire to be good and seek an honorable life,  
> Cherish the cleanliness of body and soul.

The precepts of the Fathers are boundaries for those who follow them. Concerning these the Lord speaks through Moses:

“Cursed is everyone who transgresses the boundaries of his neighbor” (Deut. 27:17).

Since this aforesaid monk was not afraid to cross the boundary of the commandment, he rightly received the sentence of the curse in the very matter in which he had transgressed.

This is also why the rich man who is said to have been buried in hell confesses that he burns more in his tongue than in his other members. Hence the saying of a certain wise man:

“By the things through which a person sins, by those same things he is tormented.”

The apostle James likewise says of the tongue:

“The tongue is a fire, the universe of iniquity. The tongue is set among our members; it defiles the whole body and sets on fire the wheel of our birth. The tongue is a restless evil, full of deadly poison” (James 3:6, 8).

And the psalmist says of it:

“The Lord will destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue” (Ps. 9:14).

Likewise, through Ezekiel:

“I will make your tongue cling to your palate, and you will be mute” (Ezek. 3:26).

Would that the tongue were mute and the person not separated from the company of the faithful! For what, I ask, is excommunication except separation from the good?

Among his other precepts, blessed Benedict placed under excommunication what he said concerning silence, and left it under no prior’s discretion. Therefore, whoever has attained the heights of monastic life should weigh carefully what he is doing and make himself a stranger to excommunication itself.

Let him always keep in his heart what happened to those two virgins who treated blessed Benedict’s command negligently, concerning whom blessed Gregory speaks in his *Dialogues*.

But we have lingered sufficiently over these matters. Let us now pass on to others.

# BOOK THREE

[Note: In the Compendian manuscript, and likewise in the oldest Silviniac manuscript, there is no division of the book here; everything is contained in two books.]

## The Death of the Monks of Saint Martin

1. At the same time, while our father was instructing us in regular discipline, he had made a practice of telling us, in careful narration, not merely about the death but about the miserable end of many monks, so that he might restrain the impulses of youth within us and, as though under a shepherd’s rod of fear, lead us toward Elysian joys.

One day, while he was explaining such matters to us, I submitted to his fatherly authority and began to ask him to tell us whether the monastic order had collapsed only within the boundaries of Italy, or whether it had likewise fallen away in the regions of Europe, and how, in what manner, or when this had happened.

Then he began to explain these matters to us:

“Some years ago, while the monastic community remained at the church of blessed Martin at Tours, they began to abandon their proper discipline and customs and to corrupt their life and profession according to their own wills. Abandoning their native and customary clothing, they began to wear gaudy, loose-fitting cowls and tunics adorned with mantles. Their shoes were so colored and polished that they seemed to have taken on the appearance of glass.

They rose at daylight for the nocturnal Lauds, so that they would not stumble with any foot. They did many other things of this kind against the authority of the Rule.

When God had determined to bring these matters to an end, one night, while everyone was sleeping, one of them remained awake during that same hour and saw two men enter the dormitory. One held a sword in his hand, while the other commanded him, pointing to each monk in turn, to strike them with these words:

‘Strike this one and this one.’

When the executioner wished to attack the man who was watching these things, the latter cried out and adjured him:

‘I adjure you by the living God: do not kill me.’

Immediately the executioner withdrew his sword, and that man alone escaped from them all.”

[Note: What is to be thought of this slaughter has been said in the Eulogy of Alcuin, in Part I of the fourth century. Read what this same Saint Odo says in his little work *On the Burning of the Church of Saint Martin*, where he reproves among the Martinian canons the admission of women into the monastery and the pomp of clothing.]

## How Serious a Fault It Is to Change Monastic Clothing

2. Again I asked him what fault there was in a monk who used any garment with a pure mind. In response, he immediately set before me this example:

“At the time when the sword of the Northmen was raging through our regions, many of our order began, taking the enemy as their pretext, to abandon their own monasteries and resume everything agreeable to human use, things to which they had previously renounced.

Instead of the company of the brothers, they frequented their relatives and friends; and instead of the monastery’s possessions, they desired to enrich themselves with personal property.

At length, having worn out the clothes in which they had left the monastery, they did not put on similar garments again, but colored ones, which we commonly call *blava*—blue.

At that time a certain brother, withdrawing from this plague, sought our monastery and begged us to receive him. When we consented to his wish, he immediately renounced everything he had acquired and granted it to the monastery.

When the brothers ordered him to go and bring everything together to the monastery, he replied:

‘Let me be the one whose possessions up to now are placed under your authority, while it belongs to your power to seek them out and dispose of them. Therefore I will not leave the monastery alone; command one of the brothers whom you choose to seek them out. I, however, obeying your will, will go with him, and I will obey his orders as best I know how. But whether I remain here or travel there, from now on I shall be stripped of all things.’

The brothers’ decision remained firm, and he went with the brother to whom they had assigned this obedience.

When they had arrived at the place where the aforesaid brother had formerly lived, he was suddenly overcome by illness and died there. As he lay in his final agony, the brother who had gone with him poured out the more urgent prayers to God for his soul the nearer he saw him approaching death.

And so it happened that both of them saw the following vision:

A throne had been set on high, and blessed Benedict appeared to be seated upon it. Before him stood an immeasurable army of monks. The ascent to that throne appeared to be spread with mantles, and on the lowest step the sick brother lay prostrate, as though asking forgiveness.

The aforesaid army of monks sat on his right and left; between the two groups there was an empty path open to those ascending.

After that brother had lain prostrate for a long time, one of those standing nearby approached blessed Benedict, pleading for the brother and saying that he was worthy to be raised by his presence [perhaps *jussione*, “by his command”], so that he might say what he wished.

Benedict appeared to reply that he saw the man but did not recognize his habit; therefore, since he was a man of another order, he ought neither to investigate his case nor judge his life.

When the brother of our order heard this, he stripped himself and clothed the sick brother in his own garments, compelling him in the same vision to ask forgiveness again.

When this had been done, a voice came from above commanding him to rise and ascend upward.

Then our brother awoke from sleep. He immediately carried out in deed what he believed he had been doing in his dream, and, now almost confident about his brother’s soul, protected his passing with prayers as best he could and fortified him with holy Communion.

Consider, therefore, my son, the judgment of the Apostle who says:

‘Faith without works is dead’ (James 2:26).

And as it is written elsewhere:

‘Whoever says that he knows Christ ought to walk as he walked’ (1 John 2:4, 6).

Likewise, whoever professes to be a monk ought to imitate Father Benedict in deed and in mind, because it is written:

‘It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers’ (Rom. 2:13).

For it is not enough for a monk to have purity of mind alone if the evidence or signs of other works are lacking. Of this the Lord says:

‘Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven’ (Matt. 5:15).

Blessed Gregory speaks more fully about this in the first part of his commentary on Ezekiel. From his discourses we shall offer one testimony:

‘Just as there are two ways of departing from God, so in two ways people become apostates from God. Each person either departs from his Creator in faith or in deed. Therefore, just as one who departs from the faith is an apostate, so one who returns to the very work he had abandoned is without any doubt judged an apostate by almighty God, even if he appears to retain the faith. One without the other cannot be beneficial: neither faith without works nor works without faith.’

Therefore no one should be horrified by what we have said: that the aforesaid brother could not receive forgiveness or deserve to ascend until a change had been made in his clothing.

No one doubts that the Law prescribed what garments the sons of Levi were to wear, without which they did not dare enter the sanctuary. Who would dare say that they used the *rationale* (breastpiece) in place of the humeral garment, or wore a linen ephod in place of a fine-linen tunic? Each has its own color, function, and variety.

The devil also opposed Jesus the great priest until he had been clothed by the angel in other garments. And David, when he wished to rise against the people of Amalek, consulted God twice and did not receive the command to go. The third time he was clothed in the ephod, and immediately he heard the voice of the one commanding him.”

## Punishment for Monks Who Ate Meat

3. He said this, and afterward added:

“Do you wish me to show you by other examples that what greatly dishonors and corrupts a person may be something very small?”

When I replied that I desired this with all eagerness, and he saw that I was burning with enthusiasm for his authoritative teachings, he briefly related the following examples.

“These days two brothers were carried off by an exceedingly swift death, though not in the same place or on the same day.

One of them came to the house of a certain sister of his and said that he was extremely hungry and asked for food. His sister immediately replied that she had an abundance of fish for him to eat, of whatever kind and at whatever hour he wished.

But he, as though indignant, replied that he was disgusted with fish, adding that he had eaten them continually for so many years and saying that he could no longer bear to see them.

His sister replied:

‘Look, we have meat ready. Eat, then, whatever you like.’

[Note: Peter the Venerable relates these examples and presses them forcefully in Book VI, Letter 15, to his Cluniacs.]

He then ordered a shoulder of some animal to be roasted for him. But, unable to endure the delay of roasting, he cut off a small piece and threw it onto the coals. Then he ordered wine to be brought and greedily took a bite of meat. But what he took did not pass through his throat, nor could he vomit it up; he lost his life together with the food.”

4. “The other came at dawn to the house of one of his relatives and immediately asked whether they had anything to give him to eat.

When they replied that it was not yet time to eat, he added indignantly:

‘Alas! I labored all night riding because of the obedience imposed upon me, and I did not rest; and now you are forcing me to fast? Bring me, then, whatever you have.’

When they said that they had fish, he became even more indignant. Filled with arrogant disdain, he began to cast his eyes about in every direction.

A flock of crows, which we call hens (*gallinae*), was walking around his feet. Then, as though furious, he seized a stick, struck whichever hen pleased him, and said with a raging mouth:

‘This will be my fish today.’

The others who were standing nearby began, with some embarrassment, to say to him:

‘Perhaps you are permitted to eat meat, Father?’

But he replied:

‘A bird is not meat. Birds and fish have one origin and an equal creation, as our hymn contains.’

At his words they all fell silent.

Meanwhile, the roasted hen that he had killed was placed before him. He took a morsel from it and bit it. He could neither spit out nor swallow the bite, and it deprived him of life. Before he died, however, he received blows with fists and blows to the neck as the reward for his wickedness, to his disgrace.

If your mind is troubled by the death of these two brothers, consider that, just as in the case of the first and as we have now shown you by example, they were worthy of the death by which they were entangled.

For a few grains of lentils, Esau lost his birthright. Likewise, while the Israelite people were being fed with manna, they turned their hearts back toward Egypt, craving the pots of meat that they had recently eaten under the yoke of evil servitude.

The apostle Paul mentions them:

‘Let us not be desirous of evil things, as they also desired them’ (1 Cor. 10:6).

These men said that they were disgusted with fish; those others murmured, saying:

‘Our eyes see nothing but manna.’

We say this not because we condemn foods, but those who use them wrongly. Hence Paul also says:

‘Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires’ (Rom. 13:14).

What he forbids in the sphere of desire, he grants in the sphere of necessity.

Three young men sent into the furnace of Babylon, renouncing royal foods, escaped from such a great fire unharmed. That same fire burned and killed as many Chaldeans as it found.

Likewise, Nebuzaradan, chief of the cooks, destroyed the walls of Jerusalem.

Therefore let no one be troubled by the fact that Elijah was fed with meat morning and evening during a time of famine; let the one who seeks the food consider the minister. Demons often assume the form of these birds. Such food from ravens was suitable for his service, and its being supplied in the evening and morning earned him hunger. But when he ate bread, he had an angel as its bearer, and he was so strengthened that for forty days he had no need of nourishment from food.

We have said all this to demonstrate more fully that the fault is not in food but in appetite.

Nevertheless, the death of these men brought about the amendment of many people’s conduct. Thus the order of monks fell among us; thus it was corrected, and is frequently corrected by many miracles, so that, by God the author, it may persevere.”

But while we had resolved to recount our father’s life and teaching more fully, like imprudent men we somehow fell into these digressions and therefore wandered far from our purpose. Let us quickly turn our pen back to it.

## Punishment of Another Whose Vein Was Cut

5. Our brothers who stood before our father often used to confess that there was a certain brother from our father’s congregation who had submitted himself to phlebotomic treatment at a permitted time.

His action angered our father, because although necessity had compelled him, he ought not to have presumed to do it without his permission.

Immediately, the vein through which the blood had previously flowed burst, and no medicine could staunch it until he gave up his spirit.

They added that, whether he had pronounced something favorable or adverse concerning anyone, that person could in no way escape it. Would that one of our own brothers had not experienced this in himself.

But happy were those who deserved to see his presence while he lived. Unhappy am I, who did not deserve to serve him for two full years.

## Odo’s Fear of Sins Against an Abbot

6. As the time approached when, according to God’s dispensation, we were to be separated from the sight of his body—and his absence, which was about to occur, was to kindle a more intense fire of love in my mind—one day, when he saw me exceedingly sad, he began, in his customary manner, gently to console me.

But when he saw that he could not even in this way satisfy my wretched mind, he began, after the manner of the patriarch Jacob, taking his starting point from past events, to foretell the future to me with a prophetic spirit:

“My dearest son, listen to what I tell you. I give thanks to God because, of all the sins I committed from my youth, I have already received punishment in this life, except for those which I committed against my abbot. I have always awaited that day and hour, praying to God that he would not reserve them for me in the future.

And now I believe that I have been heard, because what I did against him I have received back from you. But you should know that they are not repaid to you singly, but tenfold. Be strong and patient, so that by bearing them quietly you may be able to endure them.”

He said this with tears, then kissed my head and commended me to the Lord.

But you, almighty Lord, mercifully spare the priest Caesarius, who repaid me in return a hundredfold and with heavier burdens; and, if anything remains for my grieving troubles, turn it away in your mercy. [Note: In the printed editions, the material found in the preceding book in the Compendian manuscript is inserted here, namely, from number 14 through number 23.]

## The Monks’ Greed for Meat

7. At that same time, the aforesaid Alberic, prince, granted us the monastery of Saint Elias, called Subpentonia, which blessed Gregory mentions in the *Book of the Dialogues* [Note: Namely, in Book 1, chapter 7, where he places this monastery near the city of Nepi, in Etruria. Gregory returns to this monastery in the following chapter.].

But, as that same blessed Gregory says, it is difficult for an old mind to contemplate new things. Thus we were unable to withdraw the monks whom we found there from eating meat.

Our father appointed one of our brothers, Theodard by name, as prior in that monastery. When he saw that by neither virtue nor holiness could he restrain them from this same vice, he began to buy fish from the neighboring regions, so that in this way at least he might satisfy their wishes.

For this reason, the horses that our father had left him had become completely exhausted, running here and there. The aforesaid brother repeatedly took pains to inform our father of their wickedness and of his own labor.

Meanwhile, as he was asking the Lord for help, the valley itself—above and between which the monastery stood—closed up where the nearby hills joined together, not very far away, and blocked the passage of the tiny stream that flowed through it.

Then, when a multitude of waters had gathered, it produced a lake and relieved the brother of his labor, because from then on he no longer needed to buy fish.

But certain ignorant people did not know the merit of this event, because they had not seen publicly by what means it had happened, nor had they heard with their own ears our father’s prayer.

This is characteristic of hypocrites, not of the faithful: they fail to understand what the psalmist sings:

“The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; your ear has heard the desire of their heart” (Ps. 10:17);

and again:

“He will fulfill the will of those who fear him, and he will hear their prayers” (Ps. 144:19).

He had acted similarly earlier when he was in France with blessed Benedict. We can relate the reason for this all the more confidently because in this matter we have that same father as a faithful witness.

But first, in faithful speech, we must explain how he received the aforesaid monastery, so that our pen may reach what follows as though by a straight line.

## The Monastery of Saint Benedict at Fleury Reformed

8. After the end of the persecution that took place in the regions of Gaul under the most savage Northman king, Nortmund, the Lord fulfilled for his Church what he had once foretold through Isaiah:

“For a brief moment I abandoned you, and with great mercies I will gather you. In a moment of indignation I hid my face from you for a little while, but in everlasting mercy I will have compassion on you” (Isa. 54:7–8).

The brothers who had formerly been scattered here and there from the monastery of blessed Benedict out of fear of the enemy gathered together in one place and recovered their own monastery. But—something we cannot say without grief—their bodies were united while their minds were divided, and they occupied that most holy place only physically. We pass over this in a brief account, lest our pen linger over the life of such men.

What we earnestly desire to narrate openly is how the most blessed father Odo was called, chosen, and indeed preordained by blessed Benedict.

One day, while the aforesaid brothers were residing within the cloister and gnawing at one another, one of them, returning from an obedience, encountered Father Benedict before the monastery gate.

Benedict immediately commanded him:

“Go,” he said, “and tell these brothers that they do not allow me to rest. Behold, I am leaving these buildings, and let them know that I will not return to this place until I bring here from the regions of Aquitaine a certain man who is according to my heart.”

When that brother wished to ask his name, Benedict answered his hesitation:

“I am he, brother Benedict.”

He said this and began to depart.

The brother therefore announced what had been commanded him. But the wretched men, deprived of such a great father, did not resort to tears and prayers, which often appease the Lord’s very threats. Instead, mounting their horses, they began to rush here and there to find him and, once found, to bring him back by force or entreaty.

When they found no one, they later began incessantly to mock that brother.

At that time a man named Elisiardus, then a distinguished count but now living in the monastic habit, heard of these monks’ disgrace. He asked King Rudolf of the Franks for the aforesaid abbey, received it, and handed it over to our father.

Then, taking with them two counts and likewise two bishops, they set out together with our father Odo.

When the brothers learned of their arrival, some took up swords and climbed onto the roofs of the buildings, as though about to hurl stones and missiles from the heights at their enemies. Others, equipped with shields and girded with swords, guarded the monastery entrance, declaring that they would rather die than allow them to enter or accept an abbot from another order [Note: That is, from another monastery or congregation, as is explained below.].

Meanwhile, coming to their senses, they said:

“Now we see what blessed Benedict recently threatened us with. Alas, what grief! Why did we not believe our brother? Everything he told us he has fulfilled in deed. Is this not that Odo of Aquitaine whom we often suspected blessed Benedict meant? Alas! Why did we not send for him earlier and invite him willingly?”

Meanwhile, they searched for a way to drive them back, turning here and there.

There was among them a young man named Brother Vulfaldus, of good character. While he moved among them, they sent him certain royal commands stating that no one from another congregation was ever permitted to assume the priorship of that place.

Our father said to him:

“Come peacefully. I come in such a way that I harm no one and injure no one, but that I may correct the uncorrected according to the Rule.”

With these and similar words, though conveyed through intermediaries, he continually soothed their minds.

But when they saw that their ingenuity was in no way prevailing, they turned to other arguments: at one moment they invoked the king, at another they threatened to kill him. This continued for three days.

Afterward, while everyone was unaware, Father Odo mounted a little donkey and began to proceed rapidly toward the aforesaid monastery.

The bishops and the counts who were with them, together with their attendants, ran after him, crying:

“Where are you going, Father? Are you perhaps seeking death? Do you not see that they are prepared to kill you? The moment you approach them, you will die. Do you wish to give them joy at your death and bring deadly grief upon us?”

They shouted these and similar words after him. But, as Scripture says:

“The righteous is as confident as a lion, without fear” (Prov. 28:1).

They could not divert him from his chosen path.

I am about to tell of something marvelous. As he approached and was recognized by those who had known him previously, the men who had been resisting were immediately moved and transformed, so that I can say without doubt:

“This is the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 76:11).

Indeed, they immediately threw down their weapons, went out to meet him, and embraced his feet. That day brought no small joy to everyone.

They therefore received Father Odo within the cloister of the monastery; all the others returned to their own places.

## Meat and Property Only with Difficulty Abandoned; Bishops’ Concourse to Odo

9. During these days he began to persuade them to abandon the eating of meat, to live sparingly, and to possess nothing as private property. Whatever they secretly possessed, they were to renounce before everyone, after the manner of the apostles.

But because they had by no means held the monastery’s possessions in common, having divided them among themselves according to their ability and pleasure, when they saw that what had once been permitted was no longer permitted, they preferred to give away unjustly to their supporters—indeed, to their squanderers—the things they had unjustly possessed, rather than renounce them lawfully and according to the Rule.

By a mere declaration, they undertook to consume by eating the very things they had renounced, together with the other provisions our father had brought with him, so that, once everything had been consumed, he would at least be compelled to grant them meat, even against his will.

For this reason they continually demanded fish. In contrast, the merciful father supplied everything to them appropriately, in order to restrain them from one thing.

And so it happened that, while he was giving and they were eating, nearly everything was consumed.

Our father persevered, fearless in faith, secure in hope, and fortified by charity, knowing that, in accordance with the Gospel promise, he would by no means be abandoned:

“Do not be anxious about what you will eat, or what you will drink, or what you will wear” (Luke 12:22).

Meanwhile, while these things were taking place, Saint Benedict appeared in a vision to a certain brother and, among other instructions, commanded him to tell our father not to be at all afraid because of a lack of money or anxious about acquiring supplies.

Then he added:

“Tomorrow I will send him one hundred solidi, and in the following week I will provide him with such relief in various necessities as may suffice for the brothers’ needs over a long time.”

And so it happened.

10. Moreover, very many people from the surrounding regions began to hasten to the blessed man’s footsteps and to take up, under his instruction, the path of obedience pleasing to God, so that afterward they might deserve to ascend to the dwelling-places of heaven. His reputation for holiness spread so widely that not only laymen or canons flocked to him, but certain bishops as well abandoned their own sees and joined themselves to his community. Meanwhile, one might have seen that place, like earth cultivated after thorns had been cleared, bringing forth new shoots as though new crops, and, as though from a threshing floor, bringing into the Lord’s granary the grain separated from the straw of vices by the frequent blows of words.

Done on the solemnity of Saint Benedict.

[Col. 0082C] 11. At another time, too, the feast-day of blessed Benedict was approaching. Our father, who was then staying at a certain monastery, resolved to proceed to the aforesaid monastery, so that he might devoutly keep vigil there through the night before the body of the blessed man; and so he did. On that night preceding the solemn day, it happened that the morning office was celebrated before sunrise. For when one of the brothers, wearied by the night vigil, had again given himself over to sleep, blessed Benedict deigned to appear to him. After first making himself known to him, he immediately added:

“Tell the brothers,” he said, “that on this night I could not be with them, but today I shall certainly be.”

“And where were you, lord?” he asked.

Blessed Benedict replied: “On the island of Britain.”

“What did you do there?” he asked.

He answered: “Brother Leutfred, who, because of his pride, abandoned this place and crossed the seas, died this night and was received by demons. I engaged them in combat and freed him from their power.”

[Col. 0082D] When he heard this, the brother began, stunned, to marvel at what had happened. The holy father again said to him:

“If you marvel at this event, hear another. Know for certain that from the day on which this monastery was built, all the brothers who have died here have been received into eternal rest.”

[Note: [Col. 0081D] One should not place excessive trust in privileges of this kind. Saint Odo himself speaks especially aptly to this point in his sermon on [Col. 0082D] Saint Benedict, where he discusses Fleury: “Consider, then, whoever you are, to whom a place so greatly desired everywhere by so many is not denied, how highly it ought to be esteemed and with what reverence it ought to be honored. For the weight of any guilt is usually assessed not only from the understanding of the person who bears it or from the time, but also from the place. Otherwise, whoever is not moved to reverence by the presence of so great a father seems to share in the spirit of Judas.”]

Then the brother added: “Lord, since you said that you must be with us today, who will make known to us the hour of your arrival, so that we may go out to meet you?”

“No one,” he said, “but I shall show everyone such a sign [Col. 0083A] that no one will doubt my presence.”

The brother added: “And with what preparations shall we be able to receive so great a father, or with what services shall we attend him?”

Blessed Benedict replied: “If you are concerned about more sumptuous foods, you have fish in abundance.”

“By no means, lord,” he said.

“Let the fishermen,” said the saint, “be ordered not to go fishing in the bed of the Loire, but in this marsh, which flows beside the monastery.”

After hearing this, the brother awoke from sleep. When it was time to speak, he took care to make known to the brothers everything that had been commanded him. Thus, assured of the father’s arrival and instructed by the admonition of our father Odo, each of the brothers strove to offer the spiritual father spiritual gifts from his own heart. It therefore happened that they spent that very day in spiritual hymns and prayers.

Meanwhile, the monastery servants whose duty it was to fish did not go into the marsh, as they had been ordered, but into the river Loire, from which they had been expressly barred. It happened, therefore, that after laboring without any profit, they returned to the monastery at about the third hour. When they were asked why they had returned empty-handed, they were ashamed, confused by the presumption of their disobedience, to confess what they had done. But the silence imposed by shame was disclosed by the redness of their faces.

The steward said to them: “I know your presumption. But since you previously rejected what was commanded, now go back a second time to the marsh for the purpose of fishing.”

And so it was done. Indeed, they suddenly drew so many fish from that fishing-place that scarcely anyone could doubt that he who, in the desert region, had given quails to the people was at that time also causing fish to flow into the same marsh. For they became so abundant there that, plainly, they never at any time failed from it. Thus it happened that the marsh, which had previously been accustomed to boil over with frogs, afterward abounded in fish.

Our father himself published this miracle in the book which he wrote about the arrival of the body of Saint Benedict at Orléans, with the same meaning, though [Col. 0083C] not in the same words as the other accounts, and with the greatest perspicacity.

[Note: [Col. 0083D] That book of Saint Odo has disappeared. Would that someone, if it exists anywhere, might bring it to light.]

A considerable crowd of people from the surrounding regions had therefore gathered for that same solemnity.

[Note: [Col. 0083D] Odo speaks of this crowd in his sermon on the translation of Saint Benedict, which I believe was delivered on that day.]

Among them were very many blind and lame people, as well as paralytics and persons afflicted with various illnesses, awaiting the time of refreshment. Father Odo had ordered that none of them should be given food before the time of Mass. When the appointed hour had come, they all entered for Mass. The church is so large that no one was forced to remain outside.

Indeed, when they began to sing the angelic hymn—that is, “Glory to God in the highest”—

[Note: [Col. 0084D] In former times it was not permitted to every private priest to sing this hymn at Mass. See the letter of Pope Agapitus in volume I of the *Metropolis Salisburgensis*, p. 150, and the diploma of Callistus II on this matter for Franco, abbot of Tournus, in Chifflet, p. 403.]

the church doors were suddenly shaken and thrown open with a great crash, but only so far that everyone looked behind him, struck with a certain horror. In that very crash, all the sick who were present were restored to their former health: the blind received sight, the deaf hearing, and the lame their ability to walk. Indeed, all the lamps of the church were also lit.

[Col. 0083D] Then everyone understood that Benedict had arrived there, as he had foretold. Spiritual devotion filled the hearts of all to such an extent that, overcome by immense joy, they could not restrain their tears. Father Odo, however, refused to disclose to me the names of the brothers who had witnessed this. Hence it is uncertain whether he himself or someone else was the person who saw these things.

Saint Odo, ill at Rome, obtains an extension of life. He reaches Tours on the feast of Saint Martin. He dies on the octave of Saint Martin.

12. Now when the moment of his death was already at hand, and, as we have related above, Christ owed him the crown of blessed recompense for his pious deeds, he was staying at Rome when he was seized by a sharp and continuous fever. His limbs were broken by pain; a cold fire consumed his very marrow together with his flesh; and various and manifold kinds of suffering rose up in one man to such a degree that it was truly the case that he was already, at any moment, being called by the Lord and stripped of the clothing of the earthly man.

What could the holy man do? A faithful imitator and representative of the apostle, he now desired to be dissolved and longed with all his wishes to live with Christ. He had run through the contest of the saints’ labors and completed the distinguished course of every virtue, so that, with good reason, he trusted with complete confidence of hope that, through the grace of divine mercy, a crown of righteousness had been laid up for him in heaven.

Moreover, while he was held in suspense concerning this calling of his, he desired first to revisit his own Martin, in whom, so to speak, he had imbibed with his mother’s milk the heat of an inexhaustible love, in order to receive from him the grace of prayer and to entrust his final breath to him together with the ashes of his own body.

Since the mercy of almighty God always deigns to attend pious wishes, it was soon present also in the case of our Odo, whom He had set apart from his mother as another vessel of election. For the man beloved by God saw, on the following night, a man of remarkable appearance and grace, who said these things to him in a vision:

“O holy soul beloved of God, your calling and the final dissolution of your body are indeed at hand. But Martin postpones you by his prayers, and grants you both a return to your homeland and strength. When, however, you have arrived with him, life will immediately be given you in place of death, and Christ will repay you with the blessed fellowship of the elect for your pious labor.”

The signs immediately gave confirmation to the vision: the bodily illness abated somewhat, health returned with haste, the difficulty of the journey immediately overtook him, and, paying no regard to his aged and half-dead limbs, he overcame the harsh labor. His excessive ardor for Martin made him all the more devoted to spiritual service, the more secure he was regarding his reward.

When the road involving so great a labor had been completed, he arrived at Tours, while the feast of the blessed bishop was already at hand—the feast on which that victorious spirit had departed from the body. Then the city experienced a double rejoicing, as both Martin’s annual celebration was renewed and the long-desired presence of Odo, a fellow citizen, was reverently embraced by everyone in common.

It is beyond our ability—crushed as we are by dullness of mind and rusticity of speech—to unfold how devout the holy man was during that sacred festival, what prayers mingled with tears he poured forth to Martin, or what sacrifices of a contrite heart he slaughtered upon that saving altar like a living victim. For, anxious about his own calling, his mind was fixed upon God; already forgetful of earthly things, with the pure gaze of his mind, like a true servant of Martin, he contemplated only heavenly things with the greatest attention.

Thus he was held suspended in such expectation throughout the entire celebration of the blessed bishop. But, contrary to his hope, he anxiously lamented that the promised gifts had been delayed for three days. Then, behold, on the fourth day after the festival had ended, the fever flared up again; cold blood soon crept into his heart and consumed his strength with a bitter wound.

Now that he had attained the object of his desire and was certain of God’s mercy, his weary spirit indeed languished in his sick body.

But his joyful mind sees God, sighs, and breathes longingly;

his final voice resounds: “You, Christ, spare the redeemed.”

He repeats Martin’s name, looks up to Martin, and prays.

He instructs the monks who came from every direction, as they mourned his calling beyond remedy; he commends them to God in fatherly prayers, protects them with blessings, and bids them farewell with devout sobs.

It was already the fourteenth day before December, which is also reckoned as the octave of Martin’s celebration, when that blessed spirit, refreshed by that divine and saving richness and strengthened by the life-giving drink, was released from corruptible flesh, migrated freely to the heavens, and, with Martin as his guide, faithfully presented the manifold fruit of the talent entrusted to him.

From him he himself received the worthy reward of his pious labor and, joined to the assemblies of the saints, shines with the brightness of blessed immortality, through Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0085]

## THE SECOND LIFE OF SAINT ODO

By Nalgodus, a Cluniac monk of the twelfth century.

(According to Mabillon, from manuscript codices.)

### AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE

Nalgodus revises John’s account.

[Col. 0085B]

1. The persistent urging of religious older men moved me to put the finishing hand to the writing of the life of blessed Odo, the first founder of the Cluniacs. I could not refuse what such commanding charity demanded. Yet, driven both by what they ordered and by the zeal of a new devotion, I came upon John, who was found to have written about him.

I read his work with the diligence it deserved and went through the pages he had offered in sequence. There was such confusion of words, such scattered prolixity, and such disordered and inverted arrangement of the narrative that the very sequence of the account scarcely cohered with itself either in reason or in time. It displeased me greatly; and I was deeply grieved that the illustrious deeds of so worthy a man should be oppressed by a cloud of obscurity unworthy of them.

My vexation was increased by a greater freedom of spirit, and, transferring myself with pious confidence into the favor of the blessed man, I resolved to write. I shall therefore write in my own ordinary manner of speaking, and from that vast mass of words I shall try to draw out a pure and simple truth.

Nor will it be necessary for our labor to be adorned with civic elegance for the benefit of future readers. So great is the brightness of this blessed man before God and human beings that, if the polish of urban eloquence were added to it, it would seem rather to obscure his splendor than to make him brighter.

The glorious nakedness of his deeds proceeded in its own character. To have thought rightly and spoken truly about him will constitute for him the highest magnificence of renown.

Certainly, among the malicious examiners of another’s efforts, let your devotion, rising simply from the root of charity, hold me excused. For I was moved not by the profit of glory but by the cause of public usefulness: I removed the cloud from the disorderly account and restored our magnificent sun, who until today had scarcely appeared, to the eyes of readers.

But enough of this. May the Spirit of truth Himself graciously assist this work, making me concise and compact in what I say and efficient in the truth of my writing.

## HERE BEGINS THE LIFE OF SAINT ODO, ABBOT OF CLUNY

Published by Nalgodus, a Cluniac monk, a man of simple and honorable life.

[Col. 0085]

### Odo Is Obtained from Heaven by Pious Parents

[Col. 0085C]

2. Venerable Odo derived the origin of his flesh from a military family of the Franks, but he shone more brightly with the light of faith than with the splendor of his birth. His father, named Abbo, is reported to have possessed such honesty and prudence that, although pursuing a lay vocation, he lived not in a merely lay manner and was regarded among his own people as a man of counsel and foresight. Thus, winning great favor among his household, he enjoyed especially with William, duke of Aquitaine, the privilege of familiar association.

Joined to his wife by the law of marriage, although they had despaired of the gift of offspring, he preserved the good of marriage with remarkable moderation of continence. He exercised himself in honorable occupations and spent the nights at the vigils of the saints with his customary assiduity in devotion.

Thus, while keeping the night of the Lord’s Nativity sleepless and celebrating vigils for the Virgin’s childbirth, amid tears and sobs he asked, with a contrite spirit, that a son be given him. Conceiving, in great faith, hope of receiving offspring, he revived his wife’s lifeless womb in the customary manner of a husband.

The Lord made the desire of both prosper and satisfied their chaste petitions, giving them a son named Odo, an heir not of succession but of virtue. In him, indeed, the beginnings of the grace that would follow were already shining, since he who would become an instructor in sobriety and holiness was already known through prayer and continence.

### Offered to Saint Martin as a Child

3. While he was still a tiny infant lying in his cradle and being cared for by the diligence of his nurse, his father entered the room secretly one day and found him alone, without the care of a guardian. Looking around and finding no one present, he reverently took up the little child in his hands and lifted him from the cradle. Presenting him upward as though to be offered, raising the eyes of his heart and the child’s body toward heaven, he said:

“Gem of bishops, O Martin, receive this child, to be cherished in the lap of your providence.”

Having said this, he placed the child in the cradle and, as quietly as he had entered, the father went out again. That he had done this by divine rather than human inspiration is made clearer than light both by Odo’s devotion to Martin that followed and by Martin’s grace toward Odo.

### Entrusted to a Priest for Instruction. Adopted by Peter and Paul

[Col. 0087A]

4. When the infant had been weaned and removed from his nurse’s cradle, he was handed over to a priest who lived some distance away, to be brought up. The priest received the child gently and kindly, as his weaker age required, and, while instructing him, also ordered that his untutored infancy be introduced to the rudiments of letters.

The priest used a twofold diligence toward the child: in his conversations he impressed upon him the path of honorable conduct, and he poured the streams of knowledge into his tender yet receptive memory. While serving this instruction with every effort, he saw in a night vision the leaders of the Church, Peter and Paul, who demanded the child from him almost by force.

The astonished priest suffered an excess of bewilderment over that demand. As best he could, he asked what they intended to do with or to the child, and whether they were considering restoring him to his father’s household.

They answered his question briefly:

“Not to his father’s house, but to the farthest regions of the East shall we bring the child.”

The anxious priest, scarcely possessing his own spirit, begged them with fearful steadfastness not to take away the child entrusted to him. He declared that he would be brought to trial, held guilty before the father’s favor, and marked among the child’s relatives with the disgrace of betrayal if the child did not appear.

He fell at the knees of the blessed men and repeated his prayers, asking them to deign to moderate the misery of his disaster. At last, the most merciful exactors, moved by the priest’s supplication, promised, in a voice of mercy, that they would release the child, but only for a time.

After his rest, the priest awoke and, wondering at what he had seen, restored the child to his father, reporting the vision by which he had been instructed.

O discerning kindness toward an age not yet capable of discernment! The child, who did not yet possess knowledge of his election, was being drawn by the demand of holy spirits into the lot of God’s elect. This vision of the priest is not to be measured by the customary rule of dreams. In this likeness, the future expression of the truth itself was not unworthily prefigured: namely, by which agents, under whose guidance and through whose grace, that child was to be led eastward into holiness and righteousness.

### Living as a Cleric, He Is Directed by His Father toward Military Life, against God’s Will

5. When the period of childhood had passed and he was being formed toward the fuller maturity of adolescence, he devoted himself to clerical studies, destined to become a cleric. His stature was solid and well-proportioned in the balanced build of his whole body, and his appearance was developing toward such beauty that he would be praised among his foster-brothers and contemporaries [f., *coaevis*, “those of the same age”].

His carnal father, loving the flesh in him more and caring less for the spirit, looked upon the fleshly qualities of the young man, led by the impulse of nature. He noticed in his son the elegance of his body, the advance of his age, the fullness of his strength, and the firmness of his limbs.

He turned these things over in his mind and reflected upon them in thought. Wrongly foreseeing that they would all be useful for the purposes of the flesh, paternal pretense flattered him. His impatient mind, as though deliberating according to reasoned judgment, now decided that his young son should be trained in quite different arts. It was less fitting, he thought, that nature’s power, so effective and overflowing in body, should serve clerical trifles and idleness; that hands made soft and slack should weaken a spirited and courageous disposition by being given over to letters; that an outstanding youth, commended by nature for strength and made praiseworthy by virtue and grace, should be assigned to military service.

Everything that could be observed in him with the eyes, he thought, demanded a soldier’s life and altogether rejected the clerical state. Paternal folly followed its own judgment and recalled his now-grown son from the clergy. He sent him to Duke William to serve, intending that in time he should be advanced by him to military service.

His training having been changed, Odo put aside the clerical life, entered upon the ways of the world, and strengthened himself in the military career proposed to him, both in action and in appearance. To engage in hunting, to occupy himself with frequent fowling, and to carry hawks and falcons on a gloved fist had become habitual for him.

But the hand of the Lord, turning away from its deserter and renegade, withheld prosperous success from each undertaking he attempted. He was terrified in dreams, pressed by visions, and warned by revelations to reject the vanity to which he had clung and return to the true freedom of the Lord’s service.

Yet his youthful and unformed mind could not be emptied of the scent of military life with which it had once been imbued.

### Recalled by a Vision

6. After time had run its course, the solemn and holy day of the Lord’s Nativity arrived. The opportunity provided by his father’s invitation stirred Odo’s negligence, so that he himself might honor the vigils of the Virgin’s childbirth by his own watchfulness.

Father and son set out by mutual agreement and, with the humility that was fitting, devoted themselves to heavenly vigils. The awakened devotion of the clerics resounded with praise and thanksgiving to God who had been born. Then the young man of good character turned his heart toward the Virgin, whose childbirth illumined that night with divine splendors.

Before the Mother of the Lord he poured out his heart and spoke to her as though he were present in the church where she was. Before her face he disclosed his ways, confessing the sins of his youth and his ignorances. As a penitent young man, he begged from the Mother of Mercy a place of compassion and pardon.

He brought in as mediator the Angel of Great Counsel born from her and made him his advocate. He declared that he prayed and desired that the Angel should both instruct his will according to his good pleasure and direct his actions.

The night, passed amid heavenly praises, brightened into day, and clerical devotion had performed the mysteries of light according to custom. During the celebration of the solemn high Mass, when the voices of the singers repeatedly offered glory to the newborn King in the highest, the young man, touched by another spirit, sprang into the midst of the rejoicing church and began to offer the first fruits of his praise to the Son of the Virgin in a voice of freedom.

### Seized by Headache, He Becomes a Cleric

[Col. 0088C] 7. Divine vengeance immediately followed the rash presumption. Shaken by a headache, he wasted away and, pressed by sharper suffering, unwillingly bore witness that praise is not comely in the mouth of a sinner and renegade.

After a short while the pain subsided and, once calmed, seemed for a moment to have withdrawn its attack upon the presumptuous man. But after the Gospel reading had been completed, he was troubled by a similar headache and vanished from sight; he had collapsed entirely and would almost have fallen to the ground had he not been held up by those who ran to him.

Led home in the hands of those supporting him, he suffered for nearly three years from that most severe affliction of pain. Medicine procured at a price could not grant the sick man even a momentary relief. Almost continuous pain pressed upon the invalid, and his inability to be cured seemed nearly to constitute a form of despair.

Nevertheless, it had been easy to infer for what merit or fault he was being punished with such sufferings. Among those whose minds were sounder, it was said that Martin was acting and striving to reclaim the one entrusted to him, and that the whole cause of the loss was this: the imprudent young man had withdrawn himself from Martin’s service.

“Let Martin’s rightful claim be restored,” they said, “and the grace of healing will not be lacking to the sick man.”

At last, his own distress forcing him and perceiving that Martin was indignant with his son, the father had no further escape. He made satisfaction for the presumption he had committed and, having his son carried to the church in the hands of others, surrendered him from that time onward to Martin’s service and to the protection of his care.

The invalid immediately felt Martin’s favor present with him. Recovering from his affliction, he put on clerical dress and, under an outstanding teacher, obtained the dignity of a canon.

### He Lives Piously. At Last He Rejects the Poets and Virgil

8. Having been promoted to the canonry, the young man grew to such a height of spirit that he trampled the glory and pride of this life beneath the foot of humility. He chose poverty of spirit for himself and, becoming a lover of its beauty, espoused it in the faith (*fide*; the printed text reads *nive*) of marriage.

Content, according to the Apostle, with food and clothing, Odo desired nothing else. In order to live for God, he had cast his thought upon the Lord. Spending almost uninterrupted nights in prayer, he occupied the hours of the day in the study of reading.

He was led by such a great love of knowledge that he was carried away to read the empty productions of poets by the elegance of their embellished language. His intention was to read Virgil Maro’s book through in order.

On the following night, when he was relaxing his limbs into sleep, he saw in a vision a great vessel, wonderfully beautiful and attractive on the outside but seething within with innumerable serpents. Leaping out of the vessel, they surrounded him, although they did him no harm.

When the blessed man awoke and prudently considered the vision, he understood the poetic fictions in the serpents and recognized Maro’s book in the vessel: outwardly colored with civic eloquence, but inwardly befouled by the vanity of filthy meanings.

From then on he renounced Virgil and his ornaments, excluded the poets from his room, and chose to feed upon the truth of the divine Scriptures.

### He Visits the Tomb of Saint Martin at Night

9. He made a small cell for himself far from the noise of the world. There, devoting himself alone to solitary quiet and longing only for heavenly things, he was drawn by the sole desire for the Creator to the fragrance of spiritual ointments.

He pursued with the greatest eagerness and zeal the constant practice of prayer, which he had joined to himself in the highest holiness of friendship. He regularly visited the tomb of blessed Martin, which was almost two thousand paces distant from his cell, to offer nightly prayers.

Once, as the blessed man was completing that journey of prayer alone at night, he experienced the poisonous cunning of the ancient serpent in the following manner. An army of little foxes came directly toward the man of God, blocking his path. They surrounded him at the side and from behind, pressed heavily upon him, and tried to turn him aside from that virtuous journey.

When they could not overcome him, they rushed miserably into his very face, yelping something dreadful and unfamiliar. Odo recognized that the deceitful tricks of demons were being represented under the appearance of foxes and repeatedly held out the sign of the cross against those pressing upon him.

A wolf also came running to assist the struggling man, drove away those foxes by charging them, and offered the man of God the security of companionship and consolation all the way to the place of prayer.

The man of the Lord, for whom even savage beasts served, passed unmoved in the same frame of mind with which he had begun, while the vanities of filthy phantoms were overcome.

### He Leads a Rigorous Life

10. Excluding the enticing appetites of the flesh and renouncing costly clothing, he was content with the frugality that scarcely sufficed. Having placed a mat upon the bare ground, he removed the ambitious furnishings of a bed.

For three years he lay in clothing suitable to the season, an imitator of monastic religion and discipline. Having nothing in his cell that an emulous hand might steal, he guarded it with no protection against beasts.

As a lover of fasting, he cared for his flesh with such sparingness of food that half a pound of bread sustained his daily hunger. He softened the necessity of thirst and the dryness of his parched throat by drinking water in moderation.

When you considered how inhuman he was toward himself, you might have feared that he was raging only against himself. Yet what was almost miraculous in him was that neither frequent fasts in his spirit nor harsh bedding upon his limbs dissolved the fair beauty of his body: unfailing holiness preserved his limbs in the man of God unharmed and whole.

### He Listens to Remigius

11. In those days the honorable young man, inflamed with a love of learning, went to Paris, the city of the royal seat. There Remigius of Auxerre, a praiseworthy man who at that time possessed many treasures of knowledge, labored to direct and govern studies.

Studies flourished under him—studies that had already grown obsolete through time—because they were then being born for the first time from his teaching. Odo attached himself to him and for a long time had him as his teacher in the liberal arts. Through him, advancing greatly in dialectic and philosophy, especially in the works of Martianus, he rose to the summit of great learning.

### He Gives His Garment to a Freezing Man

12. One day, as he himself related under the name of another while concealing his own name, he rose early from his bed so as not to be absent from the gathering of his fellow students. The severity of winter had become so intense that even wrapped in thick skins they could scarcely moderate the harshness of the cold.

In the church atrium he found a naked poor man suffering miserably from the cold. Taking pity on the wretched man who was wasting away, he secretly removed his own tunic and clothed the freezing man.

He entered to join his fellow students, but, unable to endure the merciless cold any longer, was compelled by the harshness of the chill to return to his bed. He had already reached the first part of his room when, setting himself down in its midst, he encountered a pound of gold that had been placed there.

He understood the heavenly gift and joyfully received the weight that had been offered.

O virtue hitherto unknown to the disciplines of the schools! The philosopher-hermit grasped his God, whom he had not found in Socrates and Plato amid the golden flowers of reason and eloquence, naked in the naked poor man.

He lent to the Lord at interest and, in exchange for a worthless tunic, received back a great price in gold. Such was the custom of our God’s generosity: to grant more than had been given.

He repaid the loan that the poor man had received and added so much from grace that the scholar could both provide for himself and assist the needs of the poor.

The man of the Lord often repeated that this had happened to him under the name of another, because, fleeing human glory, he had been a true seeker of the glory that belongs to God. He was a great suppressor of his own deeds and a magnificent praiser of those of others; he attributed his own deeds to others as well, in order to receive from Him who sees in secret the reward of having avoided human favor.

Whoever wishes to know his progress in knowledge and the liberal arts should read through and reread his books; he will not deny him the distinction of a master.

### After His Studies He Lives More Uprightly

13. Returning from his studies, the man of God added to fullness of knowledge the height and progress of virtue. Crowds from the neighboring regions flocked to him in the grace of visiting him.

As they hung upon his words and reached out toward them, he instilled such an abundance of heavenly teaching that, proposing to each person what was suitable for that person, he poured forth the sweetness of God’s word abundantly from the storehouse of his divine heart.

An abundant grace was present in his words, bringing edification to his hearers and sending them back to their own affairs made more eager. A more wonderful life commended his remarkable eloquence; and, living better than he spoke, he surpassed the dignity of his speech by the more worthy discipline of his life.

### He Abbreviates the *Moralia on Job*

At that time blessed Odo was compelled by the insistence of his fellow canons to compress the *Moralia on Job*, which had been extended to excessive length, into a shorter epitome.

He replied that what they requested was beyond his strength and that he was not permitted to diminish the celebrated extent of so distinguished a work. Humble brotherly affection, and therefore true charity, excluded the little request of his brothers. A kindly answer broke the persistence of their pious importunity: they asked him continually, while he always refused those who asked.

The dispute of piety found its resolution in the following conclusion. One night, while he was occupied at the church of blessed Martin with private prayer, the weariness of the flesh compelled him to sleep. A vision followed, destined to bring the matter to an end.

He saw companies of saints descending into the same church and sitting in orderly fashion along the benches. After they had waited a little while, one of them asked what they were awaiting.

The answer was that the assembled crowd, held in suspense, was waiting for the arrival of their lord, Pope Gregory.

When venerable Odo heard this, he turned his inquisitive eyes around in every direction, hoping to see Gregory. Nearby stood a figure far more illustrious than the others, both in the elegance of his dress and in the dignity of his distinguished face.

The others rose to greet him as he approached, and, bowing, poured forth the requested blessing. The blessed pope, superior to the others and standing in a more elevated place, addressed Odo, who was prostrate on the ground:

“Rise, brother Odo,” he said. “Do not be afraid.”

The kindly voice of the one commanding dispelled the fear of the trembling man and gave him greater courage to contemplate heavenly things. Odo rose and, fixing his eyes upon the speaker’s face, marveled at the almost angelic bearing he saw in him.

The pope removed the feather that was attached to his own ear and, holding it out to Odo, said:

“Take, brother, this little feather and undertake the work assigned to you by the brothers. My book will always remain in its honor and glory, but your labor will not lack the fruit and reward of recompense.”

Warned by this vision, blessed Odo embellished the book of the *Moralia* and confined its excessive length within the abridgment of a handbook.

### He Obtains Healing for Count Fulk

[Col. 0091B]

14. The star that had been kindled could no longer remain hidden, and the holiness long enclosed within the walls of a cell shone forth through the rays of his merits even to those far away. Count Fulk of Anjou, driven headlong by the madness of unrestrained desire, stole two golden vessels from the church of blessed Martin; but, surrounded by the scourge of God, he was brought to the point of death. He ordered himself to be carried to the tomb of blessed Martin, but, unworthy of Martin’s remedy, he did not recover. A divinely inflicted affliction had nearly brought him to his final hour when the man of God entered to visit him. He rebuked him harshly in his weakness and reprimanded him as he burned in the extremity of his sufferings; then he softened his threats with a promise, assuring him that, if he returned the vessels, he would immediately be recalled from the threshold of death to the world of the living. Grace flowed from his words and compelled the wretched man, wandering between hope and fear, to return. He restored Martin’s vessels, [Col. 0091C] promising that, if he escaped that danger, he would give much more. At the blessed man’s command, the sick man was placed before Martin’s tomb; there, at once, satisfaction followed his guilt, and complete recovery followed his satisfaction. Indeed, so that the holiness of the blessed man might be made conspicuous even by the slightest excess of speech, the Lord attended his promise with its fulfillment. Immediately the Lord fulfilled what his faithful servant had pledged, so that he might preserve the dignity and glory of his servant unharmed. When the count returned home, he told his friends about the health divinely bestowed upon him and confessed that he had perceived a wonderful efficacy in Odo’s words: they had both changed a stubborn will for the better and eased the distress of his affliction. In this deed the power of both men shone forth: Martin’s merit gleamed in the count’s recovery, while the truth accompanying Odo’s promise revealed how highly Odo’s humility had been regarded by God. Nevertheless, we believe that both Martin and Odo cooperated in bringing salvation to the suffering wretch.

**Adegrinus joins him.**

[Col. 0091D]

15. The sign of holiness that had occurred in Fulk was carried by public report into almost everyone’s ears. Adegrinus, a soldier who was the most noble and eminent among the aforesaid count’s counselors, could not remain unaware of the report that had been placed on many lips. He was so moved by it that, abandoning the pomp of the princely court, he turned to the poverty of Christ. Renouncing everything that belonged to the world, he had himself tonsured before blessed Odo and, in a good exchange, laid aside at once his former mind, hair, and clothing. He put on the habit of canonical religion and, destined to share in the reward, labored alongside Christ’s soldier in the struggle. They lived together and were confined within the same narrow cell. You might have seen these practitioners of divine apprenticeship take up the weapons of poverty and continence in order to fight against spiritual wickedness. Although they did not yet shine with the perfection of monks, they already possessed the highest zeal for attaining monastic perfection.

**They withdraw to Balma.**

16. Not much time had passed when both, lifted by a greater desire for heavenly things, were drawn with more devoted affection to undertake greater works. They saw that the world lay in wickedness and, resolving to leave Babylon even bodily, aspired to the safer refuge of cenobitic life. They contemplated something higher and more divine in that life: if they pursued it earnestly and wholeheartedly, the farther they were from the world, the nearer they would be considered to the angels. Together, by agreement, they set out through Gaul, visiting houses of religion and monasteries, so that wherever the rigor of the order was greater, there they might fix the goal of their purpose. Finding no place where their foot could rest, they agreed with equal eagerness to go to Rome for this purpose, in case they might find along the way a place where their desire could reach its fulfillment. They hastened their journey, accelerated their undertaking, and [Col. 0092B] reached the monastery commonly called Balma, in Lyonnais Burgundy.

**Abbot Berno.**

17. The monastery of Balma was governed by Abbot Berno, a man who acted honorably in all things. He followed with distinction the vigor of discipline that he had received from Euticius, the founder of the place, as a worthy successor to his virtue. That place was famous: everywhere, it was commonly held that the discipline of the cenobitic order was fervent and that the inhabitants possessed mutual integrity. Received as guests, they examined the virtues of the place; with faithful eyes and truthful reports they absorbed the quality of its discipline and the reality of its order. What modesty prevented them from asking openly, they drew out through familiar inquiries. The secluded situation of the place seemed good, but the integrity of its inhabitants and the censorial rigor of its order pleased them even more than its location. After deliberation, both agreed that there they should assume the heavenly belt of service in which they would serve perpetually.

**Saint Odo and Adegrinus are vainly assailed by false brothers.**

18. The ancient enemy was grieved, envying them for what they already were and distressed by what they would become to his disgrace. He sharpened his forces, unfolded his designs, and spread his poisons; he incited certain monks, agents of his iniquity, to try to recall those neophytes from their purpose. The guests were secretly summoned and cautiously led aside; poisonous deception demanded that they listen more patiently to this supposed counsel for their salvation. They were told that prudent men ought to measure the outcome of things, lest, if they attempted something destined to have a perverse outcome, it should be shameful and disgraceful that they had begun it. What they desired was exceedingly difficult in a foreign and wooded land. They were about to assume monastic life under a barbarous and harsh man, yet, once they regretted taking it up, they would not be able to lay it aside themselves. Berno’s barbarity, they said, was so inhuman and cruel that he should be regarded as a robber, not a monk; a tyrant, not a father; a gladiator and executioner, not a corrector or nurturer. He added blows to insults and wounds to blows, and was accustomed not to attend to his sons’ progress but to satisfy himself with their punishments and deaths. They themselves would soon depart, since under him they could find neither a place of rest nor salvation.

At once the venerable Adegrinus perceived the hidden deceits in these words of cunning and recognized that the serpent’s poisons were being concealed beneath the flatteries of seduction. The holy man’s gentleness, embittered by the objections of the pretenders, he recalled by divine reasoning to the firmness of steadfastness: a house of discipline and order could not stand for long unless it were supported in its superiors and leaders by censorial rigor. If a shepherd were lax and negligent, the spirits of his subjects would be dissolved through sluggishness and carelessness. What they should pursue in Berno with favor, he said, was precisely that he could not be broken from vigor and inflexible purpose, rather than treating it as madness. They should not flee his yoke for that reason, nor avoid his commands; instead, with firm courage, wise men ought to embrace them. In this way the blessed man was satisfied, and the gentle spirit, wounded at the time by their words, was restored to itself, soothed by the abundance of their reasoning.

**How the novices conduct themselves.**

19. After entrance had been obtained through prayers, they were regularly admitted into the fellowship of the brothers; and, after making their initial profession, they were transformed into the true fullness of Christ. It was possible to see men already worn out by labor, who in due course ought to have been teachers, descending to the very beginnings of learning virtue. They were instructed by men whom they surpassed in the privileges of their merits, and they asked others to point out to them, as though they were inexperienced, the paths of virtue that they themselves had often already trodden. Those who had hitherto lived according to their own way now lived according to another’s; and they were often restrained by the commands of their elders from things they believed good and useful. They had placed men over their heads, and therefore this law [lex] of living had until then been unfamiliar to them. Everything advanced their merit; everything contributed to their glory. To those for whom lack of possessions had earned the merit of virtue, true and perfect humility enlarged their glory.

20. After receiving the monastic habit, blessed Odo remained almost exactly what he had been: the same frugality of abstinence, a similar manner of life, but an incomparable desire for purity and holiness. Patience and humility in him were beyond ordinary human measure. With unwavering stability of mind, he preserved the vigor of obedience continually and unshaken. He seemed to differ from his former self only in this: having reached the summit of perfection, he had no higher grade of profession by which he could become more worthy.

**Saint Odo directs the school.**

21. Because he excelled especially in piety and purity, his abbot thought that the boys’ school could be entrusted to Odo’s care. The duty was imposed upon him; he did not refuse it, and, undertaking the difficult care of those of tender age, he watched over the boys’ discipline. One night he led one of them out to relieve himself without a light of his own, believing that the common light illuminating the interior of the dormitory was sufficient. He seemed to have exceeded the custom of the place.
