At the following chapter he was brought forward and, by common judgment, condemned as guilty under the rule [Note: [Col. 0093D] That is, the rule and observance customarily maintained in the congregation.].

For it is almost characteristic of monks to become insolent over the smallest matters: when the voices of all had risen together, they shouted at the man, overwhelmed the innocent with words, and tore the guiltless man apart with abuse. The abbot himself pursued the public uproar with grave indignation and attacked Odo no less than the others, so that the firmness of his manly spirit, tempered by insults, might appear all the brighter. But the man of God, whose mind was founded on solid ground, endured the reproaches of the shouting men with such complete equanimity that he was neither moved by the injuries inflicted upon him nor failed to calm the agitation of those who injured him through his humility. Abbot Berno recognized in the servant of God something remarkable in patience and virtue. Foreseeing that he would become an outstanding member of the body of the Church, he thereafter held him in reverence and honor.

**Willelmus reveals his plan to found a monastery at Cluny. A privilege is granted.**

22. At that time Aquitaine was governed by Duke William, distinguished in virtue and powerful in arms; in him the splendor of military service and a remarkable likeness in faith were joined at the highest point. The devotion that occupied his manly heart overflowed toward the poor. He resolved to build a monastery for monks whose diligence would serve the gathering and support of the poor. His devotion, winged by desire and fervor, longed to burst into action. The appointed day had dawned, and Abbot Berno, invited by the duke’s letter, had presented himself at the triumphant court. The festive assembly lacked no multitude of priests, while an uncertain number of nobles and magnates filled the vastness of the palace in the sight of all.

Duke William disclosed the nature of his plan and explained the character of his deliberation in the ears of those present:

“I have conceived in my mind a bare and simple intention which, if clothed in the work of choosing and carrying it out, will not lack the rewards of life. The mystery of my plan is that I should build a monastery on my own estate, in which monks serving the Lord may purchase for themselves, in exchange for the expenses of this present time, eternal support. The Lord has for a long time opened his hand toward me and poured forth an abundance of benefits from the vessel of his goodness. Others have often received evil in exchange for good; I have more frequently, indeed almost always, received the richer portion of good. Through the Lord’s work my boundaries have been extended to the point of wonder, my territories enlarged to astonishment, and whatever I have undertaken prosperously has succeeded even more prosperously. He has given me such abundant munificence that I must now return an answer in the form of a work. It is a good order that, after care has been taken for the body and material abundance has been supplied, redemption for one’s soul should not be denied. It is good that the flesh, which is insufficient for everything, should not consume all things, but that one may rejoice to have reserved something for the consolation of one’s final need.”

The favor of the bishops and the assent of the entire court supported and elevated the piety of the prince’s plan. Duke William summoned Abbot Berno before everyone and, by solemn donation, placed in his hand the valley of Cluny, with its dependencies, which he possessed by allodial right in the territory of Mâcon. In letters of testament he also confirmed the donation already made and, in the manner of a privilege, guaranteed its complete freedom from every person, ecclesiastical or secular. The work was hastened, foundations were laid, and buildings were completed, so that he might see at least the beginnings of fulfilling, after a long time, his desire. He appointed Abbot Berno administrator of the monastery of Cluny for as long as he lived; after his death, he granted the monks free power to substitute regularly whomever they wished, provided he was suitable. The deed was made public [Col. 0094C] on the seventh day before the Ides of September at Bourges, in the presence of the bishops and magnates whom the dignity of the prince had invited to settle his affairs.

**The beginnings of the monastery under Berno, and its freedom.**

23. In the year 910 from the Lord’s Incarnation, the glorious Duke of Aquitaine built a venerable monastery for the venerable apostles Peter and Paul in the valley called Cluny. There he appointed the venerable Berno abbot. The distinguished founder himself established the complete and unbroken freedom of that monastery in its very foundations, and Gregory VII of blessed memory and Urban II confirmed it with the most extensive privileges [Note: The privileges of other pontiffs preceded these, as was stated in the preceding eulogy.].

At this, they say, certain most devout whisperers are stirred—those who, for example, accommodate themselves to episcopal losses—and who say that it is contrary to both secular and divine reasoning that pontifical churches should deprive the diocesan churches subject to them of the dignity of their own jurisdiction. To these we briefly reply with two points. They ought not to die to the good fragrance of Christ by envying the freedom of a lesser church, nor be inflated by the wind of pride so as to oppose the justice of the Roman See in a presumptuous spirit. They do not deny that it is good to provide for the peace of the good, unless they wish to be insane; and although they think perversely, they hesitate to bring forward openly the claim that the sanctions of the Apostolic See are unjust.

First, therefore, let them beware lest, if they perish because of the good of the Church, they prove themselves not good but impious. Second, let them see to it that, if they dissent from apostolic decrees, they do not become heretics by failing to agree with the justice of Rome. Its authority does not, as they chatter, diminish the principal churches; rather, it rightly arranges and orders their honor. For in the spirit of rectitude it sometimes subjects a lesser church to a greater, and sometimes raises with greater authority above another the church that had happened to be subject to it [Col. 0095A]. It has always been permitted to that See to do what is and will be permitted to it, though it was permitted to no other and will be permitted to none. All other churches are daughters, called to obey their mothers, not to command them; called to share in solicitude, not in the fullness of power.

Having refuted them with this twofold argument, the conclusion itself will not be at issue, but rather the consequence of the argument: that those who rage vainly and utter illicit whispers should henceforth keep quiet and speak no further. Now let humble prose return to the author of our freedom, our most blessed father Odo.

**The deed concerning the crumbs.**

24. It was an established custom in the church at Balma, observed almost as a right, that each of the brothers should carefully gather up the crumbs left by those reclining at table, lest the fragments of the blessing be lost through negligence. One day blessed Odo was sitting at table and was so carried away by the sweetness of reading that, being transported into a kind of ecstasy by the sound of heavenly harmony, he had forgotten to collect the crumbs placed before him according to custom [Col. 0095B]. The end of the reading recalled him from his ecstasy, and, seeing the crumbs lying before him, he was terrified. He was not permitted to collect them according to custom. Finding nothing else to do, he filled his fist with the crumbs.

After the verse had been recited [Note: [Col. 0095D] That is, the thanksgiving customarily said after the meal; Saint Benedict uses this expression in chapter 43 of the Rule.], he went to satisfy the abbot for his negligence and to present the evidence of his guilt before the assembled community. As the brothers were leaving the oratory, the saint threw himself at their feet. It was noticed that he had committed some fault. Brought into the presence of his abbot, he confessed his guilt with his body prostrate, extended his hand, and opened his fist to display the signs of his negligence. What may seem even less credible to relate: when he was about to show the crumbs, he brought forth pearls.

Those present, beside themselves when they learned the truth of what had happened, proclaimed in divine utterances that negligence had been changed into a miracle. O change wrought by the right hand of the Most High! In Odo’s hand every lowly and insignificant thing is changed into something precious, and the tiny fragments are formed into precious stones. Truly he was just and rich in grace before God: while attempting to show himself negligent and guilty, he was proved just and innocent by the testimony of a miracle. The power of his humility expiated his fault in him, cleansed his guilt, and transformed fragments of no value into wondrous pearls through an astonishing novelty.

This miracle suggests two things to us that must not be despised: the remnants of the blessing should be gathered lest they perish, and the holiness of the most blessed man should be proclaimed to succeeding ages. But the man of God, a distinguished despiser of temporal things and seeker of future ones, lest any present reward of glory follow him, transferred to another what belonged to him. Concealing his own name, he attributed to another person what was his own; and, by God’s will, the more diligently he avoided being believed the performer of the miracle, the more clearly he was regarded before everyone as the author of this deed. The abbot ordered the aforementioned pearls to be fastened into a golden fabric, lest the memory of so great a novelty be erased by some accident.

**He converts his parents to monastic life.**

[Col. 0095D]

25. The force of nature compelled him to offer his parents, whom he had left struggling amid the dangers of this world, the duty of his visitation. He sought and obtained permission, and, after receiving the blessing, departed. The Lord directed his journey and gave such efficacy to his words that, at the first encounter of their conversation, he made his father a monk and committed his mother to join the number of women religious [Note: Neither of these authors mentions the monastery in which Odo’s mother took the veil. That his father became a monk at Cluny is established from John, Book I, no. 35.]. He also took away, by a praiseworthy theft, a maiden—the daughter of one of his hosts—who could not free herself from his entreaties and tears, and committed her, dedicating the first fruits of her virginity to the Lord, to the vocation of a nun. Thus, as a minister of virtue and grace, wherever opportunity presented itself, he delighted in the advancement of religious life and the increase of chastity.

**He is ordained to the priesthood. He writes three books on the priesthood.**

26. Abbot Berno, observing in the man of God an abundance of virtues and a wealth of graces, declared him worthy of a higher rank and decided to advance him to the office of priest at the sacred altars. Though Odo resisted with all his strength and was unwilling, Berno compelled him through the final necessity of obedience. After summoning the archbishop of Besançon [Note: Rather, of Limoges, named Turpio, as was established in the preceding eulogy.] and completing the solemn consecration, he clothed him with the dignity of a priest.

The night following the day of his consecration, the man of God awoke after resting and, not even remembering his consecration, found the priestly stole wrapped around his neck. He stiffened with fear and was suffused with such deep shame that for many days he hesitated to enter the very doorway of the cloister. He also gave himself over to heavy lamentation and, sparing no tears, dissolved into weeping because something unfortunate had happened to him.

At last an opportunity arose for him to be sent to the bishop who had promoted him. Speaking to him privately, he disclosed the causes of his sorrow. Repeating Jeremiah’s denunciation of priests, he explained with remarkable eloquence that the burden of the priesthood is heavy. The bishop asked him to arrange in the form of a book what he had said there, or whatever better thoughts might occur to him. He completed the assigned work in three little books. In them his good spirit burst forth into such fullness of truth that the Church received those books with love for reading and rejoiced greatly that it had read them.

**Berno appoints his successors: Guido at Balma, Odo at Cluny.**

27. Meanwhile Abbot Berno, weakened by the burdens of advanced old age and struck down by a deadly illness, lay bedridden. He was pressed by a double affliction, illness and age [Col. 0096C]; disease and old age fought together in the same body to remove his life from the world. He summoned neighboring bishops and invited men of counsel, whose wisdom and responses might both provide for him as he was about to depart and make provision for the discipline of his sons.

With great groaning and many tears, he brought his years into public view and complained that he had uselessly spent the past of his life in negligence and torpor. He had been an abbot in name, not in merit; in office, not in virtue. He had occupied the place of governance fruitlessly and for a long time. Therefore he was liable to the torment of condemnation, because, filling the place of a shepherd as a hireling and the place of innocence as a guilty man, he had exercised the office of dignity through unworthy actions.

He said that hope of a remedy remained: while his mind was still free, he should renounce the pastoral chair, vacate the seat of authority, and give place to a better man. This was what he desired and earnestly requested: that, once the fruitless and barren man had been removed, someone more worthy and suitable should be appointed to the care of spirits and the governance of souls. Let the chaste freedom of the Church provide a guardian of its chastity, one joined to its purity by the integrity of his merits and virtues. Let the pure devotion of the sons choose for itself a father whose sobriety would produce imitation, whose teaching instruction, and whose mastery discipline. Let them appoint their own leader; let the holy establish their own teacher. Under his command, let virtue flourish, the honor of justice revive, and the discipline of the whole order grow warm again.

Nevertheless, unless his judgment differed from the common opinion, it seemed to him that the great burden of pastoral care ought to be divided between two men, so that one might rest in the other and neither be overwhelmed by the intolerable weight. Let the church of Balma, in accordance with custom, have its husband, while the rights of marriage should not be denied to the daughter, Cluny, already grown to maturity [Col. 0097A].

Each approved what had been said, and all favored it, marveling at the truth of the wise man’s counsel. The priests who were present, by their authority, and the sons, by their supplications, insisted that he himself should choose according to his judgment those whom he considered suitable and appoint one administrator for the mother and another for the daughter. He, who had better tested whether the spirits of his subjects were from God, could more truly judge who was worthy of so great an office. For it was certain to them that a man endowed with such virtue in giving counsel could not lack the spirit of wisdom in doing what he had said.

Overcome by the reverence of the priests and the prayers of his sons, the old man made his venerable nephew Guido abbot of the church of Balma. Over the monastery of Cluny he placed the holy Odo, with God working more beneficially for us, so that the house of grace and virtue, later to spread throughout the whole world, might receive in its first shepherd a foundation of holiness and a steadfastness of religious life.

**Odo’s promotion becomes material for advancement.**

[Col. 0097B]

28. Once Odo had been appointed abbot, he made that promotion material for advancement, not for decline; an occasion of glory, not of ruin. Superior to others in position, but lower through the grace of humility, he exercised the office of leadership, beloved by God because of merit and virtue rather than because of title or power. He did not attain higher ranks for the sake of honor; rather, from the summit of his authority he cast himself down to the lowest and humblest places and strove day by day to grasp better charisms. The Lord, who had directed his way in his own sight so that he might also make it wondrous in the sight of men and render his servant renowned, graciously added the working of marvelous and splendid deeds through him.

**The buildings are advanced with the help of Saint Martin, whose patronage flourished there for 200 years. What was needed for the church’s dedication is supplied.**

[Col. 0097C]

29. While blessed Odo was devoting his diligence to constructing the regular buildings, the funds for expenses ran out. The treasury of poverty was completely emptied and had nothing to place in the hands of the most generous giver. The blessed man’s mind was agitated and tortured by a twofold anxiety: he feared both dismissing the workmen without payment and interrupting the work that had begun. Yet he did not fall into distrust. Returning to familiar sources of help, he awaited the wage of blessing from the treasury of divine goodness.

The eighth day after the passing of blessed Martin was being celebrated according to ecclesiastical custom. The brothers’ devotion had completed the night Lauds, and the abbot, returning to his bed, withdrew to his little couch and fell asleep. In a dream he saw a man of dignified appearance, blooming with mature white hair and dressed in an especially pure stole. Carrying a bishop’s staff in his hand, he wore a cope. Asked respectfully who he was, he declared that he was the bishop whose eighth-day feast was being celebrated.

He also began to cast his eyes around the building and to inspect more closely how the structures that had been erected were arranged. Finally he turned to the man who was watching him from a distance and seemed to order him, on his authority, to stir up the diligence of his brothers to complete the buildings that had been begun. They should not think that funds would fail them, he said, because he himself would provide sufficient expenses for completing the work. For, returning from Rome, he would pass through Gothia and Aquitaine, from where he would send them an abundant blessing.

When he awoke, the abbot recounted the vision he had seen to the brothers, not omitting the caution he customarily observed in suppressing the name. The brothers rejoiced over Martin’s promise and, at the benevolence of his intended visitation, triumphed in still greater joy. Nor did the good promiser delay; he brought the truth corresponding to his pledge close at hand. Within a short time, approximately three thousand solidi were brought to the brothers from Gothia. The succession of the elder men of Cluny that has come down to us is also accustomed to report openly that scarcely ever thereafter did the octave of their patron pass without some blessing from Martin’s benefaction overflowing upon them. Thus, for nearly two hundred years, our excellent provider both displayed the truth of his grace toward the church of Cluny and revealed the fullness of his love toward his fosterling Odo, by whose merits we live.

The church of Cluny, now completed and finished in all its parts, sought the grace of consecration. The man of God invited a bishop-priest who was to dedicate the church. When invited, the bishop, as is customary with the wealthy, who always wish to travel more gloriously when surrounded by attendants, brought with him a large retinue. The greater influx and the insolence of the episcopal servants demanded abundant and splendid preparations. The new abbot and the uncultivated barbarism of the dry valley did not possess delicacies to set before refined men; anxiety and shame [Col. 0098B] distracted the mind of the blessed man.

Nevertheless, he cast the anchor of his hope upon the Lord, whose generosity does not allow his servants to lack anything. As the day of consecration was breaking into evening, an enormous boar emerged from the nearby forest and made its way at a full run toward the monastery. The church’s custodian, alarmed by the beast’s ferocity, withdrew inside the doorway and barred it behind him by setting the bolts in place. But the boar laid aside its ferocity and, as though softened by a domestic spirit, took up its position at the church doors. It struck the door with its foot and, standing persistently before the entrance, begged admission in its customary manner of speaking.

Meanwhile, as the bishop’s household was leaving its lodgings and hurrying to the divine offices, it encountered the boar lying at the church door. They rose together, all shouted, and, joining clubs from the neighboring houses, sentenced the beast—which had offered itself voluntarily—to death. Its flesh, prepared by the cooks’ skill, both satisfied the bishop’s delicacies and wonderfully relieved the abbot’s embarrassment.

**Saint Odo’s charity toward the poor.**

[Col. 0098C]

30. Because those who fear God lack nothing, the blessed man never lacked the means both to care for the brothers and to relieve the need of the wretched. The poverty of the afflicted was like a furnace for him, in which his inward parts were melted toward pity and compassion for their misery. Whenever either need in the poor or the possibility in his own resources seemed to call for it, he opened the lap of his generosity to those who asked. No one who was empty found him empty; rather, it was especially his concern to fill what was empty and heap up what was lacking.

He restrained the private murmurs of those who called his very great generosity indiscriminate expenditure, using words of moderation and examples from the ancients brought forward for consideration. The immeasurable breadth of his heart created opportunities and occasions for giving. Becoming all things to all people, he eagerly sought to benefit everyone in every way through solemn acts of generosity.

**On his way to Rome, he frees a demoniac.**

31. Once, for the sake of his customary prayer, the blessed man set out for Rome to visit the thresholds of the apostles. He had crossed the Alpine ridges when, among the precipices by which the descent into Italy is made, he encountered a woman who was being miserably tormented by a demon. The harmful guest had filled the mad woman’s inward parts and, as though arranging her lower limbs from a royal tribunal, cruelly used the enslaved woman subjected to him as he pleased. The blessed man pitied such great misery and, after first offering the support of prayer, shook off the captor and freed the captive woman from his tyrannical invasion.

**How, as the pope’s legate, he helped the needy.**

32. At about that time Pope Leo of the Roman Apostolic See entrusted the blessed man with the role of papal legate, so that he might labor to establish peace between Hugh, king of the Lombards, and Albert, ruler of the Roman state. When the peace envoy reached Siena, he was surrounded on every side by a multitude of poor people oppressed by lack of bread [Col. 0099A]. The man of God’s steward, who had been entrusted with the provision purse, had scarcely thirty solidi left for expenses. As though looking after the business committed to him, he left the city and withdrew from the necessity of the poor.

The needy surrounded the blessed man and, beating upon the door of his compassion with a loud cry, moved his merciful heart. The steward was summoned, but he was unable to answer because he was not there. At once the blessed man understood the imprudent caution of the dispenser, extended his hand, and signaled to the poor to follow him ahead. He also saw three men of respectable appearance who were being pressed by the common hunger but, out of shame, did not know how to beg. He accepted, at an assessed price, bowls full of berries that had been placed before them—not because he needed the berries, but because by this device he wished to help the beggars.

When the steward returned, he bestowed a stipend of blessing upon the needy. To the men mentioned above he sent back the berries together with their price. Finally, when they complained that their supplies of food had run out, he said: “We shall not fail, but shall be sufficient for everything.” One is at hand for him, as though within reach, from whose resources fainthearted spirits ought to draw life.

He had spoken, and, moving forward, encountered a priest named Peter. Receiving his offering, he both strengthened the brothers’ weak faith and supplied abundant resources for completing the journey.

**He gives his clothes to a shivering man.**

33. He had completed the business of the legation entrusted to him and was hastening his return along the maritime regions. He had reached a place called Burianum when a poor man, half dead, met him. A severe winter had set in, and among the Alps the snow had piled up into immense drifts. The poor man, lacking clothing, had no protection with which to defend himself amid the terrible dangers of mountains and snow.

The most blessed man stopped when he saw him. After sending his companions ahead on the road, he removed his own tunic, clothed the poor man, and kindly added money sufficient to meet his needs [Col. 0099C]. One of his companions, who was a very careful investigator of such matters, turned back and asked the poor man where he would find lodging that night, since there was no place to turn aside in the wilderness. He replied that he would easily reach by daylight the fortress called Pastorale.

But daylight was closing into night, and the stretch of road that the poor man had promised to complete in less than an hour had scarcely been completed by them in the entire span of the day. Neither then nor afterward, as he himself related, could John, the companion of whom we speak, remember the poor man’s appearance or face. Hence it seems most probable to me that the one who appeared was something greater than a human being.

**He repays evil with good.**

34. When the king of the Lombards had surrounded Rome with a siege, blessed Odo, who was placing himself between the two tyrants in order to preach peace, was passing near the monastery of blessed Andrew called at the Clivus Scauri [Col. 0099D], walking with his head bowed. A rustic had struck at the man of God with a stone, but, checked by the cry and intercession of those standing around, the missile aimed at his head vanished. The man of God, however, accepted money and rewarded the undeserving man in return, agreeing with Scripture that he should repay good to those who rendered evil to him.

**He does the same for a thief. The religious devotion of a brother.**
35.

At one time the blessed man Odo was staying in Rome for the sake of prayer. It seemed good to him that one of the brothers should be assigned to guard his horses, which were grazing in a meadow plain. It was night, and the men responsible for the horses had relaxed into sleep. A thief arrived, mounted a horse, and was preparing to flee, but, restrained by Odo’s merits, he could go no farther. The brother keeping watch over the horses was occupied in prayer, and preferred to lose the horse rather than interrupt his prayer or violate the silence. When daylight had appeared over the earth, the thief [Col. 0100A] was found and seized upon the horse, to be condemned by the abbot’s judgment. But when he was brought before him, the man of compassion and grace not only spared him punishment but also rewarded his laborious night watch with five solidi.

### Medicine Wrongly Extorted from the Sick

36. In the monastery of Cluny, two brothers were suffering from serious illness. By pressing their request insistently, they had extorted permission from the blessed man to take a potion. “Go,” he said, “and know that your illness cannot be cured by any medical treatment.” And so it happened: they continued to apply remedies for a long time, yet remained incurable until the end of their lives.

### A Brother Devoted to Solitude Is Rebuked

37. A certain novice brother, inflamed with initial fervor, had renounced the common studies and resolved to devote himself to compunction and tears. The man of God privately asked him [Col. 0100B] why he was abandoning the institutions of common life. The brother opened his heart and explained what goads were driving him. The elder rebuked him and declared that such a plan was closer to vanity than to justice: one should not abandon the common things for private ones, but private things ought to be subordinated to the common.

At that moment the brother lost the spirit of his compunction, so that thereafter he rejoiced in being occupied with the public observances of the church. Nevertheless, after half a year, at the prayer of the holy man, who was powerful even in spiritual matters, the brother in question confessed that he had recovered the spirit he had lost.

### He Foretells the Consecration of John as Bishop

38. John, the future bishop of the church of Nola, had twice come to Rome for consecration, but twice had suffered a serious rejection because of the opposition of his rivals. At last, confused and ashamed within himself, he went to the man of God and told him that the Roman see had rejected him twice in a failed undertaking. The man of the Lord kindly [Col. 0100C] consoled him and urged him to return to Rome a third time, promising that the grace of consecration would not be denied him. It happened as he had said, and John was appointed bishop, bearing witness that the most blessed Odo shone with the spirit of prophecy.

### He Learns from Heaven of the Death Agony of His Brothers

39. The solemn day of the Assumption of the Mother of God had dawned. The man of the Lord entered the monastery on the Aventine to pray, intending to celebrate a public Mass, and was pressed by the prayers of Abbot Baldwin to celebrate the solemn service. But the spirit of prophecy that was in him answered that he could not do so, because two of his brothers lay at the point of death and were awaiting from him the viaticum of life; a messenger was already at hand to summon him to the funeral rites of his brothers.

With these words, the messenger arrived. They hurried to Saint Paul, and the viaticum was given to those at the point of death. One of the two immediately departed; the other, preserved for life, died piously in the Lord on the following eighth day.

### He Frees His Nephew from the Normans by Prayer

[Col. 0100D]

40. The savage people of the Normans were ravaging the province of Tours. The venerable Odo had entered the region of Tours when he was told that his little nephew, not yet reborn from water and the Spirit, had been carried off with his nurse in an enemy raid. He grieved from the heart and could not endure equally that the soul of an innocent child should perish without the remedy of baptism. He devoted himself to prayer, labored with tears, and appealed to God in prayer, refusing to give his spirit rest until he had recovered the stolen innocent.

After eight days the enemy had left Tours, crossing a river with their captives. Its depth made it impossible to ford or cross by boat. The infant’s nurse conceived the courage to act. She lifted the child, broke through the middle of the enemy ranks, crossed the river almost on dry ground, and, completing in three days a journey that had taken eight days, brought the child back to the blessed man. He received him, had him regenerated in Christ, and obtained by pouring out prayer [Col. 0101A] to the Lord that the little boy should depart this life after three days.

O miracle worthy of admiration for the many new things contained in it! The power of a single prayer obtained three things together: rescue for the body, regeneration for the spirit, and, for both at once, freedom unto everlasting salvation.

### He Is Rescued from a Shipwreck

41. On one occasion the blessed Odo was crossing the Rhône by boat, a river whose entire course rushes headlong. One restless horse struck at another with its hoof, but the blow missed and struck the boat at the place from which a branch seemed to project. As they tried to shave the place of the impact more smoothly, they cut the branch off at its base. Once the knot had been torn away, the force of the river found an opening, and the boat filled with water to such a degree that one might almost have thought it a miracle that it floated rather than sank.

The man of the Lord stood unmoved, and his composure bore witness that the boat remained afloat through his merits. The boat was carried to the harbor, and, after everyone had been put ashore, Odo, the author of their salvation, was the last to leave. Once deprived [Col. 0101B] of the protection through which it had been saved, the boat sensed that the man of the Lord was gone; following the nature of the element, it disappeared and sank in an instant before the eyes of those watching. For reason demanded that, since everything else obeyed his commands, the rivers too should not fail to pay him the reverence due.

### Also from a Precipice

42. On one occasion the blessed Odo was traveling through the Apennine Alps. There such a great mass of snow had accumulated that the public roads were no longer open to those wishing to cross. When the man of the Lord entered this dreadful danger, and the whole mountain thickened after midday with gloomy darkness, he entrusted himself to the hands of the Lord.

His companions went ahead; as usual, the man of the Lord followed alone. Suddenly the horse he was riding veered aside and immediately set its feet upon a vast precipice, where he was about to be torn apart. The man of God released the reins, raised his palms to heaven, invoked the name of the Lord, and prayed for help from heaven. Nor was heavenly assistance lacking for the suppliant. [Col. 0101C]

Suddenly a branch appeared between the arms of the man of God. He leaned upon it until those going ahead, recalled by his cries, came back and lifted him unharmed from that fearful danger. The branch that had appeared immediately vanished, and the horse he had been riding was nowhere to be found.

### He Converts Robbers

43. The blessed man endured various hardships of travel for various reasons and hurried here and there as the affairs of life compelled him. It happened one day that forty robbers fell upon him. They were driven by such fury to seize spoils and tear people apart that their brutality spared no one.

Their leader, who was foremost and greatest in wickedness, fixed his eyes upon the servant of God. Admiring in him the reverence of his countenance and his constant prayer, he was moved to compunction and proved greater in mercy. Then he turned to his companions:

“I do not remember ever having seen men of this [Col. 0101D] sort. It would not turn out well for us if we attempted anything hostile against them. He is a man of great reverence and splendor, whom I see surrounded by heavenly weapons.”

When the others were in no way softened from their fury by these words and threatened to kill the holy man and drag his companions away as plunder, he said:

“It will not happen so, and not a hair of them will fall to the ground unless, after first attacking me with your swords, you spill my life together with my blood.”

He spoke, and, after dispersing his companions in every direction, he threw himself at the feet of the holy man and promised that from then on he would put an end to his crime.

44. Another robber, then moved to compunction of heart, was received as a monk by the blessed Odo after countless rejections and was assigned to guard the storeroom. After some time, struck by bodily illness, he was being led toward death. He confessed to the man of God that he had sinned during his monastic life.

With tears he declared that he had given his tunic without permission to a naked poor man and had drawn out a rope from the storeroom [Col. 0102A] and tied it around his belly. He also stated that on the preceding night a majestic lady had appeared to him in a vision. Calling herself the mother of mercy, she had announced that he would depart this life on the third following day.

The man of the Lord was astonished, thrust in his hand, tore away the rope wrapped around the man’s flesh together with the pus, and, proclaiming God wondrous in the robber, celebrated the funeral rites of the deceased brother on the third day.

### A Book Remains Untouched by the Rain

45. At Rome, near Saint Paul, the abbot’s prayers urged Odo to apply the correcting hand to a little book that Postumianus and Gallus had published concerning the Life of Saint Martin. He consented and devoted himself to the assigned work, bringing obscure passages into the light by adding glosses.

The evening synaxis recalled him from his study, and the book was left in a corner of the cloister. During the following night, rain poured down so abundantly throughout that building, yet the book endured it with such evenness that, although the margins were scarcely touched, the writing remained undamaged.

The next morning the miracle was noticed: the book was floating [Col. 0102B] in the rain yet remained untouched. Some people’s admiration broke out in favor of Martin, while others attributed the miracle to Odo’s merits. We, however, assign the sign equally to both, so that Martin’s providence preserved the codex of his own Life, while Odo’s virtue ensured that the book entrusted to him did not perish.

### Odo’s Devotion to Saint Martin

46. It is scarcely, or hardly, possible to say how devoted the holy Odo was or with what love he burned toward Martin. His whole mind and all his affection depended upon Martin’s grace. He had made him his patron and chosen him as his teacher. He proclaimed Martin in word and deed, and, adhering to him without distinction, he was often seen to perform extraordinary miracles together with him.

To enlarge Martin’s memory and plant love for him in the faithful, Odo himself composed those solemn antiphons [Col. 0102C] to be sung at the passing of Saint Martin; they are celebrated with festive rejoicing throughout nearly the whole Church.

### The Sudden Death of an Insolent Monk

47. The fame of religion, virtue, and faith that had shone wondrously in Odo spread everywhere and increased day by day. Monasteries of monks that had fallen away from the strictness of their purpose came to him, so that through him they might be formed anew in integrity of life and the order of discipline.

He had arrived with his companions at one of these monasteries entrusted to him. As Saturday evening approached, the customary rule was being prepared. One of the brothers of that place saw one of Odo’s companions washing his footwear according to the Cluniac custom. He took offense and, turning his spirit of arrogance into words of blasphemy, said—although everything there was done in silence:

“Did Benedict ever intend or command that sandals be washed?”

The brother to whom this was said gave a humble answer by a sign. But the other, cruelly enraged, began to assault the innocent man with insults and pour out curses [Col. 0102D] upon him.

At the following chapter meeting, the blessed man reproved him for this. When the monk responded still more impatiently, Odo postponed the sentence because it was Sunday, lest anyone should be saddened on a day of rejoicing. But the Lord, whom the man had not feared to provoke in his servant, did not delay his vengeance. He deprived that contemptuous man of the use of his tongue and, three days later, condemned him to a lamentable death without the remedy of confession.

### Another Case

48. Whoever presumed to do anything against Odo’s will immediately felt his offense punished by divine vengeance.

A certain brother had let blood without permission. The most blessed man took this badly, and punishment immediately followed the presumption: the vein that had been cut improperly burst so violently that it could not be healed by any medicine, until the brother breathed out his spirit.

Another man, while at his sister’s house, had ordered meat to be roasted. Driven by gluttony, he did not wait, but eagerly bit into a piece [Col. 0103A] that had been thrown onto the coals and was insufficiently cooked. Unable either to swallow the bite or spit it out, he ended his wretched life by a miserable death.

Another, with excessive greediness, attempted to eat a hen that he himself had killed and that had been set before him. Unable to swallow the morsel, he met a wretched end to his life.

### A Fishpond Obtained

49. At a place called Suppentonia, the most blessed Odo took charge of a monastery entrusted to him. He admonished the brothers that, while preserving the order of their life, they should abstain from eating meat according to the Rule.

When the brothers objected that fish could not be found among them, divine mercy, through the merits of the blessed man, formed a fishpond for them in the following manner. A small stream flowing through the valley below the monastery found no outlet. Blocked by the mountains opposing it, it gathered into a lake and became a fishpond.

In a single day mercy accomplished two notable things there: it reduced the steward’s labor and removed from the brothers the occasion for murmuring. [Col. 0103B]

### The Monastery of Fleury Reformed

50. The monastery of Fleury, where common opinion holds that Saint Benedict rests, had completely fallen away from religious observance. Virtue had failed there; justice had withdrawn from that place to such an extent that Saint Benedict himself appeared, through nocturnal visions and daytime manifestations, to show that he was abandoning those seats and moving elsewhere.

The noble man Elisiardus, wisely perceiving this, handed over to the most blessed Odo the monastery of Fleury, which had been given to him by royal authority, so that Odo might restore it to regular order.

He arrived there with a strong force of bishops and nobles. When access was denied him for three days, he finally entered alone and presented himself. By the mere appearance of humility that he displayed, he turned the turbulent madness of the monks into domestic peace and quiet. Almost all of them threw themselves at his feet and earnestly begged [Col. 0103C] the man of the Lord to preside over them and benefit them.

After arranging everything with complete propriety—for the place had indeed needed to be entirely set in order—he exercised the still-untutored minds of his sons in divine instruction.

### The Feast and Presence of Saint Benedict There; A Fast Ordered for Mass

51. It was the day on which the feast of blessed Benedict was publicly celebrated with a votive gathering and the well-attended presence of the people. A great multitude of sick people was present; burdened with different diseases and various afflictions, they had flocked there to obtain the aid of blessed Benedict.

The blessed Odo, who presided over the entire monastery with the dignity of abbot, entered to offer the solemn sacrifice. He issued an order that all who had come, and especially those weighed down by illnesses, should attend the sacrifice fasting.

When everyone had entered and stood suspended in expectation of the divine mysteries, the venerable abbot began the angelic hymn, “Glory to God in the highest.” [Col. 0103D] The doors of the church were shaken by an enormous crash, the bars were released, the defenses were thrown apart and sprang open, lamps were lit, and the afflicted and sick recovered in complete health.

Terror arose among the people; sudden amazement seized everyone. Through Odo’s interpretation they learned that the presence of blessed Benedict had been there. Such devotion and such a fervor of grace filled every heart that scarcely anyone could restrain his tears.

O what dignity! Benedict the father, winning heavenly minds to himself by so great a marvel, had promised that he would depart from that place; recalled by Odo’s grace, he gave fitting signs that he had come.

In this deed Odo’s merit shines forth more purely: by the abundance of his virtue, he both restored Benedict to favor with the sons who had rejected him and obtained heavenly relief for those oppressed by so many kinds of disease.

### Epilogue

[Col. 0104A]

52. By continuing the course of his life through these and other great works, the blessed Odo is shown, by many necessary proofs, to have been most dear to God and worthy among human beings of honor and favor.

He lived in such a way that God was his life; he performed such works that no one could doubt that God worked through him and in him. Much more would remain to be said about him, if wearisome prolixity did not prevent it. He performed more works than the order of our account contains—some he himself suppressed in order to flee glory, while human diligence omitted others lest it incur the stigma of superstition.

The few things we have said may suffice both for the glory of the blessed man and for our example.

### Odo’s Illness at Rome, His Return to Tours, His Final Words, Death and Burial, and the Year of His Death

53. The most blessed Father Odo, full of days and of life, had completed his course amid exercises of holiness and virtue and had led his temporal life to its fulfillment. The time was approaching, the day was at hand [Col. 0104B] when, taken away from exile and suffering, he would exchange earthly dwelling for his homeland, labor for rest, and misery for glory.

While he was at Rome, he was seized by a violent fever. Amid the sharp flames of its raging attacks, innocent yet guilty before God, he was tormented by the harsh afflictions of suffering. Some interpreted matters as they wished, tempering his present pain with the joy of the salvation that was to follow. He bore this kind of consolation with difficulty and announced that he would soon be dissolved.

He was touched by the memory of his Martin in the depths of his heart, whose love and favor he had almost deserved to drink in together with his mother’s milk. He resolved to visit Martin’s tomb, so that he might die for the one for whom he had lived and entrust to him the remains and ashes of the flesh to whom he had dedicated his spirit.

Then a conspicuous figure appeared in a vision, displaying the white garment of heavenly glory. It indicated that the time of his calling was at hand, but that it was being delayed by Martin’s prayers. “Take up your spirit again, sharpen your strength, and hasten your journey. When you have presented yourself before your teacher, rest and a crown will be given to your long labors.”

Signs followed [Col. 0104C] the vision, so that faith might be added to what had been seen. His illness grew milder, and the holy man recovered more in spirit than in body. He undertook the journey and arrived at Tours on the feast of blessed Martin, making the joyful day brighter by the doubled joy of the blessed bishop’s death.

He spent that day in joy and tears, and, offering himself as a living sacrifice, he longed for the hour of his departure to the Lord with desire held in suspense.

The fourth day after the feast dawned, when the returning fever grew hot and forced the man of the Lord to the point of death. He summoned the brothers and arranged the monasteries entrusted to him. He committed the monastery of Cluny to God, who had founded and built it.

> [Note: [Col. 0103D] Nearly the same account is read in his eulogy from the Cluniac chartulary. Although Aymardus seems to have been appointed in his place before Odo’s death, as will become clear in Aymardus’s eulogy.]

He retained only his own chapel for the celebration of Mass and sent everything else back to Cluny. He exhorted his sons who were attending him to advance in God. He tempered their tears and sighs with the compensation of the glory to come.

Recalling Martin in his mind, uttering his name with his mouth, and repeating it in his words, he inculcated especially this phrase:

> “You, Christ, spare the redeemed.”

At last [Col. 0104D] he extended the hand of blessing over his sons and said his final farewell to those standing by. Thus that blessed spirit, fortified with the spiritual viaticum, laid aside the burden of the body on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December and departed freely to heaven.

He was buried in the church of Saint Julian, which he himself had built from the foundations. There the Lord made clear by evident signs how great a glory Odo had received as his crown and how great a reverence he deserved among human beings.

Thus the glorious Father Odo departed in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 945, in the eighteenth year of his ordination, at the city of Tours, while the Lord Jesus Christ reigned, to whom are honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

> [Note: [Col. 0104D] We demonstrated above in his eulogy that this calculation is false, and that the year 942 should be substituted for the year 945, as Frodoard and others attest.]

# The Thirty-Five Books of the Morals on Job by Saint Odo, Second Abbot of Cluny

> [Note: [Col. 0105B] Saint Gregory’s Morals on Job, abridged by Saint Odo, second abbot of Cluny, is attested by Dom John the Italian, a Cluniac monk and author of his Life, in these words:
>
> “At that time, he was asked by the brothers who loved him to condense the Morals of blessed Pope Gregory for them into a single volume. He, however, professed that he could not possibly do this, adding that even if he possessed the ability to do it, he ought nevertheless not to do so, lest he seem to alter in any way the labor of so great a man or the value of so great a work, or to remove anything from it.
>
> “They replied that it was better to succumb beforehand than to be crushed by such great labor, [Col. 0105C] and they judged that it would be preferable to abandon it entirely and pass on to the other Scriptures than to perish beneath it as under a heavy burden. Every day there was no small dispute among them about this matter.
>
> “I know, however, that many will be indignant about this matter, and, in order to calm them, I would like to insert the following explanation. This was not done out of arrogance, but by the Lord’s arrangement, so that the lamp that had been hidden under a bushel might be placed upon a mountain.
>
> “The matter we have mentioned will nevertheless become clearer from what follows as an example. While they persisted in this request, it happened one night that Dom Odo was engaged in his customary prayer inside the church of Saint Martin. Suddenly sleep stole upon him, and in the same vision he saw a choir of saints coming down from above into that same church. First they blessed the Lord [Col. 0106B] and then they sat down in order on the benches.
>
> “After a little while, one of them stepped forward into the middle and said: ‘Why are we lingering in this place?’ The others replied that they were waiting for Pope Gregory.
>
> “Hearing this, our Father Odo, like an eager investigator, began to look around in every direction, wondering from which side he might see Gregory coming. Then, raising his eyes upward, he saw blessed Gregory as though sent from heaven, more splendid and adorned than all who had preceded him in countenance, appearance, and character.
>
> “As soon as he came, they all rose and, bowing their necks, asked for his blessing. He did not descend all the way among them, but stood above the ambo of the church. Calling our father, who was prostrate on the ground, he said: ‘Rise, Brother Odo; do not be afraid.’
>
> “When he had risen, he saw what seemed to be a pen, in the manner of a scribe’s pen, attached above Gregory’s ear. It had been drawn out and sharpened like a teacher’s instrument, and was fixed at the top. Blessed Gregory [Col. 0106C] took it and handed it to him, saying: ‘Go forward confidently, then, and complete the work that has been assigned and commanded to you. The book you compose will not be erased; mine, however, will stand forever.’
>
> “Immediately he awoke and understood what he had seen. He then took that great volume, read through it carefully, and composed in one volume the portion he judged sounder. In this way he silenced their murmuring.”]

First recovered from an old manuscript and published through the study and diligence of Dom Martin Marrier, a professed monk of the monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs in Paris, of the same order.

*(From the Lyon edition of the* Bibliotheca maxima Patrum, *vol. XVII.)*

## To the Reader

> [Col. 0105A] In preparing for publication the work on Job by our most holy prelate Odo of Cluny, second of that name, it should briefly be explained through which meanings holy Mother Church, the Catholic Church, usually reveals and teaches her meanings and conceptions to her members in more than one manner. The principal point is that, following the example of that great Gregory, he gave this writing the title *Morals*. In it, besides the moral sense, he uses the allegorical, typical, tropological, mystical, and other senses of that kind.
>
> In sacred Scripture itself, I have found eight senses specially commended in their proper places: the literal, or historical; the allegorical, or parabolic; the tropological, or etymological; the anagogical, or analogical; the typical, or exemplary; the anaphoric, or proportional; the mystical, or apocalyptic; and finally the boarcademic, or primordial. Their examples and locations follow.
>
> To make them better understood, it is also necessary to confirm them all from one passage of Scripture, with explicit testimony from the same Scripture in other passages. The passage to which all these examples must be referred is Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, chapter 4, where he says: “Now these things were spoken by allegory.”
>
> From that passage, therefore, we already have two senses explicitly expressed: first, the literal; second, the allegorical. Allegory is a perpetual and continuous parable, namely, when one thing is said and another is understood.
>
> These two senses are proved from the third chapter of John, where he says: “Search the Scriptures.” For there the literal sense is commended. The allegorical sense is proved by many passages of the prophets and evangelists, where it is said: “I will open my mouth in parables,” and, “He spoke to them only in parables.” It is therefore evident that these two senses are contained in Scripture.
>
> From the same passage the third sense is derived, namely, the tropological sense, where he says that we are children of the free woman, so that, just as Isaac was Abraham’s heir, we too may be heirs of the promise. Tropology is a kind of moral comparison, extending from the deeds of former times to our own age, so that we may act in the same way. In a single phrase, tropology is a discourse on morals.
>
> This sense is confirmed by the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 15, where he says: “Just as we have borne the image of the first man, Adam, so we must also bear the appearance of the second Adam, the new man.”
>
> From the same passage follows the anagogical sense, that is, the sense that leads back from earthly things to heavenly ones. It is contained where he says that there is an Israel of God and an Israel according to the flesh: just as the sons of that Abraham were heirs according to the flesh in obtaining the land that God had promised him, so the sons of God will be heirs of his kingdom according to the spirit, in obtaining the promise of eternal life, which is the land of the living.
>
> This sense is confirmed by the Apostle Paul in Romans 8, where he says that God’s elect will be glorified.
>
> The fifth sense is the typical sense. From this same passage, that is, in one person there is a representation of another person. It operates as follows. Just as Abraham had two sons, so God, of whom Abraham was a type, has two covenants of spiritual fellowship with human beings, from which different free persons are born. Under the covenant of the Law, slaves are born, whose type was Ishmael and his descendants, perpetually enslaved. Under the covenant of the Gospel, free persons are born, whose type was Isaac and his descendants, endowed with the freedom of piety for the kingdom of God.
>
> In this same matter another type succeeded its own type: Jacob corresponds to the elect with God, while Esau corresponds to the reprobate.
>
> This sense is confirmed by the Lord Christ when he says of John the Baptist: “If you are willing to receive it, he is Elijah.” Yet he was not Elijah except typically, for Pythagorean metempsychosis must be rejected; some Jews too were troubled by that false opinion. Elijah is therefore typical because, in the spirit and power of Elijah—that is, in the same manner as Elijah—he restored the people through his baptism in preparation for receiving the Messiah in his own time.
>
> The sixth sense follows, the anaphoric sense, which is relative to times: what the times were under Isaac and Ishmael, such are they under the Church and the Synagogue; and just as Ishmael persecuted Isaac, so the Synagogue persecutes the Church.
>
> This sense is proved by the Lord when he says: “When you see the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place,” and so forth, “as was foretold by Daniel.” By these words he shows that such times will come.
>
> The mystical sense remains. That sense is entirely divine, and in this passage too it is contained in the glory of freedom, which cannot be compared with any human or created thing. The mystical sense is the same as the ineffable sense, in which it is declared that something cannot be conceived by the human intellect, still less by the angelic. For whatever a human being can conceive in the intellect, he can also express in speech.
>
> It is proved absolutely where Isaiah says: “What God has prepared for those who love him cannot enter into the heart of man.”
>
> The final sense is the boarcademic sense, that is, the sense by which the very principles of things are compared with eternal blessedness and with the whole dispensation of salvation—as when speaking of the kingdom of God, to which all things will return, from God himself having proceeded.
>
> This sense is proved in 4 Esdras 13, where, in comparison with God’s elect, it says that gold comes from a small particle of dust and a little clod in the bowels of the earth, because God created what is most excellent very rarely. But this sense is used only among Jewish Kabbalists.
>
> Other senses are renowned among the teachers: the literal in Jerome, the allegorical in Gregory, the tropological in Ambrose, the anagogical in Augustine, the typical in Basil and Bernard, the anaphoric in Clement, successor of Peter, and the mystical in Nazianzen.

# Preface of Saint Odo

> [Col. 0107C] As I diligently devoted myself to sacred reading according to the capacity of my smallness, one day a book composed by blessed Gregory on the history of the most holy Job came into the hands of my smallness.
>
> That outstanding teacher, inspired by the divine Spirit and drinking from the heavenly fountain, poured himself like a radiant river into the History of the aforementioned man. He extended it with such eloquent speech that from it, like brilliant suns, he produced thirty-five books, which he decided to compress into six codices.
>
> But as I read through the first part of these, my mind was kindled by excessive love and so captivated by a certain sweetness that, if it could, it wished to devour the whole book with understanding. Yet because of the abundance of eloquence of the aforementioned man, I began to fail at the food by which the strong are nourished, like a little child accustomed to milk.
>
> For this wondrous teacher, enriched by divine rains [or: “enriched by divine showers”], endeavored in brilliant speech to unravel the thoughts of the Fathers that occurred to his mind in exposition. From these he condensed numerous volumes into the aforementioned history. Those who are not strangers to sacred Scripture know that the holy man Paterius extracted them by a wondrous work and restored them to their own volumes, setting aside clear volumes for himself.
>
> From these, two years earlier, I too had gathered all the sayings of the Fathers, especially those of the most holy Father Gregory, in the Book of Kings, and joined them into a single little book, which I do not think should be despised.
>
> Therefore, consulting the weakness of my understanding, the frailty of my body, and the usefulness of people like me, I rose up against myself—not swollen with the pomp of arrogance, nor puffed up with the spirit of pride, nor, as God knows, relying on empty applause—but burning with the fire of reading the aforementioned history and laboring with all my strength to retain it in memory as I had understood it. Thus I condensed this little work.
>
> In this work, as I believe, I have mixed in no discourse darkened by my own opinion. Rather, as I examined the sayings of that venerable man, I retained only those that I specified above, which had been expounded at length in various books. I did not reject the others as faulty; I keep them separately as useful. I briefly drew out the meaning, not in my own words, but in the words of the man so often mentioned above, as best I could.
>
> For the sake of brevity in reading, I also appended to each saying the mystical and moral sense as I found it, so that the wandering mind, while searching here and there for the meaning—as it often does—would not lose the understanding.
>
> I also wished to write the first letters of the historical text in red ink as a means of distinction, so that, when the history is recognized, its exposition might be more usefully gathered, lest, while the plainly expressed sense is unknown to the unlearned, it become more obscurely entangled.
>
> Therefore, I leave to those who have the ability the task of gathering numerous volumes, whose understanding and meaning are vigorous, and who are able to recognize what has been unfolded clearly as well as what has been expressed in a riddle. Let them at least allow me and people like me to meditate upon this little book, begun because of the poverty of the work.

# The Same Author’s Metrical Preface

> [Col. 0109B]
>
> When I began to traverse the shining fields of holy Gregory,
>
> his saving words indeed glittered like the stars of heaven,
>
> composing our morals—words that know how
>
> to soften minds that are excessively hard
>
> and, with brilliant light, drive away dreadful darkness.
>
> From his mouth a river flows through the crossroads of the world;
>
> practical wisdom (*Pronesiae* [*Phronesis*]) and wisdom alike shine brightly,
>
> clearer than gold, brighter than every piece of glass,
>
> surpassing all things fragrant with a honeyed taste.
>
> O mind too worthy of lament, if it withdraws itself from these
>
> honey-flowing waters, abandoning what comes from heaven
>
> and following what perishes, which has never benefited anyone.
>
> O if I had a thousand thousands of learned tongues,
>
> and my throat could utter a thousand sounds,
>
> and an airy voice could give me words of iron,
>
> so that I might sing the praise of the man whom the whole world celebrates,
>
> and compose a poem worthy of recounting even a little
>
> of so great a prelate—
>
> he who deserved to understand all the thoughts of human beings,
>
> and was able by his words to reveal depraved morals,
>
> who taught people to cut away evil impulses from the body
>
> and urged them to store peaceful morals in the mind,
>
> unlocking at once the fountain of virtues and of vices—
>
> this man turned back briefly from traversing the sacred
>
> History of Jobab, whose venerable praise shines
>
> through the crossroads of the world,
>
> whom the Church, stretched across the bright regions of the earth,
>
> praises with a resounding voice;
>
> the Judge himself, praising him with his own mouth,
>
> commanded that he be revered throughout the world.
>
> From that history he wondrously composed three times two volumes
>
> and handed them on to the Church as many distinct little books.
>
> Whether they are green meadows supported by varied grass
>
> and scattered with flowers, beautiful and fragrant to behold:
>
> here violets gleam, here lilies shine white,
>
> here the rose springs forth, or the narcissus, or nard, or amomum,
>
> while balsams joined with various perfumes give off their fragrance—
>
> these flower-bearing fields I desired to traverse,
>
> continually plucking their many kinds of flowers.
>
> With outstretched hands I strove to gather them, and already,
>
> when suddenly my feet stiffened like marble,
>
> my hands grew rigid, and my face began to grow pale.

And [his] understanding was terrified and, uttering frequent sighs, cried out in a loud voice, as though under a burden:

“Who,” he said, “could traverse these fields of human beings,  
or who could pluck all these flowers,  
so that he might go forth well supplied and rest joyfully forever?”

[Col. 0110C] “My strength is not equal to this, nor is there enough power in my breast for me, poor and insignificant, sprung from wretched stock, to gather such extraordinary treasures. Let those who are eloquent strive after these things, those who seek great matters, whose understanding is strong and whose breath is ample. Let the small vessels that are mine suffice for me, able to contain only little things, lest, seeking what is great, I lose what is modest. Therefore, leaving the great aside, I began this small work, not with a heart on stilts; the heavenly Judge knows this, he who perceives the stars. Let the lowly, therefore, not despise this, nor let the lofty despise that. Let the dull-witted hold to this, but let the discerning hold to that as well. Let the young learn that, and let the learned finally study this: the former, indeed, know how to nourish the great, while the latter knows how to feed the small; the former provide banquets, while this one knows how to offer milk.”

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0109]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0109D]

### VERSE 1. “There was a man in the land of Hus, whose name was Job.”—

For this reason the holy man’s place of habitation is mentioned, so that the excellence of his virtue may be expressed. For who does not know that Hus is the land of the Gentiles? The Gentile world, however, was bound by vices because it ignored the knowledge of its Creator. For it is not greatly praiseworthy to be good among the good, but to be good among the wicked. Hence this same man bears witness concerning himself, saying: “I was a brother to dragons and a companion of ostriches.”

We believe that these things happened according to the historical account; but let us now see how they have already been fulfilled according to allegory. For Job means “sorrowing,” while Hus means “counsellor.” Whom else does blessed Job express by his name than him of whom the prophet says [Col. 0110D]: “He himself bore our sorrows” (Isa. LIII, 4)? He inhabits the land of Hus because he reigns in the heart of the people of the Counsellor. For Paul calls Christ “the power of God and the Wisdom of God” (I Cor. I, 24). And this same Wisdom says through Solomon: “I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel, and I am present among learned thoughts” (Prov. VIII, 12).

Figuratively, then, if Job is called “sorrowing” and Hus “counsellor,” anyone instructed in the faith is not inappropriately represented by both names: he inhabits a counsellor’s mind and, sorrowing over present things, hastens toward eternal ones. When he sees how eternal is what he has lost, sound counsel teaches him to despise this temporal thing through which he is passing. Hence Solomon rightly says: “Whoever increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccl. I, 18).

It follows: “Simple and upright.”

Some are so simple that they do not know what is upright. But they abandon the innocence of true simplicity insofar as they do not rise to the virtue of uprightness. Since they do not know how to be cautious through uprightness, they cannot remain innocent through simplicity. Hence Paul admonishes the disciples, saying: “I want you to be wise in what is good, but simple concerning evil” (Rom. XVI, 19). Hence Truth says: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. X, 15).

But since justice is signified by uprightness and gentleness by simplicity, the incarnate Lord maintained simplicity together with uprightness: neither in the gentleness of mercy did he lose the strictness of justice, nor again in the strictness of justice did he lose the virtue of gentleness. Hence the prophet says to him: “Attend, prosper, and reign. You have loved justice” (Ps. XLIV, 5, 8).

Figuratively, whoever longs for the eternal homeland undoubtedly lives simply and uprightly: simple in conduct, upright in faith. But whoever, in the good deeds he performs, seeks inwardly not a reward but outwardly the favor of others is not simple. Hence a certain wise man says: “Woe to the sinner who enters the land by two ways” (Eccli. II, 14).

It follows: “Fearing God and turning away from evil.”

To fear God is to omit none of the good things that ought to be done. Hence Solomon says: “Whoever fears God neglects nothing” (Eccl. VII, 19). But because some do good while nevertheless failing to turn away from certain evils, it is rightly said after “fearing God” that he is also “turning away from evil.” For it is written: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI, 27). And James says: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all of it” (Jas. II, 10).

But this is rightly said in the voice of our Redeemer. According to the nature of his humanity, he feared God, because, in order to redeem the proud human being, he assumed a humble mind on his behalf. For it is written of him: “And the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. XI, 3). He turned away from evil—not from evil that he had committed, but from evil that he rejected when he encountered it.

The holy Church of the elect also begins the ways of its simplicity and uprightness with fear. It turns away from evil completely when, through love of God, it has begun no longer to wish to sin. But whoever does good out of fear has not entirely turned away from evil, because he sins by the very fact that he would wish to sin much, if he could [the printed reading is *multae*, perhaps *multum*, “much”]. It follows:

### VERSE 2. “And there were born to him seven sons and three daughters.”

Often the abundance of offspring leads a parent’s heart toward greed. Therefore, to show how holy blessed Job’s mind was, he is both called righteous and said to have been the father of many children.

**MYSTICALLY.** What is understood in the number seven except the fullness of perfection? From the number seven one rises to twelve. For if four is multiplied by three, or three by four, seven becomes twelve. Thus, in the seven sons is represented the order of preachers. Hence the holy apostles, who were sent to preach the Trinity in the four parts of the world, were chosen as twelve [Col. 0112A]. In the three daughters, a multitude of hearers is signified. Even if they do not remain with strong virtue through perfection of conduct, they nevertheless steadfastly hold the faith in the Trinity once they have come to know it.

The three daughters may also designate the three orders of the faithful: pastors, the continent, and the married. Hence the prophet Ezekiel declares that he heard of three men who were delivered: Noah, Daniel, and Job.

Seven sons are also born to us when, through the conception of good works by the Holy Spirit, seven virtues arise within us. Of these the prophet says: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding,” and so forth (Isa. XI, 2).

Three sisters are also born, because whatever manly understanding these virtues accomplish, they join to faith, hope, and charity. For the seven sons do not attain the perfection of the gift unless everything they do is done in faith, hope, and charity.

It follows:

### VERSE 3. “And his possessions were seven thousand sheep, and three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred she-asses, and a very great household.”

We know that greater losses stir the mind to greater sorrow. Therefore, to show how great his virtue was, it is said that he possessed much, which he lost all at once. Nothing is ever lost without sorrow unless it is possessed without love.

What, mystically, are we to understand by the seven thousand sheep except the Hebrews coming innocently from the pastures of the Law to the faith? What else is represented by the three thousand camels except the whole vice-ridden condition of the Gentiles coming to the fullness of faith, laden with the worship of idols [Col. 0112C]?

Camels may signify the life of the Samaritans, since the camel is a common animal. They are like camels in chewing the cud because they receive some of the words of the Law; and they are like camels in not dividing the hoof because they partly despise it. They also carry a heavy burden because they labor without hope of resurrection.

But because the incarnate Lord brought both the people of the Hebrews and some of the Samaritans to the faith, he possessed seven thousand sheep and three thousand camels. In Sacred Scripture, the name “camel” sometimes expresses God himself, as in the saying: “Straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel” (Matt. XXIII, 24). At other times it expresses the Gentile people. Thus Rebecca, coming to Isaac and bearing the figure of the Church, is led upon a camel’s back.

**MORALLY.** We also possess sheep when we possess harmless thoughts. We possess camels if we humbly set down whatever lofty thing we understand, bending our thoughts toward compassion for our brother’s weakness. We cannot do this without knowledge of faith in the Trinity.

Camels may also be understood as the good administration of earthly things. For since the soul does not entirely separate itself from every earthly activity, it does not divide the hoof, but it chews the cud, because, while rightly administering temporal things, it hopes for heavenly ones. When we entrust these things to the Trinity, we possess camels.

It follows: “Five hundred yoke of oxen, and so forth.”

In Sacred Scripture, the name “oxen” sometimes signifies the life of those who work well, as in the saying: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it treads out the grain” (Deut. XXV, 4; I Cor. IX, 9; I Tim. V, 18). At other times it signifies the dullness of fools, as in Solomon’s saying: “Immediately she follows him, like an ox led to the slaughter” (Prov. VII, 22).

The name “asses” sometimes designates the laziness of fools, as in Moses’ saying: “You shall not plough with an ox and an ass together” (Deut. XXII, 10). At other times it signifies the unrestrained lust of the wanton, as in the prophet’s words: “Whose flesh is like the flesh of asses” (Ezek. XXIII, 20). At other times it signifies the simplicity of the Gentiles; hence, as he proceeded toward Jerusalem, the Lord is said to have sat upon a young ass.

For what was the ox except the Jewish people, whose neck the yoke of the Law wore down? And what was the ass except the Gentile world, which any deceiver mounts, laying it beneath whatever error he wishes, like a brute animal [Col. 0113B]?

What else is signified by the number five hundred—which is completed from fifty, when seven weeks and one additional day are added—except rest? What else is expressed by ten except the fullness of perfection? Therefore, since the Jewish and Gentile peoples are gathered, on behalf of the elect, into eternal rest, it is rightly said that he possessed five hundred yoke of oxen and five hundred she-asses.

**MORALLY.** Yoke of oxen also serve our possession when harmonious virtues plough the hardness of the mind. We possess asses when we restrain wanton impulses or govern simple thoughts within us. When, from what we wisely understand or what we humbly do not know, we seek the rest of eternal peace, we hold it, as it were, within the number of the jubilee [*jubilaei*].

It follows: “And a very great household.”

Since the foolish things of the world were first gathered for the knowledge of the faith, so that afterward its clever things too might be called, the multitude and household of animals are mentioned at the end. Paul bears witness to this, saying: “Not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the strong” (I Cor. I, 26).

**MORALLY.** We possess a very large household when we restrain innumerable thoughts under the rule of the mind. For just as, when the mistress is absent, the tongues of the maidservants clamor and they neglect their duties, but when the mistress suddenly arrives, their clamoring tongues fall silent and they return to their work, so, if the reasoning faculty of the mind departs, the clamor of thoughts multiplies; but when reason returns, it restrains the tumultuous crowd of thoughts [Col. 0113D].

It follows: “And that man was great among all the Easterners.”

Who does not know that Eastern men are exceedingly rich? He was therefore great among the Easterners because he was richer even than the rich.

**MYSTICALLY.** “The East” is said of our Redeemer, as in the prophet’s words: “Behold the man; Orient is his name” (Zech. VI, 12). Therefore all who stand in faith upon this East are rightly called Easterners. But because all other men are merely human, while he is the East, God and man, it is rightly said: “He was great among all the Easterners.”

**MORALLY.** We become great among all the Easterners when, with the spirits who cling to the eastern light, we join ourselves, as far as we are able, through the rays of our discernment, the dense mist of carnal corruption having been pressed down. As Paul says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20).

It follows:

### VERSE 4. “And his sons went and held a banquet in their houses.”

O immeasurable praise of paternal instruction! The father is called rich, and the sons are harmonious.

**MYSTICALLY.** The sons went through the houses to hold banquets when the apostolic preachers, in different regions of the world, served the banquets of the virtues to their hearers as to those who were eating. Hence it is said to these same sons, while the peoples were hungry: “Give them something to eat yourselves” (Matt. XIV, 10).

For if the obscurity of ignorance is undoubtedly night for the heart, understanding is rightly called day, as Paul says: “One person judges one day to be above another; another judges every day alike” (Rom. XIV, 5). Thus each son provides a banquet on his own day, because every holy preacher, according to the measure of the understanding granted him, feeds the minds of his hearers with the banquets of truth.

Paul did this when he said: “They will be happier if they remain as they are, according to my counsel” (I Cor. VII, 40).
