The sons call their sisters to the banquet because the holy apostles preach the joys of heavenly refreshment to their weaker hearers, feeding minds hungry for the nourishment of truth with the banquets of divine speech. For Sacred Scripture is sometimes food, as in the prophet’s words: “The little children asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lam. IV, 4). At other times it is drink, as in the prophet’s words: “All who thirst, come to the waters” (Isa. LV, 1). And in the Gospel: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink” (John VII, 37).

**MORALLY.** The sons hold a banquet throughout the houses when the individual virtues feed the mind according to their particular gift.

“On his own day.” The day of each son is the illumination of each virtue. Wisdom holds a banquet on its day because it fills the mind with hope and certainty concerning eternal things. Understanding does so when it penetrates what has been heard and enlightens the darkness of the heart. Counsel holds a banquet when it prevents us from acting rashly. Fortitude does so when it fears no adversity and sets out the food of confidence. Knowledge holds a banquet because it overcomes the fast of ignorance. Piety does so when it fills the inward parts of the heart with works of mercy. Fear prepares a banquet on its day when it restrains the mind from becoming proud of present things and strengthens it with the food of hope concerning the future.

The sons also call their sisters to the banquet when our virtues bring hope, faith, and charity into everything they do, so that faith, hope, and charity may rejoice in the good work administered by each virtue.

It follows:

### VERSE 5. “And when the days of the banquet had gone around, and so forth.”

When he says, “He would send and sanctify them,” it is clearly shown what discipline he exercised toward them while present, and how he did not fail them in solicitude while absent. The holy man knew that banquets could scarcely be celebrated without fault. For when the body is relaxed in the pleasure of eating, the heart is loosened into empty delight. Hence it is written: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. XXXII, 6).

The fact that blessed Job offers sacrifice on the eighth day celebrates the mystery of the resurrection [Col. 0115A].

**MYSTICALLY.** The days of the banquet go around when the ministries of preaching are carried out. After the banquets had been completed, Job offered a holocaust for his sons because, on behalf of the apostles returning from preaching, the Redeemer implored the Father. Job sends and sanctifies the sons because, through the Holy Spirit who proceeds from him, our Redeemer cleansed from the hearts of the disciples whatever guilt they might have had. He offers holocausts at dawn because by his intercession he enlightened the darkness of the human mind.

**MORALLY.** When the cycle of the days of the banquet is completed, to send for the sons and sanctify them is, after perceiving the virtues, to direct the intention of the heart, lest things that are evil be judged good. We rise at dawn when, suffused with the light of compunction, we abandon the night of our humanity [Col. 0115B] and open the eyes of our mind to the rays of the true light. We offer a holocaust for each son when, for each virtue, we sacrifice to the Lord the offerings of our prayer.

A holocaust is called something wholly burned. To offer a holocaust is to set the whole mind ablaze with the fire of compunction.

It follows: “He said, ‘Perhaps my sons have sinned,’ and so forth.”

He had taught them to be perfect in deed and speech, yet he feared for them only in thought. So that we may not rashly judge the hearts of others, we recognize this in the words of the holy man, who did not say, “Perhaps they have blessed,” but “Perhaps they have blessed” with uncertainty. Hence Paul says: “Do not judge before the proper time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring the hidden things of darkness to light and disclose the counsels of hearts” (I Cor. IV, 5).

**MYSTICALLY.** To bless God—that is, to curse him—is to claim glory for oneself from his gift. Hence, when the apostles returned from preaching, the Lord washed their feet, because often, in a good work, the dust of an evil thought is taken up. In saying “perhaps,” he takes account of our ignorance, as in the saying: “When the Son of Man comes, do you suppose he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke XVIII, 8).

**MORALLY.** The sons curse God in their hearts when our outwardly upright works arise from thoughts that are not upright, when our minds judge that they possess from themselves what they are, and when they seek their own praise from good works.

It follows: “Thus Job did all his days.”

For it is written: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22). In the sacrifice, holy action is expressed; in “all his days,” perseverance in holy action is expressed.

**MYSTICALLY.** Without interruption our Redeemer offers a holocaust, because without ceasing he displays to the Father his incarnation on our behalf, which is the cleansing of our offering.

**MORALLY.** Good is done in vain if it is abandoned before the end of life. Hence it is said to the reprobate: “Woe to those who have lost endurance” (Eccli. II, 16). And Truth says to the elect: “You are those who have remained with me in my trials” (Luke XXII, 28).

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0115]

[Col. 0115C] ### VERSE 6. “And when one day the sons of God had come to stand before the Lord, Satan also was present among them.”

Divine Scripture expresses the qualities of things and the limits of causes. Sometimes it does so from the position of a place, as when Israel could not hear the words of God on the mountain, since afterward it would not believe (Exod. XX, 19). Sometimes from the position of the body, as when Stephen saw Jesus standing (Acts VII, 55); for standing is characteristic of one who fights. Sometimes from the quality of the air, as in the Gospel: “It was winter” (John X, 22), signifying that no one believed. Sometimes from the quality of time, as when Judas went out at night to betray the Lord.

Therefore, because blessed Job’s temptation is led toward victory, it is said to have begun “on a day.” The sons of God are called the elect angels, who come outward to us through spiritual presence and yet are not deprived of the joys of inward contemplation. Thus they come, as Paul says: “Are they not all ministering spirits sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Heb. I, 14). Yet they do not depart from God, as God says: “Their angels always see the face of my Father” (Matt. XVIII, 10).

Satan came among those from whom he had departed through pride because, although he lost blessedness, he did not lose a nature like theirs. For in the same way that God beholds all spiritual beings, he also saw him, as in the saying: “The eyes of the Lord observe the good and the evil” (Prov. XV, 3). He was seen, but did not see, as a blind man is bathed in the sun’s rays while he himself does not see the light.

God says to him: “From where have you come?” God’s not knowing is the rejection of the wicked, as in the saying: “I do not know you” (Matt. XXV, 12).

**ALLEGORICALLY.** Satan is said to have come on a certain day—not because the passage of time, with the alternation of day and night, varies for God, but because Sacred Scripture, speaking through temporal events, uses temporal expressions. The unclean spirit is penetrated by the power of this justice, because the hearts of the clean spirits are filled with it. The Lord saw Satan on the day because, in the incarnation of his Wisdom, he condemned his ways. To say, “From where have you come?” is to expose the ambushes of the hidden enemy.

The sons of God are all the elect who have been gathered by God for the calling of the eternal homeland and who inwardly stand in the presence of the divinity.

**MORALLY.** He is present even among the sons of God because the ancient enemy often subtly attaches himself to our good thoughts, which are sown in our heart through the operation of the Holy Spirit’s coming, so that he may disturb what has been well conceived. Thus, to say to him, “From where have you come?” is to disclose his ambushes to us.

It follows:

### VERSE 7. “I have gone around the earth and walked through it.”

Satan therefore goes around the earth in labor because he disdained to stand in repose at the summit of heaven. He goes around it not flying over it but walking through it, because he is weighed down in the depths by the burden of sin.

**ALLEGORICALLY.** Satan goes around the earth because, from Adam until the Lord’s coming, he dragged all the nations of the Gentiles after him. He went around and walked through it because he impressed the traces of his iniquity upon the hearts of the nations.

**FIGURATIVELY.** For Satan to go around the earth is to search out carnal hearts and investigate where he might find an opportunity for accusation. He goes around by circumventing, so that he may take away good and implant evil.

It follows:

### VERSE 8. “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth, a simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil?”

We must examine what kind of speech this is. For neither the Lord, who is the supreme and unbounded Spirit, nor Satan, who is clothed in no bodily nature, speaks in the human manner of one drawing an airy breath in through the belly. Rather, God speaks to the angels when they read, in the very contemplation of truth, whatever they ought to do. What is inspired to those who see is spoken, as it were, to those who hear.

The voice of the angels is the very wonder of inward contemplation in the praise of the Creator—the miracles of divine power. The words of souls addressed to God are their desires. For if desire were not speech, the prophet would not say: “Your ear has heard the desire of their heart” (Ps. X, 16). God speaks to souls when he confirms them in the certainty of retribution.

God’s speaking to the devil is to rebuke his ways and activities through the judgment of hidden strictness. Thus he says here: “From where have you come?” The devil’s responding to him means that he can conceal nothing from the omnipotent majesty. Hence he says here: “I have gone around the earth and walked through it.”

God speaks to the devil in four ways, and the devil to God in three. The devil indicates his ways when he says: “I have gone around the earth.” He accuses the innocence of the elect when he says: “Does Job fear God for nothing?” He asks that Job be tested when he says: “Stretch out your hand,” and so forth.

God’s saying, “From where have you come?” is his rebuke. God’s saying, “Have you considered my servant Job?” is his making such elect people that the devil can envy them. God’s saying, “Behold, all that he has is in your hand,” is his releasing him for the testing of the faithful. God’s saying, “But do not stretch out your hand against him,” is his restraining him from excessive temptation.

Thus the devil undertook a contest not against Job but against God. Blessed Job was placed in the middle as the material of the contest. And if we say that Job sinned in his speeches amid the scourges, we say that God was defeated in his promise.

**ALLEGORICALLY.** Job means “sorrowing.” He is truly called sorrowing figuratively because, as the prophet bears witness, he is said to bear our sorrows. There is none like him on earth. Although every adopted son may advance toward receiving divinity, he nevertheless did not receive this in such a way as to be God by nature; he is called a servant, according to the Apostle’s words: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” and so forth (Phil. II, 7).

Coming among human beings as the mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus was simple in offering an example of life to human beings; upright in refusing to spare evil spirits; fearing God in overcoming pride; and turning away from evil in cleansing the impurity of life in his elect.

Of him Isaiah says: “And the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. II, 3). And Peter says: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (I Pet. I, 22).

God’s figurative speech to Satan—“Have you considered my servant Job?”—marvelously displays the only-begotten Son to him in the form of a servant.

**FIGURATIVELY.** “Have you considered my servant Job?” The divine inspiration strengthens him against the enemy; God praises him, as it were, in Satan’s hearing. To praise him is both to grant good things beforehand and to preserve them after granting them.

### VERSE 10. “Have you not guarded him, his house, and all his substance on every side? You have blessed the works of his hands, and his possessions have increased in the land?”

It is as though he openly said: “Since he receives so many good things on earth, what wonder is it if he conducts himself innocently in return for them? He would truly be innocent if he remained good amid adversity.”

**ALLEGORICALLY.** Since the ancient enemy saw the Redeemer as capable of suffering, he believed that he was not God by birth but guarded by the grace of God. Hence he says: “Does Job fear God for nothing?” He says that God has surrounded him and his house with a wall because, by tempting him, he could not penetrate his conscience. He says that his substance was enclosed because he did not dare to invade the Redeemer’s elect. He complains that God blessed the works of his hands and caused his possessions to increase on earth because, while the apostles preached his faith, the innocence of human beings was multiplied. His possessions are said to increase while the number of the faithful grows daily through the labor of the preachers. Thus, for the devil to say these things is to suffer inwardly withering grief over them.

**FIGURATIVELY.** “Does Job fear God for nothing?” It is as though he said: “Why do you praise one whom you strengthen by protecting him? A man would be worthy of your praise, despite my contempt, if he stood by his own strength.”

It follows:

### VERSE 11. “But stretch out your hand a little, touch all that he possesses, and so forth.”

When Satan desires to tempt the holy man, yet says to the Lord that he should stretch out his hand, it must be noted that he does not attribute to himself the power to strike. Hence the legion said in the Gospel: “If you cast us out, send us into the swine” (Mark V, 12).

He asks that the hand be stretched out a little when he seeks the destruction of external things, because he does not think he has done much unless he wounds the soul, so that by striking it he may recall it from the heavenly homeland.

“His face” signifies the regard of his grace. “Unless he blesses you to your face” means: “Take away the things you have given. For if he loses what he has received, he will not seek the regard of your grace once temporal things have been removed. If he does not possess the things in which he delights, he will disregard even your favor by cursing you.”

**ALLEGORICALLY.** Our Redeemer, whom Satan believed to have been guarded by God’s grace in a time of tranquility, he thought capable of sinning through suffering. It is as though he said: “When questioned through afflictions, the one who is regarded as God in miracles is recognized as a human being and a sinner.”

**FIGURATIVELY.** Often, while we produce the fruits of virtue abundantly and flourish in continual prosperity, the mind is raised somewhat, so that it thinks the good things it possesses arise from itself. The enemy desires to touch these goods, but God grants them only benevolently. By a wondrous dispensation of mercy, it comes about that the place from which the wicked enemy tests the heart in order to destroy it becomes the place from which the merciful Creator instructs it so that it may live. Thus, having recognized its weakness, the soul may be established more firmly in hope of divine help.

It follows:

### VERSE 12. “Behold, all that he has is in your hand, and so forth.”

God’s dispensation of mercy must be considered: how he permits and restrains our enemy, releases him and reins him in. He exposes the substance but protects the body, intending afterward to hand it over to the persecutor. He does not release the enemy against everything at once, lest, striking from every side, he break the citizen. Hence Paul says: “God is faithful; he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (I Cor. X, 13).

It may also be understood in another way: the Lord wished to divide the combats for his warrior, so that the enemy, once defeated, might return again, and then the Lord might grant the warrior another victory over him. Thus the servant would be the more wondrous a victor because the defeated enemy prepared to fight him again.

**ALLEGORICALLY.** Satan’s hand is understood not as power but as temptation. Our Redeemer, therefore, first lost Judea, which had formerly been his substance, through unbelief; afterward his flesh was fastened to the gibbet of the cross. Thus he first lost what he had possessed and afterward endured the wickedness of the adversary in himself.

**FIGURATIVELY.** It is as though he said: “I grant that the goods of each of the elect be tested externally, but you yourself know that I preserve that person steadfastly in the root of his mind.”

It follows: “And Satan went out from the presence of the Lord.”

How does one go out from him who is everywhere? Hence he says: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXIII, 14). But as long as Satan, constrained by the power of the divine majesty, was unable to exercise the desire of his malice, he stood, as it were, before the face of the Lord. He went out from the face of the Lord because, once divinely released from the confinement of inward restraint, he came to the accomplishment of his desire.

**MYSTICALLY.** As above, he went out from the face of the Lord because he reached the fulfillment of his own desires.

**MORALLY.** He went out from the face of the Lord because, since he is by no means permitted to prevail as far as the heart’s fulfillment, he is excluded from the interior and occupies himself externally. Even if he often disturbs the powers of the mind, he is nevertheless outside for this very reason: with God assisting, he does not wound the hearts of the good unto destruction.

It follows:

### VERSE 13. “Now, when his sons and daughters were eating and drinking on a certain day, and so forth.”

The devil chose that moment for his work of temptation when he found blessed Job’s children at a banquet. This is disclosed to us by God’s providence because the joy of fellowship foretells tribulation. The oxen are reported to be ploughing, so that the remembered fruit of labor might increase the cause of sorrow [Col. 0120A]. The measure of the groans was also increased by the succession of the messengers.

**TYPICALLY.** We said that the sons and daughters of blessed Job represented either the order of the apostles or the multitude of all the faithful. But who should be understood as the elder son of the Lord except the Jewish people, generated by the teaching of the Law once given to it? The younger is the Gentile people, gathered at the end of the world.

The sons feast in the house of their firstborn brother because the holy apostles—who had been told, “Do not go on the road of the Gentiles” (Matt. X, 5)—were still feeding upon the banquets of Sacred Scripture within the gathering of the Jewish people alone. Thus it is said: “The sons of the bridegroom will not fast while the bridegroom is with them,” and so forth (Matt. IX, 15).

### VERSE 14. “The oxen were ploughing, and the she-asses were grazing.”

What else do we understand by oxen except those who work well? What else by she-asses except certain people who live simply? They rightly graze beside the oxen because the slower, joined to the prudent, are nourished by their understanding, trusting their own good qualities to them through brotherly charity.

The Sabaeans are interpreted as “captors.” By the name of captors are designated unclean spirits, who lead into unbelieving captivity those whom they subject to themselves. They also strike the children with the sword because they wound with the darts of their temptation those whom youthful steadfastness does not yet preserve as free or strong.

The boy who announces the news while escaping is the prophetic word, which, when all the evils it foretold come to pass, returns to the Lord as though unharmed.

**FIGURATIVELY.** In the heart of the elect, wisdom is born as the firstborn offspring of the good things that follow. This is our faith, as the prophet says: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. VII, 9). Thus the sons feast in the house of their firstborn brother when our virtues are filled with the nourishment of Sacred Scripture in the dwelling place of faith.

What else are the oxen ploughing except our weightier thoughts? What else do we understand by the she-asses grazing except the simple impulses of the heart? But often the crafty enemy corrupts weightier thoughts through the pleasure of lust; and, though he does not destroy the simple impulses of the heart, he harms them by creeping in through the praise of subtlety.

Alternatively: the oxen ploughing are thoughts of charity, by which we try through preaching to benefit others. The she-asses can signify patience and gentleness. But the evil one removes the oxen ploughing when he plunges us into sluggishness, so that we no longer wish to benefit others, even when we are free from our own concerns; and when he disturbs the endurance of our thoughts even for a moment, he rejoices as though he had taken the she-asses away from the field of the heart.

While the others perish, one returns to the house when, though the impulses have been disturbed in temptation, discernment runs back to the conscience, so that what it considers itself to have lost when the mind was caught off guard by sudden assaults, it may recover through the diligence of compunction.

It follows:

**VERSE 16.** While he was still speaking, another came and said: “The fire of God fell from heaven and struck the sheep,” and so forth. [Col. 0121A]—It should be observed how cunningly he says, “the fire of God.” It is as though he were saying: “You are suffering the punishment of the one whom you wished to appease with so many sacrifices; you endure the anger of him whom you served daily with toil.”

**TYPICALLY.** In this passage we may appropriately understand heaven as the priests, or the Pharisees, or the teachers of the Law, as Moses says: “Attend, O heaven, and I will speak.” They appeared to shine above others by reason of their heavenly office. But because they were exceedingly stirred against our Redeemer, it was as though fire fell from heaven, when the flame of envy blazed forth against the unlearned people even from those who were thought to teach the truth.

What else are the sheep and the children than innocent people, if we understand them as still weak? Because they feared enduring the opposition of the Pharisees and rulers, they were consumed by the burning of unbelief. The flame of envy fell from the hearts of the shepherds of the sheep and burned whatever good was arising among the peoples. One escaped, because, when the aforesaid cause of malice was fulfilled, the prophetic word escaped the destruction of deception—the word that says: “And now fire consumes the adversaries” (John XIX, 6). [Col. 0121B]

**MORALLY.** What is signified by the sheep except innocence of thought or the purity of good hearts? And because, from the powers of the air—which is called heaven—a flame of spite rushes against the purity of our thoughts, fire comes from heaven and is called the fire of God, because, although it is not generated by God’s action, it is nevertheless generated by God’s permission. But one escapes when discernment does not succumb amid disturbed thoughts, so that it may report the losses it has suffered to the mind and, as it were, summon its lord to lamentation. It follows:

**VERSE 17.** “The Chaldeans formed three bands.”—Behold, once again he announces that bands of Chaldeans have rushed upon him, lest he should have felt any less sorrow from human adversity. [Col. 0121C]

**TYPICALLY.** “Chaldeans” is interpreted as “ferocious”; by this name the authors of the Lord’s persecution are signified, those who said: “Crucify, crucify” (Luke XXIII, 21). The three bands are the Pharisees, the Herodians, and the Sadducees. They seize the camels when, by persuasion, they drag the Samaritans, certain people from Judaea, and the twisted minds of the weak toward destruction. They also strike the boys with the sword, because if any among the people had already become capable of using reason, they opposed them—not by the strength of reason, but by the authority of power. The boy who escaped from them and reports the event flees because, while they are committing their wicked deeds, the prophetic word grows strong after abandoning them, saying: “And those who held the law did not know me” (Jer. II, 8).

**TROPOLOGICALLY.** By the camels, which possess something clean because they ruminate, but something unclean because they do not divide the hoof, we said above that good administrations of temporal affairs are understood. [Col. 0121D] The more widely our concern is dispersed among these things, the more abundantly the enemy lies in wait for us. Everyone who presides over the administration of earthly matters lies more broadly exposed to the darts of the hidden enemy.

It is, as it were, to make three bands against the camels when the efforts devoted to administering earthly affairs are laid waste—now by an unlawful action, now by excessive speech, now by disordered thought. But one who has fled returns because the reasoning of discernment comes before the eyes of our mind, and the soul, watchful over itself, understands what it has inwardly lost through the sudden impulse of temptation. It follows:

**VERSE 18.** “He was speaking, and behold, another entered and said: ‘While your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine,’” and so forth. [Col. 0122A]—Satan secretly suggests that the elements themselves were moved against him by the one who permitted them to be moved. Although, once he had received power from the Lord, he was also able to shake the elements for the purposes of his wickedness.

It should be noted that he brought death upon the children at the end, so that the father would not consider the loss of insignificant possessions if he heard that he had already been deprived of them. For although banquets can scarcely take place without fault, far be it from us to suppose that the sons of so great a man devoted themselves to gorging their bellies through banquets. Thus he overwhelmed the sons on the day of their eldest brother, because the ancient enemy seeks, through the negligence of their elders, an opening for overthrow in the death of the younger.

**MYSTICALLY.** The sons and daughters signify the apostles who preach and the peoples, who are said to be feasting in the house of their eldest brother because they were still feeding upon the delights of sacred preaching within the habitation of the Jewish people. [Col. 0122B] The region of the desert is the heart of unbelievers; when the Creator abandons it, no inhabitant cultivates it. A violent wind rushes in from the region of the desert because, in the passion of our Redeemer, a powerful temptation against his faithful came from the hearts of the Jews.

Or certainly, the region of the desert is the multitude of unclean spirits, who stirred the hearts of the persecutors. The house is the synagogue. Its four corners are the four orders of rulers: priests and scribes, the elders of the people, and the Pharisees. From the unclean spirits the wind—that is, temptation—rushed in and stirred the minds of the four orders with the malice of persecution.

The house overwhelmed the children because, when Judaea fell through unbelief and persecution of the Lord, it buried the faith of the apostles beneath the fear of despair. [Col. 0122C] One escaped because the prophetic word that had announced these things is shown to have grown strong, saying: “My beloved has committed many crimes in my house” (Jer. XI, 15); and again: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Matt. XXVI, 31).

**MORALLY.** The house is our conscience. Its four corners are the four virtues: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice. The region of the desert is the unclean spirits who have been abandoned by God.

Thus a violent wind shakes the four corners of the house because a strong temptation assails the four virtues through hidden movements. When the corners have been shaken, the house collapses, because conscience is thrown into confusion when the virtues are assailed. Within these four corners of the house the children feast, because within the secret places of the mind the heart is principally raised by these four virtues to the summit of perfect uprightness, and the remaining virtues, like offspring of the heart, nourish one another. [Col. 0122D]

Once the house has been overturned, the children die because, when conscience is disturbed by temptation, the virtues generated in the heart are crushed. With them the three sisters also fall, because sometimes charity is disturbed in the heart by afflictions, hope is shaken by fear, and faith is assaulted by questions. One escapes because discernment of mind remains unharmed even amid temptations, so that the sorrowful spirit may preserve through repentance the strength that it had almost begun to lose. It follows:

[Col. 0123A] **VERSE 20.** “Then Job arose, tore his garments, and, falling upon the ground with his head shorn, worshiped.”—Some people consider it the mark of great steadfastness and philosophy if, corrected by the harshness of discipline, they do not feel the blows of scourges and pains. Others, however, feel the lashes of blows so excessively that, shaken by immoderate grief, they even slip into an outburst of speech.

Of the former the prophet says: “You struck them, and they did not grieve; you crushed them, and they refused to accept correction” (Jer. V, 3). Of the latter the Psalmist says: “They will not endure in miseries” (Ps. CXXXIX, 11). Blessed Job, therefore, because he held to the rule of true philosophy, preserved himself wonderfully against both extremes. By tearing his garments, he felt the pain of the scourge; by worshiping, he did not rebel against the judgment of the one who scourged him. [Col. 0123B]

There are two commandments of charity: love of God and love of neighbor. To fulfill love of neighbor, he offered mourning; in order not to abandon love of God, he completed prayer amid his groans.

It was the custom of the ancients that whoever preserved his hair by letting it grow should cut it off in a time of affliction, while whoever cut his hair in a time of tranquility should let it grow during affliction. Blessed Job is therefore shown to have preserved his hair in a time of tranquility, while he is remembered to have shorn his head in grief.

**MYSTICALLY.** The Lord’s rising signifies his showing that he will not abandon sinners when he judges with strict judgment. He arose because he demonstrated that he would abandon his persecutors in judgment.

What else is the Lord’s garment than the synagogue? For just as he is now clothed by those who love him, as Paul says: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. V, 27), [Col. 0123C] so, when Judaea, as the prophets proclaimed, believed that he would become incarnate, it was nevertheless a garment by clinging to him.

But he tore the garment when in Judaea he lifted some from unbelief and left others in unbelief. It was a torn garment of which the Evangelist says: “Some were saying, ‘He is good’; others said, ‘No, but he deceives the crowds’” (John VII, 12).

What is signified by the cut hair except the subtlety of the sacraments? What by the head except the summit of the priesthood? Hence it is said to the prophet Ezekiel: “You, son of man, take for yourself a sharp sword that shaves the hair; take it and draw it over your head and your beard” (Ezek. V, 1).

What is expressed here by earth except sinful humanity? For it was said to the first man: “You are earth, and into earth you will go” (Gen. III, 1). [Col. 0123D] Therefore, by the name earth, sinful gentile humanity is signified.

Our Mediator therefore fell upon the earth as though with his head shorn, because he removed the sacraments of the Law from the priesthood of the synagogue and, abandoning it, came to the knowledge of the gentiles. The Lord is said to fall, as in the passage: “The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it fell upon Israel” (Isa. IX, 8).

It is rightly said that, as he fell, he worshiped, because, when he assumed the humility of the flesh, he infused into those who believe in him the vows of humility. He did what he taught should be done, just as it is also said of his Spirit: “He pleads for us with ineffable groanings” (Rom. VIII, 26). He also entreated the Father for us before his passion.

**MORALLY.** After hearing of adversities, to rise is to prepare the mind more firmly for combat after experiencing temptations. [Col. 0124A] We tear our garments when, by discernment, we review our deeds. That our deeds cover us before God like garments is stated by the angel: “Blessed is the one who watches and keeps his garments, lest he walk naked” (Rev. XVI, 15).

What do we understand morally by hair except the thoughts that flow abundantly through the mind? What is signified by the head except the mind itself? To shave the head, therefore, is to cut off superfluous thoughts from the mind. And he falls upon the earth with his head shorn: he humbly recognizes, after restraining the thoughts of his presumption, how weak he is in himself.

Thus the head is shorn after adversities are heard, when, as temptations rush in violently, the mind is stripped of the thoughts of its presumption. [Col. 0124B] It should be noted that, falling upon the earth, he worshiped. For the one who offers true prayer to God is the person who humbly sees that he himself is dust. It follows:

**VERSE 21.** “Naked I came forth from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there.”—Since the earth has given birth to all of us, we rightly call it our mother, as it is written: “A grievous yoke is upon the sons of Adam, from the day of their going forth from their mother’s womb until the day of their burial in the mother of all” (Ecclus. XL, 1). It is as though he were saying: “The earth brought me here naked when I entered; naked the earth will receive me when I depart.”

**MYSTICALLY.** The mother of the Redeemer according to the flesh was the synagogue, from which he came to us visibly through the body. But he came forth naked from his mother’s womb because, proceeding in the flesh from the synagogue, he came visibly to the gentiles. [Col. 0124C]

This was well signified by Joseph, who fled after leaving behind his cloak. He returns naked to his mother’s womb when, at the end of this world, the one who, having become human in the world, is despised, is revealed as God before the eyes of his synagogue, existing before the ages. Hence Paul says: “Blindness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the gentiles enters; and then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. XI, 24).

**MORALLY.** The tempted spirit, detected in the poverty of its weakness, may say: “The first grace of faith gave birth to me naked; that same grace will save me naked in the assumption.” It is a great consolation for a troubled spirit that, when assailed by vices and seeing itself apparently stripped of virtues, it may have recourse to the sole hope of mercy and not allow itself to be stripped in that respect in which it humbly considers itself naked of virtues.

It follows: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away.”—The holy man had lost everything when the adversary tempted him, but, knowing that Satan would not have the power to tempt him unless God permitted it, he did not say, “The Lord gave, and the devil took away,” but, “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away.” [Col. 0124D]

It might indeed have been a cause for grief if the enemy had taken away what the Creator had given. But since the one who gave it himself took it back, he did not take away what belonged to another; he took back his own.

He adds: “As it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened.”—If, then, we know that only just things please the Lord, and that we can suffer only what pleases the Lord, everything we suffer is just. It is therefore exceedingly unjust if we murmur against a just suffering.

It follows: “Blessed be the name of the Lord.”—Behold, he concluded everything he rightly felt with the blessing of the Lord. [Col. 0125A] Thus the adversary may see, to his own punishment, what should make him ashamed: he himself, rebellious toward God, existed even when created in blessedness, while a human being, though struck down, offers God a hymn of glory.

Our Redeemer, in that he is said to give everything with the Father, gives all things; but in that he is human, he receives all things from the Father. Let him therefore say concerning Judaea, when it believed that the mystery of his incarnation would come: “The Lord gave.” Let him say concerning Judaea, when it despised the awaited presence of the Incarnation: “The Lord has taken away.”

That the Lord gave thanks, the Gospel attests: for it reports that, having taken bread, he gave thanks (Luke XXI, 19). Therefore he gives thanks who received the scourges of another’s iniquity and who, though he displayed nothing deserving punishment, humbly blesses amid punishment. [Col. 0125B]

By this he shows what each person ought to do under the scourge of his own fault, if he bore with equanimity the scourges belonging to another’s fault—and what a servant ought to do, if the one equal to the Father did this.

**MORALLY.** The person instructed by temptations grows, recognizing both the generosity of the giver in the virtue he possesses and the power of the one who takes it away amid disturbance. Yet this strength is not removed; it is disturbed, provided that it is diligently guarded by a humble mind.

When we are shaken by inward disturbance, it is right that we have recourse to the judgment of the Creator, so that our heart may offer greater praise to him through his help precisely where, having been assailed, it more truly weighs the weakness of its infirmity. It follows:

**VERSE 22.** “In all these things Job did not sin with his lips,” and so forth. [Col. 0125C]—Since we can sin through the silent movement of thought without speaking, and it is said of blessed Job that he “did not sin,” it is clear that he restrained the fault of murmuring from his thought. And when it says, “He did not speak foolishly,” it is evident that he restrained guilt from his tongue. Thus he neither sinned nor spoke foolishly, because he neither swelled silently within his conscience nor released his tongue into rebellion. [Col. 0126A]

**ALLEGORICALLY.** That the Lord neither sinned nor spoke anything foolish against God, Peter attests, saying: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (I Pet. I, 22).

**MORALLY.** A grieving spirit must guard itself with vigilant care, lest, when temptation goads it inwardly, it break forth in words of unlawful speech. It must not murmur against its testing; it must not turn the fire that burns it like gold into the ash of straw through an excess of unlawful speech.

Nothing prevents us from understanding what we have said about virtues also of those gifts of the Holy Spirit that are bestowed for the manifestation of virtue: “To one are given prophecy, to another kinds of tongues, to another powers of healings” (I Cor. XII, 10). [Col. 0126B]

But it is clearly shown that these gifts themselves are not always present in the mind in the same way: sometimes they are usefully withdrawn, lest the mind exalt itself in presumption.

For some gifts of the Holy Spirit are such that without them one cannot attain life—meekness, humility, faith, hope, and charity. Others are those by which the holiness of one’s life is displayed for the benefit of others—prophecy, the power of healings, and kinds of tongues. The former cannot be lost without danger; the latter are often withdrawn without loss.

But when they are withdrawn, let us say: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away. Blessed be the name of the Lord.” [Col. 0126C]

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0125]

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0125C]

**VERSES 1–3.** “It happened, when on a certain day the sons of God had come and stood before the Lord, that Satan also came among them and stood in his presence. And the Lord said to Satan: ‘Where have you come from?’ He answered and said: ‘I have gone around the earth and traversed it.’ And the Lord said to Satan: ‘Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth, a simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil?’”—Since we discussed these matters at greater length above, it is better to pass over them in silence. [Col. 0125D]

Although the question put to him—“Where have you come from?”—is not expressed as before, it is as though the voice of God were saying: “Behold, you are overcome by one person, placed in weak flesh, although you attempt to raise yourself against me, the author of all things.”

Immediately, when the Lord again spoke of the good qualities of blessed Job, he added, enumerating them as triumphs of victory: “Still holding fast to his innocence.” It is as though he were openly saying: “You have indeed exercised your malice, but he has not lost his innocence.”

It follows: “But you have moved me against him, so that I might afflict him without cause.”—Let us therefore ask how this was without cause and how it was not without cause. Since God is just, he cannot afflict without cause. Yet, since he is truthful, he could not have said otherwise than what he did. [Col. 0126C]

For it was necessary that the holy man, known in his strength only to God and to himself, should become known to all for imitation. He would not have offered others an evident example of virtue if he had remained without temptation. Thus he was struck without cause, since no fault was punished in him, and not without cause, since his virtue was increased for merit. [Col. 0126D]

What does he mean by saying, “You have moved me”? Does truth become inflamed by Satan’s words amid the torments of those subject to God? Far from it. But because we do not know how to strike except when moved, the divine striking itself is called “being moved”; and divine speech descends to the level of our words so that his action may in some way be understood.

But since we have already discussed these matters allegorically above, we shall avoid repeating them. From this point, therefore, we begin. He says: “You have moved me without cause.”

Since Job bears the likeness of our Redeemer and shares one substance and one power with the Father, how does he assert that he was moved by Satan against him? Satan then moved the Lord to afflict him when, through the fault of disobedience, he cast the first man from the height of justice in paradise. [Col. 0127A]

For unless the first Adam had drawn death into his soul through voluntary sin, the second Adam would not have come voluntarily to the death of the flesh without sin. Concerning him it is rightly added: “without cause.” He was afflicted without cause because he was burdened by the punishment of guilt but was not stained by the contagion of guilt.

Hence a certain wise man says to the Father: “Although you are just, you dispose all things justly” (Wis. XII, 15), even condemning one who does not deserve to be punished. It follows:

**VERSE 4.** “Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his life.”—Often, when we see a blow coming against the face, we place our hand before our eyelids to defend our eyes from the blow, exposing one part of the body to injury so that we may not be wounded in a more tender part. [Col. 0127B]

Knowing that such things are often done, Satan says: “Skin for skin.” It is as though he were openly saying: “Job endures so many scourges outside himself with equanimity because he fears being struck himself.”

**VERSE 5.** “But stretch out your hand and touch his bone and his flesh,” and so forth.—Above he said, “Touch all that he possesses”; now, as though he had forgotten his earlier proposal, defeated in that matter, he asks for another.

**MYSTICALLY.** The evil spirit, seeing our Redeemer shine forth with miracles, cries: “We know that you are the Holy One of God” (Mark I, 24). In saying this, he fears while recognizing the Son of God. Yet, ignorant of the power of heavenly mercy, whenever he considers him passible, he sometimes supposes him to be merely human.

He had learned that many people, established in pastoral office under an appearance of substantial worth, because alienated from the inward compassion of charity, regarded the losses of others as of very little account. [Col. 0127C] Thus, taking him to be one of these, and seeing that he had not been overcome by the removal of many things, he burned to reach his flesh through the touch of suffering, as though saying: “Skin for skin,” and so forth.

It is as though he were openly saying: “They neglect to be moved by what is outside themselves; but the truth of who someone is is recognized when he experiences in himself something that causes pain.”

When Satan himself desires these things to happen, he says them not in words but in desires. Through his members he brought them about both in words and in desires. For he himself speaks when, in the words of the prophet, his followers say: “Let us put wood into his bread” (Jer. XI, 19). It follows:

**VERSE 6.** “Behold, he is in your hand; nevertheless preserve his life.”—The holy man is delivered into the hand of the adversary, yet he is held inwardly in the hand of his helper. [Col. 0127D] He belonged to those sheep of whom the Truth says: “No one will snatch them from my hand” (John X, 28).

And yet it is said to the enemy who seeks him: “Behold, he is in your hand.” Thus he is at once in God’s hand and in the devil’s hand. The merciful helper held the one whom he permitted to be touched; by giving him over, he did not surrender him, but concealed him from the darts of his adversary.

Satan is said to preserve his life in the sense that he is not permitted to break into it, just as we say to the Father: “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matt. VI, 18).

**MYSTICALLY.** Pilate was a member of the devil, while the chief priests were his body. When, therefore, the Lord delivered himself into the hands of Satan’s members for our redemption, what else did he do than permit Satan’s hand to rage against him? [Col. 0128A]

If Satan’s power is understood as his hand, then Christ endured that hand in the flesh, enduring its power over his body through spitting, blows, scourges, the cross, and the spear. Hence he also said to Pilate: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given to you from above. But preserve his life” (John XIX, 11).

This does not mean that Satan was forbidden to test it, but that he was shown to be unable to test it. For the soul of our Redeemer was not disturbed by the necessity of temptation as we are shaken by temptation. Although he deigned to accept temptation externally, his mind, adhering inwardly to his divinity, remained unshaken.

His soul may also signify the life of the elect. When Satan is permitted to strike the Redeemer’s flesh, he is separated from the soul, because, when he receives his body for suffering, he loses his elect from the authority of his power. [Col. 0128B] And when his flesh dies through the cross, the minds of the elect are strengthened against his covenants. It follows:

**VERSE 7.** “Satan went out from the presence of the Lord.”—These matters have often been said above.

“He struck Job with a most grievous ulcer, from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head.”—Many scourges are often lightened by their quality, if, although numerous, they are not severe; and often severe scourges are lightened by their quantity, if, although heavy, they are not numerous.

But the adversary burned against the holy man not only through the malice of quality, as in “he struck Job with a most grievous ulcer,” but also through the weight of quantity, as in “from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head.”

**MYSTICALLY.** The body of the Lord consists of all the elect. From the very beginning of the world, therefore, the adversary attempted to attack the body of our Redeemer. He inflicted a wound from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head when, beginning with pure people, he raged onward until he reached the very head of the Church. [Col. 0128C]

No one of the elect has come into this life without enduring the adversities of this enemy.

**MORALLY.** Divine mercy abandons us in such a way that, by abandoning us, it protects us. It protects us in such a way that, while permitting a moment of temptation, it nevertheless shows us the condition of our weakness.

The enemy wounds us from the sole of the foot to the crown because, when he receives permission, he begins with the lesser and advances to the greater. He rends the body but does not reach the soul when, amid all the wounds of the pleasures it undergoes, the inward intention of a hidden purpose resists. [Col. 0128D] Thus, although pleasure bites the mind, the resolve of holy uprightness does not allow it to bend softly into consent. It follows:

**VERSE 8.** “He scraped the discharge with a potsherd while sitting on a dung heap.”—What is a potsherd except clay? What is discharge except clay? With clay, therefore, he wiped away clay.

The holy man considered from what had come the thing he carried, and he treated the body that had once been subject to him in health, though now struck, with a fragment of baked clay. He placed his body on a dung heap so that his mind might carefully consider what the substance of the flesh was, since it had been taken from the earth. [Col. 0129A]

It is pleasing to contemplate why almighty God so greatly despises in this world those whom he chose so sublimely before the ages. He presses us down so severely in lowly places because he sees how he will reward us in the heights. Let each person therefore infer what those whom he rejects will suffer there, if here he so torments those whom he loves.

**TYPICALLY.** What else is the potsherd in the Lord’s hand than flesh taken from the clay of our substance? A potsherd is hardened by fire, and the Lord’s flesh became stronger through suffering, as the prophet says: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. XXI, 16).

The discharge is therefore the corruption of blood; and sins of the flesh, worsened by long continuance, are a more grievous discharge. A wound turns into discharge when neglected guilt is made worse through habit.

Our Redeemer, therefore, delivering his body into the hands of his persecutors, scraped away the discharge with a potsherd because he blotted out our sins with his flesh. He came, as it is written, “in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Rom. VI, 5), in order to condemn sin through sin. [Col. 0129B] The discharge is scraped away with the potsherd when guilt is overcome through the flesh.

He does not sit in the forum, where the law resounds, but on a dung heap, because, as Paul testifies: “He chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (I Cor. I, 17). Behold, he sits grieving on a dung heap because, after sins have been committed, he willingly possesses the hearts of the penitent.

As they consider their evils with weeping, they heap up excrement before themselves, as it were, by casting themselves down. Hence it is said through the prophet: “Upon whom shall I look, except upon the humble and quiet?” (Isa. LXVI, 2).

Even now he daily endures the perverse, when his elect are torn apart by the reprobate. Many pursue the life of the Redeemer in the Church through depraved behavior—not with swords, but with evil deeds. They not only bring themselves into wicked action, but also strive to bend the uprightness of the just toward perversity. [Col. 0129C]

**MORALLY.** What is understood by the potsherd except the force of strictness? What by the discharge except the turmoil of unlawful thought? We scrape away the discharge with the potsherd when, after the pollution of unlawful thought, we cleanse ourselves through harsh struggle.

Alternatively, the fragility of mortality is understood by the potsherd. To cleanse the discharge with the potsherd is therefore to weigh the course and frailty of mortality. When a wicked thought flows into the mind, discharge runs out as though from a wound. But the discharge is wiped away more quickly if, in our consideration, fragility is held like a potsherd in the hand.

The discharge is wiped away when guilt is cut off not only from action but also from thought. [Col. 0129D] Hence the Lord says: “I tell you that whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V, 28).

He sits on a dung heap who carefully regards his own weakness and does not exalt himself because of the good things he receives through grace. For us, to sit on a dung heap is to turn back the eyes of the mind in repentance toward the things we have done unlawfully. It follows:

**VERSE 9.** “His wife said to him: ‘Do you still persist in your simplicity? Bless God and die.’”—The ancient enemy is accustomed to tempt the human race in two ways: either to break the hearts of those who stand firm through tribulations or to soften them through persuasion. Against blessed Job, therefore, he exercised himself vigorously in both ways.

First he brought losses of property upon the head of the household; then, defeated, he turned to subtler methods of testing. [Col. 0130A] He seized the woman’s heart and found, as it were, a ladder by which he could climb to the heart of her husband, but he gained nothing through this art.

For when the ancient enemy does not overthrow our heart through his own persuasion, he secretly approaches it through the tongues of those who cling to us. Hence it is written: “Beware of your sons, and take heed of your household” (Ecclus. XXXII, 26). And again: “A man’s enemies are those of his household” (Matt. X, 36).

**MYSTICALLY.** Whom does the woman who gives wicked advice signify except certain carnal people placed within the bosom of the Church? The more they are inwardly present through the words of professed faith, the more severely they oppress the good through their unreformed conduct.

Sometimes they persuade us with words; sometimes they entice us by examples. They attempt the same thing sometimes through fear, sometimes through boldness. [Col. 0130B] Peter and the son of Zeruiah represented these people: the former when he tried to prevent the Lord’s passion, the latter when he wished to destroy the man who was cursing the king. But those who succumb to this fault through pride rather than fear are far worse.

**MORALLY.** The wife who gives wicked advice is carnal thought harassing the mind. Often we are worn down outwardly by scourges and inwardly wearied by carnal suggestion. Hence Jeremiah says: “Outside the sword kills, and inside there is a death like it” (Lam. I, 20).

But these things take place differently in the reprobate and in the elect. The hearts of the former are tempted so that they consent; the latter indeed receive temptations, but they resist them. It follows:

**VERSE 10.** “Job answered and said: ‘You have spoken as one of the foolish women.’”—Behold, everywhere the enemy is broken and everywhere overcome. [Col. 0130C] Since it is the understanding of the wicked woman, not her sex, that is at fault, he does not say, “You have spoken as one of the women,” but “as one of the foolish women,” so that it may be shown that what she thinks perversely belongs to the folly that has entered her, not to created nature.

It follows: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?”—He calls good things the gifts of God, whether temporal or eternal, and evil things present scourges. Concerning these the Lord says through the prophet: “I am the Lord, and there is no other; forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evil” (Isa. XLI, 7).

Great indeed is the consolation of tribulation if, while suffering adversities, we recall the gifts of our Creator. [Col. 0130D] What confronts us through pain does not break us if what lifts us through grace comes more quickly to mind. Hence it is written: “On the day of good things, do not be forgetful of evil things; and on the day of evil things, do not be forgetful of good things” (Ecclus. XI, 17).

**MYSTICALLY.** When holy men are caught in the battle of tribulations and at one and the same time feel some enemies striking and others persuading, they oppose the former with the shield of patience and hurl against the latter the darts of instruction. By teaching, they correct the weak; by enduring, they overcome the hostile.

They despise the enemies who rise against them through patience, while, by compassion, they lead their weakened fellow citizens toward salvation. Since it is said to the elect, “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Ps. XVI, 4), [Col. 0131A] minds of carnal people who serve God with an unstable intention are rightly called women.

It is as though one were saying: “If we are striving toward eternal goods, why should it be surprising that we suffer temporal evils?” Hence Paul says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18).

**MORALLY.** Whoever desires to subdue vices and advances with the steps of true intention toward the heights of eternal recompense, sees himself surrounded on every side by the battle of vices and therefore girds himself more vigorously with the armor of virtues. The less he fears the darts, the more firmly he fortifies his breast against the darts that come against him.

It follows: “In all these things Job did not sin with his lips.”—We sin in two ways with our lips: either by saying what is unjust or by keeping silent about what is just. For if silence were never a fault, the prophet would not say: “Woe is me, because I was silent” (Isa. VI, 5). [Col. 0131B]

Blessed Job did not sin at all with his lips in everything he did because he neither spoke proudly against the one who struck him nor kept silent against the one who persuaded him.

**MYSTICALLY.** When holy men suffer persecution outwardly and inwardly, they not only do not exceed the bounds of propriety in matters touching God’s honor, but they also do not hurl insulting words against the adversaries themselves. Hence Peter says: “Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or a reviler” (I Pet. IV, 15). A reviler suffers as such when, at the time of his passion, he is carried away into insulting his persecutor, even if only in words. It follows:

### VERSE 11

Accordingly, when Job’s three friends heard of all the evil that had befallen him, and so forth.

Those who come by agreement to console the afflicted thereby demonstrate how great their charity was both among themselves and toward the stricken man. Although the fact that Scripture testifies that they were friends of so great a man also shows that they possessed good zeal and upright intention, nevertheless this very intention was darkened by the indiscretion that arose in them before the eyes of the strict Judge when they burst forth into speech.

**MYSTICALLY.** Job’s blessed friends, although they come to him with good intention, nevertheless represent heretics, because by speaking indiscreetly they slip into guilt. Thus Holy Church, when she endures wounds and grieves over the falls of her members, also has to endure other enemies of Christ under Christ’s name. To increase her sorrow, heretics too assemble in controversy and strike her, as though with certain arrows, with irrational words.

It follows: **They came from their own place.** The place of heretics is pride itself, just as, conversely, humility is the place of the good, according to Solomon: “If a spirit possessing power rises up against you, do not leave your place” (Eccles. 10:4). Heretics therefore come from their own place, because they are moved by pride against Holy Church.

Eliphaz is interpreted as “contempt of God.” Baldad, however, means “mere antiquity.” Since heretics neglect conversion to the new life and direct their attention solely to antiquity, this is what they represent. Sophar means “dissipation of the watchtower,” or “dissipating the watchman.” The mountains of the faithful rise toward the contemplation of heavenly things; but when heretics seek to pervert those who contemplate what is right, they attempt to destroy the watchtower.

The places from which they come are also aptly described in accordance with the actions of heretics. He is called a Themanite, “south wind” (*auster*); a Suites, “speaking”; and a Naamatite, “beauty.” First, disordered heat inflames heretics; then the brilliance of loquacity raises them up; and finally hypocrisy makes them appear attractive to human beings.

It follows: **For they had agreed together to come and visit him and console him.** Heretics agree among themselves when they hold certain wicked opinions against the Church in harmony and, in the matters in which they depart from the truth, agree with one another in falsehood. Heretics who desire to teach Holy Church their own doctrines approach her as though they were offering consolation. Nor is it surprising that they are called friends, since even to the betrayer it is said: “Friend, for what purpose have you come?” (Matt. 26:30).

**MORALLY.** Friends come to offer consolation but break out into insults: these are the vices lying in wait for us, which assume the appearance of virtues but strike us with hostile assault. Often immoderate anger wishes to appear as justice; lax indulgence as mercy; and incautious fear as humility. It is rightly said: **For they had agreed together.** Pride is near to anger, and laxity to fear. They come by agreement, because through a certain perverse thought these things ally themselves against us.

It follows:

### VERSE 12

**And when they had lifted up their eyes from afar, they did not recognize him.**

The order of consolation is this: when we wish to lift someone afflicted out of sorrow, we should first strive to harmonize ourselves with his grief by grieving with him. One who does not agree with the grief cannot console the grieving. Yet in this matter it must be understood that the person who wishes to console the afflicted must set a measure to the sorrow he takes upon himself, lest he not only fail to soothe the grieving person but, by grieving immoderately, press the afflicted soul beneath the weight of despair.

Job’s blessed friends, however, grieved in their consolation more than was necessary. They saw the blow but did not know the mind of the one who had been struck; and so they turned to an immense mourning, as though a man of such great strength, struck in body, had also fallen in heart.

**MYSTICALLY.** Heretics lift their eyes when they consider the deeds of Holy Church, because they themselves are situated in low things. Holy Church desires to receive evils here so that, purified, she may reach the reward of eternal recompense. Since heretics desire present things as something great, they do not recognize her when she is placed amid wounds.

What they see in her they do not retain in the knowledge of their own hearts.

It follows: **And having torn their garments, they scattered dust upon their heads toward heaven.**

Just as we understand all the faithful as the garments of the Church, according to the prophet: “You shall clothe yourself with all these as with an ornament” (Isa. 49:18), so all who agree with heretics belong to them; by clinging to their errors, they are wrapped in them. Since they daily rush toward worse things and divide themselves in many ways by thinking worse thoughts, it comes about that, when their followers are torn apart, the malice of their thinking is revealed. Deceit exposes the discord that a grievous fault of agreement had closed up.

By dust we understand earthly understanding; by the head, the mind; and by heaven, the command of heavenly speech. Therefore to scatter dust upon the head toward heaven is to corrupt the mind with worldly understanding and to draw earthly meanings from heavenly words. They scatter dust upon their heads because, in the commandments of God, they strive through earthly understanding beyond the strength of their minds.

**MORALLY.** Vices do not recognize us when we are afflicted, because as soon as they knock, a sorrowful heart rejects them; and although they had seemed to know us when they penetrated us in our joy, they cannot recognize us in our sorrow, because they are broken by the very firmness of our soul.

**They cried aloud and wept.** Piety is signified by weeping, discernment by the tearing of garments, and the affection of works by dust upon the head.

It follows:

### VERSE 13

**They sat with him upon the ground for seven days and seven nights, and so forth.**

We do not know whether they sat with afflicted Job for seven successive days and seven successive nights, or whether throughout as many days and nights they remained attached to him by frequent and earnest visits. Scripture, however, often places the whole for a part and a part for the whole.

It must be observed that some people begin to speak hastily and carry out what they have begun with even greater recklessness; others begin to speak slowly, but once they have begun, do not know how to moderate their speech. Job’s blessed friends, seeing his grief, remained silent for a long time; but although they began late, they spoke indiscreetly, because they were unwilling to spare the grieving man. Therefore we must consider not only what we do but also with how much discernment we do it.

**MYSTICALLY.** By day we recognize the things we see; by night we either see nothing because of blindness or are obscured by uncertainty. Day therefore signifies understanding, while night signifies ignorance. The number seven expresses the totality of the universe, for this entire period of time is completed in seven days.

What, then, does it mean to sit upon the ground for seven days and nights, except that heretics, whether in those matters in which they understand the true light or in those in which they suffer the darkness of ignorance, pretend to stoop to the weakness of Holy Church and, under the appearance of flatteries, prepare the deceits of deception?

To sit together upon the ground is to display something of the image of humility, so that, while they exhibit humble things, they persuade others of the proud doctrines they teach.

The ground may also signify the Incarnation of the Mediator himself. Hence it is said to Israel: “You shall make an altar of earth for me” (Exod. 20:24–26). To sit upon the ground therefore means that heretics, either in what they understand of the fullness of truth or in what they are blinded by the darkness of their folly, cannot deny the mystery of the Incarnation and, together with Holy Church, believe the true flesh of the Redeemer.

**MORALLY.** Vices sit upon the ground with us when we are afflicted, displaying an image of humility in order to take away the desire to be useful, so that, while each person considers himself unworthy, he fears to administer those things by which he could benefit his neighbors.

It follows: **And no one spoke a word to him.**

We have adversaries silent when, by preaching, we neglect to beget true children of the faith. But if we begin to speak rightly, we soon experience grievous insults in their response. Sometimes, however, when heretics observe that the hearts of the faithful are sluggish through inertia, they do not cease, by speaking, to scatter the seed of error.

When they see that the minds of good people understand lofty things and grieve vigorously over the misery of this exile, they restrain their tongues with anxious caution. They see that, when they speak in vain against grieving hearts, they quickly fall silent.

Hence it is immediately added: **For they saw that his grief was very great.**

**MORALLY.** If the heart truly grieves, vices have no tongue against us. For when a life of rectitude is sought completely, the superfluous suggestion of depravity is made hard and powerless. Often, if we restrain ourselves firmly, we transform vices into instruments of virtue. When we subject anger to reason, we turn it into the service of holy zeal; when it rises with pride, we transform it into the defense of justice; and when bodily strength entices us, we gain the profits of devotion.

## BOOK FOUR

### CHAPTER 3

Whoever considers the text but does not understand the sense of sacred reading instructs himself less by learning than he confuses himself through ambiguity. For behold, blessed Job is described as cursing his day, saying:

### VERSE 3

**Let the day perish in which I was born.**

Who does not know that the day on which he was born could not then continue to exist? Why, then, would so great a man curse something that he certainly knew could not subsist? If he cursed something that existed, he acted wickedly; if he cursed something that did not exist, he acted pointlessly. Therefore even apparently pointless words must be feared as though they were harmful. Hence it is written: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it” (Matt. 12:36).

It follows:

### VERSE 4

**Let that day be turned into darkness; let God not seek it from above, and let it not be illuminated by light.**

The day is known to have passed away in the course of time. Why, then, is it said to be turned into darkness? Since it does not remain, how can it be rolled about like a shadow? Or what night does a dark whirlwind possess, when no fixed state holds it? Or how can that be wished solitary which, by passing away, had already become nothing? Or how can that which lacks perception await light?

It follows:

**Why did I not die in the womb? Why, coming forth from the womb, did I not immediately perish? Why was I received upon the knees? Why was I suckled at the breasts? For now I would be sleeping in silence, and I would rest in my sleep.**

### VERSES 11–13

If he had perished immediately after coming forth from the womb, would he have received the merit of recompense from that very destruction? Do aborted children enjoy eternal rewards? What baptism accomplishes among us was accomplished among the ancients either by faith alone in the case of infants, by the virtue of sacrifice in the case of adults, or by the mysteries of circumcision.

It is written: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities,” and so forth (Ps. 50:7). But the Truth says: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he does not have eternal life” (John 3:5). What does he mean by asserting that he would be at rest, if the divine sacraments had not freed him from the guilt of original sin?

It follows: **With the kings and rulers of the earth.**

Who does not know that kings and rulers are far from solitude, or how difficult it is for them to advance toward rest? As it is written: “The severest judgment will be upon those who rule” (Wis. 6:6); and again: “From the one to whom much has been given, much will be required” (Luke 12:48).

It follows:

**Or with princes who possess gold.**

It is exceedingly rare for those who possess gold to advance toward rest, since the Truth says: “It is difficult for those who have money to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 15:23; Mark 10:25).

Since these words, on the surface, disagree with reason, the letter itself now indicates that something further is intended. But what is meant by the fact that David, who did not return evil to those who repaid him with evil (Ps. 7:5), nevertheless cursed the mountains of Gilboa (2 Sam. 1:21)? What had the mountains of Gilboa done wrong when Saul died?

From this and other curses in Sacred Scripture we learn what we should seek in blessed Job’s language of cursing. Let no reader, without understanding, presume to rebuke one whom God rewards after his blows. But it must be understood that Scripture mentions a curse in two ways: one which it approves and another which it condemns. One is uttered by the judgment of justice; the other by the spite of vengeance.

Hence it is written: “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. 12:14); and: “Nor will those who curse inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10). Elsewhere: “Cursed is the earth in your work” (Gen. 3:17).

From this it must be considered that when holy men pronounce a sentence of cursing, it does not burst forth from a desire for vengeance but from the judgment of justice—as in the case of Peter against Simon and of Elijah against the captains of fifty.

Nor should we pass over the reason why he says “after this,” namely, after those things that happened to him. It is therefore utterly unfitting for us to suppose that, without anyone provoking or pressing him, he burst out in a word of cursing from impatience, when we know that, amid so many blows, he humbly proclaimed the greatness of the Creator.

**ALLEGORICALLY.** **Let the day perish in which I was born.** By the day of birth the whole period of our mortality may be understood. Whoever already sees the day of eternity supports with difficulty the day of his mortality.

It should be noted that he does not say, “Let the day in which I was created perish,” but, “in which I was born.” Humanity was created in the day of justice, but was already born in the time of guilt. It is as though he were saying openly: “Let the day of mutability perish, and let the light of eternity break forth.”

Since we speak of something perishing in two ways—either when we wish it not to exist or when we wish it to exist in an evil condition—it is clearly shown here that this day is not wished to perish so that it may not exist, but that it may perish in the sense of becoming evil. Hence a little later it is said: “Let darkness obscure it, and let it be wrapped in bitterness.”

This time of mutability, however, will not pass away in order to become evil, but so that it may not exist at all. Thus the angel says: “By the one who lives forever, because time will be no more” (Rev. 10:6–7).

The human soul and the angelic spirit are both immortal in a mortal way and mortal in an immortal way. For they lose blessed living, whether through vice or through punishment; but they do not lose essential existence, either through vice or through punishment.

Therefore, under the name of “day,” the holy man wished to express the apostate spirit, which continues to exist in the essence of life even while dying. The ancient enemy is day by nature, since he was created good, but night by merit, since he fell into darkness. He is day when he promises good things, but night when he obscures the minds of those who consent to error with darkness. Paul says of him: “Although he is an angel of darkness, he disguises himself as an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11:14).

It is as though he were saying: “Let the ancient enemy perish, the one who displays the light of promise but brings the darkness of sin.” “Let him perish,” that is, let him lose the license to tempt.

**MORALLY.** Prosperity in this world is like a certain day for us when it smiles upon us; it ends in night because it often leads us into the darkness of tribulation. Hence the prophet says: “I did not desire the day of man; you know it” (Jer. 17:16). Again, the Lord says through the prophet: “Until night my kidneys reproved me” (Ps. 15:7).

Day may also be understood as the delight of sin and night as blindness. He therefore wishes the day to perish, so that everything that appears attractive in guilt may be destroyed when the strength of justice intervenes. He also wishes the night to perish, so that the mind which, even through consent, commits what it has conceived may extinguish it through the correction of repentance.

But we must ask why a human being is said to be born in the day and conceived in the night. Sacred Scripture calls a human being by that name in three ways. Sometimes it means nature, as in: “Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). Sometimes it means guilt, as in: “But you shall die like human beings” (Ps. 81:7). Paul likewise says: “Since there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not human beings?” (1 Cor. 3:3). Sometimes it means weakness, as in: “Cursed is the one who places his hope in a human being” (Jer. 17:5).

A human being is therefore born in the day but conceived in the night, because he is not carried away by the delight of sin unless he has first been weakened through the voluntary darkness of the mind.

Let the delight, then, perish which carried the human being away into guilt. Let the heedless weakness of mind perish which blinded him even to the darkness of perverse consent.

It follows: **Let that day be turned into darkness.**

The day is turned into darkness when the malignant enemy is perceived to be, according to his deserts, such as he is when he rages, though he lies hidden in flattering words. This day seems to shine when his persuasion of depravity is believed to promise prosperity. But when his wickedness is recognized as it truly is, the day of false promise is darkened by shadows.

The day is turned into darkness when, from the very beginning of its delight, guilt is seen to the end of destruction toward which it carries a person. We turn the day into darkness when, punishing ourselves strictly, we torture the very flatteries of evil delight through the harsh lamentations of repentance, pursuing with tears whatever we silently sinned in our hearts through delight.

It follows: **Let God not seek it from above, and let it not be illuminated by light.**

Almighty God created two creatures capable of knowing him: the angelic and the human. Pride strikes both. Yet, in his mercy, he ought to redeem the one who, in committing guilt, is known to have possessed some weakness. Hence the prophet says: “He remembered that they were flesh” (Ps. 77:39).

He ought to repel the apostate angel all the more completely because he bore nothing weak from flesh. There is also another reason why fallen humanity ought to be restored, while the proud spirit cannot be restored: the angel fell through his own malice, whereas another’s malice overthrew humanity.

It is as though this were said of him: “Since he himself brought in darkness, let him endure without end what he has done; let him never recover the state of his former light, since he lost it without having been deceived.”

**MORALLY.** God “seeks” what he examines in judgment; he does not seek what, by forgiving it, he has already left unpunished in his judgment.
