This day, that is, this delight of sin, will not be sought by the Lord if it is punished by voluntary correction, as Paul bears witness: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged by the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:31).

When the Lord appears in judgment, he illuminates with light everything that he then reproves. Whatever is not recalled to the judge’s memory is, as it were, hidden under a certain darkness. For it is written: “Everything that is reproved is made manifest by the light” (Eph. 5:13).

Therefore, since everything that is covered is hidden as though in darkness, on the day of the final judgment whatever is not examined by punishment is not illuminated by light. For it is written: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. 32:1).

It follows:

### VERSE 5

**Let darkness and the shadow of death obscure it.**

The shadow of death should be understood as forgetfulness, because just as death destroys life, so forgetfulness extinguishes memory. Since the apostate angel is handed over to eternal forgetfulness, he is darkened by the shadow of death. It is as though he said: “May the blindness of his error overwhelm him, so that he may never again rise to the light of repentance through the memory of divine regard.”

**MORALLY.** Darkness obscures the day when the lamentations of repentance inflicted upon the mind pierce through its delight. Darkness may also signify hidden judgments. Hidden judgments are like darkness before our eyes, because they cannot be searched out. Hence it is written of the Lord: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. 17:12).

Darkness therefore obscures the day when, by weeping, the inscrutable judgments of God mercifully conceal from the ray of righteous correction the joy of our delight.

In Sacred Scripture, the shadow of death sometimes means forgetfulness of death, as in: “To enlighten those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death” (Luke 1:79). Sometimes it means imitation of the devil. Of him it is said: “Is not Death his name?” (Rev. 6:8). Hence it is written: “For those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, light has risen” (Matt. 4:16).

Sometimes it means the death of the flesh, as in: “You humbled us in a place of affliction; the shadow of death covered us” (Ps. 43:20). True death occurs when the soul is separated from God. Since the Redeemer accepted on our behalf only the death of the flesh, he endured the shadow of death and hid from the eyes the guilt that we had committed.

It is as though he said: “Let the one come who, in order to free the debtors from the death of flesh and spirit, pays the debt of fleshly death although he owes none.”

It follows: **Let darkness seize it, and let it be wrapped in bitterness.**

Because the ancient enemy fell from the light of inward order, he now confounds himself inwardly with the darkness of error. After this he is wrapped in bitterness, because, on account of the merit of his voluntary darkness, he is tormented by the eternal punishment of Gehenna.

Because the eye is confused in darkness, the confusion of our mind through repentance is itself called darkness. For just as misty darkness obscures the day through a thick mass of cloud, so confusion darkens the mind with disturbed thoughts.

Hence it is written: “And confusion brings glory” (Ecclus. 4:15). This darkness had oppressed the minds of those to whom Paul said: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6:21).

The day is wrapped in bitterness when, as the mind returns to reflect upon its thoughts, the flatteries of sin are followed by the torment of repentance. Whatever is wrapped is covered on every side. We therefore wrap the day in bitterness when we see from every side what punishments follow the joy of evil delight and surround it with bitter tears.

It follows:

### VERSE 6

**Let a dark whirlwind possess that night.**

It is written: “Fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm around him.” A dark whirlwind therefore possesses this night because that storm, bringing eternal punishments to be feared, carries the apostate spirit away from the sight of the strict Judge. This night is possessed by a whirlwind because its proud blindness is struck by strict correction.

**MORALLY.** The agitated spirit of sorrow is like a certain whirlwind of a storm. When a person understands the sin he has committed, sorrow darkens his mind; and, as though the air of serene joy had been shaken, the whirlwind of repentance destroys all tranquility of heart within him.

Hence it is written: “With a mighty spirit you will crush the ships of Tarshish” (Ps. 47:8). Tarshish is interpreted as “examination of joy.” This means that the flatteries of secure repose should not nourish the perpetration of guilt, but that the devout and raging bitterness of repentance should break in.

It follows: **Let it not be counted among the days of the year, nor numbered among the months of the year.**

We may appropriately understand the year as the preaching of heavenly grace. Just as time is completed in a year through the accumulation of days, so a manifold life of virtues is completed in heavenly grace.

The year may also signify the multitude of the redeemed. Just as a year is named from the multitude of days, so that innumerable community of the elect is completed through the gathering together of all good people. Hence Isaiah says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” (Isa. 61:1), and shortly afterward adds: “To proclaim an acceptable year of the Lord” (ibid. 61:2).

What are the days except the individual minds of the elect? What are the months except their multiplied churches, which make one catholic Church?

That night is therefore not counted among the days of the year because the ancient enemy, pressed down by the darkness of his pride, sees the coming of the Redeemer but does not return to forgiveness with the elect. Hence it is written: “For he did not take hold of angels anywhere, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham” (Heb. 2:16).

Those who remain in inward light may be called angelic spirits; the months may be understood as their orders and dignities. Each spirit, because it shines, is a day. But because they are distinguished by certain dignities, so that some are Thrones and others Dominations, they are called months.

Since the ancient enemy is never restored to the merit of light or to the order of the heavenly ranks, he is numbered neither among the days of the year nor among its months.

**MORALLY.** The year of our illumination is completed when, with the eternal Judge appearing, the life of Holy Church’s pilgrimage is brought to an end. Then she will receive the recompense for her labor, when, after this time of warfare has been completed, she returns to her homeland, according to the prophet: “You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness” (Ps. 64:12).

The days of this year are the individual virtues; its months are the manifold deeds of virtue. It is as though she were entreating the strict Judge, saying: “When, after the time of Holy Church has been completed, you reveal yourself in the final examination, reward the gifts you have bestowed in such a way that you do not seek out the evils we have committed.”

If that night is counted, everything we have done is confused by the estimation of our wickedness; and the days of the virtues no longer shine if, before your sight, the dark confusion of our numbered night obscures them.

It follows:

### VERSE 7

**Let that night be solitary.**

That night becomes solitary because, by perpetual strictness, it is separated from the company of the heavenly homeland.

Alternatively: it had made human beings companions for itself in destruction, but the grace of the Redeemer restores them. The night therefore becomes solitary when, after those who are elect have been removed, the ancient enemy alone, together with his body, is consigned to the eternal fires of Gehenna.

It follows: **And not worthy of praise.**

When the human race, pressed by the darkness of error, believed stones to be gods, what else did it praise except the darkness of night? Hence Paul says: “We know that an idol is nothing” (1 Cor. 8:4). But the things that the nations sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons.

Behold, we now see that this night is recognized as unworthy of praise when the worship of idols is rejected by the redeemed human race. The night is left solitary because it does not go to punishment with the condemned apostate spirit.

**MORALLY.** There are some who not only fail to grieve over what they do but do not cease to praise and defend it. Indeed, when guilt is defended, it is doubled. Against this it is rightly said: “Have you sinned? Do not add again” (Ecclus. 22:1).

It is as though he said: “Let the guilt we have committed remain alone; let it not be praised and defended, lest it bind us more severely in the sight of the Judge.” We ought not to have sinned, but would that at least we did not anoint or adorn what we have done, and thus leave it alone.

It follows:

### VERSE 8

**Let those who curse the day curse it.**

In the Old Translation it is said: “Let those who cursed the day curse her, who is about to capture the great sea creature.”

In these words the future destruction of Antichrist is foreseen. The malignant spirit, who is night by merit, pretends to be day at the end of the world, when he displays himself to human beings as though he were God. He curses the night who curses the day, because the one who now destroys his malice will then, by the illumination of his coming, extinguish even the power of his strength.

The strength of this sea creature is captured in the waters because the cunning of the ancient enemy is overcome by the sacrament of baptism.

This is also said concerning his elect angels: the proud spirit wished to display himself as day even to the angelic powers, raising himself above the others as though in the power of divinity, and dragging so many legions after him into destruction. But those who remained with humble hearts in their Creator, perceiving that his error contained night, trampled upon the day of his brightness by thinking humbly of themselves. They now reveal to us the darkness of his deceit and demonstrate how greatly that fabricated brightness should be despised.

**MORALLY.** Those truly correct past evils through the correction of repentance who are no longer carried away by any delight toward deceptive goods. If other harmful things still delight those who deplore their past deeds, it is false that they are grieving over what they have committed.

Alternatively: those truly punish past sins who detect the snares of the malignant seducer within the very flattering suggestion.

It follows: **Who are ready to awaken Leviathan.**

Leviathan is interpreted as “their addition,” namely, the addition of human beings, because after introducing the first guilt through an evil suggestion, he does not cease daily to increase it through more serious persuasions.

Or else, by way of reproach, he is called “the addition of human beings.” He found them immortal in paradise, but by promising divinity he cunningly took away their immortality.

The elect spirits restrain the proud apostate because, in their humility, they refused to follow him; and through their ministry it is arranged that he will one day be recalled for complete destruction, when he is prepared for the end of the conflict.

**MORALLY.** All who trample upon worldly things in their minds and desire the things of God with full intention awaken Leviathan against themselves, because they inflame his malice through the provocation of their way of life. Those who are subject to his will are possessed by him as though by a tranquil right. He seems to sleep while, lulled to rest in their perverse hearts, he remains quiet within them.

But he is awakened for conflict when he has lost the right of perverse domination. Those therefore rise up against sin with the strong judgment of strictness who do not fear to awaken the ancient adversary in their temptations.

It follows:

### VERSE 9

**Let the stars be darkened by his gloom.**

In Sacred Scripture the justice of the saints is sometimes signified, as the Apostle Paul says: “In the midst of a wicked and perverse nation, among whom you shine like lights in the world” (Phil. 2:15).

At other times the pretense of hypocrites is indicated, as in: “The dragon cast down his tail and dragged away a portion of the stars” (Rev. 12:4).

It is as though he were saying: Against those who shine before human eyes as though by good works, let the dark malice of the ancient enemy prevail, and let them lay aside the light of praise that they had assumed before human judgment. [The phrase *quante* is evidently corrupt or incomplete in the transmitted text.]

**MORALLY.** The stars are darkened by the gloom of night when even those who already shine with great virtues continue to bear something of the darkness of guilt: they shine with great brightness and yet, unwillingly, still drag along what remains of the night.

Hence, in the promised land, in the midst of the tribe of Ephraim, [the transmitted wording here is corrupt: “the singing tribe … talarius is left”]. Alternatively: night is consent to guilt, which has been propagated to us through the transgression of our first parent. We, condemned to this life after that punishment, came into it with the deserving of death.

Nevertheless, many people in the darkness of the present life, while displaying higher examples in themselves, shine upon us from above like stars. Yet however greatly they kindle themselves with the fire of compunction, as long as they remain burdened by corruptible flesh they cannot see the eternal light as it is.

Let him therefore say: **Let the stars be darkened by his gloom.** That is: let even those who spread the rays of their virtues over the human race in the darkness of this life still feel, in their contemplation, the darkness of the ancient night.

It follows: **Let him await light, and not see it.**

The light is the Lord. He himself says: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). The night is the dark enemy together with his members; it awaits the light and does not see it.

Those who retain faith without works, trusting that they can be saved by that faith at the final judgment, will find their hope frustrated. Likewise, those who display themselves in good action for the sake of human praise will vainly hope for recompense for good works when the Judge comes, as the Truth bears witness: “Truly I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 7:2).

It follows: **And let it not see the rising of the dawn.**

The dawn is called the Church, which is changed from the darkness of her sins into the light of justice. Concerning her it is said: “Who is this that comes forth like the rising dawn?” (Song 6:9).

In that light which will be revealed at the coming of the strict Judge, the body of the condemned enemy does not see the rising of the dawn, because every wicked person, weighed down by the darkness of his merits, does not know with how great a brightness Holy Church rises into the inward light of the heart.

In the judgment the Church will still be dawn, but in the kingdom she will be day. The rising of the dawn is therefore the beginning of the Church as she grows bright, which the reprobate cannot see, because, pressed down by the weight of their evils before the sight of the strict Judge, they are dragged into darkness. Of them the prophet says: “Let the impious be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of the just” (Isa. 26:10).

Alternatively: Judea awaited the light and did not see it. It awaited the coming Redeemer of the human race through prophecy, but did not recognize him when he came. It also did not see the rising of the dawn because it disdained to honor the weak beginnings of Holy Church.

**MORALLY.** However earnestly the mind still engaged in pilgrimage may strive, it cannot see the light as it is, because the blindness of its condemnation hides it from the mind.

The rising of the dawn is the new birth of the resurrection of the Church. Hence the Lord says: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty” (Matt. 19:28).

But however brightly the elect now shine through virtue, they cannot penetrate what the glory of that new birth will be, by which they will then rise in the flesh to contemplate the light of eternity.

It follows:

### VERSE 10

“For he did not close the doors of the womb that bore me, nor remove evil from my eyes.”

What the womb of a mother is for each individual human being, that supreme paradise was for the whole human race. For from it the human race came forth as from a womb. But the serpent opened the doors of this womb when, through cunning persuasion, he dissolved the heavenly commandment in the human heart.

Nor should it trouble us that he is said not to have closed what he is condemned for having opened. “He did not close” means “he opened,” and “he did not remove evil” means “he inflicted it.” For he would have removed it, so to speak, if he had remained inactive; and he would have closed it, as it were, if he had ceased from breaking in.

**MORALLY.** The doors of the womb are the desires of carnal concupiscence, concerning which the prophet says: “Enter into your chambers, and close your doors” (Isaiah 26:20). Night is the guilt of sin, which opened the doors of the womb, because, once a human being had conceived sin, it unlocked the desires of concupiscence. It did not close them; as above, it opened them, and it did not remove them but inflicted them.

It follows:

### VERSE 11

“Why did I not die in the womb?” and the rest.

Sin is perpetrated in the heart in four ways, and brought to completion in action in four ways. In the heart it is perpetrated by suggestion, delight, consent, and the boldness of self-defense. By the same four ways sin is brought to completion in action. First, the hidden fault acts; afterward the guilt is revealed before human eyes without shame; then it is turned into a habit; finally, it is nourished either by the seductions of false hope or by the obstinacy of miserable despair.

Let blessed Job, therefore, contemplate the fall of the human race and say: “Why did I not die in the womb?” That is: in the very hidden perpetration of sin, why did I not choose to be put to death with respect to the life of the flesh?

It follows:

“Coming forth from the womb, why did I not perish at once?”

That is: after I came out into open iniquity, why did I not then at least recognize that I was lost? For he would have perished in his own judgment if he had recognized that he was lost.

It follows:

### VERSE 12

“Why was I received upon the knees?”

That is: after open guilt, why did habit itself still receive me, so as to make me stronger for wickedness, and, sustaining me in depraved impulses, cherish me?

It follows:

“Why was I suckled at the breasts?”

That is: after I had entered into the habit of guilt, why did I nourish myself toward more atrocious wickedness, either with confidence in false hope or with the milk of miserable despair? Guilt is increased when it is nourished by favor. Hence Solomon says: “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent” (Proverbs 1:10).

It should also be understood that those three movements of sinners are more easily corrected in the order of their progression, but this fourth is more difficult to amend. Hence our Redeemer raises the girl in the house, the young man outside the gate, and Lazarus from the tomb, but does not raise the fourth dead person.

Alternatively: “Why did I not die in the womb?” That is: when the serpent’s suggestion conceived me, would that I had then recognized the death that would follow me, lest the suggestion drag me as far as delight and bind me more tightly to death.

It follows:

“Coming forth from the womb, why did I not perish at once?”

As if he were saying: Would that, when I came forth into external delight, I had recognized that I was being deprived of the inner light, and had at least fallen in that very delight, lest death punish me more severely through consent!

It follows:

“Why was I received upon the knees?”

As if he were saying: Would that consent had not received me subject to depraved senses, and that consent itself had not dragged me still more disastrously toward boldness!

It follows:

“Why was I suckled at the breasts?”

That is: would that, at least after perpetrating evil, I had wished to flatter myself, lest I bind myself to it so much more wickedly the more softly I cherished myself in it!

It follows:

### VERSE 13

“For now I would be sleeping and silent, and I would rest in my sleep.”

Humanity had been placed in paradise for this purpose: that, if it bound itself to its Creator, it might eventually pass without bodily death into the heavenly homeland of the angels, where it could neither sin nor die.

Humanity possessed this silent rest when, against its enemy, it received free choice of the will. But because it willingly succumbed to him, it immediately discovered within itself something that clamored against it. Hence Paul says: “I see another law in my members” (Romans 7:23). The very suggestion of the flesh is like a certain cry against the mind’s quiet, which humanity did not experience before the transgression.

It follows:

### VERSE 14

“With the kings and consuls of the earth.”

We rightly understand the kings as the spirits of the angels: the more familiarly they serve the Author of all things, the more fully they govern what has been subjected to them. They are appropriately called “consuls,” because, when we recognize the will of the Creator through their announcements, we undoubtedly find in them counsel against the distress of our tribulation.

Humanity would sleep with them because it would rest with them, if it had not wished to follow the tongue of the persuader.

Alternatively: The kings are the holy preachers of the Church, who know both how rightly to order those entrusted to them and how well to govern their own bodies. While they restrain the movements of desire within themselves, they reign over their subordinate thoughts by the law of virtue.

They are also rightly called “consuls of the earth,” because, once sins have been extinguished, they provide counsel for life. Through the counsel of their exhortation they draw earthly minds toward heavenly things. For a consul was the one who said: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give my judgment” (1 Corinthians 7:25).

It follows:

“Who build themselves solitudes.”

All who either desire unlawful things or wish to appear as something in this world are compressed within their hearts by dense tumult of thought. While they stir up throngs of desires within themselves, they trample down their prostrate minds beneath the foot of wretched activity.

But holy men, because they desire nothing of this world, are assuredly oppressed by no tumult of thoughts in their hearts. To build solitudes, therefore, is to drive the tumult of earthly desires from the heart’s secret place and, with a single intention toward the eternal homeland, to yearn for the love of inner rest.

Had he not driven all the tumult of thoughts from himself who said: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord” (Psalm 26:4)? And again: “Behold, I have gone far away in flight, and I remained in solitude” (Psalm 54:8). Jeremiah also says: “I sat alone because of the threat, for you filled me with denunciation” (Jeremiah 15:17).

It follows:

### VERSE 15

“With princes who possess gold and fill their houses with silver.”

Whom else does he call princes except the rulers of the holy Church? Divine providence continually appoints them in the place of the preachers who came before. Concerning them the Psalmist says to that same Church: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you,” and the rest (Psalm 44:17).

What, moreover, does he call gold except wisdom? As Solomon says: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Proverbs 21:20).

What are designated by houses except consciences? Hence it is said to a certain healed man: “Go to your house” (Matthew 9:6).

What is signified by silver except the divine utterances? Concerning them the Psalmist says: “The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, silver tested by fire” (Psalm 11:7).

For if our first parent had not been corrupted by the rot of sin, he would never have begotten children of Gehenna from himself. Instead, those who are now to be saved through redemption would have been born from him as the only elect. The holy man therefore looks upon these same elect and considers how he could have rested with them.

It follows:

### VERSE 16

“Or, like a hidden miscarriage, I would not have existed.”

A miscarriage is something that comes forth before the full time and, having immediately died, is hidden. He calls all those with whom he could have rested “miscarriages”: those who arose from the beginning of the world before the time of redemption, yet took care to put themselves to death with respect to this world.

Although they did not possess the tablets of the written Law, they were dead, as it were, from the womb, because they feared their Creator according to the natural law. That time, therefore, which, near the beginning of the world, brought forth our fathers dead to this age, was like a miscarrying womb. Abel, Enoch, and Noah were there; Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were there.

Because the multitude of the good produced from the beginning of the world is largely withdrawn from our knowledge, it is called “a hidden miscarriage.” For we must not believe that only as many righteous people existed up to the reception of the Law as Moses touched upon in his very brief account. It is said that they did not endure because, although a few are enumerated, the multitude of them is preserved in no written record of memory among us.

It follows:

“Or those who, having been conceived, did not see the light.”

Those who were born into this world after the reception of the Law were conceived for their Creator through the admonition of that same Law. Yet they did not see the light after being conceived, because they could not reach the coming of the Lord’s incarnation, although, awakened by the clear voices of the prophets, they faithfully believed in it.

The incarnate Lord says: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). And the Light himself says: “Many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Matthew 13:17).

It follows:

### VERSE 17

“There the wicked cease from turmoil.”

The hearts of sinners are oppressed by a heavy tumult of goading thoughts because the clamor of desires possesses them. But in this light the wicked ceased from turmoil, because the gentile peoples found the advent of the Mediator as the rest of their life, as Paul testifies when he says: “What Israel was seeking, it did not obtain; but the elect obtained it” (Romans 11:7).

In this light the wicked cease, when minds that had been perverse, having come to know the truth, flee the laborious desires of the world and submit to the tranquility of inner love. Hence the Light himself says: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:28–29).

It follows:

“There the weary rest from strength.”

All who are strong in this world are strong, as it were, through strength, not weary from strength. But those who are strengthened in the love of their Creator, the more they grow strong in the strength of God whom they desire, the more they fail with respect to their own strength.

Hence the Psalmist says: “My soul has failed for your salvation” (Psalm 118:81). And again: “My soul has desired and failed in the courts of the Lord” (Psalm 83:3). It is as though he plainly said: There the rest of light rewards those whom advancement, inwardly refreshing them here, makes weary.

It should be noted that he does not say “in this light,” but “there.” For he sees that this light contains the elect, and he recognizes it as our place. Hence the Psalmist says: “But you are the same, and your years will not fail. The children of your servants will dwell” (Psalm 101:28–29).

It follows:

### VERSE 18

“And those once bound are together without distress.”

Although no tumult of carnal desires possesses the righteous, the distress of their corruption nevertheless binds them, placed as they are in this life, with hard fetters. For it is written: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wisdom 9:15).

They endure one thing in mind and another in body, and every day they labor against themselves in inward conflict. We are therefore rightly called “bound,” because we do not yet have free movement of our desire toward God. Hence Paul says: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23).

He had seen that these bonds would be broken in the resurrection who said joyfully: “You have broken my bonds,” and the rest (Psalm 115:17).

It is rightly said, “those once bound,” because, when that joy which is always present is seen, everything that will be and passes away appears already to be past. For when the end of things is contemplated, everything that passes away is reckoned as though it had already existed.

It follows:

“They did not hear the voice of their exactor.”

That exactor is the importunate persuader who once gave the human race the coin of deception and therefore does not cease daily to demand the debt of death. Concerning him Truth says: “The judge will hand you over to the exactor” (Luke 12:58).

His voice is the temptation of miserable suggestion. We hear his voice when we are struck by temptation, but we do not heed it when we resist the tempter. The righteous did not heed his voice; indeed, although they hear his suggestion when tempted, they do not obey it, because they disdain to consent.

It follows:

### VERSE 19

“The small and the great are there, and the servant is free from his master.”

Because in this life there is a distinction of works, there will undoubtedly be in that life a distinction of dignities: just as here one surpasses another in merit, there one will surpass another in reward.

Hence Truth says: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John 14:2). Hence the Psalmist says: “Your eyes saw my unfinished state, and in your book they are all written” (Psalm 138:16).

For such is the power of that peace which unites us that each person rejoices in having received through another what he did not receive in himself.

## BOOK FIVE

### VERSE 20

For blessed Job, when contemplating the heavenly rest, had said: “The small and the great are there, and the servant is free from his master.” Immediately he adds: “Why is light given to the miserable?”

In Sacred Scripture, prosperity is sometimes designated by the name of light, while adversity is designated by the name of night. Hence the Psalmist says: “As is his darkness, so is his light” (Psalm 138:12).

Light is given to the miserable when those who, contemplating sublime things, recognize that they are miserable in this pilgrimage do not receive the splendor of passing prosperity; and when they mourn deeply because they are slow to return to their homeland, they are nevertheless compelled to bear the burdens of honor.

It follows:

“And life to those who are in bitterness of soul?”

All the elect are in bitterness of soul, because they do not cease to punish by weeping the things they have done wrong, or because they afflict themselves with heavy sorrow, since, cast far away from the face of their Creator, they are not yet in the joys of the eternal homeland.

Solomon aptly speaks of their heart: “The heart that knows the bitterness of its own soul will not share its joy with a stranger” (Proverbs 14:10).

It follows:

### VERSE 21

“Who wait for death, and it does not come.”

The saints desire to mortify themselves completely and to extinguish themselves from every life of temporal glory. Yet, often by the hidden judgments of God, they are compelled either to preside in governance or to be occupied with assigned honors. They endure the losses of their desires so that they may bring greater gains to others who have been converted.

It follows:

“As those who dig for a treasure.”

Those who dig for a treasure work more energetically as they approach the object of their digging. So those who fully desire their own mortification seek it as people digging for a treasure, and they labor more joyfully in that work insofar as they already regard the rewards as drawing near, like a treasure.

Hence Paul says: “Not abandoning our assembly, as is the custom of some, but comforting one another all the more as you see the day approaching” (Hebrews 10:25).

Alternatively: We die to the world if, abandoning visible things, we are hidden in invisible things. We dig for a treasure when we seek wisdom, concerning which Solomon says: “If you seek her like money and dig for her as for treasures” (Proverbs 2:4). He finds her easily who drives away from himself the mass of earthly thought.

It follows:

### VERSE 22

“And they rejoice greatly when they have found a tomb.”

Just as a body is hidden in a tomb, so the soul is hidden in divine contemplation. We still live for the world when we wander outwardly in mind; but we are dead and hidden in a tomb when, mortified externally, we are concealed in the secret place of inward contemplation.

Hence Paul says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3).

Alternatively: We joyfully seek a treasure in a tomb when, seeking wisdom, we turn over the pages of Sacred Scripture, and when we examine the examples of those who came before us. We draw joy, as it were, from a tomb because we find the riches of the mind among the dead.

It follows:

### VERSE 23

“For the man whose way is hidden, and whom God has surrounded with darkness?”

A man’s way is hidden from him because, although he already considers the quality of life in which he stands, he nevertheless does not know toward what end it is tending. Although he already desires heavenly things and seeks them with complete desire, he does not know whether he will remain in those same desires.

There is also another concealment of our life: sometimes, even regarding the things we rightly believe we are doing, we do not know whether they are right in the judgment of the strict Judge. Solomon testifies to this when he says: “There is a way that seems right to human beings, but its end leads to death” (Proverbs 14:12).

It follows:

“And God has surrounded him with darkness.”

A human being is surrounded with darkness because, although he burns with heavenly desire, he does not know inwardly what has been determined concerning him.

It follows:

### VERSE 24

“Before I eat, I sigh.”

To eat is for the soul to be nourished by contemplation of the heavenly light. He therefore sighs before eating because he is afflicted by the groaning of tribulation and afterward is satisfied by the refreshment of contemplation.

It follows:

“And my roaring is like waters overflowing.”

When waters overflow, they come with force and swell as their many currents increase. So, when the elect set the divine judgments before the eyes of their minds, when they tremble at the hidden sentence concerning themselves, when they recall their past deeds and grieve over them, and when they fear the future things they do not know, certain currents gather within them like waters. These flow into roars of sorrow as into the shores below.

It follows:

### VERSE 25

“For the fear that I feared has come upon me.”

The righteous therefore grieve and tremble, and torment themselves with great lamentation, because they fear being abandoned. Although they rejoice in correction, correction itself disturbs their trembling minds, lest the evil they endure be not the loving blow of discipline but the punishment of just vengeance.

As in the Psalmist: “Who knows the power of your anger?” (Psalm 89:11).

It follows:

### VERSE 26

“Have I not dissembled? Have I not been silent? Have I not rested? And indignation has come upon me.”

Although, wherever we may be placed, we sin by thinking, acting, and speaking, the mind is nevertheless carried away without restraint in these three ways when it is lifted up by the prosperity of this world. When the tongue is restrained by no one in the authority of speech, it runs more freely and recklessly down precipices.

But when holy men are supported by the power of this world, they restrain their hearts from contemplating their own glory, hold their tongues back from immoderate speech, and guard their actions from wandering restlessly. When power is possessed, it must be considered for usefulness and concealed for the sake of avoiding pride.

Alternatively: To be silent is to restrain the mind from the voice of earthly desires. Those rest who set aside the noise of earthly activities for the love of God. For they know that the mind is never lifted to heavenly things if it is continually occupied below by the tumult of cares.

What can an occupied mind obtain concerning God, when even in its free moments it struggles to grasp something of him? The Psalms rightly say: “Be still and see that I am God” (Psalm 45:11). For whoever neglects to be still for God hides from himself, by his own judgment, the light of God’s vision.

It follows:

“And indignation has come upon me.”

With great skill in teaching, he placed blows before righteous deeds, so that each person might consider what punishments await sinners afterward, if such powerful scourges chastise even the righteous here.

Hence Peter says: “And if the righteous scarcely will be saved, where will the impious and the sinner appear?” (1 Peter 4:18).

### CHAPTER IV

### VERSES 1–2

Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: “If we begin to speak to you, perhaps you will take it amiss.”

For in the Latin language, *Eliphaz* means “contempt of the Lord.” And what else do heretics do except, while holding false opinions about God, contemptuously despise him in their pride?

Eliphaz, who represents the type of heretics, begins by speaking gently. He is the first of the friends to speak, and, because he neglects the restraint of speech, he goes so far as to insult the afflicted man, saying: “The tiger perished because it had no prey” (Job 4:11).

Heretics fear exasperating their hearers at the beginning of their speech, so that they may be listened to attentively; and almost always the things they propose are flattering, while those they introduce afterward in their argument are harsh.

It follows:

### VERSE 4

“Behold, you have instructed many,” and the rest.

This was a man of great eminence, who, amid the care of his household, the guardianship of many possessions, affection for his children, and the demands of his labors, devoted himself to instructing others. He arranged temporal matters to be governed and proclaimed eternal things through preaching.

But whether they are heretics or any other perverse people, when they recount the good deeds of the righteous, they twist them into an argument for accusation. For it follows:

### VERSE 5

“But now the scourge has come upon you, and you have failed.”

But once the wicked have spoken of the good deeds of the righteous, the righteous person's life may be condemned as guilty by the testimony of its own tongue; they immediately turn even the good they recognize in other righteous people into an accumulation of reproach.

It follows:

### VERSE 6

“Where is your fear, your strength, your patience, and the perfection of your ways?”

He joins all these things to the preceding statement. Yet it must be carefully observed that, although he began inappropriately, he nevertheless recounts the order of things fittingly.

For he distinguished the life of blessed Job by enumerating its virtues in four ways, joining fear to strength, strength to patience, and patience to perfection. In the way of God, fear produces strength, as Solomon says: “In the fear of God is confidence of strength” (Proverbs 14:26). When our mind is joined to the Creator of all things by a right fear, it is raised above all things by a certain power.

Strength, however, is shown only in adversity. Therefore patience is immediately added, and directly after patience the perfection of the ways is introduced. For the person who is not impatient toward the imperfection of his neighbor is perfect.

It follows:

### VERSE 7

“Remember, I beg you: Who ever perished though innocent?” and the rest.

Often even the innocent perish here, but by perishing they are preserved for eternal glory. That the innocent perish here, the prophet affirms: “The righteous perishes, and no one takes it to heart” (Isaiah 57:1). Concerning the upright, Wisdom says: “He was taken away lest wickedness change his understanding” (Wisdom 4:11).

It follows:

### VERSES 8–9

“Rather, see those who work iniquity and sow sorrows, and reap them, perishing when God blows.”

To sow sorrows is to utter deceit, and to reap is to prevail by uttering it. Or certainly, they sow sorrows when they do perverse things, and they reap them when they are punished for that same perversity. The fruit of sorrow is the recompense of condemnation.

“Therefore,” he says, “they sow sorrows and reap them,” because what they do is wicked, and in that very wickedness they prosper, as the Psalmist says: “His ways are polluted at all times” (Psalm 9:25).

The blowing of God is called the vengeance of retribution. Thus it is rightly said that those who sow sorrows perish when God blows, because from the source from which they outwardly do perverse things, from within they are rightly struck.

To blow is spoken of as anger, because the one who is tranquil in himself appears turbulent to those who are perishing.

It follows:

### VERSE 10

“The roar of the lion and the voice of the lioness, and the teeth of the lion’s cubs are broken.”

What does he call the roar of the lion except, as we said a little earlier, the severity of the man? What does he call the voice of the lioness except the loquacity of his wife? What does he call the teeth of the lion’s cubs except the voracity of his children? Because the sons were killed while feasting, this is indicated by the gnashing of teeth.

Eliphaz rejoices—or, as another reading has it, exults—when all these things are broken, declaring them condemned by right. He redoubles the harshness of his rebuke when he adds:

### VERSE 11

“The tiger perished because it had no prey, and the lion’s cubs were scattered.”

Whom does he indicate by the name “tiger” except blessed Job, marked by signs of variety, or covered with the spots of pretense? Indeed, every hypocrite is a tiger, because while a clean outward color is produced by dissimulation, it is varied by the blackness of vices breaking through.

Often, while he exalts himself over the purity of chastity, he is defiled by the filth of avarice. This tiger seizes prey because he claims glory for himself from human approval. Since he is lifted up by praise that he has seized, he is, as it were, satiated by prey.

The translation of the Seventy Interpreters, however, does not have “tiger,” but “the ant-lion (*mirmicoleon*) perished.” The *mirmicoleon* is a very small animal hostile to ants. It is called in Latin “the lion of ants,” or “ant and lion.”

What does Eliphaz rebuke in blessed Job under the name *mirmicoleon* except fear and boldness? As if he were openly saying: “You were not struck unjustly; against the powerful you were timid, but against those subject to you you were bold.”

**TYPICALLY.** The lion signifies the Lord on account of strength, and the devil on account of savagery. Concerning the Lord: “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Revelation 5:5). Concerning the devil: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion” (1 Peter 5:8).

The holy Church is sometimes signified by the name “lioness,” because she is bold in adversity, as Job himself says: “The lioness did not pass through it” (Job 28:8). At other times Babylon is signified by it, on account of its monstrous savagery.

The lion’s cubs are all the reprobate, begotten for an iniquitous life through the error of evil spirits. Holy men carefully guard themselves lest that ancient enemy, the lion, kill them under some appearance of virtue; lest the voice of the lioness resound in their ears; lest the glory of Babylon turn their minds away from love of the heavenly homeland; and lest the teeth of the cubs bite them—that is, lest the persuasion of the reprobate grow strong in their hearts.

But heretics are already, as it were, secure concerning their sanctity, because they suppose that by the merits of their life they have surpassed everything. Under the name “tiger,” too, he not incongruously signified, on account of the variety of multiform cunning, the one whom he had earlier signified by the lion. For Satan sometimes persuades the minds of fools gently, and sometimes drives them toward guilt by terrifying them.

Likewise, he is signified by the *mirmicoleon*, because he is a lion to the carnal but an ant to the spiritual.

It follows:

### VERSE 12

“Moreover, a hidden word was spoken to me.”

Heretics pretend that they hear a hidden word, so that they may cast a certain reverence for their preaching over the minds of their hearers. To be able to display marvelous things, they always seek what is new, as Solomon says: “Stolen waters are sweeter,” and the rest (Proverbs 9:17).

**TYPICALLY.** The hidden Word is called the invisible Son, concerning whom John says: “In the beginning was the Word,” and the rest (John 1:1). This hidden Word is said to come to the minds of the elect when the power of the only-begotten Son is revealed to believers.

The hidden word may also be understood as the intimate address of inward inspiration, concerning which John says: “His anointing teaches you about everything” (1 John 2:7). This inspiration, touching the human mind, raises it up and inflames it through inward desires.

To hear the hidden word, therefore, is to perceive in the heart the speech of the Holy Spirit. This cannot be known except by the one by whom it can be possessed. It is called a hidden word because what some undoubtedly perceive in their hearts is unknown to the greater part of humanity.

Or certainly, the breath of the Holy Spirit is a hidden word, because it can be felt but cannot be expressed by the noise of speech.

It follows:

“And my ear received, as though furtively, the veins of its whisper.”

He furtively received the veins of the divine whisper who, in order to perceive knowledge of its power, abandoned the door of public preaching and sought cracks of perverse understanding, concerning which the Lord says: “He who does not enter by the door into the sheepfold of the sheep is a thief and a robber” (John 10:1).

**TYPICALLY.** The ear of the heart furtively receives the veins of the heavenly whisper because the inspired mind suddenly and secretly recognizes the subtlety of inward speech. Withdrawn from visible things, it beholds invisible things; filled with invisible things, it perfectly despises visible things.

The whisper of the hidden Word is this very speech of inward inspiration. The veins of the whisper are called the origins of the causes by which this inspiration itself is led to the mountain. For it is as though he opens the vein of his whisper when he secretly reveals to us the ways by which it comes to the ear of our understanding. Sometimes he pierces us through love, sometimes through fear.

Alternatively: One who whispers speaks secretly and does not express his voice, but imitates it. When the Almighty reveals himself to us through the cracks of contemplation, he does not speak to us but whispers, because he does not disclose himself fully; nevertheless, he reveals something of himself to the human mind.

Then he no longer whispers but speaks, when his definite appearance is revealed to us. Hence the Lord says: “I will announce the Father to you openly” (John 16:25). And John says: “We shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

It follows:

### VERSE 13

“In the dread of a nocturnal vision, when sleep usually overtakes human beings.”

In a nocturnal vision things are seen uncertainly. Heretics therefore claim that they perceived the cracks of the whisper in the fear of a nocturnal vision, because, in order to show others that what they teach is lofty, they declare that they themselves can scarcely grasp it. From this, however, it must be inferred how the things they themselves saw uncertainly can be certain for those who hear them.

**TYPICALLY.** The terror of the nocturnal vision is the fear of hidden contemplation. For the more highly the human mind is raised to consider eternal things, the more gravely it trembles and fears concerning temporal deeds.

It follows:

“When sleep usually overtakes human beings.”

As if the heretics were saying: “While human beings sleep below, we remain awake to perceive heavenly things.”

Figuratively, sleep is understood in three ways. Sometimes it means the death of the flesh, as Paul says: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep,” and shortly afterward: “So also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus” (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14).

Sometimes it means the torpor of negligence, as in: “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Romans 13:11), and: “Awake, you righteous” (1 Corinthians 15:34).

Sometimes, when earthly desires have been trampled underfoot, it means the rest of life, as in: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song of Songs 5:2). Whoever desires to perform the things of the world is, as it were, awake; whoever seeks inward rest and flees the tumult of this world is, as it were, asleep.

Since inward knowledge is in no way conceived unless one ceases from outward entanglement, it is rightly said here: “When sleep usually overtakes human beings,” as the Lord says: “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24).

It follows:

### VERSE 14

“Fear seized me, and trembling, and all my bones were terrified.”

Because heretics desire to appear remarkable on account of the loftiness of their teaching, they are as though afraid of what they say.

**FIGURATIVELY.** What should we understand by bones except strong deeds? Concerning them the prophet says: “The Lord guards all their bones” (Psalm 33:21). It is as though he were saying: “While perceiving the secrets of inward subtlety, from the very place where I believed myself to stand firm before myself, I staggered before the sight of the Judge.”

For when we contemplate the strictness of justice, we rightly fear even concerning the very works that we thought we had performed strongly.

It follows:

### VERSE 15

“And when the spirit passed before me, in my presence, the hairs of my flesh bristled.”

To make it appear that they had known incomprehensible things, he says that the spirit did not stand but passed before him.

Mystically, the spirit passes while we are present when we recognize invisible things and yet see them not solidly but fleetingly. The spirit therefore does not stand but passes, because the mind, fixed in the sweetness of inward contemplation, does not remain long; soon it is called back to itself, struck back by the very immensity of the light.

The hairs of the flesh are any superfluous things belonging to human corruption, or thoughts of the former life. When the spirit passes, therefore, the hairs of the flesh bristle, because before the force of compunction superfluous thoughts flee, so that nothing fleeting is pleasing. The severity of inward visitation, having breathed upon the mind, inflames it even against itself.

It follows:

### VERSE 16

“He stood, whose face I did not recognize.” Heretics pretend that they saw an unfamiliar face, so that they may show themselves to be known to him who cannot be known by the human mind.

**TYPICALLY.** We say “a certain one” only of someone whom we either do not wish or are unable to identify. But the sense in which “a certain one” is said here is explained immediately by what follows: “whose face I did not recognize.” For when the mind, setting aside all things, considers the image, appearances, and substance of realities—always as they are, identical with themselves and present everywhere—it beholds this. Even if it has not yet grasped what this is, it has certainly recognized what it is not.

It is well said: “He stood.” Every creature, since it was made from nothing, tends through itself toward nothing. To stand, therefore, belongs solely to the Creator, through whom all passing things pass away, and in whom some things are held fast so that they do not pass away.

It follows: “An image before my eyes.” Heretics often fashion for themselves an imaginary image of God, whom they cannot behold spiritually; and they claim to hear his voice as though it were a light breeze. They rejoice as though they were more familiar than others with knowing his secrets. For they do not teach what God proclaims publicly, but what, as if secretly, breathes into their ears.

**MYSTICALLY.** The Son is the image of the Father, as Moses says concerning the formation of the human being: “He made him in his own image” (Gen. 1:27). And the Apostle says: “Who is the radiance of his glory and the likeness of his substance” (Heb. 1:3). Therefore, whenever eternity is discerned insofar as the capacity of our weakness permits, his image is set before the eyes of our mind.

But because, when we direct our attention to the Father, we see him insofar as we have received him through his image—that is, through the Son—the Lord himself says: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6).

It follows: “And I heard a voice as of a gentle breeze.” What is signified by the voice of a gentle breeze except knowledge of the Holy Spirit? Proceeding from the Father and receiving from what belongs to the Son, he is poured delicately into the knowledge of our weakness. Since the human mind, however greatly it strains with its powers, scarcely grasps the outermost aspects of inner realities, it is rightly said here: “And I heard a voice as of a gentle breeze.” It follows:

### VERSE 17

“Will a human being be justified in comparison with God?” Human righteousness, when compared with divine righteousness, is unrighteousness. A lamp is seen to shine in darkness, but when placed in the sun’s radiance it is darkened.

He rightly adds: “Or will a man be purer than his Maker?” A man considers himself purer than his Maker if, in response to the scourge, he prepares a complaint against him, and thus undoubtedly places beneath himself the one whose judgment he rebukes on account of his affliction. He who wondrously made the human being from nothing does not afflict what he has made unjustly. Therefore the person who thinks himself righteous is wrong, because he does not know the rule of supreme righteousness.

It follows:

### VERSE 18

“Behold, those who serve him are not steadfast.” Although the angelic nature, by cleaving to its Creator in contemplation, remains immutably in its own state, nevertheless, precisely because it is created, it possesses within itself the alternation of mutability. To be changed is to go from one thing to another, and thus not to be stable within oneself. Only the incomprehensible nature does not know movement; it cannot be changed from what is always the same.

He speaks of this mutability in the angels, although they are immutable in the sense that they are bound by ties to him who is always the same.

It follows: “And he found perversity in his angels.” This is said concerning the apostate spirits. In a wondrous manner, almighty God created the nature of the highest spirits good but mutable, so that those who did not wish to remain might fall, while those who persisted in their created condition might remain in it all the more worthily because they stood by their own choice.

It follows:

### VERSE 19

“How much more those who dwell in houses of clay.” We dwell in houses of clay because we subsist in earthly bodies, as Paul says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7). And again: “We know that if our earthly house is dissolved,” and so forth (2 Cor. 5:1).

It follows: “Who have an earthly foundation.” The earthly foundation is the substance of the flesh, as the Psalmist says: “My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret, and my substance in the lower parts of the earth” (Ps. 138:15).

It follows: “They will be consumed as by a moth.” A moth is born from clothing, and in being born it corrupts the very clothing from which it arises. The flesh, as it were, is a kind of clothing of the soul. From it, surely, carnal temptation arises like a moth, and through it the soul, torn apart, arrives at destruction.

It is as though he said: If those spirits cannot be immutable who are not weighed down by any weakness of the flesh, with what presumption do human beings confidently suppose that they can remain steadfast in goodness?

The angels may also be understood as holy teachers, according to the prophet’s words: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2:7). They cannot be entirely without fault while they walk the path of the present life, however brightly they may shine in virtue, because their steps are touched either by the mud of illicit action or by the dust of thought.

They dwell in houses of clay who delight in this seductive life of the flesh. Paul had rejected dwelling in it when he said: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). “Those who serve him are not steadfast,” because when the mind strives toward higher things, it is scattered by thought of its own flesh.

Thus perversity is found even in angels when the burden of a deceptive life sometimes weighs down those who proclaim the truth. It is as though he said: If the elect are struck by the iniquity of this world, by what blows are the reprobate pierced?

A moth causes damage, and damage that is not customary. Thus the minds of the wicked, because they neglect to consider their losses, lose their integrity as though unaware of it. They lose innocence from the heart, truth from the mouth, continence from the flesh, and, as time advances, the very span of life. Yet they do not perceive these losses.

It follows:

### VERSE 20

“From morning until evening they will be cut down.” The sinner is cut down from morning until evening when, from the beginning to the end of his life, he is wounded by the commission of iniquity, as the Psalmist says: “Men of blood will not halve their days” (Ps. 54:24).

It follows: “And because no one understands, they will perish forever.” “No one understands” means either none of those who perish, or none of those who perish while imitating the ways of the perishing. Thus it is said: “The just man has perished, and there is no one who reflects” (Isa. 57:1).

“Morning” may also signify prosperity, and “evening” the adversity of this world. From morning, therefore, until evening the reprobate are cut down, because they waste away in prosperity through wantonness and, in adversity, rise up into madness through impatience. Fault would never cut them down from morning until evening if they either regarded prosperity as nourishment or considered adversity to be the cutting of their wound.

It follows:

### VERSE 21

“But those who remain will be taken away from them.” By “those who remain” he means the despised of this world, whom the present age does not choose for any use of glory but leaves behind as insignificant and unworthy. Yet the Lord does not disdain to choose these people, as Paul bears witness: “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise”; and: “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1:27).

It follows: “They will die, and not in wisdom.” Here, when Eliphaz had spoken of the elect—“those who remain will be taken away from them”—and immediately added, “They will die, and not in wisdom,” he returns at once to what he had said more wisely concerning the reprobate: “And because no one understands,” and so forth.

The reprobate flee both death and wisdom alike, but they entirely abandon wisdom, while they do not escape the snares of death. And although, when they were about to die, they could have lived by dying, because they fear death, which will certainly come, they lose both life and wisdom.

It follows:

## CHAPTER FIVE

### VERSE 1

“Call, then, if there is anyone who will answer you.” Almighty God often abandons in distress the prayer of one who despises his commandments in tranquility. Hence it is written: “Whoever turns away his ear so as not to hear the law, his prayer will be accursed” (Prov. 28:9).

For us, to call is to entreat God with humble prayer. For God to answer is to grant effectiveness to prayers. It is as though he said: However loudly you cry out in affliction, you do not have God answering you, because your voice in tribulation does not find the one whom your mind despised in tranquility.

It follows: “And turn to one of the saints.” It is as though he were mocking him and saying: You are also unable to find helpers among the saints in your affliction, although you did not wish to have them as companions in your joy.

It follows:

### VERSE 2

“Anger kills the foolish man.” This statement would indeed be true if it had not been spoken against the patience of so great a man. For it is written: “But you judge with tranquility” (Wis. 12:18).

We should know, however, that whenever we restrain the turbulent movements of the soul through the power of gentleness, we try to return to the likeness of the Creator. We lose this likeness when anger disturbs the tranquility of the mind.

Through anger wisdom is lost, as it is written: “Anger rests in the bosom of a fool” (Eccles. 7:10). Through anger justice is abandoned, as it is written: “The anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God” (Jas. 1:20). Through anger the light of truth is lost, as it is written: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. 4:26).

Anger is conquered in two ways. The first is to place before oneself every insult that one may be able to endure. The second is, when we observe the faults of others, to consider our own sins—those by which we have sinned against others.

We should also know that there is one kind of anger aroused by impatience and another formed by zeal. The former arises from vice, the latter from virtue. Of the latter the Psalmist says: “Be angry and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5). Of the latter Solomon says: “Anger is better than laughter” (Eccles. 7:4). Of the former it is said: “Anger kills the foolish man” (Job 5:2).

It is as though he said: Anger arising from zeal disturbs the wise, but anger arising from vice slaughters the fool.

It follows: “And envy kills the little one.” We cannot envy anyone except those whom we think better than ourselves in some respect. The one killed by envy is therefore “little,” because he himself bears witness that he is less than the person whose success torments him. If he were not inferior, he would not grieve over another’s good.

Hence it is written: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wis. 2:24). For when envy has consumed the mind, it destroys everything good that it finds, as Solomon says: “The health of the heart is the life of the flesh, but envy is the rottenness of the bones” (Prov. 14:30).

Therefore, whoever desires to be wholly free from the plague of envy should love the inheritance that is not diminished by the number of coheirs. The diminution of envy is thus an affective impulse pressing toward inner sweetness, while its complete death is perfect love of eternity. For when a person desires nothing earthly, there is nothing that can oppose his charity toward his neighbor.

## BOOK SIX

[Col. 0155]

[Col. 0155D] ### VERSE 3

“I saw the foolish man with a firm root, and immediately I cursed his beauty.” The foolish man was the Jewish people, who rejected the very incarnation of eternal Wisdom. It grew strong as though with a firm root because, by putting to death in time the Life who had chosen it, it overcame him.

But Eliphaz despises this people by cursing it, because, in truth, all the heretics whom we have said are represented by the friends of blessed Job, while boasting of the name of Christ, condemn the faithlessness of the Jews on the authority of Scripture.

**MORALLY.** The fool is fixed in the earth as though by a firm root because he is made solid in earthly love with all his desires. Those who behold the strong glory of such a person immediately consider what punishment follows that glory, and inwardly despise him in silent thought.

To curse the beauty of the fool is to judge his glory in light of the damnation that has been considered. “Immediately,” as though he said: I did not delay in cursing the beauty of the fool, because when I saw it, I also saw at once the punishment that would follow. I would not have cursed anyone immediately if some delight in that person’s glory had held me.

It follows:

### VERSE 4

“Let his sons be far from salvation.” His sons are all those who are generated by the preaching of his faithlessness. They are far from salvation because, even if they receive temporal life without affliction, they are punished with a more grievous eternal retribution.

As is said of these same sons: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who traverse sea and land to make one proselyte; and when he has been made, you make him a son of Gehenna twice as much as yourselves” (Matt. 23:15).

**MORALLY.** The sons of the fool are those who, by imitating him, are nourished on the ambition of this age. They are made farther from salvation insofar as they are struck by no weakness in the perpetration of their wickedness.

It follows: “And they will be crushed at the gate, and there will be no one to rescue them.” Who should be understood by the name of “the gate” except the Mediator between God and human beings? He says: “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10:9).

The sons of this fool are therefore cast outside the gate and crushed at the gate, because the wicked descendants of the Jews flourished in observance of the law before the Mediator’s coming, but in the very presence of our Redeemer they fell, rejected from the service of the divinity on account of the merits of their faithlessness. There is no one to rescue them, because, when they tried to destroy the Redeemer himself by persecuting him, they concealed from themselves the remedy of deliverance that had been offered to them.

**MORALLY.** Just as the entrance to a city is called a gate, so the day of judgment is the gate of the kingdom, and through it all the elect enter into the glory of their heavenly homeland. Hence Solomon says: “Her husband is noble at the gate, when he sits with the elders of the land” (Prov. 31:23). And again: “Give her from the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her at the gates” (Prov. 31:31).

The sons of this fool are therefore exalted before the gate but crushed at the gate, because lovers of this age are proud in the present life, but at the very entrance to the kingdom they are struck by eternal punishment. Eternal Truth rescues those whom it disciplines amid temporal prosperity. Whoever now refuses to be pressed down will then be unable to be rescued.

It follows:

### VERSE 5

“His harvest the hungry will eat.” The harvest of this fool was the sayings of the sacred law. The hungry will eat it, because the gentile people learned the words of the law by understanding them, while the Jewish people labored at them without understanding. Hence Truth says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6).

**MORALLY.** The hungry person also has a harvest when some wicked person receives the gift of right understanding. The hungry person eats it because the one who breathes after God with holy desires learns what he hears and does what he has learned. When wicked teachers are refreshed by upright preaching, what else is happening than that fools are filled with grain?

It follows: “And the armed man will seize him.” The ancient enemy seized the Jewish people as an armed man, because through deceitful suggestion he extinguished the life of faith in them as though with darts.

**MORALLY.** The ancient enemy is conquered as unarmed when, suggesting open evils, he tries to destroy all good things in the human mind at once. But he comes armed when, leaving some good things untouched, he secretly corrupts others.

It follows: “And the thirsty drink his riches.” The thirsty drink the riches of this fool because the minds of the gentiles are watered by the streams of sacred speech, which the Jewish people possess in proud display. Hence the prophet says to them: “All you who are thirsty, come to the waters,” and so forth (Isa. 55:1).

**MORALLY.** Often the fool possesses a fountain of inward liquid but does not drink, because he receives the talent for understanding yet disdains to know the judgments of truth by reading. The words of sacred speech are also the riches of the mind; but the fool looks upon these riches with his eyes and scarcely takes them up for use in the mouth of his mind.

For he makes no effort, through the devotion of love, to grasp the words. Another person, by contrast, is thirsty, and often, by studying the instruction of divine law, comes at last to understand what the intellectually gifted person fails to know through negligence. Hence Solomon says: “The lizard grasps with its hands, and it dwells in kings’ palaces” (Prov. 30:21). For very often birds, whose wings lift them for flight, remain among thorns.

It follows:

### VERSE 6

“Nothing on earth happens without cause.” The sluggish person often receives intelligence for this reason: that he may be punished more justly for his negligence. He scorns to know what he could have attained without labor. The diligent person, on the other hand, is pressed by slowness of understanding so that he may find greater rewards in recompense, insofar as he labors more intensely in the pursuit of discovery.

It follows: “And suffering does not come forth from the ground.” Suffering comes forth, as it were, from the ground when a human being, created in the image of God, is scourged through insensible things. But because visible scourges proceed from the hidden merits of minds, suffering does not come forth from the ground in the sense that our wickedness demands that we be struck by insensible things.

Punishment does not arise from the creature that strikes; it undoubtedly arises from the one that, by sinning, has extorted the power to strike.

It follows:

### VERSE 7

“Human beings are born for labor, and birds for flying.” A human being is born for labor because the one endowed with reason recognizes that it is entirely impossible for him to pass through the time of his pilgrimage without groaning. Yet when the flesh is afflicted by scourges, the mind is lifted toward higher things, as Paul bears witness: “Although our outward person is being corrupted, yet the inward person is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4:16).

The mind flies upward to the highest things from the very place where the flesh labors more harshly in the lowest. The term “human being” may also signify the life of the carnal, as Paul says: “Since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not human beings and walking according to the human way?” (1 Cor. 3:3).

In this life, therefore, a human being is born for labor because each carnal person pursues vices against himself and afflicts himself with the weight of his desires. The more greedily a person desires the good things of this world, the more truly he experiences its evils. Conversely, the mind withdraws itself from the labor of affliction insofar as hope lifts it toward the highest things.

Was Paul not born like a bird for flying, when, enduring so many adversities, he said: “Our citizenship is in heaven”? (Phil. 3:20).

It follows:

[Col. 0159B] ### VERSE 8

“Therefore I will entreat the Lord, and I will set forth my speech before God.” It is as though he openly said: I pray to the one through whom I know these things have been allotted.

It follows:

### VERSE 9

“Who does great things.” Who could be sufficient to investigate the wonders of almighty God? He created all things from nothing; he arranged the very structure of the world with wondrous power; the heavens are suspended above the air, and the earth is balanced above the abyss.

He rightly added: “And unsearchable.” It would have been less remarkable to do great things if what had been done could nevertheless have been investigated.

It follows: “And marvelous things without number.” His greatness would be less if the few things he had made were unsearchable. But amid these matters we must understand that divine miracles should always be considered through study, yet never dissected by the intellect.

For it often happens that when some people consider the bodies of the dead reduced to dust and cannot gather from reason the power of resurrection, they despair that these bodies can return to their former state.

It follows:

### VERSE 10

“He gives rain upon the face of the earth,” and so forth. Almighty God gives rain to the earth when he drenches the dry hearts of the gentiles with the grace of heavenly preaching. He waters everything with water because, by filling the lost human being with the Spirit, he transforms barrenness for fruitfulness, as Truth says of itself: “Whoever drinks the water,” and so forth (John 4:13).

The term “the whole” signifies the human being, because in him the true form and great sharing of the whole universe are displayed. Hence Truth says to the disciples: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15).

The term “the whole” can also be understood here in another way. When God calls rich and poor, strong and weak, wise and foolish spirits to the knowledge of himself, he waters the whole with water.

The term “all” may also designate the very differences of character. One person is lifted up by pride, another inflamed by lust, another pants after avarice. Yet God waters all with water because he shapes the power of his word in each person according to the diversity of character, so that each one finds in his speech that by which he may bring forth the necessary seed of virtue.

It follows:

### VERSE 11

“Who sets the humble on high and raises the mourners to safety.” The humble are set on high because those who are now despised for the love of God will then come as judges with God. Hence the Lord said: “You who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty,” and so forth (Matt. 19:28).

Then the Lord will raise the mourners, because those who, in longing for him, flee prosperity and endure the tortures of their persecutors will then receive a higher well-being in proportion to the devotion with which they now die to all the joys of the world.

Hence Solomon says: “The heart that knows the bitterness of its own soul will not share its joy with a stranger” (Prov. 14:10).

There is also no obstacle to understanding this of God’s elect in the present life. The humble are set on high because, when they prostrate themselves in humility, they pass beyond all temporal things through the judgment of a lofty mind.

Let us look at the humble Paul. He says: “We do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord; and ourselves as your servants through Christ” (2 Cor. 4:5). Let us see him already set on high: “Do you not know that we will judge angels?” (1 Cor. 6:3). And again: “He raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places” (Eph. 2:6).

The Lord also raises the mourners to safety when he lifts his afflicted ones to the glory of true joy through steadfastness. They are raised to safety, not to madness, because, established in good works, they rejoice in their firmness in the Lord.

Some people commit iniquities and nevertheless do not cease rejoicing. Of them it is said: “Who rejoice when they have done evil,” and so forth (Prov. 2:14). These are certainly not raised to safety but to madness: they grow proud when they ought to be afflicted.

It follows:

### VERSE 12

“He frustrates the thoughts of the wicked, so that their hands cannot accomplish what they had begun.” The minds of the reprobate are always intent upon perverse thoughts, but heavenly providence often opposes them. Although they do not correct the wickedness of their counsel even when broken by adversities, their strength is nevertheless restrained so that they cannot prevail against the good.

It follows:

### VERSE 13

“He catches the wise in their own craftiness and frustrates the counsels of the wicked.” The Lord catches the wise in their own craftiness when he preserves human actions in accordance with his plans even when those actions resist him.

The brothers of Joseph craftily attempted to change God’s plan. But by divine judgment they served, through their resistance, the very thing they tried to avoid. Joseph was sold by them so that he would not be worshiped (Gen. 37:28). But he was worshiped precisely because he was sold. Thus the divine plan is fulfilled while it is being avoided; human wisdom is caught while it resists.

The Lord also catches the wise in their craftiness when he turns even the unbelief that has burned against him toward the service of his compassion and the increase of our salvation. Hence the Psalmist says: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his purposes” (Ps. 110:2). Hence Solomon says: “There is no wisdom, no prudence, no counsel against the Lord” (Prov. 21:30).

It follows:

### VERSE 14

“By day they will encounter darkness, and at midday they will grope as though in the night.” They encounter darkness by day when, in the very presence of truth, they are blinded by the error of faithlessness.

The persecutors of our Redeemer, although they saw the miracles of divine power, nevertheless doubted his divinity. They therefore suffered darkness in the daytime, because they lost their sight in the light. Hence it is said concerning Judea: “The sun went down while it was still day” (Jer. 15:9).

Again the prophet says: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night? Morning comes, and also night” (Isa. 21:11–12). The watchman comes from the night because the protector of the human race appeared openly in the flesh, yet Judea, oppressed by the darkness of its faithlessness, did not recognize him.

A new light also shone upon the world through his presence, yet ancient blindness remained in the hearts of unbelievers. The Jews saw the manifest miracles of God, but still sought him as though groping when they said: “How long will you take away our souls? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (John 10:24).
