**MORALLY.** When the mind of wicked people is distressed by another’s improvement, it is darkened by the ray of light. They grope at midday as though in the night because, unable to accuse the good that they see, blinded by malice they seek to accuse the evil that they do not see.

They openly see the good in their neighbors, but investigate whatever evils may lie hidden. This is well expressed when the Sodomites, with the angels protecting Lot, could not find the door of his house.

It follows:

### VERSE 15

“But he will save the needy from the sword of their mouth, and the poor from the hand of the violent.” He is the poor man of whom Paul says: “For your sake he became poor, although he was rich” (2 Cor. 8:9).

The sword of the mouth may signify the tongue of the accusing Hebrews, of whom the Psalmist says: “The sons of men— their teeth are weapons,” and so forth (Ps. 56:5). They themselves cried out: “Crucify, crucify!” (John 19:6).

By “the hand of the violent” is signified the very gentile power that crucified him and carried out in deed the cries of the Hebrews in the death of the Redeemer. Our Redeemer endured both the strength of the gentiles and the tongue of the Hebrews in the humility of his death, but by the power of his divinity he overcame them by rising again.

**MORALLY.** The poor person is anyone who is not proud in himself. Hence Truth says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” and so forth (Matt. 5:3). The sword of the mouth is the wickedness of persuasion; the hand of the violent is the adversity of power.

It is as though he said: The Lord also strengthens the minds of human beings within themselves, so that neither the enticements of persuasion draw them into wickedness nor the pains of punishment break them.

It follows:

### VERSE 16

“And there will be hope for the needy.” When the poor man has been saved, the needy receives hope, because, when the flesh of the Lord rose again, every believer grew strong in confidence in eternal life. Hope lifts the soul toward eternity, and therefore it does not feel the external evils that it endures.

It follows: “But iniquity will draw in its mouth.” Iniquity still opens its mouth wide because the tongue of the human race does not cease attacking it with the insults of unbelievers. But then it will draw in its mouth when, through punishment, it closes what it was unwilling to close through discipline.

Alternatively: When the miracle of the Lord’s resurrection became manifest and a great multitude of unbelievers believed, they ceased from the insults and reproaches directed against their Redeemer. The mouth that they had opened to mock God they contracted by believing.

**MORALLY.** Now the wicked disparage the good, and what they neglect to do rightly they do not cease to tear apart through slander. But then iniquity will draw in its mouth when it recognizes how great a glory the just desire as their recompense. Then the tongue of the wicked will be bound for the recompense of deserved punishments.

It follows:

### VERSE 17

“Blessed is the man who is corrected by the Lord.” The first virtue is that sins should not be committed but avoided. The second is at least to correct sins once committed. Yet often we not only fail to avoid impending faults, but also do not recognize those we have committed.

Nevertheless, a corrupt mind is touched by a blow so that it may be exercised, in order that the person who, secure in his own uprightness, has lost his proper standing may, once afflicted, consider where he lies. Hence Solomon says: “The Lord chastises the one whom he loves, and he scourges every son whom he accepts” (Prov. 3:12).

It follows: “Therefore do not reject the correction of the Lord.” The person who is struck because of guilt but slips into complaint about his being struck rejects the Lord’s correction, because he accuses the Lord of treating him unjustly.

Those who are struck not to purge a crime but to test their strength, however, are not rightly said to reject the Lord’s correction when they inquire into the cause of their being struck, because they strive to find within themselves what they do not know.

It follows:

### VERSE 18

“For he wounds and heals; he strikes, and his hands will heal.” Almighty God wounds those whom he intends to lead back to salvation in two ways.

Sometimes he strikes the flesh, and the hardness of the mind melts in fear of him. He therefore recalls people to salvation by wounding them when he afflicts his elect outwardly so that they may live inwardly. Hence through Moses he says: “I kill,” and so forth (Deut. 32:39).

At other times he inflicts wounds inwardly, because he strikes the hardness of our mind with desire for him. Yet he heals by striking, because with the dart of his terror he calls us, pierced through, to an awareness of righteousness. Hence the bride says: “I am wounded by love” (Song 2).

It follows:

### VERSE 19

“In six tribulations he will deliver you, and in the seventh evil will not touch you.” The number six signifies the activity and course of the present life. On the sixth day he completed all things, creating the human being, and rested in himself. Therefore the number seven signifies rest.

The Father’s compassion wears us down through the discipline and labor of the present life, but at the coming of judgment it hides us from the scourge, so that it may then present us with salvation in proportion to the severity with which the scourges now cut us.

It follows:

### VERSE 20

“In famine he will rescue you from death, and in war from the hand of the sword.” Just as bodily famine is the withdrawal of the body’s support, so famine of the mind is the silence of divine speech. Hence it is rightly said through the prophet: “I will send famine upon the land” (Ezek. 14:13)—not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God.

We suffer war when we are attacked by the temptations of our flesh. Concerning this the Psalmist says: “You have overshadowed my head on the day of battle” (Ps. 139:8).

Since the reprobate, while they languish from famine of the word, are also pierced by the sword of battle, the Lord makes the minds of his elect strong against bodily temptations while he refreshes them with the nourishment of his word.

It follows:

### VERSE 21

“You will be hidden from the scourge of the tongue.” The scourge of the tongue is the reproach of illicit insult. The wicked strike the good with the scourge of the tongue because they persecute their works with ridicule. Hence it is written: “He himself will deliver me from the snare of the hunters,” and so forth (Ps. 90:3).

The holy soul is hidden from the scourge of the tongue because, while it is in this world, it does not seek the honor of praise and does not feel the insults of detraction.

It follows: “And you will not fear calamity when it comes.” Holy men possess nourishment against famine of the divine word, the shield of continence against the sword of battle, the protection of patience against the scourge of the tongue, and the help of inner love against the loss caused by outward calamity. The more numerous the ways in which the crafty enemy tests them, the richer the soldiers of God become in divine virtues through their vigilance.

The scourge of the tongue may also be understood as the sentence of ultimate punishment, because the strict Judge will say to the reprobate: “Depart from me,” and so forth (Matt. 25:41). But every just person will then be comforted amid such strictness of judgment by the gentle voice of the Judge, when he says: “I was hungry, and you gave me food,” and so forth (Matt. 25:3); and: “Come, blessed,” and so forth (Matt. 25:34).

It follows:

### VERSE 22

“In devastation and famine you will laugh.” Then famine will kill the reprobate because the Redeemer will hide his face from them. For he said of himself: “I am the living bread,” and so forth (John 6:51). And it is written: “Let the impious be taken away, lest he see the glory of God.”

Devastation torments because Gehenna burns. Hence the Psalmist says: “You will place them like an oven of fire,” and so forth (Ps. 10:10). But then the just will laugh because, when extreme vengeance strikes all the wicked, he will rejoice in the glory of the Lord as a worthy recompense. Hence the Psalmist says: “The just will see and fear,” and so forth (Ps. 51:8).

It follows: “And you will not fear the beasts of the earth.” The crafty adversary is called a beast of the earth because, at the time of death, he rages with violent savagery to seize the souls of sinners. Yet it is said concerning the Church: “The evil beast will not pass through it” (Isa. 35:9).

Those who fear the beast of the earth at death are the ones who, while living, do not fear the power of their Creator. Holy men, because they submit themselves from the depths of their being to divine fear, cast away every burden of fear concerning the adversary’s coming.

Hence the Psalmist prays, saying: “Lest at any time he seize my soul like a lion” (Ps. 7:3). It is as though he said: Because you are now overcome by the enemy’s flattering, you will not afterward fear him when he rages.

### Verse 23

“But with the stones of the regions your covenant.” What else, then, are the stones of the regions but the chosen members of the Churches? To them it is said: “You also, like living stones, are being built up” (1 Peter 2:5). Of them the Church is promised: “Behold, I will lay your stones in order” (Isaiah 54:11). Whoever therefore lives rightly joins himself by covenant to the stones of the regions; without doubt, he binds his life to the imitation of the saints who went before him.

It follows: “And the beasts of the earth will be peaceful toward you.” He does not say *pacatae* (“pacified”), but *pacificae* (“peace-making”), because they do not merely possess peace but make peace.

The beasts of the earth therefore become peace-making toward the elect, because when evil spirits press down noble hearts by opposing them, they nevertheless drive those hearts, against their will, toward the love of the Lord. The more laboriously the afflicted mind lives in this sorrowful exile, the more intensely it directs itself toward a return to the eternal homeland.

The beasts of the earth may also be understood as the movements of the flesh. By suggesting irrational things, these movements assail our mind and rise up against us in beastly fashion. Yet the heart is restrained under the divine law even when the impulses of the flesh subside; and although they roar in order to tempt us, they nevertheless do not rise to the fury of open bites, as it were, so as to reach the accomplishment of deeds. They are therefore peace-making, because although the movements of the flesh throb through desires, they do not openly attack us by contradiction.

Or certainly the beasts of the earth make peace with us because, when the movements of the flesh assail us by tempting us, they drive us toward the love of inward rest.

It follows:

### Verse 24

“And you will know that your tent has peace.” In Sacred Scripture, complete peace is spoken of in one way, and peace begun in another. Of the former it is said: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace” (Luke 2:29). Of the latter: “I give you my peace,” and so forth (John 14:27). Our peace begins with the desire for the Creator and is perfected in manifest vision.

The tent of the righteous is therefore said to have peace because his body, which is inhabited by the mind, is restrained from the perverse movements of desire under the ordering of justice.

It follows: “And when you visit your appearance, you will not sin.” Our appearance is called our neighbor, because in him we see what we ourselves are. Someone therefore visits his own appearance when he advances on the paths of love toward one whom he recognizes as naturally like himself, so that, considering himself in the other, he may gather from himself how he ought to accommodate himself to the other’s weakness.

Hence Paul says: “I became as a Jew to the Jews, so that I might win the Jews; to those who are under the law, as though I were under the law (although I myself was not under the law), so that I might win those who were under the law; to those who were without the law, as though I were without the law (although I was not without the law of God, but was in the law of Christ), so that I might win those who were without the law. I became weak to the weak, so that I might win the weak. I became all things to all, so that I might save all” (1 Corinthians 9:10, 22). Sin is then fully conquered when each person, from his own likeness to another, considers how he may be enlarged in love of his neighbor.

It follows:

### Verse 25

“And you will know that your seed will be numerous.” When the flesh is restrained from vices, when the mind is exercised in virtues, it remains for each person to teach by speaking the life that he preserves in his conduct. For the one who first sows the seeds of good action gathers abundant fruits of preaching. His preaching is granted greater fruitfulness in proportion as it is preceded in his heart by the cultivation of perfected action.

It follows: “And your offspring will be like the grass of the earth.” It is born from his imitation, because, abandoning the withering glory of the present life, it grows green through hope in the eternal. Or certainly the offspring of the righteous arises like the grass of the earth because, by living, he shows what he asserts by preaching, and an innumerable multitude of followers rises up.

It follows:

### Verse 26

“You will enter the grave in abundance.” What is signified by the name of the grave except the contemplative life? The active life is also a grave, because it covers us, dead to evil works. But the contemplative life buries us perfectly, because it completely separates us from all the actions of the world.

Hence Paul said to those who had been buried: “For you have died,” and so forth (Colossians 3:3). Hence Abraham buries his dead wife in a double grave. The perfect man enters the grave in abundance because he first gathers the works of the active life and afterward, through contemplation, hides completely from the world the sense of the flesh, dead to it.

The time of action comes first; that of contemplation is last. Therefore it is necessary that each perfect person first exercise his mind in virtues and afterward store it in the granary of rest. Hence Jacob served for Rachel and received Leah.

The grave may also be understood not only as contemplation in this life, but as the rest of eternal and inward recompense. He therefore enters the grave in abundance who, after amassing the works of the present life, has died completely to his mutability and is hidden in the secret place of the true light. Hence it is said through the Psalmist: “You will hide them in the hiding-place of your face,” and so forth (Psalm 30:21).

It follows: “As a heap of wheat is brought in at its proper time.” Grain is touched by the sun in the standing crop because, in this human life, the soul is illumined by the attention of the heavenly light. It receives rains because it is enriched by the word of truth. It is shaken by winds because it is tested by storms; and it carries with it the chaff growing alongside it because it daily endures the more wicked life of sinners against it. Once brought to the threshing-floor, it is pressed by the weight of threshing so that it may be released from its connection with the chaff.

Thus our mind, subjected to heavenly discipline, withdraws purer from the fellowship of the carnal when it receives the scourges of correction; and, leaving the chaff behind, it is led to the granary. For while the reprobate remain outside, the elect soul is raised to the eternal joys of the heavenly dwelling.

They feel blows in an alien season, but in their own season they rest from blows. For the present life is an alien season to the elect. Hence Truth says to certain unbelievers: “My time has not yet come, but your time is always ready” (John 7:6).

It follows:

### Verse 27

“Behold, this is what we have investigated, and so it is.” It is plainly evident that nothing in these words is said by him according to the surface meaning, because what is investigated does not lie openly before the face. By indicating that he has investigated these things, he shows that he has sought inward realities in outward words.

It follows: “What you have heard, consider carefully in your mind.” However great the learning with which a mind may be endowed, it is a grave ignorance for it to wish to teach one who is better. Thus even those things that have been correctly spoken by enemies are judged incorrect by the inner arbiter. They lose the force of their correctness because they do not suit the hearer.

## BOOK SEVEN

### CHAPTER VI

### Verses 2–3

“Would that my sins by which I deserved anger, and the calamity that I suffer, were weighed in the balance! It would appear heavier than the sand of the sea.”

By the name of the balance, God and the Mediator of human beings is represented. He came to weigh the merit of our life and brought with him both justice and mercy. By making the scale of mercy outweigh our sins, he lightened them through pardon.

The calamity appeared heavy in the balance because he recognized the evil that he had suffered only in the presence of the Redeemer. The sand of the sea is indeed of great weight, but the calamity of a human being is said to be heavier than the sand of the sea because the punishment is shown to have been severe when guilt is lightened by the Judge of mercy.

It follows: “Therefore my words are full of sorrow.” The words of the righteous are full of sorrow because, as long as he endures the present things, he sighs through his speech for something else. Whoever loves pilgrimage in place of a homeland does not recognize even pain amid pains.

It follows:

### Verse 4

“For the arrows of the Lord are in me.” Sometimes the words of preaching are signified by the name of arrows. Of these the Psalmist says: “Your arrows are sharp,” and so forth (Psalm 44:6). Isaiah likewise says: “I will send some of those who have been saved to the nations by sea, to Africa, to Lydia, bearing arrows, to Italy and Greece” (Isaiah 66:19).

Sometimes a sentence of punishment is signified, as it is said through Elisha to King Joash: “Shoot an arrow” (2 Kings 13:17). When he had shot it, he said: “You will strike Syria until you consume it” (ibid.). It is as though he said: I do not rejoice in the exile of condemnation because I recognize the force of the blow.

It follows: “Their indignation has drunk up my spirit.” What is the spirit of a human being except the spirit of arrogance? The arrows of the Lord drink up the human spirit when the sentence of heavenly punishment restrains an afflicted mind from arrogance; when the heavenly sentence wounds the elect whom it finds in sins, it changes them, so that the pierced mind may abandon its hardness and the blood of confession may flow from the saving wound.

It follows: “And the terrors of the Lord wage war against me.” The mind of the righteous not only weighs what it endures but also fears what remains. It sees what it suffers in this life and fears that it may suffer worse things after this life. Hence the Psalmist says: “Your wrath passed over me, and your terrors troubled me” (Psalm 87:17).

**Morally.** We now live through faith in the Mediator, yet we still endure, as arrows of the Lord, the harsh scourges of inward punishment for the purging of our vices. But behold, we are pierced by the stroke of divine correction, and nevertheless what is more grievous is that we fear, in terror of the Judge who is to come, the eternal punishment that awaits us.

It follows:

### Verse 5

“Will the wild ass bray when it has grass? Or will the ox low when it stands before a full manger?”

By the wild ass, the ass of the wilderness, the Gentile people are signified. By the ox, the Jewish people are represented. Subjected to the yoke of heavenly dominion, and gathering proselytes in hope, it drew along the hearts that it was able to plow with the law.

We learn from these words that many among the Gentile people and among the Jews desired the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation. Of them the Lord says: “I tell you, many righteous people and prophets desired to see what you see,” and so forth (Matthew 13:17).

The wild ass found grass when the Gentile people received the grace of the divine incarnation. The ox likewise did not have an empty manger when the law displayed the Lord’s flesh to the Jewish people, whom it had long awaited and prophetically foretold. Hence the newborn Lord is placed in a manger. He, assuming flesh from our substance, willed to become hay—the one who offered himself as food to the minds of mortals, saying: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:56).

It is as though he said: The Gentiles groan because the grace of their Redeemer has not yet refreshed them; and therefore Judea extends its lowing, because, holding the law but not seeing the author of the law, it stands hungry before the manger.

**Morally.** Who else are designated by the name of wild asses except those who, established in the field of faith, are bound by no reins of office? By the name of oxen he designates those whom, within the holy Church, the yoke of their received order presses into the office of preaching.

The grass of the wild ass and the fodder of the ox are the inward refreshment of the faithful people. Because we are placed far from inward wisdom and do not see the eternal inheritance, we fast, like brute animals, from the food we desire. Of this grass the Redeemer’s voice says: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved,” and so forth (John 10:9).

It follows:

### Verse 6

“Or can one eat what is tasteless, which has not been seasoned with salt?”

Whoever, intent upon carnal observances, refuses to understand the law spiritually—what else does he eat but tasteless food? But because the Gentiles refused to submit to its commands, which imposed harsh requirements, they did not wish to eat tasteless food. Before receiving the seasoning of the Spirit, they feared to preserve the force of the letter.

But Truth placed salt in this food and taught that the taste of hidden understanding lies concealed in the law, saying: “If you believed Moses,” and so forth (John 5:46). And again: “Have salt in yourselves.” And: “Have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:50).

**Morally.** The words and behavior of carnal people thrust themselves into our minds like food and are swallowed in the belly of pleasure. But a learned person does not eat tasteless food, because, judging the words and deeds of the wicked, he rejects them from the mouth—or, as the text perhaps reads, “from the ear”—of the heart. Hence the Psalmist says: “The wicked have told me their stories,” and so forth (Psalm 118:85).

It follows: “Or can anyone taste what, once tasted, brings death?” The law, tasted carnally, brought death because it bound the offenses of transgressors with harsh punishment: through the commandment it made guilt known, but through grace it did not erase it, as Paul testifies, saying: “The law brought nothing to perfection” (Hebrews 7:19).

But the Gentile people, converted to Christ, although it understands him still to resound through the words of the law, is constrained in its desires.

**Morally.** When holy men therefore yearn for eternal things, they raise themselves to such a height of life that they already regard hearing whatever belongs to the world as a heavy and burdensome weight. They consider everything that does not sound like what they love inwardly to be utterly intolerable.

Often the mind desires heavenly things and foolishly despises what is below, yet it still does not gird itself, for love of truth, to endure the sufferings of the present life. For it is difficult to desire what causes suffering and to follow what puts life to flight.

It follows:

### Verse 7

“What my soul formerly refused to touch, these are now my food because of anguish.”

Far be it from us to think that the holy man, established in the security of his state, ever despised the words of his friends. But because blessed Job is a member of the holy Church, he also speaks with its voice. The Gentiles, converted and anxious in the fever of their love, hunger for the food of the Old Scripture, which they had formerly despised in their pride.

Alternatively: Judea, because it despised having fellowship with the Gentiles, was disgusted at taking tasteless food; and because the divine sentence had forbidden the people of Israel, under penalty of death, to form a covenant with foreigners, it did not wish to taste what, once tasted, brings death.

But when Judea came to the grace of the Redeemer and was rejected by unbelieving Israelites, it expanded through the holy apostles toward the gathering of the Gentiles. As though hungering for this food, it received what it had previously regarded with disdain as unworthy; and because of anguish it ate the food that it had formerly despised. Rejected by the hardness of the Jews, it desired to receive the Gentile peoples whom it had despised.

**Morally.** The progressing mind, which formerly, while caring only for its own concerns, was unwilling to bear those of others, draws near to bearing the weaknesses of its neighbor. Thus, for love of truth, it later eagerly seeks the sufferings of the present life, which, when weak, it had previously fled. Because of anguish, it eats what it formerly refused to touch.

It follows:

### Verse 8

“Who will grant that my petition may come, and that the Lord may give me what I seek, and that he who began may himself crush me?”

He does not ask through defiance to be destroyed so as to accuse the justice of the one who strikes him, as he demonstrates in the words that follow: “I will not contradict holy words” (Job 6:10).

We should know, however, that sometimes the adversary crushes us, and sometimes God does. Through the crushing inflicted by the adversary, we fall away from virtue. Through the Lord’s crushing, broken in our vices, we labor in virtue. Hence it is written: “You will rule them with an iron rod” (Psalm 2:9). When he afflicts us outwardly, he refreshes us inwardly.

And because the Lord often begins the crushing of vices within us, but when the mind becomes proud from the very beginning of its progress gives the adversary an entrance, the holy man therefore prays:

### Verse 9

“Let him who began crush me himself.”

It is as though he said: Let him not cease, by striking, to complete what has begun in me, lest, abandoning me, he hand me over to the adversary for crushing.

It follows: “Let him release his hand and cut me off.” To release the hand means to exercise its effect. But when the Creator sees us becoming proud and does not exercise his love toward us through blows, he binds his hand against striking our vices.

When, while we are secure and lifted up by an abundance of virtues, the pain of a blow or the trial of illness suddenly strikes us, the exaltation of our mind is immediately cut down from the summit of its position and falls. Thus it dares nothing from itself but, struck down by the blow of its weakness, seeks the hand of the one who raises it.

Hence holy men desire to be tested and long to be scourged, saying: “Test me, Lord, and try me” (Psalm 25:2); and: “I am ready for scourges” (Psalm 37:18).

It follows:

### Verse 10

“And let this be my consolation: that, afflicting me with sorrow, he does not spare.”

It is as though he said: He does not spare here so that he may spare forever. I am consoled by affliction because, knowing the corruption of human beings, I am made certain by the wound of my hope of salvation.

The elect waste away in great fear when they know that they have committed forbidden things, but, searching themselves, they discover that they have suffered no adversity for those forbidden things.

It follows: “Nor will I contradict holy words.” God’s words to us are the effects of his actions. He therefore speaks to us in what he silently does toward us. Blessed Job would contradict God’s words if he murmured against his blows. But he indicates what he thinks about the one who strikes him: the one whose blows he endures, he calls holy.

It follows:

### Verse 11

“For what is my strength, that I should endure, or what is my end, that I should act patiently?”

We should know that the strength of the righteous is one thing, and that of the reprobate another. The strength of the righteous is to conquer the flesh, resist their own pleasures, and extinguish delight in the present life. Hence it is said to the saints: “Act manfully,” and so forth (Psalm 30:25).

The strength of the reprobate, however, is to love transitory things without ceasing and to persist insensibly against the scourges of the Creator. Of them the prophet says: “Woe to you who are mighty at drinking wine,” and so forth (Isaiah 5:22). And: “Behold, they have seized my soul, and the mighty have rushed upon me” (Psalm 58:4).

They are mighty because they endure the evils of the world for the sake of the world; seeking its joys, so to speak, they lose them, yet they do not grow weary even in losing them.

It is as though the holy man said: I cannot endure the evils of the world for the sake of the world, because I am no longer strong in its desire. When I see the end of the present life, why should I suffer for the world, whose desire I trample underfoot?

It follows:

### Verse 12

“Is the strength of stones my strength, or is my flesh bronze?”

What is signified here by bronze or stones except the hearts of insensitive people, who do not grow soft under any blow? In contrast, it is said to the elect: “I will take away from you your heart of stone,” and so forth (Ezekiel 36:26).

Paul likewise says: “If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels,” and so forth (1 Corinthians 13:1). Whoever grows hard against the commandment of compassion is like a stone; when struck, he does not give back the sound of humble confession.

Some, however, differ in no respect from bronze metal. When they receive the blows of heavenly punishment, they emit the sound of devout confession. But because they do not utter words of humility from the heart, once they have been restored to a state of salvation they do not know what they promised.

It is as though the holy man said: Under the scourge of discipline, I have not become hardened like the reprobate, like stones, so that I fall silent concerning the ministry of confession; nor do I resound like bronze with the voice of confession while remaining ignorant of the meaning of that voice.

It follows:

### Verse 13

“Behold, there is no help for me in myself.”

It is already clear toward whose likeness the struck man’s spirit turns, since he declares that he has no help in himself. Often inherited virtue kills more seriously than if it were absent, because, while it raises the mind to confidence in itself, it pierces it with the sword of pride.

It follows: “And even those close to me have withdrawn from me.” Whoever reveals himself to be weak in himself is deprived even of those closest to him, so that he may attain a greater merit of strength.

It follows:

### Verse 14

“He who removes mercy from his friend abandons the fear of the Lord.”

By the name “friend” in this passage, any neighbor is designated. There are two commandments of charity: love of God and love of neighbor. Through love of God, love of neighbor is generated; through love of neighbor, love of God is nourished. Hence it is written: “Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees,” and so forth (1 John 4:20).

This divine love is born through fear, but as it grows it is transformed into affection. For it is written: “A friend will not be recognized in good fortune, and an enemy will not be concealed in misfortune” (Sirach 12:8). Whoever despises his neighbor because of adversity plainly shows that he did not love him in prosperity.

Since almighty God strikes some people in order to educate those who are struck and to provide those who are not struck with an occasion for good works, whoever despises the one who has been struck drives away from himself an occasion for virtue. He rises against the Creator all the more wickedly because he recognizes neither the Creator’s compassion in his own salvation nor his justice in another’s wound.

It follows:

### Verse 15

“My brothers have passed me by like a torrent that quickly passes through the valleys.”

Often the reprobate retain the faith that we hold: they receive the same sacraments and are contained within the truth of the same religion. Yet because they do not know the inward compassion of suffering, they do not recognize the force of the charity with which we burn toward the Lord and our neighbor.

They are rightly called “those who pass by,” because through faith they emerge with us from one womb of the mother, but they are not fixed in one devotion of charity toward God and neighbor. Those who love earthly things abandon hope of the heavenly homeland, as though they descended from the mountains toward the valleys like a torrent.

Winter multiplies them, as it were, in the present life, but the summer of the coming judgment dries them up and turns the joy of the reprobate into aridity. A torrent quickly passing through a valley signifies the minds of the wicked descending without obstacle or difficulty toward their lowest desires. For every ascent is laborious, but descent follows the will.

Alternatively: If we understand the valleys as the lowest places of punishment, each unjust person passes quickly, like earthly things, toward the valley, because in this life—which they pursue with all their desires—they cannot for long [the text appears to lack a word]. For however many days of life they receive, they advance daily toward the end by so many steps. They prolong their desires for pleasures, but suddenly they are brought to the gates of hell.

It follows:

### Verse 16

“He who fears the frost will have snow fall upon him.”

Frost freezes below, whereas snow falls from above. Often some people, while fearing temporal adversities, cast aside the severity of eternal punishment. Of them it is said: “There they trembled with fear,” and so forth (Psalm 13:5).

Others fear human beings on earth because of the truth, and from heaven they endure the wrath of that truth. Still others fear suffering want on earth and cut themselves off forever from the abundance of heavenly refreshment.

It follows:

### Verse 17

“At the time when they are scattered, they will perish.”

Those whom the anxiety of the present life orders, loss scatters. Then they also perish outwardly who had already perished inwardly by neglecting eternal things.

It follows: “And when they have grown hot, they will be dissolved from their place.” Each wicked person is dissolved from his place when he has grown hot, because, as he approaches the judgment of inward severity and begins to boil through awareness of his punishment, he is separated from the pleasure of the flesh that had formerly clung to him.

Hence the prophet says concerning the reprobate: “Only affliction will give understanding to hearing” (Isaiah 28:19). He holds on to the present life through desire, but he is dissolved from his place when, desiring the pleasures of the flesh, he is melted by punishment through the hardness of that flesh.

It follows:

### Verse 18

“The paths of their steps are entangled.”

Everything that is entangled folds back into itself. There are some who, after deliberating, desire what is right, but always return to their customary evils; stretched, as it were, outside themselves, they return in a circuit to themselves. They desire good things but never depart from evil.

They want to be humble, but without contempt; content with their own possessions, but without necessity; chaste, but without mortification of the body; patient, but without insults.

Alternatively: Often some people gird themselves vehemently against certain vices but neglect to subdue others. Since they do not rise up against the latter, those vices restore against them the ones they had subdued.

One person conquers lust in the flesh but does not restrain his mind from greed. When he remains in the world to exercise greed, once an occasion breaks out, he also falls into lust, which he had seemed to have subdued.

Sometimes, when the paths of one’s steps are entangled, one fault is overcome but another is committed through it. Theft is often joined to denial, then increased by the guilt of perjury, and one fault is added to another. What else do the steps of the wicked bind than entangled paths and knotted bonds?

Hence Isaiah says: “And it will be a lair of dragons and a pasture of ostriches, and demons will meet there; the onocentaur and the hairy one called to one another” (Isaiah 34:13).

What is signified by dragons except malice? What by ostriches except hypocrisy? Since in Greek *onos* means “ass,” lust is signified by the ass; by the bull the neck of pride is indicated, as in: “Fat bulls have surrounded me” (Psalm 21:13).

The onocentaurs, therefore, are those who, subjected to the vices of lust, raise their necks from the very place where they ought to have been humbled.

“Hairy one” is called in Greek πάνας (*pānas*), in Latin *incubi*. Their form begins with a human figure but ends in a bestial extremity. Often the pleasure of eating serves gluttony and pretends to serve necessity. When it stretches the belly into voracity, it raises the limbs into lust.

The hairy one calls to another when one wicked deed provokes the commission of another.

It follows: “They will walk in emptiness and perish.” They walk in emptiness who carry nothing with them from the fruit of their labor. For when they die, they abandon all the things that they desired while living unjustly.

In contrast, the law says: “You will not appear empty before my face” (Exodus 23:14). And of the righteous it is said: “Coming, they will come with rejoicing,” and so forth (Psalm 125:6). Since no unjust person provides, by doing good, the merit by which life is earned, he appears empty in the sight of God.

It follows:

### Verse 19

“Consider the paths of Thema, the roads of Saba.”

*Thema* means “south,” while *Saba* means “net.” What is signified here by the south, whose warm breath loosens the limbs, except a flowing laxity of life? What by the net except the bondage of action?

Those who, with a relaxed mind, desire earthly things and do not advance toward God on free steps bind themselves by their disordered efforts.

There are many who not only do not desire what belongs to others but also abandon everything they had possessed in the world. Yet, while they serve indiscriminately the love of their relatives, they often return through affection for kinship to the things they had condemned.

Where, then, do such people walk except in a net? The perfection of a life already begun had freed them in the present age, but disordered love of earthly kinship binds them.

Hence Truth says: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:26).

It is therefore rightly said after the paths of Thema that the roads of Saba are remembered, because those whom the south of reprobate time has loosened are held by the entanglement of the net.

Describing the works of the wicked, he rightly urges us to consider them, because we love to commit perverse deeds but judge them when we see them in others. We recognize that the things we believe require less judgment in ourselves are shameful when performed by others. Thus the mind returns to itself and becomes ashamed to do what it condemns.

It follows: “And wait a little.” Often, while the brevity of the present life is loved as though it would endure, the spirit is broken away from eternal hope. But suddenly, when life ends, it encounters eternal punishments that it can no longer avoid.

Hence it is said: “Woe to those who have lost endurance” (Sirach 2:16). When the mind is fixed on present things, life comes to an end, and suddenly it reaches unforeseen punishments.

Hence the Psalmist says: “A little while, and the sinner will be no more” (Psalm 36:10).

It follows:

### Verse 20

“They are confounded because I hoped.”

When the reprobate inflict evils upon the good, they rejoice in the effect of their deception if they see the good shaken from their inward hope. But when the inward hope of good works is fixed and is not bent downward toward the depths by outward evils, confusion seizes the minds of the wicked. Unable to reach the inward being of the afflicted, they are ashamed that their cruelty has proved fruitless.

It follows: “They have also come as far as me, and they have been covered with shame.” The reprobate come as far as the holy Church on the day of judgment because they are brought far enough to behold its glory, so that, rejected for the greater punishments of their guilt, they may see what they have lost.

Then shame covers the wicked when the witness of conscience brings them into the presence of the Judge. Every guilt is then brought back before their eyes, and the mind is tormented by its own more grievous fire than by the burning of Gehenna.

Of them the prophet rightly says: “Lord, let your hand be exalted, so that they may see and be confounded by what they see” (Isaiah 26:11).

All these things may also fit the friends of blessed Job. It is as though he said of them: Since they cannot bend me toward despair by their foolish reproofs, let them themselves be confounded by the madness of their rashness, seeing the wounds of my body but not knowing the conscience of my mind.

When they dared to accuse me of injustice, they had not yet come as far as me. But while they assailed me with harsh invective, they became ashamed as though they had come to me when they discovered, amid adversity, that my spirit was victorious.

It follows:

### Verse 21

“Now you have come, and now, seeing my wound, you are afraid.”

It is as though he openly said: I feared God then, when, supported by prosperity, I did not experience the losses inflicted by scourges. You, who do not fear God out of love, fear him only because of his blows.

It follows:

### Verses 22–23

“Have I said: Bring me something from your substance and give it to me? Or: Deliver me from the hand of the enemy and rescue me from the hand of the mighty?”

The preaching of heretics may appropriately be understood as carnal substance. By supporting perverse things with it, they display themselves as rich, so to speak, in words. The holy Church does not seek it precisely because it rises above it through spiritual understanding.

He calls the hand of the enemy the power of Satan, and the hand of the mighty the strength of evil spirits. He calls them mighty because, having been created without the weakness of flesh, they encounter no weakness that would oppose their perverse assertions.

The following passage, however:

### Verse 24

“Teach me, and I will be silent; and if I have perhaps been ignorant of anything, instruct me.”

It seems uncertain under which division of the sentence this should be placed: whether it belongs to what he had introduced—“Have I said?”—or whether the statement is brought forward separately from the preceding words, as though spoken by way of reproof: “Teach me,” and so forth.

Nevertheless, it suits either division, since neither departs from the sound path of understanding.

Thus blessed Job answered as a poor man against the rich of the world, as an oppressed man against the powerful, and as a fool against the wise. He seeks neither their substance as a poor man, nor assistance against the mighty as an oppressed man, nor the teaching of carnal wisdom as a fool.

For the holy man, because in mind he is beautifully carried beyond himself, is not constrained by poverty, suffers nothing as an oppressed man, and, willingly foolish, does not admire carnal wisdom.

It follows:

### Verse 25

“Why have you undermined the words of truth, when there is no one among you who can reproach me?”

It is as though it were openly said: With what rashness do you criticize what you have heard, when you do not know the causes of my being struck?

The one who takes care to correct the faults of others must himself be pure. Hence it is said to David: “You will not build a temple for me, because you are a man of blood” (III Kings 8:9).

It follows:

**VERSE 26.** You compose speeches merely for the sake of reproving.---

There are two harmful kinds of speech among humankind: one that takes pains to praise even what is adverse, and another that is eager always to rebuke even what is right. By the character of this latter kind, therefore, blessed Job reproves his friends for having been such. It follows:

“And you bring forth words into the wind”—for to bring forth words into the wind is to speak idle words. Often, when the tongue is not restrained from idle speech, it is also driven headlong into the rashness of foolish reproach. First, one takes pleasure in speaking of other people’s affairs; afterward the tongue gnaws by detraction at the lives of those about whom it speaks; and sometimes it bursts forth into open insults. Hence Solomon says: “He who lets water loose is the beginning of quarrels” (Prov. XVII, 14). And again: “He who imposes silence upon a fool appeases anger” (Prov. XXVI, 10). Isaiah likewise says: “The cultivation of justice is silence” (Isa. XXXII, 17).

An idle word is one that lacks either the reason of just necessity or the purpose of pious usefulness. Very often, those who are excessively silent, when they observe the evils of certain people and nevertheless press their tongue into silence, become authors of death precisely because they were unwilling to expel by speaking the poison they could have driven out. Hence the prophet says: “Woe is me, because I was silent” (Isa. VI, 5). But when the just person recognizes the appropriate moment, setting aside the restraint of silence, he devotes himself to useful service by speaking what is fitting. Hence it is said: “The wise man will be silent until the proper time” (Ecclus. XX, 7).

## BOOK EIGHT

**VERSE 27.** You have rushed upon the orphan, and you strive to overthrow your friend.---

He indicates the great weakness under which he labors by calling him an orphan; yet, because love does not know how to withdraw even when wounded, he complains that they wish to overthrow him, and nevertheless testifies that he is their friend.

**TYPICALLY.** The people of the holy Church, whose father is one who has died, may appropriately be called a son and an orphan. They already follow the life of the one who has risen through faith, but do not yet behold it in vision. Heretics rush upon the orphan when they afflict the humility of the faithful people with importunate and false arguments. Yet he whom they strive to overthrow is their friend, because the faithful people of God, by loving them, do not cease to call even their persecutors—whom they endure—to the truth. It follows:

**VERSE 28.** Nevertheless, complete what you have begun.---

As if he were saying openly: “I am not frightened by the troubles already inflicted, nor do I conceal the remedies of correction from ungrateful hearers, because I am exercised by being pressed by the wicked, and I grow by kindly extending mercy to my very persecutors.” Since “charity is patient and kind” (I Cor. IV, 4), and when either one of these is absent, there is no charity, it is necessary, if charity is truly to be held by us, that patience support kindness and kindness support patience.

Therefore, because blessed Job is patient, let him say: “Nevertheless, complete what you have begun.” And because he is endowed with kindness, let him say: “Give ear.” It follows:

“And see whether I am lying.”---

As if he were saying openly: “Do not believe what I assert merely on the authority of my assertion, but weigh by reason whether it is true.” For the holy Church, instructed in the discipline of humility, does not command as though by authority the right things that it says to those who are in error; rather, it persuades by reason. It follows:

**VERSE 29.** Answer, I ask, without contention.---

For heretics do not strive to attain the truth through their inquiries, but to appear victorious. Hence they seek the contests of disputation, and, since they do not know how to speak peacefully about God, “who is our peace” (Eph. II, 14), they become inventors of quarrels out of the very business of peace. To them Paul rightly says: “But if anyone seems to be contentious, we have no such custom” (I Cor. XI, 16).

It follows:

“And when speaking what is just, judge.”---

The person who speaks, while awaiting the judgment of his hearer, as though submitting himself to that person’s decision, is in turn judged by the one who hears him. Therefore, whoever fears rejection of his words ought first to examine what he says, so that a fair and discerning judge may sit between his heart and his tongue, carefully weighing whether he is offering words that are right and that, once profitably received, his tongue may convey to the judgment of his hearers. It follows:

**VERSE 30.** And you will not find iniquity in my tongue, and foolishness will not resound in my jaws.---

As if he were saying openly: “If you weigh your own words more carefully, you will assess those of others more truthfully. And when what you say begins to be right, you will recognize that what you have heard is just.”

Thus the holy Church first strives to show that the assertions of its enemies are false, and then to disclose the teachings of virtue. Open speech is signified by the tongue, while hidden reflection is signified by the jaws. Since the things that the holy Church proclaims through public speech it already preserves through inward faith, iniquity does not resound in its tongue, nor foolishness in its jaws. Whatever flows forth through the tongue of preaching, it tastes inwardly through the jaws of silent expectation. It follows:

## CHAPTER VII

**VERSE 1.** Human life upon earth is a warfare.---

Another translation has “temptation,” but the meaning of both words is apparent. For what is expressed by the name “temptation” except a struggle against wicked spirits? And what is indicated by the designation “warfare” except an army deployed against enemies? Temptation itself, therefore, is warfare, because while a person keeps watch against the snares of wicked spirits, he certainly sweats in battle array.

Human life is said to be temptation because, having fallen from the state of its creation and having been subjected to the corruption of its decay, it generates troubles for itself from itself; that is, it has already become what it endures. Human life is therefore temptation, because even when we restrain ourselves from committing iniquity, our good works are nevertheless darkened—now by the memory of evil, now by the obscurity of seduction, now by the interruption of our own intention.

Temptation, therefore, is that which, being alien to virtues, cannot rise to the heavenly reward, or which, enriched with spiritual gifts, sometimes falls more disastrously through the occasion of its virtues. Human life is also warfare, because each person, while tending daily toward the end of life through the increase of time, ceases to live by increasing life. And while he desires the spans of time to grow, he passes beyond, by growing, the very span that he gathers by extending it. For as the place in the order of military service increases, the whole of a person’s life simultaneously diminishes. It follows:

“And his days are like the days of a hired laborer.”---

A hired laborer longs to reach the reward of his labor more quickly. The days of the wise man’s eternal life are therefore rightly compared with the days of a hired laborer, because they regard the present life as a road, not as a homeland; and the hired laborer toils in the possessions of another, but nevertheless prepares a reward for himself.

The voice of the Redeemer says: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John XVIII, 36). All, therefore, who are endowed with hope of heavenly things and are worn down by the labor of the present life, work in what belongs to another. We are fatigued by labor that belongs to another, yet we receive our rewards; and we reach what is our own by faithfully administering what belongs to another. In contrast, Truth says to certain people: “If you were not faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?” (Luke XVI, 12).

It should also be known that a hired laborer carefully takes care that no day is ever empty of work. Hence the elect proceed toward their rewards with all the greater confidence in hope, the more vigorously they now persevere in increasing labor. They count their days by their works and fear that the moments of their life may pass empty of labor. Hence they say: “For your sake we are put to death all day long” (Rom. VIII, 36). And: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain” (II Tim. I, 12). It follows:

**VERSE 2.** As a stag longs for shade.---

For a stag to long for shade is for a person, amid the heat of temptation and the sweat of labor, to seek the rest of eternal refreshment. Hence it is written: “My soul thirsted for the living God,” and so forth (Ps. XLI, 3). And: “Alas for me, my sojourn has been prolonged” (Ps. CXIX, 5). And: “I will enter the place of the tabernacle of the Wonderful One,” and so forth (Ps. XLI, 5).

It follows:

“And as a hired laborer awaits the end of his work.”---

A hired laborer considers what is burdensome in his work to be light in view of his remuneration. Thus what is shown by pain to be exceedingly difficult for the elect is lightened by prudent consideration of the reward. Hence Paul indicates how grievous were the things he endured, testifying that he had been “more abundantly in prisons, above measure in beatings, frequently in deaths” (II Cor. XI, 23). He declares that he was burdened beyond his strength, saying: “We were burdened beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we were weary even of living” (II Cor. I, 8). But considering the reward, he says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18).

It follows:

**VERSE 3.** So I have had months of emptiness, and I have counted for myself nights of labor.---

The elect serve the Creator of all things, and are often confined by poverty of worldly goods. Those who do not seek present things through their actions therefore spend empty months, measured by the world’s advantages. They also endure laborious nights who carry the darkness of adversities not only to deprivation but often to bodily torment.

It may also appropriately be understood that every holy person spends empty months like a hired laborer: he already bears the labor but does not yet possess the reward. He endures the one and awaits the other. He counts laborious nights because, by exercising himself in virtues, he heaps up for himself the adversities of the present time.

**MYSTICALLY.** The Church has empty months when it bears in its weak members earthly actions that flow away without the reward of life. It has laborious nights when it carries multiple tribulations in its strong members.

The name “months” signifies a collection and totality of days. Thus one action can be expressed by a day, while the completion of actions is understood by months. We therefore speak not only of empty days but of empty months when we judge that we have labored fruitlessly in earthly actions, considering not their beginning but their end.

For when adversity follows our labors, the months of our life are, as it were, condemned as empty, because from the completion of an action it becomes known how uselessly one was occupied in those actions.

But because in sacred Scripture “night” is sometimes used for ignorance, as Paul testifies when he says to those who know the coming life: “You are all sons of light and sons of day; we are not of night or of darkness” (I Thess. V, 5), this passage may be understood as the voice of the holy Church speaking in the person of those who, after the darkness of their ignorance, return to the love of righteousness and, illumined by the rays of truth, atone with tears for having gone astray.

In them, therefore—in those through whom it returns to life—the holy Church compares its labor to that of a servant burning with heat and a hired laborer longing for the end, saying: “As a stag longs for shade,” and so forth.

For the one who burns with heat, it brings forth empty months, because the more earnestly eternal refreshment is sought, the more one recognizes how fruitlessly one labors for the present life. To the one who awaits the end, it adds laborious nights, because the more clearly we look toward the reward that we are to attain at the end of our work, the more deeply we lament that we have long been ignorant of what we seek.

For the more truly we return to God, the more subtly and sorrowfully we weigh the labors that we endured in this world through ignorance. It follows:

**VERSE 4.** If I sleep, I will say: “When shall I rise?” And again I will await evening.---

If these words are considered only according to the historical sense, they certainly express the mind of one who is grieving and show how it is driven into different states by the various movements of desire. In the night, day is sought; in the day, evening is desired, because sorrow does not permit what is present to be pleasing.

**OTHERWISE.** The holy Church, as long as it bears the life of corruption, does not cease to mourn the losses caused by its mutability. As if it were saying: “In sleep I desire the resurrection, but in the resurrection I await evening, because in repose I seek the exercise of action, and when exercised I seek the leisure of repose.”

Humanity was created so that it might never turn away from the love of its Creator. But when it moved its foot toward sin, it immediately fell away from love of its Creator into itself and lost the strength of its salvation.

**OTHERWISE.** To sleep means to lie in sins. Hence Paul says: “Awake, you just,” and so forth (I Cor. XV, 34). And again: “Rise, you who sleep, and rise from the dead,” and so forth (Eph. V, 14).

Therefore, whenever an elect person is weighed down by the sleep of sin, he strives to rise to the vigils of righteousness. But often, when he has risen, he feels himself lifted up by the very greatness of his virtues. Hence, after attaining virtues, he desires to be tested by the adversities of the present life, lest he fall more disastrously through confidence in his virtues. Hence it is written: “Test me, Lord, and try me” (Ps. XXV, 2).

In the sleep of sin, the light of righteousness is sought; and when prosperity in virtue lifts the mind, adversity is desired as a helper. We await prosperity and fear adversity. The just man therefore awaits evening, because when it is necessary for him to be exercised by tribulation, the adversity itself becomes prosperity for him.

The name “evening” may also designate the temptation of sin. Hence Moses says: “There was morning, and there was evening” (Gen. I, 5). Morning is led toward evening because, plainly, the shadow of temptation follows the light of righteousness.

After sleep, therefore, the elect desire the resurrection, because they awaken from sin to the light of righteousness and, placed in that very light of righteousness, continually prepare themselves against the allurements of temptations. They do not fear these temptations but await them, because they know that even trials contribute to the usefulness of their righteousness. It follows:

“And I will be filled with sorrows until darkness.”---

Because at one time rising vices stir up a battle in the flesh, and at another the vices that have been conquered call the mind to pride, the life of the good is filled with sorrows until darkness. For as long as it passes through the time of corruption, it is shaken by inward and outward affliction and does not find security of salvation until it has completely left behind the day of temptation. It follows:

**VERSE 5.** My flesh is clothed with decay and the filth of dust.---

As if he were saying openly: “The carnal life that I endure is either polluted by the slippery stain of evil action, or oppressed by the darkness of miserable thought arising from the memory of vices.” By consenting to vices we are worn down by decay; by tolerating the images of vices in our hearts, we are defiled by the filth of dust.

**OTHERWISE.** There are many in the holy Church who, while serving the love of the flesh, rot in the stench of lust; and there are some who abstain from the will of the flesh but nevertheless lie with their whole mind in earthly actions.

As if he were saying: “In those whom I endure as morally slippery, I lament flesh that is decaying. In those whom I endure as seeking the earth, what else do I carry but the filth of dust?” It follows:

“My skin has dried up and has contracted.”---

In the body of the holy Church, those who serve only external concerns are appropriately called “skin.” This skin is drawn tight as it dries, because the minds of carnal people, while they love present things and desire what is, as it were, placed beside them, do not wish to reach toward future things through perseverance.

While they neglect the richness of inward hope, they dry up so that they may be drawn tight. For if despair did not dry out their hearts in this way, the heat of faintheartedness would not contract them. The Psalmist had feared this contraction when, dreading dryness, he said: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Ps. XXVI, 9). It follows:

**VERSE 6.** My days have passed more swiftly than a web is cut from the weaver.---

By a very suitable comparison, the life of the flesh is likened to a web. Just as a web advances by its threads, so mortal life advances by its individual days; but insofar as it advances toward increase, it moves toward being cut, because as the times already received pass away, those yet to come grow shorter.

The days therefore pass more swiftly, because a web has the slowness of progress, whereas the present life has no delay in its decline. We reach the end of our journey even while resting, and through the course of our passage we advance even while sleeping. It follows:

“And they have been consumed without any hope.”---

As if it were said openly: “I have not placed the confidence of my mind in the present life, because I have despised by trampling upon it everything that passes away.”

The mind of the reprobate binds the present days to itself through love, so that they always desire to live here in such a way that, if they could, they would wish never to bring the course of their life to an end. In contrast, the mind of the upright is directed toward eternity even when the present life accompanies it happily. It follows:

**VERSE 7.** Remember that my life is a breath.---

As if it were said openly: “Look kindly upon me as one who passes swiftly, for I ought to be regarded by you with all the greater mercy because I myself do not turn my eyes away from considering my shortness.”

Those who do not consider the eternity of the life that follows love the life of the flesh as though it were permanent. But holy men, because they raise their hearts to eternal things, weigh how brief is what is enclosed by an end. What passes away becomes worthless in their judgment, while what, once received, never departs shines and gleams upon their understanding. It follows:

“Nor will my eye return to see good things.”---

An eye extinguished does not return to see good things, because, once the flesh has been removed, the soul does not return to perform righteous works. Hence Solomon says: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do it earnestly, because there is neither work, nor reason, nor knowledge, nor wisdom in the underworld to which you are hastening” (Eccl. IX, 10). It follows:

**VERSE 8.** Nor will the sight of man look upon me.---

The sight of man is the mercy of the Redeemer, which softens the hardness of our insensibility when it looks upon us. Hence the Gospel testifies: “Jesus looked upon Peter.” And: “He remembered the word that Jesus had spoken.” And: “He went outside and wept bitterly” (Luke XXII, 61, 62).

But the sight of man does not look upon the soul once it has been stripped of the flesh, because after death he does not liberate the person whom grace did not restore to forgiveness before death. Hence Paul says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time” (II Cor. VI, 2), and so forth. Hence Solomon says: “Where the tree falls, whether toward the south or toward the north, there it will remain” (Eccl. XI, 3).

The holy man therefore considers the losses of the human race: how it is taken from the present age without recognition of the Redeemer and is irreparably buried in eternal fires. Speaking in its person, he says: “Nor will the sight of man look upon me.”

It follows:

“Your eyes are upon me, and I will not remain.”---

As if he were saying openly: “When you come in judgment, you do not look upon me in order to save me; you look upon me in order to strike me. For the one whom in the present life you do not regard with the mercy of your dispensation, by regarding him afterward you destroy through justice.”

Then the sinner does not remain, because when the strict Judge carefully investigates his merits, the guilty person is unable to withstand the punishments. Yet this may also appropriately correspond to the voice of the just, whose minds are always attentive to strict examinations. They consider how strictly he judges good works and how subtly he weighs them, and they foresee without doubt that they will perish if they are judged with mercy removed.

Expressing well the course and decline of the elect and of the human race, he says:

**VERSE 9.** As a cloud is consumed and passes away, so one who descends to the underworld does not ascend.---

A cloud is lifted to higher places, but when thickened it is driven by the wind so that it runs, and it is dispersed by the heat of the sun so that it vanishes. Such, plainly, are human hearts. Through the intelligence bestowed upon them, they rise toward lofty things; but when driven by the breath of the wicked spirit, they are dragged here and there by the perverse movements of their desires.

Yet, under the strict regard of the heavenly Judge, they melt as though by the heat of the sun; and once they have been handed over to places of punishment, they do not return again to the practice of action.

The name “underworld” may also designate the sinner’s despair, of which the Psalmist says: “But in the underworld, who will confess to you?” (Ps. VI, 6). And again: “When the wicked comes into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. XVIII, 3).

Whoever succumbs to impiety certainly abandons the life of righteousness by dying. Whoever, after sin, is overwhelmed by the weight of despair, what else is he than one who is buried after death in the punishment of the underworld? From that place the path of return is cut off.

The hearts of the despairing are rightly compared with clouds, because they are darkened by the gloom of error and thickened by the multiplicity of sins. But they are consumed and pass away, because, irradiated by the brightness of the final judgment, they are dispersed. It follows:

**VERSE 10.** Nor will he return any longer to his house.---

Just as the house of the body is a bodily dwelling, so for each person the mind makes a house of whatever he habitually inhabits through desire. Therefore he does not return any longer to his own house, because once someone has been handed over to eternal punishments, he is in no way recalled to what he had clung to through love.

The house may also be understood as the dwelling place of the heart. Hence a certain healed man is told: “Go to your house” (Matt. IX, 6). When despair overwhelms someone, it casts him out from the dwelling place of his heart; and he cannot return inward, because, driven outward again toward worse things, he falls daily. It follows:

“Nor will his place know him any longer.”---

A person’s place—not a local place, but the Creator himself—was the one who created him so that he might stand in himself. Of this place the Psalmist says: “The children of your servants will dwell there” (Ps. CI, 29).

Man abandoned this place when, listening to the words of the seducer, he departed from love of the Creator. Therefore, in the judgment, each person is not recognized by his Creator with all the greater severity insofar as he is not now recalled to the grace of restoration even through gifts.

The strict Judge, coming to the final examination, said to those who remain in iniquity: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire” (Matt. XXV, 41). “I do not know you, where you are from” (Matt. XXV, 12). It follows:

**VERSE 11.** Therefore I will not spare my mouth.---

A person does not spare his mouth when he is not ashamed to confess the evil he has committed. Hence the Psalmist says: “Let us come before his face in confession” (Ps. XCIV, 2). Again it is written: “He who conceals his crimes will not prosper” (Prov. XXVIII, 13).

It follows:

“I will speak in the tribulation of my spirit.”---

The tongue stirs up the tribulation of the spirit, so that the voice of confession may oppose the guilt of an evil deed. It should also be known that the reprobate often confess their sins but refuse to mourn them. The elect, however, pursue with the tears of strict correction the faults that they disclose by the words of confession. Hence the Psalmist says: “I will declare my iniquity,” and so forth (Ps. L, 5).

For the person who discloses the evils he has committed but refuses to weep is like someone who pulls away a garment and exposes a wound but, with his mind numb, does not apply medicine to the wound. It follows:

“And I will converse with the bitterness of my soul.”---

Afflicted by fear of the strict Judge, while we mourn certain things badly done, the force of our own bitterness arouses us more vigilantly to examine ourselves, and we discover in ourselves other things for which we should mourn even more. Often a fault that was hidden from those who were numb becomes known more subtly to those who are weeping.

The bitterness of the soul has its own tongue in the hearts of the just. With it, the afflicted mind severely reproves itself, sometimes by recalling God’s gifts, sometimes by considering its own actions. Hence it does not say merely “I will speak,” but “I will converse,” because the force of sorrow, reckoning each sin, forms words of conversation with the dormant soul and rouses it to lamentation. It follows:

**VERSE 12.** Am I the sea, or a sea monster, that you have surrounded me with a prison?---

As if he were saying openly: “The sea—or the sea monster, namely the wicked and their author, the evil spirit—because they desire to run unrestrained toward the mere license to commit iniquity, are rightly confined in the prison of their punishment. But I, who already desire the freedom of your eternity, why am I still oppressed by the prison of my corruption?”

A human being is surrounded by a prison because, although he often strives to rise toward lofty things through progress in the virtues, he is nevertheless impeded by the corruption of his flesh. For it is written: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. IX, 15).

By the name “sea,” the hearts of carnal people, tossed about by swelling thoughts, are signified. By the name “sea monster,” the ancient enemy is expressed: by entering into and possessing the minds of worldly people, he swims, as it were, in their slippery thoughts. Cast down into lower regions, he is confined by the weight of his punishment so that he cannot fly toward heavenly things.

Hence Peter says: “God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but, hurling them into the underworld and delivering them to Tartarus, committed them to be kept for judgment and punishment” (II Pet. II, 4).

The sea monster and the sea are therefore pressed by the encircling prison, because either the evil spirit or his followers gather themselves within the minds of the wicked and stir up within them a wave of swelling thoughts. Yet they are confined by heavenly strictness, so that they cannot accomplish the evils they desire. It follows:

**VERSES 13–14.** If I say, “My bed will console me, and I shall be relieved by speaking with myself in my resting place,” you will terrify me through dreams, and through visions you will shake me with horror.---

In sacred Scripture, a bed, couch, or resting place commonly signifies the secret place of the heart. Hence it is written: “On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves” (Song III, 1). And in the Psalm: “The saints will exult in glory; they will rejoice upon their couches” (Ps. CXLIX, 5).

What else should we understand in this passage by dreams or visions except images of the final and strict judgment? We perceive it now to some extent through fear, but we do not yet see it truly as it is.

Holy men therefore always return to the secrets of the heart when, in this world, they suffer either prosperity beyond their desire or adversity beyond their strength. Wearied by external labors, they seek the couches or beds of the mind as though they were a resting place.

As if he were saying openly: “If, fleeing external things, I return inwardly, and in some measure desire to rest in the couch of my heart, there, when you set before me the contemplation of your strictness, you greatly terrify me through the very images of my own forethought, showing how strict a Judge you will come.”

“And I shall be relieved by speaking with myself.”---

For when, wearied, we return to the silence of our mind, we turn over within ourselves the hidden words of our thoughts, conversing as though upon a bed.

It should also be known that the images of dreams sometimes arise from fullness or emptiness of the stomach, sometimes from deception, as in Solomon’s saying: “Dreams follow many cares” (Eccl. V, 2). Sometimes they arise through revelation, as when Joseph was warned in a dream to flee to Egypt. Sometimes they arise through thought together with revelation, as in Daniel’s words: “You, O king, began to think upon your bed what would be after you, and he who reveals mysteries showed you what is to come” (Dan. II, 29). It follows:

**VERSE 15.** Therefore my soul chose hanging, and my bones chose death.---

What is signified by the soul except the mind’s intention? And what by the bones except the strength of the flesh? The soul therefore chooses hanging so that the bones may die, because when the mind’s intention lifts itself toward lofty things, it kills within itself all the strength of external life.

Holy men raise their minds to lofty things and gird themselves in the pursuit of virtues for love of the heavenly homeland. They pursue through the bond of humility what had previously made them strong in the world. Hence Paul says: “I live, yet no longer I,” and so forth (Gal. II, 20). Again: “A Hebrew, descended from Hebrews; according to the law, a Pharisee” (Phil. III, 5). And again: “But whatever gains I had, these I considered loss for the sake of Christ” (Phil. III, 7). It follows:

**VERSE 16.** I have despaired; I will certainly live no longer.---

For the just person to despair means to reject the goods of the present life by choosing eternity, to seek what will remain, and to place no confidence in temporal things.

There are some of the just who desire heavenly things while still retaining the temporal honors bestowed upon them; they do not covet what belongs to others, but lawfully use what is their own. There are also some of the just who, girded to attain the summit of perfection, abandon everything outwardly while inwardly seeking higher things. Of such Paul says: “For you have died,” and so forth (Col. III, 3). It follows:

“Spare me, Lord, for my days are nothing.”---

Far be it from us to think that the holy man despairs of the abundance of divine mercy, since he desires to be spared. Rather, by abandoning through despair the good things of the passing life, he rises more firmly in hope to obtain what remains.

The more truly holy men recognize supreme things, the more sublimely they despise earthly things. For this reason they perceive the days of the present life as nothing: they fix the eyes of their illumined minds upon the contemplation of eternity. It follows:

**VERSE 17.** What is man, that you magnify him, or why do you set your heart upon him?---

God magnifies man because he enriches him with the abundance of reason, visits him by the infusion of grace, and exalts him through the honor of virtue bestowed upon him. But the Lord sets his heart upon him because, after granting gifts, he establishes judgment, carefully weighs merits, and rigorously examines the burdens of life.

As if he were exclaiming openly: “Man is magnified by a spiritual gift, but he is nevertheless flesh. You strictly examine his ways after granting him gifts; yet if he is judged with your mercy removed, even the weight imposed by your scrutiny cannot be borne by the spirit, though it has been raised toward righteousness.” It follows:

**VERSE 18.** You visit him at dawn.---

We are pressed by the darkness of night when we are darkened by the commission of iniquity. But night is turned into light when the darkness of our error is illumined by the recognition of truth. The Lord therefore visits us at dawn when he enlightens the darkness of our error with the light of his knowledge. It is called dawn when the nocturnal times are already being changed into the love of light. It follows:

“And suddenly you test him.”---

For by approaching, he advances our hearts toward virtues; by withdrawing, he permits them to be shaken by temptation. If the mind were not shaken by any temptation after receiving the gifts of virtues, it would boast that it possessed those virtues through itself. Hence Paul, having been caught up to the third heaven, grieves that he has a law opposing him in his members. It follows:

**VERSE 19.** How long will you not spare me, nor release me so that I may swallow my saliva?---

Saliva flows into the mouth from the head; from the mouth it is carried to the stomach when it is swallowed. What, then, is our head except divinity, through which we receive the beginning of our existence and are creatures? Hence Paul says: “The head of man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God” (I Cor. XI, 3).

By the name “stomach,” the mind is designated. When it receives understanding from above, it undoubtedly governs the members of all actions after they have been cut away. Hence Solomon says: “The lamp of the Lord is the breath of man, searching all the hidden places of the stomach” (Prov. XX, 27).

By the name “saliva,” the taste of inward contemplation is understood. From the brightness of the Creator, while we are still placed in this life, it barely touches us through a taste of revelation. We cannot swallow it, because we are not permitted to be satisfied with the good of heavenly brightness.
