As if it were said openly: “You then truly spare man when you admit him to the perfection of your contemplation, so that, caught up inwardly, he may see your brightness, and the corruption of his flesh may not repel him. Then you permit me to swallow my saliva—when you have filled me with the taste of your brightness even to abundant satisfaction.” It follows:

**VERSE 20.** I have sinned; what shall I do to you, O guardian of men?---

Behold, he confesses the evil he has committed, but he does not find a good that he ought to offer to God in recompense. Thus, when it is said, “What shall I do to you?” the point is that the very good works we are commanded to perform benefit not the Commander but us. Hence it is written: “You have no need of my goods” (Ps. XV, 2).

God is called a guardian because, if his protection does not defend us, the watchful eye of our vigilance sleeps before the snares of the hidden enemy. Hence the Psalmist says: “Unless the Lord guards the city,” and so forth (Ps. CXXVI, 1).

It follows:

“Why have you set me against you, and have I become burdensome to myself?”---

God set man against himself when man abandoned God by sinning. Captured by the serpent’s persuasion, he became the enemy of the one whose commands he had despised. But this very opposition produced the weight of punishment for man and placed it upon the neck of his heart to be lifted up: he who refused to be subject to divine commands laid himself low beneath his own necessities.

He grows weary through idleness, fails through work, is restored by food, and undergoes other things of this kind. His mind is sometimes deceived by hope and sometimes troubled by fear. Often it loves what it had despised and despises what it had loved. In the flesh, man endures afflictions; and in the mind, anxieties. He carries himself as a heavy burden.

Hence it is written: “A heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam, from the day of their departure from their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all” (Ecclus. XL, 1).

As if he were saying openly: “Why do you despise man as though he were opposed to you, when I know with certainty that you do not wish even the one whom you are believed to despise to perish?” It follows:

VERSE 21. Why do you not take away my sin, and why do you not remove my iniquity?—By these words, what else is suggested than longing for the awaited Mediator? Of him John says: “Behold the Lamb of God,” and so forth (John 1:29). Or certainly, sin is then fully taken away from the human race when our corruption is exchanged for the glory of incorruption. Thus he desires the grace of the Redeemer, or the solidity of the resurrection, who hopes that his iniquity will be utterly removed. It follows:

“Behold, now I shall sleep in the dust, and if you seek me in the morning, I shall not remain.”—To the first man after his sin it was said: “You are dust, and to dust you shall go” (Gen. 3:19). “Morning,” however, signifies that manifestation of minds which, at the Judge’s coming, is displayed when thoughts are opened, as after the darkness of night. Hence the Psalmist says: “In the morning I shall stand before you and shall see” (Ps. 5:5). For God to seek a person is to examine him by a subtle interrogation and, by examining him strictly, to judge him. It is as though he openly lamented, saying: “At present I am already suffering the death of the flesh, yet I still dread from the coming judgment a more grievous death—the sentence of your strictness.” It follows:

# CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0186A]

VERSES 1–2. But Bildad the Shuhite answered and said: “How long will you speak such things, and [how long will] the spirit of your mouth be abundant?”—The words of the just are always burdensome to the unjust, and whatever they hear spoken for their edification they bear as though a weight had been laid upon them. The force and fullness of speakers’ expression are distinguished in four ways. For there are some whom breadth both of thought and of speech expands. There are some whom poverty both of thought and of speech constricts. There are some who possess effectiveness in speaking, but lack sharpness of thought. And there are some who are supported by keenness of thought, but fall silent through poverty of expression. But when blessed Bildad attributes “multiplicity” to the spirit of the mouth, he plainly censures poverty of heart. It is as though he openly said: “You are lifted up by an abundance of spirit in the speech of your mouth, but you are constricted by a poverty of understanding.” It follows:

VERSE 3. “Does God subvert judgment, or does the Almighty overturn what is just?”—Blessed Job had neither denied these things when speaking nor failed to know them when silent. But insolent people ostentatiously bring forward even what is well known, so that by speaking they may appear learned. It should be understood, however, that they praise the rectitude of divine justice when their prosperity raises them up to joy. But if the force of heavenly correction touches their life even briefly, they immediately reproach the decision of the divine examination when struck by it. It is therefore no wonder that this man praises divine justice, since he was suffering nothing adverse from that justice. It follows:

VERSE 4. “Even if your children sinned against him, he delivered them into the hand of their iniquity.”—It is as though preachers were proclaiming this error to afflicted Catholics: “Take care for your lives, and recognize how perverse are the things you hold by considering the condemnation of those who have died among you; for if your faithlessness had not displeased the Creator of all things, he would certainly not have taken such numerous peoples away from you through the violence of destruction.” It follows:

VERSE 5. “But if you will rise early to God and entreat the Almighty.”—Because heretics think that they possess the light of truth, they call the holy Church, as though placed in the night of error, toward the dawn of truth, so that by the knowledge of God they may rise, as it were, at dawn, and by prayers wash away their sins through repentance. It follows:

VERSE 6. “If you will walk pure and upright.”—Pure, that is, in thought; upright, in action. It follows:

“Immediately he will awaken for you.”—It is as though he openly said: “He who now does not exercise the power of your protection amid your tribulations sleeps, as though hesitating to come to your aid.” It follows:

“And he will make peaceful the dwelling of your righteousness.”—He again points to the adversities of the present life, so as immediately to demonstrate the security of tranquility. It follows:

VERSE 7. “So that your former things were small, and your latter things were multiplied exceedingly.”—Because the perverse consider temporal joy their sole good, they promise this to others as something very great. But if “the dwelling of righteousness” signifies the counsel of the mind, the teachers of error, addressing afflicted Catholics, promise them a peaceful dwelling of righteousness, as though they were drawing them over to their own side; and when they have done so, they fall silent concerning strife. They also promise that the riches of understanding will increase for those who follow, saying: “So that your former things were small.” It is added:

VERSE 8. “For ask the former generation, and diligently investigate the memory of the fathers.”—They admonish them to look into, not merely see, the former generation and the memory of the fathers, because they do not wish that to be noticed in it which is plainly evident to everyone. It follows:

VERSE 9. “For we are of yesterday, and we do not know how our days upon the earth are like a shadow.”—The former generation is therefore proposed for interrogation, so that the passing of the present life may be shown to be like a shadow. For if we recall to memory the things that existed and have already passed away, we plainly recognize how swiftly this too flees which we now possess. It follows:

VERSE 10. “They will teach you, and from their heart they will bring forth words.”—It should be noted that above he had said: “The spirit of your mouth.” But now, recalling the fathers to memory, he says: “They bring forth words from their heart.” It is as though heretics, detesting the life of the holy Church, were saying: “You have multiplicity of spirit in your mouth, but you do not have it in your heart.” Yet those ought to be heard against you who, bringing forth words from the heart, taught by living rightly. It follows:

[Col. 0187C]

VERSES 11–13. “Can the reed live without moisture, or can the rush grow without water?”—Bildad himself immediately discloses what he compares to the reed or rush when he adds: “While it is still in flower and has not been cut by hand, before all the grasses it withers; so are the ways of all who forget God, and the hope of the hypocrite will perish.”—By the name of the reed or rush he signifies the life of the hypocrite, which indeed possesses the appearance of truth, but does not yet possess, through the use of the hand, the useful fruit of benefit. Remaining dry through the work of sterility, it grows green only in the color of holiness.

Yet neither the reed without moisture nor the rush without water makes progress, because the life of hypocrites receives an infusion of heavenly light for good works, but, seeking outward praise in everything it does, is emptied of the fruit of the infusion it has received. Concerning such people Truth says: “Many will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in your name?” and so forth (Mark 7:22).

The reed is “in flower” when the hypocrite is in praise. But the rush, rising with sharp angles, is not cut by hand, because when his perceptions have been made harsh by arrogance, the hypocrite scorns being corrected for his perversity. In his flower he wounds the hand that cuts him, because when the hypocrite is placed in praise, if anyone dares to correct him, he immediately cuts the corrector with his harshness; and, as from the hand of one cutting, so from the mind of the corrector there flows, so to speak, a kind of blood of sorrow. Hence Solomon says: “Do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he mock you” (Prov. 9:9).

According to the flesh, the just are grasses, as the prophet testifies, saying: “All flesh is grass” (Isa. 40:6). But the reed is said to wither before all the grasses, because while the just remain in their goodness, the life of hypocrites dries up with respect to the greenness of the righteousness they have assumed. The grasses also wither, together with everything else, because the works of the just fail along with the life of the flesh. But the reed precedes the drying of the grasses, because before the hypocrite departs from the flesh, he abandons the deeds of virtue that he had displayed in himself. Hence it is written: “Let them become like the grass of the housetops, which withers before it is pulled up” (Ps. 128:6).

What does he hope for from all his works except the reverence of honor, the glory of praise, to be feared by those who are better, and to be called holy by human beings? But the hope of the hypocrite cannot endure, because, not seeking eternity, he flees from what he possesses. Concerning such people Truth says: “They have received their reward” (Matt. 6:16). It follows:

VERSE 14. “His folly will not please him.”—For it is great folly to undertake laborious things while panting after the breath of praise; to serve the heavenly commandments through vigorous work, but to seek the reward of an earthly recompense. Nevertheless, he is nourished by this very folly, because he is honored by everyone for his good work. For the time being this folly pleases him, but it will not please him when the time of recompense arrives. In punishment, what was foolish in him becomes displeasing. It follows:

“And his confidence is like a spider’s web.”—The confidence of hypocrites is rightly said to be like spiders’ webs, because everything for which they sweat in order to obtain glory is scattered by the wind of mortal life. Since they do not seek eternal things, they lose temporal goods along with time.

It should also be considered that spiders draw out their threads in an orderly fashion, because hypocrites arrange their works as though with discernment. A spider’s web is woven with care but scattered by a breath of air, because whatever the hypocrite accomplishes with labor is carried away by the breath of human favor. Hence Truth says: “For they disfigure their faces,” and so forth (Matt. 6:16). Now he places his confidence in holiness in the mouths of human beings; but when the witness of the heart appears, everything that outwardly trusts in human favor passes away. It follows:

VERSE 15. “He leans upon his house, and it will not stand.”—Our house is any matter which the mind inhabits through delight. Thus the hypocrite’s house is the delight of favor, which he inhabits as though at rest, because through all his works he reclines inwardly upon it. But the house cannot stand, because praise passes away with life, and human favor does not endure in judgment. Hence the foolish virgins, troubled, will say: “Give us some of your oil” (Matt. 25:8). It follows:

“He will prop it up, and it will not rise.”—For what cannot stand by itself is supported so that it may stand, because when the hypocrite sees his life tottering in judgment, he strives to establish it by propping it up with a reckoning of his works. Hence some will say: “Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in your name?” and so forth (Matt. 7:22). But the house of praise, supported by so many claims, will not rise at all, because the Judge immediately says: “I never knew you; depart from me,” and so forth (Matt. 25:12). The hypocrite’s house therefore cannot rise, because through everything he was able to do according to the heavenly commandments, he never lifts his soul away from earthly things. It follows:

VERSE 16. “He appears moist before the sun comes.”—Often in sacred eloquence the Lord is represented by the name “sun,” as it is said through the prophet: “But for you who fear the name of the Lord, the sun of righteousness will rise” (Mal. 4:2). Thus this reed is moist during the night but is dried when the sun comes, because the hypocrite is believed holy by human beings in the darkness of the present life, but when the strict Judge comes, it will appear how iniquitous he is. It follows:

“And at his rising his shoot will come forth.”—Every grass is produced by being born from the earth; afterward it is touched by air and heat, and only then is it opened to bring forth the shoot of its seed. But the reed is born with its flower, and as soon as it rises from the earth, it produces with itself the shoot of its seed. Thus the various grasses appropriately signify the holy, while the reed signifies the hypocrite: just men first arise in the work of their manner of life and, coming to their eternal homeland, enjoy the awaited recompense. The hypocrite, by contrast, who is born immediately in a good work, strives to receive the glory of the present world. Thus “the shoot at its rising” signifies recompense at the beginning. It follows:

VERSE 17. “Its roots will be thickened upon a heap of stones, and it will dwell among the stones.”—What are we to understand by “roots” except hidden thoughts? These emerge secretly, but rise openly in the display of works. By the name “stones,” however, Scripture designates human beings, as it says concerning the holy Church through Isaiah: “I will make your battlements of jasper and your gates of carved stones” (Isa. 54:12).

This reed, therefore, which dwells among the stones, thickens its roots upon a heap of rocks, because every hypocrite multiplies his thoughts in seeking the admiration of human beings. For in everything hypocrites do, they seek human praise through hidden thoughts, just as the roots of the reed send their roots into a heap. The reed also dwells among stones, because the hypocrite stands where he makes firm the intention of his mind. For when he seeks to receive the testimony of many, he remains, as it were, in a contest. It follows:

VERSE 18. “If it is swallowed up from its place, it will deny him and say: ‘I do not know you.’”—The hypocrite is swallowed up from his place when, at death, he is separated from the favors of the present life. But the inward Judge denies the one who has been swallowed up and declares that he does not know him, because Truth, justly rejecting the life of pretenders, does not recognize it, nor acknowledge the good things he did, since he did not bring them forth from a right intention. Hence, coming in judgment to the foolish virgins, he says: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12).

But would that the hypocrites’ own destruction were sufficient for them, and that their perverse pursuits did not spur other ardent persons toward life by their duplicity [duplicatis; the precise force is uncertain]. For each person ordinarily wants others joined to him who are of the same character as himself. It follows:

VERSE 19. “For this is the joy of his way, that others may again spring up from the earth.”—It is as though it were openly said: “He does not recognize the Judge who is coming, but receives him in many ways, because he rejoices more joyfully in his own iniquity insofar as he has also been wickedly propagated in others.” For whoever is not satisfied here with his own iniquity must necessarily be tormented there also by the guilt of another. It follows:

VERSE 20. “God does not cast away the simple, nor does he extend his hand to the malicious.”—For when he appears strict in judgment, he both raises up the despised simple by glorifying them and crushes the glory of the malicious by rejecting it. Hypocrites are called “malicious” because they do good things badly and perform every upright act under the pursuit of praise.

By “extending the hand,” we mean that we raise someone from the depths. God therefore does not extend his hand to the malicious, because he leaves those who seek earthly glory below and, however upright their actions may appear, does not advance them to the joys above. Hypocrites are surely called malicious for this reason: they display kindness toward their neighbor while revealing the deceits of their own iniquity. Against such people it is rightly said through Moses: “You shall not wear a garment woven from wool and linen together” (Deut. 22:11). For wool signifies simplicity, while linen signifies subtlety. It follows:

VERSE 21. “Until your mouth is filled with laughter and your lips with jubilation.”—It is as though it were openly said: The life of the simple does not abandon them even before the judgment, and by abandoning them it does not cease to strike the minds of the malicious before that time appears. The mouths of the just will then be filled with laughter when their hearts, after the tears of their pilgrimage have ended, are satisfied with the exultation of eternal joy. Concerning this laughter the Lord says to the disciples: “The world will rejoice, and you will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be changed into joy” (John 16:20).

We call it “jubilation” when we conceive in the heart such great joy as the power of speech cannot express; nevertheless, the exultation of the mind sounds through the mouth what speech cannot explain. The mouth is therefore rightly said to be filled with laughter and the lips with jubilation, because in that eternal homeland, when the minds of the just are received into exultation, the tongue is raised in a song of praise.

When it says “until,” this does not mean that Almighty God will not raise the malicious until he has taken his elect to the joys of jubilation, as though afterward he might rescue from punishment those whom, abandoning them earlier in their guilt, he condemns. Rather, he will not do this before the judgment, when it might remain doubtful to human beings whether it will happen. For in the jubilation of his elect, since he does not extend his hand to the malicious, it is already evident from the very strictness of the final examination. Thus the Psalmist also says: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Ps. 109:1, 4). It follows:

VERSE 22. “Those who hate you will be clothed with confusion.”—At the final examination, confusion clothes the enemies of the just, because when they see their past evils overflowing before the eyes of their minds, their own guilt, pressing them down on every side, clothes them. Then they endure the memory of their deeds as punishment—those who now sin joyfully, as though estranged from the sense of reason. There they see how greatly they ought to have fled from what they loved. It follows:

“The tent of the impious will not endure.”—A tent is built so that the body may be defended from heat and cold. What, then, is expressed here by the name “tent” except the construction of earthly happiness? Through it they multiply what will fall upon them, so that they may defend themselves from the necessities of the present life as from heat and rain. They seek to be occupied with honors so that they may not appear despised. By accumulating earthly things they heap them up, so that they may not waste away in the cold of poverty. Wherever, therefore, they construct a dwelling for the mind, there they have undoubtedly fixed their tents.

The just, by contrast, neither admire offered goods nor greatly fear inflicted evils. Even when they make use of present goods, they fear future evils. And while they groan over present evils, they are consoled by love of the goods to come. It is therefore rightly said: “The tent of the impious will not endure”—because lovers of the fleeting life, while they diligently build themselves up in present things, are suddenly snatched away to eternal things.

# BOOK NINE

[Col. 0191]

# CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0191B]

VERSES 1–2. But Job answered and said: “Truly I know that it is so, and that a man placed beneath God is not justified.”—A person subjected to God receives justice; a person setting himself on an equal footing with God loses it. For whoever compares himself with the Author of good things deprives himself of the good he has received. It follows:

VERSE 3. “If he wishes to contend with him, he will not be able to answer him one thing for a thousand.”—In sacred Scripture the number one thousand commonly signifies totality. Hence it is said: “The word that he commanded for a thousand generations” (Ps. 105:8). And John says: “And they will reign with him for a thousand years” (Rev. 20:6).

Because one, multiplied, is brought to ten, and ten, multiplied by itself, tends toward one thousand, we proceed from one until we arrive at one thousand. What, then, is signified here by “one” except the beginning of right living? And what by the breadth of the number one thousand except the perfection of that same good life?

To contend with God is not to attribute glory to him but to arrogate to oneself the glory of one’s virtue. Whoever contends with the Creator is unable to answer one thing for a thousand, because the person who exalts himself on the basis of perfection does not even show that he possesses the beginning of right living. It follows:

VERSE 4. “He is wise in heart and strong in power.”—God is called wise because, knowing our hidden things with subtlety, he strikes them. Now, as the wise one, he sees all things invisibly and cannot be deceived by us; then, as the strong one, he punishes without any obstacle those whom he rejects, and he cannot be avoided. It follows:

“Who has resisted him and had peace?”—He who creates all things wondrously orders them so that the things created may be harmonious with one another. Therefore, wherever resistance is offered to the Creator, the harmony of peace is shattered. For the perverse mind is confused within itself precisely where it rises up against the Author. We say that someone resists when he strives to oppose God’s dispositions. Our weakness does not, in fact, obstruct his unchangeable sentence; nevertheless, it attempts what it cannot accomplish. It strives to oppose him, but is broken by the very sword of its opposition. It follows:

VERSE 5. “He removes mountains, and they do not know those whom he overturns in his anger.”—In sacred Scripture the name “mountains” often signifies the multitude of preachers. Concerning them the Psalmist says: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people” (Ps. 72:3).

But Truth removed the mountains when it withdrew holy preachers from Jewish obstinacy. Hence it is said: “The mountains will be transferred into the heart of the sea” (Ps. 46:3); and they themselves say: “It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you first,” and so forth (Acts 12:46). Yet those who were overthrown in the Lord’s anger did not know this very transfer, because when the Hebrews expelled the apostles from their territories, they considered themselves to have gained something by losing the light of preaching. It follows:

VERSE 6. “He shakes the earth from its place, and its pillars tremble.”—The earth was shaken from its place when the Israelite people, torn away from the boundaries of Judea, submitted its neck to the nations, because it had refused to be subjected to the Author. That earth had pillars, because its stubborn structure, destined to collapse, had risen up in the priests and rulers, the teachers of the law and the Pharisees.

But when the mountains were transferred, the pillars were shaken, because, after the apostles had been withdrawn from Judea, those who had expelled the preachers of life from it were not themselves permitted to live there. For Judea was immediately destroyed through the Roman ruler Titus and, scattered among all the nations, was dispersed. It follows:

VERSE 7. “He commands the sun, and it does not rise; he seals up the stars as though under a seal.”—At times in sacred eloquence the name “sun” signifies the brightness of preachers, as it is said through John: “The sun became like a sackcloth made of hair” (Rev. 6:12). The preachers themselves are also signified by the name “stars,” concerning which it is said: “The stars of the rains have been restrained” (Jer. 3:3).

Holy preachers become a sun to our eyes during the day when they open for us the contemplation of the true light. And they shine like stars in darkness when, through the active life that benefits us, they arrange earthly affairs for our needs.

But after the preachers had been expelled, there was no one to show the Jewish people, remaining in the night of their faithlessness, either the brightness of contemplation or the light of the active life. Truth, which had abandoned them after being rejected, deservedly blinded them through the withdrawal of the light of preaching because of their perversity, and sealed up the stars as though under a seal: while keeping its preachers within itself through silence, it concealed heavenly light from the blind minds of the wicked.

Thus he who now withdraws his preachers from the eyes of Judea but later displays them has, as it were, sealed up the stars under a seal, so that, when the rays of the spiritual stars are first hidden and afterward flash forth, Judea may neither see the night of its faithlessness now, while rejected, nor fail to recognize it then, when enlightened.

Hence Isaiah says: “Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Isa. 10:22). And Paul says: “Until the fullness of the nations enters, and thus all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11:25). For this reason those two outstanding preachers were withdrawn through a delayed death, so that they might be recalled to the work of preaching at the end. Concerning them it is said: “These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands in the presence of the Lord of the earth” (Rev. 11:4). It follows:

VERSE 8. “He alone stretches out the heavens.”—What is signified by the name “heavens” except this same heavenly life of the preachers? Concerning them the Psalmist says: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 19:2). Thus they are remembered both as heavens and as the sun: heavens, because by interceding they protect; the sun, because by preaching they display the power of light.

When the earth was shaken, the heavens were stretched out, because when Judea raged against the force of persecution, the Lord extended the life of the apostles throughout the knowledge of all the nations. The heavens had been narrow when one people held so many outstanding preachers; but God alone stretched out the heavens, who, through the marvelous dispensation of his hidden counsel, caused his preachers to be extended to the very ends of the world from the place where he had permitted them to be oppressed within one nation. It follows:

“And he walks upon the waves of the sea.”—What is signified by the name “sea” except the bitterness of this world, raging against the death of the good? Hence it is written: “Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin” (Ps. 33:7).

The Lord therefore walks upon the waves of the sea, because when the storms of persecution rise up, they are broken by the astonishment produced by his miracles. He who calms the swellings of human madness treads, as it were, upon waves raised into a heap. For the Lord has placed as many steps upon these waves as he has displayed miracles to proud persecutors. Hence the Psalmist says: “The swellings of the sea are wondrous; the Lord on high is wondrous” (Ps. 93:4).

The Lord rightly says through Jeremiah: “I set the sand as a boundary for the sea, an everlasting commandment that will not pass away; they will be moved, but they will not prevail; its waves will swell, but they will not pass over it” (Jer. 5:22). The Lord placed sand against the sea when, to break the glory of the world, he chose the despised and the poor. But the waves cannot pass over the sand, because they are broken by the miracles and humility of the despised. It follows:

[Col. 0194A]

VERSE 9. “He makes Arcturus and Orion.”—The discourse of Truth does not follow the empty fables of Hesiod, Aratus, and Callimachus, so that, when it names Arcturus, it might suppose the extremity of the seven-starred tail of the Bear, or imagine Orion, armed like a madman, holding a sword. These names of the stars were invented by worshipers of carnal wisdom.

But sacred Scripture uses these same names so that the realities it wishes to suggest may be expressed through familiar designations. What, then, is expressed by the name “Arcturus,” which, established at the summit of heaven, shines with the rays of seven stars, except the universal Church, which is represented in John’s Apocalypse by seven churches and seven lampstands?

While the Church contains within itself the gifts of the Spirit’s sevenfold grace, radiating with the brightness of supreme virtue, it shines as if from the pole of truth. And just as Arcturus is always turning and never sets, so the holy Church continually endures the persecutions of the wicked, yet persists without failing until the end of the world. Thus Arcturus is raised while it turns, because the holy Church is more powerfully strengthened in truth when it is more ardently wearied for the sake of truth.

Orions, at their rising, stir up storms and disturb seas and lands. They signify the martyrs, because when the holy Church is raised to the condition of preaching, those who will suffer the weight and hardships of persecutors come, as it were, in winter to the pole of heaven. The heavens therefore brought forth Orions when the holy Church sent forth martyrs.

Winter shuddered because of the Orions, since, as the steadfastness of the saints increased, the cold mind of unbelievers roused itself toward the storm of persecution. What, then, is signified by the name “Hyades” except the teachers of the holy Church? When the storm of persecution had been removed and the long nights of unbelief had ended, they arose within the holy Church at the time when a brighter year was also opened through the springtime of faith.

They are called by the Greek word *hyetos* (ὑετός), “rain.” They are therefore aptly expressed by the name “Hyades,” since they bring the rains of holy preaching to the condition of the universal Church. Hence Moses says: “Let my speech be awaited like rain,” and so forth (Deut. 32:2). And Isaiah says: “I will command my clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isa. 5:6).

With the heavens stretched out, the Lord formed Arcturus, because, having brought the apostles into heavenly honor, he founded the Church in a heavenly way of life. Having formed Arcturus, he also made the Orions, because, once the faith of the universal Church had been strengthened, it brought forth martyrs against the storms of the world. Having brought forth the Orions, he produced the Hyades, because, as the martyrs grew strong against adversity, he bestowed the teaching of masters to irrigate the dryness of human hearts. It follows:

“And the inner chambers of the south.”—What is designated by the name “south” except the fervor of the Holy Spirit? When someone is filled with it, he burns with love for the spiritual homeland. Hence it is said: “Rise, north wind, and come, south wind,” and so forth (Song 4:16).

The inner chambers of the south are those hidden orders of angels and the most secret recesses of the heavenly homeland, which the warmth of the Holy Spirit fills. The souls of the saints reach there, both those now stripped of their bodies and those later restored to their bodies, and are hidden like stars in secret places. It follows:

VERSE 10. “He does great and unsearchable things, and wonders of which there is no number.”—Great in power, unsearchable in reason, innumerable in multiplicity. For we more truly comprehend the works of divine strength when we recognize that we cannot know them. We speak more eloquently when, being struck with amazement at them, we remain silent. Hence the Psalmist says: “Praise him in his powers,” and so forth (Ps. 19:7). It follows:

VERSE 11. “If he comes to me, I shall not see him; and if he departs, I shall not understand.”—The approach and withdrawal of God from our mind are not recognized at all so long as the outcome of changing circumstances remains unknown. For in temptation it is uncertain whether he tests or destroys; and concerning gifts it cannot be discerned whether they reward those who have been abandoned here or nourish them on the way so that they may lead them to their homeland.

It is as though he openly lamented, saying: “After I once willingly lost my eyes, how do I endure the blindness of the night I have sought, recognizing neither the rising nor the setting of the sun?”” It follows:

VERSE 12. “If he suddenly questions, who will answer him?”—God questions suddenly when he calls us, unprepared, to the strictness of his examination. But a human being is not sufficient to answer his questioning, because if he is examined then with mercy removed, even the life of the just succumbs in that examination.

Or certainly, he questions when he strikes us with harsh persecutions, and often the one who is struck groans. But he is not sufficient to answer, because the adversity of the blow itself displeases him, yet the person remains silent and fears to scrutinize divine judgments, recognizing that he is dust. Hence Paul says: “O man, who are you to answer God?” (Rom. 9:20). It follows:

“Or who can say to him: ‘Why do you act in this way?’”—The deeds of the Author must always be revered without investigation, because they can in no way be unjust. To seek an explanation for his hidden counsel is nothing other than to grow proud against his counsel. In the blow, therefore, let the mind return to itself and not seek what it cannot grasp. Hence Paul says: “Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it: ‘Why did you make me like this?’” (ibid.). It follows:

VERSE 13. “God, whose anger no one can resist.”—It is greatly to be wondered at how it is said that no one can resist divine anger, when the examples required by the matter show that many have often resisted it, such as Moses, Aaron, Phinehas, and David.

But if we weigh the matter subtly and recognize the truth, both statements are true: divine anger cannot be resisted, and many have often resisted it. For all the saints who oppose God’s anger receive from God himself the ability to stand against the force of his striking. They rise up, so to speak, with him against him; and what is imposed by him to be done is opposed to him as though against his will.

But when he prevails, human indignation cannot restrain him. Thus Moses was unable to repel from himself the anger of the punishment that had been decreed, so as to enter the promised land, although, with the Lord willing, he had removed that anger from the people. Divine anger can therefore be resisted when the one who is angry himself gives assistance; but it cannot be resisted at all when he both arouses himself to vengeance and does not inspire the prayer poured out to him.

Hence it is said to Jeremiah: “Therefore do not pray for this people, nor take up praise and prayer for them, nor intercede with me, because I will not hear them in the time of their cry to me” (Jer. 7:16). Again it is written: “Why do you cry out over your wound? Your pain is incurable” (Jer. 30:15). It follows:

“And under him those who bear the world are bent.”—Those bear the world who endure the cares of the present age. Hence among the Greeks rulers of the earth are called *basileis* (βασιλεῖς). For *laus* is interpreted as “people.” *Basileus* is therefore interpreted in Latin as “basis of the people,” because the one who governs the people, fixed by the weight of that power, supports the people upon himself.

It is as though he openly said: “You strictly abandon those who were once subject, and mercifully bend the powers of the nations that have raised themselves up.”

Alternatively: angelic powers bear the world, administering the cares of governance, as Paul testifies, saying: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Heb. 1:14). It is as though he were saying: “Which weak human being could confront your clouds, when even the angelic powers bend themselves in fear of you?”

Or certainly, those most subtle spirits would be upright if they fully grasped the power of his majesty. But those who bear the world are bent beneath God, because even the angelic powers do not comprehend the height of his divinity, though they behold it while raised up. It follows:

[Col. 0196C]

VERSE 14. “How much less am I, that I should answer him and speak with him in my own words?”—It is as though he openly said: “If that creature, which is not burdened by flesh, is not sufficient to contemplate him, with what mind do I dispute about his judgments, when I am constricted by the weight of corruption?”

God’s words addressed to us are his judgments, which pronounce the sentence concerning our actions; and our words addressed to God are the works that we present. But a human being cannot speak with God in his own words, because before his subtle judgment he possesses no confidence concerning his deeds. It follows:

### VERSE 15

“For even if I have anything just, I shall not answer, but I shall entreat my judge.”

All human justice is proved to be injustice if it is judged strictly. Therefore, after justice, it needs entreaty, so that what, when examined, might have succumbed may recover strength solely through the judge’s mercy. As if he were saying: “Even if I advance toward life through the work of virtue, I shall recover strength not through merits but through pardon.” Therefore, when we do what is right, we must lean upon prayer, so that everything we live justly may be seasoned with humility. It follows:

### VERSE 16

“And when he has heard me calling, I do not believe that he has heard my voice.”

For often the mind is kindled by the fire of divine love and is lifted up to contemplate heavenly and hidden things; but, struck by sudden temptation, it is pierced by the enemy’s thoughts and bent down—though it had been raised toward God with strong intention. Indeed, it is often brought to the point of wondering how it has comprehended such lofty things, when illicit thought has defiled it, and, conversely, how it receives illicit things, when the powerful fervor of the spirit carries it above itself. Hence it is written: “They ascend to the heavens and descend to the abysses” (Psalm 106:26).

The mind, then, becomes anxious through its very mutability, and because it unwillingly suffers what it suffers, it supposes that it has been rejected and cast down, and so the certainty of being heard is darkened for it. It follows:

### VERSE 17

“For in the whirlwind he will crush me.”

Every sinner is worn down in the whirlwind: he who seemed to stand upright in tranquility is killed by the severity of the final judgment, after having long been tolerated by heavenly patience. Hence the Psalmist says: “God will come manifestly, our God, and he will not be silent. Fire will burn before him, and a mighty tempest will surround him” (Psalm 49:3).

The just person, however, is not then crushed for this reason: here he always anxiously fears lest he be crushed. It follows: “And he will multiply my wounds even without cause.”

For some are taken away from the present light before they reach the active performance of good or evil merits. Since the sacraments of salvation do not free them from the guilt of original sin, they have done nothing here from their own initiative, yet they arrive there at punishments. For them, one wound is being born corruptible, another is dying bodily. But because eternal death also follows death, their wounds are multiplied by a hidden and just judgment, even without cause. They undergo everlasting torments, including those who have sinned nothing by their own will.

Hence it is written: “There is none clean in his sight, not even an infant of one day upon the earth.” Hence Truth itself says: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5). These words also aptly apply to blessed Job. Therefore, when he declares himself wounded without cause, he speaks outwardly of himself what Truth testifies inwardly concerning him, saying: “You have moved me against him, that I might afflict him without cause.” It follows:

### VERSE 18

“He does not allow my spirit to rest, and he fills me with bitterness.”

Often, for the just, the exercise of virtue consists solely in enduring adversities outwardly. But so that struggle may train their strength through complete testing, sometimes torments tear them outwardly while the adversary’s torments afflict them inwardly. Hence the holy man declares that he has been filled with bitterness. It follows:

### VERSE 19

“If strength is sought, he is most powerful; if the equity of the judge is sought, no one dares give testimony on my behalf.”

For he examines the causes of life who does not investigate them through another’s testimony. He who is eventually revealed as the strict bringer of punishment had long existed as the silent witness of guilt. Hence it is said through the prophet: “I am judge and witness” (Jeremiah 29:23). Again he says: “I was silent, I was always still; I was patient; like a woman in labor I shall speak” (Isaiah 42:14). It follows:

### VERSE 20

“If I wish to justify myself, my mouth will condemn me; if I show myself innocent, it will prove me perverse.”

As if he were openly saying: “Why speak of others, when I myself cannot give testimony on my own behalf?” He adds:

### VERSE 21

“If I am simple, my soul itself will not know it.”

As if he were openly saying: “With what audacity do I rebuke the judgments of my Creator, when I myself do not know myself because of the darkness of infirmity?” Hence it is said through the prophet: “The abyss gave forth its voice” (Habakkuk 3:10), and so forth.

For often, if we know the good things we do, we are led to pride; and if we know them, we do not preserve them at all. Who does not become at least somewhat proud of the awareness of his virtue? Or who, conversely, would preserve in himself a good thing that he does not know? In opposition to both dangers, what remains except that we should know and yet not know the right things we do, so that we may judge them both right and insignificant? It follows: “And my life was wearisome to me.”

The just person is wearied of living, because, while doing his work, he does not cease seeking life, yet he is unable to discover the merit of that same life. It is added:

### VERSE 22

“One thing is what I have said: He himself consumes the innocent and the impious.”

As if it were openly said: “This word of thought have I uttered within myself: neither shall I appear innocent if I am strictly examined, nor, if I wish to hide within myself, shall I be concealed from the acuity of the heavenly examination.”

The innocent, therefore, is consumed by the Creator, because however great his simplicity may be, it is devoured by the simplicity of divine greatness. The impious, too, is consumed by the Creator, because, with God ordering all things, his impiety is judged through his own cunning. Or certainly he is said himself to consume both the innocent and the impious because, although they are divided in the merits of their life, they are equally dragged from the first merit of guilt to the destruction of the flesh.

Hence Solomon says: “The learned man dies in the same way as the unlearned” (Ecclesiastes 2:16). And again: “All things are subject to vanity, and all proceed to one place. They were made from the earth, and together they shall return to the earth” (Ecclesiastes 3:19–20). It follows:

### VERSE 23

“If he scourges, let him kill once for all, and let him not laugh at the punishments of the innocent.”

Who would not believe that these words were spoken through pride, unless he heard the sentence of the judge, who says: “You have not spoken rightly before me, as my servant Job has” (Job 42:7).

But we, who have already withdrawn from God in mind and return in the flesh to dust, are bound by the punishment of a twofold death. Yet he came to us who would die for us in the flesh alone, who would join his single death to our double death and free us from both. Concerning him Paul says: “For the death that he died, he died to sin once for all” (Romans 6:10).

Every desire, when it is desired, is a punishment. Hence Solomon says: “Hope deferred afflicts the soul” (Proverbs 13:12). God’s laughing means his refusal to have mercy on the human soul, as in: “I too will laugh at your destruction” (Proverbs 1:26).

As if, therefore, he were speaking in the voice of those who desired the mystery of the Incarnation, he says: “Because our life is daily worn down by the scourge of vengeance for guilt, let him now come who will die once for all on our behalf without guilt, and let it no longer be said that he laughs at the punishments of the innocent, if he himself appears in a passible body, in whose desires our mind chastens itself.”

Or certainly, he calls God’s laughter joy. The Lord is said to laugh at the punishments of the innocent because the more ardently he is sought by us, the more sweetly he rejoices over us. We make a kind of joy out of punishment when, through holy desires, we chastise ourselves in his love. Hence the Psalmist says: “Appoint the solemn day amid the dense foliage,” and so forth (Psalm 117:27). It follows:

### VERSE 24

“The earth has been given into the hands of the impious; he covers the face of its judges.”

By the name “earth,” Christ’s flesh is expressed; by the designation “impious,” the devil is signified. The hands of this impious one were those who raged in the death of our Redeemer. The earth, therefore, was given into the hands of the impious because the ancient enemy could not corrupt the Redeemer’s mind by tempting him directly, but was permitted to extinguish his flesh through his agents for three days.

The judges of this earth were the priests and rulers, Pilate and the mockers. The face of the judges was therefore covered by the malice of the impious, because the minds of his persecutors, though able to hold him in the flesh, did not recognize God even through his miracles. Hence Paul says: “To this very day, when Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart” (2 Corinthians 3:15).

It follows: “But if he is not that one, who then is he?”

As if he were saying: “Who should ever be considered impious, if that people which persecuted piety itself is not impious?” For suddenly he is handed over by the devil to his followers. It follows:

### VERSE 25

“My days were swifter than a courier.”

The duty of a courier is to announce what follows. Therefore, all the elect who were born before the Redeemer’s coming—because they announced him either merely by seeing him beforehand or also by speaking of him—were like couriers in the world.

But because they were foreseen to be taken away before the awaited time of the Redeemer, they grieve that they pass more quickly than a courier, and lament that their days are not extended as far as seeing the Redeemer’s light. It follows: “They fled and did not see the good.”

All things that have been created are good, as in: “God saw all that he had made, and it was very good” (Genesis 1:31). But this Good is principally good, through which all these things are good. Hence Truth says: “No one is good except God alone” (Matthew 10:18).

As if, therefore, he were saying: “Those who could not reach the Redeemer’s presence passed away before the awaited time.”

#### Morally

For this purpose man was created: that he might be able to see the Good that is to be seen, and that, through the increase of time, his life might be extended toward it, not rolled away from it. But he who willingly fell into guilt suffered the passage of what he had touched as forbidden; and he who did not wish to stand in the light lost his eyes by fleeing, because guilt began to run downward and struck him with blindness, lest he see the light within. It follows:

### VERSE 26

“They passed by like ships carrying apples.”

Those who cross the seas carrying apples themselves enjoy the fragrance of the fruits, but carry food from those same fruits to others. Who, then, were the ancient Fathers except ships carrying apples? By prophesying the mystery of the divine Incarnation, they themselves were refreshed by its fragrance, but carried to us the fruit of the same hope.

What they tasted by awaiting, we are filled with by seeing and receiving. Hence the Lord says: “Others have labored, and you have entered into their labors” (John 4:38).

Or certainly, those who carry apples in ships mix apples with straw so that they may remain unharmed. In the same way, those who preceded us, when they announce the mysteries of spiritual life, preserve them by interspersing the straw of history, and carry to us the hidden fruit of the spirit while speaking of carnal things.

#### Morally

When ships carry apples, they bear the fruits of the earth across the waves. The earth, moreover, was a paradise for man; and the apples were the word of the commandment, the permitted possibility of action implanted in nature, and understanding of the Creator.

But because through the mystery of the cross we are recalled to the innate goods of nature, we carry apples, as it were, through the wood. And while we still try to preserve so many gifts amid temptations, we are driven by the breath of the present life and wearied by the waves of our mutability.

#### Another interpretation

When ships carry apples, they possess the sweetness of fragrance but do not possess the heaviness of weight. So the human race, when it raises itself again toward the heavenly things, burns with the fragrance of remembrance but does not bring forth the fire, because of the weight of life. We remember the height of paradise together with the recollection of its ardor, and we endure in the flesh the troublesome waves of temptations.

It is added: “Like an eagle flying to its food.”

For just as an eagle flies up to the heights and yet seeks the earth in order to take flesh, so were the ancient Fathers. Insofar as human weakness allowed, they contemplated the Creator’s light with an upright mind; but, knowing beforehand that he would become incarnate at the end of the world, they lowered their eyes from the sun’s rays toward the earth, as it were. When they saw him destined to suffer and die for the human race, they refreshed themselves, as it were, by his death.

#### Morally

For an eagle is suspended in a very lofty flight, but because of the appetite of its belly it seeks the earth. So too the human race, in its first parent, fell from exalted things to the depths. But because it touched the forbidden food, it came down to earthly things through the desire of the belly, and is fed, as it were, on flesh when it rejoices in bodily pleasures below. It follows:

### VERSE 27

“When I say, ‘I will certainly not speak in this way,’ I change my face and am tortured by grief.”

The Jewish people did not wish to speak as before; it denied whatever it had foretold. But it is tortured with a changed face because, when it defiled through the ugliness of faithlessness the appearance of its inner person by which it could have been recognized by the Creator, it condemned itself beneath eternal vengeance, beginning with present evils.

For it is not recognized by the Author with a changed face, as it were, when it is rejected after losing the faith of a good conscience.

#### Morally

Often we are pressed by silent thoughts: Why did almighty God create man when he foresaw that he would perish? Why did he not wish to make him such that he could not perish?

But when the silent mind asks these questions, it fears lest it break out into the boldness of pride. We say that we ought by no means to speak in this way when, passing beyond the measure of our weakness through inquiry, we correct ourselves in fear.

Thus the face is changed, because the mind—which previously sought the highest things while grasping them—begins, upon recognizing its weakness, to revere what it did not understand. But there is grief within the very warning, because it is deeply afflicted that, through the merit of the first guilt, it is blinded from understanding the things that concern him. It imposes silence upon its mouth, but the grief awakened by the very restraint is increased. It follows:

### VERSE 28

“I feared all my works.”

What the blessed Job’s works were, the sacred text of this history shows. What works, then, did he fear, when he always performed those by which God is accustomed to be appeased concerning iniquity?

From this we gather that, if we truly desire to please God, after we have subdued perverse things we must also fear the good things we have done. In good works, what must be feared before God is sloth and deceit. Hence the prophet says: “Cursed is everyone who does the work of the Lord deceitfully and negligently” (Jeremiah 48:10).

A lesser love of God increases sloth. Possessing deceit with an evil mind, self-love creates it. Against this it is said: “He shakes his hands free from every gift” (Isaiah 33:15). A gift from the heart is favor captured by thought; a gift from the mouth is glory through approval; a gift from the hand is reward through exaltation.

As if, therefore, it were said in humble confession: “I see what I have done openly, but I do not know what I have secretly endured in these things.” It follows: “Knowing that you would not spare the delinquent.”

For if the delinquent is not spared, who is rescued from eternal death, when no one is found free from delinquency? Or will he spare the penitent but not spare the delinquent? Are we not delinquent when we lament our offenses? And when Peter, denying him, is looked upon and called to tears? Why did Paul, when he was trying to extinguish the Redeemer’s name on earth, deserve to hear his words from heaven?

Yet guilt was punished in both. The Lord, therefore, does not spare the delinquent because he does not leave guilt without vengeance. Either the person himself punishes it in himself through repentance, or God strikes him by avenging it together with the person. It follows:

### VERSE 29

“But if I am impious even in this way, why have I labored in vain?”

For if we are examined with piety removed, our work is worthy of punishment, though we await rewards for it. This does not mean that he regrets having labored, but that he is uncertain about rewards and grieves amid his labors.

It must be understood that holy men are uncertain in such a way that they trust, and trust in such a way that nevertheless they do not grow sluggish through security. It follows:

### VERSE 30

“If I wash myself as with waters of snow, and my hands shine as though most clean…”

The waters of snow are the lamentations of humility. This humility, because it surpasses the other virtues before the eyes of the strict Judge, shines white, as though with the color of great merit.

There are, however, some who have lamentation but do not have humility. These indeed have water, but they do not have water of snow. Concerning these waters of snow someone says: “A contrite and humbled heart,” and so forth (Psalm 50:19).

Or certainly, water from a spring or river arises from the earth, whereas water of snow falls through the air. Those who are pierced with compunction in prayer for earthly goods are drenched with water from the earth. But those who weep because they desire heavenly rewards are washed by water of snow, because heavenly compunction is poured into them.

By “hands,” what else is designated except works? Hence it is said through the prophet concerning certain people: “Your hands are full of blood” (Isaiah 1:15).

It should be noted that he does not say, “If they shine as pure,” but “like the purest,” because as long as we are bound by the punishment of corruption, however rightly we may live, we do not attain true purity but imitate it. It follows:

### VERSE 31

“Yet you will dip me in filth.”

God is said to dip us, that is, to reveal us as dipped in filth, because the more truly we rise toward him through good works, the more subtly we recognize the filth of our life by which we differ from his purity.

As if he were openly saying: “Although I am steeped in the lamentations of heavenly compunction, although I am exercised through devotion to right action, nevertheless I see in your purity that I am not clean.”

It follows: “And my garments will abhor me.”

By the name “garment,” the body is designated, by which the soul is clothed and covered so that it may not appear naked in the subtlety of its substance. Hence Solomon says: “Let your garments be white at all times” (Ecclesiastes 9:8). And Isaiah: “The garment mixed with blood shall be for burning” (Isaiah 9:5).

In the manner of sacred speech, our garments are said to abhor us because they make us abominable, as it is said through Peter concerning Judas: “This man, having acquired a field from the reward of iniquity…” (Acts 1:18). Although, when he died, he could not himself possess the field, he is said to have possessed it because he caused it to be possessed.

Paul feared this filth of garments when he said: “I see another law in my members,” and so forth (Romans 7:23). It follows:

### VERSE 32

“For he is not a man like me, that I might answer him, nor one who could be heard with me on equal terms in judgment.”

When we contend with someone on equal terms in judgment, we recognize what is said against us and hear it in what we ourselves say. Since the invisible Judge sees what we do, he hears, as it were, what we say. But because we do not fully perceive what displeases him, we are ignorant, as it were, of what he has said. It follows:

### VERSE 33

“There is no one who can rebuke both of us and place his hand upon us both.”

It sounds harsh to say that God rebukes, but it will not seem harsh if we recall what he himself says through another prophet: “Cease to act perversely,” and so forth (Isaiah 1:16). And again: “Come, and let us argue together, says the Lord” (Isaiah 1:18).

In commanding that he himself be rebuked, the Lord openly shows how much confidence he grants to good actions. Hence the Lord says: “I sought a man who would interpose a hedge and stand opposed before me, lest I destroy it, and I found none” (Ezekiel 22:30).

But although they oppose the movements of present punishment, they are nevertheless unable, by their own power, to drive the penalties of death away from the human race. The Redeemer of the human race alone appeared just among human beings: he rebuked man so that he would not sin, and stood before God so that he would not strike.

He placed his hand upon both, because he provided human beings with examples to imitate, and by dying displayed in himself works by which God might be reconciled to humanity. It follows:

### VERSE 34

“Let him take away his rod from me, and let not his terror frighten me.”

Through the Law God had terrified us with the rod when he said: “If anyone does this or that, let him die.” But when he became incarnate, he took away the rod because he showed the ways of life through gentleness.

Hence it is said to him: “Direct, proceed prosperously, and reign, because of truth and gentleness and justice” (Psalm 44:5). He did not wish to be feared as God, but, as Father, inspired love.

Paul clearly says this: “For you did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the spirit of adoption as sons, in which we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:15). It follows:

### VERSE 35

“I shall speak, and I shall not fear him.”

For the holy man, seeing the Redeemer of the human race coming in gentleness, receives not fear from the Lord but affection from the Father, and despises fear because through the grace of adoption he rises to love. Hence John says: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18).

Fear could not raise us from the death of sin, but the grace of gentleness, desired for the state of life, lifted us up. It follows: “For I cannot answer while afraid.”

We say that we answer someone when we repay his deeds with deeds that correspond to them. To answer God, therefore, is to return our service for his preceding gifts. He bestows gifts upon us—his kindness—and he exercises it even toward the wicked.

Man ought to answer so many benefits, yet he cannot answer while afraid, because whoever still fears the Creator of the human race in a slavish manner certainly does not love him. For we render true service to God only when, through the confidence of love, we do not fear him, and when affection rather than fear directs us toward good works. It follows:

## CHAPTER X

### VERSE 1

“My soul is weary of my life.”

For when our mind is kindled in love for its Creator, every desire for the present life becomes light. Delight turns into weariness, and the mind endures it with error, though previously conquered it had served a reprobate love. It follows: “I will let loose my speech against myself.”

He uses his speech, as it were, on his own behalf who tries to defend by excuses the wrong things he has done. But he lets loose speech against himself who begins to accuse in himself that in which he has gone astray. It follows: “I will speak in the bitterness of my soul.”

Whoever speaks while detesting his sins must necessarily speak of them in the bitterness of his soul, so that this very bitterness may punish whatever the tongue accuses through the judgment of the mind. It follows:

### VERSE 2

“I will say to God: Do not condemn me.”

He who declares himself a sinner in bitterness of soul says to God nothing other than that he should not be condemned, because the bitterness of present repentance extinguishes the punishments of the wrath to come. For in this life God judges in two ways: either by beginning already through present evils to inflict the torments that follow. Hence it is written: “A second time he destroyed those who did not believe” (Jude 5). And in the Psalm: “Let them be clothed with confusion as with a double garment” (Psalm 118:29). Or he extinguishes future torments by present scourges. Hence Paul says: “When we are judged by the Lord, we are corrected, so that we may not be condemned with this world” (1 Corinthians 11:32). And elsewhere: “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise” (Revelation 3:19). It follows: “Show me why you judge me thus.”

As if he said: “Since you judge me by scourging, show that through the scourge you make me secure for judgment.” Otherwise: often the just person receives scourges for testing, but does not know for what particular fault he is struck; and he trembles the more under the blow because he does not know its cause. He asks that the Judge disclose him to himself, so that what the Judge strikes in punishing, he too may chastise in himself by weeping. It follows:

### VERSE 3

“Does it seem good to you that you should calumniate and oppress me, a poor man?”

As if he said openly: “You who are supremely good, I know do not judge it good to oppress a poor man by calumny. Therefore I know that what I suffer is not just, and I grieve the more because I do not know the grounds of justice.” When, however, he calls himself poor rather than innocent, he no longer takes boldness from his manner of life, but shows how weak he sees himself to be. It follows: “The work of your hands.”

As if he said openly: “You cannot oppress wickedly one whom you remember that you made gratuitously.” It follows: “And assist the counsel of the impious?”

Whom does he call impious here, except malignant spirits? Since they themselves cannot return to life, they cruelly seek companions for death. Their counsel, indeed, was that divine correction should touch blessed Job, so that he who had been just in tranquillity might at least sin under scourges. But the Lord did not heed the counsel of the impious, because he gave the flesh of the just man over to their temptations but withheld his soul. The Lord also continually destroys this counsel, because the merciful Creator tempers scourges according to strength, lest the punishment of persecutors exceed the virtue of the just and human weakness be overcome by the cunning of the strong. Hence Paul says: “But God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able,” and so forth (1 Corinthians 10:13). It follows:

### VERSES 4–7

“Do you have eyes of flesh, or do you see as man sees? Are your days like the days of man, or are your years like human times, that you seek out my iniquity and scrutinize my sin, although you know that I have done nothing impious?”

As if he asked humbly: “Why do you examine me in time by scourges, when with you you knew me perfectly even before time? Why do you question my faults by blows, when by the power of your eternity you were not ignorant of me even before you created me?” Eyes of flesh know deeds done in time only in time, and human sight follows any work; it does not run through it. The days and years of human beings differ from the days and years of eternity, because our life begins in time and ends in time. With God, neither things past pass away, nor are things still to come absent as though they did not appear. For he who has being always sees all things as present to himself, since in seeing he is not extended backward or forward. It follows: “When there is no one who can rescue from your hand?”

As if he said openly: “What remains for you except to spare, whose power no one can resist? For the more there is no one who can restrain your punishment by the merit of his own strength, the more readily your mercy requires of you that you spare.” It follows:

### VERSE 8

“Your hands made me and formed me wholly round about, and do you suddenly cast me down?”

As if he said humbly: “Because what I have done is not worthy of your favour under strict examination, weigh mercifully lest what you made should perish.” By these words, too, the perverse doctrine of the Manichees is destroyed: falsely maintaining that there are two principles, it tries to assert that the spirit was created by God, but the flesh by Satan. He called himself formed in respect of the image, but said that he was made wholly round about inasmuch as he consists of the garment of flesh. It should be noted that, in declaring himself formed by God’s hands, he sets the dignity of his creation before the Judge’s mercy. As if he said openly: “Why do you despise with such lowliness one whom you created with such dignity? And why do you subject to pain one whom you set above other things by reason?” It follows:

### VERSE 9

“Remember, I pray, that you made me like clay.”

As if he said openly: “Relax the weakness of the flesh and the guilt of iniquity.” Thus man was made like clay, taken from mud, because, as it were, water is poured into dust when the soul moistens the flesh. For clay is made when water is mixed with earth. What is said of the outward person can also apply to the inward person. The inner person was like clay because, when the Spirit of grace is poured into the earthly mind, it is raised to the understanding of its Creator. Human thought, which had dried up through the barrenness of its sin, grows green through the power of the Holy Spirit. It follows: “And you will bring me back into dust.”

As if he plainly asks, saying: “Look, I pray, upon the matter of my origin and the punishment of my end, and spare faults that pass away quickly.”

#### Morally

When, through the withdrawal of the Spirit, an elect mind is for a little while left to temptation, the earth is, as it were, dried from its former moisture, so that, being forsaken, it may feel its weakness and recognize how greatly man has dried up without the infusion of heavenly grace. It follows:

### VERSES 10–11

“Did you not milk me like milk and curdle me like cheese? You clothed me with skin and flesh; you bound me together with bones and sinews.”

Man, when formed, was made like clay; when propagated, he is milked like milk by seed and curdled in flesh like cheese. He is clothed with flesh and skin and supported by bones and sinews.

#### Morally

When the mind is withdrawn by the grace of the Holy Spirit from the practice of its old way of life, it is milked like milk, because it is formed in a certain tenderness and subtlety of new beginning. It is curdled like cheese because it is bound fast in the solidity of a thought growing rich, so that it no longer flows away through desires but, gathering itself in one love, rises to solid renewal. The inner person is clothed with skin and flesh because, when raised to things above, it is surrounded by the siege of carnal movements. We are clothed with flesh and skin, but bound together with bones and sinews, because, although we are shaken outwardly by an onrushing temptation, the hand of the Creator nevertheless strengthens us inwardly against temptations. It follows:

### VERSE 12

“You have granted me life and mercy.”

The praise of God would indeed be too limited if it were confined to the formation of the created body, unless the wondrous inspiration of life-giving were subsequently also expressed.

#### Morally

Life is granted when kindness is breathed into evil minds. But life cannot be received without mercy, because the Lord does not help us attain the goods of righteousness unless he first mercifully remits our past wickedness. Or certainly, he grants us life and mercy because the mercy by which he anticipates us for living well he also subsequently preserves. Unless he adds mercy, the life he grants cannot be preserved. It follows: “And your visitation guarded my spirit.”

For the Creator grants us good things in vain unless he himself guards everything that he has granted.

#### Morally

Heavenly visitation guards the human spirit when it does not cease either to strike it with a scourge, enlarged by virtues, or to pierce it with love. It follows:

### VERSE 13

“Although you hide these things in your heart, nevertheless I know that you remember all.”

As if he said openly: “Why should I tremble about myself, when I know that you gather all nations? Yet you hide this in your heart because you do not yet reveal it in open speech. But because you remember all, you undoubtedly make me certain of pardon.” It follows:

### VERSE 14

“If I have sinned and you spared me for a time, why do you not permit me to be clean from my iniquity?”

The Lord spares sin for a time when he washes away the guilt of fault by tears granted. But he does not permit us to be clean from our iniquity because we committed the fault willingly, yet sometimes unwillingly endure its memory with delight. “My scars have putrefied and festered because of my folly” (Psalm 37:6). As if he said openly: “If pardon has removed the fault, why does it not also wipe it from memory?” It follows:

### VERSE 15

“And if I am impious, woe is me; and if I am just, I shall not lift up my head.”

The impious person has woe, the just person misery, because eternal condemnation follows the reprobate, while each elect person is purified by the pains of transitory adversity. The impious lifts his head, but, being exalted, cannot escape the woe that follows. The just person, afflicted in the contest of his labour, is not allowed to lift his head, but, oppressed, is freed from perpetual affliction. As if he lamented openly, saying: “Either, laid low by the desires of the flesh, I am subjected to eternal punishment; or, resisting unlawful movements, I am tormented by present punishment.” It follows:

### VERSE 16

“And because of pride you will seize me like a lioness.”

When a lioness seeks food for her cubs, she falls greedily into a pitfall. Thus the human mind was captured: created in freedom of choice, it desired to feed the desires of the flesh, sought food for its cubs like a lioness, and fell into the pit of its capture when, at the enemy’s urging, it stretched out its hand to forbidden food. Thus he was captured like a lioness through pride, because the discipline of correction presses him down from the very point at which, not fearing the transgression of the commandment, he boldly leapt into the pit. And when any one of us desires something through fault, what else does he desire but prey in a pit? Yet heavenly mercy lifts him, captured, from the pit, because, once he knows his weakness, it brings him back to pardon. When he is puffed up by strength, he is bound in humility, fallen into desires. It follows: “And, returning, you torment me wonderfully.”

When we leave the Creator, we do not in any way feel even the losses of abandonment itself. For the farther the Creator withdraws, the more our mind hardens into insensibility. But if it is touched by the breath of the Holy Spirit, it immediately wakes to reflection, stirs itself in the search for heavenly things, and burns with the heats of highest love. For almighty God, by the very means through which, visiting our mind, he raises it to his love, afflicts it more heavily through tears. And when the mind, filled with that breath, is drawn up to things above, it marvels joyfully at the punishment of its compunction. It follows:

### Verse 17

“You renew your witnesses against me, multiply your wrath against me, and punishments wage war against me.” [Col. 0207C]

God’s witnesses are those who, through the practice of good works, testify to the rewards of truth that will follow the elect. Hence we also call those whom we recognize as having suffered for the truth *martyrs* in Greek, μάρτυρες—that is, “witnesses.” The Lord renews his witnesses against us when he multiplies the lives of the elect before our wickedness, to accuse and instruct us, so that those whom precepts do not kindle may at least be roused by examples.

It follows: “And you multiply your wrath.”

God’s wrath is said to be multiplied insofar as it is shown to be manifold, because from the life and labor of the good we now learn how great a blow we shall suffer after judgment if we do not wish to be corrected while there is still time. We see God’s elect both performing devout deeds and enduring many cruel things. From this, therefore, we infer with what strictness the Judge will strike those whom he rejects there, if here he torments those whom he loves, as Peter testifies when he says: “It is time for judgment to begin from the household of God” (1 Peter 4:17). “And if it begins with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the gospel of God?”

It follows: “And punishments wage war against me.”

When we consider God’s witnesses, punishments wage war against us, because, while we behold their marvelous deeds, we torment our own life—which displeases us in comparison with theirs—with deliberate affliction, so that lamentation may wash away whatever our deeds have polluted in us.

It follows:

### Verses 18–19

“Why did you bring me forth from the womb? Would that I had been consumed, so that no eye might see me!”

In his first speech he had already brought this forward, saying: “Why did I not die in the womb?” (Job 3). Here too he adds: “I would have been as though I had never existed, carried from the womb to the tomb.” In other words, he says: “As a hidden miscarriage I would not have continued, like those conceived who never saw the light” (ibid., 16). Since we have explained these words at length above, we avoid repeating the exposition, lest we weary the reader.

It follows:

### Verse 20

“Will not the shortness of my days soon come to an end?”

He shows himself to live cautiously and anxiously. Considering the brevity of the present life, he sees not its use but its end, so that from its conclusion he may understand that nothing which passes away is truly delightful. Hence Solomon says: “If a person lives for many years and rejoices in them all, he must remember the time of darkness and the many days which, when they come, will prove the past to have been vanity” (Ecclesiastes 11:8).

It follows: “Leave me, therefore, that I may mourn my sorrow for a little while.”

As though he plainly said: “Temper the scourges of your blows, so that through measured pains I may grow strong in estimating by tears the evils I suffer.” For just as measured affliction draws out tears, excessive affliction takes them away, because sorrow itself becomes almost sorrowless when, devouring the afflicted mind, it removes the awareness of pain. One cannot weep for one’s sorrow who strives to resist a wicked habit but is still burdened by desires of the flesh as they continue to grow. Unless we are mercifully released from the guilt that binds us, we cannot perfectly weep over what we grieve within ourselves and against ourselves. [Col. 0208C]

It follows:

### Verse 21

“Before I go—and do not return—to the land of darkness and covered with the shadow of death.”

What is signified by the name “land of darkness” except the prison of Tartarus? The darkness of eternal death covers it, because it separates the condemned forever from the light of life. Hell is not improperly called a land, because all who have been seized by it are held there permanently. For it is written: “One generation passes away, and another generation comes, but the earth stands forever” (Ecclesiastes 1:4).
