He does not mean that the one who mourns his guilt is going to the land of darkness, but undoubtedly that the one who neglects to mourn is going there.

It continues: “And I shall not return.”

For the mercy of the one who spares never again frees those whom the justice of the Judge has once condemned to places of punishment. [Col. 0208D]

It follows:

### Verse 22

“A land of misery and darkness.”

“Misery” refers to pain, and “darkness” to blindness. The place that holds those expelled from the sight of the strict Judge is therefore called a land of misery and darkness, because pain tortures them outwardly, while blindness, which divides them from the true light within, obscures them.

Yet “a land of misery and darkness” can also be understood in another way. This land in which we are born is indeed a land of misery, but it is not a land of darkness, because here we suffer many things from our corruption, while nevertheless, through the grace of conversion, we still return to the light. Truth urges us to this when it says: “Walk while you have the light, lest the darkness overtake you” (John 12:35).

That other land, however, is simultaneously a land of misery and darkness, because whoever descends into it to endure its evils never again returns to the light.

It follows: “Where there is the shadow of death and no order.”

Just as outward death separates flesh from soul, so inward death separates the soul from God. The shadow of death is therefore the darkness of separation, because every condemned person, while being kindled by eternal fire, is darkened with respect to the inner light.

The nature of fire is to provide both light from itself and burning. But that avenging flame of transgressors has burning without light. Hence Truth says of the reprobate: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire,” and so forth (Matthew 25:41). Hence also the Psalmist says: “Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun” (Psalm 57:9). [Col. 0209B]

It is very surprising that it says, “where there is no order.” For the omnipotent God, who punishes evils well, does not in any way allow punishments to be without order. How could there be no order in punishments, when retribution follows each condemned person according to the measure of his crime? Hence it is written: “The mighty will suffer mighty torments” (Wisdom 6:7), and a stronger torture awaits the stronger.

But after mentioning the shadow of death, the holy man adds how great the confusion is in the minds of the condemned. The punishments themselves, which come in an ordered manner through justice, are certainly not ordered in the hearts of those who die. Thus there will be no order among those rejected into punishments, because in their death the confusion of mind itself rages more cruelly.

What marvelous power of the Judge’s equity it is that punishment orders the soul in such a way as to confuse it as though it were disordered! Or, alternatively, punishments are said to lack order because, when various things arise for punishment, their proper character is not preserved.

It follows: “And everlasting horror dwells there.”

In the torments of this life, fear contains pain, but pain does not contain fear, because once the mind begins to suffer what it feared, the disturbing force no longer torments it. Hell, however, is both darkened by the shadow of death and inhabited by everlasting horror, because those delivered over to its fires feel pain in their punishments and, in the anguish of pain, are continually struck by fear that assails them. Thus they endure what they fear and, again, continually fear what they endure.

Of these it is written: “Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished” (Mark 9:48). Therefore, although death destroys and does not extinguish, pain torments without driving away fear, and flame burns without dispelling darkness, it follows from what can be gathered from our present life that those punishments have no order because they do not preserve their own character in every respect. [Col. 0210B]

Yet there the fire does not shine for consolation, while nevertheless it shines in order to increase torment. For the reprobate will see, through the flame illuminating their fellow followers in torment, those whom they loved and for whose sake they sinned. Thus those who loved their lives carnally, against the commands of the Creator, will be afflicted by the destruction of those same people, to the increase of their own damnation.

We have gathered this from the testimony of the Gospel, in which Truth reports that the rich man who descended into the torments of eternal fire is described as remembering his five brothers.

Therefore, just as heavenly fire knows how to burn for the consolation of the young, so as to consume their bonds, but does not know how to burn for punishment, so as to consume their garments, in the opposite way the flame of Gehenna neither shines for the reprobate as a grace of consolation, nor does it fail to shine for punishment. It shines so that, before the eyes of the condemned, the fire of punishment may glow without any brightness and yet, for the accumulation of pain, may reveal how those whom they loved are being tormented. [Col. 0210C]

## BOOK TEN

[Col. 0209]

## CHAPTER XI

[Col. 0209C]

### Verses 1–2

“Then Sophar the Naamathite answered and said: ‘Will the one who speaks much not hear? And will a verbose man be justified?’” [Col. 0209D]

It is customary for the insolent always to respond in the opposite way to correct statements, lest, if they agree with what has been said, they appear inferior. To them the words of the just, however powerfully they may have sounded, are many [or: mute], because they burden the hearing of those whose vices they cut away. Thus what is proclaimed rightly against crimes is itself dragged into accusation.

Sophar did not express a false judgment in saying that a verbose man cannot be justified, because, when someone pours himself out in words and loses the dignity of silence, he loses [something of] the mind. (Some substantive noun is missing here.) Hence it is written: “The cultivation of justice is silence” (Isaiah 32:17). Solomon says: “Like an open city, without the encircling of walls, is a man who cannot restrain his spirit in speaking” (Proverbs 25:28). [Col. 0210C]

But the virtue of a true judgment is lost when it is not uttered under the guardianship of discretion. [Col. 0210D]

It follows:

### Verse 3

“Will people be silent for you alone? And when you mock the others, will no one refute you?”

As we have said, an untrained mind bears the judgments of truth with difficulty and regards silence as punishment. It cannot endure a voice because it hurts, as though tested in the wound of its guilt; hence it immediately prepares itself for defense, so that it may conceal the shame of its guilt through words of wicked refutation. The perverse regard the voice of correction as an insult of mockery.

It follows:

### Verse 4

“For you have said: ‘My speech is pure, and I am clean in your sight.’”

How could blessed Job say that he was clean, when he said: “If I wished to justify myself, my mouth would condemn me” (Job IV, 20)? [Col. 0211A]

Such is the malice of the wicked: when they refuse to mourn their own true evils, they fabricate those of others. For they use this almost as a consolation for their crime, if they can stain the life of the one correcting them with false accusations.

It follows:

### Verse 5

“And would that God spoke with you and opened his lips to you.”

A person speaks to himself when, through what he perceives, he is not at all separated by the divine Spirit from the understanding of carnal prudence. Hence Truth still says to Peter, who was wise in earthly things: “You do not understand the things of God, but those of human beings” (Matthew 16:23). Yet to him, when he confesses rightly, it is said: “Flesh and blood has revealed this to you,” and so forth (Matthew 16:17).

What are God’s lips, then, except his judgments? God opens his lips when he shows human beings his will through manifest judgments. He speaks, as it were, with his mouth opened, when, removing the obscurity of his hidden dispensation, he does not conceal what he wills.

For he does not disclose his meaning to us, as though with closed lips, when he conceals his hidden judgments and why he does what he does. As though, therefore, he were patiently saying: “I pity your ignorance more than your punishment, because I recognize that, endowed only with carnal prudence, you are empty of the spirit of truth. If you knew God’s hidden judgments, you would not utter such insolent judgments against him.” [Col. 0211B]

It follows:

### Verse 6

“That he might show you the secrets of wisdom and how manifold his law is.”

The public works of heavenly wisdom are those in which the omnipotent God governs those whom he creates, perfects the good works he begins, and helps by inspiration those whom he illumines with the light of his visitation. [Col. 0211C]

The secret works of heavenly wisdom are those in which the Lord abandons those whom he created, does not complete by continued action the good works that had begun to arise, and does not preserve the gifts he has bestowed.

Paul directed himself toward the secrets of that wisdom when he said: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom of God,” and so forth (Romans 11:33).

It follows:

“And how manifold his law is.”

What should God’s law be understood to mean here, except love? Through it the precepts of life are continually read in the mind, so that they may be kept in action. Of this law Truth says: “This is my commandment, that you love one another” (John 15:12). Paul says of it: “Love is the fullness of the law” (Romans 13:10).

But this same law is called manifold because, through diligent care, love expands into every work of virtue. It begins with two commandments but extends itself into countless others. The beginning of this law is love of God and love of neighbor.

The love of God is distinguished into three forms, while love of neighbor is derived into two commandments. Yet when these two are considered with careful attention, they direct the heart toward innumerable mysteries of virtue, so that the restless mind may neither burn with desire to do what it ought not nor grow slack through idleness in doing what it ought.

Paul aptly enumerates the manifoldness of this law when he says: “Love is patient, love is kind, it is not jealous, it is not puffed up,” and so forth (1 Corinthians 13:4).

It follows: “And you would understand that you are asked by God for far less than your iniquity deserves.” [Col. 0212A]

Pain is tempered by the scourge when guilt is recognized. If we weigh our faults, we certainly endure the scourges with equanimity; the mind does not fall from pain into impatience when conscience subjects it to its own judgment.

But Sophar knew what he was saying and did not know to whom he was saying it. He was not free from great iniquity when he rebuked a just man by accusing him of iniquity. Although Sophar called iniquitous the one whom the heavenly judgment had praised, he was not thereby excluded from forgiveness, since he was moved to words of insult by zeal for divine love. For a fault is more quickly forgiven when it is not committed through a deliberate desire for evil.

It follows:

### Verse 7

“Perhaps you will grasp the footsteps of God, and will you find the Almighty unto perfection?”

What does he call “footsteps” except the kindness of God’s visitation? By these we are summoned to advance toward heavenly things when we are touched by the breath of his Spirit and, lifted beyond the narrowness of the flesh through love, recognize the form of our Creator that we ought to contemplate and follow.

When love of the spiritual homeland inflames our mind, he insinuates himself, as it were, into the path of those who follow. What we do not yet see must therefore be sought through the footsteps of his love, so that the mind may eventually arrive at the vision of his form, whom it now explores through holy desires, following him as though behind his back.

Hence the Psalmist says: “My soul clung after me” (Psalm 62:9). The Almighty is then found openly, when the corruption of our mortality has been utterly trampled down and he is seen by us, who have been taken up, in the glory of his divinity. [Col. 0212C]

But now the grace of the Spirit poured into us lifts the mind from carnal thought and exalts it into contempt for passing things. It attempts to behold the radiance of the unbounded light but cannot, because the mind, weighed down by weakness, neither penetrates it nor ceases to love it when repelled.

It follows:

### Verses 8–9

“He is higher than heaven, and what will you do? He is deeper than hell, and from where will you know him? His measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea.”

These words must be understood spiritually to the extent that it is impious to think of anything concerning God according to bodily dimensions.

He is higher than heaven because, by the unboundedness of his Spirit, he transcends all things. He is deeper than hell because, by transcending it, he raises those below. He is longer than the earth because, through the eternity of his permanence, he surpasses the measure of creation. He is broader than the sea because he so governs and possesses the waves of temporal things that, by constricting them under the complete presence of his power, he surrounds them.

“Heaven” may also designate angels, and “hell” demons; “earth” may signify righteous human beings, and “sea” sinners.

He is therefore higher than heaven because even the elect spirits do not perfectly penetrate the vision of such sublimity. He is deeper than hell because, in judging and condemning them, he penetrates the cunning of malignant spirits far more subtly than they themselves imagined. He is longer than the earth because divine patience surpasses the length of our endurance. He is broader than the sea because everywhere he condemns the deeds of sinners by the retribution of his vengeance. [Col. 0213A]

The eminent teacher aptly discloses his power to us when he briefly says: “That you may be able to comprehend, with all the saints, what is the breadth, length, height, and depth” (Ephesians 3:18).

God has breadth because, in his love, he extends even to the offering of love toward persecutors. He has length because, by patiently enduring us, he leads us to the homeland of life. He has height because, in the heavenly assembly, he transcends even the understanding of those who have been received there. He has depth because, below, he incomprehensibly brings forth the judgment of his strictness against the condemned.

As though, therefore, the despised man were being told: “How much are you capable of knowing his depth and excellence, when you neither possess the virtue to be lifted to the heights nor know how to rebuke yourself in temptations?” [Col. 0213B]

It follows:

### Verse 10

“If he overturns all things or gathers them into one, who will contradict him?” (Or: “Who can say to him, ‘Why do you do this?’”)

The Lord overturns heaven when, through a terrible and hidden dispensation, he destroys the loftiness of human contemplation. He overturns hell when he allows anyone’s mind, fearful amid its temptations, to fall even into worse things. He overturns earth when, as adversities rush in, he cuts off the fruitfulness of good work. He overturns the sea when he pierces the wavering of our hesitation with sudden fear that overwhelms us.

Heaven and hell are also gathered into one when one and the same mind is both illumined by the elevation of contemplation and darkened by the persistence of temptation. Light arises from heaven, while hell is possessed by darkness.

Earth and sea are likewise gathered into one when one and the same person is strengthened by the certainty of solid faith and yet, through some mutability of unbelief, is tossed by a breeze of doubt. Hence he says: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (Mark 9:33).

Divine judgment can neither be diminished by adversity nor understood through investigation.

It follows:

### Verse 11

“He knows the vanity of human beings, and, seeing iniquity, does he not consider it?”

We act vainly whenever we think about transitory things. Hence that which is suddenly removed from the eyes of those looking at it is said to vanish. The Psalmist says: “Every living human being is altogether vanity” (Psalm 18:6).

Iniquity is aptly added immediately after vanity, because while we are carried away transiently by certain things, we are harmfully bound by others. When the mind does not retain a state of immutability, it flows away from itself and breaks out into vices.

Thus “vanity” may be understood as a fault, while “iniquity” indicates a more serious guilt. If vanity were never a fault, the Psalmist would not say: “Although a person walks in the image of God, he is nevertheless troubled in vain” (Psalm 38:7).

From vanity, therefore, as was said above, we are led into iniquity: first we drift into lighter offenses, and, once habit has made everything seem light, we no longer fear committing even graver ones. Solomon says: “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Ecclesiasticus 19:1).

If we neglect to care for small matters, we are imperceptibly deceived and boldly perpetrate even greater ones.

It should be noted that the text says not that God “sees” but that he “considers.” God therefore knows human vanity and considers iniquity, because he neither overlooks the many lesser offenses nor fails to prepare himself more intently to strike the greater ones.

It follows:

### Verse 12

“A vain man is lifted up into pride.”

The end of vanity is that, when it wounds the mind with sin, it makes it bold through guilt, so that, forgetful of its guilt and not grieving that it has lost innocence, it is blinded by a just judgment and loses humility as well.

It follows: “And, like a wild ass’s colt, he thinks himself born free.”

By the wild ass’s colt every kind of beast of the field is represented. Animals of the field have the freedom both to go wherever they wish and to rest when they grow weary. Yet what is permitted to brute animals is often not permitted to human beings.

Whoever seeks, through unrestrained freedom, to fulfill everything he desires—what else does he long to resemble but a wild ass’s colt? He wants the reins of discipline not to hold him, but to run boldly and wandering through the forest of desires.

Therefore, if we no longer wish to be like a wild ass’s colt, we must first seek, in everything we desire, the decision of the inner dispensation.

It follows:

### Verse 13

“But you have hardened your heart and stretched out your hands toward him.”

“You have hardened your heart” is not said of virtue but of insensibility. Whoever grows hardened through obstinate insensibility confirms himself, as it were, so that the arrows of heavenly fear may not pierce him. Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “I will take from you the heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 11:19). [Col. 0214C]

Hands signify works. To stretch one’s hands toward God in guilt, therefore, is to grow proud of the strength of one’s works against the grace of the giver. Whoever, speaking in the sight of the divine Judge, attributes the good things he does to himself, stretches his hands toward God in pride.

Thus the reprobate rage against the elect, and heretics against Catholics, so that those whom they cannot accuse on account of weakness in action they may accuse on account of the crime of rumor.

It follows:

### Verses 14–15

“If you remove from yourself the iniquity that is in your hand, and injustice does not remain in your tent, then you will be able to lift your face without stain.”

Every sin is committed either by thought alone or by thought together with action. Iniquity, therefore, is in the hand; guilt is in the deed. Injustice is in the tent; iniquity is in the mind.

Our mind is not improperly called a tent, since within it we hide ourselves from ourselves, while outwardly we are not seen in action. He first advises that iniquity be removed from the hand and afterward that injustice be cut away from the tent, because whoever has now cut away outwardly the evil works he has done must surely return to himself and carefully examine himself in the intention of his mind, lest the guilt he no longer has in action continue in thought.

Hence Solomon says: “Prepare your work outside and diligently cultivate your field, so that afterward you may build your house” (Proverbs 24:27).

If we cleanse these two things perfectly, we immediately lift our face to God without stain. The inner face of a human being is the mind, in which we recognize that we are loved by our Creator. To lift this face is to raise the mind toward God through the practices of prayer.

But a stain defiles the lifted face if the consciousness of guilt accuses the mind that is intent upon God. Confidence in hope is immediately broken when, while one is devoted to prayer, the memory of an unconquered fault gnaws at the heart.

Hence John says: “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God, and whatever we ask of him, we shall receive” (1 John 3:21–22). Hence Solomon says: “Whoever turns away his ear so as not to hear the law,” and so forth (Proverbs 28:9).

Therefore, for the face to be lifted without stain in prayer, one must always carefully examine before the times of prayer whatever might be condemned in prayer. We then truly lift our face without stain when we neither commit the forbidden evils nor retain, through personal zeal, the wrongs committed against us. [Col. 0215B]

It follows: “And you will be steadfast, and you will not fear.”

Each person trembles less before the Judge the more firmly he stands in good deeds. The one who preserves stability overcomes fear, because, while he carefully strives to perform what the gentle Creator commands, he confidently considers even what the Creator threatens terribly.

It follows:

### Verse 16

“You will also forget misery, and remember it as waters that have passed away.”

As though he plainly said: “If you taste the joy that remains within, everything that suffers outwardly immediately becomes light. The evils of the present life are felt all the more harshly by the mind the less it considers the good that follows.”

If someone once raises himself toward eternal things, he sees that almost nothing here exists except what runs toward its end. He endures the adversities of the present life and regards everything that slips away as almost nothing.

He aptly compares the miseries of the present life with passing waters, because passing calamity does not overthrow the elect mind through its shock, although it does pour sorrow [or: pain] into it through contact. It threatens through the blood of a wound, yet does not break the certainty of salvation.

It follows:

### Verse 17

“And, like the noonday brightness, you will rise at evening.”

The noonday brightness is the renewal of virtue in temptation at evening, so that the mind may grow strong through a sudden fervor of love, after fearing that the light of grace had already set.

It follows: “And when you think yourself consumed, you will rise like the morning star.”

Often so many temptations surround us that their very number almost inclines us toward the fall of despair. But the Creator sees the darkness of our sorrow and pours into us rays of the withdrawn light, so that the mind immediately grows strong through the gifts of grace—the same mind that shortly before the contending vices were pressing down with the heel of pride.

Thus, when the just person thinks himself consumed, he rises like the morning star. As soon as he begins to grow dark beneath the shadow of temptations, he is restored to the light of grace, and in himself he displays the day of righteousness—he who shortly before feared that he would fall into the night of guilt.

The life of the just is rightly compared with the morning star. The morning star announces the sun by going before it. What else does the innocence of the saints proclaim to us except the brightness of the Judge who is to come? In our admiration of them, we see what we should think about the majesty of the true light. [Col. 0216A]

Alternatively: the sinner’s light is present in the daytime, but darkness comes at evening, because in the present life he is lifted up by prosperity, while at the end he rages amid the darkness of adversity.

For the just, however, the noonday brightness rises at evening, because he recognizes how much brightness remains for him when the light has already begun to set. Hence it is written: “It will be well with the one who fears the Lord at the end” (Ecclesiasticus 1:13). And the Psalmist says: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” (Psalm 126:3).

Even while still engaged in the struggle of this life, when the just person thinks himself consumed, he rises like the morning star. Though falling outwardly, he is renewed inwardly; and the more truly he endures adversities outwardly, the more brightly he flashes with the light of virtue inwardly. Paul testifies to this when he says: “Although our outward person is being corrupted, yet the inward person is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16).

It follows:

### Verse 18

“And you will have confidence, with hope set before you.”

Hope in God rises more firmly in proportion to the greater hardships each person has endured for him, because the joy of eternal reward is never gathered unless it is first sown here through devout tribulation.

Hence the Psalmist says: “Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds; but coming, they will come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Psalm 125:6). Paul says: “If we die with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him” (2 Timothy 2:12).

The greater the affliction that constrains the mind for the sake of truth, therefore, the greater the confidence that strengthens it. [Col. 0216C]

It follows: “And, buried, you will sleep securely.”

Just as present security produces labor for the wicked, so present labor produces perpetual security for the good. The one who already knew that, once buried, he could sleep securely was the one who said: “For I am already being poured out, and the time of my release is at hand. I have fought the good fight,” and so forth (2 Timothy 4:6).

Alternatively: occupied with transitory things, we neglect to consider through how many things we are being weighed. But if, by restoring the care of consideration, the field is opened with the plow, whatever lay hidden in the mind is found.

Those who have been dug out therefore sleep securely, because, while they vigilantly penetrate their inner selves, they are concealed from the burdensome labors of the world in the repose of quiet.

It follows:

### Verse 19

“You will rest, and there will be no one to terrify you.”

Whoever seeks present glory certainly fears contempt. But whoever fixes his desire upon eternity among the people is neither lifted up by prosperity nor shaken by adversity. When he has nothing in the world that he desires, there is nothing in the world that he fears.

Hence Solomon says: “Whatever happens to the just will not grieve him” (Proverbs 12:21). And again: “The just will be like a lion, without terror” (Proverbs 28:1).

It follows: “And many will entreat your face.”

Righteous men do not guard the narrow paths of innocence in order to be entreated by others. But heretics and other perverse people, because they live among human beings as though innocently, wish to appear intercessors for others. When they speak of holy things that they themselves desire, they promise these things to others as though they were of great value.

It follows:

### Verse 20

“But the eyes of the wicked will fail, and refuge will perish from them.”

By the name “eyes,” the force of intention is expressed. Through the Gospel, Truth says: “If your eye is simple, your whole body will be luminous” (Matthew 6:22).

The eyes of the wicked are therefore the intentions of their carnal desires. They fail because they neglect eternal things and always await only transitory ones. The life of the flesh fails moment by moment, yet carnal desire grows.

Their eyes then fail through heavenly vengeance because they were unwilling here, by their own judgment, to cease from earthly pleasure.

Hence the Psalmist says: “On that day all their thoughts will perish” (Psalm 145:4). All refuge also perishes from them, because their wickedness finds no place where it can hide from the judgment of the strict Judge.

For now they have as many refuges as they prepare pleasures for themselves. But eventually refuge perishes from them, because, having lost everything, their mind sees only itself and the Judge.

It follows: “And their hope will be an abomination to the soul.”

What does this sinner hope for with all his thoughts except to surpass others in power and become admired by all through the abundance of his possessions? Their hope is rightly called an abomination to the soul, because spiritual people oppose, by the judgment of uprightness, the things that carnal people pursue.

What sinners regard as pleasure, the just undoubtedly regard as punishment. For just as the flesh is nourished by soft things, so the soul is nourished by hard things.

The hope of carnal people is therefore called an abomination because the spirit perishes forever precisely where the flesh lives sweetly for a time.

## CHAPTER XII

### Verses 1–2

“Then Job answered and said: ‘Are you alone human beings, and will wisdom die with you?’”

Whoever thinks that he surpasses everyone in understanding—what else does he exult in than that he alone is human? It often happens that when the mind is raised up by reputation, it is lifted into contempt for humanity and admiration of itself.

Knowledge arises in the thought of self-approval, and the mind flatters itself on account of the singularity of its wisdom. Whoever thinks that he alone is wise therefore considers that this same wisdom arose with him.

It follows:

### Verse 3

“But I have a heart as you do, and I am not inferior to you.”

To correct the pride of his friends, blessed Job does not say that he is superior. By comparison, not by self-preference, he indicates that those who are far inferior to him may learn from him.

It follows: “For who is ignorant of these things that you know?”

As though he plainly said: “Since what you say is known to everyone, why do you swell up as though the knowledge of teachers belonged uniquely to you?”

It follows:

### Verse 4

“The one who is mocked by his friend, like me, will call upon the Lord, and he will hear him.”

Often a weak mind, when the concern for human approval attends its good deeds, is led toward external joys. When it eagerly awaits the voices of praise, it abandons what it had begun to be. It is separated from God precisely where it had appeared worthy of praise in God.

Sometimes, however, the mind steadfastly rests upon a right work and is nevertheless pressed by human mockery. It establishes itself all the more robustly in God because it finds no place of rest outside. It becomes closer to God in proportion as it is estranged from the favor of human beings.

It immediately pours itself into prayer, and, pressed outwardly, speaks more purely in order to penetrate the things within. While it girds itself in compunction through prayer, it is thereby joined within itself to heavenly hearing. Thus it is separated from human praise outside itself.

It should be noted how carefully the phrase “like me” is inserted. There are some whom human mockery depresses, yet they are not heard by divine ears. Hence Elijah said to certain people: “Cry out with a louder voice, for he is a god; perhaps he is speaking, or is staying in an inn” (1 Kings 18:27).

Human mockery makes someone close to God only when the innocence of his life keeps him separate from human wickedness. [Col. 0218B]

It follows: “The simplicity of the just is mocked.”

The wisdom of this world is to conceal the heart through schemes, to veil one’s meaning with words, to present false things as true and true things as deceptive. In contrast, the wisdom of the just is to fabricate nothing through display, to disclose one’s meaning in words, to show things as they are, to avoid falsehood, to offer good freely, to endure evils more willingly than to do them, to seek no revenge for injury, and to regard suffering insult for the truth as gain.

But this simplicity of the just is mocked because, by such wise people, the virtue of purity is believed to be foolishness. Everything done innocently is undoubtedly considered stupid by them.

It follows:

[Col. 0218C] **VERSE 5. “A lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich.”**—What is signified here by the name “rich,” if not the arrogance of the proud? They do not have the Judge’s coming before their eyes, while they swell with proud thoughts within themselves. Therefore, whoever is not humbled by love of the life to come, sacred Scripture calls “rich” in this passage, since, in the vengeance of judgment, it makes no difference whether they are swollen with pride in their morals alone.

Thus the simplicity of the righteous is rightly said both to be a lamp and to be despised. A lamp, because it shines inwardly; despised, because it does not shine outwardly. Within, the flame of charity burns; outwardly, no glory of adornment gleams. The righteous person, therefore, is a despised lamp, because the proud, unable to weigh the good things that follow, scarcely value those whom they do not see to possess what they love.

David had been a lamp through his innocence, yet he was greatly despised, because he did not shine to those who observed only external things. What, then, was Paul if not a despised lamp among the assemblies of the rich? Concerning him they said: “His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible” (2 Corinthians 10:10).

It follows: **“Prepared for the appointed time.”**—The appointed time of the despised lamp is the predetermined day of the final judgment, when it will be shown with what power each righteous person who is now despised shines. For then those who are now unjustly judged on God’s behalf will come as judges with God. Hence Truth says to his elect: “You who have followed me, in the regeneration …” and so forth (Matthew 19:28).

**MYSTICALLY** [Col. 0219A] our Redeemer also became a lamp for us: dying on the cross for our redemption, he poured light through the wood into our darkened minds. Hence it is written: “The true light, which enlightens every person …” and so forth (John 1:9). Yet the Evangelist saw him despised among the thoughts of the rich when he said: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1:11). And again: “Herod, with his soldiers, treated him with contempt and mocked him” (Luke 23:11). These things were prepared for the appointed time, concerning which it is written: “When I receive the appointed time, I will judge justly” (Psalm 74:3). The lamp that is now despised is therefore prepared to come at the appointed time, because the one who now bears the mockery of sinners is himself the one who judges sins on the last day. Hence the Prophet says: “I was silent, I was always quiet, I was patient; like a woman in labor I will speak” (Psalm 42:14).

# BOOK ELEVEN

[Col. 0219]

## CHAPTER XII FOLLOWS

[Col. 0219B]

**VERSE 6. “The tents of robbers abound, and they boldly provoke God.”**—The wicked are often more arrogant toward God the more they are enriched by his generosity and contrary to their deserts; and those who ought to have been summoned by gifts to better things become worse through those gifts.

But we must understand how they are called robbers, when it is immediately added: **“Although he himself has given everything into their hands.”** If they are robbers, they have taken things by force. There is no doubt that God is not the helper of those who use violence. How, then, does he himself give what those who are robbers wickedly seize?

We should know that one thing is what almighty God mercifully bestows, and another is what, in anger, he permits someone to possess. What robbers perversely do, the most just Disposer permits to happen only justly: the one who is allowed to rob may increase his guilt through a darkened mind, while the one who suffers the robbery may already be struck, in the loss caused by that same robbery, for another fault he previously committed.

This may also be understood of spiritual things. Often some receive the gifts of teaching, but swell with pride because of those same gifts and want to appear greater than others. To provoke almighty God is to grow proud among one’s neighbors because of his gifts. Such people are also rightly called robbers, because while they speak what they do not practice, they take away the words of the righteous in the use of their own speech.

It follows:

**VERSES 7–8. “Indeed, ask the beasts, and they will teach you; the birds of the sky, and they will tell you; speak to the earth, and it will answer you, and the fish of the sea will recount it to you.”**—What should we understand by “beasts” if not slower senses? What by “the birds of the sky” if not those wise in lofty and exalted things? Of the beasts—that is, of slower senses—it is written: “Your animals will dwell in it” (Psalm 67:11). And because those who are wise in lofty things soar through the words of our Redeemer, it is written: “So that the birds of the sky come and dwell in its branches” (Matthew 13:32).

What, then, should we understand by “the earth” if not those who are wise in earthly things? Hence it was said to the first human being, who had abandoned heavenly things: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis 3:19). What by “the fish of the sea” if not the curious people of this age, of whom the Psalmist says: “The fish of the sea that pass along the paths of the sea” (Psalm 8:9)? They lie hidden, as it were, in the concealed waves of their great investigations into things.

What all these creatures teach when questioned, he adds by saying:

**VERSE 9. “Who does not know that the hand of the Lord has made all these things?”**—It is as though he plainly said: Whether you seek those slower in understanding, or those wise in lofty matters, or those devoted to earthly actions, or those occupied with the investigations of this world, all confess God, the Creator of everything, and agree in their judgment concerning his power, although they do not live in agreement beneath it.

This can also usefully be understood according to the mere outward sense of the text: every creature, by its very appearance, gives a kind of voice bearing witness to itself, because, while presenting its forms to our eyes, creatures testify that they do not exist from themselves. By the very fact that they are creatures, they return to their Creator, through their visible form, something like a voice of confession. Since he created all things, he also determines how they ought to be governed.

It follows:

**VERSE 10. “In whose hand is the soul of every living thing and the spirit of all human flesh.”**—“Hand” expresses power. The soul of every living thing and the spirit of all human flesh are therefore in the power of him from whom it comes that he provides for the being of what previously was not.

“The soul of every living thing” may, however, signify the life of animals. Almighty God gives the soul of animals life only as far as bodily sensation, whereas he extends the human spirit to spiritual understanding. Thus the soul of every living thing and the spirit of all human flesh are in his hand: in the animal he grants the soul the power to enliven the flesh, while in the human being he gives life to the soul so that it may reach the understanding of eternity.

In sacred Scripture, “the spirit of a human being” is sometimes used for the soul, as in: “He bowed his head and gave up his spirit” (John 18:30); at other times it is used for a spiritual effect, as it is written: “He makes his angels spirits” (Hebrews 1:7). In this passage, if “the soul of every living thing” signifies the very life of the body, “the spirit of all human flesh” expresses the effect of spiritual understanding.

It follows:

**VERSE 11. “Does not the ear discern words, and the throat of the eater, taste?”**—Almost no one is unaware that our body’s five senses—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—draw from the brain the power of judgment and sensation in everything they perceive and discern.

From these bodily and external things, therefore, we must gather what is internal and spiritual. We should observe that, although wisdom is one, it dwells in one person less and in another more. It grants one person this, another that, and, as if in the manner of the brain, uses us as various senses, so that although wisdom itself is never unlike itself, it nevertheless always accomplishes diverse and unlike things through us.

In these words blessed Job also seems to suggest something concerning the elect and the reprobate. The words of wisdom that the reprobate hear, the elect not only hear but also taste, so that what merely sounds in the ears of the reprobate becomes sweet in the hearts of the elect. In these words blessed Job also censures the ignorance of his friends and the arrogance of those who are puffed up by the teaching of wisdom.

It follows:

**VERSE 12. “In the ancient is wisdom, and in length of days understanding.”**—Those sayings are firmly rooted in wisdom that grow strong through the practice of life and the experience of actions.

It follows:

**VERSE 13. “With him is wisdom and strength; he has counsel and understanding.”**—We may appropriately understand this of the Only-Begotten of the Most High Father, so that we recognize him as the Wisdom of God. Paul also bears witness to our understanding when he says: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God, because he is always with him” (1 Corinthians 1:24), “because in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John 1:1).

God has counsel and understanding: counsel, because he orders his own affairs; understanding, because he knows ours. The word “counsel” may also signify the hidden movements of judgment, or the fact that he sometimes strikes those who sin only later—not because the guilt of the wicked is unseen, but so that the delay of their condemnation, which is postponed to allow repentance, may seem to proceed slowly from counsel.

It follows:

**VERSE 14. “If he destroys, no one can build.”**—Almighty God destroys the human heart when he abandons it; he builds it when he fills it. He does not destroy the human mind by conquering it, but by withdrawing, because a mind left to itself is sufficient for its own ruin.

Hence it often happens that, when the grace of almighty God does not fill a hearer because of his deserving faults, the preacher’s external admonition is useless. Every mouth that speaks is mute if the one who inspires the words being heard does not cry out inwardly in the heart. The Prophet says here: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Psalm 126:1).

It follows: **“If he shuts a person in, no one can open.”**—Through whatever he does wrongly, every person makes for himself nothing other than the prison of his conscience, so that the guilt of his soul weighs upon him even if no one accuses him outwardly.

When, by God’s judgment, a person is left in the blindness of his wickedness, he is shut within himself, as it were, and finds no way of escape—a way he has by no means deserved to find. Often some wish to leave their evil actions, but because they are weighed down by the burden of those same actions, they are enclosed in the prison of evil habit and cannot escape from themselves.

For just as no one obstructs the generosity of the one who calls, so no one opposes the justice of the one who abandons. To shut in, therefore, is for God not to open what has been closed. Hence it is also said to Moses concerning Pharaoh: “I will harden his heart” (Exodus 7:3).

It follows:

**VERSE 15. “If he holds back the waters, everything will dry up.”**—If water is understood as the knowledge of preaching, as it is written: “Deep water is words from a man’s mouth, and a flowing stream is a spring of wisdom” (Proverbs 18:4), then, when the water is held back, everything dries up. For if the knowledge of preachers is withdrawn, the hearts of those who could have flourished in hope of eternity immediately wither, so that they remain in desperate dryness while, loving what passes away, they do not know how to hope for what endures.

The grace of the Holy Spirit may also be signified by the name “water.” Hence Truth says: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38). If, therefore, the grace of the Spirit is withdrawn from the mind of the hearer, the one who seemed already to be flourishing through hope in the listener immediately withers.

The text speaks not of “water” but of “waters,” and by the plural designation returns to the sevenfold grace of spiritual gifts.

It follows: **“If he releases them, they will overturn the earth.”**—When the grace of the Holy Spirit is poured out through the heavenly gift in accordance with the preacher’s voice, the earth is immediately overturned, because the hardness of the sinful mind is changed from its stubborn immobility, so that afterward it submits itself to the Lord’s commands with as much weeping as previously it had raised its neck against the Lord in pride.

It follows:

**VERSE 16. “With him are strength and wisdom.”**—Because almighty God, through the mystery of his mercy, became human, he first brought forth the teaching of gentleness and afterward showed in judgment how great his strength is. Thus wisdom is rightly mentioned before strength above, when it is said of the Father’s Only-Begotten: “With him are wisdom and strength” (Daniel 2:20).

But because, coming to judge, he will appear in the terror of his power, and, after rejecting the reprobate, he showed his elect in the eternal kingdom how he is the Father’s wisdom, the following statement rightly says that strength is first with him, and afterward wisdom.

It follows: **“He knows both the deceiver and the one who is deceived.”**—The Lord will indeed say to the wicked: “Depart from me, for I do not know you” (Matthew 25:41). But since God’s “knowing” sometimes means recognizing and sometimes approving, he knows the wicked person because he recognizes and judges him. For he could not have judged any wicked person if he did not recognize him. Yet he does not know the wicked person in the sense of approving him, because he does not approve his deeds. Thus he knows him because he detects him, and does not know him because he does not approve him.

He knows the deceiver because he often sees his earlier evils and, by a just judgment, permits him to fall into still other sins. It is written: “Let the one who does harm do harm still, and let the one who is filthy be filthy still” (Revelation 22:11).

He also knows the one who is deceived, because people often commit evils they know, and for that reason are permitted to be deceived, so that they may fall into evils they do not know as well. This sometimes happens to those who are deceived for their purification, and sometimes as the beginning of punishment.

It follows:

**VERSE 17. “He leads counselors away into a foolish end.”**—He leads counselors into a foolish end when they do something good without a good intention, but direct it toward the repayment of temporal reward.

We may also rightly understand “counselors” as preachers, who offer their hearers counsel for life. But when a preacher proclaims eternal things in order to obtain temporal gain, he is certainly led into a foolish end, because through labor he is heading toward the place from which, by uprightness of mind, he ought to have fled.

It follows: [Col. 0223B] **“And he brings judges to bewilderment.”**—All who preside over the examination of other people’s conduct are rightly called judges. But when the one who presides does not carefully examine the life of his subjects and does not understand how to correct them, the judge has been brought to bewilderment. For he who ought to judge evil deeds does not recognize the things that must be judged.

It follows:

**VERSE 18. “He loosens the belt of kings and girds their loins with a cord.”**—What is understood by “cord” if not sin, as it is said in Solomon: “His iniquities capture the wicked, and he is bound by the cords of his sins” (Proverbs 5:22)? In “loins,” the pleasure of the flesh is understood.

He therefore loosens the belt of kings when, in those who seemed to govern their members well, he destroys the belt of chastity because of the guilt of pride, so that the pleasure of sin rules over their members.

It follows:

**VERSE 19. “He leads priests away dishonored, and overthrows the mighty.”**—The great glory of a priest is the uprightness of his subjects. Hence the distinguished preacher rightly says to his disciples: “What is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Is it not you before the Lord?” (1 Thessalonians 2:19).

But when priests neglect the life of their disciples and bring no fruit of their progress before God, what else are they led away as but dishonored? Before the strict Judge they then find no glory which, through the zeal of preaching, they do not now seek in the conduct of their subjects.

It follows: **“And he overthrows the mighty.”**—When, by a just judgment, he abandons the mind of rulers, it does not seek the inward reward of recompense and is overthrown by the very deception through which it rejoices in temporal authority instead of eternal glory.

It follows:

**VERSE 20. “Changing the speech of the truthful and taking away the teaching of the elders.”**—When a priest does not do the good things he speaks, speech is also taken away from him, lest he dare to say what he does not practice, as it is said through the Prophet: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteous acts and take my covenant upon your mouth?” (Psalm 49:16).

Often, when a teacher dares to teach what he neglects to do, once he has ceased speaking the good things he disdained to practice, he begins to teach his subordinate the wicked things he himself does.

Thus he changes the speech of the truthful: those who were previously truthful in preaching heavenly things fall toward earthly things when they come to love temporal matters, and the speech of the truthful is changed. The teaching of the elders is taken away because, loving temporal things, [lacuna] they follow the precepts of their own people so that they may hold the place of governance as a source of pleasure, not as an opportunity for labor.

This may, however, be understood more plainly of the Jews. Before the Lord’s incarnation they were truthful, because they believed and proclaimed that he would come. But after he appeared in the flesh, they denied that he was the one. The speech of the truthful was therefore changed, because they denied as present the one whom they had said would come; and the teaching of the elders was taken away, because they did not follow in faith what they remembered their fathers had foretold.

But if we understand “elders” also as those same Jews, who, persuaded by unbelief, tried to oppose the word of Truth, the teaching of the elders was taken away after the Church from the Gentiles—the youthful Church—received it, and she says through the Psalmist: “I have understood more than the elders” (Psalm 118:100).

It follows:

**VERSE 21. “Pouring contempt upon princes and loosening those who had been oppressed.”**—While the Jewish people remained within the commandment of the Law and the entire Gentile world knew none of God’s precepts, the Jews seemed to rule through faith, while the Gentiles lay pressed down in the depths through unbelief.

But when Judea denied the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation and the Gentiles believed, the princes fell into contempt, while those who had been oppressed under the guilt of unbelief were raised into the freedom of true faith.

Alternatively: “Princes” are rightly called those who always rule their own thoughts and restrain all foolish impulses by the power of wisdom. But it often happens that, secretly, the mind is lifted up in the arrogance of pride because of its own wisdom and falls beneath the very vices over which it had rejoiced to be victorious.

Sometimes, however, those who seem to lie in vices run to the mourning of repentance and rise up against the faults to which they had been subject; afterward they press down beneath themselves the movements of their flesh by which they had previously been oppressed.

It follows:

**VERSE 22. “He reveals deep things from darkness and brings the shadow of death into the light.”**—When even mystical things are recognized by believers from the hidden words of the prophets, what else are they than deep things revealed from darkness? Hence the Lord says: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light” (Matthew 10:27).

The shadow of death was the severity of the Law, which decreed that every sinner should be punished with bodily death. But after our Redeemer tempered the harshness of the legal decree through gentleness, he no longer appointed the death of the flesh as punishment for sin, but indicated how greatly death should be feared. He brought the shadow of death into the light.

That death in which the flesh is separated from the soul is the shadow of the death in which the soul is separated from God. The shadow of death is therefore brought into the light when, once spiritual death is understood, bodily death is not greatly feared.

Alternatively: The Lord reveals deep things from darkness when he judges by an open sentence from his hidden counsels, showing what each person feels. Since the Creator now sees everything while he himself is not seen in his counsels, the Psalmist rightly says of him: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Psalm 17:12).

The shadow of death is evil action, which is expressed through imitation of the ancient enemy as though from the features of a body. Of him it is also said under a certain figure: “And its name was Death” (Revelation 6:8). Often his evil thought lies hidden from human minds, and through remaining unknown it prevails more powerfully.

The shadow is therefore brought into the light when the evil action of the ancient enemy is disclosed to the minds of the saints so that it may be destroyed.

It follows:

**VERSE 23. “He multiplies nations and destroys them, and, when overturned, restores them to wholeness.”**—This may perhaps be understood in the sense that the Lord multiplies and destroys nations because each day they are born to die. He will restore to wholeness those who have been overturned because the dead rise again.

We understand this better, however, if we consider how it takes place in their minds. He multiplies and destroys nations because he extends them through the fruitfulness of offspring while leaving them in their own unbelief. But he will restore to wholeness those who have been overturned because, at some point, he will bring back to the state of faith those whom he had left fallen in unbelief.

It follows:

**VERSE 24. “He changes the heart of the princes of the people of the earth and deceives them, so that they wander fruitlessly among one another.”**—The hearts of the princes of the earth were changed when, in Judea, the chief priests and elders of the people tried by their counsel to resist the one whom they had previously proclaimed to be coming.

When they attempted to extinguish his name by persecuting him, deceived by their own wickedness, they tried fruitlessly to proceed among one another.

It follows:

**VERSE 25. “They will grope as in darkness and not in light.”**—Whoever trembles amid so many manifest miracles gropes as if in darkness, because he does not see what he touches.

Everyone who goes astray is led now here, now there. At one time they seemed to show belief when they said: “If this man were not from God, he could do nothing” (John 9:23). At another time they denied that he was from God, contemptuously saying: “Is this not the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary, and his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas? And are not all his sisters with us?” (Matthew 13:55).

It follows: **“And he will make them wander like drunkards.”**—They saw him raise the dead and yet saw him as mortal. Why, then, did they not believe that he was God, whom they saw raising the dead? But again, when they saw him as mortal, they disdained to believe that he was the immortal God.

By displaying himself to their eyes in such a way that he could both show divine things and suffer human things, almighty God makes them wander like drunkards. Their pride preferred to despise rather than follow the mystery of his incarnation, and, while exalting itself against his humanity, it was made to wonder amid the shining power of his divinity.

Since all these things were made present to the eyes of blessed Job through the spirit of prophecy, it rightly follows:

# CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0226A]

**VERSE 1. “Behold, my eye has seen all these things, and my ear has heard them.”**—In him, the things that were to follow stood present before his sight. For to the one before whom neither future things arrive nor past things depart, everything stands simultaneously before his eyes.

But words have no usefulness if they lack understanding.

It follows: **“And I have understood each one.”**—When something is shown or heard, if understanding is not given, it is not prophecy. Pharaoh saw in a dream what was going to happen to Egypt (Genesis 41:17). But because he could not understand what he had seen, he was not a prophet. King Belshazzar saw the joint of the hand writing on the wall (Daniel 5:25), but he was not a prophet, because he did not receive understanding of the matter he had seen.

Therefore, to testify that blessed Job possessed the spirit of prophecy, he asserts that he not only heard and saw everything, but also understood it.

It follows:

**VERSE 2. “According to your knowledge I also know; I am not inferior to you.”**—These words make clear how humble he was: he denies that he is inferior to those whose lives he had far surpassed by holy living. He also affirms that he knows according to their knowledge, since, by knowing heavenly things, he surpassed their earthly thoughts through the spirit of prophecy.

It follows:

**VERSE 3. “Yet I will speak with the Almighty, and I desire to argue with God.”**—We speak with the Almighty when we implore his mercy. We argue with him when, joining ourselves to his justice, we examine our deeds with careful investigation.

Or certainly, to argue with God means that the one who obeyed his commands here comes afterward with him as judge to judge the peoples, as the preachers who left everything are told: “You who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28).

Thus speaking belongs to prayer, while arguing belongs to judgment. The holy man therefore now speaks to the Almighty so that afterward he may argue with the Almighty. For the one who will later come as judge with God is the one who has now been made intimate with him here in prayer.

It follows:

[Col. 0226D] **VERSE 4. “First, showing you to be fabricators of falsehood and worshipers of perverse doctrines.”**—It is clear that those who are called worshipers of perverse doctrines do not represent Catholics. In this matter, we must also note that they are called fabricators of falsehood. Just as a wall is built from stones, so falsehood is fabricated from words.

It follows:

**VERSE 5. “Would that you were silent, so that you might be thought wise.”**—Just as, when a door is closed in a house, it is unknown what members are hidden inside, so often, if a fool remains silent, it is concealed whether he is a fool or wise—provided no other deeds emerge that reveal the understanding even of one who is silent.

Hence Solomon says: “If a fool remains silent, he will be thought wise” (Proverbs 17:28).

It follows:

**VERSE 6. “Hear, then, my reproaches, and attend to the judgment of my lips.”**—He rightly brought forward reproach first and judgment afterward, because unless the swelling of a fool is first subdued through reproach, the understanding of a just judgment is not recognized.

It follows:

**VERSE 7. “Does God need your falsehood, so that you may speak deceitfully on his behalf?”**—God does not need falsehood, because truth does not seek to be supported by the aid of falsity. Heretics, however, because they cannot defend from the truth what they wrongly understand about God, seek falsity as though to prove a ray of light.

It follows:

[Col. 0227B] **VERSE 8. “Do you accept his person and strive to judge on God’s behalf?”**—When fools observe the deeds of the prudent, all these deeds seem reprehensible to them. Forgetful of their own ignorance and weakness, they judge the faults of others all the more intently the less deeply they understand their own.

The righteous, by contrast, even when they rebuke the deeds of the wicked, remain conscious of their own weakness. Although they rage outwardly, they rebuke others with inward compassion, because it belongs only to the one who, through the omnipotence of his nature, does not know how to sin to examine human sins without compassion.

Since the friends of blessed Job had criticized his deeds as though they themselves possessed nothing reprehensible, it follows:

**VERSE 9. “Will he be pleased with one whom nothing can escape? Or will he be deceived like a human being by your frauds?”**—Heretics offer fraud to God when they assert things that do not please the one on whose behalf they speak. While attempting, as it were, to defend him, they offend him, falling into opposition to the one whom they seem, through their preaching, to serve.

Hence the Psalmist says: “That you may destroy the enemy and the avenger” (Psalm 8:3). Since nothing can be hidden from God, he judges in them what they feel inwardly, not what they appear outwardly to profess.

It follows:

**VERSE 10. “He himself will rebuke you, because in secret you accept his person.”**—There are some who feel the truth in their hearts and yet speak outwardly what is false about God. So that they may not appear defeated, they recognize the truth inwardly and nevertheless oppose it [outwardly]. It is as though he said: You are all the more blameworthy before him for falsehood because you see within yourselves what is true.

There are also some who, when they return to their own minds, contemplate God’s justice and rectitude and tremble as they pray and weep. But once contemplation has passed, they return to iniquity so boldly as though, placed behind his back, they appeared to see his justice by its light.

Such people, secretly within themselves, accept the face of God as though he were bodily present and seeing.

It follows:

**VERSE 11. “As soon as he moves, he will trouble you, and his terror will fall upon you.”**—Although the Almighty is immutable by nature, he is not disturbed in the anger of judgment. In human language, however, God is said to be moved: this means the severity of his rectitude by which human wickedness is struck.

The righteous fear God before his anger is moved against them, and, lest they experience him as moved, they fear him as tranquil. The perverse, by contrast, fear being struck only when they are struck; his terror awakens them from the sleep of their time only when punishment disturbs them.

Hence it is said through the Prophet: “And only vexation will give understanding to hearing” (Isaiah 28:19).

It follows:

**VERSE 12. “Your memory will be compared to ashes.”**—All who are conformed to this age through earthly thought try, in everything they do, to leave behind a memory of themselves in this world. Some do so through records of wars, others through the lofty walls of buildings.

The breeze scatters ashes, as it is written: “Not so the wicked, not so, but like dust that the wind drives from the face of the earth” (Psalm 1:4). He therefore rightly compares the memory of fools to ashes, because it is placed where the breeze carries it away.

It follows: **“And your necks will be reduced to mud.”**—Just as sight is signified through the eye, so pride is usually signified through the neck. The neck is therefore reduced to mud when each proud person is humbled in death and the haughty flesh dissolves in decay.

Let us consider what kind of corpses of the rich lie in tombs.

It follows:

**VERSE 13. “Be silent for a little while, so that I may speak whatever my mind suggests to me.”**—He indicates that they have spoken according to the sense of the flesh. Silence restrains them for this reason: so that he may say what his mind suggests to him.

It is as though he plainly said: I do not speak carnally but spiritually, because through the perception of the spirit I hear what I utter through the ministry of the body.

It follows:

**VERSE 14. “Why do I tear my flesh with my teeth?”**—In sacred Scripture, “teeth” sometimes signify holy preachers, as in: “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing” (Song of Songs 6:5). At other times they signify inward senses, as in Jeremiah: “He broke my teeth with gravel” (Lamentations 3:16).

Since in this passage we understand “teeth” as the inward senses—which, as it were, chew and grind each thing they think about and send it into the stomach of memory—we must carefully consider what the righteous customarily do. Often, if they discover anything even slightly carnal within themselves, they reconsider it through their inward senses and vehemently pursue it within themselves. They wear themselves down through affliction and judge even the smallest faults in themselves with great torment, condemning them through repentance.

They do this so that, as far as possible, they may themselves be found irreproachable in the sight of the eternal Judge, and so that those who see them judging themselves in this way may burn with eagerness to correct themselves from more serious faults.

It follows: **“And I carry my soul in my hands.”**—To carry one’s soul in one’s hands is to display the intention of the heart in one’s actions.

Thus blessed Job says against his friends: Why do I tear my flesh with my teeth and carry my soul in my hands? That is: Why do I either strictly judge myself before people or show in my actions what I seek, if I do not benefit my neighbors by judging evil or displaying good?

It follows:

**VERSE 15. “Even if he kills me, I will hope in him.”**—The virtue of patience is never found in prosperity. Truly patient is the one who is worn down by various trials and nevertheless is not bent away from the rectitude of his hope.

Of the mind of the reprobate it is written: “He will confess to you when you have done good to him” (Psalm 48:10).

It follows:

**VERSE 16. “Nevertheless, I will reproach my ways in his sight, and he himself will be my Savior.”**—Since the apostle Paul says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Corinthians 11:31), the Lord is found to be Savior more readily when, through fear of the Lord, we more severely rebuke our sin by ourselves.

It follows: **“For no hypocrite will come into his sight.”**—We should know that we come into the Lord’s sight in two ways.

One is that, carefully weighing our sins here, we place them before his sight and judge them with weeping. For whenever we bring the power of our Creator back to mind, we stand in his sight. Hence it is rightly said through the man of God, Elijah: “The Lord, the God of Israel, lives, in whose sight I stand” (1 Kings 17:1).

In another way we come into the Lord’s sight when, at the final judgment, we stand before his tribunal. The hypocrite therefore comes before the Judge’s sight at the final examination. But because he now pretends not to consider and mourn over his faults, he refuses to come into the Lord’s sight.

It follows:

**VERSE 17. “Hear my speech, and receive the riddles with your ears.”**—By calling them “riddles,” he shows that his expressions are figurative. Hence, appropriately, what follows is also spoken by the voice of the faithful people:

### VERSE 18

“If I am judged, I know that I shall be found righteous.” This is entirely consistent with the person of blessed Job, since he himself speaks outwardly about himself what Truth had said inwardly about him to his adversary: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth?” (Job 1:8). Yet there is a question in these words. For later he says: “You have sealed up my sins as in a bag.” Sin and righteousness cannot exist together at the same time. But the holy man, attributing iniquity to himself and his cleansing to almighty God, recognizes that he is a sinner by what comes from himself, and does not fail to recognize that he has been made righteous by grace. The text continues:

### VERSE 19

“Who is there who can be judged with me? Let him come.” Holy men guard themselves in their works, with God as their author, in such a way that no grounds for the accusations brought against them outwardly are found at all. The text continues:

### VERSE 20

“Why am I consumed in silence?” He is consumed in silence who, reproaching himself for foolish thought, is gnawed inwardly by the tooth of conscience. It is as though he were saying openly: “Just as I have lived so that I would fear no accuser outwardly, would that I had lived so that I would not have an accusing conscience within myself!” He is consumed in silence who finds within himself something over which he may be angry. The text continues:

“Do not do two things to me, and then I shall not hide myself from your face.” In this passage, what should we understand by God’s face except his punishment, in which he punishes while he regards sins? No one, not even a righteous person, is hidden from it if the two things he requests are not removed. The text continues:

### VERSE 21

“Withdraw your hand from me, and let your dread not terrify me.” In these two requests, what else does the voice of prophecy seek than the time of grace and redemption? The Law held the people under the vengeance of punishment, so that whoever sinned under it was immediately punished by death. Nor did the Israelite people serve the Lord out of love, but out of fear. Yet righteousness can never be fulfilled through fear, because, in the words of John: “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18).

It is as though he were saying: “Remove the harshness of punishment; take away the burden of fear. But, with the grace of love shining upon me, pour into me the spirit of security, because if I am not freed from punishment and fear, I know that I shall not be hidden from the strictness of your judgment. For no one can be righteous in your sight who serves you not through love, but through fear.” The text continues:

### VERSE 22

“Call me, and I shall answer you; or certainly, I shall speak, and you answer me.” When our Redeemer appeared to human eyes through the flesh he assumed, he disclosed to human beings the sins that they both committed and did not know.

Alternatively: God calls when he regards us with love and chooses us. We answer when we obey his love through good works. Hence it appropriately adds: “Or certainly, I shall speak, and you answer me.” We speak when, through desire, we ask for his face. God answers those who speak when he appears to us who love him. The text continues:

### VERSE 23

“Make known to me how many iniquities and sins I have, my crimes and my offenses.” In this life the labor of the righteous is to discover themselves and, having discovered themselves, to lead themselves toward better things through weeping and correction.

Although the apostle John declares that there is no difference between iniquity and sin, saying: “Iniquity is sin” (1 John 3:4), yet in ordinary speech *iniquity* sounds like something greater than *sin*. Every person freely admits that he is a sinner, but is sometimes ashamed to say that he is wicked.

There is, however, this difference between crimes and offenses: a crime sometimes exceeds even the weight of sin, since when the Law commands a sacrifice to be offered, it plainly prescribes one both for sin and for offense. A crime is sometimes found in an action, whereas an offense is often found only in thought. The text continues:

### VERSE 24

“Why do you hide your face and consider me your enemy?” In paradise the human race possessed contemplation of the inner light. But, pleased with itself, it withdrew from itself and lost the light of its Creator; it fled from his face among the trees of paradise, because after its sin it feared to see the one whom it had been accustomed to love.

But behold: after sin came punishment, and from punishment it returns to love. Whoever has fled finds the fruit of sin, and, awakened by punishment, seeks the face he feared in sin, so that he may now flee the darkness of his blindness and dread intensely the very fact that he does not see his Creator. The text continues:

### VERSE 25

“Do you display your power against a leaf carried away by the wind, and pursue a dry stalk?” What is a human being except a leaf? The one who fell from the tree in paradise—what is he except a leaf? He is carried away by the wind of temptation and lifted up by the breezes of desire. The human mind suffers as many temptations as though it were moved by that many gusts and disturbances.

After the leaf, the human being is aptly also called a stalk. In his creation he was a tree; in temptation he made himself a leaf; but after his fall he appeared as a stalk. Because he fell from a height, he is a leaf; but because through the flesh he was close to the earth even when he seemed to stand, he is also remembered as a stalk. Yet because he has lost the greenness of inner love, he is now a dry stalk.

It is as though he were openly lamenting: “Why do you attack with such severity the one whom you recognize as so weak in temptation?” The text continues:

### VERSE 26

“You write bitter things against me.” Everything we say passes away; what we write, however, remains. God is said not to speak but to write bitter things when his scourges endure over us for a long time. For it was said once and for all to the sinful human being: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3:19). This sentence, pronounced in paradise concerning the death of our flesh, has not been changed from the beginning of the human race to the end of the age. “For who is the person who lives and shall not see death?” (Psalm 88).

The text continues:

“And you wish to consume me for the sins of my youth.” Behold, the righteous man, because he does not find that he sinned in his youth, fears the deeds of his adolescence.

Or certainly, because adolescence is the first age suited to good actions, righteous men sometimes advance with great maturity of mind and recall the beginning of their conduct, reproaching themselves for their beginnings in proportion to how far they have progressed in the gravity of their mind. They discover that they were undiscerning to the extent that they later attained more fully the summit of discernment. Thus it is rightly now, through the voice of the holy man, that the sins of adolescence are feared. The text continues:

### VERSE 27

“You have put my foot in the stocks, and have watched all my paths, and have considered the traces of my feet.” God has put a human being’s foot in the stocks because by the sentence of his strict judgment he has bound that person’s perversity to its allotted punishment. He watches all his paths because he judges each of his actions with subtle scrutiny.

A path is usually narrower than a road. Since roads may be understood as actions, we rightly understand paths as the thoughts behind actions. God therefore watches all paths because in each of our actions he weighs our thoughts. He considers the traces of our feet because he examines how rightly the intentions of our works are placed, lest even what is done well be done without a right desire.

The traces of the feet may also signify certain evil deeds. The foot is in the body, while the trace is on the road; and often, when we do certain things perversely, we provide a bad example to our observing brothers. Because, when our feet bend outside the road, we leave distorted tracks behind, through our works we provoke the peaceful hearts of others to scandal. Almighty God examines all these things subtly and repays each one in judgment.

But when can a human being, constrained by the weakness of his flesh, rise up carefully against all these things and hold to righteousness with an unshaken mind? The text continues:

### VERSE 28

“I shall be consumed like rot, and like a garment that is eaten by the moth.” Just as a garment is eaten by a moth that arises from it, so a human being has within himself the rot by which he is consumed. This is what consumes him, so that he ceases to exist.

Alternatively: A human being is consumed like rot when, crushed by the corruption of his flesh, he is attacked by an unclean temptation that arises not from elsewhere but from himself. Like a moth, temptation consumes the flesh as a garment from which it emerges. The text continues:

## CHAPTER 14

### VERSE 1

“A human being, born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries.” In sacred Scripture, *woman* is used either for sex or for weakness. It is used for sex, as it is written: “God sent his Son, born of woman, born under the Law” (Galatians 4:4). It is used for weakness, as a certain wise man says: “Better is the iniquity of a man than a woman doing good” (Sirach 24:14).

In this passage, therefore, what is signified by the name *woman* except weakness, when it says: “A human being born of woman”? It is as though it were said more plainly: “What strength does one possess who has been born of weakness?”

Behold, in the words of the holy man, the punishment of human beings is briefly expressed: life is made narrow for them, while misery is made broad. If everything done here is considered carefully, it is punishment and misery. For even being subject to the corruption of the flesh for necessary and permitted things is misery. The text continues:

### VERSE 2

“He comes forth like a flower and is crushed; he flees like a shadow and never remains in the same condition.” He comes forth like a flower because he shines in the flesh, but he is crushed because he is reduced to decay. What are human beings born into the world except certain flowers in a field? Hence Isaiah says: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field” (Isaiah 40:6).

A human being emerges like a flower from a hidden place and suddenly appears in public; immediately, through death, he is withdrawn from public view into secrecy.

One may ask why he compares the course of human life to a shadow rather than to the sun.
