The reason is that, having lost love of the Creator, he lost the warmth of his heart and remained only in the coldness of his own iniquity. For, in the words of Truth: “Iniquity has abounded, and the love of many has grown cold” (Matthew 24:12). Whoever therefore does not possess the warmth of the heart in the love of God, yet cannot retain the life he loves, flees plainly like a shadow. Hence it is rightly written of him: “For he followed a shadow.”

It is also rightly said: “And he never remains in the same condition,” because, as infancy passes into childhood, childhood into adolescence, adolescence into youth, youth into old age, and old age into death, in the course of the present life he is driven toward decline by the very stages of his growth. The text continues:

### VERSE 3

“And do you think it worthy to open your eyes upon such a one and bring him with you into judgment?” He has considered above both the power of almighty God and his own weakness, and has brought them before his eyes. He has weighed himself and the Lord, asking who is coming with whom to judgment. On one side he saw a human being, on the other the Creator—that is, dust and God. And he rightly says: “And do you think it worthy to open your eyes upon such a one?” The text continues:

### VERSE 4

“Who can make clean one conceived from unclean seed? Is it not you alone?” He who alone is clean in himself has the power to cleanse the unclean.

A human being living in corruptible flesh has the uncleanness of temptations imprinted within him, since he has plainly drawn them from his origin. His very conception is unclean because of the pleasure of the flesh. Hence the Psalmist says: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother bore me in sins” (Psalm 50:7).

## BOOK TWELVE

### VERSE 5

“The days of a human being are short; the number of his months is with you.” He considers it as though it were nothing to us because it passes with such speed. But because even things that slip away are present to almighty God, he declares that the number of our months is with him.

Or certainly, the brevity of time is signified by days, while the spaces of days, as though multiplied, are signified by months. Our days are short. But because our life is displayed before God, the number of our months is said to be known. Hence Solomon also says: “Length of days is in his right hand” (Proverbs 3:16).

The text continues:

“You have appointed his limits, which cannot be passed.” Nothing that happens to human beings in this world comes about without the hidden counsel of almighty God. For God, foreknowing all that would follow, decreed before the ages how everything would be ordered throughout the ages.

It has already been determined for each person how much prosperity in this world will follow him or how much adversity will strike him, lest excessive prosperity lift up his chosen ones or excessive adversity weigh them down.

This can also be understood according to the spirit. Sometimes we strive to advance in the virtues and receive certain gifts, while, rejected from others, we lie in the depths. No one grasps as many virtues as he desires, because almighty God, discerning the inner person, sets a measure even upon spiritual progress. Thus, because a person attempts to grasp something and cannot, he does not exalt himself in the things he can grasp. The text continues:

### VERSE 6

“Withdraw from him a little, that he may rest, until his desired day comes, like the day of a hired laborer.” Here *withdraw* means: remove the force of the scourge. For who can rest when God withdraws, since he alone is rest? The farther someone is from him, the more restless he becomes. Thus, when it is said, “Withdraw from him,” one must understand: by striking him, withdraw.

The farther a hired laborer is from the end of his work, the farther he is from the repayment of his wages. In the same way, each holy man placed in this life, when he sees himself far from the end of the present life, groans that he is far from eternal joys. The text continues:

### VERSE 7

“There is hope for a tree: if it is cut down, it sprouts again, and its branches put forth shoots.” In sacred Scripture, the name *tree* sometimes signifies the cross, as in: “Let us put wood in his bread” (Jeremiah 11:19). At other times it signifies a righteous or even an unrighteous man, as in the prophet: “I am the Lord; I have humbled the lofty tree and exalted the lowly tree” (Ezekiel 17:24). At still other times it signifies the incarnate Wisdom of God, as in: “She is a tree of life to those who grasp her” (Proverbs 3:18).

In this passage, when the tree is set before the human being, what is meant by the human being except every carnal person? And what is signified by the name *tree* except the life of each righteous person?

A tree has hope: if it is cut down, it sprouts again. When it suffers death for the sake of truth, it is restored in the greenness of eternal life. The one who flourished here through faith flourishes there through sight.

“And its branches put forth shoots,” because often, through the passion of a righteous person, faithful people also multiply in love for their heavenly homeland and receive the greenness of spiritual life, rejoicing that he acted bravely for God. The text continues:

### VERSES 8–9

“If its root has grown old in the earth, and its trunk has died in the dust, at the smell of water it will sprout and produce a crown as when it was first planted.”

What is the root of the righteous person except holy preaching, since he arises from it and remains in it? And what is understood by the name earth or dust except the sinner?

The root of the righteous person therefore grows old in the earth, and his trunk dies in the dust, because his preaching is regarded as despised and exhausted of all strength in the hearts of the wicked. His trunk dies in the dust because his body is examined amid the hands of his persecutors.

“At the smell of water he sprouts,” because, through the breathing of the Holy Spirit, he produces the shoot of virtue in the hearts of the elect by the example of his conduct. For a cut-down trunk to produce a crown means that, when the righteous person has been extinguished bodily, he awakens the hearts of many through the example of his passion and displays the greenness of truth through right faith.

It is aptly said: “As when it was first planted.” Everything done here by the righteous is a second planting, because the first planting is not in the works of the righteous but in the foreknowledge of the Creator.

The root of the righteous may also be understood as the very nature of humanity from which he subsists. This root grows old in the earth when the nature of the flesh fails, reduced to dust. Its trunk dies in the dust because the extinguished body is dispersed from its form. But it sprouts at the smell of water because it rises again through the coming of the Holy Spirit. And it produces a crown as when it was first planted because it returns to that form for the attainment of which it had been created, if, having been placed in paradise, it had not wished to sin.

This may perhaps be understood of the Lord, since although he could be killed through his passion, through the glory of the resurrection he came again to the greenness of life. His branches put forth shoots because, multiplied through his resurrection, the faithful grew far and wide.

His root in the earth grew old, as it were, because his preaching was despised by the unbelief of the Jews. His trunk died in the dust because, in the hearts of his persecutors, which were lifted up by the wind of their unbelief, he was regarded as contemptible and despised, since he could be killed in the flesh.

But he sprouted at the smell of water because, through the power of God, his dead flesh returned to life, in accordance with what is written: “Whom God raised from the dead” (1 Thessalonians 1:10). And he produced a crown as when he was first planted because the weakness of the apostles, which feared and denied him at his death and withered through denial, flourished again into faith through the glory of his resurrection. Hence it adds:

### VERSE 10

“But when a human being has died, and has been stripped bare and consumed, where, I ask, is he?” No human being is without sin except the one who did not come into this world from sin. And because we are all bound in guilt, we die through the loss of righteousness itself. We are stripped of the garment of innocence first granted in paradise, and we are also consumed when the destruction of the flesh follows.

Thus the sinful human being dies in guilt, is stripped of righteousness, and is consumed in punishment. The father graciously chose to cover the nakedness of the sinful son, who, when he returned, said: “Quickly bring out the first robe” (Luke 15:22). The first robe is the garment of innocence, which the well-created human being received, but lost after being wrongly persuaded by the serpent.

Against this nakedness it is likewise said: “Blessed is the one who keeps watch and guards his garments, lest he walk naked” (Revelation 16:15). We guard our garments when we preserve the commands of innocence in our minds, so that, when guilt strips us naked before the judge, repentance may cover us as we return to the innocence we lost.

The sinful human being did not wish to remain where he was created; here, where he fell, different things are forbidden him. He willingly lost his homeland and is unwillingly expelled from the exile he loves. Where, then, is the one who is not in his love, where true being consists? The text continues:

### VERSES 11–12

“As the waters depart from the sea and the river, emptied, dries up, so a human being, when he has fallen asleep, shall not rise again.” The sea is the human mind, and the thoughts of the mind are like the waves of the sea. At times they swell through anger, become calm through grace, and flow away with bitterness through hatred.

But when a human being dies, the waters of the sea depart, because, in the Psalmist’s words, “On that day all their thoughts shall perish” (Psalm 145:4). And again it is written concerning the dying person: “Love and hatred shall perish together” (Ecclesiastes 9:6).

The river, emptied, therefore dries up because, when the soul has been withdrawn, the body remains empty. The lifeless body is like the empty channel of a river.

But in these words it seems very harsh that a human being, when he has fallen asleep, shall not rise again. Why then do we labor if we are not striving toward the reward of the resurrection? How, moreover, can it be said that he shall not rise again when it is written: “We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:51)?

The sentence that follows indicates what distinction is concealed in the preceding statement. For it adds:

“Until heaven is worn away, he shall not awaken, nor rise from his sleep.” It is clear that he shall not rise until heaven is worn away, because, unless the end of this age has come, the human race will not awaken from the sleep of death to life. Therefore the meaning is not that he will not rise in any way at all, but that the human race will not rise before the destruction of heaven.

The text continues:

### VERSE 13

“Who will grant me this: that you protect me in the underworld?” Before the coming of the Mediator between God and humanity, it is beyond doubt that every human being, however clean and proven his life might have been, descended to the prison of the underworld.

Yet we do not say that the souls of the righteous descended to the underworld in such a way that they were held in places of punishment. Rather, the higher regions of the underworld are to be believed to exist, so that the righteous might rest in the higher places and the unrighteous be tormented in the lower ones.

Hence the Psalmist says that God’s grace came before him: “You have rescued my soul from the lower underworld” (Psalm 81:13). Blessed Job, therefore, knowing that before the Mediator’s coming he would descend to the underworld, asks there for the protection of his Creator, so that he might remain separate from the places of punishment.

The text continues:

“And hide me until your anger passes.” The anger of almighty God exercises the force of his strictness every day in this: he plunges those who live unworthily into punishments. This anger is now passing, but it passes toward the end, because it is active now but is completed at the end of the world.

Nevertheless, this anger passed away as far as the souls of the elect were concerned at the coming of our Redeemer, because the Mediator between God and humanity, when he mercifully descended there himself, led them from the prison of the underworld to the joys of paradise.

The text continues:

“And appoint for me a time when you will remember me.” “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of woman, born under the Law, to redeem those who were under the Law” (Galatians 4:4–5).

Foreseeing this redemption, through which many from among the Gentiles were to be set free, the man of the Lord says: “Although this is hidden in your heart, yet I know that you remember all things” (Job 10:13). He asks almighty God that a time of remembrance be appointed for him.

For this reason the Lord says in the Gospel: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32)—that is, all the elect. The text continues:

### VERSE 14

“Do you suppose that a dead human being will live again?” Righteous men often present, as though in doubt, something they themselves feel to be certain and firm, so that they may take upon themselves the words of the weak.

Yet, by a strong declaration, they completely contradict the doubt of the weak. In this way, by appearing to speak doubtfully, they condescend to the weak to some degree; and by presenting a certain judgment, they draw doubtful minds toward firmness. The text continues:

“All the days in which I serve, I wait until my change comes.” By longing so greatly for his change, he indicates how certain he is of the resurrection. He also makes known how much he despises the course of the present life when he calls it misery.

Through evil, one always moves toward the end, and each day the termination of the conclusion is awaited. He therefore despises the course of this life and seeks a state of stability; because, by serving in a mutable condition, he hastens to reach his change. The text continues:

### VERSE 15

“You will call me, and I shall answer you.” We say that we answer someone when we return corresponding actions in response to his deeds.

In that change, therefore, the Lord calls and the human being answers, because the incorruptible human being is displayed after corruption, before the glory of incorruption. For now, so long as we are subject to corruption, we do not answer our Creator at all. Since corruption is far from incorruption, there is no fitting likeness for our answer.

Concerning that change it is written: “When he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

The text continues:

“Stretch out your right hand to the work of your hands.” It is as though he were saying plainly: “For this reason a corruptible creature can persist toward incorruption: it is raised up by the hand of your power and held by the grace of your regard so that it may persist.”

The Son may also be signified by the name *right hand*, because “all things were made through him” (John 1:3). Almighty God therefore stretched out his right hand to the work of his hands, because, in order to raise the human race, cast down and lying in the depths, to the heights, he sent the Only-Begotten in the flesh. Through his incarnation it has been granted to us that, although by our own will we fell into corruption, we may at some time answer God, who calls us, to the glory of incorruption. The text continues:

### VERSE 16

“You have indeed counted my steps, but spare my sins.” God counts steps when he marks each of our works for the sake of repayment. For what is signified by steps except each of our actions?

Almighty God therefore both counts our steps and spares our sins: he carefully considers our deeds, yet mercifully releases them for those who repent. The text continues:

### VERSE 17

“You have sealed up my offenses as in a bag, but you have healed my iniquity.” Our offenses are sealed up as in a bag because what we do outwardly, unless we wash it away through repentance, is kept in the secrecy of God’s judgments under a certain concealment, so that one day it may emerge from the seal of secrecy into the public judgment.

Hence he also says through Moses: “Are these things not gathered up with me and sealed in my treasures? On the day of vengeance I shall repay them” (Deuteronomy 32:34–35).

But when we are crushed by the scourge of discipline for the evils we have committed and we mourn them through repentance, he both seals and heals our iniquity: he neither leaves it unpunished here nor preserves it to be punished in judgment.

Or certainly, our sins are sealed in a bag when we continually weigh the evils we have committed with an attentive heart. For what is the human heart except God’s bag? When we carefully observe how greatly we have sinned, we carry our sins as though they were sealed in God’s bag.

It is as though he were saying: “When you seal them so that I may see them in repentance, you act, without doubt, so that they may not be seen in repayment.” The text continues:

### VERSES 18–19

“A mountain falling decays, and a rock is moved from its place. Waters hollow out stones, and by their flooding the earth is gradually consumed; thus you will also destroy a human being.”

It often happens that, when cliffs fall, a rock is moved to other places, waters hollow out stones, and the earth is gradually consumed by floods. But what follows must be examined with great care: “Thus you will also destroy human beings.”

What is meant by the destruction of human beings in relation to the falling mountain, the moved rock, the hollowed stone, and the earth consumed by flooding, except that it plainly reveals that there are two kinds of temptation?

One kind takes place suddenly in the mind even of a righteous person, so that he is tempted all at once, shaken and overthrown by an unforeseen event, and does not see his fall until after he has fallen.

The other comes gradually into the mind, infecting the resisting spirit through gentle suggestions and consuming all its strength for righteousness not through its intensity but through its persistence.

Since one temptation often overthrows the righteous through a sudden assault, let it be said: “A mountain falling decays, and a rock is moved from its place”—that is, the holy mind, whose place had been righteousness, is suddenly moved to guilt by an abrupt impulse.

Again, since another temptation gently pours itself into the human heart and corrupts and consumes all the hardness of its strength, let it be said: “Waters hollow out stones.” For continual and gentle blandishments of lust absorb the hardness of the mind, and a slow and subtle vice corrupts the mind’s firm and strong purpose.

Hence it adds: “And by their flooding the earth is gradually consumed.” Just as earth is gradually consumed when water flows into it, so, when vice quietly steals upon it, even a strong mind is gently absorbed.

Hence it is rightly added: “Thus you will also destroy human beings”—that is, because when, by a just judgment, you permit temptation suddenly to dominate the mind of one who appears to stand on high, you make that mind fall and decay; and the will is changed into vice, as a rock is moved to another place.

The text continues:

### VERSE 20

“You have strengthened him for a little while, so that he might pass away forever.” A human being has been strengthened for a little while because he has received strength to live for a short time, so that he might pass into eternity, where no limit will bring his life to an end.

The text continues:

“You will change his face and send him away.” A human being’s face is changed when his appearance is worn down by death. He is sent away because, against his will, he is compelled to pass from the things he held willingly to eternal things. The text continues:

### VERSE 21

“Whether his sons were noble or ignoble, he does not know.” Just as those who are still alive [variant: *vivi*, or perhaps *in vivis*] do not know where the souls of the dead are held, so the dead do not know how the life in the flesh of those who come after them is ordered.

This, however, should not be understood of holy souls. Those who see the glory of almighty God within cannot in any way be thought to be ignorant of something external. But concerning all carnal people, who lavish their principal love upon their children, blessed Job asserts that they later do not know what they loved intensely here.

If this is to be understood spiritually, the name *sons* may appropriately signify works, just as Paul says of the woman that she will be saved through the generation of children. The sons are therefore noble when they perform righteous works, but ignoble when their deeds are perverse.

Often a person strives to do various good things with good intention, yet, because many things creep in, it is uncertain how his deeds are regarded before almighty God. The text continues:

### VERSE 22

“Yet his flesh, while he lives, will suffer, and his soul will mourn over himself.” Paul says concerning married couples: “Yet such people will have tribulation in the flesh” (1 Corinthians 7:28). Whoever desires to rejoice in himself is already in mourning for the very reason that he has withdrawn from true joy. For the Creator is true joy to the mind.

## CHAPTER 15

### VERSE 1

“Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said.” We have often said that blessed Job represents the type of the holy universal Church, while his friends represent heretics. As though in defense of the Lord, they find an opportunity for foolish speech and hurl insulting words against the good. Everything perceived by the faithful displeases them as though it had been spoken into the wind.

Hence it is now said:

### VERSE 2

“Will a wise man answer as though speaking into the wind?” They do not regard the words of the good as statements of reason, but as goads of partiality. Hence it adds:

“And fill his stomach with heat.” They always strive, as has been said, to cloak even what they know how to say insultingly under the pretext of defending the Lord. The text continues:

### VERSE 3

“Do you rebuke with words one who is not your equal, and speak what is not expedient for you?” They consider no one to possess the fear of the Lord except one whom they have been able to draw into the foolishness of their own confession. Hence he adds:

### VERSE 4

“To the extent that it lies with you, you have emptied out fear, and removed prayers from before the Lord.” *You have removed* means *you have taken away*.

It is as though he were saying plainly: “Relying on your own righteousness, you disdain to implore the grace of your Creator.” When heretics cannot find genuine evils against the good, they invent things to rebuke so that they may appear righteous. Often this leads them to open words of insult. Hence it adds further:

### VERSE 5

“For your iniquity has taught your mouth, and you imitate the tongue of blasphemers.” Iniquity teaches the mouth when, from an evil life, it conceives something worse to say. It is as though he were told plainly: “You learned to speak perversely from a still more perverse life.”

But because the holy Church, confessing the true flesh and true death of the Lord, is considered by heretics who deny these things to be directing insult against God, it is now said: “And you imitate the tongue of blasphemers.” The text continues:

### VERSE 6

“Your mouth will condemn you, and not I; your lips will answer you.” Because they think that the evils of adversity arise from an erroneous confession, they assert that the person’s own lips answer him, so that the guilt of his speech is the cause of his scourging. The text continues:

### VERSES 7–8

“Were you the first human being born, and were you formed before the hills? Have you heard the counsel of God, and is his wisdom inferior to you?” It is as though he were saying in plainer words: “You who speak about the eternal, consider that you are temporal. You who debate his wisdom, consider that you do not know his counsel.” The text continues:

### VERSE 9

“What do you know that we do not know? What do you understand that we do not?” These words plainly show from what arrogance of mind proceeds everything that sounds as though it were spoken in defense of the Lord. The text continues:

### VERSE 10

“Among us are both the old and the ancient, much older than your fathers.” John testifies that all heretics have gone out from the holy universal Church, saying: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19).

But so that they might commend what they assert to the foolish minds of people as though it derived from antiquity, they claim to have ancient Fathers and call those very teachers of the Church masters of their own confession. When they despise present-day preachers, they glory in the teaching of the ancient Fathers with false presumption, so that people may admit that even the ancient Fathers held what they themselves say. The text continues:

### VERSE 11

“Is it a great thing that God should comfort you, but your perverse words prevent it?” It is as though he were saying plainly: “If you were corrected in your profession of faith, you could long ago have had consolation in your scourges.” The text continues:

## Book Thirteen [Col. 0247]

**Verse 12.** “Why does your heart exalt you, and, as though thinking great thoughts, keep your eyes fixed in astonishment?” — The mind of the just is often so suspended in contemplating higher things that their outward countenance seems stupefied. But because heretics do not know that this power of contemplation works inwardly, they think that what the just and rightly wise do arises from hypocrisy rather than truth. It follows:

**Verse 13.** “Why does your spirit swell against God, so that you utter such words from your mouth?” — The just, oppressed by certain necessities, are often compelled to confess their deeds. Blessed Job had done this, though scourges pressed upon him after his righteousness. But when the unjust hear their words, they judge them to have been uttered through pride rather than truth. For they weigh the words of the just by their own hearts, and do not judge true good things capable of being said humbly. It follows:

**Verse 14.** “What is man, that he should be without stain?” — In the very word *man* (*homo*), his earthliness and weakness are expressed; for *homo* is named from *humus*, earth. How can one who, made from earth, has voluntarily fallen into weakness be without stain? It is added: “And how can one born of woman appear just?” — For woman first offered injustice to man in paradise. How, then, can he appear just who is born of her who proved the purveyor of injustice? It follows:

**Verse 15.** “Behold, among his holy ones none is unchangeable, and the heavens are not clean in his sight.” — By the name “heavens” he repeats what he had first signified by the designation “holy ones.” For it is written of these same saints: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 18:2). By nature all possess in themselves their own mutability. Yet, while they desire always to cling to unchangeable truth, by clinging they bring it about that they become unchangeable. As they hold to it with all their affection, they sometimes receive the grace, raised above themselves, to overcome that mutability which they had in themselves. The heavens are not clean in his sight because, by themselves, even those who become preachers of purity cannot be perfectly clean before the strict judgment. John attests this when he says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8), and what follows. It follows:

**Verse 16.** “How much more is man abominable and useless!” — Abominable, of course, because of the uncleanness of stain; useless because of the injustice of an imperfect life. Yet “abominable and useless” may also be understood otherwise. A perverse man sometimes seems to do certain things rightly, but through the things that are wicked, even those things of his which are right are destroyed. Since evils greatly displease God, neither do the things which seem good please him. Therefore, one who is abominable to God in his evils is useless in his good deeds. It follows: “Who drinks iniquity like water.” — Iniquity is drunk like water when fault is committed by a foolish man without any reconsideration. It follows:

**Verse 17.** “I will show you; listen to me: what I have seen I will tell you.” — All arrogant persons share this trait: if they perceive anything right, however little, they turn it to the use of pride; and from what makes them higher in their own estimation through understanding, they fall through the swelling of pride into a pit. To claim stronger authority for himself, he says: “What I have seen I will tell you.” Yet heretics are sometimes confuted by the condemned parties among themselves, and nevertheless bring forward their opinions as though with authority; by their folly they are deservedly rejected. It is added:

**Verses 18–19.** “The wise confess, and do not conceal their fathers, to whom alone the earth was given, and no stranger passed through them.” — They think that the earth was given to their fathers alone because they suppose that only the teachers of their errors truly governed the Church. Who is called a stranger but the apostate angel? Hence the Psalmist says of all malignant spirits together: “How strangers have risen against me, and the mighty have sought my soul” (Psalm 53:5). Heretics therefore deny that the stranger passed through the hearts of their teachers, because they think those hearts were not subject to the apostate angel. For this stranger to pass through each person is to send wicked thoughts into that person’s heart. It follows:

**Verse 20.** “The impious man is proud all his days.” — Even the elect are accustomed to be proud in certain thoughts and acts; but because they are elect, they cannot be proud all their days, for before they end their lives they turn their hearts from pride to the goal [or, as the text has it, “fear”] of humility. But the impious man is proud all his days because he ends life without at all withdrawing from pride. Hence it is well added: “And the number of the years of his tyranny is uncertain.” — He ought not to have been proud even if he could have known the definite number of his years, so that, knowing how long he would live, he might foresee when to remove himself from pride. But since life is always uncertain, death that steals upon us must always be feared in proportion as it can never be foreseen. He rightly calls the pride of the impious “tyranny.” Strictly speaking, a tyrant is one who rules unlawfully in a commonwealth. Yet every pride exercises tyranny in its own measure: the Lord considers not how much evil each person is able to do, but how much he would wish to do. Where outward power is lacking, a person is a tyrant within himself if iniquity rules within. It follows:

**Verse 21.** “The sound of terror is always in his ears, and when there is peace, he suspects snares.” — Nothing is happier than a simple heart, because, as it shows innocence toward others, it has nothing to fear suffering from them. By contrast, a crooked mind is always in toil: it either devises evils to inflict or fears that they will be inflicted on itself; and whatever it devises against its neighbours, it fears its neighbours devise against it. It becomes suspicious and trembling on every side. Everyone who comes to mind is believed to be seeking hostile things. Therefore one who lacks the tranquillity of security undoubtedly has the sound of terror always in his ears. Often such a person’s neighbour speaks simply and thinks nothing hostile; yet, though there is peace, he suspects snares, because one who always acts deceitfully does not think that others act simply toward him. And because it is written, “When the wicked man has come into the depth of sins, he despises” (Proverbs 18:3), entangled in the darkness of his iniquity he now despairs of light. Hence it follows:

**Verse 22.** “He does not believe that he can return from darkness, looking round on every side for the sword.” — Since he believes that snares threaten him on every side, despairing of salvation he continually grows in wickedness. It follows:

**Verse 23.** “When he sets himself to seek bread, he knows that the day of darkness is ready in his hand.” — Bread signifies the provision of this present life, and the day of darkness the time of retribution. In this life, which [lacuna], this perverse man at times perceives the present wrath of the heavenly Judge, yet does not turn from evil so that he may be turned even from his own destruction. Though his conscience accuses him and he fears to be struck, he nevertheless continually increases what will be struck. He despises his return, despairs of pardon, and is proud in fault. It follows:

**Verse 24.** “Tribulation will terrify him, and distress will surround him like a king prepared for battle.” — In everything the wicked man does, he is surrounded by tribulation and distress, because his heart is confounded by anxiety and suspicion. We should also know that a king prepared for battle is so suspicious of the enemy that he fears even the army he leads may be shaken, lest, deprived of soldiers, he lie exposed to the enemy’s missiles. Thus the wicked man is surrounded by distress like one preparing for battle, because, acting falsely and speaking falsely, he fears to lose his soldiers—that is, the arguments of falsehood—and to lie exposed to the darts of truth if perhaps he lacks something deceitful to oppose. It follows:

**Verse 25.** “For he stretched out his hand against God, and was strengthened against the Almighty.” — These words are more plainly understood of Antichrist himself, the head of the wicked. Raising his hand against God, he is said to be strengthened because he is permitted to be exalted for a short time; allowed briefly to glory, he may be punished more harshly forever. But since all wicked people are his members, let us see how what he alone will do in the end of the world is now done by individual evil persons. To stretch out one’s hand against God is to persist in wicked action despite God’s judgments. God is then more angry when he permits to be fulfilled what ought not even to have been conceived in thought. This wicked person is strengthened against the Almighty because he is allowed to prosper in evil action, so that he may do perverse things and yet live happily. Of him it is further added:

**Verse 26.** “He ran against God with uplifted neck.” — To run against God with uplifted neck is boldly to commit what displeases the Creator. He is rightly said to have run: that is, he had no obstacle from adversity in his evil work. It is further added: “And he was armed with a fat neck.” — A fat neck is wealthy pride, supported, as it were, by much flesh through abundant possessions. Thus the powerful wicked man is armed with a fat neck against the Lord because, puffed up by temporal goods, he rises against the precepts of truth as though through the greatness of flesh. It follows:

**Verse 27.** “Fatness covered his face.” — Sight is in the face, which is also the more honourable foremost part of the body. Therefore the attention of the mind is rightly signified by the face: wherever we turn it, there we see. Fatness covers the face because desired abundance of earthly things weighs down the eyes of the mind and defiles before God what ought to be honourable in them, burdening it with many cares. It follows: “And fat hangs from his sides.” — Since fat is the richness of flesh, we customarily call the dependants whom we see joined to rich persons their “sides.” Fat hangs from his sides because whoever clings to one who is powerful and wicked likewise swells from that person’s power as though from the richness of possessions. Following the iniquity of his perverse patron, he does not fear God; he afflicts as many poor persons as he can, and lifts his heart through temporal glory. It follows:

**Verse 28.** “He dwelt in desolate cities and deserted houses, which have been reduced to heaps of ruins.” — Since a city is named from the intercourse of those living together, desolate cities are the very bands of perverse followers, by whose cries this perverse man is praised as he is swept through wickedness into depraved works. Deserted houses are the wicked thoughts inhabited by this wicked man, since in everything he does he longs to please the thoughts of all wicked people. They are called deserted and desolate because almighty God deserts both the associations and the thoughts of such persons. The fallen buildings of houses and cities make heaps of ruins. Thus, when perverse persons join themselves in confused actions to perverse works, they plainly show that the buildings of life have fallen. It follows:

**Verse 29.** “He will not be inhabited [some manuscripts: ‘enriched’], nor will his substance endure, nor will he send his root into the earth.” — Where the text here says “he will not be inhabited,” I have found “he will not be enriched” in certain manuscripts. The sense does not differ, though the wording does. For one whose mind is not inhabited by almighty God falls away from virtues. Since the thought of the proud does not receive the grace of its Creator as an inhabitant, it is certainly not enriched with virtues. Therefore, because he is inwardly empty, it is said, “he will not be enriched” [or “inhabited”]; but because he outwardly swells only temporarily, it is rightly added: “Nor will his substance endure.” Every proud person, strengthened against the Lord, running with uplifted neck and raising himself against his Creator with fat neck, seems to stand like a tree; but his standing is without root, because his life is uprooted by the hidden judgment as by a light breath. If, however, we understand earth here as the reward of eternal life, of which the Prophet says, “My portion in the land of the living” (Psalm 141:6), this wicked man does not send his root into the earth because he never directs the thought of his heart toward the desire of eternal life. For what the root is to a tree, a person’s thought is to each human being. It follows:

**Verse 30.** “He will not depart from darkness.” — If this proud man wished to return from fault to righteousness, he would depart from darkness; but because he does not seek the light of righteousness, he does not depart from darkness. It follows: “Flame dries up his branches.” — Those joined to him also burn with earthly desires; and, while the flame of desire kindles the minds of his dependants, it dries up his branches, so that they do not bear the fruit of good work. It follows: “And he will be taken away by the breath of his mouth.” — The more powerful every proud person is in this life, the more boldly he loosens the reins of his tongue to speak whatever perverse things he pleases. He will be taken away by the breath of his mouth because he receives the sentence of punishment precisely because he did not restrain his breath under divine fear. It follows:

**Verse 31.** “Deceived by error, he does not believe in vain that he must be redeemed by some price.” — Whenever we give alms after sin, we give, as it were, a price for wicked acts. Hence the Prophet says of one who does not do this: “He will not give his propitiation, nor the price for the redemption of his soul” (Psalm 84:89). Proud rich persons sometimes oppress inferiors, seize what belongs to others, and yet bestow certain things upon others as though generously. But he does not believe in vain that he must be redeemed by a price, because the almsgiving of a proud rich man cannot redeem him when the robbery of the poor which he has committed also does not allow it to rise before God.

This may perhaps be understood otherwise. Proud rich persons often give alms, not from desire for eternal life, but to extend temporal life. They believe they can postpone death by gifts. But, deceived by error, let him not believe in vain that he can be redeemed by any price, because by an offered gift he cannot obtain escape from his appointed end—indeed, his wickedness cuts short his life. Hence it is added:

**Verse 32.** “Before his days are fulfilled, he will perish, and his hand withers.” — The individual days fixed by God’s foreknowledge can neither be increased nor diminished, unless it happens that they are foreknown as longer with better works or shorter with worse ones. Thus Hezekiah deserved an increase of days through the outpouring of tears; and it is written of the perverse: “Death meets the undisciplined” (Isaiah 38:5).

Yet though long periods of life are not predestined for the wicked person in God’s hidden foreknowledge, because he desires to live carnally he sets long days before his mind; and because he cannot reach the time he expects, he perishes as though before his days are fulfilled.

Otherwise: some return to themselves after a ruined life and, as conscience accuses them, leave perverse paths, change their deeds, oppose their old depravity, flee earthly occupations, and pursue heavenly desires. But before they are made firm in these holy desires, through sluggishness of mind they return to what they had begun to condemn and run back to the evils they had resolved to flee. Even if one perhaps begins to do some good, before he grows strong in it through length of time he slips back to outward things and perversely abandons what he seemed to have begun rightly. [The preceding appears to require the plural.] Hence it is aptly added: “His hand withers.” For, being untimely entangled in outward actions, he is dried up from every good work. It is therefore further well said:

**Verse 33.** “His cluster will be harmed like a vine in its first blossom.” — If excessive cold strikes a flowering vine through an unfavourable change of weather, it immediately dries it of all its green moisture. Some persons, after perverse paths, long to follow holy ways; but before, as we have said, good desires are strengthened in them, some prosperity of this present world overtakes them, entangles them in outward concerns, and, withdrawing their minds from the warmth of inward love, extinguishes them as by cold and kills whatever seemed to appear in them from the blossom of virtues.

At times it is not cold but heat that dries a vine. When it is touched by excessive heat, the blossom falls away and the cluster wastes. Often those who do not come to good works with a right intention, when they see that they please people, are kindled more vehemently to perform those same works; they anxiously strive to do things pleasing to human eyes and burn, as it were, with holy desire. What, then, touches these persons in blossom except heat? It follows: “And like an olive casting off its flower.” — When the olive is in flower, if excessive mist touches it, it is emptied of the fullness of its fruits. So whenever beginners in good works begin to be praised by observers and take delight in their praises, a mist of understanding arises in their thought, so that they can no longer discern with what intention they do anything; and they lose the fruit of their work as though through the mist of favour. It follows:

**Verse 34.** “For the gathering of hypocrites is barren.” — He would not lose the good he had begun if he were not a hypocrite. Hypocrites gather good works, but their very gathering is barren because by what they do they do not desire to receive fruit in eternal recompense. They seem fruitful and green in their works to human eyes, but appear unfruitful and dry in the sight of the hidden Judge. It follows: “And fire will devour the tents of those who gladly receive gifts.” — As the body dwells in a tent, so the mind dwells in thought. Fire devours tents when the heat of avarice devastates thoughts. It often happens that a hypocrite despises gold or any bodily goods offered by people; but because he does not receive these, he seeks to receive greater praise from them. Or, if we should understand their tents as those in which their souls dwell, fire devours their tents because those who burn here in mind with the fire of avarice are also there burned in flesh by the fires of Gehenna. It follows:

**Verse 35.** “He conceived pain and gave birth to iniquity, and his womb prepares deceits.” — He conceives pain while thinking perversely; he gives birth to iniquity when he begins to fulfil what he thought. By envying he conceives pain; by disparaging he gives birth to iniquity. The mind is rightly understood by the name “womb,” because, as offspring is conceived in the womb, so thought is generated in the mind; and as foods are contained in the belly, so thoughts are contained in the mind. The womb of the hypocrite prepares deceits [the text reads *vetus*, evidently an OCR error for *uterus*], because the more he seeks to appear more innocent than all others, the greater malice he continually conceives in his mind against his neighbours.

## Book Thirteen

### Chapter XVI

**Verses 1–2.** Job answered and said: “I have often heard such things.” — The elect frequently hear the evils of others as though they were their own, and are accused by those who themselves perpetrate the crimes of which they are accused. In this answer, blessed Job signifies that period of the Church when, oppressed by adversaries through their temporal power, she is regarded as though cast down. Hence it follows:

“You are all wearisome comforters.” — Whether they are heretics or any other wicked persons, when they see the good suffering in adversity, they try to persuade them to evil precisely when they wish to console them. Their consolation therefore rightly becomes burdensome to the minds of the good, because amid words of sweetness they desire to administer the poison of error. It follows:

**Verse 3.** “Will windy words have an end?” — Windy words are those that serve temporal inflation rather than uprightness. Often the wicked also say good things; but because they do not say them well, they utter windy words. For even when their statements are sound in content, they are nevertheless inflated by arrogance. It follows:

“Or is anything burdensome to you if you speak?” — Wicked men quickly fall silent when they utter abusive words to others like themselves, because they immediately hear from them the same things they say to their listeners. But when they assail good men with vicious words, no annoyance arises from the abuse, because they speak against those who remain silent. Nor do they compel the just to hear what they are, since the just do not return abuse, even when forced to hear what they are not. It follows:

**Verse 4.** “I too could speak like you.” — The just man states what he could do; but, so as not to abandon justice, he avoids doing what he could do. It follows:

**Verses 5–6.** “Would that your soul were in place of my soul! I too would comfort you with words and shake my head over you. I would strengthen you with my mouth and move my lips as though sparing you.” — At times, when wicked minds cannot be corrected by human preaching, one must benevolently wish for divine scourges to afflict them. When this is done with great devotion of love, it is not the punishment of someone who has gone astray that is sought, but his correction; and it is shown to be prayer rather than a curse.

It should be noted that he does not say, “Would that my soul were in place of your souls,” but, “Would that your soul were in place of my soul.” For he would certainly curse himself if he wished to become like them; whereas he desired better things for those whom he sought to make like himself.

We console the wicked when they are under the scourge by showing that, through their outward affliction, inward well-being is growing stronger in them. We also shake our head when we bend the mind, which is our principal faculty, toward compassion; and we strengthen them amid their scourges when we soothe the force of their pain with gentle words. There are some who, because they do not understand inward realities, are driven to despair by outward evils.

He does not say “sparing,” but “as though sparing you.” I do not think this should be passed over carelessly. The holy Church, preserving the rigor of discipline together with an admixture of gentleness, at times spares the wicked as though sparing them, and at times spares them as though not sparing them. Thus, when the holy Church, through her preachers, rebukes certain acts of the wicked with the measured severity of denunciation, she moves her lips as though sparing them; yet, by sparing them, she does not spare them, because she does not remain silent about guilt in general even when she is silent about it in particular. It follows:

**Verse 7.** “But what shall I do? If I speak, my pain does not cease; and if I am silent, it does not depart from me.” — Everyone knows how this suits the person of blessed Job. But if it is applied to the type of the holy Church, her pain does not cease when she speaks, whenever she sees that the wicked are not corrected by her speech; and when she is silent, her pain does not depart, because, even if she turns away and becomes silent, she groans all the more at this very silence, since she sees the crimes of the wicked increasing while she remains silent. It follows:

**Verse 8.** “But now my pain has oppressed me.” — The holy Church is weighed down by her pain when she sees the wicked increasing in their malice. And because, when the wicked increase, even the weak who are within her are provoked to pursue the practices of evil, it is rightly added:

“And all my limbs have been reduced to nothing.” — Just as the strong are usually signified by bones, so the weak are signified by limbs. The members of the Church are therefore reduced to nothing when, through imitation of the wicked who prosper in this world, the weak are shaped for the worse. Seeing the prosperity of the wicked, they often slip even from the very state of faith. It is rightly said, “But now,” because the present is the time of the Church’s sorrow, whereas the time of joy will come afterward. It follows:

**Verse 9.** “And my wrinkles testify against me.” — What is signified by wrinkles except duplicity? The wrinkles of the holy Church are all those who live within her in a double manner: they proclaim faith with their voices but deny it by their deeds. Yet the holy Church does not have these wrinkles in her elect, for they do not know how to display one thing outwardly while possessing another inwardly. Hence the excellent preacher rightly says: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27).

It is as though she were saying: “Those who now pursue and rebuke me are themselves placed within my body, yet do not correct in themselves the wickedness of their duplicity.” It follows:

“And the liar rises up against my face, contradicting me.” — Even in the time of her peace, the holy Church suffers false speech, since many within her distrust the promise of eternity while pretending to be faithful. Because they do not dare openly to contradict her preaching, she suffers their false speech not against her face but, as it were, behind her back. But when the time of wickedness breaks forth, the one who now detracts through fear comes before her face to contradict her, because he resists the words of true faith with open utterance. It follows:

**Verse 10.** “He gathers his fury against me.” — The devil now has fury against the holy Church, but his fury is scattered, since the temptations he stirs in individuals remain hidden. When he breaks out against her in open persecution, he gathers his fury against her, because in afflicting her he concentrates his whole intention. It follows:

“And, threatening me, he gnashes his teeth against me.” — Of this it is also added:

“My enemy has looked upon me with terrible eyes.” — That ancient enemy gnashes his teeth against her and looks upon her with terrible eyes, because through some he carries out cruel deeds, while through others he plans what deeds to carry out. The teeth of this enemy are the persecutors and executioners of the good, who tear apart his members when they afflict the elect through their persecutions. The eyes of this enemy are those who plan the evils to be done against her and, by their counsels, inflame the cruelty of her persecutors. Thus the ancient adversary gnashes against her with his teeth when, through cruel reprobates, he persecutes the life of the good within her. He looks upon her with terrible eyes because, through the counsels of the wicked, he never ceases to seek evils by which he may continually afflict her more grievously. It follows:

**Verse 11.** “They opened their mouths against me, reproaching me.” — The reprobate open their mouths in reproach when they are not afraid to preach the evils of their error and envy the teachings of right faith. It follows:

“They struck my cheek; they were satisfied with my sufferings.” — The cheeks of the Church are her holy preachers, as Jeremiah says under the figure of Judah: “She wept bitterly in the night, and her tears are on her cheeks” (Lamentations 1:2). The wicked strike her cheek when they persecute good preachers, and the reprobate think they have accomplished something great when they kill the lives of preachers. The punishment that chiefly chastises the mind of the Church satisfies them. It follows:

**Verse 12.** “God has confined me with the wicked and delivered me into the hands of the impious.” — The people of the elect are confined with the wicked when their flesh is temporarily given over to the persecutions of the ancient enemy. They are delivered not to the spirit but to the hands of the impious, because, insofar as the wicked cannot grasp them in mind, they burn more fiercely against their flesh. It follows:

**Verse 13.** “I, once prosperous, have suddenly been crushed.” — By saying that he was suddenly crushed, he portrays the unprepared mind of the weak. Since they cannot foresee the evils that are to come, those evils become more grievous to them because they endure them unexpectedly. Adversity does not come suddenly upon firm minds, because it is foreseen before it arrives.

Yet the holy Church also suffers this now in certain people who previously lay hidden. After flourishing in doctrine, they are sometimes crushed beneath subordinated vices, so that they fall into certain evils as though they had never possessed the nourishment of the word. It follows:

“He seized my neck, broke me, and set me up as though for a target.” — In the wicked, the neck signifies pride; in the good, freedom and uprightness. Because, during persecution, some of the weak do not dare freely to preach what they truly believe, it is rightly said of this enemy: “He seized my neck and broke me.”

Perhaps, however, those are signified by “neck” who, during the time of his peace, become more uplifted than is fitting and, under the pretext of defending what is right, serve the vice of arrogance. They therefore feel adversity more keenly during persecution because they are exalted by prosperity.

Clearly, a target is set up so that it may be struck by the discharge of arrows. The faithful people are set up as a target for their enemy because he continually afflicts them with his persecutions. Whoever endures continual evils in this life receives the attacks of those who inflict them as though placed upon a target. It follows:

**Verse 14.** “He surrounded me with his spears, pierced my loins on every side, did not spare me, and poured out my entrails upon the ground.” — These words might seem capable of fitting blessed Job according to the literal sense if what is said, “He surrounded me with his spears,” were followed by the statement that is not found written there: “He poured out my entrails upon the ground.” Since we cannot find this according to the literal sense, we must seek, according to the spirit, those things that sound in his words according to the historical sense.

The holy Church is surrounded by spears from her enemy when she is hindered in her members by the darts of temptation from her crafty assailant. We rightly speak of being surrounded by spears, because the ancient enemy attacks us on every side with the wound of his intention.

“He pierced my loins on every side.” — Lust is signified by the loins. Hence the one who wished to extinguish the pleasure of lust from his heart preached, saying: “Gird up the loins of your mind” (1 Peter 1:13). When the ancient enemy drags the faithful people into lust, he undoubtedly strikes them in the loins.

It should also be noted that he does not say “he wounded,” but “he pierced my loins on every side.” Just as speaking is sometimes the act of one person, while conversing is the act of two or perhaps many, so the ancient enemy, because he does not drag us into guilt without our consent, is said not to wound but to pierce our loins on every side. What he wickedly suggests to us, we fulfill by following it through our own will. It follows:

“He did not spare.” — It is as though he were saying: “He did not cease.”

“And he poured out my entrails upon the ground.” — What else should we understand by the entrails of the holy Church except the minds of those who contain certain of her mysteries within themselves and serve her innermost sacraments? When the ancient adversary drags certain faithful people, who seemed to serve the inner sacraments, into worldly affairs, he undoubtedly pours out her entrails upon the ground. It follows:

**Verse 15.** “He cut me down with wound upon wound.” — The holy Church is cut down in her weak members with wound upon wound when sin is added to sin, so that guilt is intensified all the more. When avarice draws someone to robbery, and robbery leads to deceit, so that the guilt already committed is also defended by falsehood, what is he except one cut down by wound upon wound? Hence it is also said through the prophet: “Cursing, lying, murder, theft, and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood” (Hosea 4:2). It follows:

“He rushed upon me like a giant.” — An enemy can easily be resisted if one does not consent to him for long, whether in many matters or in one. But if the soul becomes accustomed to being subject to his persuasion, the more frequently it submits to him, the more intolerable it makes him to itself, so that it cannot resist him. It follows:

**Verse 16.** “I sewed sackcloth upon my skin and covered my flesh with ashes.” — What should be understood in sackcloth and ashes except repentance? What in skin and flesh except the sin of the flesh? When some people return to repentance after the fall of the flesh, sackcloth is, as it were, sewn upon the skin and the flesh is covered with ashes, because the guilt of the flesh is covered by repentance, so that it may not appear for punishment in the examination of the strict Judge. It follows:

**Verse 17.** “My face swells with weeping.” — The face of the Church consists of those who appear first because they are placed in positions of governance, so that the faithful people’s honor derives from their appearance, even if something deformed lies hidden in the body. These leaders of the peoples lament the faults of the weak and grieve over the falls of others as though they were their own. It follows:

“And my eyelids have grown dim.” — Those who keep watch to provide for the paths of the feet are rightly called eyelids. But when even vigilant superiors do not understand God’s hidden judgments, the eyelids of the holy Church grow dim. It follows:

**Verse 18.** “I have suffered these things without iniquity in my hands, while my prayers to God were pure.” — He endured this without iniquity in his hands who “committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22). Yet he endured the pain of the cross for our redemption. He alone offered pure prayers to God on behalf of all, because even in the pain of his Passion he prayed for his persecutors, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). It follows.

Vers. 19. “May the earth not cover my blood, and may my cry find no place in you to hide.” — To sinful man it was said: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. III, 19). Yet this earth did not conceal the blood of our Redeemer, because every sinner, receiving the price of his redemption, confesses and praises it, and makes it known to whatever neighbours he wishes. Nor did the earth cover his blood, because the holy Church has proclaimed the mystery of his redemption throughout all the regions of the world. For the blood of redemption that is received is the cry of our Redeemer. Hence Paul also says: “And the sprinkling of blood speaking better than Abel” (Hebr. XII, 24). His cry finds a place to hide in us if our tongue is silent about what the mind believes. But lest his cry remain hidden in us, each person must, according to his measure, make the mystery of his vivification known to those nearby. It follows:

[Col. 0252B] Vers. 20. “For behold, my witness is in heaven, and my confidant in the heights.” — When the Son was being shaken on earth, he had a witness in heaven. The Father is the Son’s witness, of whom he himself says in the Gospel: “The Father who sent me, he himself has borne witness concerning me” (John V, 37). He is rightly also called his confidant, because the Father always works with the Son by one will and one counsel.

This may perhaps also be referred to the voice of his body. For this reason the holy Church endures the adversities of the present life: so that heavenly grace may lead her to eternal rewards. She disregards the death of her flesh because she looks toward the glory of the resurrection; the things she suffers are transitory, while those she awaits are everlasting. She has no doubt concerning these perpetual goods, because she already holds the faithful testimony of the Redeemer’s glory. He is rightly called her confidant, because he knows our nature not only by creating it but also by assuming it. For his knowing consists in having taken our nature upon himself. Hence it is also said through the Psalmist: “For he himself knows our frame” (Ps. CII, 14).

Yet this utterance may also correspond to blessed Job in each one of us. Whoever seeks human praise for what he does looks for a witness on earth; but whoever hastens to please almighty God by his actions considers that he has a witness in heaven. It follows:

Vers. 21. “My friends are wordy; my eye drips toward God.” — What is signified by the eye except the mind’s intention? As it is written: “If your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light” (Luke XI, 34). Therefore, when his friends are wordy—that is, when even those who share his faith disparage him—it is necessary for the eye to drip toward God, so that our whole intention may flow out in the compunction of inward love. It follows:

Vers. 22. “Would that a man might be judged with God as the son of man is judged with his companion.” — We always acknowledge that we are sinners, yet, when placed under the scourge, we often do not know for which sin we are being scourged. We ourselves also examine the matter by subtle inquiry, so that we may investigate, as far as possible, the cause of our persecution. When this is often hidden from us, our blindness becomes a burden, and we grieve more over what we suffer.

[Col. 0253A] But whoever comes to judgment with his companion both says what he feels and acknowledges whatever is contradicted; if he wishes, he knocks, and he knows why he is being struck. For one who is struck by divine correction knows indeed that he is being beaten, but does not know why he is being beaten. It is as though he says what he feels but does not know what is said against him: he groans beneath the blow, but God does not openly declare for what punishment he is striking him. It follows:

Vers. 23. “For behold, the brief years pass, and I walk the path by which I shall not return.” — Everything that passes is brief, even if it seems to reach its end only slowly. We walk along the path of death by which we do not return—not because we will in no way be restored to the life of the flesh through resurrection, but because we do not return again to the labors of this mortal life [Col. 0253B], or to the acquisition of rewards through labor. It follows:

CHAPTER XVII

Vers. 1. “My spirit shall be weakened.” — The spirit is weakened by fear of judgment, because the more the minds of the elect feel themselves drawing near to the final judgment, the more terribly they tremble as they examine themselves. If they ever discover in themselves any carnal thoughts, they consume them in the heat of repentance and do not allow their thoughts to expand through carnal pleasure.

It follows: “My days shall be shortened, and the grave alone remains for me.” — Whoever considers what he will be in death always becomes fearful in his conduct; and from the point at which he already seems, in his own eyes, almost not to live, he truly lives in the eyes of his Creator. It follows:

[Col. 0253C] Vers. 2. “I have not sinned, and my eye remains in bitterness.” — As though he plainly said: “I have not committed guilt, yet I have received scourges.” But this raises a question: since he confesses in many places of the narrative that he has sinned, why does he now deny that he has sinned? The answer quickly presents itself: he did not sin so greatly as to deserve scourges, yet he could not be without sin.

The Redeemer, too, coming for our deliverance, did not sin and nevertheless endured bitterness, because without guilt he accepted the punishment of our guilt. It follows:

Vers. 3. “Deliver me, and set me beside you, and let any man’s hand fight against me.” — He himself did not sin in thought or deed; he himself remained in bitterness through his Passion; he himself was delivered through the resurrection. He was set beside the Father through the Ascension, because, going up into heaven, he sits at God’s right hand. And because Judea was stirred up against the persecution of his disciples by the glory of his Ascension, it is rightly said here: “And let any man’s hand fight against me.” It follows:

Vers. 4. “You have made their heart far from discipline.” — If they had known the keeping of discipline, they would by no means have despised the commandments of our Redeemer. The mortality of their flesh itself would have stirred them to love immortal life. For the fact that we are subject in this life to corruption is already part of the scourge of discipline. To be disturbed by heat and cold, hunger and thirst, to be afflicted by illnesses, and finally even to die—what are these things other than the scourges of sin?

This is not said as though almighty and merciful God himself makes the human heart distant from discipline, but because, in his judgment, he permits the one who has fallen voluntarily to remain where he fell. It follows: “Therefore they shall not be exalted.” — Since, abandoned to lowly pleasures, they continually desire earthly goods, they never raise their hearts to heavenly joys. They would be exalted if they lifted their minds toward hope of the heavenly homeland. But those who make no effort to preserve life through discipline always lie low through their desires. It follows:

Vers. 5. “He promises spoil to his companions, and the eyes of his sons shall fail.” — After blessed Job had spoken his judgment concerning the multitude of the wicked—that is, concerning the body of the ancient enemy—he immediately turns his judgment toward their prince himself, the head of all the lost, and returns from the plural number to the singular.

This perverse author of error would promise spoil to his companions, because he sends the souls of the wicked to the malignant spirits, to be seized at their end. “And the eyes of his sons shall fail,” because, by stirring human intentions to hope for earthly things alone, he makes them love what they cannot possess for long.

The companions may perhaps also be understood as the most cruel people, already filled with every kind of wickedness. The sons, however, are those who, still deceived by the promises of the deceiver, are being nourished for the increase of wickedness. But the eyes of his sons shall fail, because the intentions of the wicked fall. It follows:

Vers. 6. “He has made me as a byword of the people, and as an example before them.” — Let blessed Job speak these words from himself; let him speak them from the voices of all the elect. Everyone who is struck by a scourge is made as a byword of the people, because whenever a foolish person desires to curse someone, he takes his curse from the likeness of the one whom he sees struck temporarily. He wishes upon his adversary the punishment that he sees has befallen the righteous, and thus the upright man becomes an example to those who do not judge rightly. It follows:

Vers. 7. “My eye has grown dim with indignation [or: from indignation], and my limbs have been reduced as though to nothing.” — The eye grows dim from indignation when even those who possess the light of truth in the Lord’s body—that is, in the Church—become troubled by wonder at the hidden judgment, seeing themselves despised and rejected for so long, and are unable to penetrate God’s secret: why the wicked are permitted to prevail against the innocence of the good.

By the name of limbs the weakness of the infirm is expressed. When they see the wicked prospering and the righteous being tortured, they sometimes reach the point of regretting that they have even begun to do good. It follows:

Vers. 8. “They were astonished at this, and the innocent was stirred up against the hypocrite.” — Here “innocent” means one who is not yet a perfect righteous person. He is still beginning to do good: although he does not know how to harm others, he is nevertheless entirely unable to perform perfect works himself.

The innocent is stirred up against the hypocrite when even someone who is accustomed to harm no one envies the hypocrite’s glory. But if here “innocent” means anyone perfect in goodness, the innocent is stirred up against the hypocrite when he sees him flourishing and nevertheless despises him together with his flourishing. It follows:

Vers. 9. “And the righteous shall hold to his way, and he who has clean hands shall add strength.” — When he has considered the hypocrite, the righteous holds to his way. Seeing that the hypocrite, through perverse intention, obtains the things of this world, the righteous is bound more firmly to the love of heavenly things, knowing that eternal rewards will not be lacking for good desires, since temporal goods are not denied even to the wicked and double-hearted.

For this reason he who has clean hands will also add strength, because, seeing the wicked attain earthly glory, he advances his good works toward perfection and despises temporal things all the more deeply the more he sees that even the wicked abound in them. It follows:

[Col. 0255B] Vers. 10. “Therefore, all of you, turn and come.” — These words of exhortation are directed especially toward the elect, whom he calls to eternity. They are invited in two ways: both to turn and to come. They are to turn through faith and come through works. Or certainly, they are to turn by abandoning evil and come by doing good, as it is written: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI, 27).

It follows: “And may I find no wise man among you.” — What does it mean that he calls them to wisdom and nevertheless wishes not to find them wise, unless that those who are deceived by confidence in their false wisdom cannot come to true wisdom? Of such people it is written: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isa. V, 21). It follows:

Vers. 11. “My days have passed, my thoughts have been scattered, tormenting my heart.” — The holy Church of the elect sees the spans of her life pass through the times of day and night, because she is accustomed to have night in adversity and day in prosperity. For light rises for her from the tranquility of peace, and night from the pain of persecution.

But when, after the leisure of rest, she returns to the labor of growing persecutions against her, she declares that her days have passed. In those days, however, she is accustomed to be burdened by more serious cares, the more, amid the tranquility of peace itself, she considers that subtler accounts will be demanded of her by the Judge. But when temporal happiness passes from good minds, the concern for earthly administration that seemed to torment them in their thoughts is also withdrawn from them. It follows:

[Col. 0255D] Vers. 12. “They have turned night into day.” — For scattered thoughts turn night into day, because sometimes the righteous prefer to endure greater evils through adversity than to be wearied by the concern of earthly administration through prosperity.

It follows: “And again, after darkness I hope for light.” — Light is hoped for after darkness, either because eternal light is received after the night of the present life, or because adversity and prosperity alternate here in such a way that they never cease to succeed one another in turn.

Thus it happens that even in light there is fear of night, and in night there is hope of light, as it is written: “In the day of good things, do not be forgetful of evils, and in the day of evils, do not be forgetful of good things” (Ecclus. II, 27). It follows:

Vers. 13. “If I wait, hell is my house; in darkness I have made my bed.” — The saints of former times could both endure adversities and yet, once led forth from their bodies, could not be freed from the places of hell, because the one who would descend there without guilt had not yet come, in order to free those who were held there because of guilt.

A man made his bed in darkness when, by consenting to the crafty persuader, he abandoned the light of righteousness. And because even the souls of the righteous were held in those regions of hell without torment, they descended there because of original guilt, while they did not suffer punishment for their own acts. To have made one’s bed in darkness is to have prepared rest for oneself in hell.

For the elect it was a grave weariness, after the dissolution of the flesh, still not to see the appearance of the Creator. Blessed Job rightly calls this weariness “darkness.” It follows:

Vers. 14. “I said to corruption: You are my father; to the worms: My mother and my sister.” — What does he mean by saying to corruption, “You are my father,” except that every human being descends from an origin already corrupted? Hence it is added: “My mother, and my sister, to the worms.” For we come into this world both from corruption itself and with corruption.

As far as the substance of corruptible flesh is concerned, worms are our mother and sister, because we have proceeded from corruption and have come with the corruption that we bear. If this is understood spiritually, nature may rightly be called mother and habit sister, because we are with the latter from the former.

This mother and sister are worms because, through corruptible nature and perverse habit, we are compelled to be wearied in the mind by restless thoughts, as though by worms. For the corrupted nature of the flesh and perverse habit generate countless cares in the heart of our weakness; they are rightly called mother and sister worms. Cares bite the mind when they trouble it. It follows:

Vers. 15. “Where, then, is my hope now?” — What could have been the hope of the righteous except the righteous and justifying God, who would willingly descend to the punishments of the human race in order to free the captives of death by the power of his righteousness?

They did not cease eagerly to await his presence in thought. They knew that he would come at some time, but they sought that he should come sooner. It follows: “And who considers my patience?” — He expressed the desire with which one placed in the flesh hastens to be redeemed and recalled from the lower regions to the heights.

It was indeed the concern of only a few people to reflect on these matters, so that they might know how to think about the labors of the present life and about the love that would follow after death. Before the coming of our Redeemer, the righteous grieved that they had to endure both. Hence it is rightly said: “And who considers my patience?”

There is certainly one who considers patience, but because he does not answer more quickly, God is said, as it were, to be considering it less. The redemption of the human race that came at the end of the world was believed only slowly by those who had gone before from the beginning of the world, because they were separated for a long span of time from the heavenly reward. This is testified by the Truth, who says: “Many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Luke X, 24). It follows:

Vers. 16. “All that is mine shall descend into the deepest hell.” — Since it is certain that the righteous were held among the dead not in places of punishment but in the higher bosom of rest, a great question arises for us: what does blessed Job mean when he says, “All that is mine shall descend into the deepest hell”?

If, then, this dark air is hell in relation to the height of heaven, and the earth lies lower than the height of that same air, it may be understood as both hell and deep. But in relation to the height of the earth itself, those regions of the lower world that are higher than other receptacles are designated by the name “deepest hell.” What air is to heaven, and earth to air, that the higher bosom of the lower world is to the earth.

But it is very remarkable that he adds: “All that is mine shall descend.” Since only his soul was going to descend to the regions of the dead, what does the holy man mean by declaring that all of him descends there, except that he sees himself to be wholly present wherever he understands the weight of his reward to be?

For he does not feel himself to be that which, insensible, he leaves behind on earth until he returns to the incorruption of the resurrection. Or certainly, all that belongs to him descends into hell because the recompense of all his labors was still expected to be received only in the rest of the lower world. As it were, everything he did descends there, because there he finds the rest due to him for all of it.

It follows: “Do you suppose that at least there I shall have rest?” — In these words he both makes known what he desires and yet shows himself uncertain about receiving rest, lest, because so many scourges followed his holy works, hidden judgment by the heavenly Judge should cause lasting torments to follow his temporal scourges as well.
