In this matter we must consider with great fear who among us can already be secure of eternal rest, if even he trembles—he whose praises of virtue the Judge himself proclaims—who says: “If the righteous man will scarcely be saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?” (I Pet. IV, 18).

BOOK FOURTEEN

[Col. 0257]

CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 0257C]

Vers. 1, 2. “Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said: Understand first, and then let us speak” [up to: “How long will you cast out words? Understand”]. — All heretics think that the holy Church is proud in matters unknown to them, and they suspect that she understands certain things not at all. It follows:

Vers. 3. “Why are we counted as beasts and considered impure before you?” — It is characteristic of the human mind to suspect that the same thing is being done to it that it does itself. They think they are despised because they are accustomed to despise the conduct of the good.

And because, in matters that can be grasped by reason, the Church shows the heretics that what they assert is unreasonable, they suspect that they are being judged by her as beasts. It follows:

[Col. 0257D] Vers. 4. “You who destroy your soul in your fury.” — Heretics regard either zeal for uprightness or the spiritual grace of holy preaching not as the weight of virtue but as madness of fury. In this fury, they suppose that the souls of the faithful perish.

It follows: “Will the earth be abandoned for your sake?” — What, then, does it mean to say, “Will the earth be abandoned for your sake?” except what they often say to the faithful: “If what you say is true, the whole earth has been abandoned, since we already possess it by reason of our multitude”?

It follows: “And will the rocks be moved from their place?” — Heretics call “rocks” those whom they consider to surpass others in the human race by the loftiness of their understanding; they boast that these are their teachers.

But when the holy Church strives to gather perverse preachers into the bosom of the true faith, what else does she do than move them from their proper places, so that those who previously stood rigid in their perverse opinions may lie humbly within her, thinking rightly? Heretics wholly resist this happening and, because of her voice, oppose the rocks’ being moved from their proper place. It follows:

Vers. 5, 6. “Will not the light of the impious be extinguished, and will the flame of his fire not shine?” — If he declares this concerning the condition of the present life, he is mistaken, because prosperity is often seen to belong even to the wicked, while the darkness of obscurity and poverty conceals the godly.

But if his speech is directed toward showing what the wicked suffer at their end, it is truly said: “Will not the light of the impious be extinguished?” Every impious person has a flame of his own fire, which he kindles in his heart from the heat of temporal desires. Yet his fiery flame does not shine when, on the day of his departure, all external beauty is taken away and he is burned only by his inward heat.

The flame is thus withdrawn from the fire when external glory is separated from his eternal burning. The righteous also have a flame of their own fire, but theirs indeed shines, because their desires illuminate good works.

It follows: “The light grows dark in his tent.” — If darkness often signifies sadness, we should rightly understand light as joy. The light in his tent therefore grows dark because, in the conscience that he inhabits wickedly, the joy derived from temporal things fails.

It follows: “And the lamp that remains over him shall be extinguished.” — To speak according to common usage, the lamp is light in a vessel of clay, and joy in the flesh. The lamp that is over him shall therefore be extinguished because, when the recompense of his evils follows the wicked man, carnal joy is dispersed in his mind.

For earthly joys possess the mind of the wicked in such a way that they are above it, not within it. It follows:

Vers. 7. “The steps of his strength shall be confined.” — Now he seems to put forth the steps of his strength whenever he exercises the violence of his power. But the steps of his strength shall be confined because punishment later restrains the powers of his wickedness that he now displays in his pleasures.

It follows: “And his own counsel shall cast him down.” — Every wicked person now has the policy of seeking present things, despairing of eternal ones, doing what is unjust, and mocking what is just. But when the Judge of the righteous and the unrighteous comes, each wicked person is cast down by his own counsel, because, through what he chose to seek here, he is plunged by perverse thoughts into the darkness of eternal punishment.

The one whom temporal glory exalts here is pressed there by punishment without end. It follows:

Vers. 8. “For he has sent his foot into the net, and he walks in its meshes.” — Whoever puts his foot into a net cannot withdraw it whenever he wishes. Likewise, whoever throws himself into sins does not rise as soon as he wishes. Whoever walks in the meshes of the net entangles his steps by walking, and when he strives to free himself in order to walk, he is bound so that he cannot walk.

It often happens that someone, persuaded by the delight of this world, reaches the glory of honor through it; then, once he possesses it, he learns by experience how worthless was the thing he desired. Recalled to himself, he seeks how he may flee without guilt from what he sees he has attained. But the very dignity that entangled him holds him fast, and he cannot escape without other sins from the place to which he came without guilt. It follows:

Vers. 9. “His foot shall be held by the snare.” — For the cord is tightened in the snare of sin, and the enemy of the human race, loving the life of each person in guilt, anxiously pants for that person’s death.

It follows: “Thirst shall burn against him.” — Our ancient enemy, when he entangles life in sin, thirsts to drink the sinner’s death.

This can also be understood in another way. When a perverse mind realizes that it has entered into sin, it seeks, by a certain superficial movement of thought, to escape the snares of sin. But, fearing either the terrors or the reproaches of men, it chooses to die eternally rather than endure some temporary adversity. Thus it abandons itself wholly to the vices by which it already feels itself bound.

Therefore, when someone’s life is held in guilt to the end, his foot is held by the snare. In whose mind thirst burns against him, because he is vehemently inflamed to drink down evils in the same direction in which he has been accustomed to act perversely. For the wicked, to thirst means to desire the goods of this world. It follows:

Vers. 10. “His trap is hidden in the earth, and his snare is on the path.” — The trap is hidden in the earth when guilt is concealed beneath earthly things. The enemy lying in wait shows the human mind what it desires in earthly profit, while concealing the snare of sin by which he binds its soul.

A trap is so called from deceiving; and the ancient enemy places a trap on the path when, in the activity of this world that the mind desires, he prepares the snare of sin. It would not easily deceive if it could be seen. A trap is placed in such a way that, while the bait is displayed, the trap itself is not seen by the passerby.

Profit with guilt, and worldly prosperity with iniquity, are like bait in a snare. The enemy therefore places his trap where he sees that the path of the mind lies, because he inserts the danger of deception there where he finds a road open to the mind’s inclination.

And because the perverse person fears even to suffer everything he does, it rightly follows:

Vers. 11. “Terrors shall frighten him from every side.” — Such a person suspects that everyone is toward him what he himself strives to be toward everyone. It follows: “And they shall entangle his feet.” — Perverse desires draw a person toward the worst action, and the worst action confines him in fear.

This fear entangles the feet so that they cannot proceed into an upright action. It often happens that someone fears being good lest he himself suffer at the hands of the wicked what he remembers having done to the good. While he fears suffering what he has done, he is frightened and suspicious on every side, as though he had entangled feet. It follows:

Vers. 12. “Let his strength be weakened by hunger, and let indigence invade his ribs.” — In the manner of sacred Scripture, he seems to wish for what he foresees will happen—not with the mind of one cursing, but of one prophesying.

Every human being consists of soul and flesh and is therefore composed, as it were, of strength and weakness. The strength of a human being is the rational soul, which is able through reason to resist the vices that attack it.

Thus the strength of the wicked is weakened by hunger because his soul is nourished by no refreshment of inward food. Of this hunger it is said through the prophet: “I will send a famine upon the land, not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God” (Amos VIII, 11).

The ribs of each person are the faculties of the soul, which protect hidden thoughts. Indigence therefore invades the ribs when, with all spiritual nourishment withdrawn, the faculties of the mind fail and are unable to govern or protect their thoughts. It follows:

[Col. 0260D] Vers. 13. “May the beauty of his skin be devoured, and firstborn death consume his arms.” — The beauty of the skin is temporal glory, which, when desired outwardly, is held like an appearance in the skin.

By the name of arms, works are appropriately designated, since bodily work is performed with the arms. But what is death except sin, which kills the soul by separating it from inward life? If sin is death, “firstborn death” may fittingly be understood as pride, because it is written: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. X, 15).

Therefore firstborn death devours the beauty of his skin and his arms because pride overthrows the glory and activity of the wicked. It follows:

[Col. 0261A] Vers. 14. “May his confidence be torn away from his tent [printed: allevatur; corrected: avellatur], and may the king of destruction trample upon him.” — Here the name “destruction” designates the enemy of the human race, who brought destruction.

This destruction, therefore, tramples upon the wicked man like a king on the day of his departure, because the one whom it first deceives with flattering persuasions it finally drags to punishment by violent force.

But if by “destruction” we should understand not the devil openly but sin, from which it happens that the reprobate are dragged to destruction, then such destruction tramples upon the mind like a king when it possesses the mind that does not resist.

Temptation to sin cannot be absent from a person placed in this life. But it is one thing to resist sin when it tempts, and another to serve it when it rules. The confidence of such a person is torn from his tent when a perverse man who had prepared many things in this life according to his wishes is suddenly scattered by death. It follows:

Vers. 15. “Let the companions of him who is not dwell in his tent.” — That is, let apostate angels dwell in his mind through the most wicked thoughts. They are the companions of him who now is not, because the highest Being has departed from him, and through this, as his defect increases daily, he tends toward nonbeing, having once fallen from him who truly is.

It follows: “Let sulfur be scattered upon his tent.” — What else is sulfur than the fire of springs? Yet it nourishes fire in such a way that it exhales a most foul odor. What, then, are we to understand in sulfur except the sin of the flesh? By filling the mind with this as with foul odors, it prepares eternal fires.

Sulfur is therefore scattered in the tent of the wicked whenever perverse pleasure of the flesh rules in his mind. It follows:

Vers. 16. “Let his roots dry up below, and let his harvest be destroyed above.” — What are we to understand by the name “roots,” which are placed in secret and bring forth a shoot into the open, except thoughts? Although they are not seen in the heart, they produce visible works.

Thus by the name “harvest” the same outward activity is designated, which is produced from the hidden root. But when the perverse person places his thoughts in weak and transitory things and neglects to seek the joys of everlasting freshness, what else does he do than permit his roots to dry below?

His harvest is destroyed above because all his activity is judged as nothing by the heavenly judgment, even if it appears good before human eyes. It follows:

[Col. 0261D] Vers. 17. “Let his memory perish from the earth, and let his name not be celebrated in the streets.” — We must observe that Bildad the Shuhite speaks of an individual in such a way that his words secretly turn toward the head of all the wicked.

The Greek term for “streets” derives from breadth. The Antichrist strives to establish his memory on earth when he desires, if it were possible, to remain forever in earthly glory. He rejoices in celebrating his name in the streets when he extends the activity of his iniquity far and wide.

But because this iniquity is not permitted to rise for long, it is said: “Let his memory perish from the earth.” It follows:

[Col. 0262A] Vers. 18. “Let him be driven from light into darkness.” — He is driven from light into darkness when he is condemned from the honor of the present life to eternal punishments. Hence it is more clearly added: “And let him be transferred from the world.” He is transferred from the world when, with the heavenly Judge appearing, he is removed from this world in which he perversely glories. It follows:

Vers. 19. “There shall be neither seed nor offspring for him among his people, nor any remnant in his regions.” — For it is written that the Lord Jesus “will kill him with the spirit of his mouth and destroy him by the brightness of his coming” (II Thess. II, 8).

When his iniquity therefore comes to an end together with the condition of the world, his offspring is not left among his people, because his people themselves are driven with him together to punishment. All the wicked who were born through his perverse persuasion into wicked acts will be struck, together with their head, by the brightness of the Lord’s coming and eternal destruction. It follows:

Vers. 20. “The latest shall be astonished at his days, and horror shall seize the first.” — At that time his iniquity will rage against the righteous with such unrestrained force that even the hearts of the elect will be struck by no small fear. Hence it is written: “So that, if it were possible, even the elect would be led into error” (Matt. XXIV, 24).

This is said not because the elect will fall, but because they will tremble amid great terrors. At that time the last and the first elect are said to have a contest of righteousness against him: those who are found elect at the end of the world are to be struck down in the death of the flesh, while those who had gone before from the earliest ages of the world—namely, Enoch and Elijah—are recalled to the midst and will suffer his cruelty in their still mortal flesh.

The latest are astonished at his powers, unleashed in such great might; the first are afraid. It follows:

Vers. 21. “Therefore these are the tents of the wicked, and this is the place of him who does not know God.” — Above he had said: “Let him be driven from light into darkness, and let him be transferred from the world.” When he added the wicked man’s evils, he also added: “These are the tents of the wicked, and this is the place of him who does not know God.”

He indicates that the one who now exalts himself by not knowing God reaches his own tents then, when his iniquity plunges him into punishments. He finds his own place at last in darkness, whereas, while he rejoiced here in the false light of righteousness, he occupied another’s place.

For in everything they do through simulation, the wicked strive to occupy, as though it were another’s place, the name and glory of the righteous. It follows:

CHAPTER XIX

Vers. 1, 2. “Then Job answered and said: How long will you afflict my soul and wear me down with words?” — As we have often already said, the utterances of holy men must sometimes be understood as spoken in their own person, sometimes in the voice of the Head, and sometimes in the figure of the universal Church.

The souls of the righteous are therefore greatly afflicted when those who do not know how to live well hurl severe judgments against the good and claim righteousness for themselves in words while opposing it by their conduct. The good are worn down by the words of the wicked when the wicked swell up against them in speech.

It follows:

**VERSE 3.** “You have reproached me ten times.” — By counting the speeches of Job’s friends, we recognize that they had as yet spoken only five times. But because he had heard five reproofs from them, and had himself replied five times to their reproofs, he declares that he has been reproached ten times: for he suffered severely both because he was reproved without cause and because he spoke words of instruction to those unwilling to listen. But if we refer these words to the type of holy Church, it is clear that keeping the precepts of the Decalogue is a great joy. Yet the wicked reproach her ten times, because in every sin they commit they abandon the precepts of the Decalogue through their perverse conduct. It follows:

“And are you not ashamed to oppress me?” — There are some whom a sudden outbreak of wickedness invites to commit evil, but whom human shame nevertheless restrains; and often, because they are ashamed outwardly, they return within themselves and pass judgment upon themselves inwardly. There are others who, after despising God in their minds, scorn human judgments even more. Hence it is said of certain people who sin with shameless boldness: “They proclaimed their sin like Sodom” (Isaiah 3:9). Such are often the adversaries of holy Church, who are restrained from committing evil neither by fear of the Lord nor by shame before human beings. It follows:

**VERSE 4.** “Indeed, even if I have been ignorant, my ignorance will be with me.” — Heretics have this characteristic: they are puffed up by the arrogance of their empty knowledge, often ridicule the simplicity of those who believe rightly, and consider the life of the humble to be of no value. Holy Church, by contrast, humbly subdues her understanding in everything she truly knows, lest knowledge inflate her, lest inquiry into hidden matters make her presumptuous, or lest she dare investigate things beyond her powers. For she more usefully strives not to know what she is unable to investigate than boldly to define what she does not know. It is written: “As it is not good for one who eats much honey, so one who is a searcher into majesty is overwhelmed by glory” (Proverbs 25:27). The sweetness of honey, if taken in excess, kills the life of the one who eats it by the very thing that delights the mouth. The investigation of majesty is also sweet; but whoever desires to scrutinize it more deeply than human understanding permits is overwhelmed by its very glory, because, like honey taken in excess, it breaks apart the mind of the investigator when it cannot grasp it.

What is for us is said to be with us; conversely, what is against us is said not to be with us. Since, therefore, the heretic’s knowledge inflates his heart, while faithful recognition of his own ignorance humbles him, blessed Job may say in his own voice—and the universal Church may say in confession as well—“My ignorance will be with me.” And because heretics receive the very things they seek to know only for the use of their pride, so that they may appear learned in opposition to the faithful and humble, it is rightly added:

**VERSE 5.** “But you rise up against me.” — As though it were said more plainly: “You who ought, because of my persecution, to have risen up against yourselves.” For the proper order of rising up in goodness is first to rise against ourselves, and afterward against the wicked. Whoever rises against the good is puffed up through pride. We rise against ourselves when, recognizing our own evils, we punish ourselves with the strict vengeance of repentance; when we do not spare ourselves in our sins and are not bent by any flattering thoughts toward ourselves.

If, then, we first pursue our own evils strictly within ourselves, it is also right that we should usefully rise up against the evils of others, and that by rebuking in others what we punish in ourselves, we should overcome them.

It follows: “And you reproach me with my reproaches.” — All the reprobate regard temporal evils as a grave reproach, and believe that each person is despised by God in proportion as they see him afflicted by the scourge of blows. They seek nothing in conduct, nothing in actions; but anyone whom they see struck down in this life they already judge condemned by divine judgment. It follows:

**VERSE 6.** “At least now understand that God has afflicted me with an unequal judgment.” — O how harshly sounds the voice of a righteous man afflicted by blows—yet it was not pride but grief that uttered it. But a man is not righteous if he abandons righteousness in grief. Blessed Job, however, possessed a gentle heart and did not sin in this harsh utterance. For if we say that he sinned in these words, we assert that the devil fulfilled what he had proposed when he said: “Touch his bone and his flesh; if he does not bless you to your face” (Job 2:5).

A difficult question therefore arises. If he did not sin in saying, “At least now understand that God has afflicted me with an unequal judgment,” we appear to agree that God—something which it is impious to say—acted unjustly. Blessed Job had considered his life and weighed the blows he was suffering; he saw that it was not equitable for such blows to be inflicted upon such a man. And when he says that he was afflicted by an unequal judgment, he spoke willingly what the Lord had said secretly about him to his adversary: “You have moved me against him, to afflict him without cause” (Job 2:3).

Thus Job spoke the truth when he weighed his life against the scourge; and God did not afflict Job by an unjust judgment, because through the scourge he increased his merits; and the devil did not fulfill what he had promised, because blessed Job, even amid words that sound harsh, did not depart either from the truth of his judgment or from the mind of the humble.

It follows: “And has girded me with his blows.” — To be struck by blows is one thing; to be girded by them is another. We are struck by blows when, even in our sufferings, we possess consolation from other things. But when such affliction weighs us down that the soul cannot draw breath from the consolation of anything, then we are not merely struck by blows but also girded by them, because we are surrounded on every side by the blows of tribulations. Paul had been girded with blows when he said: “Outwardly, conflicts; inwardly, fears” (2 Corinthians 7:5). It follows:

**VERSE 7.** “Behold, I will cry out while suffering violence, and no one will hear; I will cry aloud, and there is no one to judge.” — Almighty God, knowing what will profit us, pretends not to hear the voice of those who suffer, so that he may increase their benefit and purify their life through punishment, and so that the tranquility of rest, which cannot be found here, may be sought elsewhere. “And there is no one to judge” is said when he pretends not to judge.

**VERSE 8.** “He has fenced in my path, and I cannot pass through; and he has placed darkness upon my road.” — He saw his path fenced in by blows when, desiring to pass over into security, he could not escape the scourges. And because he saw himself being struck, yet found no life in himself deserving of such striking, he found, as it were, the darkness of ignorance in the road of his heart, unable to penetrate why he was being scourged.

This may also appropriately be referred to the weaker members of holy Church. Since sin is often committed through weakness and sometimes through ignorance, it is said from the perspective of the weak members: “He has fenced in my path, and I cannot pass through.” Of those who are blind even to the good work they should choose, it is added: “And he has placed darkness upon my road.” He finds darkness on his road because, in the things he desires to do, he does not know what he ought to choose. Against both of these conditions the Psalmist says: “The Lord is my light and my salvation” (Psalm 26:1).

**VERSE 9.** “He has stripped me of my glory and taken the crown from my head.” — There is no doubt that all these words suit the person of the blessed man placed in affliction. But since the historical sense is evident, they do not require a literal exposition. We must therefore investigate them through mystical meanings: righteousness has been taken away from the weak—righteousness which could not be taken away from them, but which could be removed because it clung outwardly like a garment.

In this regard, we must ask how those who were able to lose the righteousness they appeared to possess can be called members of holy Church. We should know that righteousness is often temporarily lost by her weakened members; afterward, through recognition of their fault, they return to repentance and bind themselves to that same righteousness more firmly than had been expected.

It follows: “And he has taken the crown from my head.” — Just as the head is the first part of the body, so the mind is the principal part of the inner person. The crown is the reward of victory, placed above so that the one who has fought may be rewarded. Since many, crushed by adversities, do not persevere in the contest, holy Church, as it were, loses the crown from her head in them. The crown on the head is the heavenly reward in the mind. There are many who, while afflicted by adversities, neglect to think about heavenly rewards and cannot attain the perfection of victory. In them, therefore, the crown is taken from the head, because the heavenly and spiritual reward is removed from the mind’s contemplation.

Or certainly, we may rightly understand the priests as the head of the faithful, since they are a part of the members of the Lord who receive rewards. Hence the prophet says that “head and tail” will be exterminated (Isaiah 9:14). The crown is therefore taken from the head when even those who appeared to preside in the body of the Church abandon the rewards of heavenly recompense.

**VERSE 10.** “He has destroyed me on every side, and I perish; and like a tree torn up by the roots, he has taken away my hope.” — The Church is destroyed on every side, as it were, and perishes in her weaker members when those who appeared strong themselves fall, when the crown is removed from the head. A tree is driven by the wind so that it falls; and when threats terrify someone into collapsing into injustice, what has he endured but the wind’s assault upon the tree, losing the uprightness of his standing?

**VERSE 11.** “His fury has become angry against me, and he has treated me as his enemy.” — Through the testimony of the preacher we have learned: “God is faithful, and he will not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can bear, but with the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that we may be able to endure” (1 Corinthians 10:13). The Lord also says through the prophet: “With the wound of an enemy I have struck you, with cruel chastisement” (Jeremiah 30:14). Whoever is struck in such a way that his strength is overcome by the blow is struck by the Lord not as a son through discipline but as an enemy through anger.

**VERSE 12.** “His robbers came together and made a way for themselves through me.” — His robbers are evil spirits, who occupy themselves with seeking the deaths of human beings. They make a way for themselves into the hearts of the afflicted when, amid the adversities they suffer outwardly, they do not cease to inject perverse thoughts.

It follows: “And they surrounded my tent in a circle.” — They besiege the tent in a circle when they surround the mind on every side with their temptations. Yet, as we have already said, these words also fit blessed Job according to the historical sense: when he gathered before his eyes the evils he had suffered, he showed that he had been struck not as a son but as an enemy. His robbers also made a way for themselves through him, because the evil spirits received permission to strike him. They besieged his tent in a circle because, after his possessions and children had been taken away, they also covered his entire body with wounds.

But it is very surprising that, when he called them robbers, he added “his.” He thereby showed that these same robbers belonged both to God and to him. For in them there was an unjust will but a just power; hence they are called both his and God’s.

But because, as we have often said, the holy man, placed amid the sufferings of punishment, sometimes uses his own voice, sometimes that of the Church, and sometimes that of our Redeemer, and often narrates his own experience in such a way that through the type he expresses what belongs to holy Church and to our Redeemer, let us set aside for a little while the historical interpretation and show how what follows accords with the voice of our Redeemer.

**VERSE 13.** “He has put my brothers far from me, and my acquaintances have withdrawn from me like strangers.” — We can show this more clearly by bringing forward the testimony of John, who says: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1:11). His brothers were indeed put far away and his acquaintances withdrew because the Hebrews, who held the Law and knew how to prophesy, did not recognize the One who was present. Hence it is rightly said:

**VERSE 14.** “My relatives have forsaken me, and those who knew me have forgotten me.” — The Jews were relatives according to the flesh and acquaintances through instruction in the Law. They were, as it were, forgetful of the One whom they had prophesied: they had proclaimed in the words of the Law that he would become incarnate, yet denied him in his incarnation through words of faithlessness.

**VERSE 15.** “The inhabitants of my house and my maidservants have treated me as a stranger.” — The priests had been inhabitants of God’s house; their lineage, already assigned by office to a condition of servitude, was held in God’s service. The maidservants may appropriately be understood as the souls of the Levites, serving more familiarly in the tabernacle’s secret places, as in the interior of a chamber. Yet they were unwilling to recognize and venerate the incarnate Lord whom they had long before foretold through the words of the Law.

It follows: “And I was like a stranger in their eyes.” — When our Redeemer was not recognized by the Synagogue, he was like a stranger in his own house. The prophet openly testifies to this, saying: “Why will you be like a sojourner in the land, and like a traveler turning aside to stay?” (Jeremiah 14:8).

**VERSE 16.** “I called my servant, and he did not answer.” — For what was the Jewish people except a servant, who obeyed the Lord not with the love of a son but with servile fear? In contrast, Paul says to us: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:15).

The Lord therefore called this servant because, by bestowing gifts—as though sending out calls—he sought to lead him to himself. But he did not answer because he scorned to return worthy works for his gifts. The Lord calls us when he anticipates us with gifts.

It follows: “I pleaded with him with my mouth.” — As though it were said more plainly: “I, the One who before my incarnation had commanded him through the mouths of the prophets to observe so many precepts, came to him in the incarnation and pleaded with him with my own mouth.” Hence it is said through the bride: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song of Songs 1:1). It is rightly said “I pleaded,” because, revealed in the flesh, he humbly spoke the commandments of life and, as it were, begged the proud servant to live.

**VERSE 17.** “My wife abhorred my breath.” — Who is meant by the Lord’s wife except the Synagogue, subject to him in the covenant of the Law according to carnal understanding? Breath proceeds from the flesh; but the faithless people understood the Lord’s flesh carnally, because they believed him to be merely a human being. His wife therefore abhorred his breath because the Synagogue was afraid to believe that the man whom it saw was God.

It follows: “And I pleaded with the sons of my womb.” — In the womb offspring are conceived and brought forth into this life. What, then, should we understand as the Lord’s womb except his counsel, in which we were conceived before the ages through predestination, so that, created through the ages, we might be brought forth? God, therefore, who remains before the ages, pleaded with the sons of his womb because, having created by his power those whom he had established through his dignity, he came in the incarnation and humbly entreated them.

**VERSE 18.** “Even fools despised me.” — After the wise had fallen away from faith in the truth, “even fools” is rightly added, because, while the Pharisees and teachers of the Law despised the Lord, the multitude of the people followed their unbelief and, seeing in him a human being, despised the proclamations concerning the Redeemer of the world.

It follows: “And when I had withdrawn from them, they slandered me.” — The Lord was, as it were, approaching the hearts of the peoples when he displayed miracles to them, and was, as it were, withdrawing when he showed no signs. But they slandered the withdrawing Lord when they refused to believe in him as he ceased from miracles.

**VERSE 19.** “My counselors once abhorred me, and the one whom I loved most opposed me.” — The scribes and teachers of the Law, who were accustomed to instruct the peoples unto life, were surely counselors of the coming Redeemer. Yet when they saw the Lord incarnate, they divided many from faith in him by their counsels, although they had previously appeared to teach many to believe in his incarnation through the words of the prophets. The very order that had once been especially loved because it served in the labor of preaching turned away from faith in the truth through the persuasion of faithlessness.

**VERSE 20.** “My bone has cleaved to my skin, with my flesh consumed.” — In bone strength is signified; in flesh, the weakness of the body. Since Christ and the Church are one person, who is signified by the bone except the Lord himself? Who by the flesh except the disciples, who at the time of his Passion understood things weakly? And by the skin, which remains outwardly upon the flesh in the body, who else are signified except those holy women who ministered to the Lord in outward services, preparing what was needed for his body?

When his disciples, although not yet strong, preached the faith of the truth to the peoples, the flesh clung to its bone; and when the holy women prepared the things that were necessary, the skin remained outwardly upon the body. Thus, as though the flesh had been consumed, the Lord’s bone cleaved to his skin, because, when his disciples fled at the time of his Passion, he found the women beside him.

It follows: “And only my lips remain around my teeth.” — What do we have around our teeth except lips, even when we suffer no blows? But what is signified by the lips except speech, and by the teeth except the holy apostles? At the time of his Passion, these teeth lost, through fear of death, the bite of correction; they lost the confidence of strength and the effectiveness of every kind of action. Thus, after his death and resurrection, two of them were walking and speaking on the road, saying: “We had hoped that he was the one who was going to redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21). It is therefore rightly said: “And only my lips remain around my teeth.” They were still speaking about him, but they no longer believed in him.

Having completed what he spoke in the voice of the Head, he returns to the blessed Job’s own words, saying:

**VERSE 21.** “Have pity on me, have pity on me, at least you, my friends, because the hand of the Lord has touched me.” — It is characteristic of the minds of the godly that, when they suffer injustice from their adversaries, they are moved not so much to anger as to prayer. They choose to ask rather than to become angry, so that the perversity of their opponents may be moderated peacefully.

It should also be noted that the blessed man’s public words correspond to what had been done secretly before God. He had been struck by Satan, yet he did not attribute his striking to Satan; rather, he called it the touch of the Lord’s hand, just as Satan himself had said: “Stretch out your hand and touch his bone and his flesh” (Job 2:5).

**VERSE 22.** “Why do you persecute me like God, and are you satisfied with my flesh?” — It is not contrary to the language of piety that he declares himself persecuted by God. There is a good persecutor, as the Lord says of himself through the prophetic mouth: “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I persecuted” (Psalm 101:5).

When any holy person is permitted to be scourged, he knows that he suffers persecution against his committed faults through an inward dispensation. But the cruel minds of persecutors, when they seek the power to strike against the lives of the good, are inflamed not by a desire for purification but by the forces of envy. They do what Almighty God permits to be done; but although one action is carried out with God in the same matter, the will in that matter is not the same. The Almighty, in love, provides purification; the perversity of the unjust, in rage, exercises wickedness.

This may also be understood in another way: Almighty God strikes the faults of others all the more justly because he has no faults in himself. When human beings strike others through discipline, they ought to strike another’s weakness in such a way that they also know how to turn their eyes back toward their own. As though it were said openly: “You afflict me because of my weaknesses as though, in the manner of God, you yourselves possessed no weakness.”

Hence it is added: “And are you satisfied with my flesh?” Those whose minds hunger for the punishments of their neighbors plainly seek to be satisfied with the flesh of others. We should also know that those who feed upon slander against another’s life are undoubtedly satisfied with the flesh of others. Hence Solomon says: “Do not be among the banquets of drunkards, nor eat with those who bring flesh for food” (Proverbs 23:20).

**VERSES 23–24.** “Who will grant me that what I have suffered may be written in a book with an iron stylus, or on a sheet of lead, or certainly engraved upon flint?” Because by the strong judgment of the Fathers [lacuna] that grave people of the Jews recognized it, it was written with an iron stylus and on a sheet of lead; but because the hard hearts of the Gentiles also came to know these things, what else do we see them as except engraved upon flint?

It should be noted that what is written on lead is erased more quickly because of the metal’s very softness. On flint, letters can indeed be impressed more slowly, but they are more difficult to erase. Not without reason, therefore, is Judea represented by a sheet of lead: it received God’s commandments without labor and lost them with speed. The Gentiles are rightly represented by flint: they could scarcely receive the words of sacred speech, which had to be preserved, yet once received they preserve them firmly.

What else is signified by the iron stylus except the strong judgment of God? Hence the prophet says: “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, with a diamond point” (Jeremiah 17:1).

We may also rightly understand by the sheet of lead those whom the weight of greed burdens, to whom the rebuking Prophet says: “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Psalm 4:3). Lead, whose nature is heavy in weight, specifically signifies the sin of greed, which makes the mind it has infected so heavy that it cannot rise at all to desire lofty things. Hence it is written in Zechariah: “Lift your eyes and see what this is that is going out.” And I said, “What is it?” And he said, “This is the ephah going out.” And he said, “This is their eye in all the earth”; and behold, a talent of lead was being carried (Zechariah 5:5, 7).

These words also suit blessed Job in relation to holy Church, which, preserving the two Testaments of sacred speech, asks to write according to its own words. Because it speaks with a strong judgment sometimes to those made heavy by the weight of greed and sometimes to hard hearts, it writes with an iron stylus on a sheet of lead—or certainly upon flint.

**VERSE 25.** “For I know that my Redeemer lives.” — By not saying “Creator” but “Redeemer,” he openly declares that this is the One who appeared incarnate among us in order to redeem us from captivity and, through his Passion, free us from everlasting death. Notice also the firmness of his faith in the power of Christ’s divinity, of whom Paul says: “For although he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives by the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4).

He says: “For I know that my Redeemer lives.” As though he were saying openly: “Let every unbeliever know him as scourged, mocked, struck with blows, crowned with a crown of thorns, smeared with spittle, crucified, and dead; but I firmly believe that he lives after death.”

But, blessed Job, since through his resurrection you also trust in the resurrection of your own flesh, declare this openly, we ask. It follows:

“And on the last day I shall rise from the earth.” — For he will one day accomplish in us the resurrection that he displayed in himself. He promised us the resurrection that he displayed in himself, because the members follow the glory of their Head.

But behold, I hear of the resurrection; I nevertheless ask about the nature of its effect. I believe that I shall rise, but I wish to hear what I shall be like. It follows:

**VERSE 26.** “And again I shall be surrounded with my skin.” — Since skin is plainly mentioned, every doubt about the reality of the resurrection is removed. For our body will not, as Eutychius, bishop of Constantinople, wrote, be impalpable in the glory of that resurrection, subtler than winds and air. In the glory of that resurrection our body will indeed be subtle through the effect of spiritual power, but palpable through the truth of its nature.

Hence our Redeemer, when his disciples doubted his resurrection, showed them his hands and side and offered his bones to be touched, saying: “Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me having” (Luke 24:39).

It follows: “And in my flesh I shall see God.” — Behold, he openly confesses the resurrection, the skin, and the flesh. What, then, remains by which our mind could doubt? If this holy man believed that the effect of the Lord’s resurrection would be the restoration of flesh to its complete condition, what guilt will attach to our doubt if the true resurrection of the flesh is not believed even after the example of the Redeemer?

**VERSE 27.** “Whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another.” — If, as certain followers of error suppose, the body will not be palpable after the resurrection, but the subtlety of an invisible body will be called flesh, although it is not the substance of flesh, then certainly one person dies and another rises. But blessed Job destroys this opinion with a truthful voice when he says: “Whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another.”

Following the faith of blessed Job, and truly believing that our Redeemer’s body was palpable after the resurrection, we confess that our flesh after the resurrection will be different and the same: the same in nature, different in glory; the same in reality, different in power.

It follows: “This hope of mine is laid up in my bosom.” — We believe that we possess nothing more certain than what we hold in our bosom. He therefore kept his hope deposited in his bosom who confidently anticipated the hope of the resurrection.

**VERSE 28.** “Why, then, do you now say, ‘Let us persecute him and find the root of a word against him’?” — In the first statement he reproves the deed of the wicked; in the next he makes known the punishment arising from divine judgment. He says: “Why, then, do you now say, ‘Let us persecute him and find the root of a word against him’?”

Whenever the perverse hear something well spoken with evil intent and seek to find in the righteous person’s speech the basis of an accusation, what else are they doing than seeking a root of speech against him? From it they may take the beginning of an utterance and extend the branches of perverse talk into an accusation.

**VERSE 29.** “Flee, then, from the face of the sword, because the sword is the avenger of iniquities; and know that there is a judgment.” — Everyone who acts perversely, by despising this very fact, does not know that there is a judgment of God. For if he knew it by fearing it, he would not do the things in him that must be punished. There are many who know in words that there will be a final judgment, but by acting perversely they show that they do not know it. Whoever does not fear it as he ought has not yet understood with what terrible tumult it will come. If he knew how to weigh the burden of the trembling examination, he would certainly anticipate the day of wrath by trembling.

To flee from the face of the sword also means to appease the sentence of strict punishment before it appears.

**BOOK FIFTEEN**

[Col. 0271]

Because the words of Zophar the Naamathite testify that the friends of blessed Job could not have been perverse—for, having heard from his mouth the terror of the coming judgment, he immediately adds:

**CHAPTER XX**

**VERSES 1–2.** “Therefore my varied thoughts follow one another, and my mind is carried in different directions.” — As though he were saying openly: “Because I consider the terror of the final judgment, I am thrown into fear by the tumult of my thoughts.” The mind tears itself apart all the more in thought the more it considers how terrible is the thing that threatens.

**VERSE 3.** “I will hear the teaching with which you reproach me, and the spirit of my understanding will answer me.” — As though he were saying openly: “I hear your words, but by the spirit of my understanding I discern whether they have been spoken rightly.”

**VERSES 4–5.** “This I know from the beginning, from the time when the human being was placed upon the earth: that the praise of the wicked is brief, and the joy of the hypocrite lasts for the space of a moment.” — It is now clear that, puffed up by the spirit of his own understanding, he turns the judgments he pronounces against the wicked into rebukes against blessed Job.

He had seen Job first doing what was right and afterward enduring punishments, and he judged that everything he had seen in him was hypocrisy, because he did not believe that a just servant could be afflicted by a just God.

But let us consider how true his words would be if he were speaking against the wicked. Since the wicked love the present life, they are undoubtedly lifted up by it and seek to receive praise; they are exalted by the favor of tongues and desire not to be good but to be called good. They think this praise will be long while they are attaining it, but understand that it was brief when they lose it.

At the end it is shown to them how worthless was the thing they loved. Often the hypocrite, while pretending to be holy and not fearing to display himself as wicked, is honored by everyone, and the glory of holiness is bestowed upon him by those who see outward things but cannot look into the interior. But what will their joy be when compared with eternity, when, at the arrival of the moment of death, it is consumed as though it had never existed at all? The delight of that joy passes away, but the punishment remains; and when the thing is lost, the cause endures.

**VERSES 6–7.** “If his pride ascends to heaven and his head touches the clouds, he will perish at the end like dung.” — The hypocrite’s pride is said to ascend to heaven when his arrogance appears to lead a heavenly life. His head also touches the clouds, as it were, when the principal part of him—namely, his understanding—is believed to equal the merits of those who came before among the saints. But he will perish at the end like dung, because, when he is led to torments at his death, full of the dung of vices, he is trampled underfoot by evil spirits.

The joys of the present life, which the unjust regard as great goods, the righteous count as dung. Hence it is written: “The lazy man is stoned with the dung of oxen” (Sirach 22:2).

It follows: “And those who saw him will say, ‘Where is he?’” — Often the life of hypocrites is recognized as blameworthy even by human beings at the end, so that clearer signs may now reveal what they were. Those, then, who saw this man exalted will say of him when he has perished: “Where is he?” For he is seen neither here, where he had been exalted, nor in the rest of eternity, where he had been thought to be.

Hence it is added:

**VERSE 8.** “Like a flying dream he will not be found; he will pass away like a vision of the night.” — What is the life of the hypocrite except a kind of phantom vision, which displays in an image what it does not possess in reality? It is therefore rightly compared to a dream, because all praise and glory are lost as soon as they seem to be possessed.

Often, in a nocturnal vision, poor people marvel that they have become rich; but suddenly waking, they discover how false was the thing in which they rejoiced. They regret having awakened because, once awake, they possess real poverty.

So the minds of hypocrites, while what they do is one thing and what they show to human beings is another, receive praise from their very display of holiness. But amid these things the hour of their hidden calling steals upon them; when they close the eyes of the flesh, they open the eyes of the mind; and as soon as they receive eternal punishments, they see how, in dreams, they had been rich in the estimation of their virtues.

**VERSE 9.** “The eye that saw him will not see him, nor will his place look upon him any longer.” — What is the hypocrite’s place except the heart of flatterers? He rests there wherever he finds applause. Therefore the eye that saw him will not see him, because, laid beneath death, he is hidden from his foolish admirers, who were accustomed to gaze upon him with wonder. Nor will his place look upon him any longer, because the tongue of flatterers does not follow him with its applause to judgment.

**VERSE 10.** “His children will be crushed by poverty.” — It is written: “Wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul” (Wisdom 1:4). And the Psalmist says: “The rich have become poor and hungry” (Psalm 34:11). The children of this hypocrite will therefore be crushed by poverty, because those who are born into hypocrisy through imitation of him, since they do not hold the solidity of truth, fail through poverty of heart.

It follows: “And his hands will repay him his pain.” — What is signified by hands except works? His hands will therefore repay him his pain, because he will receive just condemnation from his wicked actions.

It follows:

### Verse 11

“His bones will be filled with the sins of his youth, and with him they will sleep in the dust.” [Col. 0274A]

What, then, is the youth of this hypocrite except the beginning of depravity? For in youth lust already begins to grow hot, and the hypocrite has his youth when he begins to desire and embrace the lust for glory. While the flattering encouragements of his admirers multiply this lust in him, they make it stronger and, as it were, turn it into bones. For what began badly he strengthens daily through habit, and these bones will sleep with him in the dust, because sinful habits remain in him until they lead him to the dust of death.

Alternatively: when the hypocrite, light-minded and changeable, does many childish things, he becomes soft in vice even in the things he has done bravely. These, plainly, are his bones; they will sleep with him in the dust, because, just as all the pretense he practices is dust, so whatever strength he possesses is emptied of all solidity, so that through the virtues of his arrogance he also loses whatever virtue may have been in him. It follows:

### Verse 12

“For when evil is sweet in his mouth, he hides it beneath his tongue.” [Col. 0274B]

Evil is sweet in the hypocrite’s mouth because iniquity is pleasant to him in his mind. The mouth of the heart is thought, concerning which it is written: “Deceitful lips have spoken evil with a double heart” (Ps. 11:3). But this evil, which is sweet in the hypocrite’s mouth, is hidden beneath his tongue, because the harshness of the malice concealed in his mind is covered beneath the cloak of pleasant speech. Evil would be in the tongue and not beneath the tongue if the hypocrite, while speaking, openly revealed the malice of his perversity. It follows:

[Col. 0274C] ### Verse 13

“He will spare it and will not abandon it, and he will conceal it in his throat.”

The evil he loves “spares” him because he does not pursue it within himself through repentance. Hence it is added: “He will not abandon it.” For if he wished to abandon it, he would certainly not spare it, since he would pursue it. But he conceals it in his throat because he preserves it in his thoughts, so that he may never bring it forth in speech. It follows:

### Verse 14

“His bread will be turned in his belly into the gall of asps within.”

What bread is in the belly—that is, what satiety is in the belly—is the satiety of temporal pleasure in the mind. Let the hypocrite now be satisfied with the praise he has received and delight in honors; his bread in his belly will be turned within him into the gall of asps, because the satiety of passing pleasure is turned into bitterness at the end of retribution. And the gall of asps—that is, the persuasion of evil spirits—is recognized as what was here believed to be praise of glory.

Or certainly, since “bread” can suitably be understood as the meaning of Sacred Scripture, which refreshes the mind and supplies it with strength for good works: often the hypocrite also strives to be instructed in the mysteries of sacred speech, yet not so that he may live by them, but so that he may appear to other people to be learned. While he boasts of his knowledge of sacred law, however, he turns the drink of life into a cup of poison for himself; and he dies condemned from the very source from which he seemed to be learning for life.

Nor is it inappropriate to understand this in another way: sometimes, while the hypocrite pursues the word of doctrine for display, he is blinded by divine judgment and perversely understands the very word he wrongly seeks. When he slips into the error of heresy, it happens to him that, just as he dies from the gall of asps, so the wretched man dies from bread, and finds death in his teaching, because he did not seek life at all in the words of life. [Col. 0275A] It follows:

### Verse 15

“He will vomit up the riches he swallowed, and God will draw them out of his belly.” [Col. 0275B]

The hypocrite wants to know the divine utterances but not to practice them; he wants to speak learnedly but not to live. Since he did not say what he knows, he loses even what he knows. The riches of sacred law that he swallowed by reading, he vomits up by forgetting; and God draws them out of his belly because, by a just judgment, he tears from his memory what he refused to preserve, so that he may not even retain on his tongue the commandments of God that he does not keep in his life.

Hence the prophet says: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteous acts and take up my covenant in your mouth?” (Ps. 49:16). It follows:

### Verse 16

“He will suck the head of asps, and the tongue of the viper will kill him.” [Col. 0275C]

The asp is a small snake; the viper has a longer body. It is called *viper* because it gives birth by force (*vi pariat*). What, then, are signified by the small asps except the hidden suggestions of unclean spirits, which first creep into human hearts through a small persuasion? And what is signified by the tongue of the viper except the violent temptation of the devil? First it creeps in gently; afterward it drags violently.

Thus he sucks the head of asps because the beginning of the hidden suggestion is first born small in the heart; but the tongue of the viper kills him because the mind, once captured, is afterward slain by the poison of violent temptation.

Perhaps, however, we can understand these same things through the contrary interpretation. Since the asp kills swiftly with its poison, while the viper kills more slowly, the asp signifies a violent and sudden temptation, and the viper a gentle and prolonged one. Hence death is said to be in the uprising of the head for the asp, but in the tongue for the viper: sudden temptation often kills an unsuspecting mind as soon as it arises, whereas prolonged temptation, because it suggests evil by persuading over a longer time, kills as though from the tongue of a viper. It follows:

### Verse 17

“May he not see the streams of the river, the torrents of honey and butter.” [Col. 0275D]

In the Gospel the Lord says: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38).

The streams of the river, therefore, are the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Charity is a stream of the river; faith is a stream of the river; hope is a stream of the river. But since no hypocrite loves either God or his neighbor, when he seeks the passing glory of the world he does not see the streams of the river, because he is not thoroughly watered by the irrigation of charity.

It should be noted that he says not “rivers” but “streams.” The streams of the river can be understood as spiritual gifts that flow so subtly from heavenly things in the mind of one who loves that they cannot be contained by the mouth of the flesh.

The river, however, is a torrent: it is the very inundation of the Holy Spirit, gathered into the soul of one who contemplates through an overflowing infusion, when the mind is filled with more than it is capable of understanding.

Honey falls from above, whereas butter is gathered from the milk of animals. Honey, then, is from the air, and butter from flesh. The Only-Begotten of the supreme Father, although he is God above all, became human among all things. When he filled us both with the sweetness of his divinity and with the mystery of his incarnation, he satisfied us with honey and butter alike.

Therefore, because the Spirit of Christ gladdens the mind he has filled both with the sweetness of Christ’s divinity and with faith in his incarnation, these streams of the river are remembered as being streams of honey and butter together. It follows:

### Verse 18

“He will repay everything he did, yet he will not be consumed.” [Col. 0276A]

In torment he pays for the desires he unlawfully preserved here; and, handed over to avenging flames, he is always dying because he is always kept in death. He is not consumed in death, for if the life of the one who is dying were consumed, his punishment would end together with his life. But so that he may be tortured without end, he is compelled to live without end in punishment: his life was dead here in guilt, and there his death lives in punishment.

It follows: “According to the multitude of his inventions, so also will he endure.”

For whoever devised many things for guilt is tortured in punishment by new inventions. What he could not suspect here, he experiences there when handed over to punishments. Just as those practiced in good works sometimes strive to do more than the Lord has deigned to command them, so often the wicked are exercised in evil actions, discovering more to do in perverse conduct than they could have learned from the customary wickedness of the reprobate. Therefore they are struck with the torment of a greater retribution. It follows:

### Verses 19–20

“Because, crushing the poor, he stripped them; he seized a house and did not build it, and his belly was not satisfied.” [Col. 0276B]

He crushes and strips the poor man’s house because he is not ashamed, after crushing the man through power, also to despoil him through greed. “He seized it and did not build it.” It is as though it were said openly: the one who ought to have built this house instead seizes it. Thus he seized it and did not build it, because he not only contributed nothing of his own but also took what belonged to another.

The belly of the wicked is greed, because everything swallowed by perverse desire is gathered into it. It is clear that greed is not extinguished by the things desired but increased by them. For, like fire, when it receives the wood it consumes, it grows.

It follows: “And when he has obtained what he desired, he will not be able to possess it.”

It is a sign of greater anger when even what is wrongly desired is granted, and sudden vengeance follows because he has obtained what he coveted while God was angry. Hence the Psalmist says, when the people are said to have wrongly desired meat: “While the meat was still in their mouth, the anger of God rose against them and killed many of them” (Ps. 77:38). It follows:

### Verse 21

“Nothing remained of his food.” [Col. 0276D]

His food is everything he coveted through perverse desire. But nothing remains of the hypocrite’s food, because when he himself is led to eternal punishments, he is separated from all the goods he possessed here.

Hence it is added: “Therefore nothing will remain of his goods.” [Col. 0277A]

If anything remained of his goods, he would take with him what he had possessed. But because, coveting everything, he refused to fear the Judge, he is taken from this life and goes naked to the Judge. It follows:

### Verse 22

“When he is satisfied, he will be confined.”

First he pants through greed to gather what he desires; and when, as though in a certain belly of greed, he has amassed many things, he is satisfied and confined, because while he is anxious about how to guard what he has acquired, his very satiety constricts him.

It follows: “He will burn, and every pain will rush upon him.” [Col. 0277B]

At first he experienced pain in the very weariness of his desire: how he might seize what he coveted, how he might take some things by flattery and others by threats. But after he has reached his desire through the things he acquired, another pain tires him: he must guard with anxious fear what he remembers acquiring through great toil.

After this he is led to Gehenna and handed over to eternal torments. Every pain, therefore, will rush upon him: here, first, the punishment of desire; afterward, the care of guarding what he acquired; and there, finally, the punishment of vengeance will burn him. It follows:

### Verse 23

“Would that his belly might be filled, and that He might send upon him the anger of His wrath, and rain His warfare upon him.” [Col. 0277C]

The Lord rains his warfare upon this hypocrite when he strikes his works with the swords of his judgments. For God’s raining warfare is to drive the life of the wicked from above toward destruction by strict sentences. It follows:

### Verse 24

“He will flee iron weapons and rush upon a bronze bow.”

It should be understood that greed sometimes creeps in through arrogance and sometimes through fear. There are people who, while desiring to appear more powerful, are inflamed with the pursuit of other people’s possessions. There are also people who, while fearing that they lack the necessities of support, relax their minds into greed and pursue what belongs to others, suspecting that their own possessions cannot suffice for them.

Every necessity is not improperly called iron, because it tortures the life of the poor with the wound of sorrow, just as it is written concerning the man who was sold by his brothers and led an afflicted life: “Iron passed through his soul” (Ps. 104:18).

What, then, are iron weapons except the necessities of the present life, which press harshly and pursue the poor man’s life? Rust consumes iron, whereas bronze is ordinarily more difficult to consume. Iron, therefore, signifies present necessity, which is passing; bronze signifies the eternal sentence. [Col. 0277D]

And because the heavenly judgment is not considered by the mind of the wicked, it is rightly compared to a bow: it strikes as though from ambush, while the one struck does not expect it.

He will therefore flee iron weapons and rush upon a bronze bow, because, while fearing present necessities and seizing many things through greed, he places himself before the strict blows of the final judgment. It follows:

### Verse 25

“Drawn out and coming forth from its sheath, and flashing in its bitterness.” [Col. 0278A]

This wicked man lies in wait to plunder his neighbors. But while he devises evil in thought, the sword is, as it were, still in its sheath. When he wickedly carries out the evil he has conceived, it comes forth from its sheath. For through the iniquity of evil action what was hidden in the concealment of his thought is opened; in his work he is shown to be what he had remained in thought.

It should be noted that he says: “Drawn out and coming forth from its sheath.” “Drawn out,” namely, by the seducer; “coming forth,” through his own will.

Lightning, when it suddenly comes from above, flashes with terror before the eyes: it displays brightness and strikes what is set before it. So the wicked man, when he has assumed the glory of the present life, is made conspicuous by power in this world, and from that very source many are struck.

For the wicked man to flash means to shine in the honor of this life. But because the splendor of his glory is handed over to the eternal punishments of Gehenna, it is rightly said here that he is “flashing in his bitterness.” For although he now rejoices as he strikes with terror and brightness, from that very source he thereafter endures eternal punishments. [Col. 0278B]

It follows: “Terrible ones will go and come upon him.”

What are “terrible ones” called here except evil spirits—those who are to be feared and fled by good minds? Since each evil spirit is believed to serve a particular vice, when this perverse man appears for a time to abandon certain vices but begins to practice others, terrible ones go and come upon him. For although the wicked abandon some evils, others take possession of their minds. It follows:

### Verses 26–27

“All darknesses are hidden in his hiding places.” [Col. 0278C]

Although the hypocrite displays good actions on the surface, certain darknesses of evil works nevertheless appear in him. Yet he reveals less in his actions than lies hidden in his thought. For the one who does not complete everything at once in action silently holds in his mind everything that can cause harm.

It follows: “Fire that is not kindled will devour him.”

In a remarkable manner the fire of Gehenna has been expressed in very few words. Bodily fire requires bodily fuel in order to remain fire. When it must be preserved, it is undoubtedly nourished by accumulated wood; it cannot exist unless it is kindled, nor endure unless it is replenished.

The fire of Gehenna, by contrast, although bodily and although it burns the reprobate bodily within itself, is neither kindled by human effort nor nourished by wood. Once created, it remains unquenchable; it does not need kindling and does not lack heat. For the justice of the Omnipotent, foreknowing future things, created the fire of Gehenna at the very beginning of the world, so that it would begin once to exist in the punishment of the reprobate but would never bring its burning to an end, even without wood. [Col. 0278D]

It follows: “He is afflicted, abandoned in his tent.”

The tent of the wicked is the flesh, because he inhabits it joyfully and, if possible, desires never to leave it. When he receives this flesh again in the resurrection, he will burn with it after being handed over to the fires of Gehenna. Then he will want to be taken out of it; then he will seek, if he can, to escape its torments. Then he will begin to want to avoid what he loved. But because he placed that flesh before God, when God judges him he is made to suffer more severely in the fire through it.

Here, therefore, he does not wish to leave it, yet he is taken away from it; there, he desires to leave it, yet he is kept in it for the sake of punishment. Thus, for the increase of his torments, here he is unwillingly drawn out of the body, and there he is unwillingly held in the body. It follows:

### Verse 28

“The heavens will reveal his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him.” [Col. 0279A]

What do we understand by the heavens except the righteous, and by the earth except sinners? Hence in the Lord’s Prayer we ask: “Your will be done in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 6:10).

When this wicked man is brought to that terrible judgment, the heavens reveal his iniquity, and the earth rises against him, so that the life both of the righteous and of sinners may accuse him in that fearful examination—him who here spared neither the good nor the wicked. This is especially grievous if anything harms the righteous more than the sinners.

Hence the prophet says: “His blood is in his midst. He poured it out upon the most polished rock; he did not pour it out upon the earth, so that it might be covered with dust” (Ezek. 24:7). [Col. 0279B]

The earth, however, may be understood not as sinners and reprobates but as those who, occupied with earthly activities, reach eternal life through the help of almsgiving and tears. Concerning them the Psalmist says, when the Lord’s coming to judgment was announced: “He summoned heaven above and earth, to judge his people” (Ps. 49:4).

The heavens of this hypocrite therefore reveal his iniquity, and the earth will rise against him when both those who come as judges with God and those who are delivered through judgment stand as witnesses to his perversity. It follows:

### Verse 29

“The offspring of his house will be exposed; it will be removed on the day of God’s wrath.” [Col. 0279C]

The offspring of his house is exposed when every evil that was growing in his conscience is revealed. For now the offspring of the hypocrite’s house remains hidden: although his action appears in a good guise, his intention lies concealed.

The offspring of his house is therefore exposed in this hypocrite because the perverse thought in his mind is disclosed; and it will be removed on the day of God’s wrath because, once the Judge’s anger has been revealed, he is handed over to avenging flames and separated from the Judge’s sight.

It follows: “This is the portion of the impious man from God, and the inheritance of his words from the Lord.”

If he had wished to act well while placed in this life, he would have had a portion with the Lord, a share in the heavenly kingdom. But because he chose to submit to perverse desires, he finds his portion from the Lord in torments, because he did not seek to share in the grace of that same Lord. [Col. 0279D]

The one who is plunged into punishment for great evils might perhaps be thought not to be judged at all for the words he had spoken wrongly. But when the strict justice of almighty God exacts punishment from the reprobate for their perverse actions, he repays them with evils even to the point of retribution for their words.

Holy men, however, desire not to receive a portion from the Lord but to have the Lord himself as their portion. Hence the prophet prays, saying: “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. 118:57).

But the wicked man, who did not seek to have the Lord himself as his portion, finds his portion outside the Lord—in fire.

Sophar introduced these words in such a way that, through what he had said against the hypocrite, he might strike at the life of blessed Job. He supposed that the one struck by the Lord had not performed all the good he had done with a sincere mind. Seeing him struck, he believed that he had displeased God.

But blessed Job, after the manner of the holy and universal Church—which patiently endures the darts of perverse words and, when it hears the speech of the proud, does not abandon the path of its humility—added the following with great humility of heart:

## Chapter XXI

### Verses 1–3

“Listen, I beg you, to my words, and repent.”

When he said “listen” and added “I beg you,” he indicates with what great humility he speaks: while opposing the proud, he begs them to lead their understanding toward the teaching of salvation.

It follows: “Bear with me, so that I too may speak; and afterward, if it seems appropriate, laugh at my words.” [Col. 0280A]

When good people speak, they attend to two things in their speech: that they may benefit either themselves and their hearers, or themselves alone if they cannot benefit their hearers. When the good things they say are well received, they benefit both themselves and their hearers. When they are mocked by their hearers, they have nevertheless benefited themselves, since they have made those hearers free from guilt.

It should also be noted that, when he was about to add “repent,” he first said “listen.” And when he was about to add “afterward, if it seems appropriate, laugh at my words,” he first said “bear with me.” Listening belongs to one who is willing; bearing belongs to one who is unwilling. Therefore, if his friends desire to be taught, let them listen; but if they are ready to mock, let them bear what is said. It follows:

### Verse 4

“Is my dispute with a man, so that I should not rightly be sorrowful?” [Col. 0280B]

Anyone who pleases God and displeases human beings has no cause for sorrow. But the one who pleases human beings and displeases God—or believes that he displeases both God and human beings—if sorrow does not affect him, is estranged from the virtue of wisdom.

Blessed Job, however, believed amid the scourges that he had displeased God, and therefore summoned his spirit to sorrow, because he feared that he had displeased one whom he ought not to have despised. It follows:

### Verse 5

“Look at me and be astonished”—that is, consider what I have done and marvel.

It follows: “And place your finger upon your mouth.” [Col. 0280C]

As though he were saying openly: knowing the good things I have done and considering the evils I suffer, restrain yourselves also from the guilt of words, and fear your own losses in my persecutions.

Or certainly, because we distinguish things with our fingers, “finger” may suitably signify discernment. Hence the Psalmist says: “Blessed is the Lord my God, who trains my hands for battle and my fingers for war” (Ps. 143:1).

The finger is placed upon the mouth when the tongue is restrained through discernment, lest, by what it says, it fall into the guilt of folly. It follows:

### Verse 6

“And when I remember, I am afraid, and trembling shakes my flesh.” [Col. 0280D]

The conclusion of his speech shows that blessed Job had not forgotten his deeds. Thus he now says to his friends: “And when I remember, I am afraid.” It is plainly said ironically, as though he were saying openly: If I remember that I possess anything of the hypocrite, I immediately tremble in the tears of repentance.

He says that his flesh is shaken with trembling if he remembers it—that is, the weakness of his work, wearied by fear of punishment. It follows:

### Verse 7

“Why, then, do the wicked live, are lifted up, and strengthened by riches?” [Col. 0281A]

If divine patience did not tolerate them, they would certainly not continue long in a life of sins. They are lifted up by riches when they begin to become powerful. They are strengthened when they are permitted to remain for a long time in this life. Those whom possessions lift up are strengthened in the pride of their power by the length of their days.

Or certainly, they are said to be lifted up and strengthened because they are lifted up by honors and strengthened by possessions. It follows:

### Verse 8

“Their offspring remains before them.”

In the increase of great happiness, heirs are granted to them with a large inheritance. And lest even the passage of time remove from their eyes those in whom their spirit rejoices, it follows: “A crowd of relatives and descendants is in their sight.” [Col. 0281B]

Behold: life is present, honors and riches are present, sons are present, and grandchildren are present. It follows:

### Verse 9

“Their houses are secure and peaceful, and the rod of God is not upon them.”

They are secure and peaceful because they live while sinning, perform deeds worthy of mourning, and do not abandon their joys; nor does the rod of heavenly discipline strike them. It follows:

### Verse 10

“Their ox conceives and does not miscarry; their cow gives birth and is not deprived of her offspring.” [Col. 0281C]

It is common usage to call the male a “bull” and the female a “cow,” but the language of Scripture uses a common-gender term. Hence it now says: “Their ox conceives and does not miscarry,” and so forth.

The first happiness of owners of herds is that the flock, without sterility, conceives; the second is that what has been conceived reaches birth; the third is that what has been born is brought to maturity through nourishment.

To demonstrate that all these blessings are present together among the wicked, blessed Job asserts that their herds conceived and did not miscarry, gave birth, and were not deprived of their own offspring.

### Verse 11

“Their little ones go forth like flocks, and their children exult in play.”

And lest we think the very play of infants in the houses of the wicked to be too insignificant, he adds:

### Verse 12

“They hold the tambourine and the lyre, and rejoice at the sound of the organ.” [Col. 0281D]

As though he were saying openly: while their masters swell with honors and possessions, their dependents rejoice in playful activities. It follows:

### Verse 13

“They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment they descend to the underworld.”

Blessed man, you had described their joys as lasting a long time; how can you now assert that they descend to the underworld in a moment? It is because every length of time in the present life is recognized as a moment when it ends with death.

We place and lift the stylus at a point. Thus he touched life, as it were, at a point, because he received it and lost it.

This “moment” can also be understood to mean that those who have long been tolerated in iniquity are often snatched away by sudden death, so that they are not even allowed to mourn before death for the sins they have committed. [Col. 0282A] It follows:

### Verse 14

“They said to God: ‘Depart from us.’”
