Even fools scarcely presume to say these words aloud, but all the perverse say to God—not in words but in conduct—“Depart from us.” They say this because they refuse to provide him access to themselves and attack him through perverse actions, even if they appear to praise him in words.

They also say: “We do not want the knowledge of your ways”—by the very fact that they disdain to grasp his knowledge.

The way of God is peace; the way of God is humility; the way of God is patience. But because the wicked despise all these things, they say to God: “We do not want the knowledge of your ways.”

While they are proud in the present life, while they are inflated by honors, and while they desire honors even when they do not possess them, they despise the ways of God in their thoughts. It follows:

### Verse 15

“Who is the Omnipotent, that we should serve him?” [Col. 0282B]

The human mind, poured outward in an evil way and scattered among bodily things, is so dispersed that it neither returns inward to itself nor is capable of considering the invisible one. Hence carnal men, despising spiritual commands and not seeing God bodily, eventually reach the point of suspecting that he does not exist at all.

Therefore it is written: “The fool said in his heart: There is no God” (Ps. 13:1).

It follows: “And what does it profit us if we pray to him?”

When God is not sought in prayer, the mind quickly grows weary in prayer. For when someone asks for things that God perhaps refuses to grant according to his hidden judgment, the one who does not wish to give what is loved himself also becomes wearisome.

The Lord wishes himself to be loved more than the things he created, and eternal things to be requested rather than earthly things, as it is written: “Seek the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6:33). It follows:

### Verse 16

“Yet, because their goods are not in their hand, let the counsel of the wicked be far from me.” [Col. 0282C]

One possesses goods in his hand when, by despising temporal things, he holds them beneath the authority of his mind. Whoever does not love them in the least subjects them to himself rather than subjecting himself to them.

And what is the counsel of the wicked except to seek earthly glory, neglect eternal salvation, desire temporal things at the cost of interior loss, and exchange passing pains for eternal groans?

The holy man, therefore, observing these thoughts of the wicked, rejects them and says: “Let the counsel of the wicked be far from me.” It follows:

### Verse 17

“How often is their lamp extinguished?” [Col. 0282D]

Often the wicked regard the life of their children as their light. But when a greatly loved child is taken away, the lamp of the wicked, which seemed to shine, is extinguished.

Often the wicked consider the glory of present honor to be their lamp. But when he is cast down after his dignity has been removed, the lamp that shone for him according to his desire is extinguished.

It follows: “And inundation will come upon them, and he will divide the pains of his wrath.”

Inundation comes upon the wicked when they suffer waves of pain from some adversity. It is well said: “He will divide the pains of his wrath.” For the one who reserves eternal pains for the wicked in retribution and sometimes pierces his mind even with temporal pain divides the pains of his wrath over the wicked, because he strikes both here and there.

Present punishment, which does not change the unjust person’s mind from its perverse desires, does not free him from eternal punishments. Hence the Psalmist says: “He will rain snares, fire and sulfur upon sinners, and the spirit of storms is the portion of their cup” (Ps. 10:6).

By saying “snares, fire, sulfur, and the spirit of storms,” he introduced many pains. But because the sinner who is not corrected is called from these pains to eternal punishments, he said that these pains are no longer the whole cup but a part of the cup, because their suffering begins here through pains but is completed in perpetual vengeance.

Concerning their end he adds:

### Verse 18

“They will be like chaff before the face of the wind, and like ashes that the whirlwind scatters.” [Col. 0283A]

When the wicked man is seen in power and becomes greatly unrestrained in oppression and violence, he is regarded as exceedingly heavy by the thoughts of the weak and as though rooted in this world.

But when the sentence of the strict Judge arrives, all the wicked will be like chaff before the wind. They will be suddenly lifted up, so to speak, by the breath of wrath and carried away to the fire. Once, in their oppressive judgments, the tears of the needy lying beneath their mass of heavy weight could not move them; but before the hand of the judgment that carries them away, they are light—though through their injustice they had been heavy to their neighbors.

It follows: “And like ashes that the whirlwind scatters.”

Before the eyes of almighty God the life of the wicked is ashes, because, even if it appears green for a moment, it is already seen as consumed by his judgment, since it has been assigned to eternal destruction. The whirlwind scatters these ashes because “our God will come openly, and he will not be silent” (Ps. 49:5), and so forth. It follows:

### Verse 19

“God has stored up the pain of the father for his children, and when he repays it, then he will know.” [Col. 0283B]

Again it is written: “The soul that sins shall itself be punished” (Ezek. 18:4).

We draw original sin from our parents, and unless we are released through the grace of baptism, we also bear the sins of our parents, because we are still, in a certain sense, one with them. He therefore repays the sins of fathers in their children when, because of the parent’s guilt, the soul of the offspring is punished for original sin.

And again he does not repay the sins of parents in their children because through baptism we are freed from original guilt and no longer bear the sins of our parents but those which we ourselves commit.

This can nevertheless also be understood in another way: whoever imitates the iniquity of a wicked parent is also bound by that parent’s offense. Whoever does not imitate the parent’s iniquity is not burdened by the parent’s offense. [Col. 0283C]

It follows: “And when he repays it, then he will know.”

The wicked man does not know the evils he has done until he has begun to be punished for those same evils. Hence the prophet says: “And only affliction will give understanding to what is heard” (Isa. 28:19).

Then he understands what he heard, when he grieves that he is already being afflicted for his contempt. It follows:

### Verse 20

“His eyes will see his slaughter, and he will drink from the fury of the Omnipotent.” [Col. 0284A]

If, while placed in this life, he had wished to see his guilt, he would not afterward have drunk from the fury of the Omnipotent. But because here he turned his eyes away from consideration of his crime, there he cannot evade the sentence of condemnation. It follows:

### Verse 21

“For what does he care about his house after him? And if the number of his months is cut in half?” [Col. 0284B]

We must not understand this to mean that after this wicked man has been condemned to eternal punishments he will think nothing of his house—that is, of the relatives he has left behind. For Truth itself says that the rich man, who had been buried in hell, even while placed in punishment cared about the five brothers he had left behind (Luke 16:28).

Every sinner will be prudent in punishment who was foolish in guilt. Here he desires, as his supreme good, to have a house or family as the offspring of his lineage, to be filled with wealth, and to live for a long time in the corruption of the flesh.

But if something should perhaps come to satisfy his desire, although he cannot obtain it without offending the Creator, his mind is briefly disturbed. He thinks that if he does what incurs the offense of his Creator, he will be struck in his house, in his children, and in his life.

But immediately provoked by his pride, he hardens himself. However much he may feel a blow in this life, he does not care, provided that he fulfills what he has conceived and does not cease to complete his pleasures for as long as he lives.

Thus the sinner rises against God precisely where almighty God breaks his rising. The blow inflicted does not humble the mind that obstinacy against God has hardened in its deliberation. It follows:

### Verse 22

“Will anyone teach God knowledge, who judges those on high?” [Col. 0284C]

When we are uncertain about what is being done concerning us, we ought to look upon other things that are certain for us and quiet the complaint of thought that has arisen from our uncertainty.

Behold: the judgments of almighty God concerning us are exceedingly hidden, yet they are not unjust. Scourges recall the elect to life, while scourges do not restrain the reprobate from evil actions. Let us therefore turn the eye of the mind toward higher things.

In them we see that we have no just cause for complaint against God concerning ourselves. For almighty God, discerning the merits of the angels, established some to remain without falling in eternal light, while others, who of their own accord fell from the state of their high rank, he cast down into the punishment of eternal damnation. [Col. 0284D]

He therefore does nothing unjustly with us, since he has justly judged a nature more subtle than ours. It follows:

### Verses 23, 24, 25

“This man dies robust and healthy, rich and prosperous. His inward parts are full of fat, and his bones are moistened with marrow. But another dies in bitterness of soul, without any possessions.”

Since these things are so, who can investigate within the secret counsel of the Almighty why he permits them to be so? Yet the life of the elect and of the reprobate is indeed different, while the corruption of the flesh in death is not different. Hence it follows:

### Verse 26

“And yet together they will sleep in the dust, and worms will cover them.”

What wonder, then, if they run for a moment in different ways amid the prosperity or adversity of the present age, when through the corruption of the flesh they return alike to the earth? That life alone, therefore, is to be contemplated in which, together with the resurrection of the flesh, one reaches a different end of recompense. It follows:

### Verses 27, 28

“Certainly I know your thoughts and your unjust opinions against me. For you say: ‘Where is the house of the prince? And where are the tents of the wicked?’”

They had believed him wicked because they saw him temporarily overthrown from prosperous circumstances. But the holy man judges them with a discernment proportionate to the depth of his consideration, since amid the losses he had suffered he stood with unbroken uprightness. For what harm had the loss of external things done him, when he had not lost the one whom he loved inwardly?

### Allegorically

“His inward parts are full of fat.”

Just as fat arises from abundant food, so pride arises from an abundance of possessions; it makes the rich man’s mind heavy when the spirit of the proud is lifted up. The pride of the heart is, as it were, a kind of fatness and thickness. Hence, because many commit sins from abundance, it is said through the Prophet: “Their iniquity has come forth as from fat” (Psalm 72:7).

The lovers of this age have bones when they possess the strength of dignities in this world. But if earthly and domestic riches are lacking to their external dignity, then, according to their own judgment, they indeed have bones, but they do not have marrow in their bones. Since, therefore, this lover of the world is supported by external power and is also fattened by the abundance of an earthly household within, it is said: “And his bones are moistened with marrow.”

Or certainly, the bones of this rich man are his wicked and hardened habits. The marrow in the bones is the evil desire itself for living, which is not satisfied even by fulfilling its wickedness. These marrows, as it were, moisten the bones when those evil desires preserve their perverse habits in the delight of pleasures.

There are also some who do not possess riches in this world but desire to possess them; they long to be exalted, although they cannot obtain in this world what they desire. Though they are supported by no possessions or honors, nevertheless, through evil desires, conscience declares them guilty in the sight of the inward Judge. Such a person is often afflicted precisely because he cannot become rich and proud.

“To sleep in the dust” is to close the eyes of the mind amid earthly desires. Hence it is said to every sinner who sleeps in his guilt: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Ephesians 5:14).

The worms that arise from the flesh cover them together, because carnal cares weigh upon the mind of both rich and poor. Although the poor man and the reprobate rich man are not supported by equal prosperity in earthly affairs, they are nevertheless troubled by equal anxiety: what the one already possesses with fear, the other desires with anguish, and because he cannot possess it, he grieves.

But since it is written, “Who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him?” (1 Corinthians 2:11), why is it now said, “Certainly I know your thoughts”? The spirit of a human being is unknown to another when it is not revealed by words or possessions. But since it is written, “You will know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7:16), whatever lies hidden is disclosed through what is done outwardly.

Accordingly, blessed Job, when he said that he knew the thoughts of his interlocutors, added, “and your unjust opinions against me,” so that he might show by an evident matter that he had discovered what lay hidden in them. It follows:

### Verses 29, 30

“Ask any one of the travelers, and you will learn that he understands these same things: that the wicked man is kept for the day of destruction and is led to the day of wrath.”

Often divine patience endures for a long time those whom it has already condemned to punishments foreknown by it; it permits those whom it still sees committing worse deeds to flourish. Because it sees toward what pit of damnation they are tending, it considers of no account that these perverse people multiply what must be left behind here.

A traveler is one who regards the present life as a road, not a homeland. He disdains to fix his heart upon the passing world; he desires not to remain amid passing things but to reach eternal realities. Hence Moses says: “Passing by, I will see this vision” (Exodus 3:2). Hence Jeremiah says: “All you who pass along the way, attend and see,” and so forth (Lamentations 1:12).

Since, therefore, “the wicked man is kept for the day of destruction and is led to the day of wrath,” only one who is a traveler understands this; for the one who fixes his heart on present things does not discern what punishments follow the wicked.

It follows:

### Verse 31

“Who will rebuke his way before him, and who will repay him for what he has done?”

Often the wicked man experiences, even while placed in this life, the indignation of his Creator, which he will suffer eternally, when he loses the prosperity he loves and encounters the adversity he fears. And although the tongue of teachers can rebuke him for his wickedness even amid prosperity, we know nevertheless that when a person’s deeds bring him down, the rebuke of the righteous grows strong.

But why are these things said, when even without the righteous speaking it is known that the way of the wicked is rebuked here as often as his prosperity is disturbed by the intrusion of adversity?

Blessed Job, however, while speaking about the entire body of the wicked, suddenly turns his words toward the head of all the wicked. For he saw that, at the end of the world, Satan would enter a human being whom Holy Scripture calls the Antichrist. He is lifted up with such arrogance, rules with such power, and exalts himself through such great signs and wonders in a display of holiness that his deeds cannot be rebuked by human beings, since signs of displayed holiness are joined to the power of terror. Thus he says:

“Who will rebuke his way before him?”

That is, what human being would dare rebuke him, whose appearance he fears to endure? Yet all the elect rebuke his way—not only Elijah and Enoch, who are brought forward to reproach him, but also all the elect—when they despise him and resist his wickedness by the strength of their minds.

But because they do this by divine grace and not by their own strength, it is rightly said here: “Who will rebuke his way before him?” For who but God can do so—the God by whose help the elect are strengthened so that they may resist?

Many now correct the ways of the Antichrist when they judge them, but they do this as though he were absent, since they rebuke one whom they do not yet behold personally. But when he comes in that condemned man, whoever resists his presence will rebuke his way before him, because he sees and despises his powers.

Or certainly, “to rebuke his way” means to disturb the prosperity of his course by the intervention of eternal punishment. Since the Lord alone will accomplish this by his own power, of whom it is written, “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the manifestation of his coming” (2 Thessalonians 2:8), it is rightly said: “Who will rebuke his way before him?”

Hence it follows: “And who will repay him for what he has done?” Who indeed but the Lord, who alone will repay that lost man for what he has done, when by his coming he crushes his exceedingly strong power through eternal damnation? It follows:

### Verse 32

“He himself will be led to the tombs, and he will keep watch in the heap of the dead.”

Since tombs cover the dead, what else is signified by tombs than the hearts of the reprobate, in which souls extinguished to the life of blessedness lie hidden as in graves? This wicked one, therefore, is led to the tombs because he will be received into the hearts of the perverse, just as they alone receive him in whom souls dead to God are found.

Concerning him, while his punishments were being described, the Prophet rightly says: “Around him are his tombs, all the slain and those who have fallen by the sword” (Ezekiel 32:22). They are there beside him in hell.

Therefore, for Satan “to keep watch in the heap of the dead” is to exercise the cunning of his wickedness in the hearts of the reprobate. It follows:

### Verse 33

“He was sweet to the pebbles of Cocytus.”

In Greek, *Cocytus* means “lamentation”; this is generally understood as the lamentation of women or of any weak persons. The wise men of this age, excluded from the light of truth, tried to grasp, as it were, certain shadows through their investigation of truth. Hence they thought that the river Cocytus flowed in the underworld, signifying that those who perform works worthy of suffering descend into hell for lamentation.

For it is written: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Psalm 31:25). Those who refuse to be strengthened in the Lord turn toward lamentation through weakness of soul.

We customarily call pebbles the little stones of rivers, which flowing water carries along. What, then, are signified by pebbles except the reprobate, who, devoted to their pleasures, are continually dragged downward? Those who do not firmly resist the pleasures of this age become the pebbles of Cocytus, because by their daily falls they move toward lamentation, so that afterward they may mourn eternally—those who now relax themselves pleasurably in their desires.

And because the ancient enemy enters that reprobate man as his vessel, bestows gifts upon the perverse, raises them to honors in this world, and displays wonders before their eyes, while unstable minds marvel at and follow him in his wonders, it is rightly said of him: “He was sweet to the pebbles of Cocytus.”

When the elect despise him and trample him underfoot in their minds, those who follow him love him. They are dragged, as it were, from the water of pleasure toward perpetual lamentation; through earthly desire they slide downward in daily falls like pebbles.

It follows:

“And he will draw every human being after him, and innumerable ones before him.”

Here “human being” means one who thinks in a human manner. But since “all” is more than “innumerable,” we must ask why he is said to draw innumerable ones before him and all after him. The reason is that, when the ancient enemy enters that reprobate man, he seizes under the yoke of his dominion all whom he finds to be carnal.

Even now, before he appears, he draws innumerable people, though not all who are carnal, because many are recalled daily from carnal works to life, and others return to the state of righteousness through brief or lengthy repentance. Even now he seizes innumerable people, although he does not display to human beings the astonishing signs of his falsehood.

But when he has performed wondrous signs before the eyes of carnal people, then he draws after him not innumerable people but all of them. Delighted by present goods, they submit to his power without hesitation.

Blessed Job, who spoke so wonderfully against the prince of the wicked, who is permitted to be exalted in this life but will be destroyed at the Lord’s coming, clearly demonstrates by this that he did not receive the Lord’s scourges because of an offense. For if some wicked person is permitted to prosper in this life, it is necessary that God’s elect should be held beneath the heat of the scourge. For this reason he rebukes his friends, saying:

### Verse 34

“How, then, do you comfort me in vain, when your answer has been shown to oppose the truth?”

The friends of blessed Job could not comfort him, because in their words they opposed the truth. And when they called him a hypocrite or a wicked man, by the guilt they themselves committed through lying they undoubtedly increased the punishment of the righteous man afflicted by wounds.

## Book Sixteen

### Chapter 22

Those who fail against the words of truth through lack of argument often repeat even familiar things, lest they appear defeated by their silence. Thus Eliphaz, pressed by the words of blessed Job, says things that no one is unaware of. He says:

### Verses 1, 2

“Can a human being be compared with God, even when he has perfect knowledge?”

In comparison with God, our knowledge is ignorance. We gain wisdom through participation in God, not by comparison with him. It follows:

### Verse 3

“What profit is it to God if you are righteous, or what do you contribute to him if your life is blameless?”

In everything good that we do, we help ourselves, not the Lord. Hence the Psalmist says: “I said to the Lord: You are my God, for you have no need of my goods” (Psalm 16:2).

It follows:

### Verses 4, 5

“Will he rebuke you because he fears you, and will he come with you to judgment?”

Who, even if foolish, would think that the Lord rebukes out of fear or brings his judgment against us out of dread? But because they do not know how to measure their words, they undoubtedly slip into idle speech; and if they do not immediately recognize their error in these things, they at once rush into harmful and insulting words.

Thus Eliphaz, who had introduced hateful accusations, immediately burst into insulting words, saying: “Is it not because of your very great wickedness and your countless iniquities?” It follows:

### Verse 6

“For you took away the pledge of your brothers without cause.”

In Holy Scripture, the word “pledge” sometimes signifies the gift of the Holy Spirit, as in Paul: “He gave us the pledge of the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 5:5). At other times it signifies confession of sins, as it is written in the Law: “If your brother owes you a debt, and you take a pledge from him, return the pledge to him before sunset” (Deuteronomy 24:12–13).

Because, therefore, Holy Church commands those returning from the heretics to the truth of faith first to confess the guilt of their error, it persuades them; and in the guise of the heretics, Eliphaz is made to say: “You took away the pledge of your brothers without cause”—that is, from those who come to you from us, you unnecessarily demanded a confession of error.

But if, as we have said, we understand “pledge” as the gifts of the Holy Spirit, the heretics say that Holy Church has taken away the pledge of their brothers, because they suppose that those who come to her lose their spiritual gifts.

Hence it follows: “And you stripped the naked of their clothing.”

Those whom the heretics draw through perverse preaching they regard as possessing the precepts of their teaching as though they were garments. They think that these people remain clothed so long as they observe what the heretics have preached to them. When some of them return to Holy Church, the heretics immediately suppose that they have lost the garments of their teaching.

But since a naked person cannot be stripped, we must ask how they are said to have first been naked and afterward stripped. We should understand that everyone who enjoys purity of heart is naked precisely because he has no covering of duplicity. There are some among the heretics who possess purity of heart but nevertheless accept the perverse doctrines of their teaching. These are naked because of their own purity and are clothed, as it were, by the heretics’ preaching. It follows:

### Verse 7

“You did not give water to the weary, and you withheld bread from the hungry.”

Because the heretics do not possess the solidity of truth, they sometimes strive to appear more talkative and boast, as though through knowledge of doctrine, against the faith of Catholics. They seek to draw to themselves through perverse words all whom they see, and they think they are acting energetically because by this means they enlist others for destruction.

We call weary those who are exhausted by labor under the burdensome weight of this age. Hence Truth himself says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11:28).

The heretics, therefore, who do not cease preaching their doctrines ridicule Holy Church as though she were ignorant, saying: “You did not give water to the weary, and you withheld bread from the hungry.”

They think they give water to the weary when they offer the cup of their error to some who labor beneath an earthly burden. They suppose they have not withheld bread from the hungry because, even when questioned about invisible and incomprehensible things, they respond with proud audacity; and they consider themselves learned above all precisely when they presume most disastrously to speak about things unknown.

But when Holy Church sees someone hungry for what it would not benefit him to receive, she either modestly restrains what is already known to her or humbly acknowledges what still appears unknown. She recalls them to an ordered sense of humility when, through her preacher, she says: “Do not think more highly than it is necessary to think, but think with sobriety” (Romans 12:3). And again: “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Romans 11:20). It follows:

### Verse 8

“By the strength of your arm you possessed the land, and as the most powerful you held it.”

It is as though he openly said: “You occupied the whole earth through your preaching; it was the power of strength, not the reason of truth, that did this.” Because they see Christian rulers holding to his preaching, they suspect that what peoples believe about him is not the virtue of uprightness but the result of secular power. It follows:

### Verse 9

“You sent widows away empty, and you crushed the arms of orphans.”

The peoples subject to the preaching of the heretics receive, through carnal understanding, the perverse seeds of their errors and join them in their own damnation.

But when Holy Church receives the preachers of those errors—either after they have been defeated by reason or when, hardened by their devotion to perversity, she restrains them under the bond of her discipline—the deprived heretics see that the peoples remain with them without preachers. What else do they lament concerning Holy Church except that widows have been left empty?

And because, once the heretical teachers have been removed, they suppose that their disciples have been weakened in their works, they complain that the arms of the orphans have been crushed by the Church.

Or certainly, because Holy Church, when she receives some who come from the heretics, plainly contradicts their former error, the heretics detest the fact that she recalls them from the carnal intention of their superstition. When they see these people living differently from what they taught, they claim that the Church has crushed their arms with respect to the works they previously upheld. It follows:

### Verse 10

“Therefore snares surround you, and sudden fear troubles you.”

Sudden fear troubles the one who neglects to consider what threatens him from the strictness of the coming Judge. Because the heretics believe that the faithful people are oppressed by the guilt of unbelief, they accuse them of being surrounded by snares; and because they suppose that such a person does not foresee the future in his affliction, they think him troubled by sudden fear. It follows:

### Verse 11

“And you thought that you would not see darkness, and that you would not be overwhelmed by the rush of overflowing waters?”

It is as though he openly said: “You had set before yourself, in hope, the security of peace, and therefore you rejoiced in your presumption as though in light; nor did you ever think that you could be overwhelmed by tribulations.” It follows:

### Verses 12, 13, 14

“Do you not think that God is higher than heaven, that he is exalted above the summit of the stars? And you say: ‘What does God know? And he judges as though through darkness. The clouds are his hiding place; he does not consider our affairs, and he walks around the hinges of heaven.’”

Many are so dull that they know how to fear only what they see bodily. Hence they do not fear God, whom they cannot see. But because the heretics consider themselves wise, they utter words of mockery against Catholics. They suspect that Catholics do not fear one whom they cannot see bodily, so that, through a kind of dullness of sense, they imagine that their Creator—because he is higher than heaven and exalted above the summits of the stars—cannot see from afar.

And because aerial regions lie between us and the heavenly seat, they imagine that he judges through darkness while hidden in a cloud, and that, intent upon higher things, he considers lower things less carefully; and while he encompasses the hinges of heaven by walking around them, they think he cannot see inward things.

But who, even if foolish, could suspect such things of God? Although he is always omnipotent, he attends to everything in such a way that he is present to each thing; and he is present to each thing in such a way that he is never absent from all things at once. For even if he abandons certain sinners, he is nevertheless present to those same people through judgment, although he appears absent from them in assistance. It follows:

### Verse 15

“Do you wish to keep to the path of the ages, which wicked men have trodden?”

Just as the path of our Redeemer is humility, so the path of the ages is pride. Wicked men tread the path of the ages because they walk in exaltation through the desires of this life. It follows:

### Verse 16

“They were taken away before their time, and a river overturned their foundation.”

Since the time of our life is certainly fixed by divine foreknowledge, it must be asked why he now says that the wicked are removed from the present age before their proper time.

Although Almighty God sometimes changes his sentence, no one is ever removed from this life at a time other than that which, by divine power, was foreknown before the ages. We should understand that Almighty God, creating and ordering us, arranges things according to the merits of each person: he determines that an evil person should live briefly, lest he harm many who are doing good, or that a good person should remain longer in this life, so that he may assist many through good works. Yet Almighty God foreknows the time of each person’s death—the time at which his life ends. No one can die at any other time than the time at which he dies.

Since this is so, what does it mean to say that the wicked are taken away before their time, except that all who love the present life promise themselves longer stretches of that life? But when death comes and removes them from the present life, it cuts short the span of their life which, in their thoughts, they had been accustomed to extend as though it would last longer.

The wicked, because they neglect in their hearts to pass over to eternal things and do not perceive that all present things are fleeting, fix their minds on love of the present life. They build foundations for themselves in it as though for a long dwelling, because they are made firm by their desires in earthly things.

And because, through the daily passage of time, the mortality of the present life runs its course, and the destruction of the reprobate destroys them by removing them, it is rightly said of the wicked: “And a river overturned their foundations”—that is, the very course of mutability overturns within them the structure of their perverse construction. It follows:

### Verse 17

“Those who said to God: ‘Depart from us.’”

Who could doubt that blessed Job also said these things? We avoid repeating what we have explained in his words, out of consideration for the reader’s weariness.

It follows: “And they considered the Almighty as though he could do nothing.”

Here, therefore, the wording changes, but not the meaning. For what was said through blessed Job—“What is the Almighty, that we should serve him?” (Job 21:15)—is said here through Eliphaz: “And they considered him as though he could do nothing.” It follows:

### Verse 18

“Although he had filled their houses with good things.”

The Lord fills the houses of the wicked with good things because he does not deny his goods even to the ungrateful, so that they may either be ashamed of the Creator’s kindness and return to goodness, or, if they entirely refuse to return, be punished more severely for that very reason.

It follows: “Let their opinion be far from me.”

This too was said through blessed Job, for he says: “Let their counsel be far from me.” Yet “opinion” can mean one thing and “counsel” another. An opinion is expressed in the mouth, whereas counsel lies in thought. It is clear that the former wishes to be unlike the wicked in their words, while the latter wishes to be unlike them even in thought. It follows:

### Verse 19

“The righteous will see and rejoice, and the innocent will mock them.”

When the righteous see the wicked erring here, they cannot rejoice in the error of those who are perishing. If they rejoice in their errors, they are not righteous. Again, if they rejoice through insult because they are not what they see others to be, they are altogether proud.

Hence the Pharisee lost his justification: rejoicing in the merits of the tax collector, he set himself above him, saying: “I give you thanks because I am not like the rest of humanity: robbers, unjust, adulterers, or even this tax collector” (Luke 18:11).

When, then, will the righteous see the destruction of the wicked and rejoice? Only when they have clung to the strict Judge with perfect security and exultation, when in that final examination they see the damnation of the wicked and have nothing more to fear for themselves.

Now, therefore, they look upon the reprobate and groan; then they will see them and mock them, because they will despise with exultation those whom now they see committing iniquity neither without groaning nor dying for iniquity without fear. It follows:

### Verse 20

“Has not their exaltation been cut down, and will fire devour their remnant?”

Here the wicked are exalted because they rise up in wicked actions: they do perverse things and yet are not struck for their perverse deeds. But their exaltation is cut down when they are dragged either from the present life to destruction or from the sight of the eternal Judge to the eternal fire of Gehenna.

And although here they leave behind their dead flesh, they will receive that same flesh in the resurrection, so that they may burn with the flesh in which they sinned. For just as their guilt was in mind and body, so their punishment will be in soul and body alike.

It follows:

### Verses 21, 22

“Submit, therefore, to him and have peace, and through this you will receive the best fruits. Receive the law from his mouth, and place his words in your heart.”

It is the fault of pride to teach one who is better. How often the heretics commit this fault, presuming to teach Catholics concerning the things they perversely believe. They think that they submit to God if they can induce others to consent to their perversities; and they promise peace to those who submit because they then cease quarreling against those who agree with them.

They promise the best fruits to those who consent to them because they think that only those perform good works whom they rejoice to draw to their doctrines.

This agrees with what follows: “Receive the law from his mouth,” because they suppose that what they believe proceeds from the mouth of God. “And place his words in your heart.” It is as though he were asserting: “Until now you have held them in your mouth, not in your heart.” Because he rejects their perverse doctrines, they accuse him of having the words of God not in his understanding but merely in outward display. It follows:

### Verse 23

“If you return to the Almighty, you will be built up, and you will remove iniquity far from your tent.”

The heretics think that the faithful people have departed from God when they see them resisting their preaching, as though they openly said: “Because you have withdrawn from God by resisting our doctrines, you have therefore been destroyed from the building of righteousness.”

The tent sometimes signifies the tent of the body, and sometimes the dwelling place of the heart. For just as we dwell in the body through the soul, so through thought we dwell in the mind.

Iniquity in the tent of the mind is a perverse intention in the pursuit of thought; iniquity in the tent of the body is a carnal action accomplished through deeds.

It is as though Eliphaz openly said: “Whoever returns to God after errors is cleansed both in thought and in deed.” It follows:

### Verse 24

“He will give you flint instead of earth, and streams of gold instead of flint.”

What is signified by earth except weakness in action? What by the hardness of flint except strength? What by streams of gold except the teaching of inward brightness?

The Almighty Lord gives flint instead of earth to those who turn to him, because instead of weak action he grants the strength of robust works. He also gives streams of gold instead of flint, because in place of robust works he multiplies the teaching of clear preaching. It follows:

### Verse 25

“And the Almighty will be against your enemies, and silver will be heaped up for you.”

What other enemies do we suffer more than the evil spirits who besiege our thoughts? The Psalmist testifies that sacred utterances are signified by the name “silver,” saying: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire, proven on the earth” (Psalm 12:6).

Often, when we devote ourselves to the sacred utterances, we endure the snares of evil spirits more severely, because they sprinkle the dust of earthly thoughts upon our minds, so that they may obscure the eyes of our attention from the light of inward vision.

What else had the Psalmist expressed when he said: “Depart from me, you evildoers, and I will search out the commandments of my God” (Psalm 119:115)?

But because no one overcomes his enemies by his own strength, Eliphaz says: “The Almighty will be against your enemies, and silver will be heaped up for you.” It is as though he openly said: “When the Lord has driven the evil spirits away from you by his own strength, the bright treasure of divine speech will increase.” It follows:

### Verse 26

“Then you will abound in delights upon the Almighty.”

To abound in delights upon the Almighty is to be filled with the feasts of Holy Scripture in love of him. In its words we find as many delights as we receive varieties of understanding for our advancement. Hence it is also written in admiration of the bride: “Who is this that comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights?” (Song of Songs 8:5).

It follows: “And you will lift your face to God.”

To lift one’s face to God is to raise the heart to investigate sublime things. For just as a human being is known and visible to another human being through the face of the body, so we are known and visible to God through the inward person.

When we are weighed down by the guilt of sin, we fear lifting the face of our heart to God. But when guilt is washed away by the tears of repentance, and what has been done is lamented in such a way that it is no longer done, great confidence arises in the mind, and the face of our heart is lifted to behold the joys of heavenly recompense.

It is as though the heretics openly said to the faithful people: “As long as you do not follow our preaching, you press your heart down among lowly things.” It follows:

### Verse 27

“You will entreat him, and he will hear you.”

They entreat the Lord but do not deserve to be heard when they despise the commandments of the Lord who commands. Hence it is written: “The prayer of one who turns his ear away from hearing the law will be accursed” (Proverbs 28:9).

It follows: “And you will fulfill your vows.”

One who makes vows but cannot fulfill them because of weakness is dealt with through the punishment of sin: the ability to do good is taken away from one who desires it. But when the guilt that obstructs him is wiped away in the sight of the inward Judge, the ability to fulfill the vow immediately follows the vow. It follows:

### Verse 28

“You will decree a matter, and it will come to pass for you.”

It is characteristic of the weak to consider someone just in proportion as they see him obtain everything he desires, although we know that earthly goods are sometimes withheld from the righteous and bestowed generously upon the unjust.

But if Eliphaz has spoken these words about spiritual gifts, we should understand that a matter is decreed and comes to pass when, by God’s generosity, the virtue sought through desire also advances the affection that seeks it.

Hence he adds: “And light will shine on your ways.”

For light shines on the ways of the righteous when they spread the brightness of their clarity through wondrous signs of virtuous works, so that wherever they proceed in their purpose, they drive away the night of sin from the hearts of those who observe them and pour into them the light of righteousness by the example of their works. It follows:

### Verse 29

“For he who has been humbled will be in glory, and he who has lowered his eyes will himself be saved.”

This judgment does not differ from the word of Truth, who says: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted” (Matthew 23:12). Hence Solomon says: “Before he is crushed, the heart of a person is exalted, and before he is glorified, he is humbled” (Proverbs 18:12).

It is rightly said: “He who has lowered his eyes will himself be saved,” because, insofar as it can be discerned through the service of the bodily members, the first manifestation of pride is usually found in the eyes. Hence it is written: “And you will humble the eyes of the proud” (Psalm 18:27).

To lower one’s eyes, therefore, is to despise no one by looking down upon him, but to regard oneself as lesser and inferior to all whom one sees. The one who lowers his eyes will therefore be saved, because whoever abandons the false summit of pride ascends to the height of truth. It follows:

### Verse 30

“But the innocent will be saved by the purity of his hands.”

If this statement promises recompense in the heavenly kingdom, it is supported by the truth, because since it is written of God, “He will repay each person according to his works” (Romans 2:6), the justice of the eternal Judge saves at the final examination the one whom his mercy here frees from unclean works.

But if someone is believed to be saved here by the purity of his hands so that he becomes innocent through his own strength, this is certainly an error. For if heavenly grace does not first forestall the guilty, it will never find anyone innocent whom it can reward.

Hence, by the truthful voice of Moses, it is said: “No one is innocent before you by himself” (Exodus 34:7).

Nevertheless, all these things agree with the promises of the heretics in their allegorical sense. When they find the faithful afflicted in the present life, they suppose that they have been struck because of the guilt of unbelief, and they promise them, if they follow their doctrines, the salvation of innocence through the purity of good works.

It follows:

### Chapter 23
## CHAPTER XXII

### Verses 1–2

Job answered and said:

“Even now my speech is in bitterness, and the hand of my affliction is heavier than my groaning.”

As is his custom, blessed Job begins in more straightforward words, but brings his statements to completion through the profound unfolding of their mystery. The pain of the afflicted ought indeed to have been relieved by the consolation of his friends, but their consolation broke out into the flatteries of deceit, because the intention of their disordered consolation multiplied the blow that it ought to have lessened.

In these words, too, through the figure of the holy Church, the pain of the faithful is expressed: they groan all the more when they see the wicked flattering, because, in the words of Paul, “through sweet speech and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent” (Rom. 16:18).

The “hand of affliction” is the force of the blow. The elect consider their first affliction: they have been separated from the vision of their Creator, and therefore do not enjoy the brightness of inward illumination; rather, confined in the exile of the present life as though in a place of blindness, they groan. Thus, in this life, they always have the hand of affliction upon their groaning; but when adversities additionally come upon them even in this life, the hand of their affliction is made heavier than their groaning.

It continues:

### Verse 3

“Who will grant me that I may know and find him, and come even to his throne?”

If the elect person had not known the Lord, he would certainly not love him. But it is one thing to know through faith and another through sight; one thing to find through belief and another through contemplation. Hence it comes about that all the elect long to see through sight the one whom they have known through faith. They burn and languish with love for him because, through the very certainty of their faith, they already taste the sweetness of his delight.

For what is the throne of God except those angelic spirits who, as Scripture testifies, are called Thrones? When he wishes to come even to the throne of God, what else does he desire than to be present among the angelic spirits, so that he may no longer endure the passing moments of temporal decline but, in abiding glory, rise into the contemplation of eternity?

It continues:

### Verse 4

“I will set judgment before him, and I will fill my mouth with rebukes.”

To set judgment before God is, within the secret place of the mind, through contemplation by faith, to open the eyes of our consideration to the awe-inspiring examination of his majesty; it is to attend to what sinful humanity deserves and to consider how terrible the Judge who is now hidden and silent will appear afterward.

For whoever sets judgment before himself in the sight of God fills his mouth with rebukes, because, while he contemplates the searching examination of the fearsome Judge against himself, he assails himself severely with the reproach of repentance.

It continues:

### Verse 5

“That I may know the words that he will answer me, and understand what he will say to me.”

We lament our sins when we begin to weigh them; but we weigh them more carefully when we lament them more earnestly. From our lamentations there arises more fully in our hearts what divine severity threatens those who sin: what reproaches there will be for the rejected, what terrors, what rejection by the unappeasable Majesty.

For then the Lord, in his anger against the rejected, will say as much as, in his justice, he will have permitted them to suffer.

It continues:

### Verse 6

“I do not wish him to contend with me with great strength, lest he crush me by the weight of his greatness.”

For every mind of the just, if it is judged strictly by the almighty Lord, is crushed beneath the weight of his greatness.

It continues:

### Verse 7

“Let him set equity against me, and let my judgment come to victory.”

For who else is designated by the name of Equity except the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus? Of him it is written: “He was made for us by God wisdom and righteousness” (1 Cor. 1:30).

When this righteousness came into the world against the ways of sinners, we conquered the ancient enemy by whom we were held captive. It is as though he said: “Let him send the incarnate Son to rebuke my ways, and then, through the judgment of my acquittal, I shall victoriously exclude the adversary who lies in wait.”

It continues:

### Verses 8–9

“If I go to the east, he does not appear; if to the west, I shall not understand him; if to the left, what shall I do? I shall not apprehend him; if I turn myself to the right, I shall not see him.”

The Creator of all is not in a particular part, because he is everywhere; and he is found less readily when the one who is wholly everywhere is sought in a particular part.

It continues:

### Verse 10

“But he knows my way.”

It is as though he plainly said: “I am unable to see the one who sees me, and I cannot look upon the one who observes me with such subtlety”—thereby showing that he must be feared all the more because he is not visible. For the one who looks upon us in such a way that he cannot be seen by us is to be feared all the more, since he sees everything while himself being scarcely seen.

Alternatively: We go toward the east when we raise our mind in consideration of his majesty, but he does not appear, because mortal thought cannot prevail to see what he is in his nature. We go toward the west when, after the eye of our heart has been lifted toward God but has been struck back by the very immensity of the light, we draw it back to ourselves. Weary, we learn that what we were seeking is far above us; considering our mortality, we discover that we are still unworthy to see the immortal one.

To go toward the left is to consent to the delights of sins. It is therefore evident that the person who still lies on the left side in the pleasure of sin cannot apprehend God.

He undoubtedly turns toward the right who is lifted up by virtues; but he cannot see God if he rejoices in good deeds with private delight, because the swelling of pride weighs down the eye of his heart.

“He knows my way,” as though he plainly said: “I examine myself strictly, and yet the one whom I cannot see subtly sees everything that I do.”

It continues:

“And he will test me like gold that passes through fire.”

Gold advances toward the brightness of its nature in the furnace when it loses its impurities. Thus the souls of the just are tested like gold passing through fire: through the burning of tribulation, their vices are removed and their merits increased.

It continues:

### Verse 11

“My foot has followed his footsteps.”

The works of God that we see may be called certain steps of God: through them every good and wicked person is governed; through them the just and unjust are ordered according to their proper arrangements; through them every subject is daily led toward better things, while the one falling toward worse things is tolerated.

Concerning these steps the Prophet said: “Your footsteps were seen, O God” (Ps. 67:25).

When we contemplate the power of his patience and mercy and, in contemplating them, strive to imitate them, what else do we do than follow the traces of his footsteps? For we imitate certain outward aspects of his work.

The Truth admonished us to imitate these footsteps of his Father when he said: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. 5:44), and so forth.

Blessed Job may nevertheless be directing his attention to the future work of the Wisdom who was to become incarnate, just as we see by faith the past works of that same Wisdom. When blessed Job, filled with the heavenly Spirit, observed his life with attentive concern, foreseeing the future humility of his gentleness, he returned, as it were, to an example set before him, so that whatever he did in this life he might bind to the traces of that one’s imitation.

Concerning these footsteps, Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2:21).

It continues:

“I have guarded his way, and I have not turned aside from it.”

He guards and does not turn aside who practices what he has set his attention upon. To guard through intention is not to turn aside through action.

This is the concern of the just: daily to examine their deeds according to the ways of truth, and, setting those ways before themselves as a rule, not to deviate from their path of uprightness.

It continues:

### Verse 12

“I have not departed from the commands of his lips.”

Just as servants who obey well are always intent upon the faces of their masters, so that they may hear quickly whatever their masters command and strive to fulfill it, so the minds of the just attend upon the almighty Lord through their intention. In his Scripture they behold, as it were, his mouth, so that—because through it God speaks everything he wills—they differ from his will no more than they recognize that same will through his speech.

It continues:

“And I have hidden the words of his mouth in my bosom.”

We hide the words of his mouth in the bosom of our heart when we hear his commands not merely in passing but with the intention of fulfilling them in deed.

For this reason it is written of the Virgin Mother herself: “But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2:19).

It continues:

### Verse 13

“For he alone is, and no one can turn aside his thought.”

Are angels not beings? Are human beings, heaven and earth, air and seas, all flying creatures, four-footed animals, and reptiles not beings? And certainly it is written: “He created all things that they might exist” (Wis. 1:14).

Since there are so many things in the creation of the world, why does the voice of the blessed man now say, “He alone is”?

But to be is one thing, to be in the primary sense another; to be mutably is one thing, and to be immutably another. All these things exist, but they do not exist in the primary sense, because they do not subsist in themselves; and unless they are held by the hand of the one who governs them, they cannot exist at all.

Hence it is said to Moses: “I am who I am.” And: “He who is has sent me to you” (Exod. 3:14).

No one turns aside his thought, because no one can resist his hidden judgments. For although there were some who seemed to have turned aside his thought through their prayers, his inward thought was such that they were able, by entreaty, to turn aside his sentence; and from him they received what they were to do with him.

Let him therefore say, “No one can turn aside his thought,” because judgments once fixed cannot be changed at all. Hence it is written: “He established a command, and it shall not pass away” (Ps. 148:6).

It continues:

“And his soul does whatever he wills.”

Although God is outside all bodies and within all minds, that way of his by which he penetrates all things disposes everything; it is called his soul. Nothing resists his will—not even those things that appear to happen against his will. For sometimes he permits even what he has not commanded to happen, so that through it what is commanded may be fulfilled more certainly.

The perverse will of the apostate angels is evil, but it is nevertheless wonderfully ordered by God, so that even their snares serve the benefit of the good whom they tempt in order to purify them.

It continues:

### Verse 14

“When he has fulfilled his will in me, many other things like these are also ready for him.”

It is as though he plainly said: “I already consider what I am suffering, but I fear what I may suffer. He fulfills his will in me because he afflicts me with many persecutions; but many things like these are ready for him, because if he considers striking me, he still finds room for the blow to increase.”

It continues:

### Verse 15

“And therefore I am troubled at his face, and when I consider him, I am shaken with fear.”

The one who places the terror of his majesty before the eyes of his heart is rightly troubled at the face of the Lord; he is shaken by fear of his righteousness when he sees that he is not capable of rendering an account if he is judged strictly.

It is rightly said, “When I consider him, I am shaken with fear,” because whenever a person does not consider the force of divine punishment, he fears it scarcely at all. He is as secure as possible in this life insofar as he is estranged from consideration of inward severity.

It continues:

### Verse 16

“God has softened my heart, and the Almighty has troubled me.”

The heart of the just is called soft through a divine gift because it is penetrated by fear of the heavenly judgment. What can be penetrated is soft; what cannot be penetrated is hard.

Hence Solomon says: “Blessed is the person who is always fearful; but whoever is hard of mind will fall into evil” (Prov. 28:14).

The hearts of the good are not secure but troubled, because, while they consider the weight of the future examination, they do not desire to have rest here. They disturb their own security through consideration of inward severity.

It continues:

### Verse 17

“For I have not perished because of the darknesses that threaten, nor has gloom covered my face.”

The person placed under the scourge who perishes from bodily salvation because of threatening darknesses is struck for what has already been done so that he may be hidden from future punishments.

The scourges of the good either cleanse sins that have been committed or prevent future sins that might have been committed.

But blessed Job, because, though placed under the scourge, he was neither cleansed of preceding sins nor removed from those that threatened, but his virtue alone was increased through the scourge, says confidently: “For I have not perished because of the darknesses that threaten, nor has gloom covered my face.”

The person who has always looked upon the weight of divine fear has not had the face of his heart covered by the darkness of sin; and the one whom no punishments followed did not lose bodily salvation because of threatening darknesses.

## CHAPTER XXIV

### Verse 1

“The times are not hidden from the Almighty. But those who know him do not know his days.”

What are his “days” except his very eternity? This is sometimes expressed by the mention of a single day, as it is written: “One day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83:11).

At other times, through its length, it is signified by the designation of many days, concerning which it is written: “Your years are from age to age” (Ps. 101:25).

We, then, are carried within times because we are creatures. But God, who is the Creator of all, comprehends our times in his eternity, because he sees our things in a comprehensible manner, whereas we are entirely unable to comprehend what belongs to him.

But since God’s nature is simple, it is very remarkable that he says: “Those who know him do not know his days.” For he himself is not one thing and his days another. God is what he possesses: he possesses eternity, but he himself is eternity.

What, then, does it mean to say, “Those who know him do not know his days,” except that they both know him and still do not know him? For those who already hold him by faith still do not know him by sight; and although we truly believe that he himself is eternity, we nevertheless do not know how he is eternity itself.

It continues:

### Verse 2

“Others have moved the boundaries, seized flocks, and pastured them.”

Whom does he designate by the name “others” except heretics, who exist as outsiders from the bosom of the holy Church?

They move the boundaries because, by transgressing the ordinances of the Fathers, they pass beyond them. Concerning these ordinances it is written: “Do not move the ancient boundaries that your fathers established” (Prov. 22:28).

They seize flocks and pasture them because they draw the ignorant to themselves by perverse persuasions and nourish them with deadly doctrines for their destruction.

It continues:

### Verse 3

“They drove away the ass of the orphans, and took the widow’s ox as a pledge.”

Whom do we understand here by the orphans except God’s elect who are placed in the tenderness of mind, nourished by the great grace of faith, and who do not yet see the face of their father, who has already died for them?

There are some who, although they themselves cannot practice spiritual things, nevertheless gladly provide assistance to those striving toward the heights. An ass is accustomed to carry human burdens. Thus, as it were, the ass of the elect is the person who, serving earthly things, carries burdens for human needs.

Often, when heretics turn such a person away from the bosom of the holy Church, they drive away, as it were, the ass of the orphans.

And who is the widow except the holy Church, which is for the present deprived of the vision of her slain husband? The ox of this widow is each preacher. It often happens that heretics, through their perverse doctrines, draw away even those who appeared to be preachers.

They therefore take away the widow’s ox when they remove even a preacher from the holy Church. It is rightly added, “as a pledge.” For when a pledge is taken, one thing is held, but another is still sought; and often they try to take away those who preach so that they may also draw away their followers.

The widow’s ox is therefore taken as a pledge when the preacher himself is received for the purpose of having others follow.

It continues:

### Verse 4

“They overturned the way of the poor and oppressed together the meek of the earth.”

The name “poverty” often signifies humility; and sometimes those who appear meek and humble fall through the examples of others if they do not know how to preserve discernment.

It continues:

### Verse 5

“Others, like wild asses in the desert, go out to their work.”

A wild ass is an untamed ass. Heretics are rightly compared here to wild asses because, released into their own pleasures, they are alien from the bonds of faith and reason.

Hence it is written: “A wild ass accustomed to the wilderness, in the desire of its soul, draws in the wind of its love” (Jer. 2:24).

They do not carry out God’s work but their own, since they follow not sound doctrines but their own desires. For it is written: “He who walks in an immaculate way served me” (Ps. 100:6).

It continues:

“And, keeping watch for prey, they prepare bread for their children.”

They keep watch for prey who are always trying to seize the words of the just for their own meaning, so that through them they may prepare the bread of error for their perverse children.

Concerning this bread, it is said by Solomon through the words of a woman representing the type of heretical perversity: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasant” (Prov. 9:17).

It continues:

### Verse 6

“They reap a field that is not theirs, and they gather the grapes of the one whom they have violently oppressed.”

The name “field” can signify the breadth of sacred Scripture. Heretics reap a field that is not theirs because they take from it opinions far removed from their own meanings.

It is also expressed by the name “vineyard,” because through its statements of truth it produces clusters of virtues. Yet they violently oppress the Creator of this vineyard—that is, of sacred Scripture—because they forcibly strive to bend its meaning into the words of sacred speech.

He says: “You have made me serve in your sins; you have given me labor in your iniquities” (Isa. 43:24).

They gather the grapes of the same vineyard when, according to their own profession of understanding, they heap up clusters of interpretations from it.

The name “field” or “vineyard” can also signify the entire Church. Perverse teachers reap it, and they gather its fruits by oppressing its author in his members. For, while persecuting the grace of our Creator, when they snatch away from it certain people who appeared upright, what else do they take away than ears of grain or clusters of souls?

It continues:

### Verse 7

“They leave people naked, taking away their clothing; they have no covering in the cold.”

Just as clothing protects the body, so good works protect the soul. Hence it is said to a certain person: “Blessed is the one who keeps watch and guards his garments, lest he walk naked” (Rev. 16:15).

When heretics destroy good works in the minds of some, they plainly remove the coverings of clothing. The covering pertains to righteousness; the cold pertains to guilt.

There are some who commit sins in certain matters but follow upright works in others. Whoever sins through some actions but performs good deeds through others—what is he except one who is clothed and shivering in the cold? Through one work he grows warm toward righteousness, while through another he grows cold toward guilt.

But when heretics take good works away from such people, they ensure that, in the cold, they have nothing with which to clothe themselves.

Alternatively, “cold” may designate desire, and “clothing” action. Many still burn with perverse desires, but while waging spiritual battle against themselves, they oppose those desires with upright works and cover with good deeds what they feel arising within them as something leftward through temptation.

Thus, in the things they desire badly, they grow cold; but in the things they do well, they are clothed. When heretics, through perverse arguments, remove the works of right faith from them, what do they accomplish except that those who still feel the cold of carnal desires die without the clothing of good deeds?

It continues:

### Verse 8

“Those whom the rains of the mountains water embrace rocks, having no covering.”

The rains of the mountains are the words of teachers. Concerning these mountains the voice of the holy Church says: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains” (Ps. 120:1).

The rains of the mountains water these people because the streams of the holy Fathers satisfy them.

As we have already said, we understand the covering as the protection of good works, by which each person is covered so that the foulness of his perversity may be hidden before the eyes of almighty God. Hence it is written: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. 31:1).

Whom do we understand by the name “rocks” except strong men within the holy Church? Through the first shepherd it is said to them: “You also, like living stones, are being built up” (1 Pet. 2:5).

These people, who place no confidence in any work of their own, run for protection to the holy martyrs and persist in tears before their sacred bodies; they pray that, through the martyrs’ intercession, they may obtain pardon.

What, then, do they do in this humility except embrace rocks, since they do not have the covering of good action?

It continues:

### Verse 9

“They used violence, plundering the orphan, and they stripped the poor common people.”

Heretics make their way by plundering orphans because they attack the weak minds of the faithful with violence of words and deeds.

The poor common people are the uneducated populace. If they possessed the true riches of wisdom, they would not lose the garment of their faith.

Within the holy Church, true teachers are, as it were, senators. As they multiply knowledge in their hearts, they abound in true riches among themselves.

But heretics strip the poor populace, because they cannot overcome the learned; through their pestilential preaching they strip the uneducated of the covering of faith.

It continues:

### Verse 10

“They took away ears of grain from the naked and from those walking without clothing, and from the hungry.”

What he says with “the naked,” he repeats with “those walking without clothing.” But being naked is one thing, and walking naked another.

Everyone who practices neither good nor evil is naked and idle. But the person who does evil walks naked, because he proceeds along the path of perversity without the covering of good works.

There are some who desire the words of sacred speech. Whenever they turn over the sayings of the Fathers in their thoughts for the building up of minds, they carry away ears of grain, as it were, from a good harvest.

Heretics therefore take ears of grain from the naked, from those walking without clothing, and from the hungry. Whether such people are idle and exercise themselves in no good deeds, or proceed along the path of shamelessness without the covering of good works, even when they already desire to return to repentance and hunger for the nourishment of the word, the heretics take ears of grain from them in their hunger, because through harmful persuasions they destroy the sayings of the Fathers in their minds.

It continues:

### Verse 11

“Among their heaps they rested at midday, those who thirst while treading the winepresses.”

All who persecute the holy Church—what else do they do but tread the winepress? By divine dispensation this is permitted to happen, so that the clusters of souls may flow into spiritual wine and, stripped of corruptible flesh, may hasten, as though into a storehouse, to the heavenly kingdoms.

But all who persecute the life of the faithful both tread and thirst: they become more savage for carrying out cruel acts, and, blinded by the merits of their impiety, they strive to do more serious things precisely because they have already done serious things.

Heretics, however, since they do not themselves possess the power of persecution, stir up the powerful of this world. They draw their minds toward persecution and inflame them with whatever persuasions they can.

When they see those powerful people acting cruelly against the life of Catholics, they rest, as it were, in the very heat of the sun.

It continues:

### Verse 12

“From the cities they made men groan.”

Because cities are named from peoples living together, the name “cities” rightly designates the Churches of the true faith. Established in the various parts of the world, they form one catholic Church in which all the faithful who think rightly about God live together in harmony.

Heretics, therefore, because they often cling to the perverse powers of this world and persecute the communal life and concord of the good, are rightly described in the words: “From the cities they made men groan.”

Blessed Job rightly calls these people “men,” because heretics strive especially to extinguish those who run through the way of God with perfected steps—not feebly and weakly, but manfully.

It continues:

“And the soul of the wounded cried out, and God does not permit it to go unavenged.”

The soul of the just is wounded when the faith of the weak is disturbed. For such people, to cry out is already to waste away from the fall of another.

But God does not permit it to go unavenged. Although he permits something to be done unjustly according to an unjust order, he nevertheless does not allow the injustice he permitted to go unpunished. For, through the injustice of the rejected, he strikes certain faults that he observes to be present in the elect; yet he does not neglect to strike, with eternal justice, the injustice of those who inflict it.

It continues:

### Verse 13

“They were themselves rebels against the light.”

Often the perverse recognize the right things they ought to follow, yet disdain to follow what they recognize. They are therefore rebels against the light, because, following their own desires, they despise the good they know.

It continues:

“They did not know his ways, nor did they return by his paths.”

Those who first become rebels through knowledge later proceed as though they did not know, as it is written concerning certain people: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (Rom. 1:21).

A little later it is added: “God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do things that are not fitting” (Rom. 1:28).

A path is narrower than a way. Those who refuse to practice the more manifest good deeds do not reach an understanding of the more subtle ones.

Almighty God waited for them to proceed by his paths. But would that they had at least wished to return by them, so that they might follow the roads of life through repentance, which they had refused to follow through innocence.

It continues:

### Verse 14

“In the early morning the murderer rises; he kills the needy and the poor, but at night he will be like a thief.”

Since a murderer usually commits murders against his neighbors especially in the silence of night, why is he said here to rise early in the morning to kill the needy and the poor, while at night he is said to be like a thief?

But when the words of the letter do not agree among themselves, we are recalled to investigate the secrets of the spirit.

In sacred Scripture, “morning” sometimes signifies the advent of the Lord’s incarnation, as in the prophet’s words: “Morning came, and also night” (Isa. 21:12). For the beginnings of new light shone in the presence of our Redeemer, yet the darkness of their faithlessness was not wiped away from the hearts of the persecutors.

At other times, “morning” signifies the advent of the already terrible and strict Judge, as in: “In the morning I was killing all the sinners of the earth” (Ps. 118:8), and: “In the morning I shall stand before you and see” (Ps. 5:5).

At still other times, it customarily signifies the prosperity of the present life, as Solomon says: “Woe to the land whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning” (Eccl. 10:16).

For it is written: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15).

The murderer therefore rises early in the morning because every perverse person is raised up in the glory of the present life, while the life of those who thirst for the glory to come is brought low; they seek, as it were, to be satisfied in the evening.

Every wicked person who seizes the dignity of temporary power in this world expands himself toward the performance of evil all the more fiercely because he loves no one through the bowels of charity.

With all his thoughts he rages against the good and destroys the life of innocence.

“But at night he will be like a thief.”

In the night of tribulation and his own delight, although he cannot exercise the hand of cruelty, he nevertheless offers counsels of perversity to those whom he sees prevailing. He runs here and there and suggests whatever he can to harm the good.

It continues:

### Verse 15

“The eye of the adulterer watches for darkness, saying, ‘No eye will see me.’”

There is no obstacle to understanding this literally as well: the person who desires to commit adultery seeks darkness.

But since the statement is made against heretics, it is appropriate to understand what is said mystically. For Paul says: “We are not like the many, adulterating the word of God” (2 Cor. 2:17).

An adulterer in carnal intercourse seeks not offspring but pleasure. Thus every perverse person who serves empty glory is rightly said to adulterate the word of God, because through sacred speech he desires not to beget children for God but to display his own knowledge.

The lust for glory draws him to speak; he devotes himself more to pleasure than to generation.

The statement that follows is appropriate: “No eye will see me,” because the adultery that takes place in the mind is very difficult for human sight to penetrate. The perverse mind commits it all the more securely because it does not fear being seen by human beings whom it would be ashamed to face.

It continues:

“And he covers his face.”

The adulterer covers his face so that he will not be recognized. Everyone who lives wickedly in thought or action covers his face because, through the perversity of his doctrine or conduct, he strives to ensure that he cannot be recognized by almighty God in the judgment.

Hence at the end he will say to certain people: “I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity” (Matt. 7:23).

What is the face of the human heart except the likeness of God? The perverse person covers this face so that he may not be recognized when he confounds his life either through evil deeds or through the error of faithlessness.

It continues:

### Verse 16

“In darkness he breaks into houses, as they had agreed by day, and they did not know the light.”

What is designated here by the name “houses” except consciences, in which we dwell while considering what we do? Hence it is said to a certain person who had been healed: “Go to your house, to your own people, and announce to them how much the Lord has done for you” (Mark 5:19).

When the prosperities of daylight shine upon the just in the present world, the teachers of error fear to make their perverse suggestions to them. Instead, they seek opportunities and eagerly await the collapse of their prosperity, so that in the darkness of adversity they may pierce their minds with persuasion—those to whom, while they lived prosperously, they did not dare to speak perversely.

As soon as they see them in adversity, they rise up and insist that such things are happening to them only because of the merit of sin; for, loving only the glory of the present life, they consider the scourge a condemnation.

They therefore break into houses in darkness because they strive to corrupt the minds of the good through the very adversity they suffer.

It continues:

### Verse 17

“If the dawn suddenly appears, they consider it the shadow of death.”

The dawn is the mind of the just, which, abandoning the darkness of sin, is already breaking forth into the light of eternity. Thus it is also said concerning the holy Church: “Who is this who advances like the rising dawn?” (Song 6:9).

The more each just person is exalted in the present life by the honors that shine with the light of righteousness, the more he becomes, before the eyes of the perverse, the darkness of death.
