For those who remember that they have acted perversely fear to be corrected. They always desire to give free rein to their perversities and to live without correction.

It continues:

“And so they walk in darkness as though in light.”

Perverse minds rejoice in crimes; through their guilt they are daily led toward punishment, yet they remain secure.

Hence Solomon says: “There are wicked people who are so secure as though they possessed the deeds of the just” (Eccl. 8:14).

Again it is written of them: “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2:14).

Thus they walk in darkness as though in light because they rejoice in the night of sin as though the light of righteousness were surrounding them.

Or certainly, because darkness appropriately expresses the present life, in which the consciences of others are not seen, while our homeland is eternal light, in which, as we look upon faces, we see our hearts in one another.

But the wicked love the present life so greatly and embrace the times of this exile as though they were already reigning in their homeland. Hence it is rightly said: “They walk in darkness as though in light.”

It continues:

### Verse 18. “He is light upon the face of the water.”

He returns from the plural number to the singular, because often one person begins evils and many follow by imitation; yet the fault belongs chiefly to the one who offered examples of wickedness to those who followed perversely. Hence the sentence frequently returns to the one who became the originator of the fault.

The surface of the water is driven here and there by the breeze and moves without being made firm by any stability. Therefore the mind of the wicked is lighter than the surface of the water, because whenever the breeze of temptation touches it, it draws it along without any delay for reconsideration. For if we think of the shifting heart of any perverse person, what else do we see than a surface of water set in the wind?

It follows: “Let his portion be accursed upon the earth, and let him not walk by the way of the vineyards.”

Whoever acts rightly in the present life and endures adversity is indeed seen to labor under adversity, but is brought to completion for the blessing of an everlasting inheritance. Whoever, however, acts perversely and nevertheless receives prosperity, and is not restrained from evil deeds even by the generosity of gifts, is indeed seen to prosper, but is bound by the guilt of everlasting curse.

The way of the vineyards is the uprightness of the churches. In this matter, it may be understood either of heretics or, without objection, of some carnal person: the way of the vineyards—that is, the uprightness of the churches—is lost when either right faith or uprightness in justice is not maintained. For he walks by the way of the vineyards who, weighing the preaching of the holy universal Church, deviates neither from the rectitude of faith nor from the rectitude of good works.

It follows:

### Verse 19. “Let him pass from the waters of snow to excessive heat.”

For this reason wickedness is compared with cold: it constricts the sinner’s mind with torpor. Hence it is written: “As a cistern makes its water cold, so malice makes the soul cold” (Jer. VI, 7). In contrast, charity is heat, because it kindles the mind that it fills. Concerning this it is written: “Iniquity will abound, and the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. XXIV, 12).

There are some who, while avoiding the coldness of their iniquities, come to the true faith or to the manner of life of holiness. But because they presume upon their own understanding more than is necessary, they often wish to investigate in the faith they receive those things they cannot comprehend, so that they may be held in God more by reason than by faith. Since the human mind cannot investigate divine secrets, they disdain to believe whatever they cannot investigate by reason, and through excessive inquiry they fall into error.

Thus, before they believed, or while they were still occupied with the work of iniquity, they were waters of snow; but when, abandoning carnal deeds, they desire to investigate more than they comprehend in the faith to which they have been led, they become hotter than they ought to be. Accordingly, this is rightly said concerning any such perverse person—not as a wish, but merely as the prophet’s statement: “Let him pass from the waters of snow to excessive heat.”

It follows: “And his sin as far as hell.”

For the sin that is not corrected before the end of the present life through reproof and repentance is led as far as hell. Concerning this sin John says: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (1 John V, 15). It is a sin unto death, a sin extending to death, because forgiveness is sought in vain for the sin that is not corrected here. Concerning this it is further added:

### Verse 20. “Let his mercy forget him.”

The mercy of almighty God is said to forget the one who has forgotten the justice of almighty God, because whoever does not fear him as just now cannot afterward find him merciful. This sentence is directed not only against the one who abandons the teachings of the true faith, but also against the one who, established in right faith, lives carnally, because the vengeance of eternal judgment is not escaped, whether one sins in faith or in conduct.

It follows: “His sweetness is worms.”

Whoever in this world desires to prosper, surpass others, and swell with possessions and honors finds in this worldly concern his delight and in rest his labor. For he is greatly wearied if the worldly concern by which he is wearied should be absent. Since it is the nature of worms to move incessantly at every moment, the restlessness of thoughts is appropriately signified by the name “worms.”

Thus the sweetness of the perverse mind is a worm, because it is pleasantly nourished by that through which it is ceaselessly agitated in restlessness. The flesh, too, may be more plainly signified by the name “worm.” Hence it is said above:

[Note: [Col. 0307] Indeed, below, namely in the following chapter, 6, verse 6.]

> “Man is rottenness, and the son of man a worm.”

[Note: [Col. 0307] More properly, perhaps, this should be in the genitive or dative.]

The blindness of any sensual person devoted to the pleasures of the flesh is therefore demonstrated when it is said: “His sweetness is worms.” For what is flesh except rottenness and a worm? And whoever breathes after carnal desires—what else does he love than a worm? The tombs testify to what the substance of the flesh is. What parent or faithful friend can touch, however dearly loved, the flesh of one whose body is teeming with worms? When the flesh is desired, therefore, let it be considered what it is when lifeless, and then it will be understood what is being loved.

## Book Seventeen

[Col. 0307]

In the preceding words the holy man, through distinct and carefully considered sayings of wisdom, set forth the faults of any wicked person and expressed how deserving of condemnation his conduct is. Concerning his punishment he now adds, saying:

[Col. 0307D]

### Verse 20. “Let him not be remembered, but let him be crushed like an unfruitful tree.”

Whoever remains subject to vices until the end of life is not brought into the remembrance of the Creator. For if the remembrance of heavenly regard touched him, it would undoubtedly recall him from iniquity. His merits demand that he be utterly erased from the Creator’s remembrance.

It must be understood, however, that God is not properly said to remember. For one who cannot forget, how can he remember? But because we embrace those whom we remember and withdraw from those whom we forget, God is said, in human usage, to remember when he grants gifts, and to forget when he abandons someone in guilt.

Concerning this unfruitful tree John says:

> “For now the axe is laid at the root of the tree. Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Luke III, 9; Matt. III, 10).

Here, however, to signify eternal punishments for the reprobate, it is not said that he is cut down but that he is crushed. For death of the flesh cuts off the reprobate, but the punishment that follows crushes them. He is, as it were, cut down here when he is separated from the present life; but in Gehenna he is crushed when he is tormented by everlasting damnation.

It follows:

### Verse 21. “For he fed the barren woman who does not bear, and he did no good to the widow.”

What is called “the barren woman” in this passage except the flesh? Since it desires only present things, it does not know how to give birth to good thoughts. And what is called “the widow” except the soul? Since the Creator wished to join it to himself, it came from the bridal chamber of the womb of the flesh, as the Psalmist testifies:

> “And he himself comes forth like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber” (Ps. XVIII, 6).

It is rightly called a widow, because its husband suffered death for it and now lives in the recesses of heaven, hidden from its eyes, as though in a region belonging to another.

The wicked, therefore, feeds the barren woman and neglects to do good to the widow, because by serving the desires of the flesh he despises the care and life of the soul. The flesh is called not only barren but also “one that does not bear,” because by its own inclination it is unable even at the end to give birth to good thoughts.

This may also be understood of heretical preachers. For every preacher of error, while teaching a people placed outside the unity of the Church, feeds a barren woman, one unable to bear, because he devotes the work of his labor to one that in no way yields spiritual fruits. He does not do good to the widow, because he refuses to live for and serve the holy universal Church, whose husband endured the adversities of death. To do good to the widow is to labor for the consolation of one who is crushed by the death of her husband.

Often, however, a preacher of error joins himself to the rich of this world. Hence it follows:

### Verse 22. “He drags down the mighty in his own strength.”

In the strength of his wickedness he drags down the mighty when, through the craft of his error, he seizes the powerful of this world. Concerning these it is said through Paul:

> “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Cor. I, 27).

The strength of the perverse preacher is an exalted knowledge of speech, by which, puffed up, he despises others and, in contempt of everyone, swells with the belief that he alone is learned.

It follows: “And when he stands, he does not believe in his own life.”

Every perverse preacher stands in this world as long as he lives in an earthly body, but he refuses to believe in his own life because he scorns knowing the truth about God. He would believe in his own life if he rightly understood the substance of his Creator.

For every perverse person, even if he appears to hold right faith within the bosom of the Church, stands and does not believe in his own life. The things he understands about the Creator through faith are indeed right, but he nevertheless scorns the works of faith and is convicted of unbelief, because by his manner of life he is rejected by the one whom he displays himself as believing.

Hence John says:

> “Whoever says that he knows him and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John II, 4).

It follows:

### Verse 23. “God gave him a place for repentance, and he abuses it for pride.”

Whenever someone sins and continues to live, divine providence tolerates him in his iniquity in order to restrain him from iniquity. But one who is tolerated for a longer time and nevertheless is not restrained from iniquity receives the gift of heavenly patience, yet by the bonds of his guilt binds himself more tightly through that very gift.

Hence Paul says:

> “Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God” (Rom. II, 4–5).

It follows: “His eyes are upon his ways.”

The sinner looks upon his own ways because he strives to think about and see only those things that support his temporal advantage. Hence Paul says:

> “All seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. II, 21).

The way of the arrogant is pride; the way of the robber is greed; the way of the wanton is carnal desire. Thus every wicked person lowers his eyes upon his own ways, because he directs his attention solely to his vices in order to satisfy his mind through them.

Hence Solomon says:

> “The eyes of fools are at the ends of the earth” (Prov. XVII, 24).

It follows:

### Verse 24. “They are exalted for a little while, and they will not endure.”

Although the glory of the wicked often extends over a multitude of years, it is judged by weak minds to be long and almost stable. But when a sudden end cuts it short, it unquestionably proves that it was brief. Its limit makes clear that what could pass away was little.

They are therefore exalted for a little while and do not endure, because, precisely by desiring to appear exalted, they become far removed from the true essence of God through their arrogance. They cannot endure because they are separated from the solidity of eternal being. They suffer this first downfall because through private glory they fall within themselves.

Hence the Psalmist says:

> “You cast them down when they were exalted” (Ps. LXXI, 18).

When the holy man had examined the glory and downfall of the wicked, he immediately directed the eye of his mind to all things, saying: “They will be humbled like all things and will be taken away.”

He plainly means all earthly things, as though he said: “They cannot stand in any way, because even the things on which they lean are themselves fleeing. While they love temporal things, they pass away with them through the turning of time.”

But one may ask: Since Solomon says, “A generation passes away, and a generation comes; but the earth remains forever” (Eccl. I, 4), why does blessed Job assert that all things are humbled and taken away?

We can easily resolve this if we distinguish how earth and heaven pass away and how they remain. Both pass away in the appearance they now possess, yet in their essence they subsist without end. Hence Paul says:

> “For the form of this world is passing away” (1 Cor. VII, 31).

It follows: “And they will be crushed like the tops of ears of grain.”

The tops of ears of grain are awns. The awns emerge joined together in the ear, but as they grow they gradually become distinct from one another, bristling and stiff. What, then, should I call the wicked rich of this world except certain awns of the human race? While they grow proud against one another yet unanimously afflict the life of the good, they are divided against one another, but together press the grains downward.

The time of threshing, however, will come. It will break the stiffness of the awns but will not crush the solid grains. When the awns are broken, the brightness of the grains is revealed, because when the wicked fall into eternal punishments, the truth of the saints’ righteousness is shown in all its clarity.

It follows:

### Verse 25. “But if this is not so, who can prove me a liar?”

Why, then, is it said, “If this is not so, who can prove me a liar,” when we know that anyone may rebuke a falsehood? But if we examine the speaker’s meaning through careful questioning, we quickly discover how correct are the things he has uttered.

For although a just person may at some time speak while committing a fault, it is not fitting that he be judged by unjust people who live perversely. It is as though he said: “Everything is as I have stated; yet if it were not so, you could not prove me wrong, because while you yourselves are still overcome by your own faults, you cannot rebuke another’s falsehood.”

It follows: “And set my words before God.”

To set words before God is, with the inner judge taken into consideration, to weigh outward speech. The holy man therefore does not think that his proud friends are able to place his words before God. It is as though he plainly said: “You cannot place what I say before the judge because, by your sins, you hide his face from yourselves.”

This may also, without objection, be understood figuratively of the holy Church. When she is criticized for the weakness of her members by the mockery of heretics, she disdains the cunning of their mockery itself.

## Chapter 25

### Verses 1–2. “Then Baldath the Shuhite answered and said: ‘Power and terror belong to him.’”

It is as though he plainly said: “He alone truly terrifies mortal hearts who truly possesses them by the power of his divinity. For what terror does human power inspire, when it does not know when it may lose the right to that same power?”

It follows: “Who makes peace in his high places.”

Almighty God advances the good toward merit when he permits the wicked to rage against their life, and the highest things are brought into harmony while the lowest are confounded. For in the heavenly places he joins his elect to the choirs of angels, while in earthly and lowly matters he bears, according to his will, the conduct of the reprobate who oppose them.

Yet amid this one may ask: If supreme peace is maintained in the heights, what does it mean that the angel says to Daniel, “I have come because of your words. But the prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me for twenty-one days” (Dan. X, 12–13)?

Since definite angelic ministries have been appointed for the administration of each nation, whenever the conduct of those subject to them requires the assistance of the spirits placed over them, the spirits who preside are said to come against one another. When the guilt or righteousness of a particular nation is brought before the council of the heavenly court, the one appointed over that nation is said either to have prevailed in the contest or not to have prevailed.

It follows:

### Verse 3. “Is there a number of his armies?”

Within the knowledge of human reason there is no number for the heavenly spirits, because no one knows how great is the multitude of that invisible army. Concerning it Daniel says:

> “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. VII, 10).

The number of the heavenly citizens is expressed as both infinite and determinate, so that what is countable to God may be shown to be uncountable to us.

We rightly call the angelic spirits the soldiers of God, because we know that they fight against the powers of the air; yet they carry out these battles not by labor but by command. The number of elect human beings is also joined to this army: those who, through the lofty desire of the mind, are freed from slavery to earthly conduct. Concerning them Paul says:

> “No one serving as a soldier for God involves himself in worldly affairs” (2 Tim. II, 4).

Although they now appear few, they will reign innumerably in the invisible homeland.

It follows: “And upon whom does his light not rise?”

The light of God is preceding grace. Unless it arose freely in our heart, our mind would undoubtedly remain darkened in the shadows of its sins.

It follows:

### Verse 4. “Can man be justified when compared with God?”

This verse was spoken earlier by blessed Job and is now repeated as a reproach against him. Every just person is just through God’s illumination, not by comparison with him. For human justice, compared with its creator, is injustice, because even if a human being remained in the condition in which he was created, a creature could not be made equal to the Creator.

It follows: “Or can one born of a woman appear clean?”

It is as though it were plainly said: “So that a human being may not grow proud against his Creator, let him consider from where he came here and understand what he is.”

It follows:

### Verse 5. “Behold, the moon does not shine, and the stars are not clean in his sight.”

What is signified by the moon except the Church as a whole? What by the stars except the souls of individuals who live well? While they shine forth with great virtues amid the conduct of wicked people, they shine as though in the darkness of night. Hence Paul also says to the disciples:

> “Among whom you shine like lights in the world” (Phil. II, 15).

That the holy Church is expressed by the name “moon” the Prophet testifies, saying:

> “The sun was lifted up, and the moon stood in its order.”

The moon therefore does not shine, and the stars are not clean in his sight, because the holy Church does not glitter with so many miracles by its own virtue unless the gifts of preceding grace pour over it; nor are the minds of individuals who live well clean from the stains of sin if they are judged apart from mercy. For in the eyes of the strict judge each person’s corruptibility defiles him unless the grace of the one who spares wipes him clean each day.

It follows:

### Verse 6. “How much more man is rottenness, and the son of man a worm!”

It is as though it were plainly said: “If even those who shine with virtues amid the darkness of the present life cannot exist without contamination, how great is the guilt that binds those who still live carnally? If those who already live in heavenly desires cannot be free from sin, what burdens of sin do those endure who, devoted to the pleasures of their flesh, still bear the yoke of rottenness?”

Hence Peter says:

> “If the righteous person is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?” (1 Pet. IV, 18.)

Man is rightly called rottenness, but the son of man is called a worm. The first man was rottenness, not a worm, because although he rotted through death, he did not come from rottenness by birth. But the one who is a son is called a worm because he is already propagated from the corruption of mortal bodies.

## Chapter 26

### Verses 1–2. “Then Job answered and said: ‘Whose helper are you? Is it the weak man? And do you sustain the arm of one who is not strong?’”

To help the weak is charity; to wish to help the powerful is pride. It is as though he plainly said: “While you strive to help one beneath whose greatness you collapse, all the assistance you offer proceeds from display, not from compassion.”

Yet it must be understood that we often humbly assist even God, who is certainly not weak. Hence Paul says:

> “For we are God’s fellow workers” (1 Cor. III, 9).

When we join him with the voice of exhortation—him who himself pours out his grace inwardly—we assist externally through the ministry of our voice what he accomplishes within through the Spirit.

It follows:

### Verse 3. “To whom have you given counsel? Perhaps to one who has no wisdom.”

To give counsel to a fool is charity; to give it to a wise person is display; but to give counsel to Wisdom itself is perversity.

It follows: “And you have displayed your very great prudence.”

Anyone whose prudence is sound does not have very much prudence, because, in Paul’s words, he “does not desire to be wise beyond what it is necessary to be wise” (Rom. XII, 3). But whoever has very much prudence does not have sound prudence, because when it is extended beyond measure, one turns aside into fault on every side. Those display their prudence as very great who desire to appear wiser than others.

It follows:

### Verse 4. “Whom did you wish to teach? Was it not the one who made the breath?”

Through breath we live; through prudence we are wise. Living, however, comes first for us, and wisdom afterward, because before we can be wise, we must first be made to exist. Therefore the one who gave life undoubtedly also bestowed prudence.

Baldath, however, who believed that blessed Job had been scourged because of guilt, attempted through proud boldness to penetrate the hidden judgment of God, which he ought humbly to have revered. Thus he set himself above the one whose judgment he judged by failing to understand it.

It follows:

### Verse 5. “Behold, the giants groan beneath the waters.”

It was fitting that he first blunt the swelling of earthly wisdom through reproof and afterward pass by instruction to words full of mysteries. The giants may, without objection, be understood either as apostate angels or as certain proud human beings.

Hence the Prophet says:

> “The dead will not live; the giants will not rise” (Isa. XXVI, 14).

And again it is written:

> “The man who strays from the way of instruction will dwell in the assembly of giants” (Prov. XXI, 16).

It is as though he said: “Why should a human being grow proud of knowledge, when an abyss of ignorance weighs down even the most arrogant spirits among the angels?”

If, however, the powerful of this age are signified by the name “giants,” the peoples may be signified by the waters, as John testifies:

> “The waters are the peoples” (Rev. XVII, 15).

It is rightly said against the proud: “Behold, the giants groan beneath the waters.” For all the exalted, while in this life they desire to attain the heights of honors, groan beneath the burdens of the peoples. The higher anyone is raised here, the more heavily he is burdened by cares; and in thought he is subjected to those very peoples over whom he is set in dignity.

It follows: “And those who dwell with them.”

It is as though he said: “Those who are joined to their glory through delight groan together with them.”

It follows:

### Verse 6. “Hell is naked before him, and there is no covering for perdition.”

Paul also says:

> “For all things are naked and open to his eyes” (Heb. IV, 13).

By the names “hell” and “perdition” he signifies the devil and all the companions of his condemnation.

It follows:

### Verse 7. “He stretches out the north over emptiness.”

In sacred speech the devil is often called by the name “north,” because, wishing to constrict the hearts of the nations with the cold of torpor, he said:

> “I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north” (Isa. XIV, 13).

He is stretched out over emptiness because he possesses those hearts that are not filled with the grace of divine love.

It follows: “And he hangs the earth upon nothing.”

What is signified by the name “earth” except the holy Church? When it receives the words of preaching, it produces the fruit of good works. Concerning it Moses says:

> “Let the earth hear from my mouth” (Deut. XXXII, 1).

And what is signified by “nothing” except the Gentiles? Concerning them the Prophet says:

> “All the nations are regarded by him as nothing and emptiness” (Isa. XL, 17).

Therefore the earth is suspended over nothing, which was previously held empty by the north, because the hearts of the Gentiles, previously pressed down by the lukewarmness of the devil, have been filled with the love of God.

Alternatively: Since the hearts of the Jews, empty of faith, are subjected to the devil, he stretches out the north over emptiness. But since there are no merits, as it is said, “You will save them for nothing” (Ps. LIII, 6), the Lord founded the Church over the Gentiles, who have been called “nothing” by the Prophet. Appropriately, he added what follows: “He hangs the earth upon nothing.”

It follows:

### Verse 8. “He binds the waters in his clouds, so that they do not burst forth together below.”

What does he call “water” here except knowledge? What “clouds” except preachers? Hence it is written:

> “Deep water is the word from a man’s mouth, and a flowing torrent, a fountain of wisdom” (Prov. XVIII, 4).

Isaiah says:

> “Who are these who fly like clouds?” (Isa. LX, 8.)

But so that inexperienced hearers may be refreshed not by an inundation of knowledge but by the measured dripping of preaching, God binds the waters in the clouds so that they do not burst forth together below. He moderates the preaching of teachers so that the weakness of their hearers, nourished by the dew of words, may grow strong.

Hence Paul says:

> “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal people, and so forth” (1 Cor. III, 1).

The waters would burst forth together if, before weak hearers, as much knowledge as there is flowed from the speaker’s mouth—if the whole fullness of preaching poured itself out at once, reserving nothing for those who were making progress through it.

It follows:

### Verse 9. “He holds the face of his throne and spreads his cloud over it.”

Knowledge is usually represented by the face. Therefore the face of his throne is held, because in this life we do not recognize the glory of his kingdom to the extent that it exists inwardly. A cloud is rightly said to be spread over it, because the glory of the heavenly kingdom is not seen as it truly is. For:

> “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. IX, 15).

A cloud is therefore sprinkled over us for seeing him, because we are darkened by the obscurity of our own ignorance. Hence the Psalmist rightly says:

> “Darkness is beneath his feet” (Ps. XVII, 10).

He therefore holds the face of his throne because he conceals the power of his majesty from mortals.

But if we understand his throne as the angelic powers, he also presides over them as over a royal seat and holds the face of his throne from us, because as long as we remain in mortal flesh we do not see what and how great those ministries of the angels are. He spreads his cloud over it because, undoubtedly, he lifts our heart to seek, yet acts with such hidden moderation that it is restrained by the very immensity of its inquiry.

Hence it is written:

> “The abyss gave its voice, from the height of its imagination” (Hab. III, 10).

Or, certainly, because we ourselves are the throne of God, he is not improperly said to hold the face of his throne when our knowledge is prevented from advancing to higher things. God is said to sprinkle his cloud over that throne because, while remaining invisible, he exercises hidden judgments over us, so that what we can see may be accomplished in visible things, while the origin of what has been done remains hidden in secret, and we must not know why it is done.

It follows:

### Verse 10. “He surrounded the waters with a boundary, until light and darkness come to an end.”

The Lord surrounds the waters with a boundary because he moderates the knowledge of the human race, so that, until the alternations of changing times pass away, it may not attain perfect knowledge of inward brightness.

If, however, by “light” we understand the righteous and by “darkness” sinners, there is no objection to understanding the passage in the sense already stated, because perfect knowledge of eternity is granted to no one until the course of the righteous and the unjust comes to an end.

It follows:

### Verse 11. “The pillars of heaven tremble and are afraid at his nod.”

What else does he call the pillars of heaven except either the holy angels or the highest preachers of the Church? Upon them, as the whole structure of the spiritual edifice grows in the heavenly places, the entire building has risen, as Scripture elsewhere testifies:

> “Whoever conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God” (Rev. III, 12).

We may also, without impropriety, understand the churches themselves as the pillars of heaven. Hence Solomon says:

> “Wisdom built herself a house and carved out seven pillars” (Prov. IX, 1).

It is as though he said: “Even those who behold and proclaim the rewards of his will are often unable to attain the height of that will. Indeed, the heavenly powers themselves, which behold him without ceasing, tremble in that contemplation; yet their trembling is not one of fear but of wonder.”

It follows:

### Verse 12. “By his strength the seas suddenly gathered together, and by his wisdom he struck down the proud one.”

What else is signified by the name “sea” except the present age, in which the hearts of people who seek earthly things swell with various waves of thought?

But now the seas have been gathered together by his strength, because, when the Lord was incarnate, the discordant hearts of worldly people believe together in harmony.

Who is called “the proud one” here except the one who said:

> “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 14),

and concerning whom God says:

> “He was made so as to fear no one, and he is king over all the sons of pride” (Job XLI, 24–25).

It should be noted that he did not say “his strength,” but “his wisdom struck down the proud one.” For although, as has been said, because of God’s simple nature strength is wisdom, the Lord nevertheless overcame the devil, insofar as he is considered with respect to his appearance, not by force but by reason.

The devil, having supplanted us in that root of our first parent, held the human being under his captivity as though justly, since the human being, created with free will, yielded to him when he offered an unjust suggestion. But when he rashly desired the one in whom he had no claim, he justly lost the one whom he had held as though justly.

He was therefore struck by wisdom, not by force: when he was released to tempt God, he was restrained from possessing the human being, so that he might lose the one who had been under him precisely where he had presumed to contend with the one who is above him.

It follows:

### Verse 13. “His spirit adorned the heavens.”

Which heavens except those concerning which it is written:

> “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. XVIII, 2)?

The Spirit adorned them when he filled them with what we learned through Luke’s account. He says:

> “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a violent, rushing spirit, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And divided tongues appeared to them as if of fire, and one came to rest upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts II, 2–4).

It follows: “And by his hand acting as midwife, the twisting serpent was brought forth.”

Who is called by the name “serpent” except the ancient enemy, slippery and twisting, who spoke with a serpent’s mouth when he deceived the human being? Concerning him the Prophet says:

> “Leviathan, the twisting, barred serpent” (Isa. XXVII, 1).

The hearts of the wicked were the caverns of this slippery creature. Since he drew them toward their own perversity, he rested as though in their dwelling. But when the Lord’s hand acted as midwife, the twisting serpent was expelled from its own caverns, because while divine grace heals us, the ancient enemy who had held us is driven away from us.

As the incarnate Truth says:

> “Now the prince of this world is cast out” (John XII, 31).

From that time onward he possesses the saints not by holding them but by tempting them. Since he does not reign inwardly in them, he fights against them outwardly.

It follows:

### Verse 14. “Behold, these things have been spoken in part of his ways; and when we have scarcely heard a small drop of his words, who will be able to behold the thunder of his greatness?”

What does he call “ways” here except the actions of the Lord? Hence the Lord says through the Prophet:

> “For my ways are not like your ways” (Isa. LV, 8).

In recounting the Lord’s coming, he had related the ways of God only in part, because one was his action when he created us and another when he redeemed us. He therefore diminishes what he says about the Lord’s action by comparison with the final judgment, saying: “Behold, these things have been spoken in part of his ways.”

He also calls it a small drop of his words, because whatever is lofty and terrible that we, placed in this life, know through contemplation of him flows toward us from the immensity of the heavenly mysteries like a thin drop of heavenly liquid.

“And who will be able to behold the thunder of his greatness?” It is as though he plainly said: “If we scarcely endure the things worthy of wonder in his humility, with what strength will we endure the resounding and terrible arrival of his majesty?”

The Psalmist David also announces the thunder of his coming, saying:

> “God will come openly; our God, and he will not be silent” (Ps. XLIX, 3).

## Book Eighteen

[Col. 0317]

## Chapter 27

### Verse 1. “Job continued, taking up his parable, and said:”

This verse clearly shows how mystically the sayings of this most holy man were uttered, since he is said to have taken up a parable—that is, a likeness—although he speaks of nothing inferior by comparison or likeness. Everything must therefore be referred to that likeness by which the Church is figuratively signified. At the very beginning of his speech the sayings are plainly expressed, but they are entangled in the obscurities that follow.

It follows:

### Verse 2

“God lives, who has taken away my judgment, and the Almighty, who has brought my soul into bitterness.”

By these words blessed Job both recounts what concerns himself and signifies the afflicted times of the Church, in which she is pressed by the manifest obstinacy of unbelievers and troubled by the bitterness of persecution. For the Church is accustomed to be tested by adversaries in two ways: either to suffer persecution through words or through swords. Here, however, he speaks of that persecution in which she is assailed not by swords but by false assertions.

Thus the holy man, bearing the figure of the holy Church, confesses that God exists when he says, “God lives.” But to show that God cares for human affairs, he adds: “Who has taken away my judgment, and brought my soul into bitterness.” He testifies that what he suffers does not happen by chance but by God’s ordering of all things; he does not attribute the power of his bitterness to his tempter, but to its author. It follows:

### Verses 3–4

“For as long as breath remains in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils, my lips shall not speak iniquity, nor shall my tongue meditate deceit.”

What he first called “iniquity,” he later repeats as “deceit.” For every deceit is iniquity, and every iniquity is deceit, because whatever differs from the truth plainly departs from righteousness.

There is, however, a great difference between what he says about speaking and what he subsequently adds about meditating. Sometimes it is worse to meditate deceit than to speak it. Speaking is often the result of haste, whereas meditating indicates deliberate wickedness, although sometimes a kind of deceit may be a lighter fault when someone lies through precipitancy.

But because it is written, “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11), and, “You will destroy those who speak lies” (Ps. 5:7), perfect men flee even this kind of deceit with the greatest care, so that no one’s life may be defended through their falsehood, nor may they harm their own souls while striving to spare another’s flesh. It follows:

### Verse 5

“Far be it from me to judge you righteous; until I die, I will not depart from my innocence.”

He would indeed depart from innocence if he judged good what was evil, as Solomon bears witness when he says: “He who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the righteous are both abominable before God” (Prov. 17:15).

There are some who, when they exalt people’s evil deeds with praise, increase what they ought to have rebuked. Hence it is said through the prophet: “Woe to those who sew little cushions under every elbow of the hand and make pillows under the head of people of every age” (Ezek. 33:16). It follows:

### Verse 6

“I have begun to hold fast to my justification; I will not abandon it.”

He would abandon the justification he had begun if he turned aside to praise sinners. It follows:

“For my heart does not reproach me throughout all my life.”

It is as though he plainly says: “I ought not to be dragged into guilt on your account, since I have feared to sin in my own affairs.”

It should be understood that whenever anyone departs from the Lord’s commandments in action, he is reproved and confounded in his heart whenever he hears them, because he is reminded of what he has not done. For in whatever he recognizes that he has gone astray, his own conscience secretly accuses him.

Hence the prophet David prays, saying: “Then I shall not be confounded when I look upon all your commandments” (Ps. 118:6). Everyone is gravely confounded when, whether by reading or by hearing, he looks upon God’s commandments, which he despised in his life.

Hence John says: “If our heart does not reproach us, we have confidence toward God” (1 John 3:21). And: “Whatever we ask, we shall receive” (John 13:14). It is as though he said: “If we do what he commands, we obtain what we ask.” For these two things necessarily correspond with one another before God: prayer must be supported by action, and action by prayer.

One may therefore ask how he denies that his heart reproves him, when earlier he accuses himself of having sinned, saying: “I have sinned; what shall I do for you, O guardian of mankind?” Or again: “If I wished to justify myself, my mouth would condemn me.”

But it should be understood that there are sins which the righteous can avoid, and there are some which even the righteous cannot avoid. The mind of the righteous, although free from perverse action, nevertheless sometimes falls into perverse thought. It therefore falls into sin, because at least in thought it turns aside; yet it has no cause for later reproaching itself with tears, because it restores itself before it falls through consent. It follows:

### Verse 7

“Let my enemy be as the wicked, and my adversary as the unjust.”

In sacred speech, “as” and “like” are not always used to express similarity but sometimes truth. Thus it is said: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father” (John 1:14). Here too, “as” and “like” seem to be used more for affirmation than for comparison.

There is sometimes this difference between “wicked” and “unjust”: every wicked person is unjust, but not everyone who is unjust is wicked. “Wicked” is used of an unbeliever, that is, one alienated from religious devotion; “unjust” is said of one who departs from righteousness through the perversity of his actions, even if he perhaps bears the name of the Christian faith.

Blessed Job, therefore, speaking typologically as the holy Church, confesses that he has as an enemy one who contradicts right faith, since he endures such people. But because he suffers others, who are inwardly placed under the pretext of faith, persisting in evil works, he denounces his adversary as unjust [or: testifies that his adversary is unjust].

If, however, we should understand “as” and “like” more strictly as expressions of similarity, then the holy Church marks as resembling the wicked those whom she tolerates within herself while they live according to the flesh. The enemy is within who affirms himself faithful in words but denies it in his conduct. It follows:

### Verse 8

“For what is the hope of the hypocrite, if he greedily seizes, and God does not deliver his soul?”

The hypocrite, who in Latin is called a *simulator*, does not desire to be righteous but to appear righteous. Therefore he is a greedy plunderer: while he acts wickedly, he desires to be honored for holiness; he seizes the praise belonging to another’s life, while, because he loves present things, he scarcely hopes for future ones. It follows:

### Verse 9

“Will God hear his cry when distress comes upon him?”

The Lord does not hear his cry in the time of distress because, in the time of tranquility, he himself does not hear the Lord crying out in his commandments. For it is written: “He who turns his ear away so as not to hear the law—his prayer shall be accursed” (Prov. 28:9).

Hence the Lord says: “At the end the foolish virgins come, saying, ‘Lord, Lord, open to us’” (Matt. 25:11). And the answer is given to them: “Amen, amen, I say to you, I do not know you.” It follows:

### Verse 10

“Or can he take delight in the Almighty?”

One who is overcome by love of earthly things can in no way take delight in God. The soul can never exist without delight. It delights either in things below or in things above. The more intensely it is exercised in striving toward the highest things, the more greatly it grows dull with disgust toward the lowest; and the more fiercely it burns with care for the lowest things, the more it grows cold toward the highest through damnable sluggishness. For the two cannot be loved simultaneously and equally.

The hypocrite, therefore, cannot delight in God, because heavenly desires do not arise in his mind, which the thorns of earthly love press down. Of this it is plainly added:

“And call upon the Lord at all times.”

The hypocrite calls upon God when the distress of earthly things constrains him. But when he finds in this world the fulfillment of the happiness he sought, he does not seek the author who granted that very happiness. It follows:

### Verse 11

“I will teach you by the hand of God what the Almighty possesses, and I will not conceal it.”

Blessed Job speaks in his own words in such a way as to signify something concerning us. For the holy Church, teaching insofar as it is useful to know, conceals nothing of the truth.

Because the Son is called the hand of God—for “all things were made through him” (John 1:3)—he declares that he will teach by the hand of God those whom he saw remaining foolish in their own wisdom. It is as though he plainly says: “Of myself I know nothing; whatever I perceive from the truth, I grasp through the generosity of that same truth.” It follows:

### Verse 12

“Behold, you all know; why then do you speak vainly without cause?”

It is written: “The servant who knew his master’s will and did not act according to his will shall be beaten with many blows. But the one who did not know and did what deserved blows shall be beaten with few” (Luke 12:47). Again it is written: “Therefore, for one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin” (James 4:17).

Thus, to increase the weight of their guilt, the holy Church declares that her enemies both know what they ought to follow and refuse to follow what they know. It follows:

### Verse 13

“This is the portion of the impious man with God, and the inheritance of violent men which they will receive from the Almighty.”

He immediately indicates what this portion and inheritance are when he adds:

### Verse 14

“If his sons are multiplied, they shall be for the sword, and his descendants shall not be satisfied with bread.”

It is not inappropriate to call heretics “the impious,” since through the error of their perverse doctrine they are alienated from knowledge of the truth. In the following words he also calls them “the violent,” since they violently strive to bend the statements of Scripture, which contain right doctrines, toward a perverse interpretation.

They are therefore violent—not necessarily against people’s possessions, but certainly against the meaning of the commandments. The sons of the violent are the followers of heretics: by consenting to their error, they are, as it were, generated from their preaching.

“But if they are multiplied, they shall be for the sword,” because although they now increase in immense numbers through a destructive freedom, they will nevertheless be struck by the judgment of the coming Judge. Hence the Lord says through Moses: “My sword shall devour flesh” (Deut. 32:42).

The descendants of heretics are those born from the preaching of erring sons. Bread does not satisfy them, because while they seek to understand more in the nourishment of the sacred word than they are capable of grasping, they remain perpetually famished for knowledge of the truth. It follows:

### Verse 15

“Those who remain of him shall be buried in destruction.”

Those left from the people of heretics shall indeed be buried in destruction, because, since they do not return to the light of truth, they are brought down into eternal punishment by their earthly understanding. It follows:

“And his widows shall not weep.”

Whom should we understand as his widows except the peoples subject to him, who are happily deprived of him by his death? For, as we have often said, when the preacher of error is carried away to eternal punishment, the peoples subject to him often return to the grace of true knowledge.

That perverse preacher presided over these peoples as a husband, because he had been wrongly joined to them and clung to them as a corrupter of their minds. His widows, therefore, do not weep or lament, because through the death of the wicked teacher they find the way of truth, though they had seemed capable of being afflicted by his destruction.

Or certainly the widows do not weep because, remaining in their error, they think their preacher was holy and are comforted by a false hope, lest they mourn. It follows:

### Verses 16–17

“If he heaps up silver like earth and prepares garments like clay, he will indeed prepare them, but the righteous shall wear them, and the innocent shall divide the silver.”

Silver commonly signifies the brightness of sacred speech, as it is said elsewhere: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire” (Ps. 11:7).

Their silver—that is, the speech of heretics—is compared to earth because, in order to know something from sacred Scripture, they labor out of a desire for earthly praise. They also prepare garments like clay, because they weave the testimonies of sacred Scripture, by which they wish to defend themselves, in a loose and defiled manner.

“He will indeed prepare them, but the righteous shall wear them.” The righteous, therefore, will wear the garments that the unrighteous prepared, because the holy man uses those same statements for the truth by which each perverse person strives to display himself as learned against the truth.

“And the innocent shall divide the silver.” To divide the silver innocently means to explain the words of the Lord in small portions and with discernment, and to apply to each person what fittingly corresponds to him.

For what is called silver or garments here is elsewhere called spoil. The Psalmist also testifies to this by comparison, saying: “I shall rejoice over your words, as one who finds great spoil” (Ps. 118:162). It follows:

### Verse 18

“He built his house like a moth, and like a watchman he made a shelter.”

A moth builds a house for itself by corrupting it. No better comparison could have been found for the heretic, who establishes the place of his unbelief only in minds that he has corrupted. He also promises his followers that they will be free from eternal fire.

He promises them the refreshment of eternal rest, but his words have no solidity because they lack the fullness of truth. Hence it is added:

“And like a watchman he made a shelter.”

The watchman’s shelter is not made firm by any foundation but is soon destroyed as time passes. Likewise, the rest promised by heretics is destroyed with time and is nowhere found after this life. It follows:

### Verse 19

“The rich man, when he sleeps, does not take anything away with him; he opens his eyes and finds nothing.”

The Psalmist agrees with this statement when he says: “All those rich in heart were troubled; they slept their sleep, and all the men of wealth found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 75:5).

He would carry his possessions away with him when he died if, while living, he had carried them to himself at the call of the powerful one. For all earthly things that we lose by keeping, we preserve by giving.

But because a human being consists of soul and body, when sleep is attributed to one, the wakefulness of the other is indicated. When the body falls asleep in death, the soul then wakes to true knowledge.

The rich man therefore sleeps and opens his eyes, because when he dies in the flesh, his soul is compelled to see what he disdained to foresee. He opens his eyes and finds nothing, because there he opens for punishments the eyes that here he kept closed to mercy. He opens his eyes and finds no fruit of compassion, because while he lived he kept them closed to those in need. It follows:

### Verse 20

“Need shall seize him like water; a storm shall oppress him by night.”

Let us now consider the poverty of the burning rich man, whose abundance had been only that of a feaster. For he says: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am being tormented in this flame” (Luke 16:24).

That poverty is not inappropriately compared to water, because that which torments in hell, swallowing up those it receives in the depths, is customarily denoted by the name of a lake. Hence, in the voice of the human race, the prophet says: “My life has fallen into the pit” (Lam. 3:53).

By the name of the storm he signifies the whirlwind of judgment, as the Psalmist also testifies: “Our God will come openly; our God, and he will not be silent” (Ps. 49:3).

Because ignorance of the coming end itself is called night, “a storm shall oppress him by night”—that is, the whirlwind of divine judgment seizes him while he is unaware. It follows:

### Verse 21

“A burning wind carries him away.”

What is called a burning wind here except the evil spirit, who kindles the flames of desires in the heart so that he may drag it toward eternal punishments? The burning wind is therefore said to carry away any perverse person, because the malicious spirit who sets the living on fire for vices drags the dying to torments.

Hence Jeremiah says: “I see a boiling cauldron, and its face is turned from the face of the north” (Jer. 1:13). It follows:

“And like a whirlwind it snatches him from his place.”

The place of the perverse is love of temporal life and pleasure of the flesh. Each person is therefore snatched away from his place like a whirlwind when, terrified by the final day, he is separated from all his delights. Concerning that final day he appropriately adds:

### Verse 22

“And he will send it upon him and will not spare.”

Whenever God corrects a sinner by striking him, he sends the scourge for the purpose of sparing him. But when, by striking, he brings to an end a life that persists in sin, he sends the scourge but does not spare. He who sent the scourge in order to spare sends it at some point so that he may no longer spare.

In this life the Lord strives all the more to spare the more he scourges by waiting. It follows:

“Fleeing from his hand, he shall flee.”

The one who flees from the hand of the one striking is the person who corrects the wickedness of his conduct. Or certainly, because in sacred speech the hand commonly signifies action, he flees from the hand of the one who struck him when, seeing the destruction of the wicked, he abandons the ways of wickedness.

Hence it is further added:

### Verse 23

“He clenches; he will clench his hands over him.”  
[Note: [Col. 0323D] This verb is absent from the biblical books.]

To clench the hands is to strengthen the works of one’s life in righteousness. Hence Paul also says: “Raise your drooping hands and your weakened knees” (Heb. 12:12).

When people behold another’s destruction, they are recalled to their own hearts so that they may consider their own fate; and from the place where one person is led to torments, another is delivered from torment.

He therefore clenches his hands over him because he sees in another’s punishment what he should fear, and, when he observes the sinner struck down in this way, he restrains his weakened works with the strength of righteousness. Hence it is written: “The righteous shall rejoice when he sees vengeance” (Ps. 57:11), and so forth.

It follows:

“And he will hiss at him, looking upon his place.”

What is expressed by hissing except the intention of astonishment? If, however, another meaning is sought in the hissing, then, when the sinner dies, those who behold his destruction purse their lips in a hiss as they turn toward spiritual words from the things they had despised. Thus they begin to believe and preach what previously they did not believe when they saw the wicked flourishing.

Hence Solomon says: “When the pestilent man is punished, the simple will become wiser” (Prov. 21:11).

After the holy man has sufficiently described the punishments of the powerful who are exalted in the world, he again turns his words toward the pride of heretics, who are exalted in eloquence. For it follows:

## Chapter 28

### Verse 1

“Silver has the beginnings of its veins, and gold has a place where it is smelted.”

Silver commonly signifies eloquence, and gold the brightness of the wisdom of life. Because heretics are so proud of the brilliance of their eloquence that they are not made firm by the authority of the sacred books—and because these books are, as it were, veins of silver for our speech, since we draw the origin of our language from them—he recalls them to the pages of sacred authority, so that, if they truly desire to speak, they may take from there what they should say. Thus he says:

“Silver has the beginnings of its veins.”

It is as though he plainly says: “Whoever prepares himself for words of true preaching must take the origins of his arguments from the sacred pages.”

The true wisdom of the faithful, for whom the universal Church is the place, suffers tribulation from you who persecute it, but it is cleansed by the fire of your persecution from all the filth of sins. Hence it is written: “Gold and silver are tested in fire, but acceptable people in the furnace of humiliation” (Sir. 2:5).

This passage may also fittingly be understood as rebuking the heretics for their foolish passion. For they often suffer much for the name of Jesus Christ our Lord and Redeemer, and hope that through these sufferings they will become his martyrs. To them the voice of the holy men now says:

“Gold has a place where it is smelted.”

For, as has already been said before us: “Whoever suffers outside the unity of the Church may suffer punishments, but cannot become a martyr,” because “gold has a place where it is smelted.”

What do you say to this, heretics? You wish to be smelted through affliction of the flesh, or even through martyrdom, but you do not know the place where you ought to be smelted. It follows:

### Verse 2

“Iron is taken from the earth.”

Heretics commonly boast of their exaltation over us on account of their own righteousness, and vaunt their works through the inflation of ostentation. As we have said, they accuse us either of being or of having been unjust.

Against them, therefore, the holy man speaks through humble confession and truthful defense, saying: “Iron is taken from the earth.”

It is as though he plainly says: “Those who are strong, who become iron with the sharpest swords of their tongues in this battle for the defense of the faith, were once earth in lowly actions.”

For it was said to the sinner: “You are earth, and to earth you shall return” (Gen. 3:20). But iron is taken from the earth when a strong defender of the Church is separated by his conduct from the earth that he previously held.

Therefore, no one should despise in him whatever he was, since he has now received the condition that he was not before. It follows:

“And the stone, loosened by heat, is turned into bronze.”

The stone is loosened by heat when a hard heart, cold from the fire of divine love, is touched by that same fire of divine love and melts in the fervor of the spirit, so that it burns with the heat of its desires for the life to come, though previously it remained insensible even while hearing of it.

Through that heat it is softened toward love and made effective for action, so that, just as it had previously been hard in its love of the world, it may afterward exercise strength in the love of God. What it previously refused to hear, it begins to believe and preach. It follows:

### Verse 3

“He has set a time for darkness, and he himself considers the end of all things.”

“He has set a time for darkness”—that is, he has set a limit for the wicked, so that they cease to be wicked. Hence the Apostle says to them: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:10).

To other disciples the same outstanding teacher likewise said: “The night has passed, and the day has drawn near. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. Let us walk honorably as in the day” (Rom. 13:12–13).

By the phrase “all things” he wished the elect and the reprobate to be included. God does good things and orders them; he does not make evil things, but he himself arranges the evil done by the wicked so that it may not occur disorderly. Thus he considers the end of all things, patiently tolerates everything, and observes the end of the elect: how they are changed from evil to good.

He also observes the end of the reprobate: how they are dragged from evil work to the punishment they deserve. It follows:

### Verse 4

“He divides the stone of darkness and the shadow of death from the people who wander.”

What was harder than the unbelief of the Jews? What people, who refused to see the author of life when he came in the end—the one whom they had foretold through the prophet—was the stone of darkness? He was hard through cruelty and clouded through unbelief.

He is also called by another name, “the shadow of death.” A shadow is expressed through wings, whose outlines correspond to the thing from which it is cast. Who, however, is called by the name “death” except the devil? Concerning him it is said through a certain representation of his minister: “His name was Death” (Rev. 6:8).

That people became his shadow because, by following his iniquity, they impressed his image upon themselves.

What else is called by the name “torrent” except the fire proceeding from the sight of the terrifying Judge through the final examination, dividing the elect from the reprobate? Hence the prophet says: “A swift fiery river came forth from before him” (Dan. 7:10).

But what people wander in this world except those who, hastening toward the lot of the elect, know that they have their homeland in heaven? They hope all the more to find their own things there insofar as here they consider everything that passes away to be alien to them. Hence Paul says: “While we are in this body, we are exiles from the Lord” (2 Cor. 5:6).

Perhaps the name “torrent” may also be understood as the very irrigation of holy preaching, according to what is said through Solomon: “The eye that mocks a father and despises the birth of his mother—the ravens of the torrents shall pluck it out” (Prov. 30:17).

The preaching of the saints abandons the hardened minds of the reprobate and turns toward the devout hearts of the humble. It follows:

“And those whom the foot of the needy man has forgotten, and the impassable ones.”

Who else is understood here as the needy man except the one of whom Paul says: “For your sake he became poor, though he was rich” (2 Cor. 8:6)?

The feet of this needy man were the holy preachers, through whose progress and presence he went around the gentiles and traversed the whole world.

But the foot of the needy man forgot those who had become the shadow of death and the stone of darkness. At the very beginning of the Church’s birth, when the holy apostles wished to preach the kingdom of heaven to Judea, they saw that they accomplished nothing at all among them and turned to preach to the gentiles, as they themselves say in the Acts: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first. But since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

He rightly also calls them “impassable,” because, hardened by their unbelief, they refused to provide a way to the heart for the words of life. It follows:

### Verse 5

“The earth from which bread came forth in its place was overturned by fire.”

Judea was accustomed to give bread because it proclaimed the words of the law. But this earth was overturned by fire in its place, because, seeing the signs of the faithful, it burned itself with the burden of envy.

Since envy ordinarily arises from pride, it perished by fire in its place: it burned with envy because it did not abandon pride. It follows:

### Verse 6

“Her stones are the place of sapphire, and its clods are gold.”

What should we understand by stones here except the minds of the holy and strong? In sacred Scripture, stones are sometimes understood in an evil sense and sometimes in a good one.

Hence John [Luke] says: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Luke 3:8). Hence Peter says: “You also, like living stones, are being built into spiritual houses” (1 Pet. 2:5).

The sapphire stone has the color of the sky. Since holy souls who lived a heavenly life were never absent from Judea, it is said: “Her stones are the place of sapphire.”

And to show with how great a brightness of life and wisdom it shone through faith, he adds: “And its clods are gold.”

What are signified by clods except collections of the individual orders and multitudes? Clods are compacted from moisture and dust. All those, therefore, who, watered with the dew of grace, confessed with true knowledge that they were dust under the sentence of death, while shining through the power of life, lay there like golden clods.

This earth possessed clods in the prophets, clods in the teachers, and clods in the ancient Fathers, who held together in unity of confession and conduct through a great infusion of grace. It follows:

### Verse 7

“The bird does not know the path, nor has the vulture’s eye seen it.”

Who is signified here by the name “bird” except the one who, by ascending into the heavens, carried upward the fleshly body he had assumed?

He is appropriately also described by the name “vulture.” Remaining in the height of his divinity, he saw, as if in a lofty flight, the corpse of our mortality below, and lowered himself from the heavenly places to what was lowest.

He deigned to become human for our sake. In seeking a dead animal, he found death among us, though with himself he was immortal.

But the eye of this vulture was the purpose of our resurrection, because, having died for three days, he freed us from eternal death.

That faithless people of Judea therefore saw him as mortal, but paid no attention to the fact that by his death he would destroy our death. It saw the vulture but did not see the vulture’s eye. Since it refused to consider the paths of his humility by which he raised us to the heights, it did not know the path of the bird.

It did not take care to consider that his humility would raise us to heaven, and that the purpose of his death would restore us to life. It follows:

### Verse 8

“The sons of merchants have not trodden it, nor has the lioness passed through it.”

In all the Latin books we find *institores*—“merchants”—but in the Greek books we find “traders.” Whom are the merchants called here except the holy prophets, who took care through prophecy to instruct the ways of the Synagogue toward faith?

Their sons are called the holy apostles. They were generated for the same faith through the preaching of the prophets, so that they might believe that God had become human.

The sons of the merchants would have trodden it if the holy preachers had pressed down the vices of that same Synagogue with the heel of virtue.

But if we understand these merchants as the preachers of the holy Church, nothing prevents us from understanding their sons as pastors and teachers who followed the way of the apostles. They did not tread upon the Synagogue because, when their fathers—that is, the apostles—were rejected by it, they too ceased to be associated with its calling.

The lioness did not pass through that Synagogue because the holy Church, devoted to gathering the gentiles, no longer occupied itself at length with that Jewish people.

The Church is rightly called a lioness because, through the mouth of holy preaching, she kills those who live wickedly in vices. The Church therefore passed through the Synagogue, but did not pass through it, because she snatched only a few from it into the faith. It follows:

### Verse 9

“He stretched out his hand to the flint; he overturned the mountains from their roots.”

He stretched out his hand to the flint because he sent the arm of his preaching toward the hardness of the gentiles. Hence blessed Job, foreseeing that the history of his passion would be made known to the gentiles, says: “Let these things be written with an iron stylus on a lead tablet, or certainly let them be carved in flint” (Job 19:24).

What should we understand by mountains here except the powerful of this world, who swell with pride over earthly substance? Concerning them the Psalmist says: “Touch the mountains, and they shall smoke” (Ps. 143:5).

But the mountains were overturned from their roots because, when the holy Church preached, the powerful of this world fell from their inmost thoughts into the worship of almighty God. It follows:

### Verse 10

“In the rocks he cut out channels”—that is, in the hard hearts of the gentiles he opened rivers of preaching,

as it is also said through the prophet concerning the watering of the aridity of the gentiles: “He made the desert into pools of water, and the dry land into outlets of water.”

It follows:

“And his eye saw every precious thing.”

It should be understood with the greatest care that each soul becomes more precious before God’s eyes insofar as it becomes more despised in its own eyes for the sake of the love of truth.

In sacred Scripture, “to see” God sometimes means “to choose.” He saw what was precious when, by the illumination of his grace, he regarded the human soul that had become wise after despising itself. Concerning this soul the prophet says: “If you separate what is precious from what is vile, you shall be as my mouth” (Jer. 15:19). It follows:

### Verse 11

“He searched out the depths of the rivers, and brought hidden things to light.”

What else are the rivers called here except the words of the ancient Fathers?

Judea held the appearance of these rivers while retaining only the surface of the letter and not knowing their depths. But when the Lord came, we seek their inner spiritual meanings and examine their depths.

The Lord is said to do this himself because we are able to do it through his gift. Through us, therefore, who follow not the letter that kills but the spirit that gives life (2 Cor. 3:6), the Lord searches out the depths of the rivers and brings hidden things to light, because spiritual exposition now illuminates the words of the law, which an exceedingly obscure history had concealed.

Hence Truth, speaking in parables in the Gospel, commands the disciples, saying: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the housetops” (Matt. 10:27). It follows:

### Verses 12–13

“But where is wisdom found, and where is the place of understanding? Man does not know its price.”

What wisdom, then, does the holy man contemplate except that of which the Apostle Paul says: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24)?

Concerning it Solomon says: “Wisdom has built herself a house” (Prov. 9:1), and the Psalmist says: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103:24).

Man does not know the price of this wisdom because he finds nothing worthy of its valuation. It is not that this price is both said to exist and said to be unknown; rather, it is said to be unknown because it is lacking. This is the manner of speech in which someone pressed by difficulties, when he finds no remedy of assistance, is accustomed to confess that he does not know what to do.

To fail to know the price of this wisdom therefore means not to find the worthy merit of works by which one may receive it. For we give a price in order that, in exchange for it, we may possess the thing we desire.

But what have we not given so that we might deserve to receive this wisdom, which is Christ? We were redeemed by grace. Hence Paul says: “While we were still sinners, at the appointed time Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom. 5:8–9).

It follows:

“Nor will it be found in the land of those who live in pleasure.”

What is signified by the name “land” here except the human soul? Concerning it the Psalmist says: “My soul is like a land without water for you” (Ps. 142:6).

This wisdom cannot be found in the land of those who live in pleasure, because whoever is still nourished by the pleasures of this life is separated from understanding eternal wisdom.

For if he truly possessed wisdom, expelled from inward joys he would mourn over the blindness of his exile in the place where he fell. Hence Solomon says: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccl. 1:18). It follows:

### VERSE 14

“**The abyss says: It is not with me.**” What else does he call the abyss here but human hearts, which are fluid through their falling and dark with the gloom of duplicity? This abyss plainly professes that this wisdom is not within it, because an unrighteous mind, while carnally desiring to be wise, thereby shows itself foolish with respect to spiritual things. For, as Paul testifies, “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” [Col. 0328C] (1 Cor. 3:19). The more anyone strives to appear wise outwardly, the more foolish he becomes inwardly.

It follows: “**And the sea says: It is not with me.**” What is signified by the name “sea” except the bitter unrest of worldly minds? While they attack one another with hostilities, they collide like waves opposing one another. The life of worldly people is rightly called the sea, because, while it is agitated by the stormy movements of its actions, it is separated from the repose and stability of inward wisdom. In opposition to this the prophet rightly says: “Upon whom does my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2). It follows:

### VERSE 15

“**Refined gold will not be given in exchange for it.**” What else is designated by refined gold except the holy angels [Col. 0328D], who are rightly called both gold and refined gold? Gold, because they shine with the splendor of righteousness; refined gold, because they have never had any taint of sin. Righteous human beings, however, so long as they live mortally in this corruptible flesh, can indeed be gold, but they cannot at all be refined gold, because “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation depresses the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9:15). For although in this life they shine with the great splendor of righteousness, they are by no means wholly free from the filth of sins, as the apostle John attests, saying: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

But because no angel was to be sent as the redeemer of the human race on account of this wisdom, lest anyone place his hope in those angels whom we have learned often to have appeared in aid of human beings, it is said: “Refined gold will not be given in exchange for it.”

It follows: “**Nor will silver be weighed in exchange for it.**” Since divine utterances are often signified by silver, the writers of that same utterance may also be understood by the word “silver,” for their life shone among human crowds with the light of virtues. But because the law could judge sins, not remove them, neither any of the ancient Fathers nor the lawgiver Moses became the redeemer of the human race. Silver, therefore, is not weighed in exchange for this wisdom, because although any of the saints could have been holy, in comparison with the Only-Begotten Son each is reckoned to have possessed no merit. It follows:

[Col. 0329B]

### VERSE 16

“**It will not be compared with dyed colors from India.**” What is understood by India, which sends forth a black people, except this world, in which human life is born darkened by guilt? The dyed colors of India are the wise people of this world, who, although foul through unbelief and often through their conduct, are nevertheless darkened before human eyes by a superimposed color of outward respectability. But the coeternal wisdom of God is not compared with dyed colors from India, because whoever truly understands it recognizes how far removed from it are all those whom the world has honored as wise.

It follows: “**Nor with the most precious sardonyx or sapphire.**” The sardonyx resembles red earth, while sapphire has the appearance of the sky. Thus, in the sardonyx, human beings may be designated through red earth, and in the sapphire angels through the vision of the sky. Since the sardonyx has the appearance of red earth, it not improperly signifies the human being, because Adam, who was created first, is called “red earth” in the Latin language.

What, then, does it mean that this wisdom is not compared with the sardonyx or sapphire, except that he who is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24), namely, “the mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5), so greatly surpasses all things that neither the first human beings on earth nor the angels in heaven can be compared with him? Hence the Psalmist says: “Who among the clouds can be equaled with the Lord, or who will be like God among the sons of God?” [Col. 0329D] (Ps. 88:7).

The Fathers of the Old Testament may also be expressed by the sardonyx stone, and the preachers of the New Testament by the sapphire. It is as though he plainly says: He who is seen as a human being among human beings is equaled by no one, either among the ancient Fathers or among the new, because from his divinity he possesses what no one has in common with him in his humanity. It follows:

### VERSE 17

“**Gold or glass will not be equaled with it.**” We know that the metal gold shines with greater brilliance than all other metals; the nature of glass, however, is that, while seen from outside, it shines within with pure transparency. What else, then, do we understand by gold or glass except that heavenly homeland, that society of blessed citizens [Col. 0330A], whose hearts both shine toward one another with splendor and gleam with purity? John had seen this in the Apocalypse when he said: “The structure of its wall was of jasper, and the city itself was pure gold, like pure glass” (Rev. 21:18). It follows:

### VERSE 18

“**Nor will vessels of gold, lofty and exalted, be exchanged for it.**” Elijah was a lofty vessel of gold; Jeremiah was a lofty vessel of gold; the earlier Fathers were lofty and exalted vessels of gold. But this wisdom of God appeared in the flesh in order to redeem us from carnal conduct, and whoever did not truly recognize it thought that Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and human beings, was one of the prophets. The Church, however, did not exchange lofty and exalted vessels of gold for this wisdom, because it believed that Christ the Son of God was not one of the prophets, but the Lord of the prophets.

It follows: “**Nor will they be remembered in comparison with it.**” All the elect saints of the heavenly homeland are indeed holy and righteous, but through participation in wisdom, not through comparison with it.
