For what are human beings when compared with God? Light, however, is called wisdom, and servants of wisdom are also customarily called light. But wisdom is illuminating light, while they are illuminated light, as it is written: “That was the true light which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9). To them alone it is said: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14).

It follows: “**Wisdom is drawn from hidden things.**” Wisdom is drawn from hidden things because, being invisible, it is found only invisibly. It is also rightly said to be drawn, because just as we draw in breath so that the body may live, so the spirit of wisdom is drawn from the innermost places so that the soul may endure in life. Hence the Psalmist says: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Ps. 118:131). It follows:

### VERSE 19

“**Ethiopia’s topaz will not be equaled with it.**” What do we understand by Ethiopia except the present world? Through the blackness of its color it designates the sinner polluted by the foulness of his deeds. At times, however, the name Ethiopia is used specifically to designate the Gentiles, previously black through the sins of unbelief, whom the prophet Habakkuk saw terrified with fear at the coming of the Lord, and said: “The tents of the Ethiopians will tremble; the tents of the land of Midian” (Hab. 3:7).

Topaz is a precious stone, and because in Greek *pan* means “everything,” since it shines with every kind of radiance, topaz is called as though it were *pan-topazion*—“all-shining.” When the Gentiles were converted and came to believe in God, many among them were enriched by the gift of the Spirit so that they shone, as it were, with many colors—that is, with many lofty virtues.

It is as though it were said to them: However full of every virtue any of the saints may be, nevertheless, gathered from the blackness of the world, he cannot be equaled with him of whom it was said: “The holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

It follows: “**Nor will the purest dyes be combined with it.**” Those who are truly humble and truly holy are called the purest dyes. They know that they do not possess the appearance of virtue from themselves, but that they hold it from the gift of the grace that comes upon them [Col. 0331A]. They would not be dyed if they had possessed holiness by nature; but they are the purest dyes because they humbly preserve within themselves the resplendent grace of virtue that they have received.

It must be considered with the greatest care what is here sought from the holy man: from where wisdom comes. For it comes from the one from whom it originated. But because it is born from the invisible and coeternal Father, its way is hidden. Hence the prophet says: “Who will recount his generation?” (Isa. 53:8).

The place of its understanding, however, is the human mind, which this wisdom of God makes holy when it fills it. Therefore, because the one from whom it proceeded is invisible, and because it is uncertain in whose mind it comes to rest when understood, it is rightly said now:

### VERSE 20

“**From where, then, will wisdom come, and where is the place of understanding?**” [Col. 0331B]

But what immediately follows is very remarkable:

### VERSE 21

“**It is hidden from the eyes of all living things.**” If wisdom, which is God, were hidden from the eyes of all living things, then certainly none of the saints would have seen it. Yet I hear John agreeing with this statement when he says: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18).

But according to the statement of blessed Job, wisdom, which is God, is hidden from the eyes of all living things because, for those established in this mortal flesh, it could be seen through certain circumscribed images, but it cannot be seen through the uncircumscribed light of eternity. If, however, some who live in this corruptible flesh can see the eternal splendor of God through a certain sharpness of contempt, while nevertheless growing through immeasurable virtue, this too does not conflict with blessed Job’s statement, which says: “It is hidden from the eyes of all living things.”

Whoever sees this wisdom, which is God, dies utterly to this life, so that he may no longer be held by love of it. No one sees it who still lives carnally. Hence it is said to Moses: “A human being shall not see me and live” (Exod. 33:20).

## BOOK NINETEEN

[Col. 0331]

[Col. 0331B]

### VERSE 21

“**It is also hidden from the birds of heaven.**” In sacred Scripture, birds are sometimes understood in an evil sense, sometimes in a good one. For by birds, the powers of the air opposed to the pursuits of the good may sometimes be designated. On the other hand, birds are customarily placed in a good sense: “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, which a man took and put in his garden; and it grew and became a great tree, and the birds of heaven rested in its branches” (Luke 13:19).

Therefore, after it had been said in this passage concerning wisdom, “It is hidden from the eyes of all living things,” it is rightly added: “It is also hidden from the birds of heaven,” because those established in this corruptible flesh do not, even by living, penetrate its power of nature—not even those who now fly through the merit of holy contemplation. Appropriately it is added:

### VERSE 22

“**Perdition and death said: We have heard the report of it with our ears.**” What are designated by the names “perdition” and “death” except evil spirits, who became the inventors of death and perdition? To see the coeternal wisdom of God perfectly is the same as possessing it. Therefore the wicked spirits do not see this wisdom, because, repelled through pride, they could not possess it. They closed the eyes of their hearts to its light, resisting while its rays poured over them.

Thus, for evil spirits to have heard the report of wisdom means that they did not see that same wisdom: they recognized its power from its virtue, yet refused to remain humbly under it. Hence the Truth says: “He was a murderer from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44). It follows:

### VERSE 23

“**God understands its way, and he himself knows its place.**” The place of wisdom is the Father. The place of wisdom is spoken of, as Wisdom herself testifies: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10–11).

Wisdom therefore has a way in one respect and a place in another: a way through the passage of humanity, but a place through the state of divinity. It is as though he plainly said: Human thought does not know either when Wisdom will come to human beings through the flesh or how, while invisible with the Father, it continues to exist even when it has appeared outwardly.

This can also be understood in another way. For her way may suitably be understood as the very fact that she comes to the heart and pours herself inwardly into us. Her place, however, becomes the heart, to which she comes and in which she remains. Of this way of hers it is also said: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord” (John 1:23).

And because it is uncertain to human beings either in whose heart she comes or in whom, after coming, she remains and rests, it is rightly said now: “God understands its way, and he himself knows its place.” For it belongs to divine vision alone to see either by what means the understanding of wisdom, once received, does not admit destructive thoughts.

It follows:

### VERSE 24

“**For he himself looks upon the ends of the world, and he sees all that is under heaven.**” To look upon is proper to God when he restores to his grace those things that had been lost and ruined. Hence it is written: “The king who sits on the throne of his judgment dispels every evil by his gaze” (Prov. 20:8). It follows:

### VERSE 25

“**He who made a weight for the winds.**” In sacred Scripture, souls are customarily designated by the speed and subtlety of winds, as the Psalmist says of God: “He walks upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. 17:11)—that is, he surpasses the powers of souls.

He therefore made a weight for the winds because, while heavenly wisdom fills souls, it makes them weighty, clothed with maturity—not with the heaviness of which it is said: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Ps. 4:3). For it is one thing to be weighty through deliberation and another through sin; one thing to be weighty through steadfastness and another through guilt.

Or certainly, to make a weight for the winds means to temper, by mingling weakness with it, the glory arising here from virtues that has been granted to the elect.

It follows: “**And he weighed the waters by measure.**” In sacred Scripture, waters sometimes signify the Holy Spirit, as in the saying: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38). At times they signify corrupt knowledge, at times sacred knowledge, as in: “He gave them to drink of the water of saving wisdom” (Sir. 15:3). They signify corrupt knowledge in Solomon’s saying: “Stolen waters are sweeter” (Prov. 9:17) [Col. 0333B]. At times they signify tribulation, as in: “Save me, God, for the waters have entered my soul” (Ps. 68:2). At times they signify flowing peoples, as in the Apocalypse: “The waters are peoples” (Rev. 17:15). At times they signify the minds of those who follow the faith, as the prophet says: “Blessed are you who sow beside all waters” (Isa. 32:20).

What, then, are signified by the name “waters” in this passage except the hearts of the elect, which through the understanding of wisdom have already received the hearing of the heavenly voice? Of these it is rightly said: “He weighed the waters by measure,” because the saints themselves, who are lifted up by the Spirit and carried to the heights, are restrained by certain temptations so long as they are in this life, lest they become proud through exaltation. Thus they cannot advance as far as they wish. But so that they may not be lifted up by pride, a certain measure of their virtues is present within them.

It follows:

### VERSES 26–27

“**When he established a law for the rains, and a way for the resounding storms; then he saw it and recounted it, prepared it, and investigated it.**” The sayings of preachers are customarily signified by rains. Hence Moses says: “Let my speech be awaited like rain” (Deut. 32:2). Their words are rains when they persuade gently; but when they thunder terrifying things concerning the coming judgment, they are storms.

It should be noted that a law is established for the rains so that a way may be opened for the resounding storms. A law has indeed been established for preachers themselves: they must fulfill by their manner of living what they hasten to persuade others to do by their speech. For the authority of speech is lost when the voice is not supported by conduct.

He established a way for the resounding storms when he gave his holy preachers access to the hearts of human beings struck with fear of the coming judgment. In the customary language of sacred speech, God is said to see when he causes us to see, just as the Lord says to the righteous man: “Now I know that you fear God” (Gen. 22:12). And the Israelites are warned: “The Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love him” (Deut. 13:3)—that is, to make you know.

When, therefore, he established a law for the rains—that is, when he gave the preachers a command to observe—he caused this incarnate wisdom to be seen and recounted by the preachers, and to be prepared and investigated by the hearers. Whoever prepares it for himself prepares it favorably for the way of judgment by living well.

It should also be noted what four things are said about it. For he says: “He saw, recounted, prepared, and investigated.” He saw it because it is appearance; he recounted it because it is word; he prepared it because it is remedy; he investigated it because it is hidden.

It follows:

### VERSE 28

“**And he said to human beings: Behold, the fear of the Lord—that is wisdom; and to depart from evil—that is understanding.**” It is as though he plainly said: Return to yourself, human being; search out the secrets of your heart. If you discover that you fear God, it is entirely clear that you are filled with this wisdom. Even if you cannot yet understand what it is in itself, you already understand for the moment what it is within you. Hence it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:11).

But because the one who truly understands the force of divine fear is the one who guards himself from every evil deed, it is rightly added: “And to depart from evil—that is understanding.”

## CHAPTER TWENTY-NINE

### VERSE 1

“**Job also continued, taking up his parable.**” Since a parable is called a likeness, it is clear that the one who is said to have taken up a parable for speaking expresses mysteries through the form of outward words. When he recounts his own experiences, he announces what is destined to happen to the holy Church; and through what he himself suffers, he indicates what the Church will suffer.

But all the elect who, at the end of the world, will be caught up in that tribulation during the time of Antichrist remember the times in which the Church now holds the peace of faith and crushes the proud necks of heretics—not by the power of high rank, but by the yoke of reason. Through the voice of blessed Job she says:

### VERSE 2

“**Who will grant me that I might be as in former months?**” Since a fixed number of days is called a month, what is signified by the name “months” except collections of souls? When days are gathered together, they are counted in months. So also in this present time, while the holy Church gathers souls shining with the light of truth, she hides them in her inmost places.

At times, moreover, a month is used for perfection, as the prophet says: “Month after month” (Isa. 66:23)—that is, perfection for those whose perfection will then be in rest, just as their perfection is now in activity.

Let her therefore remember her former perfection [Col. 0334D], bring to mind what great profits she brought back through her preaching from the souls she had gathered, and, oppressed by tribulations, say: “Who will grant me that I might be as in former months?”

It follows:

### VERSE 3

“**According to the days when God guarded me, when his lamp shone over my head, and I walked by its light in darkness.**” Then she sees the tumult of the weak fall away from her under the compulsion of persecution—those whom she now cherishes as a mother within the bosom of peace and keeps in the tranquil cradles of faith. Mixed with the strong, they are nourished by that very tranquility of faith.

Then she considers herself to be falling in those whom she now sees guarded among the mixed multitude. The name of a lamp signifies the light of sacred Scripture. Hence the Psalmist says: “Your word is a lamp for my feet, Lord” (Ps. 118:105).

Because our ruling faculty is called the head, the Psalmist says: “You have anointed my head with oil” (Ps. 22:5)—as though he plainly said: You have filled my mind with the richness of charity.

Now, therefore, the lamp shines over the head of the Church, because the sacred utterances illuminate the darkness of our mind, so that in this shadowy place of the present life, while we receive the light of God’s words, we may see what ought to be done.

Now she walks by the light in darkness, because although the holy universal Church does not penetrate the hidden thoughts of others—since she does not, as it were, recognize a face in the night—she nevertheless sets the steps of good works in place, directed by the light of heavenly speech.

It follows:

[Col. 0335B]

### VERSE 4

“**As in the days of my youth, when God was secretly in my tabernacle.**” The age of the holy Church is described just as the age of each individual human being is described. She was then small, when, newly born, she could not preach the word of life. Hence it is said of her: “Our sister is little, and she has no breasts” (Song 8:8).

The Church is called mature when, joined to the word of God and filled with the Holy Spirit through the mystery of preaching, she bears children in conception whom she brings forth through exhortation and gives birth to through conversion. Of this age of hers the Lord says: “The young women loved you” (Song 1:3).

When, therefore, in those days the Church, weakened as though by old age, cannot give birth to children through preaching, she remembers her ancient fruitfulness.

What else do we understand by “tabernacle” here except the dwelling place of the mind? For through everything we do in thought, we dwell in the counsel of our heart. Whoever silently thinks upon God’s commandments has God secretly in his tabernacle. He had seen the dwelling place of his heart to be before God’s eyes who said: “And the meditation of my heart is always in your sight” (Ps. 18:15).

Thus the holy Church, caught in great tribulations at that time, when she sees many depart from God through evil thought, clearly sees that their dwelling place of the mind, as God departs, remains empty; and rightly lamenting, she says: “How secretly God was in my tabernacle.”

These words also appropriately lament the pretense of religion, because even now some people do not desire to be Christians, but only to appear so. For them God is in public, not in secret. But the holy Church desires to have God in secret, because she regards as truly faithful those whom she knows to remain with a full heart in the life of faith.

It follows:

### VERSE 5

“**When the Almighty was with me, and my young servants were all around me.**” They are called young servants because they serve the heavenly commandments. Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “Behold, I and the children whom God has given me” (Isa. 8:18). And again in the Gospel: “Children, do you have anything to eat?” (John 21:5).

Now, therefore, young servants are around her, because in nearly all nations there are people who keep the heavenly commandments and obey the rules of spiritual discipline [Col. 0336A]. They were absent from service then, when those who are found to be wicked despise her spiritual commandments.

It follows:

### VERSE 6

“**When I washed my feet in butter.**” Since we have often already said that Christ and his Church are one person—Christ the head of this body, and the Church the body of that head—these words must be understood in one way according to the voice of the head and in another way according to the voice of the body.

Whom, then, do we understand as the Lord’s feet except the holy preachers? Of them he says: “I will walk among them” (2 Cor. 6:16). The feet are therefore washed in butter because the holy preachers are filled with the richness of good works. For, as we have already said above, scarcely any preaching passes without some offense being committed. Hence James says: “We all stumble in many ways” (Jas. 3:2).

The feet are therefore washed in butter because the dust gathered from the glory of preaching is infused and cleansed by the richness of good works.

Or certainly, the feet are washed in butter when the listeners provide the holy preachers with the support due to them. When the labor of preaching imposed upon them fatigues them, the richness of good works displayed by their disciples comforts them—not because they preach in order to be fed, but because they are fed in order to preach, that is, so that they may continue preaching.

If, however, we should understand these words as spoken by the body alone, then the feet of the Church are surely the ministers of lower works, who, while carrying out externally what is necessary for practical purposes, cling to the earth like feet through their lowest ministry.

But those who preside and devote themselves to the work of teaching must carefully seek out the hearts of those occupied with such tasks and, through frequent admonition, pour into them the richness that they themselves receive in leisure. They wash their feet with butter because they supply the wounds of these people with the ointments of repentance.

Let the Church, therefore, severely afflicted at that time, remember how in the time of her peace she cleansed even her lowest members within herself through the word of prayer, and let her say: “When I washed my feet in butter.”

It is remarkable to contemplate how this applies to blessed Job. Amid so many affections for his children and so many practices of sacrifice, he preached the good things of the life to come to those subject to him, however lowly they might be, so that he might instruct in heavenly things those who served him in earthly works.

It follows: “**And the rock poured out streams of oil for me.**” Since Christ is understood by the name “rock,” the outstanding preacher testifies, saying: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4).

This rock now pours forth streams of oil for the holy Church, because the Lord, speaking in her, causes the teachings of inward anointing to flow out. From this rock there issued a stream of oil: the book of Matthew, the book of Mark, the book of Luke, and the book of John. In the various regions of this world, however many teachings he produced, this rock poured forth that many streams through the mouths of all the apostles.

They are called streams of oil because they flow downward and anoint; whoever is dipped in them is anointed, and whoever is dipped within is enriched inwardly.

It follows:

### VERSE 7

“**When I went out to the gate of the city, and they prepared a seat for me in the square.**” It was the custom of the ancients for elders to stand at the gate and judge the cases of those entering. We are certain that blessed Job did this in devotion to justice.

But what is signified by the gate of the city except every good action, through which the soul enters into the assembly of the heavenly kingdom? Hence the Prophet says: “You lift me up from the gates of death, that I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Ps. 9:15).

What else is signified by the seat except the authority of teaching? In Greek usage, the word *platea* means “breadth” or “wide place.” The Church now goes out to the gate of the city because she exercises herself in holy actions in order to receive access to the heavenly kingdom. A seat is prepared for her in the square because, in the breadth of great authority, she displays the freedom of her teaching. Whoever publicly preaches what he rightly thinks sits, as it were, on a seat in the square.

It follows:

### VERSE 8

“**Young men saw me and hid themselves, and old men rose and stood.**” If we attend to the historical sense, we believe what he said; if to the allegorical sense, we see what he foretold.

People are customarily called young because they are weighed down by the gravity of no counsel. Scripture, however, does not customarily call people old merely because of the length of time they have lived, but because they are mature through the greatness of their character. Hence a certain wise man says: “Old age is honorable, not because it lasts long, nor is it measured by the number of years. The gray hairs of human beings are understanding, and an undefiled life is the age of old age” (Wis. 4:8–9).

Now young men see the holy Church and hide themselves, while old men rise and stand before her, because the immature fear her strength and uprightness, while the mature glorify her. All who are frivolous flee from her, but the grave and perfect honor her by rising before her through the merits of their lives.

It follows:

### VERSES 9–10

“**Princes ceased speaking and placed a finger upon their mouth. Leaders restrained their voice, and their tongue clung to their throat.**” Who else can be understood here by the other leaders or princes except the authors of heretical perversity? Of them the Psalmist says: “Contention was poured out upon princes, and they led them astray in a trackless place and not in the way” (Ps. 106:40).

Now the princes of heretical crowds, weighing the authority of the holy Church, cease speaking and, as it were, place a finger upon their mouth. By their false complaints they indicate that they are restrained not by the reason of speech but by the hand of virtue [Col. 0337D].

The leaders restrain their voice because those who try to drag erring peoples behind them now dare not speak perversely; they are curbed both by the weight of authority and by the force of reason.

Their tongue clings to their throat because, although they do not dare to speak perversely in an unrestricted voice, inwardly they nevertheless conceal within themselves all that they falsely endeavor to propose against the true faith.

The Church, having been caught in the subsequent tribulation of those times, recalls and laments them.

It follows:

### VERSE 11

“**The ear that heard blessed me, and the eye that saw bore witness to me.**” When blessed Job declares that he was blessed by those who heard him and received testimony from those who saw him, the kind of person he was in speech and in conduct is revealed.

If we refer this to the voice of the holy Church [Col. 0338A], he blesses her words who completes in action what he has heard. He bears witness to her who responds to the examples of her life by living well.

It follows:

### VERSES 12–13

“**Because I delivered the poor man who cried out, and the orphan who had no helper. The blessing of the one who was perishing came upon me, and I comforted the heart of the widow.**”

These are works of great mercy: to deliver the poor man who cries out, to provide help to the orphan, to rescue the one who is perishing, and to comfort the widow’s heart.

Blessed Job both performed these things for his subjects and signified that they were to be performed through the holy Church. She now exercises them without ceasing in various ways, feeding her children by speaking and protecting them by defending them.

The holy Church both performs the works of piety mentioned above bodily and does not cease to perform them spiritually. She delivers the poor man who cries out when she releases the sins he has committed for the sinner who begs for pardon. Of such poor people it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3).

She delivers the orphan who has no helper when each person, having lost the ancient father, the devil, runs to the bosom of the holy Church and finds in her the help of sound exhortation, having already fled the desires of the world that pursues him.

The name “orphan” can also signify any believer because of the death of the good Father, deprived of whose vision he has been left, though not deprived of consolation. The blessing of the one who is perishing also comes upon her when she forestalls the sinner’s destruction and leads him back from the pit of guilt through holy exhortations. Hence it is written: “Whoever brings a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (Jas. 5:20).

She comforts the widow’s heart when, by recounting the Lord’s eternal rewards to each faithful soul, she recalls to its memory, as it were, the good things of its husband. Because the soul has been joined spiritually to him, it is called a widow after his death, but through the words of the holy Church it is revived by his resurrection.

It follows:

### VERSE 14

“**I clothed myself with righteousness, and it clothed me as with a garment.**” When we are clothed with a garment, we are surrounded on every side. Therefore the one who is clothed with righteousness as with a garment is the person who protects himself on every side with good works [Col. 0338D] and leaves no part of his conduct naked through sin. A person who is righteous in some actions but unrighteous in others has covered one side, as it were, and left another naked.

It follows: “**And with judgment as my diadem.**” The judgments of the righteous are rightly compared to a diadem, because through the glory of great work they lead to the crown of recompense. These judgments they conduct inwardly with themselves each day: they carefully consider what they owe to God and to their neighbor, vigorously kindle themselves to do good, and strictly rebuke themselves for the evils they have committed.

Hence Solomon also rightly says: “The thoughts of the righteous are judgments.”

It follows:

### VERSES 15–16

“I was an eye to the blind, and a foot to the lame; I was a father to the poor, and I investigated most diligently the case that I did not know.”

At this point the reader’s mind may perhaps ask why blessed Job enumerates his virtues so minutely. It is characteristic of holy men to conceal the good they have done, lest they happen to incur the downfall of pride. But when holy men are compelled to speak of the good they do, they do not serve pride but usefulness. Thus blessed Job discloses his good deeds in speech to his friends, who were unjustly reproaching him and therefore ignorant of them, so that they might learn not to rise up against his life with accusations, but to imitate it in silence.

We must first observe the proper order of his account: works of justice are described before works of mercy. For the person acts well in matters of compassion who knows first to preserve what is just, so that the stream of mercy poured out upon one’s neighbors may be drawn from the fountain of justice. Many people indeed bestow upon their neighbors what seem to be works of mercy, but do not abandon acts of injustice. If they truly desired to show mercy to their neighbors, they ought first to show mercy to themselves by living justly. Hence it is written: “Have mercy on your own soul, pleasing God” (Sirach 30:24).

If we refer these words, by a typological interpretation, to the voice of holy Church, she herself is the eye of the blind, because she shines through the word; she herself is the foot of the lame, because she supports through assistance. By preaching she illumines the blind, and by helping she sustains the lame. The blind person is one who does not yet see where he should go. The lame person is one who cannot go where he sees.

But because holy Church gathers within herself two peoples, namely the Jewish and the Gentile peoples, the Gentile people may rightly be signified by the blind, and the Jewish people by the lame. The Gentile people had, as it were, no eyes, because, having not received the Law, they did not see where they ought to go. The Jewish people, on the other hand, had eyes but were lame, because they held the Law by knowing it, yet did not extend their step into right action. When holy Church receives this people coming to her, because she joins the New Testament to the Old Testament already held by it, she adds, as it were, another foot in order to direct its steps.

This faithful people of holy Church rightly continues: “I was a father to the poor.” For the humble, who are called “poor in spirit” (Matthew 5:3), are generated through her preaching. Yet people often give much to the poor, not because they love those poor people, but because, if they give nothing, they fear the anger of the heavenly Judge. Since it is one thing to do a good work from commandment, and another to do it also from affection, the holy man does not testify that he was the patron, neighbor, or helper of the poor, but their father. For he turned the great charitable duty of mercy into the affection of nature, so that through love he might regard as sons those over whom, as a father, he presided through protection.

He continues: “And I investigated the case that I did not know.” He was indeed diligent in the affairs of the poor. For whoever thinks about the goods of eternal recompense must necessarily apply himself to every case that may lead to the reward to come. Hence Solomon says: “Whoever fears God neglects nothing” (Ecclesiastes 7:19).

In this matter I see that we must take care never to be too hasty in pronouncing judgment, lest we rashly condemn what has not been examined; lest any evils we hear about move us; lest we casually believe statements without proof. We fear committing such things if we weigh more carefully the deeds of our Creator. For although “all things are naked and open to his eyes” (Hebrews 4:13), he nevertheless did not wish to judge the evils of Sodom merely from what he had heard. He said: “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grave. I will go down and see whether they have completed in action the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Genesis 18:20–21).

These words may also, not inappropriately, be referred typologically to the voice of the Church. When she judges the evils of carnal people, she investigates what she does not know, because she investigates through corrective judgment the evils that she does not know through personal experience.

### VERSE 17

“I broke the jaws of the wicked, and snatched the prey from his teeth.”

The Church has taken prey from the teeth of the wicked as often as, by preaching, she has snatched a soul from the bite of error. For who can more truly be called wicked than the devil? We break his jaws when, abandoning his snares, we expose his hidden devices against us; and we take prey from his teeth when we restore to the salvation of life the mind that he had already wounded and seized by breaking it down into sin.

By the jaws his hidden snares are signified; by the teeth, his openly perpetrated deeds. Concerning these jaws and teeth of enemies the Psalmist writes: “But God will crush their teeth in their mouth; the Lord will break the jaws of lions” (Psalm 57:7).

It is first necessary to expose the hidden devices of his counsels, so that afterward we may be able to recall our hearer from an openly manifested fall. Against this lion holy Church, because she sees his snares, fortifies the folds of faith. She breaks his jaws as often as she destroys the arguments of heretics, and snatches prey from his teeth as often as by preaching she converts someone from error.

### VERSE 18

“And I said: ‘In my little nest I shall die, and like a palm tree I shall multiply my days.’”

What is expressed here by the word “nest”? That great multitude of good people who were found during times of persecution believed that they would complete the days of their nourishment, as it were in a nest, in a place of rest. Hence it is written: “Indeed, the sparrow has found a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest” (Psalm 83:4).

The palm tree grows slowly, but remains green for a long time. Holy Church came to the state of faith through many difficulties, and, because of the gathering of so many people, desires to remain longer in the glory of that same faith. Thus she believed that she would multiply her days like a palm tree; but when a sudden time of temptation arose, she grieved that the grace of her peace—which the faithful had attained slowly—was taken away more quickly by the unfaithful.

Nor is the life of the just compared to a palm tree without reason. The palm is rough to the touch below and wrapped, as it were, in dry bark, but above it is beautiful to the eye with its fruits. Below, it is narrowed by the layers of its bark; above, it spreads out in the breadth of its beautiful greenness. So the life of the elect is despised below but beautiful above. Here below it is wrapped, as it were, in many layers of bark, while it is constricted by many tribulations; but in that highest realm it expands like the leaves of beautiful greenness, in the breadth of recompense.

Moreover, in the fact that the palm begins with lesser breadth at the bottom and rises with greater strength toward branch after branch, the advancing life of the just is signified. They are not strong in earthly pursuits and weak in heavenly ones; rather, they show themselves more diligently devoted to God than they remember having been to the world. Even if one begins tepidly at first, he completes his final stage more fervently. He always considers himself to be beginning, and therefore remains tireless in renewal.

Observing this constancy of the just, the prophet says: “Those who trust in the Lord will renew their strength; they will take wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary; they will walk and not faint” (Isaiah 40:31).

### VERSE 19

“My root was opened beside the waters.”

A root is opened beside waters when the mind’s thought joyfully expands to receive the streams of truth. If these words are referred to the voice of holy Church, her root should be understood as the very incarnation of the Redeemer. It was opened beside the waters when the invisible God, through the assumption of his humanity, became manifest to the sight of our vision. Hence it is written: “And he shall be like a tree planted beside running waters” (Psalm 1:3).

He continues: “And dew will remain in my harvest.” The sense is: “I said.” The harvest of holy Church may appropriately be understood as perfect souls withdrawn from their bodies and descending to the heavenly storehouses like ripe crops cut from the earth. Dew falls from above; the harvest is gathered below. Thus dew remains in the harvest, because grace coming from above brings it about that we are worthy to be gathered from below. Hence Paul says: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15:10).

### VERSE 20

“My glory will always be renewed, and my bow will be restored in my hand.”

Holy Church laments a glory that has, as it were, been lost when she sees her faithful returning to their former life. She says: “And I said: ‘My glory will always be renewed.’” For she recognizes that those whom she believed were serving the new life within her are serving old desires.

In sacred speech, the name “bow” sometimes signifies the snares of the wicked, as in: “They stretched their bow for a bitter matter” (Psalm 63:4). Sometimes it signifies the day of judgment, as in: “You have given a sign to those who fear you, that they may flee from before the bow” (Psalm 59:6). Sometimes it signifies the sacred words themselves, as in: “He stretched his bow and prepared it” (Psalm 7:13).

What, then, should the name “bow” mean in this passage except sacred speech? In the string, the New Testament is understood; in the horn, the Old Testament. In a bow, when the string is drawn, the horn is bent. So, when the New Testament is read in this same sacred speech, the hardness of the Old Testament is softened.

It is not inappropriate to say that the string corresponds to the New Testament, which certainly came into being through the Lord’s incarnation. Thus the string is drawn and the horn is bent, because, when the incarnation of the Mediator is recognized in the New Testament, the rigor of the Old Testament is inclined toward spiritual understanding.

He holds the bow in his hand who completes through action the divine words that he knows through understanding. Thus the bow is restored in the hand when whatever is learned through study from sacred speech is fulfilled in one’s life.

Hence Solomon, describing strong warriors in spiritual battle, says: “All holding swords and most skilled in war” (Song of Songs 3:8). But since “all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 2:21), the writings of God are found everywhere and set before people’s eyes, yet people disdain to know them; scarcely anyone seeks to understand what he believes.

Therefore the multitude of those who preceded us in goodness should grieve that its bow is being destroyed, since it believed that sacred speech would always be restored through the study of those who followed.

## BOOK TWENTY

[Column 0341]

Holy Church, pressed by the tribulations of heretics and carnal people, recalls former times, when everything she said was heard with fear by the faithful. Lamenting the insolence of her adversaries, she says:

### VERSE 21

“Those who heard me waited for my judgment, and, attentive, they kept silent at my counsel.”

As though she were openly saying: “Not like these insolent and arrogant people, who, while refusing to accept the words of truth, anticipate the judgment of my preaching as though they were teaching.”

At that time the disciples kept silent, attentive to his counsel, because they dared not oppose his words but believed them.

### VERSE 22

“They dared to add nothing to my words.”

For when heretics are unrestrained against her with the worst kind of freedom, they presume to add something to her words when they attempt, as though correcting them, to amend the rectitude of her teachings.

He continues: “And my eloquence dropped upon them.”

What else is understood by this dripping of eloquence except the measure of preaching? The grace of exhortation must be bestowed upon each person according to the capacity of his understanding. Hence, at the Lord’s command, not only bowls but also cups are prepared for the table of the tabernacle.

### VERSE 23

“They waited for me as for rain, and they opened their mouths as for the late rain.”

We await the words of holy preaching as rain when, with true humility, we recognize the dryness of our heart, so that we may be watered by the drink of holy preaching. Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “My soul is like earth without water for you” (Psalm 143:6).

When, at the final part of the age, we receive the words of holy preaching, we open the mouth of the heart as for the late rain. For if there were no mouth in the heart, the Psalmist would not say: “Deceitful lips are in the heart, and they have spoken evil things with the heart” (Psalm 12:3).

Hence it is written: “I will give you the early rain and the late rain” (Deuteronomy 11:14).

### VERSE 24

“If ever I laughed with them, they did not believe.”

If we understand this according to the words of the historical account, we must believe that the holy man showed himself such to his subjects that even when he laughed he could be feared. What else are we taught by this except that the administration of authority ought to be such that the person in charge governs himself among his subjects with such moderation that, while smiling, he may still be feared, and while angry, he may still be loved—so that neither excessive cheerfulness makes him contemptible nor immoderate severity makes him hated?

What follows may also appropriately be understood according to the historical sense: “And the light of my countenance did not fall to the ground.” For it is written: “The eyes of fools are at the ends of the earth” (Proverbs 17:24). Again Solomon says: “The eyes of the wise are in his head” (Ecclesiastes 2:14). Paul also says: “The head of the man is Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:3).

The wise person’s eyes are therefore in his head when he continually contemplates the works of his Redeemer, which he ought to imitate. Thus the light of his countenance did not fall to the earth, because he did not look upon earthly things through desire.

But because often the voice of the head passes into the voice of the body, and the voice of the body into the voice of the head—and since those who are in one flesh may fittingly share one voice—let the head speak of his elect; let the Church speak:

“If ever I laughed with them, they did not believe.”

God laughs when he makes the paths of the saints prosper through favor. The same expression is commonly used of those who are accompanied in this world by the flatteries of prosperity. Time smiled upon them, but we do not believe in our Redeemer as he smiles upon us, even though many gifts already testify to him and we receive the grace of his favor; we still waver under his judgment because of our weakness.

Hence Solomon says: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful, but whoever is hard of heart will fall into evil” (Proverbs 28:14).

What is called “earth” except the sinner, to whom the first sentence was spoken: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis 3:19)? The light of the Lord’s countenance therefore does not fall upon the earth, because the brightness of his vision does not appear to sinners. For it is written: “Let the wicked be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of God.” It would be as though light fell upon the earth if, coming in the final judgment, he revealed the brightness of his majesty to sinners.

If we receive these words from the voice of holy Church, we may appropriately understand that the light of her countenance does not fall upon the earth because, when people are occupied with earthly actions, she avoids proclaiming the highest mysteries of her contemplation. She forbids strong things to be told to the weak, lest, when they hear what they cannot receive, they be crushed by the words of preaching through which they ought to have been lifted up.

### VERSE 25

“If I wished to go to them, I sat first.”

In the hearts of the reprobate, the actions of the flesh occupy the first place, and the actions of the soul the second. Therefore, in their thoughts Christ does not sit first but last. The elect, however, because they think before all else about eternal things, arrange whatever temporal matters there are with secondary concern. To them Truth says with authoritative voice: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:33). Thus the Lord sits first in their heart.

He continues: “And when I sat like a king with the army surrounding me, I was nevertheless the comforter of the sorrowful.”

The Lord sits like a king in the heart because he governs the tumultuous movements of our minds within our thought. In the mind that he inhabits, he rouses what is sluggish, restrains what is restless, kindles what is cold, moderates what is kindled, softens what is rigid, and restrains what is uncontrolled. From this very diversity of dispositions, an army, as it were, surrounds him.

Or certainly, he sits like a king with an army surrounding him because, when he presides over the minds of the elect, a host of virtues surrounds him. He is also the comforter of the sorrowful through the promise in which he says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5:5). And again: “I shall see you, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John 16:22).

Nothing prevents us from referring what we have said about the head of holy Church also to the voice of the Church herself. In her, the order of teachers presides like a king, surrounded by the multitude of the faithful. This multitude of the faithful is rightly called an army, because it is continually prepared each day, in the formation of good works, for the battles against temptations.

Holy Church also comforts the hearts of the sorrowful when she considers the minds of the elect afflicted by the hardship of their present pilgrimage and makes them rejoice through the promise of their eternal homeland.

We should know that, even according to the historical sense, this can greatly edify the reader if he considers how both the authority of governing and the kindness of consoling are joined in good rulers. He says: “And when I sat like a king with the army surrounding me.” Behold the authority of government. “I was nevertheless the comforter of the sorrowful.” Behold the ministry of compassion.

Discipline or mercy is greatly weakened if either is held without the other. In relation to their subjects, rulers ought to possess both mercy that consoles justly and discipline that acts sternly with compassion.

## CHAPTER 30

### VERSE 1

“But now the younger in time mock me.”

All heretics, when compared with the universal Church, are appropriately called younger in time, because they went out from her, not she from them. Hence John rightly says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19).

The younger mock holy Church when those who have gone out from her despise her teaching. Concerning them he continues: “Whose fathers I would not have placed with the dogs of my flock.”

What is the flock of holy Church except the multitude of the faithful? And who else are called the dogs of this flock except the holy teachers, who have been guardians of these faithful? While intent upon vigils by day and night for their Lord, they uttered great, as I may say, barking sounds of preaching. Concerning them the Psalmist says to that same Church: “The tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him” (Psalm 67:24).

We call the fathers of heretics those whom we call heresiarchs. From their perverse preaching—that is, from the seed of their speech—following peoples have been generated in error. Holy Church therefore disdains to place the fathers of heretics with the dogs of her flock, because by judgment she rejects the inventors of errors and refuses to count them among the true fathers.

### VERSE 2

“Whose strength of hands was regarded by me as nothing, and they were considered unworthy of life itself.”

Strength is in the hand; greatness is in action. But the strength of the hands of heretics is regarded as nothing by holy Church, because, having lost the true faith, she sees that whatever they do possesses no merit. They abandon the love of God and neighbor: they think falsely about God and divide themselves from their neighbors through quarrels.

Sometimes heretics even perform signs and miracles. But because they do not agree with the same signs they display through any humility, it is rightly added: “And they were considered unworthy of life itself.” Or certainly, holy Church declares all heretics unworthy of life itself, because under the name of Christ they fight against the name of Christ. Concerning them he continues:

### VERSE 3

“Barren through poverty and hunger.”

All heretics become barren through their hunger when, in sacred speech, they strive to investigate more of God’s secrets than they are capable of grasping. They do not seek those things from which they may educate themselves toward humility, order their conduct in tranquility, preserve patience, and display forbearance; they seek only those things that show them to be learned and eloquent, and desire to know those things by which they may appear uniquely instructed.

The excellent preacher restrains their boldness well when he says: “Do not think more highly than one ought to think, but think with sobriety” (Romans 12:3).

### VERSE 4

“Those who gnawed in the wilderness, squalid with calamity and misery, and ate herbs and the bark of trees.”

What is usually gnawed is what cannot be eaten. Heretics, however, because they attempt to understand sacred Scripture by their own strength, are plainly unable to grasp it. Since they do not understand it, they do not, as it were, eat it; and because they cannot eat it without the help of heavenly grace, they gnaw it, as it were, with certain efforts.

Those who have been separated from the fellowship of the universal Church are therefore said to gnaw not in any ordinary place but in the wilderness. They are rightly described as squalid with calamity and misery, because they are despised both for the ruin of their morals and for the perversity of their understanding.

They also eat herbs and the bark of trees, because, repelled by the obstacle of their pride, they cannot grasp great and inward things in sacred speech. They scarcely recognize certain tender and external matters in it. Herbs signify clearer sayings; the bark of trees signifies the external words of the Fathers.

Or, alternatively, to eat herbs means to observe the smallest commands of sacred Scripture while despising the greater ones. Truth rightly rebukes such people, saying: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who tithe mint, dill, and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law” (Matthew 23:23).

They eat the bark of trees because some people venerate only the surface of the letter in the sacred books and preserve nothing of the spiritual meaning, supposing that nothing more exists in God’s words than what they hear outwardly. Hence Paul says: “For such people do not serve Christ the Lord but their own belly” (Romans 16:18).

Alternatively: What else does the wilderness signify in this passage except the deprivation of goodness? Thus, under the figure of Judea, Jeremiah laments the soul of the sinner, saying: “How the city sits alone, full of people!” (Lamentations 1:1).

But when it is said through blessed Job concerning the wicked, “They gnawed in the wilderness,” it is worth considering also what is said through the Psalmist: “His enemies shall lick the earth” (Psalm 72:9).

There are two kinds of people who serve their ambition. One always uses the flatteries of the tongue for greed; the other openly devotes his life to plunder. All who desire what belongs to others but cannot seize by force what they desire, and who nevertheless try to draw it away through flattering words and a sort of sweetness, what else do they do than lick the earth?

Those who are supported in this world by some position of power, however, and who desire what belongs to others, disdain to flatter through fraud because, even by unjust strength, they can accomplish what they want. They do not lick what they desire but gnaw it.

The Church speaks, as it were, about these people: They would not gnaw what belongs to others by violently seizing it unless they themselves first remained alone and empty within, deprived of the cultivation of virtues.

Human nature, therefore, was well created, but, having fallen into weakness through the fault of its own will, it fell into calamity, because, oppressed by innumerable necessities, it found in this life nothing except what would afflict it. But when we usually serve the necessities of our nature more than is fitting, neglect the care of the mind, and add the squalor of negligence to our weakness, we add misery to our infirmity.

What else is it to turn the cause of necessity into an occasion of pleasure than to join the squalor of misery to one’s calamity?

What is signified by herbs except the tender and earth-near life of those who are making a good beginning? And what is signified by the bark of trees except the external works of those who already desire higher things?

When the wicked see people beginning what is right, they oppose them either by mocking them or by pretending to offer advice. But when they observe that some are already advancing toward the heights, because they cannot completely destroy their progress, they divert them from their works in various ways.

Thus to eat their herbs and the bark of trees is to destroy, through the pestilential persuasions of their evil—as though with certain teeth—the efforts of those who are beginning well or the works of some who, like trees, are already reaching toward higher things. The reprobate eat herbs when they consume the beginnings of the weak by mocking them.

Or certainly, to eat herbs means to imitate certain smooth and tender things from the ancient Fathers. To eat the bark of trees means to perform their works only outwardly, while failing to maintain a right intention in those same works.

He continues: “And the root of junipers was their food.”

The juniper tree has prickles instead of leaves. What it produces is so bristly that it can prick the person who touches it like thorns. Every sin is a thorn, because, while it draws the mind toward pleasure, it wounds it as though by pricking. Hence the voice of the just and penitent says: “I was turned in my anguish when the thorn was fixed” (Psalm 32:4).

What is signified by the root of juniper except greed, from which the thorns of all sins are produced? Paul says of it: “The root of all evils is desire” (1 Timothy 6:10).

Since heretics often provide instruction but do not abandon the teachings of error, and since they wish to receive payment as teachers, the holy man rightly says of them here: “And the root of junipers was their food.” For while they think about greed with all the faculties of their mind, they feed, as it were, on that nourishment from which the prickles of subsequent sins undoubtedly tend to grow.

Alternatively: Those who do not desire the fruit of divine speech but serve the pursuit of temporal things are not satisfied with wheat bread but with the root of juniper. Since they despise God, they do not perceive here how great is the evil they commit. They still eat the root of juniper but do not consider how rough the branches of this root will be. For an evil deed now pleases like a root in guilt, but afterward pricks like branches in punishment.

### VERSE 5

“Those who, snatching these things from the valleys, whenever they found anything, ran about with shouting.”

They snatch these things from the valleys because, with proud spirit, they gather them from the humble sayings of the Fathers; and, while boasting that they have discovered them for their own side, they run toward them with shouting. For they strive to broadcast to human ears everything they think, driven by their desire for praise.

Alternatively: In comparison with heavenly things, the whole of the present life is a valley. These people cannot contemplate the lofty mountains—that is, the mighty deeds of the saints—but live in low places through pleasure, as though in valleys. Whenever they find any profit or even a small payment, they run with shouting, because they strive to extract it even by quarreling.

To run with shouting over each thing found in the valley is to quarrel even over a small payment when opportunities for lawsuits arise.

Through herbs and the bark of trees, not only the works of good people, as stated above, but also the consolations and prosperities of this life may be understood. Often almighty God enriches the elect with inward gifts and also raises them up through outward honors. By placing them above others and making them honored, he makes them more widely worthy of imitation.

But sometimes certain wicked people despise their life while longing to obtain prosperity in this world. Since they seek here the flatteries of passing consolation, they eat herbs; since in their thoughts they meditate upon the outward glory of the saints, they eat the bark of trees. And since in all these matters they devote their entire intention to greed alone, they are filled with the root of juniper.

They snatch all these things from the valleys because they burn with immense desires out of love for this low and corruptible life. Whenever they find anything, they run toward it with shouting, because, although they do not seek to attain the merits of the holy Fathers, they strive to seize their places and offices; and when they cannot attain them peacefully, they often attempt to obtain them by breaking the peace of concord.

### VERSE 6

“They lived in the deserts of torrents, in caves of the earth, or upon gravel.”

The inventors of perverse doctrines are rightly called torrents, because, cold from the warmth of love, they grow as though in the torpor of wintertime. They do not flow with perpetual fullness but are dried up by the arguments of Catholics as by the heat of the sun.

The inventors of perverse doctrines who arose against holy Church have indeed been extinguished by the fervor of truth, but their disciples nevertheless do not cease to hold and defend what those teachers taught. Those who follow their errors therefore live in the deserts of torrents—that is, they trust in the preaching of those whose words have already been dried up by the responses and reasoning of Catholics.

What else should we understand by “caves of the earth” except the hidden preachings of heretics? Heretics gather together in secret assemblies in such a way that they offer their error the reverence they cannot obtain through reason by means of concealment.

By “gravel” we mean those very small stones carried along by flowing water. The teachers of perverse doctrines therefore dwell upon gravel because they draw along the minds of people who are not solidified by any stability of seriousness, carrying them continually from place to place like rivers of error.

Hence the excellent preacher, wishing his hearers not to be carried about temporarily but to be established with firm seriousness, warned them, saying: “So that we may no longer be children, tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine” (Ephesians 4:14).

Alternatively: In a good sense, we rightly understand torrents as holy preachers, who, while they flow into us with divine words in the present life, are gathered like a multitude of waters in winter. They withdraw when the summer sun arrives, because, when the light of the eternal homeland appears, they will cease preaching.

The deserts of these torrents are the advantages of temporal life. They abandon them and turn themselves toward gaining heavenly rewards. The torrent who had left all these things behind said: “For which things I have suffered the loss of all things and regard them as refuse” (Philippians 3:8).

But because the minds of the wicked desire to attain in this life the things that the just, despising them, abandon, they are said to live in the deserts of torrents. They greatly desire to receive the things that are unworthy of the saints.

The caves of the earth are evil thoughts in which they hide themselves from human eyes. The wicked, being what they are, avoid being seen by people.

Gravel is the present life, which is continually carried toward its end by the very force of its mutability, as though by the current of a river. To dwell upon gravel is to cling to the flow of the present life and to place one’s purpose where one cannot establish one’s step firmly by standing still.

There is another feature of gravel that should by no means be passed over in silence. When a foot is placed upon its surface, it slips because of the gravel’s instability and rolls down to the depths. The life of the wicked is in no way different from this. When, for love of the world, they strive to do certain lawful and honorable things, they place their foot, as it were, upon a level surface; but suddenly the foot slips downward, because their action, while always desiring more, descends even to wicked and unlawful things.

### VERSE 7

“They rejoiced among such things and considered it a delight to be under thorns.”

What else do we understand by the name “thorns” except the prickles of sins that we mentioned above? Since perverse minds rejoice in the iniquities over which they ought to weep, all heretics raise themselves up in such empty joy as they grow stronger in worse things. They consider it a delight to be under thorns because they derive perverse joy from the very things through which they bear the thorns of sins.

Alternatively: The wicked rejoice among such things because they pay attention to the passing things they receive and neglect to contemplate the permanent things they lose. While they burn with love for temporal matters, they desire true joy but do not know it.

They rejoice, therefore, but under thorns, because they take pleasure in temporal things, yet, since they cannot manage those temporal things without tribulation, they are pricked by the very care through which they are burdened. They remain under thorns and consider this itself a delight: they endure harsh things out of love for the present life, yet, bound by the effect of excessive desire, they regard the labor of that endurance as pleasure.

**Verse 8. “The sons of fools and of the ignoble.”** — Namely, the sons of those who were teachers of errors. They are therefore called sons, not begotten from their seed, but generated by imitation: by teaching perverse things they were fools through ignorance, and by living wickedly they were ignoble through their conduct. They are united to our Redeemer by no wisdom and by no knowledge of life. Concerning this, in Solomon’s praise of the holy Church, it is said: “Her husband is noble in the gates” (Prov. 31:23). Thus those who have followed the perverse examples of the erring are remembered as “sons of fools and of the ignoble.”

It is rightly added: “And utterly not appearing on the earth.” For while they desire to be regarded here as something, they are plainly excluded from the land of the living.

Alternatively: We must understand that within the holy Church some are called fools, yet noble, while others are fools and ignoble. They are called fools, but cannot be ignoble, who despise the wisdom of the flesh, seek the folly that will profit them, and are raised by the power of renewal to the nobility of inward offspring. They despise the foolish wisdom of the world and desire the wisdom of God’s foolishness. For it is written: “What is foolish of God is wiser than men” (1 Cor. 1:25). Paul urges us to grasp this foolishness, saying: “If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool, so that he may be wise” (1 Cor. 3:18).

Those who followed this foolishness perfectly deserved to hear the voice of Wisdom: “You who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit over the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28). Behold: by abandoning temporal things, they purchased the glory of eternal power.

Conversely, there are fools and ignoble people who flee from heavenly wisdom by following themselves, and are lulled in their ignorance as though in the baseness of rejected offspring. They are therefore fools and ignoble whom slavery of mind excludes from a share in the eternal inheritance. For it is written: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34). When many imitate their conduct, they become sons of fools and of the ignoble; and because they follow them in understanding and behavior and are themselves fools, they do not understand true wisdom, and they are ignoble because they are renewed by no freedom of spirit.

For just as many are on the earth and, through the baseness of their rejection, are hidden from human knowledge as if by some covering spread over them, so there are some in the Church who, while submitting themselves to the rejection brought about by wicked works, are not known to the divine gaze. To them it will eventually be said: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know you” (Luke 13:27).

To be on the earth and to appear is therefore to display the nobility of the mind in the right faith through the power of works. But to be on the earth and not to appear at all is to stand within the Church by faith, yet to demonstrate nothing worthy of the faith in one’s works. It follows:

**Verse 9. “Now I have become their song, and I have become their proverb.”** — In these verses the period of the holy Church is expressed which is publicly mocked by the reprobate, when, as the wicked increase, faith and truth will become a reproach. Thus, in the time of affliction, the holy Church of the elect is made [becomes] a proverb to the perverse, because when they see the good dying amid torments, they take from them an example of cursing.

It follows:

**Verse 10. “They abhor me and flee far from me, and they do not hesitate to spit in my face.”** — All the wicked flee far from the holy Church, not in the distance of their steps but in the quality of their conduct. They flee far, not in place but in merit, when, as their pride increases, they despise her even by open reproach. To spit in her face means not merely to slander the good in their absence, but also to refute every just person in his very presence. When the wicked then openly mock and despise them, they discharge against them, in their insults, fluid words like flowing saliva.

It follows:

**Verse 11. “He opened his quiver and afflicted me.”** — What is signified by the quiver except a hidden purpose? The Lord shoots an arrow from the quiver when he brings forth an open sentence from a hidden purpose. We know that someone is scourged, but we do not know for what reason the scourge comes. When correction of life follows the scourges, the power of the purpose itself is also revealed. The closed quiver, then, is the hidden purpose; but we are afflicted by the opened quiver when, through what follows the scourge, we see by what purpose we are scourged.

Thus the holy Church of the elect, enduring the insolent voices of her adversaries, sees that her preaching is not received and, abandoning the obstinacy of certain people, moderates the words of her preaching. For when she perceives that her persecutors are too hardened for the voice of exhortation, she prefers to remain silent; and when she sees that those who hear are unworthy, she restrains her preaching by drawing over it the veil of silence. Hence it is aptly added: “And he put a bridle in my mouth.”

As though she openly confessed, saying: “Because I saw no progress in certain people, I restrained the force of my preaching among them, so that at least through patience they might learn my life, since they were unwilling to receive my words through the preaching offered to them.”

It follows:

**Verse 12. “At the right hand of the one rising, my calamities immediately arose.”** — Calamities would arise at the left if she suffered the adversities of persecution from people placed outside religion and openly denying Christ. But when she suffers the torment of temptation from some who appear to be faithful, her calamities arise, as it were, at the right hand, because those who serve under Christ’s name attack Christ’s name in her.

By the ordinary usage of speech, we call that the right which we value highly, and the left what we despise. Zechariah plainly indicates this, saying: “And the Lord showed me the high priest standing before the angel of the Lord, and Satan stood at his right hand to oppose him” (Zech. 3:1).

This same right hand is appropriately called “of the one rising.” For it is written concerning his very head: “His name is the Rising One” (Zech. 6:12). Since light rises from the east, he is rightly called the Rising One, whose light of justice illumines the night of our injustice. Therefore calamities arise at the right hand of the Rising One, because those too rush forth to persecute who were believed to be the chosen members of our Redeemer.

He rightly asserts that these calamities arise immediately, because those who persecute were not outsiders: evil suddenly comes forth from among them, and they immediately become evil. But if those who are truly faithful are called the right hand, calamities arise at the right hand of the Rising One because, when the moment of persecution breaks out, the just suffer the cruel assaults of the wicked.

It follows: “They overturned my feet and overwhelmed me like waves with their paths.” — What is signified by the feet of the Church except her lowest members? While they serve earthly works, they can be deceived by adversaries all the more quickly because they understand sublime things less. The adversaries overturn these feet when they draw her lowest members into the error of their doctrine. The life of the wicked, troublesome through its insolent restlessness, pours in like a storm to overwhelm, so to speak, the ship of the heart. Concerning this storm Solomon says: “Like a passing storm, the wicked will not be” (Prov. 10:25).

It follows:

**Verse 13. “They have broken up my paths; they have lain in wait for me and prevailed, and there was no one to bring help.”** — Blessed Job may say this concerning the evil spirits, namely, hidden enemies. The universal Church may say it concerning wicked persecutors, namely, open adversaries.

They break up her paths when by cunning persuasion they disturb the ways of truth in the minds of certain weak people. They prevail while lying in wait when they corrupt those whom they cannot openly draw into evil by pretending to be good.

But it is very surprising that he adds: “There was no one to bring help,” since the Psalmist cries out concerning divine assistance: “A helper in times of tribulation” (Ps. 9:10). Why, then, is it now said that there was no one to bring help, except because almighty God sometimes abandons for a time those whom he loves eternally? Hence it is written: “For a brief moment, in a little while, I abandoned you; but with great mercies I will gather you” (Isa. 54:7).

It follows:

**Verse 14. “As though a wall had been broken and a gate opened, they rushed upon me, and were cast down into my miseries.”** — What is called a wall in this passage except the Redeemer of the human race? Concerning him, for the building of the holy Church, the prophet says: “A wall and an outer wall are placed in it” (Isa. 26:1).

The wall is broken, as it were, when faith—which is in our Redeemer—is scattered in the heart of some by the persuasions of the wicked. When power is granted to the perverse in this life, what else is opened than a gate of error? Thus, as though the wall had been broken and the gate opened, the wicked rush upon the good when, having received temporal power, they also try to destroy the fortifications of faith in the hearts of some.

Concerning them it is plainly said: “And they rolled down upon my miseries.” For they had first fallen into their own miseries. Unless they had fallen into their own miseries by living perversely, they would never afterward have persuaded others to fall into them.

The word “wall” may also be understood as the fortification of discipline, as Solomon testifies when he says: “I passed by the field of a lazy man and by the vineyard of a foolish man, and behold, it was completely filled with nettles; thorns covered its surface, and its stone wall had been destroyed” (Prov. 24:30).

Thus an enemy enters when, through the cunning persuasion either of evil spirits or of wicked people, the defenses of discipline are scattered in the heart.

It follows:

**Verse 15. “I have been reduced to nothing.”** — We are reduced to nothing in the estimation of the wicked when we do not possess the temporal goods that they themselves value as supreme.

It follows: “You have taken away my desire like the wind.” — The faithful people declare that they suffer what they grieve to see those whom they love suffering. The wind takes away desire when any transient thing destroys the longing for eternity. Hence he appropriately adds: “My salvation has passed away like a cloud.”

A cloud rises high, but the breath of wind drives it along its course. Such, plainly, such are the temporal goods of the wicked. They appear to live on high through the elevation of honor, but every day they are driven along the course of their life by, as it were, the various breaths of their mortality.

It follows:

**Verse 16. “Now my soul withers within me, and the days of affliction possess me.”** — The soul of the elect now withers because afterward it will grow green in eternal rejoicing. The days of affliction possess them now because days of joy follow afterward. For it is written: “It will be well with the one who fears the Lord at the end” (Ecclus. 1:13). And again it is said concerning the Church: “She will laugh on the last day” (Prov. 31:25).

Yet these matters, which we have briefly surveyed through allegorical inquiry, must also in every respect be held according to the historical sense. I pass over them now for this reason: I do not fail to recognize that they are clear to readers.

It follows:

**Verse 17. “And by night my bone is pierced with pains.”** — What is signified by bones except the strong members of the holy Church? Like bone joined to bone, they hold the members together while they steadfastly bear the habits of the weak.

But when the force of the final tribulation grows hot against her, her bones are pierced by pains in the night, because sometimes even those who seemed to hold others in the faith fall away into unbelief, overcome by torments.

It follows: “And those who consume me do not sleep.” — The evil spirits, who consume even the carnal people of the Church, are all the less able to rest from temptation because they are burdened by no weight of flesh.

It follows:

**Verse 18. “In their multitude my garment is consumed, and they have girded me like the collar of a tunic.”** — If we attend to the historical sense, what else do we understand blessed Job’s garment to be except his body? His garment is consumed when his flesh is tormented.

According to the mystery of the allegory, however, the garment is the life of the faithful of the holy Church. For just as the whole Church together is Christ’s, so each of the faithful is reckoned a garment of that same Church. Hence Paul says: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5:27). Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “As I live, you will be clothed with all these as with an ornament” (Isa. 49:18).

But when the storm of her persecution arises, many of the faithful are separated from her love, though they had seemed to cling to her diligently. The collar of a tunic surrounds the neck of the wearer; and when the neck is constricted, the power of speech and the breath of life are choked. Thus the reprobate constrict the holy Church as with the collar of a tunic when, through their persecutions, they try to extinguish within her the life of faith and the voice of preaching.

It follows:

**Verse 19. “I have been compared with mud, and likened to ashes and cinders.”** — In the judgment of the reprobate, the holy Church of the elect is compared with mud because, trampled down temporally, she is despised. She is likened to ashes and cinders because, since they do not see her inner goods, they think she has come down to nothing but the evils that they see her outwardly displaying.

It follows:

**Verse 20. “I cry to you, and you do not hear; I stand, and you do not look upon me.”** — In the time of her persecution, the holy Church stands by faith and cries out through her desires. Yet she grieves as though she were not regarded when she sees her prayers delayed amid tribulations.

It follows:

**Verse 21. “You have changed toward me into a cruel one.”** — As though she openly said: “Although you yourself possess nothing of cruelty, you appear cruel to me, whom you do not allow to breathe freely from the blows.” God cannot be cruel, just as he cannot in any way be changed.

But because cruelty and mutability never exist in God, by saying “to me” she shows that she does not perceive God in himself as either cruel or changeable. For when certain prosperous and adverse things vary around us, we suspect that his disposition toward us has changed because we ourselves change. He, however, remaining unchangeable in himself, is perceived differently by human beings according to the quality of their merits.

It follows: “And with the hardness of your hand you oppose me.” — God’s hand is considered hard when, by striking and pursuing what displeases him in us, it opposes our will and multiplies the scourges while the grieving soul awaits mercy.

Yet these words also aptly correspond, according to the mystery of the allegory, to the speech of the holy Church, arising from the voices of the weak, who often think that they are struck more than they deserve and regard the most just strictness of judgment as though it were the judge’s credulity. When a sick person’s wound is cut away by a medical instrument, the physician is called cruel; yet through the hardness of the hand that cuts, he opposes the wound but agrees with the patient’s health.

It follows:
