**Verse 22. “You have lifted me up, and, as though placing me upon the wind, you have struck me down violently.”** — The glory of the present life is seen, as it were, on high, but is established by no stability. Whoever rejoices in transitory prosperity is lifted up and placed upon the wind, as it were. For the fleeting breeze of happiness raises him only so that it may suddenly cast him down more disastrously into the depths.

Since the holy Church is held in honor by all, her weak members who rejoice in transitory successes appear to be lifted up upon the wind, do they not? When the breeze of prosperity passes during the ensuing time of persecution, their elevation immediately collapses; and, suddenly falling, they learn that they had first sat upon the wind.

These words also specially correspond to the person of the holy man—not with respect to what he was, but with respect to what he appeared to be. He was struck down violently as though placed upon the wind, because, supported by external possessions, he seemed to have fallen from the very things by which he had been thought to rise.

It follows:

**Verse 23. “I know that you will hand me over to death, where a house is established for every living person.”** — Blessed Job also rightly corresponds to this according to the historical sense, since it is certain that before the grace of the Redeemer even the just were led to the chambers of hell. That reception in hell is the house of all the living; [the transmitted clause is corrupt: *non illuc ipsa corruptionis suae conditione pertransiit*]. No one comes to it who has not proceeded to the death of the flesh through that same condition of corruption.

Concerning this death the Psalmist says: “Who is the person who will live and not see death?” (Ps. 88:49).

**Allegorically.** — These words aptly correspond to the voice of the holy Church in the person of the weak. For when she sees many people devoted to pleasures within her and already foresees their destruction, she reckons that, on the road of the present life, they serve their own desires, but that all who live carnally within her nevertheless arrive at the house of death.

It follows:

**Verse 24. “Yet you do not send out your hand for their destruction; and if they fall, you yourself will save them.”** — In these words we must carefully understand that blessed Job, while recounting his own experience, represents others in himself.

The Lord does not extend his hand for the destruction of sinners when he corrects them from their sins by striking them; and he saves those who fall when, by wounding those who fall into guilt for the salvation of the body, he causes them, though laid low outwardly, to rise inwardly. Thus those who were lying in body return to their interior state, whereas while standing outwardly they had been lying fallen from the state of the mind.

It follows:

**Verse 25. “I once wept over the afflicted, and my soul had compassion on the poor.”** — We must know that the one who gives perfectly is the one who extends his hand to the afflicted while also taking the afflicted person’s spirit into himself: first transferring the sufferer’s pain into himself, and then confronting that pain through his service.

For often, as we have said above, abundance of possessions makes a person generous in gifts, but not the virtue of compassion. Therefore, when the holy Church is overtaken by the tribulation of the final persecution, she recalls the good deeds she performed in the time of peace, saying: “I once wept over the afflicted, and my soul had compassion on the poor.”

It follows. **[Note: Here the author passes over two verses, namely verses 26 and 27.]**

**Verse 28. “I walked mourning, without anger; rising up among the crowd, I cried out.”** — According to the historical sense, I carefully observe that the holy man who shortly before said, “You have lifted me up,” adds below, “I walked mourning.” For in a wondrous order, honor at the summit outwardly and the sorrow of inward humility often coincide in the actions of good people at one and the same time.

Frequently the tumult of seditious people harasses the minds of their superiors, and by disorderly movements they exceed the bounds of their proper order. Often those who preside, unless they are restrained by the bridle of the Holy Spirit in the mouth of the heart, rush forward in the ferocity of anger and retribution; and however much they are able to do, they think they are permitted to do that much to their subjects.

But the good, in opposition to the conduct of many insolent people, possess a cry but not anger, because they do not cease to teach those whom they patiently tolerate.

Yet what we have said historically about one person must, according to the allegory, be understood of the various elect of the Church. The Church herself walks mourning in her elect even amid prosperity, because she does not truly regard anything as prosperous for herself until she grasps the good that she seeks in security.

She also rises and cries out among the crowd without anger, because she pursues the life of the wicked with the zeal of right emulation, not with the madness of rage. She becomes angry and loves; she rages and remains tranquil.

It follows:

**Verse 29. “I was a brother to dragons and a companion of ostriches.”** — What is signified by the name of dragons except the life of malicious people? Concerning them the prophet says: “They drew in the wind like dragons” (Jer. 14:6). The perverse draw in the wind like dragons when they are inflated by malicious pride.

Who, however, are usually understood by the designation “ostriches” except hypocrites? The ostrich has feathers but cannot fly, because hypocrites have the appearance of holiness but do not possess the power of holiness. The appearance of good action adorns them, but the feather of virtue does not lift them from the earth.

Thus the chosen people of the holy Church, because in the time of her peace she suffers certain malicious and hypocritical people within her, may say: “I was a brother to dragons and a companion of ostriches.” This also specially corresponds to blessed Job’s words, because the good man was among the wicked at the summit of great strength.

It follows:

**Verse 30. “My skin has become black upon me, and my bones have dried up from the heat.”** — We do not trouble to consider these words according to the historical sense, because the force of the speech is evident from the suffering inflicted.

But since, as we have often said, blessed Job frequently narrates events in such a way as to announce what must yet be done, this aptly corresponds to the words of the holy Church. She feels the pain of the final persecution heavily among the weak; and when others perish from it, her stronger members are tortured by grief.

Her outward concern is the administration of earthly affairs; her inward concern is heavenly care. By the name “skin,” therefore, the weak are signified, those who now serve her outward usefulness. By “bones,” her strong members are represented, in whom the entire structure of her body is made firm.

It follows:

**Verse 31. “My harp has been turned into mourning, and my organ into the voice of those who weep.”** — Since the organ sounds through pipes and the harp through strings, right action can be signified by the harp, and holy preaching by the organ. By the pipes of the organ we may appropriately understand the mouths of preachers; by the strings of the harp, the intention of those who live rightly.

When this intention is stretched toward the other life through affliction of the flesh, it sounds like tightened strings on a harp, through the admiration of those who observe it. A string is dried so that it may produce a fitting song on the harp; likewise holy men chastise their bodies, subject them to servitude, and are stretched from lower things toward higher ones.

It should also be considered that if a string on a harp is stretched too little, it does not sound; if it is stretched too much, it sounds harshly. Thus the virtue of abstinence is either entirely absent if a person does not subdue the body as much as he is able, or extremely disordered if he wears down the body beyond his capacity.

Therefore the holy Church, pressed by the final persecutions, may confess, saying: “In the time of my peace, through some I preached little, as with a harp, and through others I preached greatly and sonorously, as with an organ. But now the harp and the organ have been turned into mourning, because, seeing myself despised, I lament those who do not hear the song of preaching.”

The holy Church will do these things through some of her members at the end; she has already done them through others at her beginnings.

# Book Twenty-One

## Chapter 31

With what strength, therefore, the holy man bound his outward members against every fall by the discipline of inward watchfulness, he makes known, saying:

**Verse 1. “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think about a virgin.”** — Although the soul is invisible, its heart cannot be touched by delight in such things unless, being joined to the body, it possesses in the body’s senses certain openings through which it may go out, as it were. Sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch are like roads of the mind by which it comes outward and desires the things that are outside its substance.

Through these bodily senses, as through certain windows, the soul looks upon outward things, and in looking desires them. Hence Jeremiah says: “Death has climbed through our windows; it has entered our houses” (Jer. 9:21).

Whoever looks carelessly outward through these windows of the body often falls into the delight of sin even against his will; and, bound by desires, begins to want what he did not want. Therefore, so that the holy man might keep the thoughts of his heart pure, he made a covenant with his eyes, lest he first look carelessly at what he would afterward love carelessly.

And because he extinguished within himself not only the act but also the thought of lust, he added: “That I would not even think about a virgin.”

It follows:

**Verse 2. “For what portion would God have in me from above, and what inheritance would the Almighty have from the heights?”** — As though he openly said: “If the mind has polluted itself in thought, I can in no way belong to him who is the author of purity.” For all other good things are nothing if they are not approved before the eyes of the hidden Judge by the testimony of chastity. As though he openly confessed, saying: “The creator refuses to possess me as his property among the heights if my mind languishes before his sight in feeble desires.”

It follows:

**Verse 3. “Is there not destruction for the unjust, and estrangement for those who work iniquity?”** — For the consolation of the good, the end of the wicked is considered without delay. When they see, from the destruction of the wicked, the evil that they themselves escape, they regard as light whatever adversity they suffer in this life.

Let the reprobate go on now and fulfill the desires of their pleasures; at the condemnation of their end they will learn that, by living wickedly, they had loved death. The word “estrangement” would sound harsher if the translator had preserved it in the language of his own speech. What is “estrangement” among us is called *anathema* among the Hebrews.

Estrangement will therefore come upon the reprobate when, in the inheritance of the strict Judge, they see that they are accursed, because here they despised him by their perverse conduct.

It follows:

**Verse 4. “Does he not himself observe my ways and count all my steps?”** — What is indicated by the name “ways” except actions? Hence Jeremiah says: “Make your ways and your practices good” (Jer. 7:3).

What do we understand by the designation “steps” except movements of the mind or advances in merit? By these steps the Truth calls us to himself, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. 11:28).

The Lord observes each person’s ways and counts his steps in such a way that not even the smallest thoughts or the most insignificant words—which among us have become cheap through common usage—remain unexamined in his judgment. Hence he says: “Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matt. 5:22).

It follows:

**Verses 5–6. “If I have walked in vanity, or if my foot has hastened in deceit, let him weigh me in a just balance, and let God know my simplicity.”** — God is said to know when he makes us know. Who is designated by the name of the balance except the mediator between God and human beings? In him all our merits are weighed on an equal scale, and in his commandments we recognize what we lack in our life.

We are weighed in this balance whenever we are summoned to the examples of his life: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps; he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:21–22).

As though he openly said: “If I have ever done anything frivolously or perniciously, let the mediator of God and human beings appear, so that in his life I may learn whether I was truly simple.” Vanity pertains to frivolity, while deceit pertains to malice. Often some people reach certain malicious acts because they do not first avoid frivolous ones.

It follows:

**Verse 7. “If my step has turned aside from the way.”** — Our step turns aside from the way whenever our thought abandons the path of uprightness through the sense of error. We place as many steps outside the way as we separate ourselves from the delight of heavenly life through perverse desires.

As we have said above, while we are still weighed down by the burden of corruptible flesh, we cannot live in such a way that no guilty pleasure can assail us. But it is one thing to be touched unwillingly, and another for a consenting soul to be destroyed.

It follows: “If my eye has followed my heart.” — Behold, again he returns from the guarding of inward strength to discipline over the outward members, so that if the heart should perhaps desire something illicit, the eye, restrained by the instruction of discipline, would refuse to look.

Just as temptation is often drawn in through the eyes, so sometimes what has been conceived inwardly compels the eyes to serve it outwardly. Often some object is looked upon with an innocent mind, but by the very act of looking the soul is pierced by the sword of desire.

For example, David deliberately looked upon Uriah’s wife; [the causal linkage in the transmitted text is defective:] whenever watchfulness is neglected even slightly, the impurity of thought immediately passes into action. Hence he adds at once: “And if a stain has clung to my hands.”

Because the holy man has introduced all the preceding statements conditionally—if he had ever done these things—he binds himself with a sentence of cursing, saying:

**Verse 8. “Let me sow, and let another eat; and let my offspring be uprooted.”** — In the manner of sacred speech, we call it “sowing” when we preach words of life. Hence the prophet says: “Blessed are you who sow beside all waters” (Isa. 32:20).

“To eat” means to be satisfied with good works. Hence the Truth says of itself: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34).

If, therefore, he neglected to do what he had taught, he says: “Let me sow, and let another eat.” As though he openly said: “Let another, not I, carry out what my mouth speaks.”

The offspring of a teacher is uprooted when the one born through the word is killed through example: the negligence of life kills the person whom an attentive tongue has stimulated. We must not pass sluggishly over the fact that, according to Solomon, a woman killed her son, whom she had attempted to nurse while awake, when she was asleep (1 Kings 3:19).

It follows:

**Verse 9. “If my heart has been deceived concerning a woman, and if I have lain in wait at the door of my friend.”** — The tongue of the distinguished preacher testifies that the guilt of fornication is distinguished from the guilt of adultery; among other things it says: “Neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:9–10).

Yet sometimes the guilt of fornication is by no means distinct from the guilt of adultery, since the Truth says: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28).

Because in the Greek word *moichos* (μοιχός) “adulterer” is meant, and because the prohibition concerns not merely another man’s wife but a woman, the Truth plainly shows that adultery is committed even by the mere sight of a woman when she is desired shamefully or foolishly.

Nevertheless, this is often distinguished by the situation or status of the one who desires: deliberate desire in a sacred rank stains one person just as the guilt of adultery stains another.

By saying these things, blessed Job makes it plainly known that he was free from the guilt of adultery. If he had ever done this, he asks that the same guilt be turned against him as punishment, saying:

**Verse 10. “Let my wife be another man’s prostitute, and let others bow down over her.”** — Since we often fail to recognize, while committing an act, how serious it is, but assess its gravity when we suffer it, he reveals how great a crime this is by declaring what the guilty person ought to endure, saying:

**Verses 11–12. “For this is a wickedness, and a very great iniquity. It is a fire that devours unto destruction and uproots every crop.”** — The distinction between sin and crime is this: every crime is a sin, but not every sin is a crime. In this life many can be without crime, but no one can be without sins.

Thus the holy preacher, when describing a man worthy of priestly grace, did not say, “If anyone is without sin,” but rather, “If anyone is without crime” (Titus 1:6). Who could be without sin, when John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us”? (1 John 1:8.)

In considering the distinction between sins and crimes, we must understand that some sins pollute the soul, whereas crimes destroy it. Hence blessed Job, defining the crime of lust, says: “It is a fire that devours unto destruction.” The guilt of grave offenses does not merely stain unto pollution; it devours unto destruction. And because whatever other good works there may be are overwhelmed by the enormity of this crime if the sin of lust is not washed away, he adds: “And uproots every crop.”

The crops are the soul’s good works. Yet if the flesh dominates it in a perverse order, the fire of lust burns up everything that has been brought forth well.

It follows:

**Verse 13. “If I have refused to enter into judgment with my male servant and my female servant when they disputed against me.”** — Whoever does not refuse to be judged together with male and female servants clearly shows that he was never arrogant toward any neighbor.

Here it is worth inquiring with what great discretion the holy man guarded his life in every respect. A little earlier he said: “Young men saw me and hid themselves, and old men rose and stood” (Job 29:8). Who can worthily contemplate the lofty moderation of this man’s virtues? He possessed such authority of governance that leaders were restrained into silence, and such humility of heart that female servants were permitted to come to judgment on equal terms.

It follows:

### Verse 14

“For what would I do when God rises to judgment, and when he asks, what would I answer him?”—Whoever considers the Judge who is to come prepares the causes of his account for the better day by day without ceasing. Whoever gazes upon the eternal Lord with trembling heart is compelled to moderate the rights of temporal dominion over those subject to him. And because each person is lifted up in proportion as he sees himself above others, he who is set over them ought always to look upon the One who is above him, so that, through fear of him who is above all, he may suppress the growing inward swelling of his spirit. It follows:

### Verse 15

“Did not the One who made me in the womb also make her, and did not one and the same fashion me in the belly?”—For powerful men it is a great virtue to consider the equality of our condition. By nature we are all equal human beings; but, by an arrangement of providential order, it has come about that some appear to be placed over others. If, therefore, we press down in our minds what has been added temporally, we quickly discover what we are naturally. It is as though he openly said: Why should we not be examined equally in the judgment of every matter, since by the power of the Creator we were made equal?

It follows:

### Verse 16

“If I denied the poor what they desired, and made the eyes of the widow wait.”—By these words the holy man is shown not merely to have helped the poor, but also to have abandoned the desire to possess. But what if the poor themselves desired things which perhaps it would not be advantageous for them to receive? Or, since Scripture commonly calls the humble “poor,” should only those things be considered which the poor wish to receive, which the humble request? Without doubt, whatever is sought with true humility ought to be given without hesitation—that is, what is asked not from desire but from necessity. For it is already a great act of pride to desire something beyond the limits of want. Hence it is said to those who ask through pride: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (James 4:3).

Since, therefore, those are truly poor who are not puffed up by the spirit of pride—those whom the Truth plainly describes when it says, “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matthew 5:3)—the holy man rightly says here: “If I denied the poor what they desired,” because those who desire things which clearly are not beneficial to them are no longer poor by the very fact that they swell with the spirit of pride.

He did not wish to make the widow who asked him wait, so that he might increase the merit of his good works not only by the gift itself but also by the promptness of the gift. Hence it is written: “Do not say to your friend, ‘Go and return, and tomorrow I will give you,’ when you can give immediately” (Proverbs 3:28).

It follows:

### Verse 17

“If I ate my morsel alone, and the orphan did not eat of it.”—He considered that he would wrong piety if he alone ate what the Lord of all had created for common use. This sharing of life ought certainly to exist with such people within the household, so that the merits of eternal recompense may grow through them.

It follows:

### Verse 18

“For compassion grew with me from my childhood, and it came forth with me from my mother’s womb.”—Compassion was indeed subject to his will in that it grew along with him; yet it is clear that it was not subject to his will that it should come forth with him from the womb. It is therefore evident that he attributes nothing to his own virtue, since he plainly testifies that he received it as a gift of his condition.

But we must consider what he asserts: “It grew with me.” For in some people, when age begins, their character declines from innocence. In the elect, however, while bodily age declines outwardly, the age of virtue grows inwardly.

It follows:

### Verses 19–20

“If I looked upon one passing by because he had no clothing, and upon the poor man without covering; if his sides did not bless me, and he was warmed with the fleeces of my sheep.”—That he did not despise the poor man displayed the virtue of humility; that he covered him displayed compassion. These two virtues ought to be so joined to one another that they are always supported by mutual assistance: humility, when it honors a neighbor, must not abandon the grace of generosity; and compassion, when it gives, must not swell with pride.

It is as though blessed Job openly said: In love of my neighbor, suppressing both the vice of pride and the failure of compassion in one and the same manner, I neither despised someone passing by while looking upon him humbly, nor failed to make him my equal through mercy. Whoever exalts himself arrogantly over one to whom he gives something commits a greater fault inwardly through pride than he diminishes inwardly through generosity.

It follows:

### Verse 21

“If I raised my hand against the orphan when I saw myself superior in the gate.”—Among the ancients it was customary for elders to sit at the gate and distinguish the disputes of litigants through judicial examination, so that those who were at odds would not enter the city in which they ought to live in concord. Hence the Lord also says through the prophet: “Establish judgment in the gate” (Amos 5:15).

What, then, does the word “gate” signify in this passage except what was done at the gate? Just as we say “the army fights,” meaning that the fighting is done by the army, so the judgment which was customarily conducted at the gate is called “the gate.” He sees himself superior in the gate who desires, with the merit of justice, to belong to the better side in judgment.

Thus blessed Job openly says: I did not wish to exercise my interests against the orphan by force, even when I saw myself superior to him in judgment by reason of justice. But because the human mind often refuses to believe in goods which it does not know how to practice, he immediately pronounces a sentence of malediction upon himself if he did not fulfill in practice any of the things he had said, declaring:

### Verse 22

“Let my shoulder fall from its joint, and let my arm be broken together with its bones.”—Since bodily work is performed through the shoulder and arm, if he did not fulfill in action the good things he had spoken with his mouth, he wishes his shoulder to fall and his arm to be broken. It is as though he openly said: If I refused to practice the things I have said, let me lose the bodily member given to me for working, so that the part of my body which I refused to employ for usefulness may fall away from the body.

But if this sentence of malediction is to be referred to a spiritual interpretation, it is clear that the arm is joined to the body through the shoulder. Just as good action is signified by the arm, so the fellowship of social life is signified by the shoulder. Hence the prophet, looking upon the peoples of the universal Church who would serve God in concord, also says: “And they shall serve him with one shoulder” (Zephaniah 3:9).

In saying, “If I raised my hand against the orphan when I saw myself superior in the gate,” he asserts that he preserved the remarkable virtue of patience: he did not shrink from being burdened by insignificant persons, nor did he act against what could justly have belonged to him. But if he had failed to do this, he adds: “Let my shoulder fall from its joint.” For whoever has scorned to preserve patience soon abandons social life through impatience.

The shoulder falls from its joint when the mind, unable to bear some adversity, abandons fraternal concord. A member is, as it were, separated from the body when one who could have performed good works is cut off from the fellowship of all good people. Concord can never be preserved except through patience alone.

It is rightly added, when the shoulder has fallen: “And let my arm be broken together with its bones.” For all our activity, however much it may appear to be accompanied by various virtues, is dissolved unless patience is preserved through the bond of charity. Whoever refuses to endure the faults of others loses his own good works.

But the holy man’s shoulder does not fall from its joint, because his love does not withdraw through impatience from the concord of social life; nor is his arm broken, because all his activity is preserved in conjunction with the shoulder—that is, in the bond of charity.

It follows:

### Verse 23

“For I always feared God, as though waves swelling over me.”—Let us consider, if we can, from the terror inspired by so great an image how great the fear was in the holy man. When waves swell, they hang above those below; and when they threaten the death they carry, sailors have no concern then for temporal possessions, nor is any delight of the flesh brought back to the mind. They even throw from the ship the very things for which they undertook long voyages; all possessions fall into contempt in the mind because of the love of life.

Thus he feared God as waves swelling over him: while desiring the true life, he despised everything which he carried here as its possessor.

There is another matter which should be carefully observed concerning the shaking of the sea. When a storm arises, first light waves are stirred, and afterward larger swells. Finally, the waves rise high, and by their very height overturn all the sailors. So the final storm hastens upon souls, a storm that will overthrow the whole world.

Now it shows us its beginnings through wars and disasters, as through certain waves; and the nearer we come each day to the end, the more grievous billows of tribulation we see rushing upon us. Finally, when all the elements have been shaken, the heavenly Judge comes and brings the end of all things, because then the storm raises its waves into the light.

Hence it is said: “Yet a little while, and I will shake not only the earth but also heaven” (Haggai 2:7). Those who watch for this storm, like waves swelling over them, are daily terrified by it, and from the tribulations that strike the world they foresee what will follow.

It follows: “And I could not bear its weight.”—When the mind tries, by contemplating, to investigate the force of the proud Majesty who comes to judgment and the terror of so great an examination, it immediately retreats into itself and is frightened to discover what it is.

But amid these matters we must consider that blessed Job speaks of these things concerning himself after having been both praised and scourged. If, then, he who feared in this way was struck for the advancement of his merits, how will the one who despises be struck? How will God’s judgments crush those who exalt themselves, if they temporarily humble even those who always fear them in humility? How will one who despises God be able to bear his weight, if even the one who foresaw it through fear endured it under the rod?

We must therefore fear above all that examination of such strictness. It is clear, however, that in this life, when God strikes, if correction follows the blow, it is the discipline of a father, not the anger of a judge; it is the love of one who corrects, not the severity of one who punishes.

From the present blow, therefore, we must weigh the eternal judgments. For by this we ought to consider above all how that anger which condemns will be borne, if the anger which purifies can scarcely now be borne.

## Book Twenty-Two

[Column 0363]

### Verse 24

“If I thought gold was my strength, and said to fine gold, ‘You are my confidence.’”—We call *obrizum* “fine gold,” or gold in its raw state. Thus the holy man did not believe that gold itself was his strength—that is, that a mass of raw gold was his confidence—because, placing his hope and delight in the grace of the Creator alone, he committed no sin either through the quantity of his gold or through its appearance. To have despaired of the Creator would have been to place hope in a creature.

### Allegorically

What do we understand by gold in this passage except the talent of a brilliant understanding? And what by fine gold except the mind? When it is refined in the fire of love, it always preserves within itself the brightness of beauty through the daily renewal of fervor. A mind that strives always to begin anew through desire does not know how to grow old through sluggishness.

Hence Paul says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Ephesians 4:23). Just as gold is placed beneath an ornament so that an arrangement of jewels may be set above it, so the clear understanding of the saints is humbly placed beneath divine gifts, and receives above itself the distinct gifts of grace. Unless gold possessed something similar together with wisdom, a certain wise man would not have said: “Hidden wisdom and unseen treasure—what advantage is there in either?” (Ecclesiasticus 20:32).

It is as though he openly confessed, saying: I did not attribute to my own talent what I truly understood; nor, if I happened to have done anything good, did I attribute it to my own mind; nor did I regard myself as its source. He further and more subtly conveys to us the humility of his heart, adding:

It follows:

### Verse 25

“If I rejoiced over my many riches, and because my hand had found very much.”—In the anguish of their pilgrimage, holy men are not yet permitted to contemplate fully the appearance of their Creator in all that they desire. They count all the abundance of the present life as poverty, because nothing outside God is sufficient for the mind that truly seeks God. Often their very abundance becomes exceedingly burdensome to them, because they endure with difficulty the fact that, while hastening toward their homeland, they carry many things along the road.

What do we understand by “many riches” in a figurative sense except an abundance of human reflections? The hand of the seeker finds these when the thought of one who considers a matter produces them. Contemplating these riches of wisdom, Solomon says: “The crown of the wise is their wealth” (Proverbs 14:24). Since he calls prudence riches rather than earthly metals, he immediately adds by contrast: “The folly of fools is imprudence” (ibid.).

Hence Paul says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Corinthians 4:7). We find many riches within ourselves when, by investigating the divine utterances, we receive gifts of abundant understanding and perceive many things in them which nevertheless are not mutually contradictory.

It is a secure joy in the divine writings to understand either what is profound or what is abundant, but to preserve what has been understood. It is as though it were openly said: I did not consider myself rich in righteousness because I correctly understood many things that I ought to do; nor did understanding lift up my heart, because proper consideration of the action owed held it down.

It follows:

### Verses 26–28

“If I saw the sun when it shone, and the moon proceeding brightly, and my heart rejoiced in secret, and I kissed my hand with my mouth—which is a very great iniquity and a denial against the Most High God.”—It is certain that these two luminaries, assigned to human service, are called the army of heaven. We know from the testimony of Scripture that many have fallen into their worship, as it is written: “They worshiped all the army of heaven” (Deuteronomy 17:3).

Since the sun and moon are seen in one way for use and in another for veneration, blessed Job declares that he had not looked upon the sun and moon in the manner in which they are customarily venerated by their worshipers; nor had his heart rejoiced, nor had he kissed his own hand with his mouth. What else does this kissing signify except the veneration of thanksgiving? If he had ever done this, he would call it a very great iniquity and a denial of God.

But after he has recounted such lofty peaks of virtue concerning himself in the preceding passages, what is surprising now if he declares that he did not worship the sun and moon? We must therefore consider that, after testifying that he had placed no confidence in gold and had not rejoiced in many riches, he is led still higher, so that he may instruct us all the more by recounting more subtle things about himself.

He says: “If I saw the sun when it shone, and the moon proceeding brightly, and my heart rejoiced in secret.” What does “to see” mean here except to gaze upon something with desire? Hence the Psalmist says: “If I have regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear” (Psalm 65:18). Such iniquity could not be expressed by the mouth if it had not first been seen in the heart.

But seeing by judgment is one thing, and seeing by desire another. Blessed Job therefore declares that he did not see the shining sun or the brightly proceeding moon, to show that he did not desire the appearance of the present light, as though he were plainly expressing contempt for his earthly abundance. What should I say? I did not rejoice in gold, since I did not even delight in bodily light itself. Hence the prophet says: “You know that I did not desire the day of man” (Jeremiah 17:16).

### Allegorically

The sun is in brightness; a good work is in manifestation. For it is written: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). Again: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke 12:35). What is signified in this passage by the shining sun is signified in the Gospel by burning lamps.

When a good work shines among the faithless, the lamp burns in the night; when it shines within the Church, the sun shines in the day. If a good work is still of such a kind that only the wicked admire it, it is a lamp in the night; but if it advances so far that the good and the more perfect can admire it, it is truly a sun in the day.

Since blessed Job had recounted many good works of hospitality and mercy concerning himself—works which were still all the more insignificant because he knew them in a bodily way—he renews the eye of his mind toward the summit of spiritual virtues. He recalls the perfection of himself and calls the light of his examples, which he gave to others, the sun.

It is as though he openly said: Even when I gave others the light of my example through my work, I did not attend to taking it for myself; because, fearing to be exalted by it, I turned my eyes away from contemplating it.

After mentioning the sun, he appropriately adds the moon proceeding brightly, because after a good work there follows a praiseworthy reputation, through which a celebrated name is possessed in the night of the present life. If it is true, as some think, that the moon receives the illumination of its hidden circle from the sun’s ray, so that it may display light during its nocturnal courses, this interpretation also does not depart from the order of that symbolism.

Reputation receives strength from a good work and scatters the grace of favor like the brightness of light. There is another feature of the moon which corresponds to the good reputation that sheds light. Its light shows the way to those traveling even in the time of darkness, because when the light of praise shines forth from another’s life, it illuminates others for the practice of good works. When that person’s reputation is known to be bright, it provides the light of an example to one proceeding as though along a road.

Those who gaze upon the moon proceeding brightly are people who, amid the darkness of this life, fix their mind upon the brightness of their reputation, lose the grace of humility as though from nocturnal light, and, while looking at the moon, do not see themselves, because they begin not to know themselves when they fix the eyes of their mind upon passing favor.

Those who are lifted up when they hear their own praises, yet do not go so far as to express their elation in words and do not show that they rejoice in such things, nevertheless rejoice in them secretly in their hearts.

The hand signifies action, while the mouth signifies speech, as Solomon says: “The lazy person hides his hand under his armpit, and is weary if he brings it to his mouth” (Proverbs 26:15). He kisses his own hand with his mouth who praises what he does and attributes the virtue of his action to himself through the testimony of his own speech.

Who is despised in this matter except the One who grants the very gifts by which we act? Hence the distinguished Preacher rightly says: “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

He immediately adds: “Which is a very great iniquity and a denial against the Most High God.” For it is clear that he denies the One whose grace he despises and arrogates to himself the strength for a good work. This is rightly called a very great iniquity, because every sin that arises from weakness does not entirely lose hope, since it seeks pardon from the heavenly Judge. But presumption in one’s own virtue is all the more gravely a cause of despair the farther it is from humility.

It follows:

### Verse 29

“If I rejoiced at the ruin of the one who hated me, and exulted because evil had found him.”—Only the guardianship of charity proves that we are disciples of Almighty God. Hence the Truth himself says: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35).

This love, if it truly fills our heart, is customarily shown in two ways: if we love our friends in God and our enemies for God’s sake. But we must know that love toward an enemy is truly preserved when we are neither grieved by his advancement nor rejoice at his downfall.

If someone is grieved by another’s prosperity and rejoices at the calamity of one who hates him, it is clear that he does not love the person whom he does not want to become better. Even while that enemy stands, he persecutes him by his desire, though he rejoices that he has fallen.

And to show that blessed Job was free even from the guilt of cursing, he continued:

### Verse 30

“For I did not give my throat to sin, so as to await the cursing of his soul.”—He would have sinned if he had wished God to do what he himself either could not do at all or, if he could, would not say. For those who attack an enemy with curses—what else do they wish God to do to him except what they themselves either cannot do or are ashamed to do?

It follows:

### Verse 31

“If the men of my tabernacle did not say, ‘Who will give us his flesh, that we may be satisfied?’”—This sentence can also be understood mystically as spoken by the voice of the Redeemer. The men of his tabernacle desired to be satisfied with his flesh—either the Jews who persecuted him or the Gentiles who believed.

The former plotted to consume and destroy his body; the latter, through the daily sacrifice of his immolation, desire to satisfy their hungry minds with his flesh.

But now, following only the force of the historical sense, let us consider with what strength the holy man, concerned both outwardly and inwardly, endured everything. If he had ever yielded either through silence to those acting unjustly or through uprightness failed to draw them after him, he certainly would not have had adversaries. But because he held to the way of life, he found outside himself people desiring his death and patiently endured adversaries hidden within.

### Verse 32

“The stranger did not remain outside; my door was open to the traveler.”—Since, according to Paul, charity is described as patient and kind (1 Corinthians 13:4), through patience it tolerates the faults of others with equanimity, and through kindness it mercifully provides its own good things.

Hence blessed Job patiently endured members of his household who cursed him, and kindly received travelers and strangers into his presence: to the former he gave examples of good conduct, and to the latter he offered assistance through outward aid.

It follows:

### Verse 33

“If I concealed my sin as a man, and hid my iniquity in my bosom.”—These are the marks of true humility: that each person recognize his iniquity and disclose what he has recognized through confession. In contrast, it is the customary vice of the human race both to commit sin by falling, to conceal the sin committed by denying it, and to multiply the sin recognized by defending it.

We derive these increases of wickedness from the fall of the first man, from which we drew the very root of guilt. Since this fault of concealment has grown so greatly among humanity, blessed Job rightly inserted “as a man” when he said, “If I concealed my sin.” He recognizes as proper to man what descends from imitation of the former parent. He appropriately adds: “And hid my iniquity in my bosom.”

Holy Scripture is accustomed often to use “bosom” for “mind,” as the Psalmist says in the voice of the Church concerning our persecutors, who are related to us by nature but separated from us in life: “Repay our neighbors sevenfold into their bosom” (Psalm 78:12).

Since the bosom signifies the mind’s secret place, to hide iniquity in the bosom is to conceal it in the hiding places of the conscience, not to expose it through confession, but to cover it through defense. Against this James says: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James 5:16). Solomon likewise says: “Whoever hides his crimes will not prosper; but whoever confesses and abandons them will obtain mercy” (Proverbs 28:13).

Yet amid these matters we must know that people often both confess their sins and remain without humility. Blessed Job therefore shows how great his humility was: he knew that he lived even among adversaries, yet he was not ashamed to disclose his faults openly in confession.

But it should be noted that above he speaks of his virtues, while below he confesses his sin. By this he clearly demonstrates how truthfully he had spoken of his good deeds, since he did not wish to remain silent about his evils.

It follows:

### Verse 34

“If I was afraid of the great multitude, and the contempt of my relatives terrified me, and I rather remained silent, and did not go out of the door.”—It is as though he openly said: While others were disturbed outwardly against me, I myself remained undisturbed within.

What else should we understand by “door” in this passage except the mouth? Through the mouth we go out when we disclose the secrets of our heart through whatever words we can use; and as we remain within in our conscience, so we go forth outwardly through the tongue.

Some people are altogether afraid of being despised and, lest they perhaps be judged worthless, desire to appear wise. They are forced to go out through the door, because, provoked by insults, they reveal in speech how great they imagine themselves to be inwardly. Defeated by impatience, they disclose certain things about themselves that had been unknown, and thus go out, as it were, through the door of the mouth.

Hence blessed Job, about to say that he had not gone out through the door of the mouth, first said, “I remained silent.” For if he had not known how to remain silent, he would have left the house of his conscience after being disturbed by impatience.

It should also be noted that blessed Job says, “If I was afraid of the great multitude,” so that the steadfastness of his character may be recognized. The number of people outside does not terrify one whom no crowd of vices devastates within.

In this life, whoever desires no prosperity undoubtedly fears adversity.

If we draw these words toward a mystical understanding, we quickly find them fulfilled in the work of our Redeemer. He did not fear the great multitude: when his persecutors came “with swords and clubs” (Luke 22:52), he struck them with a single reply, saying, “I am he” (John 18:5).

The contempt of his relatives did not terrify him; freeing us from eternal punishments, he calmly received blows upon his face. He remained silent and did not go out through the door, because, at the very hour of his Passion, while he endured the weakness of his humanity, he did not wish to exercise the power of his divinity.

For the Mediator of God and humanity would, as it were, have gone out through the door if, when he was being held as a man, he had wished to display the power of his majesty and, through the greatness of his divinity, pass beyond the weakness of the flesh he had assumed. In order that the open man might be able to die, God remained hidden, “for if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8).

He therefore did not go out through the door: when questioned by Pilate, he was silent (Matthew 26:63); and amid the hands of his persecutors he both offered to suffering the body he had assumed for the elect and showed, to those resisting him, what he was.

Hence the Psalmist also says: “They made me an abomination to themselves; I was handed over, and I did not go out” (Psalm 87:9–10).

It follows:

### Verse 35

“Who will grant me a helper, so that the Almighty may hear my desire?”—After the holy man had recounted the lofty deeds of so many of his virtues, knowing that he could not reach the heights through his own merits, he seeks a helper. And whom does he contemplate except the only-begotten Son of God?

When he assumed human nature laboring in this mortality, he helped it. He helped humanity by becoming human, so that for the pure human being the way of return might be made through the human God.

He knew that prayers for the repose of eternal liberation could not be heard except through his Advocate, of whom the Apostle John says: “If anyone sins, we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:1).

A helper is therefore sought so that the desire may be heard, because unless the intercession of the Mediator intervened for us, the voices of our prayers would undoubtedly be silent before the ear of God.

It should also be noted that he does not say “my prayers,” but “so that the Almighty may hear my desire.” True petition consists not in words of the mouth but in the thoughts of the heart. For words do not make our voices stronger before the most sacred ears of God; desires do.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Enter your room, and, having shut your door, pray to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matthew 6:6).

It follows: “And let the one who judges write the book himself.”—Because the law was transmitted through a servant to a people still living in fear, while the grace of the Gospel was bestowed through the Lord upon loving sons, and because, coming for our redemption, he established a New Testament for us, but will also come as Judge to examine us according to the command of that same Testament, there is no need for exposition to make clear what is meant by “Let the one who judges write the book himself.”

For the Truth himself says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). The author of judgment, therefore, will then be the one who is now the author of the book, so that then he may strictly demand what he now commands with gentleness.

The prophet Ezekiel aptly announces that the Redeemer of the human race himself would establish the book of the New Testament at the end, saying: “Behold, six men were coming from the way of the upper gate, which looks toward the north, and each one had his instrument of destruction in his hand. And one man among them was clothed in linen, with a writer’s inkwell in his hand” (Ezekiel 9:2).

It follows:

### Verse 36

“So that I may carry it on my shoulder and surround myself with it as with a crown.”—To carry the book on one’s shoulder is to fulfill Holy Scripture through one’s actions. Notice the orderly sequence: first it is carried on the shoulder, and afterward it surrounds one like a crown. For if the commands of sacred speech are now carried well in action, they later present us with the crown of victory in recompense.

It follows:

### Verse 37

“On each of my steps I will proclaim it.”—Concerning these steps of merit the Psalmist says: “They shall go from virtue to virtue” (Psalm 83:8). Again, contemplating Holy Church, he says: “God shall be known in her steps, when he receives her” (Psalm 47:4).

For, as has been said, no one reaches the heights suddenly; the mind is led to the loftiness of virtue by successive increases. He truly ascends to the teaching of God who bursts forth to obtain it through the steps of holy action. He proclaims the book upon each of his steps who demonstrates that he has received its knowledge not only through words but also through deeds.

Hence he adds: “And I will offer it as to a prince.”—Whatever we offer, we hold in our hands. Therefore, to offer the book to the prince who comes to judgment is to hold the words of his commands in action.

It follows:

### Verse 38

“If my land cries out against me, and its furrows weep with it.”—What does it mean for the land to cry out, for the furrows to weep, and for someone to eat its fruits by purchase, when he never needs to buy what is his own? Who has heard the land crying out? Who has seen its furrows weeping? And since the furrows of the land always come from the land, what does it mean that the land is denied to have cried out with distinct utterance and that its furrows wept along with it?

But since the historical sense fails, a mystical meaning must be sought.

Everyone who either governs a domestic household by private right or presides over faithful peoples for the common good, in possessing the rights of governance over those entrusted to him, holds nothing other than land to be cultivated. For by divine dispensation each person is placed over others so that the minds of his subjects may be made fruitful, like soil laid beneath the seed of his preaching.

But the land cries out against its possessor if either a private household or Holy Church murmurs against the one who presides over it because of something just.

Some people have been cut open by no plow of reading or exhortation, yet they produce from themselves certain good things, however small—as land not yet plowed. Others are always attentive to hearing and retaining holy preaching and meditation. Cut from the former hardness of their mind by a kind of plowshare of the tongue, they receive seeds of exhortation and return the fruits of good works through the furrows of voluntary affliction, being continually admonished about spiritual matters as well as bodily ones.

When the land cries out, to make the furrows weep is for people of fuller life to come to lamentation through the very matter in which the body of the faithful justly brings a complaint against its ruler. Thus the furrows come from the land, and yet they are distinguished from the land by name, because those in Holy Church who cultivate their minds through the labor of sacred meditation are better than the other faithful in proportion as, having received the seeds, they return fruitful works.

Therefore, whenever one who presides exercises perversity among his subjects, the land cries out against him and the furrows weep. For against his injustice the unlearned people break out in the voices of murmuring, while all the more perfect afflict themselves with tears over his evil work. What the unlearned cry out without grieving, those of more proven life who are subject to him grieve and keep silent.

It follows:

### VERSE 39

“If I have eaten its fruits without payment.” To eat the fruits of the earth without payment is to receive the Church’s provisions, yet not offer the same Church the price of preaching, concerning which the Author’s voice says: “You ought therefore to have put my money with the money-changers, so that when I came I would at least have received what was mine with interest” (Matt. 25:27). Thus he eats the earth’s fruits without payment who receives the Church’s benefits for bodily use but does not provide the people with the ministry of exhortation. It follows:

“And has afflicted the souls of its farmers.” The farmers of this earth are those placed in a lesser position, who desire, with as much zeal and work as they can, to cooperate in the instruction of Holy Church through the grace of preaching. Not to afflict these farmers of this earth means not to begrudge their labors, lest the ruler of the Church, while claiming the right of preaching for himself alone, oppose through the bite of envy others who preach correctly. For the devout mind of pastors, since it seeks not its own glory but that of the Author, wishes to be helped by others in what it says. The faithful preacher desires, if it could be done, that the truth which he alone is not sufficient to speak might sound from the mouths of all. Hence, when Joshua wished to oppose the two men who had remained in the camp and were prophesying, Moses rightly said through him: “Are you jealous on my behalf? Would that all the people might prophesy, and that the Lord would give them his Spirit!” (Num. 11:29). It follows:

### VERSE 40

“Let a thistle arise for me instead of wheat.” As though he plainly said: If I have acted unjustly toward my subjects; if I have exacted what was owed, while I myself have not rendered what I owed; if I have begrudged others the practice of good works, then for the good things that refresh in eternity, let the evils that prick be repaid to me in judgment. Let a thistle arise for me instead of wheat, and a thorn instead of barley, when, in the final recompense in which the reward of labor is sought, the wound of pain is found.

It should be noted that just as barley differs from wheat, although both provide nourishment, so a thistle differs from a thorn, although both prick; for the thistle is softer, whereas the thorn is always harder for pricking. As though he openly said: I know that I have done both great and small good works; but if this is not so, let small evils answer me for great good works, and greater evils for small good works.

Yet this may also be understood in another way. In wheat is represented spiritual work, which refreshes the mind; in barley, however, is represented the administration of earthly affairs. In that administration we are often compelled to serve the weak and carnal, as though preparing food for beasts of burden, and even the use of our works contains something mixed with chaff. It often happens that a ruler, while exercising injustice against his subjects, while never refreshing the good with kindness, and—what is more serious—while afflicting all who work well out of envy, even if he sometimes performs certain good deeds, as though sowing wheat, nevertheless mixes himself from time to time in the earthly affairs of this administration—not from a desire for avarice, but for the benefit of the carnal—and thus expects the fruit of the same labor, as it were a barley harvest.

But his subjects, because they are burdened by him in the greatest matters, cannot listen to his small good deeds; for they do not approve even the work that another work’s injustice pollutes. What earthly administration is believed to be undertaken for the benefit of subjects when the one who rules appears to be panting with avarice? Thus it happens that even the few good deeds they observe being performed amid many evils produce not praise but fear, and they murmur in their weakness when they perceive that what they see is not the work of purity.

As though he plainly said: If I have not carefully done the great things I ought to have done, I shall receive from my subjects the prickings of their murmuring; and if I have neglected to provide what encourages, then, justly bursting forth into complaint, let their tongue prick me even because of the good I have done.

In this matter it must always be weighed with vigilant consideration lest either those who rule offer their subjects examples of evil conduct and, by the sword of their wickedness, destroy their life, or those who are subject to another’s rule dare too readily to judge the deeds of their rulers and, by murmuring against those set over them, oppose not merely a human order but the divine order of God, who arranges all things.

# BOOK TWENTY-THREE

## CHAPTER XXXII

### VERSE 1

“Now these three men ceased answering Job, because he seemed righteous to himself.” When it is said of him, “because he seemed righteous to himself,” the sacred writer of this history referred this matter to the judgment of Job’s friends; the writer, however, did not condemn blessed Job for the swelling of pride. It follows:

### VERSE 2

“And Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram, was angry and indignant.” These names—whether of Elihu himself, of his father, of the place, or of the family—aptly express the character of the action they signify. Elihu, when interpreted, means “My God is this,” or “My God.” By him is signified the right faith of arrogant people placed within the Church. For although they do not live according to the Lord’s commandments, they nevertheless acknowledge that God is Lord, because in the truth of the flesh they also understand the form of the Godhead, as the Prophet says: “Know that the Lord himself is God” (Ps. 99:3).

Barachel is said by interpretation to mean “blessing of God”; Buzite, however, means “contemptible.” Both meanings aptly correspond to arrogant preachers, because in the eloquence of preaching they indeed receive the blessing of divine grace, but by their exalted conduct they show that it is held in contempt.

Ram is interpreted as “exalted.” Exalted is the people of the faithful, who despise the low and worthless things of this life, concerning whom it is said: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Thus Elihu is said to be of the family of Ram because every arrogant preacher placed within the universal Church is joined to holy peoples by the truth of faith, although he is separated from their life by the perversity of pride. It follows:

### VERSE 3

“But he was angry against Job because he said that he was righteous before the Lord. Moreover, he was indignant against his friends because they had not found a reasonable answer, but had merely condemned Job.”

It must be carefully observed that blessed Job was reproved because he said that he was righteous before God, whereas his friends were rebuked because, while condemning him, they did not give a reasonable answer against him. These indications clearly show that the appearance of lovers of empty glory is represented through him. Job is reproved for presumed righteousness, and his friends for foolish argument.

For all who pursue empty glory, while setting themselves above everyone else, reproach some for foolish opinions and others for unworthy conduct—that is, they judge some to know nothing and others not to live well. And although they rightly rebuke all who are outside the Church for holding perverse opinions, they nevertheless despise even those who are within it by looking down on their way of life. It follows:

### VERSES 4–5

“Now Elihu had waited for Job to speak, because those who were speaking were older. But when he saw that the three could not answer, he was exceedingly angry.”

Although Holy Church is unquestionably older than its adversaries, because they came from it and it did not come from them, as John says concerning them: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19), Elihu is nevertheless rightly described as younger than those same adversaries. For arrogant men, inflated by the pride of knowledge, began to exist in Holy Church after the battles with heretics had arisen.

When it is said that Elihu waited for Job to speak, and so forth, blessed Job is clearly shown to have held himself back not out of reverence for himself but out of reverence for his friends. For arrogant people within the Church despise the same Holy Church they defend, and it often happens that they honor the abilities of those who think badly more than the simple life of the innocent. It follows:

### VERSES 6–7

“Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said: I am younger in age, but you are older; therefore, lowering my head, I was afraid to declare my opinion. For I hoped that greater age would speak, and that a multitude of years would teach wisdom.”

Elihu was wiser as long as he remained silent out of regard for his age. But when, setting himself above others, he despises the multitude of their years, he shows how childishly foolish he is. For against his opinion both greater age speaks and wisdom is taught through the multitude of years, because although longevity does not prove understanding, experience nevertheless trains it vigorously. It follows:

### VERSE 8

“But, as I see, there is a spirit in human beings, and the inspiration of the Almighty gives understanding.”

He would have said this correctly if he had not arrogated that same understanding to himself above others. There are four forms by which the pride of all arrogant people is revealed.

The first is when they think they possess goodness from themselves, against whom it is said: “What do you have that you did not receive?” and so forth (1 Cor. 4:7).

The second is when they believe that what has been given to them from above was received on account of their own merits. Against them Paul says: “You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast” (Eph. 2:8–9).

The third is when they boast of having what they do not have, as it is said to the angel of the church of Laodicea: “Because you say, ‘I am rich and have grown wealthy, and I need nothing,’ you do not know that you are wretched and miserable, poor, blind, and naked” (Rev. 3:17).

The fourth is when, despising others, they seek to appear uniquely to possess what they do possess, as the Pharisee says: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity” (Luke 18:11).

Thus, although Elihu confesses that wisdom is given by the Lord, he nevertheless falls into this form of pride: he rejoices in being wiser than others. It follows:

### VERSES 9–12

“The aged are not wise, nor do the elders understand judgment. Therefore I shall speak: Listen to me; I too shall show you my opinion. For I waited for your words; I heard your prudence while you debated in speeches, and while I thought you were saying something, I considered.”

As far as the intention of the literal text is concerned, Elihu’s speech reveals how proudly he had kept silent. When he says, “I waited for your words,” and “I thought you were saying something,” he openly declares that he remained silent before the words of the elders more from a judge’s impulse than from a speaker’s desire.

Yet these words more fittingly signify the life of arrogant people. Sometimes, when placed within Holy Church, they see the adversaries of that same Holy Church and customarily weigh not the years of the ages but the purpose of their words. However ancient the heretics may be in comparison with these arrogant people, the latter boldly suppress them when they detect perverse doctrines in their words.

It follows:

“But, as I see, there is no one who can reprove Job and answer his words among you.”

### VERSE 13

“Lest you perhaps say: ‘We have found wisdom; God has cast him down, not man.’”

Heretics, because they are accustomed to be despised even by human beings, often see Holy Church honored by nearly all peoples and attempt to tear apart its reputation with whatever slanders they can, saying: “Temporal goods abound for it because the rewards of eternal gifts have been withdrawn from it.”

Elihu counters their voice, saying: “Lest you perhaps say, ‘We have found wisdom; God has cast him down, and not man.’” As though arrogant people within Holy Church, yet still faithful, were saying against the heretics: “Because you see Holy Church flourishing temporarily in human honor, do not believe that it has been cast down by the Lord. Its Redeemer knows both how to grant it comforts while it comes along this journey and how to reserve heavenly rewards for it when it reaches its eternal homeland.”

You say in vain, therefore, that God, and not man, has cast it down, when you see it honored by nearly all human beings; for earthly glory is granted to it in such a way that through this it may be carried all the more abundantly toward heavenly things. It follows:

### VERSE 14

“He has said nothing to me.”

What does “He has said nothing to me” mean? Does Holy Church, when it sees arrogant people within it, fail to instruct and reprove them through righteous preachers? No. All arrogant people hear the voices of Holy Church, but they pretend that those voices are not addressed to them when they disdain to correct the vice of pride. They do not wish to think that they are being rebuked for pride, because they consider themselves humble; indeed, they despise being rebuked because they think themselves wiser even than those who rebuke them.

It follows:

“And I shall not answer him according to your words.”

For arrogant people placed within Holy Church answer against it, but not as heretics established outside it do. They do not contradict it by preaching perverse doctrines, but by living perversely. They do not, like heretics, hold unworthy opinions about God, but they form an opinion of themselves that is more exalted than necessary. It follows:

### VERSE 15

“They were afraid and did not answer further; they withdrew their words from themselves.”

It is fittingly reported that Elihu caused Job’s friends to fear, because sometimes the arrogant defenders of the Church, although they do not keep silent about the order of their speech, nevertheless disturb their adversaries by the very force of what they say. It follows:

### VERSE 16

“Since I waited and they did not speak, they stood still and did not answer further.”

The end of the speech of the wise is usually reached when they have spoken far enough to impose silence on their adversaries. For they do not wish to display themselves, but to restrain those who teach what is wrong.

But since Elihu continues to multiply his words while his friends remain silent, it is clear that the arrogant man, representing in himself the form of arrogant people, hastens not to overcome the words of his adversaries but to display his wisdom. It follows:

### VERSE 17

“I too shall answer my part, and I shall show my knowledge.”

Every arrogant person considers this his portion: not so much to possess knowledge as to display it. Against this Moses says: “The vessel that has no covering or binding is unclean” (Num. 19:15).

Holy preachers, however, regard this as their portion: that they themselves rejoice inwardly in wisdom and restrain others from error outwardly. They do not go forth from themselves by speaking in such a way that they place the joy of the mind in the display of eloquent speech. Rather, they meditate on the good things of knowledge in the secrecy of the heart, and they rejoice where they receive them, not where they are compelled to become known amid the snares of temptations. It follows:

### VERSE 18

“I am full of words, and the spirit of my mouth constrains me.”

Sometimes arrogant men, when they see holy preachers speaking great things and being honored because of their speech, imitate the sublimity of their utterance rather than the usefulness of their purpose. Often wise men, when they see that they are not being heard, command silence to their mouths; but frequently, when they see the crimes of the wicked increasing while they themselves remain silent and do not rebuke them, they endure a certain force of their spirit, so that they burst forth in open speech of correction.

Hence Jeremiah says: “I will not remember him, nor speak any longer in his name” (Jer. 20:9). And he adds: “And it became in my heart like a burning fire, shut up in my bones, and I grew faint, unable to endure it” (ibid.).

But because vices often pretend to be virtues—such as extravagance sometimes appearing to be mercy, stinginess sometimes appearing to be frugality, and cruelty sometimes wishing to appear as justice—so, very often, the anxiety of empty glory, unable to contain itself within silence, inflames the mind toward an impulse to speak, as though with the fire of charity. The force of the desired display drives it toward unrestrained speech, and under the pretext of offering counsel, the desire to appear breaks forth. Such a person does not care, by speaking, what may be useful, but what may be noticed.

It follows:

### VERSE 19

“Behold, my belly is like wine without an opening, which bursts new wineskins.”

If we must understand this spiritually, here he calls the recess of his heart his “belly”; in the new wine, the fervor of the Holy Spirit is understood. Concerning this the Lord says in the Gospel: “New wine into new wineskins” (Matt. 9:17).

By the little wineskins we may suitably understand weak consciences in their humanity, or certainly these earthly vessels of bodies. Concerning them the Apostle Paul says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7).

Elihu, however, stretched out by the inflation of pride, as though he were kindled to speak by the fervor of the Holy Spirit through the grace of charity, compared the spirit of his understanding, in what he had kept silent, to wine without an opening. New wine bursts the little wineskins because the power of its fervor exceeds even spiritual hearts. For the fervor of the Holy Spirit is scarcely contained not only by an old life but even by a new one. It follows:

### VERSE 20

“I shall speak and breathe a little; I shall open my lips and answer.”

He rightly says, “I shall breathe,” because it is the labor of the righteous to see what is wrong and not correct it; so heavy is the labor of the arrogant if they do not display what they know. They can scarcely bear the force boiling within them if everything they feel is made known even slightly later.

Therefore, whenever a good deed is performed, its pride must first be conquered in the heart, lest, if it proceeds from the root of a wretched intention, it produce the bitter fruits of wickedness. Those who are still subject to the battle of vices ought by no means to preside over the instruction of others through the practice of preaching. Hence, according to the voice of divine administration, the Levites serve the tabernacle from their twenty-fifth year, but become guardians of the vessels at fifty.

It follows:

### VERSES 21–22

“I shall not accept the person of a man, nor equate God with man; I do not know how long I shall endure, and after a little while my Maker may take me away.”

It is a sound consideration that he does not equate God with man because he does not know how long he will remain here or when he will be taken away by God in judgment. And he rightly says, “After a little while my Maker may take me away,” because however long the time of the present life may be, it is short precisely because it does not remain.

It follows:

# CHAPTER XXXIII

### VERSES 1–2

“Therefore hear, Job, my words, and listen to all my speeches. Behold, I have opened my mouth; let my tongue speak in my throat.”

The distinctive feature of arrogant teaching is that it does not know how to introduce what it teaches humbly, and cannot rightly administer the truths it understands. It is rightly said to such people through the Prophet: “You ruled over them with harshness and with power” (Ezek. 34:4).

True doctrine, by contrast, flees this vice of pride all the more vigorously in thought the more ardently it pursues the teacher of pride with the arrows of its words. Its teachers strive both to speak of humility, the teacher and mother of all virtues, and to display it in their lives, so that among the disciples of truth they may express it more through conduct than through speech. Hence Paul says: “We became little ones in your midst” (1 Thess. 2:7).

To speak in the throat is to speak quietly, not to shout with cries. By these words he signifies arrogant people placed within Holy Church. They are said to speak as if in the throat when they do not shout against adversaries living outside, but rebuke certain people within the bosom of Holy Church, as neighbors and those placed close by.

Often, too, arrogant people show that they are fleeing the very arrogance they possess. While acting in such a way that they remain hidden from no one, they tell each person about this perversity as though secretly, so that they may boast not only of the understanding of their intellect but also of their contempt for arrogance in the eyes of human beings. It follows:

### VERSE 3

“My words are from my simple heart, and my pure lips shall speak judgment.”

The simplicity of speech is a praise of great virtue. Because arrogant people do not possess it, they assert with particular insistence that they do, so that they may be heard more securely. They announce that they will speak purely because they fear that the malice of their duplicity may be detected.

Often they also mix truths with falsehoods, so that their lie may be believed more quickly because an affirmation of truth is recognized to be present in them. It follows:

### VERSE 4

“The Spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life.”

Before he is about to say something true, he has first uttered something proud. Such, indeed, such is the madness of arrogant minds: even in what they rightly understand, they are corrupted by the strength of their pride. Thus even their correct statements do not instruct their hearers, because through what they think in a swollen manner they call them not to reverence but to contempt.

Hence Moses says: “Whoever suffers an emission of seed shall be unclean” (Lev. 15:2).

In a good order he asserts both that he was made and that he was given life: made through the spirit and given life through the breath. For concerning Adam, after he had been made, it is written: “He breathed into his face the breath of life, and the man became a living soul” (Gen. 2:7). It follows:

### VERSE 5

“If you can, answer me and stand against my face.”

Behold, while recounting the order of true creation, he suddenly bursts into the proud arrogance of self-exaltation. It follows:

### VERSES 6–7

“Behold, God made me as he made you, and I too was formed from the same clay. Nevertheless, let not my miracle frighten you, and let not my eloquence be heavy for you.”

What does it mean that Elihu recognizes the order of true creation but does not understand the manner of right speech, except that all arrogant people remember that they were created equally with all human beings, but in the pride of knowledge disdain to have their hearers either be or consider themselves their equals?

Arrogant people also have this characteristic: before they speak, they always consider that they are about to say marvelous things, and they anticipate their speech with admiration, because in the sharpness of their understanding they do not recognize how great a folly their pride itself is.

It should also be noted that Paul, while wonderfully exhorting the Hebrews, added: “I ask you, my brothers, to bear with the word of consolation. For I have written to you very briefly” (Heb. 13:22). Elihu, however, brought forth empty words and, as though offering consolation, added: “Let not my miracle frighten you, and let not my eloquence be heavy for you.”

Hence Solomon says: “Before destruction the heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled” (Prov. 16:18). It follows:

### VERSES 8–11

“You have spoken in my ears, and I heard the sound of your words.”

Adding the same voice, he says:

“I am clean, without fault, blameless, and there is no iniquity in me. Because he found complaints against me, he considered me his enemy. He put my feet in fetters and watched all my paths.”

Then, presenting his own judgment against what he claimed blessed Job had said, he added:

### VERSE 12
