“Therefore, this is the point in which you are not justified.”

Blessed Job had truly said that he had been scourged without guilt. He himself had said of himself what the Lord said about him to the devil: “You have moved me against him, to afflict him without cause” (Job 2:3).

But Elihu did not believe that he could have been scourged when guilt had ceased. He did not know that the scourges did not cause his vice to suffer but increased his merit. Because Job had said that he had been scourged without fault, Elihu rebuked him with this judgment: “Therefore, this is the point in which you are not justified.”

Arrogant people have this characteristic: they desire more to accuse than to console, and they suppose that whatever happens to human beings has happened solely because of their iniquities. They do not know how to investigate hidden judgments subtly or humbly examine what they do not understand, because the pride of their own knowledge often drives them away from investigating the secret judgments of God while it exalts them.

It should also be noted that blessed Job said that his foot had been placed in fetters, but he never said that he was clean in this world, as Elihu charges him, or that he was without sin, blameless, and without iniquity. But Elihu, while striving to rebuke what had been said with severity, falsely added things that had not been said. Those who always desire to rebuke and never to encourage often lie in the act of rebuking; for in order to appear learned in accusation, they sometimes invent things to condemn.

It follows:

“I shall answer you that God is greater than man.”

Someone might perhaps say: Who does not know this, even without hearing it? But surely this knowledge is considered worthless unless it is weighed from the root of the speaker’s intention. Elihu was speaking to one who had been scourged, who had received the blows of punishment but did not know the causes of those blows. Therefore he added: “I shall answer you that God is greater than man,” so that the scourged man, considering that God is greater than he in everything he suffers, might subordinate himself in judgment to the One whom he does not doubt is greater than he. It follows:

### VERSES 13–14

“You contend against him because he has not answered you in all things. God speaks once, and does not repeat the same thing a second time.”

As though he said: God does not answer the hearts of individuals with private voices, but has established an utterance by which he satisfies the questions of all. If each of us seeks our own causes in the utterance of his Scripture, we find them there; there is no need for each person to seek a special divine voice answering what he particularly endures. In that Scripture we all receive a common answer concerning what we individually suffer.

There the life of those who came before becomes a pattern for those who follow. He no longer satisfies the thoughts or temptations of individuals indiscriminately through the voices of prophets or through angelic services, because Holy Scripture encompasses whatever can happen to individuals and has taken care to shape the life of those who follow through the examples of those who came before.

This may also be understood more subtly: the Father begot the only-begotten Son, consubstantial with himself. For God’s speaking is the begetting of the Word. To speak once is to have no other Word besides the only-begotten. He does not repeat it a second time because he begot this very Word—that is, the Son—only once.

That he uses not past but future tense is clear to everyone, because neither past nor future properly applies to God. Any tense may therefore be freely assigned to him precisely because none truly applies. The Father begot the Word without time. Who could worthily speak of that ineffable birth: that the one born from the eternal is coeternal; that the One existing before the ages begot an equal; that the One begotten is not later than the Begetter? We can marvel at these things, but we are entirely unable to behold them.

It follows:

### VERSE 15

“Through a dream.”

What does it mean that the speech of the Godhead becomes known to us through a dream, except that we do not know God’s secrets unless we keep watch inwardly through our desires? In sleep, the external senses rest, and inward things are seen. If, therefore, we wish to contemplate what is within, let us sleep with regard to external entanglements.

The voice of God is heard as if through a dream when, with a tranquil mind, we rest from the activity of this world and weigh the divine commandments in the silence of the mind itself. When the mind is lulled away from external activities, then it more fully recognizes the weight of God’s commandments; then the mind penetrates God’s words more vividly, when it refuses to admit into itself the tumult of worldly cares.

A person is badly awake when the heat of worldly affairs disturbs him insolently. While the crowd of earthly thoughts clamors, it closes the ear of the heart. It follows:

“In a night vision.”

In the light of day we see more clearly, but in a night vision we see under certain images. Night is the present life. All the saints, as long as they are in this life, behold the secrets of the divine nature as though under a certain image, because they do not yet contemplate them more clearly as they are. Hence the Prophet says: “My soul desired you in the night” (Isa. 26:9).

It follows:

“When sleep falls upon human beings.”

To cease from external activity is to sleep. It follows:

“And they sleep on their bed.”

For holy men, to sleep on a bed means to rest within the chamber of their mind. Hence it is written: “The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice upon their beds” (Ps. 149:5). It follows:

### VERSE 16

“Then he opens the ears of men.”

When they are lulled away from external activities, they hear, with the ear of inward examination opened, the causes of things. While they carefully consider either public scourges or hidden judgments, they do not cease to afflict themselves with weeping.

It follows:

“And, instructing them, he teaches them discipline.”

For to the mind that considers and tears itself through repentance, the laments of compunction are like certain wounds inflicted by blows. Hence Solomon also rightly joins together the force of both kinds of striking when he says: “The bruise of a wound wipes away evils, and blows reach the innermost parts of the belly” (Prov. 20:30).

Because compunction itself tears the mind, he not incongruously calls that same compunction discipline. There are four conditions by which the soul of righteous men is deeply affected in compunction:

- when it remembers its sins and considers where it has been;
- when, fearing the sentence of judgment and asking itself, it considers where it will be;
- when it carefully attends to the evils of the present life and mournfully considers where it is;
- or when it contemplates the good things of the heavenly homeland and, because it has not yet attained them, sees brightly where it is not.

It follows:

### VERSE 17

“That he may turn a man away from the things he has done and free him from pride.”

What has a human being done from his own resources except sin? And it is written: “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Sir. 10:15). It is therefore rightly said that when a person is turned away from the things he has done, he is freed from pride.

To be proud against the Creator is to transgress his commandments by sinning. But whoever desires to avoid what he has done recognizes what he has been made by God and humbly returns to the order of his creation. By fleeing his own works, he loves himself as he was made by God. It follows:

### VERSE 18

“Rescuing his soul from corruption, and his life, so that it may not pass into the sword.”

Every sinner is compelled to pass from the corruption of vices here to the sword of punishments there; from what he wickedly delighted in here, he is justly tormented there.

It should therefore be noted that God, speaking to us through a dream, first frees us from corruption and afterward from the sword. For he rescues from the vengeance of punishment there the life of the one whose mind here he withdraws from the delight of sin. It follows:

### VERSE 19

“He also rebukes through pain upon the bed.”

In Holy Scripture, a bed, couch, or resting place sometimes signifies the pleasure of the flesh, as in: “Rise, take up your mat and go to your house” (John 5:8).

Sometimes it signifies repose in good works, as in the Acts of the Apostles: “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed” (Acts 9:34). To rise is to abandon the evils one has committed; to make one’s bed is to perform the works that provide the grounds for reward in which one ought to rest.

At other times it signifies temporal rest, as it is written: “You have transformed his entire bed in his sickness” (Ps. 41:4). As though he said: Everything that he prepared here for himself as a place of rest, you have changed by hidden judgment into disturbance, because in the rest of the present life you trouble us either with the goads of temptation or with the affliction of a scourge.

“And he makes all his bones wither.”

In Holy Scripture we understand bones as virtues, as it is written: “The Lord preserves all their bones; not one of them shall be broken” (Ps. 34:21).

And because we prepare for ourselves in this rest a holy rest from this world, we are afflicted by the scourge of temptation. We are weakened by the weariness of recognized infirmity, for perhaps we could have become inflated by our virtues.

When we advance toward the Lord as we desire, if no temptation were to assail our progress, we would believe ourselves to possess some strength. But by the divine dispensation it is arranged that, because we forget our weakness as we advance, we may remember it when tempted; and that in our progress we may learn what comes from the divine gift, while in temptation we learn what we are from our own strength.

Thus all that had been a fat and flourishing celebration of our strength is dried up by the sorrow of anxiety. It follows:

## Verse 20

**“Let his bread be loathsome to him in his life.”** — What else is understood by “bread” than the delight of the present life [Col. 0382C]? It is as though he were saying: The afflicted mind considers that whatever previously tasted sweet and pleasing to it has been turned into bitterness.

In Sacred Scripture, the Lord himself is sometimes signified by the name “bread,” as he says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51). At other times it signifies the grace of a spiritual gift, as in the prophet’s words: “He who stops his ears so as not to hear of blood”—that is, who does not consent when sins urge him—“and closes his eyes so as not to see evil” (Isaiah 33:15)—that is, who does not approve anything opposed to righteousness—“he shall dwell on high,” that is, he has fixed his mind on lofty things. “The sublimity of the rocks shall be his fortress,” that is, he is raised toward the heavenly homeland through the examples of the Fathers who preceded him. “His bread shall be given to him” (ibid., 16), that is, the refreshment of spiritual grace.

Sometimes “bread” means instruction in divine teaching, as is said through the prophet: “You who dwell in the land of the South”—that is, in the Church filled with the Holy Spirit—“meet the fugitive with bread” (Isaiah 21:14), that is, when someone strives to escape his evils, offer him counsel through the word of instruction.

Sometimes, too, it signifies the preaching of heretics, as Solomon says in the voice of the Church concerning heretics: “Eat hidden breads willingly.” And again: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and concealed bread is more pleasant” (Proverbs 9:17).

At times “bread” means the support of the present life. Hence Jacob says: “Lord God, if you give me bread to eat,” and so forth (Genesis 28:20). And the Lord says: “You seek me not because of me, but because you ate of the loaves and were satisfied” (John 6:26).

Further, it sometimes denotes the delight of human pleasure. Hence Jeremiah says: “All her people groan and seek bread; they gave their most precious things for food, to revive the soul” (Lamentations 1:11). The people groan and seek bread when the perverse multitude is afflicted because it is not satisfied according to its desire with the delight of the present life. But it gives “its most precious things for food,” because it bends the virtues of the mind toward the appetite for transitory pleasure; and it strives to revive the soul because it attempts to satisfy its depraved desires.

It follows:

**“And the food of his soul, formerly desirable.”** — Everyone, when prosperity in good living smiles upon him, becomes cheerful; and cheerfulness itself refreshes the mind like desirable food [Col. 0383B]. But when he is struck by temptation pressing upon him somewhat more severely, all joy is rejected from his mind through the disgust of sorrow. The mind that previously rejoiced, as though satisfied by that same joy, now takes pleasure in nothing except recognizing and mourning itself.

It follows:

## Verse 21

**“His flesh shall be consumed, and his bones, which had been covered, shall be laid bare.”** — When all outward pleasure is worn away beneath pressing scourges, the bones of inward strength are laid bare. By “flesh,” carnal delight itself is understood. Or what is signified by “bones” except the virtues of the soul?

Thus the flesh wastes away and the bones are exposed because, while carnal delight is diminished by chastening scourges, the strong virtues that had previously lain hidden, as it were, beneath the flesh are revealed. No one knows how far he has advanced except amid adversity.

It follows:

## Verse 22

**“His soul shall draw near to corruption, and his life to those who bring death.”** — The soul of every just person who is tested is said to draw near to corruption when, lest virtue exalt it, it is compelled by scourges to recognize what it ought to acknowledge from its own weakness.

It draws near to corruption because it knows that, by its own strength, it is close to destruction, so that whatever keeps it far from destruction it may attribute not to itself but to the Lord. It draws near to those who bring death because, through the weakness of the flesh, it sees itself close to sins that bear death; and it is made farther from them by divine grace precisely as it discovers itself to be close to them through its own merits.

David had drawn near to corruption by contemplating his condition when he said: “Remember, Lord, that we are dust; man’s days are like grass” (Psalm 102:15). Paul, too, had drawn near to those who bring death by contemplating his own weakness when he said: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members. Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:23–24).

# BOOK TWENTY-FOUR

[Col. 0383]

[Col. 0383C] Thus, while Elihu shows above the human being under trial, he reveals the situation in which the human race is placed amid that trial. Therefore he immediately adds a general remedy, saying:

## Verse 23

**“If there is for him an angel speaking.”** — Who is this angel except the one who is called through the prophet “the Angel of great counsel”? Since in Greek “to evangelize” means “to announce,” the Lord, announcing himself to us, is called an angel; and he rightly says: “If there is for him an angel speaking,” because, as the Apostle says, “he also intercedes for us” (Romans 8:34).

It follows:

**“One among those like him.”** — It is the practice of medicine sometimes to cure like with like, and sometimes opposites with opposites. Therefore, when our physician came to us from above and found us all oppressed by illnesses, he applied something like us and something contrary to us.

Because he came to human beings as a human being, he agreed with us in the truth of nature; but because he came to sinners as a just man, he differed from us in the strength of righteousness. Thus, because the Lord was truly born, truly died, and truly rose again, he nevertheless differs from us in all things by the greatness of his power, while agreeing with us only in the truth of his nature.

By this he speaks to the Father on our behalf: he deigned to show himself as a human being for all human beings. It follows:

**“To announce righteousness to human beings.”** — Unless he had become like human beings, the righteous human being would not have appeared before God. From the point at which he deigned to assume our weakness, he announces our righteousness.

It follows:

## Verse 24

**“He will have mercy on him and say: Deliver him.”** — The mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, has mercy on the human being insofar as he assumed the form of a human being. By this mercy, once the human being has been redeemed, he says to the Father: “Deliver him, so that he may not descend into corruption.”

As we have already said above, his saying “Deliver him” means that, by assuming human nature, he demonstrates that the human being is free. From the flesh that he assumed he also shows that the flesh he redeemed is free, as he himself says: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John 8:36).

Earlier it had been said: “His soul has drawn near to corruption”; afterward it is said: “Let him not descend into corruption” [Col. 0384D]. It is as though he were saying: Because, by recognizing his weakness, he does not fail to understand that he is close to corruption, let him therefore not descend into the destruction of corruption.

He would descend into corruption if he judged himself to be far from corruption by his own strength. But because he has humbly drawn near to corruption, he ought to be mercifully delivered from it, so that he may be strong against attacking vices precisely because he recognizes himself to be weak by his own merits.

It follows:

**“I have found one in whom I may be gracious to him.”** — As though the mediator between God and human beings were openly saying: Since there was no human being who could appear before God as a just intercessor for all, I made myself human in order to show mercy to human beings; and, by presenting myself as a human being, I found in myself the just human being in whom I might show mercy to human beings.

And because, by assuming weakness, the Lord endured our punishment in dying and changed our corruption by rising again, this angel rightly adds the scourges of mortality and has mercy on them, saying:

## Verse 25

**“His flesh has been consumed by punishments; let him return to the days of his youth.”** — It is as though he were saying: He has been cast down by the punishment of his mortality into a kind of old age; let him return to the days of his youth, that is, let him be renewed in his former integrity, so that he may not remain where he fell but return, once redeemed, to the purpose for which he was created.

Sacred Scripture often uses “youth” for newness of life. Hence it is said to the bridegroom who is coming: “Young women have loved you” (Song of Songs 1:3). The old age of the old human being, wasting away amid vices, was mourned by the one who said: “I have grown old among all my enemies” (Psalm 6:8). Conversely, another, urging joy in virtues, says: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth” (Ecclesiastes 11:9).

It follows:

## Verse 26

**“He will entreat the Lord, and he will be favorable toward him.”** — He first speaks of the angel’s asking, and afterward of the human being, because unless the Lord himself, by his incarnation, first interceded with the Father and requested life for us, our insensibility would never rouse itself to ask for those things that are eternal.

The intercession of his incarnation came first, so that the awakening of our sluggishness might follow.

It follows:

**“And he will see his face with rejoicing.”** — A person is moved to compunction in one way when, contemplating inward things, he is terrified by fear of his evils; he is moved in another way when, looking upon heavenly joys, he is strengthened by a certain hope and security.

The fire of tribulation is first cast into our mind through consideration of its blindness, so that all the rust of vices may be burned away. Then, once the eyes of the heart have been cleansed, the joy of the heavenly homeland is opened to it, so that we may first cleanse by mourning what we have done and afterward contemplate more clearly, through joy, what we seek.

“Rejoicing” is spoken of when an unspeakable joy is conceived in the mind—one that can neither be hidden nor disclosed in words, yet is revealed through certain movements, although it cannot be expressed in any precise terms. Hence it is written: “Blessed is the people that knows rejoicing” (Psalm 88:16).

Because we recognize anyone by his face, we rightly call the knowledge of God “face.” Hence, after Jacob had wrestled with the angel, he said: “I have seen the Lord face to face” (Genesis 32:30), as though he were saying: “I have come to know the Lord because he himself has deigned to know me.”

Paul testifies that this knowledge will be made complete at the end, saying: “Then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known” (1 Corinthians 13:12).

It follows:

**“And he will restore his righteousness to the human being.”** — Our righteousness is called “ours,” not because it originates from us and is ours by nature, but because it becomes ours through divine generosity, just as we say in the Lord’s Prayer: “Give us today our daily bread” (Luke 11:3).

The Lord restores his righteousness to the human being—not a righteousness that the human being possessed from himself. God therefore restores to the human being that righteousness for which he was created: that he should delight in cleaving to God, fear his threatening judgment, and no longer believe the flattering promises of the cunning serpent.

It follows:

## Verse 27

**“He will look upon human beings and say: I have sinned.”** — But how would he recognize himself as a sinner if he did not possess righteousness? No one detects his own strength unless he has begun to be upright. For one who is altogether perverse cannot even see what he is; but whoever understands that he is a sinner has already begun, in some measure, to be righteous, and from what is righteous in him he accuses what he has done unjustly.

Sacred Scripture sometimes uses “human beings” for those who possess merely human wisdom, as Paul says: “Since there is jealousy and envy among you, are you not carnal? Are you not human beings?” (1 Corinthians 3:3). Because they also yield to carnal affection, they are no longer called human beings but beasts. Hence David says: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with beasts,” and so forth (Psalm 48:13).

At other times, when Scripture says “human beings,” it distinguishes them by reason from beasts, to whom the Lord says through the prophet: “You are my pasture, flocks, you human beings” (Ezekiel 34:31).

It is therefore rightly said of this penitent: “He will look upon human beings and say: I have sinned.” It is as though it were said: He looks upon the examples of holy men and, measuring himself against them, discovers that he is wicked.

Whoever desires to understand fully what sort of person he is must surely look upon those who are unlike him, so that from the form of the good he may measure how deformed he is through having abandoned the good. Hence it is also said through Ezekiel: “Son of man, show the house of Israel the temple, and let them be ashamed of their iniquities; let them measure its structure and be ashamed of all that they have done” (Ezekiel 43:11).

The temple is shown when the soul of the righteous, shining with such holiness, is displayed to sinners for their shame. To measure its structure is to weigh carefully the life of the righteous.

It follows:

**“And truly I have transgressed, and I have not received what I deserved.”** — Often even those who do not believe themselves to be sinners confess that they are sinners. For it frequently happens that people openly admit that they are wicked, but when they hear their sins truthfully reproved by others, they defend themselves with all their strength and try to appear innocent.

Everyone placed under a scourge considers his sins insufficiently if he thinks that he has been struck either as much as or more than he deserved. But this man, the more he considers the examples of the greater, the more strictly he examines himself; and he recognizes that he has been struck less than he deserved, because in their righteousness he sees how serious his guilt was in having gone astray.

Therefore he does not regard what he suffers as excessive, because he knows how strictly to weigh what he has done.

It follows:

## Verse 28

**“For he has delivered his soul from going into destruction.”** — Because divine grace goes before us and our free will follows in good action, we are said to deliver ourselves when we consent to the Lord who delivers us.

Hence Paul, after saying, “I labored more abundantly than all of them,” immediately added, lest he seem to attribute his labors to himself: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10).

It follows:

**“But, living, he will see the light.”** — The light of truth, which the dead could not see with the heart; or certainly because the Lord said: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12).

The dead will also see the light when all the unjust behold him coming to judgment in human form. But the living person then looks upon the light who, with the free eyes of the heart, attends to him in the form of his divinity.

It follows:

## Verse 29

**“God does all these things, three times for each person.”** [Col. 0387B] — It is as though he were saying: What I have said once concerning one person is carried out three times for each person.

But we must carefully consider what these three occasions are on which each human being is afflicted with anxious sorrow and, after sorrow, is immediately summoned to the security of joy. If we attend vigilantly, we find these three occasions of sorrow and joy alternating in the soul of each of the elect in the following ways: conversion, temptation, and death.

In the first, which we have called the occasion of conversion, there is great sorrow when each person, considering his sins, desires to break the fetters of worldly cares and to walk along God’s path through the breadth of a secure way of life.

It can therefore rightly be said of this embittered person: “His bread becomes loathsome to him in his life, and the food of his soul, formerly desirable. His flesh wastes away, and the bones that had been covered are laid bare. His soul has drawn near to corruption, and his life to those who bring death,” as was said above (Job 33:20, 22).

But because divine grace does not permit us to be afflicted by these difficulties for long, once the bonds of our sins have been broken it quickly leads us, through consolation, to the freedom of a new way of life. Immense joy arises in the heart because, through the hope of security, it is already drawing near to the one whom it desires.

Thus it is rightly said of this person: “He will entreat God, and he will be favorable toward him; he will see his face with rejoicing, and he will restore his righteousness to the human being. He will look upon human beings and say: I have sinned, and truly I have transgressed, and I have not received what I deserved. He has delivered his soul from going into destruction, but, living, he will see the light” (ibid., 26, 28).

After the first occasion of sorrow and joy, which each person recognizes through the effort of conversion, a second arises: lest he be dissolved by negligence born of security, he is afflicted by the force of temptation.

At the very beginning of conversion, each person is often received by great sweetness of consolation, but afterward experiences the hard labor of testing. There are three stages of those who are converted: beginning, middle, and perfection.

At the beginning come the blandishments of sweetness; in the middle come the struggles of temptation; at the end comes the perfection of fullness. First, therefore, they receive sweet things that console them; afterward bitter things that exercise them; and finally pleasant and lofty things that strengthen them.

Often a convert is stirred by such goads of temptation as he remembers never having experienced before the grace of conversion. This is not because the root of that temptation was absent then, but because it was not apparent.

The human mind, occupied by many thoughts, often remains in some way unknown even to itself, so that it does not know at all what it is enduring. Amid these things, therefore, the discovered mind is pulled this way and that and scattered by the many waves of temptation. It is so constricted by the movements of temptation roaring around it that it may rightly be said of it: “Let his bread be loathsome to him in his life,” as above.

But because merciful God permits us to be tested by temptations, not rejected, as it is written: “God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Corinthians 10:13), the work of consolation quickly comes to meet us. It calms the goads of temptation as they rise and stills the movements of hostile thoughts with inward peace.

Then the soul receives immense joy from heavenly hope when it sees the evil it endured conquered, so that it may rightly be said of this person who has been tested and delivered: “He will see his face with rejoicing, and he has delivered his soul from going into destruction, but, living, he will see the light.”

After the struggles of conversion and the distress of testing, a harsh temptation still remains. For no one can come to the joys of perfect freedom unless he has first paid the debt of the human condition.

Each convert, watchfully concerned for himself, does not cease silently considering within himself how strict the eternal Judge will be when he comes. Each day he looks toward his end and reflects what account of his life he will have to give before such severe justice.

He considers that we cannot pass through the way of the present life without guilt. He considers that even what we have done commendably is not without some guilt if we are judged without mercy. For who among us could surpass or even equal the life of the Fathers who preceded us? And yet David says: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant” (Psalm 142:2).

As the dissolution of the flesh approaches, therefore, the soul even of the just is sometimes disturbed by fear of punishment; and whatever tranquility it may have been able to taste in this life is shaken when the moment of death intervenes, so that it may rightly be said: “His bread becomes loathsome to him in his life,” and so forth.

But because the souls of the righteous are often cleansed from lesser contagions by the very fear of death, they begin to receive the joys of eternal recompense from the moment of the dissolution of the flesh itself. Often, indeed, they receive some foretaste of eternal recompense even before they are stripped of the flesh.

They grow joyful, and while paying the debt of their old condition, they already enjoy the gladness of a new gift. Hence it is rightly said: “He will see his face with rejoicing.”

It follows:

## Verse 30

**“To recall their souls from corruption and enlighten them with the light of the living.”** — The light of those who are dying is the light that we see with bodily eyes. Those who still live for this world are darkened by the light of the dying.

But they are enlightened by the light of the living who, scorning temporal light, turn toward the splendor of inward brightness, so that they may live there where, by perceiving it, they may see the true light; where there is not one thing called light and another called life, but where the light itself is life.

There the light surrounds us outwardly in such a way that it fills us inwardly; it fills us inwardly in such a way that, while unbounded, it encompasses us outwardly. They are therefore enlightened by this light of the living, which they then perceive with greater subtlety in proportion as they have first lived toward it here.

It follows:

## Verse 31

**“Attend, Job, and hear me; be silent while I speak.”** — By these words he reveals what sort of person he is in his own estimation. For it is immense arrogance to demand reverence from an elder and to command silence to one who is better.

It follows:

## Verse 32

**“But if you have something to say, answer me; speak. For I desire you to appear just.”** — When just preachers correct various people, they often return, through the grace of humility, to the depths of their own thoughts. In the very matter they correct, they inquire whether they themselves might perhaps be mistaken, and they grant those whom they have corrected permission to declare whether they themselves hold a more just view.

The arrogant sometimes desire to imitate this. For, setting aside the outward appearance of pride in their words for a little while, they seem to seek the righteousness of those whom they correct, if it can perhaps be found. They do this not because they truly think so, but because they desire to adorn themselves with the appearance of humility. They fear that, because they are proud and swollen, they may be seen to be so.

It follows:

## Verse 33

**“But if you do not have anything to say, hear me, be silent, and I will teach you wisdom.”** — Those who truly seek to hear what is just patiently wait to hear what they seek. But Elihu, who had not truly spoken the words of inquiry, did not permit Job to say what he had sought. Instead, what he had harbored within burst forth immediately, and he showed what he was in his own eyes, saying: “Be silent, and I will teach you wisdom.”

For arrogant men, when they speak with some appearance of humility, do not long remain within that appearance. Although they may perhaps ask to hear, they immediately obstruct the answer by speaking, lest they be deceived.

# CHAPTER THIRTY-FOUR

## Verse 1

**“Thus Elihu, proclaiming, also spoke these words.”** — What else is shown by the term “proclaiming” than an inflation of pride? The words that came from the lofty root of arrogance proceeded with a certain apparent elevation and distinction.

It follows:

## Verses 2–3

**“Hear my words, you wise men, and listen to me, you learned ones. For the ear tests words, and the throat judges foods by taste.”** [Col. 0389D] — It is as though he were saying: Just as the ear does not recognize foods and the throat does not recognize words, so no fool understands the judgment of a wise person.

Therefore, wise and learned men, hear what I say—you who are able to understand what is spoken. Let us see how much he fears: he thinks it proper that his words should be heard only by the wise.

But the true preacher of wisdom says: “I am a debtor both to the wise and to the foolish” (Romans 1:14).

It follows:

## Verse 4

**“Let us choose judgment for ourselves, and among ourselves let us see what is better.”** — Whether he sought this judgment with a humble heart we can easily recognize if we weigh his subsequent words.

It follows:

## Verses 5–6

**“For you said, Job: I am righteous, and God has overturned my judgment. In judging me there is falsehood, and my arrow is violent, though I am without any sin.”** — He complains that blessed Job said these things, although the words of sacred history, carefully examined, testify that he did not say them at all.

But the one who had fairly sought judgment immediately pronounces sentence from the fault he has invented. For it follows:

## Verses 7–8

**“What man is like Job, who drinks mockery like water, who walks with those who practice iniquity?”** — Behold, while seeking judgment, he has pronounced judgment; and, without awaiting any judgment from blessed Job after presenting his accusation, he judged him worthy of condemnation through association with the rejected.

For he says: “What man is like Job?”—so that we should understand, “No one.” And he adds: “Who drinks mockery like water.”

When water is drunk, it is taken in so fluidly that nothing about its thickness delays swallowing. To drink mockery like water is to mock God without any obstruction of thought, so that neither tongue nor conscience offers any hesitation to what is uttered in pride.

How far this judgment of his concerning blessed Job departs from the path of truth we also learn from the testimony by which the Lord says to the devil: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth?” (Job 1:8).

Behold, the Truth calls him incomparably righteous, while Elihu asserts that he is incomparably sinful.

Such is often characteristic of arrogant preachers: they desire to rebuke their afflicted hearers more harshly than to console them gently. They strive more to denounce evils by reproving than to strengthen good things by praising. Hence it is written: “In the mouth of a fool is the rod of pride” (Proverbs 14:4).

Sometimes even just preachers strike severely; but it is one thing when righteousness urges, and another when pride inflates. When the just correct severely, they do not lose the grace of inward sweetness. Often, to restrain the restlessness of the wicked, they assume the harshness of strict vigor; but inwardly they are melted by the fire of charity and burn with love for those against whom they rage with harsh correction.

Hence it is written: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deep” (Ecclesiastes 12:11).

It follows:

## Verse 9

**“For I said: A man will not please God, even if he has run with him.”** — Anyone who reads the words of blessed Job recognizes that he certainly did not say this. But one who speaks in order to display himself and grow proud—what wonder if he invents in another what he may condemn?

It follows:

## Verse 10

**“Therefore, men of understanding, hear me.”** — Behold, again inflated by the arrogance of pride, he seeks only those who might seem capable of understanding him worthily.

## Verse 11

**“Far be impiety from God, and iniquity from the Almighty; for he repays a human being according to his work, and restores to him according to the ways of each.”** [Col. 0391A] — He rightly praised God in saying that there is neither iniquity nor impiety in the Almighty. But in this life what he adds is by no means always carried out: that he repays each person according to his work and according to his ways.

For he freely goes before many who commit unlawful and perverse deeds and turns them toward holy works. He also strikes some devoted to upright actions with a scourge, afflicting them as though they were displeasing even when they are pleasing.

Solomon bears witness to this, saying: “There are righteous people to whom evils come as though they had done the works of the wicked, and there are wicked people who are so secure as though they possessed the deeds of the righteous” (Ecclesiastes 8:14).

Elihu would therefore have spoken more truthfully if he had said that there is no impiety or iniquity in the Almighty even when he does not appear to repay human beings according to their own ways. For even what we do not understand proceeds from the just balance of hidden judgment.

It follows:

## Verse 12

**“Truly God will not condemn without cause, nor does the Almighty overturn judgment.”** — The Lord says to the devil: “You have stirred me up against him, to afflict him without cause” (Job 2:3).

These statements seem contradictory unless they are weighed with careful consideration. For it is one thing to condemn and another to afflict. He afflicts, in a certain respect, without cause, but he does not condemn without cause.

Had he not afflicted Job without cause in one respect, when he was not destroying his vice but increasing his merit? He cannot condemn without cause, because condemnation cannot be made partially or with respect to only one matter. Condemnation at the end punishes everything that each person has committed here.

Nor does the Almighty overturn judgment, because even if the things we suffer appear less than just, they are nevertheless rightly decreed in the hidden tribunal.

It follows:

## Verse 13

**“Who appointed another over the earth, or whom did he place over the world that he fashioned?”** — We are to understand: “No one.”

He rules the world by himself, having created it by himself; and he does not need another’s assistance to rule what did not require assistance to be made. These points are gathered together so that he may clearly indicate that, if almighty God does not neglect to rule by himself what he created, then he certainly rules well what he created well. For he who created it lovingly does not govern it wickedly.

It follows:

## Verse 14

**“If he should direct his heart toward him, he would draw his spirit and breath to himself.”** — The heart is bent when it seeks lowly things; it is directed when it is lifted toward things above.

Therefore, if a human being directs his heart toward the Lord, the Lord draws his spirit and breath to himself. “Spirit” signifies inward thoughts; “breath,” by which the body is moved, signifies outward actions.

For God to draw a human being’s spirit and breath to himself is to change both our inward and outward aspects toward the conversion of desire for himself, so that nothing external pleases the mind and the flesh, even if it desires something below, does not strive to obtain it.

Rather, the whole human being should burn inwardly by desiring the one from whom he exists, and outwardly restrain himself by subduing himself.

It follows:

## Verse 15

**“All flesh would perish together, and the human being would return to ashes.”** — All flesh perishes together when it no longer serves any of its own impulses, because the presiding spirit restrains all its volatility and, with a certain sword of its strictness, kills everything in it that was living wrongly.

Jeremiah killed himself with this sword of discipline when he said: “After you converted me, I repented; and after you showed me, I struck my thigh” (Jeremiah 31:19).

What is understood by “thigh” except the pleasure of the flesh? And what does he mean by “After you showed me, I struck my thigh,” except that, after seeing heavenly things spiritually, he extinguished everything lower that lived carnally within him?

When a person is placed in sin, he forgets his mortality and does not remember that he is earth, because he is still swollen with pride. After the grace of conversion, when he is touched by the spirit of humility, what else does he remember himself to be than ashes?

Abraham had returned to ashes when he said: “I will speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Genesis 18:27). Hence David says: “You take away their spirit, and they perish,” and so forth (Psalm 63:29).

It follows:

## Verse 16

**“If, therefore, you have understanding, hear what is said and listen to the voice of my discourse.”** — All arrogant people have this characteristic: when they perhaps perceive something sharp, they immediately burst from it into the vice of pride, despise everyone’s understanding in comparison with their own, and in their own judgment place themselves before the merits of others.

Behold how Elihu gradually advances into arrogance through the growth of his words. He had often said: “If you have something to say, answer me,” and so forth (Job 33:32). It is as though he were saying: “Say something, if indeed you can be worthy to say it.”

But now he says: “If you have understanding, hear what is said.” It is as though he openly said: “Hear me, if indeed you can be worthy to hear.”

These are the daily declines that occur in the hearts of the rejected, by which they descend continually toward worse things.

It follows:

## Verse 17

**“Can one who does not love judgment be healed? How then do you condemn him who is righteous to such an extent?”** — He spoke a good judgment, but it ought not to have been directed against blessed Job.

In everything that is said, we must carefully consider what is said, to whom it is said, and how it is said. Elihu considered what he should say, but he did not consider to whom he should say it.

Blessed Job loved judgment because he knew how to weigh his causes carefully with God. He had not condemned him who is righteous; rather, while placed in suffering, he humbly sought to know why he had been struck without sin.

Whoever carefully examines his ways and, entering the secret chamber of his heart, weighs what the Lord himself gives and what he himself owes to God, loves judgment.

After accusing blessed Job of not loving judgment and of condemning him who is righteous, he immediately adds the righteousness of that same righteous one—that is, the Lord’s righteousness.

It follows:

## Verse 18

**“He who says to a king: Apostate; who calls rulers impious.”** — We often know that many who are in authority demand from their subjects an excessive and disordered fear of themselves. They wish to be honored not so much for the Lord’s sake as in place of the Lord.

Within themselves they exalt themselves through the swelling of their hearts and despise all their subjects in comparison with themselves. Hence it is written: “They have appointed you ruler; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Sirach 32:1). This is rightly said against them.

**“He who says to a king: Apostate.”** — Every proud ruler falls into the guilt of apostasy as often as he delights in ruling human beings and rejoices in the singularity of his honor. He does not consider under whom he stands, and he exults as though he were not equal to those who are his equals.

They would lead others along the way of piety if they displayed examples of humility to the eyes of their subjects. A ruler is impious who departs from the path of truth and, while rushing headlong himself, invites those who follow him onto the precipice. A ruler is impious who, through examples of arrogance, shows the way of error.

Paul feared being an impious ruler when he restrained the height of his authority, saying: “Not seeking glory from human beings, neither from you nor from others, although we could have been burdensome as apostles of Christ; instead, we became little ones in your midst” (1 Thessalonians 2:6–7).

# BOOK TWENTY-FIVE

[Col. 0393]

[Col. 0393B] The very nature of the human condition shows how far humanity surpasses other things. For when reason is attributed to human beings, it declares how greatly rational nature exceeds everything that lacks either life, sensation, or reason. Yet because we close our eyes to what is inward and invisible and feed upon visible things, we often honor a person not for what he is in himself but for what surrounds him. Since we do not consider what he is, but what he can do, in showing partiality we are guided not by persons themselves but by the things adjacent to them. Thus even the person who is honored outwardly comes under examination among us inwardly, because, while he is regarded as honorable on account of what pertains to him, he is placed beneath his possessions in our judgment. But, on the contrary, it is said of God:

[Col. 0393C] **VERSE 19. “Who accepts not the person of princes, nor regards the tyrant, when he contends against the poor.”** — By “prince” or “tyrant,” any proud person may be understood; by “the poor,” the humble may be represented. Therefore almighty God does not regard the tyrant contending against the poor, because He declares that in the judgment He does not know all the proud who now oppress the humble, saying: “I know not from where you are” (Luke 13:25). And because He destroys powerfully when He wills, just as He powerfully created when He willed, the reasoning appropriately continues: **“For all are the work of His hands.”** And immediately it adds:

**VERSE 20. “Suddenly they shall die, and in the middle of the night the peoples shall be bowed down and pass away.”** — However late the wicked are taken from this life, they are taken suddenly and unexpectedly, because they cannot foresee their end by reflection. What is sudden is what one could not consider beforehand. That foolish rich man was taken suddenly: he abandoned the storehouses he had prepared and found the place of hell which he had not foreseen. Therefore it is said to him: “This night they shall demand your soul from you” (Luke 12:20). But of the righteous it is said: “But you, brethren, are not in darkness, so that that day should overtake you like a thief” (1 Thess. 5:4).

In the middle of the night those who, through the negligence of their darkness, are snatched away into humiliation will be bowed down and pass away. Then those who now neglect to bow themselves through humility of heart will be bent by the sentence of the Judge. But the elect, so that they may not be unwillingly bent in death, bend themselves willingly in humility. Hence it is said to the holy Church concerning the converted offspring of persecutors: “The sons of those who humbled you shall come to you, bending low” (Isa. 60:14).

And he rightly does not say of the dying peoples, “they shall pass,” but “they shall pass away,” because even while living we move daily toward our end in time and, as though by subduing it, pass through the present life as though along a certain road. For this very living of those who are dying is like going toward death; and as many days of life as we complete, by so many steps, as on a journey toward our appointed destination, do we draw nearer to that place.

It continues: **“And they shall take away the violent man without a hand.”** — Understand: “the divine judgments.” Without a hand they shall take away the one who was violent with his hand. They shall take him away without a hand because, when a sudden departure presses upon him, he is invisibly snatched away, although he visibly used violence against others. It continues:

[Col. 0394C] **VERSE 21. “For His eyes are upon the ways of men, and He considers all their steps.”** — He seemed not to consider them when this violent man was perpetrating every evil he could with impunity. God was thought not to see the deeds of the unjust because He delayed condemning them justly, and His great patience was regarded as a kind of negligence. The wicked man himself likewise believed so many times that he was not seen by God, as often as he sinned with impunity. To him a certain wise man says: “Do not say, ‘I have sinned, and what sad thing has happened to me?’” (Sir. 5:4).

He does not wish to correct the wickedness for which he has not yet brought forth a fitting punishment. By “the steps of men” he means either the individual actions on which we rely, or the alternating movements of our inner thought, by which, as if by steps, we either recede far from the Lord or draw near to God in devotion. For the mind approaches God by as many steps as it advances through good movements, and again becomes distant by as many steps as it declines through evil thoughts. It continues:

[Col. 0394D] **VERSE 22. “There are no darknesses, and there is no shadow of death, where those who work iniquity may hide.”** — What did he intend to designate by “darkness” except ignorance, and by “the shadow of death” except forgetfulness? Concerning the ignorance of certain people it is said: “Having their understanding darkened” (Eph. 4:18). And again, concerning the forgetfulness that occurs in death, it is written: “On that day all their thoughts shall perish” (Ps. 145:4). Since, therefore, whatever is thought while living will be handed over entirely to oblivion through death, it is, as it were, a kind of forgetfulness and shadow of death.

It is as though he said: No one is hidden from His judgment for this reason: no one can either fail to see what we have done or forget what He sees. Yet “darkness” and “the shadow of death” can also be understood in another way. Every change is, as it were, a change of death. For that which changes something kills it, as it were, with respect to what it was, so that it ceases to be what it was and begins to be what it was not. Therefore the true Light, namely our Creator, because He is darkened by no vicissitude of mutability and is overshadowed by no defects of His nature, but for Him to be is to shine without change, is said to contain neither darkness nor the shadow of death.

[Col. 0395B] Hence it is written elsewhere: “With whom there is no change or shadow of alteration” (James 1:17). And again the Apostle Paul says: “Who alone has immortality and dwells in inaccessible light” (1 Tim. 6:16). For the eternal Light, which is God, shines with such unchangeability that it is also wholly penetrating in its power. He knows no hidden things, because He penetrates everything; nor does He forget what He has penetrated, because He endures unchangeably. It continues:

**VERSE 23. “For it is no longer in the power of man to come to God in judgment.”** — Here, certainly, the judgment that punishes through eternal retribution is not being designated, but the judgment that dissolves what has been conceived in the mind through conversion. No one desires to come to that judgment who fears being condemned by it.

When it is therefore said, “It is no longer in the power of man to come to God in judgment,” it clearly shows that there is a certain judgment which even the condemned and rejected may one day desire. And what is that judgment except the one of which the Apostle Paul says: “If we judged ourselves, we should not be judged” (1 Cor. 11:31); and of which it is said through the prophet: “There is no judgment in their steps” (Isa. 59:8); and which David says: “The honor of the King loves judgment” (Ps. 98:4)? That is, the one who already honors God through faith should diligently judge what he owes Him in his actions.

Hence the prophet says: “Recall me, and let us be judged together; tell me if you have anything by which you may be justified” (Isa. 43:26). Each person’s mind ought, through anxious inquiry, to examine both its own causes before the Lord and the Lord’s causes against itself. It ought carefully to weigh either what good things it has received from Him or what evils it has perversely repaid for those good things by living badly.

The elect never cease doing this daily. Hence Solomon rightly says: “The thoughts of the righteous are judgments” (Prov. 12:5). They enter the Judge’s tribunal within the breast of the heart. They consider how severely He will one day strike who now waits patiently for a long time. They fear concerning what they remember themselves to have done; they punish by weeping what they understand themselves to have perpetrated. Nor is any ministry lacking in this judgment conceived in the mind that ought to punish the guilty more fully: conscience accuses, reason judges, fear binds, and grief tortures.

This judgment punishes all the more certainly because it rages more inwardly, since nothing external contributes to it. Since, therefore, it is now in our power to undergo within our minds a judgment against ourselves, let us recognize and accuse ourselves for what we have been; let us torment ourselves through repentance; let us not cease, while it is permitted, to judge what we have done. Let us listen carefully to what is said: “It is no longer in the power of man to come to God in judgment.” It continues:

**VERSE 24. “He shall crush many and innumerable people, and make some stand in place of others.”** — After much has been said about the punishment of the wicked, a hidden judgment is suddenly introduced, which is justly and devoutly arranged over us: some lose what they seemed to possess, while others receive what others lose through their merits.

It is clear to all that at that final reckoning almighty God will conduct a public examination, abandoning some to torments and admitting others to participation in the heavenly kingdom. But what is then displayed publicly is carried out daily now through this secret judgment. For, justly and mercifully examining or ordering the hearts of individuals, He rejects some toward outward things and draws others toward what is inward. He kindles in these a desire for inward things; the others He abandons to think about outward things for the sake of their pleasures. He raises the minds of the former toward heavenly things and plunges the pride of the latter into low desires. Those who seem, according to human judgment, already stand in the sight of the eternal Judge.

Who could have judged that Judas would lose his share in life even after the ministry of apostleship? And who, on the other hand, would have believed that the thief would find the cause of life at the very moment of death?

Those also are crushed who, abandoning heavenly things, seek the earth. What greater crushing could there be than to seek the creature after abandoning the Creator, to yearn for lowly things after abandoning heavenly joys? Hence it is rightly said through the Prophet: “He humbles sinners down to the earth” (Ps. 146:6).

By saying “He shall crush many” and immediately adding “innumerable,” he wished to express the multitude of the reprobate, which surpasses the number comprehensible to human reason. Or certainly he wished to indicate that all who perish are not counted among the elect, so that they are “innumerable” precisely because they run outside the number. Hence the Prophet, seeing so many people in the present time seeming outwardly to believe—so many that it is certain they surpass the fixed number and total of the elect—says: “They have been multiplied beyond number” (Ps. 39:5). It continues:

[Col. 0396D] **VERSE 25. “For He knows their works, and therefore He brings on night, and they shall be crushed.”** — We must understand very carefully that every wicked person is crushed in night in two ways: either when he is struck by the tribulation of outward judgment, or when he is inwardly blinded by a hidden sentence. He falls in night when, through the final judgment, he loses forever the light of life. Hence it is written: “Bind his feet and hands, and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. 22:13).

Again, the wicked person is crushed in night when, condemned by the confusion of his preceding sins, he finds no light of truth and does not recognize what he ought to do thereafter. Every sin which is not quickly covered by repentance is either sin and the cause of sin, or sin and the punishment of sin.

A sin which repentance does not dissolve soon draws a person to another sin by its own weight. Thus it is not merely sin, but sin and the cause of sin. For a subsequent fault arises from that vice by which the blinded mind is led to something worse and bound by another chain. But the sin that arises from sin is no longer merely sin; it is sin and the punishment of sin, because by a just judgment almighty God darkens the heart of the sinner, so that through the merit of the preceding sin he may also fall into others.

Hence David says: “Add iniquity upon their iniquity, and let them not enter into Your righteousness” (Ps. 68:28). Therefore, because the eye of the heart has been blinded by preceding sins, that very blindness—which confounds the sinner’s mind through the condemnation of a previously committed fault—is deservedly called night, because through it the light of truth is hidden from the eyes of the delinquent.

The Lord is said to bring on night, not because He Himself inflicts darkness, but because in His mercy He does not illuminate the darkened hearts of sinners. Thus to have blinded someone in night means that He has willed to free him from other darknesses.

It continues:

[Col. 0397B] **VERSE 26. “As the wicked He struck them in the place of those who see.”** — In sacred Scripture *quasi* (“as” or “as though”) is accustomed to be used sometimes for likeness and sometimes for truth. It is used for likeness when the Apostle says: “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (2 Cor. 6:10). It is used for truth when John says: “We saw His glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father” (John 1:14).

In this passage it makes no difference whether it is used for likeness or for truth, because, whichever way it is taken, the wicked life of evil people is plainly signified. Sacred Scripture properly calls the faithless “wicked” (*impii*). By this distinction sinners are separated from the wicked: although every wicked person is a sinner, not every sinner is wicked; for even one who is devout in faith may be called a sinner. Hence John says: “If we say that we have no sin, the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). But properly one is called wicked who is separated from the devotion of religion. Concerning such people the Prophet says: “The wicked shall not rise in judgment” (Ps. 1:5).

“The place of those who see” is called the holy Church. In it one rightly stands so as to see the true Light, which is God. Hence it is said to Moses: “There is a place beside Me, and you shall stand upon the rock when My majesty passes by” (Exod. 33:21–22). And shortly afterward: “I shall take away My hand, and you shall see My back” (ibid., 23).

Many who were placed within the holy Church under a devout appearance have been found outside the Church in ungodly conduct. Concerning them it is written elsewhere: “I saw the wicked buried, who, while they were alive, were in the holy place, and they were praised in the city as though for the works of the righteous” (Eccl. 8:10). It continues:

[Col. 0397D] **VERSE 27. “Who have withdrawn from Him as though deliberately.”** — We must understand that sin is committed in three ways: through ignorance, through weakness, or deliberately. Sin committed through weakness is graver than that committed through ignorance, but sin committed deliberately is much graver than that committed through weakness.

Paul sinned through ignorance when he said: “I who formerly was a blasphemer and a persecutor,” and what follows (1 Tim. 1:13). Peter sinned through weakness. But those sinned deliberately of whom the Teacher Himself said: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin,” and what follows (John 15:22–24).

There are therefore some in the Church who not only fail to do good things but even persecute them, and who detest in others what they themselves neglect to do. Their sin is committed not through weakness or ignorance but through deliberate intention. For if they wished to fulfill good things but could not, they would at least love in others what they neglect in themselves.

It continues: **“And they did not wish to understand all His ways.”** — They do not fail to understand through weakness; rather, they did not wish to understand, because they often disdain even to know what they scorn to do. For it is written: “The servant who did not know his master’s will and did not do what was worthy shall be beaten with few strokes; but the servant who knew his master’s will and did not act according to it shall be beaten with many strokes” (Luke 12:47–48).

They regard the impunity of sinning as a remedy for not knowing. They grow dark through the sole obscurity of pride and therefore do not discern, because it is one thing not to have known and another to have been unwilling to know. Not to know is ignorance; to have been unwilling to know is pride.

“His way” is every action of the incarnate Lord which He performed in time. “His ways” are the patterns of living that He laid out for those who came to Him. He offered as many ways to those who came to Him as He displayed examples of good living. The Prophet had seen His ways of humility when he sighed, saying: “I shall be exercised in Your commandments, and I shall consider Your ways” (Ps. 118:15).

Since, therefore, the proud despise the deeds of the Lord’s humility, it is rightly said: “They did not wish to understand His ways.” To understand His ways is both humbly to endure passing things and steadfastly to await what remains, so that, following the Lord’s example, eternal glory may be sought in exchange for temporal reproaches.

It continues:

[Col. 0398D] **VERSE 28. “So that they might cause the cry of the needy to reach Him, and that He might hear the voice of the poor.”** — When these people grow proud, those who are oppressed by their pride cry out to the Lord. Or certainly it is said that they caused the cry of the poor to reach God because, when these people fall, the poor—that is, the humble in spirit—are appointed in their place.

Since this takes place through their fall, they are said to have done it, in the manner of speech by which we say that armies fight, because the battle is fought by means of them.

Or certainly, because everything said above can also be referred to ecclesiastical rulers who, abandoning the work of preaching, become entangled in earthly affairs under the pretext of governance, the statement appropriately continues: “So that they might cause the cry of the needy to reach Him, and that He might hear the voice of the poor.” For while they themselves, occupied with worldly cares, abandon the duty of preaching, they compel the flock entrusted to them to burst forth in a loud cry of complaint, so that each subject may, as though with legitimate cause, murmur against the life of a false shepherd: Why does he occupy the place of a teacher who does not perform the office?

Yet perhaps, more fittingly, the pride of the Jews is represented by the arrogance of the powerful, and the desires of the nations by the cry of the poor, just as, with the Truth bearing witness, the Jewish people are represented by the rich man who feasted splendidly, and the form of the Gentile people is expressed by Lazarus, the wounded man whose name means “helped.”

When those people sin, therefore, the cry of the poor is heard, because, while the Jews grow proud against God, the prayers of the Gentiles reach God. It continues:

[Col. 0399B] **VERSE 29. “For when He grants peace, who is there that can condemn? And when He hides His face, who is there that can behold Him?”** — Let no one therefore inquire why, while the Jewish people remained standing in their former unbelief, the Gentiles lay prostrate; or why, when the Gentiles rose to faith, the Jewish people were cast down by the guilt of unbelief. Let no one inquire why one is drawn by grace and another rejected on account of merit.

If you marvel that the Gentiles have been taken up, then, “when He grants peace, who is there that can condemn?” If you are astonished that Judea has been lost, then, “when He hides His face, who is there that can behold Him?” Thus let the plan of the highest and hidden Power be accepted as the clear satisfaction of reason.

Hence, when the Lord spoke in the Gospel about the cause of this matter, He said: “I confess to You, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, because You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11:25).

It continues: **“And over nations and over all human beings.”** — It is as though they are plainly admonished to attend, because this judgment, which is described as occurring over one nation, is also carried out over all human beings by an invisible examination: one is secretly rejected and another chosen, but no one unjustly.

Therefore let us cautiously fear that the same thing which we see occurring among the greatest may also occur in each of us. Divine judgments are directed over one soul in the same way as over one city, one nation, and the entire multitude of the human race. For the Lord attends to individuals as though He were free from all others, and attends to all together as though He were free from each individual.

He who fills all things by governing them governs by filling them. The whole does not lack Him when He orders one thing, nor does the one lack Him when He orders the whole. Through the power of His nature, He works all things.

It continues:

[Col. 0399D] **VERSE 30. “Who makes a hypocritical man reign on account of the sins of the people.”** — Since he has now passed from the particular to the general, he turns from the general back to the particular. He did not wish a true king to reign over Judea, and therefore, because of its merits, He accepted a hypocrite from among the nations, just as the Truth also says in the Gospel: “I have come in the name of My Father, and you did not receive Me; another shall come in his own name, and him you shall receive” (John 5:43).

Antichrist, the head, may also be designated by “hypocrite.” That deceiver will then pretend to holiness in order to lead people into iniquity, but he is permitted to reign on account of the sins of the people. For at that time those who are foreknown by their Lord from before the ages to be worthy of his rule will be placed under it; by their subsequent sins they will demand that, through preceding judgments, they be ordered beneath him.

The fact, therefore, that Antichrist will then reign over the ungodly does not arise from the injustice of the Judge but from the guilt of those who suffer it. Indeed, many have not seen his sovereignty and nevertheless serve his rule because of the condition imposed by their sins: although they do not visibly behold him as their ruler, they undoubtedly honor him by living perversely.

Are not those his members who, through the appearance of assumed holiness, seek to seem what they are not? He will principally assume hypocrisy, because, although he is a condemned man and an evil spirit, he falsely claims to be God. Yet those who conceal their iniquities beneath the covering of sacred honor undoubtedly now emerge from his body, seeking by their profession to appear what they refuse to be in their deeds. For it is written: “Everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34). The more freely they carry out the perverse things they desire, the more tightly they are bound to his service.

But it may reasonably be asked how this passage says that the Lord makes the hypocrite reign, when the prophet expressly complains about this matter, saying: “They have reigned, but not from Me; they have become princes, and I did not know” (Hos. 8:4). For who, thinking correctly, would say that the Lord does what He does not know? But God’s knowing is approving, and His not knowing is rejecting.

Hence He says to certain people whom He rejects: “I know not from where you are. Depart from Me, all you workers of iniquity” (Luke 13:25, 27). At times God is also said to do something when, by becoming angry, He permits what He forbids to be done. Thus He asserted that He hardened the heart of the king of Egypt, because He permitted it to be hardened. In a wondrous manner, therefore, the Lord makes hypocrites reign and does not know them: He makes them reign by permitting it; He does not know them by rejecting them.

**THE TWENTY-SIXTH BOOK.**

[Col. 0399] [Col. 0399D] **VERSES 31–32. “Since, therefore, I have spoken to God, I shall not forbid you also. If I have erred, teach me. If I have spoken iniquity, I shall not add to it again.”** — Just as it often happens that evil people speak good things, Elihu recalls that shortly before he said many forceful things, and, since he is about to continue, he asks lest perhaps he has erred. For he would not ask this if he believed that he had erred. As I have said, it is a characteristic fraud of the arrogant that they seek to inquire about error precisely when they know that they have not erred. Conversely, when they truly recognize that they have erred, they disdain either to inquire about or to be reproved for their error.

It continues:

**VERSE 33. “Does God require it from you because it displeased you?”** — It is as though he said: I shall give an account before God. Why, then, is my iniquity reproved by you? It is clear that this will not be required of you in the judgment.

When righteous men are unjustly attacked by human beings, they take refuge in the judgment above. Hence Job himself says: “Behold, my witness is in heaven, and my conscience is on high” (Job 16:20). And because they desire above all to please Him, they seek the testimony of Him alone.

The perverse, on the other hand, because they abandon the life of the righteous but sometimes scrutinize their words, when they are reproved for their evil deeds, take as an argument in their defense what the righteous utter in testimony of their purity. Thus it has also become their custom that, if someone accuses them of their deeds, they seek God’s judgment rather than human judgment.

They fear being judged by God, even though they know they will be condemned; they are ashamed to be judged by human beings. Therefore they put forward what they fear more, so that they may more easily avoid what they are ashamed of. For it is written: “Each of us shall give an account of himself to God” (Rom. 14:12).

Because those who begin to speak in contention are usually more blameworthy than those who merely respond, he adds: **“For you began to speak, and not I.”** — He considered himself innocent because he burst forth when provoked, not knowing, evidently, that innocence is defended not by timing but by reason. For what support do his defenses provide? Although he brought no accusation against one who was silent, he nevertheless gave a perverse reply to one who had begun rightly.

**“But if you know anything better, speak.”** — Although he does not say, “because you know something better,” but “whatever better thing you know, speak,” this itself reveals excessive pride: he doubted that the other possessed better knowledge. Behold, while he seems humbly to grant blessed Job the opportunity to speak, he reveals what he harbored inwardly.

It continues:

**VERSE 34. “Let men of understanding speak to me.”** — He evidently disdained to presume to speak to blessed Job, as though Job could not understand his words. And because he judged blessed Job unworthy not only to speak but even to hear him, it continues: **“Let a wise man listen to me.”** — It is as though he said: This man is unjustly permitted to speak, although he does not even deserve to hear the words of the wise.

Then he openly reveals how contemptuously he thinks of him, saying:

[Col. 0401D] **VERSE 35. “But Job has spoken foolishly, and his words do not sound with discipline.”** — He believed that blessed Job had spoken without discipline because Job had recalled that he had been righteous in his deeds.

Yet Elihu might perhaps have spoken this way if he himself, the author of discipline, had not judged that what blessed Job had related about himself was in fact true of him. Job declares that he was innocent and had been scourged, and God Himself also testified that he had been struck without cause. Since, therefore, the voice of the one who was struck sounded proud, how did it differ at all from the sentence of the One who struck him?

The humble are incautious when they entangle themselves in falsehood while avoiding arrogance. Indeed, by lying they become proud: they rise up against the truth, which they abandon. For one who, compelled by necessity, speaks true good things about himself is joined to humility all the more because he is also joined to truth.

It continues:

**VERSE 36. “My father, let Job be tested to the end.”** — Behold, what he had conceived through the swelling of arrogance he now raises even in words of malediction. Yet perhaps he would benevolently have desired the force of testing if he had judged that Job had stood firm under the testing. But so that his malice and cruelty might plainly appear, he asks that the one whom he already complains has fallen under the blows should be tested further by blows. He first stated what he felt, so that what he desired might be recognized more clearly. He asks that the one whom he accuses of having sinned beneath the hand of the one striking him should still be struck.

These are the characteristic wishes of the arrogant: they beg that the lives of the suffering be examined more harshly. For the more righteous they consider themselves, the harder they are toward the sufferings of others. They do not know how to draw into themselves the experience of another’s weakness and to show compassion toward the frailty of their neighbor as they do toward their own.

Truly holy men recognize that someone may be scourged even for guilt; and if they correct certain disordered things in him, they nevertheless share his grief over certain painful circumstances. They know how to press down what is swollen while also knowing how to soothe what is wounded, so that, while softening what is hard in them, they may strengthen what is weak.

It continues: **“Do not cease from the man of iniquity.”** — He calls him “a man of iniquity” whom God, by heavenly testimony, declares righteous above all others.

It continues:

**VERSE 37. “Who adds blasphemy to his sins.”** — He accuses Job both of having deserved blows for his sins and of having sinned after the blows. But the Lord judges quite differently: He indicates that Job was struck without cause and repays him with double blessings after the blows. Punishment is owed to guilt, not reward.

Blessed Job is therefore shown to have spoken without guilt, since rewards follow his speech. It continues: **“Let him meanwhile be bound among us, and then let him challenge God to judgment with his words.”** — It is as though he said: Let him learn from our assertion that he is in no way adequate to divine examination.

It continues:

**CHAPTER XXXV**

**“Therefore Elihu spoke these things again.”** — Everyone who speaks at length always tries to begin again in his speech, so that by the very beginning he may hold his listeners in suspense and make them keep silence more attentively, since they seem to be waiting to hear something new. It continues:

[Col. 0402D] **VERSES 1–2. “Does your thought seem right to you, so that you say: ‘I am more righteous than God’?”** — That blessed Job did not say that he was more righteous than God is recognized by everyone who reads the text of the narrative. But he did say: “Let Him set justice before me, and let my judgment come to victory” (Job 23:7). Weighing his life and ignorant of the reason for his affliction, as has often been said, he believed that he was being scourged for the removal of sins, not for the increase of merits. Therefore he was confident that his judgment would come to victory, because he found in himself no guilt for which he ought to have been struck.

The Lord also said this about him to the devil: “You have moved Me against him, so that I might afflict him without cause” (Job 2:3).

Or certainly he could have had in view the presence of our Redeemer. For He who is the power and wisdom of the Father may also, not inappropriately, be understood as His justice. By displaying and setting this justice incarnate against wicked people fleeing from God, He immediately recalled them from iniquity.

It continues:

**VERSE 3. “For you have said: ‘What is right does not please You; or what benefit will it be to You if I sin?’”** — If the entire sequence of the book is considered, blessed Job is shown to have said none of these things.
