But when the arrogant cannot justly reproach what truly exists, they reproach by lying what does not exist.

It continues:

[Col. 0403B] **VERSE 4. “Therefore I shall answer your words, and your friends with you.”** — In the preceding statements he reported, as though they were blameworthy, certain words of blessed Job and set them before himself as material for speaking. But in the words that follow he examines with keen force what he had deceitfully fabricated as material for his speech. The sentences that follow are indeed powerful, but they do not at all suit the person of blessed Job.

It continues:

**VERSES 5–7. “Look up at heaven and see; behold and contemplate the sky, which is higher than you. If you sin, what harm will you do to Him? And if your iniquities are multiplied, what will you do against Him? Moreover, if you act justly, what will you give Him, or what will He receive from your hand?”** — Although these things should by no means have been said to blessed Job, who knew greater matters, what is said is nevertheless true: our sins do not harm God, nor do our good deeds add anything to Him.

It continues:

[Col. 0403C] **VERSE 8. “Your wickedness will harm a man who is like you, and your justice will help a son of man.”** — Amid these words, however, we must carefully consider what he says: “Look up at heaven and see; behold and contemplate the sky, which is higher than you.” By saying this, he evidently gathers that one should consider how much less one’s action can either benefit or harm God, since one cannot benefit or harm the height of heaven and sky.

Nevertheless, by “heaven” or “sky” we may understand the heavenly powers, who always cling to the divine gaze. When we see that angelic spirits are still far removed from us, we recognize how far more inwardly we are removed from the Creator and Ruler of spirits. Yet there is no obstacle to understanding this passage as referring to the bodily substance of heaven and sky. For if we attentively contemplate outward things, through those very things we are recalled to inward realities.

Hence Paul says: “His invisible things are understood and seen through the things that have been made, and also His eternal power and divinity” (Rom. 1:20). Human wickedness harms the person whom it corrupts by perverting him, and again our righteousness helps the one whom it changes from evil actions. But things that cannot be corrupted by good or altered by evil know neither harm nor help.

The heavenly powers, therefore, cannot be harmed or helped insofar as they have already received an unchangeable being.

It continues:

[Col. 0404A] **VERSE 9. “Because of the multitude of accusers they shall cry out and wail because of the strength of the arms of tyrants.”** — We may rightly call all wicked people “oppressors,” not only those who seize external goods but also those who strive to ravage our inward things through their evil conduct and the example of their reprobate life.

The former seek to invade what is external to us; the latter seek to plunder us inwardly. And because in this world there is an abundance of wicked lives that cause suffering, it is rightly said: “Because of the multitude of oppressors they shall cry out.” Whoever compels us by his example to live badly still employs within us the voice of an oppressor. Whoever, while persuading us to sin, also seeks to terrify us already rages against us with the arm of tyranny. It is one thing to persuade someone to what is worthless by living that way; it is another to terrify him by commanding it.

It continues:

**VERSE 10. “And he did not say: ‘Where is God, who made me?’”** — It is the custom of sacred Scripture suddenly to pass from the singular number to the plural and from the plural to the singular. Thus Elihu, moving from the plural number to the singular, suddenly passed to the person of every one weak individual, perhaps because whatever is heard as being said of one person is better recognized by individuals, so that each person may return to his own heart and condemn in himself what is said of each.

Whoever is broken by the tribulation of adversities does not contemplate the One by whom he was made. For He who made what did not exist does not abandon what He made without governance, and He who benevolently made the human being by no means permits him to be afflicted unjustly.

It continues: **“Who gives songs in the night.”** — A song in the night is joy in tribulation. For although we are afflicted for a time by distress, we nevertheless already rejoice in hope of eternity.

Paul proclaimed songs in the night when he said: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. 12:12). David expressed a song in the night when he said: “You are my refuge from the distress that surrounded me; my exultation, deliver me from those who surround me” (Ps. 31:7).

It continues:

**VERSE 11.** “Who teaches us above the beasts of the earth, and instructs us above the birds of the sky.”

The beasts of the earth are those who, by the practice of their carnal life, seek what is low; the birds of the sky are those who, driven by proud curiosity, investigate what is lofty. The former lower themselves by their manner of life beneath what they are; the latter elevate themselves by inquiry beyond what they can attain. To the former Holy Scripture says: “Do not become like the horse and the mule, in which there is no understanding” (Ps. XXXI, 9). The proud labor of the latter is rebuked when it says: “Do not seek things higher than yourself, and do not investigate things stronger than you” (Ecclus. III, 22).

God therefore teaches us above the beasts of the earth and instructs us above the birds of the sky. For when we recognize what we are, neither does the weakness of the flesh cast us down, nor does the spirit of pride lift us up; neither, by sinking, are we subjected to low things, nor, by growing proud, are we inflamed by lofty things. Whoever slips through the flesh is thrown down by the appetite of beasts; whoever is uplifted in mind is raised, as though by the feather of levity, after the manner of birds.

And the meaning is—understand that he also did not say this: the one who surpasses beasts and birds, he does not say is remembered in tribulation. It is as though he said: The weak person does not strengthen himself in distress because he does not exercise self-restraint even in tranquility; and therefore he does not know how to endure adversity, because, established in prosperity, he does not know how by reflection to restrain himself from the flight of birds, nor to lift his carnal impulses above the gluttony of beasts.

This can also be understood in another way: “Who teaches us above the beasts of the earth, and instructs us above the birds of the sky.” For just as the term “beasts” signifies the life of human beings still subject to the movements of the flesh, so the designation “birds” represents the exaltation of proud spirits, so that earthly human beings are indicated by beasts, and demons by birds. Thus, when the Lord said that the seeds had fallen beside the way, he added: “The birds of the sky came and ate them” (Matt. XIII, 4), clearly signifying by the birds the powers of the air.

Holy men, however, because they neither seek the weak examples of human beings nor are deceived by demonic subtlety, grow through the power of instruction above both the beasts of the earth and the birds of the sky. Paul had already been taught to rise above the beasts of the earth when he said: “Many walk,” and shortly afterward: “Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame—those who set their minds on earthly things; but our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 18). Again, he knew himself to have been instructed above the birds of the sky when he said: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (I Cor. VI, 3).

It is as though he said: The weak person, overcome by faintheartedness, did not say these things; and therefore the trial of adversity struck him, because in the times of tranquility he had not surpassed all these passing things through any perfection. It follows:

**VERSE 12.** “There they will cry out, and he will not answer because of the pride of the wicked.”

“There,” namely, in tribulation, just as, conversely, it is written concerning joy: “The children of your servants will dwell there” (Ps. CI, 29). But it must be considered that it is uncertain whether the text means that “he will not answer because of the pride of the wicked,” or that “they will cry out because of the pride of the wicked.”

It can be better understood if they are said to go unheard because of the pride of the wicked, rather than to cry out because of it. For it has already been said above that they cry out because of the pride of the wicked. Therefore this verse intimates something that must be considered somewhat more carefully: often the oppressed, when they cry out, deserve in themselves to be heard, yet their desires are delayed because of the pride of those who oppress them.

For the just Lord both permits his own to be oppressed for a time and allows the wickedness of the violent to increase wickedly, so that while the life of the former is worn away in purification, the wickedness of the latter may reach completion. It is as though he said: The guilt of the oppressors prevents the voices of the oppressed from being heard; and the just are not visibly rescued because the unjust do not deserve to be invisibly saved. Hence it is said again through the prophet: “When he sees the wise dying, together the foolish and the senseless will perish” (Ps. XLVIII, 13). It follows:

**VERSE 13.** “For God will not hear in vain, and the Almighty will regard the causes of individuals.”

It should be noted that two things are stated: he does not hear the one who cries out in vain, and yet he observes what that person suffers; he appears not to hear the voices, yet he is not ignorant of what each person endures. Therefore let no one who is heard only slowly believe that he is neglected by the care from above. Often our desires, because they are not fulfilled quickly, are heard; and what we ask to be accomplished hastily prospers better precisely through the delay. It follows:

**VERSE 14.** “Even when you say, ‘He does not consider; judgment is before him,’ wait for him.”

Perhaps, while our cry is seemingly neglected, the hope that was in our heart grows weak, and we believe that heavenly assistance will fail because we obtain it only slowly; we almost lament that those things which we endure without punishment are disregarded by God.

But when this storm of despair disturbs us, the shaken mind more quickly places itself in the harbor of hope if it carefully weighs its causes before the Lord; if it recalls his good deeds; if within itself it does not wisely accuse the evils it has repaid for his good deeds; if it considers what it has justly deserved from him and what it mercifully receives.

It is as though he said: Since God is believed not to consider because he is slow to show mercy, enter into the innermost thoughts, and there, before his eyes, submit the judgment of your causes; distinguish what you have brought upon yourself by living and what you have received in misery. For whoever does not judge himself before God does not await him when he is afflicted. It follows:

**VERSE 15.** “For now he does not bring on his fury, nor does he punish exceedingly.”

God endures wickedness for a long time because he condemns it forever; and he now refrains from bringing on his fury because he reserves it to be poured out without end in the future. For it belongs to the elect to be crushed here, so that they may be instructed for the rewards of eternal inheritance; it belongs to us here to receive chastisements by which the joy of eternity is preserved for us. Hence it is written: “He scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII, 6). Hence it is said to John: “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise” (Rev. III, 19).

It should be noted, however, that he added “exceedingly,” because although he patiently endures certain things, he nevertheless chastises some even in this life; and here he sometimes begins to strike what eternal damnation completes. Thus he strikes some things and leaves others unpunished: for if he cut off nothing, who would believe that God cares for human affairs? And again, if he struck everything here, what would remain for the final judgment? It follows:

**[Col. 0406D] VERSE 16.** “Therefore Job has opened his mouth in vain, and multiplies words without knowledge.”

By introducing these statements, blessed Job, he claims, both knew nothing and said much; and although he himself introduces at length what he thinks, he accuses Job of the fault of loquacity. But this too is characteristic of the arrogant: they believe that what they themselves have said is little, even when they have said much, and that what is said to them is much, even when little is said.

It follows:

**CHAPTER XXXVI**

**VERSES 1–2.** “Elihu continued and also said these things: Bear with me a little while, and I will show you.”

He had already said much, and still hopes to be endured a little longer, because the arrogant judge that they suffer serious loss if they restrain their knowledge by brevity of speech. For they believe themselves to appear more learned in proportion to the multiplicity of words with which they can reveal themselves.

It follows: “I still have something to say on God’s behalf.”

Because they often feel that the reverence due to silence is not accorded to them, they sometimes suggest the power of the God about whom they appear to be speaking, and under his pretext demand for themselves the silence they do not deserve. Since holy teachers, however, often repeat themselves when they say something obscure, so that what they proclaim secretly may be poured into the hearts of their hearers through the voice of repetition, the arrogant frequently attempt to imitate this as well and insolently repeat what they have said.

It follows:

**VERSE 3.** “I will repeat my knowledge from the beginning.”

But because the swelling of his heart had become evident in his voice when he named his knowledge, the arrogant man is clearly recognized, unless he is quickly covered by some disguise.

It follows: “And prove that my Maker is just.”

Thus, while he appears to speak on behalf of God’s justice, whatever flows forth arrogantly may be excused before human judgments.

It follows:

**VERSE 4.** “For truly my words are without falsehood.”

When they see that they cannot be understood by weak hearers, even the just often praise the good things they say—not because they crave their own praise, but because they kindle their hearers through the attentiveness required for understanding, so that, while their words are commended, the hearers may be seized by a more ardent affection. Hence, when Paul had said many remarkable things to the Corinthians, he added: “Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart is enlarged” (II Cor. VI, 11).

But the arrogant, because they do not understand the heart of the good and sometimes imitate only their words, exalt the things they say by praising them—not because they are displeased with the sluggishness of their hearers, but because they eagerly delight in themselves.

It follows: “And perfect knowledge will be proved to you.”

Clearly he sensed that he was about to say great things; but with his heart swollen, he could not keep silent about what he had loftily thought of himself. Therefore he anticipated what he regarded as right by praising it, because he would already have been guilty before divine judgment if he had at least silently entertained such great thoughts about himself. Before the subtle examination of truth, we are by no means secure, even if in human judgment we have nothing in us that ought to be reproved.

It follows:

**VERSE 5.** “God does not reject the powerful, since he himself is powerful.”

In the practice of mortal life, some things are harmful in themselves, while others are harmful because of what surrounds them. Some things are harmful in themselves, such as sins and crimes; others sometimes harm us through what accompanies them, such as temporal power or marital union.

Marriage is good, but the things that arise around it from the cares of this world are evil. Hence Paul says: “He who is with a wife considers the things of the world, how he may please his wife” (I Cor. VII, 33).

Temporal power too is great, because it has its merit before God when government is administered well. Yet sometimes, precisely because a person surpasses others, he swells with thoughts of exaltation, despises his subjects, and disdains to regard others as equals. Thus he is led to resemble the one of whom it is written: “He sees every lofty thing, and he is king over all the sons of pride” (Job XLI, 25); and of whose body it is said: “A generation whose eyes are lofty and whose eyelids are raised high” (Prov. XXX, 13).

He desires to imitate God who administers the height of power while attending to the usefulness of others and not puffed up by his own praises; who, placed over others, desires to benefit rather than to rule. It is the elevation of swelling pride, not the order of power, that is criminal. God grants power, but the malice of our mind invents the pride of power. Let us therefore remove what we have added from ourselves, and the things we possess by God’s gift are good.

It follows:

**VERSE 6.** “But he does not save the impious, and he grants judgment to the poor.”

Holy Scripture is accustomed to call the humble “poor.” Hence in the Gospel they are named with the addition “in spirit,” when it says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. III, 5). Because visible riches make people appear powerful, those who are not proud in their consciences are poor in themselves.

He calls impious those who are either separated from the piety of faith or contradict by wicked conduct what they faithfully believe. Almighty God destroys the proud, but by judgment he makes the humble free; or certainly he grants judgment to the poor, because those who are wickedly oppressed then come as judges over their oppressors.

It follows:

**[Col. 0408C] VERSE 7.** “He will not remove his eyes from the just, and he places kings upon their throne forever, and they are raised up.”

The Lord may be thought to have removed his eyes from the just because here they are torn apart without vengeance by the cruelty of the unjust. Yet he looks upon his servants all the more when the wickedness of their persecutor afflicts them unjustly. For when he sees that they endure humbly, he already foresees what he will mercifully repay them there.

Holy men are rightly called “kings” according to the testimony of Holy Scripture, because they know not how to succumb by consenting to the movements of their temptations, but to rule over them by governing them. Therefore, since they pass from this power of governance to the power of recompense, it is rightly said: “He places kings upon their throne forever.” By ruling themselves they have been wearied for a time, but they are placed forever upon the throne of the inner establishment of the kingdom; and there they begin to judge others worthily precisely because here they do not know how wickedly to spare themselves.

Hence it is said elsewhere: “Until justice is turned into judgment” (Ps. XCIII, 15). The addition “forever” appropriately clarifies the meaning. If he were speaking of the throne of an earthly kingdom, he would never have added “forever,” because those who seize it are placed in it not forever but temporarily.

He added well, “and there they are raised up,” as though he had anticipated the thought of his hearer by saying: Because they have been humbled here, they are raised up there. For this place is one of humility for holy men, so that the other may be one of exaltation. Hence it is written elsewhere: “You humbled us in the place of affliction” (Ps. XLIII, 20).

It follows:

**VERSES 8–9.** “And if they are in chains, and are bound with ropes of poverty, he will show them their works and their crimes, because they were violent.”

The chains of bondage are the very retention of our pilgrimage here below. Paul saw himself bound by these chains when he said: “Having the desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. I, 23). He saw himself overcome by the ropes of poverty when, looking upon true riches, he also prayed for them for his disciples, saying: “That you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints” (Eph. I, 18).

It is rightly added afterward: “He showed them their works, because they were violent.” For when we come to know heavenly glory by loving it more, then we feel that the evils we have committed were more serious. Hence Paul, after receiving the grace of heavenly things, now recognized as crimes the activities he had previously believed to be exercises of virtue, saying: “Who formerly was a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I obtained mercy, because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (I Tim. I, 13). Or certainly: “The things that were gains to me, these I considered loss because of Christ” (Phil. III, 7).

It follows:

**VERSE 10.** “He will also open their ear to rebuke them, and will speak so that they may return from iniquity.”

To open the ear is to disclose the understanding of knowledge. Each person is rebuked when the ear has been opened and inwardly perceives the desire for eternal goods.

The chains and ropes of poverty may also be understood as the punishment of temporal affliction. Often people do not hear the words of one who commands, but are admonished by the blows of one who strikes, so that punishment may draw toward good desires those whom rewards do not invite. Hence it is said through the Prophet: “Bind their jaws with bit and bridle, those who do not draw near to you” (Ps. XXXI, 9).

It follows:

**VERSE 11.** “If they hear and obey, they will complete their days in goodness and their years in glory.”

“Goodness” signifies right action; “glory” signifies heavenly recompense. Those who strive to obey heavenly commands contemplate their days in goodness and their years in glory, because they complete both the course of the present time in upright work and their consummation in a happy reward.

It follows:

**[Col. 0409D] VERSE 12.** “But if they do not hear, they will pass through the sword and be consumed in folly.”

For vengeance strikes them in tribulation, and their end is brought to completion in foolishness. There are some whom not even torments restrain from their corrupt ways. Of them it is said through the prophet: “You struck them, and they did not grieve; you scourged them, and they refused to receive correction” (Jer. V, 3).

It is therefore rightly said that they pass through the sword and “are consumed in folly,” because they increase by scourges the sins that they ought to have corrected through scourges. Here they already feel his blows, and there they do not escape the punishments of just recompense. For it is folly—indeed, the folly of their stupidity—that iniquity binds them so that not even punishment restrains them from guilt.

It follows:

**[Col. 0410A] VERSE 13.** “Hypocrites and crafty men provoke the wrath of God.”

When he said “hypocrites,” he appropriately added “crafty,” because unless they are skilled in ingenuity, they cannot suitably pretend to be what they desire to appear.

There are certain vices that are easily committed even by those of slower understanding. Anyone can swell with pride, burn with the fever of greed, or succumb to the pressure of lust, even if dull-witted. But unless someone possesses a subtler intelligence, he cannot carry out the falsehood of hypocrisy. Whoever is such a person is divided by continual vigilance in order to guard two things: he must skillfully know both how to conceal what is and how to display what is not.

To deserve God’s wrath is to sin even without knowing it; but to provoke it is knowingly to oppose his commands—to know the good but despise it, to be able to do it but not to wish to do so. Of such people the Lord says: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, because you are like whitewashed tombs” (Matt. XXIII, 27).

It follows: “Nor will they cry out when they are bound.”

Every wicked person who, though wicked, desires to appear holy is caught by the blow of the scourge and is ashamed to confess that he is wicked. We are as though free when we are chastised by no correction; we are as though bound when we are restrained by the blow of the scourge. Therefore we cry out all the more loudly when bound, the more truthfully we confess our sins while placed under the blow.

Hypocrites too, when caught by the blow of the final scourge, neglect to make a pure confession even in their affliction; therefore they disdain to cry out as though bound. Yet this can also be understood in another way. Anyone who, though wicked, does not fear being called holy by human beings may indeed condemn himself as wicked in silent thought; but when he begins more frequently to hear himself called holy, he loses what he had inwardly retained about himself.

When they are struck by a sudden blow, they are entirely unable either to confess themselves wicked truthfully or to recognize themselves as they are, because they have come to believe themselves holy through human proclamation. To them the prophet appropriately says: “Return to the heart, preachers [transgressors]” (*Praedicatores* [*Praevaricatores*], Isa. LXV, 8).

It follows:

**VERSE 14.** “Their souls will die in the storm.”

They seemed to live in tranquility when they took care to rejoice in the praise of holiness. But their soul dies in a sudden storm—the soul that had rejoiced in the worst tranquility of human praise. For the whirlwind of a sudden blow carries away those whom arrogance exalts through external favor; and while they embrace in praise what they are not, they suddenly discover in punishment what they are.

It follows: “And their life among the effeminate.”

For if they lived manfully, no passing praise would corrupt them through any vice. As the Prophet urges concerning the elect, saying: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Ps. XXX, 25).

The life of hypocrites therefore dies among the effeminate, because the luxury of praise is found to have corrupted it. In another translation, however, it is not “their life among the effeminate,” but “their life is wounded by angels.” Although the wording differs, the meaning agrees in both cases: angels wound the life of the effeminate when messengers of truth attack it with the arrows of holy preaching.

Since we have heard what happens concerning the condemnation of the reprobate, let us hear what follows concerning the rescue of the humble. It follows:

**VERSE 15.** “He will rescue the poor man from his distress.”

The poor man is rescued from his distress when each humble person is freed from the affliction of his pilgrimage here below.

It follows: “And he has opened his ear in tribulation.”

To open the ear in tribulation is to open the hearing of the heart through the blows of scourges. For when we despise the commandments, he deals strictly with us so that we may fear the scourges.

It follows:

**VERSE 16.** “Therefore he will save you from the narrow mouth into a broad place.”

Whoever abandons the way of life and casts himself into the darkness of sins has plunged himself as though into a well or pit. But if he is oppressed by the prolonged practice and habit of iniquity, so that he can no longer rise to higher things, he is constricted as though by the narrow mouth of a well.

Hence the prophet David, in the person of sinners, pleads, saying: “Let not the storm of waters overwhelm me, nor let the deep swallow me, nor let the pit close its mouth over me” (Ps. LXVIII, 16).

He is saved from the narrow mouth into a broad place when, even after the yoke of iniquities, he is led back through repentance to the freedom of good works. The prophet David had seen the confinement of a narrower place when he said: “You saved my soul from distress, and did not shut me up in the hands of the enemy” (Ps. XXX, 8–9). He knew that he had been saved into a broad place when he added: “You set my feet in a spacious place” (ibid.).

It follows: “And one that has no foundation above it.”

Every sin has no foundation, because it does not subsist by its own nature. Evil is without substance, although, insofar as it exists at all, it comes together within the nature of the good.

Whomever iniquity carries away, hell absorbs. Alternatively, hell is rightly believed to have no bottom, because whoever is carried away by it is swallowed up in immensity.

Alternatively: just as a person who sinks into a well is held by the bottom of the well, so the falling soul would settle as though in a kind of bottom if, once it had fallen, it retained itself within some fixed measure of sin. But since it cannot be satisfied with the sin into which it falls, and is cast daily into worse things, it has fallen as though into a well but finds no bottom by which it can be fixed. The well would have a bottom if there were a measure to sin.

It follows: “But the rest at your table will be full of richness.”

The rest of the table is the refreshment of inward satisfaction, which is said to be full of richness because it is prepared in the eternal will **[Note: Here a word seems to be missing.]**.

The Prophet hungered for the feasts of this table when he said: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. XVI, 25).

It follows:

**VERSE 17.** “Your cause has been judged as that of an impious man; you will receive cause and judgment.”

The cause of the good is sadness, and their cause is judged as that of an impious man, because their justice here is wearied by a fatherly scourge, so that they may be instructed toward greater vigilance—not only through receiving commandments but also through the blows of scourges.

But they receive cause and judgment because, from the justice by which they now live, they then shine at the height of judicial power, so that they may judge all things more powerfully then, in proportion as all things are now judged more subtly in them.

When Elihu introduced these things by making his assertions, blessed Job had always held them firmly by faith. It follows:

**VERSE 18.** “Therefore let anger not overcome you, so that you oppress anyone.”

The arrogant assign to the movement of anger whatever is done by the holy Church through the judgment of discipline. Because they strive always to appear kind out of a desire for human praise, they consider that no one should be corrected with the severity of strictness. Hence, as was said above, they regard as oppressed by good rulers those whom they see being forcibly restrained from vices.

But, with the Lord as author, because the holy Church has grown to the height of religion in all parts of the world, they turn this very temporal power—because it uses its power well—into the vice of pride by their slander.

Morally: Anyone through whom the vices of others must be corrected ought first to observe himself carefully, lest, while punishing another, he himself be overcome by the fury of punishment. Often the savagery of anger devastates the mind under the pretext of justice; and while it appears to rage with zeal for righteousness, it satisfies the madness of fury, judging that whatever anger wickedly dictates is just to do.

For if the one who strives to correct is overcome by anger, he oppresses before he corrects; and while he is inflamed more than he ought to be, under the pretext of just vengeance he is driven without restraint into the savagery of cruelty.

It follows: “Nor let the multitude of places incline you.”

It is as though this were said in the voice of the arrogant to the holy Church, which preserves its humility more carefully amid prosperity: Because you are honored everywhere with the reverence of faith, take care not to be lifted up by the heights of that same reverence. They see certain people swelling with the vice of pride under the pretext of religion, and what they rightly condemn in some, they unjustly extend as a charge against all.

It should be noted that he does not say, “Nor let the multitude of places exalt you,” but, “Nor let the multitude of places incline you.” For everyone who is exalted temporally is, by that very exaltation, inclined downward: when he raises himself outwardly, he falls inwardly.

Morally: We are inclined in as many places as we extend ourselves through superfluous cares. For just as a place is the bodily space of a body, so a place of the mind is each particular intention of thought. When the mind is driven here and there, if it is willingly occupied by some object of thought’s affection, it is placed as though in a certain location, so that it may rest. For whenever, overcome by weariness, we are led from one thought to another, we migrate with a weary mind as though from place to place.

Thus as many places incline the summit of the mind as arising thoughts disperse the unity of good intention. The upright mind would stand if it always clung to the one thought to which it ought to cling.

It follows:

**VERSE 19.** “Set aside your greatness without tribulation, and all the strong in strength.”

Whom else should we understand as the strong of the Church except those who grow strong in overcoming the desires of this world, both through lofty beginnings and through completed progress? Its greatness consists in the life of its strong members, because it is made more glorious when its elect contend with steadfast courage even unto death in defense of the truth.

The arrogant, therefore, seeing that the apostles have been taken from this world and the martyrs have been taken to heavenly things, and perhaps seeing that teachers and more powerful rulers abound, suspect that they alone remain within the Church. Thus, while they set themselves above it, they mock it as though offering counsel, saying: “Set aside your greatness without tribulation, and all the strong in strength.”

It is as though they said openly in reproach: Do not trust that you have any greatness, because once the former members have been taken away, you no longer have anyone whose life you may glorify.

They say this, of course, without knowing that almighty God does not abandon his Church without a worthy administration. For when he calls the strong to their reward, he strengthens the weak for struggles in their place. When he receives and rewards the former, he supplies the latter with the strength for labor that he will reward.

Concerning these it is said to the same holy Church: “In place of your fathers sons have been born to you; you will appoint them princes over all the earth” (Ps. XLIV, 17).

Morally: The strong are the movements of the heart when they perceive nothing except what belongs to virtue. But we set aside greatness and strong movements when, with vice pressing upon us, we are forced to consider what we are. We set aside strong movements when we are no longer lifted up by virtue but, by consenting to guilt, fear being overwhelmed by the very weakness with which we are shaken.

It is as though it were said openly: Restrain everything by which you had inwardly swollen over a good action, and set aside the movements of the heart that you had made strong through upright work, because now, in the very trial of adversity, you see how vainly you had previously been elated by great thoughts of yourself.

This greatness is said to be set aside without tribulation because humility is advanced by trial. Adversity itself is prosperous when it guards the mind from exaltation; yet it does not occur without great tribulation, when a tranquil mind is disturbed by an invading temptation as by a sudden enemy.

It follows:

**VERSE 20.** “Do not prolong the night, so that peoples may rise up in their place.”

It is as though the arrogant openly said: Through the darkness of your ignorance, do not act so as to substitute a multitude of weak people for the strong. “Peoples” designates those who, as though devoted to ordinary custom, live indiscriminately in all that they desire.

To prolong the night is to allow peoples to rise in place of the strong: this happens if negligence permits the places of teachers and strong men to be allotted to the unlearned and weak. Peoples rise in place of the strong when those who have learned to live wickedly receive the places of pastors. This could indeed be said rightly, if it were said humbly.

Morally: The night is prolonged when the sadness arising from temptation is not quickly allowed consolation. The night is prolonged because the sorrow of the mind is extended through confused thoughts. For when the mind placed in temptation considers that it is driven away from the former firmness of its virtue, it is blinded by superimposed habits as by certain darknesses, and the eye of its joy is closed to all light, while it anxiously trembles lest it completely lose what it had recently begun to be.

Hence it is rightly said that in this night peoples rise in place of the strong, because in this thicket of temptation unworthy and manifold thoughts leap up in the heart in place of strong movements. For when the mind sees itself in turmoil, it heaps up within itself innumerable waves and disturbances, as though it had already lost what it had been and were suffering punishment for that loss.

It is as though he said to one caught in temptation: Quickly cut through the darkness of sorrow, lest you who had thought highly of yourself in tranquility become even more disastrously confused by the darkness of thoughts in disturbance.

Elihu would have said this rightly, if he had known to whom he was speaking. For these words apply to blessed Job all the less insofar as everything is understood more profoundly by him.

It follows:

**VERSE 21.** “Beware lest you turn toward iniquity, for you began to follow it after misery.”

The arrogant call the Church’s misery what they suppose to be its being despised by God, and they despise it with all the greater exaltation because they suppose it to be utterly despised by God.

Having passed over these matters in a figurative exposition, we must now present what is understood morally, so that, having recognized the figure of the Church—which we generally believe to have been expressed—we may also hear what can be gathered individually from these words.

Morally: A person follows iniquity after misery when, after the evils he endures following correction, he is inflamed by the arrogance of impatience in a passionate heart. Elihu believed blessed Job had done this because he heard him speak freely while placed amid scourges, not knowing that everything he said proceeded not from the iniquity of impatience but from the virtue of truth; for even when he justified himself, he did not err from the judgment of the inner Judge.

What does it mean that, while he forbids turning toward it, he immediately condemns him as though he had already turned toward it, unless that arrogant men wish more to appear judges than consolers? Hence they sometimes strike with severe judgments what they suspect to have arisen in the heart, and before the guilt of the offenders is certain, they bring forth a harsh verbal attack.

**THE TWENTY-SEVENTH BOOK**

**[Col. 0413]**

**[Col. 0413D] VERSE 22.** “Behold, God is exalted in his strength, and none among lawgivers is like him.”

In this passage Elihu does not perceive the humble advent of our Redeemer humbly; he prophesies and proclaims the one whom he attacks with proud impulses. It is as though he said: He who appears humble in weakness remains exalted in strength. Paul also bears witness, saying: “For although he was crucified in weakness, yet he lives by the power of God” (II Cor. XIII, 4).

It follows: “None is like him among lawgivers.”

Moses was a lawgiver, Joshua was a lawgiver, and the prophets too were lawgivers. We can call all those lawgivers whom we know to have admonished the people to what is right from the law. But among lawgivers none is like this Mediator. For they were freely called from sins to innocence, and by preaching they lead others away from what they themselves experienced. Our Redeemer, however, is a human being without sin, a son without adoption; he never committed what he reproved, and he speaks to the world in his humanity while nevertheless ruling the same world from before the ages in his divinity.

It follows:

**VERSE 23.** “Who can search out his ways, or who can say to him, ‘You are practicing iniquity’?”

It is as though it were said: If his action cannot be searched out, how can it be reproved? No one judges well what he does not know. Therefore we ought to rest in silence beneath his judgments all the more insofar as we see that we cannot discern the reason for his judgments. Hence it is rightly added:

### Chapter XXXVI

**Verse 24. “Remember that you do not know his work, concerning which men have sung.”**

In Sacred Scripture, “men” sometimes refers to angels, and at other times to people of perfected life. That an angel is sometimes called a man is attested by the prophet Daniel, who says: “Behold, the man Gabriel” (Dan. 9:21). Again, because people of perfected life are expressed by the name “men,” Wisdom speaks in Proverbs, saying: “O men, I call to you” (Prov. 8:4).

Thus men sing of the Lord when either heavenly spirits or wholly perfected teachers make his power known to us. Yet his work remains unknown, because even those who proclaim him reverently acknowledge that his judgments are impenetrable. They therefore know what they proclaim, and yet do not know his works, because they recognize him as the one from whom, by grace, they themselves have been made.

Hence the Psalmist says: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. 17:12). And again: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. 35:7). It is as though he plainly said: Although all the strong have spoken of him, his works remain hidden from the eyes of your mind, because they transcend the measure of your understanding, since you are confined by your humanity.

**Verse 25. “All human beings see him; each one beholds him from afar.”**

Every human being, insofar as he was created rational, ought by reason to conclude that the one who created him is God. To see him already is to perceive his dominion through reasoning. To behold him from afar, however, is not yet to see him in his very appearance, but still to estimate him solely from admiration for his works.

Here even the elect behold him from afar, because they do not yet grasp his glory through the keenness of inward vision. Although they are already near him through love, they are still separated from him by the burden of their earthly dwelling. The reprobate likewise behold him from afar when they see him coming in judgment, because they see him not in the form of his divinity, but only in that humanity by which he could also be apprehended.

**Verse 26. “Behold, God is great, surpassing our knowledge.”**

Above he had said: “Behold, God is exalted.” Now he says again: “Behold, God is great.” What does it mean that, speaking of God, he says “behold,” and says it again, except that we say “behold” of something we point out in the present? Since God is everywhere present, when “behold” is said of him, his presence is proclaimed even to those who do not see him.

He rightly says that he surpasses our knowledge, although he had said that human beings see him, because even if he is perceived through reason, his greatness cannot be penetrated by any subtlety of our understanding.

It follows: “The number of his years is beyond reckoning.”

He wished, in some fashion, to express eternity, and called the very length of eternity “years.” For when we wish to expand a short span of time, we extend moments into hours, hours into days, days into months, and months into years. Since he wished to express something immense, but could find nothing broader to say, he multiplied in God years beyond any reckoning, saying: “The number of his years is beyond reckoning.” Thus, by multiplying what is extended according to our own measure, human weakness may recognize that it cannot falsely define the length of eternity.

**Verse 27. “He draws away the stars of rain and pours down showers like torrents.”**

In the face of heaven there are some stars that no rain follows, and others appear that pour rain upon the parched earth. Therefore, whenever certain people live rightly in the holy Church but do not know how to preach that same righteousness, they are indeed stars, but stars born in dry air. Through the example of good living they can shine upon others, but through the word of preaching they cannot rain.

When, however, some both live rightly within it and convey that same righteousness to others through words of preaching, stars are brought forth in the heavens as though to produce rain. They shine through the merits of their life in such a way that they also rain through the speech of preaching.

Was Moses not a star of rain in this heaven? So too were Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets. Since their souls, taken from this corruptible flesh, are removed from the present life to the heavenly judgments, the stars of rain are withdrawn, as it were, from the face of heaven; and the stars return to concealment when, having completed their courses, the souls of the saints are stored in the treasuries of the hidden ordering.

But when the Lord removed the prophets, he sent the apostles in their place, so that they might rain like torrents—that is, flow forth in more abundant preaching. The holy apostles may also be represented by the stars of rain. Concerning them it is said through Jeremiah to rejected Judea: “The stars of rain have been withheld, and the late rain has not come” (Jer. 3:3).

The Lord therefore drew away the stars of rain and poured showers like torrents, because, when he removed the apostles who were preaching in Judea, he irrigated the world with the teaching of the new grace. But after removing the stars of rain, he gave the rains of torrents to the sea: even after the apostles had been taken back to heaven, through the tongues of later interpreters he disclosed, in a more abundant outpouring, the streams of divine knowledge that had long been hidden. For what they had spoken briefly, these later teachers increased many times over by explaining it.

**Verse 28. “Which flow from the clouds.”**

These torrents flow from the clouds because, if the power of understanding had not begun with the holy apostles, it would never have flowed more abundantly through the mouths of teachers.

In Sacred Scripture, “clouds” sometimes designate changeable people, as in Solomon’s saying: “Whoever watches the wind will not sow, and whoever observes the clouds will never reap” (Eccl. 11:4). By “wind” he means unclean spirits, and by “clouds” subject human beings.

Sometimes the prophets are designated by clouds, as in: “Dark water was in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 17:12). At other times the apostles are designated, as in: “I will command my clouds not to rain upon them” (Isa. 5:6).

It follows: “Which cover all things from above.”

When clouds spread over the air above us, if we raise our eyes to heaven, we look not upon heaven but upon the clouds themselves. Since we are carnal people, when we strive to desire heavenly things, we raise our eyes, as it were, toward heaven and direct our gaze heavenward, because, pressed down by habitual concern for bodily things, we try to learn spiritual things.

But because understanding is not permitted to pass over to divine realities unless it is first formed by the examples of the holy people who came before us, our eye seems already to gaze upon heaven but sees clouds. We desire to comprehend the things of God, but can scarcely admire what has been granted to human beings.

Hence it is said elsewhere: “You illuminate wonderfully from the everlasting mountains” (Ps. 75:5). We are covered by the life of the Fathers, stretched out above us like clouds, so that we may be watered for the fruit of fruitful growth. As though looking upon heaven, we first behold the clouds, because first we gaze with admiration upon the deeds of the good, and afterward, through experience, penetrate those things that are heavenly.

**Verse 29. “If he wishes to spread out the clouds as his tent.”**

The Lord spreads out the clouds when, opening the way of preaching to his ministers, he disperses them throughout the breadth of the world. It is rightly said: “As his tent.” A tent is ordinarily set up on a journey; and when holy preachers are sent into the world, they make a road for the Lord.

Hence it is written: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way” (Mal. 3:1). And again the Psalmist says: “Make a way for him who ascends above the setting sun” (Ps. 67:5).

He makes a way through them when he pours himself into human hearts through their speech; and on this journey they are God’s tent. These same hearts of the saints shelter him, as it were, while resting along the way. Through them he comes to human minds and accomplishes what he has ordained, though he is not seen.

**Verse 30. “And makes his light flash from above.”**

What ought we to understand by flashes of lightning except miracles? Concerning them the Psalmist says: “You will multiply flashes of lightning, and you will trouble them” (Ps. 17:15). Through these clouds, therefore, he flashes his light from above, because through his preachers he also illumines the darkness of our insensibility by miracles.

It follows: “He will also cover the hinges of the sea.”

Almighty God covered the hinges of the sea with flashing clouds because, through the miracles of preachers shining forth, he brought even the ends of the world to faith. For behold, he has already penetrated the hearts of nearly all nations. Behold, in one faith he has joined the boundary of the East to that of the West.

**Verse 31. “For by these he judges the peoples and gives food to many mortals.”**

By these things—namely, the words of preachers, the drops of snow, and the flashes of miracles—God judges the peoples, because through fear of them he calls them to repentance. When they hear heavenly things and attend to wondrous works, they immediately return to their hearts. Afflicting themselves over their former wickedness, they fear eternal torments.

Yet through the same clouds by which terror is inflicted, food is also given. This is the great stewardship of preachers: they must know how to afflict the minds of the proud, while also knowing how to nourish the afflicted with the speech of consolation. Thus they both terrify sinners with eternal punishments and feed penitents with the joys of the heavenly kingdom.

Concerning this judgment it is said: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20:23). It is also said of these ministers: “Give them something to eat” (Matt. 14:16).

It is as though he said: If he spreads out his saints in the ministry of preaching, and supports their words with miracles, he summons the boundaries of the whole world. Through these means he first judges the proud, and afterward, nourishing the humble with the word of consolation, strengthens them in hope.

It should be noted that he does not say “all,” but “many,” because it is written: “Faith is not possessed by all” (1 Thess. 3:2). And to some it is said: “Therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John 8:47).

**Verse 32. “He hides the light from the proud.”**  
*[Note: [Col. 0417D] Vulgate reading: “In the hands.”]*

For the proud (*immanes*) are those who hide themselves in exalted thoughts. Against them Isaiah says: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isa. 5:21). Paul likewise says against them: “Do not be wise in your own estimation” (Rom. 12:16).

Light is hidden from these monstrous ones because knowledge of the truth is denied to the proud. Hence Truth itself says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11:25).

It follows: “And he commands it to return again.”

The light of truth, which is hidden from minds that are proud and preoccupied, is revealed to the afflicted and humbled. Light arrives when the afflicted mind recognizes the very darkness of tribulations that it endures amid perishing things. For unless it received something from the inward light, it would not see even that it had lost the light.

This may also be understood particularly of the Jews, who dared to oppose our Redeemer coming in the flesh because they were monstrous in their own estimation. Light was hidden from these monstrous ones because, while the proud persecuted the light of truth, they lost it.

But because they will be received into the faith at the end of the world, it is rightly added: “And he commands it to return again.” Hence Isaiah says: “Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Isa. 10:22). Then the light returns to them, when they themselves are converted to confess the power of our Redeemer.

If, however, we understand “in the hands” not as one noun in the dative case but as two parts of speech, it can be understood in another way: light is hidden in the hands when, before the righteous judge, the wicked are blinded in their own works. Yet it is commanded to return again, because when sinners recognize that they cannot be saved by their own powers, they receive the light of grace and are illuminated by the rays of inward protection. Thus afterward they love the heavenly homeland with greater fervor than previously they burned with desire for earthly pleasure.

But when we speak of the heavenly homeland, when we hear that the ranks of angels have been revealed as dwelling there in wondrous splendor, we bring our minds back to ourselves and consider that we bear earthly limbs. Moved by this thought, the heart, conscious of its evil, trembles and despairs that it could become a citizen of that homeland whose greatness it hears described.

**Verse 33. “He announces concerning it to his friend that it is his possession.”**

A friend of the truth is one who loves right action. Hence Truth himself says to his disciples: “You are my friends if you do what I command you” (John 15:14). A friend is indeed called a guardian of the soul.

Therefore God announces concerning the light of the eternal homeland to his friend that it is his possession, so that he may never despair because of his weakness, and may consider not what he was created as, but what he has been recreated as. He should know with increasing certainty that he will possess the radiance of that light, insofar as he now more truly tramples beneath him the darkness of the vices that assail him.

It follows: “And that he may be able to ascend to it.”

For what is more difficult than for a human being, born on earth and bearing earthly, fragile limbs, to climb to the heights of heaven and penetrate the mysteries of the heavenly spirits? Yet the Creator of those very spirits came to us and displayed himself as a human being even beneath them. Concerning him the prophet says to the Father: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8:6).

And because he found discord and an occasion of stumbling between us and those spirits, he joined us with the highest through wondrous power and even more wondrous mercy: creating what was highest, taking up what was lowest.

For this reason, when the same King was born, choirs of angels appeared at his announcement, sang a hymn, and, through the defeat of the discord of wicked life, acknowledged as fellow citizens those whom previously they had despised, proclaiming with harmonious voice: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

Thus the one who for our sake became lower than the angels made us equal to the angels through the power of his becoming lower. By dying he taught us not to fear death; by rising he taught us to trust in life; by ascending he taught us to glory in the inheritance of the heavenly homeland. Where they see the head go before them, there the members may rejoice that they will follow.

Hence it is rightly said by our same Head: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Luke 17:37).

### Chapter XXXVII

**Verse 1. “At this my heart trembled.”**

It is as though he said: “It passed over into an excess of wonder.” Since the mind had been filled with the spirit of a new hope, it abandoned the condition in which it had existed in its former way of thinking. Fear, when it strikes the mind, makes it estranged from itself. Latin interpreters sometimes call *exstasis*—ecstasy or trance—fear.

It follows: “And it was moved from its place.”

The place of the human heart is the enjoyment of the present life. But when it is touched by divine inspiration, the place of our heart becomes love of eternity. Thus, through inward consideration of the homeland, the mind is moved from its place, because, having abandoned what is low, it is set among heavenly thoughts.

**Verse 2. “Hear the sound of his voice in terror.”**

It is the custom of sacred speech, when it indicates that something is heard through hearing, to speak of that hearing itself as being heard. Thus Habakkuk says: “Lord, I heard your report, and I was afraid” (Hab. 3:2).

It should be noted that the voice of God is said to be heard not in joy but in terror. For when a sinner thinks only about earthly things, when he carries an oppressed heart amid lowly thoughts, if he is suddenly touched by the inspiration of divine grace, he understands above all that everything he does is punished by the strict judgment of the eternal Judge.

The hearing of God’s voice therefore first occurs in terror, so that afterward it may be changed into sweetness. He first chastises us through fear of strict judgment, so that, once chastised, he may restore us through the consolation of heavenly sweetness.

It follows: “And the sound proceeding from his mouth.”

The sound from God’s mouth is the force of fear rushing upon us through heavenly inspiration. For when the Lord fills us through inspiration with thoughts of what is to come, he undoubtedly terrifies us concerning the evil things we have done in the past.

The mouth of God may also designate the only-begotten Son. We rightly understand the Lord’s mouth to be the one through whom he speaks all things to us. Hence the prophet also says: “The mouth of the Lord has spoken” (Isa. 1:20).

The sound of the mouth may designate the Holy Spirit, who belongs to the same Lord. Thus it is written elsewhere, in reference to this Spirit: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a rushing mighty wind” (Acts 2:2).

The sound therefore proceeds from the Lord’s mouth when the consubstantial Spirit, coming to us through the Son, breaks through the deafness of our insensibility. Hence it is said in the Gospel: “He will take from what is mine and announce it to you” (John 16:14).

The terror of the voice may therefore be understood as the power of strength, and the sound of the mouth as the sweetness of consolation. For those whom the Holy Spirit fills, he first terrifies concerning earthly activity and afterward consoles with the hope of heavenly things, so that afterward they may rejoice in their rewards through confession, to the same degree that previously they feared when they saw only punishments.

But because there are some who do not believe that God cares for human affairs and think that such things occur through random movements, it follows:

**Verse 3. “He himself looks beneath all the heavens, and his light is over the ends of the earth.”**

The name “heavens” may designate holy preachers. Hence it is written: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18:2).

There are some who, when they hear of the wondrous works of the apostles and do not see such powers now in the Church, suppose that heavenly grace has been withdrawn from the Church. They do not know what the Apostle says: “Tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers” (1 Cor. 14:22).

When the heavens have been raised, therefore, the Lord looks upon what is below, because even when the highest preachers have been taken away, he continually cares for the lowliness of our weakness. His light looks, as it were, beneath the heavens upon the ends of the earth, because, after the exalted life of those who came before, he also embraces the conduct and actions of sinners through the illumination of his grace.

Although he does not now frequently display signs of power through the lives of the faithful, he nevertheless never departs from those same faithful through the power of their works.

It may also be understood that his light is over the ends of the earth because, when the preaching of heavenly grace gathers the nations to faith, it enclosed the boundaries of the world within itself.

Or certainly, the ends of the earth are the limits of sinful human beings. It often happens that many abandon God and spend the years of their life in carnal desires. Yet when heavenly grace looks upon them, they return to God at the end of their lives, recognize what the eternal judgments are, punish with tears all the things they remember having done perversely, and show through right actions that these judgments truly follow them. Then, when justice follows, all that they previously did wrong is entirely forgiven.

Hence Anna also says through the spirit of prophecy: “The Lord will judge the ends of the earth” (1 Sam. 2:10).

**Verse 4. “After him the sound will roar.”**

The one whom the Lord has filled by illuminating him, he undoubtedly turns toward lamentation. The more he reveals eternal punishments to the illuminated mind, the more harshly he burdens it with groans over its past wickedness.

It follows: “He will thunder with the voice of his greatness.”

God thunders with the voice of his greatness when, after preparing us well through lamentation, he reveals to us how great he is in heavenly things. Thunder seems to proceed from heaven when the sudden regard of grace strikes with fear those of us who are sluggish through carelessness and negligence. Although we are placed on earth, we hear a sound from above, because, while thinking about earthly things, we suddenly fear the sound of heavenly terror.

It follows: “And he will not be searched out when his voice is heard.”

The Lord’s voice is heard when the inspiration of his grace is perceived in the mind, when the insensibility of hidden uncleanness is broken, and when the heart, awakened to the pursuit of supreme love, is penetrated by the cry of inward virtue.

Yet the mind itself, which has been illuminated by this voice of the arriving Spirit as he enters the ear of the heart, cannot investigate it. Invisible power cannot be assessed: by what paths it flows into us, in what ways it comes from itself, or by what means it departs.

Hence John rightly says: “The Spirit breathes where he wishes, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes” (John 3:8).

**Verse 5. “God will thunder wonderfully with his voice.”**

God thunders wonderfully with his voice because, by its force, he penetrates our hearts incomprehensibly. While he presses them with hidden movements in fear, he silently cries out, in some fashion, how ardently he ought to be followed.

It follows: “He does great and unsearchable things.”

When a human being devoted to earthly pursuits and oppressed by wicked desires suddenly burns for new things and grows cold toward his customary concerns, renounces external cares, and breathes after inward contemplation—who could sufficiently consider this power of the heavenly voice? Who could comprehend it by considering it?

The Lord does great things through his voice, but they would be less great if they could be searched out.

**Verse 6. “He commands the snow to descend upon the earth.”**

The Psalmist says: “You will wash me, and I will be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 51:9). What should we understand here by snow except the white hearts of the saints through the light of righteousness?

Water drawn upward is compressed above so that it becomes snow; but when the snow itself comes down to earth, it is again changed into the liquid of water.

The waters, therefore, are the minds of preachers. When they raise themselves to contemplate heavenly things, they are solidified through a higher understanding; and when they are carried away into the highest contemplation, they receive the power of firmness.

Yet because they are still held on earth by fraternal love, they moderate themselves from their lofty understanding. Preaching humbly to the weak, they raise up, like snow melting, the hearts of the parched, so that they may bear fruit.

Snow comes down from heaven to earth when the exalted hearts of the saints, already nourished by solid contemplation, descend through brotherly love to humble words of preaching. Just as snow, while it lies, covers, but when it melts, waters, so the power of the saints both protects the sinner’s life before God through its weakness and, through its condescension, pours itself out like melted snow upon the parched earth so that it may bear fruit.

It follows: “And winter with rains.”

Winter is the present life. Although hope already lifts us toward heavenly things, the cold torpor of our mortality still constrains us, because it is written: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that considers many things” (Wis. 9:15).

This winter has rains: undoubtedly, the preachings of those who govern rightly. Concerning these rains Moses says: “Let my speech be expected like rain, and let my words descend like dew” (Deut. 32:2).

These rains suit winter and will cease in summer, because now, while heavenly life is hidden from the eyes of carnal people, it is necessary for us to be watered by the preachings of the saints. But when the heat of the eternal judgment burns, no one will then need the words of preachers. When the Judge comes, each person is brought back to his own heart, so that, since he can no longer perform holy deeds, he may at least feel them.

It follows: “And [he commands] the rain of his strength.”

The rain of God’s strength is the preaching of his divinity; the rain of his weakness is the preaching of his incarnation. Concerning the former Paul says: “What is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Cor. 1:25). And again: “Though he was crucified through weakness, he lives through the power of God” (2 Cor. 13:4).

Holy men preach the weaknesses of his humanity in such a way that they also pour the strength of his divinity into the hearts of their hearers.

Let us hear the rain of strength through the thunder of the cloud: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). Let us also hear the rain of weakness: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

It follows:

**Verse 7. “For he seals the hand of every human being, so that each one may know his own work.”**

When, therefore, the rain of strength descends upon the earth, it is sealed in the hand of each person, so that each one may know his own work. When the incomprehensible power of majesty is recognized, each person more carefully examines his own life.

The omnipotent Creator made human beings rational creatures, distinguishing them from all things insensible and irrational, so that they could not fail to know what they had done. By the law of nature, each person is compelled to know whether what he does is wicked or righteous.

For if they do not know that they do good, why do they boast publicly about certain deeds? Again, if they do not know that they do evil, why do they avert the eyes of others from those same deeds?

Precisely because God created human beings as rational creatures, he seals his mark in the hand of every person, so that each one may know his own works.

It follows:

**Verse 8. “The beast will enter its hiding place and remain in its lair.”**

Who else is understood by the name “beast” except the ancient enemy, who fiercely attacked the first human being and tore apart the integrity of his life through evil persuasion?

Against this beast it is promised, through the voices of the prophets, that the holy Church of the elect will be restored to its former state and that the evil beast will not pass through it.

But when, after the coming of the Redeemer and after the voices of the preachers—like thunder after the clouds—the beast at the end of the world takes possession of that condemned man called Antichrist, what else does it do than enter its hiding place, so as to remain in its own lair?

That vessel of the devil is the lair and hiding place of the beast. Lurking among human beings as they travel along the road of this life, it both hides there through signs and kills through wickedness.

Even now, before it appears openly, it possesses the hearts of all the reprobate. It holds their minds as its own lair through hidden wickedness, and whenever it desires to harm the good, it hides itself in their dark minds.

Were not the hearts of the persecuting Jews the lair of this beast? It lay hidden for a long time in their counsels, but suddenly burst forth in their cries: “Crucify, crucify!” (John 19:6).

Hence it is written: “He made darkness, and it became night” (Ps. 104:20).

I consider it especially important to note that this beast is said not only to enter its lair but also to remain in it. It can enter the minds of the good, but it cannot remain in them, because the heart of a righteous person is not the lair of this beast.

Those whom it possesses as its own lair it undoubtedly holds by remaining in their minds. First it leads their thoughts as far as wicked desires, and afterward it leads their wicked desires as far as the most evil deeds.

It follows:

**Verse 9. “From the inner regions the storm will enter, and from the Bear the cold.”**

Since the sun burns more fiercely in the inner regions of the south, while in the Bear it has no course at all, the people of Judea are expressed here by “the inner regions,” and the Gentile people by “the Bear.”

Those who knew the one invisible God and served his law, at least carnally, were raised up as though beneath the southern sun, burning in the warmth of faith. The Gentiles, however, because they had attained no knowledge of heavenly thought, remained cold, as though without the sun beneath the north wind.

From the Jews arose the persecuting wickedness, and from the Gentiles the oppressive power: what Judea sought to accomplish by envy—namely, to kill Christ—the Gentile judge carried out through Roman authority.

It follows:

**Verse 10. “When God blows, the ice becomes solid.”**

The more the Holy Spirit breathed upon the hearts of the faithful, and the greater the miracles of virtue he bestowed, the more heavily the torpor of envy grew in the minds of unbelievers. Thus the unbelieving people hardened themselves against God precisely where the humble people softened the narrow hardness that had bound them.

*[Textual note: The printed text has “humiles populi” (“the humble peoples”), with variants “humilis” (“humble,” singular) and “populus” (“people,” singular).]*

It follows: “And again the very broad waters are poured out.”

After the ice, the Lord poured out very broad waters, because after enduring the savagery of the Jews even to death, he immediately melted their hearts from the hardness of unbelief through the inspiration of his love.

Hence a certain Wise One says: “As ice in fair weather, so your sins will be dissolved” (Sir. 3:17).

It follows:

**Verse 11. “Grain desires the clouds.”**

For who are the elect except God’s grain, to be stored in heavenly granaries? Now, on the threshing floor of the threshing area, they endure the chaff, because in this purification of the holy Church they bear the contrary conduct of the reprobate.

But until this grain reaches the perfection of its fruit, it waits for the rains of the clouds so that it may grow. The mind of the good is watered by the words of preachers, lest it be dried by the sun of carnal desires and deprived of the moisture of love.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. Ask the Lord of the harvest to send workers into his harvest” (Matt. 9:37–38).

It follows: “And the clouds scatter their light.”

For the clouds scatter light when holy preachers spread the examples of their lives through both speech and action.

It follows:

**Verse 12. “Which illuminate all things around, wherever the will of the governor directs them.”**

The clouds of God therefore illuminate all things around because they enlighten the ends of the world with the light of preaching. But because they are subject to divine commands and cannot accomplish whatever they wish, they cannot go except where the will of the one who governs leads them.

It follows: “To whatever he commands them upon the face of the inhabited world.”

Often, when they are led according to the will of the one who governs, they desire to act in one way but are directed in another. Frequently they strive to correct certain hearers gently, yet their speech is led into severity. Frequently they wish to cut off certain others harshly, yet their force is restrained by the spirit of gentleness.

Just as they cannot go wherever they wish, so they cannot act as they wish.

It follows:

**Verse 13. “Whether in one tribe, or in his own land, or wherever he commands them to be found in the place of his mercy.”**

The Lord leads his clouds either into one tribe, into his own land, or wherever he commands them to be found in the place of his mercy.

At one time he granted the preachers of the Old and New Testaments to the tribe of Judah alone, while rejecting nearly all Israel because of the evil rule of its kings. At another time he made these clouds rain in his own land, because he restored that same chosen Israel to its ancient grace after corruption and captivity.

At another time he wished them to shine in the place of his mercy, because through holy preachers he also displayed miracles of virtue to the Gentiles, so that by mercy alone he might free from the yoke of error those whom the wrath of immense unbelief was oppressing.

“One tribe” plainly signifies Judah. “The land of God” designates all Judea together. “The place of God’s mercy” is the Gentile world, concerning which the Apostle says: “The Gentiles glorify God because of his mercy” (Rom. 15:9).

It follows:

**Verse 14. “Listen to this, Job; stand and consider the wonders of God.”**

He saw Job lying, as it were, in comparison with himself, and urged him to stand for words of such great preaching. Although Elihu does not know how to weigh the good things he says in relation to the one to whom he says them, we nevertheless ought carefully to investigate the words of his teaching.

To stand is to act rightly. Hence Paul says: “Let anyone who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10:12).

Those who consider the wonders of God while lying down are people who assess his power through knowledge but do not love it through their lives. Through contemplation they stretch their eyes toward consideration, yet through intention they do not lift themselves from the earth.

Hence it is rightly said of Balaam: “He has his eyes open when he falls” (Num. 24:16). Thus, when Elihu said these things, he certainly did not believe that blessed Job had preserved in his life what he had said.

It follows:

**Verse 15. “Do you know when God commanded the rains, so that they might reveal the light of his clouds?”**

If the clouds are holy preachers, the rains of the clouds are the words of preaching. But when clouds fly through the air, unless rain comes down, one does not know how great a mass of water they carry. Unless lightning bursts forth amid the rains, it cannot be understood how much brightness is hidden within them.

In the same way, if holy preachers remain silent and do not reveal through speech how great is the brightness of heavenly hope that they carry in their hearts, they appear either like other people or even far more contemptible than others.

But when they begin to disclose through preaching the reward of the heavenly homeland that they hold within, and when they are pressed by persecution, it becomes known to what heights of virtue they have advanced.

Yet holy preachers often wish to show themselves so that they may benefit others, but cannot; and often wish to remain hidden so that they may be at peace, but are not permitted.

No one therefore knows when they reveal the light of the rain, since no one comprehends when God grants the power of preaching so that the glory of preachers may shine.

It is as though he openly said: Although you now see preachers who will come into the world, do you understand when the Lord will impel them to preach through the fullness of the Spirit, or by what means he will make the brightness of their lives known to the world?

### Verse 16

“Do you know the great paths of the clouds and his perfect knowledge?”

These clouds have very subtle paths, namely, the ways of holy preaching. For “narrow is the gate that leads to life” (Matthew 7:14). These paths are great because, insofar as they are narrow in the present life for the sake of guarding one’s manner of living, they are widened all the more in eternal recompense.

Perfect knowledge is to know everything and yet, in a certain sense, not to know oneself to be knowledgeable; to do good diligently, but to know that none of these things is one’s own. Here Truth says: “When you have done everything that has been commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants’” (Luke 17:10). And Paul says: “If anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know” (1 Corinthians 8:2).

It is as though he were saying: You now behold the highest achievements of preachers, who, after elevating themselves to the heights through knowledge, humbly bend themselves downward through recognition of their ignorance. It follows:

### Verse 17

“Are your garments warm when the earth is breathed upon by the south wind?”

We have already often said that blessed Job represents the holy Church. The garments of the Church are all those who are joined to her in the unity of faith. Concerning these same members of the Church, the Lord says through the Prophet: “As I live, you shall clothe yourself with all these as with an ornament” (Isaiah 49:18).

By the south wind, which is certainly a warm wind, the Holy Spirit is appropriately signified. When someone is touched by him, that person is freed from the torpor of iniquity. Hence it is rightly said in the Song of Songs: “Rise, north wind, and come; blow upon my garden, south wind, and let its spices flow” (Song of Songs 4:16).

The garments of the holy Church are therefore warm when the earth is breathed upon by the south wind, because those who cling to her through faith burn with fervent works of charity when their minds are filled by the breath of the Holy Spirit.
