**MORALLY.** Whoever lives rightly and is accustomed to teach this to others has, as it were, as many garments as there are hearers who adhere to him in harmony. Like garments, they receive warmth, as it were, through the pores of the body, because they are kindled to the love of God by the example of his conduct and the force of his exhortation. He rejects what is like his own coldness when he departs from his former iniquity; he retains the warmth he receives because he grows strong in the fervor that he has gained through instruction.

When hearers are kindled by the words of teachers, the garments seem to be warmed by a living body. But when the life of the teachers also advances through the progress of their hearers, warmth returns to the body from the warmed garments. Yet teachers must not attribute to themselves the fact that they see their hearers advancing through their exhortation, because unless the Holy Spirit fills their hearts, the bodily voice of teachers sounds in vain to their hearers.

After he had boldly said these things in arrogance, Elihu immediately added words prompted by a slight movement of mockery, saying:

### Verse 18

“Did you perhaps fashion the heavens with him, which are as solid as though cast from bronze?”

By the heavens may be signified those who have been established in heavenly places, namely, the angelic spirits. Hence we are taught to say in our prayer by the voice of Truth: “Let your will be done, as in heaven and on earth” (Matthew 6:10).

Bronze by its nature is difficult to consume with rust; and the angelic powers, which remained fixed in divine love, received this as a reward when the angels who grew proud fell: that they should no longer be gnawed by any rust of creeping sin, but should remain in contemplation of their Creator without end to their happiness and endure in the eternal subtlety of that in which they were created.

The heavens may also, as we have often said, represent the minds of the elect, suspended by inward love above every earthly contamination. Hence it is said: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). They are “as solid as though cast from bronze” because no rust of changeability consumes them from the integrity of the strength they first received.

It follows:

### Verse 19

“Show us what we should say to him; for we are indeed wrapped in darkness.”

It is as though he were saying: You, who already enjoy the great light of understanding, ought to teach us, who are wrapped in the darkness of ignorance.

Then, immediately recoiling from mockery, he adds disdainfully:

### Verse 20

“Who can recount to him what I say?”

It is as though he were openly saying: Who can report to him what I say? I speak, without having heard them, of his praises, though I perceive them keenly; who can report these things even after hearing them?

It follows:

“Even if a human being speaks, he will be swallowed up.”

Everything that swallows something draws it inward, hides it from the eyes of observers, and drags into the depths what could have been seen on the surface. Thus, when a human being is silent about God, he seems to be something by the reason in which he was created. But as soon as he begins to say anything about God, it is immediately shown how insignificant he is, because he is swallowed up by the immensity of God’s greatness. He is hidden as though dragged into the depths, because, desiring to speak of the ineffable, he is himself engulfed by the narrowness of his ignorance.

But behold: eternity truly became known to human beings when it revealed itself to them by assuming humanity. Since this had not yet been revealed, it is rightly added concerning those same human beings:

### Verse 21

“But now they do not see the light.”

Concerning this it is also said through the Prophet: “The people who sat in darkness have seen a great light” (Isaiah 9:2).

It follows:

“Suddenly the air will be condensed; it will be condensed into clouds.”

The air, through its very thinness, is dispersed in such a way that it is solidified by no firmness; clouds, however, are firmer insofar as they are denser. What, then, is signified by the air if not the minds of worldly people? Given over to the innumerable desires of this life, they are scattered here and there, fluid like the air.

But the air is condensed into clouds when minds that were previously fluid are strengthened by the solidity of virtue through the grace of heavenly regard, so that, thinking rightly, they gather themselves within the heart and do not dissolve into empty thoughts.

It follows:

“And a passing wind will drive them away.”

The passing wind is the present life. Thus the passing wind drives away the clouds because mortal life, hastening onward, conceals holy preachers bodily from our eyes.

It follows:

### Verse 22

“From the north gold will come.”

What is signified by the north if not the Gentile world, constricted by the cold of sin? He held it beneath the yoke of his tyranny who, in his pride, said: “I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:13).

What, however, are faithful souls expressed by the name of gold? Concerning them Jeremiah says: “How the gold has become darkened; how the finest color has been changed!” (Lamentations 4:1).

Thus gold is said to come from the north because, through the regard of the Redeemer’s grace, the precious life of the faithful multiplies for God within the holy Church from the Gentile world, formerly cold with the torpor of unbelief. Hence Isaiah says: “I will say to the north, and I will say to the south: Do not hinder” (Isaiah 43:6).

It follows:

“And from God comes a fearful praise.”

For “from God” is said as though it were said “from those who belong to God,” that is, from the faithful. Thus, when gold comes from the north, fearful praise proceeds from God, because, while the Gentile world received the splendor of faith, the multitude of faithful Hebrews praised God while fearing the divine judgments.

But how gold comes from the north, and how fearful praise bursts forth from those who are under God, let the very history of sacred speech show us, where it narrates the conversion of Cornelius. For this reason fearful praise proceeded from the Hebrews who had already become faithful when the Gentiles were converted: Judah was rightly rejected while the Gentile world was called, and Judah feared the loss caused by its rejection when it saw the gain produced by the calling of another people.

It follows:

### Verse 23

“We cannot find him worthily.”

Even if we can now find God, we cannot find him worthily, because what we perceive in him comes from faith, not yet from sight.

It follows:

“Great in strength and judgment and justice, and he cannot be described.”

He is great in strength because he conquers the strong adversary and, taking vessels of dishonor from his house, transforms them into vessels of mercy. He is great in judgment because, although here he humbles his elect through adversity, he eventually raises them up in the glory of eternal prosperity. He is great in justice because, although he tolerates the reprobate for a long time here, he nevertheless condemns them without end.

He cannot be described; one cannot worthily perceive how great he is—how much less can one speak of him? Yet we speak of this more appropriately, however imperfectly, if we remain silent in wonder beneath the awe of contemplating him.

It follows:

### Verse 24

“Therefore men will fear him, and all who seem wise to themselves will not dare to contemplate him.”

In this passage Elihu calls those who are strong in understanding “men.” It should be noted that he does not simply say, “The wise will not dare to contemplate”; by the words “who seem wise to themselves” he means people who are indeed learned but arrogant. [Note: [Col. 0427D] A word is missing here.]

Thus, while Elihu perceives many things forcefully, at the end of his speech he has touched upon himself. For arrogant and learned men, when they do not live rightly but are nevertheless compelled by the impulse of their teaching to speak rightly, become in some way heralds of their own condemnation.

Those who seem wise to themselves cannot contemplate the wisdom of God, because they are as far from his light as they are not humble before themselves. For while the swelling of pride grows in their minds, it blunts the edge of contemplation; and by the very means through which they imagine themselves to shine above others, they deprive themselves of the light of truth.

## BOOK TWENTY-EIGHT

[Col. 0429]

## CHAPTER THIRTY-EIGHT

[Col. 0429B]

### Verse 1

“Then the Lord answered Job from the whirlwind and said.”

The Lord speaks to his servants in one way when he advances them inwardly through compunction, and in another when he restrains them through sternness so that they may not become proud. In the former they learn what they should desire; in the latter, what they should fear.

Because blessed Job needed to be humbled—he was prostrate with ulcers, yet stood firm in virtue—the Lord is therefore said to have spoken to him from the whirlwind, lest the arrows of pride pierce his exceptionally strong breast, which, as was certain, the wounds inflicted upon it had not overcome.

It should also be understood that divine speech is distinguished in two ways. The Lord either speaks by himself, or his words to us are formed through some creature. When he speaks by himself, only the force of inward inspiration is opened to us, and the heart is taught by his word without words or syllables. For God’s speech, made inwardly to us, is seen rather than heard.

When the Lord makes his will known through an angel, he sometimes demonstrates it by words and sometimes by events: by words, as in “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again” (John 12:28); by events, as with Ezekiel, who heard nothing in words but saw the appearance of electrum in the midst of fire.

In these manifestations the Mediator between God and human beings is shown sometimes by words and events together, as in the passage: “When Adam had heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden at the evening breeze,” and what follows (Genesis 3:8). Sometimes he is shown through images, as when Jacob, while sleeping, saw a ladder resting on the heavens (Genesis 28:12), and as Peter saw a sheet full of reptiles (Acts 10:11).

Sometimes God speaks through heavenly substances, as when a voice sounded from the cloud: “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 17:5). Sometimes through earthly substances, as when he rebuked Balaam, forming human words in the mouth of a donkey (Numbers 22:28). Sometimes through earthly and heavenly substances together, as when, speaking to Moses, he joined fire and a bush (Exodus 3:3).

At times God also poured the power of his inspiration into human hearts through angels, even by their secret presence. Hence Zechariah says: “The angel who spoke in me said to me” (Zechariah 1:13); and shortly afterward: “And behold, the angel who spoke in me was going out,” and what follows (Zechariah 2:3).

Whether the Lord spoke to blessed Job by himself or through an angel is uncertain. It follows:

### Verse 2

“Who is this who wraps up judgments in unlearned words?”

We say “Who is this?” only concerning one whom we do not know. To know is to approve; not to know is to reject. Hence he says to certain people whom he rejects: “I do not know you” (Matthew 25:12). But because he says “judgments” without adding what kind, we understand them as good judgments, which you claim are wrapped in unlearned words because they were uttered in boastful language.

For it is a fault of ignorance to understand what is right wrongly—that is, to incline a heavenly gift toward the desire for earthly praise. As the Apostle says: “If anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know” (1 Corinthians 8:2).

It follows:

### Verse 3

“Gird your loins like a man.”

Those are truly men who follow the ways of the Lord with strong and unwavering steps, as in: “Act manfully” (Psalm 30:25). And in Proverbs: “O men, to you I call” (Proverbs 8:4).

To gird one’s loins is either to restrain lust in one’s conduct or to restrain it in one’s thoughts. Hence it is written: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35).

Blessed Job is therefore commanded that, just as he had previously conquered the lust of corruption, he should now also restrain the lust of pride. Hence Moses says: “Circumcise the foreskin of your heart” (Deuteronomy 10:16).

It follows:

“I will question you, and you shall answer me.”

Our Creator is accustomed to question us in three ways. He questions us when he strikes us with the severity of a scourge and reveals how much patience we possess or lack, as was shown in blessed Job. Or he commands certain things that we desire and makes our obedience manifest to us, as when Abraham was commanded to leave his land and to sacrifice his only son (Genesis 22:2). Or he reveals certain hidden things to us and conceals others, making the measure of our humility known to us. Hence it is written: “His eyelids question the children of men” (Psalm 10:5).

It is as though blessed Job were being told: I rouse you through words to consider sublime things; and while you perceive that you do not know what is above you, I make you better known to yourself. You truly answer me when you understand what you do not know.

It follows:

### Verse 4

“Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?”

In sacred Scripture, what else should we understand by foundations but preachers? When the Lord first established them in the holy Church, the entire structure of the subsequent edifice rose upon them. Hence the Psalmist says: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Psalm 86:1).

The Lord is understood as the foundation in the singular, concerning which Paul also says: “No one can lay another foundation except that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Corinthians 3:11).

It is as though blessed Job were being told: Consider the virtue of the strong, and contemplate me as their Author before the ages. When you look upon those whom I created in time as wonderful, consider how greatly you ought to submit to me, whom you recognize as the timeless Author of wondrous things.

**MORALLY.** If the mind of the sinner is dust, as the Psalmist says: “Not so the wicked, not so, but like dust,” and what follows (Psalm 1:4), nothing prevents us from understanding the earth as the soul of the righteous, concerning which it is written: “For the earth that drinks in the rain frequently falling upon it and produces suitable vegetation for those by whom it is cultivated receives blessing” (Hebrews 6:7).

The foundation of this earth is faith. When faith is given to one who did not believe in eternal things, the foundation of the subsequent work is already laid. When fear of the coming judgment is suddenly infused into one who despises it and boldly entangles himself in sins of flesh and spirit, the foundations are already being constructed so that the edifice of a good life may rise.

It is as though Truth were saying to the justified sinner: Do not attribute to yourself the virtues you have received from me; do not become proud against me because of my gift.

It follows:

### Verse 5

“Tell me, if you have understanding: Who set its measurements, if you know? Or who stretched the measuring line over it?”

When the Lord came in the flesh to the Church, he measured the earth with lines, because he marked out the boundaries of the Church through the subtlety of hidden judgment.

The Apostle Paul, when he was neglecting to preach in Macedonia, saw in a vision a Macedonian man who said: “Cross over into Macedonia and help us” (Acts 16:9). On the other hand, as it is written: “The apostles attempted to go into Bithynia, and the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them” (Acts 16:7).

Thus, while holy preachers are called to Macedonia and are forbidden to enter Asia, this line of hidden measurements was drawn there and withdrawn here. Within these measurements are all the elect; outside them are all the reprobate, even if they seem to be within the boundary of faith.

**MORALLY.** Who sets the measurements of the earth—that is, of the righteous soul—if not our Creator, who, by the secret governance of inward judgment, gives one the word of wisdom, another complete faith, another the grace of healings, another the working of virtues, and another prophecy? (1 Corinthians 12:8–10.)

Thus our Creator and dispenser orders all things, so that the one who might become proud because of the gift he possesses is humbled by the virtue he does not possess. In this way each person may possess in another what he himself has not received, so that he may humbly devote to another, by possessing it, what he has received.

Hence Peter says: “As each has received grace, administering it to one another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God” (1 Peter 4:10).

For a line is stretched over this earth when the examples of preceding fathers are shown to each elect soul as a rule for living, so that from their lives it may consider what it should preserve in its own actions. For this reason the subtle life of the saints is spread out before us through the sacred words, so that our works may either advance from lesser things or be restrained from greater ones, and so that the mind may neither attempt less than it is capable of completing nor undertake more than it has received.

It follows:

### Verse 6

“Upon what were its bases strengthened?”

You should understand: upon whom but me, who hold all things wondrously and provide the primary source within for external goods?

The bases of this earth are the teachers of the holy Church. By preaching what is right and by living in agreement with their preaching, they support the entire weight of the Church through the firm gravity of their conduct.

The prophets may also be signified by the bases. Since they were the first to speak openly about the Lord’s incarnation, we see them as bases rising from the foundation and supporting the weight of the structure placed upon them. Hence, when the Lord commanded Moses to erect the boards of the tabernacle, he ordered that their bases be made of silver.

**MORALLY.** The bases of each soul are its intentions. For just as a structure rests upon columns, and columns upon bases, so our life rests upon virtues, while the virtues themselves rest upon inward intention. Since it is written, “No one can lay another foundation,” and so forth (1 Corinthians 3:11), the bases are in the foundation when our intentions are strengthened in Christ.

Anyone performs the highest works in vain if, with the whole intention of his heart, he does not seek the rewards of true life.

It follows:

“Or who released its cornerstone?”

That cornerstone is the one concerning whom it is written: “The stone that the builders rejected,” and so forth (Psalm 117:22). By receiving within himself both the Jewish and the Gentile peoples, he joined two walls in the one structure of the Church.

Hence it is written: “He made both one” (Ephesians 2:14), because he displayed himself as the cornerstone not only below but also above. On earth he joined the nations of the Gentiles to the Israelite people, and in heaven he joined both together to the angels. For at his birth the angels cried out: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

**MORALLY.** The cornerstone is the twofold understanding of sacred Scripture. It is divinely released when it is not bound by strict judgment in the darkness of its ignorance but enjoys a certain freedom, being sufficient in God’s commandments either to perform external actions or to perceive inward realities through contemplation.

The incarnate Redeemer displayed both in himself and joined both together: namely, the active and contemplative life. Our understanding would never rise to this unless he came to assume our nature.

It is as though the Lord were saying: Who released the cornerstone if not I—the only-begotten one whom I begot beyond time and revealed in time for the salvation of human beings? In his life they would learn that different ways of living are not incompatible.

It follows:

### Verse 7

“When the morning stars praised me together.”

Because the first angels were created at the beginning, they are appropriately called morning stars: by existing in the light of wisdom, they preceded the coming day of the age to come.

It is rightly added, “together,” because the elect, together with the angels and the redeemed human beings at the end of the world, glorify the generosity of heavenly grace and praise together. When the angels see us being received, they rejoice that their number is being filled, saying: “Glory to God in the highest,” and so forth (Luke 2:14).

Alternatively, the morning stars are so called because they were often sent to exhort human beings. By announcing the coming morning, they drive away the darkness of the present life from human hearts.

It follows:

“And all the sons of God shouted for joy.”

A shout of joy occurs when the gladness of the heart is not completed by the power of the mouth. Let the angels praise, for they already see the breadth of such great brightness in the heights; let human beings shout for joy, for they still endure the narrowness of their mouths below.

Because the Lord knew that these things would certainly occur, he does not so much indicate that they must be done as narrate them as already done.

It follows:

### Verse 8

“Who enclosed the sea with doors when it burst forth as though proceeding from the womb?”

What should we understand by the sea if not the crowds of persecutors? By the name “womb,” the hidden, malicious, and carnal thought of human beings is signified. Elsewhere it is said of this womb of the hearts of the wicked: “He conceived pain,” and so forth (Psalm 7:15).

The sea burst forth as though proceeding from the womb when the waves of worldly threats raged for the destruction of the holy Church. But by God’s agency it was enclosed with doors, because holy men were set against the swelling of persecutors, so that their miracles and reverence might break the anger of the persecutors.

Alternatively, by this sea we should understand the world. Against this sea the Lord placed doors a second time, because he first gave the human race the precepts of the Law and afterward the Testament of the new grace.

At first God prohibited works of iniquity, saying: “You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery,” and so forth (Exodus 20:13–14). Later he also restrained sinful thoughts, saying: “Everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her,” and so forth (Matthew 5:28), and: “Love your enemies,” and so forth (Matthew 5:44).

He also indicated the time when he said that it proceeded from the womb. At that time he confronted the human race with the precepts of the Law, when it was still leaving the condition close to its origin, as though from its own birth, and progressing toward a carnal way of life. To proceed from the womb is to appear carnally in the light of the present glory.

**MORALLY.** What is the sea if not our heart, turbulent with rage, bitter with quarrels, swollen with the pride of exaltation, and darkened by the deceit of malice? Anyone who understands the hidden temptations of his thoughts recognizes how fiercely this sea rages within him.

The womb of evil thought is youth. Concerning it the Lord says through Moses: “The sense and thought of the human heart are inclined toward evil from its youth” (Genesis 8:21).

Each of us received the evil of corruption from the beginning of our carnal desires. But the Lord encloses the sea with doors because he subjects evil impulses to barriers through the inspired fear of judgment and the dread of eternal punishment.

It follows:

### Verse 9

“When I made the cloud its garment and wrapped it in darkness as though in swaddling cloths for an infant’s face.”

The raging sea is clothed with a cloud because the cruelty of persecutors is covered by the veil of their folly. Through the intervening darkness of their unbelief, they are unable to see the clear light of truth, and they do not recognize, because of the desert of their blindness, what they do under the impulse of cruelty.

“For if they had known,” as the Apostle says, “they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8).

This cloud usually oppresses not only unbelievers who are outside, but also darkens some who live carnally within the Church. Hence it is written: “I have made a cloud stand in the way, so that prayer may not pass through” (Lamentations 3:44).

Whoever constantly thinks about earthly things endures these things in prayer because he wills them when he does not will them. The feet and arms of an infant are bound with swaddling cloths. Since the persecutors of the holy Church think like children, they always desire to harm the righteous; but, constrained by divine dispensation, they do not extend their arms as far as they wish. Even if they readily desire to perpetrate every evil, they are nevertheless not permitted to fulfill everything they desire.

Alternatively, God made the cloud a garment when he rescued the Jewish people from the error of unbelief but did not yet disclose to them the splendor of his light. He removed them from darkness but still clothed them with a cloud. He also wrapped them in the darkness of his words as in the swaddling cloths of infancy when he bound them not by the open preaching of the Spirit but by the commandments of the letter.

When the weak people unwillingly endured the swaddling cloths of the commandments, they reached a stronger condition through that very binding. Hence they were commanded in the Law to demand “an eye for an eye” (Exodus 21:24), while later, struck by revealed grace, they were commanded to offer the other cheek.

**MORALLY.** Our heart, turbulent with thoughts, is clothed with a cloud because, so that it may not clearly behold earthly repose, it is darkened by the confusion of its unrest. This sea is wrapped in darkness as in the swaddling cloths of infancy because, through the earthly senses of its weakness, it is still bound from contemplating sublime realities.

Hence Paul says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma,” and so forth (1 Corinthians 13:12); “Now I know in part,” and so forth (ibid.); and: “When I was a child, I spoke as a child,” and so forth (ibid.).

It follows:

### Verse 10

“I surrounded it with my boundaries.”

The Lord surrounds the sea with his boundaries because he moderates the anger of persecutors by the dispensation of his judgments, so that the wave of their raging and swollen fury may be broken upon the full shore of hidden providence.

Alternatively, the Lord surrounded it with his boundaries because he enclosed the unformed people within the limits of the commandments, restraining their unregulated [read: immoderate] wanderings of mind.

**MORALLY.** The Lord surrounds this sea with his boundaries because he humbles our heart, still turbulent from the trouble and care of its corruption, beneath the measure of his contemplation. Although it desires more, it does not rise beyond what is permitted to it.

Alternatively, he imposes boundaries on the raging sea because he calms our heart, swollen with temptations, through the hidden distribution of gifts: at one time preventing an evil suggestion from reaching delight, at another preventing an evil delight from reaching consent.

It follows:

“And I set a bar and doors.”

What is signified by the doors if not holy preachers? What by the bar if not the incarnate Lord?

He placed these doors against the violence of the raging sea all the more powerfully because he strengthened them by his own observance. Holy men are rightly called doors because they open an entrance to the faithful and, in turn, oppose themselves to unbelievers so that they may not enter.

Peter was one of these doors: he received Cornelius and rejected Simon, saying: “In truth I have found that God is not a respecter of persons” (Acts 10:34). The doors of this Church were also those to whom the Lord said: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them,” and so forth (John 20:22).

Alternatively, closed doors are strengthened by a bar placed across them. The Lord therefore set up the bar because he sent the Only-Begotten against the wanton impulses of the human race, and because he strengthened through action the spiritual commandments that he taught by speaking.

It follows:

### Verse 11

“Thus far you shall come, and you shall proceed no farther.”

For the measure of hidden judgment determines both when the storm of persecution will burst forth and when it will subside, lest either persecution fail to exercise the elect because it does not rage, or, if not moderated, plunge them into the depths.

It follows:

“And here you shall break your swelling waves.”

When the knowledge of faith extends even to the persecutors, fear of the turbulent sea is calmed. There the sea breaks its waves, because the one who comes to the knowledge of truth blushes for everything he has wickedly done. Hence Paul says to certain people: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Romans 6:21).

Alternatively, the sea had passed beyond its own doors because the wave of human pride was battering against the barriers of the Law placed before it. But after the world encountered the Only-Begotten set against it, it broke the force of its exaltation and could not pass beyond, because it found the boundary of its fury closed by his strength. Hence it is written: “The sea saw and fled” (Psalm 114:3).

The doors may also appropriately be understood as his manifest sufferings, against which he placed a hidden bar, because he strengthened them through his invisible divinity. The waves of the world come against them, but, broken, they rebound: the proud despise them when they see them, but fear their power when they experience it.

**MORALLY.** What is signified by the doors if not virtues? What by the bar if not the strength of charity? Every good of virtue is easily destroyed when temptation assaults the heart unless it is made firm by deeply rooted charity.

Hence Paul, when setting the doors of virtue against certain people, added the strength of the bar, saying: “Above all, having charity, which is the bond of perfection” (Colossians 3:14).

Because the Lord restrains vices arising in the heart through the strength of inspired charity, he checks the assault of the rising sea by means of closed barriers. Blessed Job, therefore, so that he may not attribute to himself the fact that he stands firmly against the storms of the heart, should hear the divine voice: “Who enclosed the sea with doors?” and what follows.

## BOOK TWENTY-NINE

[Col. 0435]

[Col. 0435C]

### Verse 12

“Have you, after your rising, commanded the dawn and shown the morning its place?”

You should understand: as I have. The rising of the Lord’s divinity has no “before” or “after.” The rising of his humanity, however, because it began and ends, received a before and an after from time.

But when he himself assumed the shadow of our temporality and infused into us the light of his eternity, the dawn rightly recognized its timeless place through this rising that the Creator granted himself in time.

Because dawn or morning is turned from darkness into light, the entire Church of the elect is appropriately signified by the name of dawn or morning: it is led from the night of unbelief into the light of faith. Hence it is written: “Who is this that advances like the rising dawn?” (Song of Songs 6:9).

Alternatively, dawn or morning announces that night has passed but does not yet display the full brightness of day. While it drives night away, it receives day and holds a light mingled with darkness.

What, then, are all of us who follow the truth in this life if not dawn or morning? We already perform certain works that belong to the light, yet we are not free from certain remnants of darkness. Hence it is written: “No living person shall be justified in your sight” (Psalm 143:2).

Paul also says: “I see another law in my members warring against” me, and so forth (Romans 7:23); and again: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near,” and so forth (Romans 13:12).

The day of the holy Church will come when the shadow of sin is no longer mingled with it. The place of this dawn is the perfect brightness of inward vision. The dawn considers its place when the holy soul burns to contemplate the face of its Creator, saying: “My soul thirsted for the living God,” and so forth (Psalm 42:3).

The Lord signifies this place when he says: “Wherever the body is,” and so forth (Luke 17:37). The blessedness of the future recompense, before he himself became known through the body, was contained in the understanding of a few.

It follows:

### VERSE 13

“Have you held the ends of the earth as they were shaken, and shaken the wicked out of it?”

The Lord held the ends of the earth because, at the end of the ages, he came to the Synagogue, which was already abandoned and subjected to foreign kings; and he shook the wicked out of it because he drove away from the glory of the carnal sacrifice those who rejected the spiritual principles of faith.

Alternatively: Because he chose from Judea a few who were rejected and humble, he held the ends of the earth. For he abandoned the teachers of the Law and held on to fishermen; and while he holds its ends, he shakes the wicked out of it, because, while he strengthens the weak faithful, he sternly condemns the unbelieving within it.

A thing that is shaken is dragged to and fro and wearied. Judea, therefore, had been shaken: through some it said, “Because he is good” (John 7:12), while through others it resisted, saying, “No, but he deceives the crowds” (ibid.).

Alternatively: He shook and held the ends of the earth because, when he terrified the weak hearts of the humble with godly fear, he did not abandon them to strict judgment. For the multitude of believers stood more firmly in God precisely because it held itself humble. Hence Solomon says: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful; but whoever is hard of heart will fall into evil” (Prov. 28:14).

Alternatively, “earth” means the holy Church. The Lord therefore holds and shakes the ends of the earth because he permits the final and most savage persecution of his Church to disturb it through the coming of Antichrist. And because there are many within the Church who, as the Apostle says, “profess that they know God, but deny him by their deeds” (Tit. 1:16), the Lord shakes the wicked out of it: those whom inward vices now possess will then fall into the abyss of open unbelief and pass into a heap of chaff.

**MORALLY.** By earth, a person who thinks of what is lowly is signified; to him, when he sinned, it was said: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19). At the end of life the Lord often shakes sinners by frightening them; by shaking them, he converts them; by converting them, he holds them; and from their hearts he tears out the wicked movements of their thoughts.

It follows:

### VERSE 14

“It will be restored like clay for a seal.”

What else did the Lord find the Israelite people to be but clay, when he found them enslaved in Egypt and devoted to the services of the Gentiles, making bricks? Yet, when he bestowed upon them the hidden mysteries and the prophets, what else did he make them than the seal of a mystery to be preserved? But when afterward it refused to believe in its Redeemer, loving earth rather than truth, it said through its priests: “If we let him go on in this way, everyone will believe in him,” and so forth (John 11:48). It lost the mysteries of the word it had received and chose to understand only earthly things, which defile.

Alternatively: Those who now appear as a seal in the bosom of the Church will then be restored before the eyes of all as clay. Sacred Scripture commonly uses “seal” for faith and “clay” for iniquity. Hence the Church is told by her Bridegroom: “Set me as a seal upon your heart” (Song 8:6). By clay, earthly contaminations are indicated, as the Psalmist testifies: “You brought me up from the pit of misery and from the mire of clay” (Ps. 39:3). Many, rescued from earthly contaminations, are marked with the sacrament of heavenly faith; but those who appear to be a seal when untested will undoubtedly be clay when tested. And here it is rightly said, “it will be restored.” For as they could have been before faith, so they will be found afterward when rejected.

**MORALLY.** The Lord made the human being, whom he created in his own likeness, like a seal of his power; yet that person will be restored as clay, because although through conversion he escapes eternal punishments, nevertheless, in punishment for the pride he committed, he is condemned by the death of the flesh.

It follows:

“And it will stand like a garment.”

Rougher and coarser garments, even when they have been put on, are said to stand because they do not cling closely when properly fitted to the limbs. Thus Judea stood like a garment with regard to knowledge of the truth, even when it appeared to serve: through outward commandments it showed that it served the Lord, but it did not wish to cling to him through an understanding of charity.

Alternatively: The holy Church is now clothed, as though with many garments, by the veneration of the faithful. Hence, when the nations have been shown to her, the Lord says to her through the prophet: “As I live, you will be clothed with all these things as with an ornament” (Isa. 49:18). Yet she is now clothed, as it were, with many who are faithful only in appearance; but then, when the force of persecution strikes, she will be stripped of them and left naked.

Here “to stand” means to persist in sin, as in: “He did not stand in the way of sinners” (Ps. 1:1). Or certainly, just as a clothed garment is stretched out, while once removed it is broken and folded up, so each person who has withdrawn from the Church will lie broken and cast aside—he who, while he was being clothed, was comely and stretched out.

But if “to stand” means “to endure,” each reprobate stands like a garment because he endures for a short time in this life, which he loves, as it says: “All things will grow old like a garment,” and so forth (Ps. 102:27).

**MORALLY.** For our clay stands like a garment when it endures empty and stripped until the time of the resurrection.

It follows:

### VERSE 15

“His light will be taken away from the wicked.”

Because the Jews refuse to believe the truth, they lose knowledge of the Law forever; and because they grow proud of the Law they received, they are blinded, plainly, by the glory of their knowledge. For it is written: “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see” (Ps. 68:24). And: “Blind the heart of this people, and weigh down its ears” (Isa. 6:10).

Alternatively: Even now God’s light does not illuminate those who cloak the wickedness of their iniquity under the name of faith. There are, however, some who truly believe the eternal things they hear, yet contradict the faith they hold by living badly. While they act perversely but think rightly about God, they are illuminated in some measure by the radiance of light, lest they become wholly dark. Those who love earthly things more than heavenly things lose, when persecution strikes, what they appeared to believe rightly. This will happen especially and with greater intensity in the persecution of Antichrist. Yet the author of the wicked already appears in those who serve him, for as he comes, John says: “Now many Antichrists have arisen” (1 John 2:18).

**MORALLY.** The death of the flesh, which restores the elect to their light, takes away the light of the reprobate. For light is the glory of the present life to those who are proud. That light is taken from them when, through the destruction of the flesh, they are summoned to the darkness of their own accounting.

It follows:

“And the lofty arm will be broken.”

The lofty arm will be broken when the proud works of the Law are rejected in the proclamation of the grace of faith, as it is said: “By works of the Law no flesh will be justified” (Rom. 3:20).

Alternatively: What else is understood by the lofty arm but the proud exaltation of Antichrist? It rises above the reprobate minds of human beings through the arrogance of worldly glory, so that he falsely claims to be God over human beings. Hence the Apostle Paul says: “So that he takes his seat in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God” (2 Thess. 2:4). “The Lord Jesus Christ,” as the same Apostle says, “will kill him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the manifestation of his coming” (ibid., 8). The lofty arm is then broken because the exaltation of the heart, violently seized beyond the order of nature, is scattered by the measure of divine justice, so that what it had perversely raised up for a brief time recognizes itself as eternally shattered beneath the weight of judgment.

It follows:

### VERSE 16

“Have you entered the depths of the sea?”

As if he were saying: “As I have.” For if, according to the usage of divine discourse, the sea is to be understood as the world, nothing prevents us from understanding the depths of the sea as the prison-houses of hell. The Lord entered these depths of the sea when he entered the lowest regions of hell to rescue the souls of his elect. Hence it is said through the prophet: “You made a way in the depths of the sea for the liberated to pass through” (Isa. 51:10).

**MORALLY.** The sea is the human mind, whose depths God enters when he recalls to memory the wickedness of one’s former life and shakes the mind, tossed about in its own confusion. God enters the depths of the sea when he changes even hearts that have despaired, or when he humbles a worldly heart, or when he does not disdain to visit minds oppressed by crimes.

It follows:

“And have you walked about in the farthest depths of the abyss?”

Repeating in other words what he had said above about the depths of the sea, he calls it “the farthest part of the abyss,” because, just as the abyss of waters cannot be grasped by any sight of ours, so the hidden regions of the underworld cannot be penetrated by any sense of thought on our part. To walk about is proper not to one confined but to one who is free. Therefore, since the Lord bore no bonds of sin, he walked about in hell: free, he came to those who were bound. Hence it is written: “I became as one without help among the dead, free among the dead” (Ps. 87:5). Peter says: “Having loosed the pains of hell, since it was impossible for him to be held by it” (Acts 2:24).

Or certainly, because by walking we are led from one place to another and are found present here and there, the Lord is said to have walked in hell so that it might be shown that he was present to the elect souls in their several places through the power of his divinity.

**MORALLY.** What is the abyss but the human mind? Since it cannot comprehend itself, it conceals itself from itself in everything that exists, like a dark abyss. Hence it is rightly said through the prophet: “The abyss uttered its voice” (Hab. 3:10). For God to walk in the farthest depths of the abyss is to convert even the hearts of the most wicked people, wonderfully to reform despairing minds by touching them with the footprints of his visitation, and, after immense crimes, to restrain the dark heart, darkened by vices, through the fear of his visitation and to summon it to the lament of contrition. Concerning these steps the Prophet says: “Your processions were seen, O God, the processions of my God” (Ps. 67:25).

It follows:

### VERSE 17

“Have the gates of death been opened to you, and have you seen the dark doors?”

The gates of death are the hostile powers, which the descending Lord opened because, by dying, he overcame their strength. They are also called “dark doors” because, while they remain unseen through the ambushes of their concealment, they opened the way of death to deceived minds. The Lord sees these dark doors because he both perceives and restrains the fraudulent wickedness of unclean spirits. We too see these dark doors when we are illuminated by the rays of heavenly light.

[Note: The substantive in the ablative is missing here; something such as “rays” may have stood.]

Hence it is said through the Prophet: “The Lord is my helper, and I shall see my enemies” (Ps. 117:7). He himself sees our enemies because by his gift he makes them visible to us.

Or certainly, the Lord sees the dark doors when, penetrating the prison-houses of hell, he strikes the cruel spirits and, by dying, condemns the rulers of death.

**MORALLY.** The gates of death are thoughts, which we open to God when we confess them with tears in repentance. Then he opens a way for himself in the gates of death, when, after confession, he comes to us once our evil thoughts have been released. The dark doors are hidden evils of death, which may also exist inwardly; the Lord sees them when, by the hidden regard of grace, he destroys them. For it is written: “The king who sits on the throne of judgment scatters every evil by his gaze” (Prov. 20:8).

It follows:

### VERSE 18

“Have you considered the breadth of the earth?”

When the Lord entered the narrow places of death, he expanded his faith among the Gentiles and extended the holy Church into countless hearts. To her it is said through the prophet: “Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out the skins of your tabernacles; do not spare. Lengthen your cords and strengthen your pegs. For you will penetrate to the right and to the left, and your offspring will inherit the nations” (Isa. 54:2–3). For while he himself was preaching, only a few from the Israelite people believed; but countless peoples of the Gentiles followed the way of life when he died and rose again.

**MORALLY.** Unless virtues enlarged the soul, Paul would never say to the Corinthians: “You also be enlarged, and do not be yoked together with unbelievers” (2 Cor. 6:13–14). Attention should be paid to the word “considered.” The breadth of good things is inward and cannot be grasped unless it is carefully considered. For often poverty humbles people outwardly and the sufferings of punishment constrain them; yet amid these things inward strength continually enlarges them toward the hope of heavenly things. Of the apostles it is written: “They went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41).

It follows:

### VERSE 19

“Tell me, if you know all things, in what way light dwells, and what place darkness occupies.”

What else is understood by the name “light” but justice, and what else is designated by “darkness” but iniquity? Hence it is said to some: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8). And of some who remain in sin it is said: “Those who sleep, sleep at night” (1 Thess. 5:7).

It is as though blessed Job were being told: If you suppose that you possess complete knowledge, say in whose heart the wickedness that now exists persists.

It follows:

“In what way light dwells”—that is, in whose mind justice comes and fills it.

It follows:

### VERSE 20

“And what place darkness occupies”—that is, in whom blind iniquity endures.

It follows:

“So that you may lead each one to his boundaries”—that is, so that you may judge whether the one who is now seen to be wicked will end his life in this wickedness, or whether the one who is seen to be just will conclude the end of his life with the perfection of justice.

It follows:

“And understand the paths of his house”—that is, consider and discern to whom a persevering good action grants an eternal dwelling in the kingdom, or whom a wicked action, binding him until his end, condemns to eternal punishment. “House” is used for dwelling, and “path” for action. A path therefore leads to a house, because action draws one toward a dwelling. But what human being can examine these things and speak confidently? Who can even hear them without fear?

For we see many shining with the light of justice, yet darkened at the end by the obscurity of their wickedness; and many covered with the darkness of sins, yet, near the end of their lives, suddenly restored to the freedom of the light of justice. We have seen many hold to the way of justice until death, and many continue to heap up the crimes they once began, without ceasing, until their departure.

It follows:

### VERSE 21

“Did you know then that you would be born, or did you know the number of your days?”

As if he were saying to him openly: What wonder if you do not understand your end, when you do not even comprehend your beginning?

Alternatively: Human beings begin to exist when they are born in their mothers’ wombs. For conception itself is called birth, in accordance with what is written: “What has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20). And therefore they do not know that they will be born, because they do not exist before they are created.

But God, who has always existed without beginning, foreknew concerning himself what he took up in the Virgin’s womb at the beginning of his human existence. And because he foreknew it, he ordained it; and because he ordained it, he certainly endured nothing in human form without his will.

It follows:

### VERSE 22

“Have you entered the treasuries of snow, and have you looked upon the treasuries of hail?”

What else should be understood in snow or hail but the cold and hard hearts of the wicked? For just as charity is commonly signified in sacred discourse by heat, so malice is signified by cold. It is written: “As a cistern makes water cold, so malice makes the soul cold” (Jer. 6:7). And again: “Iniquity will abound, and the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24:12). In the coldness of snow or the hardness of hail, what can be understood more appropriately than the life of the wicked, which grows cold through torpor and is struck through the malice of hardness?

It follows:

### VERSE 23

“Which I have prepared for the time of the enemy, for the day of battle and war?”

When our adversary, the devil, strives to tempt us, he uses the behavior of the wicked as weapons of his own against us. Through them he rages and torments us, yet unknowingly purifies us. For they become a scourge through our own sins. While we are struck by such a life, we are freed from eternal death.

Alternatively: In snow or hail we understand the cold or hard hearts of the wicked. But because almighty God chose his saints from among such people, and because he knows how many elect he still has placed amid the life of the wicked, he appropriately says that he has treasuries in snow or hail.

The word “treasury” is derived from θέσις (*thesis*), that is, “from a placing.” Treasuries are therefore found in snow or hail because many who are cold with the torpor of iniquity are taken up into heavenly grace, shine with the light of justice in the holy Church, and strike down the perverse knowledge of adversaries with the blows of their teaching. For a long time he keeps them prepared for the day of battle and war in the bosom of their knowledge. But when he suddenly brings them forth, he strikes the resisting breasts of the adversaries with their words and refutations, as with hailstones.

Hence it is written: “Before his radiance,” and so forth (Ps. 17:13). Hail, when it comes, strikes; when melted, it waters. Holy men, however, both water the hearts of their hearers by soothing them and strike them. The Prophet testifies to how they strike, saying: “They will speak of the power of your terrible deeds,” and so forth (Ps. 144:6). And he adds how they water them gently: “They will pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness,” and so forth (ibid., 7).

### VERSE 24

“By what way is the light distributed?”

He himself is the way who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). Through this way, therefore, light is distributed because through his presence the entire Gentile world is illuminated. He rightly said “distributed,” because through the voices of the apostles the light of preaching did not shine narrowly or within limits, but radiated widely.

It follows:

“The heat is divided over the earth.”

That persecution is signified by heat, the Lord testifies concerning the seed cast upon the rock, saying: “When the sun had risen, everything was scorched,” and so forth (Matt. 13:6). A little later, when he explained the heat, he called it persecution. Thus, when the light had been distributed, the heat was divided over the earth, because as the life of the faithful became bright, the cruelty of unbelievers was kindled. The heat was divided when persecution raged now in Jerusalem, now in Damascus, and now in other distant regions. For it is written: “On that day a great persecution arose against the Church that was in Jerusalem, and all were scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria” (Acts 8:1).

Alternatively: By the name “light,” justice is designated, concerning which it is written: “The people who sat in darkness saw a great light” (Isa. 9:1). Whatever is distributed, however, is not cast continuously but with a certain interruption. Light is therefore distributed in this life because the understanding of reality is not continuously possessed by everyone. For while we comprehend one thing as it is and do not know another, we see partly in distributed light and partly remain in darkness.

But then the light will no longer be distributed for us, when our mind, wholly carried away to God, shines. It is as though he were saying openly: Tell me by what order I pour justice into the hidden senses, when I do not appear through approach and yet invisibly change the visible works of human beings.

It follows:

“The heat is divided over the earth.”

For the cunning enemy strives to inflame with unlawful desires the minds of those whom he sees shining with the light of justice. Hence, after the Israelites had been called, they complained against Moses about their increasing labor, saying: “May the Lord see and judge, because you have made our odor foul before Pharaoh and his servants, and you have given them a sword to kill us” (Exod. 5:21).

Heat follows light because, after illumination by the divine gift, the struggle of temptations increases. It is rightly said that the heat is divided, because individuals are not wearied by every vice, but by certain vices that are close and adjacent to them. For the ancient adversary first observes the disposition of each person and then sets the snares of temptations. To cheerful dispositions he offers lust; to sorrowful ones, the cup of discord.

The cunning usurper divides this heat in one way, while the merciful Creator divides it in another: the former divides it in order to destroy more quickly through it; the latter, so that he may make it bearable.

It follows:

### VERSE 25

“Who gave a course to the most vehement rain?”

As if he were saying: “Who but I?” For after the heat was divided, he strengthened the course of preaching amid the very straits of persecution, so that the power of the preachers might grow all the more as the cruelty of their persecutors opposed them, in order that they might pour drops of rain upon the parched hearts of their hearers and water the dryness of unbelief with abundant moisture.

Paul endured and watered this heat of persecution when he said: “I labor even to the chains, as though I were doing evil; but the word of God is not bound” (2 Tim. 2:9). Elsewhere it is said of this rain: “I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon the earth” (Isa. 5:6). But it should be noted that he calls this rain not “vehement” but “most vehement.” A vehement rain is great force; a most vehement rain is both force and the vastness of preaching. The rain is vehement when holy preachers persuade people to believe in eternal things. It is most vehement when, for the sake of hope, they admonish people to abandon what they possess and to despise all visible things for the sake of invisible ones.

It follows:

“And a way for the sounding thunder.”

What else is understood by thunder but the preaching of heavenly fear, by which human hearts are shaken when they perceive it? At times the Lord himself, incarnate, is represented by thunder. The Prophet of the ancient Fathers was brought to our knowledge, as it were, from the shaking of the clouds; appearing visibly among us, he sounded out terrifyingly the things that were above us. Hence the apostles were called “Boanerges, that is, sons of thunder” (Mark 3:17).

At times his preaching itself is understood, through which the terror of heavenly judgments is heard. Preaching is perceived in vain by the ear of the hearer when it is said to reach the inner self of a deaf heart. But because the Lord asserts that he gives a way to sounding thunder—when he grants words of preaching, he pierces hearts through fear—Paul says: “Praying at the same time for us also, that God may open to us a door for his word, to speak the mystery of Christ” (Col. 4:3).

It follows:

### VERSE 26

“And that it might rain upon the earth without a man, in the desert where none of the mortals dwells.”

To rain upon the earth without a man in the desert is to preach the word of God among the Gentiles, who, since they held no worship of divinity, displayed no appearance of a good work within themselves. It was plainly a desert, because it had no lawgiver and because it did not rationally seek God. Thus it was as though no human being were there, and, occupied only by wild beasts, it was empty of mortals.

Elsewhere it is said of this deserted earth: “He turned rivers into a desert” (Ps. 106:33). It is fitting that, after the heat had been divided over the earth, the most vehement rain received a course so that it might rain upon the desert: after the harshness of persecution had grown fierce in Judea, each preacher sent to Israel turned aside to call the Gentiles.

Hence the holy apostles say: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

It follows:

### VERSE 27

“That it might fill the pathless and desolate land.”

What this filling produced is shown when it immediately adds:

“And that it might bring forth green plants.”

The Gentile world was pathless, because the way of God’s word had not been opened to it. It was also rightly called desolate, whether because it lacked understanding of the divine counsel or because it was deprived of the fruit of good works. But the desolate land was filled when he joined inward inspiration to outward preaching, so that the parched hearts of the Gentiles might grow green and what was closed might open.

In sacred Scripture, grass sometimes signifies the glory of temporal prosperity, as the Prophet says: “In the morning let him pass away like grass; in the morning let him flower and pass away” (Ps. 86:6). At times it signifies the devil’s nourishment, as the Lord says of him: “The mountains bring forth grass for him” (Job 40:15). At times it signifies the support of preachers, as in: “He produces hay on the mountains and grass for the service of human beings” (Ps. 146:8). At times it signifies good activity, as it is written: “Let the earth bring forth green grass” (Gen. 1:11). At times it signifies knowledge of eternal life, as is said through Jeremiah: “The wild asses stood upon the rocks; they drew in the wind like dragons; their eyes failed because there was no grass” (Jer. 14:6).

This signifies the persecution of the Jews. They stood like venomous dragons upon the rocks, not upon God, saying: “We have no king,” and so forth (John 19:15). They drew in the wind of elation; their eyes—that is, their hope, which loved temporal things—fell. The grass failed because the knowledge of eternity was absent from their hearts.

But in this passage we understand the green plants as the knowledge of holy doctrine or appropriate works, because when the Gentiles received the rain of holy preaching, they brought forth both the works of life and the words of doctrine. Hence the Prophet says: “In the dens where dragons formerly dwelt, there will arise the greenness of the reed and the rush” (Isa. 35:7). By the reed he designated writers, by the rush hearers, and by the dens of dragons the people whom the malice of the enemy possessed.

**MORALLY.** Desolate lands are those who are reckoned among the faithful and hear the words of life with their ears, but do not permit them to pass into the inner parts of their hearts. This land has no human being because their mind lacks the sense of reason; and no mortal dwells in this land because, even if rational thoughts sometimes enter their conscience, they do not remain.

But when the merciful one is shown to give a course to his rain, those who have been pierced open the ears of their hearts through inward grace to the words of life. He fills the pathless land because, when he grants hearing to the word, it is heaped up with mystery. And he brings forth green plants because, through the grace of compunction, it not only gladly receives the words but also returns them abundantly, so that what it could not hear it now desires to speak.

Hence it is written: “Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created,” and so forth (Ps. 103:30).

It follows:

### VERSE 28

“Who is the father of rain, or who begot the drops of dew?”

As if he were saying: “Who but I, who sprinkle the dry earth of the human heart with drops of freely given knowledge?” Of this rain it is said elsewhere: “You will set apart, O God, a voluntary rain,” and so forth (Ps. 67:10).

God is called the father of rain because heavenly preaching is generated for us not from our merit but from his grace. The drops of dew are the holy preachers, who, amid the evils of the present life, like the darkness of a dry night, pour the fields of our hearts, parched, with the grace of heavenly generosity.

Of these drops it is said to rebellious Judea: “Therefore the drops of rain were withheld, and the latter rain did not come” (Jer. 3:3). Paul sprinkled dew when he said to the Corinthians: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2:2). Again he poured forth rain when he said: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged” (2 Cor. 6:11).

Hence Moses says: “Let my speech be awaited like rain, and let my words descend like dew” (Deut. 32:2).

It follows:

### VERSE 29

“From whose womb did the ice come forth, and who begot the frost from heaven?”

What else do we understand in frost or ice but the hearts of the Jews, cold and bound by the torpor of unbelief? Once, through the reception of the Law, through mysteries, sacrifices, and prophecy, they were held within the bosom of grace, as within the womb of the Creator. But when the Lord came, they were bound by the cold of unbelief and lost the warmth of faith and charity. Cast out from the secret bosom of grace, they came forth like ice from the Creator’s womb.

By heaven, however, the exalted life of the saints is understood. To this heaven it is said: “Attend, O heaven, and I will speak” (Isa. 1:2). Hence the Lord says: “Heaven is my throne” (ibid.). Of this throne it is written elsewhere: “The soul of the just is the seat of wisdom.” Since God is wisdom, the seat of God is heaven, and the soul of the just is the seat of wisdom. The soul of the just is therefore heaven.

Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were heaven. But because the priests who persecuted the Lord emerged from the offspring of those fathers, cold with the torpor of unbelief, it was as though frost came forth from heaven. Yet the Lord says that he himself begot this frost for us because, by a just judgment, he permitted the Jews—whom he had naturally created good—to depart from him cold on account of their wickedness. The Lord is the author of nature, not of guilt.

Alternatively: There is no obstacle to understanding Satan in frost and ice. He proceeded, as it were, from the true God like ice, because, cold from the torpor of malice, he came forth from the warmth of God’s secrets as a teacher of iniquity. He was begotten as frost from heaven because he was permitted to fall from the heights to the depths in order to constrict the hearts of the reprobate.

**MORALLY.** When almighty God forms human minds through fear, he conceives them, as it were; and when he advances them toward manifest virtues, he gives them birth. But if they become exalted through the virtues they have received, he abandons them. Ice proceeds, as it were, from God’s womb when those who had already grown warm within become cold through the gift of virtues and, therefore, sluggishly seek outward glory, when they ought to have burned more ardently with love for inward things.

The Lord now bears this ice in his womb because he tolerates it within the bosom of the holy Church; but through the final and public judgment he will reject it, saying: “I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Luke 13:27).

Heaven is understood as sacred discourse, which opens for us the day of understanding and illuminates us with the Sun of justice. While the night of the present life holds us, it shines for us through the stars of the commandments. But because “there must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Cor. 11:19), Holy Scripture sends out from itself as cold those who desire to become proud and pursue outward favor through it. While they shine through heavenly understanding in their utterances yet remain hardened, they themselves deceive others, fall as they come down to the depths, and are both frost and a source of constraint for others. He who previously stood tractable and fluid in the heights, in the knowledge of God, falls hardened into the depths.

Nevertheless, the Lord is said to beget this frost, not because he himself forms the minds of the wicked for guilt, but because he does not free them from guilt. As it is written: “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. 4:21).

This interpretation can also be understood in a good sense without difficulty. For if the earth is watered after seed has been scattered, it is irrigated; but if it receives too much, it changes the richness and strength of the grain. If, however, the rain is pressed down by frost, so that the seed is prevented from coming forth, it is forced to take root and multiply within.

What, then, does it mean that the Lord first presents himself as the father of rains, and afterward says that ice comes forth from his womb and declares that he begets frost from heaven, except that, in a marvelous way, the Lord first pours the rain of compunction through hidden grace into the earth of the heart, so that it may receive the seeds of the word; and afterward, lest it flow forth too excessively in the virtues it has conceived, he presses it down with the discipline of inward governance? Thus, when the rain of grace received irrigates, the rigor of discipline also constrains it, lest, if the conceived virtues should emerge either before they ought or more than necessary, they turn the grain into mere grass.

Let us see what Paul says when the earth has been watered: “To will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find” (Rom. 7:18). And again: “So that you do not do the things you wish” (Gal. 5:17).

Adversity in the present life can also be signified by frost or ice. While it compresses the saints beneath its harshness, it makes them stronger. For by a marvelous plan the Lord permits the elect, even in this life, to endure the winter of adverse winds and cold, so that afterward, like summer weather, they may display the fruits they conceived here. Hence, in the voice of the Bridegroom, it is said to every soul: “Rise, hasten, my beloved, my beautiful one, and come; for winter has passed, the rain has gone and departed” (Song 2:10–11).

It follows:

### VERSE 30. “The waters are hardened into the likeness of stone.”

By “waters” we understand the apostles; by “stone,” however, because of its hardness, the pagan peoples are sometimes designated. For they worshiped stones, and concerning them it was said: “Let those who make them become like them” (Psalm 113:8). Since, therefore, Judea first believed in God, while all the pagan world remained in the obstinacy of its unbelief, but afterward the hearts of the pagans were softened for faith and the unbelief of the Jews was hardened, it is said: “The waters are hardened in the likeness of stone.”

Hence Paul says to the Gentiles: “Just as you once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy because of their unbelief, so they too have now disbelieved in your mercy, in order that they themselves also may obtain mercy. For God has enclosed all things under unbelief, so that he may have mercy upon all” (Romans 11:30–32).

Alternatively: by “water” the peoples are designated, and by “stone” the hardness of Satan himself. When, therefore, he descended to the depths, the waters were hardened in the likeness of stone, because human beings, imitating his wickedness, lost the tender inward parts of charity.

**Morally.** Waters become hard on the surface through ice, but remain fluid in their depths. What else, then, do we understand by waters except the unstable hearts of the reprobate? Although they abandon the intention of virtue, they perhaps display themselves in good works through hypocrisy; while inwardly they flow downward into vices, they perhaps pretend to be imitators of the saints. Thus the waters are hardened in the likeness of stone.

Alternatively: because fluctuating thoughts inwardly trouble the mind, yet do not draw it all the way to consent to an evil deed, the mind, as though beneath a certain hardness, conceals whatever within it becomes softened under the assault of temptation. Minds that have been fluid through prosperity become hardened when constrained by adversity; and water is brought into the likeness of stone when a weak person, through the endurance received from above, imitates the sufferings of his Redeemer.

The one who said, “I complete in my flesh what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ” (Colossians 1:24), had indeed been hardened in the likeness of stone.

It follows: “And the surface of the abyss is congealed.”

Because, beneath a kind of roof—the covering of your ignorance—the incomprehensibility of divine judgment cannot at all be penetrated by the eye of the human mind. For it is written: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Psalm 35:7).

Alternatively: one thing belonging to Satan lies hidden inwardly, while another is displayed outwardly. For “he transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Corinthians 11:14): while the appearance of his persuasion, as though solid ice above, is displayed as something apparently good, his wickedness, lying hidden in the depths, is not seen.

**Morally.** The surface of the abyss is congealed because the fluid and unstable conscience of such people is covered from human beings by an overlaid appearance of holiness. For although inwardly they are disgraceful to themselves, before the eyes of others they are clothed with a certain beauty of conduct.

Alternatively: because an evil thought, even if it reaches the stage of suggestion, does not leap as far as consent, since the rigor of holy liberation laid over it restrains the mind’s fluctuating movements. Joy commonly opens the hidden places of the mind and, by opening them, causes their loss; adversity, however, when it presses us outwardly, makes us more cautious inwardly. Therefore, after frost or ice, the surface of the abyss is congealed, because our mind is fortified by those very adversities for the preservation of the deep gifts it has received.

Isaiah covered this abyss when he said: “My secret is for me” (Isaiah 24:16). And Paul: “I refrain, lest anyone should think of me above what he sees and hears from me” (2 Corinthians 12:6).

It follows:

### VERSE 31. “Will you perhaps join together the shining stars of the Pleiades, or will you be able to disperse the circuit of Arcturus?”

The stars called the Pleiades derive their name *apo tou pleistou* [ἀπὸ τοῦ πλείστου], that is, “from multitude.” They were created so close to one another and yet so separate that they are together and nevertheless cannot be joined.

Arcturus, however, illumines the nighttime hours in such a way that, placed upon the axis of heaven, it turns through different positions and yet does not set.

What else do the shining Pleiades, which are also seven in number, signify except all the saints, who amid the darkness of the present life illumine us with the light of the sevenfold grace of the Spirit? Since they were sent to prophesy at different times from the very beginning of the world to its end, they are joined to one another in one respect and not joined in another. They are joined by the intention of the mind and separated by the division of the image that appeared at different times in Abel, Isaiah, and John. They were divided in time, but not in proclamation, since they are united both by the confession of their voice and by the unanimity of their virtues.

In Arcturus, however, which by its circuit illumines the nighttime spaces without falling, not the life of the saints produced piecemeal but the whole Church at once is designated. She suffers weariness, indeed, but does not, struck down to the point of exhaustion, bend beneath it. For while the holy Church is shaken by innumerable tribulations, the shadow of the present life is brought to an end; and while she stands, night passes away, because, while she endures in her wholeness, the life of this mortality runs its course.

Alternatively: Arcturus revolves among seven stars, at one time raising three to the heights and lowering four to the depths, and at another raising four above and pressing three below. So also the holy Church, sometimes preaching knowledge of the Trinity to unbelievers and sometimes the four virtues—prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance—to believers, as though rotated by the art of preaching, changes in some way the appearance of her position.

For when she empties out confidence in one’s own labor and exalts faith in the Trinity, Arcturus raises three stars and inclines four. Hence Paul says: “If Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before God. For what does Scripture say? ‘Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness’” (Romans 4:2–3).

And when she forbids presumption based on faith left barren, but commands that what has been prescribed be carried out more earnestly, she lowers not four but three. Hence James says: “Just as the body without the spirit is dead, so also faith without works is dead” (James 2:26).

Arcturus therefore revolves because the holy Church, in accordance with the minds of her hearers, turns about in different aspects through the art of preaching. But the Lord will one day disperse this circuit of Arcturus, because he changes the Church’s labors into rest. Then he will also join the Pleiades more fully, since all the saints will certainly be joined to one another in the form of vision when, at the end of the world, the holy Church is released from the labors that she now endures.

Thus Arcturus, because it arises from the region of cold, can signify the Law; while the Pleiades, which rise in the east, can signify the grace of the New Testament. The Law came, as it were, from the north, and afflicted its subjects with such severe rigidity. For when it commanded some to be stoned to death for their offenses and others to be punished by the sword, it pressed the seeds of its commandments with a torporing blow—as though removed from the sun of charity—and nourished them more by cold than by heat.

Hence Peter says: “Why are you testing God by placing upon the neck of the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?” (Acts 15:10).

The seven stars, certainly, express the Old Testament, as though the seventh day were held in honor of the Law and the vows of sacrifice established for the whole week extended through it. The Pleiades, however, which are seven, designate the grace of the New Testament; through it he illumines his faithful at the threshold of the sevenfold gift.

Since, therefore, Arcturus turns itself, it displays the Pleiades, because throughout everything that the Old Testament speaks, the works of the New Testament are announced. Our Redeemer, coming in the flesh, joined the Pleiades, because he possessed the operations of the sevenfold Spirit both together and abiding in himself.

Concerning him Isaiah says: “A shoot will go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower will ascend from his root, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord will rest upon him” (Isaiah 11:1). Concerning him Zechariah says: “Upon one stone there are seven eyes” (Zechariah 3:9).

By joining the Pleiades, he disperses the circuit of Arcturus, because, when he made known that the operations of the Holy Spirit were joined together in himself, made man, he released the labor imposed by the letter of the Old Testament, so that each believer might now understand with the freedom of the spirit what he had previously served in fear amid so many dangers.

It follows:

### VERSE 32. “Will you bring forth Lucifer at his appointed time?”

The Father brought forth Lucifer at his appointed time, because, as it is written: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law, to redeem those who were under the Law” (Galatians 4:4–5).

Born of a virgin, he appeared like Lucifer in the darkness of our night, because, having driven away the darkness of sin, he announced to us the eternal morning. He made himself known as Lucifer because he rose from death at dawn; and by the splendor of his light he expressed the earth of our mortality as darkness.

Hence John says: “The bright and morning star” (Revelation 21:16).

It follows: “And do you cause the evening to rise over the children of the earth?”

The Lord causes the evening to rise because, in accordance with their deserts, he permits Antichrist to rule over the unbelieving hearts of the Jews. Since they sought earthly things and not heavenly things, they willingly chose to be children of the earth and were blinded so as not to receive the brightness of our Lucifer.

Hence the Lord says: “I have come in the name of my Father, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and him you will receive” (John 5:43).

**Morally.** Lucifer rises for the elect, while, by God’s permission, evening rules over the reprobate. There is one and the same word of God in the mouth of the preacher. When some hear it with joy and others with envy, they turn the brightness of Lucifer into the darkness of evening for themselves.

Hence Paul says: “We are the good aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to the former an aroma of death unto death, to the latter an aroma of life unto life” (2 Corinthians 2:15–16).

It follows:
