### VERSE 33. “Do you perhaps know the order of heaven, and do you set out its reasoning upon the earth?”

To know the order of heaven is to see the hidden predestinations of heavenly arrangements. To set out its reasoning upon the earth is to disclose before human hearts the causes of such secrets—to investigate the mysteries of heavenly judgments either by reflection or by speech and to make them manifest. No one can do this in the present life.

Who can understand why one person lives while plotting against his neighbors, whereas another dies who would have been useful to the lives of many? No one has ascended to know these inner recesses of hidden judgments.

## BOOK THIRTY

### VERSE 34. “Will you raise your voice in the cloud, and will the force of the waters cover you?”

The Lord raises his voice in the cloud when he shapes the tongues of his preachers by exhortation for the clouded hearts of unbelievers; and the force of the waters covers him when the crowd of those who resist presses upon his members who act well.

Hence it is written:

“The word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, saying: ‘Concerning all the cities of Judah, from which they come to worship in the house of the Lord, you shall speak all the words that I have commanded you to speak to them; do not omit a word. Perhaps they will listen, and each will turn from his evil way, and I will relent of the evil that I am thinking of doing to them because of the wickedness of their practices.

“And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: If you will not listen to me, so as to walk in my Law, which I have given you, and to listen to the words of my servants the prophets, whom I have sent to you, rising by night and sending them, and you have not listened, I will make this house like Shiloh, and I will give this city as a curse to all the nations of the earth.’

“And the priests and the prophets and all the people heard Jeremiah speaking these words in the house of the Lord. And when Jeremiah had finished speaking everything that the Lord had commanded him to speak to all the people, the priests and the prophets and all the people seized him, saying: ‘He shall surely die. Why has he prophesied in the name of the Lord?’” (Jeremiah 26:2, 9).

The Lord also raised his voice in the cloud through himself when, while presenting himself as present even in the body he had assumed, he sounded forth his truth to unbelievers who would not follow him, speaking as through a cloud: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and: “Before Abraham came to be, I am” (John 8:58).

But the force of the waters immediately covered him, because the crowd of the peoples soon rose up in fury against him. For it is written: “Therefore the Jews were seeking to kill him, because he not only was breaking the Sabbath, but was also calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (John 5:18).

Concerning this force of the waters the Prophet cries out: “They surrounded me like water all day long” (Psalm 87:18); and: “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even to my soul” (Psalm 68:2).

**Morally.** Although we are faithful, when we are weighed down by certain unnecessary cares, we grow dim beneath the confusion that covers us. And when the Lord suggests to us, even in such a state, certain remarkable things to be understood about him, he raises his voice as though in a cloud: he speaks of himself to our clouded minds, and, as though in a cloud, he is heard though not seen.

For when he instills subtle truths about himself into our blind minds, he raises his voice in a cloud. But when our understanding of God is itself oppressed by the temptation of vices, God is, as it were, covered by the force of the waters in his voice. We admit as many waters over him as we turn illicit thoughts over in our hearts after the inspiration of his grace.

It follows:

### VERSE 35. “Will you send forth lightning bolts, and will they go, and, returning, say to you, ‘Here we are’?”

Lightning bolts come forth from clouds, just as wondrous works are displayed through holy preachers. They are commonly called clouds because they both flash with miracles and rain through their words.

Hence it is written: “You will multiply lightning bolts and trouble them” (Psalm 17:15).

The lightning bolts go forth when preachers flash with miracles and pierce hearts that turn back to things above. They return when they attribute to God’s power, not to themselves, whatever they recognize that they have accomplished with strength.

For what is it for them to say to God, “Here we are,” except to give praise to the grace from which they know that they received victory in the struggle?

The lightning was going forth when Peter said: “I have neither silver nor gold, but what I have I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise and walk” (Acts 3:6).

The lightning returned when he said: “Why do you marvel at this, or why do you look at us as though by our own power or piety we had made him walk?” and what follows (Acts 3:12).

Alternatively: the lightning bolts—that is, holy men—are sent and go forth when they leave the secrecy of contemplation for the public work of action, when they spread from the hiddenness of intimate contemplation into the breadth of active life. But they return because, after the external works they perform, they always hurry back to the bosom of contemplation, so that there they may renew the flame of their ardor and, as though from contact with heavenly brightness, may become inflamed.

Hence Solomon says: “To the place from which the rivers go, they return, so that they may flow again” (Ecclesiastes 1:7). They are called rivers because they water the hearts of their hearers; but because they approach, they are remembered as lightning bolts.

Hence it is said: “His lightning bolts have shone upon the world” (Psalm 96:4). Elsewhere: “The rivers have raised themselves, O Lord; the rivers have raised their voices” (Psalm 88:26).

To say “Here we are” is to show themselves present through love.

It follows:

### VERSE 36. “Who placed wisdom in the inward parts of a human being, or who gave understanding to the rooster?”

Under the name “rooster,” holy preachers are designated. Amid the darkness of the present life, they strive to announce by preaching the light that is to come, as though proclaiming it by crowing.

For they say: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near” (Romans 13:11); and: “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep” (ibid., 13:12).

Elsewhere it is said of this rooster: “There are three things that walk well, and a fourth that proceeds happily: the lion, strongest among beasts, will fear no encounter; the rooster with girded loins; and the ram—and there is no king who can resist him” (Proverbs 30:29–31).

There the lion is understood as Christ, the rooster designates preachers, and the ram designates the leaders of the churches. The fourth that proceeds happily is Antichrist, possessing all things prosperously.

It should be noted that wisdom inspired by God is placed in the inward parts of a human being, because it is given to the elect not only in their words but also in their understanding, and their conscience speaks in accordance with what their tongue says.

Understanding is therefore given to the rooster because the teacher is divinely shown the virtue of discernment, so that he may know to whom, when, and how he should bring the truth. For one and the same exhortation is not suitable for everyone.

The rooster commonly gives longer and stronger crowing in the deeper hours of the night; as daylight approaches, it forms altogether shorter and more frequent calls. In this way preachers act toward minds that are still wicked: with great cries they announce the terrors of eternal judgment. But to minds that have been enlightened they preach not only those things that are terrifying because of punishment, but also those gentler things that belong to rewards.

In the manner of the rooster, holy preachers also first rouse themselves and thus make others vigilant. For they first strive to punish their own faults with tears, and then declare what must be punished in others.

It follows:

### VERSE 37. “Who has declared the order of the heavens, and who makes the harmony of heaven sleep?”

What else is understood by the order of the heavens except the heavenly power of hidden things? By the harmony of heaven, however, the harmonious speech of preachers is signified.

Therefore, when our Creator begins to declare the order of the heavens, he makes the harmony of heaven sleep, because, when he is already displayed to us by sight, the words of preachers are withdrawn.

Hence Jeremiah says: “No longer shall each person teach his neighbor, or a man his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord’; for all shall know me, from the least of them to the greatest, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 31:34).

Or certainly the order of the heavens is that life-giving power itself which forms the spirits of angels. For the Lord, just as he is the cause of causes and the life of the living, is also the order of rational creatures.

He therefore declares the order of the heavens when he manifests himself to us in clear vision. Hence he says in the Gospel: “The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in parables, but will announce the Father to you openly” (John 16:25).

**Morally.** The Lord declares the order of the heavens when, by presently suggesting heavenly secrets, he illumines the minds of his elect. But he makes the harmony of heaven sleep when, by a just judgment, he conceals from the hearts of the reprobate the harmonious hymns of the angels and those joys of the heavenly powers.

Although this harmony of heaven remains awake inwardly in itself, it nevertheless sleeps outwardly in the ignorance of the reprobate. Thus the order of the heavenly secret is declared, yet the harmony of heaven is permitted to sleep, because knowledge of the heavenly reward is opened to some through inspiration, while the sweetness of inward praise is hidden from others.

The harmony of heavenly praise had burst into the ear of the one who said: “I will enter into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God” (Psalm 41:5).

It follows:

### VERSE 38. “When dust was poured upon the earth, and clods were compacted together.”

In its customary manner, the divine word describes things still future as though they had already passed. For it is said of him: “Who made the things that are to be.”

Dust is therefore poured upon the earth when it is brought back into solid members; clods are compacted because firm bodies, gathered from dust, rise up.

**Morally.** What do we understand by dust except sinners, who, not solidified by any weight of reason, are carried away by the breath of every temptation? Concerning them it is written: “Not so the wicked, not so, but like dust,” and what follows (Psalm 1:4).

Dust was therefore poured upon the earth when sinners who had been called and brought into the Church were solidified by the reasoning of faith, so that afterward they might stand immovable against temptations.

In this earth the clods were compacted, because sinners who had been called and infused with the grace of the Holy Spirit were united in the gathering of charity. Hence it is written that “there was in them one heart and one soul” in the Lord (Acts 4:32).

We can also distinguish these clods in the Church according to the diversity of their merits. For while one is the order of preachers, another of hearers, another of the continent, another of virgins, and another of penitents, they are like different forms of clods distinguished from one earth, since within one faith and one charity different things are displayed.

It follows:

### VERSE 39. “Will you seize prey for the lioness, or will you fill the souls of her cubs?”

This is surely the lioness of whom Job had said: “The sons of the merchants have not trodden them, nor will the lioness pass through them” (Job 28:8).

The Lord therefore seizes prey for this lioness in order to fill the souls of her cubs, because he snatched countless people from the Gentiles for the increase of this Church and, through the gain of souls, satisfied the desires of the hungry apostles.

They are called cubs because of the tenderness of their merit and the weakness of their fear; when the Lord had suffered, they remained behind closed doors. Thus it is written of them: “When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were closed,” and what follows (John 20:19).

We know that these things were done by the holy apostles, and we know that they are now also done by upright teachers. They are fathers of succeeding peoples, yet sons of those who came before. Hence they are rightly called cubs.

Or certainly, although they are teachers of certain people, they glory in being disciples of the universal Church.

The Lord therefore seizes prey for the lioness because, by the power of his inspiration, he snatches the life of sinners from error; and he fills the souls of her cubs because, through the conduct of many people, he satisfies the pious desires of teachers.

It follows:

### VERSE 40. “When they lie in their dens and lie in wait in their caves.”

When the holy apostles still did not rise up against the members of the devil with the free voice of preaching, they lay in wait against their adversaries as though in dens.

With the doors closed, as though in certain added caves of their own, the cubs lie ready to seize the world, so that afterward they might presume to snatch away the prey of souls.

To that first cub, hungry but strengthened all the more by the Gentile world spread out through the sheet, prey was shown, as it were, and it was said: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13).

Alternatively: holy teachers, when they observe things that must be rebuked but nevertheless retain them in their thoughts through silence, lie hidden as though in caves. They conceal themselves as though in dens because they are hidden within their own hearts.

But when they find the proper time, they suddenly leap forth, conceal nothing that ought to be said, and seize the necks of the proud with the bite of a harsh rebuke. For not every time is suitable for teaching.

It follows:

### VERSE 41. “Who prepares food for the raven when its young cry out to the Lord?”

What else is designated by the young of the raven except the black Gentile world of sin?

Concerning it the Prophet says: “He gives their food to the beasts, and to the young of the ravens,” and what follows (Psalm 146:9).

This raven was food when it was seeking the Church herself; but now it receives food, because it itself seeks others for conversion. Its young—that is, the preachers brought forth from it—do not presume upon themselves but upon the powers of their Redeemer. Although they hunger with pious voices for souls, they know that they can accomplish nothing by their own power: “Neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:7).

It follows: “Wandering because they have no food.”

In this wandering nothing other than the desires of preachers burning with zeal is signified. As they strive to bring peoples into the bosom of the Church, kindled by great ardor, they send their longing now to us, now to others, in order to gather them.

The fervor of thought itself is, as it were, a kind of wandering. Thus Paul desires to pass from one place to another, because the charity that fills him urges him on.

While detained at Ephesus, he writes to the Corinthians: “Behold, this is the third time I am ready to come to you” (2 Corinthians 12:14). Again, while remaining at Ephesus, he speaks to the Galatians, saying: “I wish that I could now be with you and change my voice” (Galatians 4:20).

The black Jewish people may also be designated by the name “raven,” black because of the merit of unbelief. The young are certainly the holy apostles, born in the flesh from the people of Israel. While they poured out prayers to the Lord on behalf of their nation, as young ravens they fed through spiritual understanding the parent people from whom they had been born carnally.

Thus, while the young cry out, food is prepared for the raven, because, while the apostles pray, the people who had formerly been faithless are led to knowledge of the faith. Through the preaching of the sons, Judea, hearing, was spiritually nourished now by three thousand (Acts 2:41), now by five thousand (Acts 4:4).

But the wandering young, hungry, sought food for this raven, because, when Judea refused to believe, the apostles were scattered throughout every part of the world, saying to those who resisted: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

Then the raven found food, because, after the Gentiles had been converted, the Jewish people would at last abandon the foolishness of their unbelief. As it is written: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and so all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25–26).

**Morally.** The raven, it is said, does not fully provide food for its newly born young until they have grown feathers and become black.

The raven is indeed every learned preacher who brings back to mind the blackness of his sins. Disciples are born to him in faith; but perhaps, while they turn their memory away from past sins, they do not display the blackness of humility. To them, while they seek to learn lofty things, the discerning teacher does not supply the inner mysteries.

If, however, in confessing their former life they bring forth the laments of their groaning like blackening feathers, he immediately supplies nourishment for life to his hungry disciples by speaking.

But while the young cry out so that they may be saved, food is prepared for the raven, because, while good hearers hunger for the word of God, greater gifts of understanding are granted to teachers for their advancement.

It follows:

## CHAPTER 39

### VERSE 1. “Do you perhaps know the time when the wild goats give birth among the rocks, or have you watched the does in labor?”

The southern region calls ibices birds that inhabit the streams of the Nile. The eastern and western regions, however, call small four-footed animals ibices. It is their custom to give birth among rocks; when they fall by accident, they catch themselves unharmed upon their own horns.

The custom of stags is to destroy serpents and, when crossing rivers, to carry the weight of their heads in turn.

In the does or ibices the person of spiritual teachers is signified. They give birth among the rocks when, through the teaching of the Fathers—who were called “rock” because of their firmness—they bring souls forth for conversion. They themselves suffer no harm from any fall, because whatever temporal ruin comes upon them, they receive support from the two Testaments.

Concerning them it is said: “Horns are in his hands” (Habakkuk 3:4). Paul supported himself with these horns when he said: “Whatever was written was written for our instruction,” and so forth (Romans 15:4).

They are also called stags. Thus Jeremiah says: “The doe gave birth in the field and abandoned it” (Jeremiah 14:5).

Like stags, after their vices have been destroyed as though they were serpents, they live and burn more ardently for the fountain of life. Hence it is written: “As the deer longs for springs of water,” and so forth (Psalm 41:2).

While they cross the fleeting moments of this temporality like certain rivers, they bear their burdens for one another in compassion through charity, fulfilling what was said: “Bear one another’s burdens,” and so forth (Galatians 6:2).

Since, after the Lord’s coming, spiritual teachers were scattered throughout the world so that they might bring souls to birth in the faith through preaching, and since the time of the Lord’s incarnation was not known beforehand through the voices of the prophets, although that future incarnation itself was foreknown to all the elect, blessed Job is rightly questioned about the time of the ibices’ birth and of the does.

The teachers may indeed be understood by the designation “does,” and the hearers by the name “ibices.” The ibices give birth among the rocks because they are made fruitful for the performance of holy works through the examples of the Fathers who came before them.

When they hear lofty commandments and, conscious of their own weakness, despair of being able to fulfill them, they look upon the life of their elders and, considering their strength, bring forth the offspring of good works.

For example, when someone pressed by verbal insults is unable to preserve the virtue of patience, let him recall David’s deed.

To watch the does in labor is to weigh carefully the very labors of the Fathers who have begotten spiritual children. They examine themselves with cautious attention so that they may be strong in commandments, compassionate toward weaknesses, terrifying in threats, and gentle in exhortations.

They know that through the vigor of discipline they are fathers, but through the bowels of compassion they are mothers, because they endure the labors of holy conception and, by bringing forth the children of God, carry them within the womb of charity.

It follows:

### VERSE 2. “Have you counted the months of their conception?”

You are to understand: “As I have,” for I count in the holy preachers not only the fruit of their outward work but also their prolonged thoughts, because I preserve them for recompense.

When holy men think about the progress of their hearers, they carry them as though already conceived in the womb. But when they defer certain things that must be said and seek a suitable time for their exhortations, they are lengthened, as it were, through the extended course of the months, with the birth they desire already opened before them.

The months may also signify multiplied virtues, since days are accumulated in them. In the months, moreover, the moon is renewed; and nothing prevents the creature of new regeneration from being signified through the months.

Concerning this the apostle Paul says: “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but a new creation” (Galatians 6:15).

Therefore, when the saints prepare themselves to preach, they first renew themselves inwardly through virtues, so that in living they may agree with what they teach by speaking. They take the greatest care to place patience against anger and purity of heart against lust. Thus, in the presence of holy preaching, the months of virtues come to be—months that the Lord alone counts, since he alone, who gave those good things in their hearts, weighs them.

It follows: “And have you known the time of their birth?”

You are to understand: “As I have,” for, while I count the months of virtues in thought, I know when they can give birth to what they desire to fulfill.

It follows:

### VERSE 3. “They bend down for birth, and they open—or give birth—and emit cries.”

They low when, by bending down, they give birth to the souls of their hearers in a life of light, because they cannot remove us from eternal punishments except by weeping and grieving.

Hence Paul said: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19); and: “O foolish Galatians,” and so forth (Galatians 3:1).

It should also be noted that these does bend down in order to give birth, because they descend from the immensity of intimate contemplation to our weakness.

Hence Paul says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as little ones in Christ; I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians 3:1–2).

It follows:

### VERSE 4. “Their young are separated; they go out to pasture; they depart and do not return.”

Holy Scripture calls that pasture the nourishment of eternal verdure. Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord rules me,” and so forth (Psalm 22:1), and again: “But we are his people and the sheep of his pasture” (Psalm 99:3).

They therefore go out to pasture because, departing from their bodies, they find those inner pastures of verdure. And they do not return to them, because in that contemplation they have received, they no longer need at all to hear the words of those who say:

“No longer shall anyone teach his neighbor or his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ for all shall know me,” and so forth (Jeremiah 31:34).

And the Lord says: “I will announce the Father to you openly” (John 16:25).

It follows:

[Col. 0458A] **VERSE 5. “Who sent the wild ass free into the wilderness?”**—Supply: “except me?” By the wild ass is signified the life of those who dwell apart from the crowds of the populace. It is aptly called free, because the servitude of worldly affairs is great; the mind is grievously worn down by them, even though one willingly labors in them. Thus, if someone has once shaken the neck of his mind free from the domination of desires, he already enjoys a kind of liberty. From this heavy yoke of servitude the Lord calls him back, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. 11:28). The free wild ass is therefore released, because, with earthly desires trampled underfoot, he frees the mind’s serenity from the craving for temporal things.

**MYSTICALLY.** Nor should anyone consider it unfitting that the incarnate Lord can be represented by such an animal, since in Holy Scripture he is called both a worm and a scarab. Thus: “I am a worm” (Ps. 21:7). And: “The scarab cried out from the wood.” For he is likewise compared with a lamb and a serpent. Through all these images it can be said in a singular way that nothing essential can be believed concerning any of them. The wild ass, then, can signify the incarnate Lord, for the wild ass is an animal of the fields. And because the incarnate Lord benefited the Gentiles more than the Jews, he came as though not into a house but rather into a field. Hence it is written: “The appearance of the field is with me” (Ps. 9:11). And because the incarnate Lord became a partaker of our nature, though not of our sin, he is called one released as free, because he is not held under the dominion of sin. Of him it is said elsewhere: “Free among the dead” (Ps. 87:5). For “everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34). He was released as free because, taking our nature upon himself, he was in no way held by the yoke of iniquity.

It follows: **“And who loosens his bonds?”**—Supply: “except me?” Each person’s bonds are loosened when, by divine assistance, the inner restraints of carnal desires are torn apart. God therefore loosens the wild ass’s bonds when he breaks the knots of feeble thoughts from the soul of each of his elect and, in his mercy, scatters everything that was bound within the chosen mind.

**TYPICALLY.** The Lord’s bonds were loosened when the weaknesses of his Passion were changed into the glory of his resurrection. To hunger, thirst, be assaulted, seized, scourged, and crucified was the bond of our mortality. But when, death having been completed, the bolts of hell were opened, what else were being loosened except the bonds of our weakness? Concerning these bonds Peter says: “Whom God raised up, having loosed the pains of hell, since it was impossible for him to be held by it” (Acts 2:24).

It follows:

**VERSE 6. “To whom I gave the wilderness as a house.”**—At this point should we understand the wilderness of the body or the wilderness of the heart? But what is bodily solitude if solitude of heart is absent? Someone who lives apart bodily but inserts himself into the tumult of human society and the thoughts of earthly desires is not in solitude. If, however, someone is physically pressed by crowds of people but suffers no tumult of worldly cares in his heart, he is not in the city. He drives away from the eyes of his mind all the movements of frivolous thoughts that obtrude themselves unseasonably, like swarming flies, with the hand of seriousness; and he seeks within himself a kind of secret place with the Lord, where, once outward noise has ceased, he may speak silently with him through inward desires. Concerning this secret of the heart it is said elsewhere: “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (Rev. 8:1).

**ALLEGORICALLY.** The Gentiles are signified by the wilderness. While there was no patriarch among them to understand God, there was no one who used reason; indeed, there was scarcely a human being. Hence Isaiah says: “The deserted and impassable land shall rejoice, and the wilderness shall exult and shall blossom like a lily” (Isa. 35:1). And again it is said concerning the Church: “He will make its wilderness like delights, and its solitude like the garden of the Lord” (Isa. 51:3). The Lord therefore received a house in the wilderness because, after his death and resurrection, he deigned to call the Gentiles to the grace of faith.

It follows: **“And his tent in a land of saltiness.”**—Saltiness usually kindles thirst. Because holy men, so long as they dwell in the tents of this life, are inflamed by the daily heats of their desire for the heavenly homeland, they are said to have their tents in a land of saltiness, as it is written: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness,” etc. (Matt. 5:6).

**ALLEGORICALLY.** The land of saltiness is understood as the Gentiles. Before they knew the true wisdom of God, they produced saltiness, because, producing no greenness of good understanding, they savored what was perverse. Concerning them it is written: “He made a fruitful land into saltiness,” etc. (Ps. 106:34). Our Redeemer therefore received a tent in a land of saltiness, because, having become incarnate for human beings, he took possession of the hearts of the Gentiles, which had been abandoned by God. Concerning this it is written: “He turned the wilderness into pools of water, and the dry land into outlets of water” (ibid., 35).

It follows:

[Col. 0459C] **VERSE 7. “He despises the multitude of the city.”**—To despise the multitude of the city is to avoid the perverse pursuits of human society, so that one no longer desires to imitate the depraved ways of earthly people, who are numerous because of the abundance of iniquity. They desire to enter the narrow gate with the few, rather than enter with the many upon the pleasant roads that lead to destruction (Matt. 7:13). Hence, in the Song of Songs, the bridegroom’s voice says to the bride: “Unless you know yourself, O most beautiful among women, go out and depart after the footsteps of the flocks, and pasture your young goats” (Song 1:7).

**MORALLY.** “He despises the multitude of the city,” that is, he scorned the ways of human society. Although he became human among human beings, he did not wish to retain the customs of human beings. For he became human among us so that he might not only redeem us by the shedding of his blood but also transform us by the example he displayed. Thus, by coming into our society he found one way of life, and by living in it he taught another.

All those descended from proud Adam were astonished to see people seeking the prosperity of the present life, avoiding adversity, fleeing reproach, and pursuing glory. The incarnate Lord came among them desiring adversity, scorning prosperity, embracing reproach, and fleeing glory. For when the Jews wished to make him their king, he avoided becoming king; and when they plotted to kill him, he came willingly to the gallows of the cross.

Because, then, he adopted a new way of life among human beings and did not follow their customs, it is rightly written of him: “He despises the multitude of the city.” Or certainly, because he abandoned the many wandering along the broad way and chose the few walking along the narrow one. To despise the multitude of the city is to reject from the share of his kingdom that portion of the human race which enters by the broad way and is numerous because of the abundance of iniquity.

It follows: **“He does not hear the cry of the tax collector.”**—Who else can be understood as the tax collector except the devil? Once, in paradise, he gave the human being the coin of evil persuasion, and every day he seeks to demand from him the guilt of this debt. The speech of this tax collector is the beginning of evil suggestion.

It should also be known that the vice of gluttony tempts us in five ways. Sometimes it anticipates the time of need, as Jonathan anticipated the proper time for eating by tasting honey (1 Sam. 14:27). Sometimes it does not anticipate the time, but seeks more elaborate foods, as the people in the wilderness requested the kinds of meat they considered more luxurious (Num. 11:31–32). Sometimes it seeks to prepare whatever is to be eaten with excessive care, as the servant of Eli’s sons sought not the sacrificial meat cooked in the customary manner but raw meat, which he could prepare more carefully (1 Sam. 2:15). Sometimes, regardless of what is to be eaten, the mind exceeds the proper measure of refreshment in the quantity consumed, as in the saying: “The iniquity of Sodom was fullness of bread and abundance of water” (Ezek. 16:49). Sometimes the food is despised, but is consumed more greedily, as when Esau sold the glory of his birthright for lentils (Gen. 25:34).

The speech of this tax collector is therefore nature’s necessary demand; his cry, however, is the appetite of gluttony passing beyond the measure of necessity. This wild ass hears the tax collector’s speech but does not hear his cry, because a disciplined and continent man refreshes his stomach only to the extent necessary for moderation and restrains himself from pleasure. Hence it is written: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:14).

**MYSTICALLY.** The Lord did not fear the violent movements of this tax collector when he came, as he himself says: “The prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John 14:30). The tax collector of the human race came to him because he saw that he was human; but although he believed him to be a despised human being because of the weakness he saw in him, he perceived him to possess a power above humanity.

Laban represented this tax collector when, coming in fury, he searched for his idols among Jacob’s possessions (Gen. 31:34). Concerning this tax collector, when our Redeemer was freeing the Gentiles from his dominion, the prophet says: “For you have broken the yoke of his burden and the rod of his tax collector,” etc. (Isa. 9:4).

It follows:

**VERSE 8. “He surveys the mountains of pasture.”**—The mountains of pasture are the lofty contemplations of inward refreshment. For the more holy men abase themselves outwardly by despising themselves, the more abundantly they are inwardly nourished by the contemplation of revelations. Hence it is written: “He has arranged ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears” (Ps. 83:7).

Alternatively: The mountains of pasture are also the sublime virtues of the angels. They refresh us here by ministering and assisting us because there they grow rich from the dew of inward contemplation. Since, by God’s generosity, they protect us in every struggle, they are rightly said to be surveyed.

Alternatively: The mountains of pasture may be understood as the lofty sayings of Holy Scripture. Concerning them it is written: “The high mountains are for the deer” (Ps. 103:18). For those who have already learned to make leaps of contemplation ascend the lofty powers of divine sayings as though they were mountain peaks.

**MYSTICALLY.** By the mountains we understand the proud people of this age, who held the loftiness of earthly things in their hearts. But because the Lord also takes such people, converted in heart, into the inner being of his Church, changing them from their former pride and transforming them into his members, these mountains are his pastures. For he is nourished by the conversion of the wandering and by the humility of the proud, just as he instructed the apostles when they were sent to preach, saying: “Work not for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures unto eternal life” (John 6:27). As he himself says: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34).

Concerning these mountains it is written: “The Lord will not reject his people” (Ps. 93:14), and “For in his hand are all the ends of the earth, and the heights of the mountains belong to him” (Ps. 94:4). He converts the one whom he sees, as it is written: “The Lord turned and looked upon Peter” (Luke 22:61); and as Solomon says: “The king who sits upon the throne of judgment scatters all evil with his gaze” (Prov. 20:8).

It should be noted that he does not say “he looks upon,” but “he surveys.” For the Lord became incarnate in Judea, which was situated in the midst of the nations; therefore he surveys the mountains because he gathers from the whole Gentile world the broad, [proud] mountains of this age that are situated all around. He is nourished in these mountains because he is satisfied by the good works of those who are converted, as by verdant grasses. Hence it is written: “Where do you pasture, where do you lie down at noon?” (Song 1:6).

It follows: **“He searches out every green thing.”**—Green things are all those things which, having been created temporally, dry up with the summer sun of the present life when the end comes. Those things are called green, however, which do not wither through any temporality. Thus, for the wild ass to search out green things, despising transient matters, is for each holy person to desire what will remain forever.

**TYPICALLY.** The hearts of human beings are dry when, planted in the perishable things of this age, they possess no hope of eternity; but those are green which cling to that inheritance. Concerning it the apostle Peter says: “Into an incorruptible inheritance” (1 Pet. 1:4). Therefore, whoever fears drying up inwardly should flee the outward desires of this world, which are dry. Whoever desires to seek from the Lord the eternal homeland should grow green through the inward planting of the heart.

Let what has been expounded concerning the wild ass suffice for the twofold interpretation. It must be left to the judgment of the reader which interpretation he considers preferable.

**BOOK THIRTY-ONE**

[Col. 0461]

[Col. 0461C] **VERSE 9. “Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you?”**—Supply: “I, who endured for a long time their resistance to human preaching, yet suddenly, whenever I wished, overthrew them by miracles?”

The rhinoceros is entirely of an untamed nature, so that, if it is ever captured, it cannot be held in any way. For, as is said, being incapable of submission, it immediately dies. Its name, interpreted in Latin, means “having a horn in the nose.” And what else is signified by the nose except foolishness, and by the horn except pride? That foolishness is usually understood by the nose we learn from Solomon, who says: “A golden ring in a pig’s snout is a beautiful woman who is foolish” (Prov. 11:22). That pride is signified by the horn the prophet demonstrates, saying: “I said to the wicked, ‘Do not act wickedly,’ and to sinners, ‘Do not lift up your horn’” (Ps. 74:5).

What, then, is signified by this rhinoceros except the powerful people of this age? Or perhaps the powers of the principalities themselves, who, raised up by the foolish boasting of their type, are puffed up outwardly by false honors and are inwardly emptied by true miseries? To them it is rightly said: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Sir. 10:9).

But this rhinoceros lowered its horn, wearied by striking the Church through the martyrs, when God broke the powers of this world not by words but by miracles and made them subject to himself.

Alternatively: This rhinoceros, which is also called *monoceros* in Greek exemplars, is said to possess such strength that it cannot be captured by any skill of hunters. Some say that, when a virgin girl is presented to it, she opens her lap as it approaches; abandoning all its ferocity, it lays down its head in her lap, and thus is suddenly found powerless by those seeking to capture it. It is also described as the color of boxwood, and is said to drive its horn—an enormous horn which it alone bears—into an elephant’s belly, so that it easily brings the elephant down.

This unicorn can therefore signify that people who, from the law they received, took not works but only pride among all human beings, carrying one distinctive horn among the other beasts. Hence it is written: “Deliver me from the mouth of the lion and from the horns of unicorns” (Ps. 22:22).

It is as though blessed Job, who represents the blessed Church, were told: “Will you bring under the rule of your preaching that people whom you see, in the slaughter of the faithful, growing proud through its foolish arrogance?” Supply: “I, who see it exalting itself against me with a singular horn, yet immediately subject it to myself whenever I wish?”

Let Paul, then, be brought forward as an example. When, in ignorance, he exalted himself against God as though relying on the guardianship of the law, he carried a horn in his nose. Therefore, later inclining this horn of his nose through humility, he says: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I received mercy because I acted in ignorance” (1 Tim. 1:13).

The virgin opened her lap to the rhinoceros when the incorrupt wisdom of God disclosed to Saul from heaven the mystery of his Incarnation, saying: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). And the rhinoceros lost its strength because, thrown to the ground, it lost everything that had been swelling with pride.

It follows: **“Or would it remain at your manger?”**—In this passage the manger may appropriately be understood as Holy Scripture, in which holy animals are nourished by the food of the Word. Concerning them the prophet says: “Your animals shall dwell in it” (Ps. 68:11).

But all the proud, at the beginning of the emerging Church, were all the less willing to be enclosed in the preachers’ manger, the more they had been released into the field of their despair through their own pleasures. Concerning them Paul says: “Having become without hope, they handed themselves over to licentiousness for the working of every impurity, in greed” (Eph. 4:19).

Yet when he wished, the Lord suddenly bound them to his own manger. For we see that the powerful people of this age, its rulers, willingly hear the Lord’s pronouncements, read them steadfastly, and do not depart from the manger at all, because they do not transgress in living the commandments of God that they learn either by reading or by hearing. Rather, they tolerate remaining quietly enclosed by the food of the Word, so that by eating and remaining they may grow fat.

Alternatively: This same rhinoceros also remained at God’s manger, because he did not disdain to ruminate upon the words of the Gospel. For he says: “I went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus with me; I went up according to revelation, and I presented the Gospel to them” (Gal. 2:1–2). And because he had earlier heard, while still fasting: “It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts 9:5), afterward, pressed by the wondrous power of the one who ruled him, he gained strength from the food of the Word.

It follows:

[Col. 0463D] **VERSE 10. “Will you bind the rhinoceros to plow with your rope?”**—The ropes are the Church’s precepts of discipline. To plow is, through the zeal of preaching, to cut open the human breast with the plowshare of the tongue.

We know with what cruelty this earthly ruler—the rhinoceros—formerly raged; and now, through the Lord’s action, we see with how many ropes of discipline he is bound. He not only restrains himself from evil works but also exercises himself in preaching the holy faith. When we see such people fearing God in their actions, what else do we see but that they are bound by ropes? When they now cease not to preach, through the laws they have promulgated, the faith that they once attacked by persecuting it, what else are they doing except laboring at the work of the plow?

Alternatively: The aforementioned rhinoceros is bound by ropes because at one and the same time he is bound by blindness, preaching, and baptism, so that he not only does not attack human beings with the horn of cruelty but, raging for their refreshment, also draws the plow of preaching. For he says of evangelists, as of plowers: “The one who plows ought to plow in hope, and the one who threshes in hope of receiving fruits” (2 Cor. 9:10). Therefore, the one who had formerly inflicted torments upon the faithful and afterward willingly bore scourges for the faith surely labors well bound beneath the plow toward the harvest—the one who had lived wickedly free in the field, without fear.

It follows: **“Or will he break the clods of the valleys behind you?”**—Often the rulers of the earth, bound by the ropes of faith, are seized by anger for striking; they incline the summits of their kingdoms, like a horn, toward the advancement of the heavenly kingdom.

Alternatively: The Lord had already entered the minds of certain people who truly believed him to be the Redeemer of the human race. Yet, because they did not at all depart from their former observance but guarded the harsh commandments of the letter, the outstanding preacher said to them: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5:2). Therefore, when he crushed the harshness of the law in the humble mind of believers by censuring it, what else did he do than break clods in the valley behind the Lord? He did this so that the seeds of grain, which the furrow cut by the plow of faith had received in the heart, might not perish, pressed down by the observance of the letter.

It follows:

[Col. 0464C] **VERSE 11. “Will you trust in his strength?”**—As though it were said: “I?” The Lord declares that he trusts in the strength of the rhinoceros because he has inclined to the worship of his own veneration what he temporarily bestowed upon an earthly ruler. For the more power he possesses in the world, the more he prevails on behalf of the Author of the world. Since he himself is feared by his subjects, he persuades all the more easily because, with authority, he shows who is truly to be feared.

Alternatively: God trusted in the strength of this rhinoceros because the more cruelly he endured the one inflicting harsh things upon him, the more firmly he foresaw that he would endure adversity through himself.

It follows: **“And will you leave your labors to him?”**—The Lord left his labors to this rhinoceros because, once the earthly ruler had been converted, he entrusted to him the Church that he had purchased by his death. For he committed to his hand the great care with which the peace of faith must be maintained.

Alternatively: He also left to the rhinoceros the labors he himself had endured in the flesh, because he drew that convert even to the imitation of his own Passion. Hence it is said through this same rhinoceros: “I make up in my flesh what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ” (Col. 1:24).

It follows:

**VERSE 12. “Will you believe him that he will return seed to you and gather your threshing floor?”**—What else is understood by seed except the word of preaching? As the Lord says in the Gospel: “The one who sows went out to sow his seed” (Matt. 13:3). And as the prophet says: “Blessed are you who sow beside all waters” (Isa. 32:20).

What else should be understood by the threshing floor except the Church? Concerning it, again, the Forerunner says: “And he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor” (Matt. 3:12).

Who, then, at the beginning of the nascent Church, while that untamed earthly power raged against it with so many threats and tortures, would have believed that this rhinoceros would return seed to God—that is, repay by his works the word of preaching he had received? Who could then have believed that he would gather their threshing floor? For now he promulgates laws on behalf of the Church, though formerly he raged against it through various tortures. Whatever nations he has been able to seize, he leads by persuasion to the grace of faith; and to those whom he captures he points out eternal life, while preserving their present life.

Alternatively: Let us consider what Paul had been before the faith, and we shall certainly recognize that at that time none of the faithful had believed that God would bend the force of such great arrogance beneath the yoke of his fear. Hence Ananias, trembling, said: “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints in Jerusalem” (Acts 9:13). Yet, suddenly changed, he became a preacher instead of an enemy, and throughout all the regions of the world he made known the name of his Redeemer. He endured punishments for the truth; he called some by gentle persuasion and recalled others to the faith through terrors. He gathered God’s threshing floor to the extent that he had formerly winnowed it through arrogance.

Nor is it contrary to Paul that the rhinoceros is said to be the color of boxwood. For what is expressed by the color of boxwood except the pallor of abstinence? Paul himself testifies that he clung firmly to it, saying: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude,” etc. (1 Cor. 9:27). When he reproves the gluttony of others, he strikes the elephant in the belly with his horn. Thus: “For many walk, of whom I have often told you and now tell you even weeping, enemies of the cross, whose end is destruction, whose god is their belly,” etc. (Phil. 3:18). And again: “Such people do not serve Christ the Lord but their own belly” (Rom. 16:18).

Since, then, we have recognized these things written about Paul, it remains for us to believe that they were also accomplished in others.

It follows:

**VERSE 13. “The wing of the ostrich is like the wings of the heron and the hawk.”**—Who does not know how greatly the heron and the hawk surpass the other birds in the speed of their flight? The ostrich, however, has wings resembling theirs but does not possess the speed of their flight. It cannot rise from the earth, and it raises its wings, as though for flight, only in outward appearance.

The Almighty signifies hypocrites by this bird. While they imitate the life of the good, they possess the appearance of holy vision but not the reality of holy action. They extend wings under the appearance of sanctity, but, weighed down by the burden of worldly cares, they are in no way lifted from the earth. Concerning this burden the prophet says: “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Ps. 4:3). Of them the Lord says: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitewashed tombs, which appear beautiful outwardly to human beings, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead,” etc. (Matt. 23:27).

And because the bodies of the hawk and heron are small but supported by denser feathers, they fly across the sky with speed, since there is little in them that weighs them down and much that lifts them. The ostrich, by contrast, is covered with sparse feathers and burdened with an enormous body, so that, even if it wishes to fly, the very scarcity of its feathers cannot suspend such a great mass in the air.

The person of the elect is therefore rightly signified by the heron and the hawk, because, so long as they are in this life, they cannot exist without some contamination of even the slightest fault. But because there is little in them that weighs them down and much virtue of good action supports them, they are lifted toward heaven. Hypocrites, by contrast, even if they do a few things that lift them, commit many things that weigh them down.

This very wing of the ostrich has a color resembling the wings of the heron and the hawk, but it does not possess a resemblance of their virtue. What, then, do we see in these birds except that the solid virtues of the elect fly and press down the winds of human favor? The action of hypocrites, however upright it may appear, is not sufficient to fly, because the wind of human praise passes through the feather of their insubstantial virtue.

Alternatively: What is signified by the name ostrich except the synagogue? It had wings, but, crawling in its heart among lowly things, it never lifted itself from the earth. What, then, is expressed by the heron and the hawk except the ancient Fathers, who were able not only to perceive what they could understand but also to penetrate it by living accordingly? The ostrich’s wing is therefore like the heron’s and the hawk’s because the voice of the synagogue retained the teaching of the earlier ones in speech but did not know it in life. Hence Truth says to the people of that same synagogue: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon Moses’ seat. Therefore, whatever they tell you, observe and do,” etc. (Matt. 23:2).

It follows:

**VERSE 14. “She leaves her eggs upon the earth.”**—What else is expressed by eggs except tender offspring, which must be warmed for a long time so that they may develop into living birds? Eggs are insensible in themselves, but once warmed they are changed into living birds. Likewise, it is certain that little hearers and children remain cold and insensible unless they are warmed by the careful exhortation of their teacher. They must be warmed by the continual voice of teachers until they are able to live through understanding and fly through contemplation.

Hypocrites, however, although they always practice what is perverse, do not cease to speak what is right. By speaking well they beget children in faith or conduct, but they cannot nourish them by living well, because out of an inner love they submit themselves to external things. The more they exalt themselves in these things, the less they grieve over the defect of their offspring.

To leave eggs upon the earth is therefore to provide no example of heavenly life for one’s children.

Alternatively: In eggs there is one thing that is seen and another that is hoped for; hope cannot be seen, as Paul testifies when he says: “For what a person sees, why does he hope for?” (Rom. 8:24). What, then, are signified by the ostrich’s eggs except the apostles born from the flesh of the synagogue? Although they showed themselves despised and humble in the world, they taught hope for glory in heaven. Rejected and regarded as almost worthless by the proud, they lay upon the earth like eggs; yet within them lay that by which they would live, and, lifted up on the wings of hope, fly toward heavenly things.

The ostrich leaves these eggs upon the earth because the synagogue, scorning to hear the apostles whom it had begotten in the flesh, abandoned them to the Gentiles who were to be called.

It follows: **“Perhaps you warm them in the dust?”**—As though he said: “I do so, for I warm them in the dust.” That is, I set alight with the fire of my love the souls of the little ones, who are placed in the midst of sinners. For what is signified by dust except the sinner? Hence it is written: “Dust shall be the serpent’s bread” (Isa. 65:25).

Thus we see many people living in the midst of the crowds and yet not adopting the life of the sluggish populace; so that, if I may put it this way, they grow warm in the cold. They do not remain numb, lying among lowly things, but, changed into living birds, they raise themselves toward heavenly things through contemplation—that is, through flight.

Alternatively: The Lord warms these same eggs in the dust by wondrous power because he raised up living offspring of the apostles in the Gentiles, who had formerly been cast aside. Those whom the synagogue had despised as senseless and unvivified now fly alive, through the instruction of their teaching, in the veneration of the nations.

The ostrich left its eggs in the dust because the synagogue also failed to lift from earthly desires all those whom it had begotten to become preachers.

It follows:

**VERSE 15. “She forgets that a foot may crush them or a wild beast of the field may trample them.”**—What is signified by the field except this world? Concerning it the Lord says in the Gospel: “The field is the world” (Matt. 13:38). What is expressed by the wild beast except the ancient enemy, who lies in wait for the spoils of this world and is daily satiated by human death? Concerning him the Lord promises through the prophet: “The evil beast shall not pass through it” (Isa. 35:9).

Hypocrites, like the ostrich, abandon those whom they beget as children in their way of life, and take no care lest, deprived either of the diligence of exhortation or of the protection of discipline, they be perverted by examples of evil works. If they loved the eggs they produce, they would surely fear that someone might crush them by displaying perverse deeds.

Hence Paul was afraid when he said: “Beware of the evil workers” (Phil. 3:2); and again: “Many walk, of whom I often told you and now tell you even weeping, enemies of the cross of Christ” (ibid., 18). Paul also feared this wild beast of the field for the eggs he had laid, saying: “I fear that, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ Jesus” (2 Cor. 11:3). Hence Peter says: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour; resist him, strong in faith” (1 Pet. 5:9).

Alternatively: The foot crushes the eggs and the wild beast of the field tramples them when they are abandoned upon the earth. For human hearts, when they always desire to think about earthly things and always desire to do what is below, lay themselves down to be crushed by the wild beast of the field—that is, by the devil—so that, after they have long been cast down by lowly thoughts, they may eventually be broken by the commission of greater crimes.

The synagogue therefore neglected to lift the eggs it had begotten from the earth by living well. But the omnipotent God found many of its children dead and cold in earthly desires, and yet, by the warmth of his love, gave them life from the dead. The life that the synagogue had not given its children, it later attacked when it attempted to extinguish through persecution those whom it did not remember having nourished into good works.

It follows:

**VERSE 16. “She is harsh toward her children, as though they were not hers.”**—Hypocrites live with hardened hearts. They do not acknowledge even the children they beget with any tenderness of due love; and because they always seek their own interests, they do not soften toward their neighbor through any compassion of charity.

How tender were the inward parts of Paul, who said: “Now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord” (1 Thess. 3:8); and: “God is my witness, how I long for all of you in the inward parts of Christ Jesus” (Phil. 1:8). He also says to the Ephesians: “I ask that you not grow weary in my tribulations for you, which are your glory” (Eph. 3:13).

Alternatively: She regards as though they were not hers those whom she reproves for living otherwise than she taught them. As her cruelty hardens, she brings terrors upon them and exercises herself in their torments. Inflamed by the fires of envy, she labors to destroy those whom she did not labor to make capable of living. And when she persecutes the members of the Lord, she imagines that by this she is pleasing the Lord.

Hence Truth says to those same eggs of the ostrich: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God” (John 16:2).

It follows: **“She labored in vain, compelled by no fear.”**—For “they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Ps. 13:5). Behold, the divine voice commands: “If someone takes your tunic and wishes to contend with you in judgment, let him have your cloak also” (Matt. 5:40). The apostle says: “Why do you not rather accept injury? Why do you not rather suffer fraud?” (1 Cor. 6:7).

Yet the hypocrite, having assumed the habit of holy conduct, abandons the guardianship of his children. He seeks even through quarrels to defend every temporal possession; he does not fear, by his example, to destroy their hearts, and, as though through negligence, he fears losing earthly property.

A disciple falls into error, yet the hypocrite’s heart is not wounded by any grief. He sees those entrusted to him going into the abyss of iniquity and passes over it as though he had heard nothing. But if he senses that some slight temporal loss has been inflicted upon him, he suddenly burns inwardly with anger for revenge; patience immediately breaks, and the pain of the heart runs uncontrolled into words.

Alternatively: In that labor of persecution, it is not fear but cruelty that compels her to pant. But because vices are often dyed with the color of virtues and are therefore more wicked the less they are recognized as vices, the synagogue became harsher in persecution to the degree that it judged itself to be becoming more religious through the deaths of the faithful. For this reason it could not discern at all what it was doing: through pride it had closed off from itself the light of understanding.

It follows:

VERS. 17. “God deprived her of wisdom, nor gave her understanding.” — Although “to be deprived” is one thing and “not to give” another, he nevertheless repeats the point, adding “nor gave,” where he had already said “deprived”; as if he were saying: What I called deprivation was not an unjust taking away of wisdom, but a just refusal to give it. Hence the Lord is also described as having hardened Pharaoh’s heart (Exod. IV, 21). Alternatively: The scrutiny of hidden retribution is exact; and because she knowingly loses humility, she also unknowingly loses understanding of the truth. The wounds she inflicted on the faithful at the Redeemer’s coming are less grievous than those with which she still strives to wound the holy Church through the coming of Antichrist. It follows:

VERS. 18. “When the time comes, she lifts her wings on high. She mocks the horseman [Note: [Col. 0469D] The Vulgate reads “horse” (equum).] and his rider.” — What else should we understand by the wings of this ostrich except the thoughts of the hypocrite, which, although received at the present time, are nevertheless folded up? When he finds an opportunity, he reveals them proudly, as though lifting them on high. To lift one’s wings on high is to disclose one’s thoughts through pride. But now, because he pretends to be holy, because he restrains within himself what he thinks, he folds his wings within his body, as it were, through humility.

It should be noted that he does not say, “She mocks the horse and its rider,” but “the horseman and the rider.” The horse is the body of each person’s soul, which the soul knows how both to restrain from unlawful things and to release for good works. By the name “horseman,” therefore, he expresses the soul of a holy man. Hence it is written: “The armies that are in heaven followed him on white horses” (Rev. XIX, 14). The rider of the horseman, however, is the almighty Lord, who possesses the soul of each man, while possessing his members.

The hypocrite therefore mocks the horseman, because he despises the holiness of the elect. He mocks the rider of the horseman when he proceeds even to an insult against the Creator.

Alternatively: The ostrich lifts its wings on high when the Synagogue, no longer fearing its Creator as before, but openly resisting him, contradicts him. Passing into the members of the devil and believing the man of lies to be God, it exalts itself against the faithful as greatly as it boasts itself to be the body of God. Because it mocks not only the humility of the Lord but also his divinity itself, it mocks not only the horseman but also the rider of the horseman.

For the Word of God mounted the horseman when, by creating the human soul in himself, he subjected to divine worship that soul which presides over its own flesh. The divinity assumed flesh through the mediation of the soul, and by this held the whole horseman together: not only was the soul governed by him, but he also bound to himself the flesh that the soul governed.

Judah, therefore, captured by the snare of seduction through the coming of the proud Antichrist, despises the fact that our Redeemer was humble among men and mocks the horseman. Because it contradicts his divinity in every respect, it also mocks the rider. Yet the one and same Redeemer is both horseman and rider of the horseman. When he came into the world, he raised up strong preachers against the world; and when he endures the confidence of Antichrist at the world’s end, he himself supplies strength to those who contend.

VERS. 19. “Will you give strength to the horse, or surround his neck with neighing?” — By the name “horse,” every holy preacher is understood, as the prophet testifies when he says: “You sent your horses into the sea, stirring up many waters” (Hab. III, 15). “Neighing” expresses preaching. Every true preacher receives strength before, and neighing afterward: first he extinguishes vices within himself, and then he comes to the voice of preaching for the instruction of others. He has strength because he endures adversity steadfastly; he has neighing because he calls gently toward things above.

For the Lord gives his horse both the neighing of the voice together with strength of action, and strength of action together with the neighing of the voice. Neighing is placed around the horse’s neck because, lest he proceed to perverse works, the preacher’s life is bound by his own words. Hence it is said through Solomon: “You will receive a crown of graces upon your head and a golden necklace around your neck” (Prov. I, 9).

MORALLY. To every soul over which God mercifully presides, he first grants the strength of faith. Concerning this Peter says: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls about seeking someone to devour; resist him, strong in faith” (I Pet. V, 8). Neighing is joined to this strength when what is written is fulfilled: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X, 10). It follows:

VERS. 20. “Will you raise him up like locusts?” — The implied meaning is: “as I do,” for I raise him up by lifting him toward higher things, and I permit him to be tormented by the more grievous heat of persecution.

The name “locusts” sometimes signifies the people of the Jews, as in the passage concerning John: “He ate locusts and wild honey” (Mark I, 6). Sometimes it signifies the converted Gentiles, as in: “The almond tree shall flourish” (Eccl. XII, 5), that is, the primitive Church shall flourish with the flower of virtues. “The locust shall be fattened” (ibid.), that is, the dry Gentile world shall be fattened with the richness of the earth; “and the caper shall be scattered” (ibid.), that is, Judah.

Sometimes it signifies the tongue of flatterers, as in: “The burning wind lifted up the locusts, which went up over the whole land of Egypt” (Exod. X, 13–14). Sometimes, by comparison, it signifies the Lord’s resurrection or the life of preachers, as in: “I was shaken like a locust” (Ps. CVIII, 23).

The perfection of preachers is rightly expressed by locusts. Whenever they try to rise, they fix their legs and lift their wings: by acting rightly they establish themselves, and by contemplating higher things they are raised up. Then, after their leap, they catch themselves again with their feet, when, after contemplating sublime realities, they return to active life.

Or, just as locusts scarcely lift themselves from the earth in the morning hours, but, when the heat has blazed up, fly both higher and more eagerly, so every holy preacher, when he sees times of quiet faith, is regarded as humble and despised; but if the heat of persecution grows intense, he immediately shows how great is his elevation, clinging in his heart to heavenly things.

MORALLY. Everyone who follows God is raised up at the very beginning like a locust. Although in some actions he clings to the earth with bent knees, after the manner of locusts, in others he suspends himself in the air with outspread wings. For among converts, beginnings in good conduct are mixed with evil, while a new life is already being enacted in intention, yet the old life is still retained through habit.

It follows: “The glory of his nostrils is terror.” — In sacred Scripture, the word “nostrils” sometimes signifies the stupidity of the nostrils, as in: “A golden ring in a pig’s snout” (Prov. XI, 22). Sometimes it signifies the instigation of the ancient enemy, as in: “Smoke proceeds from his nostrils” (Job XLI, 11). Sometimes it designates foreknowledge, as in the prophet: “Cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, for he is accounted exalted” (Isa. II, 22).

In this passage, however, by the name “nostrils,” the foreknowledge and expectation of the holy preacher are signified. For when he is shown that the final judgment will come and that the heavenly homeland will be granted to the righteous, he desires its rewards, as though drawing through his nostrils the breath of future things. But the glory of his nostrils is terror, because the vision of the strict Judge, which the righteous eagerly awaits, the unrighteous fears will come.

Hence Paul says: “I am already being poured out, and the time of my dissolution is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. As for the rest, there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the just Judge, will give me on that day—not only to me, but also to those who love his coming” (II Tim. IV, 6–8).

MORALLY. Since an unseen thing is perceived by its odor, the thoughts of our hope are appropriately expressed by the name “nostrils.” Through them we foresee by hope the judgment that is to come, although we do not yet see it with our eyes. Everyone who begins to live well rejoices when he hears that the righteous will be called to the kingdom at the final judgment. But because he considers that certain evils still remain in him, he fears that the very judgment whose coming he begins to celebrate may approach. He sees that his life is mixed with good and evil, and at times his thoughts are confused by hope and fear. It follows:

VERS. 21. “His hoof digs the earth.” — What is signified by the hoof except the perfection of the holy preacher’s virtues? The hoof digs the earth when, by the example of his works, he draws earthly thoughts from the hearts of his hearers and empties their hearts of worldly cares, while he himself shows by his deeds that the world is to be despised. Hence Paul says to his disciples: “Think on these things, which you have both learned, received, and heard from me, and the God of peace will be with you” (Phil. IV, 8–9); and again: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (Phil. III, 17).

Alternatively: This horse digs the earth with his hoof when every preacher, by a vigorous examination, stirs up earthly thoughts within himself and does not cease to empty himself of them through tears. Hence it is said to Ezekiel: “Son of man, dig through the wall” (Ezek. VIII, 8). Likewise the Lord says to Isaiah: “Enter into the rock; hide yourself in a pit in the earth, from the face of the fear of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty” (Isa. II, 10); that is, penetrate the hardness of your heart, and hide earthly thoughts in the humility of your mind from the anger of the strict Judge.

MORALLY. To dig the earth with the hoof is to tame the flesh by strict abstinence.

It follows: “He exults boldly.” — He exults boldly because he is not broken by adversity, nor lifted up by prosperity. Adversity does not cast down the one whom no prosperity corrupts. Therefore, lest he be crushed by adversity, he has the force of strength; lest he be lifted up by prosperity, he has the weight of the One who sits above him. In adversity he rejoices because he is glad that the merit of his virtue is increased.

Hence it is said of the apostles: “They went forth rejoicing from the presence of the council,” and so forth (Acts V, 41). Heretics commonly shelter themselves against the preaching of faith behind the defenses of worldly powers, as though behind weapons. But this horse does not fear the anger of worldly powers, because through an ecstasy of mind he tramples even the desire for the present life.

Hence it is said through Solomon: “The righteous is confident as a lion and will be without terror” (Prov. VI, 28).

MORALLY. Whoever bravely restrains what attacks him exults boldly in what he desires in eternal peace. Hence it is said through Solomon: “Diligently cultivate your field, so that afterward you may build your house” (Prov. XXIV, 27).

It follows: “He advances to meet the armed.” — We are often left tranquil and shaken alike if, for the sake of justice, we do not take care to oppose the wicked. But if the soul has been inflamed with desire for eternal life, then, insofar as the occasion permits, we ought voluntarily to offer ourselves for the defense of justice, as is written concerning Paul: “They were filled with anger and cried out, saying: Great is Diana of the Ephesians” (Acts XIX, 28); and shortly afterward: “When Paul wished to enter among the people, the disciples would not permit him” (ibid., 30).

For when they strike the justice that we love in others, they also pierce us by that same blow, even if they appear to revere it.

MORALLY. The armed enemies are unclean spirits, equipped with countless deceits against us. When they cannot persuade us to do wrong, they set wrong before our eyes under the appearance of virtues. Therefore, to advance over dug-up earth to meet armed enemies is, after conquering carnal wickedness, to undertake battle against spiritual vices.

For whoever still fights feebly with himself raises in vain against himself the wars that are positioned outside him. Or certainly, we advance to meet armed enemies when, through diligent exhortation, we forestall their snares even in another person’s heart; when, while setting aside our own concerns in an orderly way, we prevent the approach of unclean spirits to the mind of our neighbor.

It follows:

VERS. 22. “He despises fear and does not yield to the sword.” — Let us see how he despises fear, since he says: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or famine, or persecution?” (Rom. VIII, 35.) Against this horse, therefore, there are as many swords of the enemies as there are kinds of persecution.

But the holy man, because he does not fear the adversities that are to come, despises fear; and because he is not overcome when persecution arrives, he does not yield to swords.

MORALLY. He despises fear because he is not so terrified by dread of any temptation that he becomes silent; and he does not yield to the sword because, even if a violent temptation strikes him, it nevertheless does not drive him away from care for his neighbor.

Paul says what swords he receives from the enemy and shows how he does not yield to those same swords: “I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind,” and so forth (Rom. VII, 23). To the others he says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire” (Col. III, 5).

It follows:

VERS. 23. “The quiver will resound over him.” — In sacred Scripture, the name “quiver” sometimes signifies God’s hidden purpose, as in: “He opened his quiver and afflicted me” (Job XXX, 11). Sometimes it signifies the secret plotting of the wicked, as in: “They prepared their arrows in the quiver” (Ps. X, 3).

Since, therefore, the horse of God is terrified by no adversity, he is opposed all the more, so that those who approach him uselessly in open conflict may strike him from a distance through an ambush of plotting. This quiver resounded over the horse of God when forty men conspired to kill Paul (Acts XXIII, 13). The quiver therefore resounded because the cause of a hidden plot reached Paul.

It follows: “The spear and shield flashed.” — Against the horse of God, the quiver resounds because the counsels and threats of the wicked make a din. The spear flashes because open punishment seeks his death; but the shield is raised because resistance is offered to him in argument.

Holy preachers have arrows with which they strike the hearts of their hearers. Concerning these Paul said: “I suffer even to chains as an evildoer, but the word of God is not bound” (II Tim. II, 9). Against these arrows, persecutors fortify the hearts of their hearers with the shield of their disputation.

MORALLY. The cunning enemy attacks the horse of God with arrows through ambush when he conceals vice beneath the appearance of virtue. He wounds with a spear at close quarters when manifest wickedness tempts even one who knows it.

Often some, neglecting the guardianship of their life, plunge into the uncleanness of lust. Others, while fleeing the uncleanness of lust, fall through the summit of chastity into the chasm of self-exaltation. The spear is guilt arising from vice; the arrow is guilt arising from virtue. But every perfect person is protected from both.

Hence Solomon says: “The Lord will be at your side and will guard your foot, lest you be caught” (Prov. III, 26). The deceitful enemy also opposes a shield to him, so that, if he cannot pierce the breast of the one who resists by striking it, he may at least block the progress of the one advancing by certain objections.

It follows:

VERS. 24. “Boiling and roaring, he swallows the earth and does not regard the sound of the trumpet.” — To the first man, when he sinned, it was said: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III, 19). Because, therefore, the horse, inflamed by zeal for the Holy Spirit or placed amid punishments, does not cease to draw sinners of every kind to himself, he undoubtedly swallows the earth while boiling.

Trumpets sound when the powers of this world terrifyingly prohibit the saints from speaking. Since preachers do not fear the threats of persecution, they do not regard the sound of the trumpet.

This trumpet sounded from the chief priests when they prohibited the apostles, after they had been scourged, from speaking about God, as it is written: “They warned them not to speak in the name of Jesus” (Acts V, 40). But let us see how the trumpet’s sound does not terrify the horse of God. Peter says: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts V, 29). And again: “We cannot but speak the things we have seen and heard” (Acts IV, 20).

MORALLY. The sound of the trumpet rings out against the horse when, near the elect person’s mind, some fault is placed that terrifyingly tempts him in the very thing he is doing with strength. But he swallows the earth while boiling and roaring because, by excessive fervor, he examines himself and consumes whatever earthly thing he finds in himself by advancing in virtue. He does not regard the sound of the trumpet because, by considering the strong, he carefully avoids the vice that might arise from the glory of virtue.

It follows:

[Col. 0474B] VERS. 25. “When he hears the trumpet, he says: ‘Ha!’” — The horse, therefore, says “Ha!” when he hears the trumpet, because every strong preacher, when he desires the contest of suffering to draw near, exults in the exercise of virtue. He is not terrified by the danger of battle because he rejoices in the triumph of victory.
