Let us see how Paul loves what he flees and flees what he loves. For he says: “Having a desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. I, 23). Yet he also says: “We who are in this dwelling groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (II Cor. V, 4).

MORALLY. His own prosperity has laid many low, and prolonged peace has made many sluggish. The horse therefore says “Ha!” when he hears the trumpet, because the soldier of God, when he sees the force of temptation pressing upon him, considers the usefulness of the heavenly dispensation and, from the adversity itself, gains stronger confidence.

It follows: “He scents battle from afar.” — To scent battle from afar is to foresee in thought the adversities that are still far away, lest perhaps, arriving unexpectedly, they should prevail. He therefore overcomes every contest because, in his mind, he prepares for the contest before the contest begins.

Hence Paul says to his disciples: “Test yourselves, whether you are in the faith; examine yourselves” (II Cor. III, 5).

MORALLY. To scent battle from afar is to recognize, from preceding causes, what will follow in the battle against vices and, as by the breath of the nostrils, secretly indicate the wickednesses of thought that have been foreseen. Concerning this sense of smell he rightly says in praise of his Church: “Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon” (Song VII, 4).

It follows: “The exhortation of the leaders and the howling of the army.” — The leaders of the opposing side are the authors of error. Concerning them the Psalmist says: “Contempt was poured upon princes, and he caused them to wander in a pathless place and not in the way” (Ps. CVI, 40). Concerning them Truth itself says: “If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit” (Matt. XV, 14).

The army follows these leaders, namely, the crowd of the wicked, which serves their unjust commands. The leaders exhort because those who preside over unbelievers persuade, as though by exhortation, the evil things they command to the inexperienced. The army howls because the throngs of the reprobate, while panting only for rapacity against the life and conduct of the faithful, cry out as though in a howl.

But every preacher considers long beforehand either what their authors may command against the elect or how savagely the crowd subject to them may rage. Concerning these leaders Paul says: “By smooth speech and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent” (Rom. XVI, 18). He sensed these howlings when he said: “After my departure, fierce wolves will enter among you” (Acts XX, 29).

MORALLY. The vices that tempt us, which wage an invisible battle against us while pride reigns over them, advance in some cases like leaders and follow in others like an army.

For pride itself, the queen of vices, as soon as it has seized a conquered heart, immediately hands it over to the seven principal vices, as to certain leaders of its own, to be devastated by them. For “pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. X, 15). From it arise vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony, and lust. Yet each of these has its own army against us.

From vainglory arise disobedience, boasting, hypocrisy, quarrels, obstinacy, discord, and presumptuous innovations.

From envy arise hatred, whispering, detraction, rejoicing in a neighbor’s adversity, and distress at his prosperity.

From anger proceed quarrels, swelling of mind, insults, shouting, indignation, and blasphemies.

From sadness arise malice, resentment, faintheartedness, despair, sluggishness regarding the commandments, and mental vacancy concerning unlawful things.

From avarice arise betrayal, fraud, deceit, perjury, restlessness, violence, and hardness of heart against mercy.

From gluttony arise foolish merriment, buffoonery, uncleanness, excessive talk, and dullness of understanding.

From lust are generated blindness of mind, thoughtlessness, inconstancy, rashness, self-love, hatred of God, affection for the present world, horror, and despair of the future.

The leaders are rightly said to exhort and the army to howl, because the first vices present themselves to the deceived mind under a kind of reasoning, while the countless vices that follow, as they drag the mind into every madness, confuse it with something like a bestial cry.

Vainglory says: “You ought to seek greater things, so that, to the extent that you are powerful, you may surpass many and thereby also benefit more people.”

Envy says: “In what respect are you less than this person or that one? Therefore, neither your superiors nor even your equals ought to be above you.”

Anger says: “You cannot endure calmly what is done against you, because, unless you resist them with great exasperation, they will accumulate things against you without measure.”

Sadness says: “What do you have from which to rejoice, when you bear so many evils from your neighbors?”

Avarice says: “How is it a fault that you desire to possess certain things, since you do not seek to multiply them but fear to be in need?”

Gluttony cries: “God created all things clean for eating; and since he rejects what satisfies him with food, what else does he do than contradict the gift?”

Lust says: “Why do you not expand yourself in your pleasure? For if God had not wished human beings to mingle in the pleasure of intercourse, he would not have made male and female at the beginning of the human race” (Gen. I, 27).

But the soldier of God, because he strives diligently to foresee the battles of vices, scents battle from afar: with attentive thought he considers what the evils that advance before them may persuade the mind to do. By the keen perception of his nostrils he detects the exhortation of the leaders; and because he foresees from afar the confusion of the iniquities that will follow, he recognizes, as though by scent, the howling of the army.

It follows:

VERS. 26. “Does the hawk grow feathered by your wisdom and spread his wings toward the south?” — This does not refer to the period when the hawk is clothed with feathers in the nest, but to the annual molt, when the old feathers are loosened and renewed.

Domestic birds seek protected and warm places. Wild birds, however, customarily spread their wings when the south wind blows, so that the warmth of the wind may heat their bodies and loosen the old feathers. When there is no wind, they spread themselves toward the sun’s rays and, being struck by them, create a warm breeze for themselves.

What, then, is signified by the hawk except that each of the saints, warmed by the breath of the Holy Spirit, casts off the habits of his former life and assumes the form of the new man? Paul urges this when he says: “Stripping off the old man with his deeds and putting on the new, who is created according to God” (Col. III, 9); and again: “Although our outward man is being corrupted, yet the inward man is renewed day by day” (II Cor. IV, 16).

To spread our wings toward the south is, through the coming of the Holy Spirit, to open our thoughts by confessing them, so that we may no longer wish to conceal ourselves by defending ourselves but to make ourselves known by accusing ourselves.

The hawk therefore grows feathered when he spreads his wings toward the south, because each person clothes himself with the feathers of virtues when he submits his thoughts to the Holy Spirit by confessing them. Whoever does not uncover the old things by confession produces none of the works of new life; whoever does not know how to mourn what burdens him cannot bring forth what lifts him up.

It follows:

VERS. 27. “Is the eagle raised at your command and does he place his nest in high places?” — In sacred Scripture, the word “eagle” sometimes designates the powers of the present world, as in Ezekiel: “A great eagle, with great wings, long limbs, full of feathers and variety, came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar and plucked off the topmost branches” (Ezek. XVII, 3–4).

The eagle is understood as Nebuchadnezzar: the greatness of his army signifies the great wings; the long duration of time, his long limbs; his many riches, his fullness of feathers; and the countless variety of earthly glory, his fullness of variety. Because, seeking the height of Judah, he removed the nobility of its kingdom, as though taking the marrow of the cedar, the image is especially apt.

At other times the word “eagle” expresses spirits lying in wait, as in Jeremiah: “Our persecutors were swifter than the eagles of heaven” (Lam. IV, 19). At other times it signifies the subtle understandings of the saints or the flight of the Lord’s ascension, as is read in Ezekiel concerning the four living creatures (chap. IV, 5) and likewise in Revelation (chap. IV, 6–7).

In this passage, however, by the name “eagle” the subtle understanding of the saints and their sublime contemplation are signified.

The eagle is therefore raised at God’s command when the life of the faithful, obeying divine commands, is suspended in heavenly things. He places his nest in high places when, despising earthly desires, he is already nourished by hope in heavenly things and does not build the dwelling of his mind in a low and degraded way of life.

Hence Paul says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20); and again: “He raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places” (Eph. II, 6). Hence the Lord says through the prophet to the perfected soul that follows him: “I will lift you above the heights of the earth” (Isa. LVIII, 14).

It follows:

VERS. 28. “He dwells among the rocks.” — In sacred speech, when “rock” is named in the singular, whom else is understood except Christ? Thus: “The rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 4). When the word is used in the plural, the saints are expressed, those who have been made solid by his strength. Hence Peter says: “You also, as living stones, are being built into spiritual houses” (I Pet. II, 5).

This eagle is said to dwell among the rocks because he establishes the station of his mind in the sayings of the ancient and strong Fathers. When he recalls them to memory, he builds for himself, in the height of their strength, the nest of holy meditation.

The name “rocks” may also signify the exalted powers of the heavenly virtues. Like rocks in high places, they are removed from every movement of mutability and, fixed in the solidity of their height, have endured through the very eternity to which they cleave.

When the holy man despises earthly things, he lifts himself to higher things in the manner of an eagle. Raised up by the spirit of contemplation, he awaits the eternal glory of the angels; and, while a guest in this world, desiring the things he sees, he is already fixed in the heights.

It follows: “And he dwells on precipitous crags and inaccessible rocks.” — The precipitous ones are those strongest choirs of angels, because part of them fell while another part remained. They stand whole in the quality of their merit, but are diminished in the number of the heavenly host. Because of this diminution, the Mediator came, perhaps to enrich more fully the measure of the heavenly homeland.

Hence it is said of the Father: “He purposed, in the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, those in heaven and those on earth, in him” (Eph. I, 9–10).

These are also the inaccessible rocks. The glory of the angels is entirely inaccessible to the hearts of sinful human beings, because, having fallen with respect to the beauty of bodily things, they have closed their eyes to spiritual form.

It follows:

VERS. 29. “From there he watches for prey”—that is, from those angelic choirs he directs the eye of his mind toward contemplating the glory of the heavenly majesty. He hungers for what he does not yet see, and when at last he sees it, he is satisfied. For it is written: “Because his soul has labored, he shall see and be satisfied” (Isa. LIII, 11). And again: “Blessed are those who hunger,” and so forth (Matt. V, 6, 8). Likewise: “Blessed are the pure in heart,” and so forth (ibid., 8).

It follows: “His eyes see from afar.” — However greatly someone may advance in this life, he does not see God by direct vision, but through riddles and in a mirror (I Cor. XIII, 12). It is as if he were saying: They stretch the sharpness of their intention with strength, yet they do not behold as near the One whose great brightness they are by no means able worthily to penetrate.

It is pleasing to bring forward the words of Isaiah: “He who walks in righteousness and speaks truth, who rejects avarice gained through slander and shakes his hands free from every gift; who stops his ears so as not to hear of bloodshed and closes his eyes so as not to see evil” (Isa. XXXIII, 15). And again: “He dwells on high; the heights of the rocks are his fortress; bread is given to him, and his waters are sure. He shall see the King in his beauty; his eyes shall behold the land from afar” (Isa. XVI, 17).

To dwell on high is to set the heart on heavenly things. The heights of the rocks are our fortifications when we look to the examples of the strong Fathers and join ourselves to the heavenly camps. The waters are sure because the words of life that they teach before death they also demonstrate after death. Bread is given to him when he is refreshed by contemplation. They see the King in his beauty because, carried beyond themselves, they fix the eyes of their hearts upon the splendor of his divinity.

It follows:

VERS. 30. “His young ones lick up blood.” — It is as though he were saying openly: He is indeed nourished by the contemplation of divinity, but because his hearers cannot at all grasp the mysteries of the Godhead, they are satisfied with the known blood of the crucified Lord.

To lick blood is to revere the weakness of the Lord’s passion. Hence Paul says to his disciples: “I judged myself not to know anything among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Cor. II, 2).

It follows: “And wherever the carcass is, there he is immediately.” — “Carcass” derives from falling. Not improperly, therefore, the Lord’s body is called a carcass because of the fall of death. Hence Truth itself says: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matt. XXIV, 18).

Alternatively: Everyone who has fallen into the death of sin can suitably be called a carcass. He lies as though lifeless who does not possess the life-giving spirit of righteousness. But every holy preacher directs the usefulness of his preaching there where he sees that he can be of benefit, so that, from the fact that he already lives spiritually, he may benefit others who lie in death.

The food of the righteous is the conversion of sinners, concerning which it is said: “Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life” (John VI, 27).

Holy Job, therefore, did not think that his merits were increased by so strict a scourging, but that his vices were cut away. Because he recognized none in himself, he believed himself to have been struck unjustly; and to accuse the one who struck him is plainly to murmur against the striking.

But the Lord, considering that what he had said arose not from a swelling of pride but from the quality of his life, mercifully reproves him, saying [Note: [Col. 0477] The author passes over verse 31, which reads: “And the Lord continued and spoke to Job.”]:

VERS. 32. “Will the one who contends with God so easily cease? Surely the one who accuses God must also answer him?” — It is as though he were saying more plainly: You who have said so much about your own conduct, why have you remained silent about the life of the saints when you heard it? You were considering your own height, but you did not know the height of others. Having therefore heard of the virtues of others, answer with your own, if you are able.

BOOK THIRTY-SECOND.

[Col. 0479]

[Col. 0479A] VERS. 33–34. “Job answered the Lord and said: Since I have spoken lightly, what can I answer?” — It is as though he were saying: I would defend my speech if I had uttered it with the weight of reason. But since my tongue is shown to have acted with levity, what remains except that it be restrained by silence?

It follows: “I will place my hand over my mouth.” — In the usage of sacred speech, “hand” ordinarily signifies action and “mouth” speech. To place the hand over the mouth, therefore, is to wipe away the faults of careless speech by the virtue of good works.

For who is so perfect that he does not sin at least in idle speech? Jacob testifies to this when he says: “We all offend in many things” (Jas. III, 2). Hence holy Church places her hand over her mouth when, in her elect, the life of idle speech is daily covered by the virtue of good action.

For it is written: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven,” and so forth (Ps. XXXI, 1). It follows:

### VERSE 35

“I have spoken one thing which I wish I had not said, and another; I will add nothing further to them.” — If we examine the words of blessed Job that have already been spoken, we find that he said nothing wickedly. But if we bend to some fault of pride those things that he uttered truthfully and freely, they will no longer be merely two, because they are many. Yet because it is proper for human beings to disclose their mind through words, while to speak before divine ears means to show the movement of the mind through action, to speak one thing illicitly is to do things deserving punishment, and to speak another is also to murmur against the punishment.

It is as though he were saying: “I believed myself upright among human beings, but when you spoke, I discovered myself perverse before the punishments, and after the punishments I found myself unyielding. To these I will add nothing further, since now, the more subtly I understand you as you speak, the more humbly I examine myself.”

In the Church, however, the elect recognize that they have sinned both in one respect and in another, because they understand that they have sinned either in thought and deed, or through neglecting love of God and neighbor. They promise themselves that they will add nothing further to these things, because through the grace of conversion they take care, by repenting, to cleanse daily even the deeds already committed.

Every sinner, however, ought in repentance to have a twofold lament: namely, that he did not do the good he ought to have done, and that he did the evil he ought not to have done.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XL

### VERSES 1–2

“And the Lord answered Job from the whirlwind and said: Gird your loins like a man; I will question you, and you shall answer me.” — All these matters have already been treated in the Lord’s first speech.

It follows:

### VERSE 3

“Will you annul my judgment and condemn me, so that you may be justified?” — Blessed Job, then, did not find his guilt amid the punishments; yet he also failed to recognize that the punishments were the cause of increasing his merit. Since he found nothing in himself that ought to be corrected, he believed that he was being struck unjustly. For the heavenly punishments did not strike him in order to extinguish sins in him, but rather to increase his merits.

Yet, lest his very innocence bend him toward the swelling of pride, he is rebuked by the divine voice, so that, even if the heavenly judgment is not understood, it may nevertheless not be believed unjust.

It follows:

### VERSE 4

“Do you have an arm like God, and do you thunder with a voice like his?” — When a voice and an arm are attributed to God, one must be exceedingly careful lest the mind imagine anything bodily in him. For to fall into the heresy of the Anthropomorphites is to enclose him who fills and embraces all things without limitation among corporeal features.

But almighty God, drawing us toward what belongs to him, humbles himself down to what belongs to us; and, in order to convey lofty realities, he condescends in a lowly manner. Hence Scripture sometimes derives comparisons for him from bodies, as in: “Whoever touches you touches the apple of my eye” (Zech. 2:8), and: “With his shoulders he will overshadow you” (Ps. 90:4). Sometimes it derives them from minds, as in: “I remembered you, showing compassion for your youth” (Jer. 2:2). Sometimes from birds, as in: “He spread his wings and took them up” (Deut. 32:11). Sometimes even from insensible things, as in: “Behold, I will creak over you, as a wagon creaks when loaded with hay” (Amos 2:13).

When eyes, shoulders, and wings are named in relation to God, some effect of his activity is indicated. But when hand and arm, right hand or voice, are spoken of in relation to God, these names demonstrate his consubstantial Son.

He himself is the hand and the right hand, as in: “I will lift my hand to heaven” (Deut. 32:40), and: “I will swear by my right hand” (Isa. 62:8). He himself is the arm: “And the arm of the Lord—to whom has it been revealed?” (Isa. 53:1). He himself is the voice: “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 32:9).

For God, then, to have an arm is to beget the Son who acts; to thunder with a voice is to reveal his consubstantial Son in a terrifying manner. Yet, when these things are said to blessed Job, God, by rebuking him, exalts him through a marvelous dispensation of compassion.

It follows:

### VERSE 5

“Adorn yourself with beauty, and raise yourself on high; be glorious, and clothe yourself in splendid garments.” — You should supply: “as I am.” He himself adorns himself with beauty. Of him it is written: “The Lord reigns; he has clothed himself with beauty” (Ps. 92:1).

He is raised on high among us when he is shown to exist in his own nature as impenetrable to our minds. He is glorious because, enjoying himself in himself, he has no need of praise that comes from elsewhere.

He is clothed in splendid garments because he has taken up the choirs of the saints whom he created for the use of his own beauty, and presents to himself, as it were, a certain garment: the glorious Church “not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5:27). Hence the Prophet says to him: “You have clothed yourself with confession and beauty,” and so forth (Ps. 103:1).

### VERSE 6

“Scatter the proud in your fury.” — You should supply: “as I do,” since in the time of tranquility I endure them as fierce against me, but, coming one day in judgment, I scatter them in my fury.

Far be it from anyone to believe that tranquility is changed into fury within the substance of divinity. For it is written: “But you, Lord, judge with tranquility” (Wis. 12:18).

The Lord’s fury, therefore, does not mean disturbance in the divine substance; rather, it is called the examination of just vengeance against sinners who are knowingly evil.

It follows: “And, looking upon every arrogant person, humble him.” — It is as though he were saying: “As I do.” Each sinner is looked upon by the Lord in two ways: either when he is converted from sin, or when he is punished because of sin.

Concerning the gaze of conversion it is said that “the Lord looked upon Peter,” and so forth (Luke 22:61). Concerning the gaze of vengeance it is again said: “But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil,” and so forth (Ps. 33:17).

It follows:

### VERSE 7

“Look upon all the proud, confound them, and crush the wicked in their place.” — You should supply: “as I do.” The proud are confounded by the Lord’s gaze: here, when they recognize and condemn their crimes through mercy; there, when they experience punishments through justice.

The place of the wicked is pride itself, since it is written: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10:15). Wherever wickedness arises, there it is contained. Indeed, wickedness differs in no way from pride. To be exceedingly proud is to think perversely about one’s creator.

The wicked person is therefore crushed in his own place, because the very pride by which he is raised up is pressed down. Hence the Prophet says: “You cast them down when they were being raised up” (Ps. 72:18).

It follows:

### VERSE 8

“Hide them in the dust.” — It is as though he were saying: “As I do.” By a just judgment the Lord hides the proud and the wicked in the dust, because whoever still desires the things of the world does not appear, so to speak, before the face of the true light, but lies hidden beneath the dust of earthly thought.

The mind oppressed by this dust of perverse thoughts endures it, while the wind of the most wicked temptation carries it away.

It follows: “At the same time, sink their faces into the pit.” — It is as though he were saying: “As I do.” By a just judgment the Lord sinks the faces of the proud into the pit, because he casts down below the intention of their heart, which raises itself above everyone.

The face of one who looks toward the pit looks toward the depths. Their faces are therefore rightly said to be plunged into the pit, because, following what is below, they move toward the abyss of hell.

It follows:

### VERSE 9

“And I will confess that your right hand can save you.” — As though he were openly saying: “If you can do these terrible things that I have endured, then I attribute all the good things you have done to you and not to me. But if, by looking upon sinners, you cannot destroy them, it is clear that you could not free yourself from the guilt of wickedness by your own power.”

It follows:

### VERSE 10

“Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you.” — Whom does he signify under the name Behemoth, if not the ancient enemy, who, translated from the Hebrew word into Latin, means “animal”? But when it is said of God that he made all things together (Ecclus. 18:1), this indicates that he made this animal together with humanity, since it is established that he made all things at once.

The substance of things was created together, but it was not formed all at once according to its species. Insofar as it came into existence together through the substance of matter, it did not appear together through the form of its species.

But why is Behemoth mentioned specifically, when blessed Job shares with all creatures generally the fact of having been made? Through careful examination we understand that the angel and the human being were made “together”—not in unity of time, but in the consideration of reason.

They were made “together” through the image of wisdom they received, but not “together” through a joined substance of form. For it is written concerning the human being: “Let us make humanity in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). And through Ezekiel it is said to Satan: “You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God” (Ezek. 28:12).

Since, therefore, in the whole creation of things no rational creature exists except the angel and the human being, whatever cannot use reason was not made together with humanity. Therefore, when the human being considers that the one who was made rational together with him has perished, he should fear the neighboring fall into pride from the very destruction of his companion.

It must also be known that the impious doctrine of Mani is reproved here. In speaking of two principles, he attempts to assert that the race of darkness was not made. For how can he call the most wicked race uncreated, when the Lord testifies that he made Behemoth—that is, the author of wickedness—well formed by nature?

It follows: “He eats grass like an ox.” — Isaiah also says the same thing: “The lion shall eat straw like an ox” (Isa. 11:7).

What is signified by the name of grass and straw except the life of carnal people? Concerning it the Prophet says: “All flesh is grass” (Isa. 40:6).

Thus, the one called Behemoth here is called a lion there; what is called grass here is called straw there. Oxen drink any kind of water, even dirty water, but they feed only on clean grass.

What, then, does it mean that this Behemoth is compared with the ox, which eats what is clean, except what the Prophet says about this ancient enemy: “His food is the chosen” (Hab. 1:16)?

Behemoth desires to eat grass like an ox because he seeks, with the tooth of his suggestion, to crush the clean life of spiritual people.

But if the life of carnal people is signified by grass, how does the one who eats grass have chosen food? The answer quickly presents itself: some people are grass before God, yet among human beings they are esteemed under the name of holiness.

Concerning them Solomon says: “I saw the wicked buried, who, while they were still alive, were in the holy place and were praised in the city” (Eccles. 8:10).

Because they claim to live a clean life through their efforts, but do not inwardly seek to please God by it, they are rightly called his chosen food; yet this Behemoth is remembered as eating grass like an ox.

It follows:

### VERSE 11

“His strength is in his loins, and his power is said to be in the navel of his belly.” — Hence Truth says: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35). Hence Peter says: “Girding the loins of your mind” (1 Pet. 1:13).

That women’s lust is contained in the thighs and the navel, the Prophet testifies when he says: “On the day of your birth, your navel was not cut” (Ezek. 16:4).

This Behemoth, therefore, raging insatiably and seeking at once to devour the human being, sometimes raises the mind into pride, and sometimes corrupts the flesh through the pleasure of lust.

His strength is rightly said not to be in the loins or navel of those who are overthrown, because those who are deceived by the allurements of his shameful suggestions and succumb to him through the flow of lust become, properly speaking, his body.

It follows:

### VERSE 12

“He tightens his tail like a cedar.” — In sacred Scripture, the name cedar sometimes expresses the lofty excellence of heavenly glory, as in the Prophet: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree and grow like a cedar of Lebanon,” and so forth (Ps. 91:13).

At other times it signifies the rigid exaltation of the wicked, as in: “The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars” (Ps. 28:5).

What else is the tail of this Behemoth except the extremity of the ancient enemy? For he enters his own particular vessel, the lost human being who is specially called Antichrist.

Because Antichrist is permitted to exalt that person sometimes through the honors of the world, sometimes through signs arising from a pretended holiness, in the fear inspired by his power, he is rightly compared by the Lord’s voice to a cedar.

As a cedar, by growing upward, leaves the other trees behind, so Antichrist, temporarily possessing the glory of the world, surpasses human measures both in the height of honor and in the power of signs.

The spirit within him was created among the heavenly beings; even after being cast down, it has not lost the power of its nature. Its strength is therefore now displayed most forcefully because, by the dispensation of divine power, it is restrained.

Hence John says: “I saw an angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand. He seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the Devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and cast him into the abyss, and shut it and sealed it over him” (Rev. 20:1–3).

He is rightly said to tighten his tail, because all his power is gathered and concentrated in that condemned human being, so that he performs powerful and marvelous deeds through him to the extent that he incites him with all his collected strength.

#### MORALLY

He is said to tighten his tail like a cedar because, once his temptation has been received in the heart, it rules as if by right over everything that it subsequently introduces.

The head of this Behemoth is grass, but his tail is a cedar: for at the first suggestion he is laid low as one who flatters, but through habit he grows exceedingly strong and, at the end of the increasing temptation, is made firm.

He is therefore rightly said to tighten his tail. He wounds with his tooth when he binds, because the first suggestion strikes, but, as the temptation grows stronger, it binds the wounded mind so that it cannot escape.

This Behemoth first sticks out his tongue by suggesting what is unlawful; then, drawing the person toward delight, he sinks in his tooth; finally, possessing the person through consent, he tightens his tail.

It follows: “The sinews of his testicles are intertwined.” — This Behemoth has as many testicles as he possesses preachers of his wickedness. By pouring the poisonous seeds of error into human hearts through perverse persuasions, they corrupt them.

They are intertwined because the arguments of his preachers are disentangled through deceptive assertions, so that they pretend to be right even while persuading people to what is perverse. Thus the entanglement of bonds, like the confusion of sinews, may be seen but cannot be undone.

They imitate their own head, who, like a lion lying in wait, rages through the power of earthly eminence and flatters through the appearance of holiness.

Many have not seen Antichrist, yet they are his testicles, because by the example of their conduct they corrupt human hearts.

Whoever is lifted up in pride, whoever is tormented by desires for avarice, or whoever is loosened by the pleasures of lust—what else is he than a testicle of Antichrist? By willingly entangling himself in the uses of this enemy, he provides others with the offspring of error through his example.

#### MORALLY

His testicles are wicked suggestions, through which he burns in the corruption of the mind and gives birth to the offspring of evil deeds in a polluted soul; or they are the poisonous arguments of his schemes.

Through these he raises up the powers of his cunning and corrupts the unstable hearts of mortals.

The sinews of these testicles are intertwined because his arguments bind the suggestion through entangled inventions. They make many people sin in such a way that, even if they wish to flee their sins, they cannot escape without another snare of sin; thus they commit faults while trying to live rightly.

For example, someone abandons worldly things and desires to submit himself to another’s rule, but, through insufficiently cautious inquiry, fails to discern the person who ought to preside over him before God. The one chosen without judgment may then begin to rule and forbid him to do the things of God while commanding him to do the things of the world.

The subject therefore considers both the guilt of disobedience and the contagion of secular life; he fears to obey and fears not to obey.

But if there is absolutely no way of escaping without sin, one should always choose the lesser evils. For when someone flees within walls that enclose him on every side, he is trapped; in his flight he throws himself toward the place where the wall is lower.

It follows:

### VERSE 13

“His bones are like pipes of bronze.” — In the body, the bones are what contain and support it.

This beast therefore has flesh and bones, because there are wicked people who are nevertheless held in error by others, while some more wicked people both remain in error and hold others in error.

What else should we understand as the bones of Antichrist except those who are more powerful in his body? Since wickedness has grown exceedingly hard in their hearts, the entire structure of his body is sustained through them.

They are rightly compared to pipes of bronze, because, in the manner of metal, they have the sound of speech in their understanding, but they do not possess the understanding required for good living.

They assert, as though humbly speaking, what they disdain through their proud way of life. Hence Paul rightly says: “If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have love, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal” (1 Cor. 13:1).

#### MORALLY

What is signified by the bones of this Behemoth except plans? Just as the body is positioned upon bones and its strength is sustained by them, so his entire wickedness raises itself up through fraudulent plans.

For he does not overwhelm someone by force, but kills him through the cunning of a poisonous persuasion.

Again, just as marrow strengthens the bones by moistening them, so the subtlety infused into his plans through the power of the spiritual nature strengthens them.

His testicles differ from his bones—that is, suggestions differ from plans—in this respect: through the former he openly inserts harmful things, while through the latter he draws a person toward guilt as though he were also giving good advice.

They are rightly compared to pipes of bronze. Pipes of bronze are ordinarily fitted to musical songs because of their sound; likewise, cunning plans, while offering advice with a kind of flattering foresight, turn the heart away from firm purpose, and, while sounding sweetly, incline it toward what is harmful.

For example, someone is preparing to break his own desires and submit to another’s will. The cunning enemy flatters him, saying: “How many marvelous things you could have done by yourself, if you had not submitted yourself to another’s judgment!” And so forth.

It follows: “His cartilage is like plates of iron.” — Cartilage indeed has the appearance of bone. What, then, does it mean that his cartilage is compared to plates of iron, except that those who are weaker in him are more wicked in carrying out evil?

Iron cuts other metals, and his cartilage is said to be like iron because those who, within his body, are not capable of displaying virtues are inflamed more fiercely against the destruction of the faithful.

They are rightly compared not merely to iron but to plates of iron, because, while they strive to spread themselves everywhere in their belief, they stretch themselves out as though into sheets of iron.

#### MORALLY

What is signified by cartilage except his simulation? Cartilage displays the appearance of bone but does not possess the firmness of bone.

There are certain vices that display in themselves the appearance of uprightness. Often cruelty is practiced in avenging vices and is thought to be justice; immoderate anger is believed to be the merit of righteous zeal. Often lax leniency is regarded as gentleness and compassion; sometimes extravagance is believed to be mercy.

What is signified by plates of iron except the hardness of strength? Some people do weak things, but, deceived by pride, they join them to strong suspicions; and the greater they consider those things to be, the more they disdain being corrected of their wickedness.

Concerning such people Jeremiah says: “Her Nazirites were whiter than snow, brighter than milk, ruddier than ancient ivory, more beautiful than sapphire. Their appearance has become blacker than coal, and they are not recognized in the streets; their skin has clung to their bones; it has dried up and become like wood” (Lam. 4:7–8).

It follows:

### VERSE 14

“He is the beginning of the ways of God.” — What should we understand as the ways of God except his actions? Concerning them the Prophet says: “For my ways are not like your ways” (Isa. 55:8).

Behemoth is called the beginning of God’s ways because, when he was creating all things, he formed him first and made him more eminent than the other angels.

Hence the Prophet says: “The cedars were not higher than he in the paradise of God; the fir trees did not equal his top,” and so forth (Ezek. 31:8). And again: “You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of paradise” (Ezek. 28:12).

Let the human being therefore consider what he deserves when exalted on earth, if even one who was placed above the angels in heaven is cast down.

Hence the Prophet says: “The sword was drunk in heaven” (Isa. 34:5).

It follows: “His maker applied his sword to him.” — The sword of this Behemoth is the malice by which he harms.

But his sword is applied by the one who made him good by nature, because his malice is restrained by divine dispensation, lest he be permitted to strike human minds as much as he desires.

This Behemoth, because he is the beginning of God’s ways, received permission to tempt the holy man. He took everything away and killed the sons who were feasting; but his sword is withdrawn by the Creator when he says: “Spare his life” (Job 2:6).

It should also be noted that the insane doctrine of Arius is openly refuted here by sound reasoning. Arius holds that the Son of God is a creature, and behold, Behemoth is shown to have been created first among all created things.

It remains, therefore, either for Arius to proclaim that the Son was not made, or, foolishly, to think that he was created after Behemoth.

Since we know, then, how powerful an enemy we are fighting, it remains for each of us to submit himself more fully to the Creator, in proportion as he weighs the violent strength of the adversary raging against him.

# BOOK THIRTY-THREE

### VERSE 15

“For him the mountains bear grass.” — In sacred Scripture, when “mountain” is placed in the singular, it sometimes signifies the incarnate Lord, as it is written: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared at the summit of the mountains” (Isa. 2:2).

Sometimes it signifies the holy Church, as in: “Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion” (Ps. 124:1).

Sometimes it signifies the Lord’s covenant, as Habakkuk says: “God will come from Lebanon, and the Holy One from the shady and dense mountain” (Hab. 3:3).

Sometimes it signifies the apostate angel, as in: “Flee to the mountain like a sparrow” (Ps. 11:1).

When mountains are named in the plural, they sometimes signify the exalted stature of the apostles and prophets, as in: “Your justice is like the mountains of God” (Ps. 36:6).

At other times they express the pride of secular powers, concerning which it is said: “The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord” (Ps. 97:5).

The exalted people of this world bear grass for this Behemoth, because they refresh him with what they wickedly do and offer him their shifting and slippery desires.

“For people will be,” says the Apostle, “lovers of themselves, lovers of pleasures rather than lovers of God” (2 Tim. 3:2, 4).

What, then, is the grass of the mountains except the fleeting pleasure that is produced from the heart of the proud?

This Behemoth feeds on such grass because, hungering for the punishment of eternal death, he will be satisfied by their ruined morals.

It follows: “All the beasts of the field will play there.” — What are signified by the beasts of the field except unclean spirits?

Hence it is said concerning the prince of the wicked spirits against Ephraim: “The beast of the field will tear them” (Hos. 13:8). Isaiah also says: “No evil beast will pass through it” (Isa. 35:9).

What is signified by the field except the present world? Hence the Lord says: “The field is the world” (Matt. 13:38).

The beasts of the field therefore play in the grass of the mountains because the demons cast down from the heights delight in the wicked works of the proud in this world.

They play well in the grass when the reprobate spirits draw human hearts toward unlawful thoughts. Since no proud person lets any evil pass without thinking about it, there is no beast of the field that is not satisfied by the grass of these mountains.

It follows:

### VERSE 16

“He sleeps under the shadow.” — In sacred speech, overshadowing sometimes signifies the incarnation of the Lord, as in: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

Sometimes it signifies the mind’s refreshment from the heat of carnal thoughts, as in: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings” (Ps. 17:8), or: “I sat under the shadow of him whom I desired” (Song 2:3).

Sometimes we understand by shadow the departing love of a cold mind, as it is said of the sinner that he followed shadows.

Sometimes, however, by shadow—if the addition of death is made—death of the flesh is expressed, as in: “The shadow of death has covered us” (Ps. 44:20). For the death of the flesh is an image of eternal death.

Or certainly death signifies the devil, as in: “His name was Death” (Rev. 6:8).

All the reprobate are therefore the shadow of death: they imitate the wickedness of that one’s pride and reproduce his image as if it were a shadow.

In this passage, however, the shadow is understood as the torpor of wickedness. Behemoth himself sleeps in it, because he vigilantly watches against hearts that burn with brightness, but lies secure in those that are cold.

He cannot sleep in the hearts of the saints, because if he ever settles in them for a moment, as many voices awaken him as holy thoughts cry out from their minds toward heaven.

Thus, terrified by the weapons of good actions and struck by the darts of sighs, he flees and returns to the cold hearts of the reprobate.

It follows: “In the secret place of the reed.” — In sacred speech, the name “reed” or “cane” sometimes signifies the abiding Word, as in: “My tongue is the pen of a ready writer,” and so forth (Ps. 45:1).

Sometimes it signifies the expertise of teachers, as in: “And in the dens where dragons formerly lived, the greenery of the reed and rush will arise” (Isa. 35:7). There, by the reed is understood the teaching of those who write, and by the rush the greenness of those who hear.

Sometimes it signifies the mobility of the mind, as in: “What did you go out to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” (Matt. 11:7).

Sometimes it signifies the brightness of temporal glory, as in Wisdom: “The righteous will shine, and like sparks they will run through the reed-bed” (Wis. 3:7). There it calls the life of secular people a reed-bed.

In this passage, therefore, the minds of secular people are signified by the name “reed.” He silently possesses their hearts when he moves them toward the desire for temporal brightness and elevation. He sleeps there peacefully, as it were, where he does not permit those whom he possesses to rest.

For, insofar as they themselves remain like an empty reed, in the manner of destruction, they provide a place where this Behemoth may rest in them.

It follows: “In moist places.” — Moist places are the minds of earthly people, which the moisture of carnal desire fills and thereby makes fluid.

Moist places are works of pleasure. He sleeps in these moist places because he rests in the slippery activity of reprobate people.

Alternatively: By moist places the genital members—that is, lust—may be signified; thus by the reed may be expressed the glory of pride, and by the moist places the lust of the body.

These are the two vices that dominate the human race with great violence: one of the spirit and the other of the flesh.

The ancient enemy therefore casts the human race down either through pride or through lust, while he possesses some in both ways.

It follows:

### VERSE 17

“The shadows protect his shadow.” — All the wicked are shadows of the devil. By serving the imitation of his wickedness, they draw from his body, as it were, the appearance of an image.

The shadows therefore protect the shadow because sinners, in the very matter in which they are conscious of their own wrongdoing, defend another sinner when they rebuke him.

They do this with deliberate purpose so that, while the fault in which they themselves are also bound is corrected in another person, it may not eventually come back to them.

Hence the Prophet says: “Thorns, nettles, and buckthorn will arise in his houses and in his fortifications” (Isa. 34:13).

By nettles we understand the itchings of thoughts; by thorns, the punctures of vices; and by buckthorn, which is a very dense thorn, we understand the protection of the most wicked.

“They will surround him, the willows of the torrent.” — In sacred speech, the name “willows” sometimes signifies the greenness of what is good, as in the Prophet: “They will sprout among the grasses like willows beside flowing waters” (Isa. 44:4).

At other times the reprobate are signified by it, as in: “On the willows in the midst of it,” and so forth (Ps. 137:2).

The torrent signifies the course of mortal life, as in: “He will drink from the torrent on the way” (Ps. 110:7).

“They will surround him, the willows of the torrent.” Those who love mortal life, alien from good actions as from fruits, cling all the more tightly to the ancient enemy the more freely the delight of passing pleasure pours into them.

The torrent also waters them, as it were, at their roots, when the love of carnal life intoxicates them in their thoughts.

At times they have words that resemble leaves of respectability, but they display no weight of life through good works.

It follows:

### VERSE 18

“He will swallow the river and will not be astonished, and he is confident that the Jordan will flow into his mouth.” — What is signified here by the name “river” except the course of the human race?

It rises as if from the origin of its own spring through birth, but, flowing downward toward the depths, it passes away through death.

What is signified by the name “Jordan” except those who have already been imbued with the sacrament of baptism?

Because our Redeemer deigned to be baptized in this river, all the baptized ought to be represented by its name, since the very sacrament of baptism began there.

It is as though he were saying: “Before the Redeemer of the world, he swallowed the world without astonishment; but, what is more grievous, even after the Redeemer’s coming he is confident that he can gulp down some who have been marked with the sacrament of baptism.” For he trips some through error of faith and inclines others through habitual evil action.

Concerning such people it is written: “They profess to know God, but they deny him by their deeds” (Titus 1:16). And: “Whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2:4).

Alternatively: Those whom we say are expressed by the Jordan may be designated by the river. For all who have already recognized the truth through faith but neglect to live faithfully can rightly be called a river, because they flow downward.

Jordan, in the Hebrew language, is said to mean “their descent.” There are some who desire the ways of truth, cast themselves down, and depart from the pride of their former life. When they desire eternal things, they make themselves wholly alien from this world.

Hence it is said: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matt. 16:24).

But the ancient enemy does not regard this as a great matter when he holds under the law of his tyranny those who seek earthly things.

For, as the Prophet testifies, we have learned that his food is the chosen. He strives especially to seize those whom he sees despising earthly pursuits and already being joined to heavenly things.

Hence the Prophet says: “The Lord called judgment to the fire, and it devoured the great abyss and consumed a portion of the house” (Amos 7:4).

It follows:

### VERSE 19

“In his eyes he will capture him as with a hook.” — Who does not know that bait is displayed on a hook while the barb is concealed? The bait entices so that the barb may pierce.

Our Lord, therefore, coming for the redemption of the human race, made from himself a kind of hook for the death of the devil.

He assumed a body so that this Behemoth might seek the death of the flesh in him as his bait. When he unjustly desired that death in him, he lost us, whom he had held as though justly.

Humanity was present there to draw the devourer to itself; divinity was present there to pierce him.

We say that something is before the eyes when we see it placed before us.

The ancient enemy therefore saw the Redeemer of the human race placed before him. By recognizing him, he confessed him; by confessing him, he feared him, saying: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?” (Matt. 8:29). He both knew him and bit him.

It follows: “And with stakes he will pierce his nostrils.” — What else should we understand by stakes—that is, poles—which are sharpened so that they may be driven in, except the sharp counsels of the saints?

These pierce the nostrils of this Behemoth when the saints, by keeping watch, scrutinize his most subtle snares, and, by overcoming them, transfix them.

Odor is drawn in through the nostrils. The nostrils of Behemoth therefore signify the cunning snares of the ancient enemy, through which he strives most shrewdly both to discover the hidden good things of our hearts and to destroy them through an evil persuasion.

The Lord therefore pierces his nostrils with stakes because, penetrating and weakening his cunning snares through the sharp perceptions of the saints, he overcomes them.

The sharp stakes may alternatively signify, through the flesh of Christ, the manifest words of wisdom.

And because odor is drawn in through the nostrils, the nostrils of Behemoth represent the ancient enemy’s investigation. When he doubted that God had become incarnate, he sought to discover this through miracles, saying: “If you are the Son of God,” and so forth (Matt. 4:3).

But when the Truth immediately answered him: “Human beings do not live by bread alone,” and so forth (ibid., 4), and: “You shall not put the Lord your God to the test” (ibid., 7), the Truth struck the ancient enemy’s investigation with the sharp points of its sayings, as though it had pierced his nostrils with stakes.

It follows:

[Col. 0490C] **VERSE 20. “Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook?”**—The implied words are, “as I can.” Leviathan means, in fact, “their addition”: namely, of human beings, upon whom he once brought the guilt of transgression and whose guilt he daily extends toward eternal death by his most wicked suggestions. He may also be called Leviathan by way of mockery. To the first man he craftily promised that he would add divinity to him, but he took away immortality. Yet this Leviathan was caught by a hook, because, when through his agents he bit the bait of the body in our Redeemer, the barb of divinity pierced him. The line of this hook is Christ’s genealogy. For when it is said, “Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac begot Jacob” (Matt. 1:2), and so on down to the Virgin Mary, a kind of line is twisted, at whose end the incarnate Lord—that is, the hook—was fastened, and this monster, hanging in these waters of the human race, sought it with open mouth.

It follows: **“And will you bind his tongue with a cord?”**—The implied words are, “as I can.” Holy Scripture sometimes designates by the name “cord” the measure of an allotted portion, as in: “The cords have fallen to me in pleasant places,” and so forth (Ps. 15:6). Sometimes it designates sins, as in the prophet’s words: “Woe to those who drag iniquities with cords of vanity” (Isa. 5:18). At other times it customarily signifies faith, as Solomon attests: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Eccl. 4:12). Thus, in this passage, there is no impediment to understanding “cord” either as sin or as faith.

The incarnate Lord bound Leviathan’s tongue with a cord, because he appeared “in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Rom. 8:3) and condemned all his pronouncements of error, as the Apostle says: “And, because of sin, he condemned sin” (ibid.). Hence the prophet appropriately says: “And the Lord will lay waste the tongue of the sea of Egypt” (Isa. 11:15). If, however, faith is signified by the cord, Leviathan’s tongue is tightened by a cord because, when the doctrine of faith in the Trinity was extended, the pronouncements of error fell silent. Hence it is written: “You broke open springs and torrents,” and so forth (Ps. 73:15).

It follows:

**VERSE 21. “Will you put a ring in his nostrils?”**—The implied words are, “as I can.” Just as the nostrils signify ambushes, so by the ring the omnipotence of divine power is signified. A ring is put in his nostrils when the sagacity of the enemy is restrained by the encircling dread of heavenly protection, so that he cannot prevail against human weakness as far as he secretly investigates the means of destruction. The name “ring” may also signify the assistance of hidden judgment. Thus the Lord places a ring in Leviathan’s nostrils, because the power of his judgment is confined within his ambushes, so that he may not prevail as much as he wishes. Hence it is said to the king of Babylon: “I will put a ring in your nostrils” (2 Kings 19:28).

It follows: **“Or will you pierce his jaw with a bracelet?”**—The implied words are, “as I can.” By the bracelet is signified the protection extended to us by his hidden judgment. Leviathan’s jaw is therefore pierced because the power of ineffable mercy so opposes the malice of the ancient enemy that sometimes even those whom he has already seized escape him, and those who return to innocence after committing sins fall, as it were, from his mouth.

Alternatively: Leviathan is said to hold in his mouth not those whom he completely entangles in sin, but those whom he still tests by the persuasions of sin. Yet, by a wondrous order of providence, while they are tested they are humbled; while they are humbled, they cease to belong to him. Paul had indeed been received to be chewed, but not swallowed, when, after such exalted revelations, Satan afflicted him with a thorn in the flesh (2 Cor. 12:7). Thus, serving God’s hidden dispensations, the enemy willingly tests the saints for destruction, but unwillingly preserves them for the kingdom by testing them.

It follows:

**VERSE 22. “Will he multiply entreaties to you, or speak soft words to you?”**—The implied words are, “as he would to me.” If these words are referred to the person of the Son of God, he spoke soft words to the incarnate Lord when he said: “I know who you are: the Holy One of God” (Mark 1:24). He multiplies entreaties when, through the legions, he says: “If you cast us out, send us into the herd of pigs” (Matt. 8:31).

Yet it can more appropriately be understood that he multiplies entreaties to God when the wicked, who are his body, plead at the judgment that they be spared, saying: “Lord, Lord, open to us” (Luke 13:25). They are answered: “I do not know you” (ibid.). He will also speak soft words through his members when they say: “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name?” and so forth (Matt. 7:22). But immediately they will hear: “I do not know who you are” (ibid., 23).

It follows:

**VERSE 23. “Will he make a covenant with you?”**—The implied words are, “as he would with me.” It follows: **“And will you receive him as an everlasting servant?”**—The implied words are, “as I can.”

The ancient enemy is at odds with the sincerity of divine innocence, inflamed by the torch of his own malice; yet he does not depart from God’s judgment even while opposed to it. He always desires to test righteous men maliciously, but the Lord permits this to happen either mercifully or justly. This very permission to test is called a covenant: in it the tester’s desire is carried out, yet through it the will of the just disposer is fulfilled in a wondrous manner. For in a covenant, the quarrels of those who disagree are brought to their desired conclusion.

He is rightly said to be received as a servant through this covenant, because by the very means through which he exercises the anger of his wicked will, he obeys the commands of heavenly grace. He is therefore a servant by covenant who, while permitted to fulfill his own will, is bound by the will of heavenly counsel.

In this passage he is received by the Lord not merely as a servant through a covenant, but as an everlasting servant. He is not permitted to test the righteous when they are already flourishing in blessedness; rather, with his body—that is, with all the reprobate—he will be handed over to avenging flames, in which he will be tortured without end. When the righteous behold these torments, they increase in the praises of God. Therefore, if testing here and condemnation there both serve the advantage of the righteous, he is an everlasting servant.

It follows:

**VERSE 24. “Will you mock him as a bird?”**—What does it mean that our adversary is first called Behemoth, afterward Leviathan, and now compares the mockery of his destruction to a bird? Behemoth means “beast,” and he is shown as a quadruped because he is said to eat grass like an ox. Leviathan, because he is caught by a hook, is plainly recognized as a serpent in the waters. Through the folly of irrational action he is an irrational four-footed animal; through his malice in doing harm, a dragon; through the lightness of a subtle nature, a bird.

Among those whom he arouses to the folly of lust, he is a beast of burden; among those whom he inflames to the malice of harming others, he is a dragon; among those whom he elevates in pride, as though they were wise in lofty matters, he is a bird. The Lord mocked him as a bird when, in the passion of his only-begotten Son, he showed him flesh as bait but concealed the snare of divinity.

It follows: **“Or will you bind him for your maidservants?”**—The implied words are, “as I can.” In male servants, although their condition is lowly, manly strength is vigorous; in maidservants, along with their condition, sex is also mentioned. Thus the Lord bound the strength of this Leviathan by his maidservants, because, as Paul testifies, “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1:27).

Hence Solomon says: “Wisdom built herself a house, and carved out seven pillars; she sacrificed victims, mixed wine, set her table, and sent her maidservants to call from the citadel and the walls of the city” (Prov. 9:1–2). He presented weak preachers to the world, restrained the powerful who were his body by the bonds of his fear, and this Leviathan himself is bound by maidservants when the ancient enemy, while the light of truth shines through weak preachers, is not permitted to rage against the minds of the elect as much as he wishes. Yet, lest he hold captive all whom he desires under the bondage of unbelief, he is confined by signs and miracles.

It follows:

[Col. 0493A] **VERSE 25. “His companions will cut him up; merchants will divide him.”**—This Leviathan is cut up as many times as his members are separated from him by the sword of the divine word. For when the wicked hear the truth and, struck by holy fear, withdraw from imitating the ancient enemy, he is divided in his body: those who had served him wickedly are taken away from him.

Holy preachers are first maidservants through fear. Of them it is said: “Do not be afraid, little flock” (Luke 12:32). They are companions through faith, as in: “I have called you friends” (John 15:15). Finally, they are merchants through action, as in: “Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15). In the preaching of faith, a kind of business is conducted: the word is given, and faith is received from the hearers. Hence the Psalmist says: “Take up the psalm and give the tambourine” (Ps. 80:3). Again, Solomon speaks from the voice of holy Church: “She made linen garments and sold them, and delivered a belt to the Canaanite” (Prov. 31:24).

Because through God’s preachers the possessions held by this Leviathan are divided in a highly praiseworthy manner, the voice of Truth promises through the prophet: “If you separate the precious from the worthless, you will be like my mouth” (Jer. 15:19).

It follows:

**VERSE 26. “Will you fill nets with his skin, or a fish-basket with his head?”**—What are signified by nets or a fish-basket except the Church of the faithful, who form one catholic Church? Hence it is written in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind” (Matt. 13:47).

By the skin of this Leviathan we understand the foolish members of his body, and by his head the wise. Or, certainly, by the skin, which is external, are signified subjects who serve these final times; by the head, rulers. Thus, first, within the holy Church he gathered, as the devil’s skin, the lowest and weakest—namely, unlearned fishermen—and afterward subjected to himself, as its head, philosophers and wise men who had been his adversaries.

It follows:

**VERSE 27. “Lay your hand upon him.”**—That is, “as I do,” for I restrain him by strong power and do not permit him to rage more than is expedient. Or, alternatively, to lay a hand upon him means to overcome him by the power of virtue.

It follows: **“Remember the battle and do not speak further.”**—As though it were plainly said: “If you consider the battle of the hidden enemy against you, do not accuse me for anything you suffer.” The profound dispensation of God’s judgments often attacks deserving servants with threats or presses them with blows because, by wondrous power, he foresaw that if they remained peaceful and free in tranquility, unable to endure the adversary’s temptations, they would lie prostrate in mind, wounded by their injuries.

It follows:

**VERSE 28. “Behold, his hope will deceive him.”**—This should be understood of him in such a way that it can also be referred to his body, because all the wicked who do not fear the strictness of divine justice flatter themselves vainly concerning mercy.

It follows: **“And he will be cast down in the sight of all.”**—When the eternal Judge then appears in terror, while legions of angels stand by and all the elect are led to this spectacle, this cruel and powerful beast will be brought forth captive into their midst and, with his body—that is, with all the reprobate—will be delivered to the fires of eternal Gehenna, when it is said: “Depart from me, you cursed,” and so forth (Matt. 25:41).

It follows:

# CHAPTER 41

**VERSES 1–2. “I will not raise him up as though I were cruel.”**—And as though the question were immediately put to us for an explanation—“How do you not raise him up as though you were cruel, when we know that you permit him to attack and devour so many?”—the text immediately adds: **“For who can resist my face?”** and: **“Who has given to me first, that I should repay him?”**

In these two verses he has fulfilled both the power of his might and the whole force of the argument. It is as though he said: “I do not raise him up as though I were cruel, because I powerfully rescue my elect from his strength; and again, I condemn the reprobate not unjustly but reasonably. That is, I can wondrously rescue those whom I mercifully choose, and I do not unjustly abandon those whom I reject.”

No one first contributed anything to God so that divine grace might follow him. For it is written: “His mercy will go before me” (Ps. 59:11). And Paul says: “You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves: it is God’s gift” (Eph. 2:8). The good that we do belongs both to God and to us: to God through prevenient grace; to us through the free will that follows it. Therefore we give thanks to God forever, and yet we hope that rewards will be repaid to us.

It follows: **“Everything that is under heaven is mine.”**—It is clear to everyone that not only the things under heaven but also those above the heavens serve his will. Yet because he is speaking of Leviathan, who is no longer contained in the dwelling of the heavenly firmament, he asserts that everything under heaven is his, so that he may teach that even the one who fell from heaven serves his power.

It follows:

**VERSE 3. “I will not spare him, nor with powerful words nor with words composed for entreaty.”**—Whoever knows that he has read this should by no means suppose that the devil will seek pardon for his sins. Perhaps, however, this is said of Antichrist: “The Lord Jesus Christ will kill him with the spirit of his mouth” (2 Thess. 2:8), so that, terrified by the presence of such majesty, he may be inclined to entreaties.

Yet it can more appropriately be understood of all the wicked, who come late to words of petition. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “Lord, Lord, open to us” (Matt. 25:11). They are answered: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (ibid., 12).

We may also understand in the present time what we have said concerning the future. There are some who offer lengthy prayers to God but do not possess the life of those who pray. They experience tears in prayer, yet when, after their prayers have ended, they are struck by the suggestion of vices, they do not remember that they wept out of desire for the eternal kingdom. God does not spare their petitions, because their prayers are destroyed by their actions.

It follows:

[Col. 0495A] **VERSE 4. “Who will reveal the face of his garment?”**—The implied words are, “except me,” who inspire my servants with the gift of the most subtle discernment, so that, when his malice is revealed, they may see his naked face, which he conceals beneath the appearance of holiness.

For this Leviathan secretly lies in wait for the good and deceives them under the appearance of holiness, so that the evils he cannot openly inflict upon them he may introduce under the covering of good action. Hence his members often, when they cannot harm others through open wickedness, assume the appearance of good action. For it is written: “Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11:14). What wonder, then, if his ministers transform themselves as ministers of righteousness?

It follows: **“And who has entered into the midst of his mouth?”**—The implied words are, “except me,” who examine the words of his suggestions through the secret minds of the elect, so that they may not consider merely what they sound like, but what they are intended to mean.

It follows:

**VERSE 5. “Who will open the doors of his face?”**—The implied words are, “except me,” who make manifest to my elect, through clear thought, the teachers of error hidden under the appearance of holiness. For just as holy preachers are called the gates of Zion, so by the gates of this Leviathan the teachers of error are signified. When their perverse preaching is received, the way of destruction is opened to their wretched hearers.

It follows: **“Around his teeth there is terror.”**—That is, the powers of this perverse age protect the wicked preachers of Antichrist. For many of the powerful strive by violence to terrify those whom the others seek to seduce by their speech. Hence it is written in the Apocalypse: “The power of the horses was in their mouths and in their tails” (Rev. 9:19). In the mouth is represented the knowledge of teachers; in the tail, the power of worldly people.

Just as the holy Church has teeth, of which it is said: “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep,” and so forth (Song 4:2), so Leviathan’s teeth are the teachers of error, who tear apart the life of the reprobate by biting them and, having drawn them away from the integrity of truth, slaughter them in the sacrifice of falsehood.

It follows:

**VERSE 6. “His body is like molten shields.”**—In Holy Scripture the name “shield” is sometimes used for divine protection, as in: “Lord, as with the shield of your good will,” and so forth (Ps. 5:13). Sometimes it is used for human resistance, as in: “There he broke the powers, the shield and the sword” (Ps. 76:4).

Molten shields are not pierced at all by the blow of those striking them, but they dissolve into fragments through their own collapse. Thus the body of this Leviathan—that is, all the wicked—is compared to molten shields, because they are hard through obstinacy but fragile in their way of life. When they hear the words of preaching, they do not allow themselves to be pierced by any arrow of correction, because in every sin they commit they set up the shield of proud self-defense. Hence Jeremiah says: “You will repay them, Lord, according to the works of their hands; you will give them the shield of your labor” (Lam. 3:64–65).

It follows: **“He is compacted with scales pressing upon him.”**—It is said that a dragon’s body is covered with scales and is not quickly pierced by a missile. In the same way, the whole body of the devil—that is, the multitude of the reprobate—when corrected for iniquity, attempts to excuse itself by every evasion available to it and places before itself, as it were, certain scales of defense, lest it be pierced by the arrow of truth.

Whoever, when corrected, desires rather to excuse his sin than to mourn it is covered, as it were, with scales, lest he be struck by the sword of the word from the holy preachers. Paul lost these scales at his illumination. For it is written of him: “There fell from his eyes as it were scales” (Acts 9:18).

Although these scales cover almost the entire human race, they especially weigh upon the minds of hypocrites and cunning people. They refuse to confess their sins all the more vehemently because they foolishly blush to appear sinful before others. Concerning them the prophet aptly says: “There the night-monster reclined and found rest; there the hedgehog had its hole” (Isa. 34:14–15). By the night-monster hypocrites are signified; by the hedgehog, malicious people who heap upon themselves various defenses.

It follows:

**VERSE 7. “One is joined to another, and no breath passes between them.”**—Because, while they protect one another in their sins by proud defenses, they do not allow the darts of holy exhortation to reach them in any way.

It follows:

**VERSE 8. “One will cling to another, and, holding one another, they will not be separated.”**—Those who could have been corrected while divided persist, bound by the obstinacy of their sins. They become daily more difficult to separate from knowledge of righteousness, insofar as no rebuke separates them from one another. Hence Solomon says: “The assembly of sinners is collected tinder” (Sir. 21:10). Hence the prophet Nahum says: “As thorns embrace one another, so is the banquet of those who drink together” (Nah. 1:10).

It follows:

**VERSE 9. “His sneezing is the splendor of fire.”**—Sneezing rises from an inflated chest. When it finds no open pores through which to escape, it touches the brain; then, emerging in a mass through the nostrils, it immediately shakes the whole head.

As it were, inflation rises from Leviathan’s chest when pride raises itself through the power of the present age. Yet it finds no pores, because it is prevented from exalting itself against the righteous as much as it desires. It shakes the brain because at the end of the world it more violently disturbs Satan’s mind; and it disturbs the head when, through Antichrist, it violently arouses persecution against the faithful.

Then the accumulated inflation leaves through his nostrils, because all his proud iniquity is displayed through open blasts of malice. “Sneezing,” therefore, is called that final agitation of Antichrist, into whom Leviathan enters so that through him he may rule the reprobate and, if possible, disturb even the members of the Lord’s elect. He uses such great signs and wonders that he appears to shine with the power of miracles like a certain light of fire.

It follows: **“His eyes are like the eyelids of dawn.”**—By his eyes are signified his counselors, who, while they foresee through perverse schemes what should be done and how, provide his wicked workers with a path, as though one had shown it to their feet.

They are rightly compared to the eyelids of dawn. By the eyelids of dawn we understand the final hours of night. Thus the prudent who cling to the perverse counsels of Antichrist are like the eyelids of dawn, because they promise that the faith they find in Christ is like the night of error [lacuna], and that the worship of Antichrist is the true morning.

[Note: In place of these dots, the manuscript has the word *emasserunt*, but this does not appear to be Latin.]

For they promise that they will drive away darkness and announce the light of truth by shining signs.

It follows:

**VERSE 10. “From his mouth torches proceed.”**—Those who proceed are called his eyes; those who preach are called his mouth. But torches come out of this mouth because they kindle the minds of their hearers toward love of treachery. For from the very source by which they seem to shine through wisdom, they undoubtedly burn through wickedness.

It follows: **“Like torches of fire that have been kindled.”**—A torch, when lit, has a pleasant smell but an obscure light. So these preachers of Antichrist assume the appearance of holiness, yet practice works of iniquity. They smell fragrant through their likeness to righteousness, but burn darkly through the perpetration of wickedness.

It follows:

**VERSE 11. “Smoke proceeds from his nostrils.”**—The sharpness of the eyes is injured by smoke; that is, from the ambushes of his miracles a momentary cloud of doubt is generated even in the heart of the elect. Smoke comes from Leviathan’s nostrils because, from his lying wonders, a mist of trepidation confuses even the eyes of good minds. Hence it is said: “Pseudo-Christs and pseudo-prophets will arise, and they will give signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect” (Matt. 24:24).

**MORALLY.** Since this Leviathan is called a serpent and a basilisk—as Isaiah says, “From the root of the serpent a basilisk will come forth” (Isa. 14:29)—and a basilisk kills not by biting but by breathing, it is rightly said that smoke proceeds from his nostrils. Through his harmful inspirations, a perverse thought arises in human hearts, by which the mind’s sharpness is dulled so that the inner light may not be seen.

At times he also touches the eyes of the elect. Hence it is written: “My eye is disturbed because of anger” (Ps. 6:8). This smoke inserts so many unlawful desires into the hearts of the reprobate that it swells before their eyes like so many clouds of thoughts. Hence Joel says: “What the cutting locust left, the swarming locust ate; what the swarming locust left, the consuming locust ate; and what the consuming locust left, the devouring locust ate” (Joel 1:4). There lust, empty glory, gluttony, and anger are signified.

It follows: **“Like a pot burning and boiling.”**—Each soul is then like a boiling pot, enduring the assaults of its thoughts as though they were the foam of burning waves. The fire of zeal stirs it, while the oppression of temporal affairs holds what is enclosed within it, like a pot.

**MORALLY.** A pot is kindled when the human mind is driven on by the persuasions of the wicked enemy. The pot boils when, through consent, it is already inflamed by desires arising from a perverse persuasion and, boiling, casts out as many waves as the wickednesses by which it extends itself into outward actions. Hence it is written: “I see a boiling pot, and its face is from the face of the north” (Jer. 1:13).

It follows:

**VERSE 12. “His breath makes coals burn.”**—What else does he call “coals” except the minds of wicked people, kindled by inward desires? They burn whenever they seek some temporal thing. Thus Leviathan’s breath kindles coals as often as his hidden suggestion draws human minds toward unlawful pleasures; at one time he inflames them with the torches of pride, at another of envy, at another of lust.

It follows: **“And flame comes forth from his mouth.”**—The flame of his mouth is the very instigation of hidden speech, which he makes reach wickedly into each person’s mind. Hence the mind burns with desires when it is stirred by his suggestions. He suggests these things daily and does not cease suggesting them until the end of the present life.
