Yet he spreads himself more wickedly when, coming through that condemned human being, he displays himself more openly in the glory of this world.

# BOOK THIRTY-FOUR

[Col. 0497]

[Col. 0497D] **VERSE 13. “Strength will dwell in his neck.”**—What is signified by the neck of this Leviathan except the extension of pride? Rising up against God, he is exalted not only by a swelling of power but also under the pretense of holiness. Since pride is signified by the neck, Isaiah bears witness, saying: “They walked with an outstretched neck” (Isa. 3:16).

Whatever is then proudly exalted and whatever he craftily contrives, he also carries out under the power of worldly authority. The prophet Daniel, observing this, says: “Deceit will be directed by his hand” (Dan. 8:25).

It follows: **“And poverty goes before his face.”**—By the face, knowledge is usually signified. Hence it is written: “My face will go before you” (Exod. 33:14).

It must be understood, however, that in sacred speech poverty is attributed to the elect in one way and to the reprobate in another. The poverty of the elect occurs when the true riches of the heavenly homeland return to their minds and, placed in the wretched exile of the present life, they remember that they are poor. Of those riches Paul says: “So that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints” (Eph. 1:18).

The poverty of the reprobate is properly so called because, while they are filled with vices, they are emptied of the riches of virtues. Of them it is said: “You say, ‘I am rich and have grown wealthy and need nothing,’ and you do not know that you are wretched and miserable, poor, blind, and naked” (Rev. 3:17).

Poverty will therefore go before his face because no one is joined to his knowledge unless he has first been stripped either of the riches of virtues or of holy thoughts. Or, certainly, because he secretly steals upon many so fraudulently that he cannot be reproved by them at all, poverty is said to precede his face: he empties their virtues in such a way that he does not reveal the malice of his cunning. Hence it is said through the prophet: “Strangers have devoured his strength, and he did not know it” (Hos. 7:9).

Alternatively: By a terrible order of hidden dispensation, before this Leviathan appears in the condemned man whom he assumes, signs of virtue are withdrawn from the holy Church, words of doctrine fall silent, and miraculous wonders are removed. Then the ancient enemy is revealed against them through open prodigies. Nevertheless, signs will not be lacking for the faithful in his battle. But his signs will be so great that ours will appear few or none.

It follows:

**VERSE 14. “The members of his flesh cling to one another.”**—The flesh of this Leviathan is all the reprobate, who do not rise through desire toward understanding of the spiritual homeland. His members are those who join themselves to those acting perversely and precede one another toward iniquity.

By contrast, Paul says of the Lord’s body: “You are the body of Christ and members of a member” (1 Cor. 12:27). Since the wicked enemy agrees with himself in perverse action from the least to the greatest, the divine word recalls that the members of his flesh cling to one another. Thus the perverse think alike, without being divided by any dispute among themselves. For this reason they prevail so strongly against the good: they hold together in evil.

The prophet desires this harmony to be divided when he says: “Hurry, Lord, and divide their tongues” (Ps. 55:10).

It follows: **“He will send lightning bolts against him, and they will not be carried to another place.”**—What is signified by the name “lightning bolts” except those dreadful sentences of the final judgment? They are called lightning bolts because they perpetually burn those whom they strike. The lightning bolts will not be carried to another place because, while the righteous rejoice, they will then strike the reprobate alone.

It follows:

**VERSE 15. “His heart will be hardened like a stone.”**—The heart of the ancient enemy will be hardened like a stone because no repentance of conversion will ever soften it.

It follows: **“And it will be tightened like a smith’s anvil.”**—He will be confined by the bonds of hell, so that through the continual blows of eternal punishment he may be beaten like an anvil. For just as other vessels are fashioned while the anvil itself, despite so many blows, is not transferred into another vessel, so we are fashioned while he persecutes us; but he is both struck forever and never changed into a useful vessel.

We are beaten when he tests us, but we are formed by the hand of the heavenly Craftsman so that we may become suitable for the service of the heavenly household.

It follows:

[Col. 0500A] **VERSE 16. “When he is lifted up, the angels will fear, and, terrified, they will be purified.”**—In Scripture, the past tense is sometimes used for the future and the future for the past. Thus John is shown a future event as already accomplished when he sees a woman about to give birth to a male child who will rule the nations with an iron rod (Rev. 12:5); and the Psalmist says, “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. 22:16), using a future event as though it were past.

Therefore, in this passage there is no impediment to understanding past events as described in the form of the future tense. When Leviathan fell from the citadel of blessedness, even the exalted angels feared his ruin, so that, when pride cast him out from their number, fear itself might strengthen them to stand more firmly. His fall both terrified and purified them: it terrified them lest they proudly despise their Creator; it purified them because, when the reprobate had gone out, it was brought about that only the elect, who would live blessedly forever, remained.

In this passage we may also understand holy preachers by “angels.” Hence the prophet says: “The angels of peace will weep bitterly” (Isa. 33:7). Hence Malachi says: “The lips of the priest will guard knowledge, and they will seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2:7).

When the strict Judge arrives, the final condemnation of this Leviathan is signified: he is taken from this world by the anger of judgment, though now he is tolerated with wondrous gentleness and patience. So great a weight of terror is then stirred up by this that even the strength of the holy preachers who may be found in their bodies is disturbed by immense fear. They are purified by being terrified because, if any slight rust of vices can be found in them, it is burned away by this fear.

Consider, then, what those who hate the Judge’s coming will do, if even those who love it fear the terror of such a judgment.

It follows:

**VERSE 17. “When the sword has seized him, neither spear nor breastplate will be able to stand.”**—In Scripture, “sword” sometimes signifies holy preaching, as in: “The sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6:17). Sometimes it signifies eternal condemnation, as in: “If his children are multiplied, they will be for the sword” (Job 27:14). Sometimes it signifies temporal tribulation, as in: “And a sword will pass through your own soul” (Luke 2:35). Sometimes it signifies the anger or persuasion of the ancient enemy, as in: “You who deliver David your servant from the evil sword” (Ps. 144:10).

That sword of the ancient enemy is the condemned man then taken up for his service. Through the malice of deceit he sharpens it and pierces the hearts of the weak. If by “sword” his anger is signified, he is rightly said not to grasp the sword but to be seized by the sword. For he will then be turned to such madness that, desiring to dominate everyone, he will not even dominate himself. He does not possess and hold anger; rather, raging from anger, he is held by it.

By the spear are signified the darts of preaching; by the breastplate, the strength of patience. When Leviathan comes into Antichrist, he will appear with such power that, if heavenly assistance is absent, he will blunt the sharpness of preachers and destroy the endurance of patience.

It follows:

**VERSE 18. “For he will regard iron as straw, and bronze as rotten wood.”**—What he previously presented under the names of spear and breastplate, he repeats here under the names of iron and bronze. By iron, therefore, the darts of preaching are signified; by bronze, the constancy of endurance. Hence, under the figure of Asher, Moses says of the holy Church: “Iron and bronze are your footwear” (Deut. 33:25). There iron expresses strength, while bronze expresses perseverance.

But when this Leviathan has taken up the sword—that is, Antichrist—unless they are protected by divine grace, he will consume the strength of preachers like straw in the fire of his wickedness and reduce the constancy of patience to dust like rotten wood.

It follows:

### VERSE 19

“An archer did not put him to flight.” — The arrows are the words of preachers, directed from the voice of those who live well and piercing the hearts of their hearers. She had been wounded by these arrows who said: “I am wounded with love” (Song of Songs 2:5). Hence it is written: “The arrows of children have become their wounds” (Psalm 63:8); and again: “Your arrows are sharp,” etc. (Psalm 44:6).

The archer, therefore, is one who, through the bow of holy intention, fixes words of right exhortation in the hearts of his hearers. Yet the arrow of the holy preacher does not drive this leviathan from the hearts of the reprobate, because whoever is seized by him now disdains to hear the words of preachers.

It follows:

“His sling-stones are turned into stubble” [Col. 0501C]. — What is signified by the sling, if not the holy Church? For when the holy Church is led through the changing course of time, by the circuit of tribulations, as by a sling, strong men emerge from it like stones from a sling, by whose blows the hearts of the wicked are battered. Hence the prophet says: “They will devour and subdue with sling-stones” (Zechariah 9:15).

Leviathan, therefore, will reduce the strength of the saints to the softness of stubble by his contempt; yet their tongue had previously battered his breast with hard blows.

It follows:

### VERSE 20

“He will regard the hammer as stubble.” — In sacred Scripture the devil is sometimes signified by the name “hammer,” by which the sins of those who offend are struck, as in the prophet’s words: “How the hammer of the whole earth has been broken and crushed” (Jeremiah 50:23). At other times, however, a heavenly blow is understood, as in the words: “Hammer and axe and every iron tool were not heard in the house when it was being built” (1 Kings 6:7).

What, then, does it mean that this leviathan despises the hammer, except that he does not fear the blows of heavenly punishment? And why does he count it as stubble? Because he prepares himself for the weight of just wrath as though against a very slight terror.

It follows:

“And he will laugh at the one who brandishes the spear.” — The Lord brandishes a spear against leviathan because He threatens him with a sentence of judgment directed toward his destruction. But the apostate spirit, despising the author of life even in the face of his own death, laughs at the brandished spear.

It follows:

### VERSE 21

“Under him are the rays of the sun” [Col. 0502A]. — In sacred Scripture, when the sun is mentioned figuratively, it sometimes signifies the Lord, as in the words: “We have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of justice has not shone upon us, and the sun has not risen for us” (Wisdom 5:6). At other times it signifies persecution, as in the Gospel: “When the sun rose, they were scorched” (Matthew 13:6). At other times it signifies the manifest disclosure of some vision, as in the words: “He placed his tabernacle in the sun” (Psalm 18:6). At still other times it signifies understanding of wisdom, as in the words: “The fourth angel poured out his bowl upon the sun, and it was given to him to afflict people with heat and fire” (Revelation 16:8).

What, then, is signified here by a ray of the sun, if not the sharp insights of the wise? For when many in the holy Church appear to shine with the radiance of wisdom, they then submit themselves to the power of this leviathan, whether captured by persuasion, terrified by threats, or broken by tortures. Rightly, therefore, it is said: “Under him are the rays of the sun.”

It follows:

“He will spread gold beneath himself as though it were mud.” — In sacred speech, the name “gold” sometimes signifies the splendor of divinity, as in the words: “His head is finest gold” (Song of Songs 5:11); sometimes the splendor of the heavenly city, as in the words: “The city itself was pure gold, like pure glass” (Revelation 21:18); sometimes love, as in the words: “Girded about the breasts with a golden belt” (Revelation 1:13); sometimes the glitter of worldly glory, as the prophet says: “Babylon is a golden cup” (Jeremiah 51:7); and sometimes the beauty of holiness is understood, as in Jeremiah’s words: “How the gold has become darkened; how the finest color has been changed” (Lamentations 5:1).

In sacred speech, the name “mud” sometimes signifies an abundance of earthly things, as in Habakkuk’s words: “Woe to him who multiplies what is not his! How long will he weigh down thick mud against himself?” (Habakkuk 2:6). At other times it signifies a filthy mind that savors wicked doctrine, as the same prophet says: “You made a way in the sea with your horses, in the mud of many waters” (Habakkuk 3:15). At other times it expresses the desire of a sordid will, as in the words: “Deliver me from the mud, that I may not become stuck” (Psalm 68:15).

Here, therefore, gold is understood as the splendor of holiness. As for mud, it may suitably be understood either as greed for earthly things, the contagion of perverse doctrines, or the filth of carnal pleasures. For when this leviathan subjects to himself through carnal pleasures those who appeared within the holy Church to shine with the radiance of righteousness, he plainly spreads gold beneath himself as mud.

This is now occurring daily in the hearts of many, as Paul says: “So that he may be revealed in his own time. For the mystery of iniquity…” and so forth (2 Thessalonians 2:6–7). Thus he now spreads gold beneath himself whenever he lays low the chastity of the faithful through the vices of the flesh, and whenever he disperses the understanding of the continent through impure desires.

It follows:

### VERSE 22

“He will make the deep sea boil like a pot.” — What is signified by the sea, if not the life of secular people? And what is signified by the deep, if not their high and hidden thoughts? He therefore makes the deep sea boil like a pot, because it is certain that at the extreme time of persecution he will strive to stir up the minds of the reprobate against the life of the elect [Col. 0503A].

It follows:

“And he will make it as when ointments boil.” — The reprobate are so deceived that, whatever they do, they suppose they are acting from the wickedness of unbelief on behalf of the truth of right faith; thus what they exercise from religious zeal seems to them to smell sweet. Hence the Lord says: “Everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God” (John 16:2).

Thus, just as a pot boils while they persecute cruelly, ointment smells sweet among them, because their minds, deceived by empty suspicions, imagine that they are rendering service to God.

It follows:

### VERSE 23

“After him the path will shine.” — The path is said to shine after leviathan because he illuminates with their wonders those whose hearts he penetrates.

It follows:

“He will regard the abyss as growing old” [Col. 0503B]. — The Psalmist shows that God’s judgments are called “the abyss,” saying: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Psalm 35:7). “Old age” is sometimes used to signify the nearness of the end. Hence the Apostle says: “What is becoming obsolete and growing old is near destruction” (Hebrews 8:13).

He considers the abyss to be growing old who thinks that heavenly punishment will at some point come to an end. This ancient one, therefore, fixes future punishments in the minds of persuaded sinners as though they had a definite limit, so that he may extend their sins without any end of correction.

Even now there are those who neglect to put an end to their sins and suppose that the future judgments imposed upon them will eventually have an end. Against them the Truth says: “These will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25:46).

It therefore belongs to the justice of the strict Judge that those should never be without punishment whose minds in this life never wished to be without sin. No limit to vengeance is granted to the wicked, because, for as long as he had the power, he did not wish to have an end to his crimes.

It follows:

### VERSE 24

“There is no power that can be compared with him.” — His power is said to be superior to all others upon the earth, because, although he fell beneath human beings by the merit of his action, he nevertheless surpasses the entire human race by the condition of his angelic nature, even though, through the abasement of his merits, he is subject to holy human beings.

It follows:

“He was made so that he would fear no one.” — By nature he was made so that he ought to have feared his Creator chastely—that is, with the fear “which endures forever and ever” (Psalm 18:10). But through his perversity he became such that he feared no one. He disdained to be subject to the one by whom he had been made, while he desired to rule over others and be subject to no one, saying: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:14).

It follows:

### VERSE 25

“He sees every lofty thing.” — That is, he looks down from a height upon all those whom he regards as placed beneath him. Because he strives through his intention against the Creator, he is shown to regard everyone as his equal. This also appropriately applies to his members, because all the wicked, exalted by the swelling of their hearts, despise all whom they see through the arrogance of pride. To them the prophet rightly says: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isaiah 5:21). And Paul says: “Do not be wise in your own estimation” (Romans 12:16).

It should be noted that this leviathan is represented by a bodily animal, and that pride of heart, when it extends outward as far as the body, is first indicated through the eyes. Those inflated by the arrogance of their swelling look down as though from a height; and the more they abase themselves, the higher they raise themselves. Hence Solomon says: “There is a generation whose eyes are lofty and whose eyelids are raised high” (Proverbs 30:13).

It follows:

“He is king over all the sons of pride.” — For this leviathan to fall into all the things mentioned above, he is struck down by pride alone. For it is written: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclesiasticus 10:15). Through it he fell; through it he laid low the human being who followed him. He attacked the salvation of our immortality with the weapon by which he extinguished the life of his own blessedness.

But the Lord inserted this statement into His teaching so that, when He called the pride of this leviathan the conclusion of all his evils, He might show what is worse than all evils. For no other evils would come into the open unless pride secretly bound the mind. Other vices attack only those virtues that stand opposed to them: anger attacks patience, gluttony attacks abstinence, and lust attacks continence. Pride, however, which we have called the root of the vices, is not content with destroying one virtue. It rises against every member of the soul and, like a universal and deadly disease, corrupts the whole body.

Against such people Scripture cries out: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). Against the plague of this sickness the Truth says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matthew 11:29).

Therefore, lest the members of this leviathan deceive us by performing wonders, the Lord showed an unmistakable sign by which he can be recognized, saying: “He is king over all the sons of pride.”

## BOOK THIRTY-FIVE

[Col. 0503]

[Col. 0503D] Therefore, after the Lord had shown His faithful servant how strong and crafty his enemy, leviathan, is, blessed Job responded to both matters. Against his monstrous strength he said:

## CHAPTER FORTY-TWO

[Col. 0505A]

### VERSES 1–2

“I know that you can do all things.” — Against his hidden schemes he added: “And no thought is hidden from you.” Hence he immediately reproaches him for these very things, saying:

### VERSE 3

“Who is this who hides counsel without knowledge?” — Leviathan hides counsel without knowledge. Although he is concealed from our weakness by many deceits, he is nevertheless revealed to us through the holy inspiration of our protector.

It follows:

“Therefore I have spoken foolishly, and of things that exceeded my knowledge beyond measure.” — All human wisdom, however sharp its insight, is foolishness when compared with divine wisdom. Blessed Job, therefore, would have believed that he had spoken wisely in what he had said, had he not heard the words of the higher Wisdom, in whose working everything that seems wise in us is foolish.

Hence Abraham says: “I will speak to my Lord, although I am dust” (Genesis 18:27). Hence Moses, instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, says: “I beg you, Lord, I am not eloquent; for yesterday and the day before, and from the time when you spoke to your servant, I am slow and hesitant of tongue” (Exodus 4:10).

It follows:

### VERSE 4

“Hear, and I will speak; I will question you, and you answer me.” — To hear God is to perceive our impulses rising beneath Him. To speak to God, who also knows the hearts of those who are silent, is not to speak with the voice but to yearn toward Him through the desires of the mind.

And because someone questions in order to learn what he does not know, for a human being to question God means to recognize oneself as ignorant in His sight. For God to answer means that He teaches through hidden inspirations the person who has humbly recognized his own ignorance.

He says: “Hear, and I will speak,” as though he were saying: “Mercifully receive my desires, so that, as your compassion receives them, greater desires may arise from you. I will question you”—that is, “From contemplating your knowledge, I recognize myself as ignorant”—“and you answer”—that is, “Teach me as I humbly recognize my own foolishness.”

It follows:

### VERSE 5

“I heard you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.” — By these words he plainly indicates that, just as sight is superior to hearing, so what existed previously differs from what comes afterward, and that the latter advances through scourging.

It follows:

### VERSE 6

“Therefore I reproach myself.” — The less anyone sees, the less displeasing he is to himself; and the more he perceives the light of greater grace, the more he recognizes himself as blameworthy.

It follows:

“And I repent in ashes and dust.” — As though he were plainly saying: “I take no pride in any gift of my Creator, because I recognize that, having been taken from dust, I must return to dust by the sentence of the death inflicted upon me.”

To repent in ashes and dust is, after contemplating the highest Essence, to recognize oneself as nothing other than ash and dust. Hence in the Gospel the Lord says to the reprobate city: “If the miracles that have been performed in you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes” (Luke 10:13).

It follows:

### VERSE 7

“And the Lord said to Eliphaz the Temanite: My anger and wrath are kindled against you and against your two friends, etc.” — As far as human judgments are concerned, the friends of blessed Job might be thought to have said many things more correctly than he did. But the Truth, bringing forth another rule from hidden things, says: “You have not spoken rightly before me, as my servant Job has.”

“Before me,” He says—that is, inwardly, where the lives of many are often displeasing, although outwardly they please human beings. Hence it is said of the elect: “Both were righteous before God” (Luke 1:6). Hence the Psalmist prays, saying: “Direct my way in your sight” (Psalm 59).

It should be noted that He does not say merely “as Job,” but “as my servant Job.” By mentioning him as belonging to Him in a special way through the designation of servitude, He shows that everything Job had said in his own defense was spoken not with rebellious pride but with humble truth.

But what does it mean that blessed Job is praised before the enemy, reproved in himself, and nevertheless preferred to his friends? It means that the holy man surpassed all others by the excellence of his merits, yet, precisely because he was human, he could not be without reproof before the eyes of God.

Blessed Job therefore believed that he was being scourged for guilt and not for grace. He is reproved because he supposed, in his intention, that he had been scourged for another reason; yet, despite the resistance of his friends, he was preferred by the judgment of the inward tribunal.

It follows:

### VERSE 8

“Now take for yourselves seven bulls and seven rams, and offer holocausts for yourselves” [Col. 0506C]. — Behold, the just and merciful God neither leaves sins without reproof nor abandons guilt without conversion. He first made the corruption of the wound known, and afterward indicated the remedies by which salvation was to be obtained.

But since we have said that the friends of blessed Job signify heretics—who offend God while attempting to defend Him—and since almighty God nevertheless often incorporates them into the body of the holy Church through knowledge of the truth, Job bore the type of the Church. The bulls express the neck of pride; the rams express leadership.

For concerning proud heretics it is said: “The counsel of bulls among the calves of the peoples” (Psalm 67:32). And because they drag the peoples who follow them along like flocks, they are sometimes called rams. Hence Jeremiah says: “Your leaders are like rams” (Lamentations 16).

To offer bulls and rams in sacrifice is to slaughter proud leadership through the humility of conversion, so that, once the neck of pride has been subdued, those who formerly attempted to lead may learn to follow by obeying.

Their pride is also rightly expiated by seven sacrifices, because heretics returning to the Church receive, through the sacrifice of humility, the gifts of the sevenfold grace of the Spirit. Those who have wasted away through the oldness of their arrogance are renewed by the newness of grace.

We hold this with unshaken faith: those whom the Spirit of grace fills, He perfects, granting them not only knowledge of the Trinity but also the activity of the four virtues—that is, prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice.

In sacred Scripture the number seven sometimes signifies secure rest, as in the words: “God rested on the seventh day” (Genesis 2:2). At other times it signifies the totality of the present age. Thus the ark of God went around the walls of Jericho for seven days with the trumpets sounding (Joshua 6:3–4). Hence the Prophet says: “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Psalm 118:164).

At other times the number seven signifies the universality of the holy Church, as in the Apocalypse: “John to the seven churches,” and the rest (Revelation 1:4).

Let the heretics who are outside, therefore, come and first mingle with the universality of the holy Church; then let them seek pardon for the guilt of their former arrogance. Let them offer seven sacrifices for their guilt, because they do not receive absolution from their guilt unless they are joined by the sevenfold Spirit of grace to the universal peace from which they had been cut off.

It follows:

“Job my servant will pray for you, and I will accept his face, so that your foolishness will not be charged against you.” — It is as though the returning heretics were plainly told: “Join yourselves through the humility of repentance to the universal Church, and through her—by whose prayers you are not worthy in yourselves to obtain it—seek pardon from me. When through her you truly learn to think rightly, you erase from before me the foolishness of your former wisdom.”

It follows:

“For you have not spoken before me as my servant Job did.” — The Lord stated this shortly before, and yet He added it again by repetition. What does this mean except that He confirms by repeating the judgment He had pronounced once before?

It follows:

### VERSE 9

“So the three friends of Job—Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite—went and did as the Lord had spoken to them, and the Lord accepted the face of Job” [Col. 0507C]. — It should be observed how carefully the order of the pardon granted, as previously prescribed, is maintained: in the sacrifices the Lord is reported to have accepted not their face but the face of blessed Job.

It follows:

### VERSE 10

“And the Lord also turned to Job’s repentance, when he prayed for his friends.” — As he recalls above, he had already been heard on behalf of his friends. Here, however, it is plainly shown that, when he repented also for himself, he deserved to be heard all the more quickly because he interceded devoutly for others.

The sacrifice of prayer is received more willingly when, in the sight of the merciful Judge, it is seasoned with love for one’s neighbor. Hence the Lord says: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matthew 5:44); and again: “When you stand to pray, forgive if you have anything against anyone,” etc. (Mark 11:25).

It follows:

“The Lord added everything that Job had possessed, twice over.” — He received twice as much as everything he had lost, because, through the compassion of the kindly Judge, the benefits of consolation overcome the loss caused by our testing. The trial afflicts less than the reward consoles.

Hence it is also said: “For a brief moment I abandoned you, but with great mercies I will gather you” (Isaiah 54:7). And again: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Psalm 93:9).

### MYSTICALLY

The holy Church now loses many of her own through the blows of temptation, but at the end of this age she will receive twice what belongs to her, when, after the Gentiles have been fully gathered in, everyone—including Judah, which will then be found—consents to run to the faith of the Church.

Hence it is written: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and so all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25). And the Truth says: “Elijah will come and restore all things.”

Or certainly, for the holy Church to receive twice as much at her end means that in each of us she will rejoice both in the blessedness of the soul and in the incorruption of the flesh. Hence the prophet says: “In their land they will possess twice as much” (Isaiah 61:2).

It follows:

### VERSE 11

“All his brothers and all his sisters, and all who had known him before, came to him, and they ate bread with him in his house, and they shook their heads over him” [Col. 0508B]. — Having been consoled by the gifts of divine compassion, he ought also to be restored by human affection, so that joys of consolation might answer him from every side, since the adversity of sorrow had torn him from every side.

In the eating of bread, love is signified; in the shaking of the head, astonishment.

### MYSTICALLY

His brothers and sisters come to the one who has been corrected when as many as are found from the Jewish people are converted to the faith. Since that people is joined to him by kinship, those who will be strong come to him with the proper joy of faith like brothers, while the weak come like sisters.

They eat bread in his house when, setting aside their observance of the letter that lies above it, they are nourished in the holy Church by the marrow of mystical speech, as by grain.

It is rightly said, “all who had known him before.” They had known him beforehand whom, during his passion, they had despised as though he were unknown. For no one who fully learned the Law was ignorant that Christ would be born. Their former knowledge and later ignorance are aptly and briefly represented by Isaac when his eyes had grown dim. While he blessed Jacob, he foresaw what would happen in the future, but he did not know who was standing before him in the present.

But behold, at the end of the world they come and recognize the one whom they had previously known. Behold, they eat bread in his house because in the holy Church they are nourished by the grain of sacred speech.

In the head, the principal part of the mind is understood, as the Psalmist says: “You have anointed my head with oil” (Psalm 22:5). Therefore, in this passage to shake the head means both to shake off the mind’s immobility and to draw near to knowledge of the faith with steps that abandon cruelty.

The head is shaken when the mind, touched by fear of the truth, is shaken from its insensibility.

It follows:

“And they consoled him concerning all the evil that the Lord had brought upon him.” — To console someone who has been struck in his grief is to rejoice with him after his affliction because pardon has been granted. For the more someone is seen to rejoice over the restoration of his neighbor’s salvation, the more he shows that he had grieved over its loss.

### TYPICALLY

They console Christ; they console the Church—those who recover from the error of their former unbelief and abandon the wickedness of life by which they resisted those who taught what was right. The subsequent progress of hearers is a great consolation for preachers. The transformation of the one who advances is the revelation of the one who speaks.

They come to console him after the scourges because, during the time of his passion, they despised the teachings of the faith and, having recognized him as a man from his death, disdained to believe him God. Hence the Lord says: “I waited for one who would grieve together with me, and there was none,” and the rest (Psalm 68:21).

At the end of the world, therefore, believing Hebrews will gather, and to the Redeemer of the human race, now revealed in the power of divinity like a restored Job, the vows of their offerings will be paid.

It follows:

“And each of them gave him one sheep and one golden earring.” — We believe that these words are truthfully stated according to the historical sense. But what is signified mystically by a sheep, if not innocence? And what by an earring, if not obedience?

By the sheep, a simple spirit is expressed; by the earring, an ear adorned with the grace of humility. It should be noted that the sheep is offered with the earring, and the earring with the sheep, because the ornament of obedience is always joined to innocent minds. The Lord attests this when He says: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (John 10:27).

He is said to have offered a golden earring so that love might shine in the obedience being presented; love surpasses all virtues, as gold surpasses the other metals.

But because no innocence and no true obedience can exist amid the manifold divisions of heretics, let those who come to knowledge of the faith offer a sheep, but one; let them offer an earring, but one—that is, let them come as people who remain innocent and obedient in the unity of the holy Church.

It follows:

### VERSE 12

“The Lord blessed the latter days of Job more than his beginning.” — We believe that these things happened historically; mystically, we hope that they will happen. For, insofar as it concerns the reception of the Israelite people, as the end draws near, the holy Church is consoled in the sorrow of the present age by the gathering of many souls.

She will be enriched all the more abundantly as it becomes more clearly known that the temporality of the present life is being driven toward its end. The Psalmist had seen the preachers of the holy Church being enriched by the blessing of the first age when he said: “They will still increase in fruitful old age, and they will be pleasing, so that they may proclaim” (Psalm 91:20).

It follows:

[Col. 0509D]

### VERSE 13

“And he had fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand she-asses. And he had seven sons and three daughters.” — When everything belonging to blessed Job was doubled, why were as many sons restored as had been lost?

He also added sons twofold, since afterward he restored ten in the flesh. The ten who had been lost he preserved in the hidden life of souls.

In these animals we can also understand the gathered universality of the faithful. Hence it is written: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet,” and the rest (Psalm 8:8); and again: “Your animals will dwell in it” (Psalm 67:11).

Let us recognize in the sheep the faithful and innocent peoples from Judah, formerly associated with the pastures of the Law. In the camels, those coming in simplicity from the Gentiles, who previously appeared exceedingly ugly under sacrilegious worship, as though deformed in their limbs, through the foulness of their vices.

Again, the oxen may be understood as Israelites, worn down as though by the yoke of the Law; the asses may signify the Gentiles, who, while bowing down to worship stones, served any idols with an animal-like understanding.

The holy Church, therefore, which in her beginnings, oppressed by countless temptations, lost either the Israelite people or many from the Gentiles—namely, those whom she was unable to gain—receives twice as much at the end, because within her the faithful from both nations increase in manifold abundance.

The yoked oxen may be understood as preachers; the she-asses may signify the minds of the simple. The holy Church receives twice as much because the holy preachers who, overcome by fear, once kept silent during her trial, and the minds of the simple who, conquered by terrors, were afraid to confess her truth, now raise their voices in confession of her truth with greater strength, in proportion to the weakness of their former fear.

Among secular disciplines the number one thousand is considered perfect because the square of the number ten produces a solid figure. Ten multiplied by ten makes one hundred, which is already a square figure, but a plane one. To rise in height and become solid, one hundred is again multiplied by ten, producing one thousand.

The number seven is considered perfect because it is completed from the first even and the first odd number. The first odd number is three, and the first even number is four; seven consists of these two, because, when its same constituent parts are multiplied, it rises to twelve.

The number six is perfect because it is the first number completed by its own parts: its sixth, its third, and its half, which are one, two, and three; together they make six.

In sacred Scripture, however, the number six is perfect because, at the origin of the world, the Lord completed on the sixth day the work that He had begun. The number seven is perfect in Scripture because every good work is performed through seven virtues, so that it may be completed in faith together with action.

The number ten is also perfect in Scripture because the Law is contained in ten commandments, and every fault is restrained by no more than ten words; moreover, as the Truth relates, the workers in the vineyard are rewarded with a denarius (Matthew 20:10). For three and seven are joined in ten.

The human being, who consists of soul and body, is contained in seven qualities. He flourishes in three spiritual qualities and in four bodily qualities. Yet the human being is rewarded with a denarius because, in the perfection of the heavenly homeland, our seven temporal qualities are joined to the three eternal ones, so that the human being receives contemplation of the Trinity.

Or certainly, there are seven virtues through which we labor in this life; when contemplation of the Trinity is given to us as their reward, the life of those who labor is rewarded with a denarius. Each perfected person also receives a denarius in this life when he joins faith, hope, and love to those same seven virtues.

The number one thousand is perfect because its designation signifies universality. Hence it is written: “The word that he commanded for a thousand generations” (Psalm 104:8).

Blessed Job therefore received fourteen thousand sheep because, when the perfection of the virtues is brought to both sexes in the holy Church, the number seven is doubled in her. He received six thousand camels because those who had previously perished through the foulness of their vices receive in her the fullness of good works.

The holy Church also receives a thousand yoke of oxen and a thousand she-asses because, after the falls of temptations, she takes up Israelites and Gentiles, the learned and the simple, to the summit of perfection.

He received seven sons and three daughters because he joins faith and love to the minds whom he generates through the seven virtues, bringing them to the highest perfection. Thus he rejoices more truly in his offspring, the more he considers that none of the virtues is lacking in his faithful.

It follows:

### VERSE 14

“And he called the name of the first Day, the name of the second Cassia, and the name of the third Cornustibii.” — By the sons of Job we understand the whole human race. Humanity shone like day by its creation, because its Creator sprinkled it with the brightness of innate innocence; but of its own will it fell into the darkness of sin. Hence it is said elsewhere: “He followed the shadow.”

Yet the merciful Creator, who had first powerfully created humanity for righteousness, later called it back from error even more powerfully by redeeming it.

And because many things must now be displayed that were not necessary in paradise—such as the virtue of patience, labor, instruction in doctrine, bodily discipline, perseverance in prayer, confession of sins, and an abundance of tears—and because the human being received the good of salvation from the very condition of his creation, the name of the second daughter, like “Cassia,” gives off a fragrance from merit.

Thus, because the first daughter appeared as Day through the dignity of creation, the second is Cassia through the fragrance of fortitude received from the grace of Redemption. Hence the same thing is said by the prophet to the coming Redeemer: “Myrrh and drop and cassia,” and the rest.

But because, in the third order, the human race is also restored through the resurrection of the flesh and taken up into that assembly of eternal praise, the third daughter is called Cornustibii.

What is expressed by Cornustibii, if not the song of those who rejoice? There the words that are written are truly fulfilled: “Sing to the Lord a new song,” etc. (Psalm 95:1).

It follows:

### VERSE 15

“And women as beautiful as the daughters of Job were not found in all the earth” [Col. 0511D]. — The souls of the elect surpass in the beauty of their splendor the whole human race that lives upon the earth according to human ways. The more they despise themselves by afflicting themselves outwardly, the more truly they are adorned inwardly.

Hence it is written: “The king desired your beauty” (Psalm 44:12); and: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within,” etc. (ibid., 14).

It follows:

“And their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers.” — Our Father grants women as well as men rights of succession, because among the strong and perfect He admits the weak and humble to a share in the heavenly inheritance.

Hence the Lord says: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John 14:2). Paul rightly indicates that these dwelling places are distributed according to merits when he says: “There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory” (1 Corinthians 15:41).

It follows:

**VERSE 16.** “Job lived after this one hundred and forty years, and saw his sons and his sons’ sons, to the fourth generation; and he died old and full of days.”

In Sacred Scripture, “full of days” is not readily said except of one whose life is praised by that same Scripture. He is empty of days who, however long he may have lived, spends the periods of his life in vanity. Conversely, he is called full of days whose days do not simply pass away as they perish, but are preserved with the just Judge as the daily recompense of good works, even after they have elapsed.

**MYSTICALLY.** If we multiply fourteen by ten, we arrive at the number one hundred forty. And rightly is the life of Holy Church reckoned as four multiplied by ten, because, while in some manner observing the Testament and living according both to the Decalogue of the Law and to the four books of the Gospel, it is extended to the summit of perfection.

Job is fittingly said to live after the scourges, because Holy Church too is first struck by the scourge of discipline and afterwards strengthened by the perfection of life. He sees sons to the fourth generation, because, in this age—which revolves through the four seasons of the year—he continually beholds offspring being born to himself through the mouths of preachers, even to the end of the world. If, when interpreting the dream of Joseph’s cupbearer, he understood three branches as the span of three days (Gen. XL, 12), why should not the four generations also signify the four yearly seasons?

Holy Church saw her sons when she first beheld the offspring of the faithful; she saw her sons’ sons when she recognized that other people too were being begotten by those same faithful into the faith. She also dies old and full of days, because, when the light follows, in recompense for her daily works, having laid aside the burden of corruption, she is transformed into the incorruption of the spiritual homeland. Through these passing times she produces what does not pass away. Hence it is said to the apostles: “Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life” (John VI, 27).

She is said to die because, when that contemplation of eternity has absorbed her, it utterly extinguishes her from this mutability, so that thereafter nothing in her remains in any way that could impede the sharpness of inward vision. Let us therefore believe that this death and this fullness of days were accomplished in blessed Job, that is, in one member of the Church, and hope that they will likewise be accomplished in the whole Church, so that the truth of what has happened may be maintained without nullifying the prophecy of what is still to happen.

[Col. 0513]

## ON SAINT MARTIN: TWELVE ANTIPHONS BY SAINT ODO

*(In Marrier, Bibliotheca Cluniacensis, p. 261.)*

**I.** Saint Martin foresaw his death long beforehand; he gathered his disciples together and foretold that his dissolution was near.

**II.** When suddenly he began to be deprived of bodily strength, then there arose the grief and mourning of all, the voice of those lamenting, and the united prayer: “Do not, shepherd, abandon your sheep.”

**III.** “We know indeed that you desire Christ, Father, but your rewards are secure; rather have mercy on us whom you are abandoning, Father.”

**IV.** “Lord, it is enough that I have struggled thus far; but as long as you yourself command, I will serve as a soldier. And if you spare my age, it is good for me; guard those for whom I am afraid.”

**V.** Fever forced his limbs, exhausted by illness, to serve the spirit. Reclining on his bed in that noble hair-shirt, and no longer deigning to look upon the earth, he yearned wholly toward heaven.

**VI.** “Let me,” he said, “look upon heaven, so that my spirit may be directed to the Lord. The enemy will find nothing in me, but Abraham’s bosom will receive me.”

**VII.** The saint departed at midnight on the Lord’s Day, and the citizens of heaven immediately came to meet him. Many heard voices on high; and he was shown to be purer than glass, whiter than milk, and was also shown in the flesh as a gem among priests.

**VIII.** Those who were present saw the glory of the glorified man. For the flesh that ashes had always covered shone so brightly that it displayed even in extinguished flesh a certain splendor of resurrection.

**IX.** A multitude of monks and virgins was present. These, possessing a special glory, wept especially, though they felt that there was more cause for rejoicing, if the force of grief admitted reason.

**X.** Martin’s obsequies should not be called a funeral but a triumph. For the dead shepherd led before him his flocks, which under his guidance had conquered the world and, following his body to the tomb, sang and wept.

**XI.** Martin, mighty with the sign, by the radiance of his virtues himself strikes back the stars. Alone he fulfilled the diverse achievements of many; therefore he has been joined to the apostles and prophets, in the peace of all the saints.

**XII.** “O truly blessed, O ineffable man, in piety, mercy, and charity! As he always flowed wholly in the Lord with the fullness of these entrails of compassion, so may he not fail us—may he not fail us forever.”

[Col. 0513]

## FOUR HYMNS OF SAINT ODO

### I. On the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood

*(In Marrier, Bibliotheca Cluniacensis.)*

God on high teaches that the guests of the banquet should be clean,  
and the Lord washed the feet of his servants.

From various gifts, rejecting many of them thereafter,  
he brought forth this one thing for all: grain and wine.

This he consecrates, this exceedingly great thing,  
which becomes small, though it is supremely exalted;

so little when received, so easy and ready;  
yet so sublime that it possesses the whole Godhead.

This alone suffices to cleanse the guilt of the world.  
Hence this gift is pleasing, which is made one from many.

Thus the body, made one from many, cleaves to the Head,  
and the Head in turn to it.

This kind, this one thing, is pleasing; this will endure forever.  
It is easy, pure, simple, and full of divinity.

### II. On Blessed Mary Magdalene

*[Ibid.]*

Praise, mother Church;  
praise the clemency of Christ,

who cleanses seven vices  
through sevenfold grace.

Mary, Lazarus’s sister,  
who committed so many crimes,

returns from the very jaws of Tartarus  
to the rewards of life.

After the scandals of wandering flesh,  
she becomes a phial from a cauldron;

transferred into a vessel of glory  
from a vessel of disgrace.

Sick, she runs to the Physician,  
carrying a vessel of spices,

and from manifold disease  
she is healed by the Physician’s word.

The piercing of a contrite heart,  
together with a river of tears,

and the work of piety  
releases the guilty woman from sin.

She saw Jesus rising victoriously  
from the dead;

she is the first to deserve the joys,  
because she will burn more than the others.

To the one [alone] God be glory  
for manifold grace,

who forgives faults and crimes [variant: punishments]  
and grants rewards. Amen.

### III. On Saint Martin, archbishop of Tours

*[Ibid.]*

King Christ, Martin’s glory,  
here is your praise, and he is yours.

Grant that we may honor you in him  
and him in you.

You who grant throughout the world’s regions  
that a gem of prelates may shine,

grant that his far-reaching merit  
may release those whom grievous sins oppress.

Behold, here is one poor and insignificant;  
he enters heaven rich.

The cohorts of heaven meet him;  
tongues, tribes, and peoples rejoice.

As did his life, his passage shines,  
splendid in heaven and on earth;

it is holy for all to rejoice;  
may this day be salvation for all.

Martin, equal to the apostles,  
cherish those who celebrate your feast.

You who wished your disciples  
either to live or to die, look upon us.

Now do what you once did:  
now [you] glorify the prelates;

increase the Church’s honor;  
strike down [or: banish] Satan’s deceptions.

You who three times conquered the realm of death,  
raise up those sunk in guilt.

As you divided the cloak,  
clothe us in righteousness.

That you may remember your former  
special glory [spiritual grace],

now aid the monastic order,  
already almost fallen. Amen.

### IV. Hymn in honor of Saint Martin, composed by Saint Odo in his final illness

*(In Mabillon, Annales, vol. III, Appendix, p. 712.)*

Behold, Martin’s splendid day shines forth,  
on which the humble man ascends, rich, into Abraham’s bosom,

and the choir of heaven stands before him in greeting:  
let us honor him with hymns.

Jesus is vehement praise, honor, and glory.  
For he adorns the heavens and illumines the fields,

emerging like another sun from the west.  
He gives this day its splendor [variant: its envy].

Here, while still young, he had imbibed devotion to the Lord,  
and could now receive nothing except him.

Full of signs from childhood into old age,  
he became renowned through faith itself.

While not yet wet with the water of the sacred font,  
he clothed the Lord with part of his cloak;

and, chilled, he makes himself cold that he may grow warm;  
may he now cover us with his merits.

Thrice mighty in virtue, he holds sway over death;  
he shines everywhere, wholly radiant with the titles of his signs,

so that there the name of Christ shines forth,  
as he is joined to the apostles.

By heavenly inspiration, at the fourfold hinge of heaven,  
peoples, tongues, and nations diligently celebrate him,

and in rivalry a stream flows toward his tomb:  
this honor befits Martin.

This day, Martin, fills fields and heavens;  
through you may it be healthful for those for whom it is celebrated.

May it be holy to rejoice; may this be a universal good,  
through you, illustrious Father.

You restore peace; here you also migrate to the stars.  
Now reconcile us through yourself with the Lord—

this work having been composed by Odo the servant  
as he departed from the world.

Have mercy, Lord, on those whom you have piously nourished,  
ever merciful, most merciful:

on Tetolon, your servant, and on your other servants;  
have mercy, O Martin.

[Col. 0517]

# SAINT ODO, ABBOT OF CLUNY: II. THE THREE BOOKS OF COLLATIONS

[Note: **The three books of Collations.** Manuscript copies do not agree concerning the title of these books. The *Victorianus* manuscript—that is, the manuscript of the Canons Regular of Saint Victor in Paris—which also makes one book out of the three by omitting several chapters, calls it *The Book of Collations of Dom Odo, venerable abbot of Cluny*. Consequently, we too were obliged to borrow for this work a title that was absent from the copy of Jacob Sirmond, which we followed. But after that edition had already been completed, another codex was sent to us from the monastery of Silviniacum, which clearly entitles the work *The Occupations of Saint Odo* and has the following verses at its beginning:

> Full of heavenly doctrine, Odo composed this little book,  
> Taking sayings of the Fathers and examples of many pious men,  
> And rightly knew it would be useful to many . . . .

Indeed, from this time another manuscript has also been found in the Martinian house, whose preface calls the work *The Collations of Blessed Odo, Abbot*, while the beginning of the first book, which follows continuously, calls it *The Occupations*, through a change in the title; it likewise adds these verses:

> Full of heavenly doctrine, Odo composed this little book,  
> Wandering through the flower-filled meadows of learned teachers.

Nor am I unaware that this work is still distinguished by other titles in other places. Antonius Possevinus calls it *Three Books on the Prophet Jeremiah*. This is not altogether inappropriate, as can be gathered from Book II of Odo’s Life, where John the Italian expressly says that he composed three little books from Jeremiah’s prophecy. Perhaps, if conjecture is permissible, the same book should be regarded as the one entitled *On Contempt of the World* in the *Deeds of the Bishops of Limoges*, as the following note will show.]

.

*(Bibliotheca Cluniacensis, from the edition of D. Marrier, p. 159.)*

## DEDICATORY LETTER

[Col. 0517A] To the lord and father Turpio, bishop, his own most lowly monk in the Lord.

[Note: **To the lord and father Turpio.** Bishop of Limoges, who was also called Turpius and Turpinus. Although some prefer Terpio—understood as “thrice pious”—to Turpio, as though the latter were derived from *turpitudo*, “deformity.” According to the *Deeds of the Bishops of Limoges*, Turpius, or Turpio, was of a very distinguished family, being the maternal uncle of Robert, viscount of Albuci. He honored Odo, abbot of Cluny, with great affection. At Turpio’s request, Odo composed the *Life of Saint Gerald* and the book *On Contempt of the World*.

For clarification of the book *On Contempt of the World*, it will suffice to add what John the Italian writes in Book II of the *Life of Saint Odo*, in these words:

> “When that bishop, namely Turpio, had in a certain way drawn out a long discourse for his own consolation concerning the dignity of the priesthood, it happened that they began to speak together about the state of the Church. Then Father Odo began to expound to him a mournful discourse about priests from the prophecy of Jeremiah. When this had been completed, that bishop began to ask him to write down the same discourse for him and arrange it in the form of a little book. In reply, our Father Odo brought forward a precept of the Rule stating that a monk may do nothing without the permission of his prior. The same bishop therefore went to the monastery for this reason, and because he was a companion and friend of the aforesaid Father, he immediately obtained from him what he wished. Then, at his command, he composed three little books from the prophecy of Jeremiah. Their text has already been spread through various Churches.”

How well all this agrees with the present books of the *Occupations*, or *Collations*, can easily be gathered from reading the letter alone.]

You remember, my lord, what you commanded me some time ago: since, with the order of affairs disturbed, you are almost always ready for departure, and cannot turn to the consolation of the Scriptures, like Moses to the tabernacle, when your books are absent, I was to gather from the sayings of the Fathers certain passages that would suit the character of the present time and, like a small daily ration or a scant refreshment, provide something for you to take along on the road.

You asked this of me once, twice, three times, and whenever it happened that I came into your presence; and you commanded it again. I marveled at the humility of a bishop, that one so great should request anything of so insignificant a man. I certainly marveled at your zeal, that a mind divided among so many concerns should seek so earnestly that song of Job which God gives in the night of tribulation. Yet I was amazed at how you could believe that I was capable of doing this. For although the lord abbot, prompted by a message from you, finally commanded it himself, I was conscious of my own ignorance and avoided even attempting what seemed impossible to me.

After the recent solemnity of Saint Martin had passed, Dom Abbot Berno [Note: **Dom Abbot Berno.** Berno, rector of the monastery of Baume, of whom Odo was a monk and disciple.] announced to me that he would immediately send me to you. But when he learned that I had still done nothing concerning the command I had received from you—or rather from him—he said: “I grant you fifteen days for doing what you have been commanded, so that you may not be ashamed to go to the lord bishop, neglecting his command.”

Pressed by this, I confess that I took up a writing tablet; but, dull and uncertain, I hesitated over what should be written and in what order the first and last matters should be arranged. Suddenly I remembered that complaint of yours which, at the first command, I had heard you compose with deep sobs concerning the condition of this life: namely, the perversity of wicked people, who continually grow worse and utterly despise ecclesiastical discipline, cruelly afflicting the weak; and finally, those who ought to have been devoted to divine service, but dedicate themselves entirely to empty glory and falsely serve the worship of God.

Concerning these people and others like them, whom, if I remember correctly, you were then lamenting, I wrote the material of this work. Throughout its course I tried to do what might console the dejection of the afflicted and somewhat restrain the curiosity of the wicked. I send you this little work, arranged however it may be, in fulfillment of your command, so that, if it should prove altogether without usefulness, it may nevertheless excuse me before you for disobedience.

The reader may pardon my presumption on account of so imperious a command. The author’s name, however, should be suppressed, lest, if the material is sordid, it should also be burdened by the lowliness of my name.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0519B] God, the author and judge of human beings, although he justly drove our race away from the happiness of paradise, nevertheless, remembering his goodness, softens the hardships of this pilgrimage with many benefits, lest the whole of what guilty humanity deserves should overtake it. But because we take excessive delight in these same benefits, by his providence this very delight of ours is frequently worn down, lest, clinging too closely to passing goods—which flow away in the same manner—we should unknowingly be drawn into the loss of inward salvation.

Thus we do not perceive how the body grows or how the appearance of that same body changes into old age. So too our mind, without our knowing it, is frequently bent away from a state of uprightness; and, while unaware, it grows old and departs from the form of religion, according to the saying: “They struck me, and I did not feel it” (Prov. XXIII, 35); and again: “Gray hairs were scattered upon him, and he did not know it” (Hos. VII, 9).

But again, lest we fail under the rebuke of the disturbance just mentioned, he sent into the world the sanctified Scripture, which cannot be dissolved, with greater grace, so that, as Peter says, it might shine upon the feet of our actions in the dark place of this life and, amid every adversity, supply patience and consolation, in accordance with Paul’s words.

If, therefore, there is anything that can keep a wise man even-tempered amid the storms of the world, I think it is above all the meditation of the Scriptures. For every principle by which we know either God or ourselves is contained in the divine books. In this we differ greatly not only from the other animals but also from every fool; and, as Solomon says, we have gone there where life is—that is, to knowledge of the Scriptures.

That life is in the Scriptures the Lord testifies when he says: “The words that I speak to you are spirit and life” (John XIV, 10). Scripture is also the mirror in which we now see divine mysteries in an enigma and can look upon what we ourselves are, so that there it may appear how much we advance in goodness or how much we fall short. There everything that destroys is disclosed, and everything that builds up is narrated; yet most people listen more willingly to buffoonery than to this paradigm of God.

To neglect sacred reading is like refusing light in darkness, shade in the heat of the sun, or medicine in sickness. This, I say, is the voice of God, which calls back those who desert him, saying through the prophet: “Turn back, returning sons” (Jer. III, 14); and again, calling back the adulterous wife contrary to the custom of men, he says: “Hear, prostitute, the word of the Lord” (Ezek. XVI, 33), and so forth.

To show that mortals have withdrawn from him exceedingly far—not in place, but in merit—he no longer addresses them as present through words, as he once addressed the fathers. Rather, through Scripture, as through letters, he recalls those who are far away and urges his deserters to remember their former friendship. These things have been prefaced to shake off our distaste for reading, since, if I may say so with your permission, we do not sufficiently hunger for the food of sacred reading.

## I

The whole purpose of that same Scripture is to restrain us from the wickedness of this life. For this reason it pierces our heart with its terrifying judgments as with certain goads, so that a person, driven by fear, may tremble and bring back to memory the divine judgments, which he easily tends to forget when distracted either by the pleasure of the flesh or by earthly anxiety.

For this purpose it declares that each one of us will receive on the day of judgment according to what he has done. When the Apostle testified to this, he added: “Knowing therefore the fear of the Lord, we persuade men” (II Cor. V, 11). Elsewhere: “Fear God and observe his commandments; this is the whole human being” (Eccli. XII, 13). These words show that the one who does not fear God has ceased to be human.

The purpose of that same Scripture is also to strengthen us to endure every adversity through hope of the happiness that follows the present misery, since we can recover heavenly joy only through earthly bitterness. Thus the hope of abiding joy may lighten the sadness of passing distress.

For this the Apostle says: “What is at present momentary and light produces an immeasurable weight of glory” (II Cor. IV, 17). Concerning hardships, Scripture says: “Human beings are born to labor” (Job V, 7). And when the Apostle was enumerating his tribulations to the disciples, he said: “You yourselves know that we are appointed to this” (I Thess. III, 3). Job likewise says: “A human being, full of many miseries” (Job XIV, 1). This is said because it is exceedingly impossible for anyone to pass through the time of his pilgrimage without sorrow.

Hence the Author himself said: “If these things are done in the green wood, what will happen in the dry?” (Luke XXIII, 31). He is the green wood, which the rottenness of sin did not corrupt, because he committed no sin. We, however, are, as Jude declares, “autumn trees, fruitless, twice dead, uprooted.” It is as though the Lord said:

“If I myself, who committed no sin, do not depart from this life without the fire of suffering, what must be thought of those who are held bound not only by original sins but also by actual faults?”

Yet, lest we go beyond measure into the evil of murmuring because of the hardships inflicted upon us by divine providence, or neglect to restrain our wickedness amid those very hardships, he threatens transgressors with eternal Gehenna, saying: “The death of sinners is most evil” (Ps. XXXIII, 21). And again, against the murmurers among the children of Israel: “Let their murmuring cease, lest they die” (Num. XX, 6). And again: “Some of them murmured, and perished by serpents” (I Cor. X, 10).

## II

Because of these three things, which this same Scripture especially announces—namely, the hardships we suffer here, the joy that follows those who have been corrected, and the damnation that the incorrigible will incur—Ezekiel testifies that he saw a book in which were written lamentation, a song, and woe.

By this book all the divine utterances are represented. Whatever commands us to tears and mourning is referred to as written in it as lamentation. But what does the order of the words itself signify? After lamentation there are song and woe, because after the miseries of this life either eternal joy will follow for the good and patient, or eternal damnation for the wicked and murmuring.

Hence the Savior said to his disciples: “In me you shall have peace, but in the world you shall have tribulation” (John XVI, 33). It is as though he said: “From the world you will have outwardly what oppresses by its violence; but from me let there be inwardly what refreshes by consolation.”

For these three reasons also it is said that the wheels shown in a figure to Ezekiel, representing the two Testaments, had stature according to their height and a terrifying appearance. Their stature signifies the condition of this life, alternating between adversity and prosperity. For this same Scripture, demonstrating the condition of that state as though by its stature, says: “All who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution” (II Tim. III, 12).

It also declares the height of heavenly rewards when it says: “But to as many as received him, he gave power to become the sons of God” (John I, 12). What is higher than becoming sons of God?

It displays a terrifying appearance when it says of the reprobate: “These shall go into eternal punishment” (Matt. XXV, 46). And again: “Their worm shall not die” (Mark IX, 45). What remains especially for the luxurious is that saying of Job: “All their sweetness is a worm” (Job XXIV, 20). What could be more terrifying than always to receive pains from the bites of worms and never to see them end?

[Col. 0522A] III

He also recounts the deeds of strong men who patiently endured many things, so that, when we hear them, we may judge nothing impossible for us on the path of uprightness. Hence blessed Job says: “You renew your witnesses against me” (Job X, 17). For God raises up as many witnesses against us as examples of patient people he sets before our impatience.

That we ought to be liberated from the pit of worldly misery with the help both of divine admonitions and of the examples of those who preceded us is signified by Jeremiah’s rescue: when he was to be lifted from the well, ropes with old rags were lowered to him.

The ropes are the Lord’s commandments, which bind us, as it were, when by their orders they restrain us from evil actions. The old rags are works of righteousness, with which the holy Fathers clothed themselves so as not to appear naked before the eyes above. “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. CXXXI, 9).

When these rags—that is, their examples—are sent down with the ropes of the commandments to drag us from the mud of the present life, they show that the commandments themselves are possible through the examples of the Fathers, lest the divine commandments seem hard to us.

For if the saying “Be patient in tribulation” (Rom. XII, 12) seems difficult, Paul comes forward, who is not merely patient but glories, saying: “I will gladly glory” (II Cor. XII, 9). Let us therefore be bound by the commandments as by certain ropes. But let the old rags also be present, so that what we fear we cannot do because of our weakness, we may trust to be possible through the examples of the Fathers.

It should certainly be noted how mercifully God moderates the words of the Scripture mentioned above. At one time he terrifies us with harsh exhortations; at another he revives us with gentle consolations. He mixes fear with encouragement and encouragement with fear; by the fears he declares, he inclines sinners’ hearts to humility, and by the consolations he recounts, he raises up humble sorrow, so that, while both are tempered around us by a marvelous art of instruction, we may be found neither despairingly terrified nor carelessly secure.

## IV

Lamentation—that is, hardship—is difficult to endure, because, according to the Apostle, “all discipline for the present does not seem to be of joy but of sorrow.” Song, however—that is, the joy that follows—is desirable, as he safely adds there, because it yields a most peaceful fruit to those exercised in righteousness.

Woe, on the other hand, is exceedingly fearful, because, as Paul says, “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. X, 31).

If what we suffer displeases us, let us consider our striker to be just and merciful. Because he is just, he strikes only justly, as in the saying: “Is God unjust, who inflicts wrath?” It is therefore exceedingly unjust to murmur against a just striking. Let us not murmur, lest we perhaps incur the woe he threatens.

Let us also consider that he is merciful, so that we do not believe ourselves abandoned by him, as fools do, concerning whom it is said: “They shall not endure in their miseries” (Ps. CXXXIX, 11). For the Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart.

Let us consider also that what we suffer on account of our own merit he turns, through marvelous kindness, toward our benefit. Attending to this, let us not flee the scourges but rather desire them as medicines for the soul.

A sick person willingly submits himself to the surgeon’s hands and eagerly drinks cups, however bitter, when he believes that by this means he will recover the benefit of health. Let us therefore not recoil from the hands of our physician, God.

Even if he prolongs the burning of tribulation, the sick person ought not to cry out, because he sees how deeply the corruption of vices lies hidden in the wounds and must be cut away. Nor should we, like the untamed, be stunned as though something unusual or new had happened, since from the first righteous man, Abel, to the last elect, all must necessarily be held under this condition.

Hence the prince of the apostles warned the faithful not to be surprised in the fervor of temptation as though something new had happened.

## V

The kinds of afflictions are as diverse as the different forms of guilt that the heavenly physician sees to be present in us; yet they are comprehended in four ways.

Sometimes a sinner is afflicted for past sins, as the man to whom it is said: “Behold, you have been made well; now do not sin, lest something worse happen to you” (John V, 14). This command teaches that he incurred the force of suffering on account of past faults.

Sometimes affliction occurs to prevent future sins, as happened to Paul, who, lest he be exalted, received a thorn in the flesh. Certain ancient teachers said that this was a headache.

Sometimes a person is struck so that, when unexpected deliverance follows danger, the power of God the Savior may be loved more ardently. In such a striking, the grace of merit increases, as strength advances through patience. This was fulfilled in blessed Job, who was first praised in such a way and afterwards rewarded in such a way.

Sometimes, however, these three kinds converge simultaneously in a single person, so that through affliction past sins are punished, future sins are prevented, and praise of God the Deliverer is kindled by the removal of danger.

The fourth kind occurs when someone is struck in the present in such a way that he is also punished in the future. This happens only to those whose minds tribulation does not convert. Of such people is the voice of the complaining God: “In vain I struck your sons; they received no discipline” (Jer. II, 30). The wretched Antiochus and Herod incurred this kind.

For our being subject to diverse faults—to which, of course, diverse punishments are due—whether through ignorance, weakness, or sometimes presumption, does not come to us from the condition of nature but from the fault of the first transgression.

## VI

After our first parent became an adversary of the Creator through disobedience, he bent himself and all his offspring beneath this heavy yoke, so that it was truly said: “Human life upon earth is a temptation” (Job VII, 1).

Unwilling to be subject to divine commands, he prostrated himself beneath his own necessities. Free servitude had exalted him so greatly that, if he were subject to one alone, he would possess all things as subject to himself. But by raising the neck of his heart, captive freedom cast him down so far that he suffers much even from little worms and, what is more miserable, from himself.

Moreover, that great honor with which he was endowed among the other bodily creatures—namely, rational intelligence—has been so dulled in him that, although he ought to rule over every visible creature, he is now commanded to live by the example of the ant: “Go to the ant, you sluggard” (Prov. VI, 6).

The mind, which through its unstable mutability lost the one being sufficient for it, namely God, is now varied by different desires and seeks here and there, with greedy delight, something in which it may find rest. But because it was created to desire God alone, after it withdrew from him it finds nothing sufficient for it until it returns to him.

Hence it now varies among different affections, so that, when it cannot be satisfied by the nature of things, it may at least be filled by the variety of things themselves. Overcome by weariness, nature is led from thought to thought; it desires what it had rejected and rejects what it had desired. By being placed now in one thing and now in another, it plainly shows that it depends on something else.

Its first condemnation, as Augustine says, is the dreadful depth of ignorance, which gives birth to manifold loves of evil and vain things. Through these, vain joys, luxury, and countless similar desires are pursued; from them grow biting cares, disturbances, sorrows, fears, and other such things. These sprout even in infants, so that, if they are left to do what they wish, they scarcely ever arrive at anything good.

Against these tendencies, the instruction of teachers is divinely provided, so that depraved desire may be restrained and the desire for good may somehow be encouraged—if indeed, in accordance with Daniel, some teacher can still be found who instructs everyone in righteousness.

For in this age teachers more often form people contrary to the Apostle, choosing worldly things, whereas Job, although a Gentile, sanctified even his adult sons so that they did not sin even in their hearts.

## VII

Why should I say much about such evils that cause injury? If you consider carefully, you will find that even everything we do for the sake of health in this life is mixed with punishments and miseries.

Is it not misery to serve the corruption of the flesh in necessary and permitted matters? The same flesh demands clothing against the cold, food against hunger, and coolness against heat. The body’s health is guarded with great care; yet, even when guarded, it is lost, and when lost, it is restored only with great labor.

And even when restored, it is always uncertain, since the body produces so many diseases from itself that not all of them are named even in the books of physicians, and some are scarcely cured without bitterness.

Is it not also misery that a beloved friend can be offended by suspicion? We fear enemies and are not secure concerning them. Yet, so that we may not seem suspicious, we often speak to them as though they were friends. Again, while trying to be cautious, we often receive the sincere words of our neighbors—perhaps people who love us greatly—as though they were the words of an enemy. And we who wish never either to be deceived or to deceive, through our caution, more gravely er- [lacuna].

What, then, is this if not the misery of human life? Human beings have become so accustomed to their afflictions that they regard them not as hardships but as pleasures.

Having lost the heavenly homeland, they delight in the exile into which they have been driven.
