They are weighed down by cares, yet do not consider how grievous it is that the multiplicity of those very cares suffocates the mind, as it is written: “The earthly habitation weighs down the sense that thinks of many things” (Wis. IX, 15).

They are deprived of inward light, yet wish to endure their blindness in this life for a long time. Although countless deaths threaten them meanwhile through daily accidents, they nevertheless prefer to live for a long time under fear of so many deaths rather than, by dying once, fear none thereafter.

Because they presumed to transgress the command of the Creator, they rightly came to this failure of their own condition: since they preferred to their Creator the pleasure they had in external things, they now feel in those things and in themselves the hardships that, when they despised God, they foolishly thought were pleasures.

## VIII

To set forth something also concerning those things that come from outside, it must be understood that some things which we suffer come from God—namely, scourges—as in the case of Lazarus. Others come from our neighbors: persecutions, losses, or insults—as in the case of the apostle Paul. Others come from the ancient enemy, namely various temptations—as in the case of Job. Whether adversity comes through a human being or through the ancient enemy, it is nevertheless measured out by God according to our merit. For the condition of the world is disturbed in accordance with our merit, and open scourges of punishment emerge from the hidden insolence of hearts.

The Judge and Lord himself enumerates these punishments, saying: “Nation will rise against nation” (Luke 21:10), and so forth. For, as is said in the homilies, we turn everything that we have received for the use of life toward the use of guilt: human peace toward empty security; the health of our bodies toward the practice of vices; abundance not toward necessity but toward excess. We compel the very serenity and pleasantness of the air to serve our love of earthly pleasure.

It is therefore just that everything should strike us together—everything that had together been wickedly subjected to our vices—and that we who have sinned in all things should be struck in all things, so that, just as we formerly possessed so many unharmed joys in the world, so afterward we may be compelled to experience from it an equal number of torments. Hence it is said in the Book of blessed Job: “Pain does not come forth from the earth” (Job 5:6). This means that our evils demand that we be struck by insensible things.

For behold, the awaited rain is held back from the parched earth, and the darkened air is dried up while the sun burns. The sea rages with swelling storms: it destroys some whom it has taken aboard for crossing, while it denies others the journey they desire. The earth, too, consumes the seeds entrusted to it. In all these things it is plainly shown what is written about the Lord: “The whole world will fight on his behalf against the senseless” (Wisdom 5:21). This happens whenever, as punishment for sinners, the elements wage war against them, as it is likewise said: “Fire, hail, famine, and death—all these were created for vengeance”; the teeth of beasts and the attacks of scorpions, crushing and scourges.

Yet “pain does not come forth from the earth,” because the punishment which is stirred up from an insensible thing for our affliction does not arise from that creature which strikes, but from the one who, by sinning, extorted the power to strike. Hence it is likewise written: “I am the Lord, creating evil” (Isaiah 45:7). No evils, in fact, subsist as natures. They are therefore not created by the Lord; rather, he asserts that he creates evils because the things he made well, but which we desire wrongly, he turns into scourges that seem harsh and evil to us.

Hence it is that a human being dies from the poison by which the serpent lives. Hence it is that food and drink themselves, taken immoderately, weaken bodies, bring on premature old age, and even cause death, as Scripture likewise says: “The one who is temperate adds to life” (Sirach 37:34).

But God, seeing that we love perversely the things he gives us, rather than loving him who is the giver, mercifully strikes us through the things we prefer to him, so that we may recover to his love all the more quickly the more fully we have perceived that the things we desire are filled with sorrows.

Nor are we wrongly delighted only by external things. For, to come to ourselves, we frequently misuse the very members given to us by God, the good craftsman, for good purposes: our eyes, for gazing lustfully. Through them, death enters our souls. Whenever a desirable appearance presents itself to those same eyes, Adam has, as it were, the forbidden tree before his eyes. The tongue is ready to utter a lie, construct deceit, or practice quarrels; the feet are ready to run toward evil; the senses, because of the color of gold, pervert sound judgment.

And, not to proceed through every instance at length, we are injurious to God not only through the things he forbade, but also through the things he permitted. Yet a human being ought to possess divine protection within himself, lest he suffer in the body a fall which, through desiring evil, he does not fear suffering in the heart. Therefore it is fitting that, either in our proud spirit, we be compelled by God’s permission to experience many things that distress us, or that, in the delicate flesh which we frequently place before its Creator, we humbly feel his judgment.

## IX

From the malignant enemy we suffer in as many ways as he persists in our deceptions, being subtle by nature and perpetually tireless through malice. The Lord discloses to blessed Job all his contests of evasion and his schemes: what he seizes by crushing, what he circles around while lying in wait, what he terrifies by threats, what he entices by persuasion, and what he breaks by despair. He begins by saying: “Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you,” and so forth. All these matters are revealed more fully in the exposition of those words.

Here, however, only this seems worth recalling: in general, he strives to do to everyone what he did to the first human being. He seeks to tear the words of God from their hearts and to implant his own blandishments, which he deceitfully suggests. He persuades them to forget the punishments threatened by God and urges us to do what he holds out to us.

Then he said: “You will be like gods” (Genesis 3:5). Now he says: “Appear exalted in this world” (Job 40:5). Then he said: “You will certainly not die” (Genesis 3:4). Now, pretending that God is merciful, he promises impunity for crimes.

But we, who have learned from the experience of the first human being how strictly the Judge strikes sinners, must fear the threatening sentence of that same Judge and stand more cautiously and firmly against the deceit of that same enemy, paying particular attention to Job’s greater declaration: “I feared all my works, knowing that you would not spare the sinner” (Job 9:28). The Psalmist likewise says: “Cursed are those who turn away from your commandments” (Psalm 118:21).

## X

He lies in wait for each person according to the vices suited to that person. First he observes each one’s disposition, and then he sets traps of temptation close to that disposition. He would not easily capture people if he offered rewards to the lustful, or prostitutes to the avaricious. Nor would he attack the gluttonous through the glory of abstinence, or the abstinent through the weakness of gluttony. Nor would he seek to capture the meek through the pursuit of combat, or the irascible through the terror of fear.

Rather, so that he may prevail more effectively in his deception, he tests each person through the vice by which, from the quality of that person’s character, he knows that the person will consent more quickly. Hence it is written: “The heat is divided over the earth” (Job 38:24). For, cunningly bringing the heat of temptation upon individuals in this life, he divides the heat, as it were, while hiding traps corresponding to their character.

Among those subject to his will, he enjoys a kind of security, ruling over their hearts with unshaken power like a proud king. But if someone’s mind grows warm with desire for the Creator, if that person remembers the grace of the Redeemer and is ashamed to be held captive by vices, then, when the same enemy sees that he is despised and that the slave whom he formerly possessed is resisting him, he immediately rouses himself to every art of temptation. To prevent the one whom he possessed from being freed from his dominion, he struggles with manifold deceit.

Hence it is written concerning those who turn back to the heart: “Let those who curse the day curse him, who are ready to awaken Leviathan” (Job 3:8). To curse that same enemy is to execrate the sins he suggests. But whoever does this awakens Leviathan, who, as has been said, sleeps in the hearts of the wicked as though quiet and drowsing.

Therefore whoever, visited by God, desires to do what belongs to God provokes Leviathan to battle against himself and inflames his malice through his conversion. He does not greatly disturb just anyone who is wicked, since he sees that such people serve him not only through evil deeds but also through the very good works that they do insincerely. But he sets innumerable traps for those who flee to God.

## XI

To any wicked person he openly suggests any evil and, as to familiar associates, insinuates iniquities more plainly, so that they knowingly do what they do not fail to recognize as evil. To the good, however, as though they were strangers, he secretly insinuates what he cannot introduce openly, bringing it in covertly, so that those who refuse to consent to evil may either be lukewarm in good works or exceed proper measure through excessive zeal.

He often harms such people more severely through his agents than through himself: through the wicked, he either provokes the good to evil or obstructs them in doing good. Hence the prophet says: “Our enemies were swifter than the eagles of heaven” (Lamentations 4:19).

He plunges all whom he overcomes more violently through three vices: some through pride, by which they exalt themselves; others through lust, by which they serve their pleasures; and others through malice, by which they burden their neighbors. Hence he is also called by three names derived from these three activities: a bird, Behemoth, which means “beast,” and Leviathan, which means “dragon.”

Among those whom he elevates to pride on account of spiritual or temporal riches, he is a bird. Among those whom he weakens into lust, he is a beast. Among those whom he inflames to the malice of harming others, he is a dragon. Among those whom he plunges through all three together, he is at once beast, dragon, and bird.

Nevertheless, his greatest strength lies in lust. Hence it is said to blessed Job: “His strength is in his loins” (Job 40:11), evidently with reference to males. “And his power,” with reference to females, “is in the navel of his belly” (ibid.). Here it must be noted that his strength is not said to be in the loins or navel of those who are overthrown, but in the loins and navel of the devil himself, because, as is stated in Book 32 of the *Moralia*, those who succumb to him through lust properly become his body.

## XII

Yet in this lust he plunges no one as far as consent unless that person has first fallen through pride in the sight of God. The first human being demonstrated this in himself: after he sinned through pride, he immediately became ashamed of his genital members. Because he had despised God through pride, he immediately suffered combat from the flesh subjected to him.

Hence the prophet says: “The arrogance of Israel will answer to his face” (Hosea 5:5)—that is, by the merit of hidden pride, he is permitted to fall into open lust. To show that lust burst forth as the result of pride, he says: “The spirit of fornication is among them” (ibid., 4). For if the spirit of pride is held down beneath God, the flesh is not unlawfully raised above the spirit.

Therefore, whoever seeks heavenly things and is afterward overthrown by pleasure should not judge that he was defeated only when he was openly overcome. For he certainly fell into the gulf of guilt before God’s eyes at the moment when, exalting himself beyond what he ought, he secretly swelled with pride.

## XIII

Malice, then, belongs to the violent. Pride and lust, however, belong both to the violent themselves and also to others who often appear meek. For these two vices commonly flourish even in beggars and the poorest people. Pride lifts up the spirit, while lust corrupts the flesh.

Hence that wicked spirit is also said to sleep under a shadow and in the secrecy of a reed, and in damp places. For he first causes those whom he deceives to grow lukewarm toward the charity of Christ. Then, through pride—signified by the reed, which shines outwardly but is empty within—he subjects them to himself. Finally, through the genital members, understood as damp places, he casts them down into shamefulness.

Certainly, whoever wishes to overcome either these two or any other of his devices should despise him at the first suggestion. That suggestion is his head. This head is easily crushed by the foot of virtue belonging to any one of the faithful, if the first suggestion is rejected. Hence God says to that same enemy concerning every diligent soul: “She herself will crush your head” (Genesis 3:15).

His tail, however, is the completion of the deed, concerning which it is written: “He tightens his tail like a cedar” (Job 40:12). A cedar, once cut down, hardens into stone. He tightens his tail like a cedar because, if his head—which is the seductive suggestion—is once received into the heart, he thereafter rules that heart as though by right and binds it almost insolubly through a violent habit.

Hence some people strive to flee their sins but cannot escape them even while struggling to do so. For the fire of his persuasion, once received, burns more intensely in proportion as each person has made himself more yielding to consent within the vice.

But since no one in this flesh is granted to avoid being touched by the heat of his persuasion, it remains that, scorched by his evil blasts, the mind should turn without ceasing to the aid of prayer or confession. The flame of his suggestion is quickly extinguished by a flood of tears, and humble confession effectively strikes down his deceits as though they had been exposed.

## XIV

Since we are likewise going to relate some things concerning what neighbors suffer from neighbors, it seems appropriate first to recall the two generations of human beings: namely, the wicked and the good. Each person may then test to which generation he belongs when he recognizes to which of these generations the works he performs belong.

There are therefore two generations of human beings, which began from Adam’s two sons, Cain and Abel, and which continue until the last people who will be born, sometimes separately and sometimes mixed together.

Concerning the generation of the good, which begins with righteous Abel, it is said: “You are a chosen race” (1 Peter 2:9). And again: “The generation of the upright will be blessed” (Psalm 111:2). Elsewhere: “The Lord is in the generation of the righteous” (Psalm 13:6).

Concerning the generation of the wicked, which begins with Cain, it is said: “A crooked and provoking generation” (Psalm 77:8). And again: “A generation that did not direct its heart” (ibid.). And this: “It is a nation without counsel” (Deuteronomy 32:28). For what is more without counsel than not to foresee, as follows there, the things that are last?

The nation of the good has its city, Jerusalem, of which it is also a citizen: part of it already reigns in heaven, while part of it is still traveling here as an exile. It also has Christ as its humble king, of whom it is said: “Behold, your king comes to you, meek, sitting upon a donkey’s colt” (Zechariah 9:9).

That generation of the wicked likewise has its city, Babylon: part of it has been condemned in hell, while part of it is still occupied in the service of iniquity. It also has the devil as its proud king, concerning whom it is said: “He is king over all the sons of pride” (Job 41:25).

## XV

In the two human beings from whom these generations arose, what their followers would do has been made clear through provident arrangement. Let us first speak of Cain, who was Adam’s firstborn—for, as the Apostle says, “the spiritual was not first, but the natural” (1 Corinthians 15:46).

Cain himself was a farmer, and his followers seek earthly things with all their desires. They have their good here, although it is mixed with many hardships, and they rejoice in possessing that good. But what kind of joy can exist in such pleasures and possessions?

Cain offered a sacrifice to God, but not sincerely; so these people hold the faith, at least in words. They often do many good things, but they stain them either by mixing in evil or, like Cain, through hatred of their brother. They give to some and rob others; they gather wages, but, as it is written, they place them in a pierced purse, since for those gifts they seek either praise from human beings or the happiness of the present life from God.

Concerning them the prophet says: “They bring sacrifices into the depths” (Hosea 5:2)—that is, through whatever good works they seek the things that are below. For if they sought heavenly things, they would raise their sacrifices on high.

## XVI

Cain killed his brother; these people afflict their neighbors through losses or, insofar as they are able, kill them through their example. Hence it is written: “Because of the multitude of oppressors they will cry out” (Job 35:9).

Those whose wicked perversity is displeasing are rightly called oppressors—not only those who seize external goods, but also those who strive to dissipate our interior life through the example of a corrupt life. For the one who inflicts violence upon our conduct by living badly brings us a heavier oppression than the one who violently imposes losses upon our possessions.

Such a person is shown by the Lord’s words to be not only an oppressor but also a murderer. For he says of the devil: “He was a murderer from the beginning” (John 8:44)—that is, from the time when the human being whom he envied came into existence.

Observe how John describes the kind of murder. The devil did not come to the human being armed with a sword or girded with iron. Clothed in the serpent, he spoke to the woman, and through her he poisoned the man. By listening to him they died. The devil sowed a word and killed.

Therefore do not think that the person who persuades another to evil either by example or by word is not a murderer; for if he persuades his brother, he kills him. Hence Ishmael’s play with Isaac is considered by his mother not play but mockery, and by the Apostle is called persecution.

## XVII

God himself had forbidden Cain to kill his brother, but Cain scorned listening. Later, when he was questioned so that he might have an opportunity to repent, he refused to confess. Nor are such people unlike him: they knowingly do whatever has been forbidden and scorn what has been commanded.

You may see them committing every vice with shameless presumption and—something which, according to blessed Gregory, is more serious than any sin—even taking pride in their crimes after committing them, as it is written: “They rejoice when they have done evil” (Proverbs 2:14).

In such people, as in Cain, pride grows through practice, so that they do not even think that this vice exists in them, although they are full of it. Was there not immense pride in Cain when, questioned, he answered: “Am I my brother’s keeper?” (Genesis 4:9).

Thus pride is generated in the mind as darkness is generated in the eyes. The farther darkness spreads, the more intensely it obscures sight. In the same way, as this vice gradually grows, it separates the eye of the mind from spiritual understanding, so that the captive soul can suffer it but cannot see it in itself.

Because a soul that has once fallen voluntarily is never permitted to lie where it first fell, but plunges into more serious destruction, sinking more deeply the farther it withdraws from the humility of the Creator, such people are therefore blinded by God’s just judgment, so that they have a hard and insensitive heart toward his commandments.

Hence the Psalmist says: “His judgments are removed from his sight” (Psalm 10:5). Isaiah says: “Blind the heart of this people.” In contrast, it is said of the humble: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful” (Proverbs 28:14).

Through this hardness—which they incur because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God by observing his commandments—they are destroyed in such a way that they lose innocence from the heart, truth from the mouth, justice from their deeds, continence from the flesh, and the religion of faith from their understanding.

God disdains to be worshiped with pride. Thus these people, deservedly abandoned in their uncleanness on account of pride, are permitted to be deceived by demonic suggestions until they even slide into unbelief.

The Psalmist, showing how these defects are gradually constructed in them by the same evil spirits, speaks through the voice of those destroying Jerusalem: “Empty it, empty it, down to its foundations” (Psalm 136:7). Faith is the foundation, because good works are built upon it. Therefore, for perverse spirits to empty the fortress of virtue down to its foundation is, after overturning the practice of a good life, also to dissipate the strength of faith from human hearts.

Hence Jeremiah says: “They have defiled you to the crown of your head” (Jeremiah 2:6); that is, beginning with external deeds, as though with the lower members, they have proceeded in defiling all the way to the height of faith, which is the foundation of every virtue.

## XVIII

Such people may perhaps be unwilling to hear that they have lost the faith. But should those who persecute their neighbors be said to possess the faith, when the teacher of the nations says: “Whoever neglects the care of his neighbors has denied the faith” (1 Timothy 5:8)?

Certainly, it is worse to oppress brothers than to neglect their care. How, then, will the Judge of human beings condemn those who take away the food of the poor, acquired by their sweat, in order to prepare food for dogs or horses? He will cast into eternal fire those who do not feed the hungry.

Father Augustine also says in his *Letter on the Epistle of Saint John*: “Christ came in the flesh for the sake of charity alone; therefore whoever does not have charity denies that Christ came in the flesh.”

There are many things that demonstrate that certain people established in the Church are unbelievers. Many receive the person of the powerful in such a way that, to gain his favor, they deny the truth in the case of their neighbor. And what is truth except Christ, who says: “I am the Truth”? (John 14:6.)

John was put to death not after being questioned about his confession of Christ, but about the truth of justice. Therefore, whoever denies the truth so as not to offend a powerful person—if John died for Christ precisely because he incurred death for the truth—undoubtedly denies Christ, since, in order not to offend a powerful person, he is silent about the truth.

Behold: after these things, he is a Christian in the eyes of human beings; but if he is strictly judged before God, he is no longer one. In that same book many things are also said about ministers of the Church, through which they are shown to imitate Balaam and Jezebel and to be joined to the members of Antichrist.

## XIX

To come to something in which the followers of Cain more clearly reveal that they have acted in a similar way, Cain, as has been said, refused to listen when God warned him. These people despise God’s servants and rulers—indeed, they despise God himself through them, as is shown by his own words: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke 10:16).

He also granted these rulers, in the person of blessed Peter, the power of binding and loosing, and confirmed it in this way when he said elsewhere: “Concerning every matter whatever two of you agree upon on earth, it will be done for them by my Father” (Matthew 18:19).

Perhaps they therefore despise either the excommunications imposed by pastors to restrain the malice of the wicked or their admonitions because they criticize the pastors’ lives. This certainly provides a great scandal for those who mock them.

But Christ, the pastor and bishop of our souls, must not be despised. He is heard and despised in them, and, foreknowing the future, he confronts the rashness of those who despise them when he says: “Whatever they tell you, observe and do” (Matthew 23:3).

To extend the point: who was worse than Caiaphas, who prophesied about Christ? The holy Evangelist took care to show how he deserved the prophecy, saying: “Since he was high priest, he prophesied” (John 11:51).

Saul, an impious and rejected king, had ordered that no one should eat until the victory had been completed. Jonathan, unaware of the order, tasted a little honey, and immediately divine favor was withdrawn to such an extent that the victory was entirely interrupted. God made his indignation public at that time so that, throughout every age thereafter, it might be understood how greatly he is offended by contempt for rulers.

Moreover, Judas the traitor drove out demons with the other disciples of Christ, as is reported in the Book of the Letters of Saint Gregory and in Saint John Chrysostom’s sermon on the cross.

Thus Caiaphas prophesied on account of the honor of his high priesthood; and God so severely avenged Saul’s command, although it had been disregarded in ignorance, that Jonathan incurred the sentence of death unless he had been freed by the authority of the whole people. Demons were driven out by Christ’s accomplice himself out of reverence for the divine name.

Since these things are so, let those who despise pastors even when they live without the faith of Christ consider what they are doing. To put it this way, they are more audacious than demons.

## XX

Even if pastors are blameworthy, as is discussed in Book 25 of the *Moralia*, subordinates must take great care not to presume to judge their lives. They have God as their judge. Through teachers he judges the lives of the people, but by himself he examines the deeds of teachers.

The subordinates whom teachers either neglect or are unable to examine in the present life will unquestionably be reserved for his judgment. He indicates that prelates are to be judged by him alone when, with his own hand, he overturned the seats of those who sold doves.

If rulers are such men, subordinates should accuse only themselves, and not the rulers, because it is certainly their own fault that they are subjected to such people. For it is written: “I will give you kings in my wrath” (Hosea 13:11). And again: “God makes a hypocrite rule on account of the sins of the people” (Job 34:30).

If, then, while God is angry, we receive rulers according to our merits, we gather from their conduct what we should think of our own judgment or what sort of merit we possess.

Even if the life of teachers is rightly criticized, subordinates ought to endure them, even when they displease them. But this must be carefully observed: do not seek to imitate someone whom you must revere, nor refuse to revere someone whom you disdain to imitate.

A subtle path of uprightness and humility must be maintained, so that the blameworthy deeds of teachers may displease subordinates, while their minds do not depart from preserving the reverence due to the office of teacher.

Subordinates should nevertheless humbly suggest what displeases them, if perhaps what is objectionable in their prelates can be corrected. The things we feel should therefore be spoken freely, but what we say should be expressed with great humility, lest, by putting forward upright intentions arrogantly, we fail to act uprightly.

That teachers should not be reproached by subordinates was well represented by the ark of the covenant, which had been tilted by oxen that were kicking and signified the rulers. Uzzah, the Levite, believing that it was about to fall, wished to set it upright, and immediately received the sentence of death, being struck in the shoulder—the shoulder by which, according to the command of the Law, he ought to have carried it. For when subordinates lay a hand of submission against prelates whose commands they ought to bear, they are rejected from the lot of the living.

## XXI

Christ baptizes, as God the Father of John the Baptist testifies, saying: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending, he is the one who baptizes” (John 1:33). Baptism is therefore not better when administered by the hands of any holy person than when administered by the hands of a sinner, because, whatever the baptizer may be, it is Jesus who baptizes.

The same must be understood of the ministry of the holy altar: whether the priest is just or unjust, Christ himself consecrates the offering through his hands. As John explained in his homily on Judas’s betrayal, Christ himself is now present; it is not the priest himself who consecrates Christ’s body, but Christ himself through the priest.

For just as the voice of God at the beginning of the world once commanded the earth to bring forth fruit each year, and that voice continues always to effect generation, so the same voice of the man Jesus once said at the supper: “This is my body, and do this in remembrance of me.” But until, as the Apostle says, he comes to judge, this voice fulfills the efficacy of that reality throughout the entire Church.

It may indeed happen that the one who consecrates is another Judas, to whom the king says: “Friend, how did you come in here?” (Matthew 22:12). Nevertheless, he who does not lie will do what he promised.

From this, therefore, each person may understand indirectly that the force and weight of excommunication, or the weight of admonition, whoever the person may be through whom it is carried out, must be measured by the majesty of God, by whose authority the sentence is imposed.

## XXII

According to the Apostle, the spiritual person judges all things, but the natural person does not perceive spiritual things. Therefore these people, measuring nothing according to faith, neglect to tremble at the future judgment because the contempt they show is not immediately reproved by some visible sign of vengeance. They do not experience that judgment in the present, and for this reason they are quick to sin but difficult to correct.

Hence it is written that evils multiply on the earth because a sentence against wrongdoers is not quickly issued. Certainly, they are condemned by a worse vengeance when no adversity resists them. For, as is said in Book 26 of the *Moralia*, God reserves for eternal punishment those whom he does not restrain from their wickedness through temporal afflictions.

Hence it is written: “He struck his enemies in their hind parts”—not in the present—and “he gave them disgrace”—not temporal but eternal (Psalm 77:66). Hence holy Noah condemned his wicked son not in the son himself but in the posterity of his offspring.

Let rebels therefore not flatter themselves concerning impunity, because they are now permitted to prevail all the more as a punishment. It is an indication of manifest condemnation when the outcome that follows their efforts prospers without any opposing obstacle.

For, because God, as it is written, leaves no time without a testimony to his power, even in our own age he punishes many with terrifying vengeance. Such was the following case.

When, some years ago, the solemnity of Saint Andrew coincided with the first Sunday of the Lord’s Advent,

> **Note:** [Col. 0533D] Saint Andrew’s solemnity. Aymoinus, Book 4, final chapter, mentions the feast of blessed Andrew; and Book 2 of the *Capitula*, chapter 20, mentions the Mass of Saint Andrew.

a certain priest, as the precentor of the Church of Tours reports, ordered his parishioners to hear both Masses.

> **Note:** [Col. 0533D] “A certain priest [ordered] his *pagenses*”—that is, his parishioners or villagers. Although the word *pagus* sometimes means a province, as in Gregory of Tours, Book 9, chapter 9—“the Pagus of Étampes” and “the Pagus of Chartres”—and in Fredegar, chapter 57—“the Pagus of Toulouse, Cahors, Agen, and Périgueux”—and hence *pagenses* means the people of the same *pagus* or province, as also in Gregory of Tours, Book 8, chapter 18, and in Book 3, chapter 73 of the *Capitula*, nevertheless *pagus* is also frequently used for a village or parish, and *pagenses* for the inhabitants of that village or parish.

Among them was a physician who departed after hearing the first Mass. When the priest rebuked him, he gave him a harsh reply. The priest excommunicated him.

The physician, angry, went away to his house. In contempt of the excommunication, he immediately took a drink, and at once began to be afflicted until he breathed out his soul.

If these people had seen this, perhaps they would have been afraid—those to whom the reproach applies: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign” (Matthew 12:39). And likewise the words of Job: “When you see my affliction, you are afraid” (Job 6:21), because many people do not know how to fear God unless they are terrified by adversity experienced either in themselves or in others.

## XXIII

That famous emperor Theodosius, as the *Tripartite History* reports, was once excommunicated by a certain monk over a grievance which the emperor had not immediately resolved. I believe that the monk was not in his right mind.

The monk departed after writing the excommunication on a document or tablet [the reading *pictatio* is uncertain] and throwing it down where the emperor could find it. But the emperor, considering not that wandering monk,

> **Note:** [Col. 0535D] “The emperor, not that wandering monk.” Saint Benedict explains who the *gyrovagi* are in chapter 1 of his Rule, saying: “The fourth kind of monk is called a *gyrovagus*: they spend their whole life staying for three or four days at a time in the cells of different people throughout various provinces, always wandering and never stable, serving their own pleasures and the enticements of gluttony.” Peter Damian also touches on this in Letter 9 of Book 5, in these words: “In the monastic order, those whom we see regularly remaining in cloisters under the authority of an abbot we consequently call monks; but those whom we see possessing their own property, running indiscriminately here and there, and flowing away, freed from laws according to the judgment of their own will, we judge worthy to be called not monks but rather *gyrovagi*. See the chapter on *Gyrovagi* in the *Statutes of Hugh, Abbot of Cluny*.”

but rather the heavenly king, by whose authority excommunication is customarily imposed, did not dare to dine at all when the appointed hour had arrived.

Although many bishops were standing before him, and the bishop of the diocese to which the aforesaid monk belonged gave permission, he could not be compelled to taste anything until the monk had been sought for a long time, eventually found, and asked to grant the emperor permission.

I wish that such people would indirectly compare themselves with these persons, so that they might discern the matter more truthfully by contrast.

Behold: the emperor was not just anyone, but Theodosius, one who would be admired by every age after him. He observed an excommunication that had been uttered not reasonably but foolishly—not by someone who possessed even a slight authority to excommunicate, but by a foolish monk who had cast it upon him by chance.

These degenerate little men, however, who possess not even the least sign of respectability among ordinary people, despise an excommunication that is not accidental but decreed by ecclesiastical censure through bishops.

Certainly, these are evil days, in which, as the Apostle says, there exist people who love themselves, who turn their hearing away from the truth and do not receive sound doctrine. Hence they disregard the weight of divine authority, and, like Cain, they despise not only God’s ministers but also God himself, who admonishes them through those ministers.

But since we have heard about one king who observed an excommunication, though foolishly imposed, with remarkable humility, let us now hear what happened concerning another.

### XXIV

It is recorded in the history of the English people that a certain bishop excommunicated two brothers, men of the court, for repudiating their wives. It happened that the king of that people was passing by their house. Enticed by many flattering invitations to stop and dine with them, he finally agreed. When the meal was over and he was already returning, he encountered the bishop who had excommunicated those brothers. When the king saw him, he trembled; leaping from his horse in the middle of the road, as he was, he prostrated himself before the bishop.

But the bishop approached him and touched him with the staff he held in his hand, saying: “O king, it is not for me to acknowledge you, because you knowingly associated yourself with those who were excommunicated, when you acted against God. Therefore this sentence is pronounced against you: this year you must die in the very house where you despised the excommunication.”

And it happened as it is recorded there. Behold: the king could expiate this offense only by dying; behold: the bishop could not forgive even a king prostrate in the dust. From this, then, it must be concluded that even the bishop himself, whose excommunication is despised, cannot forgive such a crime without the gravest penance.

### XXV

Concerning signs, this should be known: according to Scripture, “For every matter there is its own time under heaven” (Eccles. III, 17). Hence, at its beginnings, the holy Church needed signs to strengthen the faith of its members. Now, however, since the state of faith has long been firmly established, it does not greatly require signs.

Yet, so that the inner judge might reveal the thoughts of many hearts, before the Antichrist appears the signs of virtues are withdrawn from that same Church by a terrible dispensation. Prophecy is concealed, the grace of healings is taken away, the power of prolonged abstinence is diminished, words of teaching fall silent, and the wonders of miracles are removed. This is stated in Book XXXIV of the *Moralia*.

This is permitted to happen so that, when the same Church has appeared more despised because its virtues have been withdrawn, it may become clear who pursue it for the hope of heavenly rewards and not for present signs, and who are those who neglect to follow the invisible things it promises because they are not moved to revere it by visible signs—even when the riches of miracles are withdrawn from the faithful.

Thus it is written concerning that same Antichrist: “Poverty will precede his face.” The followers of the Antichrist will perform wonders. By this circumstance it will come about that those who revere the Church solely for its miracles, abandoning reverence for it, will transfer themselves into the company of those who perform signs.

Signs, however, will by no means be lacking to the good; but in comparison with those others they will appear few or nonexistent. This is why God no longer avenges even perjuries—which he used to punish so quickly—with manifest retribution; rather, as though they were not to be punished, he permits them to multiply.

Can perjurers say that either God no longer punishes what he once used to punish, or that the saints no longer possess the same power, so that they cannot now punish perjuries committed against them as they once did? Certainly they can. But now it is time for signs to cease. It is surely no wonder if God delays avenging contempt for prelates, since he endures injuries against the saints with such great patience.

But since an occasion has arisen to speak of an oath, let us recall what Jerome says about this in Book V of his commentary on Ezekiel. King Zedekiah had entered into a pact of submission with King Nebuchadnezzar, but he acted falsely by fleeing to the king of Egypt. Ezekiel therefore says: “Shall he escape who broke the pact? As I live, says the Lord, I will bring him to Babylon, and there he shall die in the transgression by which he despised me” (Ezek. XVII, 15, 20).

There is a secular maxim that deception or valor is to be sought against an enemy. Those who say that enemies should be deceived commonly bring forward this maxim, and they say: “Let us remain at peace until you swear and enter into a pact under the name of God.” It is considered wisdom and courage either to deceive an adversary or to overcome him by whatever means one can.

But once you have bound yourself by an oath, he is no longer to be deceived as an adversary, because one must consider not to whom you have sworn but by whom you have sworn. Otherwise you despise the one by whom you swear, and the enemy proves more faithful than you, since he trusted you because of the name of God. For he who deceives the person to whom he was joined by an oath in the divine name does not deceive an enemy but a friend.

Let this be said so that a Christian who breaks an oath made to another Christian may understand from it what he deserves, if the covenant that a Jew violated against a pagan was punished in such a way that Zedekiah, after his eyes had been torn out, was led captive to Babylon with his leaders because of this transgression.

### XXVI

So that priestly dignity may be commended, on account of the majesty of faith, also by the display of a visible miracle, let the account of blessed Peter be brought forward.

This blessed Peter was bishop of Alexandria and was the first to expel the heretic Arius from his Church. Thereafter, when the moment of his passion was approaching, Christ appeared to him in a dream, shining with immense splendor. He was clothed in a very white *colobium*, but it was torn open down to the feet. Clutching this *colobium* to his breast with both hands, he somehow covered his nakedness.

Peter understood that he was Christ and, struck with great horror, said: “My Lord, who has done this?” He replied: “Arius has done this to me,” and continued with the rest of the words that Peter related with profound emotion.

During the whole time of his episcopate, Peter never wished to sit on his cathedra, but sat upon the stool of that cathedra. Because of this, the clergy and people frequently complained against him, but he never yielded. For whenever he climbed the altar, a fiery radiance appeared to come forth from the seat itself; at the sight of it the holy man was so inflamed that at times he did not know that he was still in the body.

One day, when the clergy and the bishops who were present complained about his manner of sitting, he was compelled, no longer able to conceal it, to say: “Why is my heart troubled? Do you not see the fiery power that flashes from that throne, and do you not perceive the spirit glittering?”

When all of them, having heard such a thing, remained silent with bowed heads, he continued: “Believe me, my little sons: if you saw what I see, then you would recognize what priestly power is and what grace dwells in it. In the presence of its majesty I am terrified to sit upon that cathedra.”

If this example is carefully considered, it could terrify those who now despise such authority, while those who occupy the seats of office would also tremble greatly. This is reported in the account of his passion.

### XXVII

The holy Church, therefore, will retain its power, and the impiety of the empire will be directed against it. To the faithful of that same Church it is said: “Set your hearts upon his power” (Ps. XLVII, 14)—that is, let them examine with the eyes of the mind what power exists in it, rather than judging according to what appears outwardly. For the one who promised is always present: “Behold, I am with you” (Matt. XXVIII, 20), and so forth.

Hence it follows there: “That you may declare that this is God” (Ps. XLVII, 14–15). Moreover, all the holy bishops are believed always to be present in spirit at the sees which they once occupied bodily.

If it pleases, this may also be demonstrated by an example. In that life of the blessed Gregory which the Romans use, many wonders are clearly reported to have been performed through his presence after his death in that monastery of his which he mentions in the homilies. One of these is the following.

A wicked man named Dominicus brought with him near that monastery a certain nun whom he had corrupted. Since the lodging lacked a latrine, the wretched man removed some small beams associated with Saint Gregory’s fountain and fashioned a latrine from them.

When he slept there the following night, he was seized and bound by two men who appeared to be chamberlains. When he asked them why they were binding him and striking him so cruelly, they replied: “Because of the harlot, the holy pope orders you to be brought to judgment.”

At that time the Roman bishop John had gone out against the Saracens the previous day. Remembering his absence, the accused said: “My lord the pope is not now in the city; how, then, did he order me to be bound?”

They replied: “If Pope John has gone from here, Saint Gregory has remained here. As he was making his customary circuit of the city and came here, he found that you had destroyed the enclosure of his fountain for the sake of your harlot.”

The man was awakened, and, already burning with an inward fever, expired on the twelfth day. He had despised the rebuke of Zacharias, who was in charge of the monastery; but by dying he proved—though he had not suspected it—that Gregory was present in that place and examined every matter.

### XXVIII

Whoever, therefore, lives by faith should revere the presence of Christ or of his saints and should not despise the herald—even if, God forbid, he should be contemptible in the merit of his life—but should fear the power of the judge.

For although a person may hold the place of judgment whose life is entirely unworthy of that office, nevertheless whoever receives the rank of governance assumes the place of the apostles in the authority to bind and loose.

And therefore, as Saint Gregory says in the twenty-sixth homily on the Gospels: “Whether the shepherd binds justly or unjustly, the shepherd’s sentence must nevertheless be feared, lest both the one who is subject and the one who is perhaps unjustly bound should deserve, through another fault, the very sentence of his binding.”

The shepherd, then, since he will have to render an account to the judge concerning all his judgments, should fear either to absolve indiscriminately or to bind; the subordinate, however, should fear being bound, even unjustly.

How prelates should live, both for themselves and for their subjects; how they should correct some matters more leniently and others more severely; and how they should overlook certain things without nevertheless allowing them to increase, is clearly discussed in the *Pastoral Book*.

Here, however, let this be recalled from Book XXVI of the *Moralia*: if they cease correcting the wicked, they themselves will be punished on their account. And as many subjects as each person is set over to govern, so many souls will he alone have to account for before the strict judge—when perhaps he scarcely suffices to answer for his own.

Prelates will render their subjects freer at the divine tribunal insofar as they do not leave their faults here without punishment; but they themselves become all the more bound insofar as those who commit such faults are not wounded by even the application of a word of rebuke.

### XXIX

The perversity of the wicked requires that such things be said against their contempt, taking our occasion from Cain, whose followers are those who despised the admonition of God himself. Cain did not wish to confess his guilt, but replied fearfully: “Am I my brother’s keeper?” (Gen. IV, 9).

In this act he imitated his father Adam, who, when summoned to repentance, immediately added an excuse, saying: “The woman whom you gave me gave me, and I ate” (Gen. III, 12). He secretly turned his transgression against its author, as though the one who had given him the woman had provided the occasion for sinning.

Hence, from that root, a branch of this error has continued to spread through the human race down to the present: whatever evil a person does, he attempts either to lessen by making excuses or to defend by argument.

Certainly we ought not to have sinned; but would that, after our fall, we might strive to rise again and not multiply our guilt by defending it. Yet, in a pitiable manner, the more the spirit is separated from the truth by sinning, the more wickedly it becomes hardened. The guilt that ought to have terrified the mind instead makes it more arrogant.

Let us say something further about Cain against his imitators. He lived wandering and exiled, and of these people it is said: “They will walk in emptiness and perish.” They walk in emptiness who carry nothing with them after death from the fruit of their labor. They are also exiles, because, pursuing the present life, they flee the other; finding this one, they lose that one.

One longs for honors, another for multiplying possessions, another for winning praise; but each either loses all these things before death or abandons them when dying. He therefore labors in emptiness and passes through his life as a wanderer who carries nothing with him before the judge by which to win salvation for his soul.

However guilt may emerge, they are always so subjected to it that either they do not begin rightly, or, if they have begun, they return, broken in the very attempt, to their customary wickedness.

Cain called his firstborn Enoch and named the city he founded after him. *Enoch* means “dedication.” And the more all the wicked are separated from the heavenly inheritance, the more deeply they fix the root of their hearts in this life, which is first.

Although it is written, “Do not recline in the first place” (Luke XIV, 8), they dedicate themselves at the beginning, so that here they may flourish for a moment and wither utterly from the homeland that follows.

### XXX

Their pursuits are these: they become hardened against the commands of the Creator, inflamed by wicked desires, and at times they spare not even their own deaths. They seek empty glory even at the cost of their lives.

They persecute the good by words and deeds, and even with swords. They place their hope in themselves and become insensible to the scourges of the Creator. They think of mortal things without mortality; they bring their desire for possessions to no end through any accumulation of profits.

Amid every bitterness they return to the pleasure of carnal desire. As far as they can, they nourish the body with a variety of banquets and soothe sadness with the allurements of places. So that they may not appear despised, they exalt themselves through dignities; they strive to surpass everyone in power.

Those who are more cunning learn to conceal their hearts by schemes, to veil their meaning with words, to return wrongs inflicted upon them in multiplied form, and to mock the simple. This is the prudence of the old man: it is learned from children for a price and strengthened in young men through use. Those who know it despise others; those who do not know it consider it refinement in others.

They neither mourn nor reflect upon the heavenly things they have lost. They do not recall the freedom originally given to them but abandon themselves to those things into which they have been cast. They love the exile they suffer as though it were their homeland; and although they are miserable, they love their very miseries and think themselves well off amid them.

Thus, persisting in iniquity from the beginning of life to its end, they continually multiply the blows against themselves through the growth of wickedness; struck down by these blows, they fall eternally. They do not love the eternal homeland because they think it enough for them to possess the temporal goods they desire. When these increase for them, they consider themselves happy and secure; and thus, where their flesh finds rest, there they bury and extinguish their minds.

Whoever therefore detects these things, and many others which we omit because of their length, in himself should recognize that he has not yet put off the old man with his arguments. Even if he cannot bear to hear it, his deeds prove that he belongs to that city whose king is the devil.

### XXXI

Just Abel, just as he signified in himself Christ, the king of the heavenly Jerusalem, together with the whole assembly of the elect, so in the lamb he offered he expressed the innocence of those same elect.

To say something about the practices of this innocence: all who among them are perfect imitate nothing through cunning dissimulation, because they do not know how to speak deceitfully. They do not strive to support themselves with an abundance of possessions, to display themselves as honorable through worldly dignities, to parade themselves through the adornment of clothing, or to glory in things external to them.

They fear being honored, but not being despised. They make their bodies lean through self-restraint, while growing rich in mind and character. They rejoice to receive insults for the sake of justice; they consider it gain not to inflict injuries but to endure them.

Living in these and similar ways, they please God, but offend the eyes of Cain, because the wise and worshipers of this world regard those who seem rejected and almost dead—those whom they do not see living carnally with them—as worthless.

This is signified by the young man whom the Lord, after freeing him from a demon, allowed to lie for a little while, so that many said he was dead. For those who do not know how to live spiritually consider the person who is free from unclean desires entirely useless and extinguished.

Hence Job says: “The simplicity of the just is mocked” (Job XII, 4), because, since the same just person does not shine outwardly with temporal glory, he is despised by those who know how to value no good except carnal goods.

Thus Moses aptly said in the voice of the elect: “We shall sacrifice to the Lord the abominations of the Egyptians” (Exod. VIII, 26). The Egyptians disdain eating sheep; but what they abominate the Israelites offer to God, because the simple life of the humble becomes a sacrifice to God, while the proud and deceitful consider it foolishness.

Cain, breathing murderous hatred against his brother Abel, persuades him to go outside. To go outside is to seek external things while neglecting heavenly goods. Some who succumb to the appetite for earthly things commonly try to bend those who appear to pursue eternal things, either by their example alone or also by their words.

The wife of blessed Job clearly represented such people when she urged her husband to speak words of blasphemy. For these people, because of their professed faith, have been mingled with the faithful within the bosom of the Church; and they make the faithful almost imitators of themselves, insofar as the faithful receive them even into the chamber of faith.

But whoever wishes to escape the cruelty of Cain should strive to be joined to inward desires and cease pursuing external things through the examples of the wicked. The man in the Gospel would not have fallen among robbers if he had not gone out from Jerusalem, which means “vision of peace”; nor would the king of the land have violated Jacob’s daughter if she had not gone out to see the women of that region.

Hence it is said of that same Jacob: “He was a simple man, dwelling in tents” (Gen. XXV, 27). Esau, however, whom God hated, was a man skilled in hunting.

### XXXII

God permits innocent Abel to be slaughtered by the wicked Cain, yet receives Abel himself, because it belongs to the elect to suffer evils here and to endure scourges of various kinds here, so that they may be reserved to rejoice in the eternal inheritance.

“For if children, then heirs.” We are recognized as children through affliction itself, according to the saying: “He scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII, 6). Although not everyone who is scourged is a son, nevertheless no son exists who is not scourged.

The wicked, however, are left without the rod, so that, as is said in Book XXIV of the *Moralia*, “at least they may lead this life without punishments, those who by doing evil hasten toward torments without end.”

The joy of eternal recompense is never reaped unless it is first sown here through devout tribulation. Let the reprobate therefore go on and consume their desires without punishment; for God certainly turns even the time he grants them for repentance into testimony against their guilt, and someday pours out irrevocably the wrath that he now restrains.

This is inferred from the affliction of the good, whom we see both doing what is devout and enduring many cruel things. If the strict judge strikes those whom he rejects with such great severity there, how strictly does he chastise here those whom he loves?

Hence Peter says: “It is time for judgment to begin from the house of God” (I Pet. IV, 17). “And if it begins with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel of God?”

Divine severity does not permit sins to remain unpunished, but begins here with our correction through the wrath of judgment, so that it may come to rest in the condemnation of the reprobate.

For both groups Job says: “If I am wicked, woe is me; and if I am righteous, I shall not lift up my head” (Job X, 15), being filled with affliction and misery.

The wicked lifts his head here because he is supported by prosperity here, but he will not escape what follows; his pride is struck by eternal vengeance. The righteous, oppressed by misery, is not permitted to lift his head, but, purified by passing pains, is freed from eternal punishment.

### XXXIII

The head of the righteous Abel is therefore pressed down into death, while the wicked Cain is permitted to go on in the unrestrained freedom of his will, so that in the one the blessed adversity of the good and in the other the unhappy prosperity of the wicked might be displayed.

It often happens that, just as Cain did then, so now each wicked person, when he has shaken the neck of his mind free from the yoke of divine service, is permitted to have the opportunity to carry out any kind of offense.

When he is not restrained by divine commands and enjoys impious freedom in doing evil, he sometimes thinks everything whatsoever is permitted to him. Thus it is rightly written of him: “He considers himself free, like a young wild ass” (Job XI, 12).

A *onager* is called a wild ass. Wild animals have the freedom both to go where they wish and to rest when they wish. Whoever therefore seeks to fulfill the evils he desires through unrestrained freedom wishes to be like a young wild ass. Such a person is not restrained under discipline, like a wild beast, because he is not reserved for anything else.

But human beings are said to be destined for the life to come. It is therefore necessary that in all their movements they be bound under the arrangement of discipline, serve like a domestic animal tied with reins, and live restrained by eternal ordinances.

### XXXIV

The true Abel himself, consoling all the hardships of our tribulation, endured everything by his power with wondrous compassion that he knew we would have to endure by necessity. Thus we human beings should not flee what we suffer because of the merit of our guilt, when he who is God deigned, solely out of condescension, to suffer so much.

I do not think anyone could be so presumptuous as to claim, as though relying on unique merit or a superior nature, that the present life should be arranged for him without hardships, when even the author of life did not leave this life without the pain of passion.

Whatever virtues he may possess, what is the worthiness of a sinner’s life if his life for us was subjected to the scourge, although it was subject to no sin?

To give an example: the divine voice rebuked Baruch, the disciple of the prophet Jeremiah, because, while the others were migrating into captivity, he presumed to seek rest for himself.

Otherwise the Christian soldier travels by a different road if he seeks joys and pleasures, while his leader has shown him the ways of bitterness. Concerning these ways it is written: “They were unwilling to understand all his ways” (Job XXXIV, 27). That is, the proud despised imitating the examples of humility that he provided.

Every action that Christ, the Wisdom of God, performed through the mystery of his incarnation is a way and a rule of life. To those who came to him he offered as many ways as he displayed examples. Concerning this Wisdom it is written: “She cries out, standing in the midst of the paths” (Prov. VIII, 2), which we would have had to seek if she had wished to hide herself.

But now she plants her step in the midst of the paths, so that we may be enriched by her even unwillingly, and, though we neglect to see her, may encounter her by stumbling.

What kind of way did he show? Certainly, the way of humility. Of it he himself says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI, 29).

What else did he display in this life to the eyes of those who looked upon him except abasement? The origin of our destruction was the devil’s pride. Therefore, so that the humility of God might become the instrument of redemption, he appeared not only visibly but also despised. For this he endured the mockery of insults, the disgrace of derision, the torments of suffering, and death, so that humble God might teach human beings not to be proud.

For the sole purpose of teaching humility truly, he who is great in estimation above all things deigned to become small among all things.

These, then, are his ways, which the proud do not wish to understand, because they disdain to suffer the lowly things that he endured. But for every humble person to understand these same ways is to know that through these lowly things one passes to the highest; to know that adversity must be endured patiently and lasting things awaited perseveringly, so that, following the example of him who had to suffer and thus enter into his glory, eternal glory may be sought in exchange for temporal reproaches.

### XXXV

These two generations, or two cities, which, as has been said, arose from the two sons of Adam, are divided into four generations. According to the example in which Cain, the author of evil, was the firstborn—and each of us is first evil and afterward becomes good through the grace of baptism—we shall now speak first of the generation of the wicked.

It is itself divided into two kinds. It openly includes the wicked, such as all the powerful oppressors of the poor. It is characteristic of these people either to expand themselves through pleasures, to use the power divinely granted to them to injure others, or to dissolve themselves in indulgence. Even when the means of acting is lacking, the will to act is always present in them.

Thus guilt is always present in them, because they are continually entangled in wicked desires. And because they despise the poor, it is rightly written of them, as stated above: “A despised lamp in the thoughts of the rich” (Job XII, 5).

In this passage, by the name “rich” all who swell with proud thoughts within themselves are designated. Many are enriched by possessions; but when they see themselves abounding in works, they do not seek the true riches of God. Those who, having been enriched beyond their deserts with goods, ought to have been moved by them to love the Creator instead fight against him with his gifts.

Others do not possess earthly goods, yet are proud within themselves and continually burn with love of riches. Because the love of the life to come does not humble them, the insolence of their character allies them with the wicked rich.

But, as is said in Book X of the *Moralia*, nothing differs in the retribution of judgment according to whether they swell with possessions or with character alone. Such people either oppress or despise the humble, who possess earthly things for use rather than desire and love the life to come; while they themselves die either through earthly possessions or through desires alone.

### XXXVI

Concerning these it is written: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation in the present” (Luke VI, 24). These people, disdaining what belongs to them, covet what belongs to others; or, unable to obtain what they covet, they are devastated by the turmoil of avarice that drives them on.

Concerning them Book IV of the *Moralia* says: “How difficultly do those make their way toward rest who, amid such harsh tumults of thought, are constricted in heart while they wish to be exalted in this world!”

Hence it is written: “Woe to him who multiplies what is not his own. How long will he burden himself with dense mud against himself?” (Hab. II, 6). Earthly things are represented by mud. He therefore burdens himself with dense mud who multiplies earthly possessions, who constricts himself under the oppression of avarice, which is the service of idols.

Again: “The strictest judgment will be upon those who rule” (Wis. VI, 6). Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “To whom much has been given, from him much will be required” (Luke XII, 48).

It is therefore exceedingly rare for those who possess gold to make their way toward rest, since Truth itself says: “It is difficult for those who have money to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX, 23).

For those who here yearn to multiply riches, what hope do they have of the joys of the other life? To show that this is indeed very rare, yet nevertheless possible through a miracle, our Redeemer said: “With human beings this is impossible, but with God all things are possible” (Luke XVIII, 27), and so forth.

He is powerful enough to restrain the swelling of their hearts and bridle the ambition of their desire. It is shown that this can occur only through a divine miracle, since what is entirely impossible is brought forward as an example when the Lord says: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX, 24).

### XXXVII

There is also another kind of wicked people: those who assume the appearance of religion but either openly submit themselves to many vices or secretly surrender themselves to certain ones.

Hence blessed Job, speaking in the voice of the grieving Church, says: “I have poured out my entrails upon the earth” (Job XVI, 14). Since the entrails are inward parts of the human body, those who, clothed in the appearance of religion, ought to serve its innermost mysteries are called the entrails of the Church.

When the malicious enemy draws some of them toward secular desires or affairs, he pours the entrails of that same Church upon the earth, because he tramples in low places those who were called to cling to spiritual things.

Again it is written: “Under him are the rays of the sun” (Job XLI, 21). This happens when those who within the holy Church appear to shine with a higher rank or keener wisdom submit themselves either to diabolical persuasions or to earthly powers acting wickedly, and, forgetting heavenly things, pursue earthly ones.

Again it is said: “He spreads gold beneath himself like mud” (Job XLI, 21)—that is, he tramples those who appear spiritual as though they were carnal.

Moreover, by the name of gold the brilliance of temporal glory is expressed, as the prophet says: “Babylon is a golden cup” (Jer. LI, 7). For what is designated by the name Babylon except the glory of this world? It is called a golden cup because, while it displays temporal things as beautiful, it intoxicates foolish minds with their desire, so that they pursue temporal things that only falsely appear beautiful and despise the invisible things that are truly beautiful.

Eve was the first to be intoxicated of her own accord by this golden cup; and all who, placed within ecclesiastical disciplines, receive every kind of secular allurement as she did in paradise imitate her.

Thus Leviathan, who is said to do these things, spreads either the rays of the sun or gold beneath himself like mud whenever he causes someone in the appearance of religion to fall through certain vices as though he were a secular person.

Again he says: “He will swallow the river and not be astonished, and he trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth” (Job XL, 18). Secular people are signified by the river, and ecclesiastical men by the Jordan.

He does not consider it a great thing if he devours those who, driven by earthly desires, flow downward like a river. But he strives with great effort to swallow those placed in an ecclesiastical rank, whom he sometimes kills through the snares of his cunning, gulping them down like the Jordan.

Again it is said that the fire which the Lord called to judgment consumed part of his house, because Gehenna also devours those who live negligently in the appearance of religion.

### XXXVIII

The generation of the elect is likewise distinguished into two kinds. One kind consists of the perfect, of whom it is said: “The meek increase strength in the Lord” (Isa. XXIX, 19); and again: “The righteous will hold to his way with clean hands” (Job XVII, 9).

The other consists of those who are not yet perfect, concerning whom the Church says to its Redeemer: “Your eyes saw my imperfect state” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 16), as though it were saying: “You do not repel from the gaze of your mercy even those who, in my body, cannot fully attain the ways of perfection.”

Observing that both kinds belong to the heavenly rest, Job says: “The small and the great are there” (Job III, 19).

All who are more perfect amid the troubles of this life do not rush into murmuring. If riches flow to them, they set their hearts on them not at all, but regard both prosperity and adversity as things that will quickly pass.

They consider from what snare they fell: from what blessedness, and into how great a misery, they fell in their first parent. Therefore they despise the prosperity of this life as brief and impoverished.

Although they grieve over present hardships, they consider what the strict judge threatens sinners with in the future Gehenna. They endure these hardships with all the greater patience because, after this exile, they fear that an eternal death will follow if they murmur.

They do not exalt themselves over whatever good they may perhaps have done, because they carefully consider what sort of people they will stand before what kind of judge, and how subtly that same judge examines good deeds and how strictly he punishes evil ones.

As is discussed in Book VIII of the *Moralia*, they know with complete certainty that they would perish if they were judged without mercy.

And because they know with absolute certainty that in this life they neither ought to have rest nor can have it, they meanwhile adopt this salutary counsel: abandoning earthly desires, they raise themselves toward heavenly things.

Yet while doing these things they still feel the scourges of the Father, so that they may come to the heavenly inheritance all the more perfect, insofar as the discipline that strikes them piously also purifies them daily from their smallest faults.

### XXXIX

Because of what they suffer in the present and what they fear in the future, but also because of the salutary counsel they discover, as has been said, Jeremiah rightly says to the Lord in their person: “I sat alone because of the threat of your hand, for you filled me with threat” (Jer. 15:17). A person is recognized by the face; the hand signifies an action. He sits alone who is not surrounded by the tumult of carnal desires.

Thus God’s face is called knowledge, and his hand the experience of being struck, because, as he had threatened, he punished humanity for original sin and also cast it into the tribulations of this life. The threat, however, is the terror of the punishment still to come, which he holds over sinners. Therefore, because of his threat, he sits alone before the face of the Lord’s hand who, through experience of that vengeance inflicted on mortals for original sin, recognizes how greatly the punishment that follows must be feared—the punishment threatened against those who do not repent—and therefore no longer dares to become proud or mingle with crowds of carnal desires.

Job says, because of the stings of present distress: “The arrows of the Lord are in me”; but concerning what follows he adds: “His terrors are arrayed against me” (Job 6:4). Hence the Psalmist, referring to both, says: “Your wrath has passed over me, and your terrors have troubled me” (Ps. 87:17). This is said because we already suffer something else from condemnation: namely, wraths, but passing ones, since these pains soon come to an end. Yet what makes this more grievous is that amid these pains we fear the eternal punishments he threatens, whose terrors rightly disturb us.

Whatever, therefore, afflicts perfected men, they flee that much less insofar as they believe it to be an expiation of their sins. Everything that passes away, even if it is prosperous, becomes that much more worthless in their judgment insofar as it is transitory and they themselves are striving toward something else, something which, once attained, is never lost.

They therefore neither receive the good things offered here as something very great nor fear the evils inflicted here very much. They use temporal assistance as a traveler uses either shade or a bed: he rests his body, but with his mind directed elsewhere he hastens to depart. So too these people refuse to fix the step of their hearts upon transitory things, lest the pleasure of the journey remove them from the dwelling-place of eternal habitation. For they desire to rejoice in their own home, and therefore refuse to be happy in the place of their pilgrimage.

This is why, among the offspring of the elect, Enoch—whose name is interpreted as “dedication”—is born seventh: for after the six ages of this life, the elect will be dedicated in the Jerusalem above like living stones. Cain, however, as stated above, calls his firstborn Enoch, because the wicked dedicate themselves, as it were, at the beginning, when they plant the root of their hearts in this life.

The Lord says: “When you are invited to a wedding, do not recline in the first place” (Luke 14:8).

### XL

There is also another kind of good people, but they are less perfect: unable to penetrate spiritual realities, they are weighed down by the five bodily senses. Joshua aptly represents these five senses—which the army of Christians, under the leadership of Jesus, ought to repress within its own body—for he killed the five kings who had long ruled in the promised land after they fled into a cave, as into the cavern of the body.

But while the imperfect still succumb to these same senses, they love the one who made all things that much less insofar as they are more tightly bound to created things. They do not seek what belongs to others, and they bear injuries inflicted upon them, even unwillingly. They are content with their own possessions and live humbly; yet they still care for their household, think about their children, and preserve an inheritance for them.

Among these, however, those who are more conscientious remember the divine judgment and show mercy to the poor. If they cannot leave everything, they at least become merciful to the extent of their ability and divide their care between the flesh and the soul.

But what will become of them if no one reaches the kingdom except one endowed with the highest virtues? They too have their consolation. When Solomon’s royal litter was described as a type of the Church—among the wood of Lebanon, the silver columns, the golden backrest, and the purple ascent, by which the more excellent people serving in that same Church are signified—it was added that “he paved its middle with love, because of the daughters of Jerusalem.”

Since this is said on account of our weakness, it is plainly evident that love is said to be present not because of the sons but because of the daughters of Jerusalem. For what else is signified by the female sex than weakness of mind? Whoever, therefore, is weak in mind should possess love, loving God and neighbor as much as he can and doing good works with great love. For although he is entangled in external things, if he possesses love he will nevertheless belong to God’s litter, as the Psalmist says: “He blessed all the little ones together with the great” (Ps. 113:13). For those who are imperfect and little, if they love God and neighbor insofar as they are able, are also to be placed—though in a lesser position—in the building of the holy Church.

Let each of the faithful, then, examine himself; and if he finds anything stored in his heart from the fruits of love, let him not doubt that God is in him.

### XLI

Since an opportunity has presented itself, it seems appropriate to say something about love in the words of blessed Augustine:

“He comprehends without error the manifold abundance and very broad teaching of the divine Scriptures, and preserves it without any labor, whose heart is full of love. Therefore, whoever wishes by the new commandment to extinguish the old sin should hold fast to love, which is opposed to desire; for the one who preserves love in his conduct holds both what is manifest and what is hidden in the divine words.”

Jerome reports in his letter to the Galatians that when the holy John the Evangelist was already an old man and was carried to church by the hands of his disciples, he always said only this in the assembly: “Little children, love one another.” The disciples, weary of hearing the same thing continually, said: “Teacher, why do you always say this?” He answered them with a saying worthy of John: “Because it is the Lord’s commandment, and if it is the only thing done, it is sufficient.”

It must certainly be understood that, just as in our times almost everything has lost its proper order, many call extravagant expenditure of their possessions “love,” although things lavishly distributed for empty glory, or eating or dissipation, should be called wastefulness rather than love.

The Lord himself teaches to whom possessions should be distributed, saying: “Do not invite those who will invite you in return” (Luke 14:12). Yet almost everyone, while he scarcely bestows even a little clothing or food on Christ in the poor, still distributes even borrowed goods to the powerful. This is not love but wastefulness. Love is rightly to be spent on the needy alone; and benefits are to be shown not only to friends but also to enemies.
