Moreover, just as this life lies midway between heaven, where only the good dwell, and hell, to which only the wicked are delivered, so it contains the citizens of both sides without distinction. Thus both generations alike either use temporal goods or are afflicted by temporal evils, though with different faith, different hope, and different love, until they are separated at the final judgment and each receives his own end—an end without end.

Since we have brought this sequence of words, arranged however it may be, to the point where we have said that these generations, although advancing together through prosperity and adversity, nevertheless have different ends according to the diversity of their merits, let us bring this book to a close here.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0547]

The appointed days had already passed, and, I confess, I was glad that, under the pretext of a brief period, it had been possible to bring the tasks imposed by your command to a brief conclusion. For it is a kind of consolation to a fool that, if he does not know how to keep silent, at least he may speak little. Suddenly, however, winter, harsher than usual, descended and made those few days of its own so rough that we seemed to have more reason to think about sunshine than about traveling.

Then, partly because of the severity of the winter just mentioned and partly out of reverence for the holy days that were approaching, the lord abbot allowed our journey to be delayed for a while. After reading what had already been arranged and finding a few things to say against those who are made worse by the example of the wicked, it seemed good to insert some additional material.

I am not sufficiently confident that such people will even deign to hear this, since they have failed to revere the holy Gospel as they ought. Nevertheless, I shall undertake the command in the hope that, upon the mound of testimonies on which proud sons are to be stoned according to Moses’ command, I may at least rejoice that I have cast a little stone.

### I

The good, then, as we said, now experience every kind of evil or good together with wicked people, although the wicked suffer evils more harshly and more frequently, while the good make more restrained use of good things.

The good use both prosperity and adversity in such a way that prosperity consoles them, lest they be broken by adversity, while adversity exercises them, lest they be corrupted by prosperity. But the wicked desire to have a secure life so that, having destroyed their upright character and removed every harshness of trouble, they may drift away.

They do not desire peace and abundance in every kind of resource so that they may use these goods well—that is, honorably, soberly, temperately, and piously—but so that an endless variety of pleasures may be sought through insane excesses, and so that prosperity may produce in their character those evils which are worse than enemies raging against them. Their quiet life consists in this: that their wickedness may be secure.

All who are richer always strive to increase their wealth, so that it may suffice for their daily extravagances and enable them to subjugate poorer people, whom they keep obedient as clients to their own arrogance. These poorer people, because of their satiety, willingly submit themselves to them; and those whom they cannot overpower themselves, they violently oppress through the audacity of those to whom they cling.

With such retainers and those whose patronage protects them in mind, Scripture says of the rich man in both respects: “From his sides he hangs over ruin” (Job 15:27).

In such a retinue, violations multiply with impunity, joyful banquets are frequently held, and wherever people wish and are able, day and night they play, drink, vomit, squander, and dance, although it is written: “Woe to those who linger over wine” (Prov. 23:30). Again: “Do not be among those who drink at banquets” (Prov. 23:20). And: “Woe to those who bring meats together for eating” (ibid.). Again: “They spend their days in prosperity” (Job 21:13).

They should certainly have feared and, amid their cups, considered what follows there: “In a moment they descend to the underworld” (ibid.).

Such people are represented in the Gospel by the fig tree about which the Lord complains, saying: “Why does it even occupy the ground?” (Luke 13:7). For in the case of every perverse person in power, God’s demand has almost ceased. After such a person has destroyed himself, the only question is why he also burdens others unto death.

Just as the ground beneath a tree is barren when deprived of the sun’s rays, so those subjected to his influence remain alienated from the light of truth, weighed down by the example of his favor.

Such people are often abandoned by God’s just judgment in such a way that they powerfully commit every kind of perverse act and nevertheless live happily here. Scripture says of each of them: “He ran against the Lord with an outstretched neck” (Job 15:26); that is, in his evil work he encountered no obstacle from adversity.

Again: “I saw a fool with a firm root” (Job 5:3), as though the fool were lifted up with a firm root. For he is supported here by temporal happiness and is not struck down by adversity. He prevails even against the weak without resistance, contradicts those who act well by virtue of his authority and position, continually grows richer through ever-worse conduct, and lives wealthier for a time precisely where he abandons the way of life.

### II

It is customary not only for the wicked but also for the good, though they are less perfect, that their intention or judgment be shaped according to what they happen to see. When they see joyful things, they become cheerful; over sad things, they become sad.

Thus, when they behold the glory of the wicked, they take pleasure in that same glory, waver in their hearts as though it were something great, and desire to deserve such things. Hence Truth himself says: “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matt. 18:7). Likewise the Psalmist: “When the wicked man grows proud, the poor man is set ablaze” (Ps. 10:2).

And Job, speaking in the voice of the lamenting Church, says: “All my limbs have been reduced to nothing” (Job 16:8). Just as strong people are usually signified by bones, so the weak are signified by limbs.

The limbs of the Church, therefore, are reduced to nothing because, through imitation of the wicked who increase in this age, even the weak become worse. Seeing the prosperity of the wicked, they desire temporal goods; weakened by present prosperity, they neglect to desire God, who truly is.

This was also expressed historically: the citizens of Babylon carried away the sons of Jerusalem as captives; and again, the sons of God—that is, the sons of Seth—saw the daughters of men—that is, the daughters of Cain—and desired them (Gen. 6:2).

Even now these people, deceived by the appearance of external glory, love too greatly whatever they see to be beautiful outwardly. The glory of the present life appears beautiful; in the persons of the wicked, like the daughters of Cain, it displays itself before the eyes of the weak to be desired. Hence, as stated above, it is called a golden cup.

### III

Within this same glory, riches in particular appear desirable. For many have thought that wealth is preferable to health, life, freedom from thirst and hunger, homeland, relatives and friends—in short, to everything that exists.

And, as John Chrysostom says, this opinion is maintained not only on land and sea but rises even to the clouds and stars. It is no longer merely an opinion but a flame that ravages the whole world. No one extinguishes it, while everyone kindles it and makes it burn more and more fiercely.

Those who have been captured by this evil are not the only ones who encourage it; so do those who do not yet seem to have entered into it. For the rich themselves—even if it were possible for each individual to possess the whole world—would still burn with desire for more.

The poor, meanwhile, while wishing to equal the rich, suffer an insatiable frenzy of desire. They rage and rave, and the same disease generates different illnesses in different people.

So greatly does love of money weary every soul that it leaves room neither for friendship nor for kinship, and sometimes not even for love of a spouse or children—affections to which nothing among human beings is preferred.

This love appears sweeter than honey itself. Although it prepares a thousand pits for those who give it their hands, it is nevertheless sought and desired by everyone, and they rejoice through countless labors and deaths if they can at last reach even its door.

If anyone attempts to persuade them to seek better things and the kingdom of God, which is within us, they recoil, consider him insane, and, like people delirious with fever, submit themselves even more to what their madness suggests.

Thus they embrace shadows with the utmost eagerness and clasp winds, resembling children at play—or, rather, more foolish than children. Those children, perhaps, enjoy driving a flock with blows or some other game suited to their fragile age and do not wish to be torn away from it. But these are that much more inexcusable because they knowingly trust in nothing and delight in wallowing in its mud like swine—more wretched and more shameful, certainly, than those animals that feed on mud.

### IV

Would that, as Phinehas invokes against Achar’s devoted thing, only those who had decided to live according to the prince of mammon had fallen, and that the sons of light had not also been conformed to this age against the Apostle.

But, what is most grievous, they themselves eagerly embrace the daughters of Cain after abandoning heavenly goods—that is, riches, pleasures, delights, services, and the lusts of taking revenge.

Would that they were at least frightened by God’s threat: either by the statement he made then, “My spirit shall not remain in these men” (Gen. 6:3), or by what he says now: “The sons of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness” (Matt. 22:13).

And after we have once heard, “I chose you from the world” (John 15:19), let us not afterward submit to the prince of the world. For it is necessary that we belong either to the world which God reconciles to himself through the Son, or to that which, according to the Apostle John, “lies in the power of the evil one” (1 John 5:19).

For, as Jerome states in his letter to the Ephesians, as soon as the princes of darkness trip someone up, they attach him to their own world, over which they rule.

Let whoever is such a person see how much worse his final state will be than his first. To use the words of John from the book mentioned above, all those whom the glory of this world deceives must be considered almost without pardon.

For although they see that everything connected with it is bloody and full of dangers, deaths, and precipices, they nevertheless do not restrain their desire. Although they see it surrounded by the worst companions—by insults, I mean, reproaches, envy, plots, accusations, and most destructive anxieties, by continual fear, frequent dread, and a thousand other ill-fated companions of this kind, as though encircled by a crown of bloodshed—they still go mad with love for it.

They find no other fruit in it than destruction, ruin, and everlasting punishment. Yet many love this same glory while despising heavenly glory, and make it something to be awaited. They therefore deserve to be judged more harshly, since they reject God’s grace when it is offered and prefer to choose the evil they know.

So great is the stupidity of those who are deceived that no reasoning recalls them from this destruction, nor do even the obvious examples of those who are continually perishing deter them.

Rather, although they know that from the beginning of the world the same glory has deceived all who love its shadowy beauty, they still eagerly embrace it with insatiable desire. It entices them by means of a false display, like a filthy prostitute who conceals her blackness with painted colors and captivates the eyes of the lustful.

When the perfectly good, then, have been mixed among the wicked, they learn their works, in the words of the Psalmist, so that what was said may be fulfilled: “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matt. 18:7).

### V

Whoever has sound judgment ought to consider the glory of the wicked from its end. As is discussed in Book IV of the *Moralia*, they are overwhelmed by torments all the more harshly the higher they have been elevated in sin.

What is exalted passes away; what is punished remains. They are honored on the road but condemned upon arrival. They reach prison, as it were, through pleasant meadows, while through the prosperity of the present life they advance toward destruction.

When the good see any of the glorious either dying or being dishonored, they usually confess with a groan that human glory is nothing, saying: “Behold, man is reduced to nothing” (Job 16:8). They would say this more correctly if, while seeing someone in the flower of prosperity, they considered his coming destruction.

For then one must consider how swiftly happiness will fly away, when it appears powerful before human eyes as though it were permanent. Any wicked person can reflect, at the very death of a dying man, that his glory is nothing; for then they even disparage the one whom they loved while pursuing that glory up to death.

Of these people and their imitators, under the figure of that wicked generation, it is written: “May his sons be far from salvation, and may they be crushed at the gate” (Job 5:4).

The gate is the final day of judgment, because through it one enters the kingdom. Fools, therefore, or their sons—that is, their imitators—are proud before the gate, but they will be crushed at the gate: they prosper now, but they will be struck down in judgment.

Whoever then refused to have God as a father through discipline, preferring to be a son of this kingdom, will not then deserve to have a deliverer as his helper; instead, he will be crushed at the gate.

Certainly, whoever has been captured by love of either generation or either rank of this life favors its side and does not willingly listen to a word of warning.

### VI

It must be understood that these same kinds are so mixed that they are found advancing together among every degree of the faithful. Until the judge’s winnowing fan is shaken, grain must necessarily be contained together with chaff on the threshing floor of the present life.

From this point onward, however, the discussion concerns those who, while maintaining faith toward the world by their deeds, are known to lie to God through the habit of religion.

If weak believers in secular dress are made worse by the examples of the wicked, this is not altogether astonishing. But it appears utterly more detestable if professors of religion—those to whom, as the Apostle says, “the words of God have been entrusted” (Rom. 3:2)—happen to serve carnal desires, abandon heavenly things to yearn for earthly ones, and, despising God, serve mammon.

How detestable this is is plainly demonstrated by the denunciation of prophetic speech, in which God threatens, saying: “If you fornicate, Israel, at least do not sin, Judah” (Hos. 4:15).

Ten tribes of the sons of Israel once withdrew from the house of David into idolatry. Yet the tribe of Judah, remaining as it were in the house of David, retained the worship of divine service for a longer time.

Through the ten tribes, therefore, the multitude of secular people is represented; through the one, the smaller number of ecclesiastics. However far secular people may stray from the divine laws like those ten tribes, the ministers of the Church, like the tribe of Judah, ought to cling to Christ.

Concerning those ten tribes—as concerning those who now hold the faith in word but not in deed—comes God’s complaint: “Israel the adversary departed and prostituted herself” (Jer. 3:8).

Immediately afterward, to express the ecclesiastics who are made worse by imitation of secular people, he adds, showing how the house of Judah fell through the example of the Israelites: “Her treacherous sister Judah saw that the adversary Israel had committed adultery, and that I had dismissed her and given her a bill of divorce; she did not fear, but went away and herself also committed fornication” (ibid.).

All these things are now fulfilled when ministers of the Church descend to imitation of carnal people; when pride raises them up in the same way, greed wastes them away, pleasure expands them, wickedness constricts them, anger inflames them, discord separates them, envy festers them, and luxury, defiling them, destroys them.

Those through whom secular people ought to have been corrected also incite them, by their evil examples, to despise God’s commandments. Although they ought to shine, as the Apostle says, “in the midst of a crooked generation,” so that they might make them shine, they instead grow dark by following their examples. As it is written: “It shall be as with the people, so with the priest” (Isa. 24:2).

It must be carefully observed that God says: “Because I dismissed her,” and adds: “I gave her a bill of divorce” (Deut. 24:3). God dismisses either secular people, represented by Israel, or anyone placed in the religious habit, represented by Judah, when he allows them, as it is written, to follow the desires of their hearts.

But when security follows them after their sin, when no discipline or rebuke recalls them to their hearts, they also receive a bill of divorce, so that, like an adulterous wife, they may be separated from union with the Lord and do what they wish, and thus plunge more deeply into eternal punishments.

It is therefore necessary for us to consider either these people or those as all the more wretched, since we see them abandoned in their guilt without a scourge; and the more they prosper after their iniquity, the closer they are to destruction.

This is in the twelfth homily on Ezekiel.

### VII

In the previous book, when we were speaking about the violent, we mentioned pride and luxury while remaining silent about wickedness. Those who, after professing religion, descend to carnal evils are first captured by pride. In it, as it is written, “every destruction takes its beginning” (Tob. 4:14).

It especially steals upon them for this reason: as they grow fat from being enriched by the revenues of the Church or by the gifts of the faithful, they kick against discipline; and because they are not among those who labor, they are consequently held by pride.

Then, having a full hand, they fall into the vice of the rich man clothed in purple: each day they desire to feast splendidly and to adorn themselves in more refined garments.

After that, forgetting their profession, they give their hands over to luxury. Among such people, as the comic poet says, Venus would grow cold if Ceres and Bacchus did not abound.

The descent of this ruin is also shown by the arrangement of the limbs: the spirit of a man is first placed, swollen with pride; then the belly; finally the genitals. Pride belongs to the spirit; the other two belong to the flesh. Once these two have enticed a person, they are laid aside with greater difficulty the more sweetly they are indulged.

These people, living according to the flesh against the Apostle, boast of bodily nobility. If they truly believed themselves to be sons of God, they would never, after their divine birth, admire earthly nobility.

Although it is written, “Never glory in clothing” (Sir. 11:4), they nevertheless do what they dare. They are ashamed to cast off entirely the kind of garment dedicated to religion, because of human criticism, but they eagerly seek colors and softness.

Although some abbots even refuse to wear the monastic dress, namely the cowl, so as openly to protest enmity between themselves and the holy Rule.

**Note:** The monastic dress, namely the cowl. Thus Peter the Venerable, Book II of the *Miracles*, chapter 23, where he speaks of Matthew of Cluny, who was a monk and later bishop of Albano: “He was first clothed in his hair shirt, from which he had never been separated as a monk, and afterward in the monastic cowl.”

Certainly, as the *Book of the Elders* says, the same grace is given in the monastic habit as in the white garments of baptism. And, as blessed Jerome states in his letter to the daughter of Mauricius, it is a great insult to divine grace to put on worldly and secular adornment; and after the sanctification of chrism, it is a crime to adorn the head or body—already shining with heavenly splendor—with any appearance of earthly creation.

That rich man whom Christ recalls, to his great reproach, as dressed in purple and fine linen had not heard the Law or the Prophets, yet he is condemned for his desire for clothing. What, then, will that same Christ say in judgment to these people, since even monks and nuns desire what the apostles forbid not only to laypeople but even to their spouses?

Hence Peter says: “Let their adornment not be external—the braiding of hair, the wearing of gold, or the dressing in clothes—but the hidden person of the heart” (1 Pet. 3:3–4).

And Paul says: “Likewise, women should adorn themselves in decent clothing, with modesty and sobriety, not with braided hair, gold, pearls, or costly clothing, but with what is fitting for women who profess chastity and good conduct” (1 Tim. 2:9–10).

### VIII

If this is forbidden to married women, how great a crime is it for men of the holy habit or for nuns to desire it?

Saint Germanus said to Genovefa, among other things: “If even a small measure of this world’s adornment has overcome your mind, you will lack eternal and heavenly ornaments.”

Hence lord Martin, embracing the honesty of women in a brief but weighty saying, said: “The highest virtue of a woman is not to wish to be seen.”

Bishop Cyprian says this about virgins: “Dressed in silk and purple, they cannot put on Christ; adorned with gold, pearls, and necklaces, they have lost the ornaments of heart and body.”

“If,” he says, “Peter admonishes women who are accustomed to excuse their adornment by means of their husbands, how much more is it right for a virgin to observe this, since she has no pardon for her adornment and cannot transfer the falsehood of her guilt to another, but must bear it alone in her body?”

But women of this kind do not accept that holy saying of blessed Cyprian. Rather, they make the faith of Christ void and adorn themselves more for the eyes of adulterers.

These adulterers, as blessed Jerome says in his letter to mother and daughter, whenever they dare, gaze more frequently upon the wives of Christ. They speak with gestures and pursue more ardently what is less permitted.

“Less permitted,” he says, “because just as it is more detestable to violate a consecrated house than a common one, so it is more criminal to violate Christ’s bride than one’s neighbor’s wife.”

Certainly, when one of two sisters is joined to a husband and remains faithful to him, why does the other, who is betrothed to Christ, not preserve the same reverence toward him?

But, as the same letter continues: “These women dress in shining garments, forgetting that Christ is read in Zechariah as clothed in filthy garments.

“For these women, beautiful clothing is an indication of a wanton soul. It is dragged along the ground so that their stature may appear taller; it is deliberately slit so that something may appear which will attract desire.

“Black and shining shoes, with their creaking, arouse lustful eyes toward savage desires. Their hair falls slightly and is gathered up again. Their neck and throat are exposed by chance when the cloak slips, and, as though they did not wish to be seen, they hasten to uncover them.”

This is Jerome’s account. I am ashamed to report more.

But in all these matters and others like them, such people walk not according to the virgin’s Son but according to the old human being. For, as Job says, all the sweetness of such men or women is a worm.

Although in this life they eagerly adorn their flesh with excessive finery, the statement in the book of Ecclesiasticus nevertheless remains: “Sloth will be clothed in rags” (Prov. 23:21).

And as it is likewise said in that same book: “He who joins himself to prostitutes will be wicked; decay and worms will inherit him, and his soul will be removed from the number” (Sir. 19:3).

The heavenly goods of the Bridegroom, which they lose for the sake of these beggarly things, are eternal. They are such that they have not yet entered even Paul’s hearing or risen into his heart, although he was caught up to paradise.

### IX

God enclosed the beauty of the body within certain natural limits, but he made the beauty of the soul free and confined it under no necessity.

Even if the Lord had permitted us control over bodily beauty according to our own choice, excessive anxiety would burden us, and we would occupy all our time with things that offered no benefit. Consequently, the cultivation of the soul would necessarily be neglected.

Even now, when we have no power to contribute anything to bodily beauty, we nevertheless do this and strive for it: we wish, as I have said, to add to the beauty of the body in every possible way through cosmetics, the arrangement of the hair, the movement of the eyes, variety in clothing, and various other elaborate means.

How much more fitting, then, would it have been for us to devote our efforts to cultivating the soul?

Bodily beauty consists only in the skin. If people could see what lies beneath the skin, just as lynxes in Boeotia are said to be able to see the interior of things, the sight of women would nauseate them.

This beauty consists of phlegm, blood, moisture, and bile. For if someone considers what is hidden inside the nostrils, inside the throat, and inside the belly, he will certainly find filth.

If we cannot bear to touch phlegm or excrement even with our fingertips, how do we desire to embrace the very sack of excrement?

The Lord, author of nature, although he created humanity with great dignity, nevertheless permits us to suffer many things in this corruptible life by which he may blunt the pride of the flesh.

That is why a human hair found in food or drink is especially disgusting; and we are less horrified to see fleas emerging from dust upon us than lice, which arise from the moisture of our own bodies.

To understand that bodily beauty, whatever it may be, comes not from the flesh but from the soul, let us consider how pleasing a human corpse is—or rather, how much horror it inspires in those who see it.

When the most beautiful soul has departed, all the beauty it had given to the flesh departs as well.

But those who, through pride, submit themselves to the author of ugliness discern nothing according to the rule of religion or according to the propriety of reason. Therefore they have taste only for the things of the flesh, not for the things of the Spirit of God.

### X

Before the faith of Christ had shone forth, before the world knew of another life, in which the eternal kingdom is received, it was not very surprising if mortals subjected themselves to worldly enticements. But now, when not only all the saints and teachers from the beginning of the world, but also the Son of God himself, born of a virgin, restrain us from those same enticements and urge us so earnestly to desire heavenly delights, it is astonishing—or rather, pitiable—that our madness should lead us to choose to rejoice for a brief moment in beggarly and impoverished lusts rather than to be joined eternally with the saints in complete glory. But what will happen? Precisely what the Judge himself threatens when he says: “Those who despise me shall be held of no account” (1 Samuel 2:30). And again: “You have rejected all my counsel; I called, and you refused. I also will laugh at your destruction. When sudden calamity falls, when tribulation and distress come upon you. Then they will call upon me, and I will not answer, because they hated discipline” (Proverbs 1:25–29).

But, as it is also written, “tribulation alone will give understanding to the hearing,” because they despise everything they now hear in the Scriptures—things they seem not to understand—until they begin to be punished through torments. Then they will recall them; then their minds will seethe; then they will set themselves ablaze in the fires of fruitless repentance. As it is written: “Would that they understood while it is permitted, and foresaw the things to come” (Deuteronomy 32:29).

Otherwise, the situation is as though someone were offered the choice of walking a little way along a short but rocky road and then being admitted among royal boys to a royal banquet, or of proceeding with jesters and condemned men through a flowering meadow, playing as he went, and meeting death at the meadow’s end. Yet, considering not the road’s destination but its character, he chooses the pleasant path, by which he will arrive more quickly at a dreadful end.

These people do some good things and sometimes resolve to live according to discipline, but they continually return to their customary evils. They wish to be humble, but without contempt; content with prosperity, but without necessity; chaste, but without bodily mortification; patient, but without insults. They seek to acquire virtues, but cannot attain them, because they shun their labors. Hence it is rightly written: “Their paths of travel are entangled” (Job 6:18), because they either do not desire the pursuit of virtue, or, if they do desire it, being broken in their effort, they do not attain it. Hence also: “Woe to the sinner who enters by two ways!” (Ecclesiasticus 2:14).

### XI

Formerly, no law except the natural law restrained sexual violation, and yet it was cut away with such zeal that King Abimelech said: “Someone from the people might have lain with your wife, and you would have brought great sin upon us” (Genesis 26:10). Tamar, too, who had conceived by Judah, was condemned to the flames because she appeared to have committed adultery while widowed.

Lucretia, likewise, a married woman of pagan Rome, when she had been violently violated by the son of Tarquinius, disclosed the crime to her uncle and her husband so that they might pursue the violator; but she herself, unable to endure the disgrace, killed herself.

And, to come to the saints, Job, living among pagans without a legal commandment, said: “I made a covenant with my eyes, not even to think about a virgin” (Job 31:1). You should understand this not only of another man’s wife; thus even the pagans lived in this way without the law.

But these women are betrothed to Christ. Men intrude upon them irretrievably to the injury of the Bridegroom, and the women themselves shamelessly thrust themselves upon those men. O what sort of lamps these women will be when they go out to meet the Bridegroom! Certainly they will be found holding cups full of fornications, as it is written in the Apocalypse.

Job likewise says: “If my heart has been deceived concerning a woman” (Job 31:9). To show the magnitude of such a crime, he added: “For what portion would God have in me from above?” They were restrained by the force of the natural law alone. But we would be bound by many and powerful conditions, if we had not become utterly unbridled.

For, to touch briefly on many matters, Christ has now been born of a Virgin, so that he might present to himself a bride without stain or wrinkle, but a virgin, as the Apostle says, and chaste. He has now raised the sign of the cross among the nations and declares: “Whoever does not carry his cross daily is not worthy of me” (Luke 14:27).

He carries the cross who, chaste in heart and body, makes no provision for the flesh in its desires. How, then, does one carry the cross who does not crucify his flesh away from its desires? The Apostle calls those who serve their belly not bearers but enemies of that same cross.

Our parents offered us to God as a sacrifice, just as Abraham offered Isaac and Hannah Samuel. Violating the temple of God—which we ourselves ought to have been—and defiling his offering, we ourselves have become leaven.

Naaman the Syrian held in such reverence the place where the name of God was invoked that he carried away soil from Israel with mules. We, standing in the courts of a church, commit iniquity upon the holy ground, according to the prophet’s lament: “In the land of the saints he has done wickedness” (Isaiah 26:10). It continues: “Therefore he shall not see the glory of the Lord” (ibid.).

The voice to Moses says: “The place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exodus 3:5). Moses did not even dare to look toward the fire; and yet greater is what is on the altar, to which we approach impurely and irreverently. For that fire was not God but a creature through which God’s voice resounded; here, however, is the body of Christ, in which the whole fullness of divinity dwells.

Since an occasion has arisen to speak of reverence for a sacred place, it seems appropriate to relate what happened some years ago at the monastery of Carriloc. A certain vassal named Richerius had taken refuge there out of fear of his enemies. While sleeping at night in a cell adjoining the church, he wished to have intercourse with his wife. He became attached to her like a dog, so that he could not in any way be separated from her.

When he realized that he was held in this way, he cried out, and a sudden commotion broke out. Everyone came running. The two were overcome with great confusion, both from fear and from shame. They had the monks summoned and gave the holy place as many gifts as they could. After the monks had prayed for a long time, they were restored to one another. I knew his son and brothers, and I heard this from those who were present.

As the event itself makes clear, the embrace of the spouses, because it was lawful, was punished temporally on account of the illicit presumption against the sacred place where it had occurred. But incest committed in holy places is often not punished in the present precisely because it is so great that it ought to be struck not with transitory but with eternal vengeance.

Conversely, how much reverence for a sacred place avails can be clearly seen from the following example. A certain king of the Lombards, as is recorded in the history of that people, had himself buried in the cemetery of a church of Saint John, although he remained a heretic. A thief broke open his tomb and carried away the ornaments with which he had been buried as a king. Saint John then said to him in a vision: “Why did you dare to touch the body of this man? Although he did not believe rightly, nevertheless he entrusted himself to me. Since you have dared to do this, you shall never again have entry into my basilica.”

And so it happened. Whenever he wished to enter the oratory of blessed John, his throat would suddenly seem to be struck by the strongest boxer, and he would be thrown backward as though pushed.

If Saint John was so angered by reverence for a holy place against the violator of that heretic’s tomb, how much do you think God and his saints are angered against someone who defiles holy places in any manner?

The whole world is illuminated by the Holy Scripture, which forbids us to sin. The whole world is filled with witnesses of God who have observed it. Concerning them Job says, as mentioned above: “You renew your witnesses against me” (Job 10:17). That is, as many will testify against us in judgment as have observed God’s law—which we despise—even without the constraint of a commandment.

Thus, so many considerations ought to have restrained us: the covenant of imitating chastity which the Son of the Virgin, as commander and guide, made with his soldiers; the condition of carrying the cross; the consecration by which we are dedicated to God either by our parents or by ourselves; the profession of a holy purpose; the reverence due to consecrated places; the nearness of so great a majesty contained in the mystery of the altar; the authority of the divine Scriptures; and the examples of so many saints both before and after the law.

### XII

It is clear that even now, after the grace of redemption, the sentence remains by which it is said that “all flesh is inclined to evil” (Leviticus 17:14). Although the Son of the Virgin appeared for the purpose of destroying the works of the devil, and cut off from his beloved ones the lust which the patriarch Jacob, mourning his son, calls “a most savage beast,” nevertheless that same beast still rages and growls in the forests of our thoughts, so that scarcely anyone can be found who safely escapes the shipwreck of modesty.

But when the Son of the Virgin himself looks upon the soil of our hearts and makes it tremble, and says to the waves of carnal thoughts as to the sea, “Thus far you shall come, and here you shall break your swelling waves” (Job 38:11), whoever has been deemed worthy to be enlightened comes to his senses and anxiously trembles at the eternal Gehenna, which he earns in the contest [or, uncertainly, “marriage”] of pleasure.

But if he considers that the Apostle commands us to flee fornication; that Jesus could not be found in the crowd by the man whom he had healed; that, when he was going to heal another, he took him aside from the crowd; and that for this reason he wished to flee from the crowd of vices and their worst accomplices, as Lot fled from Sodom, and to withdraw elsewhere, where perhaps the sinner’s freedom might be somewhat restrained—immediately everyone, like the devil’s satellites, objects. They call him a deserter of his place.

Yet if he wishes to depart for the sake of obtaining any temporal honor, everyone approves and offers encouragement, even assistance in the form of gifts; they consider him not a deserter but a provider for his own advancement.

Certainly, the place of the faithful is paradise, or any other place in which the road by which one returns to paradise can be held more safely. We desert that place whenever we sin. No one complains about that desertion. But this other departure is opposed because, while someone’s bodily presence in such a place is cherished, no concern is shown for how far his soul is removed from the eyes above by sinning.

Nor is it surprising that the Egyptians hindered the children of Israel from being able to serve God. After the common Lord, who is served everywhere without exception, rebuked the Pharisees because they neither entered nor allowed others to enter, these people ought at least, restrained by this rebuke, to have curbed their opposition and imitated the Egyptians, who, shaken by fear of divine judgment, not only let Israel go but also supplied them with ornaments.

These discouragers, indeed, are accustomed to do the same for those who depart for some temporal advantage; as was said above, they do not consider such people deserters but providers for their own salvation.

For it is written: “You who dwell in the South, meet the thirsty with bread” (Isaiah 21:14). It is as though it said: “You who burn with the heat of charity, offer assistance to the one who strives to seek the Lord, the living fountain.”

But if Jacob, desiring to return to his father, discovers the obstinacy of Laban, who is attempting to prevent his return, he must flee from him secretly or frustrate him by human prudence. This is what it means to be prudent as a serpent, which most carefully exposes its head to injury: withdraw yourself to a place where you can preserve the head, which is Christ.

“Beware of your household,” it says (Ecclesiasticus 32:26). If they say, “You are necessary to your brothers or your relatives,” you will answer: “It is good to visit orphans, but only in such a way that you keep yourself unstained by this world.”

And when the Apostle was commanded to follow Jesus, he was not even permitted to bury his father. In the seventh book of the *Conferences*, the hermit Joseph sufficiently explains that the man keeps the faith of his profession more correctly who withdraws to the place where he can fulfill the precepts of the Lord’s faith more fully.

Indeed, what would it be like if someone discouraged a shipwreck victim from seizing even a plank, or from grasping a branch that he might catch while emerging from the whirlpool, or if he advised someone who had fallen to remain lying there thereafter simply because he had once collapsed, when the Psalmist says: “Shall one who falls not proceed to rise again?” (Psalm 40:9).

Would that we at least abhorred with such terror the place where the soul has fallen, and strove so stubbornly to rise from its fall that we avoided the place where we stumble bodily.

Let this be said against those who call deserters the people who, abandoning the place where they have freedom to sin, desire to serve God in safety.

### XIII

But let us return to the delicate daughters of Zion, who in Isaiah are called not sons but daughters because of their softness, and who are described as walking with uplifted necks and measured steps.

“It is hard,” they say, “what is commanded. We are fragile; oppressed by the incursions of pagans and by many other hardships, we are utterly unable to keep our resolve.”

But if we are fragile, then for that very reason we ought to be humble. For “what does earth and ashes take pride in?” If they are oppressed, where do banquets and costly garments come from? Does clothing, to which God gave its natural color, not suffice to ward off the cold unless it is dyed? Or can a person not live without intercourse? Perhaps someone will claim that the heat is unbearable. And where is the statement: “He will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear” (1 Corinthians 10:13)?

Let Saint Jerome answer these excuses for sins. For in his letter to Demetrias he says:

“For no other reason is the difficulty of living well so great than the long habit of sinning, which holds us so enslaved that it seems to possess a certain force of nature. We are surprised that holiness is not bestowed upon us, idle as we are, without labor, as though by someone else, though we have formed no good habit. For an old evil attacks a new will; whatever you establish in yourself first will remain. Therefore the practice arose of dedicating boys and girls to spiritual pursuits before they were enticed by worldly allurements. But, alas, with iniquity now overflowing, the situation has been turned upside down: the school of virtues has become an amphitheater of vices. Vices are learned precisely where they ought to have been unlearned.

“What is more, we evade responsibility and set the frailty of nature against God, as though he did not know what sort of beings he made, and, forgetting our human frailty, had imposed upon humanity commandments that it could not bear. O blind insanity and profane recklessness! We seem to accuse God in two ways. The just one who gave us the ability cannot command something impossible; nor would the merciful one condemn a human being for what he cannot avoid. And how could what he himself testifies stand: ‘My yoke is easy’?” (Matthew 11:30).

Let us not, then, attribute injustice to the just one or cruelty to the merciful one.

### XIV

The Psalmist indicates why many people are unable even to resist and oppose vices. As though concerned with the mother of vices alone, he says: “Let the foot of pride come upon me” (Psalm 35:12). He shows that pride itself is the cause and occasion of every ruin by adding: “There the workers of iniquity have fallen in pride” (Psalm 35:13).

Therefore, whoever works iniquity outwardly first falls inwardly through pride. In contrast, the elect say of God: “He teaches us more than the beasts of the earth and instructs us more than the birds of heaven” (Job 35:11). For while, inspired by him, they consider what they are, the frailty of the flesh does not cast them down like beasts, nor does pride of spirit lift them up like birds.

Whoever slips through the flesh into lust is thrown down like a beast; whoever is lifted up in mind seeks high things like a bird. For if the spirit is piously held down under the Lord, as was said above, the flesh cannot unlawfully rise above the spirit.

But if a person despises his creator through pride, he will rightly be despised by the flesh subjected to him. Thus the poison of lust arises from the root of, and as the deserved consequence of, arrogance. Since this is so, the soul falls through the origin of sin into lust like a beast when, by its pride, it raises itself like a bird beyond what it ought.

Hence one who seemed to stand falls, while one who has fallen cannot rise. Hence long continence is suddenly dissolved, and often virginity is corrupted in old age.

Is pride therefore supposed to have this result: that those who exalt themselves before the eyes of God through pride should outwardly be brought down to the likeness of beasts? Whoever wishes to resist vices must humble himself under the powerful hand of God.

### XV

Is there not a likeness to beasts in the lustful? Are not horse and mule without understanding, when they hope—or rather pretend to hope—that intercourse of the flesh contributes to bodily health? The prophet says: “Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed” (Jeremiah 17:14), and: “Trusting in the Lord, I shall not be weak” (Psalm 25:1). This is understood of the health of the mind, though bodily health is not thereby excluded.

Indeed, conversely, nothing weakens the flesh so much as lust. Hence Jerome says: “Those who are with men grow old quickly.” Among the pagans, those destined either to run for a prize or to wrestle in the theater wore lead plates around their groins, lest, polluted by nocturnal emission, they be weakened in strength.

But in these people, as the prophet says, love of fornication has taken away the heart. They do not even understand through Holy Scripture what the pagans knew through experience.

Christ commands that the body be handed over for the salvation of the soul; these people, conversely, hand over the soul for the salvation of the body. Yet this is actually the greater injury to the body itself.

Nor is it surprising if one who loves iniquity hates his own soul, or if one whose god is his belly, and who follows greed—which is the service of idols—seeks bodily health while despising God, like an idolater.

Those who worship the flesh by a perverse order, although it profits nothing, and neglect the spirit, which gives life, are truly “vain and deceitful sons of men,” the people of Gomorrah, as Isaiah says, “worshipers of clothing,” since God complains through Ezekiel that they use his ornaments in pride.

They also, as Josephus records that the Jews did before the destruction, wear exotic garments. For Hegesippus reports concerning them that at that time they wore women’s clothing, mutilated their beards, and whitened their faces like prostitutes.

These people, imitating the ancient custom and adopting novel fashions in dress, show that they too are inspired by the same spirit of lust, while God threatens that he will visit everyone dressed in foreign clothing.

### XVI

Let us at last be ashamed to be the worthless bench of lust. Let us break new ground for ourselves, as the prophet says, for it is time to seek the Lord. Let us resist the devil, and he will flee from us.

Let us hear blessed Jerome, who, exposing the shortness of this life, says:

“Suppose that our life were extended for a thousand years and that we reached the final day of our whole age. When the last hour has come, what benefit will there be from the fruit of prolonged pleasure, which, as soon as it ceases, will appear not to have existed? What benefit now are daily delights, linen, or purple to the man burning in hell?”

The prophet says: “In three and four acts of impiety, shall I not oppose them?” It is wicked to think evil, according to the saying: “Woe to him who devises what is useless” (Micah 2:1). But pardon is granted. More wicked, however, is to desire to carry out what one has thought wickedly. Yet even this is forgiven. The most wicked thing is to commit sin in deed. Nevertheless, the merciful Judge stretches out his hand even to such a person and exhorts him to repentance.

But if the sinner refuses to repent, the Lord is compelled to oppose him, and as a great punishment to abandon the sinner to his own will.

Adam sinned once and died; let us see what he did. Against the commandment, he ate from the fruit of the tree. Therefore, if you have despised God in anything, if he spared Adam, he will spare you. Yet he ought to have spared that first man more, since he was still inexperienced and newly created, and was held back by the example of no one who had sinned before him and died because of his sin.

But for you, whoever you are, after the law, after the prophets, after the Gospel, after the Apostles—if you wish to sin—I do not know how pardon can be granted.

Achan stole something at Jericho from the forbidden spoils, and such anger fell upon all Israel that they could not stand against their enemies, even though they were ignorant of the theft, until the accursed thing was stoned.

And what triumphs over pagans do those who devastate the property of the Church or of the poor expect? Because of their shameless greed, the prophet calls them evening wolves.

The Apostle does not permit the man who had committed fornication among the Corinthians to pray among the faithful, lest his impure voice, like a hoarse sound, defile the pure voices of the others in the ears of God.

And how does that assembly presume that its prayers please God when among them, secretly or publicly, not one but many are defiled by a similar guilt?

For the Apostle mentioned above says that anyone who nullifies the law of Moses would be punished without reprieve, as happened to the man who gathered wood on the Sabbath. “How much worse punishment,” he says, “do you think will be deserved by one who has trampled upon the Son of God?” And again, for those who sin voluntarily after receiving knowledge of the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains.

### XVII

We do not say this in order to despair of those who wish to convert. Since divine mercy is present, it always awaits the hour of our conversion; it is as ready to receive us as—would that it were so!—we were ready to convert.

Yet we do not place sufficient confidence in those who are said to be such, because those people who disdain even the purest bread of the holy Gospel care little for the crumbs of these words.

Nevertheless, we say these things because it is a kind of consolation to those who grieve if they are permitted to pour out the causes of their sorrow, according to what is written: “Cursed is he who withholds his sword from blood” (Jeremiah 48:10)—that is, his voice from rebuking sin.

We therefore say what we can, so that we may at least show that we grieve over the perversity of the wicked.

Is it not rightly a matter for grief that Christianity, which ought to have grown stronger in proportion as it advanced, is instead bent away from the state of uprightness, so that its religion seems entirely to have failed?

For we all run eagerly and headlong toward evil. As John says in the first book *On Compunction*: “We hasten toward the fire of Gehenna not through one act but through all our acts.” Such contempt for the divine commandments has crept in that we are not only unafraid to offend God through any evil deeds, but even what we appear to do in accordance with his commandments we undertake more for empty glory than for him.

[Note: [Col. 0563D] Here several words are missing.]

[Text resumes:] …would destroy it; but we, conversely, rebuild it through our deeds, our words, and even the posture of our bodies, by which the disposition of the inner person is always revealed through the outer.

We lie subject to them like purchased slaves, and the necks that were snatched from their mockery by the Lord’s cross we now subject to them in such a way that we serve them even through good works. Indeed, we are ashamed to say it, but we read that very saying of the holy Gospel—“Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Matthew 23:12)—with a certain boastfulness.

Blessed Augustine states in the book of the *Confessions* that a person sins culpably when he takes more pleasure in the melody than in the meaning of the words in the divine responses.

Saint Jerome likewise explains in his letter to the Ephesians that in the Church it is not the throat and voices that should be cultivated with sweet and theatrical modulation, because one must sing to God not with the voice but with the heart.

We, conversely, value melody more for human ears than for divine ones, although the practice of singing psalms was instituted so that, just as David by playing the harp restrained the evil spirit in Saul, so singers by their modulation might drive every diabolical desire from the hearts of their hearers.

### XVIII

It was said above that we make excuses from frailty and therefore, as though by concession, presume to eat meat. But the aforementioned Jerome, in his book against Jovinianus, states that the eating of meat was unknown until the Flood.

Afterward, he says, sinews and poisonous meats were thrust between the teeth of those who murmured, together with the giving of the law, which no one was able to fulfill; and at that time divorce was permitted because of hardness of heart.

The Apostle teaches that God the Father purposed to recapitulate all things in Christ Jesus and to draw them back to the beginning. Thus Christ himself says in the Apocalypse: “I am the Alpha and the Omega” (Revelation 22:13), that is, the beginning and the end.

After Christ therefore came at the end of the ages, and the Omega called back to the Alpha, and the end was drawn back to the beginning, we are no longer permitted either to grant divorce or to eat meat. The Apostle says: “It is good not to eat meat or drink wine” (Romans 14:21). But, writing to Timothy about wine, he says: “Use a little wine for the sake of your stomach” (1 Timothy 5:23)—a little, and for the sake of the stomach.

For Jerome himself says in his letter to the Ephesians: “Just as we cannot serve God and Mammon” (Matthew 6:24), “so we cannot be filled simultaneously with the spirit and with wine” (Ephesians 5:18).

He therefore permits wine, but only a little. You will never find such a concession concerning meat.

In the thirtieth book of the *Moralia* it is said that many, ignorant of the order of the struggle, neglect to subdue the appetite while striving to conquer the other vices. But while the belly is not restrained, all the virtues are simultaneously overwhelmed through the lust of the flesh.

Hence it was not just anyone but the chief of the cooks who destroyed the walls of Jerusalem, because when the belly is not restrained, it destroys the virtues of the soul.

Therefore we must take what the necessity of nature requires, not what the pleasure of the appetite suggests, because, as it is likewise written in the *Pastoral Rule*: “The fall of the first man is repeated as often as certain foods contrary to the soul’s salvation are taken through the lust of the flesh.”

### XIX

A carefully arranged manner of walking is greatly opposed both to religion and to propriety. For just as the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart according to the Lord’s word, so the movements of the outer person are formed from the character of the inner person.

Hence it is written: “The clothing of the body, the laughter of the teeth, and the gait of a person reveal what he is” (Ecclesiasticus 19:27).

Nature is pleased by nothing artificial. How displeasing this is to the Author of nature himself, he testifies through the prophet:

“Because the daughters of Zion have been lifted up, and walked with an outstretched neck, and went about with the glances of their eyes, and clapped and walked, and proceeded with measured steps on their feet, the Lord will make the crown of the daughters of Zion bald, and the Lord will strip their hair” (Isaiah 3:16–17),

and so forth, up to:

“And there shall be, instead of a sweet odor, a stench; instead of a belt, a rope; instead of curled hair, baldness; and instead of a breast-band, sackcloth” (Isaiah 3:24).

Saint Ambrose, in the book *On Duties*, says concerning two clerics who walked disorderly that during a procession he made them walk behind him, because he could not bear to see the bad habit which he was unable to correct in them. One of them afterward, as Ambrose himself reports, fell publicly and was removed from his rank.

Gregory of Nazianzus likewise relates the following about Julian the Apostate in his second book against the pagans:

“I had long been acquainted with the character of that same Julian, since I had come to know him more clearly at Athens. I examined the man, and not without reason. For a truly excellent prophet is one who observes well. In him there was instability of character, an excessively expansive gait, an inflexible neck, shoulders that tossed about, eyes darting here and there, restless feet, nostrils breathing contempt, and uncontrolled, almost bubbling laughter. But why do I range through all his features? I saw this man before his deeds and said: ‘What an evil is the Roman state nourishing!’”

### XX

These three vices, through which both those devoted to religion and the whole human race most greatly succumb to the evil enemy, are shown to be greatly feared by mortals not only by the pronouncements of the Old and New Testaments but also by examples themselves.

He who is the beginning of the ways of God fell first through pride. Therefore the Savior, so that the disciples would not grow proud over the power they had received to perform signs, recalls the fallen angel to their memory, saying: “I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning” (Luke 10:18).

Concerning him, God also indicates to blessed Job such astonishing things—what he was and what he lost—that he might show the terrified man what he himself would suffer for the guilt of arrogance if he became proud, since God did not spare in striking the one whom he had raised, by creating him, to such glory and brilliance.

Let a human being therefore consider what he deserves when exalted on earth, if even an angel placed above angels is cast down.

Hence the prophet rightly says: “My sword is drunk in heaven” (Isaiah 34:5), as though he were openly saying: “Consider with what anger I will strike the proud of earth, if I did not spare even those whom I created beside me in heaven when I struck them for the vice of arrogance.”

Through this, therefore, Satan fell, and through this he lays low every human being who despises him.

If pride is admitted into the heart, it not only hands a person over to every vice; it also makes the virtues themselves, if he happens to practice them, serve it, while he seeks empty glory from them.

It tests some people through temporal things and others through spiritual things. One swells with gold, another with eloquence, another with lowly matters, another with heavenly ones.

Yet the same thing is done before the eyes of God, although it is concealed in different hearts beneath different coverings, so that it cannot be recognized—unless perhaps it is more dangerous when it springs from virtues, because no one dares to rebuke it in someone believed to be holy.

Pride rules the rich more harshly, whether they are rich in possessions or in virtues, because it has greater material for swelling in them insofar as they are supported by greater power or more praiseworthy holiness.

### XXI

By these signs it is recognized whom pride has possessed. It always makes him quick to inflict insults but slow to endure them. In whatever he does not desire voluntarily, it allows itself to be bent by no exhortations.

For what he secretly desires, however, he seeks by pretense to be compelled to do, and he thrusts himself forward if it happens that no one invites him.

He always despises the works of others and always admires his own. He believes that he alone accomplishes everything, and if no one praises him, he nevertheless proclaims his own praises, either silently or even aloud through ostentation.

In sadness or joy he almost always exceeds the proper measure: loud in speech, excessive in silence, composed in words and appearance, disordered in action.

At times he assumes the appearance of humility, but either by a movement of the eyes or by his speech he soon reveals what he is inwardly. He often performs great deeds, provided he is allowed to do them according to his own judgment.

The humble, by contrast, are always fearful and always wary. Their particular characteristic is that they always regard their own works as insignificant.

Therefore, when the Judge himself praises them at the judgment, saying, “Come, blessed of my Father,” and so forth (Matthew 25:34), they will retain their customary humility and answer: “Lord, when did we do this or that?” (Matthew 25:37).

The proud, on the other hand, strive to excuse themselves even when God rebukes them.

The humble, therefore, will hide themselves in humility as though beneath a covering. They thereby fight chiefly against the severe divine retribution directed against pride, and, as though guarding the eye in their body against violent blows, they watch over humility in themselves with the greatest care, always fearing themselves amid their virtues.

Since our Redeemer governs the hearts of the humble, and since he himself says to blessed Job that Leviathan is king over the proud, let each person consider whether he possesses humility or pride.

He will easily discover, as if by a certain sign, under which king he serves, since pride is utterly the clearest sign of the reprobate, while humility is the sign of the elect.

Pride, therefore, is an abomination; humility is a sacrifice. Concerning the former it is said: “Everyone who exalts his heart is abominable before God” (Deuteronomy 22:5). Concerning the latter: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Psalm 50:19).

The poorer people are, the less often they fall into that abomination; but the rich scarcely find this sacrifice.

## XXII

Of the five forms of gluttony, which we omit because of their length, there is a discussion with great subtlety in Book XXIX of the *Moralia*. Here, however, it seems worth suggesting that each person should consider what kind of sin it was for which Adam, together with his entire offspring, was expelled from paradise; for which the people in the wilderness proceeded as far as idolatry, as the Apostle says: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (1 Cor. 10:7). And again, concerning the coveted meats: “While their food was still in their mouths” (Ps. 77:30), and what follows. For this same reason they fornicated with the Midianites. For this Esau lost his birthright. For this Sodom rushed into the fall of fornication, as God testifies, saying: “This was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: abundance of bread” (Ezek. 16:49).

The Apostle compares the guilt of this vice with faithlessness, saying that they are worshipers of their belly and enemies of the holy cross, and that their god is their belly. He declares that this belly and its foods will be destroyed, saying: “Food is for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Cor. 6:13). And what need is there to say more? Christ himself, the Creator and knower of human nature, wishing to show where all vices spring up and where they ought to be cut off, commands this alone as especially necessary: “See that your hearts are not weighed down with drunkenness and dissipation.” If these two are cut off, the rest are easily overcome.

And certainly, who would presume to count himself among the elect without restraint, when Paul himself, the vessel of election, chastises his body for this reason, lest he become reprobate? Job likewise says that “wisdom will not be found in the land of those who live in luxury” (Job 28:13). Wisdom herself testifies that God loves no one except the one who dwells with her (Wis. 7:28). Therefore, those who live indulgently should not flatter themselves, lest, if wisdom is not found among them, they should not be loved by God.

## XXIII

But concerning lust, the instigator of this same gluttony, who could say anything that would not be scorned by those who rage in its flames? For these people heed neither the voices of patriarchs, prophets, apostles, nor of all the saints who have spoken about religion from the beginning of the world. Indeed, they so despise the very Son of the Virgin that they fornicate in his courts while he himself looks on; and in those very guesthouses which the devotion of the faithful constructed for the preservation of chastity within enclosed places, they overflow so greatly with the torrent of lust that there is no place for Mary to lay down the child Jesus.

It is certainly no wonder if slaves of lust do not fear, since, as the prophet says, “Fornication takes away the heart” (Hos. 4:11). For there is no fear of God before the eyes of those whose throat is an open tomb. Yet those who still retain some reason ought to weigh the burden of so great a crime either from events carried out in the world or from the sayings of the saints. Of these, if perhaps they deign to listen, let us recall a few.

Thus, in order to show future generations of this world what most provoked him through this vice, as soon as the sons of Seth mingled with the daughters of Cain, God declared that he regretted having made humanity and threatened every creature with the Flood. For although, when Adam sinned, he cursed the earth, and when Cain committed fratricide he punished him with the spear of a curse, he did not, as here, declare himself touched by grief of heart or repentance; nor did he decree that the world should perish in a universal destruction, nor did he avenge himself with such severity for any other crime as he did for this one, when, in that notorious conflagration, he consumed five cities with fire and sulfur even before the Law. The fame of this event is also celebrated in the books of the pagans. Indeed, as Orosius testifies, even now everything that grows there is found full of ashes.

Why, however, lust is punished either with fire, which burns, or with sulfur, which stinks, we are taught more fully in the *Dialogues* of Saint Gregory. By this deed God clearly wished to instruct all future generations, so that they might know how greatly this crime must be avoided after the knowledge of faith, since he punished it with such severity even before the prohibition of the Law.

When he had decided to restore the human race to the grace of reconciliation, he immediately commanded Abraham, whom he was initiating into the beginnings of faith, to be circumcised as a sign that lust was to be cut away. Thus he then demonstrated that all who belong to him must circumcise themselves from vices and desires with the blade of the cross. But the one who, after the grace of redemption, was first found guilty of fornication, the Apostle immediately handed over to Satan—although he was accustomed to rescue others whom Satan perhaps tormented for various other crimes. For this crime, however, he consigned this man to that same Satan, even though the man might in some measure have excused himself either by the novelty of the religion he had recently adopted or by ignorance of a discipline not yet experienced.

## XXIV

To say something by way of argument: why does God, the just judge, condemn eternally an infant conceived in a legitimate marriage and at the proper time, even if the child dies before being able to sin? Since the child is in no way punished for personal guilt, it is evident that this happens because of that sin which occurs at the hour of conception.

If, therefore, guilt in marital intercourse is so great that an infant must be punished for that alone, how great is the guilt in sexual violation (*stuprum*) or in pollution, which is committed solely to satisfy lust? Rightly, then, the Apostle declares that “God will judge fornicators and adulterers.” Certainly, lesser cases are ordinarily judged by lesser judges; but when some matter arises that they are entirely unable to settle on their own, they refer it to the knowledge of the ruler. Thus, to show how great this guilt is, it is said to be referred to the judgment of God alone.

In this sense that other statement of the same Apostle must also be understood: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified” (1 Cor. 4:4). For why he does not dare to justify himself, although after baptism he is conscious of no evil in himself, he makes clear by adding: “The Lord is the one who judges me” (ibid.)—as though he were saying: Not an equal, but one whose wrath no one can resist.

Moreover, to demonstrate the enormity of so great a vice, the same Apostle adds: “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who fornicates sins against his own body” (1 Cor. 6:18). For our heart, from which the Lord declares that sins proceed, is within the body. The Apostle does not say this because fornication alone is within the body, but to show that, just as it is graver than other sins, so the inner disease differs from ulcers that are on the skin.

Does not God also confirm this, when he declared that the devil’s strength lies in this vice, saying—as was mentioned above—to blessed Job: “His strength is in his loins” (Job 40:11)? Hence also the aforesaid Apostle commands us to fight hand-to-hand against other vices, but urges us to flee fornication. He is clearly advising that, if a soldier who has often prevailed in battle against enemies should at some time encounter one so heavily armed that he dares not engage him, he should withdraw from him by flight; so every Christian, even if he has overcome other vices, should nevertheless keep far from occasions of lust, lest, if he is bound by so much as a little finger, he be handed over entirely.

## XXV

This alone conquered the strongest Samson; this did not pass David, the holiest; it utterly suffocated Solomon, the wisest, when, as it is written, he no longer possessed authority over his own body. This hurled Amnon, the son of David, into his sister. Who, then, can now rely on the gift of virtues? If it leaves stones behind, what will become of straw?

It is more dangerous for this reason: it weakens minds more quickly, because it gives greater pleasure. It is punished so strictly, however, because it can easily be subdued. This is evident from the fact that, however ardently an adulterer may rage, as soon as he is seen by someone he immediately restrains himself—although he ought certainly to have shown at least that much reverence for the divine gaze.

Yet madness is conquered, and Jerome says in his commentary on Joel:

> In this very lust, blinding the eyes of the heart, it so intoxicates the understanding that, for the sake of the shameful part of the body, it bends the precious soul toward servile allurements and resolves to incur present disgrace and future everlasting condemnation, while it abuses a moment of time in an insane itching.

For it does not constrain a person by unavoidable necessity, as other vices often do, such as hunger. Solomon shows this when he says: “It is no great crime when someone steals; for he steals to satisfy his hungry soul, yet he restores sevenfold” (Prov. 6:30). “But the adulterer destroys his own soul, and his disgrace will not be wiped away.” For such a person sins solely because of pride.

Some people do certain good things so that they may roll about with impunity in this vice. Solomon opposes them in what follows, speaking of God’s zeal: “He will not yield to anyone’s entreaties, nor will he accept many gifts as a ransom” (Prov. 6:35). Likewise in Job: “Let him not believe, deceived by a vain error, that he can be redeemed by any price” (Job 15:31).

Whenever we give alms after a sin, we give a price, as it were, for that same sin, according to the saying: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclus. 3:33). Hence Daniel said to Nebuchadnezzar: “Redeem your sins with almsgiving” (Dan. 4:24). And the lord Martin declares that old offenses are cleansed by a way of life made better. But, as is discussed in Book XXII of the *Moralia*, one who gives alms without abandoning his guilt does not redeem his soul, since he does not restrain it from vices.

## XXVI

That hermit proves this by his own deed. Although, together with a certain son who was his companion, he had withdrawn with many virtues, this thought was injected into him by the devil: whenever he was tickled by lust, he should expel semen from his genital member as though he were throwing phlegm from his nostrils.

For this reason, when he was dying, he was handed over to demons in the sight of his companion. The companion, unaware of his guilt but remembering his exercises in virtue, almost despaired, saying: “Who can be saved, then, if this man has perished?” Immediately an angel standing beside him said: “Do not be disturbed. Although this man did many things, he defiled them all through that vice which the Apostle calls uncleanness.”

Of this the prophet says: “Your hands are full of blood” (Isa. 1:15). Indeed, something of this kind happened in our own time. Yet, so that it may not seem insignificant because of its novelty, one must consider that the one who makes the newest things is he who makes the ancient things. The poet also says:

> Again miracles arise from ancient causes.

A certain priest, therefore, in the territory of Avranches, a nephew of John, the provost of Mount Saint Michael,

[Note: [Col. 0569D] In the territory of Avranches. Gregory of Tours called it *Abrincantinum* in Book II, chapter 36 of the *Miracles of Saint Martin*; some others called it *Abrincantensem*, while others used *Arboricensem*, *Arboretanum*, and *Arbrincensem*. In French, Avranches.]

from the Mount of Saint Michael,

[Note: [Col. 0569D] The Mount of Saint Michael, commonly called “in peril of the sea,” and celebrated from ancient times for pilgrimages. The *Chronicle of Saint Victor at the walls of Paris* says: “In September, King Philip of the Franks visited the Mount of Saint Michael in peril of the sea as a pilgrim.”]

had despaired of continence. He went to Rome nine times, hoping that blessed Peter would grant him immunity from his crime, as though he might deserve it on account of his frequent visits to the place.

Although he did not wish to abandon his sin, he nevertheless feared intensely. For this is the habit of the wicked: although they take pride in their guilt, although they openly do evil boldly, in their hearts they are nevertheless compelled to tremble, so that this very fear is an obvious witness to their condemnation. Hence Adam fled after his guilt into hiding and was very greatly afraid, because he answered God harshly.

This man, therefore, out of fear, offered what seemed like a religious service. But in order to show that God accepts satisfaction only for sins that are abandoned, when he returned on the ninth occasion and, as though more secure, resumed intercourse, the wretch died by divine judgment in such a way that, as an unhappy woman testified, when he discharged his semen, he breathed out his soul at the same time.

This was also demonstrated in the case of Shechem, who had violated Dinah and preferred to retain her; even circumcision did not enable him to escape vengeance for his sexual crime.

## XXVII

Perhaps someone will ask why those things that inspire terror are continued without words of consolation. But our subject now is those who, resisting the divine command, have abandoned the fear of the Lord: they incur sickness of soul, yet are not moved to compunction.

The rot of the wound must first be cut away in them with the iron of fear, lest, while the corruption of sin continually flows out, the sweetness of the ointment be rejected. For all the threats of Scripture hurl themselves against sinners so that they may repent. Conversely, all the consolations of that same Scripture flatter them from the moment when they perhaps repent.

For, as Augustine says in his letter concerning John, iron pierces leather so that linen may enter. Thus fear must pierce the mind, according to the saying: “Nail my flesh with your fear” (Ps. 118:120), so that, once an opening has been made, charity—which will endure—may enter as if through iron.

It is the habit of the wicked to refuse to hear anything by which their earthly happiness might be disturbed, but gladly to listen to those who speak agreeable things. Of them the Apostle says: “They will heap up teachers with itching ears” (2 Tim. 4:3). And the prophet gives voice to them: “Speak to us pleasing things” (Isa. 30:10).

But the Lord threatens the teachers and the listeners with terrifying words, saying through the prophet: “Those who pronounce blessed and those who are pronounced blessed will be cast down” (Isa. 9:16). “Great peace belongs to those who love your law”; conversely, “there is no peace for the wicked,” says the Lord.

Whoever does not wish even by hearing to be terrified by the threats of Scripture, how much more ought he to fear experiencing those same threats? Whoever wishes to be secure should listen to the Lord’s warning: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 33:15), so that this may come to pass: “Whoever listens to me will rest without terror” (Prov. 1:33).

Conversely, through Isaiah: “But if you do not listen to me, my sword will devour you” (Isa. 1:20). How pleasing it is to God if we reverently hear the threats of Scripture, and how insulting it is to him if we despise them, is demonstrated in the deeds of King Josiah and Jehoiakim.

When Josiah heard the book of the Law, he trembled. God immediately sent him this message: “Because you heard the words of the book, and your heart was terrified, I also have heard, says the Lord; therefore I will gather you in peace” (2 Kings 22:18–20).

Jehoiakim, however, who not only did not fear but even burned Jeremiah’s scroll, earned a divine denunciation, in which it was said to him: “There will be none of his who sits upon the throne of David, but his corpse will be thrown out” (Jer. 22:30).

## XXVIII

It is greatly grievous that they appear to apostatize from Christ through these three vices—or through the others that shame prevents us from enumerating—but much more grievous is the fact that they presume to profane that most sacred mystery, namely, the Lord’s body.

This benefit is the greatest among all the good things granted to human beings. It is what God, in his greater charity, has bestowed upon mortals, because the salvation of the world rests wholly in this mystery. And certainly, when it is handled unworthily, the divine majesty is daily insulted most of all through this very act.

This, then, is what must grieve us; this is what we must lament in every way, so that, if we cannot correct the matter, we may at least show by protesting that the feeling of grief is present in us. Otherwise perhaps the voice of Christ will accuse us, saying: “I waited for one who would grieve, and there was none” (Ps. 68:21).

In the beginnings of the Church this mystery was not celebrated as frequently as it is now; nevertheless, the rarer it was, the more reverently it was observed.
