In the time of the earlier fathers, those who were distinguished by natural simplicity were appointed to the ministry of offering sacrifice, as the history of Eusebius relates, according to the saying: “The Lord’s conversation is with the simple” (Prov. 3:32).

Those who were to participate in this mystery approached with unshod feet, on account of what was commanded to Moses and Joshua. Saint Pachomius likewise instructed the bakers that, when they baked the offerings, they should meditate on holy things and say nothing frivolous.

When this was violated once in the monastery of Tabenna, it was immediately revealed divinely to Pachomius. He promptly sent Theodore and had this negligence corrected as a transgression of the divine command.

But now it is indeed observed much, much more frequently; yet, what is very grievous, it is observed more negligently. This negligence is plainly displayed by the very appearance of the church, by the vessels of the altar, by the linens, and by everything else that belongs to the service of the Lord.

There is no need to expose every detail individually. It is sufficiently clear what the priests cultivate more diligently: what belongs to themselves, or what belongs to the altar. But when charity, which is the fullness of the Law, has now grown entirely cold, how does such constant persistence in sacrificing continue, unless the malicious enemy opposes those who sacrifice in this very matter, because he knows that they are more burdened by it?

For he did not prevent Judas from receiving the Eucharist. He knew that, just as his deceit is checked in the devout through reception of that mystery, so he is able to rage more freely in those who receive it unworthily.

Against those who neglect the outward worship of the Church, the Lord complains through Malachi, saying: “O priests, you who despise my name, you offer polluted bread upon my altar and say: ‘The table of the Lord is polluted’” (Mal. 1:6–7).

As Jerome explains, the priests pollute the bread—that is, the body of Christ—when they approach the altar unworthily. Although they do not say in words that the table is despised, nevertheless, when they do not adorn it with outward worship, they make it contemptible even to the laity, because carnal minds think the holiness of divine power is absent where they see the adornment of honor lacking.

Therefore, what is also said applies to them: “You have turned aside from the way and have caused many to stumble; for this reason I have made you contemptible” (Mal. 2:8). Finally, the fact that holy places and the ministers of the Church are now held in contempt is chiefly the fault of those very ministers.

This is evident because the laypeople who despise them ordinarily venerate without measure anyone whom they happen to find and believe to be religious. Those who wish to sacrifice to God at the altar must first, through the mortification of vices, become God’s sacrifice themselves; otherwise they are judged reckless rather than worshipers of this mystery.

Jeremiah demonstrates this through God’s reproach to such people: “Add your holocausts to your sacrifices and eat flesh” (Jer. 7:21). “Yours,” he says, “not mine, because I did not speak with your fathers, nor did I command them concerning the word of holocausts and sacrifices. But this I commanded them, saying: ‘Hear my voice and walk in every way that I have commanded you’” (Jer. 7:23).

Isaiah likewise says: “Who has required these things from your hands? Do not bring sacrifice in vain” (Isa. 1:12). And afterward: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. 1:16). And so forth.

These words show that the person who does not first walk in the way of God’s commandments and does not remove the evil of his thought from God’s sight sacrifices to his own destruction. Hence David says in the penitential psalm: “If you had desired it, I would indeed have given sacrifice” (Ps. 50:18). What sacrifice we ought first to offer, so that afterward we may celebrate the sacrifice of the altar in proper order, he makes clear by saying: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit” (Ps. 50:19)—as though he were saying: You are not pleased by the sacrifice of the altar unless you have first been appeased by the sacrifice of a contrite heart.

There is a church of blessed Gualburgis in this neighboring region, in which miracles occur. It happened, as the lord abbot Berno relates, that the relics of the same holy Gualburgis remained upon the altar for several days. But immediately the miracles ceased.

At last the virgin herself appeared to one of the sick and said: “For this reason you are not being healed: my relics are upon the altar of the Lord, where the majesty of the divine mystery ought alone to be celebrated.” When he reported this to the custodians, they removed the reliquary, and immediately miracles began to occur.

If, then, out of reverence for that mystery, the saints do not wish even their own relics to remain nearby, what must be thought concerning impurities?

## XXIX

Every faithful person is a spiritual house. The priests ought to cleanse this house from the filth of vices by preaching. But this has now fallen into such negligence that they either remain entirely silent, or judge for gifts, or pray for money.

Hence it is said through Micah: “Her priests judge for gifts, teach for payment, and divine for money” (Mic. 3:11). And Malachi says: “You do not keep my ways and you show partiality” (Mal. 2:9), after he had already said many things against the priests.

But, as Jerome explains, partiality is placed last for this reason: it is the greater sin. Hence the Psalmist asks: “Why do you accept the faces of sinners?” (Ps. 81:2). James also rebukes this sin more fully; whoever commits it should hear what God threatens such people through Malachi:

“I take no pleasure in you, and I will not accept anything from your hand, but I will cast you out and destroy teacher and disciple, and I will curse your blessings” (Mal. 1:10).

This happens when a priest presumes to offer sacrifice for someone who does not cease from sinning. Jerome says in this passage that the one remedy for a sinner is not to do the things he has done.

Hence it is written: “A saving sacrifice is to attend to the commandments and depart from all iniquity” (Ecclus. 35:2), and prayer for sins is to withdraw from injustice. Earlier it says: “Whoever keeps the word multiplies prayer” (Ecclus. 35:1).

Against the supporters of criminals the prophet says: “Woe to those who sew cushions under every elbow” (Ezek. 13:18). This is what the person does who, for someone inclining toward the love of the world as toward a bed, removes the harshness of correction and strikes him with no opposition of severity, so that he may lie softly in error.

Rulers who love themselves undoubtedly provide this for those whom they fear may harm them in their pursuit of temporal glory. On the road that leads from the monastery of Tiberina to the forum there is a church of Saint Peter called “at the Halls.” Nearby, three years ago, lived a certain robber who, wishing to rob two travelers whom he had received as guests, attempted to kill them at night. But they overpowered and killed him.

When he was carried to the church for burial, the priest began to celebrate Mass for him. When he was about to come to the words of the Lord’s consecration, a terrifying sound resounded through the roof of the church, and the altar was split down to its foundation, as remains visible to this day. Thus the priest, struck with great fear together with everyone else, fled and ceased to offer sacrifice for an apostate.

Let this be said against those who promise that, for the sake of criminals, they will pray for them out of favor toward them.

## XXX

But why do we speak of outward matters, when many are so negligent in themselves that outwardly they alter their clothing, while inwardly, through certain serious sins, they are separated from the body of Christ? And yet they do not cease to offer sacrifice.

When they use garments that are partly or entirely secular, they rightly ought to be compared with those whom the book *The City of God* calls Cynics, and not with holy Joseph, who is said to have received a long tunic from his father.

Jeremiah laments them also, saying: “How has the finest color been changed?” (Lam. 4:1). The finest color is the habit that displays a religious life, beloved by all. This color is changed when certain garments sought with a desire for display make the reputation of their wearer contemptible among laypeople.

“Whoever clings to a prostitute becomes one body” (1 Cor. 6:16), and is now not a member of Christ but of the Antichrist. Of him Daniel says that he “will be in the desires of women” (Dan. 11:37).

As Paschasius says in his book *On the Body of the Lord*: “Whoever becomes even a member of a prostitute has certainly slipped away from the body of Christ, and therefore is not permitted to touch the body of Christ.” For Christ himself shows who ought to receive it, saying: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:57).

It is as though he were saying: Unless he first remains in me, he cannot eat my flesh or drink my blood.

What, then, does the sinner eat and what does he drink? Certainly not flesh and blood to his benefit, but judgment, although he seems to receive the other sacraments of the altar together with the rest. Why? Because he does not first test himself as to whether he is in the body of Christ or not. Then, because he does not distinguish—that is, does not discern—the Lord’s body: what and how great it is, because it is a sacrament, and what the power of the sacrament is, because it is divine and spiritual.

Hence, at the beginning of this celebration, Christ threatens judgment upon those who receive it badly, when immediately after Judas received the morsel from his hand, the devil entered him. Here it is at once shown that judgment would be present in the Church.

Therefore, if anyone who has slipped away from the body of Christ and become a member of a prostitute or of the devil presumes to touch this most sacred body, there is no doubt that he will receive judgment because of it and be made liable, together with Judas, to the same guilt—both because he has fallen and because, condemned by his conscience, he has dared to profane the holy mysteries without repentance or the pardon of correction.

We also read in the same book that God gave the children of Israel bread from heaven, “having every delight,” but that “God was not pleased with most of them” (Wis. 16:20), as the Apostle testifies. For that carnal people grew tired of manna because they sought nothing but carnal things in it.

Those people died in whom God was not pleased. But whoever among them was spiritual could not die, because they ate spiritually; for that heavenly food provided them with the taste and delight of immortality.

Thus likewise now in the Church this food is life for some, but punishment for others. Therefore, human being, learn that God is spirit, and understand for this reason that this food must be considered and received not carnally but spiritually, since it is consecrated by no one other than Christ himself and distributed by no one other than Christ himself.

A visible priest indeed stands there, through whose hands it appears to be consecrated and distributed. But Christ, who both consecrates and distributes it, divinely discerns to whom it is given as a remedy and to whom as a punishment.

For the person who is held guilty with Judas through contempt and vice is condemned together with Judas; but the person who faithfully participates with Peter and the others is consecrated with him and with the other apostles in body and soul.

Thus this judgment is immediately received at the birth of the chalice, so that it may be taught what threatens those who despise it if, condemned by their conscience, they do not withdraw their foot from the Lord’s table.

Hence God says through Moses: “Say to the sons of Aaron and to their descendants: Anyone from your offspring who approaches the consecrated things in which there is uncleanness shall perish before God. I am the Lord” (Lev. 22:3).

And certainly those things were nothing other than a shadow of these. If, therefore, an unclean person was not permitted to approach the shadow, how much less may he approach the Truth itself? At the end of the prohibition he concludes: “I am the Lord”—as though he were saying: I am the one who searches hearts; I am the priest himself, who discern what kind of person each one is who approaches.

Hence Ambrose says in the first book of *The Offices*:

> The people were purified for two or three days, and they washed their garments, and they were not permitted to approach the victim in any other way. But if such observance was commanded to the people in the figure, how great must be the observance that priests must maintain in the reality itself?

Learn, therefore, priest and Levite, what it means to wash garments, lest, with the body in which the soul is clothed defiled, you presume to profane the majesty of so great a mystery.

Hence it is said in the Book of Kings: “If a man sins against a man, God may be appeased on his behalf; but if he sins against God, who will pray for him?” (1 Sam. 2:25). At that time Eli was rebuking his sons, albeit lukewarmly, for their negligence in sacrifices.

The meaning is as though he were saying: If someone despises God, the Creator of all creation, and, unworthy, presumes to communicate to his injury, whom will he have as an intercessor? Such a person neither reverences the presence of God nor fears the presence of the angels who stand there.

## XXXI

Security should not therefore creep in because divine patience spares those who receive unworthily for a time. Certainly, those who are judged unworthy of present correction will be punished more severely.

In the beginnings of the Church, it was necessary that many transgressors be punished even with bodily penalties, so that the matter might be demonstrated. Hence the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “For this reason many among you are weak and sick, and many sleep” (1 Cor. 11:30)—that is, the sleep of death.

Indeed, as Paschasius testifies in the book mentioned above, those who communicate unworthily even once would now be slain by the angels appointed for this purpose, unless the goodness of Christ, on whose judgment everything depends, were to hold back the sword and remove temporal death from some so that they might repent.

Otherwise, plagues and illnesses would never now multiply so greatly if everyone received that mystery as he ought.

Those who repent ought to have a double grief in their penance: either because they have sinned, or because they have wrongly presumed to receive the heavenly gift to their judgment. This offense will be forgiven only through Christ’s intervention.

Hence, in the Law, those who sin against consecrated things are commanded to offer a ram, by which Christ is understood, so that God the man, the eternal high priest, may be faithfully believed to intercede for him before God the Father. And he himself daily covers the charge laid against him by conduct and life [the Latin wording is textually uncertain].

Otherwise, “if he sins against God, who will pray for him?” For although someone may be unworthy because of many other sins, he is weighed down more heavily by this one if, being unclean, he touches the holy things.

This is shown by the example of Judas. Although he wavered in his heart, he was nevertheless with the apostles before receiving that mystery, and was warned by the Lord. After receiving it, however, he was handed over to Satan and immediately went out.

Therefore, whoever remembers that he received it unworthily ought, as we have said, to have a double grief, so that, after completing his penance, he may once again participate in the holy things.

For penitents were commanded that a kid should be taken along with the lamb, so that, if someone fell after the washing and could not eat the lamb with those who were standing, he might at least eat the kid, which is always slaughtered for penitents.

This does not mean that Christ is a kid, but that, according to the diversity of merits, he becomes either a lamb or a kid for each person.

Hence it is likewise commanded that whoever cannot celebrate Passover in the first month—that is, in the grace he received in baptism—should celebrate it at least in the second month, that is, in penance, which after shipwreck is the second plank; let him receive the kid of indulgence.

### XXXII

Paschasius wrote this and much more, drawing on the sayings of the Fathers, in order to commend reverence for the holy mystery and to demonstrate its majesty. Whoever, even if merely somewhat learned, reads these things will, I believe, learn so much that he will think he had previously known very little about this mystery.

Yet in our own time—which is something greatly to be lamented—we mock this most sacred mystery with such contempt, as though there were no Father who sought and judged the honor of his Son Jesus. Truth has been so prostrated that, as it is said in Daniel, we see an abomination being committed in the temple of God.

For the commendation of reverence toward this same mystery, let us offer some examples, if you please. Saint Gregory of Tours says in his *Books of Miracles* that there was a certain priest who, because of his position, had been granted permission to celebrate Mass on the Lord’s Day. As soon as he reached the time for receiving Communion, he was suddenly seized by epilepsy, fell foaming at the mouth, and spat the sacred particle from his mouth. Several people testified that he had been drunk that very night.

The same Gregory also tells of a certain disreputable deacon who, while carrying the case containing the Lord’s Body, let it slip from his hands; it returned through the air onto the altar.

Saint Jerome, in the *Lives of the Fathers*, says of the blessed Eulogius that, when he saw certain monks wishing to approach Communion, he held them back and said:

“You had a desire for fornication last night. But you said, ‘It makes no difference whether a just person or a sinner approaches the sacrament.’ And another had doubt in his heart, saying, ‘How can Communion sanctify me?’”

He therefore removed each of them from participation in the sacrament until they had been purified for a little while through repentance and tears.

The same author also relates concerning Saint Macarius that, at the time when the brothers had approached to receive the Eucharist, he saw certain Ethiopians placing burning coals in the hands of some of them, while the Body of the Lord, which the priest appeared to give, returned to the altar. In the case of others, he saw an angel of the Lord, together with the priest’s hand, give the sacred particle, while the aforementioned Ethiopians fled.

He also reports concerning Saint Piammon that, on one occasion while he was celebrating the sacrifice, he saw an angel of God standing beside the altar and writing in a book he held the names of some of the monks who approached, while he did not write the names of others. When the elder noticed them, he questioned each one privately and discovered a mortal sin in each case. After exhorting them to repentance, he wept with them until at last he saw them being entered among the others.

### XXXIII

Among all sins, however, discord and lust weigh most heavily. Concerning discord, the Lord himself says:

“If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother” (Matt. 5:23–24).

As Saint Gregory acknowledges, one must consider from this how great a fault discord is, since because of it that gift is rejected by which every other fault is accustomed to be absolved.

The danger of lust is apparent from this: no people approach this mystery more perilously than the lustful. In the enumeration of the virtues with which those who participate in this mystery ought to be endowed, chastity is placed first: “You shall gird your loins”—those which God searches, and where Satan’s power resides.

By contrast, Zechariah, marveling at the chastity of those who participate and indicating the very species of this mystery, says:

“And what is his good, and what is his beauty, except the grain of the elect and wine that makes virgins flourish?” (Zech. 9:17).

It is clear, however, that many approach this mystery like unclean swine, without fear of the judgment they incur, and trample these things underfoot. They fear carrying their shame before human eyes more than incurring the offense of presumption before the divine majesty and the presence of all the saints.

For such people, the hardening of the heart—which continues because they do not correct themselves and are not visited by God’s chastening mercy—is already the punishment of sin and of contemptuous pride. If seventy elders and fifty thousand of the people of Beth-shemesh were struck because they looked upon the ark of God, then these people, unless they repent, will much more surely be punished eternally, as God himself testifies through Moses:

“Everyone who approaches those things that have been sanctified, while uncleanness is in him, shall perish before the Lord” (Lev. 22:3).

What then if punishment is delayed? Are these things not stored up in God’s treasuries? For he considers their end and repays their enemies with vengeance.

Nor should we pass over the fact that some are deceived by such diabolical illusions that, although they lie in their sins, they believe that they are cleansed by receiving that most sacred food and drink. Against such people the prophet says:

“My beloved has done evil in my house” (Jer. 11:15).

“Will holy flesh cleanse him?”

And elsewhere, concerning those who indeed weep but stain their tears with pollution, he says:

“You covered my altar with tears, but I will not look upon the sacrifice; I will not accept anything pleasing from your hand” (Mal. 2:13).

Therefore, whoever is in filth should give honor to God and should not presume, while conscious of it, to approach his sacrament shamelessly, until, as has been said, he has washed away the stains of uncleanness through repentance, if he can in any way at last be reconciled to so great a grace after his offense.

### XXXIV

Nor should we pass over the fact that some, being evilly conscious of themselves, neglecting self-restraint, prefer to abstain from the holy mystery. It is indeed better that they abstain, but they do not live, because “unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man, you shall not have life” (John 6:54).

What benefit there is in abstaining from the sacred office when one is unworthy is shown not only by the authority of God, but also frequently by examples. Let us recall one of them.

Bego, a canon of Saint Martin, testified to me concerning a certain priest who had returned from hunting on the Lord’s Day and presumed to celebrate Mass. As soon as the time of consecration arrived, he began shouting over the holy altar the cries that he was accustomed to utter after the hunting dogs.

There was also another man named Leo who had made a habit of hunting. He nevertheless became insane and was taken through many holy places. At last, having recovered his reason, he became one of our monks. As I myself saw, he lived religiously until the end, to such an extent that, whenever he prayed alone, he frequently used to tear out his hair.

The death of another man, who had been cured by Saint Benedict, demonstrates the same point. Although Saint Benedict had forbidden him, he presumed to undertake this sacred office. He was immediately handed over to a demon and tormented until his death.

Some, devoted to the pursuit of vanity, take pleasure in celebrating this holy mystery with gilded and elaborate vestments and vessels of precious metal. They would indeed do well to adorn their hearts equally in the sight of God, as one of the Fathers says, because in this holy work it is not garments but hearts that must be changed.

For, as the blessed Jerome declares in his letter to Rusticus, no one is richer than the person who carries the Lord’s Body in a wicker basket and his Blood in a glass vessel. Such were the holy bishops Caesarius of Arles and Eusebius of Toulouse, as well as Ambrose of Milan, who stripped their churches in this way for the redemption of captives, selling even the consecrated vessels after breaking them for that purpose. They considered it entirely appropriate that, since the souls of those captives were saved from eternal captivity through that mystery enacted in the chalice, their bodies, if necessary, should be redeemed from temporal captivity by selling the chalice.

These, then, offer a worthy sacrifice who drive greed from the temple.

Whoever takes care over the beauty of vessels or vestments should do so solely for the praise of God. He must nevertheless remember that the prophet was more concerned with the purity of ministers. He did not say, “Cleanse the vessels of the Lord,” but, “Cleanse yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52:11).

Let us speak also of some among our own order. They are not permitted to control even the length of their steps or their own will, yet from their personal chests they bring out an expensive array for performing the mysteries. They acquire it contrary to the custom and sanction of the holy Fathers from the unrighteous mammon, and possess it as though they were going to leave it behind for the adornment of the church.

One of these, on whose account the following event occurred—

#### Note

The monastery of Vézelay. It is called *Vizeliacus* here; it is also called *Veziliacus* by Peter the Venerable, *Veziliacus* in a letter of John of Salisbury, and *Virzeliacus* in a diploma of Paschal II addressed to Abbot Altardus.

“As the same Paschal says, its founders were Gerald, a most noble count, and his wife Betha, who, moved by pious devotion and confirmed by their testament, offered it to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles,” in the time of King Charles the Bald, not Charles the Great, as the old fragment concerning the foundation of this monastery states.

Since Nicolaus Camuzatius, a man who rendered excellent service to antiquity, most courteously communicated that fragment to me for the public benefit, I shall insert it here in full.

**Foundation of the monastery of Vézelay, from a very old and incomplete manuscript**

“In the time of Charles the Great, emperor and king of the Franks, around the year of the Lord 821, Girard of Roussillon, count of Nevers, and Bertha his wife, inflamed by love of the divine name, built a monastery from the goods bestowed on them by the supreme giver, in a place called Vézelay in the kingdom of Burgundy, in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and blessed Mary Magdalene.

“Because the territory called Vézelay, in which he intended to build the said monastery, belonged to the royal domain of the kingdom of France, he exchanged it with the said Charles, king of France and emperor, for the territory belonging to Girard, commonly called Mont-Royal. With the emperor’s consent, the said Girard, count of Nevers, and his wife Bertha built, endowed, and founded the monastery and dwelling of the handmaids of God living under the Rule of Saint Benedict. He subjected it, together with all the possessions of that monastery, to the Holy Roman Church by his testament.

“That testament was confirmed and ratified by the unconquered and most glorious Charles, emperor and king of the Franks. By his diploma he placed and accepted this monastery and the nuns serving God there, together with their dependencies, under his protection and safeguard.

“The said Count Girard further willed and decreed in his own testament that, whenever an abbess departed this life, the community of nuns serving God there should have the power, with the counsel of holy men, to appoint another woman of good life and good reputation, chosen from that society and community, with the approval of the supreme pontiff.

“Afterward Louis, called the Pious, son of Charles the Great and his successor in the empire and the kingdom of France, approved this foundation and endowment, accepted the monastery and the handmaids serving God into his protection and safeguard, and confirmed everything that had been done by Count Girard and his wife Bertha.

“Pope Nicholas I likewise approved this foundation and donation in the year of the Lord 858, the first year of his pontificate. He accepted the monastery under the protection of the apostolic see and confirmed everything that the same count and his wife had established in the aforesaid foundation. In particular, he decreed that, when an abbess died, no other should be appointed there except one whom the consent of the nuns, in accordance with the fear of God and the regular institution of blessed Benedict, had chosen, and whom the pontiff of the apostolic see had judged suitable to be appointed, or whose appointment he had approved at the nuns’ request.

“Later Pope John VIII conferred, granted, and bestowed many other privileges, exemptions, concessions, and favors upon the abbess and convent of the aforementioned monastery. He sat in the chair of Peter during the reigns of the emperors Louis II the Pious, Charles II the Bald, Louis III the Stammerer, and Charles III the Fat. He confirmed the privileges granted to the same monastery by Pope Nicholas, except only that Nicholas had assigned it under the name ‘handmaids of God,’ or nuns, who at that time could not remain there in an orderly fashion because of the frequent attacks of the world and of the Saracens. Pope John, for the sake of greater usefulness, appropriately decreed that they should be under the monastic habit, and sent his letters to the abbot and the community of monks of that monastery.

“He further ordered that the size of the community be maintained in such a way that neither an excessive number should produce poverty nor too few inhabitants bring about the abandonment of the place. Moreover, when an abbot died, no one should be appointed there except one whom the consent of the monks, in accordance with the fear of God and the institution of the Rule of blessed Benedict, had chosen, and whom the pontiff of the apostolic see had judged suitable to be appointed, or whose appointment he had approved at the monks’ request.

“Afterward Urban II, Innocent IV, and Urban IV—who was born at Troyes of humble parentage, the son of a cobbler and secondhand-clothing dealer, and was surnamed Pantaleon, as a persistent tradition in the city of Troyes still relates. This pontiff left no other testimony of gratitude in his homeland except the church of Saint Urban. In the city of Troyes, where he had been born, he ordered it to be rebuilt on the site of his father’s house. He constructed it from living and polished stones, leaving there a modest college of twelve canons, with a dean, treasurer, and cantor among them. He endowed it with many possessions and intended, had he lived longer, to increase them still further. He wished that this church, exempt from the authority of others, should be subject solely to the apostolic see, and he declared this by his privileges.

“Aucherus Pantaleon, nephew of Pope Urban and cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, whom his uncle had elevated to the cardinalate, protected this work and enriched it with many golden and silken ornaments, images, sacred vessels of gold and silver, and extremely valuable books.

“Afterward the Roman pontiffs Eugenius, Clement, Innocent, Celestine, Adrian, Pius, Urban, and Martin granted and conceded very many privileges, liberties, immunities, concessions, favors, indulgences, and prerogatives to the same abbot and convent, to the places and members dependent upon and subject to the said monastery.

“Furthermore, the abbot and convent possess a territory divided from and separated from the territories of others by crosses or insignia and boundaries, marked and divided by fixed limits. This territory is commonly called the jurisdiction of Vézelay. Within it are situated and established parish churches. These parish churches, and each and every inhabitant both in the aforesaid city and within the boundaries and limits of the aforesaid territories, are spiritually subject to the said abbot and are subject to no one else.”

The monastery of Vézelay was recently reduced to ashes when, as we have heard, fire entered the roof from a candle that a man had carried in order to open his chest.

Against this foolish devotion—or rather, this greed—John says:

“Do nothing more than what has been appointed for you” (Luke 3:13).

Certainly no rule commands this. Rather, the naked cross cries out that it must be followed by the naked.

The following prophetic passage suits such people well:

“Come to Bethel, and act impiously; offer sacrifice from leaven” (Amos 4:4).

Cain offered a sacrifice to God, but because it had been sprinkled with the leaven of malice, it was not pleasing.

How, then, may these people leave behind for the adornment of the church something they are not permitted to have or possess? He offers a sacrifice, but one made from leaven, who offers something God disdains.

For this reason God himself testifies through the prophet that he hates robbery in the burnt offering.

For this reason King Saul was rejected, because under the appearance of offering sacrifice he preserved from Amalek what he had been ordered to destroy.

But these people, as one of the Fathers says, would rather possess their own chests, not considering, wretched men, that they are losing their souls.

### XXXV

The devil, although he is the father of lies, foretold to the blessed Pachomius that you wretched people would fall into this defect of religion.

On one occasion he appeared to him in the form of a woman, surpassing every human beauty, so that her form, appearance, and face could not be described. Recognizing that she was a phantom, Pachomius poured out prayers to the Lord that she might vanish through the power of his majesty.

Meanwhile she stood nearer and said to him:

“Why do you labor uselessly? I have received power from the Lord to tempt whomever I wish.”

Pachomius replied:

“What do you wish to be?”

She said:

“I am the power of the devil, and I envelop mortals in the darkness of a deadly will. But I cannot approach you—or even come near you—because of Christ, who became human. But will it always be so? A time will come after your death when, as I please, I shall rage among those whom you now protect by your prayers.”

Pachomius said:

“And what do you know? Perhaps those who succeed them will be better, for you have absolutely no power to foresee what belongs to God alone.”

She replied:

“Nevertheless, I recognize many future things from those that have preceded.”

The holy man said:

“And how?”

She answered:

“The beginning of every undertaking tends toward growth; afterward it declines toward deterioration. Thus, I suppose, it will happen also in this profession of yours. At first it grew strong among its vices through signs and various virtues. But when it begins to grow old, whether weakened by the length of time or diminished by the negligence of the lukewarm, it will decline from its former growth. Then I shall be able to prevail against it.”

That this would happen is sufficiently demonstrated by our own utterly unrestrained depravity.

After this vision, Pachomius prayed earnestly, troubled by what he had seen, asking the Lord to reveal to him what the condition of monks would be after his time. Through a vision granted to him, he was taught that monasteries would indeed expand in many ways and that some would live piously and chastely, but that very many would be negligent and would completely lose their salvation. The greatest evils would grow through negligent superiors, and good things would suffer decline.

When such men held positions of authority, quarrels necessarily arose; ambitious disputes over who should preside were pursued; good men were rejected and bad men chosen. Consequently, good people would have no confidence to resist, and almost everything founded upon divine rules would be exchanged for human attractions.

Then Pachomius cried out to the Lord:

“Alas for me, because I have labored in vain! If those who will rule over the brothers are to be so perverse, what will their subjects be like?”

As he pleaded with the Lord with the deepest affection, as it is written there, the Lord appeared to him in marvelous brightness, carrying a crown of thorns, and said to him among other things:

“Take courage, Pachomius, because your posterity shall not fail until the end of the age. Whoever among those who will come lives piously and chastely shall, I tell you, obtain rest.”

### XXXVI

It must certainly be understood that, just as certain words are found in both the New and Old Testaments, which heretics, misunderstanding them, have attempted to twist into the construction of their error, so also it happens with the holy Rule. Through certain of its words, those who resist it and desert it attempt to excuse their own claims of strength.

They say:

“The Rule commands that a monk have nothing which the abbot has not given or permitted. But our abbots are such that they do not concern themselves with our affairs, and for that reason they permit us to have what we need. Therefore we do not act against the Rule if we possess something with their permission.”

But if they were willing to agree with reason and truth, the answer would easily be given. First, it must be understood that, as is discussed in Book XXV of the *Moralia*, governing persons are assigned according to the merits of their subjects. Thus the actions of rulers are arranged according to the character of those under them, so that those who appear good are often changed when they receive authority, as Saul was; and even those who appear and are good may be permitted to fall into wrongdoing because of a bad flock.

This shows that the people are receiving punishment. Hence the Psalmist says:

“Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see” (Ps. 68:24).

It is as though he were saying: Because they depart arrogantly from the way of God, let them receive as rulers, by divine judgment, people who do not possess the light of truth, so that those who follow them, like bodily eyes that see badly, may stumble under their leadership and, weighed down by the burden of iniquity, lose every condition of uprightness.

It is also clear that they can permit nothing beyond what Saint Benedict permitted for sustaining the needs of nature. The one to whom we say, “Abba, Father” (Rom. 8:15), sent his disciples like lambs among wolves. He permitted them, indeed, to carry something for the needs of the time, but nothing except a bag and a purse.

Let those who on this pretext surrender themselves to greed, gluttony, and lust understand that excuses in sins will not profit them. The same thing will happen to superiors and subjects that, as we said above, God threatens through Malachi:

“I will destroy teacher and disciple, and I will curse your blessings” (Mal. 2:2, 12).

Priests bless when, by flattering the guilty, they promise them Christ’s mercy. But the Lord curses their blessings, because, as it is said elsewhere:

“Those who pronounce blessed and those who are pronounced blessed shall be cast down” (Isa. 9:26).

If, apart from the negligence of their superiors, they did not possess personal property because of their own greed, they would not presume to have other food or other clothing than what the Rule prescribes.

Finally, if superiors command anything beyond the constitution of God or the Fathers, they immediately lose the authority to command, and in that matter they must not be obeyed in any way.

The example is that of the apostles, to whom the Teacher had said concerning the Pharisees and scribes:

“Observe and do everything whatsoever they tell you” (Matt. 23:3).

But when they later ordered the apostles not to speak in the name of Jesus, Peter replied:

“We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

There are, moreover, very many among them who live well even under bad superiors. Although they are compelled, as captives, to live outside the common life or order of the holy Rule, they imitate Daniel and the three young men who lived chastely in Babylon and happily escaped the furnace of vices.

Much has already been written—and perhaps more lengthily than was appropriate—about ecclesiastical men who, by changing the conduct of secular people, are themselves taken captive like the inhabitants of Jerusalem by the Babylonians, and about the three vices through which the condition of religious life is most greatly corrupted.

But, as your tears, venerable father, bear witness, the spirit has now so failed and truth has so diminished that, as Isaiah laments, we seem to have become as we were at the beginning, when God did not rule over us.

Is it not so, when deadly hatreds follow among relatives; when hostile quarrels arise; when blind and inexplicable malice rages even to the point of bloodshed; when the wicked envy the good, the greedy envy the generous, the turbulent disturb the most peaceful, the inactive oppose the diligent, the implacable oppose the gentle, the savage oppose the tranquil, the reckless oppose the modest, fools oppose the wise, the cunning oppose the simple, and even the furious oppose the meekest?

The apostolic trumpet rebukes their madness more effectively. For when the Teacher of the Gentiles described the dangers of the last times, he added:

“For people will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace, slanderers, incontinent, savage, without kindness, traitors, reckless, conceited, lovers of pleasures rather than lovers of God” (2 Tim. 3:2–4).

Here blessed Paul gathered together in remarkable brevity what he had previously set out at length, showing that they would be such because they would be lovers of pleasures, because they would enslave themselves to the most vicious desires.

From this all evils arise. When God is despised, pleasures are loved.

Thus, as Wisdom says:

“Everything is mixed together among them: blood, murder, deception, perjury, tumult over good things, and forgetfulness of the Lord” (Wis. 14:25).

For this reason Hosea, lamenting, says:

“There is no truth, no mercy, and no knowledge in the land. Cursing, lying, murder, theft, and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood” (Hos. 4:1–2).

And so have the peoples who contradict the priest—concerning whom the Apostle gives one common verdict: not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are worthy of death (Rom. 1:32).

### XXXVII

Isaiah says:

“The angels of peace shall weep bitterly” (Isa. 33:7).

Whoever belongs to these people and not to those of whom it is said, “Ephraim is like a dove, seduced and without understanding” (Hos. 7:11), and to whom it is said, “Why did you not rather mourn?” (1 Cor. 5:2), must mourn the time of the present life.

Everything is so confused that nowhere can one see even a trace of truth, while everything appears filled with wickedness and lust, with nothing being preserved justly or rightly. One sees the humble, the weak, and the poor being crushed, afflicted, and unjustly harmed by the proud, powerful, and rich; one sees any honorable and peaceful person disturbed by many injuries. Conversely, one sees every worst person being heaped with power, becoming terrifying, and increasing in evil through his swollen success—people whom neither fear of judges nor reverence for sacred authority can restrain or in any way prevent from bringing ruin.

But why speak of judges? Those who were appointed to suppress such things themselves inflict heavier storms and more destructive ones upon the wretched.

This wicked and unjust inequality is committed and practiced not only in cities but also in the countryside, and not only on land but also at sea.

To the leaders the prophet says:

“Is it not for you to know judgment?” (Mic. 3:1).

And another says:

“Perhaps they are fools and do not know the way of the Lord. I will go to the great men; surely they know the judgment of their God. And behold, these have broken the yoke even more” (Jer. 5:4–5).

“Shall I not visit these things?” says the Lord.

He certainly will visit them. As Malachi says, he will be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, and perjurers, and against slanderers.

And, as Amos says, there will be no escape for them. If they ascend to heaven, he will bring them down from there; if they hide themselves in the depths of the sea, there he will command the serpent, and it will bite them.

Whoever considers either the condition of those who, having received God’s grace in vain and returning to the service of the devil, perish, or the miseries of those who, afflicted beyond number, fall into murmuring or despair and incur both temporal and lasting losses, has sufficient cause for sorrow and mourning.

Those who can grieve over such things imitate God in two ways: God is said to have sorrowed over the miseries of the children of Israel and to have wept over doomed Jerusalem.

### XXXVIII

For this reason iniquity boils over more abundantly, as Isaiah says, because truth is forgotten and justice stands far away. The perilous times have come, as we have already said, and the world is being driven toward its end.

Although this end follows from the order of events itself, it will nevertheless find people who are increasingly perverse, people who deserve to be crushed by its ruins, while, in turn, because of their merits, the very order of things will be thrown into confusion.

There is another reason as well. Because, after grace had been revealed, people loved darkness more than light; because, as the prophet says, they were called and did not answer; because they chose what the Lord did not wish; and because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God—for this reason God will hand them over to the desires of their hearts.

The Apostle says of some:

“So that they may always fill up their sins,”

and:

“Let the one who is filthy become filthier still” (1 Thess. 2:16; Rev. 22:11).

Because those who had been enlightened neglected to do what was just, they are justly blinded so that they may continue to do what will make them deserve greater punishment.

To bring this about, the Lord, according to the Psalmist, makes the sending of evil angels the path of his anger, so that he justly permits a heart weighed down by its former merits to be deceived also by the subsequent persuasions of wicked spirits.

Hence it is said in the Apocalypse:

“When the thousand years are completed, Satan will be released” (Rev. 20:7).

He is permitted to exercise himself with all his strength at the end of the age, either for the benefit of the elect or for the harm of the reprobate, with greater fierceness than before, just as a beast released is more violent than one bound.

Then he becomes more fervent in savagery because he senses that his punishment is near. He considers that the time is close when he will lose the permission of his most wicked freedom. The more the brevity of time confines him, the more he expands through multiplied cruelty.

An angelic voice says of him to John:

“Woe to the earth and to the sea, because the devil has come down to you, having great wrath, knowing that he has only a short time” (Rev. 12:12).

Then he stretches himself out into the fury of great wrath, lest he who could not remain in blessedness should fall with only a few into the pit of his own damnation. Then the cunning one seeks out whatever evil he is capable of accomplishing.

That these times have already come, and that the evil enemy is already working the mystery of iniquity, is plainly evident from the fact that every order of religious life and of Christianity has been altered. Impiety no longer even blushes, but, strengthened by the multitude of the wicked, appears to have raised its head everywhere.

### XXXIX

Who those are whom this same enemy subjects to his dominion is shown by the fact that he is said to be king over all the children of pride.

Pride casts down many who are occupied in secular pursuits, and many who hold a place in religious life.

Concerning these it is written:

“The dragon swept away with its tail a third of the stars” (Rev. 12:4).

This means that, through an ultimate persuasion, he entangles many in earthly loves, although they appear devoted to the pursuit of heavenly life.

Elsewhere Scripture says of them:

“Willows of the torrent surround him” (Job 40:17).

Willows are fruitless trees, but they are watered by a torrent. A torrent swells with winter rains but dries up in summer.

The willows therefore signify all secular people, alien from the good fruits of the virtues. The torrent signifies mortal glory, which is inflated by fleeting honors like winter rains but is dried up at the end of this life.

Thus willows of the torrent surround the evil spirit, because those whom love of carnal life intoxicates in their thoughts cling to him all the more tightly the more abundantly the delight of passing pleasure pours itself into them.

Like willows, they bear no fruit but grow green in their leaves, because they sometimes speak words of uprightness but display no substantial weight of life through good works.

Of them it is written:

“They imitate him who are of his party” (Wis. 2:25),

namely, by always behaving proudly and never repenting.

The following also applies to them:

“Mountains bear grasses for him” (Job 40:15).

By the mountains are expressed the swelling pride of the proud; by the grasses, their fleeting pleasures.

Thus the mountains bear grasses for Behemoth, because, always hungering for the punishment of eternal death in them, he finds them laying themselves down before him for every vice. They pass over no evil either in thought or in action. Because he continually recognizes his desires in them, he always finds on the mountains grasses with which to stretch the belly of his wickedness. Each person feeds it all the more delightfully the more filthily he defiles himself.

### XL

It must be understood that in this pilgrimage, where Babylonians and inhabitants of Jerusalem advance mixed together, the reprobate frequently become proud and the elect often become humble.

But humility is lofty for proud minds. Therefore, when they attempt to climb it outwardly, they cannot remain in it for long, because what they seek to grasp is foreign to them; and, as though from steep paths, they soon slide back.

For as long as they do not cast it aside and return to their accustomed exaltation, they suffer as though from a heavy burden in their hearts.

Thus it is said of them:

“The wicked are proud throughout the whole time of their life.”

Although they assume the appearance of humility, they do so in order to acquire empty glory. They boast of that very feigned humility, so that they even become proud because of it if they know how to argue subtly against pride.

The elect, too, sometimes become proud, but not for all time, because before they finish their lives they change their hearts from exaltation to humility.

To have become proud is to have fallen. Hence the Psalmist says:

“Let not the foot of pride come to me” (Ps. 35:12).

He says “foot,” not “feet,” for it is clear that no one walks for long on a single foot.

For this reason they are permitted to be tested by any other vice, so that they may be humbled. Once humbled, they cease to belong to the devil, whom they had served by their pride.

Hence Zephaniah says:

“Nevertheless”—that is, even if you are proud for a time—“you shall fear me and accept instruction” (Zeph. 3:7).

### XLI

But what does more grievous harm amid all evils is this: the worst practice of sin has been so strengthened by sheer habit that scarcely anyone can distinguish sin by sound judgment. Rather, just as Aaron did not resist the Israelites when they were seeking gods, so all are either wicked or yield to wickedness.

Therefore Isaiah, weeping, says of God: “Whom will he teach knowledge, and whom will he make understand the message? The priest and the prophet did not know; they were swallowed up by wine because of drunkenness. They did not know the Seer,” that is, the Lord, “and they did not understand judgment” (Isaiah 28:7, 9), that is, how to discern the weight of sin. Indeed, as is said there, the priests applauded adulterers whom they ought to have rebuked, and “my people loved such things.”

What happened to them, therefore, happens to us, as John Chrysostom says, who either suffer from frenzy or are deranged in mind. Although many shameful and dangerous things are said or done by such people, they feel neither shame nor repentance; rather, they even seem to themselves magnificent and wiser than those who are healthy and wise.

So it is with us: although we do everything contrary to health, we do not even recognize that this very condition is the more insane. Yet if some slight illness should strike the body, at once we call in physicians, spend money, and apply every form of care appropriate to medicine. We do not stop until the things causing distress have been alleviated, if this can in any way be done.

[Col. 0587C] But when the soul is wounded every day, when it is lacerated, burned, divided [*participetur*; reading uncertain], and in every way destroyed, not even a little concern for it troubles us. The reason is that disease has taken possession of everyone alike, just as, if many sick people were lying under one affliction, no healthy person were present to assist them. It is certain that neglect corrupts and consumes everyone alike, since there is no one either to provide what is timely or to prevent what is untimely.

[Col. 0587D] The same thing has happened to us: since no one is sound in heart, but all of us are sick in the health of the mind—some with a greater, others with a lesser plague—there is certainly no one to provide a cure. For if someone were present who could in any measure distinguish Christ’s commandments from our transgressions, I do not know whether he would judge anyone more opposed to his commandments than we ourselves.

### XLII

For these and similar things, which are done in the condition of our present life, now that love has grown cold and iniquity abounds, the Lord complains through Amos, saying: “Are you not like the sons of the Ethiopians to me, O sons of Israel?” says the Lord (Amos 9:7).

[Col. 0588B] After the whitening that takes place in Salmon, we return to the blackness of sin: “They shall be whitened like snow in Salmon” (Psalm 67:15). And although Scripture says, “Make the sons of Israel ashamed and reverent before all impurity”—by which expression every defilement, whether hidden or manifest, is generally included, and which, as Jerome says, is most shameful even to name—we, on the contrary, burn with the passion of desire like the nations. All of us, as Isaiah says, turn toward greed, from the greatest to the least, neighing like a released stallion, so that we deservedly hear ourselves called, as though degenerate from our heavenly Father: “Are you not wicked children, a lying seed?” (Isaiah 57:4).

[Col. 0588C] And again he himself says: “In his indulgence he redeemed them, but they provoked him to anger and afflicted his Holy Spirit, and he turned against them as an enemy” (Isaiah 63:9–10). Hence Jacob also says in his person: “I have been made without children.”

Behold what the condition of this life is—if indeed it should be called a condition, since it tends toward ruin through so many falls into sin, and since the great mass of its perversity weighs it down to the depths. For these and similar things, which are so numerous that they can better be mourned than recounted, those who await the consolation of Jesus must grieve.

[Col. 0588D] O venerable father, how good it is to be saddened by such things! Whoever he is will be called an angel of peace, according to the passage from Isaiah that we cited above: “The angels of peace shall weep bitterly” (Isaiah 33:7). He deserves to be numbered among the elect, as it is said through Ezekiel: “Mark a Tau on the foreheads of the men who mourn” (Ezekiel 9:4).

The letter Tau has the appearance of the holy cross. See, therefore, how great a good it is to grieve over evils, since anyone who grieves for them deserves to be marked with the sign [or stigma] of the holy cross.

Let this consolation remain with you for the present: while the princes of Sodom raise their heads, while the sons of Gomorrah indulge themselves, may those who have deserved to imitate righteous Lot, seeing and hearing evils and being tormented with him, hope beneath the shadow of the divine wings until iniquity has passed away.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0589]

[Col. 0589A] Having brought this little book to some sort of completion, I thought—vainly, as I now realize—that I had done enough both for you and for the lord abbot. But the lord abbot insists, too imperiously, if I may put it so, upon the commission of your embassy, which he once accepted. Although I had already declared that the little storehouse of my heart was exhausted, he nevertheless compelled me to undertake this following book just as he had compelled me to undertake the preceding one.

It happened, however, for this reason, that in the preceding two little books only a few things were said about the consolation of the afflicted, and about giving counsel to a pontiff whose mind, like that of Moses, is embittered by the wickedness of evils. I, who can neither resist the command nor report anything other than what you know better, do indeed do what I can. But while reporting such matters to you at such length, I fear that I may produce weariness.

[Col. 0589B] Should anyone dislike the course of my words, let him compare it with the lengthened wickednesses of the depraved, who, working upon the backs of Christ’s little flock, prolong their iniquity. Let him be indignant instead with those who, as Isaiah says, “drag sin along with cords of vanity” (Isaiah 5:18), and who demand that so much be said against them.

You ought therefore to have foreseen to whom and what you were giving orders. Consider these words as though they were a vessel newly poured out, and cut away with the file of discernment whatever is superfluous, like drops clinging unsightly to a vessel. Just as some ripe fruits are gathered from sour produce, so, although you may find much in this pen that ought rightly to be rejected, you will at least find a few things containing some usefulness.

### I

[Col. 0589C] Among the wondrous things by which God speaks to blessed Job in order to express the orders of the Church, naming certain animals figuratively, he also includes the ibexes. Ibexes are four-footed animals that live among rocks. If these ibexes ever fall from the high peaks of the rocks, they receive themselves upon their own flesh without injury, so that they do not feel the damage of their fall.

[Col. 0589D] The ibexes therefore signify good and prudent men who dwell upon rocks, because they strive to live according to the examples of the Fathers. They also have horns, namely the Scriptures of the two Testaments, concerning which it is said: “He has horns in his hands” (Habakkuk 3:4).

Like ibexes, when they fall they are not dashed to pieces, because if some temporal ruin comes upon them, they escape by relying upon the Scriptures of the two Testaments as upon two horns, and, lest they fail amid disturbance, they support themselves by the consolation of Scripture. Such was Paul, who, cast down amid the adversity of this world, said: “Whatever was written was written for our instruction, so that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Romans 15:4).

[Col. 0590A] Let these remarks suffice for the study of reading. Let us now undertake the matters set before our minds.

We said above that the whole family of Christ—that is, the entire assembly of the elect, whether they live in the clerical or lay order, in riches or poverty, serving the same Christ, namely the humble King, with humble hearts—is signified through Judah, that is, through the house of David.

The ten tribes, however, although they descended from the race of the patriarchs, just as the tribe of Judah did, nevertheless departed from the worship of God and worshiped calves in Samaria. These signify Christians who are indeed regenerated through the mysteries of faith, but who worship greed, which is the service of idols, or cling wrongly to other desires, and thus deny by their deeds the God whom they confess with their words.

The Assyrians signify whatever peoples did not worship God. Thus, at that time, those ten tribes were afflicted by foreigners. [Col. 0590B] So now perverse Christians are subjected to the destruction wrought by pagans. And the house of Judah, which had often followed those ten tribes in evil actions, is read to have been then grievously oppressed both by those ten tribes themselves and by foreigners.

So now also any good Christians, because they often imitate the wicked, are frequently tormented both by pagans and by wicked Christians themselves. Through those people, therefore, to whom everything happened figuratively, it is sufficiently shown that the children of the Church must suffer many things not only from pagans but also from their own fellow tribesmen.

### II

This captivity, which is inflicted outwardly, must be endured more lightly insofar as it is proved beneficial to the salvation of souls. There is, however, another devastation, namely a spiritual one, by which we are stripped not of possessions but of virtues. It is more violent in proportion as it strikes more secretly.

[Col. 0590C] This devastation is especially signified by the captivity in which the tribe of Judah was carried away to Babylon. For it is written that the king of Babylon captured King Jehoiachin and took from Judah the princes, the craftsmen and builders, the first priest and the second priest, the gatekeepers, one eunuch, five men who had stood before the king, and Sopher, who tested the recruits.

[Col. 0590D] After the king of Babylon had captured King Jehoiachin, he appointed Mattaniah in his place. Mattaniah means “mimic,” and he called him Zedekiah, which means “the righteous one of the Lord.” For, as Jerome says in Ecclesiastes, the devil, who is the king of confusion, acts so that wise and religious men are oppressed as though they were worthless, lest they appear among the people. This is represented by his taking King Jehoiachin away so that he would not appear, and by those who are slaves of vices obtaining the position of holiness through some office. This is represented by Nebuchadnezzar changing Mattaniah into Zedekiah.

Hence Solomon says: “I saw servants upon horses” (Ecclesiastes 10:7). Hence also arose that Simoniac heresy, which the chief of the apostles condemned in its author himself, and blessed Gregory condemned in its followers with a terrible anathema.

[Col. 0591A] This Mattaniah reigned for eleven years. Since the number exceeds ten, it signifies the transgression of the Decalogue. Thus, under such a king, the princes of Judah are taken captive. When the devil lies in wait in the leadership of the Church, his fraud rages through the whole flock, so that he subjects to every kind of vice those who ought to have preceded the others through the vigor of good works.

He captures the craftsmen—that is, those who ought to forge arrows of words in the fire of divine zeal and arm others for spiritual combat—and compels the talent of their intelligence to become entangled in earthly activities.

[Col. 0591B] He captures the builders, that is, those who ought to repair with the mortar of preaching the walls of virtue broken through some vice, and makes them cease from the work of correction.

He captures the first priest, that is, bishops, and the second priest, that is, men of lower rank, who fall headlong all the more easily because they follow, as though lawfully, the same bishops who have been placed before them for imitation.

He captures the gatekeepers, that is, those who possess the key of knowledge and ought to introduce the others. He so overturns them that they neither enter themselves nor allow others to enter.

He captures one eunuch, that is, those who practice abstinence. He is called one because of singular continence, and a eunuch because of his professed chastity. He often deceives such men so that they strive to please not God but human beings through the very virtues they possess.

[Col. 0591C] He also takes the five men who had stood before the king, that is, those appointed to the holy ministry of the altar, who serve as though standing nearer to God; he makes them serve the five bodily senses.

And he takes Sopher, who tested the recruits, that is, teachers of boys or converts, whom they receive into their discipleship so that they may educate them in the service of the Lord. But, on the contrary, the teachers corrupt and scatter them either through premature freedom or through bad example. Hence Sopher is interpreted as “one who scatters.”

[Col. 0591D] The king of Babylon historically captured all these people from Judah and killed some, while leading others to Babylon. So now the king of confusion, the devil, turns many who ought to support the religious order in the Church away from religion, either through himself or through the examples of carnal people.

Just as that king killed some, so the devil irrevocably slaughters some with the sword of sin. Those whom he captured signify people who are subjected to the miseries of this life as though in a foreign land, so that they may come to their senses. Therefore the prophet, promising such a person the freedom of his former righteousness, says: “You shall come as far as Babylon, and there you shall be delivered” (Micah 4:10).

### III

This devastation of vices, by whose merit the exterior devastation occurs, has now subjected the whole world to itself; everywhere it rages, everywhere it lays waste. Yet the less everyone laments over it, the more all have submitted their hands to its dominion.

[Col. 0592A] Everyone flees the exterior captivity which, as has been said, is accustomed to benefit the salvation of souls. But we ought to have labored against the interior captivity and eagerly sought refuge. Who, however, will heal those who willingly wound themselves, who more readily follow Simon Magus or Ananias, the heresiarchs of this evil, than all the saints who from the beginning of the faithful have always fought against this perversity?

We mean the evil by which the malicious enemy infects the minds of the carnal, so that they do what belongs to God not for God’s sake but for earthly profit or human praise. They imitate Simon Magus, who wished to purchase the gift of the Holy Spirit in order to sell it to others for profit; or, seduced by desire, they reclaim what they ought to abandon for God’s sake, as Ananias did.

[Col. 0592B] But lest that devastation seize the faithful, God the Father gave his Son as a wall for his city, which is the Church, according to the passage: “The Savior shall be placed in it as a wall” (Isaiah 26:1). He also gave the patriarchs and prophets, as the passage continues, as an outer wall, and the apostles, who stand upon its walls day and night and do not remain silent.

And why say more? All teachers continually fashion bulwarks and arrows of words by which this evil may be driven back from the hearts of the faithful, the evil by which they love human glory more than God’s.

Nevertheless, iniquity abounds. Since now is the hour of evils and the power of darkness, if we cannot resist the devastation already mentioned, let us at least grieve for those whom it captures, and return to what must be said about the exterior captivity.

### IV

[Col. 0592C] Our Judge is gentle and righteous; all his ways are mercy and judgment. Therefore, even in the very punishment by which he chastises the just for their sins, he mingles the sweetness of merciful consolation.

This was also demonstrated among the peoples mentioned above. When Judah was being taken captive by the Israelites, a prophet was sent who rebuked the prince and caused all the captives to be released. And when that same Judah was being led into Babylon, God caused Ezekiel to go with them, so that he might console the afflicted people. He wished Jeremiah to remain with the others who had stayed in Jerusalem. Even when they descended into Egypt, contrary to his prohibition, that same Jeremiah accompanied them.

[Col. 0592D] So now also, amid the daily pressures by which we are surrounded by pagans or wicked Christians, it is certain that some, though few, are divinely preserved. Through their examples, words, or even prayers, the afflicted are consoled and the oppressors restrained.

This happens entirely through a wondrous dispensation, so that sins are punished through the affliction inflicted, while sinners are restored to hope through the consolation granted.

O ineffable depths of divine compassion! God pursues faults, yet protects sinners. Thus, when the children of Israel wished to go up against their enemies after offending him, he prohibited them through Moses, saying: “Do not go up, lest you fall, for I am not with you” (Exodus 19:12). He shows that he is angry, yet warns them to beware the destruction they deserved.

[Col. 0593A] So a mother often becomes angry with her little child when he does wrong; she rebukes him and, in anger, beats him as though she did not love him. But if she sees him about to fall headlong, she stretches out her hand and, in loving him, holds him back, as though she had not beaten him in anger.

Therefore, venerable Father, it remains for you—whom we believe God has preserved for this moment—to devote yourself to the apostolic task: namely, to admonish the disorderly, console the fainthearted, support the weak, and be patient toward all.

As blessed Gregory says, bear some robbers patiently; oppose others with the zeal of preserving love. But do not complain about the scarcity of good brothers. Remember that Ezekiel was alone, and Jeremiah was alone, yet they did not cease speaking.

### V

For the pontiff of pontiffs to rely upon examples, it is fitting to report briefly what certain holy bishops endured or how they conducted themselves in times of distress.

[Col. 0593B] First, let us speak of Father Augustine. In his time the city of Hippo, over which he presided, was besieged by barbarians for fourteen months. Since he had no opportunity to preach to them, he instructed his fellow bishops and all others who had then taken refuge in the city to endure patiently, continually praying to God either to free the city or to deign to call him from this world.

He soon obtained the fulfillment of his prayer. In the third month of the siege he took to his bed, and among the other preparations by which he fortified himself for death, he sang the seven penitential psalms with tears. He said that, after baptism has been received, even praiseworthy Christians and priests ought not to depart the body without worthy and fitting repentance.

He restrained not only clerics but also laypeople from every oath. He also so suppressed loquacity and detraction, which commonly abound at banquets, that he wrote these verses at his table:

> Whoever loves to gnaw at the life of the absent with his words,  
> Let him know that this table is unworthy of him.

His clothing, footwear, and bedding were of moderate and suitable quality: neither excessively elegant or splendid nor excessively poor.

### VI

[Col. 0593C] I would also like to bring forward some words, or complaints, of blessed Gregory. When he undertook the final parts of Ezekiel, he was informed that Agistulfus [Agilulfus or Aigulfus], king of the Lombards, was hastening with all speed across the Po to besiege Rome.

[Col. 0593D] He says:

> No one should reproach me if I stop after this address, because, as you all see, our tribulations have increased. We are surrounded on every side; we fear the danger that threatens. Some come to us with their hands cut off, some are reported captive, others slain. I am now compelled to restrain my tongue from exposition, because my soul is weary of life. Let no one now seek from me the study of sacred eloquence, because my harp has been turned into mourning. And since I am compelled daily to drink bitter things, how can I serve up sweet ones?
>
> What, then, remains except that amid the scourges we suffer because of our merits, we should give thanks?

[Col. 0594A] To show how much he was also troubled among his own people by domestic responsibilities, let us quote what he says in the first homilies of that same prophecy, when speaking about the watchman:

> Whoever is appointed as a watchman must stand on high and rise above the works of his subjects, so that he may benefit them through foresight all the more in proportion as he does not subject his mind to earthly affairs.

And afterward:

> O how hard for me are the things I am saying, because in speaking I strike myself! Yet I will speak; I will speak, so that through me also the word of God may sound against me. For now I am compelled to examine the affairs of churches, now of monasteries; to weigh the life and actions of individuals; now to deal with certain business matters of citizens; now to fear the swords of invading barbarians; now to endure certain robbers patiently; now to oppose them with the zeal of preserving love.
>
> What, then, or what sort of watchman am I, who, still weighed down by the disturbance of so many affairs, lie in the valley of weakness?

We say nothing here of that famous and wondrous book of the *Morals*, which he composed while very ill.

### VII

[Col. 0594B] If so many and such great scourges awaited so great a man—whom even the emperor Maurice himself, who had compelled him to be ordained against his will, pressed very hard—what wonder is it if the pontiffs of our time are afflicted?

Since we have mentioned so great a patron, we should say briefly how carefully he guarded his honor and reputation. For it is written in the Roman life mentioned above that as soon as he attained the supreme pontificate, he rejected the presumptuous title “universal,” and was the first to call himself “servant of the servants of God” in his letters. As a sign of his humility, he wore modest clothing in his pontifical office.

[Col. 0594C] Indeed, recognizing that God had established him as supreme pontiff for the purpose of uprooting the roots of vices and planting virtues, in accordance with the prophetic passage, he condemned under threat of anathema all the customs that he had discovered had recently sprouted up against apostolic tradition.

Then, excluding from his chamber not only young men but all secular persons, he chose the most prudent of the clergy and monks as his familiar companions and counselors. Spending day and night with them, he lost nothing of monastic perfection or pontifical discipline, although he had been placed over nations and kingdoms.

[Col. 0594D] Thus religious monks could be seen everywhere clinging to the pontiff together with highly learned clerics. In different professions there appeared to be a uniform integrity, and such strictness cultivated the conduct of his ministers that none of them dared to introduce anything barbarous or unfamiliar to religion either in speech or in dress. Anyone who happened to lack holiness or wisdom had no confidence to stand before the pontiff.

This rebukes the wantonness of certain people who prefer to live with such men and enjoy such unrestrained freedom in speaking lightly or acting before those whom they ought to revere more, bending even those men, softened from their state of gravity, toward the allurements of their own frivolity. Thus no word of discipline is even retained in memory, contrary to the complaint of the heavenly inspector, who says: “I attended and listened, but no one speaks what is good.” They make such a din that if a poor man—or rather Christ in the poor man—cries out, he can scarcely be heard.

[Col. 0595A] Does not what Isaiah laments then appear to happen? “The timbrel and the lyre are in your feasts, but you do not regard the work of the Lord” (Isaiah 5:12).

Pope Gregory, however, served the poor in such a way that he provided them with every kind of food at the appropriate time. When undertakers found one of those poor people dead in a secluded place, Gregory thought that he had died from lack of alms and abstained from celebrating Mass for several days, as though in repentance.

He so completely despised the glory of his apostolate that an angel appeared to a certain hermit who kept a cat with him for comfort and, weary of Gregory, testified about him, saying: “You have greater love for this cat of yours than Gregory has for the whole Roman Empire.”

[Col. 0595B] He was also so humble that when a pilgrim wished to prostrate himself before him for a blessing as Gregory was proceeding in solemn attire, Gregory himself first dismounted from his horse before the pilgrim.

He never passed over crimes once heard without investigating them. He forbade a subdeacon to be ordained unless he professed continence from marriage, and he allowed no one to advance higher unless his chastity had first been proved in the subdiaconate.

### VIII

As soon as John the Merciful had been ordained, he ordered that all his masters who were in Alexandria be registered individually, so that he might give them sufficient alms according to their number.

[Col. 0595C] His ministers asked him: “Who are your masters, patriarch?”

He replied: “Those whom you call beggars.”

At a fixed time each day he also sat in the vestibule of his house so that anyone who wished could bring a matter before him without prohibition. For he said that just as we hear those who petition us, so God hears us when we petition him.

One of the taxpayers insulted his nephew shamefully. When the nephew sought vengeance against him, John kissed the man on the chest and said: “Son, if you are my nephew, imitate me.” He then ordered that the man’s debt for the entire year be remitted.

[Col. 0595D] Mercy appeared to this same John in the form of a most beautiful woman. From then on he devoted himself so greatly to almsgiving that for this reason he was called *Eleymonos*, that is, “merciful.”

Saint Ambrose says that faith is burdened by no excess so greatly as when a priest accuses an innocent poor man and excuses a guilty rich man. And whoever does not defend the needy, if he is able to do so, is like the one who harms him.

Again he says: “We favor those from whom we hope to receive a return; but it is more fitting to care for the weak, for whom Christ is the rewarder.”

[Col. 0596A] Again, in the same work:

> It is a great fault if, without your knowing it, a faithful person is in need, because this is the law of nature: that one person should confer upon another, as one part of the body confers upon another part.
