Whoever does not give to his brother is not even comparable to the beasts, which provide for their young.
>
> Nothing is so contrary to nature as harming another for your own sake. Yet if faith weighed the matter rightly, it would recognize that the cause is God’s. In your own cause you may keep silent; in God’s cause, to pretend not to see is no small sin.
>
> If you discover some vice in your brother, correct him. And if he thinks himself injured, even if the correction wounds his spirit, do not nevertheless be afraid, because, as it is written: “The wounds of a friend are better than the kisses of flatterers” (Proverbs 27:6). Although the friend may be inferior, if the matter requires him to rebuke, he should be heard as an equal and a peer.

Of chamberlains he says:

> It is proper that we associate with the most approved people and with elders, whose experience is safer. Nothing is more beautiful than to have men of good reputation as witnesses. Whoever walks with the wise will be wise; and, conversely, a man’s household are his enemies.

[Col. 0596B] He so disciplined these ministers that neither their more private bodily members nor their functions were called by the rustic names commonly used for them.

Blessed Paulinus, bishop of the city of Nola, when he feared being tortured by barbarians because of the treasure they supposed he concealed, prayed to the Lord, saying: “O Lord, let me not be tortured because of gold, for I do not love gold.”

Blessed Augustine acknowledges this in his book *The City of God*. Let these things be said about holy pontiffs, so that it may not seem recent or novel to a bishop of our time if he has endured such things—or certainly much lighter ones.

### IX

[Col. 0596C] It is not burdensome to report some words from the apology of Saint Gregory of Nazianzus:

> If there is any disease of vice in a ruler, it is transmitted much more easily to those who are present to obey him than if they see some virtue in him. Therefore it is necessary that those who undertake to instruct and care for others should not themselves be found without discipline and dripping with the sores of vices.
>
> Nor is it enough for a teacher merely not to be evil. In those who are taught, this is rightly blamed unless the teachers also excel in every good action and do not measure their lives by comparison with the imperfect. They should perform what is worthy of their position and rank, so that their advancement may entice the others to pursue virtue, and so that they may cleanse their vices and turn their purpose toward better things both by example and exhortation.
>
> Their greatest concern should be to overcome those who love themselves carnally against their own salvation, fighting against it and concealing their vices as much as they can; who hate those who rebuke them, despise their words, and—what is worse—publicly defend their sins; and who moreover excuse and protect others so that they may not be corrected.
>
> Indeed, when wicked people do not harm their prelates but even honor them, they nevertheless neglect to oppose them for the sake of justice and sometimes persecute them. This happens through the devil’s ambush, so that when the prelates themselves are shaken, they grow sluggish in supporting those who are wavering.
>
> But, as it is written, “Whoever fears God neglects nothing” (Ecclesiastes 7:19). Therefore, when true love possesses a person’s mind, if the justice he loves is struck in others, he too is pierced by the same blow.
>
> And if he himself is attacked, he does not abandon concern for another’s welfare amid the pain of his own tribulation. He is like a great physician who has been wounded: although he himself endures the lacerations of a wound, he still offers others medicines of health. So, although this man feels adversity in himself, he nevertheless anticipates the needs of others by teaching them what is necessary.
>
> It is much easier either to teach when you endure nothing or to endure when you have no need to teach. But holy men must diligently extend themselves to both, being watchful in both directions, so that they may pierce the bold before them with the arrows of their words, and defend the weak behind them—like soldiers stationed behind a shield of consolation—from either the assault of the bold or the wound of murmuring.

[Col. 0596D] Such was Paul, the soldier of the camps of God. Although he endured such great and numerous sufferings that neither he himself could recount them nor we enumerate them, he nevertheless disputed with the Greeks and overcame the Jews.

[Col. 0597A] Regarding one of these matters he says: “We were burdened beyond measure, so that we were weary even of living.” Regarding the other he says: “If I fought with beasts at Ephesus” (1 Corinthians 15:32).

Yet, being more concerned about the faintheartedness of the weak than about his own pain, he said: “Let no one be shaken by these bonds of mine” (1 Thessalonians 3:3). And again: “I beseech you not to lose heart because of my tribulations” (Ephesians 3:13).

[Col. 0597B] Job had done both things. He could say: “The ear that heard me blessed me” (Job 29:11), which pertains to preaching, because he delivered the poor man who cried out. This pertains to protection.

That a preacher, even if he himself is not hindered by wicked people, must nevertheless resist them for the sake of others is demonstrated by that voice of God which says, under the figure of preachers, concerning the horse: “It goes out to meet armed men” (Job 39:21).

[Col. 0597C] Therefore, insofar as the cause requires and insofar as the place permits, a ruler ought to expose himself for his subjects. If necessary, he should not fear opposing their hostility for the sake of fraternal peace. Nor, because of the hardness of his hearers, should he cease from the work of correction.

Elisha teaches this. In the person of Christ, he becomes angry with King Joash, as with a negligent superior, because he struck the earth—that is, the sinner to whom it is said, “You are earth” (Genesis 3:19)—no more than three times.

For he says that if he had struck it five or seven times, he would have achieved complete victory. Thus, if a ruler is able to say, “I have proclaimed your righteousness” (Psalm 39:10), even though the people themselves despise it, he will nevertheless be rewarded with a full recompense.

### X

But, as we have already said, it should not seem a new phenomenon that in our time Mother Church, her rulers, and her household suffer so much not only from pagans but also from their own children. For among the aforementioned Fathers, who shone in wisdom, virtues, and signs, persecution raged with great violence. Whoever succeeds those Fathers in faith and rank must necessarily follow them, as a people purchased to represent the mother, by enduring the same things.

That every teacher should first be spiritually concerned for himself and then for his subjects is shown by the Apostle’s words concerning the Thessalonians: “You are witnesses, and God also, how holily and justly we behaved”—understand, among you—“and you know how we testified to each one of you, like a father pleading with his children and consoling you, that you should walk worthily of God” (1 Thess. 2:10, 12). A little earlier he had said: “We became little ones in the midst of you, and as a nurse cherishes her children, so, longing for you, we eagerly desired to impart to you not only the Gospel but also our own souls” (ibid., 7–8).

Yet we utter such words with a certain embarrassment, since they seem to touch those to whom they are spoken. But if anything in the examples related above, or in any statement, appears harsh to imitate or sounds biting, it reproves only those who refuse to bear Christ’s yoke. As for ourselves, we trust that you do not wish to imitate Nabal, to whom, as Scripture says, no one could speak, but the apostle Peter. Although he was chief of the apostles, when he had publicly learned from blessed Paul, his fellow disciple, that he was blameworthy, he did not take offense; rather, he publicly praised that same Paul for the wisdom given to him.

Let us therefore say also what is utterly incompatible with the twisted dispositions of certain people, but may make those who are concerned for themselves more cautious. I know that even bodily blemishes in priests are not overlooked by the law, but that everything is scrutinized and investigated, lest a priest possess any fault—especially since death threatens him if he walks without the bells, which signify the sound of preaching. But whoever he may be who perhaps calls me presumptuous for succeeding others should remember that Moses did not despise Jethro’s counsel; indeed, Moses is said to have been vexed because of those who embittered his spirit. Every prelate will incur such vexation all the more if he does not rebuke the faults of wrongdoers.

Hence Ezekiel is told: “Son of man, do not be one who provokes” (Ezek. 2:8). For just as the wicked provoke God by doing every kind of evil, so do the good who are placed over the wicked provoke him by keeping silent about what is right. If the prophet, when he was sent to speak words, had not obeyed, he would have provoked the almighty Lord by his silence just as the people did by their perverse conduct. It is therefore a fault of the wicked to do perverse things, and a fault of the good to keep silent about what is right. In this respect, then, the good together with the wicked provoke God, because when they do not rebuke perverse actions, they grant the wicked, through their silence, permission to advance in them. Many are so foolish that they either do not recognize the evil they commit or judge their faults to be so much smaller as the rebuke that chastises them is milder. Thus, if they do not hear what is right, lying in their perversities, they are secure through ignorance.

### XI

There are many who do not even deign to hear God’s words with their bodily ears. The malignant enemy so possesses them that he does not leave them, once captured, to any dart of preaching. Thus God says to blessed Job concerning that same enemy: “The archer’s arrow will not put him to flight” (Job 41:19). The arrows are the Lord’s words, as in: “Your arrows are sharp” (Ps. 44:6).

The bow, made from horn and sinew, signifies the Old Testament because of the hardness of its severity, and the New because of the flexibility of its mercy. Whoever is completely seized by that enemy disdains to hear the words of preachers at all. Therefore, angered by their preceding sins, the Lord says through the prophet to those whom he abandons in just judgment: “I will send among you poisonous serpents, against which there is no enchantment” (Jer. 8:17)—that is, “I will hand you over to such demons that no exhortation from preachers, as though it were an enchanter’s song, can drive them away from you.”

### XII

Others are subtly led astray by the Lord’s saying: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12:47). They suppose that ignorance is an excuse for sin. They must be told that not knowing is one thing, and unwillingness another: the former is slowness, the latter pride. Such people therefore have no excuse, because, if they wished, they could know.

Against them it is said in Job concerning God: “He seals the hand of every man, so that each may know his own works” (Job 37:7). For human beings were created rational in such a way that they cannot be unaware of what they have done. By the natural law they are compelled to know whether what they do is wrong or right. For they are punished or rewarded for their deeds by the just Judge only if they could know what they did.

Those who scorn instruction are themselves witnesses against themselves, because they know how to learn what they do. Otherwise, why do they boast publicly of certain actions as though they had been well performed? And again, why are they ashamed to be seen in some of their actions? Hence a certain wise man says: “Since wickedness is fearful, conscience bears witness to condemnation.” For when fear accuses the conscience, it itself bears witness against the person, since he knows that what he fears to have known is evil.

Let the wicked therefore flee human eyes; they certainly cannot flee themselves. In the sin they commit they first encounter the judgment of reason against themselves, and afterward they are brought before the strict judgment of the eternal Judge. Perhaps this is what the Psalmist means: “Deep calls to deep” (Ps. 41:8). For deep calling to deep is to pass from one judgment to another.

Let holy preachers go forth and rebuke the deeds of sinners. Let perverse hearers despise their words, defend their perversities as much as they wish, and, by defending their shameless deeds still more shamelessly, multiply them. They are certainly witnesses against themselves in their conscience, for they have no excuse.

### XIII

Some not only despise words of admonition but also take violent offense against those who admonish them. Since scandal is exceedingly dangerous, good men often prefer to remain silent rather than scandalize the wicked by speaking. Yet they are not safe even in silence, because of the saying: “If you do not declare his iniquity to the wicked, I will require his blood at your hand” (Ezek. 3:18).

From this we must understand that, insofar as we can do so without sin, we ought to avoid giving offense to our neighbors. But if offense is taken at the truth, it is better to allow offense to arise than to abandon the truth. The teacher of truth proves this by his action: so that scandal might not arise in certain hearts, he paid a tax that he did not owe. But when he saw scandal arising against the truth in certain hearts, he allowed them to remain in their scandal, saying: “Let them alone; they are blind guides of the blind” (Matt. 15:14).

This is in Book VII of *The Homilies on Ezekiel*. Likewise, in Book X: “Do not fear,” he says, “because the house is rebellious” (Ezek. 2:6). A person ought to have been feared if he, as a human being, had feared the author of all things. For, as we said above, whoever does not fear God is not a human being. Whoever lacks the understanding of reason directed toward fear of God is less to be feared precisely because he is not what he ought to be.

Those who are members of almighty God ought indeed to be held in fear. If they are saddened, God, who dwells in them, is offended; and on earth they commonly rebuke what God condemns from heaven. But the wicked, as we have said, are not to be feared. Hence the same prophet is again told: “Do not fear them”; and because such people commonly slander, it is added, “nor their words” (ibid.), because they are unbelieving and subversive toward you. They are no more to be feared for their slanders than they are shown to be pleasing to God.

It is exceedingly foolish to seek to please those whom we know do not please God. No one can be pleasing in one and the same matter both to God and to his enemies. Therefore, whoever pleases God’s enemy denies himself to be God’s friend. Hence holy men do not fear provoking to hatred those whom they know do not love God.

Their slander is therefore a test of our life, because unless we possessed some good, we would not displease the wicked. But we must understand that, just as we ought not deliberately to stir up the tongues of slanderers lest they perish, so, when their malice has stirred them up, we ought to endure them with equanimity, so that our merit may increase. At times, however, we must restrain them, lest, while they spread evil about us, they corrupt the hearts of innocent people who might have listened to us for their own good.

For this reason John rebuked the tongue of his slanderer, saying: “The one who loves to hold the primacy among them, Diotrephes, does not receive us. Therefore, if I come, I will call attention to his works, which he performs with malicious words, prattling against us” (3 John 9–10). Thus, as far as it depends on us, as Jerome says in his letter to the Galatians, we ought to provoke no one’s hostility. But if, by speaking the truth, we happen to acquire enemies, we are nevertheless not their enemies, since they are enemies of the truth.

Hence Truth itself says to Abraham: “I will be an enemy to your enemies” (Exod. 23:22). This would certainly not have happened if Abraham had deserved their hostility through his own fault. Jerome himself likewise says in the same letter to the Galatians: “If it is possible for us to please both God and human beings, we should please human beings. But if we cannot please human beings without displeasing God, we ought to please God rather than human beings.”

### XIV

But while we say this, we are distressed even more deeply because the minds of the wicked hate what is highest all the more obstinately the more tightly they have clung to what is lowest. Nor is it enough for them to perish themselves; what is worse, when they see others being rebuked, they oppose the rebukes of those who correct them, lest at least others be corrected.

Therefore it is rightly said of their head: “The shadows protect his shadow” (Job 40:17). All the wicked are shadows of the devil; by serving as imitators of his wickedness, they draw from his body, as it were, the appearance of an image. Shadows protect a shadow because sinners defend another sinner in the very matter in which they are conscious of their own guilt.

They do this with the deliberate purpose of preventing the fault in which they themselves are bound from being corrected in others and eventually reaching them. Those whom similar guilt joins in harmonious stubbornness are also compacted by perverse defense, so that they protect one another from their crimes through mutual defense. They cover themselves when they protect others, because they foresee that their own life will be attacked, and therefore observe others being exposed to free correction.

Thus the sum of crimes increases while it is defended, and each person’s wickedness becomes easier to commit insofar as it becomes more difficult to punish. The crimes of sinners grow all the more the longer they remain unpunished through the defense of the powerful.

### XV

All who refuse to hear God’s words reveal by that very contempt that they are not on God’s side. Nevertheless, however much they rebel, they must still be admonished, lest their blood be required from the shepherd’s hand: “If you declare to the wicked,” he says, “and he is not converted, he will die in his iniquity; but you have delivered your own soul” (Ezek. 3:19).

As it is said in the exposition of this verse, the subject dies without you when, in the action that leads to death, he has you as an opponent. For you become joined to the death that you do not oppose. Let the ruler therefore act so that he does not die when his subject dies: let him oppose evil deeds, as it is written: “Run, hasten, rouse your friend” (Prov. 6:3).

If the wicked man dies while the watchman remains silent, it is certainly true that he was not worthy to receive a word from God; yet the one who killed him was the person who, by remaining silent, handed him over to death. Hence blessed Gregory adds:

“We must consider how closely the sins of subjects and rulers are bound together. That we are not worthy shepherds is due to your fault; and that you decline into iniquity is due to our guilt, because you do not have us opposing your sins. You spare yourselves and us if you cease from wicked deeds. We spare ourselves and you when we do not remain silent about what displeases us. But we have added the deaths of others to our own sins, and we have killed as many as we see dying daily while we remain silent.”

For, as that same teacher testifies, no sacrifice is so acceptable to God as zeal for souls. Because Phinehas, moved by this zeal, pierced one adulterer with a dagger, he immediately removed God’s anger from the whole people. Because Eli did not possess it, he eventually kindled God’s anger against himself inextinguishably.

And so that God might console teachers amid this difficulty of being heard, when he sent the prophet Ezekiel to the children of Israel, he frequently inserted into his speech: “If perhaps he will hear,” and, “If perhaps they will desist” (Ezek. 2:7). In this doubtful adverb—“perhaps”—we must note that the prophet is both sent and the hardness of his hearers is indicated. Through these words God intimates that the person who has undertaken the office of preaching must neither remain silent nor be saddened by the hardness of his hearers.

If God himself scarcely declares his words to be heard, why should a teacher be distressed if he is despised in his admonition?

### XVI

The hardness of the wicked has indeed become exceedingly calloused. As God says to each such person through the prophet: “I know that you are hard, and your neck is an iron sinew” (Isa. 48:4). When you consider this, I fear that it may become burdensome to you, since we magnify the office of preaching so greatly in order to stir you to action. For this reason I wish that some other avenue might have opened in this necessity.

I know that the prophet said: “Upon the willows in its midst we hung our instruments” (Ps. 136:2)—that is, among people who are exceedingly obstinate. Because willows bear no fruit of good works, we hold back the words of preaching. He himself also says: “I was mute and silent from good things, and was humbled” (Ps. 38:3).

When Jeremiah saw that he was scarcely heard, he sought silence, saying: “I will not remember him, nor speak any more in his name” (Jer. 20:9). But true preachers, when they see that the crimes of the wicked increase because they themselves do not correct them, endure a kind of force in their hearts until they burst forth into open correction.

Thus another of the same prophets, when he had said in silence because of the incorrigible, “I was silent from good things” (Ps. 38:3), immediately burned with the zeal of charity and added: “And my sorrow was renewed. My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation the fire burned” (ibid.). Another, after saying, “I will not speak any more in his name,” was immediately kindled by the same fire and added: “His word became in my heart like a burning fire enclosed in my bones, and I grew faint, unable to endure it” (Jer. 20:9). “For I heard the insults of many.”

Thus the zeal of charity in holy men increases when it is restrained. They console themselves in such a way that, bursting forth in speech, they at least do not cease to rebuke what they cannot correct.

It remains, however, as Prosper says, that those who despise words should see good works in the teacher, so that they may revere them. If it happens that the preacher is despised by the powerful or by outsiders, let him sing for himself and his own people, with Joshua: “But I and my house will follow the Lord” (Josh. 24:17). It is certain that the faithful themselves advance more through examples than through words, and the two must necessarily be joined, so that what someone preaches by speaking he may confirm by doing.

### XVII

Among those who endure hearing the words of preaching in some fashion, we must recall what God says to the prophet: “If you judge them, son of man, if you judge them, show them the iniquities of their fathers” (Ezek. 20:4). And again: “Son of man, I am sending you to apostate nations, to the children of Israel; their fathers transgressed my covenant” (Ezek. 2:3), and so forth, until he adds: “Perhaps even they will hear this” (ibid., 5).

The fact that he calls them “apostate nations” applies especially to those who, through monastic profession, relapse into worldly desires. Of them it is written: “Woe to the sinner who enters by two ways” (Sir. 2:14). For *apostate* means one who turns back. Whoever has put his hand to the plough and looks back is plainly shown to be an apostate and, as God himself testifies, is declared wholly unfit for the kingdom of God.

The ninth homily on Ezekiel likewise states that just as the person who departs from faith in God is an apostate, so one who returns to perverse action after making a profession is without any doubt reckoned an apostate from almighty God, even if he appears to retain the faith.

Is it not apostasy to despise the traditions of the Fathers concerning clothing or food, when God has forbidden the boundaries established by the Fathers to be transgressed, and when, despising the quality or quantity of food prescribed through blessed Benedict, one desires bloody feasts with the children of Israel? Those who despised the manna and the measure of an omer, and desired pots of meat, are rebuked for returning in their hearts to Egypt.

Is it not apostasy to reject humble clothing and seek splendid garments, when the perfect apostate, the angel, fell into hell because he grew proud through his beauty? And is it not apostasy to worship the belly, when Paul, weeping, declares that the “gluttons” (*ligurgitones*) are enemies of the holy cross and have their belly for their god?

These words concerning apostasy apply to us, I say, since in our own time certain wanton and insolent persons among us have dared to change the religious habit that they had retained throughout so many preceding years.

### XVIII

What will these people say on the day of judgment, or how will they appear, when religion has extended as far as them and collapsed in their hands? Let them themselves consider their hidden matters, about which it is shameful to speak. This alone is certain: they change their garments outwardly because their hearts have been changed inwardly.

God had said through Jeremiah: “See whether anything like this has happened, whether a nation has changed its gods—and certainly they are not gods. But my people have changed their glory” (Jer. 2:11). And afterward: “You broke my yoke and said: ‘I will not serve’” (Jer. 2:20). Does this not apply also to these people?

For, to put the matter plainly, all who practice any arts for the purposes of this life carry them out as they learned them from their teachers, and use the tools appropriate to the activity to which they are devoted—sailors, shoemakers, and craftsmen alike. But we monks alone cast aside the instruments of good works that Saint Benedict constructed for attaining heavenly life. We alone, deserters of our profession, cross the lines that God has shown us through teachers, now to the right and now to the left, and do not deign to use the instruments of good works as they were handed down by our teachers.

Although the cruelty of heart in such people has become calloused, and is much more obstinate and difficult to correct than that of laypeople, they too must be admonished, since as long as they live they can be changed for the better. Thus blessed Gregory admonished Venantius, who had gone from being a monk to becoming a patrician, saying:

“Whether you wish it or not, I shall speak to you, because I desire either that you be saved or that I be rescued from your death. While you can, shudder at your fault and at the severity of the future Judge, lest you then feel it bitterly, when you can no longer escape it with any tears. Consider what God will do with a perverse deed, if in his judgment he rejects some people for an idle word. You know with what death Ananias was punished, because he kept back part of the money he had vowed to God. If, then, the one who took away coins was worthy of death, consider what punishment is deserved by the one who, through forgetfulness of his profession, withheld himself from God.

“Behold, brought to sorrow by the sadness of your deed, I speak in mourning; and I confess that I marvel at heavenly mercy, since it sees you in your pride and tolerates you: it sees you fleeing from life and yet still preserves you for life.”

When that same Venantius fell into a very serious illness, Gregory, hearing of it, wrote back to Bishop John, saying:

“I have received the letter of your Fraternity, which spoke to me of the illness of my most beloved son, Lord Venantius. When I heard this, tears broke forth from me amid groans. Therefore let Your Holiness take great care of him: exhorting him, asking him, setting before him the terrifying judgment of God, and promising him God’s ineffable mercy, so that at the very end he may return to the resolution owed, lest so great a guilt stand against him in the judgment.”

It should also be considered that blessed Gregory calls him “Lord” as a term of affection.

But if they now neglect to fear God’s words, what blessed Job says of the wicked will happen to them: “When God repays him, then he will know; his eyes will see his destruction, and he will drink from the wrath of the Almighty” (Job 21:19). The wicked person delays reconsidering the evils he has done, but then he will know what he has done, when he begins to drink from the wrath of the Almighty. Then the eyes of their understanding will be opened—eyes that pride now closes.

### XIX

Alas! After the prince of this world was cast out, he has once again been admitted through us and works the mystery of iniquity in the children of distrust, who do the desires of the flesh and make themselves detestable through their pursuits—especially since the chief of the apostles says that the past time was sufficient for fulfilling their desires: “They walked,” he says, “in debauchery and drunkenness” (1 Pet. 4:3), and so forth.

The teacher of the nations likewise testified to us, saying: “I testify in the Lord Jesus that you must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, who gave themselves over to immorality. But you did not learn Christ in this way” (Eph. 4:17–20).

But we, as I see, joining together in the same confession of debauchery, shall give an account to the one who is ready to judge, as the aforementioned Peter goes on to say.

Although the time has now come when sinners are rarely struck by the miracles of former times, since those miracles were sufficient to make God’s judgments known, we nevertheless know that some of our own order have been punished by evident retribution.

For a certain man named Hucbertus, at Senones, saw two women standing beside him at night. Since he knew that they were not the women who used to come, he understood them to be phantoms. Those who were present ran up, but no one saw the women except him. He therefore fled into the church, but found it filled also with phantom women. Among them one, seated like a queen, ordered him to be seized and beaten.

When he seized the book of the holy Gospel and wished to make the sign of the cross over himself, he could not. She said: “It is too late; you have already been handed over to me.” When the bells sounded, the neighbors ran up. He had collapsed on the ground and was being beaten, and therefore cried out, saying what he saw and what he felt. When this had continued for a long time and the phantoms had departed, those outside saw a crowd of women leaving across the bridge. He died shortly afterward. Abbot Gorlantius relates this.

Therefore, whoever delights in the sweetness and embrace of a prostitute should place the bitterness of wormwood before his mind.

### XX

The superior of the monastery of Autun (*Heduensis coenobii*) eagerly devoured meat whenever he could find an opportunity. Since the brothers were entirely unable to correct this vice, on one occasion, when he wished to eat meat, he was strangled by the morsel with which he had filled his mouth and died.

Another man, who had left the monastery of Doué and gone to a certain village, asked his host for meat. When the host replied, “Look, it is already cooking,” he said, “Hurry and cook something on the spit more quickly.” The man prepared the meat on the spit, but the monk, burning with impatience, cut off a portion from the spit and threw it onto the coals. He shook it free of the ashes once it had been roasted and thrust it into his mouth, but immediately ended his life in the midst of his greed.

A certain man from Cormery, whose frivolities I myself knew—for I had known the man himself—went cheerfully to bed late in the evening and was found dead during the time of the night office. The same thing happened to Abbot Iammon, as you yourselves know. Another canon of Saint Martin’s, Lord Obertus’s chief chamberlain—that is, his chamberlain—was seized by a demon and tormented until he breathed out his spirit.

[Note: A certain man from Cormery. This was the monastery of the district of Tours, constructed in honor of Saint Paul, which the writer of the *Chronicle of Limoges* calls Cormaricense. He says that it was founded by a certain Iterius, a monk of Saint Martin, around the year 782, in these words: “At this time the monastery of Cormaricense was founded under Abbot Iterius, who received both its beginning and its subsequent growth from the Church of blessed Martin of Tours.” It is commonly called Cormery.]

### XXI

Two nuns from a women’s monastery situated near our Balma returned to secular life three years ago. The younger shortly afterward ended her life when her arm swelled up. The elder joined herself to a certain wicked man and gave birth to such a monstrous child that its neck was longer than one cubit. When she prostituted herself again, she conceived, but was unable to give birth until she died with her belly ruptured.

Until the time when they left, they had lived properly. They were permitted to leave so that they might bring something back to the monastery from the possessions of their parents, who had perhaps recently died. But after sampling the world on this pretext, they forgot God. From this it is clear how dangerous permission to sin can be.

Alipius, a friend of Saint Augustine, proves the same thing by his fall. When certain friends urged him to attend the theater, he detested seeing such a spectacle as something profane. But they dragged him there by force. Closing his eyes and unable to resist those who were pulling him, he swore that he would see nothing there. When suddenly a burst of laughter rang out in the theater, however, he forgot himself and opened his eyes. His heart was immediately enticed so strongly that only after a long time could Augustine draw him away from such entertainment.

Therefore, whoever does not wish to be burned should not allow a leaping spark to remain upon his skin, even for a little while.

Nor should we pass over what happened in the aforementioned monastery to a certain dying girl. The malignant enemy appeared to her, and, trembling violently, she remembered that she had a small needle without permission. The sisters brought it from the place where she said it was, but the demon did not depart. Recognizing that she still possessed something of her own for which the malignant enemy was pressing her, she finally remembered. “I have a silk thread at the bedrail,” she said. As soon as it was found and brought, the devil departed, and the girl died as though smiling.

These things may perhaps be judged trivial and unworthy of recounting. But if God, who, as has been said, does great and inscrutable things, has deigned to perform these deeds in our time, how highly should we esteem them, since we had not been worthy even of such signs?

### XXII

If a dream deserves belief, I am not reluctant to relate the vision that Guido, a monk from Solignac, saw. He seemed to see Ganzlinus, who had recently departed this life, being guarded in a church, dressed in a blue-gray cowl and lying in a coffin. Before a certain abbot of venerable white hair, he saw Ganzlinus prostrate and asking pardon. But the aforementioned abbot disdained him because of the blue-gray cowl in which he was dressed, saying that he did not recognize him and would not grant him pardon until he received the regular habit.

Then the aforesaid Ganzlinus rose and ran, trembling and greatly confused, to that same Guido. Nor do we disbelieve the vision. For Ganzlinus himself had recently been with the brothers of the cell at Dol, from whom he returned with the intention of immediately changing his clothing and thereafter possessing nothing as his own.

We must therefore believe that God, who judges the ends of the earth—that is, the final deeds of a human being—received him into pardon because of the good intention in which he died, and wished to show this through such a sign in order to encourage others.

We have related these signs from close at hand, so that those who do not fear ancient examples may at least fear recent ones. The men whom we said were strangled by flesh, and those whom we said were handed over to demons through lust, were punished in the present life for this reason: that those who neglect to consider the punishment awaiting them may at least be moved by the punishment through which these men were destroyed.

Who could hear without fear that a demon laid claim to a girl’s death on account of a single needle and a single thread, except perhaps someone to whom the prophet says: “A dove deceived, without understanding” (Hos. 7:11)? And hence it is said: “They did not fear, nor were they human beings.” If Ananias and Sapphira were struck down because of greed, at a time when persecutions and countless necessities surrounded the newly established Christianity, what punishment will be inflicted on those who know the sayings and examples of the ancients yet, without pressing necessity, have appropriated more than was established?

As for the quality or alteration of clothing, secular people themselves are indignant against monks, because that pride is always more detestable which displays itself where greater humility ought to reign. To those, therefore, who seek the ostentation of color in the habit of humility, the prophetic saying applies: “You have acquired the forehead of a prostitute” (Jer. 3:3).

It would have been better for them to imitate the example of Elijah and John, doing God’s will rather than their own, than to imitate the rich man, whom Christ rebukes for being dressed in purple and fine linen, or Herod, who, as we read, died struck by an angel while wearing splendid clothing.

### XXIII

From the occasion of that word in which God, speaking to the prophet, calls the children of Israel apostate nations, we have taken the opportunity to say these things against us wretched men—not monks, as we are falsely called, but *sarabaites*, that is, refusers of the rule—because we reject the yoke of regular discipline.

But what will happen when neither the examples of the patriarchs, nor the mysteries of the prophets, nor the darts of the apostles, nor the words of any of the holy Fathers, nor even the thunder of the holy Gospel can soften the hardness of our hearts? Religion is held in such contempt, and each person is ruled by whatever he pleases, that the poetic verse seems to apply to us:

> All else is a matter of concern; God alone is forgotten.

What the prophet added after the word quoted above—“if perhaps even they will then hear”—must be carefully weighed, for it has great force. “Perhaps” is a doubtful adverb. God inserts this word into his speech to indicate that there will be few who will receive his correction.

Yet he also consoles and exhorts his preachers, so that when they remember that God himself implies in his words that he will be despised, and nevertheless does not cease speaking to those who despise him, those holy preachers may not be saddened when they are despised, nor in any way cease from the duty of correction.

For the addition “even they” also carries great weight. It applies to those who remember that their predecessors were punished, yet do not cease to imitate them and immediately suffer tribulations as they did. “Even they,” he says—that is, those who could have had the example of their predecessors as an aid to correction, those who, afflicted, besieged, and confined, lost all the good things they possessed in this world; who see cities destroyed, fortifications overthrown, fields devastated, and churches undermined—yet still follow those same predecessors into iniquity and are not changed or withdraw from their pride, for which they saw them punished so many times.

[Note: Not monks, but *sarabaites*, that is, refusers of the rule. There are four kinds of monks: cenobites, anchorites, sarabaites, and gyrovagues, as Saint Benedict notes in chapter 1 of the *Rule*, where he also explains who the sarabaites are.]

## XXIV

The more powerful should be addressed with the greater caution, in proportion as they are permitted to lead a freer life and are themselves encouraged by their power—as though by a certain material for pride—not to humble themselves. To them, therefore, let the words of Gregory Nazianzen, in which he addresses Jeremiah, be spoken [Col. 0608A]:

“I turn my speech to you. What, then, will you say? Do you suppose that you will endure my dealing with you not according to your rank, but truthfully? Or will you willingly accept the fact that Christ’s law subjects you to priestly authority? For he has given us a power far more perfect than your tribunals. Or is it perhaps just that earthly things should surpass heavenly ones? Therefore, I ask you patiently: accept our freedom.

“Know that you, whoever you are, are a sheep of my flock, counted to me by Christ, the supreme Shepherd, and sealed by the Holy Spirit. Know that among the sacred altars you are reverently subjected to the hands of the priest. Know that you owe worship and faith to the blessed Trinity.

“We do not wish to appear unequal—teaching, that is, those who are lowly while trusting in your power, or using toward them but not toward you the freedom that Christ gave us in the Church. Otherwise, we would seem to care more for them, while despising and neglecting you. For whom, then, is it more fitting that we should have greater concern? For you, I say, all the more because, if you err, it affects the ruin of many; and again, the salvation of many is promoted when you uphold justice and clemency.

“You, O man, who, although set over others, are nevertheless equal to them by nature, remember how greatly you are indebted to God, who has granted you power over those equal to you. Do not consider what you are able to do, but what you ought to do. By his appointment you bear the sword—not to strike, but to threaten. Would that you might return it undefiled to Christ, its keeper! He has granted power from heaven for this reason: that those whom the authority of the holy Church is not strong enough to restrain from oppressing the poor on account of their own virtue, might be broken through the assistance of these rulers.”

For this reason God says to Job: “Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you, or will it break the clods of the valleys behind you?” (Job XXXIX, 9). Understand: “as it does behind me,” because it is the power of God, not of man, that enables any powerful person to humble the summit of his power for advancement in heavenly discipline and to restrain the oppressors of the humble like clods.

But what will happen? For, according to Isaiah, “the one who turns away from evil is exposed to plunder.” Princes are companions of thieves; they love gifts and do not judge for the orphan and the widow. To them Wisdom says: “O you who please yourselves in the crowds, power has been given to you by God, who will examine your works and thoughts, because, although you were ministers of his kingdom, you did not judge rightly, nor did you walk according to God’s will. A terrible and swift judgment will be made against those who rule” (Wis. VI, 3–6). “For the lowly are granted mercy, but a more severe punishment awaits the powerful.”

## XXV

Therefore, O rulers, lest these threats overtake you, if you are powerful, humble yourselves beneath the powerful hand of God. Remember what vices most closely accompany power. The powerful commonly grow proud, rejoice in temporal things, and, so that they may have or spend abundantly, commonly covet what belongs to others.

Against pride Scripture says: “Why is earth and ashes proud?” (Eccli. X, 9). Against temporal rejoicing it says: “Laughter will be mingled with sorrow” (Prov. XIV, 13). For how will the covetous be innocent, since the holy Apostle even compares covetousness with idols, saying: “Covetousness, which is the service of idols” (Eph. V, 5)? And Saint Gregory, discussing this, declares that whoever is subject to covetousness is not yet free from the worship of idols.

They are also commanded not to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in God, to do good, and to give readily. And, so that they may use only what is their own and not what belongs to others, John the Baptist says to them: “Shake no one violently, accuse no one falsely, and be content with your wages” [Col. 0609B] (Luke III, 14).

## XXVI

Those who feed themselves on the plunder of the poor must be confronted with greater severity. For those who do not afflict the poor themselves, but nevertheless do not take care to resist their oppressors, also sin grievously. Let such people know that they deprive God of the comfort of their assistance when they do not defend his poor. For just as he is burdened in his own people, so he is comforted in them. Hence it is written: “And in his servants he will be comforted” (II Macc. VII, 6); and he himself says: “He who is not with me is against me” (Matt. XII, 30). Paul says: “We are God’s assistants” (I Cor. III, 9). And the prophet says: “You have not gone up in opposition, nor have you set up a wall for Jerusalem” (Ezek. XIII, 5).

But let the plunderers consider that, when they harm the poor, they extend their hands even to the injury of God himself. For his own voice says: “Whatever you did for one of these least ones, you did for me” (Matt. XXV, 40). When, therefore, they afflict the poor, they certainly afflict God, as he himself testifies, saying: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts XXII, 7). He had already ascended into heaven, yet Saul’s persecution was still touching his members here below.

For just as he speaks through the good, as that same Paul says, “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (II Cor. XIII, 3), so he himself is torn in the affliction of the humble. Malachi says: “If a man afflicts God, because you pierce me, you are accursed, the whole nation of you who pierce me” (Mal. III, 9). And not only those who afflict them, but also the wealthier who sell their own goods at excessive prices, certainly sin.

Hence Amos says: “Hear, you who crush the poor, who say: ‘Let us possess the needy and sell the refuse of the grain.’ The Lord has sworn: If I forget this to the end, I will turn all your songs into mourning, and your final days into a bitter day” (Amos VIII, 4–6, 10).

Again he says: “Woe to you who are wealthy, you nobles, heads of the peoples, proceeding pompously, who sleep on ivory beds and indulge yourselves on your couches, drinking wine from bowls” (Amos VI, 1–2)—for they disdain drinking from rustic vessels—and what follows: “The Lord has sworn by his own hand: I detest pride” (ibid., 8).

Micah says: “Are not my words good, and are they not with him who walks rightly? But, on the contrary, my people has risen up as an enemy. You have driven widows from their houses, and from the little ones you have taken away my praise” (Mic. II, 7–9) [Col. 0610A]. And again: “Hear this, rulers, who abominate justice and pervert everything that is right: I will hide my face from you, as you have acted wickedly” (Mic. III, 9, 4).

To show that he is the one who suffers all adversities in his servants, he said to blessed Job: “Have you walked through the depths of the abyss?” (Job XXXVIII, 16). Understand: “as I have,” because the wicked hear the saints preaching, but do not understand; they see him suffering in the afflicted, but do not consider it.

Therefore, let them hear the counsel of Saint James: “Come now, you rich, weep and howl over the miseries that will come upon you. Your riches have rotted, and your garments have been eaten by moths; your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you and will consume your flesh like fire” (James V, 1–3).

Otherwise, when their shadowy pleasure and the affliction of the poor—which passes away—have flown by, the saying of Isaiah will come upon both: “Behold, my servants shall eat, and you shall hunger; behold, my servants shall drink, and you shall thirst; behold, my servants shall rejoice, and you shall be confounded” (Isa. LXV, 13). And why say more? Every threat in all of Scripture is hurled against them unless they come to their senses.

## XXVII

Let them not, therefore, rejoice and divide the spoils. Let the memory of that saying gnaw at them: “Woe to you who plunder; will you not yourself be plundered?” (Isa. XXXIII, 1). And it is said in Job: “The violent man is taken away without a hand” (Job XXXIV, 26).

The plunderer sees those whom he plunders, but does not see those who will plunder him at death. Thus the violent man is taken away without a hand: he who plundered visibly is snatched away invisibly when a sudden departure presses upon him. He does not see his plunderers, yet he is driven toward his end.

For now, while every violent person oppresses whomever he wishes and is permitted to carry out everything he wickedly desires, he often rushes into greater blindness of heart. Because he is not struck immediately, because his punishment is deferred to the future, he may think either that God does not see his wickedness or—worse—that God is not displeased by it. Thus he neglects to correct the same wickedness for which he does not immediately suffer vengeance.

But the preceding statement about God continues: “His eyes are upon the ways of men, and he considers all their paths” (Job XXXIV, 21). God was thought not to consider wickedness when this violent man perpetrated every evil he could with impunity, and his great patience was regarded as a kind of negligence.

But let him go now and presume to rush into whatever violence he chooses; let him fulfill the wickedness of his desires, seize what belongs to others, and glut himself on the oppression of the innocent. Because he has not yet been struck, let him suppose either that his ways are not seen by the Lord or—what is worse—that they are approved.

The eternal and sudden blow will certainly come, and then he will know that all things are seen by God, when he finds himself condemned by an unexpected departure in repayment for everything. Then, in his punishment, he opens eyes that he kept closed for a long time in guilt. Then he perceives that the true Judge considers all things, when he can no longer escape the deserts of his evil by perceiving them.

Yet, as is said in the *Hexaemeron*, the fish called the silurus (sheatfish) aptly represents any plunderer: although it continually devours other fish, it is itself caught and devoured. If only plunderers would learn, however imperfectly, what punishments await them!

The man to whom it was said, “Fool, this night your soul will be required of you; whose will those things be that you have prepared?” (Luke XII, 20), was not condemned because he had plundered what belonged to others, but because he had gloried in the abundance of his riches. Nor did the man clothed in purple perish because of plunder, but because he did not give alms.

What, then, are Christian plunderers like, and what do they deserve, when they kill their brothers for whom they are commanded to lay down their lives? They kill them, I say, when they afflict them, since not only the one who plunders but also the one who defrauds a hired worker is declared to be the equal of a murderer.

[Col. 0611B]

## XXVIII

Although the whole world was lying in wickedness, people were nevertheless persuaded to fear God—not merely to refrain from loving the world, but even to despise it—so that, for love of the life to come, they would hand themselves over to every kind of torment. But now, when everything pertaining to the instruction of Christians has been made clear both by words and by examples, all these things are nevertheless despised together, so that we demonstrate that the perversity of the Jews exists in our own conduct.

For God’s providential care was directed toward them to such an extent that, beyond other mortals, certain new and magnificent institutions of life were provided for their instruction. Indeed, almost all nature, so to speak, served their education. After all the signs of divine power, after such great glory had been given to them—glory that the whole world still marvels at—they worshiped a calf’s head. Later they had a temple and those things with which they completed daily sacrifices. They also had prophets, some dead and others still living, who instructed them about present events and reminded them of God’s ancient benefits: what he had done for them in Egypt, what he had done in the wilderness, and what he had done in the land of promise when they entered it.

Yet, amid all these things, they not only made no progress; they even worshiped idols in the very temple. Now migrating from nation to nation, now from one kingdom to another people, they were left without law, without God, and without sacrifice.

We also are “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession.” The great mystery of piety has been revealed to us: he was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, and taken up in glory. We have tasted, as the same Apostle says, the heavenly gift, and have been enlightened. We also have so great a cloud of witnesses set over us, namely, all the institutions of the Old and New Testaments.

Yet, when we ought to lay aside every weight and the sin that surrounds us, and run with endurance the contest set before us, we again fall back to the weak and needy elements. As the prophet says, we have again drawn in the winds like dragons, crucifying Christ again and putting him to open shame.

Therefore, we must fear in every way lest what the Apostle terrifyingly recalls concerning such people come to pass in us. To people of this kind the saying of Job must be addressed: “Know that there is a judgment” (Job XIX, 29). And again: “As soon as he moves, he will trouble you, and his terror will fall upon you” (Job XIII, 11). And again: “What will you do when God rises up to judge?” (Job XXXI, 14).

## XXIX

Those who are excessively delighted by present glory and the present life, of whom the prophet says, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (I Cor. XV, 32), commonly say: “Why did God create the riches of this life if we are not to use them at will?”

But the force of the saying should be sufficient: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world; because if anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (I John II, 15). And: “If anyone wishes to be its friend, he is made an enemy of God” (James IV, 4). Again: “He who hastens to become rich will not be innocent” (Prov. XXVIII, 22).

This was expressed in Esau, who, eager to seize the lentil dish, lost the birthright that he would have received in its proper time. These and many similar examples ought to be sufficient, because Scripture cannot be overthrown.

Yet, if this is measured by human experience, we must know that, after falling from the joys of paradise, we are in no way able to think about spiritual realities as they are. Hence it has happened that carnal people now know nothing except what can be known through the bodily eyes by touching, so to speak. They no longer raise themselves to the highest concern, but willingly consent to lie among the lowest things.

The blindness of their minds has become so dense that, since they cannot apprehend invisible things through experience, they now doubt whether anything exists that cannot be seen by bodily eyes—unless visible examples somehow display those invisible things to them. This is like the example blessed Gregory gives in the *Dialogues* of a mother who, perhaps pregnant, has been condemned to a dark prison and gives birth and nurses her child there. If, once the son has grown capable of understanding, she wishes to describe the forms of worldly things to him, he, who has seen nothing but darkness, can indeed hear what his mother says; but without experience he cannot understand those forms as they actually are.

Therefore, lest our blindness altogether exclude us from the understanding of higher things, divine providence chose to create in this world certain things that appear pleasing to the five bodily senses. Some please by color, some by smell, some by taste, some by sound, and some by gentle touch.

Just as hunters, having seen an animal’s footprint, learn from the evidence of the footprint what kind of animal it is, so, when we see the things that delight us in this world, we should understand how great heavenly things are, if earthly things appear to be of such importance. Desiring those heavenly things as though they were already known, we should turn away from these earthly things, like hunters hastening after an animal by following its tracks.

Otherwise, just as hunters are frustrated if, while admiring only the footprint, they do not seek the animal, so we will be useless if we cling too closely to perishable things. All the things that delight us in the world are therefore certain footprints of heavenly goods.

Let us not, then, yearn for these things, but through them learn by experience to yearn for those goods for which longing is deserved. Should someone throw himself into water merely because he needs to refresh his thirst from it? Or should he embrace fire because it is useful either for cooking or for warding off cold?

Plunderers, therefore, who afflict the poor in temporal matters, seem to choose the footprint of folly, while nevertheless, even against their will, healthfully driving the poor to seek heavenly things.

## XXX

What madness it is that they do not fear both offending God for transient things, burdening their neighbor, and losing a good measure—and that, in this very madness, they consider themselves better in proportion as they appear to surpass good and devout brothers in those same things by which they are worse.

They think they possess more in proportion as they see that they are able to do more; and although they are servants of many vices, they rejoice that they can rule over various brothers. But if they are so animal-like that, according to the Apostle, they can understand nothing spiritually, they ought at least to consider the equality of nature.

Worldly nobility was granted not by nature but by ambition. To commend unity, Eve was formed from Adam himself. Adam was greater, yet he was outside paradise, while she was in paradise. Hence it is written: “No one among kings had any other beginning of birth; there is one entrance into life for all, and a similar departure” (Wis. VII, 5).

And certainly, as Jerome says, all are made equal by divine grace whom the second birth has regenerated. Through it, both noble and ignoble become sons of God, and earthly nobility is overshadowed by the splendor of heavenly glory.

Are the poor born more filthily, when David himself laments that he was conceived in sins? Are nobles regenerated more splendidly, when, according to James, God chose the poor, rich in faith?

Job considered equality: although he was a king, he did not disdain to submit to judgment together with his servant. And Lord Martin served his servant in turn so greatly that he wiped his shoes.

Esau, whom the Lord hated, walked with four hundred men. Jacob, whom he chose, crossed the Jordan with his staff.

Consider all the books of antiquity: you will always find the more powerful to be worse. Indeed, to put it plainly, what enables the powerful to be fattened is prepared by the sweat of the poor.

Are those garments, those embroidered tents, and those exotic foods prepared by the hands of the poor? If there is any beauty or sweetness in them, the artisans should be praised, as Boethius says, not those who use them. When such people desire to be adorned with truth borrowed from external things, they reveal that their own worth is insufficient.

Hence Jerome says: “He who seeks to please by another’s scent fears to offend by his own.”

But those who embrace the winds and trust in nothing should remember that, according to Job, they will vomit up the riches they swallowed, and God will draw them out of their belly; and if they spend their days in prosperity, in a moment they will descend to the underworld.

“In a moment,” that is, because just as a stylus is raised when it is set down, so the wicked rich man loses his present joy as soon as he touches it. For however many years he may have lived happily, when he reaches the end, that long period is consumed as though it had been brief.

[Col. 0614A]

## XXXI

Meanwhile, to say nothing of the punishments that follow, should not the glory of the present life have been despised more on account of its very frailty? There were powerful, proud, and pleasure-loving people before us. But what did immoderate joy, garments and perfumes of various delights, and an abundance of possessions profit them? Where are those things now, and where are the people themselves?

Let us approach their tombs. What will we see there? Stinking remains of worms.

We shall prove true what is said of the wicked: “He will pass like a night vision” (Job XX, 8). When people placed in any punishment see themselves, perhaps in a dream, possessing the prosperity they desire while awake, once they awaken they recognize that what they dreamed was empty and of no benefit to them. So the lover and seeker of this life, when he departs from it, learns that everything that could pass away while giving pleasure was nothing: he is stripped, abandoned, and brought to nothing.

Would that all the pomp of mortals ended only in ashes and worms! But let us consider the dreadful tribunal of the Judge, the burning river, the worms that will not die, the fires of Gehenna, weeping and gnashing of teeth. Let us place these things before our eyes as though we had already come to them, and fear them as though they were already present—even though they are delayed, for they will nevertheless come.

Beyond all that we have said, there is a far graver evil: to be excluded from the everlasting goods prepared for the saints. Every torment is surpassed by being removed from that glory which you had the power to enjoy, especially by being cast out from Christ’s presence when we see others—even those with whom we have lived this life—being admitted.

Believe me, as it is said in the rebuke of the fallen, this surpasses Gehenna; it torments more severely than every punishment.

Let us grant, if you wish, one hundred years for enjoying delights, or, if you prefer, ten times that amount. But what comparison can these have with eternity?

Those who cling to such things passionately believe that we are delirious. Nevertheless, they cannot fail to know that delights pass away like a shadow and flee swiftly, while punishments remain forever. And if the time and duration were equal, would anyone be so foolish and deranged as to choose one day of punishment for one day of delights, when the pain of a single hour and any bodily torture usually consign to oblivion all the time previously spent in pleasure?

God arranged this so that the present life would indeed be a life of labor, but a brief life, so that labors would quickly end and the rewards of merits would last without end; so that the one who fears God would, as it is written, soon be secure, while the reckless would quickly lose the pleasures they prefer to him and eternally suffer the recompense they deserve.

Let us not, therefore, choose among deceptive pleasures as though to see the pleasing dream of a single hour, lest we happen to undergo eternal torments amid real miseries.

## XXXII

They must therefore be urged carefully to consider what a human being is and before what a Judge he will stand. Let them contemplate his power, weigh their own weakness, enumerate the evils of their works, and set against these the good things of his generosity.

Let them consider how strictly he examines evils, how subtly he examines good deeds, and how strict he will come against both. Let them keep in mind how great will be the arrival of that judgment; what a multitude of human beings and angels will then be present; how great the shame will be in the sight of the whole human race and of all angels and archangels; how fiercely the burning elements will fight against the reprobate; and with what force the Judge, whom the heavenly powers obey, will illuminate the secrets of every heart and bring all sins before the eyes of all.

Finally, let them weigh how terrifying will be the sentence by which the reprobate will be condemned, and what the punishments of Gehenna will be amid the heavy darkness of bitterness. After the confusion, let them consider what torment remains when guilt consumes the soul that dies immortally and Gehenna consumes the flesh that fails without failing.

Amid these thoughts, let the mind look back upon itself. On one side let it place the strictness of justice, on the other the weight of guilt, and let a person recognize without any doubt that he will perish if he is judged without mercy.

Let him turn to repentance, so that mercy may be present for definite sins—mercy that commonly rescues him from eternal punishment through present lamentation, and that judges our life when it has turned toward it in such a way that it nevertheless excuses our sins before the merciful God.

Let it become pleasing to weep healthfully over what was committed in a joy that ought to have been mourned. Although the conscience has long been polluted, it is renewed through tears as though baptized.

Hence it is written: “The Lord will judge the ends of the earth” (Ps. IX, 9), because the Lord does not judge a former life when he illumines the sinner’s later deeds by regard for heavenly mercy.

Hence Moses says: “You shall exchange the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep” (Exod. XXXIV, 20)—that is, turn the beginnings of an unclean life into the simplicity of innocence.

Again it is said: “And his light is over the boundaries of the earth” (Job XXXVII, 3), because the sinner, who is rightly called earth, if he turns to justice after wicked deeds, is separated from the darkness of his actions by divine light.

Hence the Lord says to afflicted Job: “Have you walked in the farthest depths of the abyss?” (Job XXXVIII, 16). The abyss is the human mind, darkened by the waves of vices. Since it cannot comprehend itself, it lies hidden from itself like a dark abyss.

To walk in the farthest depths of the abyss is, through wondrous mercy, to turn the minds of the worst people when they are near their end, to visit those pressed down by crimes, and to change those who have already despaired.

David and Peter are cited here as having fallen, so that, although their words forbid us to sin, their examples may cause us, if we sin, to breathe again in hope of forgiveness. For who would despair of pardon if he repented, when Peter himself urges Simon Magus to repentance?

## XXXIII

Let this never depart from the mind: whether the enemies of peace and correction endure the word or refuse to hear it, we must pray for them earnestly, following the example of our Savior and blessed Paul.

That same Paul knew that they thirsted for his blood, while no effort could persuade them toward salvation. He devoted himself to the one and only thing he could do: he wept and applied the assistance of prayer, saying: “The desire of my heart and my supplication to God for them is for salvation” (Rom. X, 1).

Let us not, therefore, fail to recognize that we ought to love enemies after his example. And if we are not such people that, according to the Apostle, we receive the plundering of our goods with joy, let us at least be such that we bless those who persecute us.

This seems difficult to the proud. Christ says: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke XXIII, 34). Stephen says: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts VII, 59). Paul says: “I could wish that I myself were accursed and separated from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Rom. IX, 3).

Moses says: “If you forgive them their sin, forgive it; but if not, erase me also from the book that you have written” (Exod. XXXII, 31–32). David says: “Let your hand be against me and against my father’s house” (II Sam. XXIV, 17). Samuel says: “Far be it from me to sin against the Lord by ceasing to pray for you” (I Sam. XII, 23).

What forgiveness, then, can we deserve if we do not imitate the example of so many servants from the Old and New Testaments, and especially that of the Lord himself? As John says in the first homily on the cross and the thief, it is better to pray for enemies than for friends.

Hence the Lord says: “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the tax collectors do this?” (Matt. V, 46). If we pray only for friends, then, we have not yet surpassed the tax collectors. When we pray for enemies, we imitate God as far as possible.

Hence blessed Gregory says that the prayer most commended to divine ears is the one that strives to intercede even for enemies.

This, however, must be practiced especially by those set over others. They know the divine commands more fully and better, and they must bear the tender and uneducated minds of their subjects like nurses or fathers.

For when they intervene before God for the sins of others, as is stated in the ninth homily of the final part of Ezekiel, they reveal their own sins more fully before God, because they justify themselves by that very charity through which, in wondrous devotion, they sacrifice themselves in lamentation for another’s iniquity.

It ought not to be burdensome for teachers to shed tears for converted sinners, when he himself who created all things, having become human, shed his blood on the cross for our iniquities.

## XXXIV

A miracle recently performed had slipped from my mind; I now wish to insert it for the correction of robbers.

There is a church of Saint Aventinus in Auvergne, beside a river called the Alerius. When merchants passing by with pigs saw some mounted men approaching them, they feared them and turned into the care of the church. One of the horsemen said to them: “Bring out the pigs.” When they refused, he compelled them, promising to give them one of the pigs.

Then he entrusted the pigs to one of his men to drive them, and began slowly to depart. But the man driving the pigs had gone only a short distance when he suddenly fell and broke his thigh.

The man who had ordered the pigs to be driven then happened to see a fox beside the road. He abandoned his horse and began to run after it. Suddenly he fell and was so crushed beneath the horse that the projecting part of the saddle completely severed his head.

The merchants, who had followed weeping, recovered their pigs and fled. The one who had been the robber did not find his folly pleasing. I learned this from his own cousin.

These things have been said about those who afflict the poor. Now we shall say what we can concerning your present condition, as though forgetting that we have already said much above for their consolation.

First, it must be made clear to them that neither prosperity nor adversity is distributed by chance, but by divine providence, both collectively and individually. Hence it is written, as we said above: “Nothing on earth happens without cause.” Through Amos it is said: “Will there be evil in a city which the Lord has not done?” (Amos III, 6). And through Isaiah: “Who gave Jacob over to plunder, and Israel to those who ravaged him? Was it not the Lord himself, against whom we sinned?” (Isa. XLII, 24).

Regarding the good, for whose benefit adversity is given, the aforementioned Amos says: “I have known only you from all the families of the earth; therefore I will visit all your iniquities upon you” (Amos III, 2).

Regarding the wicked, to whom Jeremiah offers the cup of wrath, he says: “Thus says the Lord: Drinking, you shall drink, for behold, in the city in which my name has been invoked, I begin to afflict you. Shall you be as though innocent and exempt? You shall not be exempt” (Jer. XXV, 28).

Considering these things, let us restrain the excess of murmuring in every distress, as King David did when he said: “I was silent and did not open my mouth—but why? Because you did it” (Ps. XXXVIII, 10).

## XXXV

By a hidden judgment, therefore, it happens that prosperity and adversity alternate variously among both the good and the wicked, as was said above. More commonly, however, things go badly for the good here and well for the wicked.

This perhaps occurs by a hidden judgment because the good receive here what they have done wrong, so that they may be freed more fully from eternal condemnation; while the wicked find here the good things they do for the sake of this life, so that afterward they may be led only to punishments.

Hence it is said to the rich man burning in hell: “Remember, son, that you received good things during your life, and Lazarus likewise bad things” (Luke XVI, 25).

But when things go badly for the wicked here and well for the good, it is very uncertain whether the good receive good things for this reason: that, being stirred by them, they may grow toward something better; or whether, by a just and hidden judgment, they receive here the reward of their works, so that they are deprived of the rewards of the life to come.

Likewise, it is uncertain whether adversity strikes the wicked so that, being corrected, they may be kept from eternal punishments; or whether their punishment begins here, so that, when it is eventually completed, it may lead them to the final torments of Gehenna.

Holy men therefore fear prosperity in this world more than adversity. They know that adversity, when it presses upon them, drives their minds to desire heavenly things, where there is perfect rest. But when prosperity is available, they are disturbed by fearful suspicion, dreading that, rewarded in external things, they may be excluded from inward ones.

For this reason they shun prosperity with all the greater disdain, the more fully they know that its sweetness flatters them into contempt for heavenly sweetness, and that it commonly diminishes the mind through its occupation with external things, so that they do not recognize how they have been changed.

But there are some who neglect their life, desire transient things, do not understand eternal things—or, having understood them, despise them—and neither feel sorrow for what they have done nor take care to seek counsel for recovering what they have lost.

Since they do not consider heavenly things, they do not raise the eyes of their minds to the light of truth for which they were created, nor direct the edge of their desire toward contemplation of the eternal homeland. Abandoning themselves to the things toward which they have been cast, they love as their homeland the exile they suffer.

Hence they desire the miserable happiness of this life so greatly that, even with any offense against God or injury to their neighbors, they prefer to attain it rather than be rejected from the house of God.

Whether adversity comes to us for the sake of the good, so that they may not be rewarded here by being placed in uninterrupted prosperity; or for the sake of the wicked, so that they may be corrected here; or certainly for any other reason of hidden judgment, one thing remains: in accordance with James’s exhortation, we should consider it all joy when we fall into various temptations.

Yet, as Paul says: “No discipline, for the present, seems to be a matter of joy, but of sorrow” (Heb. XII, 11). And therefore matters frequently turn in the opposite direction, so that some inexperienced people become worse through the affliction by which they ought to have become better.

For they also fall into despair, thinking that they have been abandoned by God, or into murmuring because they do not reflect that they are being afflicted by a just judgment.

### XXXVI

So that they may not fall into these two things—namely, despair or murmuring—those who are afflicted must, above all, consider two others: mercy and judgment. Hence the Psalmist says: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. 100:1); and again: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 25:10). The Creator and Judge of us all exercises these two in a marvelous way both toward the reprobate and toward the elect.

Toward the elect he displays mercy in the life to come, yet here he presses them with harsh afflictions by judgment. The reprobate, however, he tolerates here through mercy and often permits them to be supported according to their wishes by the temporal goods they desire; but by judgment he excludes them from the eternal goods which, through free choice, they despise. Both the wicked and the good commonly enjoy prosperity or adversity, as was said above, but the former in one way and the latter in another. The former are raised up by prosperity and broken by adversity; the latter are sustained by prosperity and instructed by adversity.

A certain wise man demonstrates this when he says: “Necessary for human life are water, fire, and iron, milk, bread, and honey” (Ecclus. 39:31), and so forth—mentioning some things on account of adversity and some on account of prosperity. Concerning these he also adds: “All these things will be turned into good for the holy, and into evil for the ungodly and sinners” (ibid., 33).

To understand this dispensation by which God divinely exercises either mercy or judgment, the apostle James teaches that wisdom is necessary. When speaking of the affliction of the righteous, he continues: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask it of God” (Jas. 1:5). It is therefore great wisdom to understand this dispensation, and, conversely, dangerous folly not to know it. Thus Job’s blessed wife, who urged him toward excessive murmuring, is reproved as though she had spoken as one of the foolish women; and Moses says to the children of Israel, who complained under their tribulations in the wilderness: “O foolish and senseless people” (Deut. 32:6).

For God’s plan is to lead his elect through temporal afflictions into eternal refreshment. Concerning this the Apostle says: “For I have not shrunk from declaring to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts 20:27). In order to reveal this counsel, our Head had to suffer and so enter into his glory, showing that all the members of that same Head must, as it is written, enter the kingdom through many tribulations.

To signify this counsel—that is, this dispensation—by which it is necessary for us to live in hardships from the time of baptism until the end, the children of Israel were delayed, so that they would not enter the promised land immediately after crossing the Red Sea. Rather, they remained in the wilderness for forty years and were afflicted by many hardships. Yet they murmured with disgust over the manna which, by Moses, they had been commanded to receive by the measure of a gomor, and, understanding or caring nothing about this dispensation, they desired their pots of meat.
