Therefore, as is said of them, “they did not understand the wonders of God, but soon failed and did not endure his counsel.”

Since the preceding example has supplied the occasion for what creeps through the mind to burst out again in words, let us speak of us miserable monks—or rather, Sarabaites—who, unbridled, kick against every yoke of regular discipline. We, I say, having been led out of the Egypt of this world by our professed religious life, and running through the course of the present life as through a wilderness under the mortification of the cross, ought to hasten toward the rest of the heavenly promise. But, alas, offering a spectacle ridiculous to angels and to human beings, we grow sluggish in the course we have undertaken. Just as those people, scorning the gomor and manna and desiring pots of meat, turned back in their hearts toward Egypt, so we, disdaining both the measure and the quality of food established for us by God through blessed Benedict, and desiring bloody dishes like barbarians, relapse into the apostasy of this world, refusing to endure the counsel.

### XXXVII

Yet neither the depth of judgments nor that of mercies can be penetrated completely. “The judgments of the Lord,” he says, “are a great abyss” (Ps. 36:6); and again: “Who understands the mercies of the Lord?” (Ps. 107:43). Nevertheless, it is necessary to understand this much: what we suffer is just, so that amid whatever hardships we may not murmur, but say: “You are just, O Lord, and your judgment is right” (Ps. 119:137). And again, as another prophet says: “I will endure the reproach of the Lord, because I have sinned” (Mic. 7:9).

Let us also understand, in accordance with Job, that “the afflicted person will be in glory” (Job 22:29). And let us say: “It is good for me that you have humbled me” (Ps. 119:71). For if the equity of judgment is considered, murmuring will cease, since it is exceedingly unjust for the guilty person to accuse the judge when he has received, in proportion to his deeds, what he deserved.

We, as is shown to blessed Job, are often required to suffer far less than our iniquity deserves. Job himself, although incomparably praised by the Judge’s own voice, confesses concerning himself: “When he has fulfilled his will in me, many other things are still in his presence” (Job 23:14). It is as though he said: “When, after taking away everything—possessions and children alike—and after my flesh has been consumed by worms, he has humbled me even to the dunghill, his eye still discovers many things in me that require correction. If he did not wish to spare me for these, he could justly increase my torment.”

Even after he had patiently endured such great and terrible things—things at which all generations are astonished—he does not boast of his victory, but says: “I condemn myself and do penance” (Job 42:6).

If mercy too is weighed—the mercy by which the kind Judge hides his guilty servants from eternal punishment through temporal hardships—we shall not think ourselves abandoned, as some do. They bless God in prosperity, according to the saying: “He will give thanks to you when you have done good to him” (Ps. 49:18), but fail in adversity, according to the words: “In their miseries they do not endure” (Ps. 140:11), and: “Woe to those who have lost endurance” (Ecclus. 2:16).

Rather, we shall love the Judge, who scourges his guilty servants with passing punishment as though with rods for this reason: to absolve them from Gehenna and from the gallows of the executioners. As was said above, a sick person tolerates the physician’s instrument the more patiently the more clearly he sees that what is being cut is rotten, and the more he hopes for the remedy of health through the very incision.

God is the inner physician, and he cuts away from us the contagions of sins, which he rejects as being present in our very marrow. He cuts away the poison of corruption with the iron of tribulation; and the more he appears not to heed the sick person’s cries, the more he works toward bringing the illness to an end.

That a creature neither ought nor is able to scrutinize the Creator’s judgment, the Apostle demonstrates. Speaking of the depth of divine judgments, he says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God,” and then adds: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Rom. 11:33–34). The word “man” derives from *humus*, “earth.” Therefore the one called “man” is shown to be unable to answer God, because, having been taken from the earth, he is not competent to scrutinize heavenly judgments.

Since, then, we are not sufficient to investigate these things, it remains for us humbly to keep silent under his dispositions, lest perhaps, if the reason for his strictness is examined, it be provoked still further by our examination. The power of the heavenly plan cannot be avoided; but the person who restrains himself beneath its commands lightens its weight by great strength and willingly bears it upon the shoulder of a submissive heart.

### XXXVIII

The evil of murmuring or despair, with the devil lying in wait, creeps in chiefly because the wicked prosper and the good are oppressed. From this it happens that a weak spirit either suspects that God does not care about good deeds—as the wife of blessed Tobiah, who was afflicted, openly said to him: “Your hope has proved vain” (Tob. 2:22), and so forth—or questions whether his judgment is just, as Gideon said: “If the Lord is with us, why have all these things happened to us?” (Judg. 6:13).

It is no small question why the wicked fare well and the good fare badly, since the holy prophets appear to voice a complaint about this on behalf of the weak. Jeremiah says: “Why does the way of the wicked prosper? You are near their mouths, but far from their kidneys” (Jer. 12:1). David says: “But my feet were almost shaken, because I was jealous of sinners, seeing the prosperity of the wicked” (Ps. 73:2–3). Malachi, resisting such people, says: “You have wearied the Lord with your words.” And they said: “In what way?”—“In that you said: Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and such people please him” (Mal. 2:17). Job says: “Why do the wicked live?” (Job 21), followed by much of the same kind.

Solomon also indicates this when he says: “This is the worst of all that happens under the sun: that the same things happen to the just and to the impious” (Eccl. 9:3), and so forth. Hence the hearts of human beings are filled with wickedness and contempt.

The devil knows this ordering of things: that some people are accustomed, through afflictions, to arrive either at murmuring or at despair. Therefore, when he sought the aforementioned Job for testing, he destroyed all his possessions and afflicted his entire body—not because he wished to make him poor or sick, but so that, through outwardly inflicted troubles, he might weary his conscience and, after stripping his mind of its strength, induce him to think something impious about God.

For this purpose he also craftily sent messengers, so that one might first say: “The Sabeans formed three bands, took everything, and then the fire of God fell from heaven and consumed the sheep and the servants that it struck” (Job 1:15–16). It was as though he said: “Consider that you wished in vain to appease God with so many sacrifices. You are enduring his anger, although you hoped that he would console you amid human adversities.” He wanted Job, seeing himself wounded outwardly by human beings and abandoned inwardly by God, to burst forth into insult all the more boldly because he was also more despairing.

The devil presumed that this could happen to such an extent that, speaking to God not merely about just anyone but about Job himself—who at that time had no equal—he said: “Touch all that he possesses, and then you will see that he blesses you to your face” (Job 1:11).

Yet that same Job stood firm, fortified against both dangers. Against murmuring he recalled the equity of the Judge, saying: “I know that if a man wishes to contend with God, he cannot answer one question out of a thousand” (Job 9:3); and again: “I will not answer; even if I have anything just, I will entreat my judge” (ibid., 9:15).

Against despair he remembered his burnt offerings, his compassion, his chastity, his humility, and many such virtues, so that he said: “My heart does not reproach me throughout all my life” (1 John 3:21). He was not disturbed by the prosperity of the wicked, because he considered their end, saying: “They spend their days in prosperity, and in an instant they descend into the underworld” (Job 21:13).

So also now, when the weak in mind see the wicked prospering in happy circumstances while the innocent are often oppressed by grief and poverty, they know that, as was said above, nothing happens on earth without cause. Even if God does not disclose the reasons for the scourge by which the good are oppressed and the prosperity by which the wicked are supported, he nevertheless indicates that these things are just by ordering them himself—he who is supremely just. Nothing pleases God except what is just; and we can suffer only what pleases God.

Everything we suffer is therefore just, because it happens by the ordering of him who cannot will anything unjustly. The divine judgments by which adversity comes to the good and prosperity to the wicked must not be scrutinized with bold speech, but venerated in fearful silence. Do not investigate why this happens or does not happen in this way; look to the end of both.

David labored in his investigation until he understood “their latter end” and saw that those possessed by pride are cast out even as they are exalted, and that they will suddenly be brought to desolation. But those who justify their heart and are chastised have become, for the whole day, as it were cattle; yet they will always be with the Lord.

Therefore, however variously you may be afflicted, do not despair that whatever good works there may be have displeased God. For, as it is written, when you have thought yourself consumed, you will rise like Lucifer, and the brightness of midday will rise for you in the evening.

### XXXIX

Some do not think that God cares for human affairs, because they see them appearing to occur by chance; nor do they trust that divine help is present to them, especially when their prayers are not heard. But in Job it is said: “He himself considers above all the heavens, and over the nations and over all human beings” (Job 37:3).

Hence, in Book XXV of the *Moralia*, it is said that God regards everything equally and arranges everything equally; present everywhere, he is neither confined locally nor changed by caring for different things. Thus divine judgments are directed over one soul just as over one city, and over one nation just as over the whole multitude of the human race. He governs the highest things in such a way that he does not abandon even the lowest; he is not absent from the universe when he arranges one thing, nor from one thing when he arranges the universe.

He does not therefore neglect human actions—indeed, he frequently either punishes or rewards them here—but, as has been said, he himself determines how he will deal with them either now or in the future. If he were to punish every sin now with manifest punishment, it would be thought that nothing had been reserved for the final judgment; but if he punished no sin now, divine providence would be believed not to exist.

When afflicted people cry out and are heard only after delay, when their cry seems to be disregarded, their hope is weakened and heavenly help is believed to be absent, because it is obtained only later. Against this it is written: “For God will not hear in vain” (Job 35:13). “Not in vain,” he says, “but beneficially.”

Many are heard according to their desire, but not for their salvation, as happened when Satan sought blessed Job. Others are heard not according to their desire, but for their salvation, as happened with the blessed Apostle. Hence the Psalmist says: “My God, I will cry by day, and you will not hear” (Ps. 22:2); and then: “And by night, and not for my foolishness” (ibid.). He cries by night, whose hearing is delayed. For hope deferred kills the soul.

It is as though he were saying: “You seem to abandon me when you do not hear me according to my desire while I cry out; but, by disregarding what I foolishly ask, you hear me better, because you arrange what is more opportune.”

Against the belief that God does not consider the things we suffer, Scripture, after saying, “God does not hear in vain,” adds: “And the Almighty regards the causes of individuals” (Job 35:13). For he hears the prayers which he appears not to hear, and he is not ignorant of what each person suffers.

Let the person who is compelled by the weight of the blow either to murmur or to despair consider God as the author of mercy and of his own nature. Hence King David, pressed by hardships, gathered himself back into hope, saying: “I was silent and did not open my mouth, because you did it” (Ps. 39:10). He considered that the one who had kindly created him when he did not exist had certainly struck him, once created, only justly.

Hence Moses, restraining those who murmured, said: “O perverse generation, is this how you repay the Lord?” He adds: “Is he not himself your father, who created you?” and so forth (Deut. 32:5–6). It was as though he said: “The one who kindly created you neither permits you to be tormented without cause nor allows you to perish through neglect.”

Again, in Job, the voice of one in despair did not say: “Where is the one who made me?” (Job 35:10). For, as is said in the third book of the *Moralia*, everything that happens to human beings comes by God’s hidden plan. He himself determines how much prosperity or adversity follows each person; neither does excessive prosperity raise up the elect, nor excessive adversity crush them.

Whoever is broken by despair amid pressures does not sufficiently contemplate the one by whom he was made. For, as has been said, the one who made what did not exist does not abandon what he has made without governance.

Hence Ambrose says: “If an artisan neglects care for his work, abandons and forsakes it, and does not regard as made what he himself judged ought to be made, that is the height of cruelty.”

But when this storm of despair troubles us, the shaken mind quickly places itself in the harbor of hope if it recalls God’s benefits, if it does not excuse the evils it has repaid his goodness, and if it weighs what it justly deserved from him who has given it what it received.

If, then, the afflicted person considers either the good received from God or the evils committed by himself, he will neither accuse the punishments he suffers nor grow weary of hoping for mercy—mercy that would have existed even if no benefits had preceded it.

Otherwise, how will this saying stand: “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart” (Ps. 34:18)? Blessed Martin confidently affirms it. When he was captured by robbers, his appearance did not change; when asked whether he was afraid, he replied that he had never been so secure, because he knew that the Lord’s mercy is especially present in temptations.

Blessed Antony, too, when he had been so afflicted by evil spirits that neither their assault nor his steadfastness can adequately be described, was at last refreshed by heavenly light when those apparitions vanished. He said: “Jesus, where were you until now?” And immediately the response came to him: “Antony, I was here, but I was waiting to see your patience.”

### XL

To say something further about the delay of prayers: when the afflicted cry out, they often deserve to be heard on their own account, but nevertheless their prayers are delayed on account of the guilt of those who oppress them, as it is written: “They will cry out, and he will not hear because of the pride of the wicked” (Job 35:12). It is as though he said: “The guilt of the persecutors prevents the afflicted from being heard.”

For the just and merciful God permits his own people to be oppressed for a time and allows the wickedness of violent men to increase monstrously, so that, while the life of the righteous is worn down by purification, the wickedness of the persecutors may be brought to completion.

Often the faithful, caught in tribulation, receive heavenly consolation even during their temporal suffering. When almighty God frees them by some miracle, he makes his power known even to their persecutors, so that by the means through which he saves his own temporarily, he may redeem their adversaries eternally.

Hence the Prophet says: “Deliver me because of my enemies” (Ps. 69:19). It is as though he said: “I do not seek to be delivered from temporal tribulation for my own sake, but I desire to be delivered because of my enemies, so that, when they see me saved miraculously, they may be converted from their hardness by the very sight of the miracle.” For those who are not held by faith in invisible things are sometimes moved by visible miracles.

But divine power is often not exercised on behalf of the afflicted for this reason: as was said above, their oppressors do not deserve to be enlightened. Whether, therefore, tribulation is prolonged on account of our adversaries or for the testing of our patience, let us not grow weary of hoping for mercy. The desire for good things is tested when some adversity resists it.

Those who have been tested, however, are heard more effectively. The Psalmist teaches that both testing and hearing take place amid hardships when he says: “I heard you in the hidden place of the storm” (Ps. 81:8)—that is, “amid the waves of affliction I tested you at the waters of contradiction.”

Moreover, as blessed Jerome states in his second letter to the Ephesians, people ask according to their weakness for what seems beneficial to them. But as regards the truth of the matter itself, it is clear that God gives more than is requested, and that our prayers are surpassed by our desires, because we do not know how to pray as we ought and often ask against ourselves, thinking that something is for our benefit.

### XLI

Divine providence has prepared for the future good things for the just, which the unjust will not enjoy, and evils for the wicked, by which the good will not be tormented. But he willed these temporal goods and evils to be shared by both, so that people would neither pursue goods too eagerly because they see that the wicked also possess them, nor shamefully avoid evils, since the good are often afflicted by them as well.

In these prosperous or adverse circumstances, which now, as we have said, occur mixed together, God’s patience or severity is arranged according to this dispensation. In prosperity, patience nurtures the good and invites the wicked to repentance; in adversity, severity trains the good in patience.

It makes a very great difference how one uses the things called prosperous and the things called adverse. The good person is neither raised up by temporal goods nor broken by evils; the wicked person is punished by adversity precisely because he is corrupted by prosperity.

It therefore makes a very great difference what sort of person is being afflicted. Just as, if ointment and mud are shaken by an equal motion, one emits a sweet fragrance while the other exhales a foul odor, so the difference among those who suffer remains even when their sufferings are alike.

And just as gold glows under fire while straw smokes, and under the same threshing grain is purified while straw is crushed, so any common tribulation purifies the good and destroys the wicked. The good praise God and accuse themselves; the wicked murmur and, with the order of the kingdom disturbed, undertake every crime with greater license, and therefore more frequently and more recklessly.

Of the good, who recognize and cleanse their sins through scourges, it is written: “If they are in chains and are bound with the ropes of poverty, he will declare to them their works, so that they may return from iniquity” (Job 36:8–9). Those who do not hear the words of the commanding God are brought close by the blows of the one who strikes, so that punishment may draw toward a good life those whom rewards do not change: “Constrain their jaws with bit and bridle,” he says (Ps. 32:9).

Concerning the wicked who do not reform, it continues: “If they do not hear, they will pass by the sword and will not be consumed by folly” (Job 36:12)—that is, they are indeed afflicted, but, because the Ethiopian does not change his skin, what is said of them earlier in the same book of Job will come to pass: “They will die, but not in wisdom” (Job 4:21).

There is a grave folly in those whom iniquity binds so tightly that even punishment does not restrain them from sin. Since they despise the scourges of correction, they must be judged there with all the greater severity, the more they trample here upon the grace of greater providence.

### XLII

The difference between the good and the wicked is marked by the words of sacred Scripture when it speaks of both under the names of their mothers—namely, Babylon and Jerusalem.

Of the former it says: “Instruct Jerusalem, lest my soul depart from you” (Jer. 6:8). Against the latter: “We treated Babylon, but she was not healed” (Jer. 51:9).

Of the former: “I will chastise you in judgment, lest you seem innocent to yourself” (Jer. 46:28). Of the latter: “With great labor it was exhausted, yet its rust did not depart from it” (Ezek. 24:12).

Of the former: “I will smelt away your dross completely” (Isa. 1:25). Of the latter: “They have become dross to me, and lead” (Jer. 22:18).

Of the former: “They will be whitened beyond snow” (Ps. 51:7). Of the latter: “The Ethiopian cannot change his skin” (Jer. 13:23).

Of the former: “I will hedge your way with thorns, and you will not find your lovers” (Hos. 2:6). Of the latter: “I let them go according to the desires of their hearts” (Ps. 81:12).

Of the former: “You will fear me and receive discipline” (Ps. 2:11–12). Of the latter: “You have turned away with a contentious turning” (3 Kings 9:6).

Of those who, through adoption, have become true sons of David, the Father’s voice promises a great gift: “If his sons forsake my law, and do not walk in my judgments, if they profane my ordinances and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod. But I will not remove my mercy from him” (Ps. 89:31–34).

Of the others: “I will not visit your daughters when they have committed fornication, nor your brides when they have committed adultery” (Hos. 4:14).

This woman is forced to respond to her tribulations and cry out: “The Lord has forsaken me, and the Lord has forgotten me” (Isa. 49:14). But God consoles her, saying: “Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have compassion on the child of her womb? And even if she should forget, I nevertheless will not forget you” (ibid., 15).

She says: “I sit as queen, and I am not a widow” (Rev. 18:7), but the divine voice says to her: “Descend, you who are more beautiful” (Ezek. 32:19). And again: “Sit in the dust; there is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans” (Isa. 47:1).

There are very many other passages of this kind. In all of them it is clearly apparent that these things, as is read in the life of blessed Martin, are common to all the saints and to all others for undergoing; yet enduring them has always been the particular virtue of the just.

We said that we would relate something for the consolation of the afflicted. But perhaps someone will say: “What consolation is there in these words?” If, however, we seek consolation in the manner of the saints, and not according to the worldly and dull opinion of carnal people, we confess, with a marvelous but truthful assertion, that not only should these words—which demonstrate that the good and righteous Lord afflicts his own mercifully and justly—be regarded as consolation, but the tribulation itself ought also to be considered consolation.

Is it not consolation to know that you suffer by God’s arrangement, who strikes us only justly? Did not tribulation itself console Paul when he said: “And not only this, but we glory in tribulations” (Rom. 5:3)? And concerning himself, when he did not refuse to rejoice on account of that ineffable tribulation of his: “For me, I will glory in nothing except my weaknesses” (2 Cor. 12:5).

Job says this even more plainly: “Let this be my consolation, that he who afflicts me does not spare me from sorrow” (Job 6:10).

It is a medicinal practice that the heat of the internal organs is often drawn out into an itching of the skin, and that one is frequently healed inwardly by the means through which one is wounded outwardly. Thus divine medicine sometimes operates so that an interior wound is removed through outward pains, and the interior corruption of vices, which might have occupied the mind, is driven away through the incisions of scourges.

Before our flesh is made firm through the incorruption of the resurrection, if it is affected by no sorrow, it runs wild in temptations. Whether, therefore, we are punished in the present for sins already committed so that we may not be punished in the future, or afflicted so that henceforth we may not continue to commit crimes deserving punishment in the future, there is sufficient reason for us to embrace the tribulations themselves joyfully and to give thanks in all things to our Judge and Physician.

It is no small matter that the Apostle not only commands us to rejoice in tribulation, but to regard it as complete joy when we fall into various tribulations. Who does not know that it is much better to be subjected to harsh human servitude than to be exposed to the flattering spirits of demons? Yet, when we are worn down under the yoke of human condition by the profound judgment of God, we leap into complaint, plainly because we pay too little attention.

If no condition of servitude oppressed us, perhaps our mind, freed from restraint, would serve many iniquities even more wickedly. We therefore believe that the things we endure are burdensome because we neglect to consider from how great an enemy we are being freed through the scourge.

Hence God says to blessed Job: “Remember the battle; do not speak further” (Job 40:27). It is as though he admonished him by consideration of the matter and restrained him from murmuring, saying: “If you consider the sword of the adversary, be silent under the discipline of the Father, who frees you from inward suffering through outward torments, in proportion as you have seen yourself weak against the warfare of that same enemy.”

The profound dispensation of God’s judgments, through marvelous power, foresees that if his servants remained quiet and free, unable to endure the adversary’s temptations, they would lie prostrate with wounds of the mind. For this reason, although they often deserve well, he either assails them with threats, presses them with scourges, burdens them with imposed loads, or entangles them in laborious occupations.

### XLIII

Let these words therefore persuade us that we suffer every kind of trouble by divine dispensation for this purpose: either that past sins may be punished in us or that future sins may be prevented.

When these two things have been considered, we shall not murmur. We shall understand that the kind Judge wishes to excuse us from the eternal punishment we deserved by means of a momentary punishment, and we shall in no way think you abandoned. For, from the very experience of the scourge, we shall recognize that God’s providence is being exercised toward us in such a way that this itself can give us hope: he loves those for whom he deigns to take care that they do not sin, according to the saying: “Those whom I love, I reprove and chastise” (Rev. 3:19).

Indeed, whenever we are afflicted by various troubles of mind and body, we desire to know the causes of those same troubles, so that in what causes us pain we may possess, from knowledge of the events that befall us, a certain kind of consolation.

But it is no longer necessary for God to answer each individual concerning what each person suffers, because he has composed sacred Scripture, in which each person, if he seeks, will find his own cause. To offer one example among many, Paul, tested by an infirmity of the flesh, heard: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9).

Paul is therefore afflicted individually in sacred Scripture so that each one of us, who does not hear this consolation, might not seek to hear it privately. Hence in Job: “He speaks once, and does not repeat the same thing a second time” (Job 33:14); nor will he answer everything.

It is as though he said: “God does not answer privately to the hearts of individuals when perhaps each person seeks to know the causes of his own distress; rather, he constructs such an utterance as satisfies the questions of all.”

God therefore no longer answers our thoughts or afflictions by the voices of prophets or through the services of angels, because the power of Scripture comprehends whatever can happen to individuals. The thing formed does not say to the potter: “Why have you made me thus?” But the servant and creature have something to say which the Son and Creator said: “Not my will, but yours be done” (Luke 22:42).

It must nevertheless be understood, as blessed Jerome argues in his book on the Psalms: “If Christ and the Church are one body, and if they are two in one flesh, it is necessary that now they share together in one suffering, and, when they have passed through it, share together in one rest. For if the sufferings are only in the Head, who is Christ, why does Paul, his member, say: ‘I fill up in my flesh what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ’ (Col. 1:24)?”

All the sufferings of Christ—who suffered in the Head, that is, in himself, and suffers in the members, that is, in us—must be borne by each of us. By bringing forward what we suffer, according to the measure of our strength, as a kind of assessment toward the common service of the republic, we pay what we owe.

Otherwise, if we are outside discipline, whose participants shall we be, as the Apostle says? Adulterers, and not sons. And if we lack discipline, it follows that we shall lack the inheritance.

In ourselves, then, we must transform what we read, so that when the mind is stirred through hearing, life may hasten to carry out what it has heard.

### XLIV

Although, then, we do not know for what fault we are being struck, and although—if it were possible—we were conscious of no evil, still it is not lawful for us to believe that our correction is either unjust or superfluous. Nor should we be altogether saddened, since it is written of the blessed Tobit that he was not grieved by the wound of blindness, even though he had feared God from childhood.

Let someone, therefore, be so just that he has no need to be scourged for any other fault. Yet he too must consider that, through the very use of human life, we grow old day by day and, under the impulse of the outward man, leave our inward state through slippery thought. For just as we were created from nothing, so by ourselves, unless we are held by the hand of our Maker, we are always tending toward nothing. That creative hand holds us when it either gives us life by pricking us toward love or restores us by scourging us toward fear. Unless it does this, the mind wholly grows old through sudden collapse—even the mind that had seemed renewed by long practice in virtue.

Is it not written: “Your visitation has guarded my spirit” (Job 10:12)? “Visitation,” he says; for the spirit is quickly stripped of virtue unless it is guarded by the giver of that virtue, either through scourges or through a visitation of remorse. Nor is it surprising that the spirit is guarded by bitterness, which is contrary to the flesh, since they are mutually opposed. For as the flesh is nourished by soft pleasure, so the spirit is strengthened by bitterness; and as hard things wound the flesh, so soft things kill the spirit. Thus the spirit perishes forever from the very source by which the flesh lives pleasantly for a time. Its care outweighs the bond of the flesh, if here it is abandoned by the author of discipline.

Indeed, when we are intent upon bodily concerns, we feel no harm at all from our very abandonment. For the farther our Creator withdraws from us, the more our mind hardens in sensible things, and becomes, in a miserable way, all the more secure the worse it is. It is exceedingly difficult for anyone, in prosperity, to recognize either what he has already done or the fault toward which his mind is gradually inclining.

Therefore he who has deigned, out of piety, to become a father to the faithful, seeing that dangerous negligence is creeping in among the children whom he calls to the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, restores them not only through gifts but also teaches them through scourges. If someone therefore seems just, let him remember the sentence already quoted: “If I am righteous, I shall not lift up my head, being filled with affliction and misery” (Job 10:15).

There is also another reason why the more perfect are rightly scourged for a time together with the weak or even the wicked, as is discussed in the first book of *The City of God*: namely, because they do not correct them, fearing either that they might offend their favor or that, through their criticisms, they might suffer damage to their good reputation. Thus they experience with them the bitterness of this life, whose sweetness they neglect to make bitter for transgressors by loving them. This fault especially involves prelates and other venerable men, who are divinely appointed in the Church for this purpose and are held under grave guilt.

Nor is one entirely free from this fault merely because he is not a superior. If, among those to whom the necessities of life bind him, he knows of many things that ought to be admonished or reproved, yet neglects them in order to avoid offending them because of those things which he uses in this life not improperly but delights in more than he ought, he too is implicated.

They are therefore scourged together, not because they lead an evil life, but because they love together the temporal life that they ought to despise, so that, if they wished to be corrected, they might attain eternal life with them.

Certainly, if someone does not rebuke because he is awaiting a more suitable time, or fears that those rebuked may become worse and harm the weak more seriously, this is not negligence or an occasion of cupidity, but the counsel of charity. For, as is said in Book XX of the *Moralia*, when holy men see that certain people despise their words, and understand that those people are being abandoned by God, they fall silent with groaning. Hence the saying: “How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?” (Psalm 136:4). It is written: “Do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you” (Proverbs 9:8). Holy men therefore remain silent, not because they fear their hatred, but lest those people become worse by hating them.

### XLV

But to speak of the more negligent: we need to be scourged all the more, both because many things in us deserve the eternal fires and because we are more inclined to commit other offenses. Indeed, even amid our very afflictions we habitually grow proud in many ways.

This twofold usefulness of our affliction is shown in the first human being. When he neglected to preserve righteousness amid the delights of paradise, God corrected him by expelling him and subjecting him to hardships; and his wife, who had likewise grown proud and fallen through the honor she had received, he made better through a useful servitude.

So he hands us over to injuries and oppresses us with hardships—we who are proud in our freedom, fattened by pleasures, and disdainful toward divine reverence—in order that the soul, driven by repeated punishments, may abandon the summit of pride and, relying upon labors and hardships, be restored to what it lost through delight.

For this reason, according to Augustine, he was placed opposite Eden, that is, opposite the seat of delights, to signify that sinful flesh must be instructed through labors, which are contrary to delights. When God sees us forgetting heavenly goods, longing for transitory things, and fearing the punishments to come little or not at all, he graciously looks upon those whom he deigns to regard with gratuitous goodness, corrects them through the intervention of the scourge, and, looking upon the earth, makes it tremble.

Then, as the scourge increases, we are compelled to consider the bitterness and strictness of the eternal judgment; brought back to our heart, we begin to think about satisfaction. Then the tongue speaks of guilt, and the mouth willingly confesses what the mind had treated lightly, like Joseph’s brothers, whom he constrained—not by mockery but by argument—until, worn down, they confessed: “We rightly suffer these things, because we sinned against our brother.”

Hence the blessed Job says: “I will speak in the tribulation of my spirit” (Job 7:11). Whatever the spirit speaks in the divine ears is speech; tribulation prompts that speech, so that the voice bursts forth into confession. Confession is followed by pardon, according to the saying: “I said, ‘I will confess,’ and you forgave” (Psalm 32:5).

And when David, in his own guilt, said, “I have sinned” (Psalm 51:6), Nathan immediately replied: “The Lord has taken away your sin; you shall not die” (2 Samuel 12:13), as is reported in Book XXXII of the *Moralia*. Whoever understands that he is a sinner has already begun to be just in some measure, and accuses what he did as an unjust person from the standpoint of what he is as a just person.

For although he is struck on account of the merit of his sin, nevertheless, if he believes that the very judgment being carried out against him is just and does not murmur but embraces it, he is joined to the divine will in his being struck. Thus he is already corrected from his injustice precisely when he either rejoices that he has been justly struck or agrees, in punishment, with the will of the judge, from which he had departed in guilt.

Great, therefore, is the usefulness of affliction, by which confession of guilt is elicited and pardon is earned.

### XLVI

The children of Israel, too, were often afflicted for their sins and compelled to return to God. To pass over their other occasions, when they abandoned God and served idols, they were delivered into the hands of the nations of Syria, Sidon, Moab, and Philistia, and were grievously afflicted for eighteen years.

At last they cried out to God, saying: “We have sinned against you.” Among other things the Lord answered them: “I will not continue to save you. Go and call upon the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you” (Judges 10:13–14). But they replied: “We have sinned; do to us whatever pleases you, only deliver us now” (ibid., 15).

Immediately afterward it says: “The Lord was grieved over their miseries and delivered them, because these things happened to them symbolically” (ibid., 16).

Let us also say to the Lord, when we are surrounded by some tribulation: “Do with us in the present whatever pleases you; only deliver us in the future.”

Since we have mentioned the children of Israel, let us hear something yet more magnificent about them, to commend God’s mercy and indicate the usefulness of tribulation. Through Ezekiel the Lord says: “The house of Israel provoked me in the wilderness, and I said that I would pour out my wrath upon them and consume them” (Ezekiel 20:13), followed by what he says concerning this.

As the blessed Jerome explains these words in Book IV of his exposition, the question arises how God fulfilled this threat against those whose corpses fell in the wilderness and, apart from Joshua son of Nun and Caleb, none of whom entered the promised land. From this we understand that they live, that they were not reserved for eternal punishments, that they were not blotted out of the book of the living, and that they were not consumed before the face of the Lord.

For if they are believed to have perished because they were not brought into the promised land, then Moses too perished, since he was not brought into that land. Otherwise, how could the prayers of Moses have been heard when he prayed that God would forgive their sin and was told: “I will do according to your word” (Exodus 8:10)?

Let us therefore understand that God’s knowledge of his children or servants is not destruction but correction. Thus far Jerome.

Through the same prophet it is said: “As I live, says the Lord, this thought of your mind shall not come to pass, when you say, ‘Let us worship wood and stones’; for I will reign over you with a strong hand and an outstretched arm and in fury, and I will subject you to my scepter, and I will bring you into second bonds” (Ezekiel 20:32–33, 37).

What greater usefulness, then, could there be than that, through wrath poured out upon them, they should be prevented from worshiping stones and wood and brought into the second bonds of God’s friendship?

### XLVII

It is remarkable how Scipio, although a pagan, understood that external discipline was necessary for preserving moral integrity. He did not want Carthage, hostile to the Romans, to be destroyed for this reason: so that it might remain for the Romans themselves to hold in check. For he knew that security is dangerous for weak minds and that terror is as necessary a guardian for them as a tutor is for children.

This was proved in reality. Once Carthage had been destroyed, such evils immediately arose from prosperity that seditions, civil wars, bloodshed, and plunder occurred so cruelly that the Roman people were ravaged more severely by their own citizens than by their Carthaginian enemies.

Scipio feared that this corruption of minds, born of favorable circumstances, and this overthrow of prosperity and moral integrity would occur. For this reason he opposed the construction of a theater at Rome. He knew that citizens could easily be corrupted through the city itself, and therefore he wanted the opportunity for amusement to be suppressed.

If that was his position, what should we do, who now contemplate eternal things with grace revealed; who are commanded to live by faith; who know that all things work together for good for those who love God; and who know that nothing happens by accidental chance, but that everything is ordered divinely?

If the flesh shrinks from discipline, let it persuade itself to endure. For when we wish to drive away illnesses, we do indeed drink a bitter potion sadly, but, certain of the health that will follow, we rejoice. Since the body cannot attain health in any other way, it drinks even what it dislikes in the potion. When the mind perceives that life is contained in bitterness, it grows cheerful even while disturbed by sorrow.

That past sins are cleansed and future ones prevented through the scourge, Solomon shows when he says: “The bruise of the wound cleanses away evil, and blows reach the innermost parts of the belly” (Proverbs 20:30). By “belly” the mind is signified, because just as the belly is enlarged by food, so the mind, raised up by wicked thoughts, expands.

The blows in the innermost parts of the belly are the hardships generated by external affliction. Evils are therefore cleansed, and the bruise of the wound and blows reach the innermost parts of the belly, because external discipline washes away sins, while remorse or the bitterness of eternal punishment pierces the mind stretched out by wicked thoughts.

Saint Jerome, in his letter to Rusticus, reports that there was a certain young man in a monastery who could extinguish the flame of the flesh by no degree of abstinence or labor. The father of the monastery preserved him by this means: he ordered one of the older monks deliberately to wear him down with frequent insults. After a year had passed in this way, the Father asked him about his former thoughts. He replied: “I am not permitted to live, and I have no desire to commit fornication.”

This man could have been submerged in wantonness if he had not been restrained in the place of tribulation.

### XLVIII

And why say more? Sacred Scripture frequently impresses upon us, in both words and examples, that prosperity is sometimes dangerous. Thus it says: “The prosperity of fools will destroy them” (Proverbs 1:32). And again: “The beloved grew fat and kicked” (Deuteronomy 32:15).

There are many examples. But, to say nothing of the reprobate, let King David, brought forward as an example, show how much prosperity is accustomed to harm even the elect, for whom all things work together for good.

As it is said in the *Pastoral*, he had pleased the judgment of his Creator in nearly all his actions. But as soon as he was free from the weight of oppression, he burst forth into the swelling of a wound. He became cruelly rigid in the death of a man, because in his desire for a woman he had been weakly indulgent; and he who had previously known how to spare the wicked mercifully afterward learned, in the killing even of the good, to rush forward without hindrance from reconsideration.

Earlier he had refused to strike a detected usurper; later, at the cost of a laboring army, he destroyed even a devoted soldier. Guilt would have drawn him far from the number of the elect had scourges not recalled him to pardon.

Holy men knew how dangerous prosperity is, and when adversity happened to be absent, they sought it in their prayers. Thus David said: “Prove me, Lord, and test me” (Psalm 26:2). Another said: “Let rottenness enter into my bones” (Habakkuk 3:16). Another said: “Though he has begun to strike me, let him crush me” (Job 6:9). Another said: “Reprove me, Lord, but not in your anger” (Psalm 6:2). Another said: “Lord, you were merciful to them” (Psalm 99:8).

He makes clear in what way he was merciful to them when he adds: “Taking vengeance on all their inventions” (ibid.), that is, punishing in the present whatever they had sinned through human weakness.

Although, therefore, we are surrounded by scourges and saddened in part according to the flesh, let us nevertheless rejoice in spirit, contemplating the usefulness of affliction. Otherwise, nature itself teaches us that we ought to spend this life in sorrow and hope for joy in the next.

Is this not suggested when each infant, born into this light, gives forth his first cry in weeping, but learns to laugh in sleep, as the blessed Augustine reports in the book of the *Confessions*? Since death is commonly signified by sleep and joy by laughter, the infant, entering the world, weeps, but while sleeping laughs. Through this law of nature it is shown that, as it is written, “Man is born to labor” (Job 5:7), and: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” (Psalm 127:2). Again: “It shall be well with the one who fears the Lord at the end” (Sirach 1:13).

Every sinner is exalted by present happiness, but, as it is written, “His steps shall be hemmed in at the end” (Job 18:7). Yet it shall be well with the one who fears the Lord at the end, because, as it is also said, “The mouths of the righteous shall be filled with laughter” (Job 8:21), and “no one shall take their joy from them” (John 16:22).

“What is present,” says the Apostle, “is the momentary and light affliction of ours, producing in us, beyond all measure, an eternal weight of glory in sublimity” (2 Corinthians 4:17).

Zoroaster alone is said to have laughed before he wept—an exceedingly evil omen, since he was the inventor of the magical arts.

Otherwise, as the blessed Jerome says, considering the miseries of this age and the swords raging everywhere, the man who does not lack bread is sufficiently rich, and the man who is not compelled to serve is excessively powerful.

### XLIX

Whoever loves present glory is refreshed by its enjoyment and undoubtedly wounded by its loss. On the other hand, whoever tastes the joy that remains within immediately considers as light whatever causes pain externally.

Hence it is written: “Nothing that happens to the just will grieve him” (Proverbs 12:21). Whoever therefore desires external things, when these are disturbed for him by any circumstance or even taken away against his will, is invaded by blind thought, and the calamity that shakes his momentary joy, although it will soon pass, is mourned as though it were infinite.

Whoever does not want to be afflicted by external pains should strive to be lifted from low things by hope in heavenly ones. But because we are not such people—because we neither despise earthly things through contemplation of heavenly goods nor even wish to experience temporal hardships for the sake of the joy of the sheaves harvested from the seed of tribulation—God, like a provident father, compels the childish and wanton son toward what is better and nearer to salvation through threats of affliction.

This was well signified by the Israelite people, when Moses called them and King Pharaoh raged. Moses was sent to call them only when Pharaoh had already been stirred up to oppress them with hard labor, so that one, by calling, might draw along the minds of the Israelites shamefully attached to Egypt, while the other, by raging, might drive them forward; thus the people, provoked disgracefully in servitude and moved by good or evil impulses, would be stirred to action.

This happens daily when, while heavenly rewards are preached, the wicked are permitted to rage against the elect, so that, if we neglect to depart for the land of promise, we may at least be driven onward by the hardships that rage against us.

This, then, is why the just are allowed to be afflicted by the unjust: so that, while they hear of the future goods they desire, they may also suffer and dread present evils, and, while love summons them toward an easier departure, torment may drive them forward.

Some travelers, when they happen to see pleasant meadows along the road, are accustomed to linger, and, delighted by their beauty, to turn aside onto byways. Our present life is the road by which we make for paradise. Therefore, having been nourished by the repose of the present as by the pleasantness of a journey, and preferring to travel longer rather than arrive sooner, we are worn down by frequent disturbances through God’s hidden counsel, lest, loving the road instead of our homeland, we forget where we ought to be going; and for this reason, as is said in Book XXIII of the *Moralia*, wherever we remain—whether in the place of any rank or in the recess of any hidden refuge—we are unable to live entirely without temptations.

Do not therefore think it negligence that we are afflicted. And when we patiently endure the grace of consolation, do not think that the wicked are advancing from evil to worse without purpose. They do not return to consider themselves; no wall of discipline stands in their way; no power of judges is present to restrain them; no punishment of the future judgment is foreseen to terrify them.

With the eyes of their hearts closed, they perpetrate temporal evils in security, while they strip the good of their possessions or even kill them. But a strict judgment is certainly being prepared for them, so that they may be struck by eternal damnation all the more harshly in proportion as they are now permitted to carry out more freely what they wickedly desire.

With the afflicted, however, God deals mercifully, so that their guilt may be cleansed here. The wickedness of the reprobate, like a threshing floor, separates them as grains from chaff by beating them, while through the things they violently inflict it compels them to hasten toward heavenly things.

### L

Since we have mentioned grains and threshing, it seems appropriate to take something further from the use of a field and to establish what we are arguing. “You are God’s cultivation,” says the Apostle (1 Corinthians 3:9). If this is so, let us take an example from it.

The grain in the field is touched by the sun; it receives the rains, while the field grows rich through the word of truth. The grain is shaken by the winds; the field is exercised by temptations. The grain bears the growing chaff of the world; the field bears the wicked life of sinners. The grain is pressed by threshing and stripped of chaff; the field is scourged by heavenly discipline so that it may be separated in heart from the fellowship of the carnal.

The grain, once the chaff has been left behind, is carried into the granary; the field, while the reprobate remain outside, is brought into the joy of its Lord.

Hence it is said to the chosen people in Job: “You shall enter the abundance of the tomb like a heap of grain in its season” (Job 5:26). The season of the reprobate is in this life; that of the elect is in the next, as their Head says: “My time has not yet come” (John 7:6). Of them he says: “Your time is always ready” (ibid.).

The tomb in its season, therefore, is like a heap of grain: every just person is brought in at his proper time, because he receives future rest who first feels here, as in a season not his own, the pressures of discipline by which he must be corrected.

The awns or the chaff signify false brothers because they grow in the same ear, as though in one faith, together with the grains. They now stand above the others because they frequently prevail over the good; they are erect and separated from one another because the wicked are proud and there are always quarrels among them. Yet they touch one another above the grains because they agree among themselves in the oppression of the good.

They are bristly and fragile, because toward the one who rebukes them, as though touching them, they are unmanageable, while they quickly yield to vices. Yet by a wondrous dispensation, when they afflict us here for our sins after we have received heavenly grace, they are like frost that checks a harvest burgeoning excessively among the grasses after rain, so that it may flourish more fruitfully in grain; they restrain us from the flow of pleasure and make us more fruitful in the harvest of eternal reward.

Let the devil’s agents go now and occupy, like awns, the higher place in the Lord’s harvest. Certainly, since they will not retain even the lowest place in the granaries, let them now be bristly and set up the little thorns of excuses against the evil of the one who rebukes them.

The judge will surely come, the one who shows no partiality, whom they continually afflict in his little ones. The iron rod will come—the rod with which he rules the nations—and with it he will crush the awns, while he stores the grains for himself after consigning the chaff to the fire.

### LI

Much has already been said against murmuring and despair. Therefore, while repeating things known to you and pressing them upon you, we fear that we may be accused of throwing a drop uselessly into a river. Let us quickly explain what remains.

We must therefore know that we are instructed in many ways toward endurance not only by commandment but also by numerous examples. The whole body of the elect, which, as Isaiah prophesies, the little child—that is, humble Jesus—leads by scourging toward the folds of the heavenly dwelling, as though driving it by threats along the narrow way, endures adversity while it lives here.

Whom, then, shall we bring forward individually, since the whole multitude of the elect is an example? Concerning them, as we have already said, the Apostle declares: “Having so great a cloud of witnesses set before us, let us run with patience” (Hebrews 12:1). Of this cloud James says: “Take, brothers, as an example of the outcome of evil and of long endurance, of labor and patience, the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord” (James 5:10).

It is as though he were saying: “So that you may endure more patiently the things that happen to you, see that those who were so holy that God spoke through them had a harsh end. For whoever proved dearer to God always experienced harsher things.”

Nevertheless, let us bring forward two examples, one from the Old Testament and one from the New: Job and John. When we recall that they were praised beyond comparison and yet suffered such cruel things, we understand appropriately what should be thought about the rest.

Job, of whom it was said, “There is none like him on earth” (Job 1:8), endured the loss of so many possessions, grieved under the deaths of so many children, and bore so many wounds. Yet he is described as sitting not on clean earth but on a dung heap. This was done so that, from the stench of the place, he might be reminded that his body would finally return to stench.

To scrape away the discharge he used neither his fingers nor a garment, but a potsherd. By this it was shown how little he valued his healthy body, since he neglected it even when it was stricken.

But as I consider the wounds and sufferings of blessed Job, suddenly I turn the eyes of my mind back to John. Not without the greatest astonishment I reflect that he who was filled with the spirit of prophecy within his mother’s womb, and, so to speak, was reborn before he was born; he who was the friend of the bridegroom; he than whom no one born of women arose greater; he who was a prophet in such a way that he was even more than a prophet—was sent to prison by the wicked and, a man of such severity, died for the amusement of the base.

What, then, does it mean that Job is preferred by God’s testimony and yet is stretched out by blows as far as a dung heap? What does it mean that John is praised by God’s voice and yet dies, as the reward for a dance, because of drunken words? What does it mean that almighty God so severely despises in this world those whom he chose so sublimely before the ages?

It means only what is evident to the piety of the faithful: that he presses them so severely in the lowest places because he sees how he will reward them in the highest; and that he casts them outward even into contemptible places because inwardly he leads them even to things beyond comprehension.

From this, then, let each person infer what those whom God rejects will suffer there, if here those whom he loves suffer such things; or how those will be struck who are to be accused in the judgment, if the life of those who are praised by the testimony of the judge himself is pressed down in this way.

### LII

Among all the sources of our consolation, this one stands out above all: our kind Creator has stooped toward us in such kindness—or, so to speak, kindness compelled him to do so—that, while granting everything salutary for sinful humanity, he also endured, out of compassion alone, everything that the same humanity deserved on account of sin.

For humanity needed not only to be redeemed but also to be taught how to live after redemption. He therefore came to his fugitive, thrusting himself before our eyes. Even if he had done nothing more, by appearing on earth he would have humbled himself greatly.

All those who, born from the stock of Adam, sought to pursue the prosperity of the present life, avoid adversity, flee reproach, and follow glory. But he, the new man who came and embraced a new life, fled what everyone seeks and sought what everyone flees.

There are two lives, the present and the future. We knew one but did not know the other; and the human race, intent upon the one it knew, was directed only toward it. He therefore assumed the life known to us so that he might reveal to us the one that was unknown.

To show that this life is contemptible and the other desirable, he neither wished to prosper in this one nor to remain in it for long. Rather, by suffering, he departed to the other and says: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John 12:26). By his example he taught us that our present life is not to be loved for its own sake but endured for the sake of the other.

Therefore, in view of that singular protection by which he redeemed us through the shedding of his blood, let that be judged most excellent which strengthened us so greatly toward repentance. To impress this upon us, he despised those things that the uninstructed regard as great evils, especially since by so many miracles he showed that he possessed such power over all things.

Let us consider, then, that while saving us through the prickings of our sins, he did not refuse to place his head beneath thorns; that while intoxicating us with eternal sweetness, he received the bitterness of gall in his thirst; that he who worshiped the Father for us, although equal to him in divinity, remained silent when worshiped amid mockery; and that, preparing life for the dead, Life itself proceeded even to death.

Why, then, is it considered harsh that a human being should endure scourges from God for evil deeds, if God endured such evils from human beings for the sake of good, in order to recall humanity to the blessedness it had lost?

Hence the prophet says: “His alien work, that he might do his own work” (Isaiah 28:21). His work is to save what he created; to be scourged is the work of sinful humanity, not of the one who committed no sin. He therefore assumed an alien work—that is, scourges—in order to save his creature in this way, which is his own work.

### LIII

Stirred, then, by so many voices of commandments and helped by so many comparisons drawn from examples, let us love God’s judgment, certain that, in the humble, the bitterness of present hardship extinguishes the punishments of abiding wrath.

Although we are surrounded by scourges and saddened in part according to the flesh, let us nevertheless rejoice in spirit, contemplating the usefulness of affliction.

We ought indeed to pray for those who afflict us. Yet if they do not repent, when, according to Isaiah, they have completed their plundering, they will become the prey of demons. And, as it is read in the Septuagint, the divine voice also consoles the afflicted concerning their destruction, saying: “Woe to those who make you miserable, for they shall be rejected.”

Again, in the same prophet: “For a brief moment and a little while I abandoned you, poor woman, shaken by the storm and without any consolation; but with great mercies I have had mercy on you” (Isaiah 54:7–8, 11). And: “I took from your hand the cup of my stupor and indignation, and I will place it in the hand of those who humbled you. But you shall not continue to drink it any longer” (Isaiah 51:22). Again: “You shall go out and leap, and you shall trample the wicked when they are ashes beneath the soles of your feet” (Malachi 4:3).

For just as a most merciful father, whose beloved son has been killed, if he should find both the murderer and the sword, kills the murderer with that same sword and breaks into pieces the sword by which his son perished, so Christ, the lover of humanity, will wipe away every tear from his own, but will cast the tormentor into the place where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth. He will crush the hammer of the afflicters in such a way that he will remove it entirely from his own and turn all its weight back upon those who wielded it.

Therefore, comforting the afflicted household through the prophet, he says: “As I swore to Noah that I would never again bring the waters of the flood upon the earth, so I have sworn to you that I will not rebuke you any longer” (Isaiah 54:9).

But to the one who places a stumbling block before his mother’s son he threatens, saying: “I will rebuke you and set before you”—that is understood, “the things you have done”—“before your face” (Psalm 50:21).

When she sees this God of gods in Zion, carrying with exultation the sheaves that she sowed in tears, she will cry out joyfully: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Psalm 94:19).

Concerning the afflicters, under the figure of Babylon their mother, it is said: “As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much give her torment and mourning” (Revelation 18:7).

Let the smoke not boast if it is exalted—that is, let the Lord’s enemies not boast if they prevail—because smoke rises only in order to cease to exist. In their voice it is said: “Exalting, you have struck me down” (Psalm 102:11).

To his little flock the Holy Spirit says: “My son, do not reject the discipline of the Lord” (Proverbs 3:11), and so forth. Again, through the Apostle: “For whom does the father not correct?” (Hebrews 12:7). And in the same passage: “We had fathers according to the flesh, and we revered our instructors; shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits and live?” (Hebrews 12:9).

Therefore, so to speak, let paternal scourges not bite harshly, but torment gently and sadden cheerfully, because “if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him.”

I call them paternal scourges because, although it is a great thing for anyone to be called a servant of God, the afflicted, as Jerome says, are not called servants, nor even friends—which is greater—but, what is greatest of all, they are called sons, and beloved sons: “He scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6). And, as is reported in Job: “Blessed is the man whom the Lord corrects” (Job 5:17).

Although blessedness and pain cannot properly exist together, nevertheless, because correction through pain is an indication of salvation, one who is corrected through suffering is rightly called blessed: for through the fact that he is afflicted outwardly, he lives inwardly.

Therefore, as blessed Gregory establishes in Book VIII of the *Moralia*, let this hope remain with you: as little as the freedom of the children of God appears amid the necessities of the present age, so little will any trace of servitude appear in those same servants of God in the glory of future freedom.

[Col. 0639]

## The Four Books of Saint Odo, Abbot of Cluny, on the Life of Saint Gerald, Count of Aurillac

*(From the Cluniac Library, edited by D. Marrier, p. 65.)*

## The Author’s Dedicatory Letter

[Col. 0639A] To Lord Aymo, abbot, to be remembered with affection for his merits, [Note: [Col. 0639B] Lord Aymo, abbot of Saint Martial of Limoges, at whose urging Saint Odo undertook to write a book on the conduct and miracles of the blessed Gerald, count of Aurillac. For the chronology of the abbots of Limoges runs as follows: “Aymo, the eighth abbot, presided for six years and died on the Nones of May. He was a friend of Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, whom he ordered to publish the Life of Saint Gerald.” Turpio, or Turpin, bishop of Limoges, whose brother he was and whom he honored with the greatest affection, calls Aymo “Aimon” in the testament concerning the restoration of the monastery of Saint Augustine. Nor is what is recorded in the *Deeds of the Bishops of Limoges*, under Turpio, any less true—namely, that “Odo composed the Life of Saint Gerald and the book *On Contempt of the World* at Turpio’s request.” For, as Saint Odo himself says, “both Lord Turpio the bishop and Aymo, the most beloved and venerable abbot, together with many others, compelled him by the force of their prayers to undertake this work.”]

Odo, a fellow-servant of the brothers, wishes perpetual salvation in Christ.

A little book, venerable father, which you recently urged me so imperiously to compose, as best I could, about the life and miracles of the blessed man Gerald, I now undertake, though trembling. For although I fear presumption, as though I were attempting something beyond my powers, I also fear, if I do not undertake it, the charge of contumacy, as though I were disobedient. Confident, however, in the obedience and goodness of Christ, as I begin, I ask you to implore the mercy of that same Christ, so that, for love of his servant Gerald, he may deign to shape my account in such a way that it will be neither wholly unworthy of the man whom he has determined to glorify nor a cause of transgression for me. To avoid that transgression, I have passed over certain matters about which you may perhaps complain, weaving together only those things that are commonly reported to me, while you yourself were present and can confirm them through reliable authorities. Farewell.

## PREFACE

[Col. 0639]

Most people are accustomed to doubt whether the things reported about the blessed Gerald are true. Some of them consider them altogether untrue and fanciful. Others, seeking excuses for their sins, indiscriminately praise him, saying that Gerald was powerful and rich, lived amid luxuries, and was nevertheless a saint. By his example they strive to excuse their own pleasure-loving lives.

It therefore seemed to us that we should respond to these people at some length, insofar as we can. For we too, having long ago heard the fame of his miracles, nevertheless doubted them—especially because in certain places, I do not know by whose rumors, popular gatherings are newly accustomed to be held about such matters, and then gradually cease as though the whole thing were a fiction.

But when the matter pressed upon us and we were going to visit the community of the monastery of Tulle, we wished to turn our attention to his tomb.

[Note: “To visit the community of the monastery of Tulle.” We have already noted that Saint Odo had charge of the abbey of Tulle in the Limousin. The Limousin Martyrology states: “Odo, the second abbot of Cluny, was first abbot of Tulle in the diocese of Limoges.” It is now sufficient to add that Tulle—which the ancient author of the Life of Saint Martial also calls Tullum—was raised by Pope John XXII into an episcopal see. In French, Tulle.]

We then summoned four men whom he himself had nurtured: namely, the monk Hugh, the priest Hildebert, Wilard, and another Hildebert, both noble laymen; and, together with many others, we investigated his character and the quality of his life up to that time. We examined eagerly what each one said, sometimes together and sometimes separately, and whether they agreed with one another in their statements, silently weighing whether his life was such as miracles might fittingly accompany.

When we discovered how religiously he had lived, and that God had shown by many signs that he was in his grace, we could no longer doubt Gerald’s sanctity. Rather, we are astonished that in our own age, when almost all charity is already growing cold and the time of Antichrist is approaching, the miracles of the saints should cease. Yet surely God remembers his promise, since through Jeremiah he says: “I will not cease to do good to my people” (Jer. 32:40).

The Apostle bears witness to this beneficence, saying that God, who in no age leaves himself without a witness, does good by filling human hearts with joy. If, then, it pleases his divine goodness that he who performed miracles with the fathers should also be glorified in our times, we ought not to be unbelieving.

That this divine dispensation is being carried out both in this age and through a contemporary man seems clearly to be because all the deeds and sayings of the saints of former times have already withdrawn from our hearts as though they were dead. When this man of God was found, like Noah in his days, to have lived according to the law, God set him before those who looked on as a witness, so that, seeing that he had lived justly and devoutly, the vision of their hearts might awaken to imitate him, as though he were shining close at hand.

Nor should observance of God’s commandments be considered burdensome or impossible, since it appears to have been observed by a layman and a powerful man. Nothing nourishes the mind’s sluggishness more than failing in the present to reflect upon the recompense for good or evil deeds that remains after this life. Scripture warns us against this, telling us to remember our last things in all our works.

God therefore exalts his servant, whom he rewards in heaven, also on earth, before those who despise him. Through what is done outwardly, the despisers of God may see inwardly that the one who serves God is not empty or futile; rather, as God himself testifies, “those who glorify me I will glorify,” while “those who despise me shall be held in dishonor.”

Since we believe that this man of God was given as an example to the powerful, let them consider how they should imitate him, who was like one of their own rank and yet set above them. Otherwise, just as the queen of the South will condemn the Jews, so he may condemn them at the judgment.

Taking occasion from his deeds, we have therefore appended, wherever the opportunity arose, something with which to admonish those same powerful men, as you requested. For the lord Bishop Turpio and my dearest and venerable Abbot Aymo, together with many others, compelled me by their urgent pleas to undertake this work.

[Col. 0642B] When I offered what I considered a genuine excuse based on my inactivity, they said it was wrong that these matters, once undertaken, should not rather be brought to light in writing. But I reflected that a pompous account is less fitting for a humble man, and I placed my trust in the statements of the witnesses.

They did not report many of the signs that the crowd values highly, but they did report numerous instances of disciplined living and works of mercy, which are more pleasing to God. For the King will say to many who prophesied and to many who performed worthy deeds, “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12). But those who practice righteousness—which Gerald cultivated above all—will hear: “Come, you blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25:34).

And truly, what are the deeds by which Job, David, Tobias, and many others are called blessed, if not those which Gerald is proved to have performed?

Having considered these matters, I have been persuaded to believe that Gerald is worthy of the company of the saints, through whom the heavenly Rewarder may also deign to work miracles. But since we have spent a long time weaving together this apologetic preface, let us now come, in Christ’s name, to the beginning of our account.

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0641]

### I

The man of God Gerald was born in that part of Gaul which the ancients called Celtica, specifically in a territory bordering Auvergne, Quercy, and also Albigeois, in the town or estate of Aurillac, the son of Gerald and Adaltrude.

[Note: “In the town or estate of Aurillac.” Below, in chapter 39 of this book, he calls it the castle of Aurillac; in Book II, chapter 4, he calls Aurillac a distinguished estate. Gerald himself calls it Aureliacum; Gerbertus calls it Aurilacum. We commonly call it Aurillac.]

In the nobility of his lineage he was so exceptionally distinguished that among the families of Gaul his ancestry appeared more noble than others both in possessions and in uprightness of character. For it is said that his parents possessed modesty and devotion as though they had received them as an hereditary inheritance.

Two witnesses arising from that same stock are sufficiently suitable to establish this: namely, Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles,

[Note: “Caesarius, bishop of Arles.” “He is said,” as Cyprian, his disciple, says, “to have been a native of the territory of Chalon. His parents, outstanding in fortune as well as in ancestry—which is an illustrious and outstanding example of nobility—excelled all their fellow citizens in faith and character.” While still young he entered the monastery of Lérins, where he later became abbot after having been a monk; and from there, after Saint Eonius, he was finally raised to the episcopate of the Church of Arles. He also had a sister named Caesaria, whom he consecrated to God as a holy virgin and placed over the convent of virgins at Arles that he had built. But how Saint Gerald, count of Aurillac, could have arisen from his lineage, as our Saint Odo notes, is certainly not yet clear to me.]

and the blessed Abbot Aredius.

[Note: “And the blessed Abbot Aredius.” A native of the city of Limoges, as Gregory of Tours says in Book X of his History of the Franks, chapter 29, he was “born not of ordinary parents of his region, but of very noble ones.” He was abbot of the monastery of Attane, which he founded and which, from his name, is still commonly called Saint-Yrieix.

A charter addressed to the most dear noble matron, drawn from the archives of Saint-Martin of Tours, recounts his descent from King Childebert of the Franks down to his own time as follows:

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. The account of the lineage of the illustrious Abbot Aredius begins thus. Suldeca, a noble woman, daughter of King Childebert and Queen Mathildis [Nanthildis], bore Astidius, bishop of Limoges. Born at Trier, he was later, by God’s favor, raised to be bishop in the city of Limoges.

Astidius had a gracious wife named Thecla before his episcopate. Her sister was the wealthy Frontunia, whose estates were at Nataliacum. Astidius and his wife Thecla begot Liverius, Adtecus, Dulcitius, Adteca, and Austiliana.

Liverius begot Sperius and Pientia. Adtecus begot Eustachius, Ruricius, and Peladia. Dulcitius begot Ambrosius, the most holy Severus, whom the people of Bourges venerate on the bank of the Loire, and Basolus of Ravenna.

Adteca begot Clarus and the martyr Ispanus. Pientia begot Perogoricus [Petrogoricus] and Leontius. Ambrosius begot Julius, Industrius, and Eusebia. Eusebia begot Savina and Salica. Savina begot Optatus, the venerable archbishop of Bourges.

Optatus begot Pomponia, wife of Godefredi of Flanders, and Ocilius, the most noble bishop of Soissons. Peladia begot Cartheria, Eulalia, and Mummulus. Cartheria begot Pelagia, most holy, and Savina, the aunt of Abbot Aredius.

Pelagia, therefore, granddaughter of King Theodebert, and her husband Jocundus, the most noble prince of the Limousin, begot Aredius, an educated man and chancellor of the aforesaid king; and his brother Eustachius, Germana, and Consortia. Consortia begot Astidius, Pientia, and Basilia. Pientia begot Ocilius. Basilia, wife of Dodo, prince of Bourges, begot Pugia and Karissima.”]

But from this no one can learn that Saint Gerald, Count of Aurillac, was begotten by the aforementioned most noble Aredius, as our Saint Odo asserts here.

And since the Lord is present in a righteous generation, while Gerald’s lineage belongs to those who seek the Lord, it follows that the lineage of the upright should be blessed.

Certainly, how wealthy these people were is shown by the estates filled with slaves, which, scattered throughout the surrounding region, came to Gerald by hereditary right. But the splendor of mind that he had drawn from his parents shone forth in him, multiplied in many ways. Indeed, his parents are made more illustrious by the fact that they deserved to beget such a fortunate child.

### II

His father, while still within marriage, took such care to practice chastity that he frequently separated his bed from that of his wife and slept alone, as though, for a time, he were devoting himself to prayer, in accordance with the Apostle.

One night, it is said, he was warned in a dream to have intercourse with his wife, because she was to bear a son. They say that he was also instructed to call him Gerald, after his own name, and that the child would be a man of great merit.

When he awoke, he rejoiced over the vision. Then, having fallen asleep again, he seemed to see a little shoot growing from the big toe of his right foot.
