It gradually grew into a great tree and then, as its foliage spread, extended everywhere [variant: gradually (*sensim*)]. He then, as though calling for workmen, ordered supports of forks or poles to be placed beneath it. Although the tree grew exceedingly large, he nevertheless felt no weight upon his toe.

[Note: “Visions of dreams.” Peter the Venerable cites this passage in Book II of his Miracles, chapter 25, in the following form: “For, as our holy Father Odo wrote in the Life of the holy man Gerald, visions of dreams are not always empty.”]

For visions of dreams are not always empty. And if credence ought to be given to a dream, this vision seems to correspond to the outcome of future events.

He therefore had intercourse with his wife, who, in accordance with the agreement of the vision, conceived a child. But perhaps this may be doubted as merely a dream. Another clear sign of power followed.

### III

When his mother was near childbirth—on the ninth day before he was born—it happened that she and her husband lay awake together. While they were talking to each other about something or other, the infant emitted a voice, which both of them heard.

Struck with amazement, they wondered what it could be. They could not fail to know that the sound had come from within the mother’s womb. The father therefore called the chambermaid and, having ordered a light to be brought, instructed her to investigate from where the cry had come.

While the woman, equally astonished, declared that there was no infant present who could have uttered that voice, the child sounded again a second time. After a short interval he sounded a third time, like a newborn child crying.

Thus he was heard three times in his mother’s womb—a thing as extraordinary as it is clearly contrary to the ordinary course of nature. Since it happened not by chance but through the arrangement of God, the ordering of all things, perhaps that voice already foretold (*praesagabat*; variant *praesagiebat*, “gave forewarning”) that within the confinement of mortal life he would possess vital activity.

For just as a fetus living in its mother’s womb is alive but has no sensation, so the entire human race, after the guilt of the first man, is held enclosed in this life as though within the narrowness of a womb. Although it lives through faith in hope of the glory of the children of God, it exercises no spiritual faculty [variant: no sensory faculty (*sensuale*)], such as seeing, nor the power of the senses that the first man possessed before sin or that the saints receive after this life, except weakly and with difficulty.

Gerald, therefore, sounded well in his mother’s womb. By exercising a faith in the Holy Trinity beyond the ordinary vigor of others, he signified through that little voice the blessed reputation with which he was to fill the world.

### IV

[Note: “When he was born.” This was in the year of Christ 856, the fifth year of Abbo’s eleventh year as the second abbot of Saint Martial of Limoges, as Ademar, himself a monk of Limoges, notes in his *Memorial of the Abbots of the Basilica of Saint Martial*: “The second Abbot Abbo presided for eleven years; in his fifth year Saint Gerald of Aurillac was born.”]

When he had been born and weaned, and had reached the age at which children’s character is usually tested, a pleasing disposition began to shine in him, by which those who watched carefully inferred that this boy would become a man of virtue.

In early childhood, as we often see, children are accustomed, under the prompting of corrupt nature, to become angry, envious, and eager for revenge, or to attempt similar things. But in the boy Gerald a certain sweetness of spirit, together with the modesty that greatly adorns adolescence, beautified even his childish actions.

By the providence of divine grace he was assigned to the study of letters, though only because his parents intended that, after he had completed the Psalter, he should immediately be trained in secular pursuits, as was customary for noble boys: namely, that he should handle Molossian hounds, become an archer, and grow accustomed to releasing hooded birds and hawks with an appropriate cast.

But so that, devoted to empty pursuits, he would not let the time suitable for learning letters pass unused, divine providence arranged that he should remain ill for a long time. It was an illness of such a kind that he was withdrawn from secular activities but not prevented from studying.

He was continually covered with small pustules, so that, because they lasted for a long time, they were thought no longer capable of being healed. For this reason his father and mother decided that he should be devoted more closely to the study of letters, so that, if he proved less suited to secular occupations, he might be made fit for ecclesiastical service.

On this account it happened that he learned not only singing but also the rudiments of grammar. This later benefited him greatly, since the edge of his intellect, sharpened by that exercise, became keener for whatever he wished to undertake. He possessed a lively intelligence and was sufficiently ready to learn whatever he desired.

### V

When childhood had passed and he was growing into adolescence, the strengthening of his limbs consumed the harmful moisture of his body. He became so swift that he could leap easily over the backs of horses.

Because he was growing vigorously agile in bodily strength, people wanted him to become accustomed to armed military service. But the sweetness of the Scriptures had already begun to captivate the young man’s mind, and he yearned for their study with increasing affection.

Thus, although he excelled in military duties, he was nevertheless enticed by the pleasure of letters. Toward military matters he was slow through deliberate reluctance; toward the study of letters he was accustomed to apply himself diligently.

I believe he already perceived that, according to the testimony of Scripture, “wisdom is better than strength” (Wis. 6:1), and that nothing is richer than she. Since she readily appears to those who love her, she took possession of the young man’s mind beforehand, so that she might reveal herself to him first and become the sweet conversation of his thoughts.

Gerald could therefore be occupied by no hindrance that prevented him from returning to the love of learning. As a result, he learned almost the entire sequence of the Scriptures and surpassed in his knowledge many clerics, however learned they might be.

### VI

When his parents died and all authority over their dominion came to him, Gerald did not swell with pride as adolescents commonly do when they mature into rulers, nor did he alter the modesty he had begun to cultivate in his heart.

The power to rule grew, but his humble mind did not become insolent. He was compelled to occupy himself with arranging and protecting the possessions that, as we have said, he had claimed for himself by hereditary right, and to leave the sweetness of heart that he had already tasted to go outward into the bitterness of earthly business.

He found it painful to abandon the secret place of his heart, but as soon as it was possible he returned to it. While he seemed to fall from the height of contemplation through earthly occupations, he escaped the ruin of inward death by returning to the love of God or to meditation on Holy Scripture—just as it is the habit of the ibex, when falling, to catch itself on its horns so that it may not die.

By that Davidic spirit, I believe, he was already inspired: the spirit by which David, burning with devotion, did not give sleep to his eyes until, freed from the day’s activities, he found a place for the Lord within himself, where, secretly rejoicing beneath his tongue, he might taste how sweet the Lord is.

Perhaps, in accordance with the saying of Job, Christ the Rock poured streams of oil upon him, lest many waters be able to extinguish within him the lamp of charity. He longed fixedly for this refreshment of heart, but household members and retainers nevertheless required him to spend his leisure and devote himself to the usefulness of others.

### VII

Against his will he admitted the biting cares occasioned by the complaints of those who protested. His people complained, saying: Why should a powerful man suffer violence at the hands of lowly persons who were plundering his possessions? They added that, once those men discovered that he did not wish to avenge himself, they would ravage whatever belonged to his jurisdiction all the more aggressively.

It was holier and more honorable, they said, that he should recognize the rights of armed warfare, draw the sword against his enemies, and restrain the audacity of violent men. It was better that reckless men should be subdued by military force than that peasants and unarmed people should be unjustly oppressed by them.

When Gerald heard this, he was encouraged not by assault but by reason, and was moved to show pity and offer assistance. Entrusting himself entirely to the divine will and mercy, he considered how he might visit orphans and widows according to the apostolic command, so that he might keep himself unstained by this world.

### VIII

He therefore began to train himself to restrain the insolence of violent men, observing above all, in earnest competition with himself, that he should promise his enemies peace and the easiest possible reconciliation.

He did this so that either he might overcome evil with good, or, if they rejected his offer, justice would already have favored his side more fully in God’s sight. Sometimes he soothed them and brought them back to peace.

But when the blatant wickedness of some mocked the peaceful man, he then revealed the severity of his heart and crushed the molars of the wicked, so that, in accordance with Job’s saying, he might take the prey from their teeth.

He was not driven by a desire for revenge, as is customary for many, nor enticed by love of popular praise, but was inflamed by love for the poor, who were unable to defend themselves. He acted in this way lest, if he had grown numb through sluggish patience, he might seem to have neglected the command concerning care for the poor. For Scripture commands that the poor be rescued and the needy delivered from the hand of the sinner.

He therefore rightly did not give the sinner power. Sometimes, when the unavoidable necessity of fighting fell upon him, he commanded his men in an authoritative voice to fight with the points of their swords turned backward, directing their spears forward.

This would have seemed ridiculous to his enemies if Gerald, strengthened by divine power, had not immediately become unbearable to those same enemies. It also seemed utterly foolish to his own men until they had proved by experience that Gerald, whom compassion overcame at the very moment of battle, was always invincible.

When they saw that, through a new kind of warfare combined with compassion, he triumphed, they turned their mockery into admiration. Even once victory was assured, they eagerly observed his commands.

For it was never heard that either he or his soldiers, who fought under his fealty, had been deceived by the outcome of battle. It is also certain that he himself never wounded anyone, nor was he ever wounded by anyone.

Christ was, as it is written, at his side. Looking into the eye of his heart, Christ perceived that Gerald was so benevolent for his sake that he did not wish to attack the enemies themselves, but only to deprive them of their audacity.

Let no one be disturbed that a righteous man sometimes practiced warfare, which appears unsuitable to religion. Whoever examines the matter with a just balance will not find that Gerald’s glory ought to be obscured even in this respect.

For some of the Fathers, although they were both most holy and most patient, nevertheless, when justice demanded it, courageously took up arms against their adversaries. Abraham, for example, routed a great multitude of enemies in order to rescue his nephew; and King David even sent legions against his son.

Gerald fought not by invading what belonged to others but by defending what belonged to him—or rather, the rights of his people. He knew that the rhinoceros, that is, any powerful man, is tied by a leather strap so that he may break to pieces the clods of the valleys, that is, the oppressors of the humble.

Nor, as the Apostle says, does the judge carry the sword without cause; “for he is God’s avenger” (Rom. 13:4). It was therefore permissible for a layman placed in the military order to carry a sword, so that he might defend the unarmed populace, like innocent sheep, from wolves, as Scripture says, and restrain by military law or judicial force those whom ecclesiastical discipline could not subdue.

It therefore does not obscure his glory that he fought for God’s cause, for which the whole world fights against the senseless. Rather, it contributes to his praise that he always won openly, without fraud or ambush, and yet was so protected by God that, as we have said above, he never stained his sword with human blood.

Moreover, whoever takes up arms against enemies after his example should, following that same example, seek not his own advantage but the common good. You can see some men boldly exposing themselves to danger for love of praise or profit, willingly enduring the world’s evils for the sake of the world. While seeking its joys, so to speak, whenever its bitterness confronts them, they lose them.

But Gerald’s work is of another kind. It is bright because it proceeds from simplicity of heart.

### IX

The ancient deceiver had examined the young man’s character and, perceiving something divine in him, burned with envy. For that reason he tried to overwhelm him with every possible deceit of temptation.

But Gerald had already learned to flee in prayer to the lap of divine mercy and, through Christ’s grace, to reject the enemy’s schemes. Since the insatiably envious enemy had discovered by experience that he could not rule Gerald through the pleasure of the flesh, he stirred up the storms of war against him through wicked men, as we said above, in order to assault through them the fortress of piety in his heart, which he could not breach by himself.

But when we return to the chastity that the same young man cherished so ardently, the exceedingly crafty enemy was inflamed most fiercely against it. It was something new and unheard-of for him that a young man should escape shipwreck of modesty unharmed.

He therefore persistently suggested lust to Gerald, that power which, for deceiving the human race, is either his greatest or his first weapon. When Gerald utterly rejected it, the enemy was tormented, because he could not even admit it through the doors of his heart.

He therefore returned to his old trick and resorted to the instrument of deception by which Adam and his descendants are usually deceived most effectively: namely, a woman.

It is said that he placed a certain young woman before Gerald’s eyes. When Gerald carelessly observed the bright color of her delicate skin, he immediately began to soften under the pleasure of looking at her.

If only he had at once understood what lay beneath the skin! For no flesh is beautiful except through the deceptive coloring of the skin. He turned his eyes away, but the appearance impressed upon them remained fixed in his heart.

Thus he was troubled, enticed, and scorched by a blind fire. At last, overcome, he sent to the girl’s mother and announced that he would come at night. Following the messenger, he was rushing violently toward the destruction of his soul.

Meanwhile, as captives in chains often sigh while remembering their former freedom, Gerald sighed and recalled the sweetness of his customary love of God. Though in distress, he begged God not to let that temptation swallow him completely.

They came to the appointed place. The girl entered the lodging, because it was cold, and stood facing the fire. But divine grace had already looked upon Gerald. The girl immediately appeared so deformed to him that he could not believe she was the one he had seen, until her father declared that she was indeed the same.

Understanding that this had happened through divine providence, because the young woman no longer possessed the same beauty in his eyes, he immediately gathered himself under Christ’s mercy. Sighing deeply, he mounted his horse in haste and, without delay, giving thanks to God, hurried away.

Perhaps an intense frost had then set in. He allowed himself to be tormented by it throughout the night, so that icy severity might punish the warmth of a small pleasure.

He immediately ordered the girl’s father to give her in marriage. He also granted her freedom and bestowed a small estate upon her by testamentary right. Perhaps, suspicious of his own weakness, he hastened her marriage. For the sake of almsgiving, and by the gift of freedom as her dowry, he ensured that her marriage would not be delayed.

But how could you, destined to become a cedar of Paradise, have been shaken in this way? Certainly, so that you might learn what you were like in yourself. For your patron, the prince of the apostles, to whom you later entrusted both yourself and all that was yours, would not have known himself sufficiently unless the moment of temptation had overtaken him.

Now that you have learned by experience what a man is by himself and what he is through God’s grace, may you not disdain to sympathize with the weakness of those who supplicate you.

Let us know, moreover, that it is not unfamiliar for saints to be tempted. They are born with the vices of corrupt nature woven into them, so that, whenever they struggle, they may overcome in the struggle and, having overcome, be crowned.

The difference lies in whether someone receives the pleasure of vice and succumbs, or resists it and conquers, occupying his mind instead with the pleasure of virtue and driving away with the antidote of devout supplication the poison of wrongful pleasure that he may perhaps have taken in for a moment.

After this experience of danger, the young man became more discerning. Like someone walking on slippery ground after striking his foot, he proceeded more cautiously, taking great care that his eyes should report nothing to his heart through which death might enter his soul by way of their windows.

### X

But the sweet and righteous Lord, who in the sweetness of his compassion had preserved his servant Gerald from fornication, did not fail to punish him for his desire by the judgment of his righteousness.

After not many days had passed, he crushed the offender through glaucoma and blindness lasting for more than a year, so that the eyes that had seen unlawful things could for a time see not even lawful ones.

No obvious defect appeared either on his eyelids or in his pupils. His household knew of his blindness, but his keen pupils carefully concealed it from outsiders. He, humbling himself beneath the hand of the striking Lord, remained silent, as though ready for his blows.

He neither rejected bodily medicine nor sought it urgently, patiently awaiting the time and manner in which his Lord, once his will to strike had been fulfilled, would wish to remove the blows.

For he knew that every son is scourged. The inward Judge also cleanses even the smallest stains in his chosen ones, so that nothing may remain in them that would later offend his eyes.

For this reason he inflicted this scourge upon Gerald, so that the young man’s mind might both be cleansed of the past and be kept purer for the future. When God had fulfilled his will in him, he removed the scourge and restored light to his eyes.

### XI

Now, as though his senses had been refined by affliction, Gerald lived a sufficiently upright life and walked the middle path of discretion, inclining excessively to neither side.

He did not fail to discharge his duties in secular affairs, nor did he allow earthly occupation to entangle him so that he abandoned religious observance. He associated more familiarly with honorable men and with clerics of better reputation, with whom at home or abroad he performed the divine office, either together or individually.

A Sunday came, and he was obliged to attend a certain *placitum*—that is, a court or judicial assembly—to which certain noblemen were to gather by appointment.

[Note: “To a certain *placitum*.” That is, a judgment or an assembly held for judicial purposes. The Third Synod of Tours, canon 35, says: “For any *placitum* or judgment, to demand gifts from any person.” And Book III of the Capitularies, chapter 84, says: “Each count shall have his *placitum* and administer justice.” Hence also *placitare*, in Geoffrey of Vendôme, Letter 24, Book II, means what the Fourth Synod of Arles, canon 16, calls “to conduct cases and disputes.” In our language, *plaid* and *plaider*.]

So that he would not seem, by arriving late, to delay those who were coming, he made an effort to travel on horseback and to depart before dawn.

In this he avoided swollen arrogance, lest he make himself late or difficult for anyone, as is now the custom of certain people who, as though emerging from a bedchamber, surrender themselves first to drunkenness before attending to their friends, contrary to the Scripture that says: “Woe to the land whose princes eat in the morning” (Isa. 5:11).

But Gerald was not like that. He considered it extremely disgraceful that one who had been placed over many and was their lord should become a slave to the rule of vices. He went fasting to the judicial assembly, lest, with sobriety submerged, he should lack the judgment of reason. He inquired what would favor Christ, peace, and the common good.

After the nocturnal praises, whenever he had to set out, the solemnity of Mass followed; thus, entrusting himself and his people to divine mercy, he departed.

On that Sunday, because it had been necessary to set out before dawn [printed *proficiscere*; corrected *proficisci*], he had missed Mass. After completing the judicial business, he hoped to hear it, but it was nowhere possible.

Very sorrowful, he went about searching for some hope of finding it. When he had searched in vain, he summoned the clerics who happened to be present, together with all the psalm-singing soldiers, and said:

“It is entirely my own fault that this holy day will pass for us in vain. But there is something we can do for God’s praise, so that we may not seem to have spent the holy day uselessly.”

Having said this, he took up the Psalter from the beginning and ran through it with them, uttering nothing mortal.

From then on he established for himself the custom of reciting the Psalter almost every day. When he had completed it, he seemed to rejoice as though spiritually feasted, just as someone rejoices after his ambition has been satisfied.

## XII

It seems worth the effort to say something about the appearance of his body. For although the flesh profits nothing, and although beauty is deceptive grace, nevertheless, since it is often fuel for lust and pride, this should be praised in the man: he was handsome, yet did not defile himself with the filth of lust.

Gerald was of medium height and, as they say, entirely *euphormis*, that is, well formed. Although the beauty of each limb enhanced its own appearance, his neck was so fair and, as it were, adorned according to the rule of perfect proportion that you would scarcely have thought you had seen anything else so graceful. The elegance of his body was adorned by the beauty of his spirit. Hence the disposition of his heart shone out upon his brow. Scripture also testifies to this, saying that the laughter of the teeth and the expression of the face reveal the quality of the inner person.

He had already tasted that the Lord is sweet, and that the embrace of the heavenly bridegroom is gracious; therefore he did not allow the beautiful appearance of his soul to be enticed in the eyes of that same bridegroom by the allurements of the flesh. His household would often kiss his neck in delight, and he did not take offense at them, because pride—which is always unapproachable—could not claim a seat for itself.

Moreover, he was exceedingly swift in bodily movement and strong in physical power. This must be mentioned so that it may be clear that the one who has material for pride yet humbles himself in humility is praiseworthy. Conversely, those are blameworthy who, possessing little or none of these qualities, swell with pride. After he had applied himself more fully to intellectual pursuits, however, that bodily agility completely withered away.

He was also most agreeable in ordinary conversation and, in handling and arranging affairs, profound in the acuity of his judgment. Although he avoided the language of buffoonery, he expressed serious matters in such a way that even his own people found pleasure in it. He was neither too talkative in uttering threats nor tenacious in retaining injuries. Nor was he readily inclined to give just any benefits, nor changeable in taking back what he had given. Whatever he said affirmatively, he fulfilled without fail—unless, of course, he recognized that it was sinful.

## XIII

He cultivated sobriety so carefully that he guarded not only himself but also his household from drunkenness. His guests were neither gluttonous nor hard drinkers. He never compelled guests to drink, nor did he drink more than the other guests. Thus he regulated the banquet so that no one rose from it drunk or dispirited.

When he had sometimes arranged for guests, to whose hospitality he devoted himself entirely, to be refreshed in the morning, he himself did not eat before the third hour of the day, or, when fasting, before the ninth [*aute*; evidently *ante*, “before”]. The blessed prince observed that command of Scripture according to which one should eat at the proper time for refreshment, not for luxury. What could he have observed more appropriately than drunkenness, which, besides being the death of the soul and excluding one from the kingdom of God, as the Apostle testifies, just as murder does, is also proved to be exceedingly harmful to the body?

From it come weakness of strength, trembling of the limbs, enervation of the senses, and untimely old age. Sight, speech, and facial expression are disgraced, and every adornment of religion is corrupted. No one can at once be filled with wine and with the Holy Spirit; nor can anyone in any way guard Jerusalem from the fire of fornication if he refuses to drive away from its siege Nebuzaradan, the chief of the cooks.

## XIV

Seats were always prepared before him for the poor, and sometimes tables were set before them, so that he might see for himself what and how much was given them for refreshment. No fixed number of recipients was maintained; if more happened to be present, provided that their persons seemed suitable to receive assistance, more were admitted to him. No one was ever excluded from the door without receiving an alms.

The servants saw to it that dishes were always at hand for him to give them. Drink was also brought; after inspecting and tasting it, he sent it on, so that they might drink first. To them he also gave half of his own bread.

Believing that he received Christ in these people, and reverently honoring Christ in them, he admitted through them to himself the one whose refreshment, according to the prophet, is to refresh the weary. Those who, although they send alms outside, do not admit the poor to themselves greatly diminish the reward of such hospitality. For they seem in this way to exclude from their houses Christ, who says: “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me” (Matt. 25:35).

And so that he might surpass the righteousness of the Pharisees, in accordance with the Lord’s command, he had a ninth part of the revenues from his lands set aside separately. From this the poor were maintained in some of his houses; from it clothing and footwear were supplied to them. He continually distributed coins, which he himself carried for this purpose, either personally or secretly through a trustworthy servant, to those he met.

Sometimes, when money was being given on behalf of someone, he himself received it together with the needy, rejoicing and desiring to be likened to the poor. He immediately gave away the money, repaying the little gift he had received with a great exercise of divine service.

## XV

At mealtimes great reverence was maintained around him. There was no prevailing talkativeness or buffoonery, but either necessary or honorable conversation, or at least words from divine Scripture.

Throughout his life he ate only once a day, except perhaps during the summer, when he would dine somewhat more freely [*prosius*; uncertain] or eat uncooked food. At his table, reading was first continued for a considerable time. But, accommodating himself occasionally to secular people, he would suspend the reading and ask the clerics what was being said in it—though he asked only those whom he knew were able to answer.

He nourished noble clerics, to whom both uprightness of conduct and learning of mind were imparted in equal measure. Toward adolescents he showed himself stricter, saying that the period of that age is exceedingly dangerous: at that time every young man, laying aside the likeness of his mother’s voice or face, begins to assume his father’s voice or appearance. Whoever strives to preserve himself at that time will afterward overcome the incentives of the flesh with ease.

When those whom he questioned about the reading asked him to speak instead, he would eventually produce what learned simplicity, not pompous eloquence, supplied him. Meanwhile, when there were always some who, as usual, introduced certain witticisms or jokes, he restrained them not with biting indignation but as though joking along with them. Nevertheless, he never allowed frivolity to be prolonged in his presence.

For he knew that all Christians are commonly commanded to eat their bread in silence. At the end of the meal, the reader always resumed the reading. Thus Gerald spent the greater part of the meal either speaking about God or listening to God speaking to him through the reading.

Let those who, contrary to the prophet’s rebuke, have harp and lyre at their banquets while they play judge this example of his. They delight in amusements and exult at the sound of the organ. They do not regard the work of the Lord, because amid the voices of those who shout loudly they do not even hear the cry of the poor.

For what? It is true that Christ, the Truth, said that “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matt. 12:34). Those who always speak of worldly matters and little or rarely of God plainly reveal what they love more, or what abounds in their hearts. Would that, like Gerald, they looked to the end and, whether they ate or drank, did everything to the glory of God, in accordance with the Apostle’s command.

Three days each week, and throughout every period devoted to abstinence, he abstained from meat. If an annual feast occurred on one of those days, he relaxed the abstinence in such a way that, on a different day when abstinence was permitted, he abstained in its place; he also refreshed an additional poor person on behalf of that feast.

If, however, a fast fell on a Sunday, he did not relax it or omit it on that pretext, but completed the solemnity of the fast on the preceding Saturday. If this observance of the holy man seems inappropriate to anyone, let the person whom it perhaps troubles know that “all things are clean to the clean”—that is, to those who eat without the fault of desire—and that the inward judge considers not the quality of the food but the need or appetite with which it is consumed. The prophet Elijah and Esau prove this by their examples.

It was therefore permitted to a layman, especially one so just, to use things that were lawful; this is not permitted to those whose profession forbids it. For the tree in paradise did not bring death because it was evil, but because it was presumptuously taken in violation of the prohibition.

## XVI

He always used woolen or linen garments—not in the manner now presumed upon and devised by the sons of Belial, who are entirely without a yoke, but according to ancient custom. They were woven so that they suggested neither affected splendor nor plebeian rusticity.

He did not seek to adorn himself with silks or costly garments, even on the occasion of any feast or in the presence of any margrave, more than usual. He took care not to change or renew the strap by which a sword is usually fastened around the loins for twenty years, if it could last that long.

What should I say about a belt, elaborate girdles, or a brooch, or about the trappings of horses, when he would not tolerate not only carrying gold but even possessing it? He did not regard gold as his strength, nor did he glory in an abundance of riches, but in God.

This is unlike the way even religious devotees commonly behave when they are urged by shameless and tireless zeal to cultivate bodily appearance. They strive with all their might to obtain from onlookers, at least under the pretext of costly clothing, the respect which they take away from themselves by their conduct. It would be more profitable for them to devote themselves instead to the adornment of the soul, which could continually grow more beautiful.

## XVII

The poor and those who had suffered injury always had free access to him, and they did not need to bring any little gift to commend their case to him. Each person pleaded his need more forcefully before his eyes, the more straitened by want he saw him to be.

His kindness was renowned not only among neighboring regions but also in distant lands. Since everyone knew how beneficent he was toward all, many settled their needs through him. He did not disdain to concern himself, personally or through his people, with the affairs of the poor and to offer assistance as far as he was able.

When he learned that harsh wars were often raging between disputing parties, on the day when the case was to be heard he had Masses celebrated for them. When he could not humanly come to their aid, he invoked divine assistance for them.

Nor did he tolerate that any lord should be able to take away a benefit from his vassal because of any fit of anger.

Once the matter had been brought forward, he restrained the anger of the exasperated man, partly by entreaty and partly by command. In this one matter alone you might have thought the vigor of his rectitude inclined toward severity.

Whenever a poor man happened to be bound to a more powerful person, he insisted on supporting the weaker in such a way that he could overcome the stronger without injury. Since he truly hungered and thirsted for justice, he did not tolerate its being violated not only among his own people but even among strangers.

## XVIII

A thirst for justice burned in him in due order, just as hunger does. Simplicity and kindness did not abandon the severity of his zeal, nor did the severity of his zeal abandon the kindness of simplicity.

As it is said of Job that he was simple and upright, so this man, although he greatly assisted the poor, did not entirely sleep when it came to punishing the guilty. He knew, of course, that some people are divinely appointed to pay by temporal punishment for a crime that cannot remain unpunished. Hence, when King David was dying, he ordered Joab and Shimei to be punished.

Some robbers had occupied a certain forest, where they inflicted robbery and slaughter upon passersby and neighbors. When Gerald heard of this, he immediately sent men to capture them. At that time a certain peasant, compelled by fear, had happened to come to them. The soldiers who captured the robbers, fearing that Lord Gerald might either release them or blame the soldiers for showing them to him unpunished, immediately tore out the eyes of all of them. On that occasion the peasant was blinded along with the others.

Afterward he withdrew to the district of Toulouse. A long time later, when Lord Gerald heard that the man had not been a companion of the robbers, he was greatly saddened and inquired whether he was alive and where he had gone. When he learned that he had departed for the region of Toulouse, he sent him, as they say, one hundred solidi, ordering the bearer to ask forgiveness from him in Gerald’s place.

## XIX

How mercifully he consoled the afflicted, and how often he pitied those in distress, may likewise be made clear by this example.

A certain priest had been so tormented by the increasing quarrel of his neighbors that they tore out his eyes. The lord consoled him greatly with words, urging him to patience. But lest the consolation of words seem too slight, he formally made a will and transferred to him a church belonging to his own jurisdiction.

Some time passed, and one of those who had inflicted violence upon the priest was arrested by the officials and shut up in prison.

> [Note: **He was arrested by the officials.** So below, chapter 41: “The officials allowed him, against his will and unwillingly, to entrust that little estate—namely, Taladiciacum—to a certain Bernard for safekeeping.”]

This was immediately reported to the lord, as though it would make him rejoice. He at once hastened toward the prison, apparently eager to punish the man. Other cases, however, had arisen that had to be settled the following day. Taking advantage of this circumstance, he ordered the accused man to remain there until then.

Late in the day, when the officials had gone away to their own affairs, he secretly instructed the guard to refresh the prisoner with food and drink. Since the man was barefoot, he ordered him to give him shoes and allow him to escape.

The next day, when people were flocking to the lord from every direction for the assembly—

> [Note: **With the people of the assembly flocking to the lord from every direction.** *Mallus* means the greater court, where major cases were customarily settled by counts and lords. The Edict of Pîtres of Charles the Bald, 864: “Let him hold his assembly in such a way that his *barigildi* and advocates, who have cases in other counties, may be able to come to his assembly.” Hence *admallare*, to come before a judge for the purpose of litigating. Marculfus, book I of the *Formulas*, chapter 21: “Because, on account of his simplicity, he is quite unable to pursue his cases or come to court.” And *mallenses*, those summoned to court to pursue and dispute their affairs.]

—he ordered the accused to be brought forward. Certain men whom the prison guard had recruited for himself, trembling, reported that the prisoner had escaped. The lord, wishing to conceal what had happened, pretended to threaten the guard. But immediately afterward he said in the same manner: “Well done; for the priest had already forgiven him the injury.”

## XX

Likewise, two prisoners whose grave guilt had subjected them to him had been brought before him. Their accusers insisted that he order them to be hanged and killed immediately. He, however, concealed his intention, because he did not wish to free them publicly. In every work of mercy he moderated himself so carefully that his mercy itself would not appear excessive.

Looking at the accusers, he said: “If, as you say, they must die, let us first refresh them according to the common judgment.” He then ordered food and drink to be brought to them and had them unbound for eating.

When they had been refreshed, he gave them his knife and said: “Go and bring branches yourselves, on which you are to be hanged.”

Not far away there was a forest that had grown dense with shoots. Entering it as though looking for branches, they gradually penetrated farther into it and suddenly disappeared, thus escaping the moment of death. Those who were present understood his consent and did not dare search for them among the thickets.

As can be inferred from the equality of the persons involved, those persons of criminals who had given themselves over to evil he either curbed by fines or branded with the mark of burning. Those who had committed some offense not through habitual wickedness but on a particular occasion he dismissed unharmed. Yet it was never heard that, in his presence, anyone was punished by death or mutilated in his limbs.

## XXI

Of his many deeds we recall only a few individual examples, which can suffice to display certain acts of mercy known to us. For this reason we also insert even the smallest details, through which the greatness of his zeal may be demonstrated.

Once, as he was walking along the public causeway, a peasant woman in a field beside the road was driving a plow. He asked why the woman had presumed to perform a man’s work. She replied that her husband had long been ill, that the season for sowing was passing, that she was alone, and that she had no one to help her.

Moved by her misfortune, he ordered that enough money be given her for the number of sowing days that seemed to remain, so that she could hire a farmer for each day and thereafter cease from the man’s work herself.

Nature, as Ambrose says, avoids everything artificial, and God, its author, abhors whatever is contrary to it. This deed is small in itself, but the upright man’s disposition, which accords with the laws of nature, makes it great.

## XXII

On another occasion, as he was likewise traveling along a road, a certain peasant was not far away harvesting chickpeas. When the young men who went ahead of the lord took some and ate them, he saw this, spurred his horse, and hastened to the man, asking whether the boys had taken the chickpeas.

“Sir,” the man replied, “I gave them freely.”

“May God reward you,” said the lord.

## XXIII

The same is shown by what happened on another occasion. When his servants were preparing a meal beneath cherry trees, the same servants had broken off branches hanging with berries that were already ripe before he arrived. After a peasant objected, he bought them from him for the price of silver.

Someone might perhaps say that such matters are unworthy of being reported. But through these small incidents we display the mind of a God-fearing man, so that it may be understood indirectly that one who did not despise small things could not gradually fall into greater ones. Was not the widow’s devotion commended by the Lord through her two small coins?

## XXIV

Toward those who belonged to his jurisdiction he was so beneficent and so peaceful that it was astonishing to those who considered it. They often reproached him for being soft and timid, since he allowed himself to be injured by persons of the lowest rank, as though he were powerless. Yet he was not easily angered, as lords commonly are, against those who reproached him, nor did he take even slight offense.

On one occasion he encountered a considerable number of peasants who—

> [Note: **Having abandoned their holdings.** A *colonia* is a small dwelling with as much land as one tenant, together with his servants, can cultivate. Flodoard, book IX of the *History of Reims*, chapter 19, speaking of Archbishop Ebo: “He organized certain church holdings, assigning tenants to them through capable men and arranging their services.” And Rudolf Glaber, book III of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 5: “That monastery too, namely Cluny, is said at first to have received no more than fifteen agricultural holdings as its endowment.” *Colonica* is also found frequently among ancient writers. The *Chronicle of Saint Benignus*: “With the servants who held seven agricultural holdings from the aforesaid estates.” The Synod of Valence under the Emperor Lothair, chapter 9: “Let them confer upon them, as a dowry, one equipped agricultural holding with three dependents.” And an even older charter of endowment of the church of Viviers: “I, Venantius, bishop of the see of Viviers, endowed the church at Luciatense in honor of Saint Mary and Saint Martin at Bessiacum; I endowed them with seventy agricultural holdings and their servants, and I left them to God and Saint Vincent.”]

—were migrating to another province, having abandoned their holdings.

When he recognized them and asked where they were going with their belongings, they replied that they had been wronged by him, although he had benefited them. The soldiers who accompanied the prince urged him to order them to be beaten and compelled to return to the little houses from which they had departed.

But he refused. He knew that their Lord and his own was one and the same in heaven, and he was more accustomed, in accordance with the Apostle, to refrain from threats and not to raise the hand of his power against the weak. Therefore he allowed them to go wherever they thought it more advantageous for themselves and gave them permission to settle elsewhere.

What I recently heard a certain chatterer say—not without embarrassment on my part—namely, that he was never accustomed to release a debtor’s *wadium* debt, is entirely false.

> [Note: **A *wadium* debt.** Book III of the *Capitularies*, chapter 19: “If a free man who has placed himself in another’s power in the place of a pledge, while remaining there, causes harm to anyone, let the person who received him in the place of a pledge either pay the damages or produce the man in court and release him, losing at the same time the debt for which he received him as a pledge.” Hence *debitum rewadiatum* in book IV, chapter 58, and *heribannum rewadiare* in chapter 70 of the same book.]

Those who often witnessed it testify that he released not only the increase of the *wadium* but also the principal debt.

> [Note: **The principal debt.** Thus *capitalis dominus*, a principal or superior lord. *Chartulary of the Affairs Relating to the Great Monastery at Vendôme*, from the library of the most illustrious president J. A. de Thou, charter 175: “The principal lords of that same land also authorized this.” And earlier, charter 121: “Solomon of Lavarzino, being the principal lord of this land, also laid his hand upon this purchase to confirm it.”]

## XXV

His peasants and clerics, who loved him affectionately as a father, often brought him little cakes of wax. He received them as though they were great gifts and returned many thanks. Yet he did not permit any of that wax to be burned for his own use. Rather, before the altar or before the holy relics—which he likewise had carried with him—he ordered all of it to be burned as lights.

When wax prepared elsewhere for his service happened to be lacking in the bedchamber, they prepared birch bark or fir torches before him and for his services. But since he took such care that private persons would not use the gifts freely given to him, how could it follow that he exacted *wadium* payments without mercy? On the contrary, he frequently released debts voluntarily, even when they were legally owed to him. In accordance with the Apostle’s command, he also remitted threats to servants. For at times he endured fraud and, as the same Apostle says, accepted the seizure of his goods.

## XXVI

This may be demonstrated by the following example. Once a thief entered his tent at night. A candle was burning as usual before his bed, and the lord happened to be awake. He was accustomed, while lying on his bed, to be nourished by the love and sweetness of Christ through the practice of prayer.

The thief, however, scanning everything with a searching gaze, was looking to see whether he might find anything worth carrying away. He noticed a small cushion whose covering was of silk. He stretched out his hand and began to pull it toward himself.

Then the lord said: “Who are you?”

The thief was frightened and stood there stupefied and hesitating.

“Go on,” said the lord. “Do what you are doing, and depart carefully, lest someone notice.”

In this way he persuaded the thief to leave freely with the stolen object. Who other than Gerald would have acted in this way? Surely it seems to me more worthy of admiration than if he had made the thief stiffen into the hardness of stone.

## XXVII

How carefully he strove to observe the Apostle’s command, “Do not defraud your brother in business” (1 Thess. 4:6), will likewise be made clear by a present example.

Once, on his return from the city of Rome, he passed by Pavia and encamped not far away. When the Venetians and many others immediately learned of this, they came out to him at once. By then he was sufficiently renowned throughout the entire journey, and famous among everyone for his piety and generosity.

As merchants, according to their custom, hurried among the tents—

> [Note: **Among the tents.** That is, among the pavilions and tents. In French, *pavillons et tentes*.]

—and made inquiries if anyone wished to buy something, certain more respectable men reached the lord’s tent and asked the servants whether the lord count—for that is what everyone called him—wanted to have cloaks or spices purchased.

He then called them to him and said: “What pleased me, I bid for in Rome; but I should very much like you to tell me whether I made a good bargain.”

He ordered the cloaks he had bought to be brought before him. One of them was exceedingly valuable. When the Venetian saw it, he asked what had been paid for it. When he learned the price, he said: “Truly, if it were in Constantinople, it would be worth even more there.”

When the lord heard this, he was frightened, as though recoiling from a great crime. Later, when he encountered some Romans whom he knew, he entrusted them with as many solidi as the Venetian had said the cloak was worth beyond the price paid, indicating where they could find the cloak’s seller.

In other kinds of sin, people commonly feel remorse and consider making amends. But rarely, or rather scarcely ever, do you see anyone besides Gerald grieve that he had committed this particular kind of sin. He knew, of course, that God is offended by every sin, and he did not wish to offend the one whom he loved with all his heart even in the smallest matters.

## XXVIII

Not forgetting that the righteousness of Christians ought to surpass the righteousness of the Pharisees, he ordered not only all his crops to be tithed with complete accuracy but also the ninths to be stored separately, to be distributed for the various needs of the poor.

When necessity required it, clothing was purchased for poor people who arrived at different times. Moreover, he continually carried coins with him, which he secretly gave, as far as he could, either personally or through anyone aware of this practice, to the needy whom he encountered.

Although the revenues from his fields and vineyards were abundant enough, it was never heard that his stewards had acquired anything. Nor did he ever acquire an estate, except for one small field that happened to be attached to one of his possessions. Wealthy people commonly burn intensely with the desire to do this, forgetting the prophet’s terrible threat: “Woe to you who join house to house and add field to field” (Isa. 5:8).

Gerald, in accordance with the command of the Gospel, was content with his wages. And just as he oppressed no one and practiced no extortion, so the Lord, the disposer of all things, preserved what belonged to him from the wicked and usurpers.

Indeed, he held so many estates in different provinces under his authority that, in truth, he could be called wealthy in the very places of which he possessed an abundance. Yet the multitude of his estates did not exalt him, because, as the psalmist says, he desired nothing from the Lord upon earth.

The Lord added all these things to him because Gerald sought first from him the kingdom of God. By God’s generosity he had grown so greatly, and remained so protected and secure, that the words spoken of Job seem applicable to him: “You have fenced him around, and his possessions have increased in the land” (Job 1:10).

## XXIX

To show how he was accustomed to overcome evil with good, in accordance with the Apostle’s command, let this deed of his be recalled as an example.

When he later came to the port of Piacenza, a certain cleric who was in charge of the port arrived. As was customary there, he was expecting a very profitable freight charge from the Romans. For some reason, stirred by bile, he hurled words of indignation and attacked the bishop of the province of Rodez and other noblemen with insulting reproaches.

> [Note: **Of the province of Rodez.** In Aquitania Prima, under the archbishopric of Bourges, Caesar and Gregory of Tours called the people *Rutheni*. Today we call them the people of Rodez.]

The man of God happened to be standing opposite. Fearing that a disturbance might arise, he restrained his fellow travelers so that they would not answer harshly. He overcame the cleric with gentle speech and gave him certain small gifts.

Seeing how easily he had restrained both the bishop and the others from answering insults, and how gently he had brought the cleric back to his senses, the cleric asked who he was. When Gerald replied that he was an Aquitanian and a person of modest standing, the cleric, considering both his appearance and his eloquence, completely bent himself toward his favor. He remitted everything owed for the freight and filled with wine both Gerald’s flasks and those of the others in his company.

That same lord had received from God the gift of being gracious, both personally and in his speech—not only to ordinary people but also to the powerful. Indeed, he was always dear and revered even to kings.

## XXX

He was rightly loved by everyone because he loved everyone. Let us relate what he did for a certain fugitive, as though for a friend.

On the same journey he encountered a fugitive who had left his municipality several years earlier. Among the people with whom he lived, the man was regarded as important and wealthy. Gerald’s servants found him and brought him, trembling and afraid, to their lord.

Gerald questioned him privately about how he was doing. When he learned that the man was held in considerable honor in that place, he said: “Nor will I dishonor you.”

He then ordered his men not to reveal what the man had formerly been in his own region. In the presence of his neighbors he gave the man certain little gifts, honored him conspicuously in conversation and at table, and dismissed him in peace.

Who other than Gerald would have done this? He did it because he was not a servant of avarice but had devoted himself entirely to mercy.

## XXXI

Likewise, on the same journey, a man from the region of Bourges had broken his hip not far from Rome. Abandoned by his own people, he remained alone with his wife.

A certain Boniface, one of Lord Gerald’s soldiers, happened to find him. When he heard of the man’s need, he brought him to Lord Gerald and said: “Behold, my lord, according to your desire I have found something that will please you and which I present to you: here is a man in need of comfort.”

The man of God then gladly received him into his protection and led him, sufficiently supported, as far as the town of Brioude.

> [Note: **As far as the town of Brioude.** In Auvergne, famous for the relics of Saint Julian the Martyr, it is called *Brivas* by Sidonius in the *Propemptic to a Little Book*, by Gregory in book X of his *History*, chapter 29, and by the ancient writer of the *Life of Saint Odilo*. Gregory also mentions another Brioude in the Limousin, which, to distinguish it from the Auvergne town, he calls *Briva Curretia* in book V, chapter 10, in these words: “Having joined the aforesaid dukes and entered the Limousin, he arrived at the town of Briva Curretia, where Saint Martin, said to be one of our Martin’s disciples, rests.” The French call it *Brives-la-Gaillarde*, though incorrectly. It should be called *Brive de Corrèze*, from the river Corrèze, which flows around it.]

He also gave him ten solidi, so that he would have assistance until he reached his own people.

These and similar deeds testify to the compassionate disposition that divine inspiration had generously awakened in him.

### XXXII

But let us understand that it is necessary for the wheat harvest to grow together with the darnel, and for the grain of wheat meanwhile to be pressed down by the straw above it; and for this reason it was necessary that the wicked Cain should exercise the just Abel in patience. Gerald, too, like Job—“a brother of dragons and a companion of ostriches”—is shown to have been frequently harassed by certain men of the provinces.

For, when the condition of the commonwealth had already become excessively disturbed, the insolence of the marquises had subjected the royal vassals [Col. 0661A] to itself.

[Note: [Col. 0660D] Royal vassals—that is, servants or faithful men who owed and were bound to render service and loyalty to the king. Aymoinus, Book V, chapter 35: “The abbots also, and the leading men of the kingdom and the royal vassals, commended themselves to him and promised him faith by oath according to custom.” This is an old French word, still retained by the French in the form *vassaux*. Hence also *vassaticum* among Gregory, Theodulf, and others, meaning *vasselage*. Every lord—count, duke, or king—had his vassals. Odo likewise says: “Nor did he tolerate this, that any lord should be able to take away a benefice from his vassal for any disturbance of mind.” *Lex Alamannorum*, title 36, chapter 4: “Whatever person he may be, whether a vassal of a duke or of a count.” And the *Lex Baiuvariorum*, chapter 2, title 15: “Whether a king’s vassal or a duke’s, let all come to the assembly.” Walafrid Strabo used the general expression “the lord’s vassals”: “The lesser chaplains,” he says, “are like those whom, in the French custom, we call the lord’s vassals.” And Book III of the *Capitularies*, chapter 73, *On the Lord’s Vassals*: “Concerning the lord’s vassals who still serve within the household, yet are known to possess benefices, it has been decreed that if any one of them remains at home with the lord emperor, he shall not retain with him his settled vassals, but shall allow them to go with the count whose dependents they are.” *Drudi* likewise derives from the German word *drow*, that is, “faith,” as Claudius Falcetus notes in Book IX of the *Antiquities of the Franks*, chapter 15. The capitularies that the bishops of the Rheims and Rouen dioceses sent to King Louis in 818: “And she will go forth naked and desolate, without the protection and retinue of *drudi* and vassals.” Likewise, *lassi* among the Saxons, as Witaldus explains, and Hucbald, abbot of Elnon, in the *Life of Blessed Lebuin*: “For there are those,” he says, “who in their language are called *Edlingi*; there are those who are called *Frilingi*; there are those who are called *Lassi*, which in Latin means nobles, free men, and servile persons.”]

It had already been demonstrated by the experience of many events that, as it is written, the Almighty was against Gerald’s enemies. He seemed so unconquerable to them that the evil they plotted to inflict upon him rebounded instead upon themselves, as it is written: “He who digs a pit for his neighbor will himself first fall into it” (Prov. 26:27).

[Note: [Col. 0661D] William, plainly duke of Aquitaine. Byname “the Pious,” and also count of Auvergne, in Abbo, Book II of the *Siege of Paris* concerning Clermont. See Frodoard under the year 824 and what we said above.]

William, plainly, duke of Aquitaine, a good man and praiseworthy in many respects, when at last he had grown very powerful, acted not by threats but by entreaties, asking Gerald to withdraw from royal service and commend himself to him. But Gerald did not consent, in any way, to the favor of the count that had recently been usurped.

[Note: [Col. 0661D] His nephew, named Rainald. Saint Gerald says in his testament: “I give to that place, namely Aurillac, half of the court of Decatucerias, and half to my nephew Rainald,” and so forth. He was the brother of Benedict, viscount of Toulouse, as Odo himself shows in Book II, chapter 28, in these words: “You knew Count Raymond, the son, namely, of Odo. This man held Benedict, the nephew of Lord Gerald, namely viscount of Toulouse, after capturing him by treachery. But Rainald, his brother, giving himself as hostage, recovered his brother.”]

Nevertheless, he commended his nephew Rainald to William with a very large number of soldiers. Yet this same William was in no way angered with him, since he did not forget that his father Bernard had commended him, while still a young man, to Lord Gerald out of affection.

[Note: [Col. 0662C] Because his father was Bernard. Count and marquis of Nevers, as we have already noted. Perhaps he was also the marquis of Gothia, of whom Aymoinus speaks in Book V, chapter 37, or, as Nithard calls him in Book II, duke of Septimania. “For,” he says, speaking of the battle of Fontenay, “when Bernard, duke of Septimania, learned that the victory belonged to Charles, he sent his son William to him and ordered him to commend himself to Charles, if he was willing to grant him the honors he held in Burgundy.” I am led to believe this for two principal reasons. First, because this Nithard testifies that Bernard, William’s father, held honors in Burgundy. Martin of Poland also calls William the Pious, founder of Cluny, prince of Burgundy. Second, because John the Italian writes that William himself ruled Gothia together with Aquitaine, in Book I of the *Life of Saint Odo*: “For this reason he was dear to all, and especially to Count William, a most powerful man, who at that time held Aquitaine and Gothia by his own right.”]

And therefore he always honored Gerald with very great affection and reverence. Whenever business required it, William came to converse with him. Sometimes, delighted by the charm of this gracious man, William would insist by entreaty that he remain with him longer. Frequently, when he had gone some distance on official business, he would make Gerald travel farther with him.

### XXXIII

On one occasion, when circumstances required it, Gerald had spent a long time with him in a certain region to which William had gone in a hostile manner. Meanwhile all the provisions that had been carried in Gerald’s pack animals gradually ran out.

[Note: [Col. 0662D] In Gerald’s pack animals. Below, Book II, chapter 18: “A certain thief stole two of his pack animals.” Also in Charles the Bald’s decree concerning the liberties of the abbey of Saint-Denis: “Likewise concerning all carts and pack animals.” In French, *sommiers et chevaux de charge*.]

Moreover, the army, turning to plunder as though pursuing William’s enemies, was laying waste to the entire region. Because of this, the inhabitants, fearing for themselves, fled after exposing their property, and no one could be found who would sell provisions to Gerald’s attendants. Since they found nothing to buy, and were not permitted to touch anything from the plunder, Gerald endured considerable want on that expedition. For he would accept nothing from those who were plundering, lest by sharing with them he should become their partner in sin.

Yet he endured the company of his friend and did not abandon him in distress. Some laughed at this, because while others were reveling in the plunder, Gerald himself and his men were in need. Many, however, who possessed sounder understanding, called him blessed, groaning more deeply because they were not capable of imitating him. Finally, from this time and thereafter, he earned the title by which all commonly called him: that Gerald was “the Good.”

### XXXIV

He was held in such high esteem by the same William that William wished to give him his sister in marriage, with Ermengard, her mother, eagerly desiring this from the outset; she loved this man with pious affection.

[Note: [Col. 0662D] To give him his sister in marriage. Ademar of Chabanais—or, as others call him, of Angoulême, or rather of Limoges—speaking of Duke William: “When he desired to join his sister in marriage to Saint Gerald, he was wholly unable to do so, because Gerald always led a celibate life. Although he was continually urged to marry for the sake of children, Saint Gerald replied: ‘It is better, he said, to die without children than to leave wicked heirs.’”]

But Christ, the Son of the Virgin, had long sweetened for him the love of chastity. From the beginning of his life he embraced it so firmly that not even for the sake of so distinguished a marriage would he endure to be separated from it.

How greatly he recoiled from the obscenity of the flesh may be perceived from this: he never experienced a nocturnal emission without sorrow. Whenever that human misfortune occurred to him while sleeping, his consecrated chamberlain would separately bring him, in a suitable place, replacement garments always prepared for this purpose, together with tow and a vessel of water. When Gerald entered that place—for he did not allow himself to be seen naked—the servant immediately withdrew after closing the door.

Thus this guardian of inward purity fled bodily defilement: he washed away the pollution that had occurred to him in sleep not only with baths but also with tears. His conduct might perhaps seem foolish, but only to those whose muddy minds exhale the filth of vices—those who defile themselves either naturally or willingly, yet disdain to wash away their own impurities.

Gerald, however, knew what is written: “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Prov. 4:23). And again: “He who despises small things will gradually fall” (Ecclus. 19:1).

I would have you consider how highly it ought to be regarded that, amid worldly riches and placed at the summit of earthly rank, he preserved chastity. What could he have done more magnificently? Seek nothing further or more excellent. For, as blessed Martin testifies, nothing is comparable to virginity.

### XXXV

[Note: [Col. 0663D] Hence Count Ademar. Namely, of Poitiers, who was the son of Emenon, count of Angoulême. The author of the *History of the Counts of Angoulême* says: “Emenon left a young son named Ademar, who in the course of time became count of Poitiers.” He was made count by King Odo after the death of Ranulf. The same author shortly afterward says: “Ademar, the son of Emenon, having married Sancia, the sister of Bernard, was most intimate with Alduin and William, loving their honors as a brother. Called to the palace by King Odo, he was advanced as count of Poitiers.” Hence I suspect that the beginning of his quarrels with Saint Gerald arose from this. For the monk who wrote the *History of Aquitaine*, a fragment of which we possess in the Pithou edition, after recounting that Ademar himself had been advanced by King Odo to the county of Poitiers, immediately adds: “After returning from the palace, Gerald secretly took Ranulf’s son away from Poitiers and entrusted him to William, duke of Aquitaine and count of Auvergne, to be raised, since he was his kinsman.”]

Hence Count Ademar also pressed him intensely to submit himself to Ademar’s authority, but could extract this from him by no means. Indeed, Gerald would not consent to commend himself not only to Ademar, but even to Duke William, who at that time possessed greater abundance of power and resources.

I believe this man was contemplating Mordecai, who disdained to submit to the proud Haman and to render the honor bestowed by God upon kings.

But although Gerald appeared to have been overcome by William’s friendship and to enjoy peace, so that persecution might not be lacking to a man living in Christ, Satan incited the aforesaid Count Ademar against him. Although Ademar attacked him with many and various temptations, he could not bring him under his power.

On one occasion, Gerald happened to be spending the night in a meadow with a few soldiers. Ademar learned with certainty through a scout both where Gerald was and how many men were with him. Greatly rejoicing that he had found a favorable opportunity to seize him, he gathered a force of armed men and directed his line toward the place.

Gerald, meanwhile, was lying with all his men in one part of the meadow, as they say, asleep. But he who guards Israel was by no means sleeping in regard to the innocent man. Just as it is written of the prophet Jeremiah that the Lord hid him, so God concealed Gerald, so that although Ademar’s men had traversed the entire meadow in a circuit and had searched back through its middle, they could not find him.

Then Ademar, frustrated in his effort and grieving that his wickedness had been mocked, withdrew. But the just man, as it is written, “adds strength to those of clean hands,” praising the Lord.

### XXXVI

Likewise, the agents of Count Ademar occupied Gerald’s castle. When Gerald heard this, he took with him the few soldiers who happened to be present and hurried to the town.

Ademar, however, was preparing to follow the invaders with a strong force. But when they were not far away, and Ademar learned that Gerald had gone ahead to besiege the castle, he held back his swiftly advancing army, saying:

“We must investigate with what number of warriors Gerald is defended, since he has dared to precede us in besieging the town. He would not have plunged himself into this danger unless he were surrounded by the assistance of some peasants.”

Having said this, he sent swift horsemen to investigate. Night had now fallen. The scouts did not delay but hurried forward and carefully examined what Gerald’s camp was like.

As happens at night, they caught sight from a distance of some whitish stones in the uncertain light and took them to be the tents of those conducting the siege. Immediately bloodless and terrified, they returned to Ademar and confessed that they had seen an enormous army in the camp.

They had in fact returned by way of a certain noblewoman, to whom they reported this. Through her, what the scouts had seen also later became known to the man of God.

Thus Ademar, shaken by divine direction, returned to his own men with his army. On the following day, the invaders of the castle, learning that Ademar was not with them, sought peace from Gerald, asking that he permit them to withdraw without disgrace.

The man of God Gerald immediately granted this. But the soldiers, excited in spirit, were displeased that the enemy should not at least be stripped of their arms. Gerald’s mercy nevertheless prevailed, and he forced his men to stand still while allowing the enemies, fleeing through a narrow passage, an avenue of escape.

He even stationed two armed men of his own, who stood on either side and took care that no one dared to seize anything from the property of those departing.

Thus Gerald triumphed over the enemies he had expelled without bloodshed. Thus Christ, in his customary manner, ennobled his soldier more gloriously through adversity itself.

### XXXVII

That Count Godefred of Turenne—

[Note: [Col. 0664D] That Count Godefred of Turenne. Turenne, or Torenne, is a city in the territory of Limoges, concerning which Odo himself says below, chapter 40: “The present Adalbert bears witness to this, namely that monk who usually preaches the word of God to the people at Limoges. He was guarding the treasure of Saint Martial at Turenne.” As for this Count Godefred of Turenne, I do not remember anyone else speaking of him anywhere, unless perhaps he is that Gozfrid whose sons are mentioned by Aymoinus, Book V, chapter 36: “In the year 878, they seized the castle and honors of the son of Odo, once count; in that same year Immo, brother of the marquis Bernard, usurping the city of Évreux, carried out many depredations throughout those regions. Therefore, Louis came as far as Tours, and, at the urging of certain counselors and friends of Gozfrid, this Gozfrid came to him, bringing his sons with him, on the condition that they restore to King Louis the castle and honors they had seized, and afterward hold them by his grant. Then Gozfrid converted some of the Bretons to loyalty to the king.” However the matter may stand, today Turenne possesses only the rank of a viscountship and is commonly called *la vicomté de Turenne*.]

—on one occasion gathered a troop of soldiers and hurried forth to harass this man of God by war or to devastate what belonged to him. It happened, however, that he was wounded by the very sword with which he had armed himself, so severely that he could not complete the journey he had begun.

At last, understanding that he had been wounded because of the injury he intended against the man of God, he ceased from his wickedness, recognizing that the Mosaic saying aptly applied to him: “Let us flee from Israel, for the Lord fights for them against us” (Exod. 14:25).

### XXXVIII

Nevertheless, the brother of the aforesaid Ademar secretly entered the town that overlooks the monastery. But since he had already learned from the experiences of others that Gerald, with God fighting on his behalf, always prevailed over his enemies, he did not dare remain there. Still, after taking everything that could be carried away, he fled swiftly.

Not long afterward, however, when certain honorable men rebuked him for this crime, he returned everything and came to the man of God to ask pardon for his rashness.

By then Gerald enjoyed such reverence among all who knew him that whoever injured him was certain not to prosper, as though he had committed sacrilege.

Indeed, although the sons of darkness harassed the son of light both through the events we have mentioned and through many others, Gerald nevertheless never failed to protect the poor wherever he could. He forgave those who harmed him so readily that one might think he was more eager to forgive than they were to be reconciled.

His concern for the poor was always more demanding than his concern for himself; his soul felt compassion for them, and he could more easily neglect his own cause than theirs. Just as a very skilled physician who happens to lie wounded nevertheless strives to heal the wounds of others, so Gerald, though he himself was being injured, did not cease to protect those who lacked power.

### XXXIX

Gerald was so unconquerable by his enemies that the evil they plotted against him rebounded upon themselves. This is proved by some of the events already related and by the present example.

[Note: [Col. 0666D] The brother of Count Ademar. Adalelmus, or Adelelmus, who later broke into the castle of Aurillac. Saint Odo himself says in the following chapter: “Adelelmus, the brother of Count Ademar, in addition to the injury he had inflicted upon Lord Gerald when he had seized the castle of Aurillac, was still raging in his wickedness.” But he did not go unpunished. For, as Saint Odo says, “on the fourteenth day afterward he died so terribly that a violent whirlwind uncovered everything beneath which he lay.”]

Adalelmus, the brother of Count Ademar, in addition to the injury he had inflicted upon Lord Gerald when he had seized the castle of Aurillac—an injury which Gerald himself had willingly forgiven him—was still seething with wickedness and was persistently incited to injure the holy man.

Having therefore gathered a band of his agents, he attempted to break into the castle, where Lord Gerald happened at that time to be attending the solemn celebration of Mass. But those who were outside saw him from a distance rushing headlong and suddenly closed the gate.

When a commotion arose in the castle, with people shouting, the soldiers who were with their lord at Mass wanted to rush out. Gerald restrained them by his words and would not allow them to leave until the service of God had been completed.

Meanwhile Adalelmus’s agents went around the circuit of the castle and found only seven horses, which they drove away. Immediately, realizing that they had broken in to no purpose, they began to withdraw, overcome by shame.

It is said that the man of God, keeping the soldiers back, quickly climbed above the gate with a psalter in hand and sang something from the Psalms to the Lord—I do not know what.

But the tyrant who had caused the just man grief was not allowed to return rejoicing. I am about to tell something marvelous, almost incredible, were it not attested by a sufficiently trustworthy witness: nearly sixty of their horses died within a short space of time.

Adalelmus himself died on the fourteenth day afterward so terribly that a violent whirlwind uncovered everything beneath which he lay. The present Adalbert—Madalbertus—bears witness to this, namely that monk who usually preaches the word of God to the people at Limoges.

He was guarding the treasure of Saint Martial at Turenne, which had previously been transported there out of fear of the pagan people. When the men who had taken the horses saw what had happened, they sent Gerald’s horses back to the man of God.

### XL

Sometimes he was unwillingly compelled to exercise the powers of his authority and to bend the neck of wicked men by military force, as happened in the case of a certain exceedingly wicked man named Arlaldus.

He held a small town called Saint Serenus, from which, like an evening wolf going out, he made raids against the household of Lord Gerald.

Although Gerald spoke to him as a peacemaker speaks to one who hates peace, and even gave him certain small gifts and weapons suitable for soldiers, in order to soften his savage ways through benefits, that foolish and brutish man attributed this not to piety but to weakness and attacked the aforesaid household more boldly.

At last Gerald, considering that the madness of a foolish man could not be restrained without the lash, gathered a troop of soldiers and marched against the castle. With an astonishingly successful victory, he drove that beast from his chamber without killing anyone.

When Arlaldus stood before him in complete confusion, Gerald addressed him—not insultingly, but with as much reasoning as the situation required:

“You have now learned by experience that you cannot stand against me by your own strength. Therefore beware of raging; beware of practicing wickedness any longer, lest it rebound more grievously upon your own head.

“And I shall release you in such a way that I will not demand from you either a hostage or any oath. Nor will I permit anything to be taken from your property, even as compensation for the plunder you have been accustomed to inflict.”

Thus he released the man after restraining him, and from then on Arlaldus took sufficient care not to presume to injure Gerald’s household.

### XLI

Now, as we said above, Gerald’s adversaries ceased, terrified by divine fear. For although, in the manner of Job, he was “a brother of dragons and a companion of ostriches,” the beasts of the field were peaceful toward him.

His allod being described as *postomia* [uncertain], and his broad estates extending one after another in such a way that, as he traveled to and fro as far as the great mountain Greon, he could always stay in his own little houses, he nevertheless did not need to entrust any estate to a powerful man for protection—except one small property called Taladiciacus.

It was isolated among very wicked neighbors and stood far apart from his other possessions. His officials brought it about that, against his wish and inclination, he entrusted it to a certain Bernard for safekeeping.

Gerald endured this patiently, indeed with a certain cheerfulness, saying: “It has turned out well for me, that I may learn that it is better to trust in the Lord than in man.”
