I have wished to recall this for the reason that it may be evident from it that whenever God permitted something to be done for Gerald’s testing, Gerald attributed it not to sadness but to humility. It also demonstrates that this man lived by faith: he understood that all things are subject to divine providence and knew that nothing on earth happens without a reason, as it is written.

### XLII

Thus far we have arranged certain matters concerning his external deeds and ordinary conduct. From these it is very easy to see that this man was a worshiper of justice and, in accordance with the apostolic command, lived soberly, piously, and justly.

Since, therefore, he exercised himself blamelessly in the ordinances of the Lord, it ought not to seem incredible if the Lord himself magnifies his mercy toward him.

Accordingly, we urge those to whom everything that report now spreads about this holy man seems incredible to reconsider his case more cautiously and carefully. If it seems to obstruct belief that he was powerful in the world, one must consider that it is a greater and more praiseworthy virtue to have possessed material for pride and nevertheless to have restrained the summit of one’s power humbly.

Power comes only from God. According to Scripture, he does not cast away the powerful, since he himself is powerful. Therefore, although Gerald was exalted by worldly glory, it ought not to seem incredible if God glorifies him—the one whom God glorified in obedience to his commandments.

Were not David, Hezekiah, and Josiah both powerful and warlike kings? In our own times also, we have heard of certain men, such as Oswald, king of the English, whom God glorifies through signs; they had striven to glorify him by observing God’s commandments.

[Note: [Col. 0667C] King Oswald of the English. The pagan Penda, king of the Mercians, killed him in a fierce battle and, after killing him, tore his body apart with the greatest savagery. Bede calls him “most Christian and beloved of God.” Bede also reports that miracles became manifest where Oswald fell, and writes more about him in Book II of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, the final chapter; Book III, chapters 1, 6, and 9–13; and Book IV, chapter 14.]

In the individual ages of this life, divine condescension performs many things that may serve to stir up religion, which has been trampled down and forgotten. Hence the Apostle says that God leaves no time without a testimony to himself.

This sometimes happens even through ungrateful people. Thus, under Moses, many signs were performed among those of whom it is written that God was not well pleased with most of them.

And trustworthy and suitable witnesses assert certain things that are scarcely credible—for example, blessed Jerome tells of a certain former violent man and robber who, after being converted to Christ, caused the sun to stand still for a long time in order to complete his journey and afterward entered bodily among his disciples through a closed door.

If, then, God, who performed wonders with the fathers, deigns in our own times to work signs through a man who, like Noah in his days, was found to be just, in order to revive affection for religion that has been trampled down, this ought not to seem incredible.

Rather, he himself ought to be glorified: leaving no time without a testimony to his goodness, mindful of his promise, he does not cease to do good to his people.

As for the deeds of this same man after he had given himself entirely to the service of divine worship, we reserve what must be said for the following little book. Here, in God’s name, let us bring this account to an end.

## Preface to Book Two

[Col. 0667]

[Col. 0667D] Consideration and examination of the quality of Lord Gerald’s life can satisfy those who rashly dispute his merits. For, as though seated in some tribunal, they decide whether he ought to be a saint or not, although this belongs to divine judgment, through which signs are often performed even by the reprobate for the benefit of the good.

Let the testimony of miracles, then, satisfy them—miracles that Christ deigns to perform through Gerald, both while he lived and after his death.

But to those who boast, saying that Gerald was powerful and is a saint, we advise them not to applaud themselves for this. Unless they are poor in spirit and, like Gerald, season their power with religion, their house cannot be small.

Indeed, by comparison with Gerald they will be convicted of having been able to live justly in the same way but of having been unwilling to do so. As for gluttons and drunkards—to speak of certain professors of religion who invent excuses for themselves in their sins and habitually confess over their cups that Gerald ate meat and is a saint—their own profession plainly condemns them.

For many things are permitted to a layman that are not permitted to a monk. Adam was condemned not because the tree in paradise was evil, but because he presumed against a prohibition.

Gerald used what was lawfully permitted to his order, since he abstained from what was unlawful and ate together with the poor. He knew that wine was created for sobriety. Elijah, too, was fed with meat and was worthy to be taken into paradise.

Yet through desire, which incites some people, Esau lost his birthright for a dish of lentils. Gerald’s case, therefore, is one thing, and theirs another.

But those who rave that Gerald can be called neither martyr nor confessor should know that he can be called both—not only Gerald, but everyone who, by resisting vices, carries the cross, or by doing good glorifies God.

God confesses through deeds, as John testifies: “By this we know that we know him, if we keep his commandments” (1 John 2:3). He is also denied through deeds, as the Apostle says of certain people: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16).

Since, therefore, a confessor is called from confessing, while God is either denied or confessed through deeds, Gerald may all the more rightly be called a confessor the more justly he confessed God by his deeds.

As for those who, like Judaizers, seek signs, what will they say about John the Baptist, of whom no sign is recorded after his birth? Although miracles are certainly not wholly absent in Gerald’s case, we answer this one thing: because he did not place his hope in money and treasures, he performed, as it is written, “wonders in his life” (Ps. 70:7).

## Book Two

[Col. 0669]

### I

The athlete of the heavenly warfare, who had long struggled in the arena of worldly conduct, bravely defeated the battalions of vices. Then, holding the word of life in the midst of a crooked nation, he shone like a certain lamp.

And because it was necessary that he be tested in the hiding-place of a storm, the malignant enemy attempted by every stratagem within his power, both personally and through his agents, to extinguish this lamp.

But just as a flame stirred by blasts is accustomed to burn more strongly, so the spark of divine love, which had grown warm in Gerald’s breast from childhood, could not be extinguished by any shower of temptation. Rather, as he matured in age and gradually suppressed every kind of vice, he grew daily stronger in virtue than he had been.

Already he was arranging certain ascents in his heart; already, in accordance with the prophetic saying, he was rising above the heights of the earth. You could see the dawn of his holiness brightening into day; you could see the lily growing among thorns; and the nearer he came to maturity, the more widely he spread the open flowers of his virtues.

Thus, situated as though at the summit of all things, he had fixed the affection of his mind upon that heavenly blessedness. Since an inner light irradiated him through heavenly desire, he was able to distinguish the darkness of worldly desire.

Should I not call earthly desire darkness, by which lovers of the world are blinded so that they love vanity? Gerald had learned to separate the precious from the worthless, and he considered it utterly unworthy to lick the earth when he knew that he had been called to the banquet of the heavenly Lamb.

He grieved especially for those who, through friendship with the world, are made enemies of God. And after he had tasted how sweet the Lord is, he disdained to lick the stolen waters that are said to be sweeter.

Rather, he mourned for those who, in the words of blessed Job, run with a shout to gnaw at the root of the juniper—that is, an appetite filled with stings.

Thus he had trampled underfoot, with contempt of mind, the worldly power that was abundantly available to him. But, as is characteristic of the prudent, he considered how to turn everything to his own advantage: how he might arrange the things he possessed temporarily so that they would benefit him eternally.

### II

Therefore he summoned the venerable and plainly praiseworthy bishop Gausbert, together with certain other honorable men, and familiarly disclosed the thought that was moving his mind.

[Note: [Col. 0669D] Bishop Gausbert. I believe he was bishop of Rodez, and he had previously accompanied Gerald all the way to Rome, as our Saint Odo notes in Book I, chapter 29.]

For this Lord Gausbert was extremely dear to the man of God, and because of their shared holiness they offered each other mutual companionship.

Gerald explained that he was disgusted with the present life and desired the religious habit; that he wished to travel to Rome and assign his estates by testamentary right to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

When the matter had been discussed for a long time, Lord Gausbert, examining it according to a higher counsel, finally advised Gerald to remain outwardly, for the common welfare of the people of the province, in secular dress, but to dedicate his possessions to blessed Peter as he wished.

Gerald consented, lest by clinging too obstinately to his own decision he should seem to have acted disobediently.

Remembering, however, the Apostle’s statement that the Jew—whose name is interpreted as “confessing”—becomes greater and better in secret than in public, Gerald was tonsured in such a way that this remained hidden from human beings but was manifest to the heavenly Inspector.

With a razor he trimmed his beard and, passing the razor around his head in the manner of a crown, also cut away part of his hair. To conceal this completely, he bound certain chamberlains who knew of it by an oath, so that as long as he lived they would reveal it in no way.

In this deed of his he seems to have secured a double reward. On the one hand, burning with love of the Lord, he offered God the work of conversion; on the other, filled with love for his neighbors, he compelled himself, for their benefit, to remain unwillingly in a form of life he did not desire.

For what kind of way of life could he have offered to God more pleasing than this—one in which he neither neglected the common consolation nor diminished anything of the perfection of his own way of life? This way of life was evidently more precious in proportion as it was more useful to many and known only to God.

He it was who, as it is written, directed Gerald’s purpose, so that although he caused him to enter into Leah’s marriage, he did not deprive him of Rachel’s desired embraces.

### III

To conceal his tonsure, he readily found a means. He cut his beard as though it were a burden, and, since the hair had fallen away from the back of his head, he concealed the tonsure on his crown, which he continually covered by wearing a tiara. Over linen garments he wore leather garments, because clerics and laymen alike commonly used this kind of clothing. He never, however, had two leather garments at the same time. Whenever it was necessary for a new one to be brought, he immediately ordered the old one to be given away.

When he rode, a sword was always carried before him by someone, although he himself never touched it with his own hand. Indeed, long before this he had ordered a golden cross to be fashioned from the equipment of the belt or girdle. He never sat upon a caparisoned horse. In these and similar matters it was sufficiently evident how greatly, devoted as he was to moderation, he despised the accumulation of his power.

[Col. 0671B] **Note on “fur garments.”** The use of furs or fur garments was formerly common to clerics and laymen, indeed especially to monks. The anonymous author of the *Life of Saint Hugh, Abbot of Cluny*: “He hastened to take off his fur garment and clothed the sick man.” The *Book of the Statutes and Customs of the Abbey of La Règle*, folio 3: “Likewise all the furriers must provide the Prior with a good fur garment each year.” And the statutes of the Cluniac congregation, issued by Peter the Venerable, chapter 17: “It has been decreed that none of the brothers of Cluny shall clothe himself in foreign skins, whether cat skins or other skins which he was accustomed to use, nor indeed in any skins whatsoever except ram, lamb, and goat skins.” Peter the Venerable should likewise be consulted, letter 28 of book I, where he defends among the Cluniacs against the Cistercians this use of fur garments and diverse skins.

### IV

After he had devoted himself entirely to divine worship, so that he might also consecrate his possessions to the Lord, he went to Rome and, having solemnly made his will, assigned to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the distinguished estate of Aureliacum, together with such extensive appurtenances that they could suffice for every support of the monks whom he had determined to gather there.

[Col. 0671B] **Note on Aureliacum, belonging to Saint Peter.** The monastery of Aureliacum, founded and built by Saint Gerald, is attested above all by the author of the *Life of Saint Genulfus*, chapter 17: “Saint Gerald also, a man of great holiness and distinguished nobility, flourished in those times; he built the monastery of Aureliacum.” And a fragment of the *History of the Franks*: “Saint Gerald founded the monastery of Aureliacum.” He founded it in honor of the apostle Saint Peter and Saint Clement, as can be learned even from Odo alone. Hence the writer of the Limoges Chronicle, and the compiler of the deeds of the abbots of Saint Martial, called it the monastery of Saint Peter; so too, shortly afterward, did Gerbert, himself a monk of Aureliacum, in letter 61 to Gerald, abbot of Aureliacum, and Ademar, who had been a monk at Limoges, called it the church of Saint Gerald of Aureliacum.

[Col. 0671C] **Testament made solemnly.** The testament of Saint Gerald concerning the endowment of this monastery founded by him deserves to be inserted here, both because it is brief and because the very learned Jean Savaron, president and glory of the Auvergne, courteously and generously supplied it to us so that it might be made public. It runs as follows.

**The Testament of Saint Gerald**

“While the end of the world draws near and ruins grow more frequent, certain signs are now clearly manifested, because when these things arrive the world will truly be judged. And if we contribute anything from our possessions to the places of the saints, we trust that the Lord will be our recompense, who says: ‘Give alms.’ Therefore I, Gerald, considering the precarious condition of human life and fearing the final, trembling day of judgment, for this reason grant to the places of the saints and to those who serve them, and for the substance of the poor, and to my relatives and faithful men—that is, first of all, to the place which I have granted for God and Saint Peter, called the monastery of Aurelhacus—what the monks themselves possess from the present day: half of the estate, and the castle itself with the lord’s farm, and two holdings at Grandemont, and the holding at Fabricas, where Rainald was seen to dwell permanently; he shall hold it while he lives, and after his death it shall remain with the community of Aurelhacus.

“Let Rainald and the monks divide the half-estate equally, and after his death let everything pass to Aurelhacum. I give half of the estate of Decatucerias to the place named above, and half to my nephew Rainald while he lives; afterward it shall remain with Aurelhacum. Let the monks have my village at Ermos. At Fraxininas let the monks have half my village and Rainald the other half; after his death it shall remain with Aurelhacum. Let Rainald have Curtogillo while he lives; afterward it shall remain with Aurelhacum. Let the monks possess the church at Glaurgo. Let Rainald hold my estate at Roacina while he lives; after his death it shall remain with Aurelhacum.

“Of what I am seen to possess at Goliacum, let the monks have half and Rainald half while he lives; after his death it shall remain with Aurelhacum. I give Boresia to Malfred [Amalfred], son of Galamon, while he lives; after his death it shall remain with Aurelhacum. Likewise, let him hold the holding at Marconi, which I bought from Adoaldus, while he lives; after his death it shall remain with Aurelhacum.

“Whatever belongs or seems to belong to the aforesaid estates, whether already acquired or still to be acquired, together with the dependents living there and their relatives dwelling outside these aforesaid estates, and with all their appurtenances, additions, and adjoining properties, I give in full to Saint Peter and Saint Clement and to those who serve them, as their own property, to have, hold, and receive its usufruct; with this condition: while I live, I shall possess it, and after our death my nephew Rainald shall have authority concerning the aforesaid monastery to appoint and remove abbots, to investigate the monks’ causes before kings, counts, and their representatives, and in various regions to hold the monks and their households under his protection.

“Let this grant made by me remain firm and stable for all time, with every security, strengthened by the hands of men and confirmed by stipulation. This grant was made in the month of September, on Thursday, in the seventeenth year after King Charles assumed the empire. Signed: Gerald, who requested that this grant be written or confirmed; signed: Fataldus; signed: Wigo; signed: Vicarnius; signed: Bladinus; signed: Tugirannus.”

[Col. 0673C] That this was not the original testament of the foundation of the monastery of Aureliacum, but rather a simple later addition to its first endowment, is made entirely clear both by the beginning and end of the testament itself and by the fact that it makes no mention of the annual tribute assigned to the shrine of blessed Peter, as Odo goes on to relate.

He also assigned a tribute to be paid annually to the shrine of blessed Peter.

[Col. 0673D] **Note on the tribute assigned to be paid annually to the shrine of blessed Peter.** William the Pious likewise ordained that his Cluniacs should pay a tribute of ten solidi to the Apostolic See every fifth year, as a fee for protection. “Every five years,” he says in the testament of foundation, “let the aforesaid monks pay ten solidi at Rome, at the thresholds of the apostles, for supplying their lamps, and let them have the protection of those apostles and the Roman pontiff as their defender.” Likewise the founder of the monastery of Vendôme wished twelve solidi of the local coinage to be paid yearly to blessed Peter, as Geoffrey of Vendôme, himself also abbot, explains in letter 9 of book I: “In the time of our predecessors the Roman Church could scarcely obtain from there even the due tribute, namely twelve solidi a year.” On this matter Jacques Sirmond made several very learned observations. But it should not be omitted that our blessed Odo himself writes below, in chapter 17, concerning the tribute customarily brought to Rome by this Saint Gerald every second year: “He had imposed this rule upon himself: every second year he would always return to the tomb of the apostles and, with ten solidi hanging from his own neck, carry them to his Lord as a humble servant, as though they were tribute.”

Thus, as he had conceived in his fervent heart, he set out according to agreement and, with God’s favor, accomplished what he had resolved. On his return he ordered stonecutters and masons to be gathered from everywhere, and commanded that the foundation be opened for the construction of a church in honor of blessed Peter.

[Col. 0674D] **Note on “masons.”** *Mactiones*: a French word, which we still retain today as *maçons*.

But Satan, envious of every good work, somehow deceived the foremen’s judgment. They laid the foundation insecurely, and when a great sum of money had already been spent and the walls had nevertheless been raised high, the joints of the masonry suddenly came apart and collapsed. Yet this man was not excessively saddened by it. For, as it is written, “Whatever happens to him does not grieve the righteous” (Proverbs 12:21). He truly trusted that, although the work had been delayed on this occasion, the reward for the lost labor would not perish. Seeing that God had permitted this loss by his judgment, he nevertheless recognized that it is almost customary in every undertaking that whatever is offered to God more acceptably is accomplished with greater difficulty. Certainly, in the natural order, what grows more quickly turns more quickly toward decline; but what is achieved with difficulty endures longer.

[Col. 0673C]

### V

The season of Lent had arrived, when the gentler weather was already favorable for building. One morning, after completing his customary prayers, Gerald went out from the town overlooking that place. After proceeding a little way, he began, looking around in every direction, to consider where the church building could most suitably be founded. At last he chose a place already foreknown by divine providence.

He therefore ordered the craftsmen to return, to rekindle their zeal, to reopen the interrupted work, and to apply themselves skillfully to the undertaking begun: to build a church of suitable size and vaulted design, like the one his father had formerly built in honor of Saint Clement. For, as we said earlier, his father too was religious, being descended from a family of religious people.

### VI

While he continued the construction of the building, he was always turning over in his mind how he might find monks who were well behaved and able to inhabit the place under a regular rule. But because the scarcity of suitable men made the search difficult, he became anxious and did not know what he should do.

[Col. 0674D] **Note on “to the monastery of Vabres.”** This monastery belonged to the Order of Saint Benedict and depended upon the monastery of Saint Victor at Marseille. John XXII eventually made it a bishopric, and Gregory XIII permitted its monks to exchange their customary habit for canonical dress. Vabres is the town of the Rutheni, called *Vabrense castrum* by Gregory of Tours in book IX, chapter 9 of the *History of the Franks*, and *Vabrium* by Bernard Gui in his account of John XXII: “Likewise, in the bishopric of Rodez he established another bishopric and placed its seat in the abbey of Vabres, erecting it as a new city.” It is commonly called Vabres.

Then he sent several noble boys to the monastery of Vabres. At that time the fervor of regular observance was growing, so that the boys might be instructed there within the brotherhood under the rule. Of these, one still survives, who relates what we are describing as having seen it with that blessed Gerald, and writes it down in his own hand.

But when the same boys were ordered to return, because teachers were lacking, they soon relaxed with childish softness and neglected the strictness of discipline. Thus it happened that the matter did not come to completion. Nevertheless, compelled by necessity, he placed one of them over the others. But when that man lived dissolutely, the man of God was deeply distressed, because he could neither correct him nor find another whom he could put in his place.

When, therefore, he saw either that man or his companions proceeding along the path of corrupt living, he would say, sighing deeply, the words of David: “O Lord, scatter the counsel of Ahithophel” (2 Samuel 15:34).

### VII

Sometimes, however, he broke into a voice of lamentation over men whom he saw inclined toward evil. Weary and groaning, as though making complaint, he lamented that those same men were perishing for love of the world, that devotion was failing, that iniquity was flooding everything, and that almost everyone had already lost innocence from the heart and truth from the mouth.

He did not wish to involve himself in their quarrels, but prayed that almighty God might pacify everyone. He ordered the solemn celebration of Masses and frequently repeated the words of Hezekiah: “O Lord, let there be only peace and truth in my days” (Isaiah 39:8); and also: “O how the holy man has vanished! O how the truths have been diminished among the children of men!” (Psalm 11:2).

### VIII

He hoped that the desire with which he burned for heavenly things and despised earthly things could be consoled if he found companions who shared that same desire. Therefore his mind burned day and night, and he could not forget his longing to gather monks, often discussing the matter with his household and close associates.

He was driven toward this with such feeling that he sometimes exclaimed: “If only someone would give me the opportunity to find religious monks under such a covenant! I would give them everything I possess, and afterward spend this life begging! I would not delay at all in making such an agreement.”

When his household members once replied to him, saying, “Are there not many monks to be found in these regions, from whom you could gather a community according to your desire?” he gave this very forceful answer:

“If they are perfect monks, they are made like the blessed angels. But if they return to worldly desire, they are rightly compared, through their apostasy, with the apostate angels who did not keep their own dwelling. I tell you plainly that a good layman is incomparably better than a monk who transgresses the rule he has undertaken.”

When they added, “Why, then, are you accustomed to bestow so many benefits, not only upon neighboring monks but also upon those from distant monasteries?” he replied, with his customary humility, making light of his own deeds:

“I do nothing. Yet if, as you say, I were doing something, I am certain that the true promiser is the one who promised to reward a cup of cold water given in his name. Let them themselves see what sort of people they are in God’s eyes. Certainly it is true that whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward.”

From these and similar words of his it is evident that he despised the pleasures of the present life, burned with heavenly desire, and wished to abandon all his possessions if there had not been a lack of people to whom he could reasonably entrust them.

The common proverb is true: the will is counted as the deed. Hence the one who hates his brother is said to be a murderer. And the evangelist John drank the cup of suffering, although he died in peace. If, therefore, the will is counted as the deed, Gerald is certainly not deprived of the reward of those who renounce the world.

### IX

He was therefore held unwillingly in the world. Although he lacked companions with whom he might renounce that same world, he nevertheless occupied himself entirely with God’s work in a remarkable manner.

He was so intent upon hearing readings and, in turn, upon prayers—now with others, now alone—that it is astonishing how he could have maintained such zeal for these practices or wished always to complete so extensive a portion of the Psalms, especially since he sometimes attended to other responsibilities. He was not obstinate, so as to occupy himself excessively with necessary business; but after giving these matters a little attention as circumstances required, he quickly returned to the sweetness of psalmody that he had tasted.

It is impossible to report adequately how reverently he stood in church. You would have thought that he was contemplating something divine and, with an astonished countenance, imitating the prophetic saying: “The Lord lives, before whom I stand” (1 Kings 17:1). To make this clear by an example, the feast day of the Lord’s Ascension arrived, and he hurried to the monastery of Sollemniacum to celebrate it, as the solemn law requires.

[Col. 0675D] **Note on the monastery of Sollemniacum.** It was in the district of Limoges. Its founder was Saint Eligius, formerly the goldsmith of King Dagobert and afterward bishop of Noyon. As Aimoinus writes in book IV, chapter 41: “While he was living a life pleasing to God and men at the palace, he had asked King Dagobert to grant him a village situated in the district of Limoges, called Sollemniacum, in which he also built a monastery and established a community of monks serving God.” After it was ravaged by the hostile incursions of pagans throughout Aquitaine, Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne, restored it, or rather rebuilt it from its foundations, as an anonymous but contemporary author who wrote his life records.

He could not tolerate the office of so great a feast being performed without festivity, or, as is the custom of many, being shortened by abbreviating the celebration. When the monks had come there, they prepared for him, as was fitting for so great and distinguished a person, a seat and a reclining place covered with ornamental fabrics. When he turned aside to it after making the rounds of the oratories, the brothers began to celebrate the office, extending it at length according to custom.

But the elder, until it was completed, stood so absorbed in contemplation that he neither sat down nor reclined even slightly upon the footstool, displaying through the immobility of his body the devotion and steadfastness of his mind.

But we are not like this. We present divine praises with a pompous voice rather than with a simple heart, as though praying to the face of God while he remains hidden. Although the understanding of the mind ought to correspond to the voice, we make the voice run after the mind’s frivolity. Gerald, however, recalling the apostolic saying, “We are manifest to God” (2 Corinthians 5:11), conducted himself as though he were in the presence of a judge who sees everything.

### X

And so, in order that divine favor might glorify him before men—because he glorified God before the disobedient by carrying out his commandments—although, with the time of Antichrist already approaching, the miracles of the saints ought to cease, nevertheless, mindful of his promise, which says, “Those who glorify me, I will glorify” (1 Samuel 2:30), God deigned to glorify this servant of his through a certain grace of healing.

The manner of healing was this: although, out of humility, he refused to lay his hand upon the sick, he nevertheless often helped them while absent and unwilling. The sick used to steal water in which he had been accustomed to wash his hands, and many were healed.

Although it may make the matter seem more credible to recall particular persons, one such case may be mentioned. A peasant near the monastery of Sollemniacum had a blind son. Groaning for a long time because blindness and poverty oppressed him alike, the man was warned in a vision to go to Lord Gerald and pour upon his son’s eyes the water with which Gerald’s hands had been washed.

The man believed the vision and, when he came, told the elder what he had dreamed. When the elder heard this, he was shaken in mind and trembled. Refusing to presume upon such a thing, he said that it had been an illusion which wished both to deceive the man and to lead him into attempting what was not permitted; the man was mistaken in asking for such things on the basis of a vain hope.

The father, distressed by his son’s blindness, groaned. Understanding that the man of God would not consent on account of his humility, he pretended to leave and obtained water from one of the servants. Returning home, he washed his son’s extinguished eyes while invoking the name of Christ, and the boy received his sight.

Another deed followed this one.

### XI

A little boy at Aureliacum was lame. He had been entrusted to a certain smith so that he might learn a craft by which he could earn a living. Meanwhile, the boy was warned in a dream that he should likewise seek the water. But the smith, knowing that the man of God was exceedingly strict in this matter, did not dare to ask for the water openly; instead, he secretly obtained it through servants.

When he sprinkled the boy’s useless limbs with that water, divine power immediately restored them to their proper function. As the event gradually became known through rumor, it reached the elder’s ears.

Struck by the novelty of the matter, he said that this had happened not through his own merit but through the faith of those who had given the water to the smith. This was carefully concealed from him. Since he could not discover who had given it, he was moved to vehement threats that no one should ever again presume to do such a thing. He declared that if a servant did it, he would be mutilated, but if a free man did it, that man would no longer be his.

For he feared nothing so much as praise. Although he was generous toward his enemies, he seemed harsh toward those who praised him.

### XII

At Postomium, a distinguished allod belonging to him in his own right, a blind woman received her sight from the water in which he had washed his hands. This became widely known, but it was carefully concealed from him, especially because of one of the servants who had given the water to the woman.

They could not disregard the danger to their lives which he had earlier threatened in this matter, knowing that the servant would not escape punishment if he discovered who had supplied the water.

[Col. 0677D] **Note on Postomium, an allod belonging to him in his own right.** He called it Postomia above, in the final chapter of book I: “Since his allod was Postomia, and his estates succeeded one another in such a way that, as he went and returned, he could always lodge in his own little chapels as far as the great mountain Creon.”

### XIII

Likewise, he was staying in the chapel situated near the village called Crucicula. Another woman, who belonged to the number of his female servants, was likewise given sight by the water in which his hands had been washed.

When he learned of this, he diligently investigated the man who had given the water, named Rabboldus. He found him and immediately dismissed him.

After some time, a certain nobleman named Ebbo approached the elder and argued with him, saying that perhaps he was acting against God’s will by neglecting, under the pretext of an unreasonable humility, a grace granted from heaven and abandoning in distress those whom he could benefit.

It would be better, Ebbo said, to employ the grace which had perhaps been given to Gerald for the sake of such people and to grant what necessity demanded to those who asked. There was no need to fear pride, since Gerald was not desirous of praise; nor presumption, since those who sought help recalled that they had been divinely admonished to do so. This was especially true since experience had already proved that the benefit of healing sought from him had taken effect, although he himself was unaware of it, more than once.

Ebbo pursued this argument reasonably. Gerald, however, sighed and wept, saying that he feared it was rather a demonic deception seeking to mislead them under this pretext, and that, if he had ever done anything good, it might be constructing a way to deprive him of the reward for that good.

At last, overcome either by prayers or by reason, he received back the man he had dismissed and ordered twelve coins to be given to the woman.

### XIV

Knowing that the state of the mind is better preserved by sometimes turning to reading after prayer, he had divine words read aloud in his presence, as we have said above. Hence he adopted the practice of having something read during his meal, and he did not allow the reader to omit it even when guests were present.

As an act of accommodation, he sometimes ordered the reader to stop and asked those who happened to know to explain the meaning of the reading. When those whom he questioned customarily begged him to speak instead, he finally answered clearly and intelligently, as a learned man would, yet in such a way that he did not embarrass the clerics.

After the guests had gone away to their own homes following the meal, those passages were likewise read aloud in his presence, especially the words that had remained after the readings recited in church.

When he was attending to the reading, no one readily dared to interrupt him for any reason. For, in accordance with the saying of Job, he was terrifying to his subjects, and the light of his countenance did not fall to the ground.

There is much to recall about his speech and conversation. In what he said with a cheerful spirit, he was extremely pleasant. But what he uttered in rebuke seemed like goads, so that they were almost more feared than words. In giving anything, he was very deliberate. But once he had given it, he did not take it back.

If he heard that a priest had a bad reputation, he nevertheless did not despise the office of Mass when performed by him, because he knew that the sacred mystery could not be made worse by a sinful man.

Although in judging the deeds of others he was either sharp or gentle according to the merits of the cases, he nevertheless disparaged his own works. These he commended all the more dearly to the heavenly observer because he himself valued them so little.

### XV

Since heavenly desire, so to speak, consumed him ever more abundantly, his mouth was so filled from the abundance of his heart that almost always the law of the Lord resounded from it.

He had marked down certain sacred words which seemed suitable to bodily activities. For example, in the morning, before he began to speak, he would say: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” (Psalm 141:3), along with other such passages which he adapted to each occasion: when he awoke, when he rose from bed, when he put on his leggings, when he took up his clothing or girdle, or when he began a journey or anything else. Thus he seemed, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying, to do everything in the name of the Lord.

Sometimes, when he happened to be sitting with a few people or alone, he would remain silent for a long time, meditating on something. Then, covered with tears, he would draw a sigh from the depths of his heart, shaking his whole body, so that anyone could easily perceive that his mind was hanging upon something else and that he found no consolation in the present.

Such was his conversation and such his silence that his mouth proclaimed the praise of the Lord, while the meditation of his heart was in his presence.

### XVI

His people knew that he desired with all his strength to wear the religious habit. But he was prudent and considered that those who profess a lofty calling, when corrupted by love of the world, fall more grievously from a height. He therefore judged it better to remain as he was than to attempt so arduous a matter without proven collaborators.

If, therefore, one considers his intention, he preserved the faith of monastic profession before Christ through his devotion. It is a very eminent praise to serve the purpose of religion while wearing secular dress; conversely, it is exceedingly disgraceful to seek the world under the clothing of that same religion.

Since, as we have said, this man had no brothers with whom he could live well and joyfully in community, he bore the habitation of this life with weariness. Just as Noah’s dove, finding no place outside where it could rest, returned to the ark and to Noah himself, so this man, amid the waves of the present world, returned to the secret place of his heart and rested in the delight of Christ.

He had not clung, like that raven, to the corpse of bodily pleasure. His soul refused to be consoled by the glory of the present life; rather, remembering his God, he rejoiced, and returning to the secret place of his heart as to an ark, he exulted under his tongue.

He did not allow iniquity to remain longer in his heart, fearing that perhaps the Lord would refuse to hear him. Rather, he always tried to recognize before his eyes the sins without which human nature cannot exist—sins that seemed light to us but heavy to him—so that he did not doubt that he would mercifully receive from God the forgiveness of the wickedness in his heart.

For this reason his king and Lord mercifully directed his way in his sight and graciously attended to the prayer of his voice.

He took such care always to lodge near a church that, throughout the course of many years, he spent no night anywhere except in an oratory, with one exception, when he was traveling on the feast of the Holy Innocents. A large number of clerics always accompanied him, with whom he continually labored in divine service.

All the necessary ecclesiastical equipment was likewise carried with him. With it, divine service was performed with great care and reverence, especially on feast days. At night he usually arrived in the oratory long before everyone else. When the office was finished, he generally remained there alone. At that time he tasted the sweetness within all the more pleasantly because it was more secret.

Sometimes he went out cheerful and lively, either to his bed according to the time or to his attendants. He had established such a manner of life for himself that every person of sound judgment would wonder that so much heavenly grace had converged in him.

He also maintained this manner of conduct in his external life, so that his servants knew how he would conduct himself during each season of the year.

### XVII

He had made it his custom to visit Rome frequently.

[Col. 0679D] **Note on “to visit Rome frequently.”** The kings of the Franks themselves, and all the leading men in Francia, formerly used to hasten to Rome for pilgrimage and prayer. The author of the *Life of Louis the Pious*: “He conceived a desire to see Rome, once mistress of the world, and to approach the thresholds of the prince of the apostles and the teacher of the nations, and to commend himself and his offspring to him. By God’s favor this matter turned out according to his wish.” Rigord, in his account of Philip Augustus: “After visiting the thresholds of the apostles, he passed through Rome and returned to Francia.” And the anonymous author who wrote the deeds of Philip III: “He came to Rome. There, after reverently honoring the apostles, he went to the city of Viterbo.”

It is said that he went there very often. Our informants, however, are certain of seven visits. Since it is a power of human nature always to wish to behold light, this man, being spiritual, desired spiritually to gaze upon the two luminaries of the world, namely Peter and Paul.

Since he did not yet wish to look upon them themselves, he often visited their tombs and churches and entrusted his possessions to that same blessed Peter. He had imposed this rule upon himself: every second year he would return to their tomb, and, with ten solidi hanging from his own neck, would carry them to his Lord as a humble servant, as though they were tribute.

But who could adequately describe how devoutly he fulfilled this? He was so generous toward the needy that his charity almost never passed by any poor person, of whom great crowds abounded there. He confidently believed that he would himself be heard if he heard the poor crying out.

He also gave much to the monasteries adjoining the road. The fame of such generosity had resounded everywhere and far and wide. Consequently, monks, pilgrims, and needy people, who diligently sought his hospitality at the time when pilgrims to Rome customarily travelled, carefully inquired whether Count Gerald was coming or when he would come.

The Marruci themselves, inhabitants of the frozen Alps, considered nothing more profitable than carrying Gerald’s baggage across the ridges of Mount Joux.

[Col. 0680D] **Note on the ridges of Mount Joux.** Peter Damian, in the *Life of Saint Odilo*, chapter 15, called them the steep slopes of Mount Joux. We commonly call it *Mont Joux*.

### XVIII

On one occasion he was traveling along this route. When he had come to a city called Asti, a thief stole two of his pack animals.

When he came to a certain stream, he could not force them to cross, until he was seized by Gerald’s men. After the pack animals had been recovered, he did the thief no harm.

### XIX

Once, while making that journey, he took with him a certain monk named Aribert, a man of great abstinence. For this was a congenial companionship to him: whenever he encountered someone devoted to the religious life, he always found especial delight in him. It happened on one occasion that there was no relish with which that abstinent man could eat his bread. The elder carefully asked whether the servants had prepared his customary food. When they replied [Col. 0681B] that they had nothing except bread, he grew anxious and said: “Oh, what has happened to us today? We all have a full meal, while this servant of God will be left weakened by hunger.”

It was, however, a day on which abstinence had been relaxed. The time for washing the hands had already come, and Samuel, who relates this incident as an eyewitness, ran to fetch water. By chance he found a little fish lying on the bank and still twitching; it had leapt out of the water before his very eyes. He seized it and joyfully ran to the elder, saying: “Behold, God is sending you this fish, for I found it lying beside the water.”

“Thanks be to God,” the elder replied. Meanwhile, while it was being cooked, he entered his tent, bent his knees, and prayed for some time with tears. For it was always his custom to place nothing before Christ, but rather to give Him devout thanks for each individual circumstance that befell him. When he rose from prayer, he appeared exceedingly joyful to everyone.

Then, when they had sat down to table, the abstinent monk ate until he had had enough. Since some of the fish still remained, the elder urged him, saying: “Why, brother, do you delay eating this little fish, when you will have nothing else?” When the monk declared that he was already satisfied, the elder tasted it to see whether it might be good. Finding it to be of excellent flavor, he himself ate as much as sufficed, and gave pieces to all who were present as a blessing. Everyone gave thanks to God, recognizing a divine gift both in the fish that had been found and in the fact that it had remained in abundance. It had been half a foot in length.

### XX

Likewise, when he was travelling to Rome and had reached the Tuscan city called Lucca, a certain woman came forward to meet him, saying that she had been admonished in a vision to have him restore sight to her son. When he heard this, he reproached the woman and, spurring the mule on which he was riding, hurried away.

The woman, however, asked everyone she could how she might obtain the favor she hoped for from the man of God. Eventually one of the servants told the woman that miracles had already been performed through the water in which the elder had washed his hands. But the elder, becoming concerned for the woman, whenever he washed his hands immediately caused the water to be poured out upon the ground before him. The woman nevertheless followed him continually, until he no longer took care to have the water poured out.

At last, without his knowledge, the woman obtained some of it, washed her blind son’s eyes, and he immediately recovered his sight. When the man of God had returned from the city, the woman brought the seeing boy before him. While everyone magnified the event, he went on silently and in tears; and while he was within hearing, no one dared say anything about this or any similar matter.

### XXI

I shall relate something marvelous, and perhaps incredible. Yet I believe it because two witnesses affirm it; they report that this same man of God, returning from Italy by the road that leads from the city of Turin to Lyons, had already crossed the Alps and was passing through certain places said to be exceedingly lacking in water, as the necessities of the journey required. It happened that their wine, too, ran out in the wineskins. Since that region had long been abandoned by the Saracens, when water was lacking and no wine could be found, they began to suffer intensely from thirst.

They tried to traverse that stretch of road as quickly as possible, if this could be done, but the foot travelers and the pack animals were failing. Therefore it became necessary for the elder to order them to delay for a little while. The sorrowful men lay down upon the grass, while the wandering pack animals, driven by thirst, searched the pastures here and there.

Then one of the clerics went to bring the pack animals back for loading, since he did not wish the halt to be prolonged. The cleric found a little hollow full of liquid. Amazed, and wishing to discover what it was, he bent down; meanwhile the liquid gave off the aroma of wine. He then hurried back joyfully to the elder and announced that he had found something resembling wine.

“What are you talking about?” the elder said. “Would that you had found water! For where would wine come from here?”

The cleric took a small vessel, drew some of the aforesaid liquid, and brought it before him. What had been brought possessed both the color and the taste of wine. Then the elder ordered the chaplains to take the cross and the little reliquary chests, and to perform an exorcism with blessed water over the hollow containing the liquid. Afterward, in the name of Christ, he ordered them to determine by tasting what it was.

When they found that it was wine, the man of God, filled with immense wonder and joy, gave thanks to God with all of them. Before drinking himself, he ordered that it be given to everyone, though he did not permit any of it to be carried away in flasks [Note: [Col. 0681D] *In flasconibus.* Hence *flacons*. An old French word.]. This account is given according to the testimony of those who assert that they saw it. Yet the things now taking place at his tomb, whether this or that, persuade us to believe what is heard about him.

### XXII

The holy man frequently travelled this road. For he no longer wished to visit royal palaces, the residences of marquises, or, indeed, the courts of princes; rather, as stated above, he eagerly desired to visit more often the consuls of heaven, Peter and Paul. Nevertheless, he also visited other places of the saints [Note: [Col. 0681D] The tomb of the most holy lord Martin. There were also frequent gatherings and acts of devotion by people of every rank and dignity, both ancient and contemporary, at the memory or tomb of Saint Martin, bishop of Tours. The author of the *Life of Charlemagne*: “From there he proceeded along the shore of the Ocean to the city of Rouen, crossed the river Seine, and went to Tours to Saint Martin for the sake of prayer.” Frodoard, under the year 938: “Rudolph returns to Tours to Saint Martin for the sake of prayer.” The *Deeds of the Counts of Anjou*, in the section on Fulk the Good: “It happened once that the king of France was present at the city of Tours with a company of noblemen on the eve of the summer feast of Saint Martin. Among the other magistrates and distinguished men, the aforementioned count was also present, radiant like a star, handsome in appearance, and tall in stature.” And Hebernus, abbot of Marmoutier, in the *Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 11: “Boniface, marquis of Montferrat, had acquired the pious custom of going every year on the feast day of blessed Martin to his holy tomb. Neither the length and hardship of the journey, nor the ambushes of enemies lying between, nor the frequent outbreak of wars, nor finally any other business could prevent him from hastening to obtain the intercession of Saint Martin.”], namely the tomb of the most holy lord Martin [Note: [Col. 0684D] Also Saint Martial, the first bishop of the people of Limoges, about whom we have written elsewhere], and likewise that of blessed Martial, with eager devotion.

I believe that in spirit he contemplated how those blessed hosts rejoice in the court of the heavenly Capitol. Since he was shortly to be joined to them, he was already in some measure tasting the joy of his Lord.

### XXIII

Beyond Sutrium there is a marshy field, beside a settlement called Saint Martin’s, where the Roman pilgrims customarily make camp. When the servants had set up the tents there, the elder happened to be standing apart. A certain man had himself brought near him and, humbly entreating him, asked that he deign to give him water touched by his hands.

The elder ordered him to remain there and keep silent. Then he entered the tent and prayed for a while before the holy relics [Col. 0683B]. Each of the servants was intent upon the task that had to be performed. When they were otherwise occupied, and he saw that the act could be carried out secretly, he summoned someone to bring the man to him without being noticed.

He then carefully washed his hands, dipped his fingers into fresh water, and made the sign of the cross over it with the holy relics. When the blind man poured it over his sightless eyes, he immediately received the ability to see. The man of God restrained his voice and prevented him from crying out; he himself gave thanks with him to the divine majesty, and secretly had him led outside the tents wearing one of his own garments, namely a *curcinbaldus*.

### XXIV

Likewise, when he was returning from the city, he came on Saturday to a certain church, near the place where sulphurous heaps are visible. When the people wished to set out the next day, he detained them, saying that out of reverence for the Lord’s Day they should remain at least until None.

Nor was this delay without a temporal benefit. After the office of the Mass had been solemnly completed, when they were preparing to begin the journey after the meal, someone came riding a horse that had been lost while he was travelling. Lord Gerald ordered that it be taken back without harming its rider.

Before they reached Abricola, a certain blind man sitting beside the road asked passers-by whether anyone in the same company was coming who was called Gerald. One of our brothers, then still a canon, happened to be walking in Lord Gerald’s company. Proceeding on foot out of devotion, he arrived tired at the blind man.

When the blind man asked him about Lord Gerald, he replied that he was following him immediately behind. “But,” he added, “why are you seeking him so urgently?”

The other answered: “It is nine years since I have been afflicted by the hardship of blindness. But last night I was instructed in a dream to come here, seek Gerald the pilgrim of Saint Peter, and ask him to wash his hands; then I was to pour that water over my blinded eyes.”

When the cleric heard this, he stopped; meanwhile the man of God Gerald came up. It was his custom to ride alone with his head covered, so that he might devote himself more freely to the singing of psalms. When he drew near, the cleric quietly said to the blind man: “Behold, he is here.”

The blind man asked him to deign to stop for a little while and then told him what he had seen in his dream. But the elder, blushing and showing by the change in his expression that he abhorred what he had heard, began to leave.

The blind man, however, uttering dreadful adjurations, begged him to stop, help the wretched man, and not refuse the benefits that had been promised. Those who were present also earnestly entreated him to do the same. After considering for a short while, remembering, I believe, that according to the Apostle he ought not to neglect the grace given to him, he replied with the words customary to him: “Come to the aid of the saints of God.” And he stopped.

Since a stream was flowing past, as commonly happens in those hills, water was immediately brought. The elder dismounted, washed his hands, and said: “Let the will of God be done.” Then he began quickly to depart.

The blind man, without delaying, poured the water over himself, and the outcome of the miracle did not disappoint him. He recovered his sight so suddenly that he immediately ran after the elder, saying: “O holy Gerald, O holy Gerald, thanks be to God—behold, I see!”

The elder drove the mule onward with his spurs so as not to hear the voices of those who praised him. He passed through Abricola, and afterward could not be caught up with by his travelling companions even on the following day.

It can indeed be observed that those hands through which this power of healing was bestowed shone with purity, and that no stain clung to them; rather, they shook off every gift. In contrast, exceedingly wretched are those whose right hand is filled with gifts. For, as it is written, fire devours those who willingly accept gifts.

### XXV

Several other incidents from his journeys are also related, but because of their length we deliberately pass over them. Yet we shall add one more, since it concerns a power of another kind.

Once, while he was travelling to Rome and was already in Italy, he heard a voice in the air calling out to him and announcing the departure of someone. It seemed to him to be the voice of a certain man named Girbald, whom he had left in his homeland.

He therefore summoned some of his people and asked whether they knew anything about Girbald. They replied that they had left him ill. The elder then ordered the time to be recorded and psalms to be recited for him.

When he returned and asked about the aforementioned man, he discovered that Girbald had died on the very day when he had heard the voice in the air.

### XXVI

When he had completed the journey of his holy devotion, he began to take pleasure in visiting more secluded places, as though following the Psalmist’s words: “I fled far away and remained in solitude” (Psalm 54:8).

There he wished to rest from the crowds of worldly people and the noise of affairs, so that he might devote himself more freely to divine service. While he was staying for this purpose near a chapel called Catuserias, the feast of John and Paul arrived.

A peasant woman entered a small garden and was doing something—I do not know what—when suddenly a large drop of blood appeared upon her hand, which immediately began to swell. Terrified, the woman ran lamenting to the man of God and, showing him her hand, begged him to have mercy on her.

He immediately ordered the clerics to attend and a Mass to be celebrated for her. He then commanded that water be exorcised and that the drop of blood be washed with that water. He himself, however, stood apart out of humility, lest the sign of that power be attributed to him.

When the woman’s hand had been washed, the blood and swelling instantly disappeared, and she departed healed.

### XXVII

Since that place, as we have said he desired, was remote and secluded, he often stayed there. Once, after celebrating the Assumption of Saint Mary, the Mother of God, in the same church, and after the solemn Mass had been completed, he went outside to his attendants.

For it was his custom, after long and continual prayers, to give himself to ordinary conversation, so that anyone who had a reason for speaking might have the opportunity to do so. When he had gone out to his people, a man in charge of preparing the food said to him:

“We are troubled, Lord, because on this solemn feast we cannot find anything for your meal except salted meat.”

“Do not concern yourselves,” he replied, “for if it pleased the Mother of God, even this would not be lacking to us on her feast.”

He had scarcely said this when a stag threw itself down from the cliff overlooking the place. The servants, rejoicing and marveling at the same time, carried it away and prepared from it a delicate dish for the elder, since at that season venison is tender meat.

It should not seem incredible that divine generosity suddenly supplied him with food, since he, acting according to the Apostle’s teaching for the glory of God, ate his morsel together with the poor [Col. 0685D]. As his disciples, who are present witnesses, attest, he never turned his ear away from the cry of a poor person. This holy man, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words, “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor” (Psalm 40:2), whenever he heard the voices of those crying out, was accustomed to sigh deeply and answer with words of compassion.

### XXVIII

You knew Count Raymond, the son of Odo. He was holding Benedict, Lord Gerald’s nephew, namely the viscount of Toulouse, whom he had captured by deceit. Rainald, his brother, gave himself as a hostage and thereby recovered his brother.

When Lord Gerald heard that Rainald had pledged himself for his brother, he was deeply moved to help his nephew. Raymond, however, delayed returning him, secretly striving to recapture Benedict and hold them both.

Seven months had already passed, and the man of God Gerald was making no progress in rescuing his nephew. One day, as he was speaking to his sister Avigerna almost in complaint about the matter, he said:

“Why do you delay praying to Christ for your son? Either we are wavering in faith, or—and this is more likely—we are not worthy to be heard.”

As he said this, he dissolved in tears. At that time, so to speak from the depths of his being, he devoted himself entirely to the Lord in prayer. He also sent Abbot Rodulf to Raymond once more. Since the abbot was still unable to accomplish anything, he turned back after going no great distance on his way.

The following night, Raymond dreamed that the man of God Gerald was standing before his bed and struck him with his hand.

“Why,” he said, “do you not hear me, when I have so often begged you? Know for certain that if you continue to hold the hostage, it will by no means turn out well for you.”

After these words Raymond awoke. Reflecting on the vision, he trembled, summoned his men, and told them what he had dreamed. One of them, who until then had opposed Lord Gerald most strongly, was likewise terrified for some reason and urged Raymond to grant Lord Gerald’s request immediately; otherwise, he declared, they would have to die.

Raymond immediately sent word to Abbot Rodulf’s lodging and ordered him to return. When the abbot came back, Raymond openly recounted how the man of God had terrified him in a vision. He immediately returned the hostage and humbly asked Rodulf to reconcile him to Lord Gerald’s favor.

Thus Gerald prevailed through divine assistance and, in accordance with the words of Scripture, humbled the proud of the earth.

### XXIX

On another occasion, when he was hastening to meet the same Count Raymond, as he approached the river called the Avarion, mention was made of the fact that he had no fish to eat that day. Those who were walking with the elder were discussing this when they saw a fish called a *capito* swimming toward them.

One of them, who reports the incident himself, extended a small dragnet and wounded the fish. After receiving the wound, it retreated a little toward the bank to which it had previously been heading, then turned back again and lingered until one of them caught it with an outstretched hand. It was not small in size.

The man of God therefore gave thanks to God, but tried to restrain the others who were extolling this as a miracle, as though it had happened by chance. Perhaps someone may admit that such a thing could occur accidentally; nevertheless, I do not think he will recall having ever seen a fish in a broad river such as the Avarion voluntarily rush upon the bank and into the hands of men.

### XXX

It is rightly counted a miracle that once a fish leapt out of the water, or that a stag unexpectedly fell from a cliff; likewise, that a fish in a river presented itself to be caught. But it is much more marvelous that on another occasion a fish was brought from heaven for the meal of this man of God.

Not far from the monastery of Friac there is a village consecrated in honor of Saint Gregory. A certain priest named Gerald was in charge of it. He was very dear and familiar to the same man of God, Gerald, because of his holiness; before the end of his life he even shut himself away as a recluse out of divine love.

The man of God Gerald once turned aside to visit him. After prayer, he kissed him and said:

“What will you give us to eat, brother Gerald? We have come to dine with you.”

He said this because the priest enjoyed familiar companionship with him. The priest replied joyfully:

“Lord, if it pleases your kindness, you will not leave hungry. Nevertheless, I have nothing to set before you except bread and wine; but I shall inquire whether I can find some cheese or eggs.”

Then the elder said:

“Do not trouble yourself, for it is a day of abstinence, and since delicacies are lacking, it will be good if on this occasion we eat more sparingly.”

While the priest was hurrying about to prepare things, he entered a room and saw a fish on a serving dish. Astonished, he secretly asked the servant who had brought the fish. The servant said that he did not know, asserting that there had been no one there who could have brought it.

The priest therefore went out and begged the elder to deign to enter the room. When the elder followed him, the priest showed him the fish. Astonished and amazed, he gave thanks to God with the priest. Yet he bound both the priest and his servant by an oath not to reveal the matter to anyone while he lived.

The event nevertheless gradually became known to many, because divine providence, which glorifies all the saints, sometimes reveals them even against their will. Truly the Lord is still mindful of His promise, and those who seek Him shall not lack any good thing. Nor should this seem incredible, since we frequently read that God has deigned to provide His servants with drink or food from heaven as needed.

### XXXI

There is a district not far from Aureliacum called Marculiscus, near which a naturally rounded stone stands. Once, as Lord Gerald was passing through the region, a certain member of his company named Adrald asserted to his travelling companions that he could leap onto that stone.

To the astonishment of everyone, he immediately did so. It was said that this same Adrald knew incantations and magic [Col. 0687D]. As the elder followed, those who had gone ahead stood waiting and told him about Adrald’s leap.

The elder, however, realizing that Adrald could not have done this by his own agility, raised his hand and made the sign of the cross. Afterward, although Adrald attempted the feat many times, he could not leap upon the aforesaid stone at all.

Thus it became known that his agility had been produced by an incantation, which could no longer assist him after the sign of the cross; and it was a great power of Lord Gerald that, after his sign, the hostile force had no effect.

### XXXII

Since we have mentioned what he did by making the sign of the cross, let us add what he did on another occasion by the same sign.

The solemnity of Saint Lawrence had arrived, and he was celebrating that feast in one of his chapels, situated not far from a village called Argentado. One of his female servants was being severely tormented there.

When he looked toward her in prayer, she was in the midst of the people, gnashing her teeth violently and raving. Everyone begged the man of God to deign to make the sign of the cross over her. Out of his customary humility he delayed for a long time. But when she did not cease raging, at last, after those present had pressed their request, he raised his hand and made the sign of the cross over her.

She immediately vomited purulent blood and was healed. While everyone resounded with praises of God and magnified him, he restrained them with great severity, saying that they should magnify only the clemency of God and of Saint Peter, whose church it was.

This was the same church where he had been staying when the blind woman mentioned above received sight through the water in which he had washed his hands.

### XXXIII

A certain man named Herloard fell from a horse and struck one of his knees violently. Because of the pain, he had already gone six days without food. Since he could find no remedy for himself, he sent to Captennac and secretly had water from Lord Gerald’s hands brought to him.

Wonderful to relate, as soon as he sprinkled the aforesaid water upon his knee, he was freed from all pain and rose unharmed.

Several other things are related about him that are worthy either of being told or of admiration. But since they are reported popularly and not affirmed by the four witnesses mentioned above, we prefer to remain silent about them, although we do not fail to recognize that he performed many deeds known either to no one or to very few.

For, as is customary among pious and good men, he always strove to preserve humility as though it were the eye of his heart. Therefore, as far as he could, he concealed his works. As for those that became known against his will, he would not tolerate hearing them praised.

### XXXIV

Let this, then, suffice concerning his miracles—miracles sufficient for those who measure the glory of any saint not by the quantity of his good works but by the number of his signs. In their view his holiness might perhaps have been considered less worthy if they had heard nothing about the miracles he performed while alive.

Those, however, who are piously devoted to him and venerate him with discerning love take greater pleasure in the works of righteousness that he practiced. But when both qualities came together in him—namely, righteousness and sanctification, along with the glorification brought by signs—they venerate him with greater confidence and more eager devotion.

If, perhaps, he had possessed the spirit of prophecy, no one, I think, would have denied that he was holy. But he accomplished something greater, because he conquered greed. What good did it do Balaam that he prophesied with such profound mystery, when he was rejected on account of his greed?

Therefore do not seek in Gerald a miracle greater than this: that he did not place his hope in money or treasures. This, as we have already said, is itself to have performed wonders. You will find scarcely anyone who does not hope that happiness lies in money; and because such people are so rare, the divine word has introduced the question:

“Who is this?”

When such a person is found, however imperfectly, he is worthy of praise, as the passage continues: “We shall praise him, for he performed wonders in his life.”

There is abundant evidence that Gerald performed wonders of this kind. It is clear that he held what had been given to him by his parents or by kings in such a way that he distributed it not as though to servants but almost as though to masters; that he increased his earthly possessions without harming anyone, yet stored up treasures in heaven; and that although he was exalted in power, he remained poor in spirit.

Therefore, as the passage continues, it should seem neither strange nor incredible if his goods were established in the Lord. Yet one thing stands out incomparably among his deeds: he remained chaste into old age. For chastity alone imitates angelic purity.

Since he conquered lust, which is Satan’s greatest power, it is not surprising that he now commands even Satan, whom he defeated by preserving chastity. It is not incredible that he now frees those possessed by demons, since he expelled from his heart the prince of mammon by conquering greed. Rightly does he now hold the spirit of pride subject, since at the very summit of earthly power he showed himself gentle.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0689]

[Col. 0689B] Since the preceding discourse has explained in greater detail that the venerable man Gerald was distinguished by the power of signs, it now remains for us to set forth in writing how he released his spiritual essence from its bodily covering.

For it is certain that although this same man had subdued his bodily appetite through frugal moderation, he nevertheless remained vigorous in strength. He was not without bodily power, nor did he lack the force of physical strength. But when the time was already near for him, as an aged man, to be discharged from completed service, he began, weakened from his customary vigor, to decline.

Nor was this hidden from him. Rather, the exhaustion of his very powers revealed to him that his end was approaching. When he saw many of those present who were accustomed to cling closely to him, he began to address them with something like a deeper and more inward sob and failing voice:

“Come, my little dependants and most beloved companions, do you not see that I have been deprived of my former strength? Understand that the lot of my deposition is near: the spirit, led by its author, is to be transferred to its appointed dwelling, while exceedingly fragile nature is reduced to dust.”

The torment of illness did not keep him from his customary abstinence. A strange thing: not even that weakness which usually overcomes the aged could, contrary to its ordinary practice, persuade his steadfast mind to give way. For bodily softness had been unable to weaken the rigor of his spirit.

As his soul was nourished by these and similar virtues, he lost his bodily effectiveness. Yet because, in despising himself in his own eyes, he did not recognize himself as a virtuous man, he did not sufficiently understand where the weakness of his powers had entered him.

By then the spiritual power that had grown fully within him had almost slaughtered his bodily strength. For this is the custom of the saints: divine power would be less strong in them if it did not weaken their bodily vigor. Thus Daniel, after seeing an angelic vision, languished for many days. Thus Jacob, having wrestled with the angel, began to limp. For whoever is filled with spiritual grace is weakened in bodily power.

And so the outward man was wasting away while the inward man was renewed from day to day.

### I

One day, while he was in a town overlooking Aureliacum, he looked toward the construction of a house and wept profusely. When one of his close companions asked why he was crying, he replied:

“Because I am unable by any means to bring to fulfillment the desire that I conceived long ago concerning this place. For this is my resting place; here I shall dwell. Indeed, with God’s favor, I have easily prepared everything else that appears suitable for the use of monks; only monks are lacking, and they alone cannot be found.

“Therefore, like a solitary and bereaved man, I am consumed with sorrow. Yet I hope that almighty God, whenever it pleases Him, will deign to fulfill my desire. Nor is it surprising if I, a sinner, am kept waiting in this desire, since King David was forbidden to build a temple for the Lord, although the Lord Himself provided the person who would complete that work after him.

“And although I do not see this in this life, the mercy of Christ will nevertheless grant what I desire, whenever it pleases Him. I would have you know that the walls of this house will often be too narrow for the crowds who will gather there.”

He did not explain at all how he had learned this. But when those who knew that he had said it saw crowds assembling in that same place, as he had foretold, the opinion arose among them that he had learned what he said by divine revelation.

His mouth was already so filled from the abundance of his heart that the law of the Lord always sounded fully within him. Moreover, following the example of the aforementioned David, whatever he foresaw to be necessary for the future inhabitants, he took care to prepare—both relics of the saints and ecclesiastical vessels and vestments, as well as revenues from fields.

### II

But, as Scripture says, “Let the one who is holy be sanctified still,” it was necessary that this man of God be stripped by scourging before his death. Like blessed Job and Tobit, he had to be tested because he was acceptable to God.

Thus for seven years and more he lost the light of his eyes. Yet he had possessed them so keenly that he seemed to suffer nothing from blindness. He not only did not grieve over this affliction, but greatly rejoiced in the Lord because He had deigned to scourge him.

For he was not unaware that not everyone who is scourged is a son, but that no son exists who is not scourged. His consolation was that the heavenly Judge had released His hand to strike him and was punishing in the present life the sins without which no one here lives.

Thus, already secure concerning the Lord’s mercy, he trusted that He would deign to free him from eternal punishment, since He had deigned to press him beneath the scourge in the present life.

If he could add anything to his former disciplines, then, to the extent that the cause of external blindness had caused him to withdraw from outward activity, he devoted himself more attentively to prayer. And insofar as he could no longer look upon the shape of the world, he applied his heart more clearly to contemplating the true light.

His activity in external matters ceased; he applied himself wholly to the practice of prayer and to constant reading.

### III

Two years before he died, he had the church solemnly dedicated [Col. 0691B]. The altars contain so many relics of the saints [Col. 0691D]—that is, relics, *chymilia*; Gregory of Tours uses the term frequently. Odo himself does so below, Book IV, chapters 8 and 12, as do others—that those who know about them find it astonishing. To those who happen to hear about them from such people, it may seem almost incredible.

For that holy father devoted himself in every way, throughout his life, whenever opportunity arose, to gathering them from every source. He obtained them both at Rome and everywhere else, as was fitting for one who was gracious in speech and countenance, generous in offering prices, and, more importantly, confident in divine grace for the task that had to be accomplished.

It is often reported that, in obtaining these relics, he gave costly tents, large and powerful horses, and many weights of money. He placed a tooth of Saint Martial in the right-hand altar, together with relics of the most blessed lord Martin and also of Saint Hilary. Although all the donors had long tried to extract it from the holy body, from the sacred jaw, none could do so; after first offering a prayer, Gerald immediately pulled it out.

On that same altar, something remarkable is said to have happened on the very day of its dedication. A certain young man, pressing himself into the crowd, took a covering cloth from above in order to return it to the servant, although the bystanders told him not to presume to do so.

But because he did not stop taking it, he was immediately seized by a violent affliction. At first his hands were flayed; then little by little his entire body was stripped of skin, so that he could scarcely recover even after six weeks.
