As he had once determined, Gerald entrusted the place to the authority of monks, although afterward he stayed there only a short time.

### IV

During the time he had remaining to him, he took the greatest care to dismiss all those dependent upon him in peace, lest an occasion for quarrel should arise among them. He left the estates and slaves that he had not assigned to blessed Peter to certain relatives and soldiers, or at least to his servants. To some he gave them on the condition that, after their death, they should return to Aureliacum. At that time alone he granted freedom to one hundred slaves. For at other places and times there were countless others whom he emancipated. Many of these, however, bound by affection for him, refused their freedom and preferred to remain in his service. From this it may be understood how gently he exercised lordship over them, since they preferred his servitude to their own freedom.

Some of his people advised him to release a greater number from the yoke of servitude, since his household was more than sufficiently numerous. He replied to them: “It is just that the worldly law be observed in this matter, and therefore one ought not to exceed the number prescribed in that law.” This has been recalled in order that it may be clear how closely he adhered to divine commands, since he submitted himself in the same way both to legal and to human ordinances.

### V

When the time of his departure was already approaching, he was staying at Cezerviacum [Note: [Col. 0691D] At Cezerniacum. In French, Cézeinac.], at a church belonging to him, which had been consecrated in honor of Saint Cyricus. There, more deeply moved than usual, he sighed with such intensity that it was quite evident that the desire of his heart was directed elsewhere and that he had no consolation whatever in the present life. Amid his sighs he was bathed in tears, and from time to time, lifting his eyes toward heaven, he prayed to be freed from this world, repeatedly saying: “Come to my aid, saints of God.” This expression had always been familiar to his lips; whenever any sudden misfortune occurred, he was accustomed to call out with it.

Not long afterward, the vigor of life began to waste away under a kind of spasm, and the strength of his limbs, together with the harmony of his whole body, gradually dissolved. Recognizing, therefore, that his dissolution was already near, he ordered Bishop Amblardus [Col. 0692C] to be summoned [Note: [Col. 0692D] Bishop Amblardus. Bishop of Clermont, forty-third in order; the foundation charter of the monastery of Cluny, to which he subscribed in 910, and the Catalogue of the Church of Clermont call him Adalardus.], so that he might strengthen his passing with his prayers and entrust to Christ, the shepherd of all, the sheep returning to the pastures of paradise.

Meanwhile, with sound judgment and unimpaired memory, he arranged everything that the funeral or the needs of those who would remain might require. Suddenly swift rumor spread everywhere that the man of God, Geraldus, was nearing his departure. Everyone hurried there as though mourning a common loss: crowds of clergy and monks mingled with noblemen, companies of the poor, and peasant populations. The weeping of some stirred up the tears of others. Amid sobs and bursting tears, as though making a lament, each person repeated cries of mourning over his piety, his charity, his care for the poor, and his protection of the helpless.

Some who were weeping said: “What a consolation the world is losing!” Others said: “O Geraldus, rightly called good, who will now be, as you were, a support for the needy? Who will be a nourisher of orphans or a defender of widows? Who will console the sorrowful? Surely, who will bend the height of his power toward the poor as you did? Who will, like you, consider and relieve the needs of each person? Most indulgent father, how gentle and gracious you have always been! You drew the favor of all to yourself; even the affection of strangers you had attracted to you through the fame of such great goodness.”

These and similar expressions, which the force of grief is accustomed to magnify amid sobs, poured forth in such mournful lamentations that one might have thought those tears could never cease. This continued day after day until the very end of his calling had arrived. Yet he could not abandon his customary practice even at the end: he ordered every stipend to be given to all who wished to receive it.

### VI

I would truly call blessed and happy the man who was such that he did not leave behind on earth the charity owed to his works, but was received into the charity of the saints in heaven. Truly happy was he who, although exalted by secular power, harmed no one and oppressed no one, and against whom no one raised even a small complaint.

For if Nathanael is truly called an Israelite because there was no deceit in him, I may rightly call this man an Israelite as well: the listening ear blesses him, and, after the example of blessed Job, the seeing eye bears witness to him.

While everyone mourned together, he alone remained joyful. He knew that for those who hope in the Lord, the brightness of midday rises into evening, and that, when he gives them sleep, this is their inheritance. Although the flesh, because of its mortal condition, may have felt fear, the spirit, fixed upon the vision of glory, rejoiced, since he confidently believed that he was already receiving in reality the hope he had long desired. For, as it is written, “the righteous trusts even in his death”; one might have thought him fixed in that hope and entirely without fear of death.

Thus he appeared joyful, since he did not admit even the slightest thing by which he might show that he was trembling in the least. Throughout the entire period of his illness, he drove his failing limbs to divine service in such a way that he would not allow even one nocturnal office to be celebrated except in the church. He listened, stationed before the altar, to one Mass appropriate to the day and another for the dead.

When his limbs had already become so stiff that he could not advance by himself even with support, his spirit nevertheless remained ardent and compelled the little body to be carried by bearers into the oratory. In this way, extending the garment of good works down to his ankle, he sang the praise of his virtue at the end.

### VII

At dawn on Friday, feeling his condition worsening, he ordered the chaplains to perform the nocturnal office before him, while the bishop and his attendants celebrated it in the church. He himself psalmodized with those singing until, after the morning office, he had completed all the hours of the day.

Then, having finished Compline, he armed himself with the sign of the holy cross and added the expression that had always been familiar to him, saying: “Come to my aid, saints of God.” Having spoken this final word, he silently closed his eyes. Those present, seeing that he had ceased to speak, summoned the bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0693D] They also placed his holy limbs in haircloth. This was an ancient custom among Christians, especially clergy and monks, to die in haircloth and ashes. The Life of Saint Arigius, bishop of Gap, says: “After his body had been stripped, while he lay before the altar of Saint Eusebius in ashes and haircloth, and had received the viaticum of Christ’s body and blood from the hand of Bishop Ysicium and the priest Dicontius, he said: ‘I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, because I now see the time of my dissolution.’” Peter the Venerable likewise says in Book I of the Miracles, chapter 4: “And when, as is the custom of Christians, especially monks, he had been laid out by the brothers upon haircloth and ashes, he lay awaiting the hour of his calling.”]

They also placed his holy limbs in haircloth. While the others were singing for his departure, one of the priests quickly celebrated Mass and brought the most holy sacrament. When some said that he had already departed, he, still retaining consciousness, opened his eyes and showed by this sign that he had not yet departed. Then he received of his own accord the Lord’s body, which he had been awaiting, and so that happy soul migrated to heaven.

By the very number of the day, as it were, he indicated the reason for his departure: he had completed well the good work belonging to the number six and shown that he had migrated to the true Sabbath, which is rest. He now sees, as we believe, what he desired; he now possesses what he hoped for. Nevertheless, he left many in no small grief. Although their sorrow was mingled with a certain sweetness, because they knew that one such as he was more to be rejoiced over than mourned, they nevertheless lamented with loud cries that they were deprived of the companionship of one whose like they did not expect to see again.

They grieved for human reasons; but the angels, as we believe, rejoiced. For if there is joy before the angels over one sinner who repents, how much more over this righteous man who grew old amid works of virtue?

The joy of his Lord, by which he was received by those same angels, faith contemplates; but for the time being it is hidden from bodily eyes. Those eyes saw only the corpse that had paid the debt of death, while it was not yet apparent how greatly the soul was being glorified in heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0694D] Geraldus therefore dies. This was in the year of Christ 907, which was the sixth year of Fulbert II, abbot of Limoges. Thus the author of the Chronology of the Abbots of Limoges says: “The sixth abbot, Fulbert, presided for twenty years. In his sixth year Saint Geraldus died at Aureliacum on the third day before the Ides of October.” I am not unaware, however, that this does not agree with the Limoges Chronicle, which says: “In the year of the Lord 917 Saint Geraldus, renowned by birth, life, and miracles, died.” It is enough to have noted the discrepancy.]

Geraldus therefore dies, but, in accordance with that saying of David, not at all as the sluggish are accustomed to die, for his lot is among the saints. And although he fulfilled the Psalmist’s words, “But you shall die like men” (Psalm 81:7), this also applies to him, which is stated there beforehand: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Psalm 81:6). The evangelist bears witness: “We are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be” (John 9:2).

Happy, therefore, was Geraldus, who separated what was precious from what was vile. After he had tasted how sweet the Lord is, he did not submit himself to the pleasures of this life, thereby showing contempt for that same Lord. He counted this life, which is precious to the reprobate, as vile for himself, and found precious the death that is most wretched to them.

Truly blessed is the man whose days passed in sorrow and whose years passed in mourning, because he has now experienced how great is the abundance of sweetness that God has hidden for those who fear him. He also reveals something of it, through individual signs, in the sight of the children of men.

O what a difference there is between him and the *vedii*, that is, the evil rich! For his tears were his bread, and he received his drink in tears and in measure. But they spend their days in good things and have their consolation in the present, according to the Gospel.

This man, however, has now passed, with a voice of exultation, into the place of God’s tabernacle. Of them it is said that they descend to the underworld in a moment. But if anyone could recount anything worthy concerning his outward conduct, nevertheless no one among us is able—not merely to explain in words, but even to grasp in thought—the delights that filled him in the Lord’s right hand to the end, unless perhaps someone experiences within himself what it is to delight in the salvation of God.

### VIII

Since God is marvelous in his saints, in whom Scripture commands us to praise him, saying, “Praise the Lord in his saints” (Psalm 150:1), therefore, blessed Geraldus, we offer him such praise for you as we are able.

We praise him because he chose you and justified you; because he made his mercy wondrous in you; because he led you along straight paths; because he himself caused the fruit of your labor to be found; and finally because he did not abandon you even into old age and advanced years. Greater still, he counted you among the children of God and, moreover, glorifies you in the sight of all.

Since praise befits the saints, we also praise you to his glory: because, according to Jeremiah, you bore Christ’s yoke from youth; because you did not despise the grace of his calling [the printed reading has *non recepisti*, “you did not receive”]; because you did not give your soul in exchange; because you did not receive his salvation in vain; because you did not cast away the innermost things you had conceived from the love of Christ; because you did not withdraw in the time of temptation; because you did not pour yourself out into the external joys of the present life; and because you did not grow weary in doing good.

Yet you, Lord God—you pardon our presumption through him. For in this account we fear that we have gone beyond what is proper, since we have attempted what we are in no way fit to undertake. Although he is worthy of praise, in whom you are praised, we, Lord, are unworthy to offer this praise, because “praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclesiasticus 15:9).

Therefore, as it is written, “Let your saints bless you, and let them declare your works to you.” But because your eyes see what is imperfect in the Church and will have compassion on its stones and earth, we ask that those who are called stones because of the solidity of their character may deign to help us, who by the perversity of our conduct are rightly called earth. May we who do not possess the garment of righteousness embrace the stones, so that through their merits we may cover our nakedness.

May this servant of yours therefore direct toward us the compassionate affection that your charity implanted within him. From that eternal council of the Capitol, where he now sits among the consuls of heaven, may he piously look upon this valley of tears from which he has escaped; may he hear the prayers of each person and obtain the needs of all before you, through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who with you and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, for endless ages of ages. Amen.

### IX

Swiftly, as is customary in the case of an eminent person, news of his departure resounded everywhere. An incredible multitude of people immediately began to rush in from every direction: companies of noblemen, countless groups of peasants and needy people, many monks, and companies of priests. All mourned him with a kind of fraternal and most tender affection; under some divine impulse, I do not know what, they grieved for him with greater compunction and sweetness, because they knew that he had pleased God.

[Note: [Col. 0695D] When, according to custom, he had been stripped for washing. This too was an ancient custom of stripping and washing bodies after death. Peter the Venerable, Book II of the *Miracles*, chapter 23, concerning the funeral and burial of Matthew, bishop of Alba, says: “It is reported that the body of the righteous man was immediately carried by devoted men into the monks’ cloister, and that psalmody was sung everywhere according to Cluniac custom. He was washed, as the common custom requires, and, in accordance with his own command, was first clothed in his haircloth, which he had never been without as a monk, and afterward in a monastic cowl.” Radulfus, a Cluniac monk, likewise says in his Life of Peter the Venerable: “The body of the holy Father was carried to the place where the bodies of the dead were washed; and there, stripped of his garments, the glory of the glorified man appeared to all who saw it, causing them wonder.”]

### X

When, according to custom, he had been stripped for washing, Ragambertus and the other attendants performing this task placed both his hands upon his chest. Suddenly his right arm extended, and his hand was applied to his genitals in such a way that it enclosed those members beneath the palm.

Thinking that this had happened by accident, they put the hand back upon his chest. But again, as before, it extended and positioned itself to cover his sexual organs. They began to be astonished; yet, wishing to understand the matter more carefully, they bent the arm back a third time and moved the hand from the chest to the other side. Immediately, with the greatest speed, it returned to the aforementioned members, as before, and covered them.

The embalmers, struck at once by wonder and fear, then understood that this could not have happened without divine power. Perhaps heaven was thereby showing that, in order to preserve the modesty of chastity, that living flesh had always been ashamed. They therefore quickly covered the little body. After he had received clothing, that hand never extended itself anywhere again.

### XI

His household, accompanied by very large crowds, carried that holy body to Aureliacum, as he himself had ordered, and placed it upon an *ariston* stone [Note: [Col. 0696D] On the left side of the basilica itself, beside the altar of Saint Peter. The Limoges Chronicle says: “Saint Geraldus died and was buried in the monastery at Aureliacum, which he had built in honor of Saint Peter.” The Chronology of the Abbots of Saint Martial says: “Buried in the monastery of the Apostle Peter, which he himself had built.”], on the left side of the basilica, beside the altar of Saint Peter, so that his tomb was on the right and he himself likewise toward the right.

But let us now end this little book, lest it displease either through rusticity or through length. If anything in it has delighted the reader, let him consider it the result of the merits of Lord Geraldus. Whatever has displeased him, let him attribute to my incompetence; nevertheless, he will find an occasion for compassion. For this reason I humbly beseech him—and, considering that I presumed to undertake this task because I was ordered to do so, I ask him to plead for me before the judge of hearts.

### XII

It would have been sufficient for blessed Geraldus that the faithful witness who is in heaven, and whom he always strove to please, should reward him in that paradisiacal region. Yet Christ, that same witness, deigns to manifest outwardly how great is the glory that Geraldus possesses within.

For it is written that God establishes his witnesses against us. Whoever keeps his commandments is his witness against us, showing that we too are able to keep those commandments as he did, but do not wish to. To speak of those like myself: we have already grown weary of reading all the sayings of devout people and neglect to imitate their examples, while we occupy ourselves tirelessly with idle or worldly words.

By acting thus, we prove ourselves to belong to those whom the apostolic voice condemns, saying: “They will turn away their hearing from the truth and turn instead to fables” (2 Timothy 4:4). To restrain this inertia, together with the other monstrosities of vice, to some extent, Christ, the disposer of the ages, establishes this witness of his against us. He also illuminates him before us with many miracles, so that, because we have closed our eyes to contemplating the examples of the devout, as has been said, we may at least look upon the brightness of this man, shining as though close at hand.

He indeed kept the divine commandments in our own time. But because the dead quickly depart from the heart, we immediately consign this to forgetfulness; and, failing to consider the reward awaiting his holy works, we grow sluggish in imitating them. For this reason he deigns to perform miracles that perhaps occur only for a time, so that we may understand, even in this way, the glory he possesses within, and direct the focus of our minds toward the works by which he was advanced to that same glory, as though they had just been set before us, and strive to grow strong enough to imitate them.

But now, with God’s help, let us recount those miracles insofar as they accord with reason.

## BOOK FOUR

### I

On the Sunday that followed his departure, he was carried to Aureliacum, accompanied, as we have said, by many crowds. While choirs of those singing psalms kept vigil around the bier throughout the night, a certain nobleman named Gibbo placed beneath that same bier his daughter, who had been seized by epilepsy. From that time she suffered none of that illness. She is now a mother of a household and herself offers her restored health as testimony to this miracle.

### II

A man named Grimaldus, living in a village, dreamed that he was trying to tear away the cover of Geraldus’s sarcophagus. When he awoke, his arms from the elbows downward, including his hands, were so dried up that he could do nothing with them. After remaining weakened in this condition for nearly fifteen days, he came to the tomb to pray and immediately recovered his health.

### III

A certain man named Lambertus had a female servant afflicted with lunacy. In a dream she was instructed to come to Geraldus’s tomb to pray. She told this to her master. Fearing that it would be an illusion and a source of ridicule if the vision were not followed by a miraculous result, he forbade her.

Afterward, when she was instructed in a vision a second and a third time, she begged her master to permit her to go there. He finally consented. The woman went, kept vigil before the tomb, and departed completely healed.

### IV

Meanwhile, a small grassy plot, round like a wheel, appeared before the crypt. Although it was covered with grass, the earth around it was bare and dusty in a circle. Those who passed through the cemetery saw the little plot and the dusty furrow surrounding it and wondered, knowing that neither man nor beast had worn down that furrow by walking upon it.

It remained for some time and then disappeared. The following summer it was seen in the same place, but much wider. As before, it had a worn and dusty rim around it. In the third summer, a similarly grassy wheel appeared, surrounded as though by a dusty path, but now much more extensive. Thereafter, spreading gradually farther year by year, it seemed to extend outward.

Those who examined the matter more carefully believed it to be some kind of prodigy, conjecturing that the green wheel perhaps represented the fame of blessed Geraldus, full of the greenness of virtue. That fame spreads continually among peoples barren from the aridity of good works, signified by the dusty circle, and fertilizes them, as it were, by his example: they undertake a devout pilgrimage and labor for love of him, offer gifts, and some return with improved morals. Thus the wheel, extending farther and farther, partly filled the aridity of the dusty circle.

Whether this was what it signified, the disposer of events knows. It is nevertheless certain that nothing occurs on earth without a cause.

### V

A cleric of good reputation lived in the city of Rodez. If dreams are to be believed, he saw the following vision:

There was what appeared to be a high place where a great splendor shone. One ascended to that splendor by four steps. Before the first step there was something like an iron barrier (*antepodium*); the second step had a bronze barrier, the third a silver one, and the fourth a golden one.

Upon the first step he saw two men of extraordinary splendor in face and clothing arrive. Two others followed them, leading a third between them by the hands. The cleric who saw this was told that the first two were Saint Paul and Saint Martial, and that the two who followed were Saint Peter and Saint Andrew. The third whom they were leading was Saint Geraldus.

The cleric had not known Geraldus while he remained in this life. But afterward, when he described the stature and appearance in which he had seen him, those who had known Geraldus recognized his features.

When they came to the first step, they sang as though singing a psalm. After it, Saint Peter said a collect. When it was completed, they responded: “Amen.” They did the same at the second, third, and fourth steps.

While the others remained standing, blessed Peter proceeded as far as the place of the aforementioned splendor. He lay prostrate on the ground, worshiping for a while. Then he rose and prostrated himself a third time. After that, a voice answering from the splendor asked what he wanted.

He replied: “Lord, I beg your mercy for your servant Geraldus.”

Then someone—or something—appeared to recite his life as though holding a book. Although he read for some time, the cleric was able to understand only this: “He who could transgress and did not transgress, and do evil and did not do it” (Ecclesiasticus 31:10).

Then a voice said to him: “Do with him what you wish.” It brought forth, as it were, a scepter and gave it to him, thereby granting him the power to exalt Geraldus. The cleric heard the voice of the giver, but saw nothing except the scepter.

Then blessed Peter returned joyfully to those who were waiting for him. At the place where they were standing, there appeared what looked like a sloping ascent extending all the way to heaven. Blessed Peter held beloved Geraldus by the hand and, beginning to ascend those steps, cried out in a loud voice: “We praise you, O God!”

And so, singing psalms, they went with him toward heaven.

After this, another sign concerning his tomb appeared visibly.

### VI

In the seventh year after his departure, the sarcophagus, which until then had been covered up to the middle of its lid with packed earth and trampling feet, gradually began to rise above that same earth. Yet the earth surrounding it appeared neither to rise nor to sink.

The inhabitants had not yet noticed this when a certain cleric arrived from the district of Limoges and asked the monks whether the sarcophagus of Lord Geraldus had risen any farther. He added that he had been warned in a dream to come to Geraldus’s tomb, because his sarcophagus had begun to appear.

The monks then went with him to the tomb and pulled away the cloth covering it. They found it exactly as the sleeping cleric had seen it. At that time it projected a little; now it appears considerably higher. Whoever recognizes this cannot deny that it is some divine power. From this point onward, miracles began frequently to occur.

### VII

The solemnity of the Lord’s Circumcision had arrived when a certain vassal named Adraldus ordered a fire of charcoal to be made in his house throughout the night. At the dead of night, demons rushed upon those guarding the fire. They were so grievously afflicted by them that one was killed and another, his limbs disabled, was deprived of bodily health.

The latter afterward spent his life begging and was brought to Aureliacum. While he was living there for several days, some violent men began presumptuously to act against the authority of that place. For this reason the monks began to sound the bells and persist in litanies.

Then the crippled man begged those standing around to carry him to the tomb of Lord Geraldus. When they had done so, he prayed that Geraldus would deign to help him. Shortly afterward he rose up sound and, with his limbs restored, recovered completely in an instant.

From that time onward miracles began continually to be performed, and the reputation of his powers resounded with greater certainty and more widely. If anyone should perhaps doubt these things because the same cures are often repeated in the sick, he can verify them by sight, through which faith in past events may be gained.

We have omitted, for the sake of brevity, the miracles that divine grace has often deigned to repeat among those oppressed by various illnesses. We have nevertheless touched upon some of them to commend the glory of that blessed man, lest we appear to have passed over them carelessly.

### VIII

It is well established that, while he was alive, this same holy man brought many relics of the saints to Aureliacum. As was said above, he was extraordinarily devoted to this purpose and had received no small grace from God for obtaining whatever he desired.

Among the other sacred treasures kept there is a certain piece of the Lord’s wood. Its power is recognized through frequent experience: if someone carries it while riding, the horse soon dies; or if someone happens to commit perjury, he becomes an *emptilentiscus* [epileptic]. Indeed, not a few have become subject to seizures because of this sin.

The inhabitants of that region were accustomed to have very savage customs, but they seem to have become somewhat gentler through the example or reverence of the holy man.

[Note: [Col. 0699D] When they establish a pact or some great oath. Among the ancients it was extremely common to swear friendship, fidelity, innocence, or anything else over the relics of the saints. Aymoinus, Book IV, chapter 64: “He promised by oath, over the body of Saint Denis, fidelity both to King Pippin himself and to his sons Charles and Carloman.” The Appendix to Gregory of Tours, chapter 54: “Godinus was brought at the command of Chlothar to the principal shrines of the saints—of Lord Medardus at Soissons and of Lord Denis at Paris—in order to give his oath under the provision that he should always remain faithful to Chlothar.” And later: “Chramnulfus, one of the nobles, and Valdebertus, the domesticus, told Godinus that he should go to the church of Saint Aignan at Orléans and to the threshold of Saint Martin at Tours to fulfill that oath once more.” Gregory of Tours himself should be consulted, Book IV of the *History*, chapter 46; Book V, chapter 23; and Book I of the *Miracles*, chapter 54.]

When they formally establish a pact or some solemn oath, they have it carried to them by any monk or cleric who nevertheless walks on foot.

### IX

Certain people, rashly disputing the glory of blessed Geraldus, assert that the grace of these cures is bestowed not through his merits but through the powers of the relics. But we, considering the matter more carefully, believe that healing benefits are granted through those holy pledges in such a way that the cooperation of blessed Geraldus’s power must not be denied.

The very character of the events encourages this belief, since Geraldus himself is accustomed to appear to the sick in visions and, especially before his tomb, to grant the benefit of health.

Such is the case of the son of John, viscount of Auvergne [*Arvernensis*], whom his father brought there mute and deaf, with one hand contracted. The father prostrated himself before the tomb and gave himself to prayer. At midnight, blood burst from the boy’s ears, and his hand was straightened; he spread it out, restored, around his father’s neck, and uttering his first word, asked his father for bread.

The father, giving thanks for his son, filled the entire church with his cries and handed over to the holy tomb an allod belonging to him.

We mention this case by name because the miracle, performed upon a person of distinction, became known to many. Other miracles, of different kinds and forms, were at first recorded by the inhabitants; but when their number grew immense, the task of counting them was abandoned.

### X

In the town of Aureliacum, before the doors of the church, there was a mounting block from which Geraldus used to mount his horse. When the sick kiss it out of love for him, they generally recover their health. For this reason the inhabitants have now moved it inside the church and covered it with a cloth in the manner of an altar.

Not far from the town that the peasants call Mulsedonum, the man of God had possessed a house. The townspeople mutually agreed to carry away his table, which was still in that house, so that they might use it for a meal. They did so. By chance, however, the bearers set it down in front of a certain house.

When someone wished to sleep upon it at midday, he suddenly became blind and insane. Then, when a dog also stepped upon the same table, all its limbs immediately became rigid. The people had not yet realized what the cause was when another man likewise threw himself upon it, and he too was immediately struck blind.

At last, understanding that they had suffered these things because of the table, consecrated by the holy man’s frequent use of it for meals, they carried it, covered with a linen cloth, to the nearby church of blessed Martin. To this day it is displayed there, hanging from the roof.

At another of his tables, which was in the village of Vaxia, a certain priest had come to a banquet with his neighbors. When, as usually happens, they began to chatter during the meal and exchange ridiculous remarks, a sudden great terror struck them all so severely that they immediately stopped their buffoonery and withdrew to another place to eat.

They carried the table to the oratory that had been built in a certain place where the bearers had set down the bier in order to change its covering. At that place, when wandering livestock happened to reach the little area where, as we have said, the bier had been placed, while grazing around it, they immediately began to suffer torments, and some died.

The inhabitants, understanding the cause from what had happened to the animals, built the aforementioned oratory there. It is certain that afterward many sick people recovered their health there.

Moreover, something marvelous and almost incredible occurred—except that experience proves it. From that time onward, a little spring began to bubble up in the same place, sufficient to provide drinking water for travelers.

### XI

[Note: [Col. 0701D] Rainaldus. The nephew of blessed Geraldus, of whom we spoke above. Saint Odo himself immediately afterward indicates this in the following words: “Although he was related by blood to the holy man, he was nevertheless far removed from his piety.”]

Rainaldus, whom the man of God suspected and had bound by an oath while still alive, as was said above, broke faith with that oath and was exceedingly hostile, together with his men, toward the household that Geraldus had assigned to the monastery.

During the raids they suffered, each of them was accustomed to call upon the name of Lord Geraldus. One night Rainaldus seemed to see the man of God standing before him. When Geraldus demanded that he keep faith with his oath, he also warned him to stop harassing the household from then on.

After being awakened, Rainaldus told his wife about the vision. She too urged him at least to keep the oath, since he had been warned. He was moved for the moment and repeated the warning to his men, ordering them—but sluggishly—not to trouble the household.

Shortly afterward, however, they returned to their customary plundering. Rainaldus did not resist them, because he was inclined toward evil. Although he was related by blood to the holy man, he was nevertheless far removed from his piety.

Then the holy man appeared to him again, threatening him. In fury he reproached him for the good deeds Geraldus had done for him, for which Rainaldus was repaying him with evil. He struck him on the head and threatened that death would soon follow for him.

### XII

In the province called Alamannia there was a nobleman possessed by demons. His parents and his soldiers led him to many relics of the saints, hoping that at least through their intercession [Column 0702D] divine grace might free him. But the dispenser of all good things, who had determined to glorify his chosen servant, reserved this power for him. The name of the blessed man had not yet been heard in that province.

As the aforementioned parents were taking him before the bodies of the saints, the demons repeatedly shouted from the man’s body that they would not leave it except through the intercession of the blessed Gerald. Then the same parents of the demoniac ran here and there, asking whether anyone had heard of the province in which the blessed Gerald was. I do not know whether a Roman or some other pilgrim told them the province [Column 0703A] and the place. They hurried to Aurillac.

As soon as he came before the tomb, the demons began to cry out through the possessed man: “O Gerald,” one said, “why do you mock us? Why do we burn at your power?” [Column 0704A] Immediately the man fell to the ground and vomited them out together with blood. From that hour onward he remained well.

[Column 0703]

## A COMPENDIUM OF THE LIFE OF SAINT GERALD

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, fifth century, p. 6.)*

### 1. Gerald, a benefactor of the Order of Saint Benedict

Although Gerald never embraced the monastic life, the Benedictine religion, to which he was always deeply devoted, owes him so much that he rightly deserves a place among the holy men of our order. It is unnecessary to reproduce here the life of Gerald written in four books by Odo, abbot of Cluny, both because it has already been published and annotated in the Cluniac Library, and because it is sufficient to extract and collect from it what pertains to monastic affairs.

In addition to these deeds of Gerald, whose author was Odo, we have found in manuscripts from Compiègne and Conques a shorter account. Since it contains nothing different from Odo’s work, we have thought it better to omit it than to burden this volume with useless writings. It will be enough to point out that the two final chapters of the Life of Saint Gerald composed by Odo, which are missing from the Cluniac Library, were sent to us from a Cistercian manuscript [Column 0703C] by John Lannoy, a Cistercian monk of blessed memory. Attached to them, without the author’s name, is a sermon written in praise of blessed Gerald and divided into eight lessons, as such lessons are customarily read at Matins.

### 2. His lineage and age

Odo of Cluny traces Gerald’s lineage from the high blood of kings through Caesarius, bishop of Arles, and Abbot Aredius; others trace it through Mathilda, daughter of Pepin, king of Aquitaine, whom they believe to have been Gerald’s grandmother. However that may be, it is certain that Gerald was born to his father Gerald, count of Aurillac—counts were sometimes called illustrious local rulers—and his mother Adaltrude, parents of the highest distinction and wealth. He was born in the year of Christ 855, as may be gathered from Ademar of Chabannes in his list of the abbots of Saint Martial of Limoges. In that same year the chronicler records that the monastery of Beaulieu was founded by Radulf, bishop of Bourges, and that all the clerics of Saint Martial were transformed from canons into monks.

### 3. Charity toward the poor; fasts

Gerald always cultivated the pious training handed down by his parents through the highest virtues. Thus, because of his charity toward the poor, “seats were always prepared for them before him, and sometimes tables were set up, so that he himself could see what, and how much, was given them for refreshment. No one was ever excluded from the door without receiving alms. Indeed, his servants took care that he always had dishes at hand which he himself could give them. Drink, too, was brought to him; after inspecting and tasting it, he passed it on so that they might drink first. To them he also gave half of his own bread, believing that in these people he received Christ.”

While he took such pains to supply the needy with what they required, he himself “on three weekdays each week, throughout the whole period appointed for abstinence, abstained from meat. If, however, an annual feast occurred on one of those weekdays, he relaxed the abstinence in such a way that, on whichever weekday had been released, he abstained in its place on another day, and also refreshed one additional poor person on account of that feast. But if a fast fell on the Lord’s Day, he did not relax it at all or pass it over on that account; instead, he fulfilled the solemnity of the fast on the preceding Saturday.”

The holy Odo here defends this highly religious custom of transferring the Sunday fast to the preceding day against the charge of singularity. There is no doubt that its observance, introduced by Gerald and other holy men, gave occasion for the practice that remains in force today.

### 4. Modesty in clothing

His charity toward the poor was nourished and increased by his love of poverty and his contempt for more elegant dress. “He always used woolen or linen garments,” says Odo, “not in the manner now adopted and devised by the sons of Belial, but according to the ancient custom. They were made so that they gave off neither the odor of ostentatious display nor the mark of plebeian rusticity. As for silken or costly garments, he resolved not to adorn himself more than usual either on the occasion of any festival or in the presence of any marquis.”

Yet—and this may surprise you—this Christian modesty never diminished the authority of the man of God. Rather, “among all who knew him he possessed such reverence that whoever injured him was certain that it would not turn out well for him, as though he had committed sacrilege.”

Count Adelelmus, then the most powerful man of the time, experienced this very thing. After unsuccessfully attempting to besiege the castle of Aurillac, he was not permitted to return rejoicing, because he “had afflicted the heart of the just man with grief”; on the fourteenth day he died so terribly that a violent whirlwind completely uncovered the whole place where he lay.

### 5. Love of chastity

The most distinguished princes sought Gerald’s friendship, indeed even kinship by marriage. Among them was “William, duke of the Aquitanians,” as Ademar relates in his Chronicle under the year 910. Since he had no offspring and wished to unite his sister in marriage to holy Gerald, he was entirely unable to do so. For Gerald, leading a celibate life, was constantly urged to marry for the sake of having children, but he replied: “It is better to die without children than to leave behind wicked heirs.”

From this love of chastity arose his profound desire for the monastic life. Although, because of various hindering circumstances, he did not undertake that way of life, he always pursued it in spirit, so that “if one considers his vow, he preserved for Christ through devotion the fidelity of the monastic profession.”

One of the principal reasons was the scarcity of reputable monks at that time. For “being prudent and reflecting that those who profess a sublime purpose, when corrupted by love of the world, fall from on high all the more grievously, he judged it better to remain thus in secular dress than to attempt so arduous a task without approved collaborators.”

### 6. The foundation at Aurillac

“After he had devoted himself entirely to divine worship, so that he might also consecrate all his possessions to the Lord, he went to Rome and, by a solemn testament, assigned the distinguished estate of Aurillac to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. He attached to it such extensive resources that they could suffice for all the support of the monks whom he intended to gather there. He also assigned a rent to be paid annually at the tomb of blessed Peter.”

Aurillac is a town—or, as Saint Odo calls it, a castle—situated among the Arverni. It formerly belonged to the diocese of Clermont and now belongs to the diocese of Saint-Flour; there Gerald founded the famous monastery bearing the same name.

The learned Aegidius Laccarius of the Society of Jesus, in his special dissertation on the day and year of Gerald’s death and birth, plausibly assigns its origin to the year 894. Since Gerald obtained a privilege from Charles the Simple in the seventh year of that king’s reign—that is, in the year of Christ 899—according to the calculation of the Transligerani, who counted Charles’s years from his restoration, and since by this privilege the possessions assigned to the monastery of Aurillac were confirmed at the request of Adelgarius, abbot of that place, and the monks, it follows that this monastery had already been built and cultivated by monks for several years.

### 7. The testament of Saint Gerald

The testament of Saint Gerald, mentioned above by Saint Odo and constituting the principal charter of the monastery of Aurillac, was published by Andreas Chesnius in his notes to the Cluniac Library. Nevertheless, this author hesitates over whether it is precisely the same testament as the one praised by Saint Odo in the Life of Gerald, because that document makes no mention of the rent assigned annually to the tomb of blessed Peter.

Certainly, the confirmation of Gerald’s testament by King Charles in the seventh year of his reign sufficiently proves that it cannot refer to the document said to have been drawn up only in the seventeenth year of his reign. I would therefore readily believe that, a few days before his death, Gerald confirmed and enlarged an earlier testament that he himself had written by means of a later one, as we often read happened. Odo’s words seem to suggest this, if I am not mistaken:

“During the time he survived, he took the greatest care to release all those dependent on him in peace, lest an occasion for dispute should perhaps arise among them. The estates or slaves that he had not assigned to blessed Peter he left to certain relatives and soldiers, or at least to servants, though in some cases on the condition that, eleven years after their death, they should return to Aurillac.”

Almost the same conditions are found in Gerald’s testament as published by Chesnius.

### 8. Confirmed by kings

Charles the Simple ratified the erection of the monastery of Aurillac by his diploma. Our Stephanotius extracted this diploma, together with another by Louis the Younger confirming it, from a manuscript at Cantoën. Since both documents are relevant to our subject, we have thought it appropriate to present them here.

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Charles, king by the favoring mercy of God. If we grant suitable benefits to the places of the saints, consecrated to divine worship, we do not doubt that a reward of eternal recompense will be paid to us by God. Therefore we wish it to be known to the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own people, both present and future, that a certain illustrious man and beloved count, Gerald, sending his envoys and monks into the presence of our highness, petitioned our majesty through them with the most humble prayers that we might receive under the protection of our immunity his monastery, situated in the district of Auvergne and called Aurillac, founded in honor of Peter, prince of the apostles, and blessed Clement, where Abbot Adelgarius presides together with the community of monks serving God there; and the possessions belonging to the same monastery, which the abbot and monks, and Gerald himself, rector and founder of that place, have held—namely, the church of Saint Peter at Exitus, and at Glinicus, and at Curtiniacus, together with the church of Saint Cyricus, with estates and slaves, from which the monks themselves are to pay five solidi each year to the authority of Saint Peter of Poitiers; and Magrinus in Condacum; and vineyards handed over there by God-fearing people; and estates or anything else belonging to the aforesaid place, whether in property or in slaves.

> “Recognizing that his petition was just, and considering also the salvation of our soul, we willingly granted our assent and decreed that this our authority should be established toward the aforesaid monastery and its rectors under the fullest protection of our immunity. By it we prescribe and command that the abbot himself and the monks dwelling there remain secure under our protection, without the authority of any judge, except that of Gerald himself and his sister Avigerna. No public judge, or anyone exercising judicial authority, may enter the churches, places, lands, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery—which they now justly and legally possess in any districts or territories within the dominion of our kingdom, or which divine mercy may henceforth wish to increase as belonging to that holy place—in order to hear cases, exact fines, demand lodging or provisions, take sureties, or distrain the men of that monastery, whether free or otherwise, who live upon its land; nor may anyone seek any returns or unlawful pretexts in our time or in the future, or presume to exact anything mentioned above.

> “Rather, let the aforesaid abbot, his successors, and the monks quietly possess the property of the said monastery under the protection of our immunity, so that it may please those servants of God who serve the Lord there to implore the mercy of almighty God for us and for the condition of our kingdom with continual prayers.

> “So that the authority of this immunity and confirmation of ours may possess greater force in the name of God, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring. Sign of Charles, most glorious king. Heriveus, notary, in place of Archbishop Folco, examined and subscribed it. Count William acted as envoy. Given on the fourth day before the Nones of July, in the second indiction, in the seventh year of the reign of Charles, most serene king. Publicly enacted at Liturnum, happily in the name of God. Amen.”

Louis’s diploma reads as follows:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen. Louis, king of the Franks by the favoring mercy of God. If we grant suitable benefits to places consecrated to divine worship, we do not doubt that a reward of eternal recompense will be paid to us by God. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, that, when we were in Auvergne besieging the castle of Nonette (Nonnette-le-Beau), the privilege of Charles, our predecessor, was brought before us. We judged it worthy of great veneration and authority, and, at the earnest petition of Peter, abbot of Aurillac, adhering to the counsel of our household, we confirmed everything contained in that privilege, together with everything granted to the church of Aurillac by the testimony of the aforesaid privilege, in all its fiefs and possessions and in everything belonging to the right of that church, as well as in whatever that church might justly and reasonably acquire; and we ordered it secured by the impression of our name.

> “We further add and absolutely prohibit anyone in our kingdom from constructing, on any pretext, any building that could in any way harm the aforesaid church, or from presuming to take away its rights or possessions. Rather, let the aforementioned abbot, his successors, and the monks improve the possessions of that monastery in whatever ways they can and quietly possess them under the protection of our immunity, so that those servants serving God there may delight in imploring the mercy of almighty God for us and for the condition of our kingdom with continual prayers.

> “So that this may remain ratified in the future, we have ordered it confirmed by the impression of our ring. Publicly enacted at Nonette in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1169, with the following persons present in our palace, whose names and signs are subscribed: Sign of our count Theobald, our steward and secretary. Sign of Matthew, chamberlain. Sign of Guy, butler. Sign of Radulf, constable. Given by the hand of Hugh, chancellor and bishop of Soissons.”

### 9. The monks of Aurillac brought from the monastery of Vabres. The abbots of Aurillac

After the monastery of Aurillac had been built, “Gerald was always turning over in his mind how he might find monks of good character who could inhabit the place under a regular discipline. But since the scarcity of such men created difficulty in finding them, he was anxious and did not know what to do. Then he sent certain noble boys to the monastery of Vabres”—which, as we shall see below, had recently been built near Rodez by Raymond, count of Toulouse—“so that these boys might be trained among that brotherhood under the regular rule.

> “When the boys were ordered to return, however, because teachers were lacking, they soon dissolved into childish softness, neglected the rigor of discipline, and so it happened that the matter did not come to fruition. Nevertheless, compelled by necessity, he placed one of them over the others. But since that man lived dissolute­ly, the man of God was deeply distressed, because he could neither correct him nor find another whom he could appoint in his place.”

I cannot easily say whether this first abbot of Aurillac, who administered the office he had undertaken so badly, was the same as Adelgarius, who is listed first in Charles’s charter and in the catalogue of the abbots of Aurillac, since Saint Odo does not mention his name here.

The Chronicle of Malleais, cited by Labbe, reports that Berno, abbot of Cluny, presided first over the monks of Aurillac before the others. But I fear this is not true, since the Aurillac chronicler published in the second volume of our *Analecta* places Adelgarius before the others and omits Berno. From the same source we also learn that John, his successor, obtained from the supreme pontiff, who was favorably disposed toward him, a privilege “that the monastery of Aurillac should be free from every domination except that of Saint Peter and the Roman See.”

The same John is also mentioned in a certain document published by the distinguished Baluzius in his notes to Regino. There he is said to have been a relative of blessed Gerald and simultaneously provost of the monasteries of Tulle and Aurillac.

### 10. Gerald’s adversities

Gerald’s holiness, confirmed by many miracles, was also tested by various misfortunes, the seizure of his estates, and the captivity of his relatives. His principal adversary was Ademar. When Ademar attempted to draw Gerald, who was devoted to Charles the Simple, over to his own side and subject him to his rule—as Saint Odo puts it—he left no stone unturned in order to crush a man wholly devoted to works of Christian piety, whether by deceit or by force of arms.

After Gerald had nobly survived these dangers and believed that an open path to the longed-for peace of his soul lay before him, he was suddenly deprived of the sight of his eyes and endured blindness with the greatest patience for seven years and more.

### 11. Piety during illness

“Recognizing that his dissolution was already approaching, he ordered Bishop Amblard to be summoned, so that the bishop might fortify his passing with his prayers. Throughout the whole period of his weakness, he so compelled his failing limbs to divine service that he would not permit even a single nocturnal office to be celebrated except in the church; and, while lying down, he listened to one Mass proper to the day and another for the dead.”

### 12. Death

“On Friday, as day was beginning to dawn, feeling that his condition was worsening, he ordered the chaplains to perform the nocturnal office before him, while the bishop celebrated in the church with his attendants. He himself sang with those singing, until after the Matins office he had also completed all the Hours of the day. Then, finishing Compline, he armed himself with the sign of the cross and added the word that had always been most familiar to him: ‘Come to his aid, saints of God.’ Having spoken this last word, he silently closed his eyes.

“Those who were present, seeing that he had ceased to speak, summoned the bishop and placed his holy limbs upon sackcloth. While the others sang for his departure, one of the priests hastily celebrated Mass and brought the most holy mystery. When someone said that he had already departed, Gerald, still retaining consciousness, opened his eyes and showed by this sign that he had not yet departed. Then he received of his own accord the Lord’s Body, which he had been awaiting, and thus that blessed soul migrated to heaven.”

Thus far Odo’s words. If you compare them with what precedes, you will readily understand the year of his death. It cannot be placed before 909 or postponed beyond 912. The first limit is ruled out by the tablets of the testament drawn up by Gerald himself in September 909; the second by the death of Adelard, or Amblard, bishop of Clermont, who was present at Gerald’s death and had Arnold as his successor in September 912.

“But,” you may object, “what prevents us from assigning Gerald’s death to 910 or the following year?” Odo’s authority. For he testifies that Gerald migrated to heaven on a Friday. Yet in none of these years, except 909, did Friday fall on 13 October, the day on which his death is nevertheless celebrated both at Aurillac and throughout Aquitaine.

I am not unaware that the Limoges chronicler assigned Gerald’s final day to the year 917. But Odo’s testimony ought to prevail over the others, since, as he himself asserts, he learned Gerald’s deeds and death from Gerald’s companions and later committed them to writing.

### 13. Burial, translation, and cult

“They carried that holy body, accompanied by very large crowds, to Aurillac, as he himself had ordered, and placed it in an *ariston* stone [read: *aristatonem*, that is, an honorable distinction], on the left side of the basilica itself, beside the altar of Saint Peter, so that his tomb might be on the right and he himself nevertheless toward the right.”

There, after it had shone forth through various miracles for seven years, “the sarcophagus, which had been covered up to the middle of its lid with earth trampled down by feet, gradually began to rise above that same earth.” The ancients regarded this as an indication of proven holiness, as we observed in the Acts of Saint Droctoveus, abbot, in the first century.

This led to the establishment of the public cult of Gerald that is still offered to him today. What a holy man had long before predicted to one of his companions also came to pass: “the walls of this house would often be too narrow for the peoples who would gather there.”

The memory of Saint Gerald is celebrated throughout the entire province. Recent martyrologies and the ancient monuments of Aurillac mention him on 13 October, from which it is clear that this is the day of his heavenly birth.

### 14. Illustrious men

In addition to the exceptional devotion of the people toward Saint Gerald and the astonishing crowds flowing together from every direction, the observance and learning of the monks made this place famous in subsequent times as well.

Jordan, bishop of Limoges, praised the abbot of Aurillac among the others at the council held at Bourges in the year of Christ 1031, because “acting according to the rule, he watched over the winning of souls rather than concerning himself with fleeting and transitory matters.”

Among men distinguished for learning, Gerbert claims no minor place for himself. He was first a monk of this place, then archbishop of Reims and Ravenna, and finally became the Roman pontiff called Sylvester. Letters survive that he sent to Girard and Raymond, abbots of Aurillac, in which both the gratitude of his spirit toward the monuments of Aurillac and his extraordinary judgments of devotion toward Saint Gerald are evident.

The same reputation for learning continued among the monks of Aurillac in the twelfth century, as may be gathered from John of Salisbury, bishop of Chartres, who praises them in Letter 60 “because they possessed knowledge and practical experience of many things.”

### 15.

In the middle of the fifteenth century monastic discipline began to decline at Aurillac. Stephen, the last regular abbot, was removed—not without suspicion of poisoning—and John, bishop of Castres, was substituted in his place. After him the place successively received commendatory abbots. Through their negligence, as the regular buildings fell into decay, the monastery eventually passed to secular canons, with Pius V approving this change.

### 16. The monastery of Vabres

As for the monastery of Vabres, where Gerald arranged for boys to be trained in monastic matters, it had been founded shortly before that time, as I have already said, near Rodez, in Rouergue, by Raymond, count of Toulouse, with the agreement of his wife Berteyza, at the Dordogne River.

The principal charter is dated “the third day before the Ides of November, in the twenty-third year of King Charles,” called Charles the Bald. He says that he was doing this for the remedy of his own soul and those of his father Fulcuald and his mother Senegundis, as well as his brother Fredelo. Therefore he grants his own property, “situated in the district of Rouergue, in the vicariate of Curia,” namely “a village called Vaber, to Abbot Adaigisus and his monks, for the construction of a monastery in honor of the holy Savior and holy Mary, Mother of God, and Saint Denis the martyr, so that they might gather in that place a community of monks who would serve there according to the rule of Saint Benedict, receive guests, refresh the poor, and faithfully pray for themselves.”

### 17.

He grants these things “in such a way that no king or any other power shall have the right to grant these properties as benefices, exchange them, or give them away, but only that they should remain perpetually under the king’s protection and immunity.” Raymond himself became guardian and defender of the place; after his death he appointed his sons Bernard, Fulcuald, and Odo as defenders in succession.

This charter was published by Catel in Book I of *On the Counts of Toulouse*, pp. 69–70. There, drawing on Abbot Agius of Vabres, he observes that Abbot Adalgisus and the monks had fled from the monastery of Palmatus, which the Marcomanni had plundered near Périgord, and had come to the attention of Count Raymond. After consulting Bishop Helisacarius, Raymond founded the monastery of Vabres to receive them.

Charles the Bald confirmed this arrangement in the fourteenth year of his reign by a royal diploma, which the same Catel reports in the same place.

The following words of Abbot Agius deserve attention:

> “At that time, therefore, there was in the province of Gaul, in the district of Périgord, a monastery called Palmatus, in which ten servants of God continually served, possessing nothing of their own except what the rule of Saint Benedict allowed. There were many other monasteries in the same province, considerably richer in worldly goods. But when the foretold plague came upon them and the danger of famine arose, the monks began to neglect the rule of Saint Benedict and, contrary to its discipline, to possess personal property. The monks of Palmatus, avoiding this, considered it wicked and unlawful.
>
> “For they themselves said that those who sought personal property on earth could in no way be monks—nor, indeed, could those who sought their own will, except insofar as they possessed their own faults and their own place. They were poor in possessions but rich in faith. Their abbot was a man named Adalgasius, venerable with white hair, upright in conduct, cheerful in appearance, born of a not ignoble lineage, and most eloquent in speech.
>
> “When he saw that he could in no way endure their savagery in the face of the present danger, he began, like a good shepherd, to traverse every region, in case he might find somewhere he could preserve his poor little sheep from the mouths of those raging against them. For it was by no means suitable for him to remain on his own soil, where he saw repeated and pitiable slaughter among his beloved disciples.
>
> “It therefore came to the ears of the distinguished marquis Raymond, who at that time held the office of ruler of Toulouse, that the venerable Abbot Adalgasius, together with his dependents, had been exiled from his native soil by an incursion of pagans.
>
> “Finally, Raymond did not cease sending urgent messages to the aforementioned abbot, appearing to beg him not to be reluctant to come to Toulouse to speak with him. But the abbot could not immediately go to him, since he was nearly sixty miles from the city of Toulouse; and, unwilling to travel to him for an uncertain matter, he sent two disciples to him.”

Raymond disclosed his plan to them. When they returned, they reported the matter to Adalgasius. Adalgasius himself went to Toulouse, and the monastery of Vabres was built. John XXII later erected it as a cathedral church, which soon thereafter became secular.

Abbot Agius, the author of the preceding fragment, was later archbishop of Narbonne at the beginning of the tenth century. We regret that Catel did not publish his letter in full.

[Column 0709]

## LIFE OF SAINT GREGORY, BISHOP OF TOURS, BY ODO

*(See among the Prolegomena to Gregory of Tours, Patrologia, vol. LXXI, col. 115.)*

[Column 0709]

# FIVE SERMONS OF SAINT ODO, ABBOT OF CLUNY

*(From the Cluniac Library and Martene.)*

## FIRST SERMON: ON THE CHAIR OF SAINT PETER

[Column 0709D]

I rejoice, dearly beloved, in the religious affection of your devotion, and I give thanks to God that I recognize in you the piety of Christian unity. For, as your very large attendance bears witness, you understand that the return of this day belongs to the common joy and that it celebrates the honor of the entire flock’s shepherd through annual feasts.

Although the whole Church of God is ordered in distinct degrees, so that the integrity of the consecrated body subsists from its various members, nevertheless we are all one in Christ. No one is so divided from another by office that the humility of any portion does not belong to the connection of the head.

In the unity, therefore, of faith and baptism, dearly beloved, we share an undivided fellowship and a common dignity, according to the words of the most blessed apostle Peter, whom this sermon must serve: “You yourselves, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Christ our Lord” (1 Peter 2:5).

The sign of the cross makes all who have been reborn in Christ kings, while the anointing of the Holy Spirit consecrates them priests. Thus, apart from this special service of our ministry, all spiritual Christians recognize that they share in royal lineage and priestly office.

For what is as royal as making a spirit subject to God the ruler of the body? And what is as priestly as dedicating a pure conscience and offering spotless sacrifices of devotion from the altar of the heart?

Since this has been made common to all through the grace of God, it is religious and praiseworthy for us today to rejoice in the advancement of our own patron. Although throughout the whole body of the Church the sacrament of the apostolic episcopate is celebrated, we have special reason for rejoicing because the oil of blessing, poured out abundantly, flowed more copiously upon the higher members and descended no less generously upon the lower.

Since, then, dearly beloved, our participation in this office provides abundant material for common joy, the truer and more excellent reason for rejoicing will be present if you do not linger over consideration of our lowliness. It is far more useful and far more worthy to raise the mind’s gaze toward contemplating the glory of the most blessed apostle Peter and to celebrate this day chiefly in his veneration.

He was cleansed by such abundant purifications that, although he alone received many things, nothing passed to anyone without his participation. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and Christ had given himself entirely for the restoration of the human race. Nothing was beyond the readiness of wisdom; nothing was too difficult for power. The elements served, angelic spirits ministered, and the sacrament could in no way be ineffective, since the unity of his divinity and the Trinity were working together.

And yet, from the whole world, Peter alone is chosen to be placed before the calling of all nations, all the apostles, and all the Fathers of the Church, so that although there are many priests among God’s people, Peter may govern them all, just as Christ principally governs them all.

Great and marvelous, dearly beloved, was the divine condescension in granting this man a share in his own power. If he wished other leaders to share anything with Peter, he gave it only through Peter; he did not deny anything to the others.

Finally, the Lord asks all the apostles what people think about him, and the common speech of those answering continued as long as the ambiguity of human ignorance persisted. But when the disciples’ understanding is examined, the first in the confession of the Lord is the one who was first in apostolic dignity.

When he had said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16), Jesus answered him: “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16:17). That is: You are blessed because my Father taught you. An earthly opinion did not deceive you; heavenly inspiration instructed you. It was not flesh and blood, but he whose only-begotten Son I am, who revealed me to you.

The most blessed Peter, therefore, prince of the apostolic order and the first to become the Lord’s confessor, was constituted the rock of the Church and the keeper of the kingdom. Hence he is given a name from his deed, and a title is imposed from the merit of his power, when he deserved to hear from the Lord: “And I say to you” (Matthew 16:18). That is: Just as my Father revealed my divinity to you, so I make known to you your excellence, because “you are Peter” (ibid.).

That is: although I am the unshakable rock, I, the cornerstone who makes both one; I am the foundation besides which no one can lay another; nevertheless, you too are a rock, because you are made firm by my power, so that what is proper to me by power may be shared with you through participation with me.

“Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (ibid.). “Upon this,” he says, “this strength, I will construct an eternal temple, and the exalted height of my Church, to be joined to heaven, will rise from the firmness of this faith.”

This confession the gates of hell will not hold, nor will the bonds of death bind. For this voice is the voice of life; and just as it raises its confessors to the heavenly places, so it casts its deniers down into the depths below. Therefore it is said to the most blessed Peter: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (ibid., 19). O immeasurable and boundless goodness, that a man placed on earth should hold heaven! [Col. 0712C] Behold, at Peter’s command the gates of the divine kingdom now stand open. For he received from Christ the keys of the kingdom of heaven, so that, once the bonds of sins had been loosed, he might open heaven to believers. O how near and profound are the remedies! The kingdom of God is close at hand for the world, if it hastens to Peter. Christ placed Peter in the world in his own stead as the keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom, so that no one might think ascent to heaven difficult for him.

The right of this power indeed passed also to the other apostles, and the constitution of this decree came to all the leaders of the Church; yet it is not without reason that what is entrusted to one is proclaimed to all. For this is entrusted particularly to Peter because Peter’s form is set before all the rulers of the Church. [Col. 0712D] Peter’s privilege therefore remains wherever judgment is rendered according to his equity. There is neither excessive severity nor excessive leniency, except what the blessed pontiff and apostle Peter has bound or loosed.

Therefore, beloved, although we ought universally to rejoice at the commemoration of all the saints, nevertheless we have good reason to exult, rejoice, and glory in the excellence of this, our patron, whom the grace of God raised to so lofty a summit among all the members of the Church that, in the body whose head is Christ, he established him as a most radiant light of the eyes. And just as we ourselves have experienced, and our forebears have proved, we believe that, in order to obtain God’s mercy, we are always to be assisted by the prayers of our special patron, so that in proportion as we are weighed down by our own sins, we may be lifted up by apostolic merits.

As the Lord’s Passion approached, and knowing that the disciples’ steadfastness would be shaken, the Lord said to Peter: “Simon, behold, Satan has demanded you, to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, and when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:31–32). The danger of fearful temptation was common to all the apostles, and they likewise needed the aid of divine protection; nevertheless, the Lord assumes a special care for Peter and makes supplication particularly for Peter’s faith, as though the condition of the others would be more secure if the mind of their leader were not overcome.

In Peter, therefore, the strength of all is fortified, and the aid of divine grace is so ordered [Col. 0713B] that the steadfastness granted to Peter through Christ may be conferred through Peter upon the apostles. Since, then, beloved, we see such protection divinely established for us, we rightly and justly rejoice in the merits and dignity of our leader, giving thanks to the eternal King, our Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ, because he gave such power to him whom he made prince and bishop of the whole Church.

If anything is rightly done and rightly discerned through us in our own times, it must be attributed to his works and his governance, to whom it was said: “And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32), and to whom, after his resurrection, the Lord said three times, in response to his threefold profession of love: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17). He himself also carries out the Lord’s command as shepherd, strengthening us by his exhortations and never ceasing to pray for us, so that we may not be overcome by any temptation.

If he extends this care of his compassion to all God’s people everywhere, how much more will he deign to furnish his aid to us, his foster-children! Let us therefore ascribe to him the anniversary of our service and this feast, under whose patronage we have been protected and have merited, through his merits, to share in such a fellowship. Let us also seek him as the helper of our prayer, through whose prayers we trust that we are delivered both from spiritual enemies and from bodily foes. Let us therefore ask him, by his intercession, to obtain for us that, once the bonds of the flesh have been destroyed, we may deserve to enter the courts of the heavenly city.

Since, then, the discourse demands an end, let us exalt the most blessed Peter in the Church of the people, and, praising him in the assembly of the elders, let us bless the Lord Jesus, who lives with God the Father and the Holy Spirit in the unity of divine majesty, throughout infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON II. IN VENERATION OF SAINT MARY MAGDALENE

Although throughout the four quarters of the world, propagated through the fellowship of the faithful, the most sacred Church celebrates the distinction of Saint Mary Magdalene as an example of devout imitation; and although, in the writings of the most blessed evangelists, her devoted service, persevering ministry, great ardor of love, and service of that holy intimacy, as well as her unspeakable steadfastness even to the triumph of the Lord’s Passion, are held in high honor—not to mention what she did at the death of her Redeemer, even when the apostles were fleeing, and the fact that the Lord himself, the angel of the great counsel, after rising from the dead first appeared to her—nevertheless, concerned for the benefit of readers, we have taken care briefly to offer beforehand those things concerning the little flowers of her virtues which, like gems, illuminate the pages of the holy Scriptures and make them bloom, as it were, through the imprint of their own radiance.

Thus, if someone should perhaps lack the leisure to travel through the vast ocean of the holy Gospel in order, in which the proclamations of such great faith are contained, let him at least not refuse, kindled by desire for her, to read this little sheet of our insignificance. According to the splendor of the world, therefore, the most blessed Mary was born of illustrious parents. As the traditions of the Fathers maintain, she was called Mary Magdalene from the town of Magdala. Not only the nobility of her birth but also the rights of her parents’ inheritance made her splendid beyond measure, so that a doubled honor spread the excellence of her name everywhere. For among human beings, the names of the rich are usually better known than those of the poor.

But because pleasure sometimes accompanies an abundance of possessions, the years of her youth surrendered themselves to slippery pursuits, with the reins of chastity loosened. She is the woman of whom the evangelist Luke writes: “There was a certain woman in the city who was a sinner; and because she loved much, many sins were forgiven her” (Luke 7:37). And of whom Mark says: “When Jesus had risen early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons” (Mark 16:9).

How compassionate and merciful God has been toward converted sinners is demonstrated by her perfection. She not only obtained cleansing from her crime but, made a companion of the apostles, was granted to be the messenger of the Lord’s Resurrection to them. Afterwards, inspired by the divine Spirit, reflecting the gaze of her mind back upon herself and unable to bear the losses of her former life, when she learned that the Lord and Creator of the entire human race had come into the house of Simon—he who had not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance (Mark 2:17)—she did not, because of the enormity of her crimes, distrust the clemency of her Creator. Taking the most precious ointment, she hastened quickly to that very fountain of mercy, falling before the Lord’s compassionate feet and intensifying the bitterness of her heart through an abundant fountain of tears.

Then, amid the tears of repentance, she began to bathe the feet of her Maker, to wipe them with the hair of her devotion, to cherish them unceasingly with kisses of true humility, and to anoint them with the purest ointment of her love. Since she was not rejected in such devoted service but rather mercifully received, trusting in the boldness of intimacy, she even poured out the fragrance of the most precious liquid over the Lord’s most holy head. The whole house was so filled with the fragrance that it smelled like spices. She said nothing with her mouth, but through the benefits of her outward service she revealed the flame of her repentance and the ardor of her love, as though she were speaking these very words:

“O most merciful Lord Jesus, who know all things and are the true examiner of hearts, who do not desire the death of sinners but rather that they should turn and live: you yourself understand what my sobs demand, what my tears, drawn from the depths, implore, and what my bitter groaning asks.
