I am a sinner and unclean, polluted by the stain of every abominable crime. But because I contaminated my life from my earliest years, I flee to you, my Lord, who are eternal life, so that you may restore the life I wickedly lost and mercifully rescue me from the jaws of the abyss; deliver me in your mercy and draw me out by your power, you who alone regard labor and sorrow.”

What she obtained through this profession of love the Lord himself makes clear. When Simon was indignant that he allowed a sinful woman to approach him, the Lord turned to him and replied, among other things: “Amen, I say to you, many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47).

Having obtained the Lord’s clemency, as Luke describes, she immediately set everything else aside and became so intimate with him that she followed him not only in mind but also in body, supplying him with food and clothing from her own resources, since she was very wealthy, fulfilling in both senses the Lord’s command: “Whoever serves me must follow me” (John 12:26).

Mystically, this most blessed woman signifies the holy Church. She is rightly said to have come into Simon’s house and, healed from all the contagions of her former life—Simon being interpreted as “obedient”—to have condemned her former errors by burning them away, to have set aside all the filth of idols, and through the water of baptism to have obtained forgiveness for her sins. Every day she follows the Lord, not by the movement of her feet but by the imitation of her works.

This woman watered the Lord’s feet with tears of repentance and anointed them with the ointment of devout confession, because the Church, believing the Lord Jesus Christ to be true Lord and true man, daily begs him, with sobs of tears, for cleansing from her offenses. And while she receives and proclaims with fitting reverence the mysteries of his assumed humanity, because he deigned to dwell among human beings, she pours upon the Lord’s feet the ointment of pure nard—that is, faithful nard.

She speaks in the Song of Love, saying: “While the king was on his couch, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song of Songs 1:11). In the literal sense, the blessed hands of Mary Magdalene fulfilled these words; spiritually, she does not cease to fulfill them every day when, gloriously proclaiming praises to the Creator throughout the whole breadth of the world, she says: “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and manifests through us the fragrance of his knowledge in every place, for we are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2:14–15).

When she confesses and proclaims, with fitting worship and reverence, the sublimity of the divine majesty that is equal to the Father, and recalls with worthy veneration how far the vigor of her natural understanding has been suffused with the illumination of heavenly light, and extends the keen sight of her mind to contemplate such power, she surely pours over his head the most precious ointment.

When Judas Iscariot is said to have become indignant against this most holy woman because of the outpouring of so much ointment, it is plainly understood that the reprobate and unbelieving daily rage against the holy Church and disparage its worship and devotion, seeing that throughout the four regions of the world, through its teaching and examples, the power of the Lord’s divinity and the mercy of his humanity have been made clear to all.

Therefore, concerning this holy woman who anticipated anointing the Lord’s body, he himself says: “Amen, I say to you, wherever this Gospel is preached in the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her” (Mark 14:9). For it is not only preached throughout the whole world of this holy woman, that she anointed the Lord’s head; the Church also performs this daily in its holy actions, as has already been mentioned.

Mary Magdalene is also rightly so called. Magdalus is interpreted as “tower,” and signifies the Church. A tower is not only a higher dwelling but also a safer one, not easily open to enemies; and thus it designates the Church, which, abandoning earthly things, desires heavenly ones, fighting against spiritual wickedness and entrusting its strength not to itself but to the Lord. It prays with the Prophet, saying: “Be to me a tower of strength in the face of the enemy” (Psalm 60:4).

This is that strong and impregnable tower to which the voice of the Bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “Your neck is like the tower of David, which was built with battlements. A thousand shields hang upon it, and every kind of armor of the strong” (Song of Songs 4:4). And concerning which Solomon says: “The name of the Lord is a most strong tower; the righteous runs to it and will be exalted” (Proverbs 18:10).

But since, compelled by the interpretation of the name, we have departed a little from the surface of the historical sense, let us look upon the Lord’s most merciful intimacy toward blessed Mary and her sister Martha, and their devout service in all things.

For we read, as the evangelist Luke relates, that “Jesus entered a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house; and she had a sister named Mary. She also sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to his word, while Martha was busy with much serving” (Luke 10:38–40). Therefore she took up a complaint not only against her sister but even against the Lord himself, saying: “Lord, is it no concern of yours that my sister has left me alone to serve? Tell her, then, to help me” (ibid.).

But he who is not a respecter of persons, who judges the merits of individuals and knows that the soul is better than the body, just as spiritual food is better than bodily food, praises the work of one without condemning that of the other. He said: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things; but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the better part, which will not be taken away from her forever” (Luke 10:41–42).

Spiritually, these two most devoted women, who received the Lord into their house, signify the Church’s two ways of life: the active and the contemplative. Through Martha, who was occupied with much service, the labor of the active life is expressed. Through Mary, however, who sat at the Lord’s feet and received his word with attentive mind, the sweetness of the contemplative life is signified. The more its flavor is tasted, the more the mind is separated from visible things and the turmoil of cares. Rejecting all temporal matters, the mind desires to be alone with God.

For it delights to hear heavenly commands, as this most blessed Mary did, sitting at the Lord’s feet and receiving his word with attentive ear. In her was fulfilled what had once been spoken through the blessed Moses: “And those who draw near to his feet will receive instruction from him” (Deuteronomy 33:3).

How pleasing she was to the clemency of her Creator through her devoted service and the unquenchable ardor of her love, the evangelist John makes clear when he describes the venerable and unheard-of resurrection of Lazarus after four days. “Jesus loved Martha,” he says, “and her sister Mary, and Lazarus” (John 11:5).

Further on he recalls that, summoned by her sister, when she came to where the Lord was, she fell before his feet, saying: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died” (ibid.). But when Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, “he groaned in spirit and troubled himself, and said: Where have you laid him? They said to him: Lord, come and see. And Jesus wept” (ibid.).

He plainly revealed the clemency of his compassion through the humanity he had assumed, when, moved by the enormity of her grief, he did not disdain to shed tears of compassion, while nevertheless preserving the divine mystery.

The sublimity of her birth and the dignity of her worldly splendor are recognized in this event concerning blessed Mary Magdalene, since, when her brother had been dead for four days, such a great multitude of noble and powerful Jews came together to console her grief. They did not allow her to hasten to her brother’s tomb without their presence, saying: “She is going to the tomb to weep there” (John 11:31).

This was arranged by the Lord’s mercy so that, as he was about to perform so great a miracle, many Jews might be present. Thus, while one person was raised in the body, many might be raised in mind and become his most ready witnesses and praisers. Therefore the same evangelist later reports: “The crowd that had been with Jesus when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead bore witness” (John 12:17).

Typologically, this woman, mourning her brother who had been dead four days, prefigures the holy Church, which never ceases to mourn on account of the peril of those held liable by crimes and buried beneath the habitual stain of human sins, who have incurred from their own persons a reputation of the worst kind. For “we are all brothers in Christ” (Matthew 23:8).

The Lord is said to weep over Lazarus’s death when, looking upon such hearts with compassion and visiting them through the grace of repentance, he bends them toward the lamentation of penitence. He is said to do what he arranges that we should accomplish most intently through the impulse of his own inspiration. The same is true of the statement: “The Spirit himself pleads for us with unspeakable groanings” (Romans 8:29).

And just as Lazarus, after the outpouring of tears, is raised bodily before the astonished crowds, so sinners, after tears of repentance and the completion of worthy mortification of the flesh, are raised in soul, while the merciful Lord promises through the Prophet: “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, all his sins will be consigned to oblivion” (Ezekiel 33:2).

But having briefly offered these preliminary remarks, we must proceed to her steadfastness in faith and the ardor of her most fervent love, as well as to what she did with special intimacy during the Lord’s Passion—something to be admired by all mortals, or rather imitated.

For, as we have already said, this holy woman followed the Lord and ministered to him most devotedly from her abundant resources. After she saw him seized, bound, scourged, and mocked with every kind of derision and insult, and finally placed upon the cross for the salvation of the human race; after she saw even the disciples who had earlier said, “Let us go also, and die with him” (John 11:16), turn their backs and flee—she herself remained with him, because she who had loved him more closely and fervently could not be separated from him even when he was dead.

Thus was fulfilled at the time of the Lord’s Passion what had once been spoken through the blessed Job: “My bone has clung to my skin, with my flesh consumed, and only my lips have been left about my teeth” (Job 19:20). For just as skin clings to bone when the flesh has been consumed, so blessed Mary Magdalene remained with the Lord while the disciples were fleeing. She remained until she saw him placed in the tomb, embalmed with various spices.

Then, grieving and inflamed with immense sorrow, she departed and went straight to the known place of her Redeemer’s tomb, where she bought spices. That very night, insofar as she was able, she prepared the ointments. On the Sabbath, in accordance with the command of the law, she remained silent. When the sun had set, she devoted herself to whatever remained in the preparation of the ointments.

At dawn on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, she came to the tomb with the spices she had prepared, desiring to anoint his most sacred body, whom she had loved with immense love while he was alive. Although the female sex is usually timid about walking in darkness, this woman, who loved the Lord with her whole heart, feared nothing.

There was in her perfect love, which casts out fear. Neither because of the weakness of her sex, nor because of the size of the stone, nor because of fear of the guards did she turn aside from the journey she had begun, until she reached the Lord’s tomb without fear.

The steadfastness of this woman was beautifully prefigured in the Book of Kings, when the Philistines yoked cows that had recently calved to a cart and shut up their calves at home. “The cows went straight along the road,” as it is written, “taking the road that leads to Beth-shemesh, and going and lowing, without turning aside either to the right or to the left” (1 Kings 6:12).

So blessed Mary Magdalene, desiring to visit the Lord’s tomb, proceeded like a lowing and groaning cow, deprived for a time of the presence of her Lord, offering all the faithful an example to imitate: that as we walk along the way of God, we should not turn aside from the journey we have begun because of the temptation of demons, the fear of human beings, or concern for our relatives. For a reward is promised to those who begin, but it is given to those who persevere.

Allegorically, darkness was in the heart of this most sacred woman when she came to the Lord’s tomb, because, ignorant of his resurrection, she was seeking the living among the dead. Then the sun rose in her mind when she not only saw that he had risen but also believed, and saw that the stone had been removed from the tomb.

Because she did not find the Lord’s body, she believed it had been stolen, and hastening, she announced to the disciples what she had seen. Concerning her, the voice of the Church truly says in the Song of Songs:

“On my bed at night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him. I will rise and go around the city, seeking him whom my soul loves. The watchmen who guard the city found me. ‘Have you seen him whom my soul loves?’ And when I had passed them, I found him whom my soul loves. I will hold him and will not let him go until I bring him into the house of my father and into the chamber of my mother” (Song of Songs 3:1–4).

As we have said, this holy woman ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved, and said to them: “They have taken my Lord from the tomb, and I do not know where they have laid him.” They ran to the tomb and found it just as the woman had said. Then the disciples departed and returned to themselves. But Mary stood outside at the tomb, weeping (John 20:2–3, 10–11).

Here we must consider how great a love for the Lord had inflamed this woman’s mind. Even when the disciples were leaving the Lord’s tomb, she did not leave. And because she did not cease searching, she deserved to be the first to see him.

She wept because she did not see the one she desired so greatly. She wept because she thought that the Lord’s body had been stolen from the tomb. While she was weeping, she bent down and looked into the tomb.

She had already seen that the tomb was empty and had announced to the disciples that the Lord had been stolen from it. What does it mean that she bends down again, except that she desires to see again? For example, when we lose something, although we may search for it by running here and there repeatedly, we nevertheless return again and again to the place where we remember having put it and look there.

So this holy woman, although she ran here and there seeking the Lord’s body, nevertheless, anxious over his absence, frequently looked toward the tomb where she knew he had been placed. Therefore, although she did not immediately deserve to see the Lord, she was not deprived of the sight of angels. For she saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain.

They said to her: “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?” (John 20:13–15.) The angels asked not to lessen her desire to seek him but to increase it. For when we weep because of a loss and someone asks the reason for our tears, the inquiry often increases our weeping. So they asked the cause of her grief in order to increase her longing through tears, knowing that blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted (Matthew 5:4).

But the woman reveals why she was weeping when she adds: “Because they have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.” After she had said this, she turned back and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus (John 20:13–14).

She is rightly said to have turned back in order to deserve to see the Lord. For one who turns back directs his eyes toward the place where previously he had his back. She turned back, as it were, when, setting aside the clouds of doubt, she began partly to believe in Christ’s resurrection.

Nevertheless, the Lord delayed revealing himself to her because, although she loved him, she did not believe that he had risen: thus she both saw him and did not recognize him. Therefore the evangelist says: “Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him: Lord, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him” (John 20:15).

The power of love has this characteristic: whoever loves someone greatly thinks that everyone else loves him as well. Yet this woman was not entirely mistaken when she supposed that the Lord was a gardener. For just as it is the gardener’s task to uproot harmful weeds so that good plants may flourish, so the Lord Jesus Christ daily uproots vices from his garden—that is, from his Church—so that virtues may grow.

Although the female sex is physically weak for carrying burdens, because of the greatness of her love she considered this task light and possible, saying: “If you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him.”

Jesus said to her: “Mary.” She turned and said: “Rabboni,” which means “Teacher.” Jesus said to her: “Do not touch me” (ibid.).

Because earlier the Lord had addressed her as a woman, using the common designation of her sex, and she had not recognized him, he called her by her own name so that she might at least recognize the one who recognized her. For he said: “Mary.”

Since the number of the elect is certain to the Lord, great grace is given to those who are shown to be known by God by their own names. Such was Moses, to whom it was said: “I have known you by name” (Exodus 33:12). Therefore, after the Lord called the woman by her own name, she immediately recognized the one who recognized her and said: “Rabboni,” which means “Teacher.”

When she said this, she immediately fell to the ground, wishing to hold his feet in adoration, recognizing him because he had called her by name. But the Lord said to her: “Do not touch me.”

It must not be thought that after his resurrection he refused to be touched by women, since it is said of the two who were leaving his tomb that they approached and held his feet. Rather, he forbade her to touch him because he did not yet find her mind perfect in faith: she had been seeking the living Lord among the dead.

Why he did not wish her to touch him is made clear when it is added: “For I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20:17). That is: Because you seek me among the dead as though I were dead, and do not yet believe that according to my divinity I am equal to the Father, do not touch me. For the Lord has not ascended to the Father in the mind of one who does not believe that he is equal to the Father.

And because blessed Mary had not yet perfectly understood the power of his divinity, she was then forbidden to touch his feet. “Go instead to my brothers and say to them: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, my God and your God.” Mary came announcing to the disciples: “I have seen the Lord, and he said these things to me” (ibid.).

The most merciful compassion of God is here revealed toward the female sex. Because death had been brought into the world through a woman, and lest the female sex should forever be held in reproach, God willed that the joys of the Resurrection should be announced to men through the female sex, through which the sorrow of death had been announced. It was as though he said: “From the hand of the one from whom you received the cup of death, hear from her mouth the joys of the Resurrection.”

And just as through blessed Mary ever-virgin, the world’s only hope, the gates of paradise were opened to us and Eve’s curse was excluded, so through blessed Mary Magdalene the reproach of the female sex was erased, and the splendor of our resurrection, arising in the Lord’s resurrection, was announced to us by her.

Thus Mary is aptly interpreted as “star of the sea.” Although this interpretation specially suits the Mother of God, through whose virginal birth the Sun of righteousness shone upon the world, it can also suit blessed Magdalene, who, coming with spices to the Lord’s tomb, was the first to announce the splendor of the Lord’s resurrection to the world.

And if the disciples were called apostles because they were sent by him to preach the Gospel to every creature, no less was blessed Mary Magdalene sent by the Lord himself to the apostles, so that she might remove from their hearts their doubt and disbelief concerning his Resurrection.

We therefore beg you, Lord, that you who bestowed upon her such great grace of your mercy may deign to be reconciled to us through her merits, so that we, buried beneath the burden of our sins and unable to obtain forgiveness, may, with her devout patronage—she who served you devotedly, indeed in a special way, in this world—be freed from the stain of all crimes through the support of her intercession. Now she triumphs in heaven, enjoying glory with the angels of splendor and shining with her accustomed radiance of love. May she lead us by her prayer to the heavenly homeland, so that, crowned, we may become sharers in her glory, with your consent, you who live, and so forth.

## SERMON III. ON SAINT BENEDICT, ABBOT

[Col. 0721D] **[Note: [Col. 0721D] The festive solemnity of Blessed Benedict. That this sermon is by Saint Odo, as are the preceding sermons on Saint Peter and Mary Magdalene, is attested by Aimoinus in Book II of *The Miracles of Saint Benedict*, chapter 4, where he says: “Yet he himself, namely Saint Odo, in the sermon which he composed with most eloquent fluency in praise and honor of that same Father, records that this legislator of cenobites shone in his own times with many signs of miracles.” He delivered it while governing Saint Benedict’s monastery at Fleury, into which he himself was also the first to introduce the Rule of this holy Father, as Asso clearly teaches in Book II of *The History of Saint Berchorius the Abbot*, in these words: “But the most prudent king, Rodulfus, in order to adorn the laws of the government entrusted to him by God, being an unconquerable pursuer of justice and an inflexible restorer of churches, by no means allowed monks who wore a merely shadowy habit to stray without the instruction of some other rule. He therefore handed over for correction to Saint Odo, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, the distinguished monastery of Fleury, renowned for the relics of the body of Benedict, the most devout father of monks. The glorious abbot, most religiously ordering the aforesaid place, as is read in his deeds, which Saint Benedict had adopted as his own, was the first to bring into that place the little book of that same Father’s Rule.”]**

The festive solemnity of the most blessed Benedict shines forth by the favor of Christ the Lord. It is accustomed both to increase the affection of devotion in the hearts of the faithful and to bring them spiritual joy. The faithful rightly rejoice together at the memory of so great a father, so that the prophetic saying may be fulfilled: “Say to the righteous: It is well” (Isaiah 3:10). And again: “The memory of the righteous is with praises” (Proverbs 10:7).

For it is clear that Christian devotion venerates each of the saints all the more greatly the more exaltedly it knows that he has been adorned by God. Therefore it loves this father with a particular devotion inspired by God and recalls his memory with greater sweetness. It is certainly not unaware that almighty God advanced him in a remarkable manner among the highest and chosen Fathers of the holy Church and raised him conspicuously among the founders of the holy faith and the guardians of heavenly discipline.

Indeed, the grace of the Holy Spirit adorned him both with signs of miracles and with an army of virtues, so that he might appear in the world worthy to be the one through whom he would instruct a multitude of the higher order. Hence, both on this solemnity and on the other feasts dedicated to his holy name, whenever they occur throughout the year in their appointed seasons, so many people hasten so devoutly and gladly, and from such distant regions, to his sacred tomb.

For it is not only the country people who gather, but also the urban populace, crowded with noblemen and adorned, as though with flowers, by the honorable presence of clerics. They come together joyfully and devoutly seek his common patronage.

For, as though God perceived that the desire of the devout would be insufficient if the faithful honored the solemnity of this father only once a year, he provided causes by which he might increase other solemnities as well, to the joy of Christians. [Col. 0722C]

These include, namely, his holy translation and burial, which many proofs of signs show to have been arranged by divine providence.

**[Note: [Col. 0722D] On his holy translation. Many writers mention the translation of Saint Benedict’s body from Cassino to Fleury, and several have even written the complete history of it. See the *Bibliotheca Floriacensis*.]**

At that place, so many and such wonderful miracles—as I may put it—are both recorded in Scripture as having occurred and recognized as having been performed before people’s eyes, that their radiance could rouse even those living far away to venerate him.

Although, now that the time of Antichrist is approaching—the one whose face, as it is written, will be preceded by want (Job 41:13)—these miracles may appear to have ceased, nevertheless a more excellent healing, that of the soul, is always granted through his merits.

The cessation of divine miracles, whether there or elsewhere, is caused by the enormity of our sins: we who, after the grace of Christ had been revealed, have turned back.

It is indeed reported of the Lord Jesus Christ that, because of the blindness of the unbelieving people, he was unable to perform any miracle in Capernaum (Mark 6:5). We, therefore, are not worthy that this holy father should cherish us with that favor, or deign to console us, with which he is accustomed to gladden those disciples whom he loves. This alone ought to seem a great thing to us: that he grants us the privilege of being able to take part in his holy solemnity and rejoice in the hope of his mercy. His power and piety are no less great than if he were performing miracles continually. Yet it is plainly necessary that, when signs cease throughout the Church, it should be made manifest who are those who honor the universal faith because of present miracles, and who honor it because of future blessedness. Moreover, as the terrifying judgment already approaches, the followers of Antichrist will rather perform signs, so that before those who sin willingly there may be placed, as it is written, a stumbling block (Ezek. 3:20). Nevertheless, those same miracles have not yet entirely ceased, since we know that they still occur at the most sacred tomb of this father, and in other places hallowed by the memory of his blessedness.

Those who inquire into signs, and judge every holy father to be powerful or powerless according to the rarity or abundance of such signs, should consider the Lord’s rebuke, in which he says: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign” (Matt. 12:39). They should also consider the rebuke of his own herald, who says: “The Jews demand signs” (1 Cor. 2:22), while elsewhere he does not fail to call them hateful to God (Rom. 1:30). Herod, moreover, who, as it is written, desired to see some sign from him (Luke 23:8), was not deemed worthy to hear even the smallest reply from him. Yet he placed the faith of the centurion above that of all Israel (Matt. 8:13): the centurion did not doubt that his servant’s healing required nothing more than Christ’s command.

These matters have been inserted here because the lukewarmness of certain people requires it, since their devotion grows cold when signs cease. For the most blessed father himself, his own distinction is entirely sufficient: he shines with so great a radiance that he illuminates even the most distant recesses of all Christendom with the rays of his blessedness. Nor do the cohorts of monks spread throughout the world remain ignorant of his greatness, since they follow his holy institution above all others. Indeed, even in the monasteries of those Fathers who faithfully and religiously promulgated the rule of the holy calling, their own clients prefer to profess this father’s rule. They rightly judge that God specially predestined him as another Moses, through whom he would establish the decrees of the monastic law.

There were, as has already been said, certain other legislators of the same holy institution; but, as was said to Moses, this one too may be addressed: “I know you by name.” He is the one who shone forth peacefully in this heavenly discipline. For before Moses, the ceremonies of sacrifice and the rites of circumcision had long been practiced; nevertheless, they were specially inculcated through that same Moses (Exod. 35:12; Gen. 8:20; Exod. 12:3). Thus, then, let the other Fathers who described the duties of the holy Rule not prejudice this most blessed legislator, but rather, as its defenders, confirm what he established. For this holy man is not compared to Moses without reason, since many great things were performed by both in almost corresponding fashion.

Setting aside the majesty of the mystery, under Moses everything happened symbolically (1 Cor. 10:11), you will find many other things that our own father performed in similar fashion, as though they had been accomplished under one spirit. This privilege is certainly common to both: they are legislators. Moses persuaded the complaining crowds of Hebrews to leave Egypt; this man leads into the land of the living many companies of the people of acquisition, drawn under his leadership, as though from the inborn darkness of carnal desires. Moses divided the Red Sea; this man, after Peter, by an extraordinary miracle caused a disciple to run over the waters. Since in both deeds it is plainly evident that the nature of things was overcome, consider which of these surpasses the other: whether it is equal to have divided the waters, or to have run over them with dry footsteps.

Moses brought water from a rock to the thirsty people in the parched fields (Num. 20:10); this man drew a spring from dry stone for the use of the monks, and it still flows today as a stream. Moses restrained with the rod of the law the brutish behavior of the Jews, whom he calls unbelieving and rebellious; this man addresses the flock of monks as obedient by willingly hearing the voice, as though they were one person because they possessed one heart, calls them “son,” and subjects them to Christ’s gentle yoke.

Many further things could be said by which the correspondence between these persons would become clear. Indeed, legislation itself specially compares this most blessed father with Moses. Yet the greatness of his virtues and signs also shows him to be joined with men of the highest excellence. Thus that remarkable narrator of his life, Pope Gregory, asserts this, equating him, on the basis of certain deeds, with several individuals named explicitly. Among other things he says:

“For in the water brought forth from the rock, I see Moses; in the iron that returned from the depth of the water, Elisha; in the passage upon the water, Peter; in the obedience of the raven, Elijah; and in the mourning over the death of an enemy, I see and recognize David. This man was filled with the spirit of all the righteous.”

Gregory also does not conceal that Benedict was remarkably perceptive in the gift of prophecy, in discerning human thoughts, and in recognizing the judgments of hidden matters. Finally, among the many charisms of heavenly gift, he joyfully recounts to delighted ears that Benedict was especially eloquent, and that he wrote the rule of the monks in brilliant speech and with exceptional discernment. I say “to delighted ears,” because this brings great joy to all who possess sound understanding: that divine providence appointed for them such a great and such a leader and teacher, whom the whole world recognizes as worthy and suitable to promulgate the law of heavenly discipline.

They rejoice, therefore, and, following him as their guide, depend upon his direction and fix the gaze of their hearts upon him. They rejoice because, through his instruction, they have been enlisted in the training of the heavenly army. They hope that, serving under his command, they will be admitted to the palace of the heavenly King. What they by no means presume to obtain through their own merits, they trust they will gain through the intercession of this same commander.

They continually turn toward this lamp, shining in the darkened course of the present life, and in it they see toward what goal their work should direct its steps. The most blessed Benedict, therefore, is a lamp—a lamp, I say, placed upon a lampstand for this purpose: that, burning and shining, as Truth testifies concerning his forerunner, he may shine upon all who are in the house of God (Matt. 5:13; John 5:35).

Did he not also burn intensely with heavenly love? Did he not also shine, both in word and deed and through the splendor of his signs? He is therefore a lamp. But how more fittingly will the legions of monks call this same teacher of theirs, indeed their lord? “Lord,” I say, since Elijah too was called the lord of Elisha. Let him therefore be called a lamp out of an affection of devotion. But since that seems too little, let him also be called a star—not just any star, but one that shines, instructing many in righteousness, according to Daniel, for everlasting ages. Let him also be called the sun, because he will shine like the sun with the righteous, both now in the Church and then in the kingdom of their Father. Let him also be called an angel, because they seek the law from his mouth. Finally, let them see and rejoice at how appropriately he is called Benedict, whom God has blessed with every spiritual blessing, and through whom they will possess so great a blessing as their inheritance.

For I confess that those who love this father are so pleased to be known by such a name that, in Christian custom, it is habitually used especially after the divine name. Who, speaking piously, would not say either “Benedict” or “blessing” under some pretext or other? Yet it would in some measure be fitting for those to resound with his praises who, according to the Apostle, know what is the hope of God’s calling (Eph. 1:18)—namely, both that calling by which they were called to the faith together with other Christians, and also that calling to undertake a higher rank, established by this same father. They do not receive this grace in vain, but know the things that have been given by God (2 Cor. 6:1).

Concerning them, because they have one heart and one soul, God speaks under the designation of one people: “They obey me by the hearing of the ear,” whom we are commanded to praise among his holy ones (Ps. 17:45; 150:1). But Scripture does not remain silent about what sort of people ought to praise him, saying to them: “You who fear the Lord, praise him”; and again: “Those who seek him will praise the Lord” (Ps. 21:24–25). In contrast, it says: “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Sir. 15:9).

What, then, should be thought of us, who are sinners beyond measure and yet presume to attempt his praises? But attending to the riches of divine mercy, we presume upon the mercy of this same most forgiving patron.

Finally, the same Scripture that says in the person of the righteous, “Let the heavens praise him,” immediately adds, “and the earth” (Ps. 68:35), so that sinners would not despair. For God so multiplies his mercy that he saves not only human beings but even beasts. Therefore, although unworthy, let us too rejoice in the praise of this same father.

Although shame prevents us from opening our mouths, let each of us nevertheless say to him that Mosaic utterance: “I know that you are merciful, Lord” (Ps. 35:8). Let us await with fear and hope whether, just as it is customary for kings to absolve the guilty on their birthdays, this prince of God might, because of the joy of his holy solemnity, loosen our bonds.

For it also comes to mind that, among the precious gifts of the children of Israel, certain people brought even goats’ hair (Exod. 25:4). Since this signifies the confession of sins, let us offer at least this one thing. But if the gold of wisdom is lacking, if the silver of eloquence rightly praising him is lacking, if the gems of various virtues are lacking, and finally if the linen of chastity is absent from the wretched, let us offer at least the aforementioned goats’ hair, because perhaps even this will please him when accompanied by a truthful confession.

It is truthful because, if someone still delights in sinning by consent, then it is false to say that he truly repents of past sins. To speak of something from ordinary human practice: whenever a master of a household returns home after some time away, the whole household usually rejoices with him; indeed, even the little dogs leap up and show by a certain movement of their limbs that they are happy.

Therefore, although we rightly deserve to be compared with unintelligent animals, if we rejoice in honor of this solemnity—which in some manner represents our own Lord to us—we may at least hope for crumbs of his mercy, like puppies beneath the table. And this hope rests not on ourselves, but on the goodness of the evangelical King, who deigned to invite the blind and the lame to his banquet (Luke 14:13).

We are therefore well treated, since this same master of the household does not disdain to allow us to take part in his solemnities. How many there are even in the most remote regions beyond the seas who would rejoice greatly if they had the opportunity of approaching his sacred tomb even once! From this we should also consider what has been given to us by God.

Let us beware lest, if we have felt his presence with insufficient reverence, or—God forbid—have come into his sight with an impure heart and empty hands, he himself should say that prophetic utterance: “My soul is not with this people” (Isa. 15:1); and again: “You are near to their mouth, but far from their reins” (Jer. 12:2).

Therefore, when he enters, after the example of that evangelical king, to see those celebrating as though they were reclining at table—for since he is filled with the Spirit of God, nothing among God’s creatures can be hidden from him—let each of us take care lest this father’s eyes be offended by the garment of our heart or of our body.

For, as he himself says: “Every exaltation is a kind of pride, by which each person becomes especially hateful, as it is written, before the Lord” (Deut. 22:5). Let us nevertheless remember that, in order to appease the heavenly Judge, or the senators of heaven, reflection upon or confession of sin is especially beneficial, according to the saying: “Declare whatever you have, so that you may be justified” (Isa. 43:26). “I acknowledge my iniquity,” he says. And therefore, as though secure, he asks: “Turn your face away from my sins” (Ps. 50:11).

Whoever among us wishes to contemplate the face of his own merit must necessarily gaze into this mirror—that is, must carefully weigh the deeds of this same most blessed confessor. For when his deeds have been examined, insofar as our smallness permits, we will be able to perceive both how far we are sunk below and how high he is raised above.

Hence it is written of every penitent: “He will look upon men,” that is, the saints, “and say: I have sinned” (Job 33:27). For he considers their beauty and recognizes how deformed he is. The benefit that proceeds from this same confession is indicated there as well, when it says: “Let us deliver him from pride and from the things he has done, so that he may not go into destruction” (ibid., 17).

But since Scripture commands: “For this is a holy day of the Lord; do not be sorrowful” (2 Esdr. 8:10), let us set aside whatever is sad in us or about us and presume to rejoice as though the Bridegroom were with us today. Offering the gift of our confession, as it were, before the feet of paternal mercy, let us raise up all that we can in his praise and admiration.

Let each person cry out his praises in a voice all the louder the more ardently he loves him, or the more perceptively he considers his life, which from its very beginning is altogether worthy of admiration. For how magnificent is it that, when he abandoned his father’s wealth, as the story relates, the Holy Spirit established for himself a dwelling in his sacred little breast; that, while still extremely tender in age, he recognized the empty studies of the philosophers; and that, already possessing a mature spirit, he then dared to enter the wilderness.

Even Martin himself, wondrous throughout the world, is not reported to have done this. And because he bore the yoke not only from adolescence but from infancy itself (Jer. 3:25), as Jeremiah continues there, he will sit uniquely in that heavenly capitol. It is clear that it was not without divine guidance that he experienced there the goads of temptation so powerfully within himself.

For just as Peter, the leader of the good, was first shown to himself and then placed over the Lord’s flock, so it was fitting that this prince of God, who was to be set over so many thousands of monks, should be tested through his own peril, so that he might learn how he ought to show mercy to those subject to him. Yet because he conquered the first assault of the struggle bravely, he never afterward experienced anything of the kind.

How obediently and eloquently each person ought to prefer the common good to his private good, this teacher of spiritual discipline demonstrates in this deed of his. As soon as he was sought out, overcoming himself, he abandoned his beloved solitude and satisfied the request of his petitioners.

But since his holy and admirable deeds are readily available, let us meanwhile remain silent about them. Let us nevertheless report this to his honor: that no other teacher of the Church arranged the life of so great a father, but that distinguished and most eloquent pope, Gregory, whose entire composition shines like gold.

For it was divinely arranged that, while this most excellent legislator was adorned by God in other ways as well, both he himself and his legislation should be strengthened by greater authority through this circumstance: that the supreme pontiff of the apostolic see arranged that life. Through the occasion of his *Dialogues*, that life would become known to many, and it would be most famous not only among Latins but also among Greeks.

Nor should we pass over the fact that we ought to rejoice in every way that so great a splendor has come, by divine direction, into this our western region. We do not believe it happened without reason that, while still alive, he sent his uniquely beloved disciple, the blessed Maurus, into these parts, and finally wished himself to be transferred here. Perhaps, when his holy mind had been so expanded that he could behold the whole world at once, he chose this place for himself by some hidden counsel as a special destination.

Let everyone, therefore, to whom a place so greatly desired everywhere by so many has not been denied, consider how highly it ought to be valued and with what reverence it should be cultivated. For the weight of every offense is usually measured not only by the understanding of the one who commits it and by the time, but also by the place.

Hence, as though from a greater reproach, the divine voice complains against the impious, saying: “He acted wickedly in the land of the saints, and he will not see the glory of the Lord” (Isa. 26:10); and again: “My beloved has acted wickedly in my house” (Jer. 11:15).

Otherwise, anyone whom the presence of so great a father does not bend toward reverence appears to share the spirit of Judas. Neither the sight, nor the speech, nor the banquet of the Lord himself softened Judas’s hardness. Let us therefore consider what has been given to us by God, and let us not receive offered grace in vain.

May so great a radiance illuminate the blindness of our minds. May so great a piety soften our hardness. May so powerful a medicine heal our wounds. If, while still a little boy, he repaired a sieve so completely that not even a crack could be seen, then we, who by grace have been called vessels for honor in the house of God, may be restored—since we have suffered many cracks through our sins—by this same physician, who has now been joined to his King.

If the blackness of our crimes has discolored us, let us not be like the Ethiopians, who do not change their skin; but, returning to his hand, let us ask from him, like that raven, for the grain of mercy. If we are also rightly counted among those who have inflicted injury, let us nevertheless ask from him that affection with which he wept for one who hated him. For he will not reject suppliants, however unworthy, since he himself mourned for one who persisted in wickedness.

Let us therefore rejoice and, with whatever effort of love we can muster, show our affection toward our Lord. For this reason many sins were forgiven Mary: because she loved much (Luke 7:47).

Moreover, everyone ought always to desire to add to the praises of this same prince of God, in accordance with the Psalmist. But we can indeed show affection; we are wholly unable to fulfill the perfection of so great a matter. Therefore his praises are not proclaimed by one voice, one congregation, one city, or one province; wherever the holy Church is spread, the praise of Benedict is celebrated through tribes, nations, and languages.

For if, as Solomon says, “in the multitude of the people is the dignity of the king” (Prov. 14:28), how great do we think is the dignity of this king, whom so numerous an army of monks follows? What king or emperor ever ruled over so many regions of the world, or gathered such great legions for himself from so many different nations, as this man, who arranges in the army of Christ people of every sex and age, voluntarily sworn to its service? Gazing upon him as though he were present and following the banner of his institution, they bravely shatter the ranks of the devil. To them may be fitted the prophetic saying: “Your eyes shall see your teacher” (Isa. 30:20).

Finally, it is a faithful belief that each of the saints will rise in the resurrection with those whom he acquired for the Lord. When all the followers of his institution have therefore been gathered together, what sign of Benedict’s apostleship will that great army then present in itself? With what joy will he then exult who has been able to mingle himself among those cohorts!

Now let all who are near to him either by place or by affection direct the gaze of their hearts toward him. For he has become all things to all people. He has the form of a child in the child, for them to imitate, so that, since they have been offered to God in the likeness of Isaac, they may take care not to ferment their beginnings. Thereafter, let each, as the succession of ages advances, become perfect in understanding, so that he may not degenerate from the paternal piety of his nurturer. Otherwise, if they fall from a higher rank, they may be dashed down more grievously.

But let all of us who have sinned in no way cease to hope for clemency, since, while still living and even after his death, he raised the dead, restored what was broken, and healed what was hopeless.

And although we have not done his will, let us nevertheless invoke him as Lord, and let our eyes be fixed upon his hands, waiting until he himself raises them over us and has mercy on us. Let Benedict always be in our heart, Benedict on our lips, Benedict in our deeds, so that, if there is any virtue or any praise of discipline, by imitating that apostolic injunction—“what we have seen in him, and heard in him, and heard from him”—we may pursue it, so that he may be with us.

May the God of peace, through him, be with us forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON IV. ON THE BURNING OF THE BASILICA OF THE BLESSED MARTIN

You, my lords, demand rich things from a poor man, eloquence from one without a tongue. For since recently the flame once again devoured the basilica of our lord Martin, and on this occasion some, as though wavering in faith, while certain foolish people chatter about why he did not restrain the fire, the grief caused by the earlier conflagration has been renewed for us. Therefore you demand that a kind of intoxicating draught of words be prepared for you, to be offered to those who mourn and to rebuke those others somewhat.

I hesitated for a long time and shrank from this task. For Martin, whose service this sermon ought to perform, is greater than can be expressed. As is said of him, God glorifies him everywhere by wondrous deeds, and also glorifies him in this respect: all who have written about him, whether in prose, verse, or rhythm, are known to have been holy and learned and to have published what they undertook in language exceedingly sweet and elegant.

Indeed, unless the authority of those commanding and the necessity of the matter pressed upon me, it would seem unreasonable for one who has nothing—or very little—to say about a man to presume to attempt it. But, turning the eyes of my heart toward our common hope, I trust that Christ, who blesses the small and the great, will not abandon this effort, by which obedience seeks to serve the command of charity.

For he himself flies upon the wings of the winds, surpassing all angelic contemplation; he himself descends to the lower regions of the earth, becoming milk for the tenderness of little ones. He makes living creatures move with the wheels that follow them; he makes the lizard, supporting itself on its arms, linger in the palaces of kings. The patriarchs and prophets sang to him, and the Hebrew children cried out his praises.

Therefore, just as he provided distinguished men who, keeping the appointed vigils, would write nobly in praise of the blessed Martin, so may he deign to grant the weak at least to bark a little on his behalf, like dogs, out of zeal for him.

When, therefore, the report of so great a calamity suddenly flew through all the neighboring and more distant provinces, immense sorrow and mourning pierced everyone’s hearts. We were told that not only ordinary peasants, who were accustomed to love the blessed man as though he belonged especially to them, but also the leading men—and even kings—were said to have wept.

What especially intensified the force of their grief was that this same building had been burned not many years before.

[Note: The basilica of our lord Martin was again devoured by flames. The church of Saint Martin was burned not once but several times before the year 1000.

First, in the time of King Chlothar, by Wilichar and his wife, as Gregory of Tours writes in Book IV, chapter 20, and Book X, final chapter, of his *History of the Franks*.

Second, by the Northmen in the year 853, as the *Annals of an Unknown Author* report in these words: “In the year 853, the Northmen, coming by the river Loire, plundered Tours, a city of Gaul, and among the other buildings they also burned the church of Saint Martin the Confessor, with no one resisting.” Sigebert of Gembloux, a monk, agrees with this in his *Chronicle*.

Third, again by the same Northmen in the year of Christ 903, as the *History of the Lords of Amboise* attests, saying: “After the death of King Odo, who reigned for ten years, in the seventh year after his death the city of Tours was burned by the Northmen Erith and Bathet, and the church of the blessed Martin, together with the entire castle and twenty-eight churches.”

Finally, as an anonymous monk of Marmoutier records: “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 994, the church of the blessed Martin was again burned, together with the castle—from the east, from the end of Saint Hilary’s district to Saint Mary the Poor; from the south, from the gate of Saint Petrutionus to the Loire.”

This sermon, however, was delivered by Odo not during the first or second burning, but during the third, which occurred in the year 903. The time at which he flourished, and the words that immediately follow—namely, that the same building had been burned not many years earlier—clearly demonstrate this.]

And now it had been repaired at great expense and through the great industry of his people.

[Note: The first restoration after the burning of Saint Martin’s basilica was carried out by Archbishop Euphronius, who covered it with tin, with the assistance of King Chlothar, as Gregory of Tours says in Book IV, chapter 20, and Book X, final chapter. The canons of Saint Martin themselves restored the second one with whatever industry and excellence they could, as Saint Odo teaches here.

For the repair of the third, when funds were already running out, appeal was made to Alfonso, king of Spain, as is evident from a letter of Alfonso dated 906. The letter, owed to the kindness of John Masson, brother of Papirius, reads as follows:

“ In the name of God, Alfonso, by the will and power of Christ king of Spain, to the most Christian flock and to the custodians of the tomb of the blessed confessor of Christ, Martin, of the church of Tours: eternal salvation in Christ and through Christ.

After your letter of holiness—which you arranged to have delivered through a station or lodging, “es datum +” [corrupt and uncertain], to the distinguished bishop, Archbishop Sisnandus of the apostolic see of James—had been graciously received by him, and after he had eagerly read it through and carefully taken pains to send it on to our clemency, we rejoiced when your written message was read aloud, rejoicing in your safety. But concerning the audacity of the Northmen, who burned the house of the blessed Martin, dug it up, and ravaged its pastures, an unbearable grief has been fixed in our heart.

Yet it is certain that, because of contempt for the divine precepts and transgression of the commandments, Judea and Jerusalem suffered the destruction of calamities, and that the house of God and the divine law were seized and burned on many occasions [stirpis +: the reading is materially uncertain]. But since the Lord is not angry forever, through Jesus the great priest, Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, all the ruins were restored for the better at God’s command, and the house of God was rebuilt.

Therefore we trust in the merit and intervention of Saint Martin, who inspired you to fortify and restore his house, so that from now on no proud eye may [conculcet: trample] it, nor any polluted person defile it.

As for the miracles performed among you, according to what your letter reports—what the Lord performs today in your church: making the mute speak, loosing those who are bound, and enabling the deaf to hear—blessed be the Lord, who through his great mercy has increased our joy a thousandfold and strengthens his Church in every tribulation.

Therefore we wish you well. Take care to prosper and to carry on in such a way, and attend to fortifying Saint Martin’s house. We rejoice greatly in what you are rightly doing. We have even greater joy when we hear that you walk in the ways of the Lord, restore the house of God, and fortify its courts, so that, by his favor, it may no longer fear ruin.

Furthermore, you have indicated again that you possess among you an imperial crown, adorned with gold and gems and worthy of our serenity; and for this reason you have approached the apostolic serenity of Sisnandus, so that he might arrange to inform us of it and express your desire that we should purchase it. The matter remains [res ista: variant reading]: if this pleases our will, we will not delay in certifying it to you by a written reply.

This, therefore, pleased our serenity, and in addition we extend an abundant favor to your counsel [variant: “to your counsels”]. Know, accordingly, that there is a naval passage between you and our friend Amalwin, duke of Bordeaux. With the help of the power of the Most High, in this year—which is the year 906 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the ninth indiction—we have decided, among other things, that in the month of May our ships, with the boys of our palace, will sail to the city of Bordeaux.

If you truly strive to fulfill this from your heart, send the crown through your most faithful brothers to Amalwin, count of Bordeaux, so that it may be there in the appointed month, by mid-May, and our boys may find it there. The arrangement is to be observed that our ships and our boys remain there with some of your brothers until two or three of those same brothers, together with a few of our boys and the crown itself, board a single ship, so that, with God’s help, they may fly more swiftly to our presence.

If this is agreeable, we shall immediately send you a fully determined agreement through them. For we seek not to diminish but to increase and enrich the interests of your church. In addition, we are endeavoring through your brothers to secure gifts for you in aid of the building works. If this is agreeable, we shall send it back safely [per: through] enriched brothers, and ob fastidium, locupletatos [the phrase is materially corrupt and uncertain].

We earnestly desire your kindness in not hesitating to send us whatever you have written concerning the miracles that, after the death of Saint Martin, have been performed in your church by his grace and merit, with God’s approval.

Although we have a written account of his miracles—those mystically performed during his life until his death—we also possess the lives, virtues, and miracles of many illustrious men, written out clearly and wisely, [emeretensum +: the reading is materially uncertain], which, as I recall, are not found in your archives. If this would be useful to you, we will arrange to send them.

Furthermore, concerning your question about whose apostle’s tomb is here among us: know with absolute certainty that we possess the tomb of the apostle James son of Zebedee, called Bonargis, who was beheaded by Herod. His tomb is in marble arches in the province of Galicia. For, with the hand of the Lord guiding it, as many truthful histories relate, his body was carried by ship all the way there and buried.

His tomb continues to shine with many miracles: demons are [lacinantur +: torn or tormented; the reading is uncertain], light is restored to the blind, walking to the lame, hearing to the deaf, speech to the mute, and many other miracles—things that we have learned and seen, and that the bishops and clergy of that place have reported to us.

For how he was beheaded in Jerusalem by Herod, transported here and buried, and at what time and in what manner, is clearly known to everyone. The truthful letters of our archbishops, the histories of the Fathers, and the testimony of many attest it.

If we wished to relate each matter to you now, our writing would be extended too far, and we would exceed the limits of a letter, especially given the haste of the carriers, who did not wish to delay. But, with God’s help, when your clerics come to us, we shall not refuse to send you everything more clearly and fully explained, without withholding anything that requires study, but setting down for you what we have received and retain from the holy Fathers.

With God’s approval and with all hesitation removed, believe with certainty that we hold what is right and just.

As for what you asked—how far his tomb lies from the Ocean Sea, and in what place it is situated—know that from the sea, through the *mari virio +* [reading uncertain], as far as the place where, under the Lord’s guidance, the two rivers that antiquity called the Volia and the Sar are found, at a place called Bisria, in the territory of your see of Iria, at the church of Saint Eulalia, there are ten miles; and from there to his glorious tomb there are twelve miles.”]

But this expression of Spanish devotion did not reach a laudable outcome. Rather, as it is related by an anonymous monk of Marmoutier, “five leading men, the clergy, and the townsmen rebuilt this church of Saint Martin, burned so many times; and, so that it might not again be overwhelmed easily, they fortified it with a wall and enclosed it with strong and most heavily fortified towers.”

Finally, the fourth burning was repaired by Herveus, treasurer of that holy bishop. Glaber Radulfus wrongly calls him both “Henricus” and “Herineus the *archclavus* (chief key-bearer)” in Book III, chapter 4.]
: and now, at great expense and through the considerable industry of his people, [Col. 0731A] it finally seemed to have been restored more beautifully. For it shone, adorned much more fittingly now than it had before that conflagration, though still far below its former condition, because it was then also lined inside with marble slabs. For at one time the reddish wall displayed a varied and quite beautiful pattern in Proconnesian marble, [Col. 0732A] at another a white one in Parian marble, and at another a green one in green (prasinus) marble; outside, it gleamed with little golden, sapphire, and mosaic stones. The roof, too, was covered with sheets of tin [stannum].

[Note: [Col. 0732D] The roof, too, was covered with tin plates. Saint Briccius, his successor in the episcopate, built the first basilica over the body of Saint Martin; he himself was also buried there, as Gregory of Tours testifies, Book X. [Col. 0733D] Because this church was far too small, Perpetuus, also bishop of Tours and second in succession to Briccius, demolished it and built another, larger one, with wondrous workmanship. The same Gregory describes it in Book II, chapter 14; Perpetuus transferred the body of that venerable saint into its apse. But when this church too was burned by Wilichar, as Eufronius, the eighteenth bishop, had made it a refuge during Chramnus’s former encirclement, Eufronius restored it to the elegance it had previously possessed; and, at the command of King Chlothar, he covered it with tin, as the aforementioned Gregory of Tours records in Book IV, chapter 20, and Book XI, the final chapter.]

There are still some indications of these things, and we saw certain very old brothers [Col. 0733A] who testified as follows: the structure of the church, shining against the sun, looked like a little golden mountain and presented so pleasing an appearance to those who saw it that it seemed in some fashion to bear witness to the glory of blessed Martin. The ancient builders, however, wished to construct it with vaulted porticoes, because that building, although extremely broad, is nevertheless accustomed to become so narrow when crowds press into it that the people at the ends of the choir and in the side chapels crush one another, even unwillingly.

I believe that the lord Martin himself finds this devout violence pleasing, after the example, namely, of his Lord, whom the crowds pressed upon. Even now, adorned with striped walls, with glass embellished by sapphire, and with little gold plates, it greatly delighted those who looked upon it.

When, as we said, news of so dreadful an event had flown everywhere, the time was already approaching when the solemnity of that same blessed Martin is customarily celebrated. At that time crowds of people rush in, some drawn by the celebration, others to see the church’s destruction. Such is the force of nature that anyone in grief longs to see with his own eyes the very thing over which he grieves. And although the sight of what has happened intensifies the sorrow of the heart, one nevertheless desires to see it, as though for consolation, in order to grieve the more deeply.

It was being reported among many people that, only three days earlier, fierce discord had arisen among the brothers, and that, indeed, on the day before the holy church was burned, someone had dishonored certain of the brothers before the holy altar, both with insults and with blows [Col. 0733C]. Saint Martin, moreover, had appeared in a dream to a certain poor man and, as if complaining, had said that he had been wronged in his own house and would soon depart from it and arrive at the village of Tulle.

Thus an immense crowd gathered, so that you might have thought that Job’s friends had agreed among themselves to visit him in his affliction. Then we too hurried there. As our eyes passed over everything, tears poured forth. As we looked upon each detail, seeing how it had been before, weeping, groans broke out. But when the blood of the heart, from which tears arise, had already been exhausted—for tears flow from that same blood and therefore, when shed out of compassion, in a certain sense imitate martyrdom—we withdrew to the audience chamber [Col. 0733D].

There we spoke for a long time—I do not know what. For it is the custom of those who grieve to repeat not what reason demands, but what sorrow extorts. At last the discussion reached the point where, to increase our grief, it was said that some people were disparaging blessed Martin, as though he were unable to restrain the fire, since he had allowed his own house to be consumed by flames so many times. Others were saying that he had already grown weary of our age and no longer listened, as was his custom, to the prayers of suppliants, since he did not show himself present through miracles [Col. 0734A].

Others, no less, seemed to ask what it meant that such abundant psalmody and such frequent celebration of Mass took place there, and that even the boldness of prayer was so greatly restrained: why had divine severity been permitted to rule so harshly, when in many other places God was served less and freedom to pray appeared more unrestrained?

Hearing this, we were struck with astonishment; stunned with grief, we immediately recognized the frauds of the ancient deceiver. For although the apostles are a good fragrance to God, that same deceiver makes them, for some people, an odor of death leading to death. We feared that this was happening to those who, from the medicine, were making their wound worse through murmuring [Col. 0734B].

But because we heard insults being directed against our most blessed lord, we began to grieve more deeply, insofar as anyone’s heart of charity could feel it. It had not been enough that, because our sins demanded it, the church had suffered conflagration, in accordance with that saying; now, alas, those for whom he had endured this wrong were striving to slander him.

Nevertheless, remembering what is said of God—that “he gives songs in the night,” that is, the consolation of the Scriptures in tribulation—we shared with one another whatever occurred to our minds as consolation. And then, by chance, an opportunity arose from what was being said, so that the matter, reconsidered more carefully, might be written down.

Therefore, in accordance with the tenor of the conversation we then had, let us begin to discuss what divine favor has now granted [Col. 0734C]. First, let us urge that, in accordance with the prophet, “at least affliction should give understanding to hearing,” so that we may fear the threats that God directs against sinners, having learned them through what has occurred. Let us ask Christ’s mercy that, in accordance with what is said in Job, he may soften our heart and deem us worthy to feed upon the bread of tears, lest it be said of us: “You have struck them, and they have not grieved” (Jer. 5:3); and again: “I struck my people, and they did not return from their ways” (Jer. 15:7).

And since our perversity makes the heart of the just man, namely our lord Martin, sorrowful—as we have said elsewhere—when he sees us rejoicing instead in the worst things, he may complain, saying: “I looked for one who would at least grieve, and there was none” (Ps. 68:21); and likewise: “There is no one who grieves over my lot” (1 Kings 22:8).

For the memory of sin did not sufficiently trouble us. This often happens to those who not only do not mourn their sins but rather multiply them, and to whom nothing sad occurs. Hence it is written: “Because sentence against the wicked is not quickly pronounced, the children of men commit evil without any fear” (Eccl. 8:11).

But the saying that applied to us was this: “They dragged me, and I did not feel it” (Prov. 23:35); [Col. 0735A] “I was reduced to nothing, and I did not know it” (Ps. 72:22); “The scourges gathered over me, and I did not know it” (Ps. 34:18).

And therefore God, who is terrible in his counsels, displayed in the burning of that holy church the vengeance we deserved, as though he were saying to the ministers of vengeance: “These are an exasperating house to me. Begin the punishment from my sanctuary, so that the fire of indignation, which is destined to burn the abyss of the human heart, may meanwhile seize part of the building. Then, when they see what is desirable to their eyes taken away from them, they may repent of having despised me as I knocked at the door of their hearts.”

Thus, through what occurred in the church, our arrogance, so to speak, answered us to our face. And we must be exceedingly careful lest, as follows there, “a spirit of fornication” be found “in our midst,” and lest the destruction caused by that fire become, for the time being, the fuel of this outward fire [Col. 0735B].

Often it happens that the worse a sinner is, the denser becomes the darkness that obscures his heart. And when he has done something good, he boasts of it inwardly, like that Pharisee, paying little attention to the fact that no good deeds please God when they are stained by an admixture of evil.

To every such person the divine voice cries out: “You say, ‘I am rich,’ and you do not know that you are wretched, blind, and naked”—naked, that is, of righteousness; blind because he does not know how to see his own nakedness.

Therefore, as it is written, the Lord poured out fire upon Zion and willed to render devastation in flame, so that through the indignation raging against the material building we might fear being an exasperating house and take heed of what we deserve in his hidden judgment [Col. 0735C].

For it is no small guilt that demands that that holy house be burned both immediately and so many times: although it had just been set alight, his fury was not turned away, but his hand was still stretched out.

Nor should it be thought that this happened by chance, in view of what Jeremiah says: “Who is this who says that it has happened, when the Lord has not commanded it?” (Lam. 3:37). And again: “Is there evil in the city which I have not ordained?” says the Lord (Amos 3:6); or, “Who gave Jacob to the plunderers, and Israel to the despoilers? Was it not the Lord, against whom they sinned?” (Isa. 42:24).

Therefore, knowing that our sins brought these things about, it follows that we should groan over the wrongs done to our lord Martin—or rather, over ourselves, because if they do this with green wood, what will happen with dry wood?

Otherwise it will be said: “They were scattered, and they were not pierced with remorse” (Ps. 34:16). And again: “You have acquired the forehead of a prostitute; you have not known how to blush” (Jer. 3:3).

But those who tremble at God’s command and know that they have been humbled beneath his powerful hand should hear the consolation that came after the destruction of Jerusalem, when the Lord said: “I will build you up and not destroy you; for I have already relented concerning the evil that I brought upon you, and I am with you” (Jer. 42:10).

And he, like the Lord, who judges with tranquillity and disposes our affairs with great reverence, will be reconciled to his servants. Nevertheless, it is our duty to praise him in all his judgments and, if there are any good works in us, to fear even in those works. “I feared all my works,” Job says (Job 9:28).

For even he, after enduring so many and such great things, although he had meanwhile become more pleasing through those very scourges, so that God deigned to come to visit him, still humbled himself, saying: “I condemn myself and repent” (Job 42:6).

After that previous burning, you enclosed the monastery with walls joined together through immense effort, wishing thereby to take care lest the holy house might thereafter be harmed by enemies. But you did not sufficiently consider how greatly this holy place had shone in reverence from ancient times. Immediately abandoning its religious character, you allowed it to become a common lodging place, so that porters do not resist women coming to draw water or going wherever they wish, although we have seen that formerly no one was permitted to enter even a little way through the monastery gates, nor did anyone dare to ride immediately across the court [Col. 0736B].

But now the place is neglected, as though that wall had been erected not to repel enemies but to exclude reverence for the site. Nor was that same wall able to prevent the fire which neglected contempt demanded should be kindled.

I say this more sharply because, to speak frankly, many hearts are saddened by the fact that they do not see the place, which is sacrosanct because of love for blessed Martin, venerated according to its ancient reverence.

Nor is it a small offense that some who were raised in that place dishonor themselves with certain lay garments, or with clothing that is excessively pompous, although their manner of life was once such that we heard it praised even at Rome. Certain Romans used to say: “There would be no need for anyone to travel to Rome if they could die near the church of blessed Martin” [Col. 0736C].

The prophet Jeremiah laments that the color appropriate to religion is changed. Elsewhere it is said: “Never glory in clothing” (Ecclus. 11:4). Let these people see, then, how foolish it is to beg for glory through the beauty of clothing while stripping the soul of the beauty of virtue.

As for those who rave about the power of blessed Martin, his lover and most eloquent narrator, Sulpicius, answered them sufficiently long ago. For once, when a fire was blowing upon his clothes as well, he immediately threw himself into the midst of it and felt it to be cold. Some people likewise took this as an opportunity to disparage him.

The answer then given to them ought to suffice these people too. They would not be astonished by this at all if they had understood the arrangement by which God governs the world. It is a small thing for them to wonder if this church, perhaps polluted by the vices of pride or luxury, was cleansed by flame when such causes, known to God, demanded it [Col. 0736D].

Let them rather examine why evil has prevailed from the beginning of the world. Why did God permit the wicked Cain to overthrow the righteous Abel? Why did Satan drive Job, incomparably righteous at that time, as far as the dungheap and the worms? Why was John, than whom no one born of woman was greater, beheaded at the request of a dancing girl?

Certainly, if these people had seen Christ upon the cross, they would not have believed, like that thief, that a kingdom remained for him. If they had also publicly seen the apostles beaten, and had perhaps witnessed Stephen exposed to wild beasts night and day, they would have thought the faith of Christ empty.

But after the world began to live by faith, anyone who reverently considers the purpose of divine providence understands that Jesus’ kingdom is not of this world, that his saints have no lasting city here, and that therefore they do not seek here the glory they hope for in the future. Nor do they ever seek any sign here except for the benefit of their neighbors.

For this reason the prophet prays to be saved not for his own sake but for the sake of his enemies, saying: “Deliver me because of my enemies” (Ps. 68:19)—that is, so that, by understanding your power through my deliverance, they may turn to you.

Knowing that they cannot pass through this life without sin, they prefer to desire that they be afflicted here for their correction. Thus the prophet prays: “Prove me, Lord, and test me” (Ps. 25:2). Another says: “Let rottenness enter my bones” (Hab. 3:16). He reveals what benefit he hoped to gain from this when he adds: “so that I may rest in the day of tribulation” (ibid.).

Afflicted Job likewise says: “This shall be my consolation: that, afflicting me with sorrow, he does not spare me” (Job 6:10).

The Apostle too does not boast that he was caught up into paradise, even to the third heaven, or that he heard ineffable mysteries there. Rather, he rejoices that he suffered shipwreck three times, was beaten with rods three times, and was stoned once.

But these querulous people, who are always seeking miracles, do not know how to attend to this dispensation. For the proud and vain always desire that to happen from which popular rumor and empty glory may increase. But all who are God-fearing desire rather that by which their sins may be cleansed and their minds defended from pride.

For if Martin had driven back the flame by his customary power, the vengeance due to sins would have remained, and impiety might perhaps have grown as though it had gone unpunished. But if the virtue of every saint is to be judged by what happens to that saint in the present, then not one alone but all the saints, not merely the ordinary but the greatest, will be dishonored.

For the holy Benedict had built a monastery, religiously and devoutly, as was fitting for one who was blessed. Yet it was revealed to him that, by divine judgment, it was to be handed over to enemies; this alone being granted him, that none of the souls should perish.

I should certainly say too little if I said that such a thing befell even outwardly a confessor, however great he might be. But I believe that even a foolish person will regard it as no small thing that the aforesaid Baptist—so powerful in miracles, sensing the Lord Christ within the womb, leading a most holy life, and falling in defense of the truth—he who was incomparably great in himself, that is, in his holy bones, endured such things as would inspire immense horror in those who heard of them. For, as Eusebius relates in Book XI of his *Ecclesiastical History*, pagans broke open his holy tomb, which stood at Sebaste; then they burned his bones, mixed them with earthly dust, and scattered them here and there across the fields. But certain monks arrived and, by divine providence, found and collected fragments of the holy body at that very hour.

An idol was also set up at the Lord’s sepulchre for many years, so that whoever bowed there would appear to have worshiped the idol. The Lord’s cross, long concealed by the fraudulent action of the Jews, was at last miraculously found and subsequently permitted to be carried away by a profane king.
