Let those investigators of secret matters consider by what dispensation of the Lord such things, and things like them, are allowed to happen.

It seems appropriate for us to do one thing: to fear the divine judgments, and, seeing what has happened, for each of us to say: “Lord, I have heard your report, and I was afraid; Lord, I considered your works, and I was terrified” (Habakkuk 3:2). And again: “I will confess to you, Lord, because you were angry with me” (Isaiah 12:1), and so forth. And because, through the material temple, he gave a sign to spiritual people that they should flee from the face of the bow, let us beseech him concerning what is stated there beforehand, so that, since he has been angry, he may also have shown mercy, saying: “I will endure the Lord’s rebuke, because I have sinned against him.”

Then let that diabolical suspicion not enter our minds—that the power of the lord Martin has failed. That power is wondrous throughout the whole world because of its greatness; that power, so to speak, has been proved by signs. Rather, we must believe that his charity—which was always inclined and beneficent even toward his rivals—moved him to obtain this from the Lord.

When we consider the deeds of certain saints who preferred to suffer injury for the sake of others, we do not arrive at this opinion without reason. Moses, indeed, begged the Lord his God to forgive the people’s offense; otherwise, he asked him to erase him from the book of life. David too, when he saw the angel striking down the people, asked that the sword be turned against him and his father’s house. After his son, the murderer, had been killed, he mourned and said: “Who will grant me that I might die for you, my son?” (2 Samuel 18:22).

Jeremiah also, when he forbade the people, from the mouth of God, to descend into Egypt, and they disregarded him, could not even then abandon them; he descended with that people and was killed by them. The Apostle Paul, the chosen vessel, also desired to become accursed for his brothers.

Certainly Stephen could not pray that he might die for those who stoned him, since they themselves were forcing him to his death; nevertheless, he offered them the one thing that remained to them, saying: “Do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:53).

But why should we speak of servants, when the Lord of all himself died for the ungodly, as the Apostle says? Hence the prophet says that he took upon himself an alien work, in order to perform his own work. To suffer, to be mocked, and to die is alien to God; to save, however, is his work. Yet what is alien to God was owed to sinful humanity. Nevertheless, he took upon himself an alien work in order to perform his own work, because he deigned to die so that he might save those worthy of death.

Let us see, then, whether something of this kind was present in Martin. Was it not this charity that urged him on when he divided his cloak with the poor man? For the command was given concerning two tunics, that one of them should be given to the one who had none. But he, far surpassing not only Pharisaic righteousness but even Christian righteousness, divided the one garment itself, together with his own nakedness.

When he was bound by a robber, he nevertheless declared himself completely secure, and said that it was rather the robber who ought to grieve: by practicing robbery, he had become unworthy of Christ’s mercy. Then, with the same love with which he burned most intensely, knowing that he could not return before the day of his death, he did not hesitate to travel farther away in order to restore peace among the clergy.

At that time, he could even have forgotten anyone else who was present. For this same charity burned most fervently at the end—which is most fitting of all—when, for the love of his disciples, he did not refuse to postpone for as long as Christ himself wished the heavenly kingdom for which he had sighed from childhood, and even the very presence of Christ.

Is that charity insignificant? Or would he neglect a human being who often extended compassion even toward brute animals? Hence a certain man called Grammaticus recently chattered that the account of the hare which Martin rescued from dogs had been included in his life unnecessarily. But for those of us who are such that, on account of our own righteousness, we possess no claim to commendation before him, no other miracle, however great, seems likely to please us more; for while in other matters he displays greater power, in this one he shows a more ardent disposition to mercy.

But why speak of weakened [variant: liberated] animals, when he even removed the sword of Maximus from the heretics themselves? Moreover, he promised pardon even to the demon itself, if it would cease attacking human beings. He said this, to be sure, in order to draw certain brothers—whose vices that demon was exposing—away from despair.

Therefore, recalling these and other things of the same kind, we firmly believe that he allowed his own house to be burned, not because of any lack of power, but for the sake of a pious dispensation. If it is asked what this dispensation was, this again comes to mind: those who had previously labored on the construction of that same house lost nothing of their reward. For although the work perished, the reward of the pious work remains, just as the divine word assures certain people who labor piously, saying: “Your reward will correspond to your work” (2 Chronicles 25:7).

Indeed, if any slight fault—something that frequently happens—had become mixed into that labor, we believe that it was purified. For even in good works sin often insinuates itself, whether through self-exaltation or through lukewarmness. That is why priests are commanded to wash their holocausts: namely, so that in the very act of doing good work each person may fear and, like one washing a sacrifice, pour out tears.

There is also another reason connected with this dispensation. Many people, both grieving over the injury done to the holy man and contributing their devout efforts or their possessions toward restoring the place, have purchased for themselves a heavenly reward. If the basilica had remained standing in its former condition, they would have done nothing of the kind; instead, perhaps they would have gazed hungrily at its paintings and laughed.

We confidently believe that something even greater—if I may say so without rashness—has resulted from this. If, thereafter, the people cease from those sins whose demands brought this about, we hope that pardon will come to them, because God does not judge the same matter twice. True also is that saying of Job: “The afflicted person will be in glory” (Job 22:29). And again, in Jeremiah, after the destruction of the temple, God speaks to the survivors of the captives: “Do not be afraid. For now I have been reconciled concerning the evil that I inflicted upon you” (Jeremiah 42:10).

In saying this, however, we are not sewing cushions on which, as Ezekiel reproves them, sinners may rest comfortably. We are speaking only of those sins which the Apostle designates by hay and straw, not of those represented by iron and lead, which fire cannot consume. As for whom this benefits and whom it harms, let him know who permits nothing to happen without a reason.

We must consider this point of Scripture: human beings cannot discover any reason for all God’s works; yet, as it is likewise written, when judgment is passed upon us, we hope for mercy.

Nevertheless, let us not forget that the ark of God, which was first permitted to be carried away by the Philistines, was afterward held in such reverence and fear by its own people after its return that, when the common people looked upon it indiscriminately, seventy of the elders and fifty thousand of the populace perished.

Therefore, the greatest care must be taken lest anyone think that the house, although handed over to the flames, should be despised. For although it may appear poor and abandoned to the storm, and although the Lord may seem for a little while to have hidden his face from it, nevertheless he will console it with many mercies, so that, according to the multitude of its sorrows, its consolations may also gladden it.

The question that troubles those who ask why vengeance more frequently rages in a place where more good things are done and fewer evils occur has often been debated by many, but has been explained fully by no one. For when the wicked prosper and the good suffer, this perhaps happens so that the wicked may receive the good things of the present, which they desire, and be excluded from everlasting happiness; while the good, who do not care to be happy here, are chastised here on account of certain sins without which they cannot live this life, so that afterward they may be admitted to abiding joys.

Yet sometimes the good prosper and the wicked suffer without distinction. Even then it is unknown whether good things are being repaid to the good as their reward, and evil things imposed on the wicked so that they may be corrected. Why this variation comes upon mortal beings is uncertain.

And this is, as Ecclesiastes says, the worst thing among all that happen under the sun: that the same things happen equally to everyone—to the just and the impious, to the good and the wicked. But, as I stated a little earlier, everything is reserved for the future, and remains uncertain.

Above all, however, people grieve over this: that the impious prevail and the innocent are afflicted. Hence Jeremiah says: “Why does the way of the impious prosper? Why is it well with all who transgress and act wickedly?” (Jeremiah 12:1). Habakkuk likewise says: “Why, Lord, do you look upon those who act unjustly and remain silent while the impious devours one more righteous than himself?” (Habakkuk 1:13). He had previously spoken in the voice of those who suffer: “How long, Lord, shall I cry to you, suffering violence, and you will not save me?” (Habakkuk 1:2).

What troubles us most, then, is that many things happen to the just—as it is written—as though they had done the works of the wicked, while the wicked are secure as though they possessed the deeds of the just.

But do not seek things higher than you, and do not pry into God’s works. Suspicion has overthrown many people. Always think about what God has commanded, because his power is great and he is honored by the humble—that is, by those who do not dare to contemplate such things, but know that the Church must sing of mercy and judgment, and must recognize both as inscrutable.

“For the judgments of God are a great abyss” (Psalm 35:7). And who is wise enough to understand the Lord’s mercies? The Apostle says: “O the inscrutable ways of the Lord!” (Romans 11:33). “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24:10).

When that same Apostle forbade us to investigate them, he said: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Romans 9:20). A human being is called *homo* from *humus*, “earth”; he inserted this name so that, in his very name, a human being might recognize that he is in no way capable of searching out God’s judgments.

Therefore, as Augustine says, if you do not wish to go astray, do not investigate why something is so, or is not so. And that sweet-speaking Gregory likewise says: Nothing can happen unless God, whether angry, permits it, or, being reconciled, grants it. What we suffer is shown by that very fact to be just, because it does not happen without the ordering of God, who can do nothing unjustly.

The force of his dispensation cannot be avoided; but the person who willingly bears it upon the shoulder of his heart makes it much lighter for himself.

The Psalmist too, seeing the peace of sinners and that they are not in human toil but possess riches in this age, almost records that his steps were shaken, because he himself had been scourged all day while their impiety flowed as though from fatness. He would have considered the nation of God’s children justified without cause, had he not understood the end of both parties.

This had been his difficulty, until, by entering into the powers of the Lord—that is, into sacred Scripture—he learned that “it will be well in the end for the one who fears God” (Ecclesiasticus 1:13); and: “Woe to the impious man for evil! The recompense of his hands will be made to him” (Isaiah 3:11); and: “If he is righteous, he will not lift up his head, sated with affliction and misery” (Job 10:15).

But if he is impious, as is stated there beforehand, woe to him, because “their image will be reduced to nothing in the city of God”; while those who in mind are like beasts “will be received with glory, and they will be with God” (Psalm 72:20).

Thus, although misguided people call that people blessed whose sons are like young plantings, whose boys leap about in play, and in whose streets there is no outcry, along with the other things said there, nevertheless blessed is the one, as the Psalmist says, “whose Lord is his God” (Psalm 32:12). And as another Scripture says: “Blessed is the person who is corrected by the Lord” (Job 5:17).

There are many other statements of this kind, by which it is shown that this question holds very many people in its grip and cannot in fact be investigated. Nevertheless, one must return to the end of both parties and know without doubt that if the righteous receives something here, the impious and sinner will receive much more in the future.

And if Babylon is now like a golden cup, intoxicating her lovers, she will nevertheless hear from the heavenly Judge: “As much as she glorified herself in luxury, so much give her mourning and woe” (Revelation 18:7). Jerusalem, however, which is now poor and shaken by the storm, will hear good and consoling words from the angel who stands among the myrtles, when he says to her: “For a little while I hid my face from you, but now I will console you with many mercies” (Isaiah 54:8).

We are therefore completely unable to give an account of this matter. For the present, however, this comes to mind: when the good suffer, while the wicked prosper, and so forth as above, one purpose is served—that, always fearing under divine judgment, we should never presume to seek things higher than ourselves.

For often the sharpness of our mind is darkened the more it strives to see. When someone stares too intently at the sun’s rays, he is forced to see nothing precisely because he is trying to see more.

But if good works abound among you, this is an old custom: the inhabitants of that place, always aided by the merits of blessed Martin and drawn by his very radiance, have been accustomed to live devoutly. For when even the most distant nations glorify him, it is exceedingly impious in the present age to possess such a man and not venerate him piously and reverently.

Yet those good works themselves are not so pure that they are entirely free from the stains of guilt. For it is written: “There is no just person who does not sin” (Ecclesiastes 7:21). “Cursed is everyone who performs God’s work deceitfully” (Jeremiah 48:10).

Private self-love performs God’s work deceitfully, while the torpor of the heart produces sluggishness. The person who desires to be praised for God’s work commits deceit in it. The person who grows lukewarm and falls away from the fervor of devotion incurs sluggishness, and performs a good work more because custom demands it than because devotion inspires it.

Since, therefore, the stealthy intrusion of guilt is scarcely overcome even in a good action, it remains that we should always fear in the very performance of good work.

Is it a slight offense to celebrate or partake of the holy mystery without immense fear and careful reverence? For, according to the Apostle, the person who does not discern this and has not been proved fit to perform it brings judgment upon himself.

If, at the beginning of the young Christian community, many were for this reason both weak and dead in body, how much more now, when the matter is clearer, is danger incurred by the soul?

For, as is found in the sayings of the Fathers, no sin is the cause of adversity becoming so frequent in the world. Is it a small matter to speak with God in psalmody, and at the same time to think, without restraint of heart, about something worthless or even shameful?

There is understanding when one speaks reverently with human beings, but no care when one prays devoutly to God. For the person who speaks about an ant has it in mind at that moment; yet the immense matter of speaking with God is carried out with forgetfulness of God himself.

Who among us does not sometimes turn his ear away from a poor person’s cry? Who does not become angry with the poor? And the person who exalts his heart is abhorrent to God. Who among us can truthfully say to the Lord: “My heart has not been exalted” (Psalm 130:1)?

Who loves every neighbor as himself? Or who glories in the Lord alone? Sometimes we glory in the work of weavers, although it is written: “Never glory in clothing” (Ecclesiasticus 11:4).

Certainly the Truth commands nothing that is not just and possible. Yet the Truth affirms that not one apex, not one iota, will pass away from the whole law without being required.

But these and similar faults commonly occur even among the good. The transgressions of the wicked are far graver: there are nations who, loving the things that belong to the world, have lost the love of the Father, and through friendship with the world have been made enemies of God.

Some make their belly their god; the Apostle, grieving over them, calls them enemies of the holy cross. The divine voice threatens woe to those who burn with wine. God will judge fornicators and adulterers.

A greedy person, as blessed Gregory says, is not yet free from the worship of idols. For if anyone is a fornicator, or greedy, or drunkard, the chosen vessel commands that one should not even eat with such a person.

To love one’s own glory is so great a sin that the Jews fell chiefly into unbelief on account of it. “How,” says the Lord, “can you believe, when you love your own glory?” (John 5:44).

“If anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him” (1 Corinthians 3:17). Although this is spoken of the spiritual house, great care must nevertheless be taken that no one makes it into anything other than what it is: namely, a house of prayer.

For it was not without reason that the Lord Christ himself drove them out. With great attention to the matter and by his own action, he expelled the merchants from the temple, and ordered not only the others but also those who sold doves for use in holocausts to depart.

Let each person consider how he honors the presence of Christ and of the saints. For he looks down from heaven to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God. Scripture says: “An intelligent minister is acceptable to the king” (Proverbs 14:35).

If someone speaks an idle word at a crossroads and will have to give an account of it on the day of judgment, how much more will those have to answer who, in the very temple of God, crow out jests or slanders?

When Moses saw the fire, his words failed him and he did not dare to look. Certainly, the majesty is greater here than there, since here is the dwelling of God and the paradise where secret words are heard—words that human beings are not permitted to speak—that is, those to whom it is said: “When there are jealousy and contention among you, are you not human?” (1 Corinthians 3:3).

Or consider the person who does not restrain his tongue but, sitting down, speaks against his brother.

We see some who frequently attend the divine mystery; yet, as the order of divine service requires, they ought first to become a sacrifice themselves, through a contrite and humbled heart. Otherwise, care must be taken lest this be said to any such person: “My beloved has done evil in my house; will holy flesh cleanse him?” (Jeremiah 11:15). And again: “He acted wickedly in the land of the saints; he will not see the glory of the Lord” (Isaiah 26:10). And again: “Why do you reject my victim with your foot?” (1 Samuel 2:29).

This happens when the Lord’s table is served negligently. Hence another prophet complains, addressing the ministers: “You despise my table, and I will make you contemptible” (Malachi 1:12).

Elsewhere he also calls them rulers of Sodom: “What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me?” he says. “Who asked this from your hands? Do not bring sacrifice in vain any longer. Incense is an abomination to me. I will not endure your new moons and Sabbaths and other festivals. Your assemblies are wicked. Your new moons and solemnities my soul hates; they have become burdensome to me, I am weary of enduring them. When you stretch out your hands, I will turn my eyes away from you; and when you multiply prayer, I will not hear. Your hands are full of blood” (Isaiah 1:11–15).

The same Isaiah, when he saw the Lord, first wished to acknowledge that he had polluted lips: “Woe is me,” he said, “for I am a man of polluted lips, and I have seen the Lord of hosts” (Isaiah 6:5).

But if the one who saw the Lord with prophetic eyes grieved that his lips were polluted, how much more ought we to grieve, who receive the Lord’s body with polluted lips—or, God forbid, touch it with hands full of blood?

The Psalmist calls those whose mouth has spoken vanity “foreign sons.” And if such great danger threatens sacred ministers from their lips, how much more from their loins? That this danger must especially be guarded against is shown by the command given to those summoned to eat the lamb: first, they were to gird their loins.

Zachariah also speaks to commend this, saying that his beautiful and precious substance is “grain and wine producing virgins.”

We have advanced too far already, but the undisciplined and irreligious conduct of certain people compels us to speak. Although by their own merits they ought to be counted among outsiders, they nevertheless approach the sanctuary as though God’s prohibition did not exist: “Whoever is an outsider approaches,” it says, “shall die” (Numbers 18:7).

Wherever these or similar things are done and guarded against, the heavenly Arbiter observes in silence. According to blessed Job, he consumes both the innocent and the impious: afflicting the innocent here, but punishing the impious in the future.

Where impiety abounds more greatly, there divine rebuke frequently rages less; and where piety reigns more fully, there divine severity presses more heavily. Blessed Job shows this when he says: “If I am impious, woe is me; and if I am righteous, I will not lift up my head, sated with affliction and misery” (Job 10:15).

The impious has woe, while the righteous has misery: for eternal damnation follows the former, whereas the latter is purified by temporary pain. The impious lifts his head here but does not escape the woe that follows, because, while he exalts himself in pleasures, he plunges himself into the punishments to come.

The righteous, however, is not permitted to lift his head; but through the misery that now weighs him down, he is freed from eternal punishment.

Thus the impious, who cannot be purified by temporal punishment, commonly enjoys present prosperity for certain good works that he performs, though he is to be handed over to subsequent punishment. The righteous, on the other hand, is oppressed because of certain slight sins, so that he may be freed from eternal punishment.

Since, then, we all offend in many ways, we should not be saddened but rather rejoice if we are afflicted in any manner, as the Apostle says: “Consider it all joy, my brothers” (James 1:2), and so forth.

That every sin is punished is shown by Job, who says: “I feared all my works, knowing that you would not spare the offender” (*derelinquenti* [variant: *delinquenti*], Job 9:28). Blessed Gregory, explaining this, says that God does not leave sin without vengeance: either the person himself punishes it in himself through repentance, or God strikes him when he condemns him.

Hence the Lord looked upon Peter, and he wept bitterly. Paul, the chosen vessel, is called such, but it is said of him: “He must suffer many things for my name” (Acts 9:16).

Thus David is told: “The Lord has transferred your sin”; yet, weeping and barefoot, he fled from his son until he had received punishment for his guilt.

Thus we are washed through the baptistery, but, because of the merit of the first transgression, we die even after having been redeemed.

Therefore he strikes with scourges even when he releases sin, because he now strives to cleanse the stains of sin from his elect—stains that he does not wish to see in them forever.

But those to whom he says through the prophet, “I know that you are hard, and that your neck is an iron sinew” (Isaiah 48:4), and again, “Can the Ethiopian change his skin?” (Jeremiah 13:23), he abandons according to the desires of their hearts. In great indignation he says to them: “I will no longer be angry with you” (Isaiah 54:9). And: “When your daughters commit fornication, I will not visit them” (Hosea 4:14).

Job says of them: “Their houses are secure and peaceful, and the rod of God is not upon them” (Job 21:9). But what remains for them? He adds: “God will preserve their pain, and they will drink from the wrath of the Almighty” (ibid., 19).

Therefore, in accordance with the Psalmist, let us be ready for his scourges, and let his judgments be joyful for us, because, as it is written: “The one who does not love judgment cannot be healed” (Job 34:17).

For this reason the Apostle commands us to glory in tribulation and to give thanks in all things. Should we not offer praise for the fact that, when he afflicts us, he shows the sign of our sonship? “He scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6).

It would have been a great thing if they had been called servants. “It is a great thing for you to be called my servant.” But it is too little to be called servants, since they are not even called friends. To show a more ardent affection toward the afflicted, the divine voice calls them sons.

Whatever works, moreover, are carried out there under the protection of blessed Martin, we must believe that they are protected through his intercession, lest either the minds of those who work become empty through continual prosperity and pride, or, if not, they should be found at the supreme judgment less stripped of their sins because the file of the scourge had been set aside.

For he knows that all our righteousnesses, according to the prophet, are like a menstruating woman’s cloth, and that the priests’ holocausts themselves require washing.

What certain people marvel at—that adversity does not usually arise there where evil works abound more and good works are performed less—is known not to human beings but to God alone.

Nevertheless, it is written concerning the devil and his body, namely, the reprobate, that “deceit is directed by his hand.” For they frequently have this characteristic: what they wickedly desire, they are able to accomplish even more wickedly. They desire things with a perverse will and complete them with an even more perverse capacity, so that no adversity hinders them in the present, since nothing of prosperity will remain for them in the future.

It is therefore more necessary, and more desirable for us, that he command and provide what advances the salvation of souls than what produces applause and admiration.

Those who murmur and complain that blessed Martin no longer frequently performs the miracles customary for him add this as well: that he is not inclined to show mercy toward us as he was toward our predecessors.

By these words they reveal both the distrust and the foolishness of their hearts. For these words do not sound like discipline; rather, they imply that either blessed Martin’s power or his charity has suffered a defect: his power, in that he has less effectiveness for performing miracles; his charity, in that—God forbid—he has forgotten to show mercy.

We first answer them that they are not Jews and must not Judaize by seeking signs. Such signs were necessary at the beginning of the newborn Church to establish the faith.

Fishermen and men taken from humble occupations were preaching the divinity of the Crucified One. Since proud kings and magistrates would regard this as utterly foolish, they were compelled, through the wonder of signs, to believe the majesty of so great a matter.

When they saw that a common and lowly person healed the sick and raised the dead—something that neither the emperor with his entire army nor the priests with all their gods could do in any way—they submitted their proud necks to Christ’s humble yoke.

Now, however, since the grace of the righteous has been raised up and he ought rather to live by faith, miracles are sought unnecessarily. The works of righteousness should be performed instead.

Many have performed signs, to whom the Judge will say: “I do not know you.” Those who perform works of mercy will hear: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matthew 25:34), and so forth.

And to come to this same blessed Martin: it pleased the divine dispensation that, both while he was alive and after his death, he should perform so many and such great miracles that the whole world would recognize his name and glory.

Hence he has been endowed everywhere with such grace that, as it is written of him, no monk and certainly no bishop can be compared with him. He is joined only to the prophets and apostles; that he is in every respect like them, Egypt acknowledges, India has discovered, Syria has heard, Ethiopia has heard, and the other kingdoms listed there as well, until the passage continues:

“How much more wretched is this region of ours, which, though it had such a great man close at hand, did not deserve to know him.”

The poet, wishing to demonstrate Martin’s glory, which has extended far away, says:

“From lofty Gaul’s lighthouse, radiance is sent to the Indians.”

And again:

And wherever Christ has a name, Martin has honor. Do not his devotees attest this, who are accustomed to flock to him from distant regions and unknown languages in order to venerate him? The devotion of the ancients, by which they very frequently devoted themselves to his reverence and love, is attested also by the countless churches that are found everywhere under his name, [Col. 0746D] so many that, after the Mother of God and Peter, the shepherd of the Church, no one seems to possess more of them. Certainly, since nothing in you happens without cause, the fact that he is so glorified and so precious throughout, so to speak, the whole world did not occur by chance, but through the impulse of him who gives grace according to measure. By making his saint wondrous everywhere, he shows through the fact that he is venerated by all how greatly his grace has poured over him. For even if all kings and Caesars, by universally published edicts, commanded everyone to venerate him, they could nevertheless in no way compel his veneration to be so universal and celebrated as it is now, when all are drawn gladly to venerate him by divine inspiration. [Col. 0747A] By making his saint wondrous everywhere, God not only worked every other kind of miracle, but even raised the dead after his death in order to commend his glory.

If, therefore, by God’s providence something happens through which that same glory appears to be diminished, one must have recourse to the greatness of the virtues that he is known to have displayed at some time, so that the ship of the heart, as though firmly moored from its prow, may in no way be torn from the shore of faith by waves of distrust that perhaps strike its stern. Christ himself wished to instruct the world in this precaution. As though he intended to signify the rejection of his death, when he said, “Blessed is the one who is not scandalized because of me” (Matt. 11:6), he first proclaimed the miracles of his power. For this reason also, when he openly told his disciples of his death, he added that he would rise again on the third day. [Col. 0747B] Likewise, to blessed Peter, whom he knew would deny him, he first showed himself transfigured on the mountain, so that, when Peter incurred distrust because of the impending death, he might have recourse to the majesty that had been shown and recover the strength of faith.

But there is yet another thing that causes miracles to cease: namely, the sin of unbelief. For this reason the evangelist Mark says of omnipotent Jesus that he could not perform many miracles in Capernaum and Chorazin, adding that he marveled at the unbelief of their hearts.

What then, whoever you are? Is Martin not glorious simply because his house was so often given over to fire? We know this happening frequently in other places of the saints as well, as recently happened to that house of the holy Theban Legion, which had been built so elegantly that the craftsmen of our own time could in no way restore it to its former beauty. So too with the church in which the most blessed Martial rests, [Note: [Col. 0747D] “So too with the church in which Blessed Martial rests.” Namely, the Church of the Holy Savior, concerning which Bernard Gui, in his catalogue of the bishops of Limoges, says: “Louis, king of the Franks and Emperor Augustus, son of Charlemagne, held a general assembly at the palace of Jocundiacum in the Limousin and ordered the royal basilica of the most holy Savior to be dedicated at Limoges with great splendor in the month of October. In it, the body of the most holy Martial, which had been raised, was placed behind the altar dedicated to that most glorious Savior, in the crypt of the greater vault, in the presence of that same emperor, in that same month.” From that time the church was also called Saint Martial’s; and Ademar, a monk of Limoges, records that it was again consumed by fire by divine judgment in the year 954.] which, together with everything within its walls, is known to have suffered the same fate.

Before its burning, this same saint appeared in a dream to someone. With a sorrowful face he declared that his servants had made that house hateful to him, and that therefore its burning, as well as the death of Abbot Stephen, [Note: [Col. 0748D] “Abbot Stephen.” The seventh [abbot] of Saint Martial’s.] would soon be fulfilled. Indeed, before the aforesaid fire consumed the basilica of the aforementioned lord Martin, some faithful people saw in a vision that [Note: [Col. 0748D] “In the church at Tulle, the same Saint Martin.” Earlier it reads: “Saint Martin also appeared in a vision to a certain poor man and, as though complaining, said that he had been wronged in his house and would soon depart from it, and would go to the town of Tulle.”] the same Saint Martin stood in the church at Tulle with Saint Michael, and that Martin, praying, urged Michael concerning the care of that monastery; and, as though somewhat saddened, added that his servants would not allow him to have rest at Tours. [Col. 0747D]

Yet if dreams are to be given no, or perhaps only rare, credence, this nevertheless remains certain: God, according to the Apostle’s statement, is provoked by sin. And whoever, as Isaiah says, acts wickedly in the land of the saints [Col. 0748A] will not see the glory of the Lord. Nor does sin grieve merely some saint to whom a place may have been consecrated; according to the testimony of the Apostle, it grieves the Spirit of God himself, the one who defiles his temple by sinning. For when he was restraining the faithful from idle words and buffoonery, he added: “And do not grieve the Spirit of God” (Eph. 4:30).

But, if I may say this with your leave, whether such conduct is customarily continued in the presence of this lord, you yourselves know better. Whatever the causes may have been for which this happened, it seems that nothing else should be thought than that this most pious father preferred to hurl this scourge against his own house rather than against his subjects. He thus imitated the example of the most pious Creator, who, when the first man sinned, cursed not the man himself but the earth that he was to work.

Does it not [Col. 0748B] appear from the very outcome of these events that only that house was burned, while the clerics’ little houses around it remained unharmed? And if Martin’s power seems to have been diminished for this reason, he will no longer be the only one whom detractors insult on this account. Many other saints too have houses that burn indiscriminately on every side; indeed, although it is impious to say so, they might even mutter against the Lord himself, since the Solomonic temple was burned not once or twice but, according to Hegesippus, frequently.

Thus contempt for holy places occurs because our sins demand it, not through any defect in the Lord’s power, with which the saints have been filled. For if Martin’s power should seem thereby to be mutilated in the judgment of the foolish, nevertheless, from his other holy places, and from the miracles recently performed by him, that same power could, if it were not tedious, be fittingly commended.

But now this sort of disparagement, whatever it may be, must end. To conclude it, let us add this: it is very necessary for us, struck down by the scourge, to turn our ways toward the ways of God’s testimonies, lest it perhaps be said of us, “We tried to heal Babylon, but she was not healed, not even by fire” (Jer. 51:9). Let heavenly indignation rage not against a material house, but against those from whom the Holy Spirit flees; and let us set Martin, drawn forth by our prayers, before the offended eyes of Christ. Seizing, as it is written in Zechariah, the fringe of the garment of the lord Martin, the truest confessor, let us approach, with such an advocate, the throne of grace, in accordance with Paul’s words; perhaps in this way we shall be able to merit mercy. And as Job bears witness, we who do not possess garments of righteousness should embrace this stone, humbly begging that he cover our nakedness by his merits, lest our shame be revealed before the heavenly Judge. [Col. 0749A] For he will certainly not forget to show mercy; but the love that compelled him, when he divided his cloak, to clothe the poor man in his nakedness will now move him much more readily, if he sees that we have been corrected, to hide us—rescued from the wrath of the Lamb—while he abounds in heavenly riches.

## SERMON V

[Note: [Col. 0749D] I have transcribed the following sermon of Saint Odo of Tours, canon of Saint Martin and later abbot of Cluny, from an old Bigotian manuscript, which also contained another sermon by the same saint, already published in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, with this heading: “The sermon of Odo, of holy and distinguished memory, recently edited—while Bishop Theothelon was praying—concerning the burning of the church of Blessed Martin of Tours begins.” Concerning Odo and his writings there is no need for me to write more, since what the *Bibliotheca Patrum* and the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis* provide on this subject is more than sufficient. —Marten.]

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT MARTIN

[Apud Marten., *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. V, col. 617, from the Bigotian manuscript.]

This sacred solemnity of today, dearest brothers, must be reverently celebrated by us with the utmost respect. On it our lord, Blessed Martin, rejoices that the crown of his most glorious confession has been bestowed upon him by the Lord Jesus Christ in heaven—although once on the Lord’s day, yet for us today. We ought to rejoice, dearest brothers, in the solemnities of the saints, but especially in that of the foremost of confessors, of whom we sing: “To him the Lord deigned to grant such great grace after the apostles that, through the power of the divine Trinity, he deserved magnificently to become the raiser of three dead men.”

For blessed Paul says of such people: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined; and those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. 8:30). Saint Martin would not have come to us from such a distant region, namely Pannonia, had he not been chosen by the Lord Jesus Christ. Nor would he have despised the command of the emperor Julian and the will of his parents had he not been predestined for us by God. Nor would the great royal honor and the sweetness of noble parents have been hateful to him had he not been called by God, chosen for us, and granted as a merciful intercessor.

This is a great consolation for us, dearest brothers. We recognize that so great a reward has been given to us, but we fear the negligence of our sluggishness and indolence. A great and immeasurable talent, therefore, and a sacred trust, has been granted to us and to you in him. When entrusted to suitable people, it can truly increase; among the negligent it cannot fail to perish. From some it will be restored with manifold grace; from others it will be demanded with interest in punishments. For Christ demands with interest the talent that he lends: he repays grace to the one who pays it back, but assigns the one who does not repay it to punishments, fires, and eternal torments.

This talent, dearest brothers, we lend to your hearts through our preaching on behalf of the distinguished father, lord Martin, so that we may assign some profit of your salvation to God. We shall have to give an account of how our preaching benefits you and how obedience bears fruit for God in your souls. For I wish you to know with certainty that, while the flesh is weakly subjected to flattering desires, the army of vices is already arming itself vigorously against the soul. [Col. 0750A]

Christ’s Church also admonishes all Catholics to place their minds less upon earthly things in proportion as they remember that they have a homeland in heaven. For this is usually the distinction between the elect and the reprobate: the elect, now pilgrims and exiles, await their homeland in the future, and the less they take pleasure in fleeting joys, the more they have desired to possess their homeland in heaven. The reprobate, by contrast, have a homeland and miserable joy here; they spend their days in wicked pleasures and in a moment descend to the realms below, as it is written: “Those who have done good will go into eternal life, but those who have done evil into eternal fire; their worm will not die and their fire will not be quenched.”

When this voice has reached anyone’s ear, that person will either be blessed because of the devotion of correction or guilty because of contempt for the proclamation. For we speak blessedness to believers and bear witness to judgment against criminals, since we exist today and do not know what the future day will bring. Therefore, while we have time, let us do good, and let us not add sin upon sin, for “not one stone will be left upon another that will not be destroyed.”

Wicked thoughts separate us from God; how much more, then, do wicked deeds? If we shall have to give an account of idle words on the day of judgment, what will become of wicked deeds? And if judgment without mercy awaits the one who has not shown mercy, what judgment will await the one who has practiced negligence?

Dearest fathers and brothers: insofar as you are righteous, you are fathers; insofar as you are sinners, you are companions and brothers. By admonishing and entreating I say: let us not harden our hearts, [Col. 0750C] because neither knowledge nor prayer nor treasures will benefit those approaching the infernal realm, since there is no redemption there, none at all.

What, then, shall we say in judgment before the one who willingly endured being beaten with rods, spat upon, crowned with thorns, struck with blows, and fastened to the cross—not only for us, but also delivered over for our crimes and sins? From these sins we have been washed through him in baptism and in penance, yet, by repeating the same sins again and again, we remain sinners still. Let us indeed say with the Apostle, and let us say it continually with frequent lamentation: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ” (Rom. VII, 2).

For we must remember that we ought to do not our own will but God’s, [Col. 0750D] because “the one who does his will remains forever.” Therefore, dearest brothers, with an undivided mind, steadfast faith, strong virtue, and perfect charity, let us be prepared for every will of God. Let us firmly preserve the Lord’s commands: innocence in simplicity, harmony in charity, modesty in humility, diligence in administration, vigilance in assisting those who labor, mercy in supporting the poor, steadfastness in defending the truth, and discipline in the severity of judgment, so that nothing may be lacking in us as an example of good works; through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with God the Father lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

---

[Col. 0751]

# THE OPUSCULA ON MUSIC OF SAINT ODO, ABBOT OF CLUNY, OR OF ANOTHER ODO, A MONK

[Apud D. Gerbert, *Ecclesiastical Writers on Music*, vol. I, p. 247.]

## NOTICE

A dialogue entitled *On the Art of Music* is famous under Odo’s name. The anonymous writer of Melk attributes it specifically to Saint Odo of Cluny: “Otto,” he says, “the venerable abbot of Cluny, the most ardent lover of monastic religion, who was the jewel of monks and the glory of his disciples, composed a sufficiently useful dialogue *On the Art of Music*.”

According to John in Odo’s Life, Odo was taught music at Paris by Master Remigius of Auxerre, among the other liberal arts, and “frequently read Martianus in the liberal arts. For Remigius was his teacher in all these subjects.” That he was seized by a passion for music from his earliest youth is likewise attested to us by the words of the holy man himself concerning the vigils he celebrated on the Nativity of the Lord:

“Amid these prayers, morning praises, and Masses, the following day had dawned. And behold, while, as was customary, during the praises of so great a solemnity a melody of diverse voices was being performed, I, like an impatient young man, leapt into their midst and began to praise the King of the world together with them. I know and confess that I acted improperly, but, nevertheless, retaining in my heart that Davidic saying which is written, I presumed, not without justification, to do this: ‘Praise the Lord, all nations.’”

At that time he had not yet been instructed by Remigius in the art of music. Once formed in it, however, he later became “master of the school and teacher of that same church of Tours,” as is recorded by the author of the *Deeds of the Counts of Anjou* under Fulk the Good. In Book III, chapter 5, of his *History*, Ralph Glaber calls him provost of the church of Saint Martin at Tours; in other sources he is called a canon and precentor of that same church, and he is frequently distinguished by the name “the Musician.” Thus he is called by John, the author of his Life, Book I, no. 10; by Sigebert, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 124, and in the *Chronicle* under the years 898 and 912; also by Robert, a monk of Saint-Marien at Auxerre; and by Bernard Gui under the year 919. Bernard adds that Remigius thoroughly educated Odo in music and dialectic. Vincent of Beauvais repeats these words in Book XXIV [Col. 0751D] of the *Speculum historiale*, chapter 55, as does the author of the *Chronicon chronicorum* under the year 913.

Trithemius calls him “an excellent musician” in Book II, chapter 53, of *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*; in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 292, and in Book I, p. 47, of the *Chronicle of Hirsau*, he calls him “a distinguished musician.” Similar commendations may be seen in the *Cluniac Library* published by Quercetanus at Paris in 1614, and in volume XVII of the Lyon *Bibliotheca Patrum*, where he is often called a musician in the testimonies prefixed to Odo’s works. Yet none of these writers attributes the work *On Music* to him.

Nevertheless, following the anonymous writer of Melk, the authors of the *Literary History of France* take this as established in volume VI, p. 246:

“Saint Odo made use of his extensive knowledge of music to write a treatise in the form of a dialogue. The work was known under its author’s name to the anonymous writer of Melk, a twelfth-century author, who speaks of it favorably. It still exists in various manuscripts, notably in that of the Vatican Library numbered 1995, and in one of those that belonged to the Queen of Sweden. Monsieur de Sainte-Palaye saw the same work in manuscript during his journey through Italy. He does not name the place, saying only that it begins with the question, ‘What is music?’ and that something is missing at the end.”

Elsewhere, when reviewing the opinion of others who attribute the same little book to Odo, abbot of Morimond, they retract—or rather suspend—their judgment:

“It is claimed” (they say in volume XII, [Col. 0752C] p. 613) “that Odo of Morimond composed an *Enchiridion*, or handbook on music, in the form of a dialogue between master and disciple. Indeed, the King’s manuscripts numbered 369 and 7211 each contain a treatise *On Music* bearing Odo’s name. But since there is no proof that it belongs to our author rather than to any other person of the same name, we suspend our judgment on the matter.”

But Odo of Morimond, a twelfth-century writer, cannot be the author, since this book is cited by writers of the eleventh century.

In Guido’s letter to Michael, near the end, I read as follows:

“Let him also read the handbook (*Enchiridion*) that the most reverend Abbot Odo composed with great clarity. I left its example solely in the figures of the sounds, because I accommodated myself to children, not following Boethius in this, whose book is useful not to singers but only to philosophers.”

Immediately thereafter, in the Saint-Emmeram manuscript, there follows a dialogue composed by Abbot Odo on the art of music, called the *Enchiridion*:

“D. What is music?  
“M. Truly, the science of singing, etc.”

The same book is entitled in an Admont manuscript: “Dialogue on the Art of Music of the Lord Abbot Odo, which he called the *Enchiridion* because of the brevity of life.” In another Admont manuscript, from approximately the twelfth century, it is attributed to “Otto, abbot of the first monastery of Cluny.”

From the prologue of this little work, which we found only in the Paris Royal Library manuscript 7211, it is clear that the author was a monk in the monastery of the Blessed Virgin Mary, but undertook the work at the command of the “common Father.” By “common Father” either the pope, a bishop, or the abbot of the monastery is meant. In that manuscript it is entitled: “The Book, also called a dialogue, composed by the lord Odo.”

Although the title “lord” properly belongs to an abbot, in the Middle Ages the title “abbot” was nevertheless often added. It was therefore easy for two authors with the same name to be confused: namely, Otto, author of the *Tonary* which we publish from a Cassinese manuscript and, as may be conjectured, abbot of Cluny; and the other, a monk, the author of the dialogue.

In our twelfth-century Saint-Blasien manuscript: “The Music of the Lord Odo.” In Vatican manuscript no. 72, formerly belonging to the Queen of Sweden, it is recorded as: “A dialogue composed by Lord Odo on the art of music.” This manuscript is mutilated at the end and does not proceed beyond the formulas of the fourth mode. The Saint-Emmeram manuscript does not reach those formulas at all, its pages breaking off abruptly. The Admont manuscript ends with these exact words: “Here ends the musical *Enchiridion*.”

In the Saint-Blasien manuscript the following continues in the same context:

“D. Come then, I beg you, and explain the modes that follow.”

Immediately afterward, beginning with the line “The discipline of the musical art must be pursued with the greatest zeal,” and so forth, the text appears in the Leipzig Paulina Library manuscript and is attributed to Berno of Reichenau. At the end of the Saint-Blasien manuscript, some material is added from the aforementioned letter of Guido to Michael, in which reference is made to Odo’s *Enchiridion* itself.

In that portion of the work which bears Odo’s name in all the manuscripts, Odo is cited. Since he may be taken to be the celebrated abbot of Cluny, there is no obstacle to my thinking that this is the Odo whom, according to Trithemius, *Chronicle of Hirsau*, under the year 994, “before entering the religious life, was a great master in the art of music and precentor of the church of Tours.”

What function is more appropriate to a precentor than to prescribe a tonary such as the one we give from the Cassinese manuscript? From this it is also clear why John and the other writers of his Life, as well as the cataloguers of his writings, make no mention of a work *On Music*: a work of the kind in question cannot properly be called a tonary. Nevertheless, this circumstance may have furnished an opportunity for attributing another Odo’s book *On Music* to this holy abbot, whose fame was conspicuous everywhere. For in that age, throughout the Middle Ages, outstanding men devoted themselves to this kind of study and labor. We have already mentioned the *Tonary*, or *Antiphonary*, of Regino, the universally celebrated abbot of Prüm, which was inscribed by its author, Archbishop Rathbod of Trier, and which, it is believed, survives in the Leipzig municipal library, copied in Regino’s own hand and even containing musical notation.

I myself handled and examined a contemporary manuscript of the *Tonary* of Berno, the famous abbot of Reichenau, which was preserved in the monastery of Saint Blaise, already consumed by fire.

I pass over others in silence. It is appropriate, however, to refer to the twenty-first letter of Saint Anselm in the new edition by Gerberon, a monk of Saint-Maur. In it Anselm asks Rodulf, whom he calls his dearest brother, to write an antiphonary with musical notation, beginning as follows:

“Reverend Lord Prior Helgotus, beloved by us and loving us and you, wishes to encourage you by his prayers to notate an antiphonary, but he considers that a considerable burden of labor is involved in the undertaking itself. Since, therefore, in venerable humility he does not wish to weigh his prayers, although he could, so heavily that they might suspend the burden imposed, he earnestly asks that you take care to add our prayers to his against the labor in question. But since neither he nor we are attempting to lighten the burden of the desired work through the petitions of friends in such a way as to try to burden you with indiscriminate entreaties, let us consider and propose to you the benefit of those nearby, as well as the reward of your charity and obedience. We therefore advise your affection to devote to this work, which you are being asked to undertake, the time that you do not begrudge spending on any other writings. If you say that this is nothing, or very little, then, just as you are certain that this nothing or very little is scarcely sufficient, so we are not doubtful that it will advance the work somewhat.”

That Saint Odo, while still young, was renowned for composing chants is clear from the account of John, the author of his Life and his disciple, Book I, no. 10. John relates that Odo was asked to revise the office of Saint Martin and shorten its antiphons, and says that he performed this task excellently. The three hymns of that office that John mentions are also touched upon by Ulrich in Book I, chapter 23, of the *Customs of Cluny*, and by Ditmar in his *Chronicle*, both cited by Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints*, fifth century, p. 154.

“Likewise,” John continues, “he composed twelve antiphons, each having three differentiae; their words and the consonance of their melodies correspond to one another so harmoniously that nothing sweeter seems capable of being found either in their meaning, whether more or less, or in the modulations of the symphony.”

The author of the dialogue *On Music*, Odo, repeatedly refers to the antiphon of this office, “O blessed pontiff!” He says:

“Since it was in the beginning and end of the second mode, it was most carefully corrected by Lord Odo into the first tone solely because of the elevation of that one voice, where it says: ‘O Martin, sweetness.’”

Nothing could provide clearer evidence that this Odo, the author of the dialogue—who, as the frequent mention of the gamma that Guido added to the monochord reveals, wrote after Guido—is different from our Odo.

In a Viennese manuscript his image is indeed depicted with a halo around his head, but with hair and without any indication of monastic dress; he stands beside a seat, holding a pen in both hands as though about to write. The manuscript of the Imperial Library is different. From it the following works occur in our collection: *Rules of the Lord Odo on Rithmomachy*, and *On the Abacus*, etc.

In the library of the monastery of Monte Cassino there is preserved a manuscript written around the eleventh century in Lombard script. It contains, arranged by chapters, a compilation on music drawn from various writers, and quite often interpolated. Its ninety-fifth chapter is entitled, in a barbarous manner like everything else in that manuscript:

“Likewise, the tonaries in order with their differentiae, which we possess honorably corrected and explained by the religious abbot Lord Odo, who was skilled in the art of music.”

It is a tonary with almost continuous ancient Lombard musical notation, which we cannot reproduce in types. Its preface also discusses the correction of the antiphon “O blessed pontiff,” [Col. 0754D] which the other Odo—the one who professes himself a monk subject to the common Father, namely the abbot Lord Odo—attributes in the dialogue *On Music*. We publish that dialogue, together with its prologue from Paris Royal Library manuscript no. 7211, from the twelfth-century Saint-Blasien manuscript, collated with the defective Saint-Emmeram manuscript and with the Admont manuscript, in which, after the dialogue, one reads: “Here ends the musical *Enchiridion*.” I think that somewhere this dialogue is also entitled *Enchiridion*.

# PREFACE TO THE TONARY OF LORD ODO, ABBOT

*(From the eleventh-century Cassinese manuscript.)*

Here begins the formula concerning the tones, explaining how each singer ought to perform in the church.

“Gloria: *e u o u a e*, that is, ‘of the ages. Amen.’”

[Col. 0755]

[Col. 0755A] I have taken care to write down for you the formulas for singing, explaining how every church singer ought to maintain the tone of antiphons, offices, or communions, or of any kind of chant he may undertake. Anyone who wishes to hold the highest position of mastery in church singing should study them with the greatest zeal.

I admonish all singers, especially those who seem to preside over the greater offices in the church, to provide these examples daily and with precision to those under them, so that, whenever the antiphons begin in church, they may not create confusion at the beginning of the psalm and wander off by starting in different places.

Whoever wishes to devote himself diligently to singing should read these formulas and the differentiae contained in them every day. When he wishes to begin an antiphon in church, he should not retain its opening but hurry as quickly as possible to its end; and, in whatever tone he finds it, he should begin the psalm in that tone. For there are many in the church—of whose number I have observed a great many—who, because of their arrogance, put themselves before others, make up their own tone, and say that such-and-such is the tone, although they are entirely mistaken. They do this for no other reason than to appear as masters before others.

Such people acquire greater condemnation for themselves thereby than reward, because blessed Pope Gregory said that, when he labored to compose chant, he was not following negligence but did this to soothe the minds of believers, to the praise of our Creator.

Finally, let no one suppose that all antiphons correspond at their beginnings with the beginning of the psalm. Most antiphons, however, require the psalm to begin at their end, as with the antiphon “O blessed pontiff,” which many assign to the second tone. But they are mistaken, since it belongs to the first tone and the seventh differentia. The same applies to many other antiphons prescribed in the formulas.

Therefore I command all singers who preside over this art to preserve with the greatest zeal the eight tones that we have explained in the figure of the eight beatitudes. If they do this, their labor here will not be in vain but highly profitable; and there is a very useful rationale in each of their differentiae for anyone who is able to grasp its meaning.

The first tone has ten differentiae; the second tone has one; the third tone appears to consist of five differentiae. The fourth is prescribed to end in nine. The fifth appears to have been constructed in two only for a single antiphon. The sixth is recognized as marked by a single differentia. We show that the seventh is written with seven differentiae. We have judged that the eighth ends in six differentiae.

The seventh and eighth seem to agree in their endings but differ at their beginnings. Therefore those who wish to begin their antiphons without error must apply themselves to them with great diligence. For sometimes, as was briefly mentioned above, they correspond with the psalm at their beginning; but many others must be begun at their end.

## THE EIGHT TONES WITH THEIR DIFFERENTIAE FOLLOW

### On the eight tonaries in order

### I

The first differentia: the Dorian tone and authentic protus; the voice is *odax*, the interval *lychanos hypaton*, the organ *anoton*, the symphony the variety of protus, and the string *scembs*, as the first tone begins, with the schema D.

We explain how each differentia [probably *quaeque differentiae*] ascends and descends individually in sounding with the voices. The first differentia begins on the fourth string, called *scembs*, and, proceeding smoothly, ascends to the eighth, called *kaphe*. Proceeding smoothly, it ascends to the third, called *re*, and rests where it began.

The chant begins:

> Seek first the kingdom of God.

The first ends; the second begins.

### II

The second differentia: the hypoiastian tone and plagal protus; the voice is *odax*, the interval *lychanos hypaton*, the organ *ysaton*, the symphony the variety of plagal protus. The string is *scembs*, and the schema D.

The second differentia begins on the fourth string, called *scembs*, ascends to the sixth string, called *neth*, and descends to the first, called *buc*, resting where the chant begins.

The following is similar to this:

> The second is like this.

The second ends; the third begins.

### III

The third differentia: the Aeolian semitone tone and authentic deuterus. The voice is *jubilo*, the interval *hypate meson*, the organ *chamilon*, the symphony the variety of deuterus, the string *kaphe*, and the schema B.

The third differentia begins on the ninth string, called *kaphe*, ascends to the eleventh string, called *suggesse*, descends to the fourth, called *scembs*, and rests in schema E.

Another chant:

> It is the third day since these things happened.

The third ends; the fourth begins.

### IV

The fourth differentia is taken as the cantus tone and plagal deuterus. The voice is *jubilo*, the interval *hypate meson*, the organ *salpion*, and the symphony the variety of plagal deuterus. The string is *caemar*, and the schema E.

The fourth differentia is taken on the fifth string, called *caemar*. It ascends to the seventh, called *uciche*, descends to the third, called *re*, and rests where it began.

Another chant:

> The fourth watch came upon them.

The fourth ends; the fifth begins.

### V

The fifth differentia: the parmenus tone and authentic tritus. The voice is *excelsa*, the interval *parypate meson*, the organ *cuphos*, the symphony the variety of tritus, the string *asel*, and the schema D.

The fifth begins on the eighth string, called *asel*, ascends to the eleventh, called *sucgesse*, [Col. 0757B] descends to the sixth, called *neth*, and rests in schema F.

The chant:

> Five prudent women entered the wedding feast.

The fifth ends; the sixth begins.

### VI

The sixth differentia: the epynician semitone tone and plagal tritus. The voice is *excelsa*, the interval *parypate meson*, the organ *bubos*, the symphony the variety of plagal tritus, the string *neth*, and the schema F.

The sixth arises from the sixth string, called *neth*, ascends to the eighth, called *asel*, descends to the third, called *re*, and rests in schema F.

The chant:

> At the sixth hour he sat beside the well.

The sixth ends; the seventh begins.

### VII

The seventh differentia: the *adonta* tone and authentic tetrardus. The voice is *stridentis*, the interval *lichanos meson*, the organ *strigon*, the symphony the variety of tetrardus, and the string *sucgesse*. It ascends to the twelfth, called *nar*, descends to the seventh, called *viche*, and rests in schema G.

The chant:

> There are seven spirits before the throne of God.

The seventh ends; the eighth begins.

### VIII

The eighth differentia begins with the thetic tone and plagal tetrardus. The voice is *stridentis*, the interval *lichanos meson*, the organ *fonicon*, and the symphony the variety of plagal tetrardus. The string is *neth*, and the schema F.

The eighth begins on the sixth string, called *neth*. It ascends to the eleventh, called *sucgesse*, descends to the sixth, where it begins, and rests in schema G.

The chant:

> There are eight beatitudes.

# THE BOOK BEGINS, ALSO CALLED A DIALOGUE, COMPOSED BY LORD ODO, BRIEFLY, APPROPRIATELY, AND DECOROUSLY COLLECTED FOR THE BENEFIT OF READERS

*(From Paris Royal Library manuscript 7211.)*

[Col. 0757]

## THE PROLOGUE BEGINS
[Col. 0757C] You earnestly requested, dearest brothers, that I should give you a few rules of music—only such rules as boys and simple people could grasp—and by which they might quickly attain, with God’s help, complete proficiency in singing. You made this request because [the transmitted *quae* is corrected to *quia*, “because”] you yourselves had heard and seen that this could be done, and had confirmed it by reliable evidence. While I was living among you, with God’s cooperation alone, through this art I taught certain boys and young men: some learned in three days, others in four [the text is corrected accordingly from *alii triduo, ut alii*], and some, after practicing this art for a week, learned many antiphons by themselves, without hearing them from anyone, relying only on the regular written notation, and shortly afterward sang them without hesitation. After not many more days had passed, [Col. 0757D] at first sight and without preparation they sang faultlessly whatever had been written according to the principles of music—something ordinary singers had never been able to do, although many of them had already spent fifty [Col. 0758C] years uselessly engaged in the practice and study of singing.

When people were carefully and inquisitively investigating whether our teaching was effective for every chant, I took a certain brother who seemed accomplished in comparison with the other singers and examined the antiphonary of Saint Gregory with the greatest care. I found that almost everything in it stood according to the rules. A few passages that had been corrupted by inexperienced singers were corrected [the transmitted *correpta* is corrected to *correcta*], with the testimony of certain singers no less than by the authority of the rule. Yet, dearest brothers, in the longer chants we found a voice belonging to a high tone, as well as elevations and descents contrary to the rule. But because common usage unanimously defended those chants, [Col. 0758D] we did not presume to correct them. We nevertheless noted them individually, lest, while seeking the truth of the rule, we should make people uncertain.

When this had been done, you were inflamed with still greater desire and pressed on with the most fervent [Col. 0759A] prayers and efforts that, for the honor of God and of his most holy mother Mary, in whose venerable monastery these things were taking place, and so that the rules might be made available as useful aids, the entire antiphonary should be written out together with the formulas of the tones.

Trusting, therefore, in your prayers and accepting the commands of our common Father, I neither wish nor am able to abandon this work. Among the wise men of this age, the teaching of this art is very difficult and extensive. Let anyone who wishes cultivate and traverse that field with laborious effort. But whoever has received this small gift of God from God himself will be satisfied with simple fruit. So that you may understand this better and accept what is necessary according to your true intention, let one of you come forward to ask questions or converse, and I will not neglect to answer as the Lord grants me ability.

## THE MUSIC OF LORD ODO BEGINS

[Note: [Col. 0759D] The Vienna Codex gives this title: “The Dialogue composed by Lord Odo on the art of music begins.” The Saint-Emmeram Codex gives this one: “The Dialogue composed by Lord Odo, abbot, on the art of music, which is called the Handbook, begins.” The Admont Codex, from about the thirteenth century, is entitled as follows: “The Dialogue on the musical art of Lord Otto, abbot of the first monastery of Cluny, which he called the Handbook because of its brevity.”]

[Col. 0759]

## SUMMARY

[Col. 0759A]

1. On the monochord and its use.  
2. On measurement.  
3. On the tone and semitone.  
4. On consonances.  
5. On the conjunctions of voices.  
6. The distinction between tone and semitone according to the modes.  
7. On the limits of the modes.  
8. What a mode is, and from what it may be recognized and distinguished.  
9. On the elevation and descent of the modes.  
10. The eight modes.  
11. The formula of the first mode.  
12. The formula of the second mode.  
13. The formula of the third mode.  
14. The formula of the fourth mode.  
15. The formula of the fifth mode.  
16. The formula of the sixth mode.  
17. The formula of the seventh mode.  
10. The formula of the eighth mode.

[Col. 0759B]

**1. D.** What is music?

**M.** The true science of singing, and an easy path to perfection in singing.

**D.** How so?

**M.** Just as a teacher first shows you all the letters on a writing tablet, so the musician indicates all the notes of a melody on the monochord.

**D.** What is that monochord like?

**M.** A long, square piece of wood shaped like a box and hollow inside like a harp; a string placed over it produces a sound, through which you can easily grasp the variations of the notes.

[Note: The Vienna Codex omits *long*, and Saint-Emmeram has *square*.]

**D.** How is the string placed?

**M.** A straight line is drawn lengthwise through the middle of the box. After leaving a space of one inch from each end, a point is placed on that same line at each side. In the spaces left at the ends, two small bridges are set, so that they hold the string suspended above the line in such a way that the string between the two bridges is as long as the line beneath the string.

**D.** How does one string produce many different notes?

**M.** The letters or signs used by musicians are set in order on the line beneath the string. As the measuring device runs along between the line and the string, shortening or lengthening the string at those same letters, it miraculously produces the whole melody. [Note: The following material is missing in the Vienna Codex.] When an antiphon is marked out for boys by means of those letters, they learn it from the string more easily and better than if they heard it from a person. After practicing for a few months, once the string has been removed, they can sing without hesitation, by sight alone, [Col. 0759D] what they have never heard.

[Col. 0760B]

**D.** What you say is extremely marvelous. Our singers, at any rate, have never been able to aspire to such perfection.

**M.** Rather, brother, they have gone astray; and because they did not seek the path, they labored in vain throughout their entire lives.

**D.** How can it happen that a string teaches better than a human being?

**M.** A human being sings as he wishes or is able; but the string has been divided by the wisest men through the letters mentioned above according to such an art that, when it is carefully observed and considered, it cannot lie.

### 2

**D.** What, I ask, is that art?

**M.** The measurement of the monochord; for what has been properly measured never deceives.

**D.** Might I perhaps learn the measurements themselves simply, in a few words?

**M.** Today, with God’s help—only listen carefully. At the head of the monochord, at the point mentioned above, place the letter Γ, that is, the Greek G. [Note: The material in parentheses is taken from the Admont Codex.] [Since it is rarely used, many copies do not contain it.] From Γ to the point that we placed at the end, divide the length carefully into nine parts; where the first ninth part ends [near Γ], write the letter A, and call this the first note. From that first letter A, divide the length similarly into nine parts all the way to the end, and at the ninth part place the letter B as the second note. Then return to the head, divide from Γ into four parts, and write the letter C as the third note. Divide similarly from the first A into four parts, and write the letter D as the fourth note. Dividing B in the same way into four parts, you will find the fifth note, E. The third note, C, likewise indicates the sixth letter, F. After this return to Γ and, beginning there and proceeding in order through the other letters that follow, divide the aforesaid line into two parts—that is, through the middle—until you have fourteen or fifteen notes apart from Γ. When you divide the notes through the middle, you must make them different. For example, when you divide from Γ through the middle, write G for Γ, place a lower-case *a* for the halfway point of A, and another *b* for B, another *c* for C, another *d* for D, another *e* for E, another *f* for F, another *g* for G, and another *a* for *a*, so that from the middle of the monochord onward the letters are the same as those in the first part. In addition, divide from the sixth note F by four and place backward another rounded *b*: both of these are taken as one note, and one is called the second ninth; neither of the two will regularly be found in the same chant.

The figures, notes, and letters are therefore placed in order as follows:

Γ. I. A. II. B. III. C. IIII. D. V. E. VI. F. VII. G. VIII. a. IX. I.b. IX. II. X. c. XI. d. XII. e. XIII. f. XIIII. g. XV a [a].

**D.** Thanks be to God. I understand well, and trust that from now on I shall know how to make a monochord.

### 3

But what is this, I ask, that I observe on a regularly measured monochord: in some places smaller, in others larger, spaces and intervals between the notes?

**M.** The larger space is called a tone. It is found from Γ to the first A, and from the first A to the second B. The smaller space, such as that from the second note B to the third C, is called a semitone, producing a more contracted elevation or descent. No space of a semitone, whether measured or calculated, reaches the extent of a tone; rather, when the divisions are made according to the method described above, tones and semitones are formed in their proper places. [Note: The material in parentheses is taken from the Admont Codex.] [If you carry all the tones to the farthest point, you will marvel that a division into nine parts is found everywhere, as from Γ to the first A and from the first A to the second B, just as you did at the beginning.] The first ninth, *b*, and the second ninth do not make either a tone or a semitone with one another. But from the first ninth *b* to the eighth note *a* there is a semitone; to the tenth note *c*, a tone. Conversely, the second ninth makes a tone with the eighth note *a*, but a semitone with the tenth note *c*. [Note: This material is from Admont.] [Therefore one of them is always superfluous; and in whatever chant you admit one, you reject the other, lest at the same place you should appear to make both a tone and a semitone, which would be absurd.]

**D.** It is especially astonishing that, after dividing only from Γ to the first A and from the first A to the second B into nine parts, I have proved that all equal tones consist of a division into nine parts. But I ask you to show me whether there are other divisions of the monochord and whether they are found everywhere or only in several places.

### 4

**M.** Besides the tone, there are three divisions that preserve the natural arrangement of the notes mentioned above. The first is a division into four, because it is divided into four parts, as from the first A to the fourth D. It contains four notes and three intervals: two tones and one semitone. Therefore, wherever on the monochord you find two tones and one semitone between two notes, you will prove that the interval between those two notes runs to its end by a fourfold division. It is therefore called *diatessaron*, that is, “from four.”

The second is a division into three, as from the first note A to the fifth E. Within its space are five notes and four intervals: three tones and one semitone. Therefore, wherever you see three tones and one semitone between two notes, the space between those notes runs to its end in three steps. It is called *diapente*, that is, “from five,” because there are five notes within its space.

The third division is that which is divided by two, or through the middle, and is called *diapason*, that is, “from all.” As stated above, you recognize it clearly from the similarity of the letters, as from the first A to the eighth *a*. It consists of eight notes and seven intervals: five tones and two semitones. It also contains one diatessaron and one diapente. From the first A to the fourth D is a diatessaron, and from the fourth D to the eighth *a* is a diapente. From the first A to the eighth *a* the diapason is found in this way: A, B, C, D, E, F, G, *a*.

**D.** In a few words I have learned quite a lot about the divisions. But I wish to hear why the same letters occur in the first and second parts.

**M.** This happens because, when the notes of the second part are made from the seventh G onward according to the notes of the first part by means of the diapason, apart from the first ninth *b*, the two parts agree with one another so closely that whatever letters make a tone, semitone, diatessaron, diapente, or diapason in the first part are proved to make the same intervals in the second part.

For example, in the first part, from Γ to A there is one tone; to B, a tone and a tone—that is, a ditone; to C, a diatessaron; to D, a diapente; and to G, a diapason. Similarly, in the second part, from G to *a* there is one tone; to the square *b* (*b quadratum*), a tone and a tone; to *c*, a diatessaron; to *d*, a diapente; and to *g*, a diapason. Thus every chant is sung in the second part just as in the first. But the notes of the first part sing concordantly with those of the second part, as masculine voices with boys’ voices.
