**D.** I understand that this was wisely arranged. Now I wish first to hear how I can mark a chant, so that I may grasp it without a teacher. When you have given examples of the rules, I shall recognize it better; and if anything should completely escape my memory, I shall be able to return confidently to such notes.

**M.** Place before your eyes the letters of the monochord as the melody proceeds through them. If you do not yet fully understand the power of those letters, strike the string according to them and hear and learn wonderfully from a teacher who does not know what he is teaching.

**D.** Truly, I said, you have given me a marvelous teacher, made by me to teach me, who himself knows nothing while teaching me. Indeed, because of his patience and obedience I cherish him greatly: he will sing to me whenever I wish, and, never angered by my slowness of understanding, will not torment me with blows or insults [Vienna: *with rods*].

**M.** He is a good teacher, but he requires a diligent listener.

### 5

**D.** In what matters must diligence chiefly be applied?

**M.** In the conjunctions of notes that produce different consonances, so that, just as they are different and distinct, you may be able to pronounce each one appropriately in a different and distinct manner.

**D.** How many distinctions are there? Please explain and demonstrate them with common examples.

[Note: In this paragraph, letters that in Migne are printed above a word have been keyed in square brackets after the word.]

**M.** There are six, both in descent and in elevation.

The first conjunction of notes occurs when two notes are joined between which there is one semitone, as from the fifth [E] to the sixth [F]. This consonance is the most contracted and narrowest of all, as in the first elevation of this antiphon: *Haec* [E] *est* [F] *quae* [E] *nescivit*—“This is she who did not know.” [G a c c] In descent, by reversal, it is as follows: *Vidimus* [F E D] *stellam*—“We saw the star.” [E F]

The second occurs when there is a tone between two notes, as from the third [C] to the fourth [D] in elevation: *Non* [C] *vos* [D] *relinquam*—“I will not leave you,” [D F D] and so forth. In descent it is as follows: *Angelus* [D C E F] *Domini*—“The angel of the Lord.” [G E D D]

The third occurs when a tone and a semitone make the interval between two notes, as between the fourth [D] and the sixth [F], in this way in elevation: *Joannes* [D D F] *autem*—“But John.” In descent: *In* [E] *lege*—“In the law.” [E D]

The fourth occurs when there are two tones between one note and another, as from the sixth [F] to the eighth [*a*] in elevation: *Adhuc* [E F] *multa* [*a a*] *habeo*—“I still have many things.” [] In descent, in this way: *Ecce* [*a F*] *Maria*—“Behold Mary.” [*a c c c*]

The fifth is made by a diatessaron, as from the first A to the fourth D in elevation: *Valde* [A D] *honorandus*—“Very greatly to be honored.” In descent it is as follows: *Secundum* [*a C D*] *autem*—“But according to.”

The sixth is by a diapente, as from the fourth D to the eighth *a*, as in: [Col. 0763D] *Primum* [D a, b a] *quaerite*—“Seek first.” [a G G] In descent, from the third C to the seventh G, as follows: *Canite* [G C D] *tuba*—“Sound the trumpet.”

No other regular conjunctions of notes are found anywhere.

### 6

Ordinary singers often fall into the gravest error because they pay no attention at all to the force of the tone, the semitone, and the other consonances. Each chooses whatever first pleases his ears or whatever happens to be easier to learn or pronounce; and a great error arises in many chants as to what mode they belong to.

By “modes” I mean all eight tones and the modes of all the chants that occur in order in the formulas, so that, if one says “tones,” there will be no uncertainty whether one is speaking of the tones of the formulas or of the tones formed by division and arrangement into nine parts.

If you ask those singers about a chant, what kind it is, they immediately answer that they do not know, as though they knew it perfectly. If you ask them for a reason by which they know this, they say hesitantly that it is because the chant resembles other chants of the same mode at its beginning and end. Yet they understand nothing at all about the mode of any chant, not knowing that a difference of a single note forces a change of mode.

Consider this antiphon: *O beatum pontificem!*—“O blessed pontiff!” It had been in the second mode at both its beginning and end, but because of the elevation of that one note where it says *O Martine dulcedo*—“O Martin, sweetness”—it was most carefully corrected by Lord Odo into the first tone.

Likewise, in the antiphon *Domine, qui operati sunt*—“Lord, those who have acted”—you can test this more carefully. If you begin it in the sixth mode, as many establish it, on the letter F, it does not depart from that mode until the semitone that occurs in *tabernaculo tuo*—“in your tabernacle”—on a single syllable. But because this is customary and sounds well, it should not be corrected. Instead, let us inquire whether it perhaps begins in another tone and is found to be consonant throughout in that mode, so that it does not need correction.

Begin it, therefore, on the letter G, that is, in the eighth mode, and you will prove that it stands regularly in that mode. Hence some begin it, *Domine*—“Lord”—as I now tell you.

From this it is understood that the musician is inexperienced who easily and presumptuously corrects several chants without first investigating all the modes to see whether a chant might stand properly in one of them. He should care not greatly about resemblance to other chants but about regular truth. If it pleases no tone, let it be corrected according to the tone in which it is least dissonant. The following should also be observed: a corrected chant should either sound more fittingly or differ only slightly from its former resemblance.

**D.** You have wisely warned me about the error of incompetent singers, and have also given useful instruction—though in few words—to those who practice as they ought: concerning the careful investigation of the regular monochord, the approval of regular chants, and the correction of false ones.

### 7

**D.** Nevertheless, add how many notes a chant ought to contain.

**M.** Some say eight, others nine, and others ten.

**D.** Why eight?

**M.** Because of the greater division, that is, the diapason; or because, among the ancients, the lyre was made with eight sounds.

**D.** Why nine?

**M.** Because of the two diapentes, which end at nine notes. Since there is one diapente from Γ to the fourth note and another from that fourth D to the eighth *a*, there are nine notes from Γ to the eighth *a*.

**D.** Why ten?

**M.** Because of the authority of David’s ten-stringed psalter, or because a threefold diatessaron is found in ten notes. From Γ to the third C there is one diatessaron; from the third C to the sixth F there is another; and from the sixth F to the first ninth B there remains a third. Therefore ten notes are counted from Γ to the first ninth B.

[Col. 0765A]

**D.** Can there also be fewer notes in a chant?

**M.** Certainly, five or four; but in such a way that five produce a diapente and four a diatessaron.

**D.** The argument you have given, and the testimony of nearly all chants, prove that what you say is true. But explain what the tone is, which you so often call a mode.

### 8

**M.** A tone or mode is a rule that determines every chant from its ending. For unless you know the ending, you cannot know where the chant should begin or how far it should be elevated or lowered.

**D.** What rule takes its beginning from the ending?

**M.** Every beginning must agree with its ending according to the six consonances mentioned above. No note can begin a chant unless it is itself the final note or agrees with the final note through one of the six consonances. Any notes that can be joined to the ending by those consonances can also serve as the beginning of a chant with that ending, except that a chant ending on the fifth note E, which is the first semitone in the third mode, is often found to begin on the tenth note C, which lies one diapente and one semitone away from that fifth note E.

It is also clear that the distinctions—that is, the places at which we pause in a chant and divide it—must end in each mode on the same notes on which chants of that mode may begin. And wherever each mode begins more often and more suitably, there it customarily begins or ends its distinctions more appropriately and decorously.

The teachers teach that more distinctions ought to end on the note that terminates the mode, lest, if more distinctions were made on some other note than on that one, they should also seek to end the chant on the same note and thereby be forced to change from the mode in which they had been.

In the end, a chant belongs more properly to the mode toward which its distinctions run more extensively. Beginnings, too, are more often and more suitably found on the same note that terminates the chant.

You may confirm this principle in the following antiphon, *Tribus miraculis*—“With three miracles”: here is one distinction, *Ornatum diem sanctum colimus*—“We celebrate the adorned holy day”; here is another, *Hodie stella magos duxit ad praesepium*—“Today a star led the Magi to the manger”; here is a third, *Hodie vinum ex aqua factum est ad nuptias*—“Today wine was made from water for the wedding”; here is a fourth, *Hodie a Joanne Christus baptizari voluit*—“Today Christ wished to be baptized by John”; here is the final one.

You see, therefore, that in a regular chant several distinctions begin and end in its own tone, so that the chants themselves also begin and end on the same note.

### 9

**D.** That it is so, as you assert, is defended everywhere by the authority of singing teachers. But continue by explaining what rule the chant takes from its ending concerning elevation and descent.

**M.** In sharp or elevated chants, such as those of the first, third, fifth, and seventh tones, no chant should rise more than eight notes above its ending. At that eighth note is the same letter as at the ending, because of the chief extent of the division called the diapason. The chant has one note below its final.

But in the lower or flatter chants, such as the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth, no descent of any note before the ending will be found that is not joined to the ending by one of the six consonances mentioned above. Their elevation from the ending proceeds through five notes according to those same consonances. Sometimes it proceeds as far as the sixth. In which notes the chants of all the modes most often begin according to present usage, you will observe in their formulas.

### 10

**D.** Since you have proved that the chants of all the modes take their rule from their endings, it is time to say how many modes or tones there are.

**M.** Some think there are four modes.

**D.** Why?

**M.** Because every regular chant can end on four notes of the monochord.

**D.** What are those notes?

**M.** The fourth D, on which the mode called *authentus protus* ends—that is, the first author or prince. The fifth E, on which the mode called *authentus deuterus* ends—that is, the second author or prince. The sixth F, on which *authentus tritus* ends—that is, the third author and prince. And the seventh G, on which *authentus tetrardus* ends—that is, the fourth author or prince. These four are divided into eight.

**D.** Why?

**M.** Because of elevated and low chants. When a chant in *authentus protus* is sharp or elevated, the mode is called *authentus protus*. But if it is grave and low in the same *authentus protus*, it is called *plaga proti*.

**D.** Why is it called *plaga proti*?

**M.** *Plaga proti*, that is, “the part of the first,” is so called because it ends in the same part—that is, the same place or note, the fourth D of the monochord—on which *authentus protus* also ends.

Similarly, when a chant in *authentus deuterus* is sharp, it is called *authentus deuterus*; but if the chant is flat, it is called *plaga deuteri*. The same terminology applies to *authentus tritus* and *plaga triti*, and to *authentus tetrardus* and *plaga tetrardi*.

Custom, however, has established that *authentus protus* and *plaga proti* be called the first and second modes; *authentus deuterus* and *plaga deuteri*, the third and fourth; *authentus tritus* and its plagal mode, the fifth and sixth; and *authentus tetrardus* and its plagal mode, the seventh and eighth.

There are therefore eight modes, through which every melody proceeds and is varied by eight different qualities.

**D.** How shall I be able to observe their differences and common features?

**M.** Through tones and semitones. Wherever tones and semitones occur together, the remaining consonances are also similar. Wherever there are two tones and one semitone, there will be a diatessaron; and wherever three tones are joined to a semitone, there will also be a diapente. The same must be understood concerning the remaining consonances.

[Col. 0767A]

**D.** Come then, I beg you, and tell me about the modes that follow.

### 11

**M.** The first tone ends on the fourth note and proceeds to the eleventh, on which the same letter *d* occurs, through tones and semitones as follows: after the ending, a tone occurs first, then a semitone, then two tones, followed again by a semitone and two tones. It descends from the ending by one tone to the third note, in this manner [the source supplies no formula here].

[Note: Admont adds these verses:

> On the fourth note the first establishes its seat;  
> Let the third note lie below, and let another, the fourth, stand above,  
> So that it may sound an intense diatessaron and diapente.]

Some wish to make a ten-stringed scale and add one note, the second B. But it is not customary for the first mode to descend to it.

A chant of this mode begins on C, as in *O beatum pontificem*—“O blessed pontiff”; more often on D, when the beginning agrees with the ending, as in *Ecce nomen Domini*—“Behold the name of the Lord”; also on E, but rarely, as in *Gaudete in Domino*—“Rejoice in the Lord”; on F, as in *Ipsi soli*—“To him alone”; also on G, as in *Canite tuba*—“Sing, trumpet”; and on *a*, as in *Veniet Dominus*—“The Lord will come,” or *Exi cito*—“Go out quickly.”

### 12

The second tone likewise ends on the same note D and ascends with it to the first ninth *b*, but does not reach the tenth or eleventh. It descends from the ending by a tone, a semitone, and a tone to the first A, and sometimes, though rarely, by another tone as far as Γ. Thus ten strings are formed in this manner [the source supplies no formula here].

[Note: Admont adds:

> The second also takes its seat and rests there,  
> To which the intense diapente sounds and the relaxed one sounds.  
> Add a ninth above the first, if you wish to proceed.]

The second tone therefore has Γ, the first A, and the second B, which the first does not have; while the first has the tenth *c* and the eleventh *d*, which the second does not have.

There are many chants that do not descend to Γ, the first A, or the second B, and do not rise to the tenth or eleventh. It is uncertain whether these belong to the first or second tone. Their distinction is as follows.

If they do not rise to the eighth and ninth, they certainly belong to the second tone. The eighth and ninth will therefore be common to both. When a chant rises to them, if it remains on them for a long time, strikes them a third or fourth time, or begins on the eighth, it will belong to the first mode. But if it begins on the lower notes and, according to the length of the antiphon, rises only very rarely [Col. 0767C] to those notes, it will belong to the second mode. Otherwise they are distinguished according to the variations and differences of the formulas.

The beginnings of the second tone are on Γ, as in *Educ de carcere*—“Bring out from prison”; on A, as in *Omnes patriarchae*—“All the patriarchs”; on C, as in *Nonne cor nostrum*—“Was not our heart”; on D, as in *Ecce in nubibus*—“Behold, in the clouds”; on E, as in *Animalia*—“Living creatures”—and *Ecce Maria*—“Behold Mary”; and on F, as in *Quem vidistis*—“Whom did you see?” On B, E, or G you will find very rare examples.

**D.** What you have said about distinguishing the first and second modes is sufficient. We must hurry on to the rest.

### 13

**M.** The third mode ends on the fifth note, the letter E, and proceeds through one diapason to the same letter, the acute *e*, through tones and semitones as follows: first taking a semitone, then three tones and a semitone, and two tones. It descends from the ending to the fourth by one tone, in this manner [the source supplies no formula here].

[Note: Admont adds:

> The third establishes its seat on the fifth note;  
> Let the fourth note lie below, and let another, the fifth, stand above,  
> So that it may sound an intense diatessaron and diapente.]

It particularly favors the second ninth because a diapente extends from it to the ending; but especially because it produces a diatessaron from it to its highest note, *e*. Since it has three tones near its ending, in descent or elevation it proceeds by leaps rather than by steps.

Its customary beginnings are these: on E, as in *Quando natus es*—“When you were born”; on F, as in *Nunc scio*—“Now I know”; or on G, as in *Multa quidem*—“Many things indeed”; on *a*, as in *Quis Deus magnus*—“Who is a great God?”; and on *c*, as in *Tertia dies est*—“It is the third day.”

### 14

The fourth mode, because it is flat, does not have three tones near its ending. Therefore it takes the first ninth *b* and ascends to the tenth *c*. After its ending it has a semitone and two tones, followed by a semitone and a tone. It descends from its ending by two tones to the third C, but usually also to the second B and the first A, by an acute semitone and a tone. Since the second B produces a diatessaron to its ending and the first A produces a diapente consonance, ten notes are formed, proceeding through tones and semitones in this manner [the source supplies no formula here].

[Note: Admont adds:

> From this seat the fourth descends as far as the first,  
> To which the intense diatessaron and the relaxed one sound.  
> You may join the tenth above any of the ninths.]

Its beginnings are found on C, as in *Hodie nata est*—“Today she was born”; on D, as in *Benedicta tu*—“Blessed are you”; on E, as in *Gaude Maria*—“Rejoice, Mary”; on F, as in *Anxiatus est*—“He was distressed”; on G, as in *O mors*—“O death”; and on *a*, as in *Rectos decet*—“It befits the upright.”

The fourth is distinguished from the third because the fourth has the first A, the second B, and the third C, which the third does not have; while the third has the eleventh *d* and the twelfth *e*, which the fourth does not have.

If an antiphon has neither the notes belonging to the third nor those belonging to the fourth, but begins on the tenth *c*, as *Vivo ego*—“As I live,” or favors the second ninth, as *Ecce quomodo computati sunt*—“Behold how they have been counted,” it will belong to the third mode; otherwise it will be assigned to the fourth if it imitates the differences of its formula.

Some, however, wish to assign the second ninth to the fourth mode, as to the third, because it is a diapente from its ending; but there is no consonance from the first ninth *b* to its ending. We have followed common usage more closely.

Moreover, in more difficult chants we find the third mode joined with the third note C, so that it becomes a ten-stringed scale. Since this happens very rarely, I do not doubt that it is an abuse. For, according to the rule of the ten-stringed scale given above, a threefold diatessaron cannot be found from the third C to the twelfth *e*.

**D.** Although there are many grammarians, books are found to be scarcely ever, or never, truthful, especially since people are so often laboring to correct them. Musicians, however, are very few, and antiphonaries have not been corrected for a long time. It is therefore not surprising if falsity is found in many places. Continue only with the rule and common usage; for an artistic rule does not ordinarily reject what happens only very rarely.

### 15

**M.** The fifth mode ends on the sixth note F, and its highest note, the thirteenth *f*, is marked with the same letter. Since the sixth F produces a diapente to the first ninth *b* and to the thirteenth *f*, the first ninth *b* will be available in the fifth or sixth mode.

It therefore has in order two tones and a semitone, followed by three tones and a final semitone over eight notes, in this manner [the source supplies no formula here].

[Note: Admont adds:

> On the sixth note the fifth establishes its seat;  
> No note lies below it, and another, the sixth, stands above,  
> So that it may sound an intense diatessaron and diapente.]

Its customary beginnings are these: on F, as in *Haurietis*—“You shall draw”; on G, rarely, as in *Non vos relinquam*—“I will not leave you”; on *a*, as in *Quinque prudentes*—“Five wise [women]”; and on *c*, as in *Ecce Dominus veniet*—“Behold, the Lord will come.” Since it has no tone before its ending, it did not look back to a tone either at its beginning or in its subsequent progression.

### 16

The sixth mode proceeds with it to the eleventh *d*, but descends from the common ending by a semitone and two tones to the third C, in this manner [the source supplies no formula here].

[Note: Admont adds:

> The sixth also takes its seat and rests there,  
> To which the intense diatessaron and the relaxed one sound.  
> Add a tone above these, making the course proceed.]

Just as the fifth has the twelfth *e* and the thirteenth *f*, which the sixth does not have, so the sixth has the third C, the fourth D, and the fifth E, which the fifth does not have—except that sometimes the fifth is mixed with the sixth, turning aside to the fourth D and becoming a ten-stringed scale. But this is rarely found, especially in antiphons.

Their distinction is as follows. If neither the descent of the sixth nor the entire elevation of the fifth is present, and if the chant begins on the tenth *c* and, according to its length, frequently strikes that note or the eleventh *d*, it will be the fifth mode. But if it does not rise beyond the first ninth *b*, it will be called the sixth mode; alternatively, the modes may be distinguished by their beginnings.

The sixth scarcely ever begins except on its own ending, as in *Verbum caro factum est*—“The Word became flesh”; or on *a*, as in *Vidi Dominum*—“I saw the Lord”; or on the fifth note E, as in *Domine, in auxilium*—“Lord, [come] to help”; or on the fourth note D, as in *Si ego verus Christi*—“If I am truly Christ’s”; or on the third note C, as in *Decantabat populus*—“The people were singing.”

**D.** What you have said about the modes proves useful, indeed necessary, for exposing the present error. Do not delay in granting me what I wish to hear about the seventh and eighth tones, as you began to do.

### 17

**M.** The seventh mode ends on the seventh note, whose highest note is the fourteenth *g*, marked with the same character as its ending. It takes the second ninth, so that it has two tones after its ending; after these come a semitone and two tones, followed again by a semitone. It descends from its ending by one tone, in this manner [the source ends here; no formula or subsequent passage is supplied].

[Note: Admont adds:

> The seventh establishes its seat on the odd-numbered note;  
> Let the sixth note lie below, and let the seventh stand highest,  
> So that it may sound an intense diatessaron and diapente.]

[Col. 0769D] If it pleases you to make it a ten-string scale, lower it still by one semitone from the end to the fifth, E; yet you will not often find this. It must be noted, however, that if the first ninth, b, is granted to it, nothing remains except that a fourth be made from the sixth to it; then it will be in every respect the first mode, because it will have a tone and a semitone, followed by two tones, a semitone, and two tones, and it is lowered from the end by one tone, as was said concerning the first mode. It will no longer be the seventh but the first.

[Note: [Col. 0770D] Admontensis: “If a fourth is made from the twelfth, e, to it, and is contracted to the path, it will be,” etc.]

For we do not, as the most foolish singers suppose, understand one mode to differ from another by gravity or acuteness. Nothing prevents whichever mode you wish from being sung either high or low; rather, the differing arrangement of the tones and semitones, through which the other consonances are also formed, establishes modes that are distinct and different from one another. Again, if it ends with only one corrupted note on the eighth, a, it once more becomes in every respect the first mode: for from the end it will have a tone and a semitone, two tones, and the remaining features belonging to the first mode.

Its beginnings are these: in F, you will scarcely find an example, such as *Qui regni claves* (“Who [hold] the keys of the kingdom”) and *Memento mei* (“Remember me”); in G, *Assumpta est Maria* (“Mary has been taken up”); in a, you will rarely find one, as in the communion *Domus mea* (“My house”), in *Dixit Dominus* (“The Lord said”); in c, *Benedicta filia* (“Blessed daughter”); in d, *Sit nomen Domini* (“May the name of the Lord be …”).

[Col. 0772A] **18.** The eighth mode proceeds together with the seventh up to the twelfth, e, but is lowered to the third, C, by a tone, a semitone, and two tones; thus it forms a ten-string scale in this manner.

[Note: [Col. 0771D] Admont adds:

> The eighth, seated there, also takes its place;  
> To it the tense fifth sounds, and the relaxed fifth sounds.  
> Add a tone above it, and you will make its course proceed.

]

We said above that such a ten-string scale does not contain three fourths, and therefore it does not receive both—the highest e and the lowest C—simultaneously in one and the same chant, as some maintain.

[Col. 0771B] It is clear, however, that in its descent from the end the eighth tone is in every respect the second. If, in its ascent, the first ninth, b, were given to it, so that from the end it had a tone and a semitone and two tones, it would remain second in its ascent as well. But the buffoonery of incompetent singers deserves ridicule: they perceive nothing of the distinction between tones and follow only what seems in some fashion to flatter the ears. They are like those who serve gluttony, deceiving the true rule of sobriety through false sweetness.

It is also found that when the eighth, descending to the fourth, D, seeks the thirteenth, f—which properly belongs to the seventh—and thus, though rarely, presumes to restore the regular ten-string scale, its beginnings are these:

[Note: [Col. 0771D] Adam has it thus: in C, *Nos qui vivimus* (“We who live”), *Dum venerit Paraclitus* (“When the Paraclete comes”); in D, *Spiritus Domini* (“The Spirit of the Lord”); in E, *Ornaverunt faciem* (“They adorned the face”); in F, *Jucundare* (“Rejoice”); in G, *In illa die* (“On that day”); in a, *Completi sunt* (“They were completed”); in c, *Ecce*, etc.]

In C, *Stabunt justi* (“The righteous will stand”); in D, *Angeli Domini* (“The angels of the Lord”); in F, *Zachae* (“Zacchaeus”); in G, *Judaea et Jerusalem* (“Judaea and Jerusalem”); in a, *Apertum est* (“It has been opened”); in c, *Ecce ancilla* (“Behold the handmaid”).

The eighth differs from the seventh in this respect: the eighth has the third C, the fourth D, and the fifth E, which the seventh does not have; while the seventh has the thirteenth f and the fourteenth g, which the eighth properly does not have.

In those chants that lie between the descent of the eighth and the ascent of the seventh, as was also said concerning the remaining modes, their tone will be determined according to the varieties of the formulas. For through these very varieties you will clearly discern the beginnings of each mode.

**D.** Since I scarcely find a few chants that oppose these rules, I have no doubt that their small number—and, so to speak, their furtive singularity—was produced by presumptuous and corrupted singers.

**M.** A rule is a common commandment of each art; singular things of this kind do not conform to an artistic rule.

**D.** But I ask you to add a little more concerning the law of the modes, according to the position of each note.

**M.** It is right to answer your request. Each note bears the likeness of one of the modes mentioned above. Thus gamma (Γ), because it has two tones before it, followed by a semitone, and adds two tones, then a semitone and a tone, not without reason bears the likeness of the seventh mode, since the final note of the seventh forms an octave with gamma.

The first note also, because it has a tone after it, but before it has a tone, a semitone, and two tones, observes the law of the first mode; hence it is not without reason called the first. The second, when it is lowered by two tones after itself and is raised before itself by a semitone and two tones, and again by a semitone and a tone, preserves the customary rule of the fourth mode.

Moreover, the third, C, since it has after itself a semitone and two tones, but before itself two tones and a semitone, followed by three tones, is supported by the character of the fifth or sixth mode.

We say that the eighth, a, occupies the first place, in the likeness of the first, with which it forms an octave. Otherwise, if you consider it together with the first ninth, b, it will have a tone in its descent, but in its ascent a semitone and three tones, in the likeness of the third mode.

The first ninth, b, contains in its descent a semitone and two tones, in the likeness of the sixth mode. In its ascent, however, whether because three tones follow, or rather because none of the following notes is joined to it by a fourth—which is the principal consonance—it bears the regular likeness of no mode. Nor can this be achieved through an octave with the notes that follow it; therefore you will find that neither a chant nor a distinction has its beginning or ending on it, unless this happens through error.

The second ninth, [unavailable sign], in the likeness of the second note B, from which it is formed by an octave, bears the image of the fourth mode. The tenth, c, in the likeness of the third C, corresponds to the seventh mode.

Otherwise, if the second ninth is removed, it will have after itself a tone, a semitone, and two tones, but before itself two tones and a semitone, in comparison with the eighth mode, from whose final note it marks a fourth. The remaining notes that follow can easily be understood through the likeness of the letters, as this figure shows.

From what has been said, the diligent investigator, with the help of divine grace, will understand many other things concerning both the tones and the remaining rules of this art. But if he acts carelessly, or presumes that he can grasp these matters not through divine illumination but through the keenness of his own understanding, he will understand nothing—or, while failing to give thanks to the Giver, he will become, God forbid, a servant of pride.

[Col. 0773A] [Note: The Codex Admontensis concludes thus:

> Now less a servant and subject to God,  
> Who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.
>
> Behold the first mode; thus the second is recognized:  
> The worn mode is received; thus the fourth also is proved:  
> This is the fifth; thus the sixth is discerned:  
> The seventh holds this harmony, and the eighth that one.
>
> The first tone from D to d;  
> the second from A to a;  
> the third from E to e;  
> the fourth from B to Greek lambda;  
> the fifth from F to f;  
> the sixth from C to c;  
> the seventh from G to g;  
> the eighth as before.]

—now less subject to the Creator, who is blessed forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0774A] **D.** Come, then, I ask you, and declare what follows concerning the modes.

[Note: [Col. 0774A] Immediately after this one reads: “Here the Dialogue ends.”]

**The Music of the Enchiridion ends.**

# ODO ON MUSIC

## NOTICE

[Col. 0773] What follows is continuously placed in the San-Blasian manuscript after Odo’s little work, or *Dialogue*, on music—namely, after these words, which are absent from other manuscripts: “D. Come, then, I ask you, and declare what follows concerning the modes.” We therefore place it here immediately, collated with the Leipzig manuscript, in which it appears under the name of Berno.

[Col. 0773B] The discipline of the musical art should be sought with the greatest zeal, especially by those who serve God in the common life. For just as it is said through the Psalmist that bread strengthens and wine gladdens the human heart, so frequent reading strengthens our spirit for the virtues, while singing gladdens the mind in the service of God.

Moreover, when we rejoice and marvel at the sweetness of the melody performed on earth, we are stirred to hasten more eagerly toward hearing that harmony of the heavenly homeland, which is as much sweeter than this as we marvel that heaven is higher than earth.

When we wish to teach children to read, we first make them learn the alphabet on a tablet, so that once they have recognized all the letters they may more easily read whatever is written in letters. In the same way, those who wish to learn song must first learn all the notes and the varieties of the tones on the monochord.

Because we do not use this discipline, we waste as much time learning the antiphoner as we might have spent learning divine authority and the rule of grammar. Worse still, we never reach such perfection in any period of time that we can learn even the smallest antiphon without the teacher’s labor; and if we happen to forget it, we are entirely unable to restore it to memory.

But let the reader not be frightened by the difficulty of this art. In the rules now before us you will find nothing except those things which, with God’s illumination, you will be able easily to grasp, and through which you may quickly attain skill in singing. For this art is shown to possess such power and scope that even children can grasp from it the means by which they may attain skill in singing, while strong minds can exercise themselves through many remarkable things.

[Col. 0773D] Now we first place the monochord before your eyes, so that whatever we say afterward about the nature of the notes may be demonstrated to the eyes if it is not sufficiently revealed by reading.

[Note: [Col. 0773D] These and the following diagrams are absent from the Leipzig manuscript, although space was left blank.]

[Col. 0774B] When, therefore, by subtracting or adding according to the letters of the string given above, you have shortened or lengthened the string itself, you will recognize all the notes by which every chant is produced, and numerically how much each note is lower or higher than another. In this matter you will be able to glorify God while admiring divine wisdom, because, just as he established all other things, so he established human voices so that they might praise him in number and measure.

[Col. 0774C] When, therefore, you have first observed the monochord, recognize that each note is separated from another by a tone or a semitone. All tones are produced by a division into nine parts. When you divide the monochord from its beginning, where the string starts, to its end, where the string terminates, into nine parts, you place the sign of the first note where the first ninth part ends.

[Note: [Col. 0774D] The material enclosed in parentheses is absent from the Leipzig manuscript.]

[That is, beginning there, if you divide again by nine all the way to the end of the string, you place the sign of the second note where the second ninth part ends.]

The Leipzig manuscript reads *secundae* (“of the second”) instead of *primae* (“of the first”).

That descent or ascent—that is, the interval itself—which extends from the first note, where A is inscribed, to the second, where B is inscribed, is the first tone. For the first note is the whole string before it is divided; hence the letter A, the first letter, is written at the head of the string, while the letter B, the second letter, is written in the second position.

[Col. 0774D] A tone, then, is said to occur whenever the space of one note up to another is carried nine times to the end of the string. Thus, whatever the eighth part of the following interval is, by that amount the earlier note appears greater than it; and, conversely, by as much as the ninth part of the earlier interval, the following one is understood to be diminished.

You will be able easily to prove this, and to recognize it once proved, if, when you have measured the distance from A to B and then carried that distance to the end of the string as though walking it out with your feet, you observe that from A to the end there are nine such spaces, but from B to the end eight.

The Leipzig manuscript reads *cum sexta* (“with the sixth”) instead of *cum* (“when”), and *deduxeris* (“you have carried it”) instead of *duxeris* (“you carry it”); it adds: “for there will be from A …,” etc.

[Col. 0776A] There are moreover ten such tones among the notes that you see on the monochord; their arrangement is described as follows.

[Col. 0775B] In each tone, whatever nine spaces the earlier note has, the later has similar—or the same—eight spaces. The Leipzig manuscript reads *habebit* (“will have”) rather than *habuerit* (“has had”).

This is an example of the tone: *Angelus Domini* (“The angel of the Lord”). Wherever you see two of those letters doubled, as they are in the figure, whether in this chant or in another, there is a tone, as here.

[Note: “An.”—that is, in this antiphon. The Leipzig manuscript adds: “the second tone.”]

The tone is *epogdous*, because musicians call a tone *epogdous*, that is, “superoctonary,” whenever the greater note, compared with the lesser, contains the whole of the lesser and in addition its eighth part. The same occurs numerically when we compare nine with eight or ten, and eight with sixteen.

[Col. 0775C] This is the *epogdous* tone whose description was given above. Five semitones are counted among these same notes. A semitone is so called as though it were a middle tone, for it is midway between two tones: namely, the interval that remains in the middle when tones are placed on either side, so that the tones of both sides, as was said, are made by division into nine parts.

[The Leipzig manuscript adds: “Or it is called a semitone because it is a half-tone and not a full tone; hence we commonly say, ‘The cup is not full,’ and similar expressions.”]

Therefore, when the first tone has been completed, if you take the fourth note—which completes the second tone and is marked by a quarter-part of the entire monochord measured from the first note—and carry it by eight all the way to the end, then add that eighth part above the fourth note, so that the parts are ninths, you will marvel to find that the last part of the second tone is the beginning and end of the first tone. The Leipzig manuscript reads “semitone” instead of “tone.”

Everywhere there are five semitones, enclosed by the final part of the first tone and the first part of the following tone, just as this figure marks them in order. In the following figure the prudent reader will find in order the numbers of all the tones and semitones, together with other useful information.

[Note: [Col. 0775D] The figure is absent from the Leipzig manuscript, where space was left blank.]

[Col. 0776C] For if you compare the first and last notes of each row with one another, you will find a fourth, which appears to contain two tones and a middle semitone. Likewise, if, descending, you compare the first note of the earlier row with the second of the next, and the second with the third, you will find two fourths; the same will occur equally in the second, third, and fourth rows. From the fourth to the fifth you will perceive the same thing. But if you consider the third in relation to the fifth, step by step, you will find a fifth. Thus, if you inquire into the measure of the monochord and are tired of reading further, this figure will indicate to you as much as is sufficient.

The Leipzig manuscript adds *ad inferiora* (“toward the lower parts”) after “descending.”

[Col. 0776D] It must also be noted concerning tones and semitones that a semitone never permits discordant tones to be joined without its midpoint—the Leipzig manuscript adds: “for example, tone, tone, tone, tone and semitone”—except for the first semitone, which has only the first tone above it. Everywhere else the semitone occurs after two tones as a moderator of the notes, lest either excessive repetition produce weariness or several gaps and extensions of the voices create dissonance.

Nor are doubled semitones ever found, lest, since they were devised to moderate and season the chant, they produce the bitterness of excessive salt when placed indiscriminately beyond what is fitting. The Leipzig manuscript reads “doubled” before “semitones.”

The two semitones that you see from the eighth string to the tenth must never be joined consecutively. Their signs are these: the eighth, a; the ninth, b; the tenth, [unavailable sign]; and the eleventh, c. They must be used as follows: when a and b join to form a semitone, understand a tone from b to c; and when b wishes to form a semitone with c, do not doubt that from a to b there is a tone.

The first of these was placed so that three consecutive tones would not occur from the sixth note, F, to the ninth. The second is formed for the same reason, so that the third would not be joined to two tones following it, as you will see in this figure.

[Col. 0777B] Furthermore, it must be understood that the first note b and [unavailable sign] are to be taken as one, namely the ninth, although it is divided into the first ninth and the second ninth, lest this appear to introduce a very great error. For otherwise it would seem that the fourth from the eighth string to the eleventh contained five notes, which is wholly absurd.

An example of this semitone is the first ascent of the antiphon *Vigilate animo* (“Watch in spirit”). It must be noted concerning the semitone that by itself it can complete no useful tone, but when joined to a tone it moderates the excessive length of its interval.

A tone, however, produces the sweetness of sound at both its endpoints, as when *Oremus* (“Let us pray”) is sung. There is only one tone there, defined at its endpoints from the sixth to the seventh note, whose euphony is completed through its descent and ascent.

Two notes also produce a certain consonance, but it is not called a chant, because a chant is completed by no fewer than the space of four notes. This kind of symphony is called a fourth, *diatessaron*, that is, “from four”: it contains two tones and one semitone, namely three intervals and four notes.

This symphony rejoices so greatly in a quadrangular arrangement through divine ordering that it contains four notes in its interval and is made by a fourfold division. For if you divide the whole interval from the first note into four, you will call the first part a fourth. Its proportion is as follows: if the first note, compared with the fourth, contains the whole of the fourth and in addition as much as the fourth part of the first or the third part of the fourth, this is a fourth.

To increase the dignity of its name, the same fourth proceeds from the first (A) or second (B) note and, then establishing itself from itself, claims eight places in pairs all the way to the end. For from the first (A) to the fourth (D) there is one fourth; from that fourth (D) to the seventh (G), a second; from that to the tenth (c), a third; and from the tenth (c) to the thirteenth (f), a fourth—everywhere, except in the final one, carrying a semitone between two tones.

[Col. 0778A] Conversely, when it proceeds from the second (B) note to the fifth (E), from the fifth (E) to the eighth (a), from the eighth to the eleventh (d), and from the eleventh (d) to the fourteenth (g), which is the last, it runs as though in four steps and contains the middle semitone only in the final part, whereas in the others it places it at the beginning.

When it proceeds from the third note (C) to the sixth (F), and from the sixth (F) to the first ninth (b), it marks the semitone neither in the first nor in the middle but at the end. Thus, with the sides changed in this threefold division, two tones and a semitone produce this remarkable consonance. However you join two tones and a semitone, you will call it a fourth.

Moreover, there is another fourth, from the second ninth ([unavailable sign]) to the twelfth (e), so that no note of the sweetest character may be deprived of its participation, as is marked in this figure.

[Col. 0778B] Examples are the incomplete chant fragment *Secundum autem* (“But according to …”), and likewise: *Christus vincit* (“Christ conquers”), *Christus regnat* (“Christ reigns”), *Christus imperat* (“Christ commands”), *Rex noster* (“Our king”). In this harmony the greater and lesser notes—that is, the fifth (E) and the eighth (a)—complete a fourth with two tones and a semitone, as was said.

If you add to this the one tone that lies from the fourth (D) to the fifth (E), you will likewise perceive the marvelous symphony of a fifth.

A fifth is called *diapente*, that is, “from five,” because it has five notes and ends from the first (A) at the fifth (E). It is defined by a threefold division of the whole string from any note to which it is compared. Thus, when the fifth note is compared with the first, the fifth of the whole string is defined from the first by a threefold division; this division is called a fifth.

[Note: The Leipzig manuscript reads: *Diffinitur autem ipsa quinta e* (“But the fifth E itself is defined”). In brackets it has: “E [is determined] from the first A by a threefold division of the whole string; this division is called *diapente*.” This is undoubtedly a scribal error; our manuscript has the correct reading through the final words.]

Wherever a tone occurs before or after a fourth and is joined to it, the fourth makes a fifth.

[Note: [Col. 0778D] Both manuscripts have this reading, but the word *tonus* (“tone”) must certainly be inserted.]

It consists of five notes, three tones, and a semitone—in other words, four intervals. In the specified notes it contains nine positions. In seven cases, since it has a tone at the beginning and at the end, if either of those tones is removed, a fourth will remain: for the fifth extending from the first (A) to the fifth (E) has a tone at both the beginning and the end.

If, therefore, you separate the first tone, from the second (B) to the fifth (E) a fourth will remain. If you remove the final tone, a fourth will likewise remain from the first (A) to the fourth (D). You will note such a fifth in this figure.

[Note: [Col. 0778D] The figure is corrupt in our manuscript and cannot be corrected from the Leipzig manuscript, where it is absent; it should apparently be corrected as we have presented it.]

Except for one, from the fifth (E) to the second ninth ([unavailable sign]), which has a semitone at the beginning, whereas the others have a tone at the beginning and end; and another from the first ninth (b) to the thirteenth, where conversely the semitone is found at the end.

[Col. 0779B] [Note: In this paragraph, letters printed above a word in Migne have been keyed in square brackets after the word.]

You will find many examples of this fifth. Among them is that song of Boethius:

> **Bel** [D E D] **la** [C] **bis** [D] **quinis** [D D] **operatus** [C D E F]  
> **annis** [E D C] **ultor** [E D C] **Atrides** [D D D]  
> **Phrygiae** [D D E] **ruinis** [F G G F D C]  
> **fratris** [F F] **amissos** [E D C] **thalamos** [D D E]  
> **piavit** [F E D D].

“The avenging Atreid, having waged wars for twice five years, by the ruin of Phrygia expiated the marriage-bed lost by his brother.”

In this melody the lower note is the third (C), while the higher is the seventh, G; these are joined by one fifth.

This is the nature of the fifth: the lower note exceeds the higher and later note by as much as the third part of the lower note itself, or the half of the later note, because when the earlier has three spaces to the end, the later is contained within two of those spaces.

[Col. 0779C] The third symphony is the octave, *diapason*, that is, the double, or “from two.” [The Leipzig manuscript adds: “The *diapason* consists of eight notes.”] It occurs whenever the greater note contains twice as much of the string as the lesser, or when the greater note, divided through the middle into two parts, terminates another note, as the first (A) does in relation to the eighth (a).

This octave is formed by the two symphonies mentioned above, namely the fourth and the fifth, joined to one another. Wherever you join a fourth and a fifth, or a fifth and a fourth, you will perceive a complete octave.

Thus, when there is a fourth from the first to the fourth (D), and a fifth from the fourth to the eighth (a), there is an octave from the first (A) to the eighth (a), that is, the half of the first (A) is necessarily obtained.

[Col. 0779D] It must be noted that the note (D) which is a fourth from the first (A), when compared with the eighth (a), makes a fifth; and (E), which is a fifth from the first (A), becomes a fourth in relation to the eighth. The interval formed by the marked fourth and fifth from the first is a tone situated in the middle of the octave.

When this is removed, a fourth is marked both above and below within the entire octave, as is clearly shown in this figure.

[Col. 0780B] There are six such patterns, in all of which the rule stated above remains fixed, as in the first.

There remains one further octave, from the second (B) to the second ninth ([unavailable sign]), differing from the preceding ones because a fifth is not found from the second. There is something divine in this symphony: its first and last notes agree with such marvelous sweetness that they seem to sound the same note, although the first is manly and the last childish. They agree as though a man and a boy were uttering the same melody in similar voices, as far as differing natures permit.

Hence, when one singer precedes another and the other follows, one sounds nothing other than what the other sounded; this is counted as an octave, that is, the eighth note. Therefore it has happened that on the monochord each note is marked with the same character as its octave, by which it is divided in the middle, although the figures differ.

Thus the note that we call the first ninth (b) appears similar to none of the preceding notes, because none of the preceding notes is joined to itself by the bond of an octave. But because it formed a semitone with the octave, it is adorned with the name of semitone.

[Col. 0780C] Concerning the octave symphony, ordinary music also proves this—namely, the flute and the cithara or fiddle—for it is a sufficiently agreeable chant, since it is contained within one octave, that is, eight notes.

Ecclesiastical custom has handed down that no chant should rise more than an octave above its final note. When this happens, the same chant rises to the octave above its final note; only very rarely, and only in longer chants, does it descend farther than the second note below the final.

If that descent is absent, the chant will have only one octave.

[Note: [Col. 0779] The Leipzig manuscript inserts: “But when both the ascent and the descent mentioned above are present, that chant will have two fifths.”]

The descent from the final note ought not to occur except when an *epogdous* tone is found from the final note to the second note to which it descends; but if it is a semitone, it will be useless.

An *epogdous* tone joined to an octave everywhere constitutes two fifths, that is, nine notes. We find ten notes rarely, and in longer chants, a practice defended by the authority of the Psalter of David. Even in these, however, one should not ascend more than to the octave above the final note; rather, that extension should be marked before the final note.

[Note: [Col. 0781] In this paragraph, letters printed above a word in Migne have been keyed in square brackets after the word: “With the letters A B C D A B C D doubled in the third ascending class.”]

[Col. 0781A] For this is not done without numerical reasoning and authority. Since ten strings are adorned by three consecutive fourths—except when the fourths are made from the third note, in which case the third fourth is not found regularly—such a ten-string scale is judged incongruous both through excess and through lack of rational basis.

Rarely, beloved reader, according to the ancient precepts, the institutions of many teachers, and common practice, will you require more notes than those we have designated. Although these are rarely found, they must not be entirely ignored. Therefore, on the monochord we judged that one note should be placed before the first. Because of its rare use and the reason stated above, we call it not the first but rather the adjunct note.

Nor do we designate it by the first letter; instead, we depict it with the Greek gamma, Γ. This is because the seventh letter of the Latin alphabet—recognized on the monochord as an octave from gamma—appears to have among us a function similar to that which gamma has among the Greeks.

When you place gamma at the head of the string, you will mark, by division into ninths, the position of the first note mentioned above. From gamma to the first there will be a tone; to the third, a fourth; and to the final note—which forms another octave from the seventh—gamma itself may be called a double octave.

Moreover, a faulty harmony, especially one that is excessively wanton and delicate, sometimes demands more semitones than those we have described and rejects those we have placed. Such a practice ought to be corrected rather than imitated.

[Col. 0781C] Care must be taken lest this happen through the negligence of the musician, when he begins and completes the chant differently from the way it was composed. For such dissonance, as the teachers demonstrate, is contrary to the rule: after two tones nothing other than a semitone should be placed, and after a semitone nothing other than two tones.

But because a fault cannot be avoided unless it has first been recognized, we place five such semitones on the monochord, outside the prescribed rule. One is placed after the first note; from it to the end stands the semitone midway after the eighth. We accept both of these, though each is formed with the character of a semitone in a different shape. Another, midway from the one after the eighth, is likewise drawn, but with a Greek character.

Likewise, another is marked after the fourth; it is connected to the one after the first by a fourfold division. From it another middle note is found after the eleventh.

These two, however, are made with the letter of aspiration, though in different forms. For this reason the Greeks call and write a semitone, *hemitonium*, with that letter. Of these, we accept the one after the eighth, or its middle form; concerning the others we advise that they be avoided rather than accepted.

We also add four notes after the final note, either because of superfluous chants—which you will scarcely, if ever, find ascending to them—or so that, when we wish one singer to precede another with a higher voice, we may have whatever notes are necessary for this purpose.

If we divide these from the eighth string, we find them easily. In whatever ways the notes from the eighth to the eleventh are compared with their preceding notes, these notes likewise preserve their positions according to the same relationships.

The Leipzig manuscript reads: “We divide all the notes up to the eleventh by the middle note just mentioned.”

Not only these notes, but every note whatsoever, will have the same proportions to the notes nearest to it as the note from which it receives the adornment of an octave has. Hence any chant, if it begins correctly on one note, even a higher one, can begin and proceed equally from another note that forms an octave with it, provided the range of the notes permits this.

Therefore the first and final notes are not improperly designated by the same letters as an octave. The same letters that occur from the first to the seventh occur again from the seventh to the final note; and the letters that occur from the eighth to the eleventh follow after the final note, so that there are three rows of similar letters.

The first row is marked with capital letters, such as we commonly place at the beginning of sentences. The second row is written with smaller letters of a different form, such as we use throughout the sequence of the book. The third row, because it is considered superfluous, is marked rather with the forms of Greek letters. It contains five notes, of which two are taken as one letter in likeness to the notes from which they are formed by the measure of an octave, although that letter is divided. This figure represents the arrangement.

[Col. 0782B] Enough has been said about the construction of the monochord for those who are either children or have not acquired knowledge of the liberal arts. But when I remember why the most foolish of grammarians is the wisest of rustics, I add one sufficiently intelligible pattern for measuring the monochord, lest I be accused of envy or deprive a rustic of our goodwill.

The arrangement is as follows. In the first row we place all the letters of the monochord in order. In the second row, whatever note is produced from any of those in the first row by division into ninths is written immediately below it; we said that this division is called an *epogdous* tone.

In the third row, whatever note is divided from any note of the preceding row by four, so that it is found below, is recognized by descending directly from the earlier note. Similarly, in the fourth row it is found by a threefold division.

In the fifth row, the division by two—or doubling, or halving—is taken from the preceding notes. We call the fourfold division a fourth, *diatessaron*; the threefold division a fifth, *diapente*; and the double division an octave, *diapason*.

[Col. 0783B] In this figure we find the measurement of each note in relation to another as follows. If you are looking for the fourth note, on which the fourth letter D is inscribed, look in the figure for that letter in the fourth row, with the number three attached on both sides. Then, ascending directly from that letter to the first row, you recognize the letter gamma.

Therefore, if you divide from gamma to the end of the monochord into three parts, you will place the sign of the fourth note mentioned above where the first third ends.

Likewise, you see the same letter in the third row, where there is the number four. When you look above it, you find in the first row the first letter A. If you divide the entire monochord into four parts, you will marvel to find the very place we mentioned.

[Note: [Col. 0783D] The material enclosed in parentheses is absent from the Leipzig manuscript.]

[You will find the same place.]

Similarly, by doing this with all the remaining notes, you will be able to discover in many ways marvelous and diverse measurements of the notes. For whatever number a letter has in its row, by that number its measurement is found in relation to the letter of the first row placed above it.

[Note: [Col. 0783D] The following words are absent from the Leipzig manuscript: “Whatever number a letter has in its row, by that number …”]

And if you turn over repeatedly in a diligent mind the things that have been said, you will be able to extend your understanding to many other and higher mysteries of numbers. We have omitted them for this reason: lest we seem to suffocate the tender reader with excessive food rather than nourish him with milk.

For when such people, in their excessive eagerness, investigate things they cannot grasp, they generally fail even to discover the matters that are easier. To such people the Apostle says:

> Do not think more highly than one ought to think, but think with sober judgment.

If anyone wishes to be sober, he will neither reject the present rules as superfluous nor desire anything more than what is necessary for attaining knowledge of singing.

[Note: [Col. 0784D] The material enclosed in brackets is absent from the Leipzig manuscript.] There are also other kinds of music, adapted to other measures; but this kind of music, which we have explained, has been perfected according to the more pleasing, more truthful, and natural method of the most expert and holiest musicians. For the most holy Gregory, whose precepts the holy Church most diligently observes in all things, wonderfully handed down to the Church an antiphonary composed according to this method, and taught it to his disciples through his own labor—although he is nowhere read to have acquired knowledge of this art by worldly learning, while it is absolutely certain that he received the whole fullness of knowledge divinely. One thing is certain: since this kind of music was divinely given to Saint Gregory, it is supported not only by human but also by divine authority. The symphony of Saint Ambrose, who was exceedingly prudent in this art, does not at all depart from this rule, except where the wantonness of excessively delicate voices distorts it. For we have learned by experience that very many dissolute-minded men, possessing voices of this kind, utter almost no song according to the rule of truth, but rather according to their own will, especially those desirous of empty glory. Of such men it is said: “Music ignored makes a jester of the singer”; and for this reason Saint Isidore says that God is [perhaps: not] served by such voices. For this reason too we have declined to discuss other kinds of music, and have accepted only that which the philosophers themselves affirm to be primary and natural. The wisest of the philosophers also asserted that the power of this art was marvelous, and that it could even change human dispositions, and that it remained so long as it was treated simply. But when it began to be treated in different ways, it lost its former power, fled far from the school of boys, and was no longer, even among adults, associated with its former intimacy to the full. We, however, shall pursue what follows, insofar as divine grace deigns to grant it.

To know in what ways voices are joined to one another is of the greatest usefulness for the science of singing. For just as two, or usually three or four, letters make one syllable, or a single letter is taken for a syllable, as in *amo*, “I love,” and *templum*, “temple,” so also in music a single voice is usually uttered by itself, while two, three, or four voices joined together usually produce one consonance, which, according to a certain analogy, we may call a musical syllable. Again, just as one syllable alone, or two, three, or even more, make one part of speech signifying something, as in “death,” “life,” “glory,” “kindness,” “blessedness,” so also one, two, or more musical syllables join a tone, a diatessaron, or a diapente. Since in them we both perceive melody and, understanding the measure, marvel at it, we may not improperly call them the parts of music that signify something. A distinction in music is the extent of any song that we continue; it is pronounced wherever the voice comes to rest. Again, just as one part of speech, or two or more, complete a sense and comprise a complete statement, as when I say, “What are you doing?” and you answer, “I am reading,” whether I affirm the reading [Col. 0785A] or ask for some statement, so one, two, or more of these musical parts complete a verse, antiphon, or responsory, without losing the significance of their numerical patterns. And just as many different statements grow together into a volume, so many different songs, gathered together, complete an antiphonary. From this it is proved that the holy Pope Gregory acquired, through divine grace, a greater mastery of this art than all others. For if you consider it, it is highly remarkable that in the nocturnal responsories he seems, in the heavy and disordered manner of the sleepy, to exhort us to keep watch; in the antiphons he sounds clear and sweet; in the introits [read: *introitibus*, “entrance chants”] he cries out to the divine service as if with a herald’s voice; in the Alleluia he rejoices sweetly; in the tract and graduals he seems to proceed with a clear, extended, and humbled voice. In the offertories and their verses, and especially in the Communions, he revealed how powerful he was in this art. In them there is every kind of elevation, lowering, doubling, sweetness for those who understand, labor for those who learn, and a wondrous lowering greatly differing from other chants, outstanding not so much in being composed according to music as in displaying music’s authority and principles. Saint Ambrose, however, labored wonderfully in sweetness alone; and very many others contributed to its treasury according to the gifts they received from the Lord. But he most directly contradicts the authority of the Church who, on account of the chants of others, entirely neglects the divine gift of blessed Gregory. For although other things must be accepted, the authority of so great a father must nevertheless be revered above all. We, trusting not in worldly learning but in the spirit with which he himself was imbued, shall pursue, as we began, whatever contributes to a speedy knowledge of this art; and, since enough has been said about music’s alphabet, let us examine its syllables.]

[Note: [Col. 0785D] The Leipzig manuscript resumes here.] A musical syllable, which is believed to be made with a single voice, requires no lengthy explanation, since what is one is sufficiently clear. One may nevertheless observe in it that sometimes a single voice, sometimes a doubled or tripled voice, is believed to form a syllable. In such syllables, two, three, or four are sometimes found placed together through the mere repetition of one voice. But as is evident in most affairs, if this occurs rarely it will be welcomed; repeated too often, it will generate disgust. Not only this, but every musical consonance is enjoyed when discreetly repeated; yet:

> Everything excessive harms; everything moderate in due measure benefits.

A musical syllable is moreover produced by two voices in four ways. For every voice is joined either to the one nearest it—that is, the second from it—or to the third, or to the fourth, or to the fifth, and produces a consonance. This occurs equally in lowering and in raising. But with the second, raising and lowering occur in two ways: by a semitone and by a tone; the semitone is the more contracted. For it does not appear to possess half of a tone within the interval in which it makes the lowering and raising, nor can it maintain its position in equal numerical steps. It is incomplete, and its raising or lowering, as occurs on a string, must likewise be extended slightly in the voice, as the first raising of this antiphon shows: “Rejoice to God.” For when you proceed from the fifth voice to the sixth, you recognize that this kind of raising is made by a semitone; you will observe its lowering by reversing the voices, as in this antiphon: “Praise to God the Father.”

A semitone syllable may also be either simple or compound. A simple one is that in which each string sounds once, whether in *arsis* or in *thesis*—that is, in raising or lowering—and it has only two voices and two movements. A compound one, although it has only two voices, contains three movements in them: one voice sounds twice and the other once. It occurs in six ways. When the lower voice sounds twice and the higher once, and then the lower voice again proceeds twice, there are two modes. But if the higher voice sounds twice and descends to the lower with a single stroke, there are again two other modes. Finally, if it ascends simply to the second and immediately returns to itself, either by the first voice descending, or if the second moves to the first and then immediately returns to itself, there are two further modes. When, in any of the preceding modes, you strike again the voice at which it ends, or return to the other, the syllable will be marked by four movements and two voices.

[Col. 0786D] Once these arrangements have been made, if you strike one or the other again, you will also discern five movements; and this can be extended to many cases. We, however, prefer all these movements to be arranged into syllables in such a way that the syllables themselves contain either one, two, or three movements, since this is more convenient for reason and has proved more useful for learners. Whenever continuations of this kind are found, they should rather be called multiplications of syllables. Thus it often happens that the same syllable is doubled and tripled, and that different syllables of two voices are set down in multiplication. When this occurs—that is, when syllables are multiplied through a few voices and many movements—we call what is then produced continuously a musical part. This part should be resolved into syllables having one, two, or three movements.

I leave it to the judgment and practice of singers to determine how these movements are distributed among syllables, so that, when there is a part of this kind in which both strings sound, it may not generate disgust through frequent repetition. Sometimes we assign the first movement to one syllable and the following three to another; sometimes we place two movements in one and two in the other; sometimes we take the first three movements for one syllable and only the fourth for another. In this way he will judge the remaining parts as well. For such great dissimilarity can be produced by this arrangement that it seems to make the same chant almost another chant, difficult and less [Col. 0787B] pleasing. If you make its syllables, parts, and distinctions similar, you will see its difficulty removed and its sweetness increased; this is especially suitable for boys. But if it is excessively delicate and easy, by creating similarity in its syllables and parts you will add weight, make it more difficult, and remove the disgust caused by extensive repetition. But lest anyone enviously suppose that this was undertaken by our own design, let our friend set against him the Antiphonary of the most blessed Gregory, in which we can prove by many examples everything that we say. It must be observed in every way that we use these rules so as in no respect to offend euphony, since the whole purpose of this art appears to serve it. *Euphonia* is Greek; in Latin it is interpreted as “good sonority,” that is, consonance, and all music treats of consonance.

As we have said, a tone is a more extended and more perfect raising and lowering; and, so to speak, the semitone is imperfect, while the tone is excessive. But when the imperfection of one moderates the excess of the other, or the excess of one moderates the imperfection of the other, perfect modulation is achieved from both sides. It is more pleasing to sonority and authority to place one or two tones without a semitone in a consonance than a semitone without a tone. An example of a tone is the first consonance in this antiphon: “The angel of the Lord.” Whatever kinds of syllables we have said are made with a semitone, we affirm are made more suitably and more frequently. Therefore, if you retain what was said above about the semitone, you need not seek anything further about the tone. Only consider this with the greatest care: if you already recognize one semitone or tone, derive the others from its likeness. For the same syllables and consonances of voices are found in all cases just as in one, differing in nothing except that one tone may be lower or higher than another. Therefore, so that by deriving one thing from another you may more easily recognize the force of things joined together and agreeing through some likeness, we depict tones and semitones in these two figures.

[Col. 0787C] Since, as in one case, so in others—even though the voice sung is changed—it will greatly benefit you to apply yourself to such figures, so that, if you think it burdensome to learn all tones and semitones separately, once their likeness is recognized you may possess them as one, and thus, with the Spirit of God breathing upon you, diligently attain skill in singing.

Moreover, when a voice is joined to the third above it, this is said to occur in two ways. In consonances of this kind the lower and higher voices are separated from one another either by a tone and a semitone or by two tones. That which is formed by a tone and a semitone is the more contracted, as in: “But when John had heard.” That which is more extended, by two tones, occurs as in the first lowering of this antiphon: “Five prudent [virgins].” Whatever was said above about the tone and semitone is said of this mode as well, except that syllables of the present mode are not found to be multiplied as much as the preceding ones. But to the extent that this mode is more extended than that one, it will be rarer in repetition and multiplication.

When a voice is joined to the fourth above it, it is adorned with all the patterns of the preceding syllables because of the dignity of the diatessaron. But just as we spoke of the voice joined to the third, so too we speak of this one. Therefore, to the extent that the one formed by a tone or semitone, or the one formed by two tones, or by a tone and semitone, appears more extended, it is content with rarer multiplication and repetition. We must by no means repeat a syllable of this kind frequently without inserting another. In such a syllable one voice is separated from the other by two tones and a semitone, that is, by the symphony of the diatessaron, as in this lowering: “The Holy Spirit.” But that they should differ from one another by three tones is supported neither by sonority nor by the authority of the rule—that is, when it is separated from it by three tones and a semitone. For it is very rarely found that this occurs through two tones and two semitones. Such a syllable is set down simply, and rarely doubled, as follows: “Seek first.”

A syllable is also formed from three voices, each having only one movement, either continuously or interruptedly. It is continuous because the three voices themselves, just as they are placed on the monochord, are placed in one syllable, with none remaining in between. This is marked in the syllable in which a fourth is joined to a third, if the second voice that remained between is taken up. Thus, just as in that syllable either two tones or a tone and semitone make the difference, so the same two species are found in this one as well. For three continuous voices enclose either two tones or a tone and semitone within their two intervals. In either species the aforesaid syllable will contain six modes. When it begins from the first voice, it either ascends directly to the second and third, or first goes to the third and then comes to the second; these make two modes. Likewise, when it begins from the second, it first goes to the first and then to the third, or first to the third and then to the first; this again makes two modes. When it begins from the third, it either proceeds first to the first and then to the second, or first to the second and then to the first; these produce the other two modes. For whichever of these syllables you add one movement to, you will observe two syllables consisting of two movements each—or, as some prefer, a musical syllable made of four movements and three voices. But if you add another movement, so that there are five movements, it will be divided into two syllables, one having two movements and the other three. This will continue to grow until such syllables usually become two, sometimes three or more.

A syllable is formed from three interrupted voices when the three voices are arranged so that one or two voices are omitted untouched from the lower to the higher—that is, when the lower and higher voices constitute a diatessaron or diapente. Of three sounding voices, either one is left out, and there are four; or two are left out, and the omitted and sounding voices together are counted as five. Four and five voices properly stand together when they form a diatessaron and diapente.

[Col. 0789C] To omit superfluous discussion of the arrangement of syllables, this will suffice for your knowledge of them: every syllable consisting of two or three voices never exceeds a diatessaron and diapente. If it consists of two voices, then, if it omits two others, it remains within the diatessaron; but if it omits three, this occurs within the diapente, and two sounding voices and three omitted voices are counted as five. If it consists of three voices, as was said above, it omits one within the diatessaron and two within the diapente. These conjunctions of voices, by which syllables are constituted, are to be observed similarly in parts and distinctions: each voice, whether in lowering or raising, is joined to the second, third, fourth, or fifth, just as was said of syllables, so that the end of some part or distinction may appear to agree with the beginning according to the modes described above.

We have said these few things about musical syllables to show in some manner how very many varieties of consonances can be produced with few voices, and to teach the person who must mark the antiphonary with the letters of the monochord how to distribute them. We have done so also because everything divided is easily grasped both through practice and understanding, whereas what is undivided is likewise confused, and confuses the mind more and envelops it in the darkness of ignorance than it imbues it with any learning or makes it clear through the light of knowledge. This is the reason why syllables, parts, and distinctions were devised in music as well.

But since we gain no small knowledge from the likeness of things—when we observe that what happens in one thing happens similarly in others, and recognize many through one—you should understand that the conjunctions of voices we have mentioned occur similarly in the monochord in their respective places, and are sung in a similar manner even when the voice is changed. Just as we did above with the tone and semitone, so now we mark in these figures the remaining conjunctions of voices that are alike. If God has granted you knowledge of them, you will never regret having undertaken this work of inquiry in vain. The first figure will teach which voices differ from one another by a tone and semitone. The second will concern those that differ from one another by two tones. The third will concern the diatessaron, and the fourth the diapente. The doubled and tripled figures concern the marvelous concord of the diapason.

[Col. 0791A] The conjunction and likeness of two voices has been sufficiently shown in these four figures.
