What more is there to say? Ships were built, shields renewed, breastplates repaired, coats of mail and helmets polished, swords and lances sharpened, and the army carefully equipped with every kind of weapon. Then, on the appointed day, the ships were pushed into the sea; the soldiers hastened gladly to them; banners were raised; sails were spread to the winds; swift wolves were carried forth to tear the Lord’s sheep, while they poured out human blood to their god Thur.”]

[Note: “He enters Gaul, besieges cities.” Many ancient writers mention this entry and ravaging of the Danes, or Normans; but they do not sufficiently agree among themselves about the time when it occurred, nor does Saint Odo himself—or anyone else—seem consistent. Therefore, what Claudius Falcetus could not accomplish without effort in reconciling this disagreement, I shall presume to attempt still less. I shall only present what a certain bishop of Utrecht wrote concerning ravages of this kind by the Danes:

“The Danes and Swedes, whom the Germans in their own language call *Northman*, that is, northern men, repeatedly devastated the provinces of Gaul so thoroughly that where once there had been most fertile fields and most splendid cities, there are now desolate haunts of beasts and birds. And where once the luxuriant abundance of beautifully blooming gardens flourished, now, on the contrary:

‘Thistle rises, and the sharp thorny paliurus.’

“For this had been brought about by the plundering of the aforesaid people, which, they say, in the very year in which four kings, begotten by one father, fighting one another with their armies, defiled [lacuna] fields with much Christian blood, a pirate fleet sailed up the channel of the river Seine. After that day, how many slaughters of Gauls they committed, how many cities and regions they burned with fire, is dreadful to write and miserable to recount.”]

It happened, however, that, after the regions of upper Gaul had been burned, Tours …

[Note: “Tours.” Geoffrey of Vendôme uses this form in Letter 12 of Book I: “When he had been stripped by thieves at Tours.” The *Annals of an Unknown Author* say: “They plunder Tours, a city of Gaul”; and Frodoard: “Rudolph returns to Tours.”

It is also said in the singular as *Turonis*, just as *Aurelianis*, *Blesis*, *Pictavis*, and *Cenomannis*. John, a monk of Marmoutier, says: “How great Tours is, and what and how excellent are its possessions.” The *Deeds of the Counts of Anjou* say: “Trusting in the aid of Odo of Champagne, who possessed Tours, Blois, Chartres, Brie, and Champagne.”

The form *Turonium* also occurs in Gerbert, Letter 61: “Your brother Godefrid and Rainherius told my Gobtherus, whom I had sent to Tours.” Indeed, *Turo* also occurs, as in the *History of the Counts of Anjou*: “It happened once that the king of France was present at the city of Tours.”

The plural *Turoni* is also found in the *Life of Charlemagne*: “He went to Tours, to Saint Martin, for the sake of prayer.” Hebernus, abbot of Marmoutier, says: “It happened at Tours that Adalaud, worn out by old age, entered upon the way of all flesh.”

Finally, there is *Turones*, as in William the Breton’s *Philippid*:

“Then he hastens his journey, swiftly, to the city of Tours.”

But this last form is more customary even among the ancients, and would require many examples.]

[Fragmentary ending: the supplied source ends after the Tours-form apparatus.]
, intending to consume it in a like destruction [or: conflagration], [Col. 0821A] would come down. Thus, after Ambazium and everything contained between the Loire and the Cher had been reduced to ashes [Note: Ambazium, and everything contained between the Loire and the Cher, having been reduced to ashes. The *Deeds of the Counts of Anjou* also remember this plundering of Ambazium by the Normans in these words: “Only the village of Ambazium, situated on a hill and possessing the ruins of an ancient castle once destroyed by the crafty Normans.” The old *History of the Lords of Ambazium* also mentions it, but at greater length and in words that vividly illuminate Odo’s account: “Thus,” it says, “ravaging everything along the banks of the Loire, they reached Ambazium. Finding the town with only a few defenders, they quickly captured it, burned it all, and destroyed the bridge over the Loire. They utterly destroyed the churches—one beyond the Loire at the entrance to the bridge, and another situated in a place called Luat. Having taken lodging on the plain near Ambazium, they stained the place called Nigron with much innocent captive blood. This happened in the time of Louis the Stammerer, surnamed ‘Nothing.’ It occurred through the folly of the people of Ambazium, who, believing they could harm the Normans, had advanced to meet them with the neighboring peoples. Because they were deceived when the Normans proceeded by another route, they lost their own fortress.”], he besieged Tours. He therefore stationed guards at the gates [Note: He besieged Tours and stationed guards at the gates. The same old *History of the Lords of Ambazium* describes both the siege of the city of Tours and the flight of the pagan besiegers through the prayers of Saint Martin, in these words: “After ravaging the fields between the Cher and the Loire and also destroying the stone bridge at Bléré, when they found nothing further that they could plunder, they gathered their armed forces and directed their march toward the city of Tours. After first slaughtering the people miserably, they destroyed everything they could find in the city’s suburb. The people of Tours, meanwhile, did not cease to tremble, gather together, close the gates, take refuge in the towers, and fortify the defenses with weapons. The enemies, battering the city gates with great tumult, confidently promised themselves entry with all their strength. Then the clerics who were present there, joining the whole body of the citizens to themselves, hastened rapidly to the church and cried out: ‘Holy Martin of God, why have you fallen into so deep a sleep? Show, we beg you, your mercy; come to the aid of the wretched and bring help. Otherwise we too shall perish, and our city shall be reduced to desolation.’ They took from the tomb of the blessed man a little chest containing Martin’s most sacred relics, and that wedge which the clerics had kept ready to avert dangers, and brought them to the city gate, already violently battered by the enemy’s assault. Then the townsmen, who shortly before had been terrified by fear of imminent death, immediately regained strength of body and mind, encouraged by the presence of so great a help. The Danes, on the contrary, were struck by profound stupor; after the stupor, fear and derangement of mind stole over them. Then, when they attempted flight, one obstructing another and they came upon the ice, you would see them fall headlong. The townsmen, therefore, perceiving that Christ had been made favorable to them through Martin’s prayers, made a sortie and pursued their enemies, killing nearly a thousand of them. Thus glorifying God’s mercy, which had granted them the unexpected palm of victory, they restored the relics of blessed Martin to their place.” The bishop of Trajectum also recounts this memorable siege and flight; if anyone desires it, his account is as follows: “When the aforesaid Danish fleet had for sixty years or more, sailing now upon the Loire, now upon the Seine, now upon both rivers, harassed their banks, it was at last proved in our own days how great was the merit of the most blessed Martin. For when, on one occasion, after the fields between those two rivers had been ravaged, they found nothing further in the neighboring regions to plunder, they gathered their armed forces and, intending to plunder whatever lay at a distance, first directed their march toward the region of Tours; after first slaughtering the inhabitants miserably, they destroyed everything they could find in the city’s suburb. When the people of Tours heard this, they began to tremble, gather together, and announce the enemy’s arrival to one another. Then, doing what the situation required, they did not cease to close the gates, take refuge in the towers, and fortify the defenses with hides and other military equipment. But since they were very few, when they saw the multitude of Danes rush forward in an assault as far as the wall, confidently promising themselves entry into the city with all their strength, they despaired of themselves and determined that salvation had to be sought in their final recourse—not in human strength, but rather in God’s aid and Saint Martin’s intervention. A few armed men resisted from the defenses, though, deeming their lives of no account, they had offered themselves to death. Meanwhile, the clerics who were present there, joining to themselves the entire weakened populace, hastened rapidly to the church and surrounded on every side the tomb of their protector, struck at once by immense fear and grief. Amid groaning old men, weeping children, and lamenting women, they cried out: ‘Holy Martin of God, why have you fallen into so deep a sleep? Why are you unwilling to awaken for our distress? Behold, we are to be handed over to the pagans; behold, we are to be led away captive, if anyone should escape the blows of the swords. And you pretend not to know all this. Show, we beg you, your mercy; come to the aid of the wretched and bring help. You who once performed many signs for others, at least now perform one immediately, so that you may free us. Otherwise we too shall perish, and your city shall be reduced to desolation.’ After these lamentations, they immediately seized from the tomb the little chest containing Martin’s most sacred relics and, amid grief and tears—which, I believe, compelled even the angels themselves to compassion—brought it to the city gate, already violently battered by the enemy’s assault. Then the townsmen, raising their hands to the stars and their minds toward divine mercy, who shortly before had been terrified by fear of what they believed to be imminent death, immediately regained both bodily strength and courage of mind, encouraged by the presence of so great a help. The Danes, on the contrary, were struck by violent fear; after their stupor came intolerable dread, and after dread, as many assert, derangement of mind. I seem to see the wretched men first trembling, then attempting flight, and immediately, as they made the attempt, being carried about in ridiculous confusion, entangled with one another, one obstructing another, and, as though they were running over ice, falling headlong and providing a spectacle for those watching them—openly showing how many troubles that *cuniculus* [perhaps “little wedge”], which the clerics had brought out to avert danger, had brought upon them. The townsmen, therefore, perceiving that Christ had been made favorable to them through Martin’s prayers, made a sortie and pursued their enemies. Finding them scattered across the fields and hiding miserably in the woods, they killed nearly nine hundred of them; then, quickly recovering the spoils, they returned to the city, loudly praising and glorifying God’s mercy, which had granted them the unexpected palm of victory. They immediately restored the body of blessed Martin to its place, offering him the greatest thanks because, through his outstanding intervention, he had helped them so solemnly, by the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.”], and took great and careful measures to ensure that no one could safely leave. He also constructed ramparts, leveled rough places, and arranged whatever might assist in capturing the city. News of another’s misfortune, when brought to the besieged, supplied fuel for the fear they had conceived. Nevertheless, they repaired the walls and patched the defenses of the towers [or: repaired both the tower and the defenses], and, after launching a hailstorm of arrows, added various assaults. By now the walls were repeatedly shaken by the battering ram and, yielding to the blows of the engines, threatened their own collapse. The besieged, divided in strength, were utterly deprived of the comfort of hope. At last, however, by divine grace inspiring them, they came to themselves, reverently seized the body of their blessed patron Martin, and carried it to the place where the violence of the battle was greatest, setting the dead man against the enemy ranks as a defender of the living. O man admirable in every respect! While he lived, he was called mighty in signs and brought the splendor of his virtues among the stars; in death, also mighty in war, he destroyed the enemy’s battalions by his mere presence. Truly, God is wondrous in his saints. [Col. 0823B] Through the intercession of the saint’s patronage, security and confidence were restored to the besieged, while no little fear and terror were inflicted upon the besiegers.

**II.** The Danes therefore fled [or: accordingly], and the people of Tours pursued them in flight. Some of the fugitives fell by the sword, some were captured and brought back, and some escaped with flight as their means of support. They pursued the Danes as far as the sixth milestone from the city, carrying with hymns and glory the body of their victorious champion, through whom triumph and victory had come to them. Therefore, in triumphant memory of that same battle, a church was built in his honor at the very place where the saint’s body had stopped; because of the outcome of the battle, it received the name Saint Martin of Battle.

At that place in the city where his body, spending the night above the wall, initiated the beginnings of victory, there were ruins of ancient walls. They said that Valentinian’s palace had once stood there [Note: They said that Valentinian’s palace had stood there. John of Paris, in his *Memorial of Histories*, says: “By the power of Saint Martin, the Danes immediately fled in terror; the people of Tours pursued them as far as the sixth milestone, where, in his memory, at the place where the holy body had stopped, a church was built in honor of Saint Martin. There, however, were ruins of ancient walls, where it was said that the palace of the Emperor Valentinian had once stood, in which, while seated, he had not deigned to rise before Saint Martin.”], and that, while seated there, he had by no means deigned to rise before blessed Martin the bishop until fire consumed the royal throne, the flames scorched the king himself on that part of his body on which he sat, he was violently thrown from his throne in his pride, and rose as Martin’s enemy.

There, the archbishop, together with the devout people, restored a church—also in honor of that same saint—which is called Saint Martin of the Basilica. Therefore, when a synod had been held, it was decreed, by the authority [the word is absent in the printed edition] of the archbishop and of the bishops who had assembled, that henceforth throughout the entire diocese the feast of this Assistance [Note: The feast of this Assistance. There are several solemnities of Saint Martin, among them this Assistance and the return of his body from Burgundy, as an anonymous monk of the Major Monastery notes in the registers of the bishops of Tours, in these words: “The solemnity of his basilica possesses a threefold dignity: namely, the dedication of the church, the translation of the sacred body, and the institution of the episcopate of that saint himself. You shall observe the first on the fourth day before the Nones of July. Know that his deposition is on the fourth day before the Ides of November, and his return from Burgundy on the Ides of December. His Assistance, by which he freed his own people of Tours from the hand of Hasting, is on the fourth day before the Ides of May.”] should be solemnly celebrated every year on the fourth day before the Ides of May [Col. 0824B], and that it should rightly be designated by no other name than Assistance.

**III.** When three five-year periods had passed after Hasting’s fires, a member of the same people succeeded him. Exiled from his own homeland by a similar fate, Rollo, a man vigorous in arms [Note: Rollo, a man vigorous in arms. He is also so called at the beginning of Book II of the *Gesta of the Norman Dukes* by the monk of Jumièges. He was that prince of the Normans who, after plundering cities throughout Gaul and burning churches, finally settled near the mouth of the Seine. He named the region Normandy after his people; it had previously been called Neustria. He compelled Charles the Simple, king of the Franks, to declare him a Christian and make him duke, to give him his daughter in marriage, and to confirm Normandy itself to him as a dowry and benefice, although afterward Rollo himself refused to promise fidelity to the king by kissing his foot. The *History of the Affairs of Ambazium* says: “When Rollo had become a Christian, Charles the Fool gave him Normandy with his daughter Gilla; he refused to kiss the foot of Charles the Fool unless he raised it to his mouth.” The *Chronicle of Anjou* likewise says: “Charles the Fool gave Normandy to Rollo with his daughter Gisla. He did not deign to kiss Charles’s foot. When the counts admonished him to kiss the king’s foot in acceptance of so great a benefaction, he replied in the English tongue, ‘Ne se Bigod,’ which means ‘Not by God.’ But the king and his men mocked him, and, corruptly repeating his speech, called him Bigod; hence the Normans are still called Bigodhi.” To these may be added what the author of the *Deeds of the Counts of Anjou* says in these words: “After Rollo, duke of the Normans, had been baptized, together with all his people, that land which they have held from that time until now was granted to them by the king of the Franks and Duke Hugh, under agreed payments for the service owed to the Franks and for the preservation of peace. For when Rollo had become a catholic Christian, he took Gilla, the daughter of Charles the Fool, as his wife, and afterward ordered the land given to him to be called Normandy.”], but inhuman toward Christians, accompanied by a multitude of infantry, a large force of cavalry, and many soldiers. After repeatedly destroying the Flemings, Normans, and Bretons in battle, reducing their cities, towns, and churches to ashes, he inflicted very great slaughter upon the people.

Afterward, when Le Mans had been besieged [Note: Afterward, at Le Mans. Thus below: “Le Mans having been captured”; Flodoard: “He gave Le Mans to Hugh, son of Robert.” Abo likewise uses the term at the end of Book I of the *Siege of Paris*: “Nor did those at Le Mans obtain anything more favorable.” Nevertheless, the singular number is also used, just as at Tours, Poitiers, and similar places. The same Frodoard has: “Le Mans and Bayeux were granted to them by a peace treaty.” This is the very city that Geoffrey of Vendôme, Letter 16 of Book III, calls *Cenomannum*, and Hugh of Cléry, in his commentary on the *Majordomate and Seneschalship of France*, sometimes calls *Cenomannica*.], he sent the commanders of his army as far as Tours [Col. 0825A], so that, after the city had been overthrown, they might plunder its abundant supply of gold and silver and its other goods, and, binding its inhabitants, lead them away and enslave them.

But by God’s merciful providence, the waters of the Cher and the Loire rose in such a flood [or: inundation] that, joining together, they formed a single sea and, by their considerable depth, kept the enemy forces from approaching the city.

Nevertheless, the Major Monastery [Note: The Major Monastery. It was built by Saint Martin, the third bishop of Tours, as Severus Sulpicius teaches; he also elegantly describes the place in his account of the life of this glorious bishop: “For a while,” he says, “he used a little cell attached to the church. Then, since he could not endure the disturbance of those who visited him, he established a monastery nearly two miles outside the city. The place was so secluded and remote that it did not lack the solitude of the desert. On one side it was enclosed by the sheer cliff of a lofty mountain; the Loire, bending its course slightly, enclosed the remaining plain. It could be approached by only one road, and that a very narrow one.” Why it was called the Major Monastery, and how it once gained precedence through the excellence of monastic life and contributed an example to the entire order and dignity of monks, is explained by an anonymous monk of that monastery in these words: “We know, on the testimony of Gregory of Tours, that the name ‘Major Monastery’ was given to this place by Martin. Since many monasteries are larger than the Major Monastery, the question arises why it claimed the privilege of so distinguished a name. There is a threefold answer to this question. It is well known, and has become sufficiently famous, that Martin, the most blessed archbishop of Tours, founded three monasteries: the first at Milan, the second at Poitiers, and the third one mile from Tours. In relation and comparison to the other two, he called the third, both in reality and in name, the Major Monastery. There is another reason why it received this name, as the trustworthy and truthful testimony of Severus Sulpicius teaches, who describes the life and deeds of the aforementioned archbishop in eloquent language. The blessed archbishop, avoiding the biting cares of a turbulent life, had withdrawn into these more secluded places as into a haven of rest. Eighty men adhered to his holy service. Like their noble master, condemning themselves to hunger and thirst, ashes and haircloth, they had crucified the world to themselves and themselves to the world. Each of them spent the whole week in prayers and fasts, separately in individual dwellings as though in a little monastery; only on Sunday did they gather at the great monastery, whose side was pierced through where the bed and dwelling of their leader and teacher adjoined it. In comparison with these dwellings, therefore, the monastery to which, as has been said, they customarily gathered was not improperly called the Major Monastery. The remainder of the proposed question is explained in a third way. Although the Church on this side of the Alps flourished with many magnificent monasteries, Martin’s monastery alone surpassed all the principal establishments of the order and of holy religion. For what church or monastery,” as Sulpicius says, “would not desire priests from Martin’s monastery?” Holding precedence over the others through the merit of its holiness and excellence, it deserved, by a certain prerogative of merit, to be called the Major Monastery. With the archbishop Martin as its leader and guide, that Major Monastery extended the branches of its religion as far as the sea and spread the growth of its holiness to the ends of the earth.”], which was not far from Tours, was utterly destroyed [Note: Utterly destroyed. The same monk of the Major Monastery also mentions this destruction: “In the aforesaid monastery, the customary succession of abbots and the vigorous daily growth of religion continued until the times of Hasting and Rollo. Their empty ferocity, laying waste the cities and churches of Gaul, utterly destroyed that monastery and rendered it incapable of habitation and religion, without inhabitants and without religious life.” A little later he says: “Hasting came into the region of Tours, and after destroying all the suburbs together with the Major Monastery and reducing them to ashes, he besieged Tours.”], and one hundred and twenty monks, less four, were struck down there by the sword, apart from the abbot and twenty-four others who escaped by hiding in caves. The abbot, however, was dragged from his hiding place and subjected to torture and torment in order to force him to reveal the church’s treasures and bring into the open the monks who were hiding in the caves.

But the man of God, Abbot Hebernus [Note: The man of God, Abbot Hebernus. The genuine and correct name of this abbot is Hebernus—not Herbertus, Hibernus, Herbenus, Erbinus, or Urbinus, as he is called, most corruptly, in the published registers of the Major Monastery. He was made archbishop of Tours after being abbot of the Major Monastery, as is shown even by his own testimony in the Book of Miracles of Saint Martin after the saint’s return from Burgundy. For in its preface he says: “It happened in the same month, while Ingelgerius was count, that Adalaudus, worn out by old age, entered the way of all flesh at Tours. Ingelgerius, the count, with God’s help, through the intercession of blessed Martin, and with the assistance of the clerics and the consent of the citizens of Tours, enthroned and elevated to the episcopal see the aged Hebernus, holy abbot and minister of the Major Monastery of blessed Martin.”], although restrained by the varied and manifold violence of torture, neither disclosed the treasures nor revealed the sons hiding in the caves. They had been preserved so that they might follow the body of their patron among strangers.

This indeed happened; but he himself rather repaid his companions for the reward of his exile. For none of them survived whom Martin did not bring forward [or: prefer] to the government of the Church and elevate to honor. When the Danes had departed, after the swelling of the river had subsided and the citizens had been given freedom to return [or: move about], the misfortune and destruction of the Major Monastery, as well as the abbot’s torture and sufferings and the precious death and passion of the monks, were reported. These things, overshadowing the joy of everyone, and especially of Saint Martin’s canons, supplied mournful sighs and offered abundant material for immeasurable grief.

**IV.** Thus clothed in the garment of sadness and sorrow, assuming a mournful expression and the attire customary among those who share another’s grief—“to grieve with those who grieve and rejoice with those who rejoice” [or: “to weep with those who weep”]—they approached the aforementioned place, grieving and weeping, while the swelling of their inward sorrow dripped out in sobs. After their outward tears had somewhat subsided, they brought out the twenty-four monks who had been living hidden in the caves, and together with them brought the abbot, with due honor and reverence, back to their own church [Col. 0827A]. Providing for them in every respect, they selected for them a house adjoining the church doors, from which a more private passage into and out of the church could be maintained.

After six months had passed, when the canons learned that Rollo, having captured Le Mans, intended to go and capture Tours [or: Turonim], they consulted with their fellow citizens and sent the precious pearl and singular treasure—the body, namely, of the most holy Martin—as far as Orléans [Note: They sent the body of Saint Martin as far as Orléans. The aforementioned monk of the Major Monastery reports the same]. The bearers and guardians of it were the aforesaid Hebernus, abbot of the Major Monastery, with twenty-four monks, and twelve canons, who were to serve God and Christ’s confessor Martin [day and night]. Twelve burghers of Château-Neuf also remained constantly attached to their company [Note: With twelve burghers of Château-Neuf. “The close proximity of Château-Neuf,” says the same monk, “contributes greatly to the aforementioned city. Its men are so distinguished that, overflowing with an abundance of gold, silver, purple, gray cloth, various spices, and every worldly glory, they walk about in purple garments.” Château-Neuf of Saint Martin is called *Castellum Novum Sancti Martini* in the *Chartulary of Vendôme*, charter 28, in these words: “But if, as he says, he wishes to learn letters, and wishes to live in the city of Tours or at Château-Neuf of Saint Martin, there too we shall provide for him and his man only three loaves of bread.”], and, devotedly serving the holy attendants, provided them with what they needed.

Afterward, informed by the report of spreading [or: traveling] rumor that the Danes had advanced into Upper Gaul, they crossed over with their treasure to Saint-Benoît. A few days later, when vigilant rumor again announced beforehand that Rollo had already arrived at Orléans, the bearers of the sacred relics came to Chablis [previously *Clabeia*, but corruptly].

**V.** Having remained there only a very short time, when fear grew strong again, they proceeded with that incomparable treasure as far as Auxerre [Note: With the incomparable treasure to Auxerre. The *History of the Lords of Ambazium* says: “After Charles the Bald had died, the Danes who remained in unbelief, ravaging Gaul with their duke Huasten for three [or: thirty; some have sixty] years, compelled the canons to transfer the body of blessed Martin to Auxerre.” The registers of the Major Monastery likewise say: “The monastery of Saint Martin itself, which stood near the city, was burned; the monks and clerics were slaughtered; and the venerable body of the holy bishop was carried to Auxerre.”—*Autissiodorum* is better. Thus Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XVI: “Having traveled the same road, he reached Auxerre.” Hence also in Frodoard, “the bishop of Auxerre,” and in Nithard, Book I, “the district of Auxerre.” It is also called *Altissiodorum*, formerly *Antricus* in Ptolemy, as Hericus teaches in his *Life of Saint Germanus*, in these words:

> In Celtic Gaul, which spreads through the middle regions,  
> The earlier Gauls established a city not unknown;  
> It is reported to have once been called Antricus by the ancients.  
> A later age added towers and battlements to its ancestral  
> Walls, defenses against harsh warfare.  
> From the enlarged walls, with the name altered,  
> Whether you call it Autissiodorum, as usage follows,  
> Or shorten the name and say Altiodorum,  
> Under a different name the same thing is made richer.  

He said *Altiodorum* instead of *Altissiodorum* for the sake of the verse.]

The bishop, forewarned by a report that had gone ahead, and the whole city, rushed out to meet them. They escorted so distinguished a guest with fitting honor and placed Martin’s body in the church of Saint Germanus, beside the bier of that same bishop, a body not inferior to his in dignity.

Through the merits of blessed Martin, countless powers and miracles occurred there. The blind received sight, the lame the ability to walk, those suffering from fever health, the withered restoration, lepers cleansing, and the paralytic restoration of their limbs. As rumor, which is accustomed to leave nothing unspoken, spread the grace of these cures throughout every region, such a multitude of sick people gathered there daily that, by an incalculable estimate of their number, the region seemed comparable to an army of any country.

Because the city, inadequate for so great a multitude, could not contain everyone, they were dispersed through the surrounding villages for lodging. For all of them, according to their desire, the hoped-for health was restored through the merits of blessed Martin the bishop. Every offering from the sick passed into the use of that bishop’s household [or: pontiff’s household]. Such a heap of money accumulated from the offerings that, because its quantity exceeded the number [or: value] of the gifts, it supplied the clerics of Auxerre with fuel for envy.

Therefore, driven on by the spur of greed and envy, they addressed Martin’s attendants as follows: “Since powers and miracles are performed equally through both our bishop and yours, it is fair that, if any profit has arisen from them, the attendants of both should share it in common.”

Those attendants, satisfying them by evident reasoning, dissolved the claim to communal sharing, which had been requested [or: formulated], in this manner, saying: “Before our Martin came here, while your Germanus was administering here [or: residing here], there was no mention of miracles. At the arrival of our bishop, however, through the power of his meritorious piety, the frequent occurrence of signs is plainly displayed, and, in consideration of the health bestowed through him, such benefits accrue to us.

“But so that every doubt about this may be removed from your minds, let this leper who is before our eyes be brought into the midst to be healed by the two bishops, if it pleases you. If the side of the leper placed next to Martin’s side recovers, while the side joined to Germanus’s side remains in leprosy, let the miracle be ascribed to Martin as its author. But if, conversely, the part of the leper placed on Martin’s side is not healed, while the part adhering to Germanus is cured, let the manifested power and miracle be transferred to the merit of Germanus.”

They readily agreed, and the judgment pronounced was approved by everyone.

**VI.** As evidence, therefore, for recognizing the truth, the leper was placed between the bishops. After that night had been spent in vigils and [prayers are absent in the printed edition, Col. 0829A], together with praises, when morning dawned and both parties assembled, the half of the man placed on Martin’s side was found healthy and unharmed. The other half, by God’s hidden judgment, was left to be saved [or: healed] later.

But so that faith might shine forth more clearly through a more evident miracle, and that it might become higher [or: so that the faith might become more certain and shine more clearly], the leper’s part still requiring healing was again turned toward Martin. When morning came, before everyone’s eyes the whole man was found completely transformed into health.

Thus this mutual dispute was laid to rest, and from that time onward the entire offering of the sick passed peacefully to Martin’s worshipers.

O Germanus, bishop of admirable graciousness, who, although he possessed such great merit that he raised the dead, showed such honor in his own house to his guest that, in the display of signs, he wished to appear inferior to him!

O praises worthy to be proclaimed of Martin, mighty in signs, who, observing everywhere and in everything the dignity of the episcopal ministry although in exile, both illuminated with the grace of miracles the city that had received him as an exile and always showed himself kind, generous, and abundant toward his followers!

After many years had passed, when peace had been restored to the Church and Rollo had been restored to the faith, the men of Tours set out for Auxerre in order to seek their Lord and patron.

### VII.

**[Note: Col. 0829C]** They therefore meet Armarius. This Armarius—Annarius, or Abnarius, or, as certain manuscripts have it, Januarius—is found neither in the registers of the Church of Auxerre nor in the *Chronicle* of Robert, the holy monk of Saint-Marien, who wrote chiefly about the affairs of the archbishops of Sens and the bishops of Auxerre. There is therefore no doubt that the name is corrupt, and that Umbaldus should perhaps be restored in its place; after Walla, the brother of Ansegisus, archbishop of Sens, he governed the Church of Auxerre. For he died around the year 900, namely three years after the return of Saint Martin’s body, which, as Saint Odo himself notes, occurred in the year 887.

They therefore meet Armarius [Januarius], bishop of that same city, so that by his permission and authorization they may be granted the opportunity to bring back their own bishop. He is said to have given them this reply:

> I do not wish my church to be defrauded of so great a treasure, since, when I became bishop, I found it endowed [invested] with him.

Seeing, then, that they were making no progress through this bishop, the men of Tours turned back to the king of the Franks, who was king at that time, hoping for a better outcome. They approached him with humble prayers and supplications, asking him to order that Tours and its Martin be restored, and that, once he had been received, the city might be changed from mourning to joy by the return of its shepherd.

The king said to them:

> Since both cities belong to the royal jurisdiction, and both serve us without distinction, we consider it unworthy to strip Auxerre, which has been legally seized of possession of this treasure, by an act of prejudice and force, and to invest your Tours, which up to now has lost its investiture in him.

The men of Tours, therefore, abandoning [their hope], returned frustrated to their own country.

They therefore convened a council with Adalaudus [Adlandus] [**Note: Col. 0829C**]—a corrupt form, and indeed even more corrupt in certain registers, which variously call this archbishop Adlandus, Adelerandus, Adelardus, Adalardus, and Aulandus. His correct and true name was Adalaudus, and he had a brother, Raimo, bishop of Orléans, as the *Deeds of the Counts of Anjou* testify in these words: “The nobles and bishops of Tours, Adalaudus and Raimo, two brothers by the same parents, nobly born in the city of Orléans.”—archbishop of Tours, Raimo of Orléans [**Note: Col. 0829D**]—the brother, namely, of Archbishop Adalaudus, whom some also call Rennerius—and Mainoldus of Le Mans [**Note: Col. 0829D**]—Mainoldus of Le Mans, incorrectly called Mannardus in the registers printed by Demochare—[and Saint Lupus of Angers], together with an assembled multitude of clergy and people, and they considered what ought to be done.

At that time the illustrious count of Gâtinais, Ingelgerius [**Note: Col. 0829D**]—the count of Gâtinais, Ingelgerius, son of Tertullus, of whom the history of Anjou records: “Charles the Bald, holding him dear on account of his merits, gave him a wife together with a considerable benefice in the castle of Landon, and also settled him with certain lands both in the district of Gâtinais and in other places throughout France”—the nephew of Hugh, duke of Burgundy [**Note: Col. 0829D**]—through his daughter Petronilla, as the same history of the counts of Anjou explains in these words: “At about that time, after Tertullus had died in France, his son named Ingelgerius remained, possessing his inheritances, though begotten under Charles the Bald. For Tertullus had married a noble woman, the daughter of the duke of Burgundy, named Petronilla, who bore him this son”—lord of Loches and Amboise [**Note: Col. 0830C**]—on his wife Adendis’s, or Adelenda’s, side, she being the niece of Adalaudus, archbishop of Tours:

> “For Adelerodus [Adalaudus],” says the *Chronicle of Anjou*, “and Raymo, two brothers by the same parents, bishops of Tours and Angers, both nobly born citizens of Orléans, gave their niece, named Adendis, to him in marriage, together with her allodial possessions, namely Amboise, Buzançais, and Châtillon.”

The *History of the Counts of Anjou* likewise testifies to this in these words:

> “The bishops Adalaudus and Raymo, two brothers by the same parents and nobly born citizens of Orléans, gave their niece, named Adelenda, to him in marriage, handing over to him, together with the girl, by the authority of the king and the nobles, their patrimonies, which had come to them by lawful inheritance in the district of Orléans and in Touraine. For the allodium belonging to their kinship was then only the estate of Amboise, situated on a hill and possessing the ruins of an ancient castle once destroyed by the cunning Normans.”

But concerning Loches, or Lochis, both writers are silent. The old history of the affairs of Amboise seems to supply the omission, saying:

> “The prudent king Charles granted to a certain nobleman of the district of Orléans, named Adalaudus, the castle of Loches and two parts of the town of Amboise.”

For if Adalaudus transferred to his niece, as her dowry, all the property he possessed in the district of Tours, it follows that he did not retain for himself Loches, or Lochia, of which he was lord.

He was vigorous in arms and endowed with the highest power and probity, and administered the countship of Anjou [**Note: Col. 0830D**]—indeed, also the viscounty of Orléans and the royal prefecture of Tours. The *Chronicle of Anjou* says: “Afterward Louis, the son of Charles the Bald, gave him the viscounty of Orléans, the prefecture of Tours, and half the county of Angers as a benefice.” And the *History of the Counts of Anjou* says: “Afterward the aforesaid king gave him the viscounty of the city of Orléans as a benefice; then, having obtained the royal prefecture at Tours, he bravely defended that land against the Normans.” It adds shortly afterward: “Half the county of the city of Angers was also given to him, because beyond the Mayenne there was another count in Anjou”—recently granted to him by royal gift.

In the city of Auxerre he also had and possessed his own palace, vineyards [**Note: Col. 0831D**]—a manuscript codex once belonging to the Parisian senator Paul Petau adds: “wine-bearing vines of the highest quality,” which most people commonly call *vin passelatin*. But since these words are absent from the old editions and from two other manuscript codices that I used, I am readily compelled to regard them as a gloss rather than as Odo’s genuine text—, and suburban estates [“he had,” absent from the printed edition].

Since so many advantages for carrying out this undertaking converged upon so great a man, everyone acclaimed him as the person to undertake the mission. When they were preparing to send messengers to him for this purpose, by the assistance of God’s grace, as we believe, he entered the church to pray to Saint Martin, as was his custom.

When he came out of the church, everyone received him joyfully, and all rendered him the honor and reverence due to him. When he had sat down among them, as though forewarned by the Holy Spirit, he burst into these words:

> Men of Tours, men abounding in riches, skilled in the rich vein of your intelligence, strong in wisdom and courage: I am greatly amazed and utterly astonished that you have neglected to bring back your bishop Martin, the joy of your city, indeed your city’s light, after he has been banished into so long an exile through your own negligence.

They answered him with tears:

> We give thanks to you, and first of all to God, who inspired [commanded] your heart to speak with us about such matters and, when we were placed in longing, to make us the desired reminder of our desire. It is not, my lord, through our negligence, as you suppose; rather, the sluggish indifference of the king of France hindered us, and the stubborn violence of the bishop of Auxerre denied us our Martin, though we sought him with great labor and persistence. Since, then, that obstinate bishop’s heart has been hardened and he has become like another Pharaoh, he refuses to let the man of God go except by a strong hand. Therefore, lord, since nobility, vigor, probity, and power are at your disposal, we ask and humbly beseech you by our common supplication: moved by zeal for God and love of blessed Martin, join yourself to this appeal, and restore both him and, with him, joy to this grief-stricken region.

### VIII.

When the illustrious Ingelgerius saw that, after God, the whole community’s hope rested entirely upon him, he took pity on the petitioners’ tears and wishes, and promised that he would carry out the task entrusted to him to the best of his ability.

He therefore gathered a considerable force both from the foreign army and from his own men, selecting with him nearly six thousand soldiers and cavalry, and came to Auxerre.

Meanwhile the men of Tours, at the command of their bishop, continued a week-long fast, praying to God with continual prayer and persistent supplication that their Martin might be restored to them.

The city of Auxerre was astonished to find itself suddenly filled with armed soldiers. At dawn on the following day, the tireless foreign count, after praying with tears in the church before the body of his beloved archbishop Martin and offering the prayers and vows of his pilgrimage, met with the bishop concerning the restoration of the deposit and said:

> Since the name and honor of bishop delight you, why, having lost the etymology of this title [pronoun], do you not build a bridge of virtues but overthrow it? Having become for your flock a model of deception and fraud, why do you cast down from the lofty road of truth those who cling to your footsteps and compel them to go into the abyss of perdition? Why, in a time of necessity, do you disdain to return the treasure entrusted to your faith, entangling the matter in delays [of affection]? Choose one of two things: either restore their Martin to the men of Tours without further delay, or answer that you will in no way restore him.

Angered, the bishop replied in these words:

> It is not proper for a foreigner to visit holy places with an armed force, nor to claim the relics of saints for himself by force and arms. Nevertheless, remain patiently today with your men; tomorrow will show you what I intend to do about this.

Meanwhile, after consulting with his fellow bishops, who happened then to be present, he inquired what the outcome or end of this action might be.

Siagrius of Autun [**Note: Col. 0832D**]—formerly Fiagrius in the printed editions, and in Paul Petau’s manuscript, “of Nevers” instead of “of Autun.” Since, however, he appears in neither the registers of Autun nor those of Nevers, it is difficult for me to believe that Nevers is intended—especially because Nevers and Auxerre belong to the same archbishop, namely the archbishop of Sens, and because Saint Odo calls this Siagrius a fellow bishop of Auxerre, which cannot be understood of the bishop of Autun, who was a suffragan of the metropolitan of Lyon—, together with Domnolus of Troyes [Trecensis] [**Note: Col. 0832D**]—called Domiollus by some, and absent from all the catalogues of the bishops of Troyes, both printed and manuscript—, answered him wisely:

> It is not proper for a bishop to seize another’s property, or to attempt to steal anyone’s deposit by fraud or violence. We know that the body of blessed Martin, brought here by the men of Tours under pressure from the hostile sword, was deposited with you by them. Therefore, restore faithfully what was entrusted to you faithfully by the faithful; repair the damage done to faith, and, soothing the angered count with gentle words and acts of courtesy, grant what is requested. For unless you restore it willingly and quickly, you will immediately see it taken from you, to your disgrace and dishonor, against your will. Make a virtue of necessity, then, and before the impending necessity extorts it from you, let discreet and prudent generosity provide it.

The bishop yielded. Having been softened by the pleasant address of the Angevin, he brought forth the desired treasure.

The abbot Herbenus [Hebernus], of blessed memory, was also present before the bishops, together with Ingelgerius, who was now without his companions. For by divine providence, aided by Saint Martin’s continual prayer, all of them individually had by then been advanced throughout the province of Burgundy to bishoprics and abbacies: so that those who had come as exiles with the exiled man, now established as bishops and abbots, might restore the exile himself to his proper place, on the very soil of his exile.

Finally, he sent orders to them through mounted couriers [**Note: Col. 0833D**]—the ancient practice of couriers, or stations for changing horses, although Philippe de Commines writes that they were first established in France by Louis XI. Besides Josephus, Suetonius, and Procopius, who mention them, nothing is more frequent in the old writers of France. The *History of the Counts of Anjou*, speaking of Fulk Nerra, says: “When the count heard this, he hastened to the aid of his men, pretending that he was going to his castle of Landon, and rode by night and day, repeatedly changing horses.” Marculf, *Book I of the Forms*, chapter 11, says: “We have sent that illustrious man to those regions on an embassy; therefore we order that, at suitable places, both transportation and hospitality be provided for him by you, that is, so many post-horses or relay horses.” He called them *veredi* and *paraveredi*, whereas Odo calls them *veredarii*; Charlemagne, in an old diploma, calls them *mansionatici* and *paraveredi*; *Book II of the Capitularies*, chapter 16, calls them *paravreda*; the *Capitula of the Bishops* for the year 880, *mansuarii* in wagons and *paraveredi*; and Procopius, *Book II of the Persian War*, calls them public horses, which, he says, they customarily call *veredi*. The word comes from *rheda*, a Gallic name; hence also *eporedicae*, good horse-breakers, in Pliny, Book III, chapter 17, and *palefridus* in Stephen of Tournai and other medieval writers, meaning a horse, a *palefroi*—, to the often-mentioned abbot Herbenus [Hebernus], ordering them to attend the expedition and to carry away the body of the aforesaid bishop; so that those whom simple monks and exiles had brought from their proper place into exile might now, having become bishops and abbots, restore the exile himself to his proper place.

And so it happened.

After the proper Mass of Saint Martin had been solemnly celebrated, Ingelgerius of Angers and Abnarius of Auxerre, taking up that noble burden and placing it upon their shoulders, began the journey homeward.

The bishops escorted the relics of the holy prelate with hymns and praises, as did the devoted clergy and the crowds of common people streaming in from every direction.

When those who had escorted Martin had returned, the army resumed the journey it had begun and attained its desired triumph. The abbot and monks, as well as the clerics, rendered God each day the due service with the greatest devotion, and Mass was celebrated daily. In that noble army there was no soft or effeminate man: no one there knew a woman, no one robbery; rather, each lived from an honest livelihood.

### IX.

When the body of the most sacred bishop Martin reached the boundaries of his diocese, both the sick sheep, in a wondrous manner, recognized the presence of their shepherd, and the shepherd recognized how much care he owed his sheep.

Although, as a foreigner among strangers, he had flourished through an abundance of miracles, among his own people—who had been commended to him by God—his grace of healing was even more abundant and, if it may be said, his benevolent goodwill more generous.

Therefore, all who suffered from any kind of illness, even those who were not brought to him and did not ask, were marvelously healed throughout the entire province, on the right and on the left.

How true is the Savior’s promise, when he says: “The works that I do, the one who believes in me will also do, and will do greater works than these” (John 14:12). For in the signs and healings that the Lord himself deigned to perform, he also willed the faith of those seeking them to cooperate, as the Gospels frequently demonstrate. Hence the saying: “Your faith has made you well” (Luke 18:42).

Through Martin, however, help came even to those who did not ask, did not come running, and—what shows greater mercy—even did not want it.

While such and so many signs of virtue were being performed, although fame could not conceal them even if it had not seen them, two paralytics, who lived by asking alms from passersby in a village called Hedera, said to one another:

> Look, brother: we live in comfortable idleness; no one troubles us, everyone pities us. Our only labor is asking for what we desire. Whenever we wish, we may indulge in sleep, and we have continual rest; in short, we spend our days in good things. This infirmity from which we lie here claims all of this for us. If it were cured—which God forbid—the unfamiliar labor of our hands would necessarily fall upon us; indeed, begging would by then be useless. And now we have heard about this Martin, in whose diocese we live: that, returning from exile, he passes no one lying sick anywhere in his bishopric without healing him. Therefore, brother, follow my advice, and let us flee Martin as quickly as possible, leaving his diocese, lest the abundance of his healings overtake us.

A truly novel plan, wishes utterly unheard of: they did not want to be deprived of such an affliction, and sought to escape having themselves restored to health.

Why delay? Both approved the plan, fitted staffs beneath their armpits, and set out in flight, crawling rather than walking.

But Martin’s swift power pursued the fugitives, caught the runaways, and, once caught and found, restored them unwillingly to health.

Experiencing this in themselves, they could neither conceal it nor dare to remain silent. For they knew that he was powerful enough to destroy the ungrateful, since he had helped even those who did not want help.

They therefore cried out, proclaiming the miracle, and invited the people of the place where it had occurred to praise Martin. They did not consider their duty complete until they had carried the staffs that marked their former weakness to Martin’s mother church, openly explaining to everyone both their flight born of faithlessness and Martin’s mercy even toward the unwilling.

The inhabitants of the settlement where this sign of healing occurred then built, in the name of the miracle-working Martin, a church that is called the White Chapel to this day.

### X.

When blessed Archbishop Martin entered the boundaries of his own parish [**Note: Col. 0834D**]—that is, after the thirty-sixth year from the time when Rollo began to ravage Gaul, as is recorded by the anonymous monk of Marmoutier: “In the thirty-sixth year,” he says, “after the kingdom of the Franks began to be ravaged by the aforementioned Danes, namely Rollo and Hastin, the body of blessed Martin was brought back with honor from Auxerre to its own place. The text of the account of its return, published by blessed Odo, first a canon and precentor of that same church and afterward abbot of Cluny, is in our possession.”—*parish* here means his diocese, as above: “When the body reached the boundaries of his diocese.” For *parish* is sometimes used for entire dioceses, and conversely *dioceses* sometimes for districts or parishes, of which there are many within one diocese. The *Capitularies*, Book VI, says: “Let each bishop have authority over his parish,” that is, his diocese and entire jurisdiction. Sidonius, Letter 16, Book IX, says: “Having perhaps traveled through the dioceses, I came home,” that is, through the parishes, as Jacobus Sirmondus noted there—, inanimate and insensible things, sensing the arrival of their shepherd, displayed wondrous signs of their joyful congratulation.

All the trees and shrubs, although winter opposed it [**Note: Col. 0835B**]—the *Chronicle of Limoges* briefly describes this and the preceding miracles of Saint Martin’s body in these words: “In the year of the Lord 879, the body of blessed Martin, carried to Auxerre because of the Normans, shines through miracles. But because of the offerings, when the monks were disputing between Martin and Germanus, a leper placed on Martin’s side was healed, and on the following night, when he had turned toward Germanus, was completely cleansed—not because Germanus lacked power, but because he honored his guest. When it was carried back to Tours with the converted Normans, everything flourished, and the two paralytics who fled before it were healed against their will”—, were clothed with renewed leaves and bloomed with flowers, demonstrating through their adornment how great were the excellence and merits of the father of his country returning home.

Likewise, on the right and left, in the churches of that same parish, signs of divine power [divinely] rang out without human assistance. Lights, both candles and lamps, were kindled by divine power, especially in two churches dedicated to his name, which are recognized [noted].

The first is called Marmoutier, in which, while alive in the body, he devoted himself to God day and night in reading, meditation, vigils, fasts, and prayers.

The other is called Saint Martin of the Rich New Castle. From this place he had first been carried away while fleeing Rollo; there, too, he was received by all the bishops of his diocese, as well as by the clergy and people, and there he remains to this day in the place where he is now worshiped.

When, therefore, Lord Martin of Tours, as we have said, entered his own Tours amid its thousands [**Note: Col. 0835C**]—“When Lord Martin entered his own Tours.” Properly “his own,” which William the Breton especially praises on account of the presence of his body in Book III of the *Philippid*:

> From there he hastens his journey to the city of Tours,  
> Which two rivers encircle with shining waters.  
> Here the Loire, there the Cher; between the two lies  
> A city bright in situation, beautiful in soil, delightful in its streams,  
> Fertile in trees, richest in grain, proud  
> In its powerful citizens, numerous clergy and people,  
> Filled with riches, shining everywhere with woods and vines.  
> The presence of the sacred body adorns it,  
> The distinguished bishop Martin, whose glory  
> Has heaped supreme honor upon all the churches.

Properly “his own,” indeed, since it was once called Martinopolis after his name. Bernard Silvestris, in the *Megacosmos*, addressed to Herricus, says:

> It shines where Martinopolis sits among the starry rivers  
> And the painted fields of the Loire.

Matthew of Vendôme, in the preface to his book of Tobit, dedicated to Bartholomew, archbishop of Tours, says:

> The sun, whose rays the city Martinopolis  
> Lends to the world, honors the whole of its realm with honor.

And the monk of Marmoutier says: “Martinopolis, also called Tours, is exalted by the excellence of metropolitan dignity”—, the whole population rushed out to meet him.

Archbishop Adalaudus [Adalandus] of Tours, his brother Raimo of Orléans, Mainoldus of Le Mans, Saint Lupus of Angers, and the suffragan bishops of the entire province came joyfully to meet him. Every sex and class alike, rejoicing, came to meet their long-desired lord, and was drenched with tears forced forth by joy.

The bishops and abbots, clergy and virgins, peoples and barons, children and old men, gloriously escorted the glorious bishop into his church with candles and crosses, hymns and praises, and installed him in the former rank of his own see with the honor due to him and the highest reverence.

**[Note: Col. 0836B]** “He was installed in the former rank of his own see.” Saint Martin’s body had been placed in the apse that blessed Perpetuus had once made. When it was brought back to Tours by Ingelgerius and the barons of the district of Tours, Bishops Adalaudus of Tours, Raimo of Orléans, Lupus of Angers, and Mainoldus of Le Mans received it with candles and crosses and honorably placed it within the enclosure of the altar. They appointed Ingelgerius himself treasurer and defender of that church.

Knowledge of this event is owed to Hebernus, in the preface to the book of miracles performed after the body’s return or deposition. It reads:

> The apse in which the body of blessed Martin was contained—the same apse that they had also carried from Auxerre—was cast from gold and silver, which is called electrum, two fingers thick. It identified its maker, blessed Perpetuus, by means of carved letters and verses, and there was no crack, hole, window, or door in it. Blessed Perpetuus had made it when he raised Martin’s body from the ground, first wrapped in red purple and carefully sewn up, and then placed it in this apse. He also made a square, hollow altar of dressed stones, covered it with a large slab, and cemented it with the others. Inside, he made another apse cast from orichalcum, copper, and tin, a palm thick, with a cast door; it was secured with bolts, hinges, and four keys. Finally, he made above it a *freda* of the finest gold and precious stones, worthy of so great a priest. At last the same count, together with the venerable bishops Adalaudus of Tours, Saint Lupus of Angers, Mainoldus of Le Mans, and Raimo of Orléans, deserved to place the body of the often-mentioned confessor Martin within the enclosure of the altar, in the second apse; and they sealed the door together with the apse, so that no access or entrance lay open. With the full agreement of all, they granted Count Ingelgerius the prebend of Saint Martin, to be possessed by him and his heirs forever. Since at that time the church of the same saint lacked a treasurer and custodian, they enthroned Count Ingelgerius, appointed him treasurer, made him defender of the church, and appointed him guardian of all its possessions wherever they might be. He held the treasurer’s seat and houses with their revenues for as long as he lived. All those who were with Count Ingelgerius and had been summoned to bring back blessed Martin’s body, especially the barons of the district of Tours, entered into the association and granted a benefice to the church.

This, then, was the glorious and solemn reception by which Martin, archbishop of Tours, returning from exile, was ceremoniously received by his foster children and, seated in his own see, as has been said, gave abundant assistance to everyone who asked him, according to his custom.

Synodal authority decreed that this celebrated feast of the reception should be solemnly observed by Adalaudus [Adalandus], archbishop of Tours, and the bishops of the neighboring provinces, on the Ides of December, in the year 887 from the Incarnation of the Lord, thirty-one years after the translation. Whenever it is commemorated, the destruction wrought by the Danes and the celebrated, joyful reception of Martin returning home by his own people are remembered.

Therefore, good Martin, pious father, shepherd, and our patron, grant your sons and foster children, as well as your venerators, good things according to your custom; remove harmful things; and by the continual urgency of your prayers obtain for us the joys of unending life.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0837]

## II. SERMON ON THE FEAST OF SAINT ODO, ABBOT OF CLUNY

(*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 1761, from an old manuscript of Saint Martin.)

**[Col. 0837B]** To add anything to the praises of Saint and most blessed Odo, our father, whose feast we celebrate today, is to take something away from them. For the grace of his virtues ought not to be set forth in words but proved by deeds.

Since Scripture says, “A wise son is the glory of his father,” how great must be the glory of this man, who rejoices in the wisdom and devotion of so many sons? For in Christ Jesus he gave us birth through the Gospel. Whatever virtue and grace can exist in this holy people flowed from him, as from a certain most lucid fountain, in the purity of all its streams.

Because he excelled in the strength of chastity, because he gloried in the rigors of abstinence, and because he possessed the charm of gentleness, he stirred the affection of all his fellow citizens toward God.

Well and fittingly, on this day, which the passage of our blessed father Odo to paradise renders joyful for us, we sang the verse of the present psalm: “The righteous man will be held in everlasting remembrance.” For he is rightly turned into the memory of human beings who has passed over into the joy of angels. Having been glorified, he has found the grace of Christ because he did not seek the glory of the world.

The divine word says: “Do not praise a man during his lifetime.” It is as though it said: Praise him after life; magnify him after completion. For two reasons it is more useful to give praise to the memory of men than to their life: so that you may extol their holy merits especially at the time when flattery harms neither the one who praises nor exaltation tempts the one who is praised.

Praise, therefore, after danger; proclaim him secure. Praise not the happiness of one still at sea, but when he has reached harbor. Praise the courage of the commander, but when he has been led to triumph.

Who among the living can safely and without trembling be praised, when he remembers that he has something from the past to erase and sees that something remains for him to fear in the future? Who among those placed in this little body ought to claim anything for himself from merits whose path is besieged by a multitude of demons, like a horde of robbers, and whose every day is surrounded by invisible enemies laying snares of soul-destroying deaths that must be feared?

As we sail across this great and spacious sea, in which are creeping things without number, small and great animals—that is, various kinds of enemies—these adversaries wrestle with us in a contest proportioned to the measure of our strength.

In the sea of this world, therefore, we must fear greatly lest either the storm’s tempest carry away our ship, the waves swallow it, or a cruel pirate lead it away as eternal plunder.

Against these manifold evils of the age, let us resist with disciplined and chaste actions. Let us confidently magnify the merits of blessed Father Odo, now placed in safety. Holding the rudder of faith manfully, he has set the anchor of hope in a tranquil station and placed his ship, full of heavenly riches and eternal merchandise, upon the desired shore. Against all adversaries he held the shield of the fear of God tirelessly until he reached victory.

For what was the whole course of his life except a single conflict with a vigilant enemy?

How many blind people here, wandering from the way of truth and already hanging from the highest cliff over the depths, did he restore to sight and give back that vision by which Christ might be seen?

Into how many ears condemned by the blockage of filth and unbelief did he pour precious hearing, so that, on receiving the voice of the heavenly commandments, they might answer God calling them to mercy through obedience?

How many people wounded inwardly did he heal by the skill of an angelic mouth and the firmness of prayers?

How many, dissolved through long neglect by the stain of sin and covered with a kind of leprous contagion, did he cleanse by purifying them through corrections and exhortations, while God worked within them?

How many souls living in the body, yet already dead and buried beneath the weight of their offenses, did he call to amendment as to the light, and God resurrected through him? Thus, as an admirable imitator of his Lord, he in turn put to death for God those who were already dead, by a life-giving death to sin.

From how many hearts possessed by shameful iniquity and impiety did he drive out lust, cast down anger, and wipe away envy? As though barbarians had disrupted an ancient house, he brought back faith, chastity, justice, and mercy, peaceful inhabitants by whom Christ, the head of these virtues, might enter the dwelling of the mind. Applying the medicines of repentance, he roused them, like a stinking man dead four days, by the roar of his rebukes; and, once amendment had been received, he snatched them from the midst of the jaws of death and restored them to life by a timely resurrection.

Having therefore performed these and many other such deeds—which you yourselves remember even more fully, and which our poor little speech cannot suitably set forth or explain—it is better that your own affection should recount them to you. With the utmost zeal and alacrity he was a cultivator and guardian of souls, cutting away desires, restraining anger, and uprooting wickedness. The most blessed Odo was especially necessary in those times, when such great iniquity, daily gathering strength as justice weakened, was growing powerful. Indeed, although he was present in this pilgrimage only in body, in thought and desire he dwelt in that eternal homeland. The world was crucified and dead to him; whatever he accomplished through the active life he transferred to that other life; and, like a good steward extending his hand toward a hundredfold return, he continually transferred from his left hand to his right and stored his labors in heaven. For even if his works appear to belong here, the merits of his works passed there.

Let us therefore follow, as far as we can, in his footsteps; by these he showed us how we should follow him as he hastened by that exceedingly narrow way toward the spaciousness of heaven. Let one person take from him the grace and appearance of compunction, another the purest pigment of shining chastity, one the pallor of abstinence, another the blush of modesty. Let another take his faith in divine matters, burning and radiant like an airy splendor; and, arranging in this way the spiritual limbs of the inner person, let him pass into the body of his people and onward to heaven. Let us adorn the whole house—that is, let us paint the entire Church of God—in accordance with that one face. And when he sees us either trembling at the eternal judgment or thinking upon the blessedness to come, may that evangelical voice of Christ be able to take us up: “Father, I ask that where I am, they also may be with me.” And when we too shall one day depart from this world, may our patron Odo receive us into his seat and bosom as Abraham received his own, and on that day may the joyful shepherd recognize his sheep safe and sound.

With the help of him who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0839]

### III. Two Charters of Louis IV, King of the Franks, and Conrad, Emperor

Concerning certain churches and estates granted to the monastery of Cluny in the time of Saint Odo, the second abbot of Cluny.

*(Bibliotheca Cluniacensis, p. 265.)*

#### I. Charter of Louis, King of the Franks, concerning Salustriacus, Chavinias, the fishery of the Osa, Camberiacus, Savigniacus, and Amberta. (Year 939.)

[Col. 0839D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Louis, the peaceful, august, and unconquered king by the grace of God.

Just as it is certain that God does not cast away the powerful—for without him there is no power—so it is also clear that he will call the works of the powerful to account. Therefore we must take the greatest care that, whenever by his disposition we are able either to benefit or to harm, we subject our power entirely to his command and zealously do whatever advances the honor of his holy Church.

Accordingly, let it be known to all, both kings and persons of every other rank, present and future, that one of our faithful, Hugh, son of Richard, a most illustrious man and marquis, asked us to release, by this charter of our authority, from every disturbance and domination of all men, just as it had been enlarged by our predecessors and freed by apostolic privileges, a certain monastery called Cluny. This monastery was built by William, a magnificent man, in honor of the chief apostles, namely Peter and Paul, through the hands of a certain venerable abbot named Berno.

Let that place therefore remain, according to what William himself established under a terrible and solemn adjuration, and subjected by testament to the Apostolic See for protection, not domination, entirely free and released from every secular lordship, whether of kings, of all princes, of William’s relatives, or indeed of any person whatsoever. Let it continue in the monastic order and be administered according to the tenor of the testament that he made concerning it. Let its inhabitants, living under the regular rule, elect for themselves from among their own number, after Odo who now presides, an abbot according to the rule of Saint Benedict.

Let them possess, hold, and administer their common goods—those which they now have or may acquire in the future, whether through our liberty [perhaps: generosity] or through the gift of anyone whatsoever—without anyone’s domination or opposition. At markets they shall pay no toll. No one shall distrain their free persons or slaves without their consent. Let them have their demesne tithes for the hospital. Let them hold and possess their churches, with all their tithes, as they acquired them through the Roman privilege and through the written grants of bishops. Let them likewise hold and possess intact the estates which they acquired through charters of our predecessors or of other kings.

These estates are named as follows: in the county of Mâcon, Salustriacus and Chavinias, and one-third of the fishpond whose name is Osa, together with the holdings and fishermen belonging to that portion; and in the county of Lyon, Camberiacus and Savigniacus, from the portion of Kings Hugh and Lothair. Likewise in the same county, Amberta, which Bernard acquired from the Emperor Louis by charter.

Moreover, let them perpetually claim as their lawful property the farms, possessions, and allods that have been donated to the aforesaid monastery at various times by different persons and faithful Christians, wherever they may lie, in whatever counties or vicariates, with all their appurtenances. Of the woods in which they have a share, and of the lands, no one shall take a land tax except with their consent.

In accordance with the excommunications of the popes inserted in the privileges, and with the adjuration pronounced by the aforesaid William, we too command and declare in the name of Christ that it shall never be subjected in any manner to any mortal person, whether king, bishop, or count. Rather, in accordance with the tradition which they appear to have maintained in our days, let them be permitted to live under it. If they should deviate, let them be reserved for the judgment of God or correction according to the rule, and let the gift made to God and his saints in no way be rescinded.

So that this may be believed more surely and observed more carefully by everyone, we have confirmed it with our own hand and ordered it to be recorded below under the impression of our ring.

The sign of Lord Louis, most glorious king.

Gerard the notary, acting in place of Bishop Artaldus, has verified this.

Done at Quercecus, near the village of Dociacus, on the river Carus, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the twelfth indiction, in the fourth year of the reign of King Louis. In the name of God, successfully. Amen.

#### II. Charter of King Conrad concerning Tusiacum in the county of Lyon. (Year 943.)

[Col. 0842B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Conrad, by the will of almighty God, most serene king.

It is fitting that each of us should exalt and assist the Church of God on behalf of himself and all his people faithful to God, so that this may be known to the memory of all our faithful, present and future.

Hugh, our kinsman and count, approached our royal majesty, asking that we grant by royal charter to the monastery of Cluny—built in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul—that which he restored to us, namely the village of Thosiacum in the county of Lyon, and whatever is lawfully seen to belong to it: lands, vineyards, meadows, woods, waters and watercourses, fisheries, and all slaves of both sexes, for the sake of our lord, King Rudolf, of blessed memory, and for the salvation of our soul. This we have done.

We wish and firmly decree that the aforesaid place possess full force, and that whatever belongs here to the aforementioned village, with all its adjoining lands and appurtenances, whether already acquired or to be acquired, be held wholly and entirely, without any impediment or opposition.

So that this charter of ours may be observed by everyone and never violated by anyone, we have confirmed it with our own hand and ordered it to be authenticated with our seal.

The sign of Lord Conrad, most devout king.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the year 943 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the … year of the reign of Lord Conrad, son of Rudolf. Successfully. Amen.

[Col. 0841]

### IV. Donation of Leotald, Count of Mâcon, Made to the Monastery of Cluny

*(Bibliotheca Sabusiana, p. 168, from the cartulary of the church of Cluny.)*

[Col. 0841D]

To the most holy church founded in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, in the county of Mâcon, in the village of Cluny, which Lord Odo the abbot is seen to possess for its governance.

I, Leotald, by the grace of God count of Mâcon, and my wife Ermengard, for the love of God and eternal recompense, so that the merciful God may deign to free our souls and those of our parents Alberic and Tholosana, Manasseh and Ermengard, as well as our friend Gerald and all faithful Christians, both living and dead, from the punishments of hell—for that love we cede and donate to that house of God something from our possessions in the county of Lyon, in the village of Dardanicum, on the river Sillia [Note: Sillia, commonly called the Seille, is a river that flows into the Saône, not far from the village of Ratenella], whether acquired or to be acquired, with all its appurtenances and the resident dependents: whatever we are seen to possess there, wholly and entirely, to that house of God, for the support of the brothers who continually serve God there.

If anyone should oppose this donation, let him incur the wrath of God and pay four pounds of gold; and let this donation remain firm, supported by a formal stipulation.

The sign of Leotald; the sign of Ermengard, who requested that this donation be made and confirmed; the signs of Count Geoffrey, Nardoin, Leodegarius, Racher, Gerald, Gothofred, Gosbert, Iwicherann, Mayol, Odeylard, Alberic, Ardrad, Wichard, Adalgarius, and Bonon.

Given through the hand of Berard on Wednesday, the second day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth year of the reign of King Rudolf.

[Col. 0843]

### V. Testament of William, Called the Pious, Count of the Auvergnats and Duke of the Aquitanians, Concerning the Construction of the Site of Cluny

[Note: Testament of William concerning the construction of the site of Cluny. Many modern writers assert that this William, or William, count of the Auvergnats and duke of the Aquitanians, was not the founder but merely the restorer of the monastery of Cluny: especially Bugnonius, William Paradinus in Book I of the *Annals of Burgundy*, Pierre Sanjulianus Baluze in Books II and III of the *Antiquities of Mâcon*, and Jacques Severtius in Part II, *Concerning the Bishops of Mâcon*. All of them say that Warin, or Guarin, count of Mâcon and Chalon, first built this celebrated monastery, and that Hildebold, bishop of Mâcon, consecrated it in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, around the twelfth or thirteenth year of Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne. But since Bugnonius adds the year 828 of Christ to an ancient diploma by which he attempts to prove this foundation, he makes the matter suspect, as Nicholas Vignier remarks in the *Chronicle of Burgundian Affairs*, especially because of what he writes about Warin himself, affirming that he was appointed count of Mâcon only after the restoration of Emperor Louis.
