It would be more credible to accept the testimony produced by Severtius from the treasury of the abbey of Cluny itself, expressed in these words: “The first founder of the monastery of Cluny was Guarinus, also called Gerinus, count of Chalon and Mâcon, during the reign of Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne, around the year 820; after it was devastated by the Hungarians, it was restored by William, duke of Aquitaine.” I say that this would be more credible if the innumerable authorities of the diplomas, charters, and even books of that same monastery did not outweigh this single testimony by an uncertain author. For Pope Agapetus II, Louis of Overseas, king of the Franks, and many others repeatedly assert in their bulls and charters that William, count of Auvergne and duke of the Aquitanians, laid the first foundations of this religious and world-famous monastery.

Saint Odilo, the fifth abbot of Cluny, in his *Life of Saint Majolus*, his predecessor; Ralph Glaber, himself a monk of Cluny, in Book III, chapter 5, of his *History of the Franks*; and likewise the writer of the *Chronicle of Cluny*, who lived under Saint Hugh, the sixth abbot, all consistently affirm the same thing. The words of the chronicle are as follows: “In the year 910 from the Lord’s Incarnation, William, duke of the Aquitanians, built the monastery of Cluny for the venerable Peter and Paul.”

Many other and very ancient authors also agree with the Cluniac records and unanimously recognize William the Pious’s original foundation: the writer of the *Life of Saint Hugh*, abbot of Saint-Martin of Autun; an old fragment of Frankish history; Ademar, a monk of Saint Martial of Limoges, in his history of Aquitaine; the *Chronicle of Saint Peter of Sens*; Martin of Opava, who nevertheless wrongly calls this William prince of Burgundy; Orderic Vitalis, a monk of Utica in the diocese of Lisieux; and the anonymous author of a history of the Franks who wrote in the time of Philip, son of Louis the Pious. The last two, however, also wrongly substitute Gerard for William. We have presented the testimony of all these writers in the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, pages 5, 7, and 8.

Let us now add two further testimonies of equally ancient writers. An anonymous but learned author of Book II of the *Life of Saint Genulphus* says: “At this time William, count of the Auvergnats, was duke of the Aquitanians; he founded the monastery of Cluny.” And a certain Ademar, son of Raymond, in his chronology of the abbots of Saint Martial of Limoges, writes: “In the nineteenth year of this abbot, namely Fulbert VI, William died, duke and count of the Auvergnats, who built the monastery of Cluny.”

Among more recent writers who mention the same foundation by Duke William there is also no small number. Platina, in the *Life of Pope Adrian III*; the *Chronicle of Chronicles*; James of Bergamo in his *Supplement*; Robert Gaguin in Book VI of his *History of the Franks*; Jean Bouchet in the *Annals of Aquitaine*; Nicholas Vignier in the *Chronicle of Burgundian Affairs* under the year 910; and Genebrard in Book IV of his *Chronology* all agree, in the clearest possible terms, on this point.]

(Year 910.)

*(Bibliotheca Cluniacensis, p. 1.)*

[Col. 0843B]

It is clear to all who consider the matter that God’s providence so assists the wealthy that, from the possessions they temporarily hold, they may, if they use them well, always earn rewards that will endure. Divine speech shows this to be possible and strongly urges it when it says: “The riches of a man are the redemption of his soul” (Proverbs 13).

I, William, count and duke by God’s gift, carefully considering this and wishing, while it is permitted, to provide for my own salvation, have judged it right—indeed absolutely necessary—to distribute something from the possessions temporarily granted to me for the benefit of my soul. For since I appear to have grown prosperous through these things, I do not wish to be accused at the last judgment of having spent everything on the care of the body; rather, when the final lot has carried everything away, I rejoice that I have reserved something for myself.

This purpose, it seems, can be fulfilled in no more fitting way than that, according to the Lord’s command, “I will make his poor my friends” (Luke 16:9), I should sustain them from my own resources, so that this work may continue not for a time but without interruption, by supporting those gathered together in the monastic profession. I do so in such faith and hope that, although I myself cannot wholly despise all things, nevertheless, when the despisers of the world, whom I believe to be righteous, shall have received [them], I may receive “the reward of the righteous” (Matthew 10:41).

Therefore, let all who live in the unity of faith and ask for the mercy of Christ, those who will succeed them and live until the consummation of the world, know that, for the love of God and of our Savior Jesus Christ, I transfer from my own lordship to the holy apostles Peter and Paul, as a gift, namely Cluny [that is, the village of Cluny], which is situated [Note: Cluny, which is situated. Ralph Glaber describes the location and etymology of Cluny as follows in Book III, chapter 5, of his *History of the Franks*, while discussing the Order of Saint Benedict:

“Finally, when the aforesaid institution was already almost exhausted, by God’s agency it chose for itself a seat of wisdom, where it might gather strength and bear fruit in abundant offspring: namely, in the monastery called Cluny. This name was also assigned to it from the sloping and low-lying situation of the place; or, what suits it better, it was derived from *cluere*, since we say *cluere*, ‘to grow.’ From its beginning the place has conspicuously increased day by day through various gifts.”

Peter Damian also offers another origin for the name in Book VI of his letters, in a letter to Hugh, abbot, and the monks of the monastery of Cluny, in these words:

“Therefore, when I contemplate you, fortunate Cluny, I perceive that this name was given to you not without the arrangement of divine foreknowledge. For the name is composed from *clunes* and *acus*, by which the work of plowing oxen is signified. The ox is pricked in the haunches with a goad so that it may draw the plow and break open the fields. There the field of the human heart is cultivated, from which the harvest is gathered and stored in the chambers of the heavenly granary.”

And shortly afterward:

“Accordingly, I may appropriately call Cluny a field, in which the Lord’s oxen plow without weariness while the goad of divine fear spurs them on. Just as the rear part of the haunches is pierced with a goad, so the human mind is terrified by fear of the final judgment.”]

on the river called Grauna [Granna] [Note: On the river called Grauna. Another manuscript has *Grannam*; Ralph Glaber calls it *Graona*], together with a farmstead and a demesne holding, and a chapel dedicated to holy Mary, Mother of God, and to Saint Peter, prince of the apostles [Note: And a chapel dedicated to Saint Mary and Saint Peter. This may perhaps be the chapel that Count Warin built and Bishop Hildebold consecrated—not, as Paradinus and Sanjulianus assert, in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, but, as William the duke’s own words state, “in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, and Saint Peter, prince of the apostles.”

I have no doubt that their error arose from this: they supposed that the monastery of Cluny itself had been built by Warin. Yet another church had already been founded at Cluny in Count Warin’s time, dedicated to Saint Romanus by a certain Flodomeus, whom Begatius states in his commentaries to have served from the beginning as guardian of Sigismund and Gothomar, sons of Gundobad, king of the Burgundians. This is mentioned in a diploma of Louis the Pious.], with all the possessions belonging to that village: villages, chapels, dependents of both sexes, vineyards, fields, meadows, woods, waters and watercourses, mills, rights of access and return, cultivated and uncultivated land, in their entirety.

These possessions are situated in the county of Mâcon or nearby, each enclosed within its own boundaries [Note: Each enclosed within its own boundaries. Peter, bishop of Albano; Pope Urban II; Pope Calixtus II; and other Roman pontiffs frequently discuss the boundaries of the sacred ban of the monastery of Cluny in their charters.]

I, William, and my wife Ingelberga give all these things to the aforesaid apostles, first for the love of God, then for the soul of my lord King Odo [Note: For the soul of my lord King Odo. This Odo was the son of Robert, count of Anjou. “The Franks,” as the old fragment of the *History* says, “although he resisted, chose him as guardian of the boy, namely Charles, son of Louis the Stammerer, and as administrator of the kingdom. Kind in spirit, he governed vigorously by crushing the enemies of the state, raised the boy excellently, and patiently restored the kingdom to the young man when he came of age and sought it back.”

At that time he was count of Paris and duke of Aquitaine, as Abbo of Fleury in Book I of *The Siege of Paris* and Ademar of Chabannes in his *History of Aquitaine* testify. Later, however, the Franks conspired against Charles, expelled him from the kingdom, and established this Odo as king in his place, as the author of Book II of the *Life of Saint Genulphus*, chapter 17, relates. This plainly became the beginning and cause of great disputes between him and Charles, as Flodoard shows in Book IV of his *Ecclesiastical History of Rheims*, chapters 2, 3, and following, although Odo himself did not remain in the kingdom even for two complete years.

William therefore calls him his lord, that is, his master, as count of the Auvergnats addressing the duke of Aquitaine—not as duke of the Aquitanians addressing the king of the Franks. For William was not duke of Aquitaine until after Odo’s death, as Abbo teaches in Book II. It is well known from ancient records that *senior* was customarily used for “lord.” The cartulary of the abbey of Marmoutier, concerning the affairs of Vendôme, charter 129, says: “Yet there is an agreement concerning all their grants, that he should cause his lord, from whom he holds these things in benefice, to approve them.” It is also used broadly for a prince or generous lord. Thus, in Berno’s testament below: “I beseech you, O princes and lords, whoever you are who judge earthly matters.” In ordinary French, they say *seigneur* and *seigneur de fief*.],

for the souls of my father and mother [Note: For my father and mother. William’s father was Bernard, as Saint Odo notes in Book I, chapter 32, of the *Life of Saint Gerald*; Guido Coquille later repeats this in his *History of Nevers*, adding that Bernard was count and marquis of Nevers. Saint Odo, in the cited passage, calls William’s mother Ermengard.], for myself and my wife, namely for the salvation of our souls and bodies; and likewise for Avana, who granted these same possessions to me by testamentary right [Note: For Avana, who granted these same possessions to me by testamentary right. By Avana he means the wife of Count Warin of Mâcon and Chalon. Louis the Pious calls her Albana and Alba in a diploma; Sigebert and the author of the *Fasciculus Temporum* call her Ava; Bernard Gui and the author of the *Chronicle of Limoges* call her Anna; Peter Sanjulianus calls her Eva; Nicholas Gilles calls her Ina; Louis Golut, in Book IV of his *Commentaries on the Commonwealth of Burgundy*, calls her Yva; and finally Johannes Trithemius, in the *Chronicles of the Monastery of Hirsau*, incorrectly calls her Avia instead of Ava.

To understand how she could have granted the village of Cluny and the possessions belonging to it to Count William by testamentary right, it should be noted, following Bugnonius, that Leduardus XIII, bishop of Mâcon, had received this Cluny—or the land on which the village was later built—from Charlemagne, as an increase to the endowment of the cathedral church of Saint Vincent. Leduardus’s successors retained it until Hildebold XVIII, bishop of that see. Hildebold exchanged the village with Warin, count of Mâcon, and his wife Avana, for certain other possessions situated in the counties of Nevers and Auvergne, as can be learned from the diploma of Emperor Louis the Pious, who confirmed the exchange by his authority in the twelfth year of his reign.

But since this diploma seems to be none other than the one whose testimony Bugnonius uses in attempting to establish that Count Warin was the first founder of the monastery of Cluny, I shall reproduce it in full from the Cluniac cartulary belonging to the library of the illustrious president Jacques-Auguste de Thou. It contains not even a word about a monastery, much less any mention of its foundation or construction. It is as follows:

**Donation of Hildebert [Hildebold], Bishop of Mâcon, received from Warin and Ava [Alba and Albana below] his wife, concerning the village of Cluny.**

“In the name of the holy Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, emperor augustus by the providence of God’s ordering. If we confirm by our edicts those things which the faithful of our empire exchange among themselves for their needs, we exercise the imperial custom, and we wish this to remain thereafter established by the firmest right. Therefore let the industry of all our faithful, present and future, know that the venerable man Hilduin, abbot and chief chaplain of the sacred palace, made known to our serenity that Hildebold, bishop of the Church of Mâcon, and the illustrious man Warin, count, had recently exchanged certain possessions among themselves for their common advantage and benefit.

The aforesaid Bishop Hildebold therefore gave, from the property of his bishopric, to Count Warin and his wife Albana [another reading: Ava], to have as their own perpetually, in the same county of Mâcon, a village called Cluny, with the church in that village, and with its houses, dwellings, buildings, vineyards, fields, meadows, woods, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, rights of access and return, and with the dependents residing there, together with all their offspring: everything belonging to them, in every respect, and wholly and entirely whatever appears to pertain to that village.

Likewise, in the county of Nevers, a village called Aptannacus, with the church built there, with its holdings, houses, buildings, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, woods, rights of access and return, and with the dependents residing there, together with all their offspring: everything, in every respect, however much appears to pertain to that village.

In exchange for this property, the aforementioned Count Warin and his wife Alba [above: Albana] gave from their own possessions to Bishop Hildebold, for the benefit of his church, in the same county of Mâcon, a village called Genuliacus, with the church built there, its holdings, houses, dwellings, buildings, vineyards, fields, meadows, woods, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, rights of access and return, and the dependents residing there, together with all their offspring: everything, in every respect, whatever appears to pertain to that village and is recognized as their possession.

And in the county of Nevers, a village called Calda Aqua, with houses, dwellings, buildings, holdings, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, waters and watercourses, rights of access and return, and with the dependents residing there, together with all their offspring: everything, in every respect, whatever appears there to be their own property.

Likewise, in the duchy of Auvergne, in the county of Donobres, a village called Lituinias, with houses, dwellings, buildings, holdings, vineyards, fields, meadows, woods, pastures, waters and watercourses, and with the dependents living there, together with their offspring: everything, in every respect, whatever is recognized as their own.

Therefore he declared that he had in hand two exchanges written in identical form and confirmed by the hands of good men. But for complete security he asked our highness to confirm those exchanges anew, more fully, by a charter of our mercy. We did not wish to deny his request; rather, know that just as we have granted and confirmed the requests of each of our faithful who ask justly, so we have granted and confirmed theirs in every respect.

Accordingly, we command and order that whatever one party has justly and reasonably transferred to the other party shall henceforth, by this authority of ours, be held and possessed by the firmest right; and that either party shall enjoy complete freedom to do or adjudicate concerning it whatever it wishes to undertake.

So that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved better for future times, we have ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.”

“Deacon Durandus, acting in place of Fridegisus, has verified this.

“Given on the third day before the Nones of June, in the twelfth year, with Christ favorable, of the empire of Lord Louis, most devout Augustus, in the third indiction.

“Done at the royal palace of Aachen, successfully in the name of God. Amen.”]

for the souls also of our brothers and sisters, nephews and all relatives of both sexes; for our faithful who adhere to our service; and for the welfare and integrity of the Catholic religion.

Finally, just as all Christians are bound together by a single bond of charity and faith, so let this donation be made for all the orthodox faithful of past, present, and future times.

[Col. 0849A] With this condition attached to the gift: that at Cluny a regular monastery be built in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and that monks living according to the rule of blessed Benedict be gathered there, who may possess, hold, have, and administer those properties in perpetuity. Only in such a way, namely, that there the venerable dwelling of prayer may be faithfully frequented with vows and supplications, and that heavenly conversion [or: heavenly way of life] may be sought and desired with every longing and deepest ardor. Diligent prayers, petitions, and supplications are likewise directed to the Lord, both for me and for all, as their remembrance has been set out above.

We therefore command that this donation of ours be especially for them a perpetual refuge: for those who, having come forth from the world as poor men, bring nothing with them except good will, so that our supplement may become their abundance. Let the monks themselves, with all the properties prescribed above, be under the authority and dominion of Abbot Berno.

[Note: “Let the monks themselves, with all the properties.” The very small number of the first monks of the Cluniac monastery is attested especially by the author of the Life of Saint Hugh, abbot of Saint-Martin of Autun. Speaking of this monastery, he says: “At the beginning, a very small company of brothers was established in this same place.” Rodulfus Glaber likewise records that only twelve came together at the beginning, but that from that very small seed an immense and abundant harvest grew without number. His words are found in Book III, chapter 5, of the *History of the Franks*: “This monastery, at first, is said to have received no more than fifteen agricultural holdings as its endowment; nevertheless, twelve brothers are remembered as having assembled there. From them, as from an excellent seed, a multiplied offspring of the Lord of hosts is known to have filled a great region of the world without number.” This offspring of the Lord was indeed multiplied to such an extent that Peter the Venerable, the ninth Cluniac abbot, testifies that, when he was appointed abbot, more than three hundred religious men were in this monastery. In a certain book of statutes that he published, he writes: “Therefore I, Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, make known to all who read this that, when I was appointed to this office twenty-eight years ago, I found a large, religious, and famous church, but extremely poor, burdened with great expenses and, when its revenues were compared with its expenses, possessing scarcely any income. There were three hundred brothers, or more, and that house could not support even a hundred from its own resources.” This was a great multitude, and it endured almost up to the year 1346 without diminution, except perhaps a small one. For in the catalogue of the abbeys and priories dependent upon this illustrious monastery it is found that “before the great mortality, which began in the year of the Lord 1346 and lasted for three years, there were ordinarily two hundred and sixty religious there.” From that time onward there was no fixed number of Cluniac monks; they were placed there according to the resources available.]

For as long as he lives, let him regularly preside over them according to his knowledge and ability. After his departure, however, let those same monks have the power and permission to choose as abbot and ruler any member of their order whom they prefer, in accordance with God’s will and the rule promulgated [or: proclaimed] by Saint Benedict; and let them not be obstructed in a properly religious election by contradiction from us or from any other power.

[Note: “Let the monks have the power to choose an abbot.” Thus Louis Ultramarine, king of the Franks, writes in his charter concerning Salustria: “Let the inhabitants living under the regular order choose for themselves from among themselves, according to the rule of Saint Benedict, an abbot after Odo, who now presides.”]

For five years, let the aforesaid monks pay ten solidi at Rome, at the threshold of the apostles, for preparing [or: continuing] their lamps; and let them have the protection of those apostles and the Roman pontiff as their defender.

[Note: “For five years at Rome, ten solidi.” Pope Agapitus says: “Certainly, in recognition that the aforesaid monastery belongs to the Holy Apostolic See for protection and support, ten solidi are to be paid for five years.” But Orderic Vitalis, Book XI of his *History of His Times*, gives a somewhat different account: “It is established, and is clearly shown by documents read by those who examine them, that G., duke of Aquitaine, built the Cluniac monastery on his own allod and, going to Rome, most devoutly entrusted it to the Roman pontiff; nor did he wish this to be done without purpose. For at that time he offered the pope twelve gold pieces, and decreed that the same number should thereafter be given each year.”]

Let the monks themselves, with full heart and mind, build up the aforesaid place to the best of their ability and knowledge.

[Col. 0851A] We also wish that, in our times and in those of our successors, as the opportunity and capacity of that place permit, works of mercy may daily be provided with the utmost devotion to the poor, the needy, strangers, and pilgrims.

It has also pleased us to insert into this testament that, from this day forward, the same monks gathered there shall be subject neither to us nor to our parents, neither to the insignia of royal greatness nor to the yoke of any earthly power.

[Note: “Nor any secular prince.” Pope Agapitus, writing to Aymard, abbot of Cluny, says: “Because you have asked us to decree by our apostolic authority that the Cluniac monastery should remain in that condition in which Duke William determined by his testament that it should remain, and so forth, yielding to your prayers, we entrust it to you to govern. Therefore let that monastery, with all its possessions, both those which it now has and those which shall hereafter be entrusted to you, be free from the domination of every king, bishop, count, or any of William’s relatives.” And Louis, son of Charles the Simple, says: “Let that place, according to what William himself established under a terrible and solemn adjuration, and subjected by testament to the Apostolic See for protection, not for domination, be entirely free and released from every secular domination, whether of kings, all princes, or William’s relatives, indeed of all men.”]

Nor shall any secular prince, any count, or any bishop, nor even the pontiff of the aforesaid Roman See, by God—and I call upon God, all his saints, and the day of the dreadful judgment as witnesses—invade the possessions of those servants of God. Let no one alienate, diminish, exchange, or grant them as a benefice; let no person be appointed over them against their will.

[Note: “Let no one exchange or grant them as a benefice.” *Procamiare* and *concamiare* are very common in ancient charters and testaments for “to exchange” and “to make an exchange.” Hence *camium*, *cambium*, *concamium*, *concambium*, and *excambium* mean an exchange or barter, which even today is commonly called *échange*. It was customary for founders of monasteries to impose this prohibition, lest those whom they appointed as protectors and patrons should ever exchange the monasteries, alienate them, or give them as benefices. Thus Henry I, king of the Franks, in a charter protecting the congregation of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of Saint Genevieve the virgin at Paris, says: “That congregation, which had formerly been founded by one of his predecessors, King Clovis of the Franks, at the urging and persuasion of blessed Remigius, archbishop of Reims, we establish, command by royal authority, and confirm by the impression of our seal, so that none of the succeeding kings or princes possessing the city of Paris may ever grant the aforesaid congregation to anyone by right of benefice, or alienate it from its protection or administration by any kind of exchange; rather, under royal defense, let it possess honorable security and, if this should ever occur, let it have from the prince’s possession both present and unfailing protection and consolation.”]

And so that this impiety may be more strictly forbidden to all rash and wicked persons, I add the following, repeating the same warning. I beseech you, holy apostles and glorious princes of the earth, Peter and Paul, and you, pontiff of pontiffs of the Apostolic See, that by the canonical and apostolic authority which you have received from God, you exclude from the fellowship of the holy Church of God and from eternal life the plunderers, invaders, and dissipators of these possessions, which I give to you with joyful mind and ready will.

Be guardians and defenders of the aforesaid place of Cluny [or: Cluniac], and of the servants of God living and dwelling there; and guardians and defenders also of all these possessions, for the almsgiving, clemency, and mercy of our most merciful Redeemer.

If anyone, which God forbid—and which, through God’s mercy and the protection of the apostles, I do not think will happen—whether among our relatives or strangers, or of whatever condition or power, should attempt by any deceit whatsoever to inflict injury upon this testament,

[Note: “Against this testament.” *Testament* is used for a command, charter, diploma, or princely instrument. Odo, abbot of Cluny, Book II of the *Life of Saint Gerald, Count of Aurillac*, chapter 4, says: “To consecrate his possessions to the Lord, he went to Rome and, by solemn testament, assigned the distinguished estate of Aurillac to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.” But this is too well known to require proof.]

—which I have established for the love of almighty God and the veneration of the apostolic princes Peter and Paul—let him first incur the anger of almighty God; let God remove his portion from the land of the living (Rev. XXII, 19), erase his name from the book of life (Rev. III, 5), and make his portion with those who said to the Lord God, “Depart from us” (Job XXI, 14), and with Dathan and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed when it opened its mouth, and whom hell absorbed alive (Num. XVI, 31). Let him incur everlasting damnation.

Let him also become the companion of Judas, the Lord’s betrayer, shut away in eternal torments; and, lest he appear to pass unpunished in the present world before human eyes, let him experience in his own body the torments of future damnation, receiving a double punishment with Heliodorus and Antiochus: the former was restrained by fierce blows and scarcely escaped half alive (II Macc. IX, 9); the latter, struck by a heavenly command, with his limbs rotting and worms swarming over him, died in the most wretched manner.

Let him be a partner also with the other sacrilegious men who presumed to violate the treasury of the house of the Lord; and, unless he repents, let him have the chief key-bearer of the entire monarchy of the Churches, with Paul joined to him as one who bars his way and opposes the entrance to the pleasant paradise—although, had he wished, he could have had them as most merciful intercessors on his behalf.

According to worldly law, moreover, let him be compelled by judicial authority to pay one hundred pounds of gold to those against whom he has brought a vexatious claim,

[Note: “To those whom he has wronged, one hundred pounds of gold.” It was customary at that time, and also later, to add a monetary penalty to the provisions of charters and testaments. Thus Emperor Otto, in a charter concerning Saint Mayolus at Pavia, says: “Therefore, if anyone breaks this decree of our stability, let him pay one hundred pounds of gold, half to our treasury and half to the Cluniac monastery.”]

and let his lawsuit, frustrated, achieve no effect whatever. But let the validity of this testament, supported by every authority, remain forever inviolate and unshaken, confirmed by stipulation.

Executed publicly in the city of Bourges.

William. I requested that this charter be made and confirmed, and I strengthened it with my own hand.

The seal of Ingelberga, his wife.

The seal of Madalbert,

[Note: “The seal of Madalbert.” Some call him Moalbert, others Maalbert. He was the fifty-first in succession among the archbishops of Bourges and held office in the time of Emperor Arnulf and Charles the Simple, king of the Franks.]

the sinful archbishop of Bourges.

The sign of Bishop Adalard,

[Note: “The sign of Bishop Adalard.” This Adalard was bishop of Clermont, concerning whom Odo writes in the *Life of Saint Gerald*, and perhaps we shall say more there.]

P. Alto, sinful bishop; the sign of Wilelon, his nephew; the sign of Armannus; the sign of Wigo; the sign of Ugbert; the sign of Stephen; the sign of Veraclus; the sign of Gotbransin; the sign of Eufred, viscount; the sign of Gentard, count; the sign of Ignard; the sign of Urso the Greek; the sign of Ratald; the sign of Rumbert; the sign of Ismengrius; the sign of Rotbert; the sign of Otbert; the sign of Guibert [Girbert]; the sign of Bermond; the sign of Girard; the sign of Amblad; the sign of Aleard; the sign of Achedeus; the sign of Windon; the sign of Grimbert; the sign of Umbert; the sign of Arnald; the sign of Armand; the sign of Walon; the sign of Robert; the sign of Bodon; the sign of Athon; the sign of Girband; the sign of Ismendon; the sign of Lotbert; the sign of Tertbert; the sign of Bernard; the sign of Gerald; the sign of Truannus.

In the eleventh year, while King Charles was reigning, in indiction 13. I, Oddo the levite, wrote and subscribed this in place of the chancellor.

[Col. 0853]

## VI. The Testament of Lord Berno, Abbot

To whom William the Pious, founder of the aforesaid monastery, first entrusted the government of the Cluniac monastery. (Year 926.)

(*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 9.)

[Col. 0853C] Since divine providence established after the Flood that one human being should provide for another, all who, according to God’s will, have presided over others, both in the Old Testament and in the New, have done their utmost, insofar as possible, to ensure that provision would be made for their subjects in the future. Many documents prove that blessed Benedict and many other founders of our order did this, and that, during their lifetime, they chose successors for themselves.

Therefore, may the whole community of royal power, sacerdotal authority, the dignity of princes, and the rest of the faithful who may happen to hear this writing pardon me. I, Berno, the least among all abbots, recognizing that my final day is already drawing near, have designated two of our brothers,

[Col. 0854C] namely Wido, my kinsman,

[Note: “Namely Wido, my kinsman.” The *Chronicle of Cluny* calls him Berno’s nephew and disciple in these words: “The venerable father Berno had holy disciples, namely Odo, Adhegrin, and the venerable Wido, his nephew, whom he made abbot of Baume.”]

[Note: “The monastery of Gigny.” Berno himself founded this monastery and was its first abbot. The *Chronicle of Limoges*, under the year 890, says: “At this time Berno, formerly a count, shone in Burgundy as abbot of the monastery of Gigny, founded by himself.” Sigebert says the same under the year 895; as do Vincent of Beauvais, Book XXIV, chapter 53; Bernard Guy in his *Chronicles*; Trithemius; and others.]

and Odo, equally beloved, with the consent of the brothers, to succeed me; and after my death I have commanded them, by God’s gift, to perform my office.

Thus, specifically, our beloved Wido is to preside regularly over the monastery of Gigny, that of Baume, that of Aethic, and the cell called Saint-Lothain, with all the properties belonging to the aforesaid monasteries, except the estate called Alafracta, certain properties of Lord Samson situated in the same district, the fourth part of the Caldariae situated in the place called Leodonis,

[Note: “In the place called Leodonis.” Pope Eugenius III calls it the borough of Ledon and mentions a donation or sale made to the Cluniac monastery by William, count of Mâcon.]

and half of the meadow that belonged to Lord Saymon [perhaps Simon].

But our dearest brother Odo is to receive Cluny, Masciacum,

[Note: “Masciacum.” A monastery in Aquitaine, which an unknown but contemporary author says was built by Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne, in his *Life* of that emperor. He writes: “Many monasteries were restored under his authority, indeed built from their foundations, but especially these: the monastery of Menat, the monastery of Saint-Savin, the monastery of Masciacum,” and so forth.]

and the monastery of Dol,

[Note: “And the monastery of Dol.” This is the monastery of Dol, or Bourg-Dieu, in Berry, which, as we read in the *Chronicle of Ademar*, “Eblo of Berry began to build in honor of the Mother of God, and afterward his son Rodulf completed it, where he gathered a great company of monks living there according to the rule.” A fragment of Frankish history calls this Eblo, prince of the people of Berry, Abbo. Bernard Guy writes that “when Paschal II came to Gaul, he dedicated this church to the blessed virgin Mary in the castle of Dol.”]

with the properties belonging to those places, so that, with God’s favor, he may regulate them according to his strength.

With these matters thus arranged, I beseech you, by the reverence that you owe to the holy faith and religion, O princes and lords, whoever you are who judge earthly affairs, willingly to hear this writing, which speaks in my place, in any of our communities. As divine law commands, consent to what is good, and agree that both the aforesaid abbots, and the monks, and the places with their possessions, remain in that condition which has long been established by royal charters and apostolic privileges and is now decreed by me.

If any dispute should arise, whether among them or elsewhere, that ought to be decided by us, uphold justice and suppress false accusation, so that what has been inserted in our charters may come to pass: just as you have been helpers concerning all the good works carried out in the aforesaid places, so may you also be able to share in them.

The estate called Alafracta, with everything belonging to it, and the fourth part of the Caldariae that we possess at Leodonis, as well as half of the aforesaid meadow, I transfer to Cluny, on the condition that twelve denarii be paid each year to Gigny as a rent for the vesting.

[Note: “Twelve denarii as a rent to Gigny.” Concerning this rent, Sigebert writes under the year 912: “Berno, the abbot, being about to die, appointed Odo, formerly a musician, abbot of the Cluniac monastery, on the condition that the church of Cluny should pay annually to the church of Gigny a rent of twelve denarii.” The same is written by Vincent of Beauvais, Book XXIV, chapter 59; the author of the *Chronicle of Limoges*; Bernard Guy; and others. But as the reputation for holiness of the Cluniac monastery grew, Gigny itself eventually became a dependency of its jurisdiction. See Peter the Venerable, Letter 33 of Book I of the catalogue of abbeys and priories dependent upon the Cluniac monastery, and various diplomas of the supreme pontiffs.]

Nor should it seem unjust that I assign these same properties to Cluny, since I have chosen my burial there, and because that place itself, like a posthumous child, is left unfinished through the death of Lord William, once the illustrious duke, and now through my own,

[Note: “And that place itself, unfinished, is now abandoned after the death of Lord William, once the illustrious duke.” From this it is clear that William the Pious, duke of Aquitaine, only began the Cluniac monastery and did not complete it. But if we believe Platina, he left responsibility for completing it to Eblo, count of Poitiers, who succeeded him in the duchy of Aquitaine and the county of Auvergne. In his *Life of Pope Adrian III*, speaking of the foundation of the Cluniac monastery, he writes: “Before his death, William left the monastery unfinished, appointing Eblo, count of Poitiers, to complete the work according to his testament.” John Bouchet gives the same account in his *Annals of Aquitaine*. A charter of Count Eblo is also found in the commentaries on Aquitanian Gaul, beginning: “E., count of Poitiers and duke of Aquitaine, having obtained the hereditary principate by the grace of God and through the donation of William, a man of glorious memory, have resolved to enlarge the monastery at Cluny.” But that charter, like many others reported there, is judged false by many. Nor do all agree about the duke William’s death. That he died before Berno is indicated by this very passage of Berno’s testament; but the year is not entirely certain. An ancient author of the chronology of the Cluniac abbots says that he died in 918. Ademar the monk, in the commemoration of the abbots of the basilica of Saint Martial at Limoges, places it under the nineteenth year of Fulbert, the sixth abbot, which was the year 920 from the Incarnation. Flodoard testifies in his *Chronicle* that he lived until 927. He died at Auvergne and “was buried at Brioude beside Saint Julian the martyr,” as the already cited Cluniac chronologist says.]

[Note: “And that place itself, unfinished, is now abandoned.” Those who called Berno the builder of the Cluniac monastery—Sigebert, Vincent of Beauvais, Trithemius, and others—are not entirely wrong. He was its first builder, with William, duke of Aquitaine, favoring him and supplying the necessary expenses. A charter of Louis, son of Charles the Simple, says: “The monastery called Cluny, which was built by the magnificent man William in honor of the first apostles, Peter and Paul, through the hands of a certain venerable abbot named Berno.” Rodulfus Glaber, Book III, chapter 5, writes: “Thus the aforesaid monastery was first built by the father of the monks of the monastery of Baume, named Berno, at the command of William, the most devout duke of Aquitaine, in the county of Mâcon, beside the little river Grosne.” Saint Odilo, in the *Life of Blessed Majolus*, says: “With William, the most Christian prince of Aquitaine, favoring him, the abbot Berno, of blessed memory, began to build a monastery in Burgundy, in the territory of Mâcon, in the district called Cluny, and strove to labor at its construction as far as he could.” But when he adds, “and by a laborious struggle brought the intention of pious devotion to a praiseworthy completion,” he seems to depart somewhat from the truth. Although the writer of the *Life of Blessed Hugh*, abbot of Saint-Martin of Autun and a contemporary of Abbot Berno, says that “the work was immediately begun and completed in a short time,” Berno himself teaches us by his death that this monastery remained unfinished, and the Italian monk John of Cluny states in Book II of the *Life of Saint Odo* that Odo, Berno’s successor, completed what had long before been begun.]

And indeed it is poorer both in possessions and in the number of its brethren. To add this point: if, after the earlier sons and the earlier place for whom and which I made this testament, divine generosity has deigned to enlarge for us both the place and the number of sons, it ought to be considered just that the later sons not be disinherited; rather, let some portion of our inheritance benefit them, who, although in another place, will nevertheless serve the same Lord, that is, blessed Peter, in whose name we built both places.

For the rest, I ask both the abbots and all the brothers, present and future, by the mercy of God, who looks upon the present, to preserve such unanimity among you that you continue thereafter to maintain the manner of life observed until now—both in psalmody and in the observance of silence, and also in the quality of food and clothing, and, above all, in contempt for private possessions—if not better, at least as you have done until now.

But if, which God forbid, any one of them should obstinately err, we command, by the authority of the holy rule, that the priors of both places mutually assist one another in correcting the error.

If anyone, which God forbid, violates this institution of ours in any respect, let the divine voice terrify him, which says: “Cursed is he who moves his neighbor’s boundary stone”—that is, the institution of his commands—and let his attempt be utterly frustrated.

May the arrangement of our affairs, which, as I believe, seeks through charity to provide for both places, remain, by God’s ordering and blessed Peter’s protection, firm and unshaken.

The sign of Berno, abbot, who requested that this charter be made and confirmed. The sign of Wido, the present abbot, who consented to this. The sign of Odo, abbot. The sign of Geoffroy. The sign of Wandanbert. In the fourth year, while King Rudolf was reigning.

## In the Year of the Lord 943. Cappidus of Stavoren, Frisian Priest

[Col. 0857]

## Historical Notice Concerning Cappidus

(*In Fabricius, Medieval and Later Latin Library.*)

Cappidus of Stavoren, a Frisian priest, is believed to be the author of the *Life of Saint Odulphus the Priest*, who lived around the year 860 and whose life was published by Surius on June 12. He is also said to have written the lives of Saints Lebuinus, Otger, and Plechelmus.

As for the *Genealogy of the Princes, Dukes, and Kings of Frisia* and the *Ecclesiastical History of the Frisian People*, which Suffridus Petri attributes to him and laments as having been destroyed by fire (*On the Writers of Frisia*, p. 57), I see that learned men are no less doubtful about these works than about many others attributed to him from the remote antiquity of the Frisians.

[Col. 0857]

## Cappidus of Stavoren, Frisian Priest, on the Life of Saint Odulphus the Priest

(*In Surius, Lives of the Saints, June 12.*)

[Col. 0857B] **I.** In the time of Louis, the most devout emperor, there was a certain venerable man born of a noble Frankish family. His name was Bodgis, and Odulphus was born from him. As soon as Odulphus had been reborn from the most sacred waters of baptism, he was also divinely watered with heavenly dew.

When he had ceased to depend upon his mother’s breasts, he was entrusted to the study of letters and commended to holy and devoted men, so that he might be instructed by them in canonical discipline. God granted him such zeal for discernment and such ease of understanding that he left far behind even those who were older than he was, and splendidly adorned his years—although not yet mature in age—with divine teachings and doctrines.

[Col. 0858B] As he grew in age, wisdom and holiness also increased in him, to such a degree that to those who at that time were striving to serve God religiously he seemed to be a new Samuel. Divine grace made him so pleasing to them that they all loved him unanimously and held him in the highest esteem because of his exemplary life. In turn, with equal affection, he loved them sincerely in his heart.

Already, while still a religious and venerable boy, at the very beginning of adolescence he showed that he was meditating upon and desiring what he afterward accomplished in fact, mindful of the Lord’s saying: “Whoever loves father more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. X); and again: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Luke IX).

While still a boy, he often remembered these words, silently turning them over within himself day and night. By holy conduct and virtuous works he firmly resolved in his heart to serve God perpetually and to cleave inseparably to the holy Church, his spiritual mother.

**II.** Thus the holy young man, especially dear to worthy men but concerned only to serve God, continually pressed upward through the stages of virtue toward higher things, until he became a perfect man. He resolved, as holy men are accustomed to do, continually to raise his mind and spirit toward heavenly things and to reject the enticements of worldly vanity and empty display, so that the words written in the psalm might also apply to him: “They go from strength to strength” (Ps. LXXXIII).

Thus, advancing in every virtue, he also climbed the degrees of the ecclesiastical orders and received the blessing of the priesthood, becoming a priest of the Most High King.

Then he immediately resolved within himself, through the pursuit of a devout way of life, to withdraw to a monastery of sacred religion. His parents dissuaded him from doing this, urging him instead to accommodate himself to their wishes and undertake the administration of the Church of Oorschot, for he had been born and raised there. At length, overcome by their entreaties, he complied with them in this matter, though unwillingly.

Not long afterward, however, he decided to visit the place of highest reverence at Utrecht, anciently called Wittenburg, with the intention and plan of faithfully serving there, for as long as he lived, the almighty God together with the other servants of God who were laboring for Christ there.

Remembering what the Savior says in the Gospel: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke IX), he put his father second, neglected his relatives, and despised his fields, household, possessions, and all his resources. Led by Christ, he set out for that place, poor in worldly goods but rich in merits.

He no longer wished to possess anything in this world, so that, according to the Lord’s promise, he might receive a hundredfold from him and deserve to become an heir of eternal life.

**III.** At that time the bishop of Utrecht was a man of outstanding holiness named Frederic. He received the man of God with great joy and honor. All the servants of God who were gathered there did the same, rejoicing sincerely among themselves that so holy and religious a servant of God had come to them.

Nor could he long conceal what had not escaped the eye of the divine majesty. After he had remained among them for some time, he shone among them all like a lamp burning with heavenly light.

He was vigorous in vigils, strong in fasting, diligent in prayer, devoted to sacred reading, generous in almsgiving, renowned for caring for the poor, fervent in hospitality, and prudent in distributing ecclesiastical goods. In short, he surpassed in a remarkable way all those over whom he had been placed after the bishop.

Accordingly, he was called by all of them, and even by the bishop himself, “Father of the monastery,” and they all desired to receive counsel from his mouth. For, with the Apostle, he had become all things to all people, so that he might win all for Christ (I Cor. IX).

IV. At that time the Frisians, a fierce people, had fallen into such shameful errors that the bishop whom we have mentioned could bring them back to the way of truth neither by himself nor through his archdeacons. Therefore, by means of a trustworthy messenger, he sent a letter to the man of God Odulph at Utrecht, asking him to cross the arm of the sea and come to him as quickly as he could. When he received that letter, Christ’s servant was extraordinarily delighted, as though he had been invited to a heavenly feast; he desired, with his shepherd, if the situation should require it, to pour out his blood for Christ in so holy a struggle.

When he had reached the bishop, the latter, seeing him, was overwhelmed with immense joy and received him courteously with the kiss of peace. Then, mutually consoling one another and, as befitted the noble heralds of the supreme King, splendidly girded with the sword of the Spirit, they began to travel together through the churches, visiting them again and again, and holding sermons to lead the people back to the truth through evangelical instruction. Finally, by frequently admonishing, reproving, and rebuking the people—who had previously been savage and rapacious like wolves—they converted them through salutary teaching into gentle sheep.

When these things had been accomplished, that bishop, after taking counsel with the clergy and with not a few laymen devoted to religion, earnestly begged the man of God to remain within the boundaries of that land and to strengthen through his instruction the people recently restored to health, rescuing them from the deadly jaws of the ancient enemy. But the man of God flatly refused, asserting that he was weighed down by age and could not bring sufficient strength to that ministry. The bishop, however, tried to bend him by his entreaties. At last the holy man yielded, undertook the commands of his shepherd, and complied with the people’s wishes, on the condition, nevertheless, that after several cycles of years had elapsed he would be permitted to revisit Utrecht, where he had promised to end his life in the service of Christ.

V. Thus, desiring not to fail in his appointed duty, the man filled with the Holy Spirit did not cease to sow the seeds of God’s word among the people, preaching the kingdom of heaven with great earnestness, and, as a prudent and faithful steward to all, providing nourishment from the divine word: solid food to the stronger and, according to the Apostle’s teaching, milk to the weak (I Cor. III). As a result, everyone was filled with joy because of his holiness.

When he had completed that ministry, he withdrew to his own people at Utrecht, praising God that, relying on His help, he had won so many souls. Although he was already greatly weakened by old age, yet in spirit overcoming his years, he relaxed nothing of his service to God or of his customary exercises of piety. For he persevered in continual fasts, in vigils pleasing to God, in holy prayers, and in the most generous almsgiving; sparing himself, but generous to all others for Christ’s name. He desired to acquire nothing earthly for himself, so that he might enjoy eternal goods.

VI. He also became renowned for the spirit of prophecy, predicting future events as though he already saw them happening before his eyes. To make this clearer and better attested, we shall present a few examples from the many.

When he was about to depart from the place called Stavoren, before setting out on his journey, a great multitude of Frisians gathered around him, wishing to be fortified by his most salutary exhortation. Commending them to the Lord, he blessed them and lovingly warned them never to turn aside from the way of truth, assuring them that, if they did so, they would not escape serious punishment.

“And indeed,” he said, “I know well that you will not remain in sound doctrine. For this reason barbarian peoples will attack you; you may confidently believe what I am now predicting to you. They will ravage your region and lead you, together with your possessions, into captivity.” Both events later occurred, just as the holy man had foretold.

VII. A huge stone lay before the doorway of his house. Pointing it out with his finger, he said to them:

“Know that this stone will come rolling down into the river without the work of any human being. There it will lie hidden beneath the waters until you have been deprived of the benefit of divine peace. When you see it emerge again upon the shore without human assistance, do not doubt that I, although already dead, will revisit you and carry to you peace obtained from God. It will remain with you until, through pride, perjuries, homicides, adulteries, and every kind of wickedness, you once more exclude it from yourselves, with God angered because of your crimes.”

Many witnesses of this prophecy and of the marvelous sign still survive today; they assert that they saw it with their own eyes. That stone also remains fixed and immovable there in the church, so that the faith of believers may be strengthened and unbelievers put to shame.

[Col. 0861C] VIII. After the bishop of the church of Utrecht had been taken from this life, the church was left without its shepherd. Soon the clergy assembled and discussed with the blessed man the choice of a successor. After they had long contended among themselves, they finally elected Crastus, the provost of the church.

But he, being very wealthy in worldly goods, said to them arrogantly and boastfully: “I have more than enough possessions. Why do you cast such a burden upon my shoulders?” Moved by these words, blessed Odulphus said: “What are you saying, most wretched man? You plainly reject what you do not deserve to obtain. If you did not wish to accept it, you should at least have said that you were unworthy of the summit of such an honor. But now, because of your immense wealth, you reject the dignity of the apostolic order; before many days have passed, you will be taken from this light.” The man of God spoke, and the man’s death declared the truth of his words.

Meanwhile, as those who had assembled from the clergy wavered in their minds, each of them chose the person whom he considered most suitable. But Christ’s priest, looking not to the person but to merit, said that someone more suitable might be found among them, although he did not disparage those whom they had chosen. He therefore pointed out to them a certain priest named Hunger, who, although deformed in appearance, was distinguished by his merits—unknown to men, but not unknown to God.

The people therefore elected him, and at the appointed time he was consecrated bishop. His life was indeed so upright that, after the holy bishops Willibrord and Boniface, no one was found in that see who was his equal in cultivating the virtues until the last day of his life. It is therefore evident that Saint Odulphus did not prefer him to the others without good reason.

IX. Old age was now weighing upon the holy man Odulphus, and he could no longer go to church without a staff. At the very top of this staff he had fastened a wax tablet on which, whenever an opportunity arose, he used to record the names of the faithful until he could write them in the book of life.

One day, however, through the vigor and liveliness of his spirit, he forgot his weakness. As he hurried to the worship of God, he left that staff in his dwelling. Shortly afterward, through the work of an evil demon, that dwelling caught fire and was consumed together with all its furnishings.

The man of God was occupied in divine praises. But when he saw that the dwelling had already been seized by a powerful fire, he turned to his customary refuge, praying to God that the flames should not invade the holy places; he was not greatly concerned about the destruction of his little cell. God heard his prayers, and the fire was soon suppressed; it burned nothing except the dwelling of the man of God.

In the midst of the flames, however, the staff remained so unharmed that the wax appeared to have been hardened by the fire, and not even the tiniest point had been erased from it. Through this remarkable miracle God wished to show how great the merit of Saint Odulphus was in His sight. The brothers fixed that staff in the tomb of the deceased man, where it remained set until the work of Bishop Ratbod of blessed memory.

X. At last, when the time was approaching in which the blessed man was to pass into the desired glory of his heavenly homeland, he was seized by a slight fever and perceived that the time of his departure had come. He therefore summoned the brothers and announced to them the day of his death.

At the very hour of his death he again wished the brothers to be present with him and to sing psalms with him in expectation of his departure. When everything had been duly carried out according to his instructions, he bade farewell to the brothers, asking them to pray to the Lord for him. He also promised that he would continually offer prayers to the Lord for them, for that place, and for its inhabitants.

Then, immediately turning toward the Lord and fearing nothing in the face of death—for he counted death itself as gain—he said with a joyful mind: “Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit” (Ps. XXX). With these words that most holy soul departed from the body. At the same time, the fragrance of an exceedingly sweet odor spread throughout the place, so that everyone was filled with indescribable sweetness. From this it was plainly possible to perceive that the most blessed angelic spirits had received the soul as it departed from the body.

His feast day is celebrated on the day before the Ides of June. Through his merits innumerable miracles are performed, not only at Utrecht, where his relics are kept at Saint Saviour’s, but also at Stavoren, in honor and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for endless ages of ages. Amen.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1446. POPE MARINUS II.

[Col. 0863]

HISTORICAL NOTICE.

(From Cocquelines, *Bullar., privileg. Romanorum pontif. ampl. Collect.*)

Marinus II, also called Martinus III, a Roman by nationality, was immediately appointed in the place of Pope Stephen. He occupied the pontificate during the reigns of Constantine Porphyrogenitus in the East and Emperor Otto the Great in the West, for three years and six months; many add thirteen days. But since Pagius demonstrates from the letters of his successor Agapetus that he was already pope on 15 June 946, the third catalogue of Vignolius, from the Vatican manuscript, appears to be preferable; in it only three years and six months are assigned. Marinus therefore died around 5 or 6 June 946.

[Col. 0863]

LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES OF POPE MARINUS II.

I. PRIVILEGE OF POPE MARINUS II FOR THE MONASTERY OF VÉZELAY. (Year 953.)

[From Acher, *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 504.]

[Col. 0863A]

Marinus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Guido, religious abbot of the monastery of Vézelay, and to the entire congregation of that monastery, forever.

Whenever we are asked to grant things that plainly accord with reason, we ought willingly to concede them and to provide appropriate assistance to the desires of those who ask. Therefore, because you requested that we should grant the monastery of Vézelay, over which you are known to preside, a privilege of the Apostolic See—this monastery having formerly been built in the kingdom of Burgundy, in the district of Avallon, by Gerard, a most noble and Christian man, and by Berta, his wife, in honor of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ and in veneration of the most blessed ever-virgin Mary, mother of that same Lord Jesus Christ, and having been bestowed by the aforesaid founders upon blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, through pious devotion and by a testamentary document—we, inclined by your prayers, have willingly decided that this should be done.

Accordingly, by our authority we establish and decree, and through this apostolic privilege we confirm, that no king or bishop, abbot or count, nor any person of great or small rank, corrupted by avaricious greed or deceived by diabolical suggestion, shall dare or presume, against your honor, venerable Abbot Guido, to rise up against you in any way during your lifetime, to inflict injury upon you concerning your dignity, or to inflict any invasion, plunder, or violence upon any of the monastery’s possessions that have been granted and confirmed to you and your predecessors by us and our predecessors through the document of privilege. Whoever does so shall, by the authority of God, Saint Peter, and our apostolic authority, be cut off from the body and blood of the Lord Jesus Christ and from entry into the church.

We also add this provision to the present chapter, so that we may exclude avarice: no king, no bishop or priest, nor any other faithful person, either personally or through an intermediary, shall dare to receive anything in any form as a gift on account of the appointment of that abbot, clerics, or priests, or on account of the distribution of chrism, the consecration of a basilica, or any other matter pertaining to that monastery. Nor shall the abbot himself presume to give anything for his appointment, lest on this pretext the offerings made by the faithful to the holy place be consumed.

Nor shall the bishop of that city or diocese celebrate public Masses there unless invited by the abbot of the monastery. Nor shall he announce stations in that monastery, lest the peace of God’s servants in any way be disturbed by a popular gathering. Nor shall he presume to demand provisions or lodging dues from it.

As for the reception of the faithful and of religious men, and the beneficence which the Apostle commands to be shown to all according to the capacity of the place and its resources, we not only do not forbid it from taking place there, but also recommend it. Yet the number of the congregation should be so regulated that neither an excessive number brings poverty upon the place nor too few inhabitants bring about its abandonment.

We also confirm by our authority the privilege granted to the same monastery by our predecessor, Pope Nicholas of blessed memory, except only that what he assigned under the name of “servants of God”—who, because of the frequent disturbances of the world, are now unable to remain there in an orderly manner—we, for the sake of more suitable usefulness, decree should appropriately be under the monastic habit.

If any king, bishop, priest, abbot, judge, count, or secular person attempts to act against this document of our institution, struck by apostolic anathema, let him lose the dignity of his power or honor, recognize himself as guilty before the divine judgment, and, unless he erases the evil things he has done, let him be separated from the most sacred body of our Lord Jesus Christ and subjected to the strict retribution of eternal judgment.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve what is just toward that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

Written by the hand of Azo, notary of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of February, in the first indiction.

Given on the second day before the Nones of February, by the hand of Benedict, bishop and librarian of the Holy Apostolic See, in the first year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord Marinus, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the most sacred see of blessed Peter the apostle, in the month of February, indiction 1.

II. PRIVILEGE OF POPE MARTINUS II FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT BONIFACE AT FULDA. (Year 943.)

[Dronke, *Codex diplomaticus Fuldensis*, p. 318.]

Marinus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hadamar, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of the holy martyr of Christ, Boniface, and through him to that venerable monastery and to your successors, forever.

Since things that accord with reasonable desires must always be granted, the authority of a pious foundation ought by no means to be denied the devotion of its founder when privileges are being bestowed. Therefore, because you requested that the monastery of the Saviour, first constructed by Saint Boniface and recently rebuilt by you at the place called Boconia beside the bank of the river Fulda, should be adorned with the insignia of a privilege of the Apostolic See and, established under the jurisdiction of our Church, which by God’s authority we serve, should not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other church, we, favoring your pious desires, commit to effect by our authority what has been requested.

And therefore we prohibit any priest or bishop of any church from exercising any jurisdiction or authority in the aforesaid monastery apart from the Apostolic See. Unless invited by the abbot of the monastery, no one at all shall presume to celebrate the solemnity of Masses there, so that, plainly, in accordance with the fact that it has been subjected to the Apostolic See through the firmness of this privilege, it may remain securely endowed with its places and possessions—both those which it now holds or possesses and those which divine piety may wish to increase in future for the rights of this venerable monastery from the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful—enjoying perpetual security without opposition from any person.

We also establish by this document of our decree that whoever, whether a prelate of any church or a person possessing any dignity, attempts to violate this charter of our privilege, which we confirm by the authority of the prince of the apostles, shall be anathema. Incurring the wrath of God, let him be excluded from the assembly of all the saints. Nevertheless, the dignity of the aforesaid monastery, granted by us, shall remain perpetually inviolate, supported by our authority.

Written by the hand of Theodore, regional notary and scrivener of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of March and in the first indiction.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, by the hand of Nicholas, first secretary of the supreme Apostolic See, in the first month, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord Marinus, supreme pontiff and universal junior pope, in the most sacred see of blessed Peter the apostle, and in the first indiction.

III. PRIVILEGE OF POPE MARINUS II FOR THE CHURCH OF BENEVENTO. (Year 943.)

[From Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. VIII, p. 50.]

[Col. 0866B] Marinus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved and deservedly honorable John, bishop of the holy Beneventan Church, and to your successors, forever.

Since the splendor of Christ’s supreme and apostolic dignity is recognized as shining forth in this divine office, and since it strives to offer the contest of its labor with especial diligence in performing the praises of God, the due care of that same apostolic pastoral solicitude has compelled us to promulgate whatever ought to be established for the stability of holy places and to confirm it by the judgment of apostolic institution.

Therefore, because you requested that it should be adorned [lacuna] of the Apostolic See, and that we should confirm the ancient boundaries granted to it by our predecessors the pontiffs, we, favoring your pious desires, commit by our authority to effect what has been requested. We grant to you and to your holy Beneventan Church whatever it is seen to possess legally and reasonably by ancient right in the time of your predecessors: namely, Bivinum, Asculum, Larinum, Sipontum, and the church of Saint Michael the Archangel on Mount Gargano, with all their appurtenances; and all estates, together with churches, male and female dependants, and estates, and every place within your diocese, we grant to your religious authority and to your successors to govern and to administer legally and canonically, with all their appurtenances—whether they are cities or whatever castles were formerly possessed and established by your predecessors the bishops.

We further establish, under the threat of divine judgment and by powerful and most severe prohibitions of anathema, that no person endowed with the power of any other dignity, whether a great or small person, or a Greek, shall ever presume to use force against your holy Beneventan Church, or in any way remove, alienate, or diminish the boundaries of anything that appears to belong to it, nor at any time inflict upon it any wickedness, breach, or injury. Nor shall anyone have permission, as has been said, to take away anything from it or from all that belongs to it, whether the person be great or small, so that the same venerable holy Beneventan Church, established in accordance with what we have decreed and adorned with apostolic constitutions and privileges, may remain secure and fully endowed.

But if anyone—which we do not desire—should presume with wicked boldness to oppose or in any way transgress what we have established for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid Beneventan Church, whether he be a Greek or any other person who, personally or through another, wishes to exercise domination or primacy in the aforesaid churches without the consent and command of the Beneventan bishop, then all such persons, together with those who may have presumed to receive them, shall remain bound by the same apostolic anathema pronounced and recorded by us as inviolable. They shall not presume to enter any church or perform any ecclesiastical office.

But those who, out of pious concern, observe and in every respect guard this apostolic decree of ours, looking toward the worship of God, shall receive manifold the grace of blessing from our most merciful God and merit becoming participants in eternal life.

Written by the hand of Stephen, scrivener of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of October, indiction 2. Farewell.

Given on the third day before the Ides of November, by the hand of Nicholas, first secretary of the Holy Apostolic See, in the second year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord Marinus, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the most sacred see of blessed Peter the apostle, in the month and indiction written above, 2.

IV. PRIVILEGE OF POPE MARINUS II FOR THE MONASTERY OF MONTE CASSINO. (Year 944.)

[Gattula, *Historia Cassinensis*, p. 94.]

[Col. 0867C]

Marinus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Baldwin, venerable abbot of the monastery of Christ’s confessor Benedict, situated on the mountain called the Castle of Cassino, and to your holy congregation and to your successors, forever.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those endowed with pious religion through benevolent compassion and to fulfill the hearts of those who ask with the supports of eager devotion. For from this, above all, we undoubtedly deserve the reward of gain from the Creator of all, God, whenever venerable places, suitably organized, have unquestionably been brought into a better condition.

Therefore, because you requested that we should confirm and grant to you the monastery of Christ’s confessor, blessed Benedict, situated on the mountain of the Castle of Cassino, where his most sacred body is believed to have been buried, together with all its possessions and dependencies or appurtenances, whether in monasteries of men or of handmaids of God, as well as cells and estates, wherever or however they are recognized to belong to the rights of that monastery—in their entirety; especially the monastery of the Lord Saviour situated at the foot of that mountain, and the monastery of Saint Mary, holy Mother and Virgin of God, called Plumbarola; likewise the monastery of Saint Mary at Cingla, which has now been built within the city of Capua; also the monastery of Saint Sophia, which has been built within the city of Benevento; and the monastery of Saint Mary situated in Beneventan territory at the place called Canneto, beside the river Trigno; as well as the monastery of Saint Mary within the city of Cosenza, belonging to God’s servants, with all, as we have said, its possessions and dependencies in various places, both in Beneventan territory and in Apulia and Calabria, and also in the territory of the March, and in the territory of the Marsi, or wherever, far and wide, in different places, together with the male and female tenants, or male and female servants of either sex, belonging to the rights of that monastery—we, favoring your pious desires, commit by this authority of ours what is requested to effect.

We establish that it shall be adorned with the insignia of a privilege of the Apostolic See, so that, constituted under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, which by God’s authority we serve, it shall not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other church. Therefore we prohibit any priest of any church from exercising any jurisdiction or authority in the aforesaid monasteries apart from the Apostolic See. Unless invited by the abbot of the monastery, no one shall presume in any way to celebrate the solemnity of Masses there.

From this present second indiction we irrevocably establish that it shall be held and governed and administered forever in the fear of God. We further decree, under apostolic censure and the threat of divine judgment, and by powerful and most severe prohibitions of anathema, that no one else, whatever dignity or power he may possess, nor any person, great or small, shall ever presume to interfere in that monastery or in its affairs, or in any way offer or alienate its possessions, estates, or churches subject to it, or anything else that appears to belong to it. Nor shall anyone inflict there any injury or loss, whether in time of peace or of barbarian disturbance. We firmly decree that it shall remain under the jurisdiction of our holy Church.

We proclaim and, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, before God, his terrible future judgment, and this apostolic privilege and decree of ours, enact that the places exchanged or granted to us by any abbot in the aforesaid monastery of Saint Benedict, as well as the other possessions of places bestowed and offered to that holy place by kings, dukes, gastalds, and other Christians, or which may later be granted to it, shall remain firm and secure, belong to the rights of the aforesaid monastery, and continue so forever.

No one shall have permission, as has been said, to take away anything from it or from all that belongs to the same monastery, whether the person be great or small. Rather, in accordance with the fact that the venerable place has been subjected to apostolic decrees and privileges, it shall remain securely endowed. The monks of that congregation shall also have permission always to elect an abbot from their own community.

You shall also have permission, for the preparation of chrism, the offering, and the ordination of priests, deacons, and subdeacons, and for the consecration of altars, to invite whatever bishop you choose. We grant that the angelic hymn may be sung at the solemnities of Mass on Sundays and feast days at all times. You shall also have permission to ring the bell whenever you wish, both at the daytime and nighttime hours, both in the aforesaid monastery and in its cells. No bishop shall prevent the people of God from entering either the monastery or its cells to hear the word of God.

Furthermore, we decree that no bishop shall presume in the aforesaid monastery or in its subject churches to excommunicate priests, summon them to a synod, or [text syntactically incomplete] the abbot and monks who may at that time be there. You shall also have permission to receive, for residence or for receiving the monastic habit together with their possessions, any cleric, priest, deacon, or subdeacon from whatever bishopric, without the prohibition of any bishop.

You and the monks subject to you shall have permission to judge both the monastery of men and the convent of women without secular authority or the prohibition of any bishop.

But if anyone—which we do not desire—should presume with wicked boldness to oppose or in any way transgress what we have established for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid monastery, let him know that, unless he repents, he is bound by the bond of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, and assigned to be burned with the devil, his most dreadful pomp, and Judas, the betrayer of Jesus Christ our Lord, in the punishment of eternal fire.

But whoever, with pious intent, observes and in every respect keeps this apostolic decree of ours and looks to the worship of God shall, through the intercession of blessed Benedict, receive manifold the grace of blessing from our most merciful God and merit becoming a participant in eternal life.

Written by the hand of Leo, notary, regional notary, and scrivener of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of January, in the second indiction written above. Farewell.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, by the hand of Benedict, bishop of the Church of Santa Rufina and librarian of the Holy Apostolic See, in the second year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord Martinus, supreme pontiff and universal second pope, in the most sacred see of blessed Peter the apostle, in the second month of January, second indiction.

V. BULL OF POPE MARINUS II FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT VINCENT OF VULTURNUM. (Year 944.)

[Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores* I, I, 432.]

Marinus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Leo, venerable abbot of the monastery of Christ’s martyr Vincent, situated in the region of Samnium, in Beneventan territory, above the source of the river Vulturnus, and, through you, to all your successors who shall regularly be promoted in that venerable monastery, forever.

Because in pious solicitude it is fitting for us always to keep watch over all the Churches of God, and with the whole intention of our mind to safeguard the integrity of venerable places, we therefore desire to confer assistance for their benefit, and especially for the repose of monks, so that we may obtain the reward of divine mercy in the heavenly palaces.

Therefore, since you have asked us to secure by the authority of our privilege the monastery of the blessed martyr Vincent, together with everything belonging to it—monasteries, cells, chapels, lands, and castles, male and female servants, with all their revenues—under the jurisdiction of the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, for that reason we grant it to you and to your legitimate successors [Col. 0870B], the abbots, to retain perpetually, so that it may not be subjected to the authority of any other Church, but may remain with all the monasteries and cells subject to it, namely:
