the monastery of the blessed apostle Peter situated beside the river Sabbatus in the territory already mentioned, Beneventan territory; the monastery of holy Mary, Mother of God, in the place called Sano; the monastery of the Lord Savior, situated at Alife; the monastery of holy Mary in the place called Apinianicus, in the territory of Marsica; the monastery of holy Mary at the Two Basilicas; the monastery of holy Mary at Castanieto; the monastery of holy Mary at Palere, in the territory of Domo; the monastery of holy Mary at Planisi; the monastery of Saint Peter at Vipera, with the estate of Leo itself; the monastery of Saint Peter at Tontole; the monastery of Saint Peter [Col. 0870C] at Trite; the monastery of holy Mary at Musano; the monastery of holy Mary at Arole; the monastery of Saint George at Salerno; the monastery of Saint Vincent at Capua; the monastery of Saint Martin and of the Holy Cross on Mount Marsico; the monastery of Saint Columba at Sora; the monastery of Saint Maurus and Saint Valentine at Atina; and the monastery of Saint Donatus with the renowned valley of Sora.

We receive all these places, together with everything lawfully belonging to them, under the protection of our apostolic see, in such a way that you may have full authority to summon whatever bishop you wish to the aforesaid venerable monastery for any Christian ministry required. Likewise, you may have authority for the consecration of churches, for ordinations of priests and deacons as circumstances require, and for completing every ecclesiastical order there [Col. 0870D].

For we declare that no bishop may summon thence a priest or deacon to his synod unless it is the person’s own wish, nor may he in any way judge or excommunicate the abbot or the monks.

We wish, and by apostolic authority enjoin upon you and your aforesaid abbots, that priests or clerics from any Church, if they come to live in the brotherhood or withdraw to receive the monastic habit, be received immediately. As for chrism, you may always obtain it from whatever bishop you wish, in accordance with what we have stated, under our apostolic authority.

We also prohibit every priest of any Church from exercising any authority in the aforesaid [Col. 0871A] venerable monastery, apart from the apostolic see, so that unless he has been invited by the abbot of the monastery, he may not presume to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass there.

Moreover, establishing this by apostolic censure and under the threat of divine judgment, and prohibiting it by firm and most severe anathemas, we forbid anyone, whatever power or dignity he may possess, ever to presume to interfere either in this venerable monastery or in its affairs, or to take away or alienate anything from its possessions, lands, or subject churches, or anything else that appears to belong to it. Nor may anyone in any way inflict there any malicious injury or loss, whether in time of peace or in barbarian times, while we decree that the aforesaid monastery shall perpetually [Col. 0871B], as stated, remain firmly established under the jurisdiction of the holy Roman Church.

Publishing this decree, and by this authority of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, before God and his terrible tribunal, through the constitution of this privilege of ours we sanction and decree that the places exchanged by any bishop or abbot, as well as the possessions of various places that have been granted, bestowed, or offered to this holy and venerable monastery by kings, dukes, princes, castaldei, and other Christians, or that may hereafter be granted or offered, shall remain perpetually the property of that monastery.

Nor shall anyone, as stated above, have permission to take away from any person, great or small, anything belonging to it or to all the dependencies of that monastery [Col. 0871C], so that it may remain undisturbed in accordance with what is right, just as the same venerable monastery stands subject to apostolic constitutions and privileges.

The same monks shall always be permitted to elect an abbot from their own congregation. The abbot himself shall be permitted to judge his monks, and not only the men’s monastery but also the women’s monastery subject to him.

If anyone, however—which we do not wish—should presume with wicked audacity to oppose or in any way transgress these provisions established by us for the praise of our God and the stability of the aforesaid venerable monastery, let him be bound by the bond of anathema and be destined to burn in eternal fire with the devil, his angels, and Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ.

But whoever, with pious regard, proves in all things an observer, guarding the constitution of this privilege of ours directed toward the worship of God, may receive manifoldly the grace of blessing from our most merciful Lord God and deserve to become a participant in eternal life [Col. 0871D].

Farewell.

Written by the hand of Adrian, scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of March, in the second indiction. Given by the hand of Stephen, chief of the defenders of the supreme apostolic see, in the second year of the pontificate of our lord Marinus, supreme pontiff, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter.

## VI. Bull of Pope Marinus II for the Church of Sabina. (Year 944.)

[Sperandio, *Sabina sacra*, p. 331.]

[Col. 0872A]

Marinus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved brother John, bishop of Sabina, and to his successors forever.

It is fitting for those endowed with pious religion under apostolic governance to come to the aid of petitioners with benevolent compassion and to grant suitable assistance to their desires. Therefore, because you asked us to grant and delimit for you the episcopate of Sabina, which is dedicated to holy Mary, Mother of God, and is situated at Foronovo, together with all that justly and lawfully belongs to it [Col. 0872B], we, moved by your prayers, confirm and strengthen the episcopate for you by this document of our apostolic command.

Its boundary on one side is the river Tiber, running as far as the Utriculan territory, where there is a stream called Votivus; from there it rises to the boundary of Narnia at a place called Prata, and from that boundary proceeds to the frontier and reaches Scapua, running along the boundary of Reate; from that boundary it comes to the mountain called Tancia; from those boundaries it comes to the Sabellian wall, and, reaching the summit of Black Mountain, proceeds to the Long Estate, to Staffilum itself; from that boundary it goes to the mountain district of Leones, then proceeds to the stream that runs beside holy Victoria of Trebula.

From there it ascends the mountain [Col. 0872C] called Carbo and, by way of Aqua Mensa, reaches the river Torritius; along that boundary it runs down to Carzoli and comes to the Sacred Field.

Thus, as we have said, these boundaries begin at the river Tiber, proceeding beside the gate of Saint Valentine, and come to the Pincian Gate; from there they proceed to the Salarian Gate, where there is the church of Saint Millitis at Rome, which belongs by right to the aforesaid episcopate of Sabina. From there they come to the Silice, which is beside Saint Lawrence; from that boundary they come to the Seven Brothers; and through those boundaries they reach the Silice beside Saint Anatolia, which lies beneath the mountain called Rasiano. There is the church of Peter, which belongs by right to that bishop. From there they reach the Silice that runs beside Saint Vincent, proceeding to Saint [Col. 0872D] Stephen at the end of the stream; then, through those boundaries, they ascend to the summit of Mount January; from there they come to the mountain called Possode; and proceeding through the lands of the mountains, they finally come to the Sacred Field.

Together with all the inhabitants and churches, and everything that appears to lie under and belong to the same bishop, whether vessels, castles, villages, and estates, or the sacred vessels of that same church—golden or silver, or made of any kind of clay—or books, vestments, or any movable or immovable goods known to belong to the same bishop, let everything remain intact. Just as it was granted to your predecessors, the bishops, and to our former pontiffs [the reading is uncertain], so we grant it [Col. 0873A] to you and to your successors to retain forever, to restore, and to administer, including both the monasteries and the other churches situated within these boundaries, together with everything listed and encompassed above.

Likewise, we decree that priests, deacons, and all clerics remaining in the minor orders, together with deaconesses and handmaids of God, shall be subject to you and your successors, as the holy Fathers established. They shall likewise remain perpetually under the law and censure of you and your successors and shall be exempt from all other powers, so that no one without your authority may constrain them or bring them before the palace for any complaint, nor may anyone demand a court from them. Since they belong to the portion of God, it is therefore not proper for them to serve in any secular matter whatsoever [Col. 0873B]; rather, they shall remain perpetually under your power and that of your successors, together with the tithes and first fruits, and whatever is bequeathed for the dead.

All these things shall remain perpetually under your right and that of your successors, so that no duke, count, viscount, or any other person, great or small, of whatever dignity or order, may presume in any way to injure, diminish, or revoke this apostolic dignity and authority of ours or this confirmation of your episcopate. If anyone does so, let him be struck by our anathema [Note: [Col. 0873D] This passage seems to us to require restoration as follows: “and let it remain … and … to be condemned, and let him receive his lot … with Christ; but whoever has been the guardian and observer [Col. 0874D] of this privilege of ours, [shall receive] blessing and grace,” etc. EDIT.], be swallowed up in the chaos of perpetual damnation, be alienated from the kingdom of God, and be condemned with the impious to eternal fire or punishment, and may he receive the lot of Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ; from our most merciful Lord [Col. 0873C] God may he deserve to obtain this fate.

Written by the hand of Leo, notary, regionarius, and scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, in the second indiction. Farewell. Given by the hand of Gregory, by God’s providence second chief notary (*secundicerius*) of the holy apostolic see, in the year of the pontificate of Marinus, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter, in the month, etc.

## VII. Letter of Pope Marinus II to Sico, bishop of Capua. (Years 942–946.)

[Tosti, *Storia di Montecasino*, I, 215.]

Marinus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Sico, bishop of the Church of Capua.

Although you were consecrated by this most sacred see of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, contrary to the provisions of the canons and the decrees of the ancient Fathers concerning the episcopal order, you ought not therefore to have set yourself against so great an authority, nor was it fitting for you to do the things, of such a kind and number, that are reported about you by the most trustworthy men who fear God.

For, as Pope Celestine confirms in his decrees, no priest is permitted to be ignorant of the canons; how much more was it fitting for you to study them, since, established at the episcopal summit, you ought first to have instructed yourself and then others.

But because, as we have learned by report, you persisted in being trained with a lay mind and manner of life in the imperial court for service [Col. 0874A], you meditate more on secular matters than on episcopal laws, and desire a gathering of laymen more than an assembly of clerics.

You have forgotten—or rather, do not know—the eighth canon of the Council of Chalcedon, which says that a bishop must in no way go to the imperial court, and the other matters in its ninth canon, that the presumption of bishops should in no way strive to go to the court, and the rest.

These and many other things you practice more against yourself than against the canons. Moreover, ignorant of literary studies, you do not spend your days with disciplined and highly learned men who could instruct you, but with the basest and most undisciplined laymen and ignorant clerics, daily meditating on wandering and secular matters.

Thus, fearing neither God nor man, you attempt to do many things against holy Scripture [Col. 0874B].

But what is astonishing is that, although even the institution of your benefactor—who bought you from the Agarene people—was binding upon you, you, driven by obstinacy and ignorance and fearing neither God nor the holy canons, dared to break it. Nor did you fear transgressing what your predecessor, the venerable bishop, who was canonically ordained, established, bound under the bond of anathema, and confirmed by canonical authority.

You treated this as nothing, so that, as the Scripture of a certain teacher testifies, you handed over the church of the monastery of Saint Angelus of Monte to your ignorant and undisciplined deacon, although it had already for many years been established under the regular discipline of monks, so that dances and amusements might take place there as once they did.

Certainly, if you held the fear of God in your heart, you ought not to have allowed this to be done but should have opposed it [Col. 0874C], even if—which we do not believe—our son, your prince, who persists in such matters like an innocent lamb, had wished to do it; and even if, God forbid, he agreed to such things, we believe that he had been seduced by your machinations.

Therefore God, who knows all things beforehand and distinguishes everything by his balance, in his just judgment mercifully stirred him against you, so that he might send you into exile—you who first plotted to kill the body and now plot to kill the soul.

Thus, since in these and other matters you show yourself ignorant, I shall remain silent for the time being about the fact that, by asking questions, you ought to have learned what the Council of Chalcedon declares about monasteries in its twenty-fourth canon; for through negligence you neither inquire nor follow the canonical order.

But because you judged that the church of Saint Angelus of Monte had been removed from the community of monks, contrary to holy institution, out of love for your deacon, we decree that this man be excluded from your fellowship, except when he renders you a lawful service in the customary manner.

We wish the church of Saint Angelus of Monte to return to the status of a monastery, but this must be strengthened by our commands [Col. 0874D].

Therefore, by the authority of almighty God, of the blessed princes of the apostles Peter and Paul, of all the saints, and of the seven universal councils, we send this letter excommunicating you, so that you may take the greatest care to avoid and amend all the matters mentioned above. You must restore, from this present hour, to the aforesaid monastery the church of Saint Angelus of Monte [Col. 0875A], which your venerable predecessor, with the counsel of your princely benefactor, gave to this monastery, confirmed by canonical authority, and moreover bound with the bond of anathema.

Then, having summoned all the orders of the Church, confirm it in such a way that it may remain a monastery forever and always be under the custody and lordship of Saint Benedict of your city, without you or your successors inflicting any disturbance there, except to the extent established by your predecessor.

But if you are disobedient to this exhortation and command of ours, then, by the authority of almighty God, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, of all the saints together, and of the venerable seven universal councils, and by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, may you be alienated from every priestly honor and title and stripped of every clerical office [Col. 0875B]. If afterward you dare, in your former manner, to touch anything belonging to the sacred ministry, may you in no way be permitted to have hope of communion or satisfaction; but, anathematized forever, may you receive the body and blood of the Lord only when in immediate danger of death.

## DOUBTFUL DOCUMENTS

### I. Privilege of Pope Marinus II for the Church of Hamburg. (Year 946.)

[Lappenberg, *Hamburgische Urkund*.]

[Col. 0875C]

Marinus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most holy Adaldag, archbishop of the holy Church of Hamburg and our brother: paternal love and perpetual blessing in Christ.

Since the desire of a pious will and the intention of praiseworthy devotion must always be assisted by apostolic efforts, diligent care must be applied so that those things which are lawfully done and accord with the form of equity may not be disturbed by any opposition, but, by God’s authority, may remain by irrefragable right.

For this reason, when apostolic sanctions are promulgated, justice demands that each person’s possessions, insofar as reason supports them, be confirmed for him to hold. And since you asked us to make a privilege for your Church and strengthen it with apostolic protection [Col. 0875D], we grant that it remain in its former state.

By apostolic right we confirm to you, to your holy Church of Hamburg, and to your successors that dignity and those proper boundaries, together with all estates and parishes and all movable and immovable goods, with slaves of both sexes, which Gregory, of blessed memory, our predecessor, granted to Ansgar, your predecessor whom he ordained archbishop in your Church, with the established legal title and all the boundaries which Louis, the emperor of blessed memory, and Louis his son, wished your Church to possess and defined by imperial authority.

We decree that you have the power to ordain bishops within your parish [Col. 0876A] and diocese, provided, however, that they remain under your authority and that of your Church, without prejudice to its dignity.

If anyone attempts to act against this privilege of our authority, or in any way strives to break it in part or in whole, let him be excommunicated from the body and life-giving blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and separated from access to and fellowship with the holy Church of God.

But whoever observes this admonition and command of ours shall have the blessing of almighty God, of the blessed apostles, and of us, who exercise their vicariate.

Written by the hand of Benedict, chancellor of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, in the sixth indiction.

### II. Bull of Pope Marinus II confirming all the rights and possessions of the Church of Adria. (Year 946.)

[Muratori, *Antiquitates Italicae*, vol. I, col. 947.]

[Col. 0876B]

Martinus, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

It is fitting under apostolic governance to come to those who ask with benevolent compassion and to grant assent to the sacred devotion of petitioners. For by this, above all, the greatest profit is first placed before God the Creator, since venerable places are thereby undoubtedly advanced to a better condition.

Therefore, because you humbly and justly and reasonably asked our apostolate to grant and confirm, by the authority of this present privilege of ours, to the holy Church of Adria of the blessed apostle Peter the Lord, all the possessions and properties of that Church of Adria—namely, the island called Adriana, together with its entire woodland and its harbors, which are the harbor of Laureto and the harbor of Gaurus—all intact as far as the sea, and from the harbor of Laureto to the Fea Channel, and as far as the Falce Channel, together with all its hunting, fishing, and bird-catching rights [Col. 0876C].

Likewise, the estate of Quinto, and the woods of Lapario and Lathualo, and the Trionis Channel, as well as the Aira Channel and the Palo Channel, or Conchagatula, as far as the fishery of Cythiu, and the Corrigio Susorum.

Also the whole island between the Athesis and the Tartarus, with its woodland and manegium, together with the estate of Gavello in its entirety, and the village of Martiana in its entirety, as well as the estate of Roda with its woodland and the valley belonging to it [Col. 0876D], as far as the valleys of Fraxinita, Lavigie, and Valentina.

Likewise Argele Major and Grignano, or the estate of Pedrulio, as well as the estate of Pontecli as far as Vibo Carario, and the estate of Lamando, and the aforesaid estate of Pedrulio, continuing as far as Stillo de Baldo.

Moreover, we confirm and strengthen in the aforesaid holy Church of Adria the parish church of holy Mary called Corna Cervina, extending from the Channel of Finale as far as Gaurus; and the parish church of holy Mary at Stornio, which the river Po destroyed, extending from the Jovian breach as far as the Opilea ditch and the Corrulo ditch, in its entirety.

Also the parish church of Saint George at Tamara, together with the estate of Copario and the estate of Ambioso, extending as far as the valley of Fraxineta, in its entirety.

Likewise, let the aforesaid Church of Adria have, hold, and possess in its entirety the parish church of Saint Martin at Roviola and the parish church of Saint Donatus at Pedrulio [Col. 0877A].

Therefore, by the authority of this privilege of ours, we confirm in the aforesaid Church of Adria the estates of Cappaciana and Lendenaria, together with their woodland as far as the river Athesis, as well as Sulicini, Tribano, Mardinagus, or Anguillaria, and Caput Argele.

Wherefore, by our apostolic command, or by the command of our most beloved son, the most serene king Hugh, we order that no person whatsoever, of whatever condition, rank, dignity, or religious status, have permission to enter upon the properties and possessions of the aforesaid Church without the consent of the bishop or of the person presiding over that Church. No one may diminish them, exercise dominion over them, or presume to impose anything by way of lodging, commendation, or any violence [Col. 0877B].

Rather, as we have said, they must remain altogether safe and unharmed forever, together with all the clerics, laymen, servants, and residents of that Church, and with all their movable and immovable goods and living creatures, so that everything may remain intact, live quietly and peacefully, and be free from the dispute of all men.

For, which we do not believe, if anyone is found to have violated the authority of this privilege of ours, let him know that he will incur the anger of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, of our son King Hugh, and of us.

Let the aforesaid Church, with its dependencies as listed above, remain under the protection of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of us and our successors [Col. 0877C].

Moreover, unless he turns back from evil, let him know that he must pay one thousand gold mancuses, half to our palace and half to the aforesaid Church.

But whoever proves in all things a guardian and observer with pious regard may deserve to possess, together with all the saints, the grace of blessing and eternal life without end, for ever and ever. Amen.

Written by the hand of Gregory, scriniarius of the Roman Church.

Given at the Lateran patriarchium, on the third day before the Ides of June. Farewell.

I, Benignus, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed with my own hand.

I, Grisogonus, bishop of Porto, have subscribed with my own hand [Col. 0877D].

In the second year of his see and the fourth of Lord Hugh, in the twelfth indiction.

And I, Dominic, by the mercy of Christ notary of the holy Church of Adria, having seen this authentic document of the privilege, written by the hand of Lord Gregory, scriniarius of the Roman Church, copied it exactly as it is contained here, adding or subtracting nothing, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 951, on the fourteenth day as the month of April ended, in the fourteenth indiction, in the time of Pope Eugenius and King Conrad.

[Col. 0878A] I, Romeus, notary of Lord King Henry, saw and read the original of this copy, just as it is contained here.

[Note: [Col. 0877D] There is a conflict between the years of Pope Marinus and those of King Hugh. In the year 944 the indiction was also running as the second, not the twelfth. Observe also the words “by the command of our most beloved son Hugh, the most serene king,” leaving aside other matters. Moreover, if this bull were to be considered genuine, we would have one thousand mancuses to pay, half to the sacred Lateran palace.]

### III. Privilege of Pope Marinus II for the Nonantulan monastery of Saint Sylvester. (Years 942–946.)

[Marini, *Papiri diplomatichi*, 11.]

Marinus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Theodoric, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Sylvester [lacuna] in the territory of Modena, and to all those subject to it, forever [lacuna].

Whatever is known to pertain to the praise of God our Redeemer and Lord Savior Jesus Christ, and whatever concerns the stability of venerable places, it is fitting for us to procure with great diligence, under apostolic and reasonable judgment, so that from this the praises of songs may be paid more effectively and continually to our propitiator, the Lord God, and that we, who, although unworthy, nevertheless by the prevenient grace of God bear the pastoral care of government, may receive abundant rewards of recompense in the heavenly palaces [Col. 0878B].

Therefore, since it is evident that your religious devotion has brought to us the command of our predecessor, Lord Adrian, and of John, pontiffs of revered memory, concerning the aforesaid monastery and all the places and possessions belonging to it, and since you asked us to confirm them by the document of our apostolic privilege, we, moved by your prayers, confirm from this first indiction and forever the aforesaid monastery [Col. 0878C] under the jurisdiction and power of your successors, the abbots. By irrefragable right we decree that it shall remain, namely, the monastery of Saint Sylvester, which [lacuna] from Nonantula in the territory of Modena.

Therefore, by the authority of the blessed apostle Peter, to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven were given by our Lord God, and to whom power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth was granted, we publish and decree, and by a firm judgment of stability establish, that the same venerable monastery, together with all places, manses, estates, houses, homesteads, dwellings, and households, hereditary servants, and likewise goods and possessions, as well as watermills, olive groves, or whatever in any [lacuna] appears or has been lawfully granted or bestowed by authority, or has justly come to it in any manner [Col. 0878D], may hold and possess them without any dispute for perpetual times.

Let no king [lacuna], bishop [lacuna], or agent, person of small or great standing, ever have permission in the aforesaid venerable monastery, or in those things that appear to belong to the same venerable monastery, to interfere in any way, make an invasion, approach [lacuna], or celebrate the solemn rites of Mass, unless he has been invited by the abbot. Thus, what we establish for the praise and benefit of the aforesaid holy monastery may remain with firm stability [Col. 0879A].

We absolutely prohibit the bishop in whose parish the aforesaid monastery appears to be situated from claiming anything for himself against the tenor of this decree granted by pious petition, and likewise from claiming baptismal churches for himself in any way.

And I, Henry, scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, together with Bartholomew, cleric of Saint Peter at the Chains, having seen and read through the authentic privileges of the aforesaid exemplars—namely, those of Lords Adrian, [Col. 0880A] John, and Pope Marinus—just as they were contained in them, so they are contained in the copies written above. I faithfully copied them and made my mark. Therefore, let no one at all be permitted to violate this document of our transcription or rashly oppose it. But if anyone should do so, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of June, in the sixteenth year of our pontificate.

## In the Year of the Lord 850. Cosmas the Iapygian of Matera.

[Col. 0879]

## Historical Notice on Cosmas the Iapygian

(From Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*)

Cosmas the Iapygian, of Matera, is said to have composed around the year 950 a certain poem in honor of Bishop Theopompus, Theonas, and Synesius, whose martyrdom, suffered during the persecution of Diocletian, is celebrated on 21 May. It begins:

> Christ bestowed pious gifts upon the ranks of brothers;

After a preface addressed to Gregory Ligus, a monk of Nonantula:

> Cosmas gave these things kindly to the monk Gregory.

A hymn follows, beginning:

> The lofty triumph of the martyrs.

Ughellus published it from a Nonantulan codex in volume II of *Italia Sacra*, in the section on the bishops of Modena, pp. 111–112.

[Col. 0879]

## Poem of Cosmas the Iapygian in Honor of Saints Theopompus and His Companions

(From Ughellus, *Italia sacra* II, 111.)

### Ughellus’s Notice

We read the deeds of Saints Theopompus and his companions in a very ancient parchment codex of the abbey of Nonantula, altogether different from those which Peter de Natalibus listed in book V, chapter 35, of his catalogue. Their beginning, after the preface and the interpretation of their names, is as follows:

> Passion of the holy Theopompus, bishop, and of Theonas, who is also Synesius.

At the end:

> The most blessed martyrs Theopompus the bishop and Theonas, who is also Synesius, were martyred under Diocletian, the most impious emperor, in the first year of his persecution, at the city of Nicomedia, on the day before the Nones of January; but our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for infinite ages of ages, was reigning. Amen.

The city of which Theopompus was bishop is not stated in the acts; it is only said that he suffered at Nicomedia during the persecution of Diocletian, together with Synesius. Their feast is celebrated at Nonantula on 4 January, the day on which they suffered, whereas the Roman Martyrology and Baronius in his notes place it on 21 May. There Baronius very elegantly demonstrates that Theopompus could not have been bishop of Nicomedia during the persecution of Diocletian, since the chronology seems scarcely to agree.

For Anthimus, bishop of Nicomedia, who during the persecution of Diocletian received the glory of martyrdom by beheading for confessing Christ, succeeded Saint Cyril as bishop of that city, as is testified by the acts of the holy martyrs Indes and Domna, which Metaphrastes recites on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, from which they are found in the *Lippomanus*, book 6, and in Surius, volume VI.

Moreover, in honor of the saints Synesius and Theopompus, a certain Cosmas of Matera, more than seven hundred years ago, sang and dedicated these verses to Gregory, a monk of Nonantula. They are indeed inept and without wit, but they breathe the air of Christian antiquity. We excerpted them from the same most ancient Nonantulan codex while we were serving there as abbot.

[Col. 0881A]

## Cosmas of Matera to Gregory Ligus

> Cosmas gave these things kindly to the monk Gregory,  
> Verses for the Levite who cleanses through his office.  
>   
> For the merit of the great and gracious bishop Theopompus,  
> And for Synesius, or Theon the aged.  
>   
> He often entreated the lofty assembly  
> That we should celebrate in writing the pious cause.  
>   
> At once we applied ourselves to the task: from a Greek source,  
> Let the Latin murmur forth the sacred deeds more swiftly and piously.  
>   
> May the Lord Christ grant us his gifts;  
> May he add aid to the prayers of the rejoicing Ligyan assembly.  
>   
> May love save the servant, great in Christ and in faith;  
> May the proper time in the world suffice for what is upright.  
>   
> Amen.

> The Iapygian Cosmas gave a poem concerning the deeds of the sacred martyrs  
> To Gregory’s prayers, with a pious mind.  
>   
> Prosperously.

> Christ bestowed pious gifts upon the ranks of brothers.  
> God bestowed the sacred rites upon the ranks.  
>   
> To take up things full of roses, but sacred relics full of violets;  
> To take up things full of roses, with martyrial wreaths.  
>   
> They are the ranks of the Lord, for they are red with sweet blood.  
> The ranks of the Lord are sacred with the fragrance of heaven.  
>   
> The martyr’s honor shines, and Theopompus shines in his limbs.  
> Antula bears the work: the martyr’s honor.  
>   
> Synesius restores riches by magical deeds, freed from dark bonds.  
> Your power, Synesius, cleansed, restores riches by magical deeds.  
>   
> Echo the hymn-like melodies, O stony Lygians;  
> Give them back through the fields: the hymn-like melodies.  
>   
> Behold, shining Nicomedia brought you splendid supports.  
> Behold, it brought its gifts, shining.  
>   
> Sing of those crowned with athletic garments and marks.  
> May salvation be for the dwellings, in athletic garments.  
>   
> The Italian assembly, always acting, appeases its stomach;  
> Let it grant annual jubilees, always acting.  
>   
> Now, companions, let us resound the songs of Theopompus from here.  
> Let the styluses sound forth what is established: now, companions, the songs.  
>   
> The order of the mound resounds, and now great Synesius goes before.  
> Your renowned holy one: the order of the mound resounds.  
>   
> Impiety raises the tenth plague in the eastern lands;  
> It raises schemes against the Christians.  
>   
> Diocletian, greedy for wealth, assails the anointed one.  
> The king desires to violate the race.  
>   
> For the foolish wicked man had made many idols for himself,  
> Giving the pagan things more widely.  
>   
> Apollo, worshiped with harmful rites, was of no avail.  
> Dread Diana was of no avail.  
>   
> The excellent one, blazing, approaches—and Theopompus presses forward.  
> He destroys the dark things while bringing consolation: the excellent one, blazing.  
>   
> These wretched, emaciated things: the empty idols stand, not gracious.  
> Wholly more harmful: these wretched, emaciated things.  
>   
> The author and almighty God is the one who alone fashions the world,  
> Holding all things by his hand: the author and almighty one.  
>   
> Three in unceasing honor—of the Son and likewise of the gracious Spirit—  
> Lives in the palace of heaven: three in unceasing honor.  
>   
> He breathes and shines upon his own, and also sends them upon the earth;  
> He renews all offspring: he breathes and shines.  
>   
> Cast away empty things, threatening one; now worship, devoted and bold, what is holy,  
> And be fruitful in your works: cast away empty things, threatening one.  
>   
> May the Lord, God Christ, rejoice in you, illustrious Diocletian;  
> O my Diocletian, may the Lord rejoice.  
>   
> The savage king was astonished and asked who he might be.  
> Speaking these things, he was afraid: the savage king was astonished.  
>   
> Theopompus, an aged man worthy of love, the Bithynian bishop, gives help to the flocks.  
> He gives help to the flocks.  
>   
> The king, in a furious manner, proclaims that this man is rather a magician,  
> And tears him harmfully apart, the king in his fury.

He pledged every scourge for pious limbs doomed to die, giving them to be laid upon their shoulders—every scourge for the pious.

[Col. 0882B] The magician stirs up wars while displaying dreadful and harsh tortures;  
overcome, he flies to the stars: the magician stirs up wars.

For he took up Theonas, the beginnings through the waters;  
Theonas indeed took up the consummation of martyrdom.

Behold, blessed one, holy Synesius gave you a noble bishop;  
read the name of the heavenly realm: behold, blessed one, for you.

The fallen sphere weighs the slain limbs of the bull,  
and entirely by your water: the fallen sphere weighs them.

The impious woman fed the holy man bitterness and gave him the taste of a sweet morsel;  
the impious creatress [or: maker] fed the man bitterness.

The madman troubles the eye, restored by the sacred Caesar,  
looking upon its origin [reading uncertain]: the madman troubles the eye.

Harsh punishments: steadfast Theopompus proceeds to the deeds;  
he proclaims them rejoicing, slight though they are: harsh punishments.

Then the holy man, slain by the sword, safely bears  
pleasant things to the place above: then the holy man by the sword.

He lives exceedingly in the citadel, and Synesius among the fields with Theonas;  
[reading uncertain: *catapalastus*] enough for the horses: he lives exceedingly in the citadel.

While the people of Nicomedia raise up and adorn the bodies of the dead,  
behold, Nonanta shines: while they raise up the bodies of the dead.

O people of Liguria, behold, they are your patrons;  
now, having been given, venerate them: O people of Liguria.

Let the heavens resound with sacred songs to God in a threefold order;  
let every human being sound forth sacred songs to God.

May the noble Three-in-One, enduring, wash away our stains;  
may the abiding Trinity itself atone for our wild deeds.

Granting kingdoms to your servants, O God, heed their prayers;  
repay the good in turn: grant kingdoms to your servants.

Amen.

## Hymn

[Col. 0882D]

Let us sing the lofty annual triumph  
of the martyrs,  
bringing to Christ  
a great song with devoted mind.

Let us now sing the battles of Theopompus,  
and the deeds of Synesius,  
of radiant virtue,  
in the service of the exalted King.

For these men, leaving behind  
the joys and pleasures  
of the present age,  
bear prepared rewards.

For the profane king drives them  
to sacrifice to filthy idols;  
nor does he bend them at the altars,  
but constrains them with dreadful punishments.

But after they had bravely endured all things,  
after the scourges, steadfastly,  
through the gift of Christ they conquered  
and hold shining crowns.

[Col. 0884A]

Therefore, suppliant brothers,  
let us ask that they make us fit  
for heavenly hymns  
and grant us a share in the kingdom.

To the Trinity be glory;  
to the Father, as to the Son,  
be praise, honor, and the greatest victory,  
with the Spirit, through the ages.

Amen.

## In the Year of the Lord 954. John the Italian, Cluniacensian Monk

[Col. 0883]

## Historical Notice Concerning John the Italian

(Oudin, *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, p. 434.)

John the Italian, a monk of Cluny, a Roman by birthplace, an Italian by nation, and a canon by profession, was brought from Rome as far as Pavia by Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, in the year 939, and there was made a monk, as is clear from John the Italian’s own words in Book I of the *Life of Saint Odo*, sections 2 and 4. After Odo had taken him with him for some time on his journey, he later appointed him prior, as is repeatedly read in Book II, sections 4, 7, and 10. Whether this occurred at Cluny, at Saint Paul’s in Rome, or elsewhere is uncertain; the doubt may arise from comparing sections 10 and 21. John himself testifies, section 21, that he was sent to Naples because of the pressing needs of his monastery. In Book III, section 5, he reckons a period of two years as the whole span of time during which he was Saint Odo’s companion.

He wrote the *Life of Saint Odo, Abbot of Cluny*, in three books, committing to writing whatever during that interval he himself had seen or heard concerning Odo’s deeds and sayings, or had later been able to learn from others. Since Saint Odo died on 18 November 942, John began writing the life of his abbot not long after that time. John the Italian dedicated this little work, which he had composed, to the monks of Salerno, once his friends and intimates; many later imitated him. Around the year 1120, Nalgodus, a Cluniacensian monk, likewise undertook to write Odo’s life, abridging John’s work and at the same time arranging it more suitably.

This *Life of Saint Odo*, composed by John the Italian, is found in the *Collectanea* of Laurentius Surius, volume VI, under 18 November. These two lives, by John and Nalgodus, are also found in the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, with notes by André Duchesne. Finally, they are found in the fifth volume of *The Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, pages 124 and following, and 150 and following. Gerardus Joannes Vossius, Book II of *On Latin Historians*, chapter 40, p. 324 in my edition; John Mabillon; and André Duchesne, in the places cited, discuss John the Italian, the author of Odo’s life.

[Col. 0883]

## II. Life of Saint Odo, Abbot of Cluny

See above in the Prolegomena to Saint Odo.

[Col. 0883]

## Prologue by John the Italian to His Book on Miracles

[Note: [Col. 0883] The work survives in a Benedictoburanus manuscript written in approximately the twelfth century, although its author does not appear to be later than the eighth or ninth century.]

(Pez, *Diplomatic-Historical-Epistolary Codex.*)

[Col. 0883B] You have often urged me, most noble man and illustrious consul, Lord Pantaleon, to translate into Latin certain things found in the books or histories of the Greeks that are not found in Latin. But I have repeatedly pleaded to you the rusticity of my speech, considering that I could not cross so vast a sea with such a small boat of knowledge, since there are so many discourses and so many books that, I confidently say, if Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, and Gregory—men most learned in both kinds of knowledge, divine and human, and in eloquence like the four rivers of paradise—were to rise again, even they would have much to do for many years. How much more would I, who am the least of all, less learned in both kinds of knowledge, whose understanding has already been diminished by age, and whose eyes have grown dim?

[Col. 0886A] Yet while I turned these matters over in my heart for a long time, not knowing whether to obey you or to conceal my ignorance in silence, at last, overcome by your exhortations and also trusting in the goodwill of the fathers and brothers into whose hands these chapters or narratives will come—for they will kindly endeavor to correct and amend them—I shall undertake this work imposed upon me, invoking as helper the Holy Spirit, who opens the mouths of the mute and makes the tongues of infants eloquent.

Therefore I beg all of you who will read this: correct what ought to be corrected; amend what ought to be amended; and, I ask you, grant me pardon.

## In the Year of the Lord 950. Laurence of Cassino, First a Monk, Later a Bishop of an Unknown See

[Col. 0885]

## Historical Notice

(From Mai, *Roman Spicilegium*, vol. V.)

Peter the Deacon, in his little book *On the Illustrious Men of Cassino*, chapter 6, writes as follows: “Laurence, a monk of the monastery of Cassino, inferior to none in the knowledge of his predecessors after the most holy Benedict, having been made a bishop, and so forth, composed an elegant sermon on the vigil of blessed Benedict.” The records of Cassino do not identify Laurence’s episcopal see; Marus nevertheless reports in his notes on Peter the Deacon that Laurence flourished around the year 950. I willingly present the following sermon from Vatican Codex 1202, formerly belonging to Cassino, written in Lombard script and wonderfully illuminated.

[Col. 0885]

## Laurence’s Sermon at the Vigil of Saint Benedict, Our Holy Father

[Col. 0885B] O most venerable assembly, as we are about to celebrate the solemn feast of our life-giving Father Benedict, let us humbly entreat the mercy of almighty God, who granted him to climb the summit of perfection, that our mind, cleansed of the rust of vices, may await the arrival of its patron with such devotion that it may deserve joyfully to embrace his presence.

For there is absolutely no doubt that this most sacred patron is present with us when we strive to honor his glorious feast with devoted affection. Indeed, although he deigns to visit those who observe his life-giving commandments with his customary goodness at all times, and never ceases to protect them, nevertheless, on this most holy solemnity of his, he will deign, with a special kindliness, to be present among his servants—those who, more specially and more devoutly than usual, diligently strive to adorn their hearts in every way [Col. 0885C] in order to receive so great a Father.

For it is certain that he is the foremost member of that Head who, speaking aloud with the evangelical voice, deigned to say: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matthew 18:20). If, therefore, Christ the Head deigns to be present with us gathered in his name, his members are certainly not absent. But if all the members—namely, all the elect—are generally present with him, how much more does our most glorious patron Benedict, clinging to him, cherish his clients and endeavor to commend their prayers and wholesome petitions to that same Most High?

We undoubtedly believe that he can obtain our salvation from that same God and Lord all the more easily because, after the blessed and holy apostles, he has been exalted above almost all earthly beings, raised high in the glory of his merits [Col. 0886C] and more splendidly elevated by the effectiveness of immense miracles. Finally, the insignia of his merits are so wholly worthy of admiration by human senses that they seem to surpass all measure.

Having received the grace of the holy Spirit in his boyhood, he became so mature in wisdom that, abandoning his paternal wealth and scorning human pomp—which those devoted especially to the liberal arts were then striving to attain—he finally rejected even the comfort of his obedient nurse and sought the arduous way of life. By the example of his deeds and the sweetness of his teaching, he made the exceedingly difficult path so easy for his followers that the lordly voice may be experienced everywhere saying: “My yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”

For through whose wondrous teaching and speech—or rather, through whose outstanding example—did so great a phalanx of monks devote themselves to the divine commandments, except through the example of him who, with God as his guide, effectively fulfilled in his deeds what he taught so clearly and sweetly? How graciously God approved his service is plainly shown by the fact that he did not permit the man whom he had determined to place before many as an example of life to remain hidden for long in the caves of the mountains.

For, as is read in the life of Benedict which blessed Gregory composed with loving care, Gregory deigned first to command a certain priest, who was preparing refreshment for himself on the solemnity of Easter, to visit his most devout servant, exhausted by hunger in the rugged cliffs; afterward he wished Benedict to be made known to shepherds and many others. [Col. 0887C] This was plainly a worthy and holy judgment, so that a lamp so resplendent with examples of virtue, and a jewel so radiant with the effectiveness of signs, would not remain hidden for long beneath the bushel of a hiding place.

Moreover, I doubt that anyone knows how great was the effectiveness of the wonders that accompanied him, since they are so remarkable that, after the holy apostles, as was said, it seems that the Savior’s words were addressed in a special way to him: “You will do greater things than these, because you believe in my name.” Truly believing in his name, he wished to display so many and such great miracles—the man who embraced him after setting aside all the prosperity of this unstable life.

Hence a lofty power was rightly bestowed upon him from heaven, by which he restored life through prayer to a corpse prepared for burial; and, among countless other things, by a mere glance he loosened the cords binding the arms of the captives. He also powerfully caused a completely empty vessel to flow with oil through suppliant prayer. Likewise, when the boy Placidus had been submerged in the watery depths, Benedict restored him safely to solid ground through the appearance of his garment [reading uncertain: *pepli*], by means of the equally blessed Maurus. I do not doubt that these and the remaining deeds are known and celebrated throughout almost the whole world.

He is therefore worthily honored by us, his little servants, with the solemnity due to him: having peacefully laid down the burden of the body, he migrated to the heavenly palaces, there to receive those ineffable rewards which, because of their greatness, cannot be fully contemplated by human estimation.

With good reason also we dance in spiritual joy at his sacred solemnity: accompanied by the service of the watchful, he ascended rejoicing to the heights of heaven along a road adorned with heavenly ornament. It is surely fitting that we embrace with devoted exultation the solemnity of him whom Christ drew from the earth and enriched with his generosity.

It is not without reason that we celebrate him more devoutly than other saints, since, by divine mercy, we experience his help every day. It is, moreover, most unfitting that his own assembly should neglect to glorify, with whatever effort it can, the man whom every foreign and distant province, illuminated by the sparks of his merits, venerates with the most devoted services.

Meanwhile, let us carefully read and examine the rule of his holy institution, to consider by what services this most blessed Father of ours is especially pleased, so that, following his path, we may vigilantly avoid every tangled thicket [reading uncertain: *deviis ... dumetis*]. Among the many most celebrated instruments of virtue that the same Father taught, he especially commended charity, which is the bond of perfection, and humility, which is acknowledged to be the guardian of all the remaining virtues.

Your Charity is certainly not ignorant how cautiously and moderately he prescribed that the office of psalmody should be performed—or, to use his own expression, with what gravity. For among other things he says: “Let us stand at psalmody in such a way that our mind agrees with our voice.” In these words he indicates more clearly than daylight that he takes pleasure not in the sweetness of voices or in song raised beyond measure, but rather in attention to the force of the words and in salutary compunction.

Let us therefore strive, dearest brothers, at this principal solemnity of his, to celebrate the memory of so great a Father, fervent in charity, distinguished by humility of mind, and salutarily moved to compunction by the sweetness of song, so that everywhere we may deserve to be fortified by his patronage.

But since, as that same most holy man says, the things that are to be done ought to be begun with prayer, let us for a little while beseech his patronage, so that what has been devoutly begun may be happily completed.

Therefore, with bowed minds, we, your *bidentes* (“two-toothed,” that is, two-year-old sheep), entreat you as our shepherd to have mercy on us and graciously offer to the all-creating God your customary prayers for your flock; kindly protect us, your little servants, from the attacks of the ancient enemy; mercifully make us strong in the virtue of charity; graciously bestow an abundance of every spiritual gift upon your clients; and do not at some time fail to gather us among your companies.

Protect me also, who presume to praise you in writing yet am insufficiently trained in literary skill, the lowliest household servant, as it were, of your servants, I beg, by your patronage, so that, enriched together by your gift, we may obtain forgiveness for our sins. Meanwhile, may the final line of our page briefly conclude the substance of this most excellent Father of ours.

But when will our sluggishness, with a witty and graceful speech, be able fully to recount the glorious marks of his merits? Even if Plato or Demosthenes, those torrents of eloquence, as they say, were to rise again from the jaws of Erebus, where they are tormented, they would be more capable of wondering at the praises of so great a Father than of speaking them.

For such great blessedness has the mercy of the Thunderer bestowed upon him that, crowned with the emblem of justice, he possesses the heavenly kingdoms in triumph, and that the kings of the earth venerate and worship, with bowed and submissive devotion, his sacred relics, by which the Cassinese monastery is blessed.

Even now he prevails at his honored shrine through such great miracles and wonders that the thunder of such renown powerfully draws overseas and transalpine princes into his service. Nor is it without reason that he is reverently honored by earthly princes: he bowed his neck to the King of all kings and strove throughout his life to serve him most worthily. For he himself deigned to promise through the prophet: “I will glorify those who glorify me.”

Truly, he has glorified and continues to glorify this most sacred Father of ours conspicuously—not only in the heavenly kingdoms, but also before human beings on earth—so that the whole world may recognize with how great a glory of blessedness he is exalted, since for his name’s sake he strove to humble himself salutarily in this life.

Behold him whom a cave once held, hiding there for a while; now paradise holds him rejoicing. And him whom the fields once held, exhausted by fasts, the joys of Olympus now embrace with dancing. Behold, the kings of the earth now offer to the footprints of him whom once only Campania knew their most devoted kisses and exceedingly generous gifts.

Now, therefore, most excellent Father of fathers, with bowed heads we beg your mercy: extend to us the right hand of your help. In your compassion, I beg you, close the cruel mouths of our wicked enemies [Codex: *cicorum*], who deceitfully strive to ensnare your little servants. Grant your comfort, Father, to your clients whom you mercifully drew along the path of imitation. Graciously reveal, we ask, the road by which one reaches the homeland, so that no one from your flock may suffer harm; so that, when you return to our common Lord the talents once entrusted to you, multiplied through us, you may deserve to receive a double reward.

May we also, though unworthy, through your intercession at least escape punishment, though we are uncertain whether, because of the quality of our merits, we shall obtain a reward. This is granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, who so exalted you, most blessed Father, that after the blessed apostles you appear inferior to none of the saints [so the manuscript]; he indeed who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## In the Year of the Lord 956. Agapetus, Pope II

[Col. 0889]

## Historical Notice

(From Mansi, *The Most Extensive Collection of Councils*, XVIII, 405.)

Agapetus succeeded Marinus in the year of Christ 946, during the reign of Constantine VIII. After many synods had been held concerning Hugh and Artald, he confirmed the adjudication of the archbishopric of Rheims to Artald. When Bruno, archbishop of Cologne and brother of Otto, requested the pallium, Agapetus granted it to him. After King Otto had defeated the Danes in a great victory and received them into the Christian religion, Agapetus congratulated the Church of Hamburg and renewed the privileges it had received from its predecessors (Adam, Book II, chapter 2).

During his pontificate, after the death of Lothair, Berengar invaded the kingdom of Italy. The emperor Otto, having been urged by Adelheid, daughter of Rudolf and widow of Lothair, and by Pope Agapetus to provide assistance, drove out the entire family of Berengar and took as his wife Queen Adelheid, formerly Lothair’s wife. He defended the kingdom with complete integrity. After Agapetus had faithfully discharged the pastoral office for nine years, seven months, and ten days, he departed this life.

[Col. 0889]

## Letters and Privileges of Agapetus II

### I. Privilege of Pope Agapetus II for the Monastery of Saint Salvator at Fulda

(Year 946.) Confirmation of the privileges that Pope Marinus II granted to the monastery of Fulda.

(Cocquelines, *Bullar., Privileg., Ampl. Collect.*, I, 250.)

[Col. 0889C]

Agapetus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hadamar, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of the Lord Savior, and through you to your successors, the abbots of that same venerable monastery, forever.

With the greatest concern for all venerable places, insofar as the possibility granted by divine assistance permits, we strive to care for their stability. Through this concern, divine mercy is appeased and praise for the Church of Christ is advanced; for with greater confidence we dare to implore eternal compassion for the forgiveness of our sins.

Therefore your Reverence requested that the venerable monastery of the Lord Savior, constructed by Saint Boniface the bishop in the place called Boconia beside the bank of the river Fulda, should be adorned with the protection of a privilege of the apostolic see and, being placed under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, which by God’s authority we serve, should not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other church.

For this reason, favoring your pious desires, by this apostolic authority we commit to effect what you request, in accordance with the text of the privilege which you have taken care to show us as having been permanently issued there by our predecessor of blessed memory, Marinus, prelate of this life-giving see.

Therefore we prohibit any priest of any church from exercising any authority or jurisdiction whatsoever in the aforesaid monastery, except the apostolic see, so that no one may presume to celebrate the solemnity of Mass there unless he has been invited by the abbot. Thus, in accordance with what has been set forth, it shall remain securely endowed by the firmness of the apostolic privilege, and it shall enjoy perpetual security, without contradiction from any person, in its places and possessions—both those which it holds or possesses at the present time and those which divine piety may in future wish to add to the rights of the monastery from the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful.

Furthermore, after deliberation, we decree that at suitable times it be reported to our ecclesiastical concern how the monastic discipline is directed according to the rule and entrusted to suitable ecclesiastical concord, lest, God forbid, under the pretext of this privilege, the mind and conduct of righteousness should in any way be turned aside from the true standard of justice.

Nor shall it be lawful for a king, any bishop, a count, or any other person, great or small, to inflict any force or bring any dispute concerning the possessions and dependents of the same venerable monastery.

By our authority we also forbid any woman ever to presume to enter there; no one may hold a public court in that venerable monastery or in any of its other places; no one may compel servants or tenants to perform any service, except those persons to whom the abbot has granted consent for the sake of his necessary business.

When it is necessary, the brothers shall have the power to choose an abbot from among themselves, according to the rule of Saint Benedict, without contradiction from any person. And to you, beloved son Hadamar, because we know you to be a well-educated and eloquent man, we both grant and command that you preach the word of God by the authority of Saint Peter.

Therefore, establishing and decreeing by apostolic censure through the text of this decree of ours, if any prelate of any church, or any person invested with whatever dignity, should presume to violate this authority of our privilege, which we confirm by the prerogative of the prince of the apostles, unless he quickly repent, let him be anathema. Incurring the wrath of God, let him be excluded from the company of all the saints. Nevertheless, the dignity of the aforesaid monastery, granted by us, shall remain perpetually inviolate, strengthened by apostolic authority.

But whoever proves to be the guardian and observer of this privilege of ours shall receive blessing and grace from the Lord.

Written by the hand of Leo, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of October, indiction 5. Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, by the hand of Stephen, first secretary of the supreme apostolic see, in the year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of Agapetus, supreme pontiff and universal pope II, in the month of October, indiction 5.

### II. Letter of Pope Agapetus II to Atenulf, Prince of Benevento

(Year 946.) He urges him to restore the monastery of Saint Sophia to the monks of Cassino.

[From Gattula, *History of Cassino*, 53.]

[Col. 0892B]

Agapetus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Atenulf, prince of Benevento: greetings and apostolic blessing.

The custom of our office demands that we admonish those who are vigilant and await the day of judgment, so that they may advance toward better things, and correct those who are negligent, in accordance with the apostolic injunction: “Reprove, entreat, and rebuke” (2 Timothy 4:2). In another place the Lord says through the prophet: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezekiel 3:18).

We have heard from our beloved son Baldwin, the abbot, of the goodwill of your disposition; we greatly rejoice that we have heard you are ready to promote the exaltation of churches. But since the pastoral care of all the churches compels us to keep vigilant watch, our spiritual son Baldwin, the most reverend Father of monasteries, has reported to your lordships that you have not continued in the good work you had begun.

We are therefore greatly saddened and grieved that you have not feared, in your time, boldly disregarding the statutes of kings and the decrees of universal apostolic men, to withdraw the monastery of Saint Sophia, situated within the city of Benevento and, from the beginning of its construction, remaining under the authority of the monks of the blessed Father Benedict established on Mount Cassino, from the authority of the monastery of Saint Benedict with unheard-of audacity.

But the same monastery, having been recalled by the most reverend abbot Baldwin through canonical authority and through the lawful commands of kings and apostles, has been restored to the jurisdiction of that holy monastery. When our predecessor, Pope Marinus, summoned you to him, you nevertheless presumed to seize that same monastery.

Therefore we admonish you in every way and beseech you for the love of Christ to restore the aforesaid monastery in its entirety to the aforementioned abbot when he requests it, and henceforth not to cause trouble for the monastery of Saint Sophia or the Cassinese monastery. If, God forbid, you act otherwise, know that, as it was enacted in the decrees of our predecessors the pontiffs, you likewise shall be bound by the bond of anathema.

### III. Privilege of Agapetus II for the Parthenon of Essen

(Year 946.) At the request of Abbess Hatewiga, he confirms the privileges of the Parthenon of Essen.

(Marini, *Diplomatic Papers*, 35.)

[Col. 0893B]

Agapetus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hatewiga, religious abbess, and to the monastery of Asinda, formerly constructed by Bishop Altfrid, and to its successors forever.

The summit of the supreme apostolic dignity is recognized to shine forth with the splendor of divine providence when it strives to display the contest of its labor more zealously in carrying out the praises of God.

Therefore, because you requested through the intervention of our lord and glorious King Otto that we should newly grant you, by our apostolic authority, the privilege given by our predecessor, Lord Pope Zacharias, to the aforesaid monastery called Asinda, constructed by Bishop Altfrid and burned by the consuming flames together with the aforesaid monastery; and because you requested the tithe which, with the permission of the aforesaid apostolic lord and the consent of the bishops and the entire clergy, Gunthar, archbishop of the Church of Cologne, had assigned for the sustenance of those nuns; and also the right of election, so that when the abbess dies the nuns may have permission to choose as abbess from among themselves whoever within that place is worthy and pleasing to God;

and because you requested that the same monastery be adorned with the privileges of the apostolic see, so that, being established under the jurisdiction of our holy Church—which, by God’s authority, we serve—it should not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other church:

For this reason, favoring your pious desires, we commit to effect what you request, decreeing by apostolic censure, under invocation of the divine judgment and threat of anathema, that no one ever presume—whatever his dignity, or however great or small a person he may be—to take away or alienate in any way anything from its goods or possessions, or anything that appears to belong to it.

Nor shall anyone presume to inflict any harm or loss there, whether in time of peace or in time of barbarian disturbance. We decree that it remain with firm stability under the jurisdiction of our holy Church.

But whoever, with pious regard, proves to be an observer of this apostolic privilege of ours shall receive abundant grace of blessing from the most merciful Lord God.

### IV. Letter of Pope Agapetus II to Leo and Benedict, Intruders into the Churches of Trivento and Termoli

(Year 947.)

[From Mansi, *Councils*, XVIII, 412.]

[Col. 0894A]

Agapetus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Leo, priest and monk, and Benedict, likewise a priest, irrationally consecrated by us as bishops and wearing the episcopal order [lacuna].

We have already sent you letters ordering you to come to us and answer the accusations and complaints which John, bishop of the holy see of Benevento, has brought against you. He appealed to us and produced privileges issued to our predecessors, the pontiffs of the Holy Roman Church and the apostolic see, with a strict anathema, so that no one might presume to diminish the boundaries of the aforesaid Beneventan church.

He also showed that the churches of Trivento and Termoli had been subject from ancient times to the bishop of Benevento, and likewise all the other churches that have been or are to be constructed within the boundaries of these and other cities and castles, and all places subject to the authority of the principality of Benevento.

And because you refused to come and give an account, we have learned that you did not enter through the door, but broke in furtively from elsewhere like thieves and robbers, and unlawfully usurped the episcopal ministry.

When a new presumption also arose, as it appears, whereby the peoples subject to the diocese and [lacuna] of the episcopate of that province of Benevento, contrary to the canonical institutions, chose you as their bishops through payment and bribery, by the simoniacal heresy, we therefore excommunicate you by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

You shall not presume to occupy the episcopal chair among those same peoples—that is, in the churches of Trivento and Termoli—nor shall you be permitted to perform any episcopal office in any other church [lacuna].

Finally, recognizing that these things had been possessed by the ancient pontiffs, we restore, renew, and confirm all the churches, parishes, and dioceses in their entirety to the principality of Benevento, for John, the bishop of Benevento, and his successors to possess forever, and for none of our successors to diminish anything thereof.

Therefore, admonishing and commanding, we excommunicate, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the clergy and the entire people of Trivento and those residing at Termoli: if [lacuna] without the gastalds and ministerial officials, either a cleric or the people of those cities should presume to seek out the aforesaid Leo the monk and Benedict, likewise a priest, and receive them in those cities to exercise the episcopal order, let them remain bound by the bond of anathema.

But if anyone, which we do not wish, should presume with audacity to oppose, transgress, or diminish in any respect what we have established for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid Church of Benevento, let him know that he is bound by the bond of anathema and condemned to eternal punishment with Judas, the betrayer of the Lord, and with all the impious.

But whoever, with pious regard, proves to be an observer and guardian in all things of this apostolic constitution of ours, directed toward the worship of God, shall abundantly receive the grace of blessing from our most merciful Lord and deserve to become a participant in eternal life.

Given by the hand of Stephen, first secretary of the holy Roman and apostolic see, in the year, by the Lord’s favor, of the pontificate of Lord Agapetus II, pope, in the most sacred see of blessed Peter the apostle, his first year, indiction 5.

### V. Letter of Pope Agapetus II to Adalgar, Archbishop of Hamburg

(Year 948.) He confirms the union of the Church of Bremen with Hamburg and the other rights of Hamburg.

[Col. 0895B]

Agapetus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most holy Adalgar, archbishop of the holy Church of Hamburg, and to your successors forever.

The apostolic moderation is bound to assist with benevolent compassion those endowed with pious religion, and to grant the requests of petitioners with eager devotion; for by this we shall undoubtedly earn the greatest reward of profit from God, the creator of all, when venerable places have unquestionably been suitably brought into a better condition. Therefore, since you requested that we confirm to you the entire archbishopric of the Church of Hammaburg, just as it was decreed by our predecessor, the lord Nicholas, of this apostolic see, moved by the prayers of Hadamar, abbot of Fulda, we grant it by apostolic authority, together with all places generally and specifically belonging to your archbishopric: namely, everything that your predecessors acquired through their labors, or that the love of the eternal homeland has bestowed or continues to bestow there through the faithful worshipers of Christ; together also with those who in their own time have now been converted to the faith of Christ by divine protection—namely, the bishops of the Danes, Norwegians, Swedes, and all the northern regions. We also decree that the pallium, and its use in the matters previously designated by the aforesaid pope, shall be held by you and all your successors in perpetuity.

[Col. 0895D]

Henceforth, moreover, we decree that no archbishop—whether the archbishop of Cologne or any other—may claim any authority for himself in your diocese. Indeed, we advise them and all practitioners of religion without exception to provide you with assistance and support in every matter, so that they may deserve to receive a full reward from the Lord for the grace of this benefaction. For whatever is shown to benefit the Church and is not opposed to divine commands, we do not doubt that it must be carried out and provided by the authority of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. By this decree, therefore, in accordance with the sanction of Pope Nicholas of good memory and the wish of the most reverend King Louis, we decree and confirm that the aforesaid dioceses—namely, Hamburg and Bremen—shall henceforth not be two, but shall be and be called one.

We strike with the sentence of anathema, and condemn to the lot of the devil as guilty of eternal punishment, anyone who opposes or contradicts this, or in any way plots against our pious efforts, so that, following the example of our predecessors, we may zealously protect the summit of the apostles and the cause of God with pious affection from adversaries on every side. Accordingly, by apostolic authority, we further order and admonish Bishop Bernhard of Halberstadt, Thidard of the Church of Hildesheim, and the other neighboring bishops to assist you in everything, so that you may more easily fulfill your priestly ministry and acquire gains of souls for the Lord Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0896B]

Therefore, by apostolic authority and ecclesiastical censure, under appeal to divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we establish that no person, great or small, whatever his order or dignity, may violate anything granted by us or by our predecessors to your Church and to you. Whoever changes it or presumes to violate it in any respect, unless he repents, shall, by the authority of God, blessed Peter, and ourselves, who exercise his vicariate, be bound by the chain of perpetual anathema. Whoever, however, proves to be its guardian and observer, may deserve to obtain the grace of blessing and heavenly recompense from the just Judge, our Lord God.

Written by the hand of Arron, regional notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of January, in the sixth indiction.

[Col. 0896C]

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of January, by the hand of Andrew, treasurer of the holy apostolic see, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter, in the sixth indiction.

## VI. Letter of Pope Agapetus II to Windilgard, Abbess. (948)

The monastery of Gandersheim, built in Saxony, is received under the protection of the apostolic see and endowed with various privileges.

[According to Coquelines, *Collection of Bulls*, I, 251.]

Agapetus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Windilgard, abbess of the venerable monastery of Gandersheim, built by Count Otto of Saxony, and to the other abbesses of her succession, forever.

[Col. 0896D]

Since those things which accord with reasonable desires must always be granted, the authority of pious preservation ought by no means to be denied to the devotion of the founder when privileges are being granted. Therefore, since the venerable abbot Hathumarus asked us, through his intervention and entreaty, to confirm to you by apostolic authority your monastery of Gandersheim, situated beside the river Eterna and established under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, which by God’s authority we serve, so that it might be subject to the jurisdiction of no other church, we, favoring your pious desires, by this our authority bring into effect what is requested. Accordingly, by our authority we prohibit any priest of any church from exercising any jurisdiction in the aforesaid monastery, except the apostolic see.

By the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, we order that no king may dare to give the monastery as a benefice to any persons without your permission, so that, in accordance with the security established by the firmness of the privilege subject to the apostolic see, it may remain undisturbedly endowed with places and possessions—both those which it currently has or possesses and those which divine goodness may wish to add to the rights of the monastery in future—and may enjoy perpetual security in gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful, without contradiction from any person.

When the abbess of that monastery departs from this world, no one shall be permitted to appoint an abbess there except from the congregation itself, if one is found who is worthy before God. If, however, none is found there, then the king shall have the power to appoint there an abbess who is able to please God and is worthy before him.

[Col. 0897B]

We also establish by the page of this decree that, if a person of whatever dignity attempts to violate this charter of our privilege, which we confirm by the authority of the prince of the apostles, that person shall be anathema; incurring the wrath of God, he shall be excluded from the assembly of all the saints, so that, nevertheless, the dignity of the aforesaid monastery granted by us may remain perpetually inviolate, supported by apostolic authority.

Written by the hand of Stephen, archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of January, in the sixth indiction.

[Col. 0897C]

Farewell. Given on the third day before the Nones of January, by the hand of Andrew, treasurer of the holy apostolic see by the grace of divine favor, in the year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of Agapetus, supreme pontiff, junior pope, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter, the second.

## VII. Privilege of Pope Agapetus II for the Monastery of Saint Boniface at Fulda. (948)

Confirms the privileges of the monastery of Fulda, “recently renewed.”

[Dronke, *Diplomatic Code of Fulda*, p. 320.]

Agapetus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hadamar, venerable abbot, and through him to the abbots who shall succeed him in the monastery first built by Saint Boniface and recently renewed, forever.

[Col. 0897D]

Since those things which accord with reasonable desires must always be granted, the authority of pious construction ought by no means to be denied to the devotion of the founder when privileges are being granted. Therefore, since you asked us that the monastery of the Savior, first built by Saint Boniface and recently rebuilt by you at the place called Boconis beside the bank of the river Fulda, be adorned with the insignia of a privilege of the apostolic see and, being established under the jurisdiction of our Church—which by God’s authority we serve—be subject to the jurisdiction of no other church, we, favoring your pious desires, bring into effect by this our authority what is requested.

Accordingly, we prohibit any priest or bishop of any church from exercising any jurisdiction or authority in the aforesaid monastery, except the apostolic see. Thus, unless invited by the abbot of the monastery, no one at all shall presume to celebrate the solemnity of Mass there, so that, in accordance with the security established by the firmness of the privilege subject to the apostolic see, it may remain undisturbedly endowed with places and possessions—both those which it holds or possesses at the present time and those which divine goodness may wish to add in future to the rights of the venerable monastery—and may enjoy perpetual security in the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful, without contradiction from any person.

[Col. 0898B]

We also establish by the page of this decree that whoever—a prelate of any church, or a person of whatever dignity—attempts to violate this charter of our privilege, which we confirm by the authority of the prince of the apostles, shall be anathema; incurring the wrath of God, he shall be excluded from the assembly of all the saints. Nevertheless, the dignity of the aforesaid monastery granted by us shall remain perpetually inviolate, supported by apostolic authority.

Written by the hand of Stephen, regional notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of January and in the sixth indiction.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of January.

## VIII. Letter of Pope Agapetus II to Gerard, Archbishop of Lauriacum. (948)

Settles the dispute between the Churches of Lauriacum—that is, Passau—and Salzburg.
