It assigns western Pannonia to Salzburg; to Lauriacum, as the older see, the precedence of blessing and rank of see, eastern Pannonia, and the regions of the Avars, Moravians, and Slavs, together with the power to preach freely throughout all the lands of the Slavs, ordain bishops there, and establish everything by apostolic authority.

[According to Mansi, *Councils*, XVIII, 405.]

[Col. 0898C]

Agapetus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved and most reverend brother Gerard, archbishop of the holy Church of Lauriacum: greetings in Christ.

Your petitions for the renewal or approval of the privileges of your Church were presented to our experience with great goodwill by Hademarus, abbot of the venerable monastery of Fulda, who came here for the sake of prayer. He also sorrowfully reported the very serious quarrels and disputes that had arisen between you and Archbishop Herold because each had assumed authority over the pallium in one province. We too deplore this with profound grief of heart as a matter entrusted to our pastoral care, and regard it as a profanation.

For the holy and universal Church, over which by God’s authority we preside, is supported as though on so many columns by its religious and peaceful priests, strengthened in sincere charity. When they are divided, however, and, puffed up by hostile pride against one another, raise their minds—especially when they are such great bishops—it is shaken from its proper condition, as though its supports had been torn away, and risks collapse, with great danger and loss of strength. Moreover, while such a stubborn contention is carried on externally among you over the honor of the pallium, the dignity of the priesthood is emptied within through fraternal rivalry.

[Col. 0899A]

Therefore, brother, recognizing that it is our duty to prevent a schism in the holy Church of God, nourished by the fuel of enmity among you, and to prevent scandal from being prolonged without regard for counsel or your benefit, we come as arbiters to separate your dispute. We are moved to this both by concern for the governance entrusted to us by the Lord and by love for you both. In this way, we shall properly satisfy justice by reasonable judgments concerning the grievance arising from your aforementioned conflict, and, with every controversy dismissed, restore you to fraternal concord under Christ’s direction.

It is known, and recorded in letters kept with us, to which ecclesiastical places the dignity of the pallium is owed by this apostolic see. We have read in authentic privileges sent to us by you that the city of Lauriacum was anciently metropolitan and the seat of an archbishop, over which your Holiness is recognized to preside. We have likewise found this in certain copies of a charter, extremely worn by age, in the archive of Saint Peter.

[Col. 0899C]

We know that, at the beginning of the Church’s birth and during the most savage persecution of Christians, it received the rudiments of the Catholic faith from the teachers of this see; thereafter the grace of that same faith spread through the successive preachers into the provinces of Upper and Lower Pannonia. Until the time of the Huns, no one other than the archbishop of holy Lauriacum presided over these two provinces and their bishops. The barbarian ferocity of the Huns devastated and utterly destroyed not only the aforesaid city of Lauriacum but also the surrounding regions.

It therefore happened that the bishops, compelled by this necessity, abandoned that deserted see and transferred elsewhere, and at the same time abandoned the archiepiscopal dignity of that see. In more recent times—not long ago—the kingdom of the Bavarians having become vacant of an apostolic representative, Arno was appointed the first archbishop of the holy Church of Salzburg. The long-standing history preserved in the sacred archive bears witness to this.

[Col. 0899D]

Now, however, since Christ has mercifully granted peace and security for dwelling to the holy Church of Lauriacum against its enemies, your fraternity’s cathedral ought to be located nowhere other than there. Therefore we re-enthrone you in that Church, carrying out the sanctions and statutes of the holy Fathers, our predecessors, and also of Pope Leo of blessed memory, from whom your Excellency received the pallium and privilege. We absolve the often-mentioned holy Church of Lauriacum by the power and in the place of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; we restore its archiepiscopal status and raise it to metropolitan rank; we secure and strengthen the privileges sent to us in your own hand and confirm them as valid. We once again grant you the pallium, previously granted according to its established use, together with the present decree, to be held perpetually by you and your successors.

With these matters thus restored precisely to justice, we have decided to end your quarrels and the dissensions arising from the aforesaid cause, and to reconcile you in fraternal love, so that the honor of the pallium now accorded to each of you may remain unharmed. We exhort you, in accordance with apostolic institution, henceforth not to remain in contention and rivalry.

[Col. 0900B]

It is established canonically that individual metropolitans are appointed for individual provinces. We therefore consider it good and peaceful to divide and define the parishes among you in this way: since the two provinces of the region of Noricum have been divided, let the care and guardianship of western Pannonia be entrusted to Archbishop Herold; but to you and your successors, because of the meritorious antiquity of the holy Church of Lauriacum—to which, by right, the younger ought to rise in reverence—let the oversight of eastern Pannonia be assigned, with precedence and authority in the order of blessing and of the see, together with the region of the Avars and of the Marahars, that is, the Moravians,

[Note: [Col. 0899] That is, the Moravians, who are also called Maravi and Maraci.]

and also of the Slavs dwelling throughout those regions, whether they are now Christians or are still to be won for Christ through baptism. We entrust to you and your successors our apostolic authority in those parts to preach and, at your discretion, to establish bishops wherever necessary, and to arrange and regulate everything with such authority and power as if we ourselves were present.

[Col. 0900C]

But if the aforesaid Archbishop Herold, or any of his successors, is not content with the boundary that has been defined and stubbornly attempts to reclaim a diocese that has been forbidden and separated from his authority, and is not restrained from the schism of forbidden contention by these our apostolic traditions and determinations, then he shall be entirely deprived of the munificence of the dignity piously granted to him. According to the former law, Upper Pannonia shall then be joined to Lower Pannonia, and both shall perpetually be subject to you and your successors’ authority.

[Col. 0900D]

We bless and approve as Catholics those who welcome and assent to these our most salutary decrees. But those who resist, or strive to weaken or wholly overturn them, we strike strictly with the anathema “Maranatha” (“Our Lord, come!”) of the Holy Trinity; by the apostolic sentence through which Ananias and Sapphira, having been punished, died, we condemn them; and we consign them to everlasting torments with the blasphemers of the Holy Spirit.

## IX. Letter of Pope Agapetus II to Aymard, Abbot of Cluny

Privilege of the abbey of Cluny.

[According to Mansi, *Councils*, XVIII, p. 408.]

Agapetus, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Aymard, venerable abbot of the monastery of Cluny, built in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and situated in the territory of Mâcon, and through you to your successors in the same monastery, forever.

[Col. 0901A]

It accords with apostolic moderation to assist compassionately and piously the wishes of petitioners, and to grant them assent with eager devotion. For by this we shall obtain the greatest reward from God, the creator of all. Therefore, since you asked us to decree by our apostolic authority that the aforesaid monastery should remain in the condition in which Duke William determined by his testament that it should remain, subject to the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, we, moved by your prayers, grant it to you to govern.

Accordingly, let that monastery, together with all its possessions, both those which it now has and those which shall henceforth be given to it, be free from the domination of any king, bishop, count, or any of William’s relatives. After your death, let no one presume to appoint a superior over them against the will of the monks. Rather, let them have the free power, without consulting any ruler, to appoint for themselves whomever they wish according to the Rule of Saint Benedict—unless, God forbid, they should prefer to choose someone who consents to their vices. Let anyone who wishes prevent this with zeal for God.

We restore to you in full the tithes that formerly belonged to your chapels and that, through a kind of modern authority or license, have been taken away by one bishop or another. If any chapels have already been built there, or are yet to be built, we permit them to remain in such a way that nothing is diminished from the tithes belonging to your churches. What our beloved son Bruno, bishop, granted to you from the aforesaid chapels, we decree shall remain valid and firm forever.

[Col. 0901C]

Moreover, we decree that whatever from vineyards or cultivated lands belongs to your share, and likewise a portion of the tithes, belongs to your hospice; likewise concerning the possessions which you are to receive. Also, concerning what Leobald left to the aforesaid monastery. Likewise, concerning that which Magiona, or concerning any possessions which ought to belong to that monastery.

By our apostolic authority we also confirm the abbey of the monastery of Cariloc, which has been bestowed upon the same monastery. We decree that the abbeys of Saint John and blessed Martin, situated in the suburb of Mâcon, shall likewise remain perpetually attached to the aforesaid place, so that no bishop, count, or any person may presume by rash attempt to arrange anything there without the command of the rector of that place.

We rule similarly concerning Celsanicas, the estate of Count Hecfred, which our son Stephen, examining the case with just judgment, assigned to the aforesaid place for the remedy of all Christians.

[Col. 0901D]

Moreover, we strengthen with apostolic firmness all the villas belonging to the same monastery of Cluny: namely, Solustriacum, Caninias, Seneciacum, Arpagiacum, Saint Victor, and Scociolas, Kaerdasemscum, Dabormacum, and Piscatoria, which is called Osa; Tosciacum and the church of Saint Desiderius; Ambariacum; and the estate of Saviniacum, which Engelbald gave; and the estate which Waldo gave when he came to conversion.

Likewise Amberia and the church of Saint Abundius, which Artald, when dying, left to the aforesaid monastery; the church of Saint Saturninus, with the entire estate which Archbishop Gerald gave to the aforesaid monastery.

[Col. 0902A]

And because the monastic order desires the highest degree of immunity, we grant you this privilege, as reverence is owed everywhere to holy places: no one shall presume in any way, without your consultation, to distrain or invade your municipal holdings or any of your possessions.

Indeed, as recognition that the aforesaid monastery belongs to the holy apostolic see for protection and support, ten solidi shall be paid every five years.

[Col. 0902B]

If anyone attempts to resist this most salutary constitution of ours, or tries to corrupt any part of it, and fails to observe everything that we sanction in this privilege, let him know that, under appeal to divine judgment, unless he repents he is eternally bound by the chain of anathema, excluded from the kingdom of God, and destined to suffer without end with the devil.

Whoever, however, proves to be the guardian and observer of this most salutary sanction of ours may deserve to obtain from Christ the Lord blessing, and from the holy apostles, judges of the world, absolution both in this life and in the future.

Written by the hand of Leo, royal notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of March, in the seventh indiction.

## X. Letter of Pope Agapetus II to Williar, Abbot. (950)

Confirms the judgment of Otto the Great concerning the immunity of Saint Maximinus.

[According to Hontheim, *History of Trier*, I, 284.]

[Col. 0902C]

Agapetus, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend abbot Williar: every expression of charity in Christ.

We received with great goodwill the messengers of your Holiness, sent to the thresholds of the holy apostles and likewise to our apostolic dignity—namely, Asolf and Gunthar—and we graciously heard their embassy in the presence of all the Roman clergy.

[Col. 0902D]

From their report we know that you have often and greatly been harassed by Ruotbert, an archbishop who, although by no means venerable in this matter, is nevertheless venerable in others, because he unjustly wished to subject the monastery entrusted to you to the church entrusted to him. You were protected, however, on the one hand by the just judgment issued from royal authority by the serene Otto, and on the other by the charters of Charlemagne and the other ancient kings, which were read aloud in their presence.

Therefore, with the assent of our apostolic dignity, the entire order of the Roman clergy decreed that concerning your monastery—the one founded near the walls of Trier in honor of Saint John the Evangelist and dedicated to the bodies of the holy confessors Maximinus, Agritius, and Nicetius—the judgments written in the charters of King Otto and his predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks, shall remain immovable. Thus, both now and hereafter, it shall remain under royal authority alone and shall never be subject to any other person, except the abbot whom the brothers of that monastery elect in common agreement according to the Rule.

[Col. 0903A]

But if the aforesaid archbishop, or any of his successors, or any other of the brothers who are or shall be in that monastery, should impiously and cruelly disturb its peace, and, after first being admonished by this present document and then by the apostolic dignity, should not repent, let him be treated not as a shepherd but as a hireling.

Therefore, if he persists in such obstinate hardness, let him ultimately be excommunicated by our apostolic authority; moreover, let him never achieve his desire against good kings and dukes and just judges who resist him.

Written by the hand of the archivist of the Holy Roman Church. Given on the second day before the Kalends of March, in the eighth indiction. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0903D] The present papal bull has always seemed to me of suspect authenticity, especially because of its form. Indeed, anyone moderately familiar with the documents of this age can easily see that it reflects little of the style and usage of that century or of the Roman curia. As for its subject matter, it cannot in any way concern ecclesiastical immunity, or exemption properly so called; for it is evident that monasteries exempt from episcopal jurisdiction were still unknown in that age. Among others, Van Espen observed and demonstrated this in *Jus Ecclesiasticum Universum*, Part III, title 12, chapter 2, §§ 21 ff. Certainly, in the Council of Confluence at Trier, held in the tenth century in the presence of Charles, king of France, and Henry, king of Germany, we read: “So that the churches of whatever monks, situated in each parish, may be divinely subject to the governance of the bishops, and may diligently render them obedience in the conduct of ecclesiastical affairs. Without doubt, the monks themselves must obey their bishops in everything.” Hence it is clear that the Fathers of this synod assumed that at that time monks were without distinction subject to their bishops, with no difference between exempt and non-exempt communities.]

## XI. Privilege of Agapetus II for the Monastery of Saints Germanus and Michael at Cuxa. (950)

Confirms the privileges of the monastery of Cuxa.

[According to D. Bouquet, *Collection of Historians*, IX, 227.]

Agapetus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gondefred, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Germanus and Saint Michael, situated in the Confluent valley, in the place called Cuxa—Saint-Michel de Cusan—and, after you, to the abbots who succeed you in that monastery, forever.

[Col. 0903C]

Since great solicitude and care continually weigh upon us, we must keep watch over all the Churches of God, lest they suffer loss and damage through any necessity. Therefore, since Soniarius, a religious priest and monk, coming into our presence as your representative, asked us to confirm to you and to your successors, the abbots, the aforesaid monastery in its entirety, with all its boundaries, limits, adjacent lands, and all its dependencies, forever, we, moved by your prayers and for the love of almighty God and Saint Peter, confirm the aforesaid monastery with its boundaries and limits as follows.

On the eastern side it begins at the front, along the summit of the Serra that runs from Bovaria to Jupiter at Celerano; it proceeds from the mountain called Laccarias, and from there runs through the Laccarias to Mount Canigou. On the south it borders Mount Canigou and descends along the Serra above Miliarias; it reaches the cross above the estates, then Chero Clarinto; it proceeds along the summit of the Serra to the river Merdarius.

[Col. 0904A]

On the west, the Serra of Chero Clarinto reaches the river Merdarius and runs as far as the river Têt. On the northern side it borders the public road leading to the Two Sisters; it follows that public road as far as Litterano, then below Saint Felix, and reaches the estate of Saint Mary.

It includes the villa of Tauriniano with the church of Saint Fructuosus, together with its tithes and first fruits; the church of Saint Martin of Clerano; and the church of Saint Andrew, founded in the villa of Catellano, with its estate. It includes the villa of Torrente with its boundaries and limits, as is set forth in your authentic documents; the valley of Taresago and its estates; the cell of Saint Vincent with its estate, as contained in your documents; the estate of Tonegale; Manzunculas; Ocenias; Tres-Valles; Lare with the church of Saint Andrew; the cell of Saint Thomas with its estate; the church of Saint Peter, founded in the villa of Inforcadis; and Laguna with its church and your estates in these places.

[Col. 0904B]

In the county of Roussillon: in the villa of Miliarii; in Camelas; in Relano; in Saint Felix; in the windy valley; on Mount Auriol; in the villa of Insula; in the valley of Locas; at Pui Nadal; in the valley of Vincano; in Saorla; in Arbussolas; in Planicolas; at Interrivos; in the valley of Molegica; in the villa of Orto Falguerias; in the villa of Arriano; in the villa of Folioliis; in Vernet; in Corneliano; in the valley of Foliano; in the valley of Savrra; in Torre Sindo; in Pino; in Campelias;

[Col. 0904C]

in Segondaniano; in Juloss; in Flazano; in Angerro; in Enne; in Porciliarios; in Evole; and in Altino.

In the county of Cerdanya: in the villa of Sallagosa; in Onzes; and in Annes.

In Fenouillèdes: in the villa of Tavernulas; in Sauriniano, or Perolas; in Vallemagna with its church; and in the valley of Stavia.

In the county of Berguedà: in the village of Gilmari; in the villa of Canes; and in all other places wherever the monastery’s possessions lie.

In the county of Roussillon, in the Confluent valley, in the county of Cerdanya, in the county of Fenouillèdes, and in Berguedà—in the places and counties named above—as much as the monastery possesses and is contained or recorded in your documents, and as much as, with God’s help, you will acquire in the future, with the boundaries, limits, and borders of your monastery.

[Col. 0904D]

We likewise grant you the first fruits, tithes, and offerings from your places, to be gathered for the aforesaid monastery with all its dependencies.

[Col. 0905A]

[lacuna] of the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve; by the tenor of this privilege we establish your monastery and the places or churches belonging to it everywhere, from the present ninth indiction and forever, for you and your successors, the servants of God dwelling there and leading the cenobitic life, to be governed and held in the fear of God, and to remain securely and peacefully under the rule and protection of the apostolic see; we subject them to no other power whatsoever.

Likewise, by apostolic authority, we order that the faithful of Christ be received hospitably and kindly according to God’s will. When you have been taken from this light, let no person be chosen as abbot there except from that congregation; let an abbot be chosen from the aforesaid congregation according to God’s will.

[Col. 0905B]

We command by apostolic authority that no person, great or small, ever presume to use force or make an invasion in the aforesaid monastery or in its possessions. Therefore, under appeal to divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we decree that no one of our successors in the pontificate, nor any person, great or small, of whatever order, shall presume to break the authority of this our apostolic privilege.

For—something we do not believe—whoever presumes to act otherwise shall know that he is excommunicated and bound by the chains of anathema, excluded from the kingdom of God, and plunged into the abyss and Tartarean chaos, where he shall perish with the impious. Whoever, however, proves to be its guardian and observer may deserve to obtain manifold grace of blessing from Christ the Lord, our God.

[Col. 0905C]

Written by the hand of Leo, regional notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of December, in the aforementioned indiction. Farewell.

## XII. Letter of Pope Agapetus II to Wisad, Bishop of Urgell. (951)

Confirms the privileges of the Church of Urgell.

[According to D. Bouquet, cited above, p. 230.]

Agapetus, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most holy Wisad, bishop of the holy Church of Urgell, and to your successors, forever.

It is fitting for the apostolic authority to come to the aid, with benevolent compassion, of those who abound in devout religion, and to grant the requests of petitioners with eager devotion. For by this we undoubtedly earn the greatest reward from God, the creator of all, when venerable places, suitably ordered, have without doubt been brought to a better condition.

Therefore, since you asked us to confirm the aforesaid bishopric of the Church of Urgell, with all its buildings, as well as its villages, churches, parishes, houses, vineyards, lands, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, willow groves, fruit trees, fruitful or unfruitful, of various kinds, wells, springs, streams, mills, fisheries, waters and watercourses, castles, mountains, valleys, hills, clearings and adjoining properties—cultivated or uncultivated—together with the appurtenances of that same bishopric, namely the districts of Cerdanya, Llívia, Berguedà, Pallars, Ribagorça, Jistavín, Cardós, Àneu and Tirbia, and the places of Santa Deodata with their boundaries, Fencris with its boundaries, and Submonte with its boundaries, [lacuna] we also confirm the third part of the toll of that same bishopric, with the appurtenances of the market, and with everything belonging generally and in full to that bishopric from all its places wherever they may be, within the aforesaid bishopric, from the territories of Urgell, Cerdanya, Berguedà, Pallars and Ribagorça.

Likewise, we confirm to you and to your successors the first fruits and tithes from the places and appurtenances of the aforesaid bishopric. We further establish that no person whatsoever shall presume unjustly to subject the clergy belonging to your bishopric to coercion or to bring them before an unjust tribunal together with a layperson.

Since the aforesaid bishopric, with all the possessions belonging to it wherever they may be, has been secured and established by the kings of the Franks through the written instrument of their decree and by royal authority, so by our apostolic authority we likewise confirm and establish that whatever you and your successors may lawfully acquire in future, from this present year of the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ 991, the tenth indiction, moved by your prayers and through your royal decrees and the text of this privilege, we confirm and establish in perpetuity for you and your successors, to hold, possess, administer with fear of God, and govern.

Thus no king, no prince, no count, no margrave, no judge, nor any person, great or small, shall ever presume to inflict violence or invasion upon that bishopric or upon its appurtenances. Therefore, under the solemn appeal to divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we decree that none of our pontifical successors, nor any person, great or small, shall dare or presume to act unjustly in any matter against this our apostolic privilege, or attempt to violate it.

If anyone, which we do not believe, should attempt to violate it in any matter, let him know that, unless he repents, by the authority of God, of the holy apostle Peter, and of us, who exercise his vicariate, he is to be indissolubly bound by the chains of anathema, excluded from the kingdom of God, and burned in the fire with the devil and his most terrible pomp and with Judas, the betrayer of Our Lord Jesus Christ; and, plunged into the infernal abyss and Tartarean chaos, let him perish with the ungodly.

But whoever proves himself its guardian and observer, may he obtain abundantly from the just Judge, the Lord our God, the grace of blessing and heavenly recompense, and deserve to share in eternal life. Amen. Farewell.

Written by the hand of Leo, regional notary and scrinarius of our holy Roman Church, in the month of December, in the aforesaid year and the aforementioned indiction.

### XIII. Privilege of Agapetus II for the Monastery of Saint Mary of Ripoll. (Year 951.)

[In D. Bouquet, cited above, p. 229.]

**Agapetus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Arnulf, the religious abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Mary, Virgin and Mother of God, our Lady, situated in the county of Ausona, in the valley of Ripoll, between two rivers, and after you to your successors in the same venerable monastery, forever.**

It is fitting for the apostolic authority to come to the aid, with benevolent compassion, of those who abound in devout religion, and to grant the requests of petitioners with eager devotion. For by this we undoubtedly earn the greatest reward from God, the creator of all, when venerable places, suitably ordered, have without doubt been brought to a better condition.

Therefore, since you have asked us to confirm to you the aforesaid monastery with all its possessions, namely churches, parishes, villages, estates, houses, farmsteads, lands, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, thickets, plots, winepresses, watercourses, mills with their headwaters and fisheries, cultivated and uncultivated, and also whatever it is known to possess in the surrounding places and throughout the circuit of that monastery, and so forth, we establish that, when the abbot of that monastery departs from this world, no abbot shall be appointed there by kings, counts, or any other person, whether for the desire of money or for any kind of empty favor or glory. Rather, a worthy person shall be elected abbot by all the servants of God of that aforesaid monastery, according to God and according to the rule of Saint Benedict the Father.

The aforesaid monastery is situated in the territory of Ausona, in the valley of Ripoll, between two rivers. We also establish for you and your successors the first fruits and tithes from the places and appurtenances of the aforesaid monastery. We further establish that no person whatsoever shall presume unjustly to inflict coercion upon the monks residing in your aforesaid monastery, or to bring them before an unjust tribunal together with a layperson.

Since the aforesaid monastery, wherever it may be, with its appurtenances, has been secured and established by the kings of the Franks through the written instrument of their decree and by royal authority, as stated above, so from now and henceforth whatever you and your successors may lawfully acquire in future, from this present tenth indiction, moved by your prayers and through the aforesaid royal decrees and the text of this privilege, as set out above, we confirm and establish in perpetuity for you and your successors, to hold and henceforth administer and govern.

Thus no king, no prince, no count, no margrave, no judge, nor any person, great or small, shall ever presume to inflict any harm or invasion upon that monastery or upon its appurtenances. Therefore, under the solemn appeal to divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we decree that no person, great or small, shall dare or presume to act unjustly in any matter against this our apostolic privilege, or attempt to violate it.

If anyone, which we do not believe, should attempt to violate it in any matter, let him know that, unless he repents, by the authority of almighty God, of the holy prince of the apostles Peter, and of us, who exercise his vicariate, he is to be indissolubly bound by the chains of anathema, excluded from the kingdom of God, burned in eternal fire with the devil and his most terrible pomp and with Judas, the betrayer of Our Lord Jesus Christ, and, plunged into the infernal abyss and Tartarean chaos, let him perish with the ungodly.

But whoever proves himself its guardian and observer, may he obtain abundantly from the just Judge, Our Lord Jesus Christ, the grace of blessing and heavenly recompense, and deserve to share in eternal life.

Written by the hand of Stephen, regional notary and scrinarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of December, in the aforesaid tenth indiction. Farewell.

### XIV. Letter of Agapetus II to Suniarius, Abbot. (Year 951.) He confirms the privileges of the Monastery of Crassus.

[In D. Bouquet, cited above, p. 231.]

**Agapetus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Suniarius, the religious abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Mary, Mother of God, our Lady, situated in the county of Carcassonne, on the River Orbieu, and after you to your successors in the same venerable monastery, forever.**

It is fitting for the apostolic authority to come to the aid, with benevolent compassion, of those who abound in devout religion, and to grant the requests of petitioners with eager devotion. For by this we undoubtedly earn the greatest reward from God, the creator of all, when venerable places, suitably ordered, have without doubt been brought to a better condition.

Therefore, since through your legate, namely Arnulf, the humble abbot of Ripoll, you asked us to confirm the aforesaid monastery, with all its possessions, namely churches, [lacuna] villages, houses, lands, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, thickets, plots and winepresses, waters and watercourses, mills with their headwaters and fisheries, cultivated or uncultivated; and also in these places, in the county of Carcassonne, the village of Agrifolio with the church of Saint Cyricus and its boundaries and limits; likewise the village of Verzeliano with the church of Saint Mary and its boundaries; and the village of Cucuniano with the church of Saint Mary and its boundaries; also half [of certain holdings], and whatever that place itself possesses in the said county [lacuna]; and in the county of Toulouse, or in its vicariates, the church of Saint Mary, and of Saint Savior, and of Saint John at Ercino, and the place called Camboni with everything belonging to it; and whatever Simplicius, the archdeacon, granted there with his relatives, as is recorded in the text of their documents, or whatever you may acquire in future in those places; and in the county of Razès whatever the aforesaid Simplicius, the archdeacon, granted there, both in parishes and in other places; also the village of Boxamaurea and Aureliosa with all their rights; and in the suburb of Peyrepertuse what Roger gave in Cucuniano, Retgas in Ollito with its church, [lacuna] in Paterno, with as much as belongs there from the village of Corneliano up to the aforesaid place, as Holiba granted there; the village of Corneliano with its church; the village of Stagello with its church; [lacuna] whatever [there is] in the village of Gologias with its church; half of Vernettum with its church; the village of Ripas Altas with its church; and Villare itself with its church; the village of Coningos with its church; and fisheries in the villages of Palsas and in the village of Canonae; and in the county of Conflent whatever you possess in meadows and in bonaria belonging to it; in the county of Girona, the church of Saint Felix in the village of Lorostaria, and its church; in the county of Besalú, the church of Saint Stephen and Saint Peregrine, as well as the villages of Enuscho and Mediano with their church and appurtenances; and what they possess in Barcelona, Oriell, Sarda, Cabast, Albi and Minerve; and in the county of Narbonne, the village of Erciam with its church; and on the island of Sici, the church of Saint Peter with its appurtenances, and whatever Remigius, the archdeacon, gave there; and in Toulouse the village [lacuna], and Palma, and in the village of Alianto, and Fabriciano, and Ferrales, Fabarios of Saint Stephen and Saint Genesius; and whatever they possess there in the village of Miliano.

In the county of Ausona, the church of Saint Martin with its tithes and appurtenances, and also in the village of R[lacuna]ano and the hamlet of Asenario whatever they possess there; and in Salmas, near Narbonne and beside the lake, whatever they possess there; together with everything belonging in full to the aforesaid monastery. We also confirm to you the pontage, carriage tax, salt tax and toll, as the kings granted them to you through the written instrument of their decree.

We establish, however, that when the abbot of the said monastery departs from this world, no abbot shall be appointed there by kings, counts, or any other person, whether for the desire of money or for any kind of empty favor or glory. Rather, abbots shall be elected by all the servants of God of that monastery, according to God and according to the rule of Saint Benedict the Father. The aforesaid monastery is situated in the territory of Carcassonne, near the district of Narbonne.

We also confirm to you and to your successors the first fruits and tithes from the places and appurtenances of that holy monastery. We further establish that no person whatsoever shall presume unjustly [lacuna] to subject the monks residing in your monastery to coercion or to bring them before an unjust tribunal together with a layperson.

Since the aforesaid monastery [lacuna] has been secured and established by the written decree of the king of the Franks [lacuna], so by our apostolic authority, as stated above, [lacuna], moved by the prayers of your aforesaid legate, Abbot Arnulf, and through the aforesaid royal decrees and other privileges [lacuna], we confirm and establish in perpetuity for you and your successors, to hold, and henceforth to administer and govern with fear of God, that no king, no prince, no count, no margrave, no judge, nor any person, great or small, shall ever presume to inflict violence or invasion upon that monastery or upon its appurtenances.

Therefore, under the solemn appeal to divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we decree that none of our pontifical successors, and, as we stated above, no person, great or small, shall dare or presume to act in any matter against this our apostolic privilege, or attempt to violate it.

If anyone, which we do not believe, should attempt to violate it in any matter, let him know that, unless he repents, by the authority of almighty God, of the holy prince of the apostles Peter, and of us, who exercise his vicariate, he is to be indissolubly bound by the chains of anathema, excluded from the kingdom of God, burned in eternal fire with the devil and his most terrible pomp and with Judas, the betrayer of Our Lord Jesus Christ, and, plunged into the infernal abyss and Tartarean chaos, let him perish with the ungodly.

Written by the hand of Stephen, notary and scrinarius of the holy and apostolic Roman Church, in the month of December, in the aforementioned tenth indiction. Farewell.

### XV. Privilege of Pope Agapetus II Granted to Maimbod, Bishop of Mâcon. (Years 946–954.) He confirms the privileges and possessions of the canons of the Church of Saint Vincent of Mâcon.

[In Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XVIII, col. 411.]

**Agapetus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy Maimbod, bishop of the Church of Mâcon, and to his successors in perpetuity.**

Since the condition of all the holy churches of God is advanced by the teachings of the blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, and since those things that have fallen are restored through his support, it is right that the holy Church of Mâcon, suffering the diminution of its diocese and deprived of the abundance of its dignities, be quickly restored, so that it may not lose its honor.

Therefore, recognizing that it has been shaken in every respect, it is fitting for us to extend our helping right hand toward its restoration, so that, having drunk from the fountain of the blessed apostle Peter, it may, with Christ’s help, be restored to its honors. And therefore let all the worshipers and faithful of the holy churches of God know that Maimbod, the beloved bishop and our spiritual son, represented to our apostolic benevolence that we should grant to his canons and to the laymen residing in the Church of Saint Vincent the Martyr that they should not appoint a bishop there from elsewhere, except one whom the canons, together with the aforesaid religious laymen, have elected among themselves, as the sacred canons decree. We also grant to him and to his successors that the honor due to them be rendered at all times.

To the aforesaid canons we grant and confirm all the possessions that have been given in that place through royal decrees or through the generosity of the faithful of Christ, both men and women, so that they may hold them irrevocably and forever, without anyone’s contradiction.

Likewise, the abbey of Saint Clement the Martyr, situated in the suburb of the aforesaid city, with all its entirety, churches, lands, female servants, male tenants and female tenants belonging to it; and also the church of Saint Desiderius situated in the village of Vergiaco, together with the small estate of Saint Peter adjoining it from the bishopric in the aforesaid village; and likewise the church of Saint Romanus situated in the village of Cathenac [or Cadeniac].

Moreover, the ninths and tithes and the revenues from the mills [reading uncertain: *ex furtis*, perhaps *ex furnis*] of the aforesaid district, and the third part of the woodland beside the River Saône, extending from the river and the village of Adolan, just as the pious King Louis, our beloved son, granted them, with the assent of the aforementioned Bishop Maimbod concerning the tithes and land, and with the joint consent of Hugh, the margrave, and Leotald, the most honorable count, whose heart burned wholly for the increase of the aforesaid church.

Therefore, through this our apostolic privilege, we grant them to be held perpetually, together with the tithes of Saint Alban the Martyr and Gisario, so that from now and henceforth they may hold and possess, without anyone’s interference or harassment, whatever has been donated or granted in that place, or whatever divine mercy may hereafter choose to increase there, by whatever person.

This, however, on the condition that no king, duke, count, tax collector or public official shall presume to impose upon them any forced service, coercion, burden or command, except whatever the faithful canons of the aforesaid place may wish to grant to any person on account of his goodness.

Establishing and promulgating this before God and his terrible judgment, by the firm foundation of this our apostolic privilege we decree, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and we solemnly charge both the future pontiffs of the apostolic see and those who perform ecclesiastical functions, as well as persons great and small, that no one, whatever dignity he may possess, shall in any way have permission to separate or alienate from the frequently named place any of all these provisions granted by us, especially those joined to the grace of apostolic intercession.

If anyone meanwhile, which we do not believe, should attempt with reckless boldness to oppose what has been piously and firmly established by our authority through this privilege, or should presume in any way to resist or transgress what has been orderly established by us for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid church, let him know that, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose unworthy vicars we are, he is bound by the bond of anathema and is to be burned with the devil and his most terrible pomp in the punishment of eternal fire.

But whoever proves himself a pious guardian and observer in all things, preserving this our apostolic decree directed toward the worship of God, may he receive eternal blessing from our most merciful Lord God and deserve to become a participant in eternal life.

### XVI. Letter of Pope Agapetus II to the Auvergnats. (Years 946–955.) Raiders are to be kept away from the Monastery of Celsinianus.

[In D. Bouquet, *Collection of Historians*, IX, 232.]

**Agapetus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the sons of the holy Church of God dwelling in Auvergne: perpetual peace and eternal salvation in Christ Jesus.**

We are suspended in immense astonishment as to why those to whom pastoral care has been entrusted among you keep the eyes of their minds closed; why they allow the holy Church, as has been reported to us, to be torn apart by the fury of the wicked, laid waste and stripped of its possessions, without presenting themselves as a wall for the house of Israel, and without standing in battle on the day of the Lord so as to oppose robbers and raiders by their authority. They see their own mother dishonored, yet remain silent and do not rebuke the perpetrators with harsh denunciation.

For we seem either to ignore or not to fear at all that terrible voice which said: “Cursed is he who withholds his sword from blood” (Jeremiah 48:10). Therefore we commiserate with all of you, fearing that God’s anger, beginning from his sanctuary—that is, from the prelates—may by a just judgment be permitted to rage against their sheep.

You know, brothers—and let anyone who does not know learn—that the place of Celsinianus, from the time it was founded, was specially entrusted to the holy Roman Church and has remained under its protection from the beginning. We decree that it should be loved with special affection and have judged that it should always be exalted with manifold honor. Nor is this without reason, for the life-giving fragrance of the monastic order rising from that place now appears, by God’s gift, to spread beneficially through our regions.

Therefore we ask, entreat and urgently beseech you to take care to show reverence to the aforesaid place, and let no one presume to disturb those who serve God there. If anyone unjustly holds any land belonging to the aforesaid monastery, or anything belonging to the monks themselves or to their household, against the will of the abbot of that monastery, we command by our apostolic authority that he hasten to restore it without delay.

If he does not do so, we order him to come before our presence and give a reasonable account. But if he also scorns to do this, let him be punished and struck down, bound by terrible anathema and our excommunication—we who, although unworthy, appear to exercise the vicariate of blessed Peter—because he did not fear unjustly to invade his [the monastery’s] lands.

Therefore, on our behalf, we specially exhort and command Lord Stephen, bishop of Auvergne, in whose diocese the monastery of Celsinianus is situated, not to delay striking with the sword of excommunication all who lay waste to the possessions of that monastery or inflict any harm upon the household of the monks residing there, and to exclude them from the thresholds of the holy Church of God until they are compelled to make amends with worthy satisfaction.

### XVII. Letter of Agapetus II to Landulf, Prince of Capua. (Years 946–955.) He warns him not to violate the liberty of the monastery of Capua.

[Gattula, *History of Cassino*, 190.]

**Agapetus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Landulf, prince of Capua.**

We have heard—and cannot speak of it without the greatest sorrow of heart—that the monks of the monastery of Cassino are behaving dishonorably and disgracefully. No faithful person is unaware how pernicious and wicked this is, for, as the Prophet testifies: “The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” (Lamentations 4:1). Those who ought to serve God in the monastery, as the rule of blessed Benedict prescribes, appear to be living while wandering through castles and streets. Thus, abandoning the regular life and serving their own will and their pleasures, as the rule of blessed Benedict prescribes, the pleasure of their desires is their law—not the Lord’s, but their own enclosures.

This evil falls upon the head of your late father Landulf, who, building what was virtually a monastery within the city of Capua, desired to subject the monastery to his own dominion—not out of reverence for God, but greedy for the honor of worldly glory and making light of the danger to souls, and perversely longing to recline with a diseased flock, so that possession of the entire aforesaid monastery might be left to his own people as though by hereditary right.

We therefore grieve exceedingly and wonder at the blind greed of so great a man, who did not reconsider that, after the church of Cassino had been burned and overturned, he took its possessions, contrary to the sentence of the Prophet who says: “All the princes who said, ‘Let us take possession of the sanctuary of God as our inheritance’: My God, make them like a wheel, and like stubble before the face of the wind, and like a fire that burns the forests, and like a flame setting the mountains ablaze” (Psalm 82:13–15). May God avert these things from him, if that is possible.

Frequently admonished while he was alive, and, as Abbot Baldwin himself testifies, in the presence of his bishop, he acknowledged himself guilty and restored the aforesaid monastery with all its possessions in full to that abbot, leaving neither to himself nor to his descendants any further power of domination.

Now, giving thanks to God, out of reverence for the blessed Father Benedict, we have decided that the aforesaid monastery of Cassino, together with that abbot, should govern the monastery of Capua and that it should be strengthened by the privilege of our authority. By the authority of God and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we establish and order that in that monastery of Capua—which was built not out of love for God but out of worldly greed—one or two, or at most three, elderly monks of unquestioned life shall remain to govern and guard it.

But all the other monks, both older and younger, together with all the possessions of the monastery, shall return to their proper monastery on Mount Cassino, there to serve God and live under the rule of that blessed Father Benedict, just as our predecessors, emperors and kings established and promulgated in ancient times: namely, that it should in no way be subjected to the dominion of any prince, duke, gastald, or any person, great or small. So too, under our protection and that of the kings, and under the governance of the abbot, it shall be perpetually governed and administered with fear of God.

For if anyone, which we do not believe, should presume to act otherwise, or attempt to make any arrangement concerning that monastery, or presume to seize any of the possessions of the aforesaid monastery, and attempt in any matter to violate this our apostolic command, let him know that, unless he repents, by the authority of God and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of us, who exercise *in caricationem* [sic], he is excommunicated, deprived of entrance into the church and of the body and blood of Christ, and separated from the fellowship of Christians. Let him know again that by the sanction of this privilege he is bound by the chains of anathema.

But whoever proves himself its guardian, observer and helper, may he obtain abundantly from Christ the Lord, our God, the grace of blessing and heavenly recompense. We order the aforesaid monastery to retain this apostolic command as a future testimony.

### XVIII. Letter of Pope Agapetus II to William, Archbishop of Mainz. (Year 955.) He grants the same privilege that Maximus II had granted to Frideric.

[In Wurdtwein, *Letters of Saint Boniface*, p. 375.]

Moved by fraternal love and surrounded by the faith of the ancients, we do not know how to deny to you and to the holy Church of Mainz, over which you preside, those things on account of which we know that you sent your messengers to the holy see of the prince of the apostles and to our apostolic dignity, and which our predecessors denied to your predecessors.

We know, however, from your letters, which report that your predecessor Saint Boniface received from Gregory II, Gregory III and Zacharias, our predecessors, and also from our predecessor Marinus, that Frideric, our brother and your predecessor, was appointed overseer of the holy see of Mainz, as apostolic vicar and legate throughout all the regions of Germany and Gaul.

Thus, if he found men deviating from the straight path of justice, whatever their status, he had apostolic authority to summon them before him, admonish and correct them wherever he wished, and establish a synod wherever he wished.

Therefore, since you profess the faith, submission and other obligations that, as you acknowledge, all the former overseers of the holy see of Mainz professed, we grant you the same power that our earlier apostolic men granted to your predecessors, so that in our place you may have authority to rebuke wicked men and those of evil life, and to recall them to the way of truth by your exhortations.

As you know, as our vicar and legate in the regions of Germany and Gaul, wherever you find bishops, priests, deacons or even monks, whatever their status, transgressing against the canons and the constitutions of the holy Fathers or against ecclesiastical rule, do not fail to correct them by apostolic authority according to the canons and the constitutions of the holy Fathers and to lead them back to the way of truth.

We also grant you, as overseer and metropolitan of the see of Mainz, authority to establish a synod wherever you please in the regions of Germany and Gaul, without contradiction from anyone.

If anyone, which God forbid, should wish to oppose you as apostolic vicar by appealing to the apostolic see, let him know that, before the time appointed by you has ended, he is to be deprived of apostolic blessing and bound by the bond of anathema.

We also draw up a privilege for the holy see of Mainz, so that if anyone, whatever his status, should wish to plunder it on account of its ancient [lacuna], he himself shall be plundered; and unless he repents, he shall be handed over, bound by the eternal bond of anathema, to the apostolic majesty, which has been given power to bind and loose. On the day of judgment—[the preceding printed words, *in die omnium proditore*, are corrupt or uncertain]—he shall render an account for it there.

### XIX. Privilege of Pope Agapetus II for the Monastery of Saints Stephen, Dionysius and Sylvester in Capite. (Year 955.)

[Note: This is an illustrious and, in many respects, important document—if only the notary Ognissanti had known or been able to read it better in the year 1277, when the original papyrus still existed. The same should nevertheless be said of the document that follows, which is in every respect the same as this one but contains very extensive variants; both contain many errors, as do all the others transmitted by those who made a profession of reading old documents in the twelfth, thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Both were known to the historian of the Church of Saint Sylvester in Capite, Giovanni Giacchetti (*Iconologia Salvatoris*, etc., Rome, 1628, p. 80, and *History of the Church of Saint Sylvester*, Rome, 1629, pp. 10 ff.), and the first also to Crescimbeni (*History of Saint Mary in Cosmedin*, p. 10), and now to Abbot Carletti, who recently published another history of that church (pp. 11, 24, 179, 181, 184, 214). They reproduce excerpts from them and the subscription of that notary. In place of *privilegio carticinio*—the privilege on paper—which someone responding to the paper document mentioned at the beginning had read, Giacchetti, who perhaps did not understand the meaning, read *privilegio exemplato*. The present bull cites Oldoino in the additions to Ciacconio, and Ughelli in the section on Sergius, bishop of Nepi.]

[Marini, *Diplomatic Papyri*, I, 38.]

In the name of the Lord. This is a copy of the privilege written below, composed on paper, whose wording is in every respect as follows, insofar as it could scarcely be read.

AGAPETUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ LEo, [Note: [Col. 0915D] An abbot of this name is mentioned in a fragmentary parchment published by Carletti (p. 186); but since in the year 988, in papyrus CVI, a Leo, abbot of St. Sylvester, is likewise mentioned, we cannot say to which of the two the parchment belongs; it might even concern a third Abbot Leo.] a religious son, priest, and monk, and abbot instituted and appointed by us over the venerable monastery of the holy martyrs of Christ, Stephen and Dionysius, and of the confessor Sylvester, which is called *cata Pauli* [Note: [Col. 0915D] That is, “at Paul’s” (*ad Pauli [domum]*); and it is known that this church really was built in the house of Pope Paul I (see Baronius under the year 761, no. 2).

Carletti (p. 11) ought not to have declared such a designation a corrupted word: it consisted, from its origin, not of one word but of two, and at that time—and for many centuries earlier—the Greek preposition *cata* was widely used in place of the Latin *ad*. In papyrus LXXV we shall find *cata ipso Zenobio* (“at Zenobius himself”); and in the Bavarian papyrus codex (p. 33), the monasteries of St. John *cata paterie* (later wrongly transformed into *in casa pateria*) ([the] bull of Alexander III in the possession of the distinguished Count Fantuzzi, *Monumenta Ravennatia*, vol. II, p. 139), and of St. Mary of the Xenodochium *cata portam S. Laurentii* (pp. 14 and 18).

Alexandria near Issus was called *cata Isson* by the anonymous Ravennate, and corruptly *Catisson* in the Peutinger Table. The Romans are also thoroughly familiar with the churches of St. Andrew *cata Barbara*, and of St. Stephen *cata Galla patricia*, as well as the cemetery *ad nymphas cata Bassi*. Two miles outside the Appian Gate they likewise had a monument, perhaps named from some low relief in which Cerberus, *cata cane tricapita* (“with the three-headed dog”), [lacuna] as a document from the Subiaco register of 850 says, published by Monsignor Galletti (*Primic.*, p. 187); although I believe that it was, or ought to have been, written *cata cane tricapite* (“with the three-headed dog”).

To these examples—which should all be added to those cited by Du Cange under the word *cata*—I shall add three inscriptions. One was cited above in the notes to papyrus IV, in which we read: *IN REGIONE QUINTA DOMV ET HORTV CATA QD ANNIBONIV* (“in the fifth region, house and garden at the former [property] of Annibonius”). The second, though incomplete, stands in the portico of St. Peter with a donation of St. Gregory, more probably II than III; it has *CATA PETRUM VESTARARIUM* (see the *Bullarium Vaticanum*, vol. I, p. 18), a name absent from the *vesterarii* listed by the aforementioned Galletti, among whom it deserved precedence by age, and *CATA GEMMULV. MAG. MIL.* (“at Gemmulus, distinguished soldier”). Of this Gemmulus there is a record in the register of the Roman Church’s patrimonies and estates, where it is said that Gregory II had indeed leased: “to the soldier Gemmulus, an estate; to Mauricius, an estate on the Via Nova, Via Prenestina, at approximately the milestone, out of the body of the Varvarian *massa* [estate]” (*Deus dedit*, in the appendix to Cardinal Borgia’s *Brief History*, p. 10).

Finally, the third inscription contains the words *ANIMA SANCTA CATA NOMEN BENEDICTA* (“holy soul, blessed by name”), which Fabretti did not understand (ch. 10, no. 469). He thought that *CATA* had to be emended to *casta* (“chaste”), and by that name called the deceased woman, who in fact was named Benedicta. The author of that brief epitaph, wishing to say something quite ordinary—namely, that she was blessed in name and in life, or in deed—used the phrase *cata nomen* appropriately.] of Paul, once pope, and to your success... [lacuna] abbots and monks dwelling in the same monastery, forever.

It befits apostolic governance to aid with benevolent compassion those distinguished by pious devotion and thereafter, through the glad devotion of the mind and perpetual assent, to gain from this venerable [lacuna] a most worthy reward and profit before the Creator of all, for those who merit forgiveness from the Lord, or, if venerable places of saints established for the better are without doubt brought to a better condition.

Therefore, since your religious devotion has humbly asked our apostolate that we should [lacuna] and confirm for you and your successors in perpetuity the aforesaid monastery, with all its churches, buildings, and appurtenances, both within it and also together around it, and the mountain called Augustus of Saint Angelus at the summit of the [lacuna] mountain, together with the vineyards and lands around the same mountain, and the church of Saint Nicholas in its entirety with all its appurtenances—as its boundaries indicate: on one side, the public road that leads beneath the arch of the aqueduct called the Virgin, and on the [lacuna] side, the aqueduct itself; the aqueduct of the Virgin itself and the mountain called Pinzi; on the third side, the wall of this city of Rome, and the Gate of Saint Valentine; and on the fourth side, the wall of this city, extending back as far as the Posterula that belongs to Saint Agatha, and the road beside the Posterula that runs beside the aforesaid church to the public road, together with the arable land held by Constantius, a noble man, and also the public road that runs through the Posterula from the Pigna, the church of Saint Blaise, and proceeds to the aforesaid aqueduct of the Virgin, with the lands [lacuna] and grants.

We also confirm for you the entire monastery of Saint Valentine.

[Note: Concerning the church of Saint Valentine outside the Gate of the People—called for that reason on some occasions Saint Valentine—and its vicissitudes and memories, see the hagiographer Enschenius in volume II of February (p. 151), where whatever is read elsewhere is stated, as well as the fact that it was one of the twenty privileged abbeys of Rome, of which John the Deacon and Peter Mallius speak in their works published by Mabillon (*Mus. Ital.*, vol. II, pp. 160, 574). Two old inscriptions of the tenth and eleventh centuries belong to it: one now existing in the portico of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, and the other in the church of Saint Sylvester in Capite, at the altar of Saint Dionysius, certainly carried there after that church was demolished. It is readily understood how one of them came to be repaired in Saint Sylvester, to whose monastery it had been joined since the time of Sergius II (Carletti, p. 179), while nevertheless retaining its own monks and abbot; the other must have been carried, Heaven knows how and when, to the vicinity of that basilica, and was found there in several pieces at the beginning of the seventeenth century, as I learn from the manuscript of the Donian Inscriptions preserved in the Barberina Library (p. 533; see Crescimbeni, p. 81). On their evidence, some uncritical writers have asserted that another church of Saint Valentine formerly existed near Saint Mary in Cosmedin. Crescimbeni could never find any record of it, and correctly realized that the two inscriptions belonged to one and the same church. But because the inscription at Saint Sylvester had not yet been properly read [Col. 0918C], and had been attributed to Nicholas I rather than to Nicholas II, he thought that the same abbot Theobald was named in both inscriptions (p. 99); this is false. It is indeed true that two Theobalds made handsome gifts and benefactions to that church or monastery, but the first is not said to have been an abbot, whereas the second was one, certainly abbot of Saint Valentine and not of Saint Sylvester, as Giacchetti thought (*History of Saint Sylvester*, p. 41), and now Carletti also thinks (pp. 34 and 179). To Carletti alone is due the accurate woodcut engraving of the inscription, although it has not always been interpreted and supplemented perfectly. But since he was convinced that the abbot named there was abbot of Saint Sylvester, he finds himself compelled to maintain that the works mentioned were all carried out in the church of that saint and not in the extramural church of Saint Valentine.]

with all its buildings and adjacent properties, and its appurtenances everywhere, namely, outside the Gate of Saint Valentine, belonging by right to your aforesaid monastery. Moreover, we grant and confirm to you the Milvian Bridge in its entirety, with all its entrance and exit, its payments and tolls, and likewise vacant arable land of approximately [lacuna] modii of wheat, with everything belonging to it, situated before the aforesaid Gate of Saint Valentine beside the frequently mentioned wall of this city of Rome. Its boundaries are: on one side, the Fossatum—that is, the Carbonaria—between that wall and the same land, which from there extends [Col. 0917C] as far as the great river [lacuna]; [lacuna]; the public road that leads to and from Saint Valentine; and on the fourth side, property belonging to the Holy Roman Church.

Likewise, another piece of arable land in its entirety, with all its appurtenances and everything belonging to it, situated on the right as one goes toward Saint Valentine, with the great arch beneath it called Passarana [lacuna], in the place called [Col. 0918A] the Fish Garden, between the following boundaries: on one side, the aforesaid public road; on the second side, the fountain of living water that is held in common between the aforesaid monastery and the heirs [lacuna] of the late Gregory [Note: Torrigio had already noted in the Vatican Grottoes (p. 527), on the strength of a badly damaged parchment from the archive of the Vatican Basilica dating from 1037, that the keepers and chamberlains of Saint Peter’s Confession formed a corporate body and were also called mansionarii of the schola of the Confession of blessed Peter, as this Gregory is called.], mansionary of the schola of the Confession of Blessed Peter; and extending as far as the head of the ancient wall; on the third side, land belonging to the venerable monastery of Saint Cyriacus, which is called Via Lata, running straight upward by the boundary across the level of the mountain called Bassitulo; and on the fourth side, the public road that descends through the valley called after the aforesaid Bussitudo and emerges onto the Flaminian Way.

We further confirm for you the entire estate called Girulo, with its various trees and everything generally belonging to it, just as the series of documents appears to show that it belongs to you [Col. 0918B]. It is situated about one mile, more or less, from the city of Rome, beyond the aforesaid Gate of Saint Valentine, between these boundaries: on one side, the public road paved with ancient flint, which descends as far as Sanguinaria; on the second side, the small channel of living water issuing below the mountain of the aforesaid Girulo, or the meadow of the venerable monastery of Saint Cyriacus; on the third side, the mountain above the aforesaid mountain of Saint Valentine, or the arable land belonging by right to your aforesaid monastery, held by the heirs of the late Romanus of the Campus Martius; and on the fourth side [lacuna].

Likewise, we confirm to you in its entirety an estate called Pelajolum, with its arable lands, fields, meadows, pastures, mountains, and plain, on which the deserted church of Saint Sylvester was situated [Col. 0918C], together with everything generally belonging to it, just as formerly Albericus, senator of all the Romans [Note: Concerning this most noble and powerful senator of all the Romans—who liked to call himself by that title—and concerning his brothers, I shall mention several matters in the notes on Pope C.], formerly gave it to your aforesaid monastery in exchange, by a charter of exchange in which he and his brothers and sisters subscribed and consented with their own hands, namely Constantius, a noble man; Sergius [Col. 0919A], bishop of the holy Church of Nepi; together with Bertha and another Bertha, on account of the valley of Saint Vitus, which the aforesaid Albericus donated to the venerable monastery of Saint Agnes. This estate, which was situated outside the Gate [lacuna], about one mile from the city of Rome beside the Tiber, had the following boundaries: on one side, the place called Gurgini; on the second side, the river Tiber, or arable land with its meadow belonging to the venerable monastery of Saint Basil, situated in the schola of the Dead, together with another piece of land; also with its meadow belonging to the venerable monastery of Saint Mary on the Aventine; and another piece of land with a meadow belonging to Gregory of the Campus Martius; on the third side, the estate of the Six Columns and the mountain called Mollario; and on the fourth side [lacuna], belonging to [lacuna].

Likewise, one entire meadow, just as you hold it beyond the Solar Bridge, in the place called Fliscari, which has the following boundaries: on one side, the Fossatum; on the second side, the meadow [lacuna]; on the third side [lacuna]; and on the fourth side, the meadow held by Benedict, bishop of Silva Candida [Note: This bishop is missing from Ughelli’s series—or, better, he is not in his proper place, since the Benedict named as bishop of Silva Candida in the year 884 is the Benedict of this bull. Nor is the bull cited by Ughelli one of Marinus I, but of Marinus II, from the year 944. See Gattola, *History of Monte Cassino* (vol. I, p. 95), and Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals* (vol. III, pp. 435, 437).].

Also an entire estate called Gallorum, or Balneolum and Paccianum, or by whatever other names it may have been called, just as it was originally, as formerly John, called Oudinus, offered it to your aforesaid monastery by a charter of donation, with arable lands, sand quarries, fields, meadows, pastures, masonry buildings and adjacent properties, plain and wells and springs, cultivated or uncultivated, with everything generally and wholly belonging to it. It is situated beyond the Salarian Bridge, approximately one mile from that bridge, between the following boundaries: on one side, the estate that belonged to Roserius Peter, remaining there; on the second side, an ancient wall and the land that formerly belonged to the late Maczo, son of the sacellarius, now held by Ylpizo, a noble man; on the third side, the land of Stephanus son of Theodorus [Note: Contelori did not know this prefect of Rome.]; and on the fourth side, the sand quarry called Serpentaria and another vacant piece of land beside it, belonging by right to the venerable monastery of Saint Vitus.

Also two entire pieces of arable land, placed there beside the same estate and beside the aforesaid quarry, on the side of that quarry, between boundaries on two sides consisting of land that formerly belonged to the aforesaid Rosa and that lies above it; on the third side, land of the heir of Leo Camburlingus; and on the fourth side, the public road [Col. 0919D] belonging by right to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Vitus.

Likewise, one entire Column [Note: Concerning the right possessed over the Antonine Column by the monastery of Saint Sylvester in Capite, see Crescimbeni (loc. cit., p. 13), Carletti (p. 182), and the fine inscription of the year 1119 in Galletti (*Roman Inscriptions*, vol. I, p. 506). The Trajanic Column also once belonged to the monastery of Saint Cyriacus; see the same Galletti (*Primicerius*, p. 323) and Martinelli (*First Trophy of the Second Cross*, p. 106).], the larger one, called the Antonine Column, in its entirety, with a chamber beneath it and vacant land around it, just as it appears to be enclosed on every side by a public road, situated inside this city.

Likewise, beyond the Nomentan Bridge, an entire estate called Lampati, with everything belonging to it, bounded on three sides by the river called the Tiverone and on the fourth side by the Fossatum and the public road belonging by right to the monastery of Saint Lawrence called Palacina.

Also one cesina of approximately [lacuna] modii, with sand quarries, divided masonry walls, and everything belonging to it, situated outside the Gate of Saint John, approximately [lacuna] miles from the city of Rome. Its boundaries are: on two sides, land belonging to Adrian, a noble man, son of the late Adrian [Note: He was an archarius (treasury official) in 943, as is established by a charter reproduced by the same Galletti (ibid., p. 198).]; on the third side, land belonging to the heir of the late Stephanus Chaumatus; and on the fourth side, an aqueduct.

Moreover, other arable lands placed there with their various trees, just as the series of documents appears to show that they belong to you, with everything belonging to them, situated beyond the aforesaid Gate, approximately six miles from the city. Their boundaries are: on one side, the land of Stephanus Denimentis [lacuna] of Theodorus the prefect; on the second side, land belonging to the heir of the late Theodorus of the Aventine; on the third side, land called Morani; and on the fourth side, the aforesaid aqueduct. Also the estate called the Seven Basins, with its appurtenances, between it and another piece of land and other arable cesinae, just as you hold them, in the place called Mil. fixo, beyond the aforesaid Gate of Saint John.

Furthermore, we confirm for you three entire estates. One is called the Ninth Bridge, within that bridge, with various arable lands and their trees, or sand quarries, its various and ruined walls [Col. 0920C], and those that are covered by construction, cultivated or uncultivated, with everything generally and wholly belonging to them. It is situated beyond the aforesaid Gate of Saint John, now called the Latin Way, approximately nine miles from the city of Rome. Its boundaries are: on one side, the aforesaid aqueduct called Claudia and the aforesaid bridge called the Ninth; on the second side, the aforementioned aqueduct called Abeberatorium; on the third side, the aforesaid Corte of Morenus; and on the fourth side, the boundary that runs beside the quarry called Ardenda, belonging by right to the Holy Roman Church.

Likewise, another entire estate called the domnical estate, in which there is a deserted church with its crypts and masonry walls, with arable lands and various fruit-bearing and productive trees of different kinds [Col. 0920D], cultivated or uncultivated, and everything belonging to it. It is situated on the aforesaid Latin Way beside the previously named estate of the Ninth Bridge. Its boundaries are: on one side, that estate; on the second side, the running stream called Papati; on the third side, the public road with ancient flint; and on the fourth side, the greater aqueduct [Col. 0921A] and the estate called the Seven Vassia, with everything belonging to it.

Also another entire estate called Casana, with various other places and their names, namely the valley of Marcianus, Pretiosa House, the mountain called Paulelli, and the field called Albanensis—or by whatever other names they are or originally were called—with arable lands, woods, various trees, and working watermills, as well as the deserted church of Saint Peter with everything generally and wholly belonging to it. It is situated on the aforesaid Latin Way, approximately ten miles from the city, between these boundaries: on one side, land where there were formerly meadows called Pauli; on the second side, the estate called Civitella; on the third side, the vineyard of the aforesaid monastery, and the public road that descends to the place called the Seat of Saint Peter; and on the fourth side, the deserted church called Saint Mary in Diaconia. From there the boundary descends through the ditch as far as the aforesaid [lacuna], or whatever other boundaries there are or originally were, belonging by right to the venerable monastery of the apostle Saint Andrew and Saint Bartholomew, called that of Honorius.

Moreover, one entire church called Saint Angelus, with vineyards or lands around it or at a distance from it, and with everything generally and wholly belonging to them, just as you hold them in your hands, situated in the Appian patrimony, in Alban territory, approximately [lacuna] miles from the city of Rome, on the mountain called Crescentulus. Its boundaries are: on two sides, the land of the Mountain belonging to the heir of the late Dominicus, who was called Cacainboctes, as indicated from the boundary [Col. 0921C] and by trees; on the second side, a boundary line running through trees and along the side of land held by Peter the physician, reaching the boundary that is beside the vineyard of the venerable monastery of Saint Mary, called that on the Aventine; and on the third and fourth sides [lacuna].

Also a vineyard of the aforesaid monastery called that on the Aventine, together with a vineyard [lacuna] in its entirety, with its entrance and its revenue at the Calcatorium, and everything belonging to it, situated in Alban territory, approximately [lacuna] miles from the city of Rome. Its boundaries are: on one side, the vineyard that belonged to Aczo Accaritus, and the vineyard of the venerable monastery of Saint Lawrence outside the walls; on the second side, the vineyard of Aczo of Albano; on the third side, the vineyard of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary of the Aventine; and on the fourth side, another vineyard of the aforementioned monastery of Saint Lawrence outside the walls, and a vineyard [lacuna].

Also four entire pieces of vineyard, with revenue at the Calcatorium and their entrance, and everything belonging to them, in the same territory, in the place called Rufi. Their boundaries are: on two sides, the vineyard of Lady Marozza; on the third side, a vineyard [lacuna]; and on the fourth side, a vineyard belonging to the venerable Saint Sabba, called Cellanova, with an entrance through that vineyard from the Greater Flint Road.

Also a vineyard [lacuna] with revenue at the Calcatorium and its entrance from the Greater Flint Road, and everything belonging to it, situated in the territory of Ariccia, in the place called Cucuruczii. Its boundaries are: on one side, the aforesaid Flint Road; on the second side, a vineyard [lacuna]; on the third side, the road leading to the wall called the Long Wall; and on the fourth side, a vineyard [lacuna].

And we grant you in its entirety the estate called Zizinni, with the church of Saint Mary, vineyards, lands, or a watermill, and quarries, just as you hold them in your hands, situated in the aforesaid Alban territory, approximately thirteen miles from the city of Rome, belonging by right to our chief vestararius, and yielding three gold solidi. Its boundaries are: on one side, the estate of Saint Euphemia and the vineyard of Ursus, formerly primicerius [Note: This often-mentioned Ursus the primicerius was known to M. Galletti from a Farfa charter that records him as dead in 1003 (p. 80).]; on the second side, the vineyard of the heir of the late Gausbertus; on the third side, the public road [Col. 0922B] and the plantation of venerable Stephanus; and on the fourth side, the estate called Luczano.

Also two pieces of vineyard in the place called Honorius, in Arician territory, just as you hold them in your hands—namely, in the aforesaid Arician territory, in the place called [lacuna], a vineyard at the foot of the Greater Flint Road. Its boundaries are: on one side, that aforesaid Flint Road; on the second side, a vineyard [lacuna]; on the third side [lacuna]; and on the fourth side, a vineyard [lacuna] belonging by right to the venerable diaconia of Saint Mary called in Cosmedin.

In the same way, we grant and confirm to you an entire half-share of one salt-pan, in the place called the Great Ditch, just as the series of documents shows that it came to the late Dominicus, who was called Cacainboctes. Its co-owners are the other half belonging to the heir of the late Leo, which together constitutes the whole salt-pan. Its boundaries are: on one side, Benedict’s salt-pan; on the second side, the salt-pan of Salinus, belonging to the aforesaid heir of Dominicus; on the third side, the aforesaid Great Ditch; and on the fourth side [lacuna].

Also the salt-pan belonging to the heir of the late John the Elder, belonging by right to [lacuna].

Likewise, another entire salt-pan belonging to Saint Sylvester, in the place called Campo Malo. Its boundaries are: on one side [lacuna]; and on the second side, another property of your aforesaid monastery.

We also confirm for you an entire working watermill in the river Tiber beside the Saxon schola, situated there, just as the late Alto Achomatus granted you that same watermill. Its boundaries are: on one side, a watermill [lacuna]; on the second side, the watermill of Benedict Virgarius of Saint Peter’s Gate, with his other co-owners; on the third side, the greater harbor of that river; and on the fourth side, the public road by which one descends to those watermills, with its fastening and entrance, and with all its equipment, together with everything belonging to it, just as our predecessor John offered it to your monastery by a written precept. Likewise, by a written privilege he granted and confirmed to you in the aforesaid river Tiber, before the sewer, with water beyond it, for the construction of another watermill.
