Within these boundaries are, on one side, the watermill of the venerable monastery of Saint Mary in the Capitol, and the watermill of Leo [Note: The very well-known chief scriniarius, who later became Leo VIII (see Galletti, cited above, p. 142).], chief [Col. 0923A] scriniarius; on the second side, half of the same river; on the third side, the watermill of Theophilatus the nomenclator [Note: Here is another nomenclator named Theophilatus, of whom the most diligent and industrious bishop of Cyrene has not spoken to us. The person who was such in the years 826 and 829 should not be mentioned in our bull (Galletti, pp. 165, 183)]; and the watermill of the venerable monastery of Saint Cyriacus, called that on Via Lata; and on the fourth side, the public road belonging by right to the person to whom it belongs.

Furthermore, the entire monastery of Saint Terentianus, with all the cells listed below, namely those of Saint Stephen and Saint Mary, as well as the cell of Saint Benedict, Saint Sylvester, and Saint Valentine, together with all its buildings, adjacent properties, and appurtenances everywhere, situated in the territory of Polimarco, belonging by right to the venerable monastery of Saint Lawrence, martyr of Christ, called Outside the Walls, of this [lacuna] [Col. 0923B] serving Roman citizen, yielding [lacuna].

Moreover, I confirm to you Paternum in its entirety, with its names; likewise, the entire Massa called Majana, with all its places and names, namely the estates of Tujanum, Pollejanum, Anticuum, Sutanum, Occanum, Betujanum, Terentianum, Centumcelle, or by whatever other names they are now called, with vineyards, lands, woods, houses, male and female tenants of both sexes residing there and belonging to it, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, willow groves, fruit-bearing and fruitless trees of various kinds, wells, bridges, streams, and permanent masonry buildings, cultivated or uncultivated, with everything generally and wholly belonging to them. It is situated in Ortan territory, approximately forty miles from the city of Rome, belonging by right to your aforesaid monastery.

Likewise, we establish for you various small estates situated inside that city of Orte [Col. 0923C], together with all immovable lands and properties belonging by right to your aforesaid monastery, both within that city of Orte and outside it in various places called [lacuna], and the charters truthfully made concerning them.

Again, in the same Ortan territory, we confirm for you the church of Saint Juvenal, martyr of Christ, with all its appurtenances in their entirety, just as it appears to belong to you from the same bishopric of Orte.

Again, we establish for you all immovable properties belonging to your aforesaid monastery within the city of Gallese and everywhere in its territory, including three estates called Cazanum, Casinianum, and Cesa of Narni.

Moreover, we grant you the entire estate called Preciliana [lacuna], with everything generally and wholly belonging to it, situated in Sabine territory, belonging by right to the Holy Roman Church. Its boundaries are: on one side, the Massa called Pausa; on the second side, the stream of Utriculum called Butino; on the third side, property of the monastery of Saint Mary; and on the fourth side, property of the monastery of Saint Saviour.

We also confirm for you the estate of Campo Morto beyond Albano, which lies between the city of Orte [lacuna].

Nevertheless, we confirm for you all properties belonging by jurisdiction to your aforesaid monastery in Nepi territory, and Casamala, namely the estate called Casanova, and Bovarico and Boltejano, together with male and female servants of both sexes residing there and belonging to the aforesaid monastery; and we also confirm for you those properties which, according to the documentary records of the same monastery, belong to you in that monastery’s aforesaid territory from the late Alto Achomatus.

Again, we confirm for you in its entirety the estate called Pacianum, with everything belonging to it, situated in Sutrine territory. Likewise, we confirm to you all properties belonging by right and authority to your aforesaid monastery throughout Collin territory, in the place called Valle and Tintoriscii, and on the mountain called Asca, as well as at Saint Cassianus, at the Estate, and at Baccaricia, with vineyards and arable lands, woods with their great marsh, together with the male and female tenants residing there and belonging to your aforesaid monastery, and the aforesaid immovable properties belonging by right to the Holy Roman Church and to the aforesaid monastery, or to other former places whose rights are established.

We also confirm to you the entire estate called Ruscitulum, with all its appurtenances generally and wholly, situated in the territory [lacuna], on the Flaminian Way, approximately fourteen miles from the city of Rome, with all its estates and names, namely Sergianum, Staturianum—which is also called Nuce—Saburia, and Pontianum, as well as Bavianum, or by whatever other names it is called [Col. 0924C], with houses, vineyards, lands, woods, and all its boundaries, termini, and boundary lines. Its boundaries are: on one side, the public road that leads into the Fossatum of the heir of the late John [Note: Add him to the very small number of tenth-century grammarians whose names have come down to us. He was alive in 906 and is mentioned by Sergius III in papyrus XXIV, and more than a century later in papyri XLVI and XLVIII.]; straight through that Fossatum to the stream that descends into the bridge called Veneno [lacuna]; on the other side, along the aforesaid public road, running straight through Montecello to the stream, and thence through arable land to the road of Solaro, and from there by the boundary to the Well, and from that Well along to the aforesaid Veneno Bridge. Or whatever other boundaries there are or originally were, belonging by right to those who possess them.

Finally, we confirm to you an entire estate called the rural villa, or by whatever other name it is called, with all its estates and names, houses, vineyards, lands and woods, fields, meadows, pastures, various trees, sand quarries, springs, cultivated or uncultivated, with all its boundaries, termini, and boundary lines, and everything generally and wholly belonging to it, situated in the territory [lacuna], approximately [lacuna] miles from the city of Rome.

Furthermore, we establish and confirm for you all the immovable properties that legally belong to your aforesaid monastery in Rome and everywhere outside Rome, so that the pensions may be paid according to the charters truthfully made concerning them.

As for the aforesaid properties on which you have until now customarily paid a pension at each indiction, we order you to continue paying it at each indiction. But concerning the other aforesaid properties from which, over the course of the years, no pension was paid either by your predecessors or by you, you shall pay nothing; and because of the negligence of the agents of this our see and of your own agents who are established in law, you shall be free from payment without opposition from your predecessors or from you, and henceforth you shall pay nothing further.

Moved by your petitions, for the inviolable restoration and stability of the aforesaid monastery, by the text of this present precept we grant and establish in perpetuity for you and for your successors, the abbots and servants of God of the same venerable monastery, the aforesaid monastery and its immovable properties, male and female servants, and male and female tenants, as they are written out above in due order from the present thirteenth indiction, to be held by you and your successors. You shall without doubt diligently provide for every improvement, construction, or defense needed by the aforesaid places, as they are written above; moreover, no delay shall arise from you in paying the annual pension. Rather, the agents of our Holy Church and of our pious places shall be paid at the proper time.

Therefore, under the dreadful and fearful day of the future judgment, and under the greatest prohibitions of anathema, by the authority of our Lord and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we decree that no one—whether any of our successor pontiffs or any other great or small person, of whatever honor or endowed with whatever dignity—may in any way, by investigation or by any contrivance of ingenuity, dissolve what we have established and confirmed through pious concern for the praise of our Redeemer. Nor may anyone remove or alienate from these same places, possessions, goods, resources, dependents, or personal property anything recognized as belonging to the same venerable monastery. Rather, all these things, as stated above, shall remain wholly and perpetually in the same holy place.

We promulgate and sanction, invoking the power of our almighty God and binding the matter under the dreadful obligation of anathema, that no one shall ever presume to inflict any opposition or malice upon the same monastery or upon its appurtenances, whether through lawsuits or in any places or against any dependents [Col. 0925D], nor hold a court proceeding or carry out a sale, except with the permission of you and your successors.

If, however, any of our successor pontiffs, or any powerful or inferior person, great or small, of whatever honor or endowed with whatever dignity, should presume, by any argument or contrived pretext, to sell, diminish, or in any way rashly oppose what we have established and confirmed for the worship of God; or should attempt to remove or alienate from that holy place any site, possession, or anything recognized as belonging to the aforesaid monastery, let him know that he is bound by an indissoluble anathema through the authority of our Lord and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and is alienated from the kingdom of God. Let him have all the saints of the same monastery, who rest there, as his adversaries; and with them, on the dreadful day of judgment, let him be dragged before the tribunal of almighty God and render an account to those same saints. Let him be assigned with the devil and his most terrible pomp, with Judas, the betrayer of God and our Saviour Jesus Christ, and with all the impious; and let him be burned forever in Tartarus, in unquenchable fire and the abyss of chaos.

But those who are found defending the monastery itself and who, while guarding all that is contained and attached in this apostolic precept of ours, preserve it intact with sincere minds, let them be found at God’s right hand, established in a place of light. Let all the saints of God who rest in the same monastery be firm protectors for them [Col. 0926C], and through their intercessions let them be helped in the present life and, in the future blessedness of the heavenly kingdom, obtain with the angels of God and all the saints and elect the joys of heaven throughout infinite ages.

Written by the hand of Leo, regional notary and scriniarius of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of April, in the aforesaid thirteenth indiction. + Farewell in good health.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, through the hands of Marinus, bishop [Note: This bishop and librarian was not unknown to Ughelli (vol. I, p. 114), through a bull of John XII; Muratori recognized him through a charter from the Subiaco register (*A. M. Ae.*, vol. VI, p. 203), as did M. Giorgi (in his critical notes on the year 955) and M. Galletti (cited above, p. 101). Through another Subiaco charter it became known that he had been bishop of Bomarzo at least from the year 942 (Muratori, cited above; see p. 773; Giorgi, cited above, under the year 942). But from the series of librarians we cannot learn of which church he was bishop, because he does not say so in another bull of the same John from the year 956. The other bull addressed to Berengar, bishop of Verdun, who died in 959 (*Gallia Christiana*, vol. XIII, p. 1180), belongs certainly to that pope, and not to John XIII, still less to the year 972, as Ciampini wrote (from the *Liber Pontificalis*, p. 23), and as it appears in the *Councils* (vol. XII, p. 879 of the Venetian edition). All these bulls, like our papyrus, were written by the same scriniarius Leo, who, I believe through the error of a copyist, is called *scriptor S. R. C.* in another bull of Agapitus from the year 955, now printed in the *History of Languedoc* (*Preuves*, vol. III, p. 95).] of the holy Church of Polimartium and librarian of the supreme apostolic see.

In the ninth year, God willing, of our lord Agapitus, supreme pontiff and universal junior pope, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter, and in the aforesaid thirteenth indiction [Note: Probably the same person who, in a parchment from the archive of Saint Mary Major dated 12 July 1309, is called “notary and now chamberlain of the notaries of the city.” Another Ognissanti Roman, in 1318, is furnished by the papyrus that follows; and M. Galletti reports the funerary inscription of one of them, who died in 1394 (*Roman Inscriptions*, vol. III, year 20, no. 42). Amidenus says that the noble family Omnia Sanctus was the same as the Mancini family. Perhaps it received this beautiful name from the exceptional goodness of one of its members, since the Latins often used, in imitation of the Greeks, who said πάντα (“all things”), ἐκάτα [sic; uncertain], πάντα (“all things”), ὁσιος (“holy”), and so forth, the expressions *omnia*, *cuncta*, *in omnia*, *per omnia*, *in omnibus*, *per cuncta*, *in cunctis*, *magnus*, *lautus*, *sublimis*, *sanctus*, and so on. The Greek expression ὕστερον πρώτερον means “later first”; Aurelius Victor said *sanctus omnia* in *Caesars* 9, and Tertullian had said *omnia sanctus* in *On Repentance*.]

I, Omnia Sanctus, judge and notary of the holy Roman Church, as I found in the said parchment privilege and as could be read in it—neither cancelled, erased, nor damaged—having seen, read, and thus carefully examined it in the presence of the discreet men Lord Presbyter Gyptius of Saint Apollinaris and Bartholomew of Saint Mary de Caccabari, rectors of the city clergy and of the Roman fraternity appointed by the Apostolic See, and by their authority, decree, and mandate, and in the presence of the learned witnesses listed below, specially summoned and requested for this purpose: namely, Lord James, archpriest of Saint Mary in Via; Lord Giles, priest and rector of the church of Saint Lucy de Confinio; Lord Raynald, priest and rector of the church of Saint Andrew de Urso; Lord James, prior of the church of Saint Andrew de Columna; Lord Thomas, canon of the church of Saint Lawrence in Lucina; Lord Angelo Ronterii, canon of that same church of Saint Lawrence; and Lord Angelo Scholarius, son of Lord James Consolinus, judge—thus, word for word, adding or subtracting nothing, insofar as it could be read, I faithfully copied and reduced it to public form. At the request of the venerable and religious man Lord Matthew [Note: [Col. 0928D] To this Abbot Matthew he addressed four letters during his brief pontificate (*Reg. in Arc. Vat.*, year 1, letters 43, 62, 207).], abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Sylvester at the Head in the City, of the Order of Saint Benedict, and also by decree of the same convent and by the authority and mandate of the aforementioned rectors, in the year of the Lord 1267, indiction 5, July 27.

In this parchment privilege there hung a leaden bull by a silk thread of violet color. On one side, around a cross placed in the middle, these letters could be read in a circle: AGAPITUS; and in the middle there was a certain sign somewhat representing a star. On the other side these letters appeared around a cross placed there: PAPAE.

Place of the notary’s sign.

+ I, Presbyter Gyptius of Saint Apollinaris, of the city clergy and rector of the Roman fraternity, having confidence in this public instrument faithfully copied, therefore subscribe my name.

+ I, Master Bartholomew of Caccabari, rector of the city clergy and of the Roman fraternity, having confidence in this public instrument faithfully copied, therefore subscribe my name.

+ I, Lord James, archpriest of Saint Mary in Via, the aforementioned witness, subscribe my name.

+ I, Presbyter Giles, rector of the church of Saint Lucy de Confinio, the aforementioned witness, subscribe my name.

+ I, Presbyter Raynald, rector of the church of Saint Andrew de Urso, the aforementioned witness, subscribe my name.

+ I, James, prior of the church of Saint Andrew de Columna, the aforementioned witness, subscribe my name.

+ I, Thomas, canon of the church of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, the aforementioned witness, subscribe my name.

+ I, Angelo Ronterii, canon of the church of Saint Lawrence, the aforementioned witness, subscribe my name.

+ I, Angelo, student of law, son of Lord James Consolinus, judge, the aforementioned witness, subscribe my name.

[Col. 0928A] + I, James Consolinus, judge and now chamberlain of the judges of the City, having confidence in this instrument and privilege faithfully copied, subscribe my name in the year of the Lord 1277, indiction 5, August 26.

+ I, Adenulf, judge and rector of the judges, having confidence in this instrument and privilege faithfully copied, subscribe my name.

+ I, Maximus, judge of Peter Odo and now chamberlain of the judges, subscribe my name to this privilege faithfully copied.

## XX. Privilege of Pope Agapetus II for the Monastery of Saint Martin de Lenis (955)

[In D. Bouquet, *Collection of Historians*, IX, 233.]

[Col. 0928B]

Agapetus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Segarius, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Martin, called Lenis, situated on the bank of the river Atax in the valley of Bolicarnea, and through him to that same venerable monastery in perpetuity.

Since the care of all churches occupies us with great solicitude, lest they suffer any loss through need, but rather receive the resources of their proper benefit, it is fitting that we should, with complete pastoral integrity of mind, provide for them and diligently confer upon them assistance for their welfare. Thus, what we have bestowed upon their venerable places for the sake of our almighty Lord, for the sanctity, honor, praise, and glory of his divine majesty, may be acceptable to him; and may the reward of such a pious work be granted to us, worthy of his most abundant mercy, in the heavenly citadels.

Therefore, since you have petitioned us that we should grant you the church of Saint Mary situated at Coronulas, with its lands and vineyards and all its revenues; likewise the church of Saint Stephen situated at Bolorda, also with its lands, vineyards, and all its appurtenances; similarly the church of Saint John situated at Combreto, with all its appurtenances; likewise the church of Saint Peter situated at Petralata, also with lands and vineyards; moreover the estate of Buxo and Petrus, with its lands, vineyards, woods, and mills; likewise, in the estate called Cassanges, houses, vineyards, and lands; and half of the estate called Barosa; also, in the district of Adasate, lands and vineyards; likewise the estate called Artosol, with all its appurtenance; and likewise within the county of Feniolot, the county of Rodez, and Roussillon, we should grant these possessions to your religious care in perpetuity—accordingly, on the condition that from you and your successors, at each indiction, ten silver solidi, in the name of the ecclesiastical due, [lacuna] twelve denarii [lacuna], without difficulty, shall be paid [lacuna], and that, without distinction, you shall be made responsible for our improvement or settlement [lacuna]. Furthermore, let no delay arise on your part in paying the annual due, but let it be paid voluntarily to the officials of our holy Church at the proper time.

We decree by apostolic censure, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and under threat of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, that no successor of ours among the pontiffs, nor any other person, great or small, shall ever presume to remove the aforesaid places from the power and jurisdiction of the aforementioned monastery. If anyone, whether great or small, should presume with reckless daring to act against this apostolic command of ours, let that person know that he is bound by the chain of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, and condemned with all the impious to the punishment of eternal fire. But whoever proves to be an observer of this command may deserve to obtain grace, mercy, and eternal life from our most merciful Lord.

Written by the hand of Leo, scrivener of the holy Roman Church, in the month of October, indiction 13. Farewell.

## XXI. Privilege of Pope Agapetus II for the Monastery of Monte Cassino (955)

He grants to Baldwin, abbot of Cassino, and to his successors, the monastery of Saint Stephen situated in the territory of Terracina.

[Tosti, *History of Monte Cassino*.]

Agapetus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Baldwin, beloved son, abbot of the venerable monastery of Monte Cassino, and to all who enter it regularly, in perpetuity.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to assist with benevolent compassion those distinguished by pious religion and to grant appropriate support to a just desire. Therefore, since you have petitioned us to grant you the monastery of Saint Stephen, protomartyr of Christ, which through great age lies in ruins and in deserted places, together with its churches or cells, waters, streams, lands, fields, pastures, woods, cultivated or uncultivated areas, and with everything generally belonging in full to the aforesaid monastery, situated in the territory of Terracina and within these boundaries:

On the first side, the estate called Vorke and the estate of Clevinus; on the second side, the foot of the mountain descends and then rises along the foot of the mountain beneath that mountain, along the foot of the mountain of Saint Lacus, and as it goes toward the mountain of Campilla, and along the stream of Balani, and the mountain of Montania, and the estate of Rustizanu and Tauri. On the fourth side, the estate of Salissanu, and Plage, and Baleranum as far as the stream of David, and it returns to the estate of Barkas.

Since it belongs to the jurisdiction of the holy Roman Church, which by God’s favor we serve, we ought to grant it to you to hold for all time. Inclined by your prayers, through the text of this command we grant to you and your successors, from the present fourteenth indiction, in perpetuity, the aforesaid monastery with everything belonging to it, as it is written above, so that you may retain it. We decree and promulgate, under the observance of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, that no successor of ours among the pontiffs, nor any other person, great or small, shall ever presume to take away what you have received from us for the restoration of that place and its return to its former condition, as a remedy for the soul of Stephania, our spiritual daughter.

If anyone—which we do not wish—should attempt with reckless daring to act against this apostolic command of ours, let that person know that, by the authority of God and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, he is bound by the chain of anathema and alienated from the kingdom of God. But whoever, moved by pious regard, proves in all things to be the guardian and observer of this apostolic decree of ours may deserve to obtain the grace of blessing and mercy from the just Judge, our Lord God.

Written by the hand of Acritioner, scrivener of the holy Roman Church, in the month of October, the aforementioned fourteenth indiction. Farewell. Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, by the hand of Andrew the divine, through the favour of grace, treasurer of the apostolic see, in the tenth year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of Lord Agapetus, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the most sacred see of blessed Peter the apostle, in the month and indiction stated above.

## XXII. Privilege of Pope Agapetus II for the Cell of Saint Mary and Saint Hunegundis at Humolarias (955)

[Colliette, *Memoirs of the Vermandois*, I, 563.]

[Col. 0930C]

In the name of the holy and inseparable Trinity: Agapetus, by the merciful assistance of Christ, bishop of the holy Roman see.

If we offer a favorable assent to holy petitions and to the wishes of the devout, we believe that we are serving the will of the Lord. Therefore, let it be known to all the sons of the Catholic mother Church that our son, the king of the Franks, Lothair, a boy of glorious character, sent to us, humbly beseeching our fatherhood that we fortify with the protection of apostolic authority a certain cell situated in the pagus of Vermandois, constructed in honor of blessed Mary, Mother of God, and of Saint Hunegundis, virgin. At the urging of his father, namely King Louis, and of the king himself, together with Count Adalbert and the highly suitable man Eibert, who possessed that same little abbey by right of benefice, he was striving to raise it to the venerable worship of sacred religion and to strengthen it by royal command.

Rejoicing in this petition, we extend the hand of ecclesiastical authority; and, supported by this authority, we command that no secular person shall ever possess the aforesaid abbey, nor shall anyone usurp anything for himself from the property of that cell—not the king, not the count, not the bishop, nor any prince whatsoever, whatever power he may possess, except perhaps for the purpose of protecting and defending it, and even then only with the permission of the regular abbot of that place.

If anyone, in order to obtain it, should give or promise money or any gift to the king or to any prince, that person shall be subject to the curse that follows. Let the same cell therefore have an abbot constituted according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, and monks subject to regular discipline; with full authority we prohibit them from suffering any loss from the property of that cell.

The possessions of that church are the estate of Humolarias, in which the cell has been constructed, with all the dwellings belonging to it; the estate of Merulfus with its appurtenances; the estate of Eudoldus with its dependencies; and Caviniacus with the manses belonging to it. In the estate called Frisia, on the river Somme, twelve manses, which it shall be permitted that same church to possess perpetually for the benefit of fishing [lacuna].

But if anyone should undertake anything against the protection of this apostolic privilege [lacuna], we excommunicate him [lacuna], so that, bound penally under the chain of this anathema, he may be anathema maranatha. Let it be done, let it be done.

# In the Year of the Lord 861. Saint Odo, Archbishop of Canterbury

## Life of Saint Odo

By Osbern, apparently, a monk of Canterbury.

[In Mabil., *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, from a manuscript of the Thuano-Colbertine codex.]

## Preliminary Observations

1. Although the antiquity of the author of this Life may be inferred from the manuscript, the Thuano-Colbertine codex from which we copied this Life neither identifies his name nor indicates his age. He seems to me to have been Osbern, a monk of Canterbury under Archbishop Lanfranc, who is mentioned by Pitseus as having written one book on the Life of Odo, archbishop of Canterbury.

It is uncertain whether William of Malmesbury had this little book before his eyes when composing the encomium of Odo that he inserted in Book I of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English*. There is reason for doubt because, in several matters—though matters of lesser importance—William does not agree with Osbern, as we may provisionally call him.

Osbern says that Odo, resisting his election to the see of Canterbury, did not consent until envoys had been sent to Fleury to summon the abbot, because Odo had been initiated into monastic life by receiving the cowl. William says that Odo, after crossing the sea, received the monastic habit at Fleury. Gervase of Canterbury supports Osbern, while Bromton supports William. Osbern adds that the dead Odo appeared to the guardian of the church so that he might restrain Elfsinus, who had been simoniacally intruded into the see of Canterbury, with his words; William reports that the apparition occurred to Elfsinus himself. William also records certain matters about which Osbern is silent, such as Odo’s translation of the relics of Saint Wilfrid and several other things.

2. Both agree that, after Wulfhelm, archbishop of Canterbury, had died and the wishes of the king and people had converged upon Odo, he resisted all the more firmly because he had not yet become a monk, lest he seem by his ambition to disturb the custom of his predecessors. “Until that time,” says William, “there had been no archbishop except one clothed in the monastic habit”—a point Osbern conveys in other words.

Godwin, a partisan, calls this an error and says it is certain that Nothelm and several other secular, as they are called, priests had presided over the Church of Canterbury before Odo. Yet Godwin cannot know this with greater certainty than Odo himself or William, who were closer to the earliest period; nor is it established that Nothelm was without monastic profession.

Bede, in the preface to his *History of the English*, calls Nothelm only a religious priest of the Church of London. But monks commonly bestowed this title upon priests, and Bede himself, in a letter to Nothelm, calls him “our venerable brother Nothelm the priest”; these words designate a monk rather than a secular priest.

Odo assumed the monastic habit and, by receiving the monastic clothing itself, made his profession around the year 937, at which time the monastery of Fleury was being restored to stricter observance of the Rule through the efforts of Odo, abbot of Cluny. Odo therefore received the monastic habit from him, passing over the monks of Canterbury and the other English monks, whose observance at that time was not held in such high regard. The same reason drew Oswald and other Englishmen to the monastery of Fleury, from which Abbo was sent to England as much for piety as for learning.

3. Among the deeds of Odo that are not mentioned in the following little book, the chief seems to be the translation of the body of Saint Wilfrid, bishop of York, which Odo is said to have arranged at Canterbury. This is recorded both by William, in his account of our Odo, and by Eadmer in his book on the *Life of Saint Wilfrid*, published in the first part of the third Benedictine century, pages 226–227.

William adds that Odo arranged for the Life of Wilfrid to be composed in heroic meter, and that a certain Fridegod carried this out. We publish his poem in volume 133 of our *Patrologia*. William further reports a synodal letter of Odo addressed to his suffragans during the reign of King Edmund, in which he urges them not to conduct themselves sluggishly or negligently in the governance of souls. In this letter, William thought, Odo displayed no ordinary learning, but an even greater degree of piety and pastoral solicitude.

I think this letter was written after the constitutions issued by Odo under the same king and published by Spelman, in which provisions are made concerning the duties of the king, clergy, and magistrates. In chapter 6, he exhorts monks to strive day and night to fulfill their vows in all humility and obedience, remaining in the fear of God in the churches where they have bound themselves by vow. Let them not be wanderers or gyrovagues—those who desire the name of monk but despise his duty—but, following the example of the apostles, let them exercise themselves through the habit of humility, the labor of their hands, sacred reading, and continual prayers.

Eadmer also mentions, in the prologue to the *Life of Saint Wilfrid*, a little book of our Odo concerning the life and conduct of Wilfrid himself. But this little book is certainly none other than Fridegod’s poem, which in some manuscripts is preceded by a letter of Odo containing these words:

“Therefore, when some people, with God’s favor—that is, from the place of his tomb—had transferred the most venerable relics of the blessed confessor of Christ Wilfrid, which were decaying in the indecent, filthy squalor of a foul pit—or rather, which it is even fearful to say, had been neglected through the bristling contempt of those in charge—I reverently received them and placed them within the precinct of the metropolitan church over which, by God’s grace, I preside. Thus, rejoicing in the nearness of so great and God-worthy a relationship, I considered it worthwhile to adorn them with a more elevated shrine and to embellish them in a new work of verse with flowers excerpted from the book of his Life.”

This was done by Fridegod; nevertheless, Eadmer, and perhaps several others, attributed it to Odo. I do not know whether the information that Pitseus gives concerning Odo’s other writings is more certain. He additionally attributes to Odo one book addressed to the monks of Fleury on behalf of his nephew Oswald; another on the real presence of Christ’s body in the Eucharist; one book of letters; and another of various poems.

4. Eadmer, William of Malmesbury, Matthew of Westminster, and others call Odo a saint, and after them Cardinal Baronius does so in volume X of his *Annals*, although Odo has no place in the Roman Martyrology. Maihew, following Capgrave and other English writers, says that he departed to the Lord on July 4, not on February 7, the day on which Molanus discusses Saint Odo in his additions to Usuard. He is highly praised in the following Life of Saint Dunstan by Osbern.

## Odo Leaves His Pagan Parents

[Col. 0933B]

1. The venerable confessor of Christ Odo, born of noble but pagan parents [Note: Namely, from Danish savagery, as William writes; Bromton says that he was Danish by nationality. Some trustworthy men, according to Maihew, attribute to him the surname Severus, but they are later writers, among them Pitseus.], flourished like a rose among thorns, or like precious perfume issuing from cheap vessels.

For he is said to have descended from that impious multitude of senators who once accompanied the most wicked pirate Inguar and were transported by naval force into the kingdom of the English. Having these men as the princes of his birth and passing his childhood under their most careful upbringing, he hastened constantly to attend the gatherings of Christians, to hear with great delight of soul the divine sermons preached by them, and, when he returned home, diligently to pour what he had heard into the ears of his parents.

At these beginnings of good studies his impious father was impiously angered and forbade him absolutely to name Christ or to alter his paternal instruction through reverence for the Christian religion. But Odo completely disregarded the command of his forbidding father. He frequented the thresholds of the Church more and more, received with attentive mind the seeds of the divine Word, and without fear reported at home what he had begun to learn.

At this the father again became exasperated beyond human measure, afflicted him with the severest reprimand, and deprived him of the right of inheritance that, under the law of primogeniture, was due to come to him. Then the boy rejoiced in the Lord because he was undergoing such proscription on earth for the Lord’s name, on account of which he considered that he ought to be enrolled in heaven. He left his parents and their wealth, fled naked and deprived of every worldly adornment.

## He Visits Athelmus and Studies Letters

2. He therefore approached a certain leader named Athelmus, who in the time of King Eluvred was both most Christian and one of the higher-ranking nobles among the other magnates of the kingdom of the English. He asked to be defended by Athelmus’s power and authority from the fury of his parents.

Athelmus rejoiced in the young man’s excellent character and judged that it was wholly unworthy for so great a distinction to serve pagan rites under his father’s authority. He received him with paternal affection, protected him, and supported him with both necessary and unnecessary assistance. Then he entrusted him to teachers to be instructed in the Greek and Latin languages, both of which were in use among many of the English people at that time, having derived from the disciples of Theodore, archbishop of blessed memory.

Odo became highly skilled in both languages, so that he could compose poems, shape prose, and express in brilliant speech whatever he had resolved in his mind.

## He Is Initiated into the Orders

3. After this, reborn through the sacrament of baptism and adorned with the clerical tonsure, he was advanced, at the urging of his lord, as far as the ministry of subdeacon. In that rank, for several years, he excelled so greatly in holiness of life and sincerity of preaching that anyone who knew him could not doubt that he was a temple of the Holy Spirit. By everyone’s testimony he was worthy to be advanced to the higher ministries of the Church, although his age, insofar as the canonical regulations were concerned, forbade this.

Therefore, when his lord urged him to allow himself to be transferred to the priesthood, so that he might daily hear the divine office from one whose most chaste life and hands full of purity he had recognized, Odo resisted as much as he could, pleading his premature age. Later, overcome by reason and by the authority of ancient examples, he yielded to his devout desire. He placed the Levitical stole around his shoulders, and after a short time he also entered upon the sacred ministry of the highest mysteries.

From that time both the leader himself and nearly all the other princes of the royal palace held him in the highest veneration. They disclosed to him the secrets of their badly conducted lives and willingly trusted his counsel concerning their amendment.

## He Goes to Rome with Athelmus and Heals Him; He Returns to England

[Col. 0935A]

4. Meanwhile, the leader informed the king that he desired to go to Rome and supplicate the holy apostles there. Soon, having received royal permission and generosity, he departed with the venerable priest Odo added to his company, together with a large retinue.

But after they had traveled some distance, Athelmus was struck by a grievous illness and began to suffer so severely that he could scarcely breathe air through his laboring breaths. When for six continuous days his weakness increased and his provisions diminished, on the seventh day he ordered the entire company to continue along the road they had begun, retaining Odo alone with him, whose help he now needed most in his danger.

After the others had been sent away, he called Odo to him in a sorrowful voice and begged him to pour out prayers to the Lord for his deliverance. He declared that he firmly believed that divine mercy would deny nothing to one whom it had accepted with great favor from childhood.

Then the venerable Odo, raising his mind to God, prostrated himself with his whole body upon the ground and shed great showers of sobs before the divine clemency. Rising from the ground, he asked that a cup filled with wine be brought to him. Having made over it the sign of the invincible cross, he humbly offered the wine to the man and faithfully admonished him to trust in the Lord in all things.

The man drank what was in the cup, and at that very moment, as he handed the cup back, he felt that complete healing had been restored to him. Accordingly, he bent his knees before the priest and gave thanks. Then, mounting his horse, he swiftly pursued the companions who had gone ahead. They had covered the road at a rapid pace, but on the following day he himself overtook them in tireless flight.

When they saw him, everyone shed tears of joy; but when they recognized the author of the health that had been granted, they marveled even more. They proceeded as far as the city of Romulus and then returned safely to their ancestral homes, bringing immense joy at their arrival both to the king and to the others living in the palace.

## He Becomes Dear to King Ethelstan

5. After some days, when the leader himself had died, and afterward the aforementioned king had been taken from this present life, Edward, the son of that same king, succeeded to the kingdom and ruled it very wisely for many years.

During his reign, the venerable Odo administered the priestly office, distinguished both by his duties and by the holiness of his life. He was known and welcomed by the king and admired by everyone, extending kindness and gentleness to all and adapting himself to the character of each, in accordance with the apostles, so that he might win everyone for Christ.

When King Edward had brought his life to an end, his son Ethelstan obtained the reins of the kingdom. The admirable Odo, conducting himself in every respect as a man of virtue, was held in high esteem by the entire people. For a city set upon a mountain, or a lamp shining on a lampstand, could not be hidden.

Thus the fame of his holiness, magnified by increasing day after day, reached even the ears of the distinguished King Ethelstan, with extraordinary praise. The king summoned Odo to himself, recognized with complete certainty that he was truly a servant of God, joined him to his circle of friends, and made him, above all others, the confidant of his secrets.

## He Becomes Bishop of Sherborne

6. Meanwhile, the episcopal see that at that time was called Sherborne and is now called Seriberic became vacant through the death of its pastor. Knowing that Odo’s life was entirely worthy of the episcopate, the king began with great earnestness to entreat him to accept the bishopric and to consent to become, in place of the deceased, the apostolic shepherd of God’s sheep.

Why delay? At last, overcome by the prayers of the Church and the king—although he declared that the office was excessively burdensome to him—he consented to administer the pontifical office after becoming bishop of the aforesaid Church of Sherborne.

At that time a good and vigorous man named Wulfhelm presided over the Church of Canterbury in position, dignity, authority, and office. Giving willing assent to this election by the king, clergy, and people, he duly consecrated Odo, with proper honor, to the dignity of the episcopate to which he had been elected.

Once consecrated and sacerdotally vested with the insignia of the priesthood, how glorious a dwelling for God he showed himself to be, and how solicitous he was for the gain of the souls entrusted to him, I do not know whether anyone, however great his intellectual skill, could adequately express.

Therefore, I do not wish to write what the simplicity of a pure mind might perceive in these matters. I merely set before consideration the works that merciful God deigns to perform, according to his good pleasure, in his servants who cling to him with a simplicity pleasing to him.

## In 938 Ethelstan Prevails over the Pagans

7. In the year 938 of the Lord’s incarnation [Note: In the same year, the Saxon Chronicle, appended to Bede, places this battle.], and in the fourteenth year of the reign of the most victorious King Ethelstan, an immense army of pagans gathered against the kingdom of the English, intending to weaken it by subjecting it to their profane laws and, by weakening it, to annihilate the most sacred laws of the Christians that the English observed.

The renowned prince, accompanied by a powerful force of armed men, met them and entered the battle. The fighting continued for a very long time and was savage on both sides. The king had taken Saint Odo with him into the battle line, trusting that he would defeat the enemy much more through Odo’s merits than through the forces of his soldiers.

While the most grievous slaughter raged on every side, a distressing and lamentable event occurred. For where the king himself was fighting, his sword broke beside the hilt and left him, as though unarmed, exposed to the enemy.

Meanwhile Odo stood some distance away from the fighting, beseeching Christ with mouth and heart for the safety of the Christian army and tirelessly raising his face, hands, and eyes toward heaven for this very purpose.

The king was therefore uncertain what he could do to save his life. He considered it wrong to arm himself by disarming one of his men. When part of the enemy observed that the king was standing unarmed with his broken sword, they turned back from the flight they had begun and attempted to avenge it through more ferocious slaughter in battle.

Then suddenly the air thundered with the shouting of the multitude, calling for God’s help and crying out that venerable Odo should hasten forward with rapid steps. He ran up and, exhausted, asked the king what he wanted him to do.

He heard the king’s answer and immediately said to him:

“What is this? What are you attempting? Your sword hangs whole at your side, and you complain that it is broken? Come to yourself; reach your hand to the scabbard, draw it out, and behold, the right hand of the Lord will be with you. Do not be afraid, for the sun will not set before flight or destruction overtakes the enemies of your Lord who have risen against you.”

At this, all who heard him, struck with great astonishment, lowered their eyes and saw the sword hanging at the king’s side, though previously they had not seen it. The king, strengthened in God, seized it and, with his right and left hands, weakened, routed, or utterly consigned to death all who came against him.

Thus, in accordance with the word of the servant of God, it happened that the sun set at the same time as victory over the enemies came to the king. Who could recount what thanks, what praises, and what vows were offered to God through his faithful servant Odo—by the king, by the victorious army, and by the entire kingdom to which the greatness of this victory was reported? The magnificence of the deed will teach those who hear of it, since scarcely anyone could readily...

From then on the glorious Odo was held in great admiration by everyone and was proven to be a truly outstanding Israelite.

## When Edmund Compels Him to the Archbishopric of Canterbury, He Refuses the Translation Unless He First Becomes a Monk
8. A few years after this notable victory, Ethelstan ended his present life with a good death [Col. 0937C] [Note: [Col. 0937D] That is, in the year 941, indeed on 27 October, according to Saxon chronology. Odo’s promotion to the see of Canterbury therefore did not occur before the following year.], and his brother Edmund became king in his brother’s place. Emulating his brother’s footsteps in goodness, he cherished every good man with the greatest devotion; having made them his intimates, he listened to them with sincere and willing spirit in matters befitting a Christian king.

Accordingly, among the others, the blessed Odo came into especially distinguished familiarity with him and was loved by him with a pure heart. In those days Wlfelmus, bishop of Canterbury, met the death appointed for all mortals. Thus, lest so great a see remain without a shepherd longer than was proper, the king approached the venerable Odo, urging him to assist the desolate Church by undertaking pastoral care over it.

Odo resisted and gave no assent to the one urging him. For he said that he was unworthy of so great a charge; and, even if the dignity in some measure invited him, he nevertheless acknowledged that the authority of the canons forbade a bishop to leave his own Church and migrate to another. In answer, the king set forth in eloquent speech both Odo’s well-known integrity and the fact that the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, had been transferred from Antioch to Rome, while many others, as the records of antiquity attest, had changed their sees for compelling reasons. He added:

“We have among us a sufficiently suitable and clear example of this very matter: I mean the holy men Melitus, bishop of London, and Justus, bishop of Rochester, who were transferred to Canterbury by a procedure like that by which we urge you to change your see.”

Overcome by these arguments, the holy bishop opposed another reason for his refusal. “When the first Fathers of this very Church,” he said, “who brought Christianity to the kingdom of the English, and all who succeeded them down to the present, have—as everyone knows—been monks, should I change, violate, and destroy so ancient, so holy, so acceptable to God a custom, strengthened by the authority of so many Fathers? Far from it. Rather, let all Britain and all the neighboring islands know that I shall never consent in any way to preside through the episcopate over the Church of Canterbury while remaining in clerical dress, since no one who was not a monk is known to have presided over it before me.

“Nevertheless, since, as appears, not you alone but many are calling me to become bishop there, it is not mine to resist them and oppose them completely, lest I offend God, who dwells in them. Therefore, commending to God my conscience, empty of every ambition for this honor, I shall at least on this occasion undertake the holy purpose of monastic religion which I desired from the beginning of my life, but which, impeded by various causes, I have not deserved to attain—so that, for the time being, it may be thought that I have undertaken it. Afterwards, let him concerning whom you are deliberating about the episcopate himself act, he who lays bare all the secrets of hearts, and let him establish in it the man whom in his wisdom he judges suitable for this.”

### He receives the monastic habit from the monks of Fleury and thereafter becomes archbishop

9. The king was greatly delighted by this decision of the man. He praised his holy purpose, praised the admirable and imitable example of his great humility [Col. 0938C], and praised his steadfast strength of mind.

Thereupon messengers were dispatched without delay to the abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict at Fleury, to obtain, for the bishop’s use and in accordance with the matter already described, the habit of holy religion. The reputation of the most religious way of life then flourishing at Fleury and spreading throughout nearly every land, together with the fact that devotion to the same religious way of life had everywhere begun to decline in England because of the many misfortunes of differing events, persuaded them that the habit should be sent from there and that the desired religious undertaking should be brought to completion through it. And so it happened.

When the abbot of that place heard the message, he was filled with joy. Taking some of his brothers with him, he crossed the sea to England on a favorable voyage [Col. 0938D]. He eagerly approached Bishop Odo, who was striving to please God in all things, and most devoutly handed him the habit of the holy purpose which he desired.

Thus the distinguished Bishop Odo became a monk by receiving the habit—he who had long before been adorned by the sacred works of the monastic life. When he was invited, indeed compelled, by king and kingdom to take up the yoke of the Lord over all England, he could no longer refuse to become archbishop of Canterbury.

Those who wish to know how he exercised the office of the government he had undertaken may, as I think, perceive it from the brief account we have given above of what his life was like both before the priesthood and in the priesthood [Col. 0939A]. For he was praiseworthy in holiness, admirable in wisdom, and singular in steadfastness.

### He anoints King Edred. He converts adversaries of the Eucharist by a miracle

10. After King Edmund had been maliciously killed in his own house, his brother Edred, having assumed the dignity of imperial rule, was solemnly anointed king by the glorious Odo, supreme pontiff of Canterbury.

At that time Dunstan, a man of outstanding integrity and most worthy abbot of the monastery at Glastonbury, was held in great esteem by the king and honored by the whole people. The blessed Odo, advanced in age and character, strong in religion and diligence, distinguished in authority and moderation, most wisely ennobled the entire kingdom by Christian laws. The king himself, fearing God and cherishing every good person with the special sweetness of love, while firmly restraining the wicked lest they disturb those who acted well through their tyranny, followed the conduct and practices of a good ruler.

At about this time certain clerics, led astray by a wicked error [Note: [Col. 0939D] Maihewvius reports this in exactly the same words from Capgrave, who therefore had already published this little work; but so far we have not been able to recover Capgrave. [Col. 0940D]], attempted to assert that the bread and wine placed upon the altar remained, after consecration, in their former substance, and were merely a figure of Christ’s body and blood, not the true body and blood of Christ.

The blessed Odo, wishing to destroy their monstrous unbelief, was one day devoutly engaged in the solemn celebration of Mass before the whole people. With abundant tears, he asked the mercy of almighty God to be present in his ministry and to reveal the substantial reality of the divine mysteries, so as to drive away human errors [Col. 0939C].

When the breaking of the life-giving bread was reached—O ineffable mercy of God, O manifestation of the eternal majesty present among them!—blood immediately began to flow drop by drop between the hands of the bishop, who was holding fragments of the body of Christ.

The bishop stood there, pouring out abundant tears of joy, and signaled to the attending ministers to bring especially close those who had recently faltered in the faith. They came quickly when summoned, and, terrified as they contemplated such great things, cried out in trembling voices:

“O you today the happiest of men, to whom the Son of God has deigned to reveal himself in the flesh!”

And again they said: “Entreat, Father, entreat the majesty of the Lord for a little while, so that this present blood may be changed back into its former appearance, lest divine vengeance pursue us because of the error of our unbelief [Col. 0939D].”

The priest therefore prayed. After the prayer he looked toward the altar and found there, where he had left the blood, the customary appearance of wine.

After receiving the heavenly sacraments, while all who had witnessed such spectacles rejoiced, the bishop ordered all the poor from every place to be gathered as a testimony to so great a power, and a solemn banquet to be prepared for them. He himself and his companions celebrated joyfully with great thanksgiving, because every error concerning the Lord’s body had been wiped from the hearts of his people, and those who had seen true blood flowing from it no longer doubted that the bread placed upon the altar was the true body of Christ [Col. 0940A].

### A marvel during the rebuilding of the church

11. He also performed another truly divine miracle in the church over which he presided—or rather, he himself did not perform it, but the One who alone possesses divinity in him did so.

The roof of that church, ruined by extreme age, hung over it, with portions throughout half-collapsed. Wishing to renew it and desiring to raise the wall to a greater height, he assembled craftsmen and ordered that whatever projected above in a loosened state be entirely removed, and that whatever the wall lacked in height be built up.

But since the clergy and people could not be without divine service, and no temple of such size could be found that seemed sufficient to contain the multitude of the numerous people, the bishop besought the Lord that, until the work begun had been completed, neither rain nor violent winds should descend within the church walls with enough force to hinder them from their sacred work.

And so it came about that during the three years in which the walls of the church were being extended upward, the entire structure remained open above; nevertheless—not merely within the enclosure of the church, but not even within the walls of the whole city—did rain ever fall in such a way as to impede the clergy standing in the church from their office or to restrain in any degree the people hastening to the church from the work they had begun.

It was a sight worthy of wonder when one saw all the orchards of the city flooded with water while its walls were not moistened by any inundation of rain [Col. 0940C].

### He attempts to correct Edwi, a lustful king, first through Dunstan and then by himself

12. When King Edred had exchanged his transitory life for eternal life, Edwi, son of the aforementioned King Edmund, was elected king. Young in character and age, he soon began to follow the counsels of the young men whom he had attached to himself as companions and attendants, scorning the older men who were known to possess great experience and authority through their life, character, and age.

When he was rebuked by Christ’s most courageous soldier, Odo, he restrained himself for a while, fearing that, if he did not listen to him in every respect, Odo might delay giving him the blessing of royal dignity beyond his desire. But once he had obtained that blessing, he immediately became, as it were, unbridled [Col. 0940D], and followed all the desires of his heart.

Thus he became a lover of pleasures rather than of God, of lust rather than of sobriety, of sexual desire rather than of chastity. He proceeded according to the wishes of his heart, and, though committing wicked deeds, received the blessing of his own people.

In addition, on the very day when he wore the crown of the kingdom upon his head in the sight of the whole Church, he brought upon both that great glory and himself a grievous mark of infamy. For when, after the ecclesiastical service, he had already dined and was seated together with the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and the other leaders of the kingdom, he suddenly sprang up, left the company of them all, and withdrew into a more private chamber. There, inflamed by lust for two women who were waiting for him, he sought an unspeakable union [Col. 0941A]. This deed cast the minds of those who trusted in him into deep grief and shame.

After they had taken counsel among themselves about what ought to be done, Dunstan, the venerable abbot mentioned above, was sent by the archbishop and the leading men to draw the king away from his illicit embraces and recall him to the royal seat among the princes. This was done.

Therefore, stirred by violent fury, the king stripped Dunstan of all his possessions, condemned him to exile, and drove him across the sea beyond England. He also committed countless other evils. Since these have elsewhere been set forth at greater length, though not all of them, I have judged it sufficient merely to touch on them briefly here.

13. The soldier of almighty God, Odo, could not endure these things with equanimity and became a public enemy of his wickedness. When he saw that Edwi would not agree to correct himself either through his admonitions, his entreaties, or his rebukes, Odo exercised his episcopal authority.

He sent soldiers from the king’s court, where one of the women in question was staying—the woman whom greater power and more shameless immodesty had dishonored and made more notorious among men, and whom the king more frequently abused in disgraceful embraces. They violently dragged her away, and he condemned her to perpetual exile in Ireland, after disfiguring her face and marking it with a branding iron.

After some interval, when the appearance of her body had already closed over into a scar, but the deformity of her shameless mind still yawned open, she left Ireland [Col. 0941C], returned to England, and reached Gloucester, steeped in the darkness of a blinded heart. There she was seized by men devoted to God and, lest she continue to wander about in the manner of a prostitute, was hamstrung. A few days later she was taken from this present life by a wretched death.

The supreme pontiff Odo was a man supported by the strength of virtues, the maturity of advanced age, and steadfastness, and he was an unbending adversary of every iniquity. Neither the allurements of any worldly pleasure, nor threats from men, nor the suffering of any loss could frighten him away from righteousness. Therefore, because he neither hoped for anything nor feared anything, he disarmed the anger of all who were powerless.

### Under King Eadgar, he consecrates Dunstan

14. After King Eadwio—if he should be called king, since he knew neither how to rule himself nor others—had been expelled from the kingdom on account of his crimes [Col. 0941D] and condemned to a wretched death, the royal throne over all England was confirmed for his brother Eadgar. [Note: [Col. 0941D] Spelmann assigns this excommunication to the year 958.]

Eadgar, surpassing nearly all his predecessors in moral integrity, suppressed, overturned, and, as far as he could, reduced to nothing all the iniquities that had arisen during his brother’s days. Moreover, as soon as he obtained the kingdom, he recalled the venerable abbot Dunstan from exile [Col. 0942A] and promoted him to the bishopric of Worcester.

The newly elected bishop came to Canterbury according to custom, to be consecrated into the rank of the honor he had received, and requested that he be consecrated by the bishop of that see, namely the blessed Odo. Odo gladly consented. Yet, so that no one might doubt that the holy bishop was endowed with the spirit of prophecy, by the working of the Holy Spirit he promoted the man who had come to be advanced to the bishopric of Worcester to the episcopate of Canterbury.

When those standing around asked why he was acting in this way, he said: “I know, my sons; I know what God is accomplishing in me. This man will have the province of Worcester as its shepherd while I am alive, but after my death all Britain will rejoice in him as its ruler; for the gift of the Holy Spirit is not bound by law.”

How true this prophecy was, the Church of God knows very well: it long afterward gloried in his rule, as the holy bishop had foretold, and to this day is protected by his most sacred intercession [Col. 0942B].

### His death

15. Thus exalted by the Lord through such gifts of goodness, the distinguished man Odo did not exalt himself at all on account of his merits or works, but always strove to advance toward better things. Forgetting what lay behind and stretching toward what lay ahead, he pursued the prize of God’s heavenly calling. Like fruitful fields, he watered the people entrusted to him daily with heavenly teaching, as though with rainlike grace, until the King brought his soul into his chamber and intoxicated it with the torrent of his delight.

Thus Odo, the brilliant star of the city of Canterbury, snatched from this world, sought the seat of the heavenly and most glorious city, while the angels rejoiced [Col. 0942C]. There he rejoices in everlasting exultation and contemplates the face of Christ with the sweetness of an ineffable delight, now secure concerning his own reward but concerned for the salvation of his children.

He died in the presence of all the sons of Christ’s Church. Even as they wept, he promised them that after his death the Lord would provide them with a good shepherd.

[Note: [Col. 0941D] Florentius of Worcester, Roger of Hoveden, and Matthew of Westminster assign Odo’s death to the year 958. But the Saxon Chronicle is preferable, in which Odo is said to have died in 961. Compare the notes on the Life of Saint Dunstan below, under the year 988. William gives Odo twenty years of rule, more correctly than Bromton, who assigns him twenty-four.]

### Elfsinus the simoniac succeeds him, insults him after his death; Saint Odo gives the church custodian commands concerning Elfsinus, who dies miserably

16. After his death, Elfsinus, bishop of Winchester, surnamed Lippe, obtained the place of supreme priest by giving money to the leading men in the palace of King Eadgar. Even before Odo, he had been driven by a great desire to seize the priesthood, but the steadfastness of good bishops had prevented him.

When, therefore, on the day of his arrival he had been received at Canterbury in solemn procession, he approached the tomb of the man of God. Standing upon it, he reproached the dead man in these furious words:

“Fool, look: you are dead and lie rotting beneath the earth, while, whenever I wish, I shall triumph powerfully over you. While you were alive, I could not become supreme pontiff of the English; now that you are dead, I have become precisely what I once desired to be. And therefore, wicked and decrepit old man, do not expect any thanks, for if you could have continued to live, you would have been willing to grant neither me nor anyone else even a share in the honor you possessed.”

He spoke thus openly in the presence of those who were there. Then, striking the saint’s tomb with his staff, he departed, inflamed by the three-pronged fury that possessed him.

But that same night, while the rest permitted to mortals was taking place, the blessed Odo appeared to the worthy custodian of the church of the Savior. His face was milk-white and his garment rose-colored. He addressed the man as follows:

“Are you asleep or awake?”

“I was asleep,” the man replied, “venerable lord, but behold, I am awake because you are speaking.”

“Go,” Odo said, “to Elfsinus, elected but not by God as bishop, and deliver this message to him in my name:

“‘The servant of Christ, Odo, commands you thus: I am not dead, but live to my almighty King and God. And so that you may experience this with complete certainty, know that just as, because of me while I was still living in the flesh, you were unable to reach the archbishopric of Canterbury, so through me, now living in the heavenly kingdom, you will soon lose the honor you have seized.

“‘Hear what I say. Yesterday you reproached me with mocking words and struck my tomb with your staff. I foretell to you that you will cross the sea and climb the Alps, but you will by no means obtain the pallium of the patriarchate of the holy Church of Dorobernia, nor will you ever sit upon its apostolic see.’”

The man who had seen these things feared the bishop’s violence and concealed the message instead of reporting it. On the following night the holy man of God appeared to him again, saying the same things he had said before. Even then the man did not dare to report what he had heard.

On the third night the man of God appeared again, clothed in pontifical dignity, and rebuked the man’s sluggishness:

“If you wish, as one who understands, to retain the prosperity of your life, I warn you not to conceal from your bishop what you heard from me a second time. For if you do so, you will learn by your punishment that you acted well.”

Then the man awoke, greatly terrified. When morning came, he went to the bishop, bowed with his whole body before him, and said:

“Reverend Father, the glorious Odo, your predecessor, appeared to me, beautiful as an angel of God, and commanded that this be announced to you:

“‘Because,’ he said to me, ‘the day before yesterday you reproached me with mocking words and struck my tomb with your staff, I foretell to you that you will cross the sea and climb the Alps, but you will by no means obtain the pallium of the patriarchate of the holy Church of Dorobernia, nor will you ever sit upon its apostolic see.’”

After these words, the bishop dismissed the reporter of the vision, making light of what he had heard as the words of an absurd threat.

But after a few days had passed, everything came to pass that the holy man of God had foretold. He crossed the sea to bring back the pallium, and after traveling for some time in prosperity, as soon as he climbed into the mountains, he was overcome by extreme cold. He ordered the horses accompanying him to be killed and thrust his feet into their bellies, supposing that the excessive cold could be driven away by such a remedy [Col. 0944A].

But the divine fury that tormented him did not cease. The impious man blasphemed the majesty of the Lord and thus breathed out his polluted spirit amid the flames.

In this way the blessed Odo showed that he lived to Christ, whom the wretched Elfsinus had dared to believe completely dead.

### After Birthelmus is removed, Dunstan succeeds him; a dove rests above Saint Odo’s tomb, and he is called Segode

17. After Elfsinus had died in this manner, Birthelmus, bishop of the province of Dorset, a man of excessive piety and simplicity, was appointed in his place to the episcopate of Canterbury. But when he was found to be altogether less vigorous than was necessary in carrying out ecclesiastical discipline, he was ordered to abandon the burden he had undertaken and humbly returned to his own flock [Col. 0944B] to live in quiet.

Thus, so that the Lord’s judgment and the prophecy of his servant, the blessed Odo, might be proved true, Dunstan, then already bishop of the Church of London, was chosen by king and kingdom and installed as the most worthy successor of the glorious Odo in the patriarchate of all Britain.

Among the other indications of the holiness and blessedness of both Dunstan and this Father Odo, whom we are discussing, there is one not insignificant sign. When Dunstan was celebrating Mass at the altar of the Lord Savior at Canterbury on the holy day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit, who had appeared above him in the form of a dove, departed after the sacrifice had been consumed toward the southern part of the altar, where the venerable Odo lay buried, and rested upon his tomb in the sight of many observers.

Dunstan held this event in such great reverence that thereafter he never passed before Odo’s tomb without bending his knees. He also used to call him thereafter by the epithet “the Good” in his mother tongue, namely Odo Segode [or Thegood], which is interpreted as “Odo the Good.” By this name he is called to this day by the English, and especially by the people of Canterbury.

With these matters thus set forth, the sequence of the event demands an end to the narration. Here we bring it to a close, and with one harmonious voice praise God, who is the end and completion of all good things, who so glorifies his name among every nation that whoever fears him and practices righteousness is acceptable to him.

To him, therefore, be praise and thanksgiving through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

> Like a rose from thorns, so Odo sprang forth among the pagans,  
> Bearing no marks of unbelief from either parent.  
> Against the vows of his fathers, he embraced the plow of faith,  
> And, like a good farmer, plowed the soil of the heart.  
> Exalted by blood, still more exalted by the order of his character,  
> Distinguished by ancestry, yet more distinguished in speech.  
> A man pure from crime, he confronted the criminal,  
> Striving to enlarge the kingdom of the Most High Father.  
> A phalanx of virtues guarded his inmost heart,  
> And did not allow vice to hold a place within him.  
> This man, pouring out prayers, drove away hostile weapons;  
> By prayer he will strike down the boar that attacks us with its tooth.  
> Odo, renowned above the stars, pray for us,  
> As we are in a region of manifold disaster.

# Letter of Saint Odo, Archbishop of Canterbury, on the Life of Wilfred, Archbishop of York

*(In Warthon, Anglia Sacra, vol. II, p. 59.)*

To those enslaved in the service of orthodox faith, and to those who preside over them in ecclesiastical purpose throughout the world, both now and in the future: Odo, shepherd of the sheep of Canterbury, offers fellowship in holy humility and rejoicing in the assembly of inexhaustible blessedness.

While the shrewd diligence of human curiosity continually piles up precautions for itself against things that slip away, philanthropy is often extended so far that, insolently passing beyond the impassable boundaries of nature, it determines that whatever can be gathered must be sought out, even by corruption.

For ever since the first settler of the earthly paradise insufficiently perceived the serpent’s deception, and, with the postponement of the briefness of death, began painfully to suffer the cleverness owed to it, the almost sleepless enormity of the world has advanced with parsimoniousness. From this, through the wild growth of more obstinate thrift, it sometimes joins together right and wrong without much discrimination.

Indeed, it is fitting for us, helmeted with the unwearied [or: unstrung] shell of truth, to mark out what must be done by regular methods, chiefly so that we may strive to adapt the hanging tufts of monastic [or: “little-cloister”] profit to prophetic harmonies.

To me they say, “It is good to cling to God”; and in this matter it is joined in direct opposition to the proposition that not serving him is good. If, then, these trifles wish to escape somewhere, I shall fasten them together in this little miscellany of arm-like bindings. I declare that no one of the same lineage is unaware that the kingdom of the English once endured innumerable conflicts, by which both the dwellings of the ancient fathers were wounded and many seeds of religious unity darkened, so as to bring the contemplative worship to completion [Col. 0946A].

[Therefore, when certain persons had transferred the most venerable relics of the blessed confessor of Christ, Wilfred, which were rotting in the unseemly filth of a muddy abyss—or rather, what is even fearful to say, neglected through the horror of the prelates—I reverently received them, with God’s favor, from that place and from his tomb [Note: [Col. 0945] “From that place” according to Mabillon, *Acta Benedictinorum*, fifth century, p. 283, where the words enclosed in brackets are found], and placed them within the boundaries of the metropolitan Church over which, by God’s grace, I preside.]

This was especially compelled by that testimony of the Evangelist, which serves as my own defense: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matthew 24:28).

Thus, delighted by the nearness of so great and God-worthy a relationship, I judged it worthwhile both to adorn them in a more distinguished reliquary and to embellish them with a new poem, using little flowers excerpted from the book of his life [Col. 0946B].

This too must be asserted in the cup, lest anyone attempt, with a most impious frowning brow, to oppose absurdly the will of God while I am made to receive—perhaps “accept,” uncertain—the capered [uncertain reading] thing; for nothing occurs on earth without a cause.

Indeed, through ignorance he avoids the comic saying, “I hold the wolf by the ears.” Moreover, I shall sweeten the bitter tricorn [uncertain] of desperation and the inserted angelic speeches with the universal poultice and ambrosial compound of language, roaring with the giant-slayer to the Lord:

> “I have hoped in the Lord.  
> Everyone who hopes in the Lord will rejoice and exult in his mercy.  
> Therefore I shall rejoice and exult in his mercy” (Psalm 30:7ff.).

# Constitutions of Saint Odo, Archbishop of Canterbury

In the time of King Edmund, approximately the year of the Lord 942. They establish regulations concerning the office of the king, magistrates, and clergy, and concerning the proper granting of the rights of the Church.

*(In Mansi, *Conciliorum amplissima collectio*, vol. XVIII, col. 395.)*

## Titles of the Chapters

I. On the immunity of the Church.  
II. On the office of secular princes and the obedience to be shown to bishops. [Col. 0946]  
III. On the office of bishops.  
IV. On the office of priests.  
V. On the office of clerics.  
VI. On the office of monks. [Col. 0947A]  
VII. On prohibiting illicit marriages.  
VIII. On preserving harmony in the Church.  
IX. On fasting and giving alms.  
X. On paying tithes.

## Preface

In the name of the holy Trinity and the one divinity.

Although, with no merits of my own, I presume rashly to teach anyone through the boldness of a pious exhortation, nevertheless, because a spiritual prize is promised by the Author of gifts, the Spirit, to those who strive and labor in the stadium of this life, and because the people of God, destined to increase in faith and number, are entrusted prudently to the care of shepherds, I, Odo, humble and least of all, enriched by divine generosity with the honor of a gracious bishop and the pallium, have decided to gather in this little document certain teachings which, if I am not mistaken, are not unworthy of any worshiper of Christ.

I have found these teachings most firmly established in the instructions of illustrious men who came before, for the consolation of my lord King Edmund and of all the people subject to his excellent rule [Col. 0947B].

Therefore I most devoutly beseech and most mercifully exhort the minds of those who hear them, that whenever they hear these things read aloud, they plant them inwardly in their hearts through frequent meditation and gather for themselves, at the time of harvest, a most peaceful fruit from the manifold gift of good works.

## Chapter I

First, we prescribe and command that the holy Church of God, founded first in the blood of Christ and whitened as a bride by the multitude of the faithful, shall not be entered by any interruption of evil men.

Nor shall anyone be permitted to impose a tax upon the Church of God, because the sons of the Church—that is, the sons of God—are free from every earthly tax in every kingdom.

Ambrose says: “The Catholic Church is free from every tax imposed by a ruler.”

In the *History of the Church*: “If any houses, fields, or estates of whatever kind have been taken away from Christians, whether placed under the royal treasury or granted as gifts, we command that all these be restored to Christians’ former right.”

For Gregory says: “If anyone strips the Church of Christ, let him be anathema unless he corrects the matter by making satisfaction.”

And again: “Whoever attempts to seize the parishes of the Church of God by plunder is to be excommunicated by the ministers of the Church and altogether alienated from the body of Christ.”

Those who disdain to obey the rules of the discipline of his Church dare do something outside the soldiers who crucified Christ; for the Church has power to bind and to loose [Col. 0947D].

## Chapter II

Second, we admonish the king, the princes, and all who are in authority to obey their archbishops and all the other bishops with great humility, because the keys of the kingdom of heaven have been given to them, and they possess the power to bind and to loose.

Nor should they think highly of themselves because of secular power, for God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble. The king should have prudent counselors, fearing God in matters concerning the kingdom, so that the people, instructed by the good examples of the king and princes, may advance to the praise and glory of God.

He must oppress no one unjustly through power; judge without respect of persons between one man and his neighbor [Col. 0948A]; be a protector of strangers, orphans, and widows; prohibit theft; punish adulteries; not exalt the wicked; and nourish the poor with alms.
