For although it is necessary for every human being to keep Christ’s commandments, it is especially necessary for kings and for all placed in high office, who on the day of the strict judgment will have to render an account both for themselves and for all subject to them to the just Judge.

## Chapter III

Third, the bishops are to be admonished to preach and display good examples to all, with complete propriety and moderation in the piety of holy religion.

They are to travel through their parishes every year with complete vigilance, preaching the word of God, lest anyone, wandering through some byway of ignorance because of the negligence of the shepherd, lie exposed to be torn apart by wolves’ bites [Col. 0948B].

No one should undertake to feed the flock entrusted to him for the sake of disgraceful profit, but in hope of eternal reward. What we have received freely, let us not delay in giving freely.

Without any fear or flattery, and with complete confidence, they are to preach the word of truth to the king, to the leaders of his people, and to all persons of rank, and never evade the truth.

They must condemn no one unjustly, admit no one to communion except justly, and show everyone the way of salvation.

## Chapter IV

Fourth, we admonish priests to teach the people of God through good examples and holy dress, and to instruct and form them through holy teaching.

Their conduct in all goodness and moderation should be superior to the character of the people [Col. 0948C], so that whoever sees a priest walking clothed according to the dignity of his priesthood may speak well and laudably of his appearance.

## Chapter V

Fifth, the clerics are to be admonished to live canonically, with complete propriety and reverence, according to the decrees of the holy Fathers, offering good examples to all.

Thus, through their good conduct, the bishop may be praised, the Church honored, the people advance to the praise of God, and the clerics themselves, according to the dignity of their name, may be made worthy to enter God’s inheritance.

## Chapter VI

Sixth, we exhort monks and all who have made a vow to God to strive to fulfill it with complete humility and obedience, day and night, remaining in the fear of God in the churches where they have bound themselves by their vow.

Let them not be wanderers or gyrovagues—those who desire the name of monk but despise his duty. Rather, following the examples of the apostles, let them exercise themselves through the habit of humility, the labor of their hands, sacred reading, and continual prayers.

With their loins girded and their lamps burning, let them await the Master of the household, so that when he comes he may make them remain forever in eternal rest.

## Chapter VII

Seventh, we prohibit and forbid all Christians to enter into unlawful or incestuous marriages with nuns, relatives, or other forbidden persons [Col. 0949A].

For Pope Gregory of holy memory, together with many bishops and other priests, established in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter:

“If anyone takes a nun, whom they call a servant of God, in marriage, let him be anathema.”

And they all answered: “Amen.”

Following the same apostolic authority, we too impose upon such persons the dart of a similar curse, unless, having been corrected, they come to make satisfaction for so unspeakable a presumption.

## Chapter VIII
In the eighth chapter we observe that, whenever we come together in any assembly, we should consider with complete attention what the Psalmist admonishes us, saying: “The Lord looks down upon the children of men” (Psalm 52), and so forth; [Col. 0949B] and again: “The Lord brings the counsels of the nations to nothing,” and so forth, “even unto an inheritance for himself” (Psalm 31). Therefore, brothers, we must see to it that there be concord and unanimity among bishops and princes, and among the entire Christian people, so that there may be unity everywhere among the churches of God, and peace: indeed, let there be one Church, in faith, hope, and charity, having one head, who is Christ. Its members ought to help one another and love one another with mutual charity, as he himself says: “By this everyone will know,” and so forth (John 14).

## CHAPTER IX

In the ninth chapter we admonish you to preserve fasting [“and prayer” to be added] together with almsgiving, carefully and vigilantly [Col. 0949C], for these are the three wings that lead the saints [Col. 0950A] to heaven. Accordingly, strive to observe with great vigilance the Lenten fast, the Ember Days, and the other lawful fasts—namely, Wednesday and Friday. Above all, take the Lord’s Day and the feasts of the saints under your most careful protection from every secular work, just as the canon and the examples of those who came before affirm; nor should you give assent to empty superstitions. You must not worship the creature instead of the Creator through magical deceptions, because those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God.

## CHAPTER X

In the tenth chapter we command, and earnestly exhort you, concerning the giving of tithes, as it is written in the Law: “You shall bring the tenth part of all your crops, or of your firstfruits, into the house of the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 12). Again, through the prophet: “Bring,” he says, “the whole tithe into my storehouse, so that there may be food in my house, and test me in this. If I do not open for you the floodgates of heaven and pour out a blessing upon you in abundance; and I will rebuke for your sake the one who eats and destroys the fruit of your land, and it shall no longer be barren in it” (Malachi 3). Therefore, with solemn adjuration, we command that all should strive to give tithes from everything they possess, because it belongs especially to the Lord God; and that they should live from the nine parts and give alms. By practicing truth, let us remain in him who is God, blessed forever and ever. [Col. 0950C] Amen.

[Col. 0949]

# SYNODAL LETTER OF SAINT ODO, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, TO THE BISHOPS WHO ARE HIS SUFFRAGANS

*(In Mansi, same work, column 398.)*

[Col. 0949D] With the wondrous mercy of the almighty Ruler of the heavens coming to my aid, I, Odo, archbishop of the Church of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and metropolitan of the city of Dorobernia, offer to my fellow bishops, fellow builders of the Catholic faith, joined by spiritual charity and also by the firmness of fellowship, my brothers, prosperity in the present life and the blessedness of heavenly glory.

If it could in any way be arranged that all the wealth of the world were placed before our eyes, so that it might universally serve us as an imperial gift, I would gladly distribute all of it and, in addition, expend myself for the salvation of your souls. For I desire and hope to be strengthened by the zeal of your holiness in that work in which the Lord God [Col. 0950D] has appointed us laborers.

[Note: [Col. 0949] I think that what is enclosed in brackets is by William of Malmesbury, who reports this letter.]

[And he added much concerning the burden of the episcopate:] Therefore, humbly, as one unworthy but devoted, I beg and exhort your holiness not to become lukewarm or negligent in the governance of souls, lest, at the time of dreadful vengeance, the Lord complain against you, saying: “The shepherds did not feed my flock, but themselves” (Ezekiel 34); and again: “They became princes, and I did not know it” (Hosea 8:4). Rather, let us care for the household of the Lord, over which he has appointed us rulers, and give it food at the proper time: a measure of wheat, that is, approved doctrine.

Although, because of the quality of my merits, I do not presume to console or exhort anyone—for I alone am unworthy and guilty of innumerable offenses [Col. 0951A]—I nevertheless rejoice that I need to be faithfully strengthened by fraternal admonitions. Yet, because of the ancient authority of my predecessors, namely blessed Augustine and the other saints, through whose zeal the rule of Christianity was first made known from this archiepiscopal see throughout all the territories of the English, I have therefore resolved to inscribe these divine words for the benefit of all of you [Col. 0952A], so that the most august king, Edmund by illustrious name, together with all his people, may rejoice to imitate what he hears in and from us, and so that all the peoples everywhere subject to his royal authority may love and delight to follow with exultation the titles of our transparent way of life.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 961: RORICO, BISHOP OF LAON

[Col. 0951]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(From Gallia Christiana, volume IX, page 520.)*

[Col. 0951B] In the year 949, “the people of Laon,” says Flodoard in his Chronicle, “who were attentive to their fidelity toward King Louis, chose for themselves as bishop Rorico, a deacon and the king’s brother, namely the illegitimate son of Charles the Simple. Archbishop Artold of Rheims consecrated him, although, since he was not received at Laon, he took up residence at the fortress of the bridge of the Aisne.”

In 955 he attended the ordination of Hadulf, bishop of Noyon. In 961, after the death of Artold, archbishop of Rheims, he exercised the office of archchancellor until Odalric succeeded Artold. In the same year he restored the monks to the abbey of Saint Vincent, removing the canons. In 962 he attended the synod of thirteen bishops in the region of Meaux, at which, together with Gibuin of Châlons, he prevented the see of Rheims from being restored to Hugh, Artold’s rival; and in the same year he laid hands upon Odalric, who had been consecrated by Wido of Soissons.

In 969, on the third day before the Nones of June, he consented to the donation of half the abbey of Saint Hilary, together with its church, to the monastery of Saint Vincent. In 973 he himself gave that monastery the church of Saint Medard in the village of Caprimiacum. In 976, “seized by a paralytic illness,” says Flodoard in his Chronicle, “after rendering many and fitting thanks to God for that illness, he departed this life, namely on the vigil of Saint Thomas the Apostle, after the morning praises to God.” The Vincentian Necrology records of him in these words: “On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, Rorico, bishop of Laon, died. He established a second rule for this monastery and gave it many goods, lands, and altars.” That he was learned is attested by the monk Atso in his book On the Antichrist, which he composed at the request of Queen Gerberga.

[Col. 0951]

# RORICO’S CONSTITUTION CONCERNING THE RESTORATION OF THE MONKS IN THE MONASTERY OF SAINT VINCENT

*(Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Rheims, volume I, page 626.)*

[Col. 0951C] With the mercy of heavenly favor assisting, I, Rorico, although unworthy, having obtained the episcopate of the holy Church of Laon, considering that the lot of the final summons awaits me as it does the rest, and reflecting upon how greatly I am weighed down by the burden of my sins, began silently to deliberate within myself about something that might benefit this see over which, by God’s authority, I preside, and which, as I believe, was especially necessary for the remedy of my own offenses.

For on the side of the mountain over which the city rises, plainly in view of it, there stands a church venerable for the worship [Col. 0952C] and honor of the distinguished martyr Saint Vincent. It was reported that in ancient times it had been notable for monastic observance; but in our own time it was sinking under the poverty of abandonment, until my predecessor Adelelm, by gathering resources from various places, established there a community of twelve canons, who were to serve in it according to a religious way of life.

After he had died, however, and the evils of various calamities had multiplied, it had almost fallen back into the ruin of its former desolation. I could not endure this patiently, especially since it was regarded as the burial place not only of the bishops of this see but also of nobles [Col. 0953A] and laypeople. I therefore summoned a general assembly and, after deliberation with its advice, resolved to restore it to the ancient state of monastic observance, as tradition reported it, and, as the opportunity of the time permitted, to gather together however small a number of monks.

Accordingly, I summoned twelve monks from the monastery of Saint Benedict situated above the Loire. I appointed the venerable Melchanus abbot over them and established him, together with the other monks, in the same monastery to serve God. Among the other benefits I conferred upon them, I approved and confirmed the dignity of second episcopal see, which had been granted to that church by our ancient predecessors. I also granted the burial place of bishops, canons, holders of benefices, custodians, chaplains and servants of the mother church, and their dependents; I also granted jurisdiction over the valley and mountain, and so forth. And so that this authority might possess firmer force, we deemed it appropriate to strengthen it below both with our own seal and with the testimony of our clergy and noble laymen.

The mark of Rorico, unworthy bishop of Laon.

We therefore decided to send it to the venerable synod held at Mont-Sainte-Marie, in the region of Tardenois, in the month of May. There it was read while Lord Adalbero the archbishop was seated with his fellow bishops, and it was confirmed by them with common consent.

I, Adalbero, archbishop of the holy Church of Rheims, have subscribed and confirmed this.

Done at Laon in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 961, indiction 4, on the fourth day before the Kalends of October, in the seventh year of King Lothair.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 961: ARTHALD, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS

[Col. 0953]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE CONCERNING ARTHALD

*(From Gallia Christiana.)*

[Col. 0953C] “Without delay,” says Flodoard, “after the death of Seulf, Count Heribert came to Rheims, summoning Abbo, bishop of Soissons, and Bovo of Châlons. Joining them to himself, he deliberated concerning the election of a ruler for this Church of Rheims and compelled both clergy and laity to act according to his will.

Following his advice, lest the bishopric perhaps be divided among outsiders, they elected his son, named Hugh, still very young, who had not yet completed his fifth year. After this had been done, they hurried to the king in order to obtain his authority. When King Rodulf learned of this election, he entrusted the bishopric of Rheims to Heribert, at the advice of the aforementioned bishops, to be administered and governed by him according to the standard of justice.

He also took care to send envoys of the Church to Rome with Bishop Abbo, carrying with them the decree of this election and seeking the pope’s approval of it. Pope John, therefore, with Bishop Abbo intervening, granted their request and assigned the bishopric of Rheims to Bishop Abbo, determining that the matters belonging to the episcopal ministry were to be handled and completed by him in that same bishopric.

Count Heribert, having obtained control of the bishopric of Rheims, unjustly deprived both me, who had not been present at the election he had arranged, and several other clergy and laymen of the benefices and possessions of the Church with which we appeared to have been rewarded by the preceding bishops in return for our obedience. He distributed these possessions according to his own pleasure to those whom he favored.

Meanwhile, in the year 927, a synod of six bishops of the diocese of Rheims was convened at Trosly by order of Count Heribert, although King Rodulf opposed it. At about the same time, Odalric, bishop of Aix, who had withdrawn from his see because of the persecution of the Saracens [Col. 0954C], was received into the Church of Rheims by Count Heribert, solely to celebrate the episcopal ministry in place of Hugh, the count’s son, who was then still a child. The same bishop was granted the abbey of Saint Timothy, together with only one cleric’s prebend.”

In the year 931, or perhaps 932, according to the Rheims Chronicle, a quarrel arose among Counts Hugh and Heribert and King Rodulf. After capturing the city of Rheims three weeks later, Rodulf, having joined to himself eighteen bishops from France and Burgundy, had a certain Artald, a monk from the monastery of Saint Remigius, ordained as bishop in that see.

But in 940, when Heribert had once again brought Rheims under his control, he compelled Artald to resign the episcopate. Then, in the following year, he convened a synod at Soissons. By its decree, Hugh, his son, with the consent of the clergy and people, was consecrated archbishop in the basilica of Saint Remigius by the bishops of the province of Rheims.

Hugh had already received the other orders: the minor orders from Abbo of Soissons, the diaconate from Wido of Auxerre, and the priesthood from Wido of Soissons. In 943, envoys of the Church of Rheims returned from Rome and brought him the pallium sent by Pope Stephen. In 943 he held the office of chief chancellor of France. In 945 he relinquished the abbacy of Saint Remigius, together with its rights and title.

In 946, Rheims was besieged by three kings: Louis the Transmariner of France, Otto of Germany, and Conrad of Cisalpine Gaul. Hugh, realizing that he could not withstand so great an army, took counsel with his kinsmen Arnulf of Flanders and Wido concerning what should be done in this danger—for an agreement had been made that his eyes would be put out if the city were captured by force. Taking precautions for himself, he escaped with his men on the third day of the siege [Col. 0955A]. The kings then entered the city and, with the bishops accompanying them, had Artald enthroned again through Robert, archbishop of Trier, and Frederick, archbishop of Mainz.

In the following year, King Louis besieged the fortress of Mouzon, which Hugh, expelled from Rheims, had retained for himself. But accomplishing nothing according to his wishes, and the Lotharingians withdrawing after several weeks of siege, he himself returned to Rheims. Shortly afterward, when he had gone to Otto around the feast of Easter, certain people suggested to Prince Hugh that Rheims could easily be captured. The prince gathered an army and, as though he were about to capture it immediately, attacked the city together with Bishop Hugh. But the soldiers of the king and of Artald resisted bravely, and on the eighth day after his arrival he withdrew in humiliation.

Meanwhile, Kings Louis and Otto discussed among themselves how to end the dispute over the archbishopric of Rheims. A meeting was announced on the River Chiers, and the bishops on both sides traveled about there; but because they had not been assembled synodically, the dispute could not be brought to an end.

Therefore, in the middle of November, a synod was announced, while during the delay the archbishopric was left in Artald’s possession and Hugh was permitted to remain at Mouzon. But Hugh, seeking revenge for his rejection, came with Theobald of Montaigu, his sister’s husband, and devastated the estates adjoining Rheims during the vintage season.

The synod was therefore held at Verdun, presided over by Robert, bishop of Trier, together with Artald of Rheims, Odalric of Aix, Adalbero of Metz, Goslin of Toul, Hildebold of the Transrhenish region, and Israel the Breton. Bruno, King Otto’s brother, was also present, as were the abbots Agenold and Odilo and several others.

When Hugh, canonically summoned, refused to come, the bishopric of Rheims was adjudicated to Artald. But because the matter was extremely tangled and did not seem capable of being conveniently settled by the bishops of the province, it was decided that a full council should be convened the following year in the church of Saint Peter near Mouzon, from the dioceses of Trier [Col. 0955C] and Rheims.

Bishop Hugh came there, however, and after speaking with Robert, archbishop of Trier, who was presiding over the council under a special legation, he refused to enter the synod. Through his cleric, who had brought them from Rome, he sent letters from Pope Agapitus to the bishops. They contained no canonical authority, but merely commanded that the bishopric of Rheims be restored to Hugh.

After the letters had been read, the bishops replied that it was not proper for them to interrupt the mandate of the apostolic legation entrusted to Archbishop Robert before kings and bishops because of these letters, which were produced by an enemy and rival of Bishop Artald. They then read chapter 19 of the Council of Carthage, “Concerning the Accused and the Accuser,” and judged that, while Artald retained the diocese of Rheims, Hugh—who had refused to come when summoned to two synods—should abstain from communion and from governing the bishopric of Rheims until he appeared before a universal synod to clear himself.

They immediately sent Hugh that chapter, written out on parchment, together with their decision [Col. 0955D]. On the following day, the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February, Hugh sent the same parchment back to Bishop Robert, adding that he would nowhere obey their judgment.

As for Artald, he is said to have been the brother of a certain Dodo. After being made archbishop of Rheims from a monk of Saint Remigius, he received the pallium one year after his ordination. It had been sent to him through envoys of the Church of Rheims by Pope John, son of Maria, who was also called Marozia, or by Alberic, the patrician, the pope’s brother.

In 933 he presided with Teutilo, bishop of Tours, at the synod of Château-Thierry. In the same year he consecrated Hibdegar of Beauvais and Fulbert of Cambrai as bishops. In 935 he held a council in the territory of Sainte-Macre and ordained the monk Wifred as bishop of Thérouanne. In 936 he anointed King Louis the Transmariner [Col. 0956A] in the city of Laon. In 939 he excommunicated Heribert, who was holding certain towns and estates of the Church of Rheims. In 940 he received from Louis the Transmariner, for himself and his Church, the mint of the city of Rheims, to be possessed in perpetuity by right; and in the same year, after he had been compelled to relinquish the see, he received the abbey of Saint Basolus and the monastery of Avenay.

In 948, after the Council of Mouzon, Pope Agapitus, having received Artald’s letters requesting restoration, sent his representative, Bishop Marinus, to King Otto to convene a general synod. It was assembled in the same year, on the seventh day before the Ides of June, in the palace of Ingelheim. There, before the kings and bishops, Artald’s letters were read.

After those letters had been read and interpreted for the benefit of the kings in the Teutonic language, a certain Sigebald entered. He was a cleric of the aforementioned Hugh and brought letters that he had carried from Rome [Col. 0956B] and had already made public at another synod at Mouzon, claiming that the same letters had been given to him at Rome by Marinus himself, who was present.

Lord Marinus then produced the letters that Sigebald had carried to Rome and ordered them to be read before the synod. When they were read, it was found—as the letters themselves acknowledged—that Bishop Wido of Soissons, Hildegarius of Beauvais, Rodulf of Laon, and all the other bishops of the diocese of Rheims had sent those letters to the apostolic see for Hugh’s restoration to the see of Rheims and Artald’s expulsion.

After they had been read, Bishop Artald rose, together with the aforementioned Rodulf, whose name appeared in the letters, and also Bishop Fulbert of Cambrai. They rejected the letters, asserting that they had never previously seen or heard of them and had not consented to their delegation.

When the cleric could not contradict them, although he loudly protested with accusations against them, Lord Marinus urged the whole synod to offer him advice and a proper judgment concerning such an accuser and an informer against a bishop.

After the informer had been publicly refuted for bringing false charges, the bishops read the chapters concerning such accusers and judged and unanimously determined that he should be deprived of the honor he enjoyed and, in accordance with the terms of those chapters, be sent into exile. Accordingly, deprived of the diaconal ministry he held, he departed rejected from the presence of the synod.

But concerning Bishop Artald, who had presented himself at every synod and had not avoided synodal judgment, they decreed, praised, and confirmed that the bishopric of Rheims should be entirely retained and administered by him, in accordance with the canons and the decrees of the holy Fathers.

On the second day of the session, after readings from divine authority had been recited and after the address of Marinus the representative, Lord Robert, archbishop of Trier, proposed that, since the bishopric of Rheims had been restored and returned to Bishop Artald according to the ordinances of sacred law [Col. 0956D], synodal judgment should be carried out against the invader of that see.

Marinus the representative therefore ordered the synod to pronounce a canonical sentence concerning this presumption. The chapters of sacred law were accordingly ordered to be brought forth. After they had been read, in accordance with the ordinances of the sacred canons and the decrees of the holy Fathers—Sixtus, Alexander, Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, Leo, Symmachus, and the other holy teachers of the Church of God—they excommunicated the aforementioned Hugh, invader of the Church of Rheims, and expelled him from the fold of the Church of God until he should undertake to come to repentance and make worthy satisfaction.

In the same year Artald attended the Council of Trier and received Louis, son of Louis the Transmariner, from the sacred font—that is, he baptized him. Here Flodoard’s history ends.

Around the year 950, the same bishop transferred the body of Saint Bertha [Col. 0957A], abbess, to Avenay. Charters from this year and from the years 938, 950, and 953 survive, from which it is clear that Artald was then chief chancellor of the kingdom.

In 952 he returned to the monks of Saint Remigius an abbey called Cosla, situated in the Vosges. In the same year he replaced secular clerics with monks at Saint Basolus. He is also said to have given those same monks of Saint Remigius the abbey of Saint Timothy, which until that time had belonged to the archbishops of Rheims; but this grant should rather be attributed to Adalbero. On this matter, see the Bollandists, August, volume IV, page 576.

In 953 he convened a synod of five bishops at Saint-Thierry in the territory of Rheims. In 954, on the day before the Ides of November, he consecrated Lothair, king of the Franks, in the basilica of Saint Remigius. In 958 he stormed and recovered the fortress of Coucy, which Count Theobald of Chartres had seized from his Church.

Finally, in 961, on the day before the Kalends of October, he was seized by illness, completed his mortal life [Col. 0957B–0958A], and was buried at the feet of Saint Remigius.

At that time, when Count Hugh, several of Heribert’s other sons, and certain bishops were striving to have the now-vacant see of Rheims restored to Hugh, Queen Gerberga and her brother Bruno raised objections, although King Lothair favored Hugh’s restoration. The matter was discussed in a synod at Matrona, in the diocese of Meaux, before the bishops who had gathered there, in the year 962.

They judged that nothing concerning Hugh’s case should be decided without consulting the supreme pontiff, especially Rorico of Laon and Gibuin of Châlons, since Hugh, having been excommunicated by many bishops, could not be restored to ecclesiastical communion. After a response had been brought from Rome, Hugh was rejected and another bishop was ordained.

Concerning Artald’s writings, see the Literary History of France, volume VI [Col. 0958B], page 297.

[Col. 0957]

# LETTER OF ARTHALD, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS, TO THE SYNOD ASSEMBLED AT INGELHEIM

*(Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Rheims, I, 614.)*

[Col. 0957C] To Lord Marinus, vicar of the holy Roman and apostolic see, and to the entire holy synod assembled at Ingelheim: Artald, by the merciful favor of God, archbishop of Rheims.

Agapitus, the lord pope, sent letters to us and to the other co-bishops of our diocese, in which he instructed us to make every effort to assemble at this council of your holiness, so instructed in all matters that the truth of the case concerning the miseries of our see, which we are suffering, might be made manifest before your holiness. Therefore we have thought it useful to disclose to your wisdom how the matter that began this litigation—which is still being most unhappily contested between Hugh and me—first arose.

When Archbishop Heriveus had died, we elected Seulf, who at that time held the office of archdeacon of our city, to the episcopate of that same see. Once ordained bishop, and taking up zeal against the relatives of his predecessor, he was unable to drive them from the place by his own efforts. Accordingly, after deliberation with certain laymen, namely his counselors, he sought the friendship of Count Heribert and obtained it through those same counselors by an oath, on the following terms: after his death, the soldiers of the Church were in no way to aspire to the election of a bishop without the advice of Heribert himself; and the count was to exclude Heriveus’s brother and his nephews from participation in the affairs of the Rheims bishopric.

After these matters had been carried out, those relatives of Bishop Heriveus were accused by the counselors of Bishop Seulf of disloyalty to their lord. Count Heribert was summoned with many of his men, and they were ordered to appear before them to give an account. Because they refused to meet in single combat with those by whom they had been accused, their possessions in the bishopric were taken from them; they were arrested and brought by Count Heribert to King Robert, by whom they were also held in custody until Robert’s death.

Finally, in the third year of his episcopate, Bishop Seulf died, as many assert, having been poisoned by Heribert’s household. Immediately afterward Count Heribert went to the city of Rheims and compelled the soldiers of the Church, together with certain clerics, to deliberate according to his counsel about the election of a ruler, as had been sworn. Going with them to King Rodulf in Burgundy, he obtained from him the administration of that bishopric, on the condition that he grant and preserve due honor to both clerics and laymen, do injustice to no one, and govern the bishopric by equal right until he presented to the king a cleric who could properly be ordained to perform the episcopal ministry.

When the count had returned to the same city, he divided the bishopric’s possessions among his supporters as he pleased, took them away from the others, and, without any judgment or legal process, stripped those whom he wished of their possessions or expelled them from the city. Finally, receiving Bishop Odalric of Aix in that city, he ordered him to celebrate the episcopal ministry there.

Thus for six years and more he claimed that bishopric under his own dominion, treating it according to his own will. He himself and his wife both occupied the bishop’s seat [Col. 0959A], until at last, in the seventh year, certain disputes arose between him and King Rodulf and Count Hugh. Then King Rodulf, together with Hugh, his brother Boso, and many others—both bishops and counts—besieged the city of Rheims. The bishops were angered against him and complained that, for so long a time and contrary to the authority of divine law, he had allowed this city to remain without a pastor.

Moved by their complaints, the king admonished the clergy and people concerning the election of a pastor and granted them the freedom to carry it out, for the honor of God and their loyalty to himself. Thus, when all the clerics and laymen who were outside the siege had agreed, and many of those held inside had also favored the same proposal, the person of my humility was elected to undertake this burden rather than honor.

At last the soldiers and citizens opened the city gates to King Rodulf; the bishops who were present—eighteen in number—conferred the episcopal blessing upon me; and the entire clergy and the remaining citizens received our humility. I was enthroned by the bishops of our diocese, and for nearly nine years I administered, as God granted, the ministry entrusted to me, ordaining eight bishops throughout the diocese and many clerics in the bishopric, as seemed appropriate.

This continued until the ninth year, after I had blessed King Louis, with Hugh’s support and that of all the chief men of the kingdom, and had likewise anointed Queen Gerberga with the sacred chrism. Count Hugh, provoked to anger because I had refused to agree or join with him in the disloyalty toward that king, took with him Count Heribert and William, prince of the Normans, and besieged the city of Rheims.

Before long—on the sixth day of the siege, in fact—I was abandoned by almost the entire body of the lay soldiery. Thus deserted, I was compelled to go out to Hugh and Heribert. They constrained and terrified me until I was forced to renounce the administration of the bishopric; then, driving me away, they arranged for me to live in the monastery of Saint Basolus. Hugh, however, the son of Heribert, who had been ordained a deacon at Auxerre, they brought into the city and took possession of it.

When King Louis returned from Burgundy, he found me at Saint Basolus. Taking me with him, together with my relatives, whose possessions Count Heribert had seized, he led us to Laon, which Heribert and Hugh were then besieging. After the siege was lifted, he entered the town and arranged quarters for us in which to live.

Meanwhile our clerics of that place, as well as certain laymen, were treated most harshly by Heribert. Some of the clerics were thrust into custody, their possessions were taken away and plundered, and robberies were committed widely throughout the whole city.

In the meantime, the bishops of our diocese were summoned by Hugh and Heribert, who were striving to obtain from them a decision concerning the ordination of Hugh, Heribert’s son. They assembled at Soissons and sent Bishop Hildegarius to me at Laon, together with certain other delegates, instructing me to come to them—namely, to consent to the perversity of this ordination.

I sent them word that it was not fitting for me to go to them, since my adversaries and enemies were assembled there with them. But if they wished to speak with me, they should come to a place where I could approach them without danger.

When they came to a place chosen by them, I went to them. On arriving, I prostrated myself before them and begged them, for the love and honor of God, to take pains to give both me and themselves the counsel that was fitting. They began to question me concerning the ordination of the aforesaid Hugh and to urge me by every means to give my consent to that ordination, promising that they would obtain for me certain possessions belonging to the bishopric.

But after I had long delayed my response, seeing that they all persisted in the intention with which they had begun, I rose and publicly forbade it in the hearing of all. By the authority of God the almighty Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, I excommunicated them, declaring that none of them should take part in that ordination or, while I lived, lay hands upon anyone for episcopal office; nor should anyone dare to receive that same blessing. If this should happen, I appealed against them to the Apostolic See.

When they raged against me, I moderated my response so that I might leave their midst and return to Laon. I told them to send someone with me who could report to them what counsel I might be able to find concerning this matter from my lady the queen and her faithful men, since the king was absent.

They sent Bishop Deroldus for this purpose, thinking that I would change my decision. When he arrived and questioned me about the matter before my lady the queen and her faithful men, I rose again and hurled against those same bishops the aforesaid sentence of excommunication. I also took care to repeat the appeal to the Apostolic See, excommunicating Deroldus himself, so that he would not conceal any of this from them but would report it openly to all.

After these events, they paid no attention to our excommunication, went to Rheims, and some of them took part in the ordination, while others are known to have withdrawn from it.

I, however, remained with the king and endured with him the hardships that he is known to have suffered. When Hugh and Heribert attacked him in war, I was with him and barely escaped the danger of death.

Having thus slipped away, with the help and protection of God, from the midst of my enemies, I wandered as a fugitive through every pathless place and forest, not daring to remain anywhere securely. Counts Hugh and Heribert addressed certain of our friends who were subject to them and urged them to find me and bring me to them, promising that they would do me good and enrich me with whatever possessions they might request.

Our friends therefore sought me and found me wandering in various places. Thus my brothers and friends brought me to the aforesaid counts. When they saw me in their power, they began to demand that I hand over the pallium conferred upon me by the Roman See and renounce the priestly ministry altogether.

I declared that I would do no such thing, not even for the love of this present life. I was therefore placed under constraint and pressure by them and finally compelled to renounce the possessions of the bishopric. Thus once again I was led to Saint Basolus, to live there as though I were without office.

I remained for a few days in that monastery, until I learned through reliable messengers from among Count Heribert’s household that he was plotting my destruction. Terrified and driven on again and again by such messages, I left the place and wandered through the hidden recesses of the forests. At silent hours, by a remote road, I returned to Laon, where the king received me and arranged for me to remain with him.

I stayed there with him and his faithful men, awaiting and beseeching the mercy of God, until God deigned to put it into the heart of Lord King Otto to hasten into France for the aid of my lord the king and of us.

Finally, after our lady the queen had left Laon to secure the release of the lord king, I departed from there and came with my lord king to Lord King Otto. Together we also approached Rheims. The city was then surrounded by armies, and the bishops who were present judged that I should be restored to my see.

Lord King Otto therefore ordered Hugh to depart and abandon the city he had seized. After hesitating for some time, and seeing that he was wholly unable to offer sufficient resistance and that the support of his friends could not help him, Hugh resolved to leave, asking that he and his men be allowed to depart freely.

He was therefore permitted to leave unharmed with all who wished to accompany him, and he carried away without opposition whatever he wished to take with him. When I entered the city with the kings, I was ordered to be restored to my place and honor.

I was received by the archbishops, Lords Robert of Trier and Frederick of Mainz, who were accompanied by the others and congratulated by both the clerics of our church and the remaining citizens; and by them I was restored to the episcopal chair.

Hugh, however, after leaving Rheims, occupied the fortress of Mouzon with his men, fortified it against the faithful of our lord king, and held it.

Finally, when a conference had been arranged between the kings—namely, my lord king and Lord Otto—over the river Chiers, both Hugh and I came to it, together with his ordainers. There the bishops heard the case underlying this dispute.

Hugh produced letters addressed to the Roman See as if they had been written in our name, supposedly as an explanation on my part, as though we had requested a suspension of the administration of our bishopric. I declared, and still declare, that I had never dictated those letters or in any way confirmed them by subscribing them.

Because no synod had yet been convened, our dispute could not be settled, since Hugh’s supporters raised this objection. A synod was then announced for Verdun, to be held around the middle of November, with the bishops of both parties agreeing.

Meanwhile it was decreed that I should govern the see of Rheims, while Hugh was permitted to remain at Mouzon.

Before long, when the season of the grape harvest was approaching, our rival Hugh came with Theobald, an enemy of the king and of our kingdom, and many other evildoers to the villages of the Rheims bishopric adjoining the city. Gathering almost all the wine from them, he had it carried off to various districts.

Many evils were then committed there. Men belonging to our Church were carried away captive and subjected to various tortures in order to force them to pay ransom.

The synod announced for Verdun was held under the presidency of Bishop Robert of Trier, by command of the lord Roman pope. Lord Bruno was also present, together with several bishops and abbots. The aforesaid Hugh was summoned to it, and two bishops, Adalbero and Gozlin, were sent to bring him there; but he disdained to come.

The entire synod decreed that I should govern the Rheims bishopric.

A synod was again announced for the Ides of January, and it was convened as had been proclaimed, in the church of Saint Peter before the sight of the fortress of Mouzon, by Lord Robert, with the others assembling.

Therefore we have learned that, through your diligence, a monastery of monks has been established at Mouzon, a fortress situated on the river Meuse, in honor of God’s mother Mary. It has been adorned with religious observance and endowed with your properties and with the lands and churches of your Church. At your request we have accepted it under the charter of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and under ours.

Moreover, you transferred to the same monastery at Mouzon a small estate which had been established by Stephen, an illustrious man, and his wife Freduide, called Tin, and had been placed under Saint Remigius. Since it could not stand on its own because of the smallness of its possessions, you gave it to that monastery, with possessions transferred in compensation to Blessed Remigius and with the consent of the brothers.

So that the whole Church may know that we unanimously approve what you have conferred or will confer, and whatever others may confer, in cultivated and uncultivated lands, vineyards, meadows, churches, male and female dependents, waters and watercourses, and in everything belonging to the aforesaid monastery, we confirm it by the decree of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and by ours, so that, free from the envy and abuse of detractors, the place may remain forever secure and inviolate.

If, meanwhile—which we do not believe—anyone should attempt, with rash audacity, to act against those things which by this our authority have been piously and firmly established through this privilege, or to break or transgress in any way what we have established for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid monastery, let him know that, by the authority of Blessed Peter, whose unworthy representative we are, he is bound by the chain of anathema and is to be burned in eternal fire with the devil and Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ.

But whoever proves in all things a faithful observer, preserving the precept of our apostolic decree concerning the worship of God, shall obtain the grace of blessing and the forgiveness of his sins, and shall become a participant in eternal life.

Written by the hand of Stephen, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of April. Given through the hands of Andrew, bishop, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the seventh year of the pontificate of our most holy lord, the thirteenth pope. In the eleventh year of the empire of the elder Lord Otto Augustus, and the fifth of the younger, in the month of April, in the fifteenth indiction.

IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 963. ODALRIC, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS.

[Col. 0963]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON ODALRIC

*(From Gallia Christiana, vol. IX, p. 56.)*

Odalric—or, as others call him, Udelric or Ulric—was the son of Count Hugh and Eva. He came from Lorraine and had parents descended from Saint Arnulf of Metz, distinguished not only by blood but also by character and piety.

After serving, if Colvenerius is to be believed, as provost of the Church of Rheims, he was elected in 962 with the support of King Lothair and consecrated in the same year by Bishops Wido of Soissons, Rorico of Laon, Gibuinus of Châlons, Hadulf of Noyon, and Wicfrid of Verdun. Having received the pallium, according to the custom of his predecessors, from Pope John XII, he soon became, on account of the distinction of his birth and the prerogative of his dignity, chief chancellor of the kingdom under King Lothair. He held that office in the years 963 and 968.

How energetic and prudent he was in defending the possessions of his Church, Flodoard briefly related in his Chronicle under the year 965. When a dispute arose over the Rheims bishopric and serious movements of war broke out between the king of France [Col. 0963B] and Heribert’s family, almost the entire province was afflicted by plundering, fires, and the destruction of cities. Certain nobles who appeared to be protecting villages held under ecclesiastical law in the king’s name had gradually drawn them to themselves as though they were hereditary possessions.

Among them was Count Theobald. Odalric summoned him, and when he refused, he pursued him with the sword of excommunication in the year 964, on account of the fortress of Codiciacum and certain other estates of Saint Remigius, which Theobald had wrongfully acquired and stubbornly retained.

Returning to a better mind, Theobald restored what had been wrongly obtained. For this reason the bishop not only absolved him but also granted the aforesaid fortress to his son Odo, who had placed himself under the bishop’s protection.

Moved by this example, Count Heribert willingly returned the village of Épernay. But Ragenold, persisting in his wrongdoing, was excommunicated on account of the villages that he likewise held unjustly. He himself, invading certain places belonging to the same bishopric with his men in a hostile manner, devastated them by plundering and burning.

In 965 Odalric attended the assembly of bishops held at Cologne, in which the foundation of the Church of Saint Martin of Liège was confirmed.

The generous bishop is praised because he gave his Church of Rheims the village of Vendenesse, situated in the county of Rethel, and because he restored to that Church, as its free possession, the valley of Rodigion, which Hugh, son of Count Roger, had donated to it but which his descendants had afterward usurped, in the year 967.

It should not, however, be concealed that, on account of the murder of one of his relatives, who had been shamefully slaughtered in the suburb of Saint Remigius, he himself burned and devastated the entire suburb and everything adjoining the fortress of Saint Remigius, and thereafter permitted no one to live there.

According to the continuation of Flodoard, he died after seven years of administration, that is, in the year 969, and was the first of the archbishops of Rheims to be buried in the metropolitan church.

The Rheims Necrology briefly records him in these words:

> “Odelric or Odalric, archbishop, died on the eighth day before the Ides of November. He gave us Vendenesse. For his soul, twenty-four coins together with an equal number of loaves and wine are given to the poor from the common funds; six poor clerics are fed in the refectory.”

Under this bishop, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April in the year 966, the celebrated Flodoard died at the age of seventy-three. He had been born at Épernay on the Marne, had first been a priest and canon of Rheims, then parish priest of Cormicy, and, according to some, afterward a monk and abbot of an uncertain monastery in the diocese of Rheims.

On him consult the abbots of Saint Basolus, the bishops of Noyon in Fulcherius, the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. VII, pp. 325 and following, the *Annals of the same Order*, vol. III, pp. 397, 511, and 512, and the *Literary History of France*, vol. VI [Col. 0964C], p. 313; nothing new occurs that needs to be added to these works.

[Col. 0963]

## SENTENCE OF ODALRIC, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS, AGAINST SACRILEGIOUS THIEVES

*(Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Rheims, vol. I, p. 621.)*

Odalric, bishop, Rodulf, archdeacon, and all the clergy of the Church of Rheims, to all the sons of the Church.

Certain wicked and criminal men enter the temple of God with an evil mind. Although they ought to implore God’s mercy and devote themselves to prayer, they do not fear, at the devil’s prompting, to pursue thefts and sacrileges.

Among them are certain men whom we do not yet know. Entering this basilica of blessed Mary, Mother of God, they did not fear to take away a pallium from above the altar of the holy cross. Moreover, certain other things have recently been stolen from there: namely, the linens from the bed of Frederick, the church’s custodian. Also, from the chapel of Saint Peter within the cloister, a priestly vestment has now been taken; in the preceding year, a missal.

We excommunicate and anathematize the perpetrators of all these acts and the sacrilegious thieves, through the power and authority of God the almighty Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; by the power of the holy cross; by the virginity of blessed Mary, Mother of God; and by the authority of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and of all the saints. They are to be excommunicated and separated from participation in the body and blood of Christ, from entry into the Church, and from every Christian society, until they come to correction and satisfaction or return to this Church the things they have taken.

AROUND THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 963. SIGEHARD, MONK OF SAINT MAXIMINUS OF TRIER.

[Col. 0965]

## SIGEHARD ON THE MIRACLES OF SAINT MAXIMINUS

*(In Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae Historica.)*

## NOTICE TO THE READER

Wikerus, who governed the monastery of Saint Maximinus at Trier as abbot from 957 to 966 [Note: *Annals of Saint Maximinus*, p. 7], urged Sigehard to append a second book on the miracles of Saint Maximinus to the saint’s Life, written perhaps by Lupus, bishop of Châlons [Note: *Acts of the Saints*, May VII, p. 20].

Although lacking confidence in his abilities, Sigehard began the work toward the end of 962 or at the beginning of 963 [Note: Year 27 of Otto I, chapter 11]. He professes that he will relate only what the abbot had thoroughly learned and handed on to him [Note: Preface; compare chapter 23—chapter 24 in the edition: “But now at last let us come to what our venerable father himself used to relate about himself”].

Nevertheless, he also seems to have consulted other monks of the monastery. For although he learned from Wikerus’s account what Duke Gisilbert had reported to Abbot Ogon [Note: Chapter 12], other matters were communicated to him by the monk Thietbert [Note: Chapter 6], the priest Ruotpert [Note: Chapter 17], Wenido the custodian [Note: Chapter 17], the priest Reginerus [Note: Chapter 21: “as he himself often testified to me”], perhaps also by Adalbert, later archbishop of Magdeburg [Note: Chapter 16], and by others [Note: Chapter 15: “as those who saw it affirm”].

All these matters Sigehard, who certainly must be regarded as a monk [Note: In the ancient Necrology of Saint Maximinus—Codex Görres, Koblenz, no. 2—on the sixth day before the Kalends of September occurs: “Sigehard, abbot and monk of our congregation.” Whether this is our Sigehard seems doubtful. I do not know why Brower (*Annals of Trier* IX, 41; I, p. 440) called him an Aquitanian], committed to writing. He did so simply and without observing chronological order [Note: Chapter 1: “We cannot preserve the order of times as events occurred, because we prefer to connect like things with like. Nor do I see what hinders the edification of readers if the times vary in an account of events of this kind, provided that what happened is not passed over in silence”], but with sufficient accuracy, good faith, and a sufficiently plausible manner of expression [Note: Yet, in the humility for which he is commended, he says at the end of the work, chapter 30: “Moreover, I beg all who deign to regard this little work without envious eyes that, when its uncultivated speech has offended them, they grant an easy pardon to ignorance, and not be astonished that a rustic man, who has scarcely learned the first rudiments of grammatical art, could not speak with an orator’s abundance. Nor do I expect anyone to accuse me of rashness, as though I had presumed to undertake something beyond my strength, because the brief preface placed above will sufficiently reveal to readers how great was the authority of the one giving the command, which finally drove me, unwilling and long resisting, to undertake these things”].

Of these matters, chapters 8–18, which shed some light on the affairs of Lorraine in the ninth and tenth centuries, ought to be presented here, while the remainder is omitted, since it scarcely—or scarcely at all—relates to history.

In the extremely rich library of the city of Trier I found five manuscripts. This year, with the permission of our colleagues Wyttenbach and Laven, the library’s prefects, who kindly favored me, I spent almost an entire month occupied in copying its manuscript books. With their help I have corrected the text in more than one place.

[Col. 0967]

1) No. 1151 (963), parchment, thirteenth century, large folio. Formerly belonging to Saint Maximinus, it contains a great collection of saints’ Lives, once arranged in seven volumes, of which four still survive. In the second volume—formerly the third—folio 125 contains the *Life of Saint Maximinus*, followed by Sigehard’s second book, which has frequently been corrected by a later hand [Note: The same hand, apparently, added on a small slip a little story about a miracle approved by the emperor Otto. It passed into the edition in chapter 25 of the *Acts of the Saints*, May VII, p. 30, but cannot be attributed to Sigehard: “But why should we review the miracles mentioned above, when new ones are close at hand? For when you, Wikerus, had been established in the burden and honor of the abbacy, the glory of our patron shone forth. Reginso, as you know, and Engela [of Branbach [Col. 0968B] “of Branbach,” added by correction, 2], born of free parents, gave themselves and their only son Adelmann to Saint Maximinus, on the condition that the boy himself, as long as he lived, and his male descendants should pay two denarii, but the females one denarius, to the altar of blessed Maximinus on the feast of Saint [Col. 0967B] Martin; after their death, whatever they possessed that was best among their livestock or clothing should pass to the Church.

“Meanwhile a certain soldier, coming into that land for the sake of plunder, secretly took away the aforementioned boy, without his parents’ knowledge, and, riding across the bridge of Trier, intended to carry him off with him. What more need be said? The boy, turning his eyes toward the monastery of the divine bishop Maximinus, cried out that the saint of God might rescue him from the soldier’s hands. The angry soldier struck the boy; but immediately, by divine vengeance, the horse’s neck was broken, and the soldier fell from the bridge into the water, while the boy remained safe and unharmed upon the bridge.

“The boy then sought the threshold of the saint and made the matter known to you, Abbot Wikerus. Giving thanks to God, you restored the boy to his parents. You also disclosed this celebrated event to the most serene king, namely Otto I, who was then staying at Trier in person, and presented the boy to his royal magnificence. You asked him to confirm by his charter the aforesaid transfer of the boy, to release both the boy and his descendants from all advocates, and to ensure that no one should make them his beneficiaries. Finally, accommodating this request out of pious good will, he decreed that it should be done and ordered a charter to be written and secured with the impression of his seal in the third year of his reign.”

I very much doubt whether Otto’s diploma from which these excerpts were taken—Hontheim, *History of Trier* I, p. 299—is genuine.]

Without doubt, the edition published under Henschenius’s direction in *Acts of the Saints*, vol. VII, p. 25, derived from this manuscript. From the same manuscript too, before those corrections and that addition were made [Note: Rivet, *Literary History* VI, 301, is mistaken if he says that this history was published from the manuscript of Saint Victor in Paris].

1o) No. 1167 (CCCXCVI), paper, late fifteenth century, formerly a codex of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Eberhard’s Clusa, was copied from it.

2) No. 1380 (1141), written elegantly in 1514 on white parchment, follows manuscript 1 for the most part [Note: From this manuscript too he took the little story mentioned under no. 15, although it is already rejected as Sigehard’s by someone else in a marginal note. It is absent from manuscripts 3 and 4], but another manuscript was also used, from which it seems to have received the divisions of the chapters and the red headings.

3) No. 1396 (1337), paper, seventeenth century, folio. Among various works illustrating the history of Trier, it also contains this book, copied from an excellent manuscript. Whatever is read correctly in manuscript 1 after correction, and better in manuscript 2, is also correctly transmitted here; other passages could be corrected only from this manuscript.

4) No. 1381 (1180), paper, sixteenth century, quarto. Although written most carelessly and corrupted by innumerable errors, it was nevertheless drawn from a good source.

Our colleague Bethmann found another manuscript, and an older one, written in the eleventh century, but apparently lacking the preface, formerly belonging to the monastery of Saint Gislenus, in the library at Mons. I trust that our edition can do without it without loss.

Hontheim supplied certain notes; he inserted fragments of the book into his collection of Trier writings, I, pp. 465–468.

## AUTHOR’S PREFACE

[Col. 0967]

Sigehard to Lord Abbot Wikerus, to be received (*suscipiendo*) with every reverence in Christ [Note: MS 3 reads *suspiciendo*, “regarded”; MS 4, *amplectendo*, “embraced”; the words *Omni in Christo reverentia suscipiendo* are absent in MSS 1 and 2] [Note: MS 4 adds: “Sigehard offers service and the due rendering of obedience”].

You ask, most beloved father—or rather, by a certain force of authority you extort from me, unwilling as I am—that I undertake to explain a work altogether arduous and beyond my powers. For you command—and MS 1 adds *-que* after *propria*, while MS 2 reads *ac propria*—and compel me by your own authority to bind in writing the miracles performed by that glorious confessor of Christ after the book on the life of Saint Maximinus published by Bishop Lupus, lest they entirely perish to the advantage of readers or hearers; and, arranging them in a suitable sequence of narrative, to complete a second little book about them after that first one, with you, naturally, supplying the material by your spoken account.

Because of this I am constrained from two sides: I fear either that, by resisting you, I may incur the crime of disobedience, or that, by trying again to obey, I may collapse beneath what I have begun. For I plainly see that the weakness of my little intellect and the small drop of my eloquence are in no way sufficient to carry out a task of this kind.

Therefore, confronted by such difficulty [Note: MS 1 reads *difficillitate*, “very great difficulty”; MS 2, *difficilitate*], from which I cannot escape unharmed, as though enclosed and surrounded on every side by a kind of circuit of walls, I have judged that the only useful thing for me to do is to choose here the place of escape where I see that the least injury can result from the precipice.

Since it is clear that contempt for one’s elders looks toward danger to the soul, while failure in what one has undertaken exposes one to ridicule [Col. 0969A], what sound-minded person would not judge it more tolerable, indeed much safer, to endure the mockery of men on account of incompetence than to condemn oneself on account of pride?

Therefore, proceed (*perge*) confidently to undertake the work so long desired [Note: MSS 2 and 3 read *pergo*, “I proceed”]. I shall assist you to the best of my ability, no longer daring to resist your holiness. Whatever you shall relate—whether, as you promise, things seen by you yourself and by those who still live with you, or things learned by you from those who saw them, persons whose testimony is credible—I shall set down in whatever style I can.

I do not rely on confidence in my own ability for this purpose; rather, I entrust so laborious a task to the merits and prayers of you and all the holy brothers.

Our illustrious Maximinus will perhaps be present here too, as he is always present in everything, and, as I trust, will easily obtain (*obtenturus*; MS 2 has *obtentaturus*, corrected in MS 1 to *obtenturus*) from Christ the Lord that, just as he was made by God the Father in the Holy Spirit the salvation and righteousness of all, so he may also make me, though without speech, a tongue.

If he deigns to do this, there is no doubt that even by a mute a clear truth will be expressed with brilliance [Note: MS 3 reads *expresum* for *expressum*].

Nor should it be concealed that, although I readily trust that this little work will be pleasing to God and to all pious people in future times, I nevertheless fear that some of those living now will disparage it and condemn me throughout the world as a foolish, lying, insignificant little man, most deserving of universal reproach [Col. 0970A].

Nor, I confess, will you, venerable father, be able to escape being involved in the plague of all this attack, even if they wish to spare you, since, according to the assertion of such men, you will have compelled me to write falsehoods and will have supplied material for falsehood to the writer.

For this reason I see that it is worthwhile—MS 1 adds *operæ* after *qua ex re*, while *præsenti* is absent in MS 2 and added after it in MS 1—to block the way to slander with this brief preface: not by resisting with elaborate defensive art, but by humbly suggesting that they remember that the first and most valiant defenders of Christ were *ydiotas* (“uneducated men”; MS 3: *ideotas*), not sophists [Note: corrected from an earlier reading by a later hand]; and that they should not expect me to declaim in the court with Mercurial charm [Note: MS 1: *lepulitate* for *lepiditate*], or with Tully’s abundance [Note: MS 1 originally *tullique copio*, corrected to *tulliique copia*; MS 2 *tullique*, corrected to *tulliique*], but to speak in the monastery cell, in pure and simple language, the truth of events drawn from the sober and truthful mouth of a pious father.

Furthermore, even if the poverty of the one laboring on this work is rightly held in contempt by them, I ask that the authority of the one who commanded it nevertheless be honored. Let them not immediately believe that our father, a man conspicuous for holy life and conduct, preferred to speak falsely rather than remain silent.

With these matters briefly set forth, Father Wikere [Note: MS 2 has *Wichere*; MS 1 was corrected from *Wikere*], let us undertake what lies before us, first entreating the divine favor, so that, with its assent, you may be able to declare by word and I to pursue in writing whatever things are worthy of it and of all the saints.

**END OF THE PREFACE** [Note: [Col. 0969] “thus” in 3; where it continues: “Here begins the second book on the miracles of Saint Maximinus, archbishop of Trier.” I had resolved to dedicate the opening of this little work to that remarkable miracle. Nearly so also 4. The other manuscripts and editions are defective at this point.]

[Col. 0969C] **8** [Note: [Col. 0969] Chapter 10 in the edition. 2 adds in red: “Those expose themselves to the gravest danger who attempt to annul the election of the abbot of this monastery”; 3: “How harshly divine vengeance punished Megingaud, duke of this kingdom, who held this abbey and blasphemed against Saint Maximinus.”] (890) In the time of Emperor Arnulf [Note: [Col. 0969] Arnolfus 1; Arnulphus 2, 3, 4.], when, alas, the condition of religious observance in this place had already declined to no small degree and the rigor of the monastic profession had begun gradually to slacken and dissolve, after the monastery’s abbot Herkenbert had died, the monks, according to custom, hastened to the palace to seek the election of an abbot. But since, because their sins demanded it, they were not permitted to hold an election [Note: [Col. 0969] “admitted” 3.], certain small properties belonging to the monastery were set aside—properties that could scarcely have provided the monks with a meager subsistence—and the emperor bestowed the abbey upon a certain Megingaud [Note: [Col. 0969] Compare Regino, under the year 892; Lamei, *Acta Palatina*, V, p. 165. Brower, *Annales*, p. 439, reports an epitaph for him found in the church of Saint Alban at Mainz.], duke of this kingdom, who happened then to be present [Note: [Col. 0969] “were present,” corrected to “was present” 1; “had approached” 3.].

After receiving it, he returned home joyfully. Displaying himself to everyone throughout the day as cheerful and delighted at the favor he had received, he went at nightfall with his wife into the bedchamber. [Col. 0969D] When they had lain down together happily and everyone else had withdrawn, he addressed the woman privately in these words: “Do you know,” he said, “what an immense gift my lord the emperor has granted me?” When she admitted that she did not know, he said: “He has bestowed upon me a very wealthy servant as a benefice; and, if you wish to know, it is Maximinus himself together with his abbey [Note: [Col. 0969] added after this in 1; absent in 2.], and I shall give him to you as well, if you wish.” On hearing this, the sane-minded woman sharply rebuked her almost insane husband, as far as she could, for his rash talk, and began to declare herself utterly unworthy of so great a benefaction [Note: [Col. 0969] “began” in 2.]. Meanwhile, there was scarcely any delay before—behold!—a fitting vengeance followed the insult done to God’s beloved Maximinus [Note: [Col. 0969] added afterward in 1.], and divine retribution seized the blasphemous mouth.

For that frail and perishable creature of earth, who in empty boasting and with a swollen spirit had exalted himself above Maximinus, the consul of heaven, suddenly contracted entirely into himself and, a little earlier in human form, rolled up into a nearly shapeless sphere or ball. [Col. 0970D]

**9** [Note: [Col. 0969] 2 adds in red: “The merciful healing of the aforesaid Megingaud after he had been gathered into a ball”; 3: “Megingaud, led to repentance, is restored by Maximinus to his former shape.”] Then Megingaud, having been chastised so harshly and for so long [Note: [Col. 0969] Thus in all the manuscripts; the edition reads “by divine power.” 2 adds “afflicted,” which was also written in 1 but later erased.], came to himself [Col. 0971A], understood what he was suffering and why, and, urged on by his wife, repented of what he had said with all his heart. He ordered that provisions be prepared and that he himself be carried with great speed to Trier.

At last they reached the monastery. He was laid before the holy altar, and the altar itself was heaped with costly gifts. The man who had earlier arrogantly proclaimed himself lord now humbly identified himself, more by gestures and hisses than by words, as the servant of Saint Maximinus. Nor was he deprived of the fruits of his satisfaction, after he had humbly fled for refuge to the mercy of the one whom he had injured with such insolence. For when the brothers poured out prayer on his behalf, the heavenly anger was calmed through Maximinus’s merits, and through the saint’s power complete health was restored to Megingaud in an instant.

Thus chastised by God with a salutary correction, so that he would not thereafter blaspheme against the saints, the man from that time onward honored Maximinus as most holy, embraced him as a father, and venerated him as a lord. He immediately reported what had happened to the emperor and pleaded concerning the election that had been denied to the brothers [Note: [Col. 0971] “denied” corrected from “being denied” in 1; “not to be denied” in 2.]. He did not cease asking and entreating the king until he had secured for the brothers, from the royal fisc, a property called Ribiniacum [Note: [Col. 0971D] Rubenach; compare Arnulf’s charter in Hontheim, *Historia Trevirensis*, I, p. 226.], for their use [Note: [Col. 0971] “acquired” corrected from “he would have acquired” in 1.].

Who, then, could sufficiently marvel at the holiness of so great and such a patron of ours, or praise it worthily? So far beyond everything else, so far superior to everything else, are all things in the merits and power of our Maximinus, that they cannot even be estimated, much less explained by any mortal. But let us return to the subject from which we have digressed into this very modest praise of the saint.

[Col. 0971C] **10** [Note: [Col. 0971] No chapter division in 1; 2 and 3 add in red: “By divine mercy, holy and religious men were never lacking in this monastery.”] Although, as we reported in the preceding chapter, the regular order and discipline in this place had earlier limped somewhat through the negligence and weakness of its superiors, nevertheless, by the divine mercy granted through Maximinus’s merits, holy and religious men were never lacking in this place, until, after abbots had again been appointed, the neglect of regular observance was corrected—by God’s favor—either to its former state or even to something better. This is clearly evident both from many matters which there is no time now to explain [Col. 0972A] [Note: [Col. 0971] absent in 1.] and also from what I shall relate at present.

**11** [Note: [Col. 0971] No division in 1; 2 and 3 add in red: “How grievously Duke Gisilbert, while wasting this abbey, afflicted the brothers of this place.”] After the aforementioned Megingaud, this abbey came under the authority and control of the dukes of this kingdom, except for those possessions which had long before been set aside for the brothers’ support; yet these too, as still happens, were entrusted by the kings to their protection.

For this reason, when Gisilbert was placed over the kingdom as a very young duke, then, as is characteristic of that age, during the first period of his rule he devoted himself to worldly pleasures, pageantry, and the enticements of sensual enjoyment, although afterward he became an outstanding man [Note: [Col. 0971] “an outstanding man” corrected from “an outstanding thing” in 1.]—he concerned himself more with his own interests than with the welfare of his subjects and grievously afflicted the monks of this monastery, taking away what had accrued to their use [Col. 0972B] and distributing it among his own followers.

At that time the most illustrious Heinricus [Note: [Col. 0971] “Henricus” in the manuscripts.], father of the most serene [Augustus [Note: [Col. 0971] absent in 2, 3, 4.]] Otto [Note: [Col. 0971] “Octo” in 1.], in whose twenty-seventh imperial year we wrote this, held the monarchy of the kingdom. He governed his subjects with the greatest moderation, through justice, peace, and clemency, and adorned the summit of imperial power with exceptional virtue, glory, and every form of honor.

[Col. 0971D] [Note: Concerning him, the *Life of Gerard of Brogne*, chapter 23, in Mabillon, *Acta*, V, p. 268, says: “Moreover, so that Duke Gislebert, whom we mentioned above, may not depart from us without praise and honor, he proved himself sufficiently humane and very generous toward the place of that same saint. He withdrew certain estates from his own military men—estates on which he had spent no little in benefits for the soldiers—and bestowed them there in perpetual right upon those who fight for Christ while serving as soldiers. Concerning this, I have one warning to give, repeating it to you, Ursidung of Cell, that is, monk of Saint Gislenus: you who live on the duke Gislebert’s most generous support, consider and attend carefully, so that you may never be found forgetful of his soul, but rather, with the most importunate prayer, knock upon the immeasurable mercy of the most kind Jesus, that he may obtain the golden rewards of eternal life. And lest you should murmur in despair that he rebelled against his lord, the Roman prince, he received—alas!—the terrible recompense of death; and the Lord Jesus does not punish the same offense twice.”]

**12** [Note: [Col. 0971] 2 adds in red: “The afflicted brothers approached the royal clemency to make complaint against the duke”; 3: “Deprived of the king’s protection, the afflicted brothers deserve Maximinus as their avenger against the tyrant.”] Accordingly, the brothers, as has been said, crushed by intolerable affliction under Gisilbert, came before the royal clemency and complained of whatever hardship they suffered from the duke [Note: [Col. 0971] “whatever inconvenience” in 2.]. Yet, having undertaken so much labor, they achieved nothing; rather, though undeservedly, they incurred the indignation of the aforesaid duke.

What else could they do? Driven at last by necessity, they were considering only withdrawal from the monastery when suddenly they recovered their courage, renewed their plan in this way: namely, with Maximinus as their patron, they would refer their case in prayer to the King of kings. When they had pursued this course for some time without slackening [Note: [Col. 0971] “they pursued” 2.], one night venerable Maximinus appeared in a vision to the duke as he slept. First he revealed who he was and on whose behalf he had come; then he reproved the guilty man for his faults; finally—and I am about to relate something marvelous, almost unbelievable except to those who do not believe that God can do all things—he beat the duke’s sides and shoulders with whips until they were livid, and immediately disappeared. [Col. 0973A]

The duke, violently shaken from both his sleep and his dream, declared to a few attendants that he had seen a dream and, as the blows testified, what he had suffered in it [Note: [Col. 0973] followed by “he saw” in 3.]; but he carefully concealed from all of them why this had happened or who had done it [Note: [Col. 0973] absent in 2.], although at that time the matter could easily have been inferred from the sequence of events.

For he immediately hastened toward Trier and, appeasing Maximinus by prayer and gifts, restored to the monks not only what he had taken away but also redeemed their lost favor by expenditures of money, of which the brotherhood stood greatly in need. From that time onward, recovering from his youthful behavior, he became an altogether magnificent man. He loved this place and its community so greatly that, through his powerful efforts, the venerable Ogone was installed as abbot of this place [Note: [Col. 0973] thus 4; absent in 1, 2, 3.] [Note: [Col. 0973] “enthroned” written “intronized” in 2, 3.], and the brightness of religious life, long too deeply obscured, at last shone forth more splendidly in our own life. (934)

He himself confessed all these events, exactly as we have related them, to the holy man Ogone. In that confession he also vowed himself as a monk to God and Saint Maximinus, if he should survive his wife and deserve to be released from the marriage bond.

**13** [Note: [Col. 0973] 2 and 3 add in red: “How a fraudulent surveyor, crossing the boundaries of Saint Maximinus’s estates, was punished” (3: “by the amputation of a finger”).] I shall relate another event which, in my judgment, should be considered scarcely inferior to this—unless one ought to regard it as diminishing Maximinus’s powers that in that miracle he is said to have had the illustrious Remigius as a partner in the deed. [Col. 0973C]

A certain count named Ruobertus [Note: [Col. 0973] “Robertus” 2; corrected to “Ruobertus” 1; “Rubertus” 4.] [Note: [Col. 0973D] He is not encountered elsewhere, unless perhaps he is the same man whom Regino mentions under the year 884.] was the brother of that Megingaud whom we mentioned above. His estates in the district of Naachgowe lay next to, and bordered upon, the estates of Maximinus and Remigius [Note: [Col. 0973D] This appears to be the church of Saint Remigius at Ingelheim.]. For this reason his servants repeatedly engaged in quarrels with the household of the saints: they wanted to cross the ancient boundaries, while the others resisted with all their strength.

Meanwhile, since the cruelty of the servants’ complaints and the rustic quarrel could not be restrained by the neighbors, and our men were protesting the covetous injustice, the case was referred to the count. He immediately announced a hearing, set a date, and arrived with a great crowd accompanying him to inspect and survey the boundaries. He ordered his own leaders to go ahead of him.

Without delay, one of them—the man who had always been the ringleader of this injustice—outstripped the others and became a fraudulent surveyor [Note: [Col. 0973] “fraudulent” written “fraudent” in 2.]. Going ahead and indicating the way, he tried, by false testimony, to transfer many portions of the saints’ estates to his own lord, crossing the ancient boundaries. He went on, with a *cirroteca*—which country people call a *wantum* [Col. 0974D] [Note: In French, *gant*, “glove.”]—drawn over his hand, indicating the boundaries as he wished, while our men followed, resisted him, and constantly cried out for the help of Maximinus and Remigius.

Meanwhile, that good and just guide pulled the *cirroteca* from his hand [Note: [Col. 0973] “glove” in 3.], but left behind in it the finger that had been amputated by divine power. [Note: [Col. 0973] “in his hand” in 3; “he should pull it off,” later corrected to “he pulled it off” in 1.] Thus convicted of his wickedness and disgracefully treated by his own lord, as was fitting, he lost his lord’s favor; and when the truth had been revealed, the entire dispute came to an end. [Col. 0974B]
