**14** [Note: [Col. 0973] 2 and 3 add in red: “How a most savage tyrant, oppressor of innocent people, miserably perished when the outpouring of his entrails brought vengeance through Saint Maximinus.”] There is a monastery estate called the church of Wimari [Note: [Col. 0974D] Weimerskirchen on the Alisontia, the Elz; Hontheim.], which a certain exceedingly cruel man—whose name has slipped from my memory—held as a benefice. Since he afflicted the saint’s household most severely and could not find anything to accuse them of, he entrusted his hawk to one of them who seemed more rustic than the others. He knew that the peasant had no knowledge whatsoever of that craft, so that, if the neglected bird should perish, he could shift the blame for its death onto the peasant.

The man resisted for a long time and earnestly pleaded his lack of skill, but at last, compelled, he had to accept responsibility for keeping the bird. What could he do? For the time being he kept it alive, although it was soon to die without food in the smoky house [Note: [Col. 0973] corrected from “smoke-filled” in 1.]. When it died, he plucked off its feathers, sprinkled it with salt, and hung it up for his master to preserve. For the foolish peasant imagined that he could escape the clever man’s cunning if, when the time of reckoning came, he were able to present him with the bird’s corpse intact [Note: [Col. 0973] “its corpse” in 3.].

When a long period of time had passed and the harsh master demanded his hawk from the peasant, the man immediately produced the corpse. The cruel man seized this opportunity and, fiercer than a wild beast, charged all the others with having insulted him through the peasant. He claimed that they had encouraged the bold deed by common counsel, and summoned them all to a hearing on the following day [Note: [Col. 0973] “palace” in 1, 2.], where they were to be stripped of all their property and subjected to many beatings.

Terrified and distressed, the wretched men gathered that night. Having completely despaired of all human help [Note: [Col. 0973] “having despaired” 1, 2.], they resolved to seek Maximinus’s aid. They selected two young men from among them, loaded them with blessed loaves, gave them their instructions, and hurriedly sent them to the monastery, while the others waited in the greatest fear for the appointed hearing.

When the young men arrived, after the brothers had celebrated the ninth-hour *synaxis* [Note: [Col. 0975] “synaxis” in 1.], they knocked loudly at the monastery gate. Since it was thought that some important person might be present, they were immediately admitted. They ran through the middle of the choir, silently placed the blessed loaves before the altar, and first beat the altar with the brooms they had brought with them. Then, prostrate on the ground, with an immense and pitiful howling, they begged Maximinus to awaken and rise to their aid against the tyrant [Note: [Col. 0975] “tyrant” in 1.].

At that very hour and in that very moment when these men were lamenting their misery here, the savage man rose from the place of the hearing, sought a privy, and there, amid indescribable torture [Col. 0975B] [Note: [Col. 0975] “describable” in 1.], discharged both the viscera of his body and the cruelty of his character.

**15** [Note: [Col. 0975] 2 and 3 add in red: “A certain wealthy man, inflamed by the torches of greed, unjustly seized the small fields of the poor.”] There was a certain noble and wealthy man named Bernaker [Note: [Col. 0975D] Compare his charter in Hontheim, *Historia Trevirensis*, I, p. 268.], who, long after the matters we have related hitherto, acquired the same estate by precarious tenure. Inflamed by the torches of avarice, he unjustly seized the small fields of the poor that lay everywhere adjacent and contiguous to the fields of that estate, because the land was fertile.

Having assembled groups of plowmen, he ordered them to plow those very fields, while the people whom he had wronged begged him by God and Saint Maximinus to let their own possessions suffice for him and not to strip them unjustly of their little holdings. When he replied that, for Maximinus’s sake, he would not grant anyone even the breadth or length of a foot of all those lands [Col. 0975C], they fled to their customary protection. In the very place where the multitude of plowmen had already sat down to eat [Note: [Col. 0975] “had sat down,” 3.], since they had no one who could provide them protection [Note: [Col. 0975] “who could be their protector” 2.], they lay prostrate on the ground and prayed with great weeping and lamentation for the help of God and Saint Maximinus.

I shall relate something marvelous. As those who saw it affirm, not even the smallest cloud appeared anywhere in the sky [Note: [Col. 0975] added afterward in 1; absent in 2.], when suddenly, in this one place alone, where the oxen with their plows were standing, such a great storm arose that the oxen and plows, lifted by the force of the winds and the whirling vortex, were spun away and hurled into a very deep valley, almost half a mile distant from that place. Immediately, however, just as there had been clear weather everywhere else, so too there was clear weather there.

When the farmers, scattered in every direction, searched for their oxen and plows and came to the valley, they found some oxen half-dead and others already dead: some with their horns torn out, others with their legs or necks broken. The plows, meanwhile, they found smashed to pieces [Note: [Col. 0975] “to fragments,” corrected to “to pieces” in 1.].

Then, deeply grieved over their losses, the farmers returned to Bernachrus [Note: [Col. 0975] “Bernachus” 2; corrected to “Bernachrus” 1; “Bernakus” 4.] and reported what had happened with heavy mourning. Terrified by great fear, and suspecting that he would soon experience an even more severe vengeance, he was frightened by Maximinus’s power and ceased thereafter to persecute the poor. [Col. 0976B]

**16** [Note: [Col. 0975] 2 and 3 add in red: “A certain tyrant named Adelbert also afflicted Saint Maximinus’s household, but in vain.”] Nor should we omit what happened to Adalbert [Note: [Col. 0975] “Abalbert” 2; corrected to “Adalbert” 1; “Ab Adalberto” 3; “Delbert” 4.], the father of our Adalbert [Note: [Col. 0975D] Henschen thought that Adalbert, apostle of the Rus, later archbishop of Magdeburg, is meant.], during Gisilbert’s dukedom. For he treated the saint’s household with utter inhumanity and could not be corrected in his wickedness, although the duke’s mother repeatedly rebuked him—since the duke’s father had already died [Note: [Col. 0975] “his father” 2.] [Note: [Col. 0975D] It is not known in what year Ragenarius died; compare Richer I, 34, who nevertheless assigns the date incorrectly. Count Ragenarius names his deceased wife Hersenda in a charter issued around 886 for the church of Gorze (Calmet, I, *Probationes*, p. 313). The other woman mentioned here must have been the one who, after her husband’s death, appears to have administered the duchy of Lotharingia for the young Gisilbert (above, chapter 2; compare Richer, cited above: “already grown young”). It should be noted that in the tenth century women often assumed the administration of duchies: in Alamannia, Hadawiga (Ekkehard, *De Casibus*, chapter 10, *Monumenta*, II, p. 122: “the widowed duke of the Suevi after Purchard”); in Bavaria, Judith (Ratherius, *Opera*, ed. Ballerini, p. CI, 382, n. 39); in Lotharingia, Beatrix (*Chronicon Senonense* in Dacherius, 2nd ed., I, p. 616: “there was a certain duchess who, widowed by her husband, governed Lotharingia according to her ability”; compare *Life of Gerard of Toul*, chapter 21, and Gerbert’s letters passim). Likewise the empresses Adelheid and Theophania governed the empire, and Theophania is more than once called emperor in Italian charters; compare *Jahrbücher*, II, 2, pp. 65–66.]—sixty men from the estate of Ramiche [Note: [Col. 0975] “Remiche” 2.] [Note: [Col. 0976D] Is this Remingen (Remich), on the left bank of the Moselle, eight leagues above Trier? Henschen.] rose up at one time—for this benefice belonged to him—and all came together here.

Keeping watch before the doors throughout the entire night, they obtained permission from the custodian and arranged twelve men below the church at three altars, intending to seek Maximinus’s assistance throughout the night with unwearied prayer. Nor did their hope in Maximinus’s mercy disappoint the petition of the wretched supplicants.

In the morning, when that lady—for she was then staying here [Note: [Col. 0975] “there” in 2, corrected to “here” in 1.]—went out to Mass accompanied by Adalbert and many other retainers, all those men who were waiting for her arrival in the church immediately, as soon as she entered, fell together upon the pavement before the sacred altar [Note: [Col. 0977] “fell” 3.]. With terrifying and very loud cries they called upon Maximinus to assist them in such great need and proclaimed that they must at last be rescued from Adalbert’s tyranny [Note: [Col. 0977] “tyranny” 1.].

Only after half an hour had passed, as they say, were those cries finally silenced. Adalbert, seeing the merciful woman deeply affected with compassion for the wretched men, began to swear by Maximinus’s power that the men had lied about everything they were saying. Girded with a sword [Note: [Col. 0977] “girded” 1.], he immediately extended his hand to the hilt and, with extreme insolence, swore by his sword that they would pay the heaviest penalties for such audacity.

He had not yet finished his threats [Note: [Col. 0977] “they had not finished” 3.] when suddenly, in full view of everyone—for at that time he was not wearing a cloak [Col. 0977B]—his belt was loosed by divine power and the sword fell from his thigh to the ground. This proved to be an unmistakable portent, showing that from then on he would be useless for military service [Note: [Col. 0977] “a clear portent,” corrected in 1; “to that same man” 2.]. Thus Maximinus, through whose power Adalbert had been publicly confounded, soon deprived him of his benefice and powerfully rescued his servants from his savagery.

**17** [Note: [Col. 0977] 2 and 3 add in red: “The miraculous replenishment of the wine.”] Then Wenido, the church custodian, whom we mentioned above [Col. 0978A] [Note: [Col. 0977C] chapter 5.], taking a small flask containing only three sextarii of wine, after obtaining Maximinus’s blessing, refreshed those sixty men, exhausted by the entire night’s vigil and weeping, very abundantly. And, so that he would not be deprived of the bodily reward of his charity as well, as soon as he returned and entered the church, he found the same flask full again, just as it had been before.

Moreover, Ruotpertus, priest and monk, who was present and saw these things, bears witness to everything we have related in this chapter.

**18** [Note: [Col. 0977] 2 and 3 add in red: “The holy conduct of Wenido.”] When I compare Wenido’s arduous way of life—which has often been described to me by those who knew him—with the fact that he shares so familiarly even in the smallest portion of Maximinus’s powers [Note: [Col. 0977] “power” in 2.], what else can I judge it to be than holy? And since we have said so much about this man, I would like to report, as an example of self-restraint for people like me—that is, those polluted in heart and body—another matter that he himself used to relate whenever he warned or rebuked the more negligent brothers.

**19.** There was in this monastery an acolyte [Note: [Col. 0977C] The author relates below several matters of no great importance concerning the monk Wenilo, the priest Reginer, whom he says “died two years ago,” the monk Richwinus, “who survives to this day,” the abbots Willerus and Wikerus (chapters 20–24), and finally the discovery, under Bishop Ratbod, of the relics of Saint Maximinus, which had been hidden during the time of the Normans (chapters 26–29). Of these, I judge that only the following passage concerning the Normans from chapter 26 should be retained: “At the time when divine judgment had subjected almost all Gaul to be ravaged by the cruelty of the Northmen, when the fury of the pagans, inflamed by the torches of its own impiety, was burning cities, villages, and all the churches of Christ with fire, it happened that this city of Trier, together with its suburbs, also fell subject to the same calamities. And because it is said that so pitiable a slaughter of the citizens and destruction of the city occurred unexpectedly and suddenly, this monastery too, among the others, was not merely burned, but filled with such a slaughter of monks and members of the ecclesiastical household that not one survivor remained who knew the location of the tomb in which the sacred relics were enclosed.”] . . . [lacuna]

**AROUND THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 963. FRIDEGODUS, BENEDICTINE MONK.**

[Col. 0977]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON FRIDEGODUS

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini.)*

Fridegodus, a Benedictine monk of the monastery of the Savior at Canterbury in Kent, around the year of Christ 960 published, in prose, under his own name, a *Life of Saint Audoenus*, archbishop of Rouen, who died in the year 677; Surius printed it under August 24. Mabillon published his *Life of Saint Wilfrid*, archbishop of York, who died in 687, written in hexameter verse for Odo, archbishop of Canterbury, in the third century of the Benedictines, p. 169, and its supplement from a Cottonian manuscript in the fourth century, p. 722. John Bale, II, [Col. 0979] 32, and, following him, Pitseus, p. 174 and following, also attribute to this Fridegodus a treatise *On the Woman Who Was a Sinner in the Gospel*, which begins: “While God, through manifold goodness…”; and another, *On the Heavenly Jerusalem and the Vision of the Blessed*, written in verse and beginning:

> Citizens of the heavenly homeland in the region above.

Finally, they attribute to him various *Contemplations*. According to the same Bale, this Fridegodus was learned in Greek, as William of Malmesbury states in his work *On the Bishops of the English*. William’s words are these, in Book I of *On the Deeds of the English Bishops*, p. 200:

> And so that he might bring forth the brightest glory of his homeland—Wilfrid—as a beacon, Archbishop Odo ordered his life to be woven in heroic meter, and so forth.

Before Fridegodus’s time, according to Leland, chapter 134, several writers composed the *Life of Saint Wilfrid*: Bede of Jarrow; Heduus, surnamed Stephen, a companion of Acca, bishop of Hexham; and Odo, archbishop of Kent. Later the same was done by Peter Blaesensis, archdeacon of Bath, a Gaul, who dedicated his little work to Galfridus Plantagenista, archbishop of York. Finally, Casimir Oudin reasonably suspects that the epic poem *On the Bishops and Saints of the Church of the York Region*, which Thomas Gale published under Alcuin’s name in the *Writers of the Fifteenth History of England*, 1691, pp. 730–732, was probably by Fridegodus. The praised Oudin proves with arguments that cannot be denied that the poem should not be attributed to Alcuin. Cointius notes, in volume II, p. 607, that the *Life of Audoenus* as published by Surius is not the genuine work of the ancient writer but an interpolated one. Add the same author, volume I, p. 754 and following.

[Col. 0979]

# FRIDEGODUS, BENEDICTINE MONK, ON THE LIFE OF SAINT WILFRID, BISHOP OF YORK

*(In Mabillon, Acta Sanctorum of the Order of Saint Benedict, third century, p. 169, and fourth century, p. 722.)*

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

[Col. 0979A] Many authors have celebrated Wilfrid, the first bishop of York to bear that name, in their writings. Above all, the Venerable Bede describes his deeds in various places in his *History*, especially in Book III, chapter 25, and Book V, chapter 20.

Bede’s contemporary, Eddi or Heddius, surnamed Stephen, is also mentioned; according to John Pitseus and other more recent writers, he is said to have composed a book on the life of Saint Wilfrid. “He was invited from Kent by the most reverend man Wilfrid, so that he might be the first teacher of singing after James for the churches of Northumbria,” as Bede testifies in Book IV, chapter 2 of his *History*. From this association he could certainly have learned the deeds of Wilfrid.

After Heddius came Fridegodus, whom Odo, bishop of Canterbury, instructed to compose the life of the same saint in heroic meter. William, the monk of Malmesbury, had read Fridegodus’s composition and offers this judgment on it in Book I of *On the Canterbury Bishops*:

> A certain Fridegodus carried out that task in verses not without merit, [Col. 0979B] except that, detesting Latin, he loves Greek and frequently uses Greek words, so that the following line of Plautus may rightly be applied to his words:
>
> “No one will read these things except the Sibyl.”

Fridegodus undertook this labor immediately after the translation of Wilfrid’s relics to the church of Canterbury. Eadmer reports that Odo himself, who governed the church of Canterbury for twenty-four years beginning in 834, also described Wilfrid’s deeds. Eadmer—or Edmerus—the monk who served as secretary to Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, later did the same in the year 1121.

Thus reads the inscription prefixed to a handwritten manuscript in the Cottonian Library:

> The Life of Saint Wilfrid, archbishop, by Eadmer of Canterbury, in the year 1121.

At the beginning and end, he approves the events he has described by “the authority of the venerable men Odo the archbishop and Bede [Col. 0980A] the priest,” without mentioning Heddius or Fridegodus, although he frequently uses Fridegodus’s very words. Hence suspicion arises that Fridegodus’s offspring may have been passed off as the work of Odo, who had encouraged the undertaking.

Nevertheless, from the preface of Odo himself, which Eadmer quotes at the end of the *Life* he composed, it has been conjectured that Odo’s work was different from Fridegodus’s composition. Gervase of Canterbury, a monk, quotes Eadmer’s fragment on the translation of Saint Wilfrid’s body in his book *On the Burning and Restoration of the Canterbury Church*; this fragment was taken from another work by Eadmer.

Eadmer’s contemporary was William, monk of Malmesbury, who likewise recounted the deeds of Saint Wilfrid in Book II of *On the English Bishops*, in the section on the bishops of York. After all these came Peter Blesensis, archdeacon of Bath, who composed a book on the life of Saint Wilfrid and dedicated it to Galfridus, archbishop of York, as may be read in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, p. 172, where a fragment from this same Peter is cited.

The English writers must also be counted among these, including Thomas Stubbes, in his book on the bishops of York; an ancient catalogue of them is preserved in Labbe, volume I of the *Bibliotheca Nova*, p. 322. Of the authors mentioned above, Bede and William are readily available to everyone.

**2.** Both the more recent martyrologies and Bede’s widely circulated *History* give Wilfrid’s feast day as October 12, although these words were inserted into Bede’s text. Abraham Wheloc placed them in parentheses; they are absent from our German copy, as well as from Alfred’s Saxon translation.

The date certainly refers to the translation of the relics: according to Eadmer, on that day Lanfranc placed Saint Wilfrid’s body in a more suitable location. But on what day the holy man departed to the heavenly realms, all the writers of his life are silent. Only one among the ancient compilers of sacred calendars assigns a date: April 24, namely the author of the metrical *Martyrology* published under Bede’s name in volume X of the *Spicilegium*, with these verses:

> Egbert, shining with the worthy glory of his virtues,  
> Reverently ascends the starry Olympus on the eighth day,  
> And on the day when Bishop Wilfrid entered the blessed heavens,  
> Carried beyond the stars of heaven by an angelic company.

The solemnity of the translation, however, appears to have been more celebrated on October 12, as is clear from the title that Eadmer placed after the preface of the *Life*.

### 3. Wilfrid lived the monastic life from the age of fourteen and propagated the rule of Saint Benedict with great distinction.

At what place, however, he first assumed the monastic habit is not entirely clear. At the age of fourteen, certainly, among the monks of Lindisfarne he diligently “both learned and endeavoured to practise those things which belonged to monastic chastity and devotion,” says Bede in Book V, chapter 19:

> “He was not yet tonsured, but, he was distinguished in no small measure by the virtues of humility and obedience, which are greater than tonsure. [Col. 0981B] While serving God for several years in that monastery, he perceived that the way of virtue taught by the Scots was not perfect; and he resolved to go to Rome and see what ecclesiastical or monastic rites were observed at the Apostolic See.”

There he acquired the complete norm of the monastic life, that is, the Benedictine norm. On his return to Lyon, he was tonsured by Dalfinus, or Annemundus, bishop of that place. Afterwards Alchfrid, son of Oswiu, king of the Northumbrians, had Wilfrid, who had returned to Britain, “as a very learned man,” says Bede, “as his teacher in Christian learning. He knew that Wilfrid’s teaching ought rightly to be preferred to all the traditions of the Scots; and therefore he had also given him a monastery of forty households at a place called Ripon.”

Bede says this in Book III, chapter 25, where he consequently calls Wilfrid an abbot; he should therefore be understood to have received the monastic insignia in that monastery. A little later, at the request of Alchfrid, [Col. 0981C] he was made a priest in that same monastery by Agilbert, a Gaul and bishop of the West Saxons. After the Scots had been refuted at the Synod of Streaneshalch, he introduced our monks into the monastery of Lindisfarne, where the Scottish monks lived. Hence, in William’s account, he boasts that he was the first in Northumbria “to teach the true Easter after the Scots had been expelled, and to order the rule of the most holy Benedict to be observed by the monks.”

He built several monasteries: Ripon and Hexham in his own bishopric; others in Kent; Selsey among the South Saxons; and others in the kingdom of the Mercians. The following verses from his epitaph refer to this:

> And in those places he gathers large companies of monks,  
> And diligently establishes what the Rule of the Fathers  
> Prescribed in its admonitions.

In this passage the rule of Saint Benedict, which Wilfrid learned and cultivated both in Britain and at Rome, is called “the Rule of the Fathers,” as it is also explicitly called by Ambrose Autpertus in his book *On the Life of Saint Paldon, Abbot, and of His Successors*.

[Col. 0981D]

### 4. As for the sequence of Wilfrid’s deeds

He was born in the year 634, or the following year, since he died in 709 at the age of seventy-five. As a boy of fourteen he sought the monastery of Lindisfarne, where he was to remain for several years. From there he went to Rome around the year 653, shortly before—or certainly shortly after—the death of Honorius, bishop of Canterbury, which Bede places in that year in Book III, chapter 20.

[Col. 0982A] After spending about four years partly at Lyon and partly at Rome, he returned to Britain, built the monastery of Ripon, and administered it under the title of abbot. Around the year 660 he refuted Colman, the leader of the Scots, at the Synod of Streaneshalch, although Bede, in Book III, chapter 26, assigns this event to the year 664.

Bede, however, is not entirely consistent with himself. In that passage he writes that Agilbert, a Gaulish bishop, attended the synod and that, at Agilbert’s command, Wilfrid, still a priest, opposed Colman; yet from chapter 28 it appears that Wilfrid was ordained bishop in Gaul at Compiègne in that very year, 664, by Agilbert, who was already bishop of Paris. In chapter 26 Agilbert is said, after the discussion had ended, to have returned home—that is, to his own bishopric among the West Saxons.

Certainly, in the Saxon Epitome appended to Bede’s *History*, Agilbert is said “in the year 660 to have departed from Cenwalh and to have assumed the bishopric of Paris in Gaul, on the river Seine.”

[Col. 0982B] Wilfrid was ordained bishop of York in 664. When he returned from Gaul and learned that Ceadda had been consecrated bishop of his church, he withdrew to the monastery of Ripon. Afterwards, summoned by Wulfhere, king of the Mercians, he came into Kent, where he “ordained priests and deacons until Theodore should arrive,” according to Bede, Book III, chapter 28, and Book IV, chapter 2. Theodore expelled Ceadda from York and installed Wilfrid in his see.

In the year 670, when Oswiu, king of the Northumbrians, wished to go to Rome, he asked Wilfrid to be his guide on the journey; but, the undertaking having come to nothing, he died, as Bede records in Book IV, chapter 5.

“In the year 673,” Wilfrid is remembered as having been present at the Council of Hertford, under the presidency of Theodore, “through his own representatives.” “In the year 677, dissension having arisen between him and King Ecgfrith, that bishop was expelled from the seat of his bishopric, and two bishops were substituted in his place: Bosa, who was to govern the province of Deira, and Eata, who was to govern that of Bernicia” (chapter 12).

Meanwhile, after two years, Wilfrid went to Rome to plead his case. When the matter had been concluded, he converted the province of the South [Col. 0982C] Saxons to Christ and built the monastery of Selsey with the favour of King Æthelwalh. Likewise, with Cædwalla’s cooperation, he instructed the people of the Isle of Wight in Christian observances, as Bede relates in chapter 16.

In 687, after the death of Cuthbert, bishop of Lindisfarne, “the venerable bishop Wilfrid administered the bishopric of that church for one year, until someone could be chosen who ought to be ordained bishop in place of Cuthbert,” according to chapter 29.

“After a long exile”—that is, of more than ten years—he was “received into the bishopric of the church of Hexham,” according to Book V, chapter 3. “In the second year” (I would prefer “the twelfth year”) of Aldfrith, who ruled after Ecgfrith—another Aldfrith, distinct from Alchfrid—that is, in the year 697, “he recovered his see and bishopric at the invitation of the king himself. But five years later he was again accused by that same king and by many bishops, and was expelled from the episcopate. Coming to Rome” around the year 703, he was acquitted by Pope John and returned to Gaul.

At Meaux, when he had been brought to the end of his life, he obtained from God [Col. 0982D] a respite of five years. Afterwards he was restored at the Council of Nidd, at the beginning of the reign of Ofred, Aldfrith’s son—that is, in the year 705. He died in the fourth year of that King Ofred, “after forty-five years of episcopate,” as Bede testifies in Book V, chapter 20, specifically on the eighth day before the Kalends of May at the beginning of the year 709.

Certainly, in his epitaph, reported by Bede, he is said to have “passed fifteen times three years as a bishop.”

[Col. 0981]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0981D]

> Unskilled, I now begin noble deeds with feeble efforts,

>
[Col. 0982D]

> The almighty Maker, the revealer of hidden mysteries,

> Phoebus cannot make his torches clear,  
> Nor Cynthia her scanty lights.  
>
[Col. 0983A]

> Earlier ages, deceived by slippery illusion,

> He shattered the varied monsters by striking down their prince,

>
> When the glorified One returned to the starry citadels,  
> He himself, ever present with his worshippers,

>
[Col. 0984A]

> Wilfrid, renowned in fame above the lofty heights,

>
> Come to our aid, O glorious witness of God throughout the regions.

>

> After the see had been left vacant by the aforesaid bishop,

[Col. 0989B]

>

>

>
> The appointed days of the orders arrived,

> Then he spoke freely to the kings:

>
[Col. 0989C]

> “For while recurrent plague and an ancient dispute remain,

>
> “The soil of Gaul has nourished me for many years [literally “harvests,” glossed *annis*],  
> And in those homes western honour is preserved.  
> Hastening there, I shall receive the sandals  
> Of the jurisdiction entrusted to me,  
> Unless perhaps the sea, compelled by a powerful storm,

### XI. He crosses the sea and is consecrated.

> They reached suitable shores and entered the harbour

> His head was enriched with freely poured oil.  
[Col. 0990A]

> The ornaments of white linen shone first.  
> Gold-flowing belts gleamed with Tyrian purple [printed *serrano*].

### XII. On his return he is tossed by a storm, attacked by pirates, and victoriously reaches harbour.

> But since temptation tests all the fortunate,  
> An inseparable companion, while they traversed the high seas

>
> Behold, the sea suddenly roared with waves from the very depths,

>
[Col. 0990B]

> Far away, beneath unknown shores, it threatened

> The dreadful costs of approaching death.  
>
> They leaned upon the oars; the weakened stern was shaken.

>
> Behold, beside the hostile shores of an ill-fated harbour  
>
> A savage people watched the disaster with weapons in their hands,

>
> In the midst of this, a young man armed his sling (*scutale*)  
> With a smooth stone and, hurling it through the air

>
> As the cunning man fell, the air seethed with cries.

> The battle lines rushed together in savage combat;  
> The king’s troops clashed with hostile cries.  
>
[Col. 0990D]

> What more need be said? Whenever the attackers provoked cruel battle,

> And they reached the desired harbour by the route they had retraced.

### XII. With Ceadda substituted at York, he withdraws to the monastery at Ripon. He is sought by Wulfhere, king of the Mercians. He ordains ministers in Kent and builds monasteries.

> Those whom the royal assembly had previously defeated  
[Col. 0991A]

> And expelled were able to obtain this only through fraud.  
>
> While, detained by the sea after travelling in Gaul,  
> He waited long for favourable weather,

>

>

> For three years of unbroken days,  
[Col. 0991C]

> Nor did he yield while stripping the citadels of the savage thief.

### XIV. He is restored to his see by Theodore.

> When the years of the aforementioned period had elapsed,  
> Theodore, a cultivator of justice and piety,

#### Source notes

The notes follow the supplied source’s order, with their relevant Latin terms retained.

1. [Col. 0983D] **II, *dedans* (“giving”).** The same word occurs below in chapter 7.

2. [Col. 0983D] [Col. 0984D] **II, life under the rule.** Namely, in the monastery of Lindisfarne, according to Bede, Book V, chapter 20, and other writers of the Life. Yet Bede, Book IV, chapter 23, numbers Wilfrid, bishop of York, among the men trained under Abbess Hilda at Streaneshalch: whether the first or the second Wilfrid is in question.

3. [Col. 0984D] **III, *Biscop Baducing*.** An unfamiliar name for Biscop, whom Bede, in the history of his monastery, and other writers also call Benedict; nowhere do they call him Baducing.

4. [Col. 0985D] **IV, *omenta*.** *Omentum*: the membrane covering the internal organs.

5. [Col. 0985D] **IV, *cliothetro*.** *Cliothetrum*, or *cliothedrum*, a folding seat. A word badly compounded from κλείω (“I close”) and ἕδρα (“seat”). Fulcher of Chartres, Book III of the *History of Jerusalem*, chapter 61: “while Bohemond was sitting on his *cliothedrum*,” etc. Read Adrien Valois’s notes on Book IV of the *Panegyric of the Emperor Berengar*.

6. [Col. 0986D] **VI, *tria lustra*.** That is, three yearly cycles, according to Bede and Eadmer.

7. [Col. 0986D] **VI, *pistrix*.** This is the name given to a sea beast of immense size. How undeservedly these descriptions are applied to the pious and holy Queen Bathild has also been demonstrated in her Life.

8. [Col. 0986D] **VI, *creagris*.** *Creagra*: a grappling hook.

9. [Col. 0987D] [Col. 0988D] **VII, *monasterium*.** Not a monastery, but the site of a monastery, which Alchfrid had shortly before given to followers of the Scots to hold as a monastery, as Bede testifies in Book III, chapter 25. Wilfrid afterwards built a monastery there. Hence his own words in a letter to Pope John, quoted by William: “I shall not lose the two monasteries situated in that province, at Ripon and Hexham, which I founded.” Wilfrid retained the government of the place until his death. After his death Abbot Tatbert, designated by him, governed the monastery, according to the *Monasticon Anglicanum*. The name Rippon now remains attached to the town above York, situated between the Ure and the little river Skell [printed *Utum et Scketf*].

10. [Col. 0988D] **VII, *hermenia*.** That is, explanations.

11. [Col. 0988D] **IX, the Easter dispute.** Bede recounts this controversy concerning Easter at length in Book III, chapter 25.

12. [Col. 0988D] **IX, *Columchilla*.** This is approximately the name given to Columba, abbot and founder of the monastery of Iona, as Bede testifies in Book V, chapter 10 of his *History*: “This Columba is now called by some Columcelli, a name compounded from *cella* and *Columba*.” His Acts are found in the Second Benedictine Century.

13. [Col. 0988D] **IX, *desmate*.** That is, with the power of binding and loosing.

14. [Col. 0989D] **X, *colla ... beari*.** That the head be consecrated.

15. [Col. 0989D] [Col. 0990D] **XI, *ormiscum*.** Episcopal shoes, or a necklace? For ὅρμος signifies both a shoe strap and a necklace. In the preceding chapter Wilfrid had said of shoes that he wished to receive in Gaul the sandals of the authority entrusted to him. Yet nothing in this passage corresponds to sandals except *ormiscum*—or should it be *hormiscum*?

16. [Col. 0990D] **XII, *marmora*.** The sea.

17. [Col. 0990D] **XII, storm and conflict.** Bede makes no mention of this storm or conflict.

18. [Col. 0991D] **XV, *picria*.** Bitterness, that is, adversity.

19. [Col. 0991D] **XV, *colurno*.** The author of the *Quirinal Bucolics* mentions *vasa colurna* (“vessels of hazel wood”) in his prologue, in volume I of Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*.

20. [Col. 0991D] **XV, *imeras*.** Ἡμέρας: days.

21. [Col. 0991D] **XV, the leaders assembling.** Peter of Blois: “He built a church at Ripon in honour of Peter. The magnates present at the consecration bestowed very many lands as an endowment upon the church, namely Rible and Hansmumdesham, etc., in the region of Duninga.”

22. [Col. 0992D] **XV, *tristatae*.** Likewise below, chapter 47: *tristatae*, that is, nobles appointed to oversee the royal hunt, as we gather from Æthelred, abbot of Rievaulx, in the last chapter of his book *On the Genealogy of the Kings of the English*: “When the king had taken his position above the others there, according to the law of hunting which the people call *trista*, he assigns separate stations to the individual nobles with their dogs, so that the beast, surrounded on every side, might find its destruction wherever it chose to make its exit.”

Source preparation: Four embedded Greek readings were recovered from the supplied local archive and translated as part of this section.

They adorned Peter’s altar “under melodious honor”; the compressed phrase *sub honore canori* does not identify securely whose honor is meant.

Standing within the chancel, he gives everyone the seed of salvation; he issued commands to kings and recovered the lands taken away. For three days he satisfied the crowd “by word or by food” (*verbo necne cibo*), the verse deliberately leaving the mode paired.

Willingly he gave all the finest gifts, offerings adorned in wonderful ways:

[Col. 0992C] fashioned in wonderful ways: reliquary-caskets and paired little gems,

a codex enclosed in gold and written in golden letters,

The following damaged line reads: “*Auctus* [sic], preserving the Gospel text within its body”; *Auctus* has no secure construction with the preceding golden Gospel-book and is therefore retained rather than resolved into a person or action.

And when he paid for everything with a kindly heart,

he was not puffed up with pride, without Jesus’ restraint.

Therefore, deservedly endowed with a worthy choir,

he flourished, like the lamp once seen in the time of Moses,

opening the path and homeland of eternal rest,

and houses of the heavenly religion dear to himself.

### XVI. He confirms the baptized. He raises a dead boy, baptizes him, and consecrates him to God.

What? Shall I speak, or shall I remain silent? Grant, Christ, the lamp of the Word.

I have said little; now let me break through the long

[Col. 0992D] delays imposed by ignorance, lest a presumptuous tongue

carry away its modesty. For no one is now sufficient

to traverse properly the sea of your virtues,

which your servants have deserved to accomplish through you.

Among them was Wilfrid, the supreme commander,

nobly leading his sheep through the pastures of the higher life.

As he drove the enemies far away,

[Col. 0993A] he showed those who were to be saved that they should be washed in clear waters,

in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and also of the gracious Spirit,

the Father himself applying the chrismal flowers.

A beautiful crowd of people surrounded him in their midst.

Behold, through the densely packed throngs a woman full of fear displays in her weary arms the funeral burden of her dead child (*defunctae funera prolis*), avoiding the bier.

Faith stands mingled with the crowds, while terror

afflicts the grieving woman’s heart with silent goads.

Then the Father approached and soon saw the pale face.

He stiffened in astonishment [Note: [Col. 0993D] So below, chapter 47, *obstipuere*, as though they stiffened like a tree-stump.] and the rash bearer halted where she stood;

she bent forward and increased her mourning with sobs.

“O Father, do not lower your raised right hand.

Why do you despise a mother bereft of her only son?

Behold, you who affirm that Christ is almighty,

[Col. 0993B] complete your faith by your deeds; give the wretched mother a pledge of her child’s life.”

She repeated her plaintive cries in urgent murmuring.

The assembly, gathered together, joined in the poor woman’s groaning.

A great lament arose. At last the lordly bishop (*herilis praesul*), moved by compassion,

offered silent thanks beneath his holy heart,

because the faithless crowd had learned to implore Jesus.

Then, fixed upon the ground, he opened the clear channels of his heart,

bathed his face in tears and pressed his breast with his palms,

and called upon Adonai with a devout cry.

Rising, the Father perceived that salvation was at hand.

[Note: [Col. 0993D] The ancients like to write *timpora* when they mean the parts adjoining the forehead, perhaps in order to distinguish it from the plural of *tempus*. This boy was called Ethelwaldus. William says that this event occurred in the village of Tiddanefrae, and that the boy later lived as a monk in the monastery at Ripon.]

And when he touched his cold temples with his hand,

the dead man moved his hair, restored to life by the breath of life.

The common people, in confused voices, gave unceasing hymns.

When these things had been accomplished, the boy was immediately

[Col. 0993C] baptized in the sacred waters, bringing joy to his unhappy mother.

At once the Father took the boy with him to be raised, ordering that he be returned to his parent after seven years.

But, compelled by her savage husband, she disregarded the command,

fleeing with her child into exile among the Britons.

It was not long before she was discovered. Afterward, unwillingly,

a certain prefect brought the boy back under the Father’s authority,

and from then on devoted him to divine service.

That boy benefited many others by his holy example.

Then a torch flashed forth and shone amid the crackling flames.

### XVII. The happy condition of England. Egfrid, king of the Northumbrians, subdues the rebellious Picts through Wilfrid’s merits.

At that time the English kingdom shone with a double lamp.

The bishops, at the king’s command, performed what was worthy;

the king, too, served the bishops with honor as to the Church.

[Col. 0993D] The people enjoyed complete peace while observing the laws.

The granaries rejoiced, heavy with fruitful harvests;

the sailors, bold in their ventures, despised robbers.

The dreadful war-trumpets were silent, and poverty was not feared:

[Col. 0994A] the Church flourished, bound together by a peaceful covenant.

The bringer of death [Note: The Devil.—Thus the manuscript codices commonly prefer *laetum*, with the diphthong *ae*, when it signifies death; some have simple *e* without the diphthong.] grew jealous and opened a thousand schemes,

so that he might rupture holy peace by a perverse schism.

The rebellious Pictish people relied upon massive ramparts,

for they could no longer endure the customary chains of the English.

Egfrid held the broad reins of imperial power.

His noble wife, Edildrid, a famous heroine,

lived in marriage as a most chaste virgin.

Therefore the prince, with a spirit inflamed,

sent against them light-armed cohorts and slaughtered the guilty with an unconquered blade.

They choked two rivers with slain enemies; the troops came to the king’s brother with spoils of war;

they spread slaughter far and wide, and the chains returned to their necks:

the victorious king enjoyed a great triumph from afar.

For he conquered not by weapons and a small band of soldiers,

[Col. 0994B] but by the power of God and the merits of the gracious bishop,

he overcame nations threatening in empty arrogance.

### XVIII. The Mercians, too, are subdued.

Nor, while the Mercian kingdoms swelled with pride,

did this king fail to lay low countless troops pierced by his spear.

Their leader yielded and fled; the next verse says that “in the following age he added northern scepters to Arctic triumphs,” but its subject and chronology remain uncertain,

supported by the magnificent request of Wilfrid.

### XIX. Wilfrid lives devoutly.

Thus no toil could slacken the man’s virtue, nor could upraised pride draw the true goad of justice away from its course.

Indeed, tirelessly ranging in thought through unknown peoples,

he everywhere extended the peoples of the divine sowing in its season,

undertaking no sluggish labor.

[Col. 0994C] Rejoicing to maintain secret vigils through the night,

he cleansed his chaste body in limpid waters.

He bathed so that “the heat of the inborn hearth” would not scorch his body; *ingeniti laris* is a compressed and uncertain image for the body’s innate heat.

Neither Phoebus’ heat nor the cold season of winter

broke the sweet courses of the discipline he had embraced,

until old age, already exhausted by apostolic commands,

deserved to be released from such hardship.

He did not decide that it was lawful for him alone to drain the cup of the river;

he gladly performed fasts,

and, going ahead of his subjects on the way, led them into a narrow path.

A throng of rulers’ children gladly gathered around him, admiring his holy integrity of conduct, whether to serve God or to learn palace life under the righteous man.

These matters also supplied material to deceitful tongues,

but the athlete of God, clothed in the fleece of peace,

[Col. 0994D] offered the incense of gentle obedience amid bitter hatreds.

### XX. He founds the basilica of St Andrew. He restores a crushed man to health.

Moreover, he built a church [Note: Namely, in the town of Haugustald, according to Eadmer, which place William calls Henglesteld. [Col. 0994D] Bede calls it Undalum in book V, chapter 20; Leland’s *Collectanea*, cited in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, names it from the province. Ethildrid is said to have granted the place there. William says at the end of the chapter on the bishops of York: “Haugustaldehem, a place fifty miles distant from York”; and below: “Now Haugustald is a village of the archbishop of York, although it was once an episcopal see.” Alcuin’s letter 32, to Bishop Aedilbert and the whole congregation serving God in the church of Saint Andrew, concerns this place. See the book *On the Miracles of the Saints of Haugustald*.], with cut stones,

[Col. 0995A] surrounding blind crypts with a curved vault,

and painting the halls, covered with gentle colors.

Soon he remembered the assistance granted to his tardy tongue,

and gave the altar the name of pious Andrew.

The poisonous breath of the deadly serpent was not absent.

For while workmen were vaulting or plastering the high work, the unstable wall is named in a corrupt construction (*muri dum futilis alta*); a brother fell headlong and his body was crushed.

His little legs could no longer carry him in walking,

and the sinews of his crushed neck [*tori*; read *colli*] withered horribly.

When he was drawing his last breaths of timid life,

sad crowds gathered for this funeral.

The Father’s prophetic mind immediately recognized what had happened in the crypts.

At once, with tears poured from his pure heart,

he urged the others, in their grief, to beseech the Lord,

so that the supreme shepherd might restore the injured sheep.

[Col. 0995B] He came, and the limbs quickly received healing;

life returned, shaming the joyful rejection of death.

Therefore they praised the gifts of mighty Christ.

### XXI. At the instigation of Queen Ermemburga, King Egfrid, with Theodore’s consent, divides Wilfrid’s diocese into three. Wilfrid appeals to Rome. He foretells the punishments of his persecutors.

The raging wrath of the demon seeks deceitfully to overcome so great a chosen power or champion—the word *gnosiu* is corrupt—by first striking down the soldier, so that it may terrify the fragile spears of the weakened army.

Preparing many things, it returned to its ancient weapons,

and morbidly corrupted the king’s fickle wife [Note: Namely Ermemburga, whom he married after dismissing Ethildrid, who, preserving her chastity, withdrew to the monastery at Ely on Wilfrid’s advice; he had inspired her with a devotion to virginity, according to Bede, book IV, chapter 19. From the book *On the Life of St Ethildrid*, Camden observes in his description of the region of York that in the church at Ripon there was once a very famous *Wilfridiacum*, that is, a narrow opening in the crypt, by which women’s chastity was tested. Those who were chaste passed through easily; those of doubtful reputation were held fast by some unexplained miracle. So he says.].

Casting from that evil quiver these venomous shafts,

she wounded the king’s heart with a twisted blow,

hostile in her rancid methods like a chattering partridge,

[Col. 0995C] and accused the just man of abusing the resources entrusted to him.

For the man possessed glory throughout all parts of the world:

many farmers, the fertile grasses of the earth,

noblemen bowed before him, a rich offspring of young men,

and, above all, the assembly of monks devoted to heavenly life.

After the deadly poison had entered their hearts,

they summoned, deceived by their treacherous words,

the teacher of truth and almost a follower of justice,

Theodore, whom the rustic Muse has celebrated above.

He wickedly approved the royal undertaking, installing three men under the title of bishop within the Father’s adjoining territory, in place of the one bishop who had ruled it.

[Col. 0995D] Eutyches [Note: Greek *eutychēs*, “fortunate,” namely Wilfrid.] heard what the king was plotting against him,

and, wishing to question the wrath without a stain of guilt,

slowly sought the lofty dining hall with sumptuous steps.

[Col. 0996A] Behold, the torches and instigators of so great a danger

grew numb with fear, while the malicious woman devised her scheme.

“Why am I injured, Father?” she said, “by those whom no concern

for our laws, as I confess, ever troubles with impunity?

‘We are carrying out the crime,’ they say, ‘although the council compels us;

nothing impious is being done if decrees are challenged.’

Thus they were able to become witnesses of their own crimes.”

But the bishop, unwilling to desist from his undertaking,

whatever false religion [Note: False religion.] wove against him,

declared that everything would be examined by the Roman judgment.

Seeing certain men insulting him with an obscene laugh, he said:

“Oh, may you happily lead joyful years of life!

But hostile fate will dissolve your joys.

Nor will these times return with the receding suns

before you pay the excessively premature penalty of a sorrowful death.”

[Col. 0996B] He said this and restrained his words behind his sober lips.

After Alfwine’s killing, the people mourned the event that had been foretold [Note: He was King Egfrid’s brother, slain by King Ethilred of Mercia, called Elwinus by Bede [Col. 0996D] in book IV, chapter 21.]. Grieving, they offered funeral rites to the slain prince [*Cliton*; Note: The English call a royal youth destined to inherit the kingdom, whom the French call the *Dauphin*, a *Cliton*, as though “illustrious.” See Spelman’s *Glossary* and William Somner on the English historians. Here understand Elfwinus, Egfrid’s brother.]; after his burial, his brother’s victory followed.

### XXII. Transported across the sea to the Frisians, he preaches the word of God.

When these things had become known, he returned, and with joyful heart revisited the sheep denied to him,

gradually restoring their parched hearts by giving them consoling words.

Meanwhile a swift skiff [boat] was launched along the slanting shore,

about to attempt the sea passages.

The monks, left on either side around it,

prayed for their father with favorable but tearful lamentations.

Then the hostile crop, destined for eternal fire,

not content to have poured out the poison of its own wickedness [*kakia*, malice],

[Col. 0996C] sent envoys to the king of the Franks and demanded the Lord’s steward, Wilfrid, after having plundered him with impunity.

But, through the mercy of the heavenly leader,

their false efforts could inflict no ruin upon Macarius.

Bishop Winfrid perceived the deadly traps

skillfully hidden in pits;

having been undone by those same intrigues, he was mocked merely through the one-letter difference of his name [Note: Namely, Wilfrid and Winfrid differ by a single letter. William writes: “Ethilred, after achieving triumph and recovering the integrity of his kingdom, expelled Bishop Winfrid, who had succeeded Cedd at Lichfield because he had supported Egfrid’s party. Having reached the Gallic shore by chance, he encountered King Theodoric and the Frankish duke Ebroin,” and so forth. Bede makes no mention of this matter.].

Moreover, when the winds had happily shifted elsewhere,

he reached the joyful harbor on the shores of the Frisians.

The pagans were greatly astonished, but the “supreme *mekotes*” [sic; perhaps greatness or loftiness, but the printed form is insecure] made the king and all his leaders well disposed.

Thus, declaring [*categorans*, i.e. preaching] the divine seed to the people,

he opened sweet streams in the false rocks.

Then the breeding of sheep became fruitful, and then the seed in the fields

[Col. 0996D] grew, and the shepherds celebrated with solemn joy.

[Col. 0997A] After a short time he granted many the baptism of salvation,

and Wilfrid founded the strongholds that Wilbrord now possesses [Note: Bede mentions Wilfrid’s stay with Willibrord in book III, chapter 13.], equaling his master only in fervor of faith.

### XXIII. Ebroin attempts to incite the king of the Frisians against Wilfrid.

An abundance of Frankish treasure corrupted the leader and inflamed him with bitter fury. Ebroin, the lover of ostentation (*philokompōs*) [Note: “A lover of display,” Greek *philókompos*. Ratherius uses the same word in his *Apologeticus*, volume II of the *Spicilegium*, and in the *Life of St Walburga* the form *philokompica* occurs. Here Ebroin is called Efruinus in an unusual form; he is also called Ebremerdus in the anonymous *Life of St Leger*.], drew up a written compact and marked out a purchasable gift, seeking deceitfully to induce King Adalgis with the wealth offered.

The envoys hastened forward and disclosed the orders in paraphrase.

But the prudent king tore up the deadly document

and, scorning them, cast it into high flames.

“Thus, I pray, may whoever seeks to dissolve the bonds of compact faith perish

in eternal heat,” he began,

[Col. 0997B] and ordered the hostile companions to return.

There is no doubt that he had been illumined by heavenly radiance: “toward the cradle of *agii* [sic], he who once shone from on high.” The terminal verse is corrupt, and *agii* and the relation of the cradle cannot be resolved securely.

### XXIV. An apostrophe to the queen.

“Foolish woman, destined to perish, why do you stir up the just man with furious weapons?

It was enough to have expelled the blessed man from his homeland.

Why do you trouble the sea? Why do you hide nets in Charybdis?

Does the fourfold mechanism of the earth obey you?

At your command, will the right-hand axis of heaven flash?

Stop; take hold of the faith, and by the same power [Note: Greek *dynamei*, “by force” or “by power.”] you will be captured.

Soon, once your husband is lost, you yourself will be changed;

you will become a pursuer of crimes, an enemy of wolves;

now, made gentler, you will feed Christ’s spotless lambs.

The man whom you now persecute, afterward you will follow in devotion,

[Col. 0997C] bringing many reminders of salvation to the peoples.”

These things I have played upon in ecstasy with a hooked stylus.

Now I am pleased to rave in my customary tragic buskin.

### XXV. Wilfrid takes refuge with Dagobert.

Spring had already dissolved the icy Alps with warm breezes,

when the bishop, having recovered his strength, left those territories and sought the Gallic countryside,

and confidently entered the known walls of King Dagobert [Note: This was Dagobert II, son of King Sigibert and grandson of the elder Dagobert. His restoration to the kingdom, obscure and indeed unknown for a long time, has recently been asserted, above all on the testimony of William of Malmesbury, a monk whom this author preceded. Bede does not mention Dagobert.].

Dagobert, as the sequence will show, provided public rejoicing when he received his patron. He said: “Lost, as you know, from the people’s wings, I once endured grievous sorrows in my tender body.” The printed *popularibus alis* is an unusual image for the support from which he had been separated.

I embarked, a trembling exile, upon a small boat with few oars,

driven as a young man among the sluggish Irish.

[Col. 0997D] Behold the man through whose protection I deserved to be restored to you.

For my sake, and for your own salvation, beloved warrior,

if there is any faith in your heart, let us preserve this friend.”

[Col. 0998A] The nobles rejoiced; for it is no light matter for subjects

to wish to move beyond the special right of a prince.

The king offered him distinguished dwellings “with immense *oromate*” [the printed word is corrupt]. The following lines read *ire catillatum … friguttire* and then “he seeks the forbidden strongholds more eagerly”; the two rare or corrupt forms do not support a secure narrative about dining or muttering.

But the great-hearted hero did not yield to royal wishes.

Rather, lightened or deprived of possessions and companions (*rebus sociisque levatus*),

and even taking Bishop Deodatus [Note: Henschenius, in book II, chapter 4 of *On the Three Dagoberts*, believes this Deodatus to be the man who, after being bishop of Nevers, became a monk of the Valley of Galilee. I, however, would rather believe him to have been Deodatus, bishop of Toul, who traveled to Rome with Wilfrid and attended the Roman council under Pope Agatho, to which he is also found to have subscribed in Spelman’s volume I of the *Councils*; others call him Adeodatus.], he went onward.

Again hastening away from the king who had prepared a place for him,

he went to his lodging. For Bertherus [Note: Eadmer calls him Bertherus, duke of Champagne; William calls him Bertharius, duke of Provence. Perhaps he was the man who was Waratton’s son-in-law and afterward mayor of the palace of King Theodoric, in the continuation of Fredegar, chapter 99.]

ruled the extensive lands with great terror.

He himself received the just man and comforted him with pious affection.

After the meal and after the welcome cups of grateful Bacchus,

the king began to tell the Father how he had seen the livid undertaking of a citizen’s evil that wished to violate him.

[Col. 0998B] “But mindful of the danger I endured in the past,” he said, “holy Father,

when once deprived of my own land,

I experienced bitter wounds while living under a foreign king.

“Though preserved ‘from the ground by a great compact’—the phrase is compressed—I escaped and departed free from savage friends. They too sought to deceive me with extensive gifts, so that by tearing the blue-gray Briton they might deceive you. But if steadfast love of a people’s loyalty scorned to sell me, I too will cherish you no less.” The subject of “scorned” remains unstated in the verse.

The trumpet sounded, and the eager king increased his companions.

Thus they hastened on swift feet toward the Roman halls.

### XXVI. In his presence a synod is convened at Rome, in which Wilfrid is restored.

But the archbishop Theodore had already sent messengers ahead.

Then the pious fame of blessed Wilfrid

[Col. 0998C] penetrated the Ausonian halls with familiar gestures.

At once all the citizens cried out “Well done!” in eager rivalry.

The most worthy man passed through or “wore down” Peter’s fir-wood doors (*exterit* permits no more precise action here).

Agatho adorned the apostolic reins,

a straightforward justice, an unfailing guardian of equity.

He issued an edict, assembled the ancestral charter,

and gathered companies of the Fathers under one crown: the verse says “four times twelve,” while its note gives “one hundred and twenty-five,” so the conflicting count is retained [Note: One hundred and twenty-five],

and spoke with one common voice:

“The ancient sanction of the Church’s worship is being disfigured,

unless ecclesiastical heat cooks the weeds that have sprung up.

We have learned that the English kingdoms are being gravely troubled,

while dissensions arise beyond their fixed boundaries.

In sharp division, brothers bring slaughter upon brothers. Weigh the ancient matters, lest they perish on untrained scales.

[Col. 0998D] The leading Italians, matured in the balance of piety,

reported such events to the learned-speaking master:

‘Begin, shepherd; you possess the decrees of the ancient men.

[Col. 0999A] Now, as is fitting, admit those whom the faith prompts

to endure the many hardships of a broad land.

In pious speech decide what the subordinate order,

and what each Church, should cultivate or is commanded to avoid;

in this way every crime will be emptied out.’”

He gave his assent, and at once Wilfrid was brought into the sacred hall

and ordered to recount his complaints.

He presented a document, clearly written, for the Fathers to read,

explaining how he had diligently managed the affairs of his homeland’s sheep,

as though they were gains of pious labor;

how envy had compelled his suspension from the consecrated sees or “doors” entrusted to him;

and—alas!—how the frauds of bishops, after the manner of suitors,

had invaded the bride adorned by her own patron.

“I do not blacken anyone with crimes already committed.

I await judgment,” he said, “from the western court,

[Col. 0999B] rather than recount everything at length.”

Both sides declared that the man had spoken sincere oracles:

that he was wholly worthy to be heard,

and that his strength, to be solidified by apostolic power,

would prevent this poison from spreading

and infecting the unwary with a diseased sap,

while the savage enemy utterly corrupted the just man.

The archbishop [the pope] agreed and ordered the legal decrees

to be recorded for Theodore and the king.

Unless they preserve the master’s commands with equal piety,

let all who seek to condemn the blessed man’s soul without cause [Note: Without reason.]

be punished with the Lord’s anathema.

### XXVII. When Dagobert is attacked and killed in war, Wilfrid, because he had saved him, is assailed with abuse.

When these matters had thus been established, lest he, like a worthless apostate

or a fugitive from the laws, should seek to perish on that charge alone,

[Col. 0999C] he crossed beyond those lands within clear boundaries.

The enemy of the human race burns,

maliciously seeking to stain the good man’s praiseworthy purpose.

For while he hastened to sweep the open spaces of the plain,

hostile companies raged, massed beneath their standards,

after royal blood had supposedly been shed.

For Dagobert, the military commander [Note: The author also uses the title “commander” for a king below, chapter 35, and above, chapter 16, for a bishop. This is an important passage, from which we learn the manner of Dagobert’s death and the year, 679, in which the Roman synod was held. Eadmer learned it from Fridegod; Fridegod, I think, learned it from Heddie.],

had felt the hands of his own countrymen, and rigid iron driven into his groin up to the hilt.

They threatened close combat with leveled spears.

One of them, having thrust aside his spear,

hurled these insults at the bishop with foul mouth:

“Reckless betrayer of your homeland, traveler about to die, you formerly violated the Gallic scepter by restoring the tyrant who has now been slain; you should rightly follow him.

‘Did I act wrongly when I restored the king?’

[Col. 0999D] he said, ‘and I rejoice to suffer for Christ’s name.’”

Immediately savage spears came rushing forward; then, after lowering them,

they bent over their shields and asked him to bless them.

I would believe that they were struck by the fire of the flashing thunderbolt—that divine light which was revealed to the world when it came forth from its mother’s womb.

### XXVIII. Returning to England, he presents the papal letters.

Fearing nothing, therefore, he crossed the grassland safely,

and confidently entered the hollow alders [ships].

[Col. 1000A] Afterward, strengthened by the many-sided prayer of the brothers,

carrying the authorized standards of blessed Peter,

he approached the royal doors, bringing joy to the just.

He offered sealed letters marked upon parchment.

Immediately learned companies gathered together,

ready to hear what the Roman summit had to say.

The chief commander [Note: King Egfrid.] looked down from his lofty throne,

daring to dictate cruel law in sacred words.

### XXIX. When these were rejected, he himself is thrown into prison.

After the Gospel’s authoritative judgment, after the causes of the apostolic see had been recited,

certain opponents could not bear to surrender the stolen prize.

They were driven by bile in an angry, furious heart,

and—an abomination!—they soothed the king

with perverse speech [*fasmate*; read *famine*],

[Col. 1000B] persuading him to reject documents obtained through hidden dealings;

they rejoiced that God’s fellow-servant should be branded a sycophant.

At last they thrust the Father into a secluded cell,

while he recalled the gentle promises of the heavenly king,

who once said, “Whoever despises you here despises me also.”

Then the queen, the grave author of this schism,

presumed to tear away the precious cases from the saint [Note: The same word is used by Anscar in the *Life of St Willehad*, bishop of Bremen, chapter 4. *Capsaces* occurs below, chapter 35. Eadmer has *capsula* for a reliquary, William *chrismarium*. Audoen also uses the word in this sense in book I, chapter 8, of the *Life of St Eligius*.],

having joined herself to so great a robbery, not with impunity.

### XXX. His speech to his companions.

Thus, despoiled of possessions and companions, the illustrious hero

uttered words from his wondrous mouth to the brothers:

“Great glory, when spoken of, must be sought with great labor.

The hoary succession of the Fathers, after enduring long sufferings,

[Col. 1000C] deserved through divine power to conquer many enemies.

The twelvefold company of heroes, through suffering,

received blessed, heavenly glory and crowns granted by Jesus,

gaining much from him in exchange for little.

Although our bodies endure a harsh lot,

our minds are pressed into the heavenly heap of wheat,

where the rich fruits of the soul will soon be gathered.

Let no one seek rewards unless he triumphs by enduring.”

He spoke, and immediately the grim abyss of the executioners

stood in the way and bound the captive in a dark cavern.

### XXXI. In prison he is illuminated by heavenly light.

“How shall I call you, shepherd, joyful or sorrowful?

You indeed rejoiced that afterward you would be *risten* [sic]; the surviving word is corrupt and is not securely equivalent to “Christ’s.”

you wept over the losses of the flock, wounded by the shepherd’s lash.

While you are confined on every side by a muddy enclosure,

[Col. 1000D] could you not obtain your customary radiance?

The enemies sharpened their slight mattocks in vain;

their double-edged swords inspected you more keenly to no purpose.

Seasonable lights are poured upon you from heaven;

the accustomed lamp hastens to you by its customary passage [*porismate*; read *meatu*],

while you keep the beloved vigils of Jesus through the night.

A guardian stands witness, watching the savage prison

shine with serene fires at the hour of night.

[Col. 1001A] In what were you inferior to Peter, for whom light shone in a narrow place?

Worthily you will afterward be given a similar garland,

for you follow him in your desire and imitate him in sufferings.

And, lest you despair, you shine with equal splendor.”

### XXXII. He does not permit the papal letters to be violated.

Meanwhile he was troubled by many frauds

and urged to condemn the sacred documents and approve violent acts.

“If the crown of my head is struck with a bitter sword,” he said,

“or if pressing spears pierce my tender ribs,

not one jot will ever be frustrated by my craft

of what the Fathers decreed while following Peter’s teachings.

Thus, although he offended the dark faces of the leaders, he did not consent to betray the apostolic rites.”

### XXXIII. He heals the prefect’s wife, who is almost lifeless.

[Col. 1001B] Then the beloved wife of the prefect was seized by a severe illness,

alas, while she was managing disastrous reins.

Her body broken and her joints loosened,

her entrails hung limp, drawn tight by contracted sinews.

Almost deprived of consciousness, with her inner organs already afflicted by condyloma [Note: That is, apparently, wasted by a condylomatous or pustular disease.],

she had brought great anxiety to the man,

who watched for the end of her life while she gave up her last breaths.

She prolonged her delays; at last the man, in humble supplication,

earnestly sought to unlock the saint’s constricting chains.

With no small number of tears he begged the healer’s aid.

Therefore the Father, trusting in his customary gift of compassion,

hastened with breathless steps to bring assistance.

He arrived and ordered the gathered crowds to be removed.

Then, after pouring out prayers, he washed her entrails with water.

Soon the life-giving warmth returned to her limbs.

[Col. 1001C] The cruel bonds did the blessed man no harm;

rather, with cheerful face, he returned to that same place,

and was not ashamed to care again for the dreadful caverns.

The prefect whom we mentioned was named Osferd [also Osfred];

his rescued wife was called Ebba,

and shortly afterward she rejoiced, enclosed beneath the sacred veil.

### XXXIV. He is bound more tightly, but in vain. He is released.

But the fearful prefect, compelled by astonishment at these events,

declared that he preferred to suffer the loss of his own life

rather than betray the just man to the savage king.

The latter, swelling with anger, ordered him to be held

more harshly in prison, condemned with rigid fetters,

after the former guard’s assignment had been changed.

The steel shackles are pressed forward to attach two-pronged forks,

[Col. 1001D] and triple-stranded ropes are joined in barren labor,

so that they might terrify the heart of the bound athlete.

But the more fiercely they pressed upon him with punishments,

the more they were astonished that they had accomplished almost nothing.

For whatever bonds they fastened to his sacred limbs

either fell away loosened or became improperly fitted;

freedom granted by the Lord came to his unharmed limbs.

O cruel race! The anvil is beaten in vain.

O criminal hand! What good does it do to injure the body?

He does not fear the noose whose neck the rope itself trembles to encircle.

The tremulous chains fled far enough from the worthy man’s steps,

[Col. 1002A] which moved peacefully along the crossroads [Note: Thus above, chapter 8, we read *competa*. We have judged that nothing should be changed.]

of life.

Thus the most gentle shepherd, caring for the joyful lambs,

instructed them fully with his tongue and baptized them with his hands.

### XXXV. The queen is punished for removing the reliquary. Wilfrid is freed, and she recovers.

While the king was passing through the towns of the realm entrusted to him, indulging magnificently in fleeting pleasures,

behold, his joys were suddenly troubled by disaster.

For while the royal wife dared to abuse the relics she had seized,

breathing the pride of impiety,

vengeful wrath arose, and Satan muttered through her entrails:

may she, intoxicated, become the guest of the one whom she worshiped.

When those present were stunned, the royal nurse approached and said:

“Are the offenses of the ancient sin not now apparent?

Foreign prisons violate the just Wilfrid,

[Col. 1002B] while your limbs are shaken by a terrifying demon.

You despised the letters issued from Peter’s summit;

behold, you receive worthy punishments from an angry judge.

You removed the venerable reliquary-caskets [*phylacteria*] from his neck;

now, dying, you yourself are bound to Baal by a bolt [Note: A little bar, French *verrou*.].

As she poured monstrous flames from her nostrils,

the king was present, and his honorable mother addressed him:

‘Now remember who you are, son; overthrow the loathsome thing.

Supreme vengeance is destroying your beloved wife.

But if you wish to strengthen your scepter-bearing right hand,

release the man bound without any crime,

and, if you can bear it in your heart, order him to depart the kingdom.’”

He agreed unwillingly; soon the prison was opened,

and the thickest cloud restored the bright star.

[Col. 1002C] Immediately the queen felt undeserved healing.

### XXXVI. Wilfrid, freed, leaves his homeland. He wanders because of the faction of his adversaries.

Therefore, leaving his homeland and related lands,

he departed and, like a stranger, sought the southern regions.

A noble traveler, meeting the exile on every road,

received him, because the supreme power of the world

had established everything by an unfailing word,

promising that nothing would be lacking for the just who suffered on his behalf.

Berthwald, royal offspring, rich in resources,

was not concealed; immediately hostile fury burst into flame.

But the Father, never failing in his customary labor,

organized monastic regulations for the scattered flocks.

Then, in the land of the man just named, the devil’s envious plague blinded the heart of the duke who had been a suitable host, [Col. 1002D] the distinguished brother of Edilred in the Mercian kingdom. In his household remained a hostile wife, the sister of the savage and arrogant tyrant Egfrid.

They did not cease assailing the tranquil man with great terror and, by wicked pressure, forced the host to dishonor the pledge he had given.

Thus they forced him to depart without the host’s assistance,

accompanied by Christ as his guide.

Indeed, after being received in another king’s halls,

he suffered the wrath of women at the instigation of the demon.

For Ermenburg, the instigator of every crime,

as the Muse sang in the preceding passage,

[Col. 1003A] tormented the great patron in many ways, driven mad by rage.

Her savage sister, the royal wife of Centwine,

expelled him unharmed, preserving no modesty.

### XXXVII. He takes refuge with the South Saxons. He wins King Edilwalch and his people for Christ. He builds monasteries.

“Why do you hiss, doomed crop, or why are you roasted

in the sulfur of everlasting hell? Behold, you will prove despised.

The bishop himself will acquire for himself a homeland lying not far away,

not yet cut by the divine plow.

It was not permitted to entrust seeds to cultivated furrows.

Is there at least time to turn over sterile clods?

He who carries Christ in his heart does not fear exile.”

Therefore there was a certain people, settled in rocky lands,

[Col. 1003B] planted amid uncultivated forests and dense thickets,

which did not easily grant access to its own fields:

a people ignorant of God and devoted to empty idols.

He approached it fearlessly, relying on sound teaching,

and, standing beside the ruler, explained the duties of Christ.

Immediately the ruler was won over by an acceptable covenant,

not by the price of gold, nor by the greedy sword of an enemy:

he swore never to dissolve the bonds they had agreed upon.

From then on Wilfrid everywhere softened their hearts with sacred words,

and, having happily won over the ruler and his wife,

an indefatigable torch shone forth amid the darkness.

The shrines perished more swiftly than the shattered altars.

He did not grieve as he overturned the oracle’s wet incense vessels.

Sweet honey was poured from the divine basket,

and the peoples were washed as they sought holy baptism.

[Col. 1003C] The noble king, too, washed in the life-giving water,

assigned estates, and the bishop adorned monasteries.

This prince is said to have been called Edilwalch,

who, through Wilfrid’s merits, came to know the heavenly realms.

### XXXVIII. After Cedwala was restored to the kingdom, he receives him into Wessex.

And I shall sing of you, exiled boy Cedwala,

whom Ciltena [Wessex] expelled from its scepters in a wooded grove.

Indeed, submit your bold mind to Wilfrid,

so that you may recover the diadems of your kingdom,

seeking to escape the destiny of great evils.

You grew strong, mighty king, patiently being nourished by the exile, Wilfrid.

After a short time you received an increase of faith.

For the head once sheltered by trembling sedge [Note: Marsh grass.]

[Col. 1003D] now shines with a crown surrounding it through the bishop’s aid.

You too enriched the bishop with extensive lands.

Happy exile, which the purple of kings seeks!

Rather, happy Father, exiled for the sake of the covenant of peace!

### XXXIX. After Egfrid’s death, he is restored to favor with Theodore.

Then rumor spread that many troops had fallen

in bloody war, devoured by mutual slaughter,

and that Egfrid, struck by the spear of a fierce Pict,

had ceased to drive the holy men into wicked exile.

Moreover, Theodore, the shepherd governing the Dorobernian cloisters,

wishing to condemn the crime once committed against the bishop,

[Col. 1004A] as old age was already approaching,

sought, rather too late, to recall the man who had been shamefully rejected.

Therefore Wilfrid returned humbly, fulfilling what had previously been required.

Among them was the venerable bishop Erchenwald.

The three bishops came together, cords of the true light,

and then the elder Theodore began to speak:

“Behold, my son, I repent that you endured so many torments.

The final boundaries of my life are hastening near.

Whatever way I have offended, I beg you, forgive me.”

The blessed Wilfrid’s deeds had terrified his mind.

Then, raising his eyes to heaven and extending his arms toward the earth,

he forgave the offense, as Jesus commanded.

Therefore, prostrate upon the ground, they sought Christ’s mercies.

And when, with perfect hearts, they forgave each other’s faults,

they rejoiced, with tears pouring from their sober faces.

### XL. He is commended to Aldfrid and others.

[Col. 1004B]

Aldfrid had now assumed the kingdom’s fasces and public scepters after his predecessor’s death.

Soon the eastern shepherd wrote

that the blessed old man, torn away from his sees,

ought to be restored after so many dangers,

the venerable disciple of Christ [*mathētēs*; Note: Greek *semnos*, “venerable”];

lest, dying, he should suffer what Egfrid had endured.

---

### Source-order apparatus register

Every note in the supplied source is retained below in source order. The lemma is the immediately preceding printed wording; manuscript spellings, references, and editorial uncertainty retain their original scope.

- **N1 · Col. 0993D · after `mox pallida conspicit ora. Obstipuit`:** source note *Sic infra cap. 47, obstipuere, quasi stipitis instar rigescere.* — As again below in chapter 47, *obstipuere* means that they stood rigid like a tree-stump.
- **N2 · Col. 0993D · after `autem praesensit adesse salutem. Timpora`:** source note *Sic antiqui amant scribere timpora, cum adhaerentes fronti partes significant, forsan ut distinguant a plurali vocis tempus. Puer iste vocatus est Ethelwaldus, ex Willelmo, qui hoc factum in villa Tiddanefrae contigisse ait, et puerum in Ripensi coenobio monachum postea vixisse.* — The ancients write *timpora* for the parts adjoining the forehead, perhaps to distinguish them from the plural of *tempus*. The boy was called Ethelwald; William locates the event at Tiddanefrae and says that the boy later lived as a monk at Ripon.
- **N3 · Col. 0993D · after `Ecclesia pacato foedere nexa. Laetifer`:** source note *Diabolus.---Sic passim mss. codices praeferunt laetum, per ae diphthongum, ubi mortem significat, aliqui cum e simplici absque diphthongo.* — The referent is the Devil. Manuscripts commonly write *laetum* with *ae* when it signifies death, while some use simple *e* without the diphthong.
- **N4 · Col. 0993D · after `Elisum sospitati redintegrat. Praeterea templum`:** source note *Nempe in Haugustaldensi oppido, teste Eadmero, quem locum Willelmus Henglesteldem appellat. [Col. 0994D] Undalum Beda in lib. V cap. 20, et Lelandi collectanea in Monastico Anglicano, a provinciae nomine. Ethildrita locum concessisse dicitur ibidem. Haugustaldehem, inquit Willelmus in fine capitis de episcopis Eboracensibus, locus quinquaginta ab Eboraco miliaribus disparatus; et infra: Nunc est Haugustaldem villa archiepiscopi Eboracensis, quae tamen quondam sedes episcopalis fuerat. Huc spectat Alcuini epistola 32 Aedilberto episcopo et omni congregationi in ecclesia sancti Andreae Deo servientium. Lege librum de Miraculis sanctorum Hangustaldensium.* — The place is Haugustald: the note records the forms Henglesteld, Undalum, and Haugustaldehem; cites Eadmer, Bede V.20, Leland’s *Collectanea* in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, William, Alcuin letter 32, and the *Miracles of the Saints of Haugustald*; and says the village was formerly an episcopal see and later belonged to the archbishop of York.
