- **N5 · Col. 0995D · after `Corrupitque levem regis morbose jugalem`:** source note *Nempe Ermemburgam, quam superduxit Egfridus dimissa Ethildrita, quae servata pudicitia in monasterium Eliense secesserat auctore Wilfrido, qui ei virginitatis studium inspiraverat, ex Beda in lib. IV cap. 19, et ex libro De Vita S. Ethildritae Camdenus in descriptione agri Eboracensis observat in templo HRipensi avorum memoria celeberrimam Wilfridiacum fuisse, id est angustum in cryptoporticu foramen, quo mulierum pudicitia explorabatur. Quae enim castae erant, facile transibant: quae dubia fama, nescio quo miraculo constrictae detinebantur. Ita ille.* — The woman is Ermemburga, whom Egfrid married after dismissing Ethildrid. The note relates Ethildrid’s withdrawal to Ely, Wilfrid’s role, and Camden’s account of the Ripon *Wilfridiacum*, a narrow crypt opening used to test women’s chastity.
- **N6 · Col. 0995D · after `usque monarchas (episcopos). Audiit Eutyches`:** source note *εὐτυχὴς, felix, Wilfridus scilicet.* — Greek *eutychēs* means “fortunate” or “happy”; the referent is Wilfrid.
- **N7 · Col. 0995D · after `coepto, Quidquid ei pravum pseudo-theosebia`:** source note *Falsa religio.* — The phrase means “false religion.”
- **N8 · Col. 0995D · after `sobrio compressit verba palato. Alfwine`:** source note *Is erat frater Egfridi regis, caesus ab Ethilredo rege Merciorum, Elwinus dictus apud Bedam [Col. 0996D] in lib. IV cap. 21.* — He was King Egfrid’s brother, called Elwinus by Bede, and was killed by Ethilred, king of the Mercians; Bede IV.21 is cited.
- **N9 · Col. 0996D · after `Inferias caeso dantes moerendo Clitoni`:** source note *Angli regium adolescentem regni futurum haeredem, quem nos Galli Delphinum appellamus, Clitonem vocant, quasi inclytum. Lege Spelmanni Glossarium et Guilielmi Somneri in historicos Anglicanos. Elfwinum Egfridi fratrem hoc loco intellige ex dictis.* — The English call a royal youth and future heir *Cliton*, compared here with the French *Dauphin* and interpreted as “illustrious.” The note cites Spelman and Somner and identifies this figure as Elfwin, Egfrid’s brother.
- **N10 · Col. 0996D · after `eisdem Perditus insidiis, tantum monogrammate`:** source note *Nimirum unica littera differunt Wilfridus et Winfridus, Willelmus: «Ethelredus triumpho functus, integritate regni recepta, Winfridum episcopum, qui Ceddae apud Licefeld successerat, quod Egfridi partium fuerat, expulit. Is Gallico littori forte appulsus, in Theodoricum regem et Ebroinum ducem Francorum incidit,» etc. Nulla hujus rei mentio apud Bedam.* — Wilfrid and Winfrid differ by one letter. The note quotes William’s account of Bishop Winfrid’s expulsion and arrival at the court of Theodoric and Ebroin, and observes that Bede does not mention it.
- **N11 · Col. 0997D · after `salutis, Et fundavit eas Wilbrordus`:** source note *De mora Wilfridi cum Willibrordo mentionem facit Beda in lib. III cap. 13.* — Bede III.13 mentions Wilfrid’s stay with Willibrord.
- **N12 · Col. 0997D · after `Implanare opibus Efruinus [Ebroinus] philocompos`:** source note *Amator jactantiae, φιλόκομπος. Eadem voce utitur Ratherius in Apologetico, tomo II Spicilegii, et in Vita S. Walpurgis philocompica nota. Ebroinus nove hic vocatur Efruinus, Ebremerdus etiam dictus in Vita S. Leodegarii auctore anonymo.* — Greek *philokompos* means “lover of ostentation.” The note cites Ratherius and the *Life of St Walburga*, and records Efruinus and Ebremerdus as forms of Ebroin’s name.
- **N13 · Col. 0997D · after `axis? Siste, capesse fidem, dynami`:** source note *δυνάμει, virtute.* — Greek *dynamei* means “by power” or “by virtue.”
- **N14 · Col. 0997D · after `atque Nota subit fidens Dagoberti`:** source note *Hic Dagobertus secundus, Sigiberti regis filius, Dagoberti senioris nepos: cujus restitutio in regnum obscura, imo multo tempore ignota, nuper asserta est testimonio in primis Willelmi Malmesburiensis monachi, cui iste auctor praeivit. Dagoberti non meminit Beda.* — This is Dagobert II, son of Sigibert and grandson of the elder Dagobert. The note discusses the obscurity of his restoration and William of Malmesbury’s testimony, and observes that Bede does not mention him.
- **N15 · Col. 0998D · after `levatus, Quin etiam sumto Deodato`:** source note *Henschenius in lib. II de tribus Dagobertis cap. 4, Deodatum hunc eum esse putat qui ex episcopo Nivernensi factus est monachus Vallis-Galilaeae. Ego vero potius crediderim esse Deodatum Tullensem episcopum, qui cum Wilfrido Romam profectus, concilio Romano sub Agathone papa interfuit, cui et subscripsisse invenitur apud Spelmanum in tomo I Conc.; aliis Adeodatus appellatus.* — Henschen identifies Deodatus as the former bishop of Nevers and later monk of the Valley of Galilee; the editor instead favors Deodatus of Toul, who accompanied Wilfrid to Rome and subscribed to the council under Agatho, also called Adeodatus.
- **N16 · Col. 0998D · after `paratum Vadit ad hospitium. Bertherus`:** source note *Eadmerus vocat Bertherum Campaniae ducem, Willelmus Bertharium ducem Provinciae. An is qui gener Warattonis, et post eum major domus Theodorici regis in continuatione Fredegarii cap. 99.* — Eadmer calls him Bertherus, duke of Champagne; William calls him Bertharius, duke of Provence. The note tentatively compares Waratton’s son-in-law and successor as mayor of Theodoric’s palace in the continuation of Fredegar, chapter 99.
- **N17 · Col. 0998D · after `quater duodena Patrum, nectente diade`:** source note *Centum viginti quinque* — One hundred and twenty-five.
- **N18 · Col. 0999D · after `plecti, Quaerentes animam sine re`:** source note *Sine causa.* — Without cause or reason.
- **N19 · Col. 0999D · after `fuso. Civiles etenim Dagobertus Marchio`:** source note *Sic etiam marchionis nomen pro rege usurpat auctor infra cap. 35, supra vero cap. 16 pro episcopo. Insignis hic locus, quo discimus Dagoberti mortis genus et annum 679, quo habita synodus Romana. A Fridegodo id rescivit Eadmerus, Fridegodus, ut puto, ab Heddio.* — The author also uses *marchio* for a king in chapter 35 and for a bishop in chapter 16. The note treats this as evidence for Dagobert’s manner of death and the year 679 and traces the account through Eadmer, Fridegod, and Heddie.
- **N20 · Col. 1000D · after `Romanus apex, audire paratae. Archistrateios`:** source note *Rex Egfridus.* — The referent is King Egfrid.
- **N21 · Col. 1000D · after `pretias [pretiosas] sancto divellere capsas`:** source note *Eadem voce usus est Anscharius in Vita S. Willehadi Bremensis episcopi cap. 4. Capsaces infra cap. 35. Eadmero capsula reliquiarum, Willelmo chrismarium. Quam etiam vocem hoc in significatu usurpavit Audoenus in lib. I de Vita S. Eligii, cap. 8.* — The note documents this word for a reliquary: Anscar uses it in the *Life of St Willehad* 4; *capsaces* recurs in chapter 35; Eadmer has *capsula*, William *chrismarium*, and Audoen uses the word in the *Life of St Eligius* I.8.
- **N22 · Col. 1001D · after `pene carens, extis jam condolomatis`:** source note *Id est condylomate seu pustuloso morbo tabefactis, ut videtur.* — That is, apparently wasted by a condylomatous or pustular disease.
- **N23 · Col. 1001D · after `Pacifice qui currebant per competa`:** source note *Ita superius cap. 8 legimus competa. Nihil [Col. 1002D] mutandum duximus.* — The same form *competa* occurs above in chapter 8; the editors judge that nothing should be changed.
- **N24 · Col. 1002D · after `Baal vinciris et ipsa veruto`:** source note *Paessulo, Gallice verrou.* — *Paessulus* means a bolt or little bar, French *verrou*.
- **N25 · Col. 1003D · after `tremula quem dudum foverat ulva`:** source note *Herba palustris.* — A marsh plant.
- **N26 · Col. 1003D · after `mathiten post tanta pericula sennem`:** source note *Σεμνός, venerandus.* — Greek *semnos* means “venerable.”

He who first wished to despoil the aforesaid patron.

This same woman immediately points him out to all his friends,

Aelflede, who, girded with maidenly modesty,

Wisely fed the shining little sheep of Jesus.

And you, prince, remember the desired patronage.

He wrote to Edilred, his kinsman [Note: That is, the kinsman of the deceased Egfrid.], sunk in death,

Who had striven to drive Wilfrid from the whole world.

Now come, excellent one, if you live according to the common wish:

Often, I confess, you obeyed my prudent words.

Now also, at the Pastor’s request, believe that the final

And highest dignity of yours, growing under sceptres,

Should preserve the lofty commands of Roman strength,

Which the Fathers who support Peter’s tribute established—

The distinguished Agatho, Benedict, and Sergius also.

The leader immediately welcomed these admonitions,

Preserving his master in the highest honor, as was fitting,

Until the final hour of his fleeting life.

### XLI. Aldfrid recalls him.

When these matters had thus been joined together, Aldfrid,

Bearing the not obscure emblems of kingship, recalled Christ’s disciple.

Then, with eager rivalry, he recovered the old estates.

[Col. 1004D] The adulterers are expelled; the residence is restored to the patron, now vacant:

The citizens applaud, proclaiming the happy event.

The shining axis of Eboracum [York] gleamed in the royal hall.

### XLII. Aldfrid again harasses him; he flees once more to Edilred.

Happy the peoples who obtained so great a shepherd!

Yet their joys scarcely lasted for a brief five-year period.

For the worn-out hydra grew again with even greater perversity.

The old fires blaze up under repeated blows;

The ship of the Church is grievously tossed by storms,

And once again the helmsman is compelled to cast the anchor,

Unless the anchor is first firmly secured in the sand.

[Col. 1005A] For the so-called king, stained with the rust of gluttons [ligurionum],

Stretches the truthful threads among various dark strands,

Alternating his allegiance: now subject beneath the Father’s wings,

Now trusting the inventions of corrupt men.

Unless I am mistaken, he lacked a faithful and steady station.

But the Father, seeking to preserve the ship unmoved,

Preferred to defer the king’s exalted arrogance.

Therefore he withdrew and abandoned the lands divided among them,

Unable to endure that the sacred rule should be divided under its shepherd,

Or that the fields entrusted to the monks should be taken away,

And not fearing to set forth the oracles of great Peter.

Soon, returning to the throne of the aforesaid Aedilred,

He was received and honored in peaceful quiet under the king,

Fulfilling his lofty office with great devotion.

### XLIII. Summoned to a council, he eludes the prepared plots.

[Col. 1005B] After so many disturbances, which they had been unable to overcome by troublesome flight,

They attempted to deceive him by a stratagem.

Finally, when royal authority pressed for it,

A synod was assembled, and a false embassy was ordered

To compel the celibate man to attend with hurried steps.

He came readily. Then savage hostility among the brothers,

Surrounded on every side by fabricated complaints, sought to assail him.

The contrivance, built not on solid ground but soon patched with mud,

Collapsed, unable to withstand the prophet uttering predictions.

For the man possessed eyes as keen as those of the lynx;

Indeed, he had drunk prophetic draughts for this purpose,

So that he might also see the efforts hidden within.

At last, rebuking the crafty deceits with their flattering insinuations,

He urged them to trust the Italian documents.

But their pagan hearts could not be softened by any wines [sic],

[Col. 1005C] And they concealed the harmful poison within their minds.

### XLIV. He does not wish voluntarily to resign the pontificate. He appeals again to Rome.

Moreover, a young man, a supporter of divine honor,

Experienced in fitting sinister accusations to a holy man,

Approached and disclosed the king’s dreadful madness,

From which the arrows of the deadly quiver were flying.

For he did not hesitate to heed the faithful, outspoken man,

Who soon explained the matter and slipped quickly within the palace.

Thus, standing permanently amid the forces of the supreme leader,

He received the resounding slings without harm to his shield,

Nor could the strong arrows pierce his sturdy buckler.

For men acting with violent hunger were pressing him,

So that the Father might be willing to cut himself off by his own decision,

And judge himself unworthy of carrying out sacred duties.

O malicious band! O fraud! O discordant decree!

You will not escape punishment; you will not be free of guilt.

He himself rejoices to endure his customary labors:

You will enter Phlegethon, and fear the dwellings of Erebus.

Then, distinguished by pious words, he opened his mouth:

“Behold, for fourteen years,” he said, “I have borne

The standards of the true Faith undefiled throughout all things,

And with my boldness I have overthrown the swarms of the perverse rustic crowd,

Preserving unconquered the celebrated sayings of eastern judgment,

Not falsely sculpted, as though by a chattering hand,

By a hostile mind soon to perish from its own poison.

Now, since I am compelled, I am cleansed by Peter’s peril.

[Col. 1006A] I do not fear threats; I accept no gifts;

I will never sacrifice myself to you with my own sword.”

Thus the Father spoke and refuted the popular claim.

### XLV. He returns to Edilred.

The unspeakable entanglement is loosened, with Jesus victorious,

And the promise of the outstanding shepherd shone forth.

Thus he returned to the gaping doors of Aedilred,

And explained to the leader the schemes of the wicked crime.

The latter, strengthening his benevolent care for the shepherd,

Ordered that the ancient agreement be violated by no frustration

Until he returned from the apostolic court.

### XLVI. He revisits Rome.

Yet the hostile angers burn more fiercely.

They were preparing, by savage efforts, to destroy

The buildings which the shepherd had founded for Christ’s worship.

[Col. 1006B] The exiles stand—or perhaps establish something—in vain by a sacred recantation,

those brothers whom the holy man had formed in chosen ranks;

the following words are corrupt: “Dulsos coenosi lychinos audititi destos” [Note: [Col. 1005D] The passage is corrupt.].

But the pious judgment of Christ, through its just winnowing fan,

Blew away the chaff, destined to burn in the heat of Cocytus,

And stored the good grain in the barns of heaven.

For the Father himself, revisiting the flocks and beloved sheepfolds,

Groaned and commended them to the Lord in fervent prayers.

Then he entered upon the accessible roads to Rome

And boarded ships prepared with a wealthy crew.

They cut through the calm waters under balanced sails,

And the powerful quarry-stone was fixed upon familiar sands.

As they conveniently traversed forgotten lands,

He nourished his faithful companions from the divine spring.

They could not go astray, nor was there any need to resort to divination,

For the rich grace of so great a leader preserved them.

For he, although devoted and needy, poured out generous expenses

With open hands.

Therefore, as the Davidic singer foretold,

An abundant store of lasting life will remain for him.

At last, having crossed the Jovian caverns in safety,

They entered the shining twin peaks of Peter of Macarius,

Where John, exulting in supreme virtue, was shining.

The relatives, stirred to action, hasten through the city with cries of “Good!”

They accompany him with melodies in an ordered arrangement;

The sacred caretaker and most agile attendant opens the solemn doors wide.

The shepherd entered, supported by a shadowy vaulted roof,

Who, lying upon the curved earth with bent knee,

Sprinkled a thousand pious waters upon him; finally, by sacred power,

[Col. 1006D] He opened the heavenly chambers of the highest heavens.

He placed harmonious hymns in the divine ears.

Rising from prayer, he is properly surrounded by companies of attendants;

He dries his cheeks and restrains his sighs.

But when it pleased him, he climbed the sacred temple.

The chief of the bishops, and likewise the assembly, rejoices—

The faithful [pistica] and the old men rushing down from the Tarpeian hill.

After the Father had mourned the internal dissensions,

He returned on slow feet to the nearby dwellings.

### XLVII. He pleads his case before the Pope, producing apostolic letters.

Meanwhile the empty embassy collapsed through the recent writings

[Col. 1007A] Of Berthwald, presenting a childish volume

Against so great a Patron, certainly in vain.

The Italian Greeks assembled, and soon the old women,

Rushing into the vestibule, reviewed the ancient decisions.

Immediately, when it was admitted, the document glittered like beryl.

When the radiance entered, it brought forth, like rich nectar of light,

A youthful little book in liquid golden color,

With these characters. Then Christ’s disciple said:

“We have granted no schism of our country, I confess, to our homeland.

Neither kings, nor the afflicted [Note: [Col. 1007D] Above: nobles.], nor clients of kings,

May come freely to the embrace of the excellent Mother.

I have chosen to approve the rights previously conferred upon me.

I sing no unknown things; I tell you what you already know:

The Fathers who ruled the Roman authority granted these rights.

The sacred observance of this holy see bears witness to it,

[Col. 1007B] Because I did not despise these things, nor did I consider them contemptible.

I have been deprived of lands repeatedly granted by peoples.

Behold those who follow me with minds gravely disturbed;

If they know of anything broken in turn through my fault

That they can bring against me, I shall be examined by your mouth.

I did not approach the precious walls with pompous bridles [reins],

Nor upon dun horses adorned with trappings of woven cloth [i.e. ambler horses];

Rather, naked, I follow the footsteps of naked Peter.

Establish by friendly laws for posterity what should endure,

And do not tear away the ancient documents.

The Fathers were astonished, imagining that such things would be.

By this beacon, the world’s raw beginning was set ablaze,

Nor will there be lacking a babbler by whom the venerable mind will shine.

[Col. 1007C] Such things are endured by the scattered fragments of a failing life,

Which rival one another, and the action of the wicked does not delay

In stirring with coils the life and morals of the good.

Nevertheless, the obstacles of this party must be investigated.

And although I am proscribed by natural hatreds,

Wilfrid, you will immediately be declared innocent by our judgment.

Nor will the Roman false witnesses go beyond their boundaries

Until they pay the just penalties for their crime by right

And learn to show deference to a man proved righteous.

This man once fed the Christian throngs

At the Latin breasts, lisping, with great sweetness.

The Fathers prayed; John himself bears witness,

Saying: ‘No one will die while he carries the lamp.’

Let all the ancient ambushes now sleep.

The dull, raging with gloomy grief, are delirious.

[Col. 1007D] It is impious to condemn Wilfrid: he, like a log,

Removed from a great fire, remains unburnt.

As Peter is Christ’s, so this man purifies the footsteps of Peter,

Never made fearful by the watery waves.

What does it profit degenerate peoples to wish to be blessed?

If any virtue pleases you, you have driven it from your ancestral shores.

Behold the radiant image [Note: [Col. 1007D] A likeness, a representation.] of supreme virtue in clear light.

Let what he decreed stand firm; let neither

The royal crown nor the ecclesiastical order ever erase these things.

Let him who bears the marks of Christ think with us,

Lest he should feel the deadly chaos and the mephitic stench to be avoided,

[Col. 1008A] Shut away in the depths of the rigid abyss.

Whatever the novel apocryphal books have fabricated,

I judge that the false embassy should be annulled by these ancient pronouncements.

Who could defame by a malicious speech

Two times fifteen, and likewise ten and five rulers?

With these words, in their presence, this man confessed the honor of the Faith.

From that time, inscribed in the book of life by merit,

He awaits the heavenly gifts on the appointed days,

So that he may receive in reality what he patiently hopes for.

Whoever disagrees with this, I say, is altogether exceedingly foolish.”

(The following material, absent from the manuscript of Corbie, was supplied by Mabillon from the manuscript of the Cottonian Library.)

They ordered these same things to be inserted into the sacred books,

Sealed with the customary seals according to princely usage [Note: [Col. 1007D] According to the custom of princes.],

And sent to kings, clergy, and people,

[Col. 1008B] So that they might settle the cruel quarrels of ancient hatred.

And after kissing his tear-wet forehead, they said to the Father:

“Return in peace; restore joy to your subjects;

Be heir of Jesus over earth and heaven.”

### XLVIII.

Thus, after defeating the bearers of false stratagems,

Beautiful with the many glory of the saints as his pledge,

He left the shores of Italy with a large company.

He sought the Alpine regions, where the Celtic fields extend.

Passing slowly through the familiar Alans [Note: [Col. 1007D] The Alans were peoples of Scythia who, stirred up by Stilicho, poured into Gaul with the Vandals; some settled by the Loire, others by the Rhône. Fridegod is referring to them here.],

At last he reached the peaceful Sicambri.

From there he was afflicted by a sharp illness throughout his limbs,

And could not cross the desired boundaries on foot.

At first he was carried on horseback; afterward, borne by his brothers,

Amid the voices and the sorrowing hearts of all the shepherds.

[Col. 1008C] They carried their beloved burden into the walled city

And carefully laid the half-dead man upon an unfamiliar bed.

Struck by fear, they dreaded to await what would happen,

Pressed by the fear of death.

For he lay, perhaps, for twice eight and four-score hours,

without nourishment for mind or body,

whether by food or by any preparation of drink.

At last, when the lights of the fifth sun were breathing,

The secret Michael was sent from the highest heaven—

Radiant, shining with a bright face.

The Father, gazing upon him, did not reject him as a phantom,

But honored him as a friend, like something gleaming and newly luminous.

“Rise, fellow citizen, no worthless part of our company.

[Col. 1008D] Although you may be counted among the starry hosts,” he said,

“You will now be recalled from the orphaned lambs.

After you have strengthened the brothers for twice two years,

I shall recall you with a good reward; but hasten

To build a worthy house of Christ-bearing Mary,

For whose love your years are surely being multiplied.

He knows what you owe to Peter, and what you owe to Peter’s brother.”

Immediately complete strength entered the holy limbs;

The heavenly angelic power returned to the upper ether.

He rose, and his sorrowful companions were rightly renewed.

“O weary man, whom the heavenly tablet wisely cares for!

[Col. 1009A] Since you avoided the joys of the deceitful age,

You have deserved the highest rewards of life in due measure.”

### XLIX.

Then he returned from there to the swelling waves of the ocean,

And restrained the surrounding currents of the vast gulf.

The shores of Kent opened pleasantly to his welcoming plow.

He ordered Berthwald to carry the apostolic book;

Berthwald received it as was fitting and fulfilled the Father’s commands.

From there he sought the holy man [reading uncertain], over whom the Muse turns,

And joyfully, with greater confidence, entered Edilred’s insolent halls.

He reported to him in turn; and both rejoiced together.

### L.

Therefore, hastening, injured by no delay,

He sent Peter’s letter to King Aldfrid.

Aldfrid regarded it as unlawful and did not receive it fairly.

He brought forth evasions, as his predecessors had done,

Unwilling to offer respect in direct words.

Therefore he suffered the deserved danger before his time.

For, enduring avenging penalties in his body,

He was pleased to see the man whom he had earlier rejected in weakness,

And, making many conjectures, he died while reviewing his evil deeds,

With witnesses summoned, after denying that he wished to restore him,

If the Lord’s accumulated help should grant him life.

Aedwilf, a diseased man, took up the empty reins,

Exercising immoderate rage against the holy man;

And within a short time he perished, driven out by the violent people.

### LI.

To take up the care of the homeland and guard it properly,

The son of the often-mentioned Alhdfrid was elevated.

He, of sound gravity, subject to the protection of Wilfrid,

Loved him greatly, because he knew him to be blessed.

He ordered as much as the circuit of his own kingdom contains;

And they came together, with Berthwald summoning them by right.

Then the king, addressing the Father, decreed, and the whole order likewise,

That they should together preserve Wilfrid’s teaching reverently.

The peoples of England were strengthened by a treaty of peace.

### LII.

From that point, the definitions of the strong athlete grew greatly,

And the wicked citizen’s evil sophisms perished;

The scar of the hydra’s offspring was utterly worn away;

And demonstrative [apodictic] victorious virtue was added to the good.

[Col. 1009D] The shepherd himself, passing through remote regions,

As a mother, nourished the teachable with the milk of instruction;

As a father, he rebuked the ignorant with sober anger,

Encouraging them all in a measured way toward the homeland of light.

Moreover, he foresaw that Michael’s prophecy was approaching,

And the old man longed for grave death to come.

He collapsed, and a sudden illness closed his plans.

Crowds gathered in mourning garments;

The pitiable multitude came together from every direction.

A grave fear arose that he might perhaps depart from them.

[Col. 1010A] But among the brothers applauding and singing hymns to Jesus,

He paused and was bathed in a joyful, unharmed atmosphere.

### LIII.

Thus far I have set forth with how much toil he built up the little chapel of exile;

Can I perhaps recount the miracles?

Even if the nine Muses [Note: [Col. 1009D] The nine Muses.] should touch the melodious lyre for me,

And the seven sisters [Note: [Col. 1009D] The seven liberal arts and likewise the seven mechanical arts.] should join together in cyclical sweetness,

Or if I were a devoted and prolific follower of high-speaking Homer,

I could not fully complete the task; I now yield to certain words.

Those whom the demon had possessed with raging anger,

He released through the power of faith and poured-out prayers.

And those whose limbs dark weakness had bound—

Whether frustrating the eye, condemning them through the murmur of the tongue,

Preventing their steps, or constricting their breasts with rheumatism—

Those deprived of their senses and exhausted by the corruption of disease.

As a brother among his companions, an obstacle to crimes, as is evident,

He teaches the surrounding ranks of Christians by practical means,

And gives the grim doctrines of the life-giving word

To the sluggish splendor of the archili [tribunes], rebuking it anew.

He had accomplished these things everywhere with diligent care.

He perceived that the long-extended period of years [Note: [Col. 1009D] A span of years.] had at last come to an end,

And foresaw that the desired transformation was approaching.

Nevertheless, he himself continued to restore everyone in due order.

He rightly testified that the heavenly life must be pursued.

Why do I trifle with words? An end will now also be given to these,

I believe, writings: as death is the strong form of love.

### LIV.

Thus frequent fevers struck the gracious man,

And monks endowed with the gift of virtue came together.

They surrounded such a great shepherd in a dense throng.

Thus enclosed by them, he raised his head and said:

“May the grace of the divine dew blossom in you.

You, brothers, formerly recalled me when I was departing.

Now spare me, I beg you; it pleases me already to ascend

To the heavenly kingdom, and I anticipate being released from fragile flesh.

I shall not be joined with you any longer in this form,

Until the elements disturb the world’s darkness

And the structure of the universe is present to the Lord’s eyes.

You know the traps which the hostile enemy sets,

Seeking to corrupt minds with enticing forms.

He introduces illicit loves through lascivious hopes.

Then he deceives foolish eyes with beautiful appearances,

[Col. 1010D] And often charms the ears with flattering harps [Note: [Col. 1009D] Commonly, harps.].

To teach fraud, he offers the richest profits.

These things I have always warned you of; these things I myself have often

Set before you. Do not delay the one who is departing.

I am being pressed; O, let me die; and, O brothers, keep watch,

Lest hot Phlegethon [Note: [Col. 1009D] A river of hell.] swallow you in its wave.”

He said this and laid his limbs down to hard rest.

Then Michael, recalling the spirit of the blessed man,

Having enclosed the body in a wicker basket,

Drained the life-giving blood worthily from a glass,

[Col. 1011A] And, amid the grieving, praying, and waiting,

He escaped swiftly, freed from the wax of the flesh [i.e. from the body].

### LV.

After they had buried his sacred limbs in a holy tomb,

the reverend brothers put on their garments.

A boy seized the undergarment of the holy man,

Still wet with his sweat, and brought it to the blessed superior,

To whom the exceptional hero had fittingly joined himself by a veil,

Having crowned her through sanctification.

A woman confined to bed, deprived of strength in her limbs,

Approached her, humbly begging to be permitted to touch it.

The maiden was afraid to reveal the secret of her faithful belief.

At last, moved by compassion for the miserable woman’s earnest plea,

She soaked the garment in water, by which the woman obtained healing.

[Col. 1011B] After this, certain men, raving with foolish hearts,

Applied fire to the roof through which he had passed.

But the power of the dead man terrified the living fire,

Making its savagery gentle and displaying signs of virtue.

When the yearly cycle had completed twice six months,

[Col. 1012A] With the Father’s supports gathered from every region,

Very wondrous signs shone beneath the stars.

For they were seeking who, with the shepherd gone,

Would receive the folds and preserve so many sheepfolds.

But Hesperus had already thickened the shadows in the air,

While the brothers, wakeful with care, looked up at the lofty sky.

A luminous circle flashed among the dark stars,

As though Phosphorus were setting the morning dawn ablaze.

This ray shone white around the monks’ monasteries,

seeming visibly to have left the city streets.

From this it became clear that the Lord’s vineyard stands firm,

Strengthened for an age by the prayer of the giant Wilfrid.

Soon they hastened to offer thanks to the supreme Apopompaeus [Note: [Col. 1011B] Apopompaeus, that is, the deliverer.],

And consistently honored the Father’s name.

A rustic pipe sang its preludes through hollow reeds,

[Col. 1012B] While old Meligor, like a countryman, sang with calloused and grinning jaws,

Weighing foreign doctrines with an enervated plectrum.

Now, industrious Odo, may you favor me with an olive branch [Note: [Col. 1011B] This is Odo, archbishop of Canterbury, to whom Fridegod dedicated this poem. Thus the poet closes the Brief Life of Saint Wilfrid in the Cottonian manuscript, in which nearly the same errors as in the Corbie manuscript are found, with the chapter headings inserted; these are absent from the older Corbie copy. The Cottonian book mistakenly has “Brunhild” for “Balthid”; Brunhild had died about forty years earlier. As for Odo, I think he wrote nothing about Saint Wilfrid apart from Fridegod’s little poem, which he himself commissioned. This may be gathered from his letter, extremely rough in style, which is prefixed to Fridegod’s poem in certain manuscripts (see above, col. 945 of this volume), beginning as follows: “To all throughout the world who are devoted to the service of orthodox faith and preside over the same ecclesiastical purpose, both those now living and those to come, Odo, shepherd of the sheep of Dorobernia,” etc. The entire letter bears Fridegod’s character and aims to attest to the translation of the relics of Saint Wilfrid and to his metrical life. You will find nothing historical in it except the few passages that follow: “Therefore, when certain persons, with God’s favor, had transferred the most venerable relics of the blessed confessor of Christ, Wilfrid—withered by the indecent neglect of a thorny abyss, or rather, which is even more dreadful to say, neglected through the shuddering of those placed in authority—from the place of his tomb, I reverently received them and placed them within the bounds of the metropolitan church over which, by God’s grace, I preside, especially compelled by that testimony of the evangelist, which is my own defense: ‘Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered.’ Therefore, delighted by the nearness of so great and worthy a relationship, I judged it worthwhile both to adorn them with a more elevated reliquary and to make them beautiful in a new work of verse, with little flowers excerpted from the book of this life.” This is more than sufficient.].

Having recounted the story from its birth, I then brought it to its close.

It does not admit of an epilogue, nor does it fear ecstasy.

Farewell, Reader, to the page; take the rest for yourself.

## In the year of the Lord 963. Pope John XII

[Col. 1011]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE

(From Mansi, *The Most Extensive Collection of the Councils*, vol. XVIII, col. 447.)

[Col. 1011C] John, son of that Alberic who ruled the City, invaded the apostolic see in the year of the Lord 965, during the reign of the emperor Constantine VIII. Although he lacked the lawful age and all the other qualifications required of a legitimate pontiff, nevertheless, after the subsequent consent of the entire clergy, it seemed preferable to tolerate him rather than divide the Church by some schism, which otherwise would have arisen. Since the whole Catholic Church knew that it was the lesser evil to produce a head, however monstrous, than to cut one body into two and give it two heads, it venerated him throughout the world as the true and legitimate pontiff.

He was indeed the first who is known to have changed his name. From Octavian, he wished to be called John—not because he had cast off tyranny, but because he had exchanged it. His father Alberic had named his son Octavian on account of his temporal dominion over the City; but when he obtained the pontificate and spiritual dominion over the whole world, he wished to be called by the spiritual name John.

The same man, breathing youthful ardor and threats of slaughter, gathered an army and auxiliary forces hired from the duchy of Spoleto and made war against the prince of Capua, Pandulf by name. When Pandulf stoutly resisted him with the help and support of the people of Salerno, John was compelled to return to his own territory and seek peace through envoys.

During his pontificate, Berengar, freed from fear of the deceased Liutholf, son of Otto, who had been sent to Italy to restrain Berengar’s tyranny, was roaming with impunity throughout Italy and laying waste indiscriminately both profane and sacred things. For this reason Pope John, no longer able to endure that tyranny, sent an embassy to Otto, king of Germany, humbly asking the king by letters and signs, as Luitprand reports, that for the love of God and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, whom he desired to be remitters of his sins, he would free him and the holy Roman Church entrusted to him from the jaws of their enemies and restore them to safety and their former liberty.

At the same time, when the people of Milan had also requested this through a deputation, Otto, before leaving Germany, held a diet at Worms. There he made his son Otto, born of Adelheid, king, and entrusted him for upbringing to William, archbishop of Mainz, his son by another wife. After fidelity and security had been pledged by oath to the apostolic see, Otto received a promise concerning the future succession in the Roman Empire and its rights and titles.

After these preliminaries, says Luitprand, the most pious king, having gathered his forces, hurried into Italy and expelled Berengar and Adelbert all the more swiftly because it is evident that he had the most holy apostles Peter and Paul as his fellow soldiers. After restoring to their proper owners whatever had been taken from them, in the year of Christ the Redeemer 962, which was the seventh year of Pope John’s pontificate, he came to Rome. There the pontiff received him with great honor and extraordinary adornment and ceremony. With the applause of the entire people, he was called and ordained emperor and Augustus and received the imperial anointing.

What Otto afterward lawfully restored to Pope John, and what gifts he added to the Roman Church, is indicated by the authentic charter of donation, written in golden letters and preserved at Rome in the castle of Saint Angelo. [Col. 1014A] In return for the favor, the pontiff and all the leading men of the City swore over the body of blessed Peter that they would never assist Berengar or Adelbert; and thus the emperor, leaving Rome, went to Pavia.

Meanwhile Pope John was solicited to revolt and, forgetting the oath he had sworn, joined Adelbert. When the emperor learned through messengers returning from every direction that this was true, Luitprand writes that he said: “He is a boy; he will easily be changed by the example of good men. I hope that by honorable rebuke and generous persuasion he will easily emerge from those evils.”

When the emperor had returned to Rome for this reason, both the pope and Adelbert fled. The citizens, says Luitprand, received the holy emperor with all his men into the City and promised fidelity, adding and firmly swearing that they would never elect or ordain a pope except with the consent and election of the lord emperor Otto Caesar Augustus and his son, King Otto. Three days after he had come to Rome, a pseudo-synod was held by Otto’s authority. At it, after John had been reduced to lay order, the false pope Leo VIII was substituted for him.

After Otto’s death, John was recalled to the City and deposed Leo as an adulterer and invader of the see, rescinding all the acts of that assembly, in which Leo had been substituted after Pope John had been removed, without preserving any order of law or antiquity.

Concerning the unhappy end of Pope John, the author said to be Luitprand writes: “One night, outside Rome, while he was enjoying himself with a certain man’s wife, he was struck by the devil in the temples so violently that within eight days he died from the same wound.” This was not because, as that author says, he had been justly condemned and justly restored, but because, warned by God through so many and such great afflictions, he did not abstain from his habitual sins.

Although the things related by Luitprand are not so much his own words as those of an opponent who attributes too much to Otto, I do not dispute their truth, since they cause no damage to the Catholic faith. Concerning that faith we unanimously profess that Peter and the successors of Peter, after receiving Christ’s promise, can fall away in morals, though not in faith.

The death of Pope John is said to have occurred in the year 964, on the day before the Ides of May, according to the continuation of Regino.

# LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES OF POPE JOHN XII

## I. LETTER OF POPE JOHN XII TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ. (Year 955.)

He indicates that his letters, addressed to Agapetus, have been delivered to him. He grieves over his sufferings.

[*Letters of P. Boniface*, ed. W., p. 376.]

[Col. 1013D]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend and dearest brother, William, archbishop of the holy Church of Mainz.

Know that we have received the letter which your fraternity sent to Pope Agapetus of holy memory, whom divine power, disposing all things, appointed to the apostolic see when he died—not through our merits, but because his mercy went before us, from whom all things that exist derive their being. We have grieved over the losses caused by sufferings and afflictions, and over the attacks of wicked men who disturb the holy Churches of God and the whole order of things, just as apostolic judgment has decreed that we should rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep.

For after the Lord, we have been made the head of all Christianity, not by any human privilege, but by the voice of the Lord himself addressed to the blessed apostle Peter, as you know well: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church,” etc. Therefore, if we learn that any member of our body is suffering tribulations or unjust afflictions, whether through letters or in any other way, we sympathize with it and are burdened by grief; and, with you, we oppose by every effort, through apostolic authority, the attacks and iniquities of those men.

Meanwhile we exhort your fraternity to take every care to resist those who wish to live obstinately and wickedly and strive to devastate the churches of the Lord, and who refuse to obey our pious commands and your admonitions. Lead them to the way of peace, truth, and justice, lest, while their wickedness grows fierce, we find them guilty before the just Judge.

Those whom you know to persist in evil deeds and who are unwilling to be corrected by your commands, send to this apostolic see, as was the ancient custom, together with your trustworthy faithful men, who may faithfully and orderly report to us their causes and everything that is being done in the regions of Gaul and Germany. For this lies close to our heart, and we greatly desire that peace and the honor proper to each person should remain with all the churches and the entire Christian people, and that all traces of evil, if any have existed until now, should be utterly removed.

## II. PRIVILEGE OF POPE JOHN XII FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT MARY OF HUMOLARIA. (Year 956.)

[Mabillon, *Acts*, century II, p. 1025.]

[Col. 1015C] John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable abbot Berner of the church of the blessed virgin Mary, Mother of God, and through him to the entire congregation, forever.

If we offer the assent of the devout to just petitions, we believe that we are serving the will of the Lord. Therefore let it be known to all the sons of the Catholic Mother Church, present and future, that our son, the boy of glorious character, namely Lothair, king of the Franks, sent to us, humbly beseeching our fatherhood that we should fortify by the protection of our authority a certain cell situated in the district of Vermandois, built in honor of the blessed virgin Mary, Mother of God, and of Saint Hunegundis the virgin.

[Col. 1015D] He is endeavoring to raise it to the venerable worship of sacred religion and to strengthen it by a royal command, at the urging of his father, namely King Louis, of Count Adalbert, and of a sufficiently suitable man named Gilbert, who possessed the same little abbey by right of benefice.

Rejoicing with him in his petition, we extend the hand of ecclesiastical authority and, by the apostolic authority on which we rely, decree that no secular person shall ever possess the aforesaid abbey, nor shall anyone appropriate anything from the goods of that cell—not a king, not a count, not a bishop, nor any prince endowed with whatever power—except perhaps for the purpose of protecting and defending it, and even then only with the permission of the regular abbot of that place.

If anyone gives or promises money or any gift to the king or to any prince in order to obtain it, he shall be subject to the curse that follows.

Let an abbot therefore be appointed to the same cell according to the rule of Saint Benedict, and let the monks be subject to regular discipline. With full authority we forbid them to suffer any loss from the goods of that cell.

The possessions of the same church are: the villa of Humolaria, in which the cell has been built, with all its dependent settlements; Merulficurtis with its appurtenances; Eudoldicurtis with its dependencies; Caviniacus with the estates belonging to it; and, in the villa called Frisia on the river Somme, twelve estates, which the same church may possess perpetually for the provision of fish.

Thus these possessions, and any others which the church may acquire for itself with the Lord’s help, it shall possess lawfully and without any contradiction, fortified by apostolic authority, etc.

Written by the hand of Leo, of the sacred scrinium of the holy apostolic see, in the month of January, in the fourteenth indiction. Given on the fourth day before the Nones of January, through the hand of George, second bishop of the holy apostolic see, in the first year, by the favor of the Lord, of the pontificate of our lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope.

## III. [Note: [Col. 1015] This bull is wrongly attributed by some to John XIII, for Bishop Berengar had already died in that year. Jaffé.] LETTER OF POPE JOHN XII TO BERENGAR, BISHOP OF VERDUN. (Year 956.)

He confirms the privileges and possessions of the monastery of Saint Vitonus.

[In D. Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, Documents, p. 369.]

[Col. 1016C]

JOHN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our brother BERENGAR, bishop of the Church of Verdun, and to all entrusted to him by God: the reward of eternal recompense.

It is fitting for apostolic authority to favor with benevolent charity those who are distinguished by devout religion, and to grant the requests of petitioners with joyful devotion. For from this, above all, we shall undoubtedly win a reward from the Lord, the Creator of all, if venerable places of the saints, suitably ordered, are brought by our authority into a better condition. Therefore, dearest brother, since among the other exercises of holy conduct [Col. 1016D] we have learned that you built a monastery in your episcopate, near the city of Verdun, namely in the church of blessed Peter, in which the bodies of the holy confessors and of the former bishops of the aforesaid Church of Saint Mary, Vitonus, Pulchronius, Possessor, and Firminus, rest, and since you have prudently strengthened that holy church with the resources of your own church, so that if at any time sons of your Church, moved by divine love and despising earthly things, should desire to flee to the perfection of the contemplative life, they might not seem wholly separated from your Church, but might find in the monastery, which is a member of that same Church, a refuge of consolation under the religious habit [Col. 1017A], and might serve the Lord there in tranquil peace:

Let the diligence of all the faithful, present and future, know that we wish the same monastery, built under your direction, together with all its properties and royal charters enacted for it with your counsel, to remain forever undisturbed—namely:

- the estate above the Scantia, with its appurtenances;
- Flaviniacum, with its adjuncts;
- the abbey of Saint Amantius, with everything belonging to it;
- Nova-Villa, with its estates;
- at Mantio’s estate, as much as pertains to you;
- Parridum, with its adjoining properties;
- the church of Marculfi-Curtis, with its adjoining properties;
- Arbordi-Villa, with its appurtenances;
- the church of Castonis-Curtis, with what belongs to it;
- the church of Marleium, with its adjoining properties [Col. 1017B];
- the church of Amonzei-Villa, with its adjoining properties, including lands, vineyards, mills, male and female slaves;
- the abbey of Peter;
- the church of Maroa;
- at Limacum, everything belonging to that place;
- at Nova-Villa in the county of Bar, everything belonging to that place.

All these aforesaid places, with all their appurtenances generally and specifically, and whatever, with God’s help, may be granted to this monastery by the devotion of the faithful, we confirm perpetually for the future by this our apostolic privilege, both to you and to your successors. Moreover, by this privilege of our authority, we decree that the following be strengthened, so that the same Church of Verdun—which until now was deprived of sons exposed in its bosom from the earliest beginnings of infancy whenever they fled to external monasteries—may henceforth glory in the holy way of life of these sons, elevated within the member subject to it, through the counsel of its bishop and the care of the glorious abbot Humbert [Col. 1017C].

If any person, whether great or small, of whatever rank or power, should presume by reckless audacity to oppose this our apostolic command, let that person know that, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, he is excommunicated, bound by the sentence of anathema, and alienated from the kingdom of God, and condemned, together with all the ungodly, to eternal fire and punishment. But whoever proves to be an observer of this our command may deserve to obtain grace, mercy, and eternal life from our most merciful Lord God.

[Col. 1017D] Written by the hand of Leo, notary of the holy apostolic see, in the month of January, in the fourteenth indiction. Farewell. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of January, by the hand of Martin, bishop and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the seventh year of the pontificate of the lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope, by God’s favor, in the most sacred see of the apostle blessed Peter, in the first month, and in the fourteenth indiction.

IV. LETTER OF POPE JOHN XII TO LANDULF, BISHOP OF BENEVENTO. (Year 956.)

[In Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, VIII, 57.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend [Col. 1018A] and most holy LANDULF, bishop of the holy Beneventan Church, and to your successors forever.

Since the summit of supreme apostolic dignity is recognized as shining with the splendor of divine advancement, and since it strives to display especially diligent labor in the exercise of God’s praises, the due care of that same apostolic pastoral responsibility has compelled us to promulgate whatever contributes to the stability of pious places and to confirm it by the judgment of apostolic institution. Therefore, because you asked us that the holy Beneventan Church, over which by God’s favor you preside, should be adorned with the privileges of the holy apostolic see, and that we should confirm the ancient boundaries granted to it by our predecessor pontiffs, we favoring your pious desires commit to effect by this our authority what has been requested [Col. 1018B].

We grant to you and to your holy Beneventan Church whatever it is seen to have lawfully and reasonably possessed by ancient right in the time of your predecessors, namely Bivinum, Asculum, Larinum, Sipontum, and the church of Saint Michael the Archangel on Mount Gargano, with all their appurtenances. We likewise grant for your religious authority and that of your successors to govern and lawfully and canonically administer all estates, together with churches, households of both sexes, and holdings, and everything within the places of your parish belonging to your ancient jurisdiction, whether they be cities or whatever castles were formerly possessed by your episcopal predecessors, with all their appurtenances.

Furthermore, by apostolic judgment, under the solemn appeal of divine judgment and by strong and most severe prohibitions of anathema, we decree that no person endowed with the power of any dignity—whether a great or a small person, or a Greek—shall ever presume to use force in your aforesaid holy Beneventan Church, or in any way to take away or alienate anything that appears to belong to it, or diminish its boundaries, nor at any time inflict upon it any injury or loss. Nor shall anyone have permission, as has been said, to take away from it, or from anything belonging to it, anything whatsoever, whether from a great or small person, so that, in accordance with what we have established, the same venerable holy Beneventan Church, established and adorned by apostolic constitutions and privileges, may remain securely endowed [Col. 1018C].

But if anyone—which we do not wish—should by wicked audacity resist or in any way transgress what we have established for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid Beneventan Church, whether he be a Greek or any other person who wishes to exercise domination or primacy, whether personally or through any other person, in the aforesaid churches without the will and command of the bishop of Benevento, then all such persons, including those who should presume to receive them, shall alike remain bound by the same apostolic and strict, indissoluble anathema of ours, and shall not presume to enter any church or perform any ecclesiastical office. But whoever, out of reverence, proves to be an observer and in all things a guardian of this our constitution [Col. 1019A], with regard for the worship of God, may abundantly obtain the grace of blessing from our most merciful Lord God and deserve to become a participant in eternal life.

Written by the hand of Leo, notary of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of December, in the fifteenth indiction. Farewell.

Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January, by the hand of Marinus, bishop and librarian of the supreme apostolic see, by God’s favor, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of our lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope XII, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter, in the month and fifteenth indiction written above.

[Note: [Col. 1019D] The words “whether he be a Greek” are repeated twice in this document because at that time the province of Benevento was being oppressed by continual incursions of the Greeks. Since they boasted that they could be struck with anathema only by the patriarch of Constantinople, the Roman pontiff nevertheless, because of that supreme authority which he had always exercised throughout the Christian world, pronounced his anathemas with that extension even to the Greeks.]

V. LETTER OF JOHN XII TO HENRY, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER. Fragment. — (Year 957.) He grants him the use of the pallium.

[In Gunther, *Codex diplomaticus Rheno-Mosellanus*, I, 127.]

[Col. 1019B]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and dearest brother HENRY, archbishop of the holy Church of Trier: for your life alone … Given on the day before the Ides of February, by the hand of John, librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the fifth year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of the lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope XII, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter, V … to the most pious lord … Otto Augustus, crowned by God, great emperor, in his first year, in the month of February, in the fifth indiction.

VI. BRIEF RECORD. How Pope John XII restrained the people of Subiaco, who were rebellious against the abbot of the monastery of Subiaco and had seized many of his goods, and compelled them to restore everything, in the year 958.

[In Muratori, *Antiquitates Italicae*, VI, 203.]

[Col. 1019C]

In the year—perhaps the third—of the lord Pope John XII, in the month of May, in the first indiction.

Since the human mind is always recognized to be engaged in difficulties, and each person’s spirit, wandering here and there amid various cares and anxieties, runs about without being able to explain everything in speech or retain future events in memory, therefore, by God’s will, the art of writing was discovered by the wisest men, so that what we cannot retain in mind we may write down in letters.

For this reason I, Leo, abbot of Saint Benedict of Subiaco, record how the lord pope, having come to our monastery for the sake of prayer, heard our complaint concerning all those residing in the aforesaid castle of Subiaco and in our other districts, because of the many persecutions and afflictions which they continually inflicted upon our monastery. Thereupon the lord pope, suddenly moved by pity and mercy, began to feel compassion for that venerable place and for our entire fraternal congregation, and for the many injuries which we had suffered from the days when the lord Alberic, of blessed memory, departed this life.

Then, when the same supreme pontiff was seated in that venerable monastery with the venerable bishops—namely Marinus of the Church of Polimartium, also librarian of the holy apostolic see; Constantine, bishop of Porto; John, humble bishop of the holy Tiburtine Church—and with the Roman judges, George, second secretary of the holy Roman Church, Leo, chief notary of the holy apostolic see, and many others [Col. 1020A], he ordered all the adversaries to come into his presence.

When they came before the lord pope together with us, they were severely restrained; and he caused all the goods, estates, and lands individually mentioned there to be restored to the monastery. He ordered the abbot to prepare a brief record of this matter and to have it subscribed by the aforesaid men and other worthy men, for the perpetual memory of the event [Col. 1020B].

VII. BULL OF POPE JOHN XII TO LEO, ABBOT. (Year 938.) He confirms the property and rights of the monastery of Subiaco.

[In Muratori, *Antiquitates Italicae*, V, 461.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to LEO, venerable priest, monk, and abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Benedict and Saint Scholastica, situated at Subiaco, and to his holy congregation, and to your successors forever.

Since the desire of a pious will and the intention of praiseworthy devotion must always be assisted by apostolic means, for the purpose of ensuring that what is lawfully done may stand with equity and firmness and not be disturbed by any opposition, but remain by inviolable right and authority, apostolic sanctions require that whatever each person is entitled to possess by reason be confirmed. Therefore, since it is evident that you have acquired very many holy places, and that everything seems to belong, in honor and utility, to your venerable monastery by right and jurisdiction, and since you appear to possess various fields together with castles, properties, and a multitude of servants, you have requested that all these places, fields, estates, and properties, with all the original servants remaining there, with male and female tenants and everything belonging to them, be confirmed by the privileges of the apostolic see for retention under the jurisdiction of your reverence, your holy congregation, and your successors, servants of God, forever [Col. 1020D].

Namely, the entire castle called Subiaco, or known by whatever other names, together with all its boundaries, limits, and landmarks; lands, houses, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, willow-groves, fruit trees, trees bearing various kinds of fruit [Col. 1021A], wells, springs, streams of perpetual water, building ruins, adjoining and neighboring properties, cultivated and uncultivated, empty and occupied, together with the male and female tenants of both sexes belonging to it, and likewise with the acorn dues, pasture dues, or any other payment belonging to the right of the castle and customarily paid to our holy Roman Church.

We confirm and securely establish all this for you, with all its appurtenances and dependencies everywhere, to be held perpetually for the use and benefit of the monastery of Saint Benedict, without any payment, together with the river as it begins at the Emperor’s Rock, proceeds straight to the Terranean Bridge through its channels, and continues to the lake below the monastery itself, with its water-mills; then straight to Silicella and Saliceto [Col. 1021B]; through the place called Mandra, with the water-mills located there; then descending by the bridge to Saint Angelo, likewise to Saint Peter, and then to the meadows of Ajano.

Likewise, the other water called Cona, situated in that river; then the water called Flumicello, together with Augusta, Bullica, and Timida, all flowing into the aforesaid river, and continuing as far as the territory of Saint Cosmas; with all the banks and shores of the places named, belonging in their entirety on both sides; with all the waters of that place where water-mills have been made or may be made, and wherever fish may be caught throughout all the aforesaid waters.

We also grant perpetually, without any payment, to you and your successors the church of Saint Felicitas, to be held for the use and support of your aforesaid venerable monastery [Col. 1021C].

Likewise, the estate called Lubenzana, and Intermarana in its entirety, with its farms, canals, and all its estates wherever they belong to that estate, namely: the farm of Canterano; Marano; Seminarum; Oricula; Arsula; Bulsinianum; Toccanellum; Marcatellum; the farm of Paternum; the farm of Aprunium; the farm of Arpellum; the farm of Lenanum; the farm of Tessina; the mountains called the Twins, descending into Trellanum; Mount Gordianus; the farm of Sassa and the hill of Ferrari; the little monastery; another little monastery; Piscano; and Colonia beside Saint Valerius on two sides; and half of Ibice.

The farm of Minianum; the farm of Castaniola; Lorillianum; Saint Cecilia [Col. 1021D]; the farm of Boberanum; the farm called Valle, with the church of Saint Eleutherius; the farm called Capramolente, with the church of Saint Anastasius; the estate called Ampolloni, with the church of Saint Martin; the farm of Paternum, called Pentima; the farm of Bruvanum; the farm of Saint Pamphilus; the farm of Daniel; the farm of Merulana; the farm of Paccanum; the farm of Tospolianum, with the church of Saint Mary and Saint Lucentius; the farm of Saint Cyricus; the farm of Cispa; the farm of Romanus, with the church of Saint Angelus and Saint Felix, bounded on one side by the river Tiber, on the second side by Papi, and on the third side by the Fulgurated Arch, descending to the mountain where the cypresses are, proceeding to the mountain called Bulturella [Col. 1022A], and descending straight through Saint Mary to Piscano. And everything belonging in its entirety to the aforesaid estate.

Likewise, the farm of Caliscano in its entirety, with the church of Saint Peter.

Also the monastery of Saint Barbara and Saint Anastasius, with two small estates—one before it and the other behind it—with their houses, farms, and estates, and everything belonging to them in its entirety, situated within the city of Tibur; and half of the church of Saint Mary there in that place, with its houses, vineyards, lands, and all its appurtenances across the Tiber near the Marble Bridge; and the entire enclosed vineyard called Valle Arcese; and the entire enclosed vineyard planted with vines, with olive trees.

And the church of Saint Sebastian, and the small vineyard in front of it with its olive grove; and the enclosed vineyard situated below the small Tiburtine gate beside the paved road called Quarrati. Likewise, the entire enclosed vineyard called Ortu Magno; the farm of Casaperta; the small enclosed vineyard called Asorbo; the portion in the Greater Meadow which belonged to Bishop Calvus; the farm of Stafilanum in its entirety; the farm of Romanianum in its entirety; the farm of Patelini in its entirety; the farm of Ozanum in its entirety; the farm of Criptula; the farm of Panzi; the farm of Dirutus; the farm of Agnaniole; the farm of Macronianum; the farm of Semissanum; the farm of Paternum; the farm of Vallelonga; the farm of Saint Mary in Pesile; the farm of Donabellus; the farm of Factor; the farm of Lucus; the farm of Catacumba, with the church of Saint Lawrence; the farm of Afri, with all the aforesaid farms in their entirety, situated in the territories of Praeneste and Tibur [Col. 1022C].

Likewise, the enclosed vineyard called Ancaranum, in its entirety, with the aforesaid trees; the land and vineyard called Pentuma, formerly belonging to the priest Tetuald; two pieces of vineyard at Saint Lawrence, in two places; and likewise the farm of Porclanicum in its entirety, with all its appurtenances; the farm of Otoranum; the farm of Arceranum; the farm of Palasanum; the farm of Cesulina; the farm of Oleanum; the farm of Campelion; the farm of Ojanum and Prianum; the farm of Cammeranum; the farm of Collemundum; Catilanum; Cocubalus; Pacuranum; and the church of Saint Angelus, with all its appurtenances, situated in the territory of Lesser Ferentinum—all in the territory of Campania.

Also the farm of Falconianum, with the church of Saint Nicholas; the farm of Fontinianum and the Hill of Morelli; the farm of Toccanellum; the farm of Capla; the farm of Orarum; the farm of Gratulianum; the farm of Cervianum; the farm of Labezanum; the farm of Casanicum; the farm called Domus, with the church of Saint Peter; the farm of Ponzia; the farm of Pozzorosanum, with its enclosed vineyard situated beside Caranicum; and a valley of four *modii* with its chestnut grove beside Saint Peter, together with lands, vineyards, houses, and woods situated in various places in the territory of Aquila [Col. 1022D].

Likewise, in the territory of Alba: the farm of Soranum, with vineyards, lands, and caves, and the church of the Four Saints; the farm of Silva Major; the portion which belonged to Bishop Florus; a piece of vineyard at Zizinni; and also the enclosed vineyard in its entirety situated in the farm of Cerasanum [Col. 1023A].

Also two small houses at the Salarian Bridge; a portion of Palmi, with lands and gardens; two meadows beside the Greater Gate; two small estates, one at Pedica called Burdunaria and the other in the Greater Field. Likewise, the entire houses with their courtyards and gardens, and the church of Saint Theodore, situated within the city of Rome near the Greater Gate, just as they belonged to Bishop Florus.

Likewise, the houses that belonged to John and Stephen of Griphi, with courtyard, pergola, and small garden near the Claudian Aqueduct; and the enclosed vineyard in its entirety, with fruit trees and caves beside the road that leads to Jerusalem. Likewise, the entire house with its courtyard, small garden, and vineyard, with everything belonging to it [Col. 1023B], situated in the Seventh Region of Rome, in which house is the church of Saint Vitus. Also the vineyard or land near Jerusalem; and the enclosed vineyard in its entirety at Alba, in the farm of Zizinni, six pieces; and the entire house with its small garden situated near Saint Martin. Likewise, the house with courtyard situated in the Subura.

Likewise, the monastery of Saint Erasmus, with all its adjoining and appurtenant properties, as contained in your charter; and likewise two pieces of the vineyard of Inostus, one in the farm of Maurus and the other in Calabricetum. Likewise, the cultivated and cleared meadow of the farm of Aguzanum.

All the properties written above, with all their farms, estates, holdings, churches, monasteries, houses, gardens, vineyards, male and female slaves, male and female tenants [Col. 1023C], rivers and water-mills, fisheries, as described above, or also in other regions or cities, wherever your venerable monastery appears to hold and possess anything by any written instrument—whether by the text of a charter or by rights of privilege, or by exchanges or donations—and everything which Christian faithful have given to your holy congregation for the remission of their sins, or whatever you appear to possess in your monastery through documents, both ancient and recent, we confirm by this our apostolic command, securely and perpetually, for you and your successors to retain forever.

Nevertheless, we confirm to you in its entirety one estate called … near Quartum, with its meadow, bounded as follows: on the first side by the estate called Barbilianum; on the other side by the farm of Munitula, extending from that meadow along its boundaries as far as the deserted walls beyond the aqueduct, emerging onto the Public Road; on the third side by that Public Road [Col. 1023D]; and on the fourth side by the farm called Decorita, with water descending along its boundaries into the Jovia aqueduct, emerging through the aqueduct and returning along the boundary beside the water as far as the aforesaid farm of Barbilianum [Col. 1024A].

Also, the entire farm of Sextum, with its meadow beside the stream, bounded on one side by the road leading to the Adenona Bridge, on the other side by the public road, and by any other adjoining properties there may be.

We, bowing to your pious requests, grant and confirm to all your pious places and to our holy Roman Church, which by the Lord’s appointment we serve, through the text of this apostolic privilege, all the aforesaid immovable properties, with all their appurtenances, as described above, from this present first indiction and forever, for you and your successors to retain for the use and benefit of that venerable monastery.

Yet on each day the priests and monks of that monastery are to cry out in the same church, for the salvation of our soul and those of our successors, one hundred times “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”) and one hundred times “Christe eleison” (“Christ, have mercy”), and the priests are to offer sacred oblations in the solemn celebrations of Mass three times each week for the absolution of our soul and those of our successor pontiffs [Col. 1024B].

We establish by apostolic judgment, under the solemn appeal of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, that no one, whether one of our successor pontiffs or any other person, great or small, shall dare or presume to act against this our pontifical privilege, or to alienate or take away any of all the aforesaid immovable properties with all their appurtenances and dependencies, as described above. Rather, we decree that they remain firm and stable for perpetual and everlasting times, just as they have been established by us.

But if anyone—which we do not wish—should become an attacker of this our apostolic privilege, oppose it in any respect, and wish to be a transgressor, let that person know that, by the authority of almighty God and of our Lord Peter, prince of the apostles, whose representative we are, though unworthy, by the Lord’s favor, he is bound by the chain of anathema and alienated from the kingdom of God [Col. 1024C].

But whoever, out of pious reverence, proves to be a true guardian and observer of this our apostolic privilege may, through the merits and prayers of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of Saint Benedict in the heavenly citadels, deserve to obtain rewards, the grace of blessing, and mercy from the just judge, the Lord our God, and eternal life.

[Col. 1024D] Written by the hand of Leo, notary and secretary of the holy supreme apostolic see, in the month of May, in the first indiction already mentioned.

+ Farewell. +

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of May, by the hand of Marinus, bishop of the holy Church of Polimartium and librarian of the supreme apostolic see, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord John, supreme pontiff and universal [Col. 1025A] pope X—[Note: [Col. 1023D] The scribe should read “universal pope XII”; for the chronological notes cannot be connected with the time of Pope John X. Ughelli, volume VIII of *Italia Sacra*, in the list of the archbishops of Benevento, reports a bull of that same pontiff, John XII, given by the hand of Bishop Marinus—that is, of Polimartium—and librarian of the supreme apostolic see, “in the year, by God’s favor” (the scribe should read “by God’s favor”), of the pontificate of our lord John, and so forth, in the eleventh year; in the month of December, in the fifteenth indiction. It should be written “first year,” if the new indiction is reckoned from September, or “second year.”] in the most sacred see of the apostle blessed [Col. 1025A] Peter, in the third year, in the month and indiction written above, the first.

Let there also be added, for the greater adornment of the monastery of Subiaco, a noble charter which is likewise preserved in its archive.

VIII. RESCRIPT OF POPE JOHN XII CONCERNING THE EXCOMMUNICATION OF ARTALD, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS, AND AMBLARD, ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS, ETC., ON ACCOUNT OF THEIR INVASION OF THE POSSESSIONS OF SAINT SYMPHORIAN. (Year 958.) Transmission of the excommunication.

[In Mansi, *Councils*, XVIII, col. 450.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 959, in the third indiction, while Michael was emperor in Constantinople, and the lord John presided as apostolic in Rome [Col. 1025B], while Lothar was reigning as king of the Franks, this excommunication was sent to the archbishops of France and Burgundy: to Artald, archbishop of the Church of Rheims, and the bishops subject to him; to Amblard, archbishop of the Church of Lyons; to Rodmund, bishop of the Church of Autun; to Achard, bishop of the see of Langres; to Frotgarius, bishop of the Church of Chalon; to Natrus, bishop of Nevers; and to Richard, bishop of Auxerre—concerning the land and allod of Saint Faustus, Saint Augusta, and Saint Symphorian, which is in the region of Provence, in the territory of the place called Magna, and which Isuard and his associates hold by force.

**Excommunication**

[Col. 1025C] By the authority of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and by the order of all the saints, and by our common excommunication, we bind and anathematize Isuard and all his associates who hold the land of Saint Symphorian.

After any of them has heard this, let none of them enter a church, hear Mass, or make peace with a Christian; let him neither eat nor drink nor sleep; if he falls ill, let him not be visited; and if he dies, let him not be buried, nor let anyone pray for him, unless he comes to amendment and satisfaction.

Concerning these lands of Saint Symphorian situated in the counties of Avignon and Cavaillon, Isuard eventually made satisfaction to Gerard, bishop of Autun (352). On Tuesday, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, in the year of the Lord 972, in the fifteenth indiction [Col. 1025D], while Conrad was reigning as king, Desiderius, bishop of Cavaillon, confirmed the restoration of the property situated in the bishopric of Cavaillon, made to Hugh, dean of the church of Saint Symphorian of Cavaillon, and to his clergy.

IX. LETTER OF POPE JOHN XII TO SAINT DUNSTAN, BISHOP OF CANTERBURY. (Year 960.) Concerning the granting of the pallium.

[In Mansi, as above.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his fellow-bishop DUNSTAN, archbishop of the Church of Canterbury [Col. 1026A]: perpetual abiding in Christ.

If shepherds of sheep are willing to endure sun and frost, day and night, for the protection of their flock, and watch with vigilant eyes lest any of the sheep perish by wandering or be carried off by the bite of beasts, with how much care and with what labor ought we to remain watchful for the salvation of souls, who are said to be their shepherds?

Let us therefore take care to perform our duty in guarding the Lord’s sheep, lest, terrified as though by the coming of a wolf, we flee, and lest on the day of divine examination we be tortured before the supreme shepherd because of our laziness and your negligence, from which we are now distinguished from the others by the reverence of honor in a higher citadel.

Therefore, we fully confirm your primacy, in which, according to the custom of your predecessors, it is fitting for you to exercise the functions of the apostolic see [Col. 1026B], just as Saint Augustine and his successors, the pontiffs of the aforesaid Church, are known to have possessed it.

As for the pallium, we commend it to your fraternity according to custom, for the celebration of the solemnities of Mass; we permit you to use it only in the manner in which our predecessors prescribed its use, with the privileges of your church remaining in their established condition.

Nor is it unknown to your prudence—or to anyone—how great and how fearsome the honor of a garment becomes when moderated by conduct. These ornaments suit the uprightness of your character, so that, by God’s authority, you may be conspicuous, and your life may be a rule for your sons. If they possess any strength, let them be directed by you while they look upon in you what they should imitate.

[Col. 1026C] And at the end of the letter:

May the Holy Trinity surround your fraternity with the protection of its grace, and direct you in the way of its fear, so that after the bitterness of this life we may together deserve to attain eternal sweetness.

And this was written by the hand of Leo, notary of the apostolic see, in the month of October, in the fourth indiction, on the first day before the Kalends of October, in the twelfth [sixth] year of the supreme pontiff John.

X. PRIVILEGE OF POPE JOHN XII FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT SAVIOR AT FULDA. (Year 961.)

[In Dronke, *Codex diplomaticus Fuldensis*, p. 328.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HATTO, venerable abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Savior of our Lord Jesus Christ and of Saint Boniface, martyr of Christ, which is situated in the place of Boconia on the bank of the river Fulda, and to you and your successors, the abbots, forever [Col. 1026D].

Since whatever accords with reasonable desires must always be granted, the authority of pious construction must not be denied to the devotion of a founder when privileges are being bestowed. Therefore, because you asked us that the aforesaid monastery of Saint Savior should be adorned with the insignia of a privilege of the apostolic see, so that, established under the jurisdiction of our Church—which by God’s authority we serve—it should not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other church, we, favoring your pious desires, commit to effect by this our authority what has been requested [Col. 1027A].

Therefore, we prohibit any priest of any church from exercising any jurisdiction or authority in the aforesaid monastery, except the apostolic see. Thus, unless invited by the abbot of the monastery, no one at all may presume to celebrate the solemnity of Mass there. Accordingly, since it is subject to the apostolic see by the firmness of privilege, let it remain securely endowed in its places and possessions, both those which it holds or possesses at the present time and those which divine piety may in future wish to increase as the property of that venerable monastery through the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful, enjoying perpetual security without contradiction from any person.

We also establish by the text of this decree that if any prelate of any church, or any person of whatever dignity, should attempt to violate this charter of our privilege, which we confirm by the authority of the prince of the apostles, let that person be anathema; incurring the wrath of God, let him be excluded from the assembly of all the saints. Nevertheless, by apostolic authority, the dignity of the aforesaid monastery, granted by us, strengthened by our authority, shall remain inviolable forever [Col. 1027B].
