Written by the hand of Leo, second secretary of the apostolic see, in the month of December, in the fifth indiction.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of December, by the hand of John, bishop and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the sixth month of the year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of the lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope XII, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter, in the fifth indiction [Col. 1027C].

XI. PRIVILEGE OF POPE JOHN XII FOR THE CHURCH OF SALZBURG. (Year 962.) He confirms the privileges and possessions of the Church of Salzburg. At the request of Emperor Otto, he grants the pallium to Archbishop Frederick. He declares that Herald, the blinded and deposed archbishop, will be anathematized unless he ceases to administer sacred rites.

[Twelfth-century copy in the Vienna archive. — In Kleinmayern, *Nachrichten von den Erzbischöfen von Salzburg*, 208.]

If priests, etc.

[Col. 1027D] Given on the seventh day before the Ides of February, by the hand of Andrew, archivist of the holy apostolic see, etc.

## XII. LETTER OF POPE JOHN XII TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, ABBOTS, CLERGY, AND PEOPLE OF GAUL, GERMANY, AND BAVARIA

*(Year 962.)* At the request of Emperor Otto I, he decrees that the monastery of Magdeburg be transformed into an archbishopric, and that of Merseburg into a bishopric subordinate to the Church of Magdeburg.

[In Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, fifth century, p. 575.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend brothers, the archbishops, bishops, abbots, monks, primates, all the clergy, and the people established in Gaul, Germany, and Bavaria. [Col. 1028A]

Whenever a privilege of concession and confirmation is requested for the advancement of the new Christianity from the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, we have always considered it worthwhile to grant it with every diligence and love, lest the envy of the crafty enemy, through negligence, continually steal away what ought to be devoted with particular care to pious desires. Therefore, dearest brothers, we must strive with all our strength so that the Christianity which almighty God daily extends and advances through his servants as a heavenly trophy may, through our assistance also, granted by him, be strengthened and remain established.

Now, through the working of God’s mercy, our dearest and most Christian son Otto, having conquered [Col. 1028B] the barbarian peoples—namely the Avars and many others—so that, for the defense of the holy Church of God, he might receive from us the crown of the triumphant summit of imperial victory from blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, approached the supreme and universal see over which, by God’s authority, we preside. Receiving him with paternal affection, we anointed him emperor, with the blessing of blessed Peter, for the defense of the holy Church of God.

And while, in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, we were discussing the condition and governance of all Christianity, so that useful matters might be treated usefully according to God, the aforesaid most pious emperor Otto made known to our paternal care how he had newly established the Slavs whom he himself had conquered in the Catholic faith, earnestly begging [Col. 1028C] and insistently requesting that the sheep whom he had acquired for Christ should not, because of the shepherd’s failure, be ruled by the deceit of the ancient serpent.

Accordingly, dearest brothers, we rightly assented to this petition. Therefore, with all the innermost affections of our heart, let us attend—as is fitting—to the planting of this new growth, so that it may be founded upon the summit of the mountain, upon the rock that is Christ. He who wishes no one to perish will grant strength.

With his mercy consenting, we wish, and by this charter of privilege we order, that the monastery of Magdeburg, constructed in the kingdom of the Saxons beside the Elbe, which the aforesaid most holy emperor built for the new Christianity, since it is nearer to the peoples, be transferred into an archiepiscopal see, so that it may be able to govern and direct the whole flock of God through subordinate suffragan bishops. [Col. 1028D]

We likewise wish, and by this charter of privilege we order, that the monastery of Merseburg, which that most pious emperor devoted to God as a future foundation because he had defeated the Hungarians, be elevated into an episcopal see subject to the see of Magdeburg, since so many peoples can scarcely be governed under a single shepherd.

We wish and decree by the privilege of our authority that his successors have the power to distribute and assign the census and the tithe of all the peoples whom that same most pious emperor baptized, or who, with God’s consent, are to be baptized through him, his son—the king, his namesake—and their successors, to Magdeburg, Merseburg, or whatever future see they may choose.

We also wish, dearest brothers, and by command of the blessed apostle Peter [Col. 1029A] we order, that the archbishops of Mainz, Trier, Cologne, Salzburg, and Hamburg remain, with all the strength of heart and body, united supporters of the transformation of the monastery of Magdeburg into an archiepiscopal see and of Merseburg into an episcopal see.

When almighty God, through the aforementioned invincible servant of his, the emperor, and through his son the king and their successors, has brought the neighboring Slavic people to the worship of the Christian faith, we wish episcopal sees to be established by them in suitable places according to need, and suffragan bishops to be consecrated for those sees by the archbishop of Magdeburg, with the consent of the aforementioned rulers, and of the archbishops and their successors.

But if the successors of the aforesaid most pious son of ours, the emperor, and of his son, his namesake the king, should [Col. 1029B] attempt to violate these decrees, or if the archbishops of the aforesaid churches and the other prelates and their successors should not be helpers and united supporters of the archbishop of Magdeburg, his successors, their suffragans, and their successors, let them be struck by the sword of anathema and receive endless condemnation from the supreme rewarder.

May almighty God grant long life to the most serene emperor Otto and to his son, his namesake the king, our spiritual sons, so that, living peacefully in this world, they may receive in the future the palm of unfading glory.

Written by the hand of Leo, notary of the holy apostolic see, in the month of February, in the fifth indiction.

Given on the second day before the Ides of February, by the hand of George, subdeacon of the holy apostolic see, in the year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the seventh year, and in the first year of the empire of our most pious lord Augustus Otto, crowned by God, the great emperor, in the aforesaid month and indiction. [Col. 1029C]

## XIII. LETTER OF POPE JOHN XII TO HENRY, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER

*Fragment.*—*(Year 962.)* He grants him the use of the pallium once again.

[In Gunther, *Codex diplomaticus Rhenano-Mosellanus* I, 127.]

John, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest and most reverend Henry, archbishop of the holy Church of Trier, for the days of your life only [lacuna]. Given on the sixth day before the Ides of January, by the hand of Leo, nomenclator of the holy apostolic see, in the year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope XII, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter, in the second year, in the month of January and the fifteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 957. [Col. 1029D]

## XIV. PRIVILEGE OF POPE JOHN XII FOR THE ROMAN MONASTERY OF THE HOLY STEPHEN, DIONYSIUS, AND SYLVESTER

*(Year 962.)*

[Marini, *Papiri diplomatici* I, 45.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Theophylact, beloved son in the Lord and abbot appointed by us, abbot of the venerable monastery [lacuna] of Dionysius and the pontiff Sylvester, which is called *Cata Pauli*, and to your successors as abbots forever. [Col. 1030A]

It is fitting for apostolic governance to assist those who flourish in pious religion with benevolent compassion and to grant the petitioner’s mind the desired assent with willing devotion. By this, above all, we merit forgiveness from the Lord, creator of all, when venerable places dedicated to the saints are undoubtedly brought into a better condition.

Therefore, since your religious devotion has humbly petitioned the apostolate [lacuna], that we should grant and confirm to you the aforesaid monastery, with all its churches, buildings, and appurtenances, both those within it and those around it, together with the whole mountain called Augusto, with the church of Saint Angelus at the summit of that mountain, along with the vineyards and lands around the same mountain; and the entire church of Saint Nicholas with all its appurtenances, as its boundaries are marked below: on one side, the public road that leads beneath the arches and the aqueduct called the Virgin; on the second side, that same Virgin aqueduct and the mountain called Pineus; on the third side, the walls of the city of Rome and the gate of Saint Valentine; and on the fourth side, the aforesaid wall of the city, returning as far as the ancient Posterula, formerly called Saint Agatha’s; together with the road from that Posterula which runs beside the aforesaid church, and the public road that leads beneath the arches, situated in the fifth region of Rome. [Col. 1030B]

Likewise, beyond the aforesaid aqueduct, the lands with their buildings, as the same monastery appears to possess them [Col. 1030C], together with the land within them at Archiones, below the vineyard formerly belonging to John, once the great [lacuna] bishop [lacuna].

Again, the entire larger marble column called Antonine, apparently sculpted in every respect, with the church of Saint Andrew at its foot, and the land around it, as it appears to be enclosed on every side by the public road, constructed within this city of Rome.

Likewise, two churches, one larger and the other smaller, called Saint Mary, situated before the gate of the aforesaid monastery; and the church of Saint Hippolytus with its appurtenance, which lies outside the aforesaid aqueduct; and the church of Saint Anastasius, with the well behind it and its appurtenance; and the church of Saint Stephen called “at the Field”; and the church of Saint Mary at the place called Archiones; and the church of Saint John situated at Pineus, with its appurtenance. [Col. 1030D]

We also confirm to you in its entirety the monastery of Saint Valentine, with all its buildings and adjacent properties wherever they appear to lie, situated outside the gate also called Saint Valentine’s Gate, under the jurisdiction of the aforesaid venerable monastery.

Furthermore, we confirm to you the Milvian Bridge in its entirety, with all its entrances and exits, payments, and tolls.

Likewise, the arable land situated outside the gate of Saint Valentine, beside the walls of this city of Rome, on the left hand, bounded as follows: on the first side, the ditch called the *carbonaria* between that wall and the same land [Col. 1031A], extending as far as the river Tiber; on the second side, that river; on the third side, the public road leading to and returning from Saint Valentine; and on the fourth side, [lacuna] belonging to the holy Roman Church. In the mountain there is also other arable land with its gardens at the entrance, together with everything belonging to it.

There, on the right hand as one goes to Saint Valentine, beneath the larger arch, within the same land called Passaranum, and the entire fishpond, bounded as follows: on the first side, the aforementioned public road; on the second side, the communal spring of living water between the aforesaid monastery and Gregory Mansonarius of the school of the confession of the blessed apostle Peter, extending from there in a straight line to the head of the ancient wall; on the third side, the land of the venerable monastery of Saint Cyriacus, situated on the Via Lata, and extending straight along the boundary upward across the Plain of the Mountain called Bossetulus, exiting onto the Via Flaminia.

We also confirm to you in its entirety the estate called Girulo, with its various trees and everything belonging to it, as it appears to belong to you according to the sequence of documents. It lies outside the gate of Saint Valentine, approximately one Roman mile from the city, and is bounded on one side by the public road, an ancient paved road descending as far as Sanguinaria; on the second side by the Formello of living water, which emerges below the mountain of Girulo, or below the meadow of the aforesaid Saint Cyriacus; on the third side, mou [lacuna], the aforesaid monastery of Saint Valentine; and on the fourth side, arable land belonging to your monastery, which the Roman heirs hold from the Campus Martius. [Col. 1031C]

Likewise, we confirm to you an entire estate called Pelajolo, with its arable lands, fields, meadows, pastures, and mountains, in which is the church of Saint Sylvester, situated in the wilderness, and with everything generally and wholly belonging to it, just as Alberic, formerly senator of the Romans, once gave it to the aforesaid venerable monastery in exchange, by a charter of exchange, to which he and his brothers [lacuna] subscribed with their own hands—namely Constantius, a nobleman; Sergius, bishop of the holy Church of Nepi; with Berta and another Berta, on account of the valley of Saint Vitus, which was situated in the venerable monastery. It lies outside the Salarian Gate, approximately [lacuna] [Col. 1031D] miles away, beside the river Tiber, bounded on one side by the estate of Gorginus; on the second side by the river Tiber itself, or the land where there are now vineyards, with its meadow, belonging to the venerable monastery of Saint Basil, situated at the Scala Mortuorum, together with other land; also with its meadow belonging to the venerable monastery of Saint [lacuna], and land with its meadow belonging to Gregory of Capo Marzo; on the third side by the estate at the Five Columns and the place called Molarium; and on the fourth side [lacuna].

We also confirm [Col. 1032A] in its entirety the estate called Gallorum, and Balleolum and Pacianum, or whatever other names they were called or originally bore, just as formerly [lacuna] by a charter of donation he offered it to your aforesaid monastery, with its arable lands, sand quarries, fields, pastures, meadows, buildings, ruined walls, additions, adjacent properties, mountains, plains, wells, springs, cultivated and uncultivated land, and everything belonging to it, situated outside [lacuna], approximately one mile from that bridge. It is bounded on one side by the estate formerly belonging to Rose Superinstante; on the second side by the ancient wall and the land formerly belonging to Azzon, son of Sacella, now held by Elpizo, a nobleman; on the third side by the land of Stephen of Theodore [lacuna]; and on the fourth side by the crypt called Serpentaricum, with other vacant land beside it belonging to the monastery of Saint Vitus.

Likewise, two entire parcels of arable land are situated there, beside the same estate and the aforesaid crypt, on this side of that crypt, belonging to the monastery of Saint Vitus. Likewise, outside [lacuna], near Nomentum [lacuna], an entire estate called Lampati, with everything belonging to it. [Col. 1032B]

Likewise, we confirm to you an entire estate called Aguzianum, situated outside the Matra Bridge. Moreover, we confirm to you three entire estates: one called the Bridge of Nono, inside that bridge, with various arable lands and its trees, or sand quarries, with deserted walls covered with [uncertain: “Sinino”] work, cultivated and uncultivated land, and everything belonging to it, situated above the aforesaid bridge of John, which is called the Via Latina, approximately nine miles from the city of Rome.

Its boundaries are: on the first side, the aforesaid aqueduct called Claudia and the aforesaid bridge called Nono; on the second side, the aforementioned aqueduct called Ebeberatorium; on the third side, the court of Morene; and on the fourth side, the boundary called “beside the crypt,” which is called Ardenda, belonging to the holy Roman Church. [Col. 1032C]

Likewise, another estate called Dominicalia, in which there is a deserted church with its gardens and ruined walls, cultivated and uncultivated land, and everything belonging to it, situated on the aforesaid Via Latina beside the aforementioned estate called the Bridge of Nono. It is bounded on one side by that estate; on the second side by a stream with flowing water called Papati; on the third side by the public road with the ancient paving; and on the fourth side by the larger aqueduct and the estate called the Seven Vassi, with its appurtenance.

Also, another entire estate called [lacuna] [Col. 1032D], with various places and names, namely the Valley of Manciaria, the Precious House, the mountain called Paulelli, and the field called Albanensis, or whatever they are now called, with their lands and arable fields, woods and various trees, working watermills, and the deserted church called Saint Peter, situated beside the Via Latina, approximately ten miles from the city of Rome.

Its boundaries are: on one side, arable land where there were formerly meadows called Pauli; on the second side, the estate of Civitella; on the third side, the public road descending to the place called Saint Peter’s Cell; and on the fourth side, the deserted church called Saint Mary in the deaconry, from which it descends by the ditch as far as the aforesaid larger aqueduct, or whatever other names they may bear, belonging to the venerable monastery of the holy apostles Andrew and Bartholomew, which is called that of Honorius. [Col. 1033A]

Moreover, an entire church called Saint Angelus, with vineyards and lands around it, situated in the Alban territory, approximately [lacuna] miles from the city, on the mountain called Crescentulus; likewise an entire vineyard with its entrance and its boundary wall, together with its winepress, situated in the Alban territory at the place called Cassa Nova.

Also, four entire parcels of vineyard, with their boundary walls, winepresses, and entrances, in the same territory at the place called Jusi; and a vineyard with its boundary wall, winepress, and entrance in the Arician territory, situated at the place called Cucurti.

We also grant you the estate called Zinziomi, with the church of Saint Mary, vineyards, lands, or watermill, and crypts, just as you hold them with your own hands [Col. 1033B] in the aforesaid Alban territory, situated approximately thirteen miles from the city of Rome [lacuna].

Also, two parcels of vineyard at the place called Honorius, in the Arician territory. Likewise, in the aforesaid Arician territory, at the place called [lacuna]um, at the foot of the major paved road [sic], belonging to the venerable deaconry of Saint Mary called *Cosmedin*.

Likewise, we grant and confirm to you an entire half-share of one strip of saltworks at the place called the Greater Ditch, as came to you through the sequence of documents from the heirs of the late lord called Cacoinbucte. Similarly, another entire strip called Saint Sylvester, at the place called the Greater Field, belonging to that same aforesaid monastery of yours.

We also confirm to you two entire working watermills in the river Tiber, [Col. 1033C] situated beside the school of the Franks, as the same watermill [lacuna] formerly belonging to Alto Amaro; and another entire working watermill, with its connecting structure, entrance, all its equipment, and everything belonging to it, just as you hold it with your own hands, or just as our predecessor, the most holy pope Agapitus, granted and confirmed it to you by the charter of his privilege, in the aforesaid river Tiber before the sewer, with the water behind it for constructing another watermill.

Its boundaries are: on one side, the watermill of Saint Mary in the Capitol and the watermill of Leo, chief seminarian; on the second side, half of that river; on the third side, the watermill of Theophylact, called the Nomenclator, and the watermill of the monastery of Saint Cyriacus on the Via Lata; and on the fourth side, the public road belonging to the jurisdiction in which it lies. [Col. 1033D]

Moreover, the entire monastery called Saint Terentianus, with all the cells listed below belonging to it—namely Saint Stephen, Saint Mary, the cell of Saint Benedict, Saint Sylvester, and Saint Valentine, or with all their appurtenances—situated in the territory of Polimarcus and belonging to the venerable monastery of the holy martyr of Christ, Lawrence.

Especially since the effort of the saints’ intercession grows strong through the work of the night [uncertain reading]. Therefore, since your religious devotion has asked us to confirm to you, in honor of God and our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, Curilianus with all its appurtenances, and since we have learned [Col. 1034A] that the estate called Ortana, or whatever other name it is called, was withdrawn from the aforesaid monastery by us for two years, we, considering the mercy [lacuna] and the poverty of that venerable monastery, and moved by the love of almighty God, for the salvation of our soul, and also for the support of the monk-brothers, restore and confirm to you and to your successors forever the aforesaid estate in its entirety, together with its estates, namely Mojana, Tojana, Occiana, Antiquina [lacuna], Suranco, Betruano, the estate of Pingiano, Terenzano, Centum Cellae, Coriliano (also Catiliano or Camilliano), Pozanelle, Genbriano, Collicello, Julianello, Sepuliano, and the well of the estate of Fuficanum, with its streams and waters; together with houses, vineyards, lands, woods, fields [lacuna], pastures, willow groves, fruit-bearing and non-fruit-bearing trees, wells, springs, streams of perpetual water, buildings, ancient ruined walls and adjacent properties, cultivated and uncultivated land, with its watermills, and also with the male and female tenants [sic], men and women, and everything generally and wholly belonging to the same estate called Ortana, or whatever other name it is called. [Col. 1034B]

Likewise, we grant and confirm to you an entire church called Saint Juvenal, with its lands, woods, and olive groves, all its trees, cultivated and uncultivated land, all situated in the aforesaid territory of Ortana, approximately fifty miles from the city of Rome.

Again, we establish for you within the city of Ortana the houses belonging to the aforesaid church of Saint Juvenal, and all immovable properties that belonged to the jurisdiction of the aforesaid venerable monastery, both within the city of Ortana and wherever else they are situated outside it in its territory.

Likewise, we confirm to you [Col. 1034C] Paternus in its entirety, with all its appurtenance, with houses, vineyards, lands, woods, meadows, willow groves, and everything generally and wholly belonging to it, both within it and outside it, situated in the aforesaid territory of Ortana. Its boundaries are: on one side, Caselle; on the second side, a flowing river [sic]; on the third side, Coreliano; and on the fourth side, the estate belonging to the Pinators and Septinianus.

Again, we establish for you all the immovable properties belonging to the jurisdiction of your aforesaid monastery within the city of Gallesana and throughout its territory, or in the three estates called Cazanum, Pusinia, and Cesa Narniense. [Col. 1034D]

Furthermore, we grant you the estate called Precilianus, with everything generally belonging to it, situated in the territory of Sabina and belonging to the holy Roman Church. Its boundaries are: on one side, the estate called Paura; on the second side, the stream of Utriculum called Butinus; on the third side, the property of the monastery of Saint Mary; and on the fourth side, the property of the monastery of Saint Saviour.

We also confirm to you the properties that belong by jurisdiction and right to your monastery in the territory of Nepi, and Casa Mala, which is an estate called Casa Nova, and Bobarica and Boltejano, together with the male and female slaves residing there and belonging to the same aforesaid monastery of yours.

We likewise confirm to you whatever, according to the sequence of documents, belonged to the same aforesaid monastery in the territory formerly belonging to Alto Amaro. [Col. 1035A]

We also confirm an entire estate called Paccianum, with everything belonging to it, situated in the territory of Sutri, as well as the cell of Saint George with what belongs to it in the aforesaid territory of Sutri.

Likewise, we confirm to you all the properties belonging by right and title to your aforesaid monastery throughout the territory of Colline, and at the place called the Valley and Tintorissi, on the mountain called Arca, or at Saint Cassianus and at the Court, and at Baccaricium, with vineyards and arable lands, woods with its great marsh, houses, and its male and female tenants residing everywhere, belonging to the aforesaid monastery of yours—all the immovable properties written above, whether belonging to the jurisdiction of our holy Roman Church, to the aforesaid monastery, or to any other pious places.

Moved by your prayers [lacuna], through intercession for souls, for the inviolable confirmation and stability of the aforesaid monastery, by this perpetual decree we confirm in its entirety the aforesaid estate called Ortana, with vineyards or lands, small estates, watermills, and all its male and female tenants and their sons and daughters residing there; also the entire church of Saint Juvenal situated beside it; and the aforementioned Paternus in its entirety, with all its appurtenances, as they are read above, from the present fifth indiction forever. [Col. 1035B]

[Col. 1035C] We grant and confirm to you, to be held irrevocably by your aforesaid monastery, everything requiring improvement or defense, which you will undoubtedly provide in every respect, so that no count, castellan, or any other person, great or small, may diminish or alienate anything belonging to the aforesaid estate or church, or to the households belonging or residing there, or produce any charter for litigation against the same venerable monastery.

Otherwise, if anyone should bring before our apostolate a claim concerning anything belonging to the aforesaid estate or the aforesaid church, or should wish to litigate against that monastery on the basis of a precept made by us, we declare that claim null and void, since it was contracted unjustly and contrary to law.

We establish, under apostolic censure and divine judgment [sic], with the authority of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and under the prohibition of anathema, that no one ever—neither any of our successors in the pontificate nor any other person, as has been stated, whether great or powerful—dare to inflict any force upon the aforesaid estate, church, vineyards, lands, or any of its appurtenances. Rather, it is to remain for all time for the use and proper benefit of the aforesaid monastery, for the support and nourishment of the monk-brothers residing there. [Col. 1035D]

But if anyone should presume, with reckless boldness, to despise this apostolic precept of our confirmation promulgated by us, let him know that he is bound by the bond of the anathema of our lord Peter, prince of the apostles, [Col. 1036A] excluded from the kingdom of God, and destined to be burned eternally with the devil and his most atrocious pomp, or with Judas, the betrayer of Jesus Christ. Together with the impious, let him perish, submerged in the abyss and Tartarean chaos.

But whoever, with pious regard, remains a guardian, obedient, and observer of this salutary precept of our confirmation may deserve to attain the blessing and grace of heavenly recompense, and eternal joys, under the just Judge, the Lord our God.

Written by the hand of Leo, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of March and in the aforesaid fifth indiction. Farewell.

+ Given on the eighth day of March, by the hands of John, bishop and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope XII, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter, in the seventh year. [Col. 1036B]

I, Cirinus, notary of the holy Roman Church, as I found it in the parchment privilege of Bishop John, neither diminished nor added anything; thus I wrote and faithfully copied it. Thanks be to God.

I, John, son of Laurence Angelo of the City, notary by authority of the holy Roman prefecture, at the request of the religious and honorable lady, Donna Jacoba de Comite, abbess of the monastery of Saint Sylvester *de Capite*, faithfully copied and reduced to public form, as I found it in the aforesaid transcript or copy written by Cirinus, formerly notary of the holy Roman Church, faithfully taken from the aforesaid parchment privilege, as far as I was able to understand it. I did so from the copy which appears to be written in the Limentan script [or, *Littera Beneventana*], in the presence of learned men, and especially of the venerable lord John, bishop of Nepi, general vicar in the City of our lord the pope, and in the presence of John of All Saints, John son of Laurence, Peter son of Laurence, James son of Nicholas, All Saints, and Francis son of Laurence Mancini, notaries, summoned as witnesses and listening—unless perhaps a letter or syllable was omitted through error [lacuna] that could alter the truth of the said instrument. I faithfully reduced it to public form, having been requested to do so, in the year of the Lord 1318, in the pontificate of our lord John XXII, pope, in the first indiction, on April 26. [Col. 1036C]

## XV. PRIVILEGE OF POPE JOHN XII FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT PETER AT BIVOR

*(Year 963.)*

[Original, Guelf. IV, 556.]

He subjects the monastery of Saints Peter, John, Vitus, Stephen, and Agatha at Bivor, founded by Count Billing, to the sole jurisdiction of the Apostolic See, and confirms its possessions, on the condition “that in each and every indiction it shall reasonably present one pound of silver on the altar of Saint Peter in the name of the payment.”

[Col. 1036D]

“With the supreme apostolic [authority], etc.”

## XVI. RESCRIPT OF POPE JOHN XII TO THE BISHOPS OF THE ROMAN SYNOD

*(Year 963.)*

[Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Leges* II, 30.]

[Col. 1037A]

We have heard it said that you wish to make another pope. If you do this, I excommunicate you by almighty God, so that you may have no authority to ordain anyone or celebrate Mass.

## DOUBTFUL ITEMS

## XVII. LETTER OF POPE JOHN XII TO JOHN THE ARCHPRIEST, AND TO JOHN THE SECOND AND JOHN THE THIRD, PRIESTS

*(Year 957.)*

[Marini, *Diplomata pontificum*, 65.]

[Col. 1037B]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, John, the religious archpriest, and John the second and John the third, religious priests, and to their brothers and their successors forever.

Apostolic governance properly comes to the aid, with benevolent compassion, of those endowed with pious religion, and grants the minds of petitioners the assent they desire. For then especially a reward is stored up with God, the author of all things, when venerable places, suitably ordered, have unquestionably been brought to a better state. Therefore, since you requested that we grant and confirm to you and your successors that the church of the holy martyr of Christ, Tryphon, should be secure and free from every obligation, together with everything belonging to it—for it has recently been built by Crescentius, the most noble prefect of the city of Rome, or by the other neighbors of that same church—we, at the intervention of the aforesaid son of ours, Crescentius, the most glorious prefect, confirm the said church to you and your successors by this privilege of our authority, so that you may remain in it perpetually and eternally offer praises to the eternal God. From the present fifth indiction we grant it to you and your successors to possess.

For on the day of the sacred dedication of that church, when we ourselves were placing the most holy body of the blessed martyr Tryphon there with our own hands, we proclaimed that, just as the other honorable Catholic churches within the city of Rome exist, so that church too should stand. For it is fitting that we serve the holy martyr Tryphon with the greatest devotion, and that the church which, under his name, has been dedicated to almighty God by us and our successors should receive its due honor; and that, at the procession or station prescribed there, the schola cantorum of our sacred palace should assemble.

That most excellent martyr offered his body to various sufferings for God’s sake, and therefore deserved the crown of the heavenly kingdom. If he sees us devoted to his service, through his intercession we shall deserve to escape the punishment of Gehenna. For he does not reserve for himself a work of little value, especially since his asylum, which until now had been small, has been built from its foundations by a splendid work, raised in height and extended in breadth. What previously appeared cramped and squalid is now, with divine clemency leading the way, seen to be bright and beautiful.

Just as this same asylum has been completed for the honor of almighty God and of the most precious martyr Tryphon, so all who have endeavored to assist in its construction will find excellent and well-decorated dwellings in the heavenly homeland. The most eminent martyr rejoices with Christ, and all his servants who render him welcome service will rejoice as well. For just as the benefits of our Redeemer increase daily in us, so we ought to perform very many services for his church.

May God also be glorified through us, his servants, in that church, so that the holy martyr, for whose love it was built, may lead to eternal glory the servants subject to him who praise God.

We likewise confirm to you and to your aforesaid church of Saint Tryphon the oratory built in honor of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, together with the books and furnishings of that oratory, its portico adjoining it, and the vacant land around it for burial.

We further confirm to you the entire postern called “at the Pila,” together with the pila itself, situated below the river Tiber within that postern, with water for constructing a watermill, and with the bank of that postern; and you shall receive from it the bank-tax from the postern of Saint Lucia as far as the postern of Saint Martin, together with everything belonging to that oratory.

We also confirm the property in the district of Campus Martius, beside the same postern called “at the Pila,” bounded on the first side by the postern itself, on the second side by the riverbed, on the third side by the city wall and the house of John the mansionarius, and on the fourth side by the public road. Just as the aforesaid Crescentius, the most noble prefect of the city, gave and granted that oratory of Saint Stephen the protomartyr at the Pila to you and to the church mentioned above by a deed of donation, so we grant and confirm it to you and your church in perpetuity, secure and free from every obligation imposed on other churches, in both temporal and spiritual matters, together with its entire parish and all its holdings and appurtenances, as stated above.

We also will, and by apostolic authority command, that whichever of our successors, the pontiffs, shall have deserved to exercise the office of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, may not for any reason or by any deception alter this privilege of our grant and confirmation, or violate it in any way.

If anyone, however—which we do not believe—should rashly attempt to act against this our apostolic privilege or presume to breach it in any respect, and should not allow what we have established above to remain as it is, let him know that, unless he repents, by the authority of almighty God, of the blessed Peter and Paul, and of us, whose vicariate we exercise, he is bound by the chain of anathema and excluded from the kingdom of God; and that he is to be burned in the fire of eternal punishment with the devil, his most dreadful pomp, and Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ.

But whoever, with pious regard, proves himself the guardian and observer of this privilege of our apostolic constitution may deserve to obtain the grace of blessing from the just Judge, the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, and from his holy mother, the virgin Mary, and eternal life with all the saints and elect of God, for ever and ever. Amen.

## XVIII. Bull of Pope John XII for the Monastery of Saint Vincent at Volturno. (Year 962)

[In Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores* I, II, 447.]

[Col. 1039B]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Paul, venerable abbot, and to the monastery of the holy martyr Vincent of Christ, situated above the source of the river Volturno in the region of Samnium, in the territory of Benevento, and through you to your successors who are to be regularly advanced in that venerable monastery, forever.

Since great concern and care insistently urge us to keep watch over all the churches of God and pious places, lest they suffer any loss through necessity but rather obtain resources for their own benefit, it is therefore fitting that, with complete pastoral integrity of mind, we should especially secure the full stability of those venerable places and diligently provide assistance for their welfare. Thus what has been bestowed upon venerable places for the honor of God’s holy name and for the praise and glory of his divine majesty may be acceptable to our almighty God, and may the reward of such a pious work be conferred in the heavenly deeds worthy of his fullest mercy.

Therefore, since you requested that we grant to you the monastery of the blessed martyr Vincent, situated above the river Volturno in the territory of Benevento, in the region of Samnium, together with its appurtenances and monasteries—namely, the monastery of the blessed apostle Peter, situated beside the river Sabatus in the aforesaid territory of Benevento; also the monastery of holy Mary, Mother of God, in the place called Sano; likewise the monastery of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, situated at Alife; and also the monastery built in honor of holy Mary, namely in the territory of Marsica, at the place called Apinianicus; moreover, the monastery of Saint Maurus within the county of Atina; and another monastery of holy Mary, Mother of God, situated in the territory of Penne, at the place called Marano; and yet another monastery consecrated in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, at the place called “Two Basilicas”—together with the other monasteries and cells, estates, houses, and farmsteads, with the male and female servants of both sexes residing there, and with everything and in every respect belonging to them, we grant them to you and to your successor abbots who shall be there in due course, so that they may be held by you under the jurisdiction of our holy church, which by God’s authority we serve, and may not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other church.

Favoring these pious desires, by this our authority we commit to you what you request. Therefore we grant to you and to your successor abbots the permission of our apostolic see that, for whatever Christian need may arise in the aforesaid venerable monastery, you may have whichever bishop you wish to invite. We grant you full power to have churches consecrated, and likewise to arrange ordinations of subdeacons and deacons from time to time, and to complete there every ecclesiastical rank in due time.

We further declare that no bishop from there may summon a subdeacon to his synod unless it is the subdeacon’s own will; nor may anyone in any way judge or excommunicate the abbot or a monk.

We also wish, and by apostolic authority enjoin upon you and your successor abbots who shall in due course be appointed there, that if a priest or cleric from any church comes to live with the community of the brothers, or comes forward to receive the monastic habit, he is immediately to be received.

As for chrism and confirmation, it shall always be permitted for you to obtain them from whichever bishop you wish; and likewise, as we have said, everything shall remain under our apostolic authority. We prohibit every priest of any church from exercising any jurisdiction or authority within the aforesaid venerable monastery, except the apostolic see, so that no one may presume to celebrate the solemnities of Mass there unless invited by the abbot of the monastery.

Furthermore, establishing this by apostolic censure under the testimony of divine judgment, and by firm and dreadful prohibitions of anathema, we forbid anyone else, whatever authority or dignity he may possess, ever to presume to interfere with that venerable monastery or its affairs, or in any way to take away or alienate its goods and possessions, its subject churches, or anything that appears to belong to them; nor may anyone inflict upon it any harm or loss, whether in time of peace or in time of the barbarians. For we have decreed that the aforesaid monastery shall remain perpetually, as stated, in firm stability under the jurisdiction of our holy church, both in time of peace and in time of the barbarians.

We further proclaim and, by the authority of the blessed prince of the apostles, before God and his dreadful future judgment, by this document of our apostolic privilege and constitution, sanction and decree that the places which have been exchanged or granted to any of you abbots in the same venerable monastery of the holy martyr Vincent of Christ, as well as the other landed possessions bestowed and offered by kings, dukes, castalds, and all Christians, or which may thereafter be granted there, shall belong by firm right to the aforesaid monastery and remain so forever.

Nor shall it be lawful, as stated, for anyone to inflict harm upon any of its possessions or upon any of the monastery’s appurtenances, or to take away what has been given to it; rather, in accordance with what is subject to the apostolic statutes and privileges granted to those venerable places, these things shall remain undisturbed.

The monks of the same community shall also always be permitted to elect their abbot. The abbot himself shall be permitted to judge his monks, both those of the men’s monastery and those of the women’s monastery subject to him.

But if anyone—which we do not wish—should presume by wicked audacity to oppose or in any way transgress what we have established for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid venerable monastery, let him be bound by the chain of anathema and assigned to be burned in eternal fire with the devil and his most dreadful pomp, and with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ.

But whoever proves in all things to be an observer with pious regard, guarding our apostolic constitution directed toward the worship of God, may obtain abundantly the grace of blessing from our most merciful Lord God and deserve to become a participant in eternal life.

Farewell.

Written by the hand of Benedict, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of July, in the fifth indiction, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter, in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord John.

## XIX. Letter of Pope John XII to Eadred, King of the English. (Year 955–963)

[In Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XVIII, col. 455.] He urges him to protect the privileges of the very ancient English monastery of Saints Peter and Paul at Canterbury.

[Col. 1041C]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Eadred, the most excellent king, and to all the bishops, dukes, counts, abbots, and the entire faithful people of the English nation: the warmest greeting and apostolic blessing.

For the advancement of divine worship, we continually devote ourselves to considering the stability of venerable places, so that, through the pious labor that comes from souls dedicated to Christ—those who have resolved to serve him there throughout the days of their lives—they may persevere undisturbed under regular discipline; and so that those things which have been built to the praise of God for the sake of religious worship may remain firmly unshaken.

Therefore I command you, illustrious king and dearest son, and all the other sons of ours in the faith belonging to the aforesaid nation, to hold under our care the monastery among you established in honor of the blessed apostles Peter, prince of the apostles, and Paul, teacher of the nations. Let no person, great or small, disturb them with unrest; rather, let the abbot and monks serving God there make use of your common assistance and freely possess whatever appears to belong to their right, so that they may more effectively lead their lives in holy conduct.

When the abbot himself happens to die, no one from elsewhere is to be appointed in his place, but someone from the same community whom they have elected by common counsel; he is to be consecrated in that place and set over the Lord’s flock.

Let no bishop usurp any authority there, nor presume to celebrate Mass there unless invited by the abbot, in every respect as our predecessors, worthy of God and of apostolic jurisdiction, conferred upon that church in their privileges.

So that no one may dare to oppose these provisions with reckless audacity, we have also taken care to add the writing of our smallness, supported by apostolic authority.

It is therefore established that the aforesaid monastery was the first, from the very beginning of your nascent Church, to be adorned by the religious observance of holy monks. Christian King Æthelbert, having been led to the faith of Christ by the blessed Augustine, disciple of Gregory of blessed memory, built it from its foundations at the exhortation of that same Father, your apostle Augustine; and there he placed Peter, a monk sent from this apostolic see, over the monks who feared the Lord as their abbot.

There also, at the command of that same Gregory, the aforesaid Father Augustine chose a place for that king, for himself, for his successors the kings, and for the archbishops, where their bodily remains might await the day of resurrection.

If anyone attempts to pollute or destroy this purpose of holy religion, let him know that he is bound by apostolic authority with the chain of anathema and is to be burned with Judas, the betrayer of the Lord, in the punishment of eternal fire.

Accordingly, we command in every way the canons of the monastery of Saint Savior who occupy that place not to presume to disturb the practice of this holy devotion. If they do so, let them be punished by the same anathema.

[Col. 1042C]

May you, lord son, fare well in Christ with all your people.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, while the most pious lord Augustus Otto was ruling, in the eleventh year of his reign, in the eleventh indiction.

## XX. To the Same King and to the Clergy of England. (Years 955–963)

[Mansi, same work.] He confirms the privileges of the same monastery of Saints Peter and Paul.

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Eadred, the most excellent king of the English, and to our most beloved son Odo, archbishop of the church of Canterbury, with all the bishops, dukes, counts, abbots, and the entire faithful people of the English nation: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Among the distinguished virtues of your sacred faith, by which you, most excellent son, have subjected to the Christian religion the kings subject to you, together with your nobles and peoples, we embrace more intimately this ardor of your charity: that the first monastery of your kingdom, situated in the suburb of Canterbury—consecrated in honor of the princes of the apostles Peter and Paul by Augustine, the first teacher and apostle of the English, and founded by the first Christian king of the English, Æthelbert, the king beloved of God, where, by apostolic authority, the bodies of the kings and archbishops of Canterbury are to be buried forever—should, at the request of your royal eminence, also be confirmed through us in its ancient dignity and liberty, just as your royal predecessors and our pontifical predecessors established by written apostolic privileges.

Therefore, graciously assenting, we decree that this apostolic church, just as it is regarded among you as the firstborn in the grace of the princes of the apostles, should likewise be the primary mother of the other monasteries of your kingdom that have arisen since or will be founded throughout all posterity. Let it be, I say, by royal and apostolic confirmation both royal and apostolic; let it be free from every secular service, so that no bishop and none of your royal successors may presume to harm or disturb it in any respect, and so that no burden of service may ever be demanded from anyone, even in the smallest matter, from the goods belonging to that church. Thus, under its king, who is its defender and not its tyrant, it may freely serve Christ alone.

We also command our beloved son and fellow priest Odo, archbishop of the church of Canterbury, in the place of the blessed prince of the apostles Peter, in all things to devote himself where required, not through the arrogance of pre-eminence but through the duty of charity. Let him regard the abbot of that church as a Roman legate and fellow minister of the Gospel of peace, and as his fraternal companion, not his subject, in every respect as Theodore, archbishop of the apostolic see, and the abbot Adrian, holy sons beloved of God, conducted themselves.

Let him seize no authority over this church, nor claim any office without the abbot’s favor, except the ordination of the abbot; nor may he accept or perform anything from its inner and private places, parishes, or any of its privileged rights without the assent of that same abbot, lest he disturb the peace of the Lord’s flock through any abuse—for to cause them to stumble is to be sunk in the depths with a millstone.

The abbot, moreover, is to be regarded as first among the others, but only so that, for the joining together of sacred faith, charity, and concord, he may shine before his brothers in the place of the firstborn and in the Roman role, with affection rather than command.

We therefore solemnly declare to all the kings, princes, and peoples of Britain that these provisions, and whatever other rights have been or shall be handed down to the end of time by you, by your predecessors, by your successors, or by any persons, are to be observed by everyone in accordance with your petition. May no transgressor—God forbid—perish, cut off by the sword of excommunication of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles; rather, may he who favors that church, admitted by its key, rejoice in the kingdom.

**On the Life of Saint Wilfrid, Bishop of York**. 979  
Preliminary observations. 979  
Preface. 981  
The life begins. 983  
I. Wilfrid is born in Britain under an auspicious light. 983  
II. Piously educated, he leaves his stepmother and seeks the palace, then enters the monastery under Cudda. 983  
III. He travels as a pilgrim to Rome; Ercombert detains him for four years. 984  
IV. At Lyon, under Dalfinus. 984  
V. He nevertheless proceeds to Rome, where he is taught by Boniface, honored with the pope’s gifts, and returns to Lyon. 985  
VI. After three years he is tonsured; Delphinus having been killed, he returns to Britain. 985  
VII. He visits the royal court, receives estates from the king, and obtains the monastery of Ripon. 987  
VIII. He is ordained priest by Ægilbert, a Gallic bishop. 987  
IX. A schism arising over Easter, Wilfrid refutes the Scots. 987  
X. He is designated bishop of York. He wishes to be ordained in Gaul. 989  
XI. He crosses the channel and is consecrated. 989  
XII. Returning, he is tossed by a storm. He is attacked by pirates and reaches harbor victorious. 990  
XIII. With Chad appointed at York, he withdraws to the monastery of Ripon. He is sought by Wulfhere, king of the Mercians. He ordains ministers in Kent and builds monasteries. 990  
XIV. He is restored to his see by Theodore. 991  
XV. He repairs the church and consecrates the basilica at Ripon. 991  
XVI. He confirms the baptized and raises a dead boy. 992  
XVII. England is in a happy condition. King Ecgfrith of Northumbria subdues the rebellious Picts through Wilfrid’s merits. 993  
XVIII. The Mercians too are subdued. 994  
XIX. Wilfrid lives piously. 994  
XX. He builds the basilica of Saint Andrew and restores Ealhse to health. 994  
XXI. At the urging of Queen Ermenburh, King Ecgfrith, with Theodore’s consent, divides Wilfrid’s diocese into three. Wilfrid appeals to Rome. He foretells punishments for his persecutors. 995  
XXII. After crossing the sea, he is carried to the Frisians and preaches the word of God. 996  
XXIII. Ebroin attempts to incite the Frisian king against Wilfrid. 997  
XXIV. An address to the queen. 997  
XXV. Wilfrid withdraws to Dagobert. 997  
XXVI. While he is present, a synod is convened at Rome in which Wilfrid is restored. 998  
XXVII. After Dagobert is attacked in war and killed, Wilfrid is assailed with insults because he had saved him. 999  
XXVIII. Returning to England, he presents the papal letters. 999  
XXIX. When these are rejected, he himself is thrown into prison. 1000  
XXX. His speech to his followers. 1000  
XXXI. In prison he is illumined by heavenly light. 1000  
XXXII. He does not allow the papal letters to be violated. 1001  
XXXIII. He heals the president’s wife, who was nearly lifeless. 1001  
XXXIV. He is bound more tightly, but in vain. He is released. 1001
